en: Oṃ.
The *Tarkasaṃgrahadīpikāprakāśikā*,
composed by Śrī Rāmānuja Tātācārya of Nāvalpākkam.
The Śrī [Tiruppukkuli] shines forth, accompanied by the commentary named *Bālapriyā* composed by Śrī Kṛṣṇatātācārya and the commentary named *Prasāraṇā*.
The introduction:
Herein is the *Tarkasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Annambhaṭṭa, together with its commentary titled the *Dīpikā*, also composed by him.
It is universally renowned that all those desiring to study the Nyāya-śāstra begin by studying [this work] first.
Apart from the *Dīpikā* on the *Tarkasaṃgraha*, there is the *Padakṛtya*.
Nyāyabodhinī, Vākyavṛtti, and Nirukti.
Numerous commentaries, such as the *Paṭṭābhirāma-ṭippaṇī* and others, are found, both printed and unprinted;
likewise, there is the *Rāmarudrī* on the *Dīpikā*.
The *Prakāśikā* composed by Nīlakaṇṭha, the *Prakāśikā* composed by Nṛsiṃha Śāstrin, and the *Prakāśikā* composed by Paṭṭābhirāma.
There exist numerous commentaries on these works, both printed and unprinted; among them,
the *Nyāyabodhinī* and the *Nīlakaṇṭhī-prakāśikā*— a commentary on the *Dīpikā*— are currently in wide circulation for study and teaching.
The very quality of being concise while yet conveying all necessary meanings is the primary reason for its inclusion within the sphere of study and teaching.
Even therein, that which is worthy of the designation *Nīlakaṇṭhaprakāśikā* and *Laghugādādharī* shines forth as the most delightful to the minds of both students and scholars.
Only those who possess a deep familiarity with works such as the Gādādharī and others are able to understand, experience, and savor the intent and aesthetic flavor of the Prakāśikā.
For a long time, no commentary whatsoever has appeared for this *Nīlakaṇṭhaprakāśikā*, one that is capable of clarifying the intended meaning of every single sentence.
Although a commentary titled Bhāskarodayā, composed by Nīlakaṇṭha’s son, was printed by the Nirṇayasāgara Press many years ago and is available, [this work is distinct].

Nevertheless, because it fails to provide explanations in the appropriate manner at points where they are required, and because it indulges in unnecessary elaborations, that work does not benefit those who are mere novice logicians.
On the contrary, failing to understand the heart of the *Prakāśikā* in many places and explaining it erroneously, it only produces further confusion.
By observing such instances, the thought also arises: "This could not have been composed by the son of Nīlakaṇṭha.
For this very reason, for those like me—

Thinking that a proper commentary should be composed for the benefit of both immature logicians and the learned, I requested the eminent scholar En. Es. Rāmānujatātācārya, a native of Nāvalpāka, many years ago.

Making this connection my pretext— namely, that I had studied the Nyāya-śāstra in their presence— I made my request. They, too, immediately accepted my request and, within the span of one year, [established] the one named Bālapriyā.
Having composed a commentary on the *Prakāśikā*, he has bestowed it upon us;
that the time for its publication has now arrived brings immense joy to my heart.
By means of this explanation,
it is certain that all even the immature logicians will receive great benefit. Now, regarding the inconsistencies found in the *Bhāskarodayā*:
We shall demonstrate this by the maxim of the grain in the cooking pot (*sthālīpulākanyāya*):

[1] In the *Prakāśikā*, regarding the reversal of the tarka—which consists in the fact that it entails the opposite of that which proves the absence of the subsumptive ground (*apādaka*)—it shows that it culminates in that very alternative, stating: "It does not exist because of the absence of perception."
A line (p. 142) is seen.

The actual meaning of this line is as follows: "If there were a jar here, then the jar would have been perceived, just like the ground"—in such a form of tarka (reductio ad absurdum), [the jar] is the *āpādaka* (the antecedent condition).
A jar is the subject; its absence is "the absence of the jar"; the proof of that [absence] is the absence of the perception of its opposite (the jar);
the counter-positive of that [absence] is indeed the perception [of the jar], which is what is to be brought about (the *āpādya*).

Thus, the nature of a *tarka* is that it brings about as its consequence (*āpādya*) the counter-positive of the opposite of its own prover (*sādhaka*), while itself being the absence of that prover. [2]
Bhāskara, however, writes something without grasping this intention.

For instance, Bhāskara’s line reads: "The absence of perception, which establishes the non-existence of the jar's existence—the very thing that would result in the occurrence of its perception—[is the probans]."

Regarding the misconception that "it does not exist," there is the misconception consisting in the absence of the perception of its counter-correlative; the perception which is the counter-correlative to that [absence] is what is to be established.
In the case of the opposite [view], because of the absence of such perception, it is in the form of a reversal that one says "it does not exist."

The collective meaning is that [the passage] "tatkoṭiparyavasāyitvaṃ nāsti" (there is no such determination by that extreme) demonstrates that the tarka (logical reasoning) terminates in the extreme of non-existence (*abhāva*). [In this context], *tarkitāḥ* means "adduced" or "brought forward."
"Because it would follow that the counter-correlate, such as a jar, possesses existence"—this is from the *Prakāśikā* (p.
142). Here, regarding the word *tarkitā*:
The meaning is "having become the object of the reduction" (*āpādana*).
According to the *Bhāskarodayā* (p. 80), it means "having become the locus of the reduction.
[3] In the section on the counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*).

In the *Prakāśikā*, the following line is seen on page 203: "The meaning is that when there exists in the subject (*pakṣa*) the cognition of another reason which is pervaded by the absence of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) in relation to a certain [subject], that is a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*)."
This is its meaning: the phrase "that which is related to it" means "that which is related to the reason.
And thus, that which is related to the reason is the probandum (*sādhya*).
The cognition of another reason which is pervaded by the absence of that [probandum] exists in that subject; this is a *satpratipakṣa* (counterbalanced) case.
In the phrase "this is a *satpratipakṣa*," by the word "that" (*tat*), [the probandum is referred to].
In the phrase "that which is related to *yat*," the reason (*hetu*) is to be understood as that which is grasped by the word *yat*.
However, in the *Bhāskārodaya*, it is stated: "By the word *yat*, there is the inclusion of the subject (*pakṣa*) intended in the context;
and in the word *pakṣa*, there is the [word] *tat* and so forth."

And thus, the following explanation is seen [on p. 116]: "The meaning is that when there is the cognition of another reason which is pervaded by the absence of that which is to be proven (sādhya) in a particular subject (pakṣa), then that [reason] exists in that subject."
In this regard, the lack of logical connection (*ananvaya*) and other defects are clear to the learned.

In the *Prakāśikā* on the *Prāmāṇyavāda*: "In the Bhaṭṭa school, however, since cognition is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), the apprehension of the initial cognition takes the form of an inference based on the mark of cognizedness (*jñātatā*); by means of that [inference], validity..."
The line "gṛhyate" is seen on page 239.
Here, *jñānagraha* means the grasping of knowledge; and since it is both [the grasping] and the first [grasping], it is a *karmadhāraya* compound.
Therefore, "being first" is a qualifier of the apprehension of cognition;
for [it is established] by qualifying the apprehension of cognition with "being first."

The intention of the *Prakāśikā* is that the second apprehension of knowledge— consisting of an inference based on the probans of activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth as accepted by the Naiyāyikas— is thereby excluded. However,
in the *Bhāskarodayā*, it is stated that due to ignorance of this principle, [the term] "first" (*prāthamika*) refers to that which occurs in the first instance.

And that cognition is of the nature of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāyātmaka*), meaning that it consists in the nature of a cognition in the form of an inference which apprehends it, because it has the form of an apprehension (*graha*)— this is some such [explanation].

This has been explained (p. 137). Likewise, in that very same work it is seen: "The formulation of the inference, however, is as follows: 'This cognition is invalid, because it generates a non-concordant activity; for whatever is not thus, is not thus. (p. 288).
In this context, regarding the phrase "due to activity that is non-concordant" (*visaṃvādipravṛtti*), the meaning is: because it generates that activity which is non-concordant.
The term "non-concordant" (*visaṃvādinī*) means "fruitless" (*viphalā*).
In the *Bhāskārodaya*, however, it is stated: "The meaning is that [it] produces activity in one who possesses contrary cognition. By this, [it refers to] those that are non-concordant.
The analysis of the term as "pravṛtti" (activity) is intended here;
in this case, the impropriety is quite evident.
For the sake of illustration:
Certain passages have been presented;
in such places, an authoritative commentary has been provided in the *Bālapriyā*. Now, at the time of the completion of this printing, by those renowned as Tiruppukkuli Svāmī—

This is the commentary named *Prakāśikā*, composed by Śrī Kṛṣṇatātācārya— who resided in Kāñcī more than one hundred and fifty years ago, was proficient in the four systems of philosophy (*catustantra*), and authored numerous marginal notes (*kroḍapatra*) on Nyāya treatises— on the work known as *Prasāriṇī*.
A single palm-leaf manuscript of the *Granthalipi* was recently obtained from Śrī Sampatkumāra Tātācārya, who resides in Kāñcī;
it was written out as a manuscript by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Tātācārya for the purpose of exposition.
This is understood from the *Tālapatragranthapuṣpikā*; furthermore, the adherence to the authority found here is likewise established by logic in the commentary on the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana*.
It is seen in the *Ratnapeṭikā*; moreover, this expansion imitates the style of another of his works.
Therefore, it must be explained.
There is no doubt whatsoever that this was composed by Śrī Kṛṣṇatātācārya;
in this exposition, there is generally a consistent application of all the defining characteristics.

Therefore, considering that this commentary would be of great benefit to those desiring to understand the path of concordance, and deeming it appropriate to publish it, I have composed this commentary as a supplement.
It has been published. Had this been discovered earlier, it too would have been published along with *Bālapriyā* from beneath those respective locations.
Or perhaps, it was found for the purpose of publication as a supplement; thus, it is like a gain of what was previously unobtainable.
The inner mind is satisfied by this work,
which consists of the *Tarkasaṃgraha-dīpikā-prakāśikā*, the *Bālapriyā*, the *Prasāraṇā*, and the *Guñjā*.
Manifestation:
"That by which those who are appointed succeed even in great undertakings."
"Know that this honor is a virtue of those lords," according to this maxim.

May those preeminent among the great sages, the most excellent of teachers, who have taken incarnation for the sake of preserving the Vedas and other scriptures, and who are pure from birth— may they, with their special glances filled with unrestrained grace since childhood, revive me along with the multitudes of their devotees.
This is the manifestation of the playful grace of my most venerable guru, the illustrious Candraśekharendra Sarasvatī, the sovereign of the Śrī Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi Pīṭha, who is worthy of being served.
To my maternal uncles,
who are foremost among the devotees of the lotus feet of the venerable Śrī Kāñcī Ācārya,
who are the preeminent bearers of the burden of protecting the Dharma, who are devoted to virtuous deeds, and who are endowed with self-discipline, tranquility, and other spiritual qualities.

This work, titled *Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-Vyāsa-Śaṅkara* and also designated by the words *Satya-Jñāna*, is offered as a commemorative mark for the great sixty-year anniversary of the illustrious Vāñchināthārya, the preeminent among the noble, who had mastered the essence of the treatises on Nyāya and other systems. It is that light which is expressed by the terms *Satya* (Truth) and *Jñāna* (Knowledge).

Having offered hundreds of prostrations at the lotus feet of those gurus who possess that very nature and reside at the venerable Kāmakoṣṭha-vara-pīṭha, I offer this with devotion and faith, seeking an excellence of proficiency in the treatises such as Nyāya and Vedānta.

This work will provide great assistance to young logicians who, fearing the study of the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*) due to the absence of a suitable and straightforward commentary; for having accepted my request despite many other duties, you have composed this highly beneficial *Bālapriyā*.
To my teachers of the science of logic (tarka-śāstra), who have favored me by manifesting as childish logicians like myself— namely, those of Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and Vyākaraṇa— [I offer my salutations].
To those who are crest-jewels of Vedānta, authors of numerous treatises,
the lords of the Śrī Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi Pīṭha, recipients of supreme grace,
at the Central Institute of Indian Languages in Tirupati.
I express my profound gratitude to the eminent scholar Śrī N. S. Rāmānuja Tātācārya, who graces the position of Professor, for this work.

I offer my heartfelt gratitude to Dr. K. Kunjunni Raja, the eminent scholar renowned for his mastery of Eastern and Western learning, who served as the Head of the Department of Sanskrit and Professor at Madras University, for having favored me by writing the foreword to this work.
I manifest my gratitude to those residents of Kāñcīpura who have been kind enough to provide me with a manuscript copy of the commentary known as the Prasāriṇī.

I express my heartfelt gratitude to the learned Śrī Villiyampākkam Sampatkumāra Tātācāryas, and to the authorities of the Adyar Library, who have been so kind as to provide me with a photographic reproduction of that very manuscript from Kākadum.
To Dr. I. Govindan, a Nyāya-Śiromaṇi, who has transcribed the manuscript in the Devanāgarī script in a very clear manner for the purpose of printing this work.
I express my gratitude to the noble-minded gentlemen,
and especially to the officials of the Ilango Printing House, who have carried out the printing at the appointed time with great skill and excellence.
With auspicious greetings, gratitude is expressed to the honorable Mr. E. S. Maniyan;
furthermore, in the introduction:

An investigation, preceded by a critical examination of ancient and modern texts of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika, concerning fifteen subjects that appear to be the most principal among those analyzed in works such as the *Dīpikā*.
I have composed this introduction in accordance with the path of my research;
it may serve as a benefit for those curious about this investigation.
[Any errors] due to oversight in printing or elsewhere—
I pray that the learned may forgive any impurities that have arisen and purify them. Thus [ends the work] of the venerable Gurus residing at the Kāmakoṣṭhavara-pīṭha,
on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha.
En. Vīlinātha, whose sole life-sustenance is the nectar of the lotus-feet [of his guru]. (21-5-1980)
Śrīḥ! [1] Herein, indeed, for the most part, is the Discourse on Auspiciousness (Maṅgalavāda).

It is universally accepted that all authors perform an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) at the commencement of their works. In this regard, what is the authority for such an auspicious invocation? Or rather, what is [the purpose]?
The purpose [of this work] is explained in the discussion on auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
The author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya* did not say anything at all concerning the performance of auspicious rites.
The author of the Nyāyavārttika also began his work without performing a benedictory invocation;
however, so did the commentator Vācaspatimiśra.
He begins the commentary precisely with an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*).

In this regard, anticipating the objection— "Even though the author of the *Vārttika* is most refined, why did he not perform an auspicious rite at the commencement of his work?"— he [proceeds as follows].
He indeed performed the auspicious rite consisting of a salutation to his chosen deity;
nevertheless, he did not include it within the treatise.
The commentator offered this resolution: "There is no insistence that everything which is performed as an auspicious rite (*maṅgalakara*) must necessarily be included in the text.
In that context—

"Even though the salutation to the chosen deity was performed by the Vārttikakāra, who is the most learned of men, it has not been included in this treatise because it was obtained through a tradition of the conduct of the learned that is free from contradiction."
By stating "niveśetiḥ," he indicates that the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is the authority for performing auspicious rites (*maṅgalācaraṇa*).

In the *Tātparyaṭīkāpariśuddhi*, the teacher Udayana states: "Desiring the completion of the work they have begun without obstacles at its commencement, discerning persons proceed [to write] after first performing a salutation to their chosen deity."
However, a frequent deviation is observed here and there,
since even for one who has performed salutation, the desired object may not be accomplished.
Furthermore, because the desired goal is accomplished even for one who has not performed a salutation;
nor is there here [a rule] such as "one desiring rain should offer the Kārīrī sacrifice," [or] "one desiring the completion of what has been begun [should worship] a deity."
There is no scriptural injunction stating "one should pay homage," by virtue of which we might assume a deficiency in the ritual action, the agent, or the means, even in the case of a deviation.
Therefore, [the statement] "The seeker of wealth and pleasure here at the banyan tree... [is not authoritative].

Thinking that this performance of an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) is merely the manifestation of an unauthentic popular tradition— just as one might say, "One should worship the chest [of a deity] while residing there"—
did the author of the *Vārttika* perhaps not perform an auspicious invocation at all?
Having provided this introduction— stating that the previously mentioned commentary-text is for the purpose of resolving such an inquiry—
one [says] "as if directly perceived."

Even the unopposed practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is indeed an authoritative means of knowledge when there exists a corresponding revealed scripture (*śruti*), because a practice of the learned cannot possibly exist without a foundation.
And likewise, in some cases, the absence of completion despite the presence of auspicious rites is caused by defects in the action, the agent, or the means;
this occurs even when no auspicious rite has been performed in this life.
Having explained that completion depends upon auspicious acts performed in other lives,

one understands Udayanācārya’s intention to be this: the Vedic scripture inferred from the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) serves as the authority for the necessity of performing auspicious rites at the beginning of a work.
And that [the benediction] has the fruit of completion:
this is the intention of the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, namely, the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*.

For by the merit produced through the act of salutation, which acts as an obstacle to unrighteousness (*adharma*), those obstacles and impediments (*vighna-vināyaka*) rooted in unrighteousness are driven away;
consequently, the completion of the treatise follows— thus [the salutation] is purposeful.
Regarding the salutation: where there is no conclusion, one may infer that the salutation was improper or that the author has a great abundance of demerit (adharma).
Even in cases where [the work] proceeds without a salutation...
The completion of the treatise is observed;
even there, a mental or physical prostration is to be inferred.
Alternatively, the dharma is to be accomplished by other means;
however, the distinction is that through verbal salutation, the accomplishment of the instruction for others also occurs.
But for one who has no unrighteousness (*adharma*) that could serve as a cause for obstacles, he too must perform prostration out of apprehension of that [obstacle],
just as one acts out of apprehension of enemies and the like.
Explaining that it is like the collection of weapons and other such items, they demonstrate the necessity of performing auspicious rites (*maṅgala*);
however, they did not set forth any proof for the necessity of performing such auspicious rites.
Bhāsarvajña maintains that the sole fruit of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) is the completion [of a work].
This is the method of the Vaiśeṣika system in the *Vaiśeṣikadarśana*.
The author of the *Upaskāra* explains that by employing the word *atha* at the beginning of the first sūtra—“Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma”—Kaṇāda performed an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*).
The commentator Praśastapādācārya, however, [begins with] “Having bowed to the Lord, the Cause... [and so forth].
Thus he performed the auspicious rite consisting of a salutation to the Lord.
In that regard, it is said in the *Kiraṇāvalī*: "And [the work] was begun by one who has performed the auspicious rite."
The ritual action is completed and accumulated.
(Accumulation refers to the uninterrupted transmission of the intended text from teacher to disciple.)

Nor should it be argued that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) cannot be the cause of completion without obstacles because of deviation from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); for a causal relationship rooted in scripture (*āgama*) is not subject to sublation. Even though...
It has been established that the absence of completion in auspicious undertakings is due to defects in the action, the agent, or the means.
Furthermore, the author of the *Nyāyakandalī*, while commenting on the verse "Having prostrated before the Lord, the Cause," states: "For at the commencement of an action..."
That the deity and the guru are saluted is this traditional practice of the learned; and the fruit of such salutation is the destruction of obstacles.
Now, one might ask: is it from salutation alone that the pacification of obstacles occurs?
Or even from something else?
There is no fixed rule that [the work] must proceed from a salutation alone; for even in the absence of a salutation, the *Nyāya-bhāṣya* and the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya* are complete. When...
Furthermore, at that time, the performance of auspicious rites from any other source would necessarily be redundant. To this it is replied:
the pacification of obstacles occurs through the act of salutation alone, as is invariably practiced by the learned at the commencement of a treatise.
This is because of the performance of that [homage];
nor is it the case that the homage was not performed by the authors of the Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā commentaries.
However, although it was composed, it was not included in the book.
If one asks how this is known, it is simply by the fact that the author himself is a learned authority (śiṣṭa).
Even a barbarian does not engage in an undertaking involving his teacher until he has paid homage to his chosen deity;
and likewise, there are those who are supreme believers.
It is impossible that Vātsyāyana and Śabarasvāmin did not perform an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*);
there is scriptural authority for the practice of auspicious rites in the Smṛtis.
Regarding auspicious conduct,
even traditional law (smṛti) is an authoritative source;
for instance, Manu says:
“One should be endowed with auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have conquered the senses; one should likewise perform recitation and offer oblations.”
Always maintaining the sacred fire without negligence—
for those who are endowed with auspicious conduct and are ever self-restrained—
"For those who recite [the mantra] and offer oblations, no downfall is found.
Thus [it is said]. Downfall (*vinipāta*).
This means "an obstacle to this.
Here, the second verse has been cited as an authoritative source by the authors of the *Maṇi* at the conclusion of their discussion on auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
In this regard, there is corroboration from traditional history (itihāsa);
for instance, in the Mahābhārata, the best of histories, [Vyāsa] was requested by the great sages who desired to hear the compendium of Vyāsa.
Before beginning the narrative, the Sauti, the reciter of the Purāṇas, says: "The primordial Person, the Lord, invoked by many, praised by many, the Truth, the single syllable, the Brahman."
The manifest and the unmanifest, which is eternal.
He who is both unreal and real, who is beyond both real and unreal,
and who is the creator of all that is high and low— the entire universe which is both existent and non-existent, and that which transcends existence and non-existence.
The ancient, supreme, and immutable.
Having paid homage to Viṣṇu, the auspicious one, the source of all auspiciousness, the most excellent, the sinless, the pure, and Hṛṣīkeśa;
To Hari, the teacher of all that moves and is immobile.
I shall proclaim the meritorious doctrine of the great-souled Maharṣi, who is honored here by all the worlds.
"Of Vyāsa, whose deeds are wondrous.
Thus, beginning the narrative with a salutation to his chosen deity, he declares the necessity of performing an auspicious invocation at the commencement of the work.
Likewise, in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Viṣṇu, the Lord who swallows the universe at its dissolution, and likewise [the one] in its maintenance and creation..."
Having prostrated before the Lord of the worlds, who is unborn, imperishable, and immutable.
"I shall relate it as it was before..."— with these words,
preceded by a salutation to Viṣṇu, he began the work.
The opinion of the jewel-makers (*maṇikṛt*): first, the jewel-makers,
following the traditional doctrine, [establish] in detail that auspiciousness has completion as its fruit.
They established this;

they also demonstrated that the very Vedic revelation inferred from the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the necessity of performing auspicious rites (*maṅgala*).
Therefore, Annambhaṭṭa’s intention was to describe in detail his own established doctrine that the fruit of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) is the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*).

The author of the Dīpikā, Annambhaṭṭa, infers from the conduct of the learned that the Vedic injunction, "One desiring completion should perform an auspicious rite," is the authority for the necessity of performing an auspicious rite at the beginning of a work.
The completion of the auspicious work is the fruit;
the destruction of obstacles is the means.
Because auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) equal in number to the obstacles is the cause [of the completion of a work], there is no positive deviation (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*);
this is so by taking into account auspicious acts performed in other lifetimes.
They define this as "deviation through negative concomitance" (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*).
In the *Prakāśikā*, the view of the author of the *Maṇi*— that the fruit of the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) is the destruction of obstacles (*vighnadhvaṃsa*)— is also included.
Scripture is not the only authority for the necessity of performing auspicious rites; rather, it is also stated that "an auspicious rite must be performed."
The authors of the *Prakāśikā* have established that the inference "because it has completion as its fruit" (*samāptiphalakatvāt*) is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard.
[2] The Discussion on Darkness (*tamovāda*).
The classification of substances as being exactly nine is inconsistent,
because [it excludes] that which is distinct from the nine substances beginning with earth.

Having raised the objection from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsaka school that darkness is a distinct substance because of the existence of a substance named *tamas*, it was established in the *Dīpikā* that darkness is not a substance separate from that [category], as it is included within the absence of light (*tejo 'bhāva*).
In this regard, the intention of the Mīmāṃsakas is as follows: the substantiality of darkness must necessarily be admitted,
because its possession of color is established by the cognition "darkness is blue."
Since darkness is perceived through the cognition "darkness moves" and is understood to possess action,

its substantiality is established by way of possessing color and possessing action— two properties that are pervaded by substantiality. Thus, darkness is a substance, because it is the object of an uncontradicted cognition qualified by blue and so forth, just like a jar.
Thus, this inference is the proof for the substantiality of darkness.
Nor is it the case that wherever there is an absence of light, there [darkness exists].

Alternatively, because there exists a pervasion (vyāpti) such that "there is an absence of being an object of visual valid cognition" or "wherever there is the nature of a cognition whose object is the absence of light, there is an absence of being a visual valid cognition," it is impossible for the cognition "darkness is blue" to be a valid cognition (pramā).
It must be stated that the reason (hetu) mentioned is unestablished in its essential nature (svarūpāsiddha),
because in light (tejas) consisting of illumination and so forth,
there exists an absence of illumination delimited by the relation of conjunction (saṃyoga). In that [case],...
Because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the fact that being an object of visual perception itself constitutes existence, the aforementioned pervasion (vyāpti) is impossible.
Nor can the pervasion be stated by introducing the qualification "being distinct from light" (tejobhinnatva);
for in whatever [place]—wherever...

It should not be argued that there is no deviation from the pervasion (vyāpti)— namely, that "the absence of light, while being distinct from light, is the absence of being an object of visual valid cognition in various locations"—
because [darkness] exists as darkness (tamatva).

For even in the absence of light—which you maintain is the cause consisting of the conjunction with light—there exists the very state of being an object of visual valid cognition; thus, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is unavoidable. Likewise, darkness is the absence of light.
The positions that darkness is the absence of the perception of form,
or that darkness is merely the blueness residing in the atoms of earth pervading space, are not tenable.
Because it is impossible for darkness— which is perceived as having a positive form, being devoid of any mention of a negative particle— to be of the nature of a non-existence;
[this applies] to that darkness which is perceived as the locus of blueness.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for [non-existence] to have the nature of a negation (*naiyārūpa*),

and because [the property of] being perceived in a positive form (*vidhirūpeṇa pratīyamānatva*) serves as a proof for its being an entity (*bhāvatva*), [this does not apply] to that which is the object of a cognition expressed by words such as "dissolution" (*pralaya*) or "destruction" (*vināśa*).
It should not be said that the non-existence of destruction is untenable; for,

just as there is a clear perception of a substance— which is the locus of qualities such as blueness and actions such as motion— as distinct from other things, so too in cases such as "the destruction of a jar on the ground," [destruction is perceived] as something distinct.
Because no other entity in the form of a positive existence is perceived, and because dissolution is of the nature of non-existence;
furthermore, because dissolution is perceived as having a counter-correlative (pratiyogin), such that one says "the dissolution of a jar" or "the destruction of a jar."
Dissolution is of the nature of non-existence;
however, because darkness is perceived as being without a counter-correlate (niṣpratiyogika), it is not of the nature of non-existence. No.

It should not be argued that if darkness were earthy, it would follow that its touch must be perceived— since there is a rule that whatever possesses manifested color must also possess manifested touch—
because sapphire gems, light, and so forth necessarily possess the quality of being earthy due to their possession of blue color.
In that case, because of the deviation [of the reason], the stated rule is impossible.
Now, one might object: "Darkness is not a substance, because, while being the object of visual perception, it possesses the absence of light, just like the absence of light."
Since the absence of substantiality (*dravyatva*) in darkness is established by this inference, how can it possess substantiality?
If you argue that the qualification "provided it possesses the absence of light" is added to prevent a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of jars and the like—
then is this inference being employed by the Prābhākaras?
Is it by the Naiyāyikas, or rather by those who maintain that darkness is merely a form (*rūpa*)? Not the first, for according to their doctrine...

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because since one does not accept the existence of an absence as a distinct entity, both the example consisting of the absence of light and the reason formulated on that basis are unestablished (*asiddha*).
In the view of the Naiyāyikas, since darkness is merely the absence of light, there is no distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Consequently,
because it ultimately results in proving that the absence of light itself is a distinct substance, this constitutes the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
[The objection] "it is a fault" [applies]. Not the third [alternative], because of the deviation [of the reason] from such things as those seen by *divābhīta* (owls) and others;
for even if it were stated that [the object] is the objective domain of human vision, [the fault remains].
Because there is deviation [from the rule] due to substances perceived by yogis;
and thus, once darkness is established as a substance, it lacks the nature of earth because it is devoid of odor, yet it possesses the quality of blue color.
And since the absence of being water and so forth is established, its status as a distinct substance is proven; thus,
the Naiyāyika position is both robust and illuminating.
Since it is sufficient to say that darkness is simply the absence of the general property of light (*tejas-sāmānyābhāva*), there is no evidence for postulating it as a separate substance; thus,
darkness is not a substance.

The inference— "because it is perceptible by the eye when assisted by light, like the absence of light"— is the proof for the non-substantiality of darkness. Here, darkness, which consists in the general absence of fire (tejas), is the subject (pakṣa).

Since the absence of a specific kind of light (*tejoviśeṣābhāva*) is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is no room for the objection that there is no distinction between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example. Alternatively, darkness (*tamaḥ*) as denoted by the word [“darkness”] is the subject, [and it is] the absence of light (*ālokābhāva*).
There is no fault in this example;
since the two cognitions "darkness is blue" and "darkness moves" are erroneous, darkness does not possess color or motion by virtue of them.
"It is established"—this is the view of the Naiyāyikas.
Regarding this, they say:
because there is the cognition of possessing form and so forth, it cannot be said that [the cognition] is an error.

Because, following the cognitions "darkness is blue" and "darkness moves," there arises no subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratīti) such as "this darkness is not blue" or "this darkness does not move," it is impossible for that [initial cognition] to be an error. Furthermore:
If darkness were of the nature of the absence of light, the cognition "darkness is blue" would have to be explained as a superimposition of some blue color residing in something else;
if that were the case, then at other times [the same cognition] would arise through the superimposition of some yellow color residing in something else.

There would also be the cognition "the darkness is yellow," just as there is the cognition "the sky is blue" or "the sky is yellow" through the superimposition of forms such as the peak of Mount Meru made of jewels.

Therefore, since it is impossible for the cognition of possessing color to be a superimposition based on the blue color belonging to something else, and since it cannot be an error, its status as valid knowledge (*pramātva*) is indispensable; thus,
by virtue of possessing a blue color and so forth...

The status of darkness as a distinct substance is indeed established. Now, if by the aforementioned arguments one accepts that darkness is a distinct substance possessing color, then [in the case of] light...
There would have to be apprehensibility by the eye assisted by light;
for it is necessary that the eye assisted by light is the cause of that which is delimited by being visible (cākṣuṣatva), by way of the relation of being a worldly object existing as a substance.
Since visual perception of darkness occurs even in the absence of light, darkness is not established as a distinct substance.
Nor is it the case that [visual perception] is restricted to the visual perception of substances other than darkness.

It should not be argued that there is no inconsistency because light itself is accepted as the cause [of the perception of darkness]; for if one were to include "being different from darkness" (*tamobhinnatva*) in the delimiting condition of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), it would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). If this is said, we reply: No; because even in your own view, in the case of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of light, there is no requirement for contact with another light.
If the eye assisted by light were the cause [of visual perception], then since it would be impossible for there to be visual perception of a substance consisting of light itself,
one must state that the eye assisted by light is the cause only with respect to the visual perception of substances other than fire (tejas). And thus:

Since the eye aided by light lacks the causal efficacy for the visual perception of fire as its object, there would otherwise result the visual perception of gold—which is itself a form of fire—in darkness; therefore, to prevent this, [the following is postulated]:
the eye aided by light is the cause of the visual perception of substances other than that fire which is distinct from gold.
Alternatively, causality must be asserted, because the resulting complexity of the delimiting condition (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for that causality is difficult to avoid;
therefore, [the cause] is distinct from darkness (*tamas*).
Since there is no deficiency even if a substance distinct from gold and distinct from fire lacks the property of being perceptible by the eye when aided by light,
the proof that darkness is a substance over and above [the other categories] is entirely unassailable.
[3] An Examination of Gold:
The Ancient Viewpoint Therein.
In the *Nyāyasūtra*, its *Bhāṣya*, and the *Vaiśeṣikasūtra*, no discussion regarding the fiery nature (*taijasatva*) of gold is observed; however, [the Vaiśeṣikasūtra states]:
"The liquefaction of tin, lead, iron, silver, and gold due to contact with fire is like that of water."
The sūtra "sāmānyam" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.7) indicates that gold possesses occasional fluidity; in that sūtra, the word "taijasānām" (of luminous substances) was present as an additional term.
It is known from the *Sarvārthasiddhi* by the Vedānta-deśikas:
"The state of fluidity in tin, lead, iron, and gold— which are composed of fire (*taijasa*)— is a commonality [they share] with water due to contact with fire."
A Vaiśeṣika sūtra has been cited;
by that, it is known that Kaṇāda also agreed with the fiery nature of gold.
In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*,
in the section defining fire (*tejas*),
fire in the form of objects is divided into four types: terrestrial, celestial, digestive, and mineral.
Only this much was stated: "Gold and so forth are mine-born (*ākaraja*). Regarding that, the author of the *Kandalī* says:
"A mine (*ākara*) is a particular location."
In that [fire], luminous substances such as gold and silver are produced.
Regarding the luminous nature of gold and the like, scripture is the authority;
furthermore, the logical reasoning has already been stated.

"By virtue of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) of enjoyers, gold and other substances are produced through the support of a great number of earth-atoms; these possess non-manifest color and touch and are capable of forming a solid mass. In that [gold], tastes and other qualities inherent in the earthly substance are perceived," so he says.
Here, by the word "āgama" (scriptural authority), the Vedic statement "Gold is the first offspring of fire" is intended;
as is [the rule] stating, "Earth and fire possess adventitious fluidity."
In the *Kandalī*, on the occasion of commenting upon the *Bhāṣya*, the reasoning establishing the luminous nature (*taijasatva*) of gold is set forth;
and that is as follows: "In gold, there is no fluidity [caused by heat]."
If it is argued that fluidity, which exists only in earth just as gravity does, is perceived in burning gold through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), we say: no.

Since the liquidity of earthy substances is seen to be reduced to ashes through absolute contact with fire, whereas the liquidity of gold is not reduced to ashes even upon absolute contact with fire, gold is not earthy.
In the *Kiraṇāvalī* as well:
"Gold and the like are not earthy, because even when subjected to intense contact with fire, they possess a color that does not change, just like water."

Thus, having established by means of inference that gold is distinct from earth, and having further established that it is distinct from water— on account of the absence of natural fluidity and coldness, as well as the non-perception of its being gathered by another substance invariably concomitant with viscidity (sneha)— [the author proceeds].

Having established that [the object] is distinct from air and the other elements because it possesses color, its nature as consisting of fire (taijasa) was proven by the method of elimination; this is the intention of the author of the Maṇi.
Even jewelers,
following the very path graced by the rays of the *kandalī* plant, have established through inference that gold is of a luminous (*taijasa*) nature.
In this regard, the distinction is that certain other inferences not mentioned [here] have been demonstrated in the *Maṇi*.
They are as follows: (1)
A substance possessing a yellow color that is in constant contact with fire is conjoined with a liquid substance that acts as an obstacle to the production of a heterogeneous color,
even though it remains in contact with fire day and night.
(1) Because it does not serve as the substratum for any color other than yellow,
like a yellow cloth situated in the midst of water that has been in contact with fire for that long;
(2) that which possesses fluidity not destroyed by intense contact with fire is composed of fire (*taijasa*).
Because it possesses color while being distinct from water and earth,
like fire;
(3) [it is] yellow.

The substratum of fluidity is conjoined with a liquid substance that prevents the destruction of its fluidity, because it is a terrestrial substance whose fluidity is not destroyed even when subjected to intense contact with fire,
like ghee situated in the midst of boiling water.
(4) That which is the subject of dispute,

being the substratum of fluidity, is fiery, because it is the substratum of fluidity that is not destroyed even when there is contact with intense fire, provided there is no contact with another liquid substance; for that which is not so [is not fiery].
That is not so, as in the case of water or clarified butter.

(5) The nature of fire (*tejastva*) does not reside solely in that which possesses a non-liquid form, because it is a genus directly pervaded by *substancehood* (*dravyatva*) that resides in that which possesses form.
Like the nature of earth; or else, like the nature of fire, which has the property of flowing.
Because it is a genus directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) that resides in that which possesses form (*rūpavat*), like the nature of water (*jalatva*).
(6) The atoms that originate gold are not earthy (*pārthiva*).
Because they possess fluidity that is not destroyed even by contact with intense fire,
like water-atoms; or else, they are fiery for that very same reason.
That which is not thus is not thus, just like a particle of clarified butter. Gold, whether originated from earth or originated from fire, is neither earthy nor fiery.
Or rather, [it is so] because it is composed of atoms that serve as the substratum for fluidity which is not destroyed even when there is contact with extreme fire;
thus Annambhaṭṭa, in the *Dīpikā*, also follows this very method regarding gold.
It establishes the luminous nature [of gold];
according to the view of a certain school, gold possesses the nature of earth.
In the *Muktāvalīvyākhyāna* by Dinakara, beginning with the words "But the moderns (*navīnās tu*)," another view is presented which establishes that gold is of an earthly nature (*pārthivatva*).

Their intention, however, is as follows: from the cognition "the gold has been melted while being drunk," it is understood that liquidity exists in gold—which possesses a yellow color—and for that very reason, in that which is earthen (pārthiva).
Furthermore, because the earthen liquidity thus perceived is not destroyed even by intense heating, [liquidity] exists therein.

The fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) is unavoidable. Nor should it be argued that such a cognition is of the nature of an error (bhrama), for there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka) to that effect.
Nor should it be asked why, despite its being composed of earth, the destruction of its color does not occur due to contact with fire;
for, by the force of experience, [the cause of destruction] is established as being identical with the substance itself (*tādātmyena*) in relation to the destruction of color.
This is because the presence of gold is accepted as being an obstructing factor (*pratibandhaka*).
Here, this must be considered:
is it the conjunction with intense fire, qualified by the absence of an obstructing factor, that destroys the liquidity of the earthy substance?
The "counter-reason" (pratihetu) refers to the necessary causal relationship; in that case,
there is an absence of the effect consisting in the destruction of non-liquidity in the earthly portion residing within the gold.
It is undisputed that [the absence of smoke] is caused by the absence of the cause, namely, the conjunction with fire characterized by the absence of an obstructing factor (*pratibandhaka*).
In that case, the absence of the cause— which consists in the absence of such a qualified entity— is not...
Because of the absence of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), since the qualificand— in the form of contact with intense fire— is present there; rather,
it must be stated that [the non-existence of the effect] is due solely to the absence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), which consists in the absence of an obstructing factor (*pratibandhaka*).

It must be stated that there exists some other liquid substance acting as an impediment therein; if that too were earth, there would be another substance impeding the destruction of its liquidity, and for that one as well,
yet another— thus there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, since it possesses liquidity that does not perish even in the absence of any other obstructing factor, it is not earth. — [The authors of the *Dīpikā*]
They accept that both the earth-constituent (pārthivabhāga) possesses fluidity and the fire-constituent (tejobhāga) also possesses fluidity, based on the natural force of the two phrases:
"the destruction of the fluidity of the yellow substance" and "another fluid substance.
However, in the *Muktāvalī*, this is addressed by the passage: "Because it is not fluid, like a powder of ink situated in the midst of water."
It has been established that there is an absence of liquidity in the earthly portion [of gold];
for this very reason, another inference proving the luminous nature (*taijasatva*) of gold based on that [absence] has been presented in the *Muktāvalī*.
Those who act for the pleasure of the foolish explain this in detail:
[4] An investigation into the direct perception of wind.

The authors of the *Dīpikā*, having established that air is cognizable through inference based on the mark of touch by means of the statement "air is to be inferred from touch" and so forth, described that air is not perceptible because it is devoid of color.
This reality is now being examined:

with respect to the general class of external sensory perception of substances, manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is the cause. Consequently, because air lacks manifest color, it does not fall within the scope of direct perception.
But rather, it is known solely through inference;
and thus says the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra: "And touch belongs to air" (Vai. Sū. 2.1.9).
By the word "ca" (and), sound, support, and motion are included.
Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is that air is to be inferred through touch and other qualities, but it is not perceptible.
And thus says the Praśastapādabhāṣya: "The object, moreover, is that which serves as the substrate for the touch being perceived."
"Touch, sound, support, and motion are its marks.
Regarding this, the author of the *Kandalī* states: "First of all, perception is not a means of valid cognition for the existence of air."
Because anything other than touch is not apprehended by the skin;
nor should it be said that air is perceptible because of the cognition "the air blows."
Because that knowledge consists of an inference based on the mark of touch;

for the pervasion (vyāpti) exists— since it is observed in the case of jars and other objects that wherever there is the state of being an object of tactile perception, there is also the state of being an object of visual perception— and thus, due to the absence of color, the state of being visually perceptible [is absent] in air.
When the pervader is absent, its pervaded quality—
tangibility— is also excluded.
Therefore, he established that air is not an object of direct perception, but rather something to be inferred.
According to the view of Maṇikāra,
with respect to tactile perception (*spārśana*) directed toward a substance, it is not merely the manifested touch (*udbhūtasparśa*) that is the causal factor;
for if that were the case, the heat of summer (*nidāghoṣman*), being the substratum of manifested touch, would [absurdly] be perceptible.
The number and other properties residing in that [substance] would also have to be perceptible,
according to the rule that a number residing in a perceptible individual possesses perceptibility.
Indeed, even when heat is touched by the hand, no one perceives the number residing therein;
nor is there perception of a substance [without its qualities].
Only manifested color (udbhūtarūpa) is the determinant; if that were the case,
then since the light of the moon and other luminaries possesses manifested color, they would be perceptible, and consequently, the number residing therein would also be perceptible.
It would follow [that this is impossible],
for even one who observes minutely does not perceive such things as number existing within the light of the moon and so forth.

Therefore, because each [factor] individually deviates from the rule, it must be stated that both "manifest touch" (*udbhūtasparśa*) and "manifest color" (*udbhūtarūpa*) together are the causal conditions for the direct perception of a substance.
The light of the moon and other such sources possesses manifest color, yet it does not possess manifest touch.
The heat of summer possesses manifested touch but not manifested color;

therefore, because those two are imperceptible, it is impossible to establish the perceptibility of the number residing therein. Likewise, air possesses manifested touch but not manifested color. Thus, it is not [the case that air is perceived].
It is perceptible.
Furthermore, with respect to the perception of a substance, an emergent touch is not the cause.
If that were the case, then while a bird's egg is moving, the direct perception of its disjunction from the eastern location and its conjunction with the northern location would not occur;
for the eastern and northern locations, which consist of spheres of light, are devoid of manifested touch. Therefore...
The masters of the tradition maintain that only manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is the determining factor for the perceptibility of a substance.
Even according to their view, the author of the *Maṇi* (Raghunātha Śiromaṇi) has established that air, being devoid of manifested color, is indeed imperceptible.
And thus,
when it has been determined that manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is the cause of the external sensory perception of a substance,
[it follows that] "air is an object of external sensory perception, because it is the substratum of perceptible touch."

In this inference, the presence of unmanifested color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*)— which pervades the probandum as delimited by substantiality (*dravyatva*), which is the property of the subject— is the limiting condition (*upādhi*). And thus,
air is not the object of external sensory perception.
The essential point of the author of the *Maṇi*’s exposition is that the imperceptibility of air is established by the inference: "Because it is a substance devoid of color, like space."
The author of the Dīpikā also followed this very path;
thus it is stated regarding wind in the Muktāvalī:
The establishment of the perceptibility [of air]:
in the *Muktāvalī*, beginning with the words "But the moderns," the perceptibility of air has been determined.

For instance— color is not the cause of that which is delimited by being a perceptual cognition of a substance produced by an external sense organ, because there is a lack of evidence [for such a claim].
Furthermore, in visual perception, color is the cause, and in tactile perception,
touch is the cause; likewise, there is no [contradiction] in the air, which is the substratum of touch, being an object of tactile perception.
There is no obstacle whatsoever;
for just as light, although devoid of manifested touch, is accepted as an object of visual perception on the strength of the experience "I see the light," so too [is the case here].
From the experience "I touch the air," what contradiction is there in the air being an object of tactile perception even though it is devoid of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*)?
In that case, [tactile perception] would reside in a fit air (*yogyavāyu*).
If it is asked, "What is the solution to the fault stated by Maṇi—that number would also be perceived?"—this is it:
due to the defect consisting in the confluence of similar [atoms], the number of air is not perceived in some cases;
however, in the absence of such a defect, the perception of number is indeed intended.
In reality, however, when a bird moves through the air, its conjunctions with and disjunctions from the points in space to the east and north are directly perceived;
therein lies the [nature of] the substratum.

Since the authors of the *Maṇi* have stated that by the reasoning that "if a portion consisting of light were imperceptible, then conjunctions and disjunctions residing therein would also be imperceptible," even though light is perceptible, air is not so; therefore, it is not possible to establish the perceptibility of air by means of the example of light.
This is possible; however, no such reasoning applies to air.
Therefore, it is clear in works such as the *Dinakarya* that air is indeed imperceptible.
Rucidatta Miśra, the author of the *Cintāmaṇiprakāśa*, establishes that air is indeed perceptible,
provided it possesses manifested color and touch.
Even though the solar radiance is perceptible, its number and other qualities are not perceptible;
let it be the same for air as well.
And if it is admitted that the number and other qualities of the solar radiance are indeed perceptible, then [the same would follow].
Or let it be accepted even in the case of air; or rather,
[let it be defined as] that which possesses an unmanifested touch in its substratum with respect to the perception of number.
The possession of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) alone is the determining factor.
Therefore, number is not perceived in air. Nevertheless, for air to be perceptible by touch, the mere possession of manifested touch (*udbhūtasparśamātra*) is the determining factor.
The tactile nature of air is established beyond dispute; thus it was described by him.
[5] An investigation into the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*) in the *Dīpikā* states: "In that which possesses it..."
"An experience possessing that mode is valid," and "an experience possessing that mode in that which lacks it is invalid"— this is the definition extracted by the author of the *Maṇi*.
Having followed the path and stated the definitions of valid cognition (*pramā*) and invalid cognition (*apramā*),
we shall now examine the intention of the earlier authorities regarding this subject and the reason for proposing new definitions.
Having stated in the first aphorism, "From the knowledge of reality comes the attainment of the supreme good" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.1),
that the knowledge of reality is the means to liberation, [the author] proceeds to explain its method in the [second] aphorism, "Suffering, birth..."
In this second aphorism, beginning with "thus," he stated that the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the remover of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).
By this, the author of the aphorisms considers the knowledge of reality to be valid cognition (*pramā*); for [he holds] that only valid cognition...
Because it is the remover of false knowledge in the form of error,
its state is "tattva"— that is, a property residing in the qualificand; the knowledge of that is "tattvajñāna" (knowledge of reality).
Knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is, in other words, knowledge whose qualifier is a property residing in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
By this [definition], it is established that [the nature of such knowledge] consists in being a cognition whose qualifier is a property residing in the qualificand.
It results in [the following] definition of valid cognition (*pramā*):

In this position, the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) occurs with respect to accurate memory (*yathārthasmṛti*), because that too is a cognition whose qualifier is a property residing in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

In the commentary on the third sutra, the author of the Bhāṣya, stating that "it should be understood from the force of the definition and the etymological explanation of the term that the means of apprehension are the instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇa)," indicates that "apprehension (upalabdhi) is valid cognition (pramā)."
In accordance with the sūtra, "Buddhi, upalabdhi, and jñāna are synonymous" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.15), the word *upalabdhi* means "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Since knowledge without an object is impossible, it follows that the nature of valid cognition (*pramātva*) consists in being a knowledge whose object is a real thing (*artha*).
For this very reason, the commentary on the first sūtra states: "That which is the cognition of the object is valid knowledge (pramiti).
However, this definition is over-extensive (ativyāpti) with respect to memory and error, because both of these also have objects as their domain and are forms of cognition.
Having considered the aforementioned lack of logical consistency, the commentator Vācaspatimiśra states:
"For the relationship between word and meaning is determined by worldly usage; and the world..."
They say: "One designates as valid cognition (pramā) an apprehension other than memory that does not deviate from the object.
The meaning of this is that valid cognition is a cognition distinct from memory which does not deviate from the object.
The non-deviation of knowledge from its object consists in its having as its content an object exactly as it exists.
Even in this view, the defect of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) persists in the case of correct memory (*yathārthasmṛti*).

For this very reason, in the *Nyāyasāra*, the term "experience" (*anubhava*) was substituted for the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), and the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*) was stated as: "Valid cognition is correct experience."
And in the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, it is stated that correctness (*samyaktva*) regarding experience consists in having the nature of a determination of the object as it actually exists;
this refers to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) mentioned in the aphorism.

Having reflected that the definition of valid cognition (*pramātva*) would otherwise over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to memory (*smṛti*), Udayanācārya stated in the *Lakṣaṇāvalī* that "valid cognition is the experience of reality" (*tattvānubhūtiḥ pramā*), and this was likewise asserted by Śivādityamiśra in the *Saptapadārthī*.
This definition was refuted after being analyzed in many ways in the *Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya*.
In the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*, the teacher Udayana states: "Valid cognition is experience that accords with reality..."

By the portion of the verse stating, "Validity is desired as non-dependence on another cognition," they asserted that the definition of valid knowledge (*pramā*) is being an experience that accords with reality.
By the inclusion of the term "experience," over-extension to memory is excluded;
for [the definition requires] that in experience, there must be correspondence with reality (yathārthatva) regarding whatever exists in whatever locus.
In that case, it is precisely the state of having that as its object. For instance, at the occasion of defining error in the *Kusumāñjali*, [Udayana] says:
"That which does not exist there..."
"It was stated that 'its apprehension [is so called] because it has the sense of error.
In the *Prakāśa*, which is a commentary on that [text], it says: 'By this, whatever exists in whatever..."

"In that regard, that cognition is also defined as valid knowledge (pramā)," so it was stated. And thus, the refined definition of validity according to the teacher Udayana is: "the state of being an experience possessing a qualifier in that which possesses that [qualifier]."
Regarding the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*):
even the authors of the *Maṇi* have accepted this definition as their own final position (*siddhānta*),
and thus the author of the *Dīpikā* has likewise proclaimed that very same definition.
Viśvanātha Pañcānana, in his *Kārikāvalī*, has stated two definitions of valid cognition (*pramā*) that are common to recollection (*smṛti*):
"But [valid cognition] is distinct from error..."
"Knowledge is here called valid cognition" (Kārikā 134); "Alternatively, that knowledge which possesses that [object] as its qualifier and has that [object] as its qualificandum is valid cognition."
(Verse 135) Thus it is said. Among these, the first definition is: being a cognition while being distinct from error.

In this definition, regarding the cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl and silver, it is accepted that this cognition is a valid cognition (*pramā*) in its aspect of having silver as its object; however,
considering that the condition of being distinct from error (*bhrama*) is absent therein, [the author] reflects upon the deficiency of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and [proposes] the second...
The definition has been followed: that is to say,
valid cognition (pramā) is a cognition which, while having that [object] as its qualificandum, possesses that [property] as its qualifier.

Regarding the doubt that, since the term "experience" (*anubhava*) is not included in either of these two definitions and only the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is included, the definition of valid knowledge (*pramā*) would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to memory (*smṛti*), the following resolution is stated in the *Muktāvalī*:
The validity of memory is indeed accepted;
therefore, since it too is characterized by the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of that definition.
If it is argued that if memory is admitted to be a valid cognition (*pramā*), then its cause would result in a fifth means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)— it is not so;
for the definition of a means of knowledge is constituted by direct experience (*anubhava*).
The definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which produces an experience of an object as it truly is.
This does not apply to that which produces memory, because memory is not a producer of [new] experience.

"Because memory lacks the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*), it does not entail the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This argumentation by Viśvanātha appears to be the most reasonable.
For the author of the *Nyāyasūtra*, "non-apprehension of reality" (*atattvajñāna*) refers to erroneous cognition (*mithyājñāna*), which is the opposite of valid cognition (*pramājñāna*).
Since the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is used commonly in the *Smṛti* [text] itself, it is intended that recollection (*smṛti*) also possesses the status of valid cognition (*pramātva*).
For this very reason, [it is stated]: "Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition" (*Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.3).

In the sūtra (1-1-3), "smṛti" (remembrance) is not included among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this indicates that the definition of a means of valid cognition must be formulated as being constituted solely by direct experience (*anubhava*). This is the conclusion of the author of the *Prakāśikā*.

Even if one were to state that "a cognition which has a qualifier in that which possesses it is valid," there would still be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the error "these are silver and mother-of-pearl" regarding silver and mother-of-pearl; for that [cognition] too...
Because it has silverness as its qualifier while having silver as its qualificand, and because it has rangness (the nature of brass) as its qualifier while having brass as its qualificand; therefore,
one must incorporate the relationship of the defined and the definer (*nirūpya-nirūpaka-bhāva*) between the qualificandhood and the qualifierhood.

Similarly, the *Prakāśikā* provides the following refined definition (*niṣkarṣa*): "The definition of valid cognition (*pramā*) should be stated as 'the state of being an experience possessing a qualifier-nature residing in that [object], which is itself determined by a qualificand-nature residing in that [same object].
This is the underlying unifying principle (*anugama*) here:
Valid cognition (*pramā*) is an experience that determines a qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) qualified by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*).

And the state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [between the mode and the qualificandum] is by way of both relations: (1) residing in something that possesses the locus of itself through its own delimiting relation (*svāvacchedaka-sambandha*), and (2) being determined by that [mode-ness].
Alternatively, valid cognition (*pramā*) is an experience characterized by a qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyitā*) that is qualified by a qualifier-ness (*prakāritā*).

And this *vaiśiṣṭya* [relation] is by way of both relations: being delimited by itself (*svāvacchinnatva*), and being determined by a qualificandum-ness that is qualified by a qualifier-ness determined by itself (*svanirūpitaprakāratāviśiṣṭaviśeṣyatānirūpitatva*).

And the qualification by the modehood (*prakāratā*) is by way of the relation of its own delimiting relation (*svāvacchedaka-sambandha*) and the relation of residing in that which possesses its own locus (*svāśrayavat-niṣṭhatva*).
Further details are to be found in the commentary known as the *Prasāriṇī*.
This must be observed;
however,
even with such a refined definition, there remains the fault of non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpaka).

Because in a non-modal cognition denoted by the term "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*), there is an absence of the definition of valid knowledge (*pramā*) which is constituted by having that [object] as its mode;
therefore, an experience that has a particular mode in that which lacks it is invalid knowledge (*apramā*).
Therefore, the definition must be stated as: "Valid cognition is an experience distinct from that [error].
However, the author of the Muktāvalī [states] that indeterminate [cognition]...
They consider it to be excluded from both error and valid cognition.
[6] An investigation into the threefold nature of causes is found in works such as the Tarkasaṃgraha-dīpikā, the Kārikāvalī, and the Muktāvalī.

In the treatises following the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika systems, causes are divided into three types— namely, the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), and the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa)— and the definition for each of these has been extracted and established; however, [the following applies]...
Some modern critics maintain that this threefold division of causes is not mentioned in ancient texts such as the *sūtras*, but was propounded solely by contemporary Naiyāyikas.
This reality is now being investigated.
"That which possesses action and qualities and is an inherent cause is substance" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 1.1.15); "the cause..."
By examining Vaiśeṣika sūtras such as "The qualities [of time] are non-inherent" (Vai.Sū.
5.2.24) and "Time [is known] through its cause" (Vai.Sū. 5.2.26), it is evident that all three types of causes [are involved].
It is understood that this is the view accepted by the author of the Sūtra;
for in the Praśastapādabhāṣya as well, three types of causes are accepted: "the simultaneous [presence] of the three—namely, the inherent cause, the non-inherent cause, and the instrumental cause."
The Bhāṣya passages beginning with "from the destruction [of the cause], there is the destruction of posteriority" should be consulted.
Although the discussion of the three causes is not seen in the Nyāsa-sūtras, [it is nevertheless relevant].

Nevertheless, there is an indication of this in the *Vātsyāyana-bhāṣya*. For instance, in the *Nyāyadarśana*, in the first section of the fourth chapter, the eighteenth sūtra states: "There is no refutation [of the opponent's position] because of the mention of a specific order."
This sūtra exists within the context of refuting the view that emptiness alone is the material cause of the world;
and therein:
The Commentary: "The constituent parts of the seed,
having had activity manifested due to some cause,"
They abandon the previous arrangement and assume another arrangement; from that other arrangement, a sprout [arises].
It arises; indeed, the parts and their conjunctions are seen to be the causes for the production of the sprout.
Thus, here,
by the phrase "due to some cause," the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) consisting of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth is indicated;
and by the phrase "the parts and their conjunctions are the causes for the production of the sprout," [the material cause is indicated].

The nature of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) as the constituent parts and the nature of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) as the conjunction of the constituent parts have been indicated. The author of the *Nyāyavārttika* also explicitly mentions these three causes in various places: "It is not a [valid] reason because it is produced by that" (*Nyāyasūtra* 4.1.21).
Thus, by stating "because it is caused by that" as found in the Sūtra, it follows that Īśvara is accepted as the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa);
and whatever is the efficient cause, that [is distinct] from the other two [causes].

"The Vārttika states: 'That which assists both the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), such as the shuttle and other tools for threads and their conjunctions';
and [the Nyāya Sūtra says]: 'The sense organs—the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear—arise from the elements' (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.12)."
Thus, it is stated in the Sūtra: "No effect whatsoever is seen to have a single cause;
for every effect, when it manifests, arises from inherent causes (samavāyi-kāraṇa), non-inherent causes (asamavāyi-kāraṇa), and instrumental causes (nimitta-kāraṇa)."
And here, a *vārttika* (critical commentary) is worthy of consideration:

thus it is established that the classification of causes into three types— namely, inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*)— is firmly rooted in the ancient texts.
In their new treatises,
they have presented the definitions of those causes after refining them;
[herein] are the arguments for accepting the three causes.

In this regard, a certain doubt may arise: just as the Vedāntins and others accept two kinds of causes, namely the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), [so too might one wonder about the present case].
Likewise, why do the Naiyāyikas not accept [this]?
To this, it is said:
The Naiyāyikas accept the whole (avayavin) as something distinct from its parts;
the Vedāntins, however, maintain that the cloth is merely a particular conjunction of threads.
They say it is distinct from that; in the view of the Vedāntins, the threads and so forth belong to the category of the effect.
[The opponent] adheres [to this view]. In the system of the Naiyāyikas, however, the whole (avayavin) named "cloth" is an effect;
it arises from a particular conjunction of threads.
Therefore, the conjunction of the threads is also a cause.
It must be accepted that,
since it is impossible for it to be an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), its status as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) has been established.
In that case, let there be a twofold division into inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) and instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa),
even for the conjunction of the threads.
If it is argued that [the self] may simply be an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), it is replied:
even when the weaver, who is the efficient cause, has perished, the effect in the form of the cloth remains;
however, upon the destruction of the conjunction of the threads, the cloth does not remain.
Rather, it perishes.

Therefore, because of its dissimilarity to the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and its dissimilarity to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the conjunction of the threads is accepted as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Why is this so?
If non-inherent causes are not admitted, it must be stated what the cause is for the destruction of a substance;
it cannot be the destruction of the efficient cause,
for [the substance would still persist] even when the potter and other such factors remain present.

Furthermore, because one observes the destruction of a jar even when the potter and other such factors have perished, and because one observes the continued existence of the jar even upon the destruction of its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the destruction of the inherent cause is not the cause [of the jar's destruction].
This is because the destruction of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) would otherwise be impossible.
For the atom is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of the dyad;
indeed, its destruction is not possible.
Because [the atom] is eternal, the destruction of the dyad cannot occur through the destruction of its inherent cause; therefore,
it must be stated that its destruction occurs solely through the destruction of the conjunction of the two atoms, which serves as its non-inherent cause.
And thus, rather than relying on the assumption that the destruction of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is the cause for the destruction of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*),

while the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is the cause for the destruction of other effect-substances (*kāryadravya*), [it is more appropriate] to regard [the destruction of the inherent cause] as the cause for the destruction of all effect-substances in general, by virtue of its universal applicability.
The acceptance of the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) is necessary;
therefore, let there be a twofold division into the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) and the non-inherent cause.

If it is argued that there should be no such thing as a *nimittakāraṇa* (efficient cause), we say: no. For if every cause distinct from the *samavāyikāraṇa* (inherent cause) were included within the category of *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause), then—

Since, according to the previously stated method, the destruction of a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) is the cause for the destruction of a substance, it would follow that even upon the destruction of the potter and so forth, the destruction of the jar would occur. Therefore,
the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) must be accepted as something distinct.
And thus, since it is consistent with reason, all three causes must be accepted; therefore, it is established that the threefold classification of causes is rooted in the ancient treatises.
(7) An investigation into indeterminate and determinate perception: perception is twofold, namely indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) and determinate (*savikalpaka*).

In the *Tarkasaṃgraha*, it is stated that knowledge devoid of qualifiers (*niṣprakāraka*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), while knowledge possessing qualifiers (*saprakāraka*) is conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

It has been stated in the *Dīpikā*: "Non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is a cognition that does not apprehend the relationship between a qualifier and a qualified; conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is a cognition that apprehends the relationship between qualifiers and a qualified, such as names, universals (*jāti*), and so forth."

Non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakatva*) consists in being devoid of the state of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*), devoid of the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*), and devoid of the state of being a relation (*saṃsargatā*);
it is the state of not having a qualificand as its determiner (*viśeṣyatānirūpakatva*).

"In the *Prakāśikā*, it is stated that determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) consists in being the qualifier of the nature of a qualifier (*prakāratānirūpakatva*) and the qualifier of the nature of a relation (*saṃsargatānirūpakatva*).
