Now, the true nature of this [definition] is [to be understood] by means of a thorough examination of earlier texts."
This is now considered:
nowhere in the Nyāyasūtra has a division of perception (*pratyakṣa*) been made by means of the terms "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*) and "conceptual" (*savikalpaka*).

By the two terms "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśyam*) and "of the nature of determinate judgment" (*vyavasāyātmakam*) found in the sūtra defining perception— "produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object"— it is intended that indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) and determinate (*savikalpaka*) perception are respectively meant.
Thus the authors of the *Tātparyaṭīkā* explain;
however, we do not find such an exposition in either the *Bhāṣya* or the *Vārttika*.
Although two types of perception— non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*)— have been established with supporting arguments in both the *Nyāyamañjarī* and the *Nyāyasāra*,...
Nevertheless, the manner in which such a distinction is obtained from the Sūtra has not been demonstrated there;
however, in the Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, by means of the term *avyapadeśya* (indescribable), [it is shown].

In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, it was established with supporting arguments that the term "of the nature of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) includes determinate perception (*savikalpaka*), as opposed to indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*).
First, regarding substance, which is of two kinds:

in the case of a large [substance], [visual perception] arises from the fourfold contact consisting of [the object's] possession of multiple substances, the presence of manifested color, and illumination.

And by the passage beginning with "In the presence of the collection of factors such as the object, there is the mere observation of its own nature," non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is demonstrated.
The phrase "mere observation of its own nature" (svarūpālocanamātra) means the apprehension of the thing-in-itself alone; by the word "mere" (mātra), [the qualifiers are excluded].
This is the exclusion of [perception] having as its object a relation such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. From that—
[it arises] from the contact of the self and the mind, depending on the qualifiers of generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*).
"An existent substance arises as a direct perception, such as: 'the earth,' 'the horned one,' 'the white cow is walking,'" according to this passage.

Perceptual cognition with conceptual content (*savikalpakapratyakṣa*) has been demonstrated along with examples; however, the terms "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*) and "conceptual" (*savikalpaka*) were not employed [by him]. Kumārila Bhaṭṭa also—
"For there exists first a non-conceptualizing awareness of mere observation,
similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and others, which arises from the pure object itself."
By this verse, non-conceptual [perception] is described;
and "thereafter, that object... [is described].
Just as [an object] is determined by the intellect through its properties such as genus and so forth,
that [intellection] also is accepted as being of the nature of direct perception.
Thus, by means of this verse,
they defined determinate perception (*savikalpaka*).
And in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*:
Cognition is held to be of two kinds: conceptual and non-conceptual;
the former has a qualified object.
"and that which has as its object something other than its own nature"—
thus he demonstrated the twofold division of perception into the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and the conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

In the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, the definition of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) was presented as follows: "Indeterminate perception is that which is devoid of association with name, genus, and so forth, does not involve the apprehension of relations (*vaiśiṣṭya*), and is free from any qualifying attributes (*niṣprakāraka*)."
"Non-involving a specific distinction" (*vaiśiṣṭyānavagāhin*) is itself explained as "devoid of a qualifier" (*niṣprakāraka*).
In indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*),
there is not only an absence of the objective relation called "qualifier-ness" (*prakāratā*), but also an absence of the objective relation called "qualificandum-ness" (*viśeṣyatā*).
Thus, it can also be said that indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is a cognition devoid of a qualificandum (*nirviśeṣyaka*).

However, for the authors of the *Maṇi* (Rucidatta), who do not say this but instead state it is "devoid of a mode" (*niṣprakāraka*), the intention is as follows: since determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), [it is distinguished] from that...
First, the cognition of the qualifier is postulated;
likewise, because it serves as the cause for non-conceptual [cognition], no other cognition is required.

The proof for the existence of such non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is the following inference: "The first perception of a cow in this life is produced by a cognition of a qualifier that is itself produced, because it is a cognition of a qualified object that is produced, just like an inferential cognition (*anumiti*)."

Just as the inference "the mountain possesses fire" has as its object a mountain qualified by fire and is produced by the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*)— which consists of the cognition of the qualifier in the form of fire— so too is the initial [cognition].

It must be stated that even a qualified perception such as "this is a cow" arises solely from the cognition of the qualifier, which is the nature of cowness (*gotva*). That very [cognition] is indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*), as it does not have the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) as its object.
Nor is there [any other cognition] therein...
It should not be argued that the recollection of the qualifier *gotva* (cowness) alone is the cause of the first qualified perception (*viśiṣṭapratyakṣa*),
and thus indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpakapratyakṣa*) is not established; for [such recollection] must have occurred previously in this very life.
Because the recollection of that [cowness] is impossible without the experience of cowness,
and because the experience of the qualifier in the form of cowness cannot be anything other than conceptual, such that it would result in the thought "this is a cow."
Let it produce a qualified perception;
and thus it must be said that the non-conceptual [perception] has already passed away.

If that were the case, then because that [non-conceptual perception] would also be a qualified cognition, it too would have to be produced by a cognition of the qualifier, and for that [qualifier-cognition] as well...
If it were so, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress;
thus, by implication, a non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpaka) having "cowness" as its object is established.
Here, this is raised as an objection:
"It was stated that because a qualified cognition is preceded by the cognition of the qualifier, indeterminate perception is established;
but that is not so. For the qualified cognition 'this is a cow' is produced by the cognition of the qualifier, because it is a qualified cognition."

Thus, in this inference, the condition (*upādhi*) is "having as its object that which is cognized by distinct causal complexes" (*bhinnasāmagrīvedyaviṣayakatva*). For it is observed that only in cases where both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are cognized by distinct causal complexes is a cognition of the qualified preceded by a cognition of the qualifier.

For example, "the sandalwood is fragrant" is a qualified perception (*viśiṣṭapratyakṣa*); for in that case, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), fragrance, is cognizable by the olfactory faculty, while the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—
Sandalwood is perceptible by the eye; because it has as its object a thing perceivable by distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*),
there is first the cognition of the qualifier in the form of fragrance within that qualified perception, and by means of that, [the cognition] "fragrant sandalwood" arises.

There occurs a qualified perception (*viśiṣṭapratyakṣa*). Since it is possible for a qualified cognition to arise at one and the same time regarding two instances of cowness cognizable by a single sense-organ, there first arises the cognition of cowness, and from that, the cognition of a cow qualified by cowness.

Such a conceptual construction is not tenable. For is it not the case that, although the qualifier and the qualified— namely, cowness and the individual cow— are objects of a single cognition due to their being suitable for apprehension by the same sense organ, their relationship is not so?
In the first cognition, the relation between those two does not appear;
that alone is non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka).

If it is argued that we accept only that cognition which does not apprehend the relation between the qualifier and the qualified as being denotable by the term "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*), we say:
no. By the word "relation," do you intend the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the objects], or rather inherence (*samavāya*)? In the first case...
If the nature of the qualifier and the qualified is apprehended, the relation is also necessarily apprehended; so where is there any non-conceptual [perception]?
In the second case, [it would be apprehended] through the sense-object contact known as "qualification of the conjoined" (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā*) by means of the eye.
According to your own established doctrine that inherence (samavāya) is perceived, since the cow,
cowness, and their inherence are all capable of being apprehended by the same sense organ, the perception of all three must necessarily occur at one and the same time.

Otherwise, even for an inherent relation (*samavāya*) that is otherwise perceptible, there would be no apprehension of it at a later time if it were not apprehended initially; and thus, indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) would fail to include the apprehension of relations.
"It is not tenable according to reason.
To this, the following resolution is offered:

in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), there exists the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the form of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, as well as the qualified (*viśeṣya*) in the form of the individual (*vyakti*).
The [individual] objects appear, but the relation does not appear;
because the cognition of the relata is a cause for the cognition of the relation, that [cognition of the relata] was previously absent.

And so, first there arises a non-conceptual (nirvikalpa) cognition of the two related entities in the form of the qualifier and the qualified; thereafter, a conceptual (savikalpaka) cognition arises that apprehends the relation between those two.

As it was stated by the teacher Udayana: "However, due to the deficiency of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-vaikalyāt*), there is no apprehension of inherence (*samavāya*) in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*).
Regarding the phrase "due to the deficiency of auxiliary factors":
The meaning is: "due to the absence of the cognition of a relation.
And thus, there is no occasion for the objection: "In that case, why does the relation itself not appear in indeterminate perception?"
As for the claim that "having as its object a thing cognizable by a distinct causal complex" (*bhinnasāmagrīvedyaviṣayakatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*), this must be said in response:
since the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*) and so forth function as causes in inference, verbal cognition, and the like, [the rule] "between two particulars... applies.

By means of logic, once the general causal relationship is established— that the cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), as delimited by the nature of being a cognition of a qualifier, is the cause for [the cognition] delimited by the nature of being a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*)— then even in cases where [objects] are cognized by a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*),
the qualified cognition is produced solely by that [qualifier-cognition], through the postulation of a cognition of the qualifier. And thus:

Because the state of having an object cognizable by a distinct causal complex (bhinnasāmagrīvedyaviṣayakatva) lacks pervasion of the probandum (sādhyavyāpakatva), it cannot constitute a limiting condition (upādhi);
all this [is as stated].
Having taken this into consideration, it is stated in the *Dīpikā*:
"If it is asked, 'What is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for non-conceptual [perception]?', we say: no. [The cognition] 'cow'..."
A qualified cognition is produced by the cognition of the qualifier, because it is a qualified cognition, like the cognition "one who possesses a staff."
Thus, because inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
the cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is also conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
"The establishment of non-conceptual perception follows from the consequence of infinite regress. Thus ends the examination of sense-object contact in the *Tarkasaṃgraha*.
In the *Dīpikā*, it is demonstrated with examples that the cause of perception is contact (*saṃnikarṣa*), which is of six kinds according to the distinctions of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.
In the *Prakāśikā*, perception is stated to be of two kinds.
It is both worldly and non-worldly.
The cause of worldly perception is contact (*saṃnikarṣa*),
which is of six kinds according to the distinctions of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.

It has been established that the non-worldly (alaukika) cause of perception consists of three types of contact (saṃnikarṣa): that characterized by the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), that characterized by cognition (jñānalakṣaṇa), and that produced by yoga (yogajadharma).
The sixfold contact (*ṣoḍhā saṃnikarṣa*), however, is introduced in the *Nyāyavārttika*;
it is not seen anywhere in either the *Sūtra* or the *Bhāṣya*. This...
Regarding the subject matter, the authors of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* reflect as follows:
The author of the *Nyāyasūtrabhāṣya*, named Ācārya Adhyayanapāda, maintains that although the meaning "relation" is already obtained by the word *nikarṣa* alone,
the prefix *sam-* serves to indicate that the relation is one that is possible (*saṃbhavī*).
It is expressed by the word "proximity" (saṃnikarṣa).
Furthermore, he demonstrated that a possible relationship is indeed of only six kinds.
That is not so;
for if that were the case, the prefix "ni" would be redundant.
Since the meaning "connection" is already obtained by the word "karṣa" itself—given that verbal roots have multiple meanings—the prefix "saṃ" [would likewise be superfluous].
If it is argued that since the sixfold nature is obtained through the power of the word itself, the word "ni" is redundant;
or if it is argued that there is no worldly convention for the word "karṣa" having the sense of "connection," [then consider] the word "nikaṣa."
You must state where there is established usage for [the word] as expressing a relation;
for in common worldly usage, the word *nikarṣa* is well known as expressing inferiority, not as expressing a relation.

Therefore, the verbal root *kṛṣ* only when joined with the two prefixes *sam* and *ni* expresses a relationship, just as the root *iṇ*, preceded by the two prefixes *sam* and *ava*, expresses a collection (*samavāya*).

Therefore, the explanation that the meaningful word "sam" is not sufficient to indicate the sixfold nature because it merely serves to signify the sense of connection to the root *kṛṣ*, and thus the sixfold nature is obtained through the power of the word "sam" itself, is not correct.

Therefore, just as light and other factors, though not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra, are accepted as causes of perception by virtue of the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), so too the causality of the six kinds of contact with respect to perception is established through the power of agreement and difference.
This matter is established by logic,
since it was not refuted by the authors of the Sūtras; therefore, it is accepted by them.
Thus it is inferred,
according to the principle of "the system's method (tantrayukti) that what is not refuted is accepted as consented to."
In the Vaiśeṣika system, however,
there is a somewhat clearer indication regarding the specific varieties of sensory contact than is found in the Nyāya Sūtras. To illustrate:
By the aphorism: "The perception of the self arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.11).

It has been stated that the conjunction of the mind (*manassaṃyoga*) is the cause for perception whose object is the self (*ātman*). By this, it is indicated that the conjunction of a sense organ (*indriyasaṃyoga*) is the cause for perception whose object is a substance (*dravya*).
From this [it follows]: "From inherence in the self, [perception arises] regarding the qualities of the self" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.15).

By this sutra, it is clearly established that in the case of perception whose object is qualities such as knowledge inhering in the self (*ātman*), the cause is the inherence-in-what-is-conjoined-with-the-mind (*manassaṃyuktasamavāya*). Likewise—
By the two sūtras, "The perception of color [occurs] due to its inherence in multiple substances and due to the particularity of color" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.7),

and "Number, dimension, and action are visible because of their inherence in substances possessing color" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.11), [the nature of] perception regarding the qualities and actions residing in substances is established.
It has been clearly stated that "the cause is the inherence in that which is conjoined with the eye.
By this, "all sensory cognition regarding quality and existence is explained" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.13).

By this sūtra, it is indicated that just as the inherence in a substance (*dravyasamavāya*) is the cause for the perception of a quality (*guṇa*), so too the inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*) is the cause for the perception of the genus residing in a quality (*guṇagatajāti*). Likewise—
By the aphorism "That object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing is sound" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.21), [the nature] of sound...

Having stated the definition as "being the object of perception produced by the sense of hearing," [the author] establishes the non-substantiality of sound through the aphorism: "It is not a substance because it resides in a single substance" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.23).
Because it is the cause of inherence in a single substance whose nature is space,
and because of its abundance and its possession of odor, earth is the primary material cause in the cognition of odor.
"Likewise, water, fire, and air [are not distinct from one another],
because there is no difference in their taste, color, and touch" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 8.2.6)—
by these two sūtras of the eighth book...
By proposing that the four sense organs— smell, taste, sight, and touch—

are elemental by nature (*bhūtaprakṛtika*), and by indicating the identity of the ear with space (*ākāśa*) through the suggestion of its permanence via the non-specification of a distinct material cause for the ear, the inherence (*samavāya*) [of sound] in the ear is established.
It is implied that [sound] is the cause of auditory perception;
by this, [the sūtra] "In the case of being a quality and being an entity" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 4.1.13) [is explained].
Thus, by the logic stated in the Sūtra, the contact known as "inherence-in-that-which-is-inherent" (samavetasamavāya) is also indeed indicated in the perception of "soundness. Likewise:
"It is non-existent..."
The sūtra "Because there is no perception of a real entity [in the case of non-existence], there is memory of a real entity, just like a perception of a contradictory [entity]" is observed.
Its meaning is as follows: the perception of non-existence, which takes such forms as "the jar is non-existent," [is established].
It is like the perception of a contradictory object, equivalent to the perception of the counter-positive, the jar;
just as the perception of the counter-positive jar is established by experience and produced by ordinary sense-contact, so too [is this].
The meaning is that even the perception of absence (abhāvapratyakṣa) is not to be denied and is produced by sensory contact; however,
in the case of the perception of absence, there are the non-apprehension of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) when it is capable of being perceived, as well as memory.
The specific point is that two types of auxiliary causes are required. Thus he says:
"Because of the absence of perception of what has occurred, and because of the memory of what has occurred.
This refers to things such as a jar that have arisen and then perished.
The meaning is: "because of the non-perception of the counter-positive and because of its recollection.

Thus, indicating that the perception of absence is produced by a sense-object contact (*saṃnikarṣa*), the author of the Sūtras [states this] because conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth are impossible [in the case of absence].
He also indicated the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) consisting of the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*). Thus,
we conclude that by the word "sixfold" (*ṣaḍvidha*), the six types of contact, though not explicitly divided, are suggested by the aphorism of the Vaiśeṣika system.

In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, at the occasion of defining perception (*pratyakṣa*), five other types of sense-object contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) are specified, excluding the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

Since there is no formal definition of the category of non-existence (*abhāva*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, there is consequently no discussion of the means of contact known as "qualifier-ness" (*viśeṣaṇatā*) therein. However, the author of the *Kandalī* [Prabhācandra] has indeed described all six types of contact, complete with examples.
He demonstrated this in the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra*,
where the author of the *Nyāyavārttika* states: "Contact, moreover, is divided into six kinds," and so forth.
By means of this text, he has clearly demonstrated the six kinds of proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) previously mentioned along with their examples.
In response to the doubt as to how this classification is obtained from the Sūtra:
Thus,
this term "proximity" (saṃnikarṣa) is employed because it encompasses conjunction (saṃyoga), inherence (samavāya), and the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva).

Thus, by employing the term "proximity" (*saṃnikarṣa*)— which is common to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth— the author of the Sūtras has indicated that all possible types of proximity are to be understood; this is the resolution.

The relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*): in the *Nyāyavārttika*, the relation of qualifier and qualified is declared to be the sixth type of proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*). And that—
It has been established that [the sense-organ] is the cause of both perception having inherence as its object and perception having absence as its object.

Regarding this, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) provides the following explanation: "By means of the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇabhāvena*), both the qualifier of that which is conjoined (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇa*) and the qualifier of that which is inherent (*samavetaviśeṣaṇa*) are subsumed."
It is observed. This is its intended meaning:
for the perception of absence (abhāva) having the ground or similar substrates as its qualificand, the contact (saṃnikarṣa) is "being a qualifier of that which is conjoined" (saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇatva).

In the case of the cognition of non-existence— such as "there is no anudātta accent in the letter *a*," where the word "anudātta" is the qualificand— the sense-object contact is the state of being an inherent qualifier (*samaveta-viśeṣaṇatva*).
In the *Nyāyasāra*, however, it is stated:

"The apprehension of both perceptible absence (*dṛśyābhāva*) and inherence (*samavāya*) occurs due to the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), which is connected through these five kinds of relations."
Thus it has been stated:
the nature of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatva) is fivefold— namely, being a qualifier of that which is conjoined (saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatva),
being a qualifier of that which is inherent in what is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavetaviśeṣaṇatva), and so forth.

His intention is that [the qualifier-relationship] consists of being a qualifier of that which is conjoined and inherent, being a qualifier of that which is inherent, and being a qualifier of that which is inherent in what is inherent.

In both the *Dīpikā* and the *Prakāśikā*, it has been established with supporting arguments that both the qualifier-ness (*viśeṣaṇatva*) and the qualified-ness (*viśeṣyatva*) constitute the nature of proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*).
The details thereof are to be seen in the *Bālapriyā*.
Furthermore, the threefold extraordinary sense-object contact (*alaukika-sannikarṣa*) is not observed in ancient treatises.
It has been discussed here and there by the authors of the *Maṇi*, such as the author of the *Muktāvalī* and others,
in the section on inference (*anumāna-khaṇḍa*) in the *Maṇi*.
The proximity consisting of the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) has been established at length; let it suffice for now.
(9) Regarding the investigation of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*):
since the cognition of absence is possible through the sense faculty itself when assisted by non-apprehension, non-apprehension [is not a separate means of knowledge].

The authors of the Dīpikā maintain that it is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*); for, since the sense organ itself— which is required for the sake of knowing the locus— can appropriately function as the instrument, it is illogical for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) to be the instrument.
This reality is now investigated and determined.
In the Nyāya-darśana:
"The [means of knowledge] are not only four, because tradition (aitihya), presumption (arthāpatti), probability (saṃbhava), and non-existence (abhāva) are also authoritative" (Nyāya-sūtra 2.2.1).

Having raised the objection that the statement "there are only four means of valid cognition" is inconsistent with this sūtra— since there exist four other means of valid cognition, namely tradition (aitihya), presumption (arthāpatti), probability (saṃbhava), and non-existence (abhāva)— it is said:

By the sūtra, "There is no refutation [of these as separate means of knowledge], because tradition (aitihya) is not distinct from verbal testimony (śabda), and because presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), probability (saṃbhava), and non-existence (abhāva) are not distinct from inference (anumāna)" (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.2),
[it is shown that] tradition is included within verbal testimony, and presumptive testimony, probability, and non-existence are included within inference.
It has been established as a settled doctrine that there are exactly four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the other three are included within inference (*anumāna*).
In this regard, what is intended by the term "non-existence" (*abhāva*),
and how is it included within inference?
Nothing regarding this subject is understood from the *Nyāyasūtra*;
however, the author of the *Nyāyabhāṣya*, on the occasion of commenting upon that sūtra—
Non-existence is the opposite of existence;
that which has not occurred is the opposite of that which has occurred; and that which is non-existent is the opposite of existing rain-activity.
This establishes the conjunction of wind and clouds;
for, when there is a supporting conjunction of wind and clouds, the falling of water due to its heaviness [is prevented].
"It does not exist," he said.
His intention was this: even non-existence (abhāva) serves as a cause for the cognition of some object, just as...

The absence of rain in the form of falling water results from the conjunction of wind and clouds; therefore, since the cognition of another object arises through this absence, the opponent's prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that non-existence (*abhāva*) is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: it is true that non-existence is a means of valid cognition.

But there is no additional means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because non-existence (*abhāva*) is included within inference (*anumāna*) by virtue of generating the cognition of another object through the mode of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
This has been established in exactly this way in both the *Vārttika* and the *Tātparyaṭīkā*.

However, in these foundational texts, there is not even a mention of that means of valid cognition called non-apprehension (anupalabdhi), which the Mīmāṃsakas designate by the term "non-existence" (abhāva).

Although there is room for the possibility that— since non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is also of the nature of the absence of apprehension— the status of that which causes the cognition of the absence of a jar and so forth as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as well as its inclusion within inference (*anumāna*), is indicated by the preceding and following positions in the Sūtras; nevertheless...
Nothing indicative of this intention is found in the Bhāṣya, the Vārttika, or other such works;
the sage Kaṇāda did not say anything specific regarding the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva-pramāṇa).

Nevertheless, the perception of non-existence is established by the sūtra: "The cognition that 'it is non-existent' arises from the absence of the perception of the real object and from the memory of the real object" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.6).

By stating that [the cognition of absence] is produced by the non-apprehension of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), it is indicated that the sense faculty, assisted by the non-apprehension of the counter-positive, is the cause for the perception of absence. Thus says the author of the *Kandalī*: "Moreover..."
When the ground is perceived through the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects, there also arises the cognition of absence,
namely, "the ground is without a jar."
"In this regard,
why is it not accepted that non-existence, like the ground itself, is also directly perceived?"—
by means of this passage.
He argued that the cognition of non-existence can be subsumed even within perception; therefore, one need not seek a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it.
Regarding the means of valid cognition called non-existence (abhāva) according to Śabarasvāmin: "Non-existence also..."

They stated: "The absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) [serves as the means of knowledge] for the object 'it does not exist,' which is not in contact [with the senses]. This is the non-existence (*abhāva*), the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), which is cognized in the form "there is no jar on the ground."
That which is not in contact with the sense organs, the means of cognition that makes it known, is called non-existence (*abhāva*).
Non-existence is the absence of the means of cognition;
the meaning is the absence of the five means of cognition, beginning with perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This very [type of non-apprehension] is subsequently designated by later scholars as "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*).
The teacher Udayana established that non-apprehension is included within perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). For instance:
Non-apprehension is sometimes the cause for the valid cognition of absence when it is known, and sometimes when it is not known.
Among these, non-apprehension that is known [serves as the cause] in inference.
Non-apprehension of the unknown is included within perception;
whereas that which has a known cause produces knowledge of the imperceptible, [that which has an unknown cause produces] knowledge of the perceptible.
Furthermore, since the capacity to produce perceptual knowledge is observed in the case of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and so forth;

an example of non-apprehension of what is known (*jñātānupalabdhi*) is as follows: a servant, commanded to bring Caitra from the house, says to his master, "I have searched the house most thoroughly, yet Caitra is not there."
"He is not perceived.
And having recognized this non-perception of Caitra in the house, the master infers: "At the time when the servant entered, Caitra was in the house..."
"It did not exist. In this case,
the non-apprehension belonging to another, being known through the word, generates a mediate cognition consisting of inference.
In the same way, the cognition of the absence [of Caitra] at the time of morning is also to be explained. For instance, when someone asks at midday, "Was Caitra in the house this morning?"—

When asked, someone might think thus: "Since Caitra was not found by me even though I had entered the house earlier that morning in search of him with great care, therefore he must have been there at that time."
"It did not exist. In this case, having personally realized one's own non-perception at another time, one infers non-existence.
Therefore, the cognition of the non-existence of what occurred in the morning arises at midday.
When it is being known, [the cognition] is of the nature of inference because it is produced by the non-apprehension of what has been known;
however, the cognition produced by the non-apprehension of what has not been known is perception.
In that regard, four reasons have been set forth:
"Because there is directness in the cognition, because the sense organ has not ceased [its function],
and because the cause is not unknown."
"And because of the mind's immersion in the [absence]. Thus,

the cognition of absence, such as "the ground is without a jar," which arises immediately after the contact between the sense organ and the locus of the ground, has the sense organ as its instrument, because it is of a perceptual nature.
Because it depends on sense faculties that are not exhausted by other functions, because its instrumental cause is not itself perceived,
and because the rule that the mind produces external experience is established only by depending on another causal factor in the form of a positive entity.

And because [the self] depends upon instruments that exist as concomitants of the mind—this is the meaning of the aforementioned verse. These reasons have been established in detail in the *Kusumāñjali* and the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*; they should be consulted therein.
Furthermore, regarding the ancient texts, the phrase "non-perception of the fit" (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is intended as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound;
it refers to the absence of perception characterized by the fit counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) as its qualifier and having the fit locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as its qualificand.
It was traditionally termed "non-apprehension of the perceptible" (*yogyānupalabdhi*).
Due to the qualification that it must have a perceptible counter-positive as its qualifier, the absence of a *piśāca* in a pillar is not perceived through direct perception.

By including the condition that the subject must be a qualified locus capable of being perceived, the absence of earthness in a water atom is not perceptible. However, the authors of the *Maṇi* [the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*] maintain that it is perceptible.

And regarding this non-apprehension as "the non-apprehension of the perceptible," intending it to be a *karmadhāraya* compound, they formulated the refinement [of its definition] in works such as the *Dīpikā*: "Perceptibility (*yogyatva*) consists in having for its counter-positive that which is implied by the implication of the existence of the counter-positive."

The etymological derivation was provided strictly according to the opinion of Maṇikṛt; it is clearly stated in Rāmarudri, the commentary on Dinakari, that even according to the ancient view, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
[10] Examination of Pervasion (*vyāpti*):
In the section on inference (*anumāna*) of the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, after restating and refuting many definitions of pervasion propounded by the ancients, [the author proceeds].
Gaṅgeśopādhyāya himself demonstrated numerous definitions of pervasion (*vyāpti*) that are free from defects. Among them [is]:

"that which is delimited by the delimiter of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that resides in the same locus as *y* (the probans), while not residing in the same locus as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*)."
"That which does not exist [in a locus] stands in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with that [locus]"— this is the primary pervasion of the established doctrine (siddhānta).
This very point has been restated in both the *Dīpikā* and the *Prakāśikā*.
The purposes of the various components of that [definition] have been analyzed.
Here, this is considered:
regarding all the definitions of pervasion (*vyāpti*) presented by the authors of the manuals (*maṇikāra*), [concerning] the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*)...

Since there is an admission of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is accepted even between a probandum and a probans that reside in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), how can there be a consistent application (*samanvaya*) in that case?
To illustrate: in the downward location...
By the swelling of a river, rain in the upper region is inferred;
by the blooming of a lotus, the rising of the sun is inferred.
Just as the rising of the moon is inferred from the swelling of the ocean,
so too is the sun above inferred by the light on the ground, and the turner from the rotation of the wheel.
The proximity of the potter;
the nearness of the rising of Rohiṇī to the rising of Kṛttikā;
and fire situated in the lower portion is inferred from smoke situated in the upper portion.
In such cases, because there is an absence of pervasion (vyāpti) involving grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), there is an over-narrowness (avyāpti) of the definition.
The resolution here is as follows:
even in the cases cited where there is a difference of locus, the river is connected to an upstream location possessing rain, because it is connected to a downstream location possessing a flood.
This time possesses the rising of the sun, because it is a time like that of the blooming of lotuses;
this place possesses the proximity of a potter.
Because such inferences as "because of being the locus of a revolving wheel" are intended [as the reason],

the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in those cases is established; for while there is spatial non-co-referentiality (*vyadhikaraṇa*) in the aforementioned instances, there is temporal [co-referentiality].
Since co-referentiality exists, pervasion must be established by accepting that the temporal relation serves as the delimiting factor for both the probandum and the reason.
(11) An Investigation into the Denotative Power of Words.
In the *Dīpikā*,

within the section on the determination of words (*śabdapariccheda*), having established the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) according to the Mīmāṃsaka view that the denotative power (*śakti*) of words such as "cow" resides solely in the genus (*jāti*) such as "cowness," [the author proceeds] by the force of the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
It has been established that the expressive power (śakti) resides solely in the individual qualified by the genus; this truth is now clarified through an analysis of ancient and modern treatises.
In this regard, first the intention of the author of the Nyāya-sūtras and others is considered:
what is the meaning of a nominal stem such as "cow" (go) and so forth? Is it...
Is it the individual (vyakti), or is it the configuration (ākṛti) consisting of a specific conjunction of parts, or is it the genus (jāti)?
This is the doubt; and the cause of this doubt is that [these characteristics] exist in an inseparable relationship.
The word "cow" is applied to individuals, forms, and universals;
in that regard, it is not known which among these is the meaning of the word.
Alternatively, it may be that all three [of them] are [the meaning]. Regarding this, the proponent of the individual (vyaktivādin) says:
"For the referent of a word must be determined by the capacity of the word's usage."
Furthermore, the employment of a word occurs only with reference to an individual;
for instance, [one says] "the cow that stands" or "the cow that sits."

Thus, attributes such as "staying" and so forth are assigned to the referent of the word *go* (cow). If the universal (*jāti*) were the meaning of the word, then because it is unitary, these attributes would be untenable,
since there is nothing else to be excluded from it.
But if the individual (vyakti) is the referent of the word,
then the qualification "stands" is appropriate for the purpose of excluding that particular cow-individual which does not stand; likewise, [one says] "the cow increases," "it decreases."

In such cases as "he gives a cow" or "he receives [a cow]," the connection with actions such as giving or receiving an increase of prosperity belongs only to the individual (vyakti), not to the universal (jāti). Similarly, in instances such as "the cow is white" or "the cow is tawny," the connection with qualities such as whiteness is possible only for the individual. Thus...

Since the genus "cowness" (gotvajāti) is a single entity, it does not possess a number exceeding oneness; therefore, if the genus were the word-meaning, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning in expressions such as "twenty cows" would be untenable.
Likewise, in compounds such as *gosukham* ("cow's happiness"), the connection of happiness and so forth can only coherently apply to the individual cow (*govyakty*).

In such expressions as "he produces a cow" (*gāṃ janayati*), the connection is with birth (*janman*) in respect to the individual cow (*govyakti*), not the universal of cowness (*gotvajāti*). Therefore, the individual alone is the word-meaning (*padārtha*).
However, the proponent of the theory of form (*ākṛtivādī*) says:
The individual is not the meaning of a word;
for the distinction among living beings such as "this is a cow" or "this is a horse" occurs only in dependence upon the form (*ākṛti*), which consists of the configuration of their parts.
Therefore, the word-meaning is the form (ākṛti). But the proponent of the universal (jāti) says: no.
Neither the individual nor the configuration is the referent of a word,
because it is impossible to grasp the word’s expressive power (*śakti*) therein due to their infinity.
Furthermore, even though both the individual and the configuration exist in a clay cow, [one does not say] "Sprinkle the cow" (*gāṃ prokṣaya*).
The sprinkling, bringing, and so forth mentioned in sentences such as "Bring the cow" are not performed;
for that same consequence would apply there as well under both the theory that the individual is the word-meaning (vyaktivāda) and the theory that the form is the word-meaning (ākṛtivāda).
However, when the universal (jāti) is the word-meaning, [this does not occur].

Because the universal "cowness" (gotvajāti) is absent in a clay cow, there is no sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth [performed for it]. However, even according to the view that the universal is the referent,
since the universal cannot be perceived when neither the individual (*vyakti*) nor the configuration (*ākṛti*) is grasped, there would be no cognition of the universal.

Since there is a rule that [words] must have individuals (*vyakti*) and forms (*ākṛti*) as their objects, it follows that the universal (*jāti*) alone cannot be the denotation of a word; thus, the objection arises:
"What, then, is the meaning of a word?"
Regarding this inquiry,
the author of the Sūtras has stated: "But [the categories are] genus, configuration, and individual."

Regarding the Nyāya Sūtra (2-2-67), "padārthaḥ," its explanation is as follows: the singular number in the word "padārtha" is used to indicate that there is a single power (*śakti*) inherent in the three [categories].
Sometimes the individual is predominant,
sometimes the configuration, and sometimes the genus; [the application of a term] follows according to whichever is predominant.
The word "tu" (but) is used to indicate a specific distinction regarding the nature of being a category (*padārthatva*).
When there is an intention to express difference and a cognition of a particular individual, as in "the cow stands" or "the cow is seated," then it is the individual (*vyakti*) [that is denoted].
The referent of a word (*padārtha*) consists of the genus (*jāti*) and the configuration (*ākṛti*) within the constituent parts.

However, when the distinction [between them] is not intended to be expressed and there is a comprehension of the universal (*sāmānya*), then the genus is the referent of the word; for example, "A cow should not be touched with the foot."
In cases such as "the tangible" (spraṣṭavya) and so forth,
or "let cows made of flour be prepared" (piṣṭakamayyo gāvaḥ kriyantām) and so forth, the word-meaning is the form (ākṛti).

Even so, for the sake of parsimony, let the expressive power reside in the genus alone; let the understanding of the other two [the individual and the configuration] arise through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
A doubt arises.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Tātparyaṭīkā*: "Immediately after hearing the word 'cow,' for a person who knows the conventional relation (*saṃgati*), there occurs a simultaneous cognition of the individual (*vyakti*), the form (*ākṛti*), and the genus (*jāti*)."
It occurs, however, not as in the cases of "A hamlet dwells in the Gaṅgā" or "The Vāhīka is a cow," where— after the comprehension of the [primary] meanings "Gaṅgā-ness" and "cow-ness"—

the connection with the sentence-meaning is untenable, either because of the impossibility of that [literal] relation or because of the presence of qualities indicated by their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
Just as a ferryman is understood [to be at the bank], so too is there comprehension here;
however, the comprehension occurs simultaneously.
Therefore, it must be inferred by means of its effect, which is the nature of comprehension.
The word-potency (padaśakti) rests upon three types of word-meanings,
because there is no distinction in their simultaneous comprehension;
such is the tradition of the ancient Nyāya texts.

The modern Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that since from words such as "ghaṭa" there arises a cognition having the individual as its qualificandum and the universal (ghaṭatva) and the configuration (ghaṭākṛti) as its qualifiers, the denotative power (śakti) of words like "ghaṭa" resides in the individual qualified by the universal and the configuration.
Because there is no universal (ākṛti) in [substances] such as the self (ātman), the expressive power (śakti) resides in the individual qualified by a universal.

In the case of words such as "ether" (ākāśa), the expressive power resides in that which is qualified by an adventitious attribute (upādhi), because the universal "ether" does not exist. This is also the case therein.

While the property of potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like, being the denotatum (*śakya*), is also accepted as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*); although the configuration (*ākṛti*)— consisting of a particular conjunction of parts— is the denotatum, it is not accepted as the delimitor of denotability.

They say that, because [the property] does not reside in the individual denotable objects through a direct relation as a universal (jāti) does, its status as the delimitor of denotability must be asserted only through an indirect relation consisting in "inherence in that which inheres in its own substratum"; thus, there is the fault of prolixity (gaurava).
Others, however,

maintain that since there is a cognition of the connection between a cow and so forth with the property of "cowness" (gotva) even when configuration (saṃsthāna) is not present, the denotative power (śakti) of words such as "cow" resides only in the individual qualified by the universal (jāti).
They say that the power [to produce cognition] resides separately in the configuration (saṃsthāna) as well;
however, in this view, the singular number found in the Sūtra becomes inconsistent.
Regarding the study of the Mīmāṃsaka position:
as for what has been stated by the Mīmāṃsakas that the expressive power (śakti) resides in the genus (jāti) alone because it is the first to be presented [to the mind],
The opposite of that [is the case],
because genus and quality are not perceived at all without the perception of the substrate;
for the individual is perceived first.

It is known; therefore, it is established by experience that the cognition of the universal (jāti), which is the manifested [object], occurs immediately after the perception of the specific form of the manifestor residing in the individual. Furthermore:
Conjunction with that which is inherent in what is conjoined (*cakṣussaṃyuktasamavāya*) is the cause of visual perception whose object is that which is inherent in what is conjoined.

Since this [inherence] is preceded by conjunction, and since conjunction of the eye is the cause of visual perception delimited by being a substance (*dravya*), [visual perception of a universal, etc., occurs] prior to the cognition of the universal and so forth.
It is impossible to deny the direct perception of a substance that arises through the power of its causal complex (sāmagrī), as in the case of [the cognition],
"This person is a staff-bearer."
Just like knowledge [of the qualifier], the cognition "this is a jar" must also be preceded by the cognition of the qualifier, because it is a qualified cognition;
and that cognition of the qualifier... [is not...]
It would have a qualified object as its domain,
which would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress;
therefore, it has only the universal (jāti) as its domain.

If it is argued that "that" must necessarily be accepted, and therefore it must be stated that the universal (*jāti*) and so forth are the first to be presented— this is true, insofar as a qualified cognition is produced by the cognition of the qualifier;
yet that very cognition of the qualifier does not have the universal alone as its object.

Since the contact that illuminates the universal (jāti)—namely, inherence in what is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya)—is itself constituted by the contact known as conjunction that illuminates the individual that serves as its substratum, it follows that the cognition produced by it must necessarily have that substratum-individual as its object, just as it has the universal as its object; this is unavoidable. Not so.
And thus there would be no infinite regress,

because even though the cognition of the qualifier has both the universal and the individual as its objects, it lacks the relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*) as its object, and therefore it does not possess the nature of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*); in that case...
Since there is no requirement for another cognition of the qualifier,
one should not harbor the hope that the universal (jāti) would be presented first by virtue of its being the cause of the cognition of the qualifier.
Thus, it is untenable that the expressive power resides in the genus alone on account of parsimony;
for in many instances, the usage [of words] is predominantly directed toward the individual.
Because it would be cumbersome to postulate a capacity for every individual instance characterized by its specific form, it is more appropriate—

given that [the former] is simpler— to accept that the capacity resides in the qualified individual, and to regard the occasional use of a word for the universal as being merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).
Because it is logical: if, in all injunctional sentences such as "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*),

the words *vrīhi* and so forth were to have their secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) as the individual instances, there would be a contradiction with the maxim that "in an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not [to be set aside] by another."

Moreover, among the means for grasping word-potency (*śakti*), such as grammar and the like, we see no evidence whatsoever for the view that words such as "cow" (*go*) have potency directed toward the genus (*jāti*) alone; this is because the rules concerning words of identical form (*sarūpa-sūtra*) and others proceed by presupposing that these words denote individuals (*vyakti*).

Because the expression "in the case of denoting an individual" (*vyaktyākhyāyām*) is not mentioned [in Pāṇini’s sūtras], [the application of] rules such as *jātyākhyāyāmekasmin* (Pā. Sū. 1.2.58), which function by presupposing that [a word] denotes a genus (*jāti*), occurs only in certain instances.
Furthermore, from the rule "jātyākhyāyām" (Pāṇini 1.2.58) and others, it is understood that in all cases the individual (vyakti) is the denoted meaning;
as also seen in the rule "cādayo 'sattve" (Pāṇini 1.4.57).
Furthermore, from such exclusions as these, it is understood that [the word] denotes a substance;
and comparison (*upamāna*), which functions by depending upon the cognition of similarity, [also establishes this].
It is not possible [for the word] to function without denoting an individual;

for, from the apprehension of similarity with respect to the individual object denoted by the word *gavaya* in the analogical statement "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow," the [word] *gavaya* [is understood].
The apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) is that "the word *gavaya* denotes this [animal]";
even the lexicon (*kośa*), which functions by prioritizing the determination of specific gender markers, implies only that it denotes an individual capable of such [denotation].
And the authoritative statement (āptavākya),
such as "Bring the cow" or "Do not drink wine," which pertains to objects associated with engagement or avoidance, reveals the capacity for denotation residing in the individual word.
Even common linguistic usage, such as the activity of bringing a cow, is only logically possible if [the word] denotes the individual;
so too is the corroborative supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*).
The passage beginning with "where other plants wither" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.11.3) and so forth confirms that [the term] denotes an individual worthy of such specific attributes as being joyful;
this is also the case for the *vivaraṇa*.
The view that [words] denote individual actions and so forth, as in "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), is their natural inclination. Furthermore,
even the proximity of well-known words— as in "here on this mango tree the cuckoo sings sweetly"— is consistent only with the position that [the word *taru*] denotes a substance (*dravya*).
Therefore, there is no inherent evidence for the view that words such as "cow" possess the power to denote a universal (jāti);
moreover, there are numerous arguments against it.
The lack of coreferentiality regarding gender, number, and so forth has already been demonstrated.

Furthermore, if the universal alone were the meaning of words such as "cow," then [one would have to accept] that "cowness resides in the individual," just as [one says] "the universal cowness resides in the individual."
Furthermore, the usage "the cow-ness residing in the individual" (*gavāvyaktiniṣṭhā*) would result as a logical consequence;
moreover, when words such as "cow" are employed with the intention of expressing the genus alone, there would be no requirement for suffixes such as *tva* or *tal*.
Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "the broken cow" (*khaṇḍo gauḥ*) or "the white cow" (*śuklo gauḥ*) would not be possible,
because properties such as being broken (*khaṇḍatva*) do not connect with the universal (*jāti*).
As for what is stated here by the Mīmāṃsakas— that there is a connection with that [universal] in the individual which is the indicated meaning—
that too is not correct.
Because in no instance is there the employment of a qualifier that conforms to the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*); for example, in such cases as "The hamlet is on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).
No qualifying attribute that is unique to the bank as the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) of the word "Ganges" is ever employed in any sentence;
on the contrary, in cases such as "the hamlet is on the deep river," it is only the connection with the primary meaning (śakyārtha) that occurs.
An adjective is employed [for this purpose].
Therefore, it is more reasonable that the power (*śakti*) of words resides in the individual qualified by the genus; thus say the Naiyāyikas.
[12] An Examination of Validity:
Having defined the intrinsic (svataḥ) and extrinsic (parataḥ) nature of validity with respect to both its cognition and its production in the *Dīpikā*,...
In the section on the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*), the extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) of both [truth and falsity] was established following a refutation of the Mīmāṃsaka position;
this reality is now [discussed] after an investigation of ancient and modern texts.
It is explained as follows:
when an object has been known and knowledge has arisen, activity toward that object does not occur without the cognition of its validity (*prāmāṇya*).
It must be stated that even the cognition of the validity residing in a [prior] cognition is a cause for purposeful activity; however,
this is not so, because there is a deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), since purposeful activity arises even without the cognition that "this cognition is valid."
It must be stated that the cognition of validity is not the cause of purposeful action;
for action toward sacrifices and the like, which are accomplished through the expenditure of great wealth and effort, would be impossible without a certainty regarding their validity.
Nor should it be argued that activity there also proceeds solely from the certainty of a necessary object;

for one must necessarily accept the principle that whatever doubt and whatever certainty of absence are obstacles to a particular cognition, the certainty of that [opposite] is the cause of that [cognition].
Just as it is accepted that when there is doubt regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*) or certainty regarding the absence of pervasion, no inference arises—
and thus certainty regarding pervasion is admitted to be the cause for inference— so too [is it with the present case].

Since activity does not arise when there is doubt regarding validity or when there is certainty regarding the absence of validity, it is established that certainty regarding validity is the cause of activity. Thus, activity is impossible without certainty regarding the validity of the cognition. And this is not [the case] regarding the cognition itself...
Since, when there is doubt regarding validity, doubt regarding the object arises,
and thus the absence of activity is logically accounted for precisely due to the absence of the cause— which consists in the ascertainment of the object— [this is] with respect to activity.

It should not be argued that the inquiry into whether validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*) is misplaced, because the doubt regarding validity does not act as an obstacle [to action], and thus the aforementioned rule does not apply; consequently, the ascertainment of validity lacks the status of being a cause for initiating action. For where...
When there is doubt regarding the validity of a specific cognition, unshakable activity therein can only be accomplished through the ascertainment that "this is exactly thus.
And that ascertainment pertains to the cognition.
Since it is not possible [to act] without the ascertainment of truth,
and because the ascertainment of validity is the cause of the ascertainment of the object that serves as the motive for activity,
the ascertainment of validity must also be brought about as a prerequisite for action.
And the inquiry as to whether that [validity] arises from itself or from another is indeed appropriate;
in that regard, concerning the cognition of validity—
Self-existence (*svatastva*) and other-existence (*paratastva*) are explained in five ways regarding the gem;
among these, only the first explanation has been restated in the *Dīpikā*.

The first form of self-validity (*svatastva*) consists in being apprehended by the same causal complex that apprehends the cognition; that is, the validity residing in the cognition is known by the very same causal complex that grasps the cognition itself.
In this regard, the Prābhākaras maintain that the form of cognition is precisely "I know the jar.
Since that cognition is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), it is itself the grasper of the cognition; therefore, they assert that validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in being grasped by that [cognition].

The Bhāṭṭas maintain that cognition is inferred through "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*); thus, an inference based on *jñātatā* as its logical mark (*liṅga*) is a cognition produced by the same causal complex that apprehends the cognition itself, and validity consists in being the object of that [apprehension].
Murārimiśra [states]: Following the cognition "This is a jar," there arises the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) "I cognize the jar.
When that cognition is thereby made an object, its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is also made an object. And thus...
In all three views, they describe the intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) of validity because validity is apprehended by the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that grasps the cognition.

Even though the causal complex that apprehends the cognition is distinct [from the causal complex that apprehends the object], the "self-validity" (*svatastva*) consisting in being apprehended by the causal complex that apprehends the cognition is common [to both]. In this regard—

If it were argued that the self-validity (svatastva) of a cognition would be undermined because its validity is not apprehended by some causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that, due to the influence of defects, apprehends its invalidity when that cognition is the locus of validity, then the qualification "apprehending invalidity" must be added to the description of the causal complex.
Even so, for one who is committed to the knowledge that "this cognition is invalid," there is the apprehension of validity— defined as having the mode of invalidity in what is invalid—
by the very same causal complex that apprehends the invalidity.
Since there would be a contradiction regarding "self-validity" (svatastva) defined as being grasped by the same causal complex that grasps non-validity (aprāmāṇya),
the phrase "not grasping its non-validity" (tadaprāmāṇyāgrāhaka) must be stated in order to avoid that [contradiction].
In that [context], [the term] "grasping non-validity" (aprāmāṇyagrāhaka) [is used].

The meaning of that is as follows: it means that [the cognition] produces a knowledge which has as its qualificandum a locus of such validity as is intended to be intrinsic, and which has non-validity as its qualifier.
This refers to the causal complex that apprehends the validity residing in the cognition "this cognition is invalid";
even though it apprehends the invalidity having this cognition as its qualificandum, it is the cognition "this cognition is invalid" which serves as the locus of the validity under consideration.
There is no fault, because [the cognition] does not produce a knowledge of invalidity (aprāmāṇya) having that [object] as its qualificandum.
Even by the Naiyāyikas, it is accepted that whatever apprehends a cognition [establishes its validity], such as: "This cognition is valid, because it produces a successful purposeful activity."
Thus, since that [cognition] is admitted to be valid by virtue of being apprehended by inference,

the qualification "as far as the entire causal complex that apprehends the cognition" (*yāvaj-jñāna-grāhaka-sāmagrī*) must also be added in order to prevent the consequence of self-validity (*svatastva*). And that [qualification] is not a qualifier of the causal complex itself.
Since no single cognition is produced by all the causal complexes [of cognition], it is not established that there is a perception produced by every complex;
rather, it is a qualification of cognition. And thus:
The resulting conclusion is that [validity] is the object of every apprehension produced by the causal complex that apprehends the cognition.

There is no fault [in this definition], because the Naiyāyikas do not accept that validity is apprehended by the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya), which is included among such apprehensions.

The author of the Dīdhiti has formulated the following definition: self-validity (*svatastva*) consists in being the counter-correlate of an objectivity (*viṣayitā*) that pervades the state of being a cognition produced by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that apprehends those various cognitions which possess as their qualifier the specific properties that apprehend the invalidity of that [cognition]. This is because [self-validity] is essentially of the nature of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*).
That summary has been restated in the *Prakāśikā*.
Now, regarding the *prāmāṇyavāda* from a comparative perspective:

The inquiry is whether the validity residing in a cognition that is of the nature of valid knowledge, and the invalidity residing in a cognition that is of the nature of non-valid knowledge, are intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
The Tīrthakaras disagree on this point;
among them, the Sāṃkhyas hold that both validity and invalidity are intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
The Vaiśeṣikas and others hold that both [validity and invalidity] are extrinsic;
the Buddhists hold that invalidity alone is extrinsic.
Validity is intrinsic and invalidity is extrinsic; this is the view of the Mīmāṃsakas and the Vedāntins. Thus, there are four positions. This is the Sāṃkhya doctrine.

Fearing that if they were to accept that validity or invalidity— which did not previously exist in the cognition— arises later through the power of causes, it would result in the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (asatkāryavāda), the Sāṃkhyas [hold otherwise].
Both validity and invalidity are inherent;
however, if both were to exist by their very nature without depending on specific causes, [then there would be no distinction between them].
In that case, there would be no established distinction such as "this cognition is valid" and "this cognition is invalid"; thus,
there is an internal inconsistency in this view.
The Buddhist doctrine is that invalidity is intrinsic (svataḥ) while validity is extrinsic (parataḥ); this is what the Buddhists maintain.
For instance: if validity were ascertained through itself alone, then, because of the ascertainment of one of the two alternatives— namely, the form of validity— this [cognition]...
The doubt as to whether a cognition is valid or invalid would not arise;
therefore, validity is determined from the knowledge of the excellence (*guṇa*) that serves as its cause, as well as from the correspondence of the resulting activity.
As it has been said:
"Even though validity exists in that [cognition],
it cannot be ascertained."
"From the subsequent knowledge of successful action,
that [validity] alone is cognized.
As for invalidity, however...
It is determined by itself alone.
Therefore, knowledge produced from the Veda is of the nature of error;
thus, the intention of the Buddhists is that the Vedas are intrinsically non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*).
This is the refutation here:

even in the view of those who maintain that invalidity is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), one must assert that in an erroneous cognition, validity is intrinsic with respect to the portion consisting of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*); otherwise, [the following would occur].
Because it would follow that there could be error without a substratum;

furthermore, statements such as "the establishment of the object of knowledge depends on the means of valid cognition" and "speech that is consistent with reason is to be accepted" are accepted by all disputants.
It must be stated that [cognition] is intrinsically valid (*svataḥ pramāṇam*).
Likewise, they accept that non-conceptual cognition, which is free from the distortion of latent impressions (*vāsanopaplava*), possesses validity intrinsically (*svata eva*).
They maintain that even determinate cognition possesses validity with respect to its own internal form, yet lacks validity with respect to its objective content;
and thus, in some cases...
The self-validity (*prāmāṇya-svatastva*) of those [cognitions] is likewise unavoidable.
Moreover, since validity exists in some respect within all cognitions, whereas invalidity is merely occasional, that [self-validity] alone [is the case].

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that validity is indeed without cause, because they establish that it is like the redness [of a flower] which has a cause such as the *kiṃśuka* tree as an adventitious condition (*upādhi*).
The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that invalidity arises from defects (doṣa) and validity from excellences (guṇa);
in no way can the intrinsic nature of invalidity (aprāmāṇya-svatastva) be established.
The Mīmāṃsaka position:
validity arises intrinsically and is also known intrinsically.
The Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that invalidity arises and is known extrinsically (parataḥ),
whereas validity arises intrinsically (svataḥ); this refers to the cognition which is the locus of that validity.

The meaning is that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer [of knowledge], and by that very same [complex], the validity (*prāmāṇya*) residing in the cognition is also produced, rather than from a quality (*guṇa*).
And therefore, regarding the validity of the cognition produced from the Veda—
Their intention is that because there is no dependence on qualities such as the speaker’s knowledge of reality, the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda remains established; thus,
its validity is known intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
By the very same causal complex through which the cognition that is the locus of validity arises, the cognition of its validity also arises.
However, validity is subsequently sublated by two factors: the cognition of a sublating cognition and the cognition of defects in the causes [of the original cognition].

And thus, in the case of the Veda, which is not of human origin, since there is an absence of defects caused by connection with unreliable persons and an absence of subverting cognition, its established validity remains exactly as it is.
And thus, the very purpose of establishing the self-validity (*svatastva*) of cognition is precisely the stabilization of the authority of the Veda;
this is the intention of the Nyāya system regarding the ascertainment of validity.
Although the investigation into whether validity and invalidity are intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*) was not conducted in the *Nyāyasūtra*, nevertheless,
[it is stated]: "And its validity is like the validity of mantras and Ayurveda, because of the validity of the authoritative person" (*Nyāyasūtra* 2.1.68).
By the rule (Pāṇini 2-1-68), extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇyam*) is indeed indicated.
The author of the Nyāyabhāṣya has set forth the very opening statement as a manifestation of this extrinsic nature of validity:

"When there is comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that means of valid cognition is purposeful because it possesses the capacity for successful action. This statement from the *Bhāṣya* was introduced by Vācaspatimiśra as follows: "Now, a scripture that teaches a method impossible to perform is useless, just as..."
The treatise that instructs on the seizure of the crest-jewel of Takṣaka, the fever-dispeller, is such;
this Nyāya-śāstra is also exactly like that.
For indeed, it is through the knowledge of the sixteen categories (ṣoḍaśapadārtha) that...
In this treatise, the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is taught;
that alone is difficult to attain,
[along with] the objects of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth.
The knowledge of the true nature of categories depends upon the knowledge of the true nature of the means of valid cognition;
for a means of valid cognition, if its own nature is not determined as such, is not capable of ascertaining its own object.
Furthermore, the determination of the true nature of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is dependent upon the determination of the true nature of the valid cognition (pramā) itself;
for one who does not determine the valid cognition as it truly is cannot possibly determine the true nature of that which produces the valid cognition.
Furthermore, the true nature of valid cognition— consisting in its non-erroneousness— cannot be ascertained either intrinsically or extrinsically,
even in the case of a cognition whose object is something like a jar and which [also] takes itself as its object.
For how indeed can that which is unable to take itself as its object apprehend its own validity?
Thus, the position of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-pakṣa*) is not tenable;
this holds even in the view that cognition is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*).

Even if it were somehow possible for knowledge to have itself as its object, it would be difficult to establish that it has as its object the state of being a valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*), which consists in its own non-deviation from reality. Even on the view that validity is known extrinsically (*parataḥ*), by the word "extrinsic" (*para*), one must refer to another cognition that takes the [first] cognition as its object.
Or, if there is a desire to know either a cognition regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) or something else,

how could the validity of the preceding cognition be known if their validity is also not ascertained within themselves? Therefore, if the validity of those [subsequent cognitions] depends on other cognitions, then for those too...
If it were so, there would be an infinite regress;
moreover, the claim that their validity is intrinsic is untenable according to the reasoning previously stated.
And thus, because the true nature of valid cognition cannot be determined either intrinsically or extrinsically, the determination of the true nature of the means of knowledge is not possible.
And because that is impossible, the knowledge of the true nature of the objects of knowledge and so forth is also not possible. Therefore:

The commentary beginning with “When there is comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition” (*pramāṇato ’rthapratipattau*) has been composed for the purpose of refuting the objection that the treatise— which teaches that the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of the reality of the sixteen categories beginning with the means of valid cognition— is useless.
The meaning of this commentary is as follows:
"Validity is purposeful" is the thesis; "because of the efficacy of purposeful activity" is the reason.
The word *pramāṇa* is a term ending in the suffix *lyuṭ* (ana) with the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).
The word *arthavat* contains the possessive suffix *matup*, which denotes constant connection (*nityayoga*). This [suffix] signifies permanence (*nityatā*).
And [this refers to] the non-deviation from the object.
Non-deviation from the object consists in having that mode (prakāra) with respect to what possesses it (tadvat).
And this [non-deviation] of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is mediated by cognition.

And thus, the meaning of the proposition is that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which generates a cognition possessing a particular qualifier (*tadprakāraka*) with respect to that which possesses it (*tadvati*); that is,
its nature is to generate a corresponding activity.

This is its meaning: if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were not non-deviant from the object, it would not produce effective purposeful activity (*samarthā pravṛtti*), just as a fallacious means of cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*) which is deviant from the object does not;
this is the negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*) here.
This is what is intended to be said:
the production of activity by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not direct, but rather [indirect].

With the intention that [the apprehension of an object] occurs by way of generating the comprehension of the object, it was stated: "when there is comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*).

Thus, the final conclusion is simply this inference: "The cognition under dispute possesses that mode in respect to that which possesses it, because it generates a successful purposive activity. And in this way:

The intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) residing in the cognition is apprehended by an inference based on the reason of being the cause of a successful activity (*saphalapravṛttijanakatva*).
[Objection: But by what is the validity residing in the cognition consisting of an inference itself apprehended?
If it is argued that [this requires] another inference, and thus there would be an infinite regress— no;
for [the object] is apprehended in the inference by the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) which has that inference as its object.
Because the validity residing in that [cognition] is also apprehended, since it is accepted that the validity of an inference is to be grasped intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
If so, [in the case of the cognition] "I know the jar,"...
If it is argued: "Since the cognition of the jar is apprehended by this after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), let its validity (*prāmāṇya*) also be apprehended;
for what purpose is there the pursuit of an inference based on the mark of the efficacy of action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*) in that case?"—[we reply: this cognition...

The authors of the *Tātparyaṭīkā* explain that [the definition of validity] is not applicable here because, while one might engage in an investigation to ascertain validity based on the doubt as to whether it is a valid cognition or not— which leads to the consideration of the reason consisting in the "capacity for successful action"— such a reason is absent in the present case.
The authors of the *Kusumāñjali* maintain that there is no infinite regress because they do not accept that validity must necessarily be cognized;
this is established by the sūtra: "And its validity, like the validity of mantras and the Ayurveda, arises from the validity of the authoritative person" (*Nyāyasūtra* 2.1.68).
"What is this caused by?
It is caused by the authority of the trustworthy ones (āpta). But what, then, are the trustworthy ones?"
What is authority (*prāmāṇya*)? It is the direct realization of *dharma*, compassion for living beings, and the desire to explain things as they truly are.
