And by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that very sūtra beginning with these words, the extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) of validity— consisting in its being produced by excellences (*guṇa*)— is indeed indicated in both its origination (*utpatti*) and its cognition (*jñapti*).
This is stated in the *Kusumāñjali*.
The state of being other has been established in detail; with reference to that as well, it has been explained at length in the *Maṇi* and the *Dīdhiti*.
And this has been analyzed in the *Gādādharī*;
furthermore, the very same demonstration found therein has been summarized again in the *Dīpikā* and the *Prakāśikā*.
[13] An Examination of Anyathākhyāti: In the treatises of the Śāstras, there occurs the designation "khyāti" (manifestation) for cognition whose nature is error.
Regarding that subject, proponents speak in many ways:
whatever knowledge anyone possesses in the world, all of that is valid cognition (*pramā*).
It cannot be so stated;
for if that were the case, the knowledge of the opponent would also be valid cognition (*pramā*), and consequently,
the opponent too would be victorious.
Likewise, it cannot be maintained that all cognition is valid;
for if that were the case, even the cognition belonging to the proponent would be invalid. And thus, the proponent—
[Otherwise] he would be defeated.
Therefore, the distinction that some cognitions are valid (pramā) and some cognitions are invalid (apramā) must be accepted by everyone.
In that regard, the Naiyāyikas, Jains, and Bhāṭṭas accept *anyathākhyāti*— the appearance of one thing as another— within a cognition whose nature is non-apprehension (*apramātmake jñāne*).

The Prābhākaras maintain that the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) alone is correct, because the practical activity [of error] can be accounted for by the very same causal complex that constitutes non-apprehension, which consists in the non-cognition of a distinction.
They hold that it is the self itself, in the form of momentary consciousness, that is perceived under the appearance of an external object.
Thus say the Buddhists, proponents of the theory of self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*),
[maintaining that] in cases of error, only what is non-existent is perceived.

The Madhyamikas are proponents of the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti). The Advaitins maintain that in an error, an indefinable entity, which is both existent and non-existent, arises and is perceived.

According to this view, there is the theory of the indefinable manifestation (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*). In that regard, it is well known that the Naiyāyikas are proponents of the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*).

In the Nyāya-darśana, having stated in the first sūtra that the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) results from the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna), the second sūtra— beginning with "suffering, birth," and so forth—
demonstrates that false knowledge (mithyā-jñāna) is the cause of saṃsāra through a causal chain. In that regard:

Vātsyāyana, stating that "false knowledge (mithyājñāna) exists in many forms— such as [the notion] that there is no self in what is the self, or that there is a self in what is not the self, or that there is pleasure in what is suffering," and so forth,
maintains that false knowledge is the cognition of something as being what it is not (atasmiṃstaditi jñānam).
The author of the Vārttika also states:
"What, then, is this error? It is the cognition that something is what it is not. Of this...
The designation "misapprehension as something else" (*anyathākhyāti*) is a subsequent one;
at present, being in doubt,
he asks about the nature of misapprehension.
But what is this "error" (viparyaya)? There is doubt because of the conflicting views of investigators; some [hold one view].
They declare that cognition whose object is the externality of its own form is an error.
Others hold that cognition has a non-existent object, while the elders maintain it to be "misapprehension" (anyathākhyāti).
From this statement,
it is understood that the Naiyāyikas hold the position of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension).
This is the summary here:
First, immediately after the sensory contact with the mother-of-pearl shell, there arises a cognition in the form "this is white and lustrous";
thereafter, from the awakening of latent impressions, there occurs the recollection of silver.
Up to this point— that there is a non-apprehension of the difference between the object present before one and the silver—
the proponents of *akhyāti* (non-apprehension) and *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) are in agreement. Beyond that, [the former hold that] "this..."

The Naiyāyikas maintain that a qualified cognition (viśiṣṭajñāna) arises in the form "this is silver," characterized by having silverness as its qualifier and a locus devoid of silverness as its qualificand; it is from this alone that purposeful activity (pravṛtti) proceeds.

The Prābhākaras maintain that since the activity and so forth can be accounted for by the perception of the object present before one and the recollection of silver— accompanied by a non-apprehension of their difference from those two factors which are considered the causes of such a qualified cognition— a distinct qualified cognition (viśiṣṭajñāna) in the interim is unnecessary.

The necessity of qualified cognition (viśiṣṭajñāna) arises because qualified cognition is the cause of purposeful activity toward a real object; likewise, even in the case of an unreal object, it is indeed qualified cognition alone [that prompts action].
Or rather, it should be stated as the instigator [of activity]. And thus:
"Non-contradictory activity is produced by a qualified cognition, because it is an activity, like a true activity."

Thus, this inference is the proof for the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*). Likewise, the cognition which has silverness as its qualifier, which generates an activity directed toward mother-of-pearl produced by a desire for silver,
and which has mother-of-pearl as its substantive object, exists in the mother-of-pearl because it is a cognition that motivates activity toward mother-of-pearl.

Inferences such as "possessing a cognition that prompts activity toward the object [mistakenly perceived as] mother-of-pearl" have also been presented by Maṇi as establishing the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*).
Likewise, perceptual awareness in the form of reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) is also a means of valid knowledge for misapprehension.
For instance, following the error "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl, there arises the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya): "I cognize this as being silver."
For its meaning is: "the vehicle of a cognition that has 'this' as its qualificand and 'silverness' as its qualifier.

In that case, if the primary cognition (vyavasāya) lacked the property of having 'this' as its qualificand and 'silverness' as its qualifier, how could the aforementioned subsequent cognition (anuvyavasāya) be possible?
On the view that there are two cognitions, the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) would take the form "I know this" and "I know silver," but not "I know this silver."
An investigation into the meaning of the term *anyathākhyāti*: *anyathākhyāti* is the cognition of a thing present before one as being qualified by a form that exists elsewhere.
However, existence elsewhere is ascertained from the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) aided by the obstruction of its manifestation; therefore,
it is impossible to establish the non-existence here of real silver that has been sublated by a mistaken cognition.
This is because there is no sublation of its functional activity (*pravṛtti*).
Nor does it follow that fire bound by mantras and so forth would be determined to be false on the grounds of sublation of its activity, such as the production of a blistering burn (*sphoṭa*).
In that regard, [it is said] "it does not exist" because there is no subverting cognition;
for even by those who maintain other theories of manifestation, when one has gone to the ultimate limit...
Misapprehension (anyathākhyāti) must necessarily be accepted;
for instance, in the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), is that which is non-existent apprehended as "non-existent" or as "existent"?

If it is argued that [the object] is non-existent (*asat*), then error (*bhrama*) would be impossible; for the appearance of a non-existent thing as non-existent is a valid cognition (*pramā*), and thus both sublation (*bādha*) and the activity [of the subject] would not be possible. If, on the other hand, it is perceived as existent (*sat*), [then the following applies]:
Since what is non-existent appears as existent, this must be *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension otherwise).

In the theory of *ātmakhyāti*, is the cognition denoted by the word "self" perceived as cognition itself, or as an object? If it is the former, there would be no possibility of error, sublation, or purposeful activity.
In the second case, since cognition would appear as having the nature of the object,
it would amount to accepting *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) even within the Prābhākara system.

Since you accept that [the cognition] consists of two cognitions— namely, perception and recollection— is that pair of cognitions perceived as two, or as one? In the first case, sublation and purposive activity would be impossible.
In the second case, because two things appear as one, there is *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension).
Regarding the position that "the cognition exists but the object does not," is the object perceived as being non-existent or as being existent?
In the first case, there is the impossibility of engagement and so forth;
for no one ever engages with an object that is perceived as being non-existent.
In the second [view], because that which is non-existent appears as if it were existent, there is "misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*).
(14) This is the examination of non-existence (*abhāva*) in the *Tarkasaṃgraha*.
In the *Dīpikā* as well, the fourfold division of non-existence (*abhāva*) and its status as a distinct category (*atirikta-padārtha*) were demonstrated.
This [point] is now briefly examined.
Regarding the sūtra, "And because non-existence is established prior to origination" (Nyāya-sūtra 2.2.12),
the Bhāṣya states:
"Indeed, there is a duality of non-existence..."
"There is non-existence prior to arising,
and there is non-existence due to the loss of the self once it has arisen."
The same is established in the Vārttika as well.

Therefore, it is understood that both the authors of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika accept that non-existence (abhāva) is of only two kinds: prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva). In that very [work]:
The author of the Tātparyaṭīkā states:
"'The non-duality of absence' refers back to the subject under discussion."
This is the demonstration of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) directed against the proponent of mere destruction (pradhvaṃsamātra-vādin) regarding the subject at hand.
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however,
duality first exists in the sense of non-existence— that is, the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) and the absence of relation (*saṃsargābhāva*).
And "existence" (bhāva):

non-existence through relation (saṃsargābhāva) is also threefold— namely, prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), non-existence after destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva), and absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva)— thus [there are] four.
He established that even the fourfold non-existence (*abhāva*)— namely, "the four kinds of non-existence"— is accepted in the Nyāya system;
for like existence (*bhāva*), non-existence as well is cognizable through the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The commentator, intending to show that the very same means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which makes a positive entity known also makes a non-entity (abhāva) known when assisted by the non-apprehension of its counter-positive (pratiyogyanupalabdhi), states: [the following].
But how, then, is the subsequent [cognition] apprehended by means of a valid cognition,
given that something is being apprehended?
"In the same way, through non-apprehension, like a lamp; thus,
the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), which illuminates what exists, illuminates even that which does not exist."
In the first sūtra, he spoke [of the means of valid cognition].
To the objection— namely, that since non-existence (*abhāva*) is also established by a means of valid cognition, why was it not taught alongside existence (*bhāva*)?— the author of the Vārttika says:
Indeed, that which exists is an independent objective support for valid cognition;
that which does not exist is dependent.
He proceeds by way of negation;
for non-existence depends upon the knowledge of both the object to be negated and the locus of that negation.

The intention of the author of the Sūtra is that, because non-existence is for the most part already known once existence is known, he did not explicitly mention non-existence; such is his underlying purpose.
In the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras as well, the acceptance of the fourfold non-existence is indicated:
"Prior non-existence [is established] because of the absence of action, quality, and designation" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.1).
Thus, the Sūtra,
by establishing the non-existence of effects such as jars prior to their production,
acknowledges antecedent negation (prāgabhāva).
Indeed, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is defined as the state of not existing prior to production;
likewise, the Sūtra "the existent and the non-existent" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.2) refers to an existent thing such as a jar.
By establishing non-existence immediately after the falling of the hammer and so forth, it indicates the non-existence known as "destruction" (dhvaṃsa).
Therefore, the sūtra "existent and non-existent" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.3) [refers to] the pot and other things being existent [as themselves], yet [non-existent] in the form of cloth and so forth.

By making non-existence known, it manifests mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), which consists in the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*). Therefore, [it is stated]: "And whatever else is other than the existent, that is non-existent" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 9.1.5).
Such is the Sūtra.
In that context, the two occurrences of the word *asat* are designations in which the state (*bhāva*) is the primary meaning.
That which is other than this *asat* is *asat*.
The logical connection is that "that is non-existent" (tat asat).
Any absence other than the three types of absence previously mentioned is what constitutes absolute absence (atyantābhāva).
This being the case, it is established that the non-separate teaching of non-existence (abhāva) is due to its dependence upon existence (bhāva), and not because it is [itself] non-existent;
so say the authors of the Nyāyamañjarī.
"But other [absences] than antecedent non-existence do not differ from it in the ultimate sense; for that..."

Mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is said to have another entity as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). That very same [non-existence], when devoid of a limit (*avadhi*), becomes absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*),
or it is the destruction of that which has arisen.
Or rather, it is simply non-arising;
in reality, it is non-existence, while other distinctions are considered to be merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). (1)
Thus, by this passage, non-existence (*abhāva*) is twofold, distinguished as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*);
[the other two types are] mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
These two are included within antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) itself;
if antecedent non-existence has another entity as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*),
it is called mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
The Prābhākaras have defined that very same [non-existence], when devoid of a temporal limit (avadhi), as absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva).
They do not accept non-existence as a separate entity;
rather, they present three positions: that non-existence is of the nature of a particular cognition, of the nature of its locus, or of the nature of a particular time.
These three positions have also been refuted in detail in the *Maṇi*,
and accordingly in the *Muktāvalī*;
however, the specific distinction is that in the *Dīpikā*, the position that [negation] consists in its locus (*adhikaraṇātmakatva*) is restated and then refuted.
Here it is considered:
even the Naiyāyikas accept that an absence whose locus is another absence has the nature of the very absence that serves as its locus. In that regard—
In the expression "there is no cloth in the absence of a jar," a relationship between locus and located is perceived;
and this occurs even though there is no difference between the locus and the located.
The distinction is established because of the difference between the delimiters of the substrata, namely "the nature of the absence of a jar" and "the nature of the absence of a cloth. Likewise,
the cognition "there is the absence of a jar on the ground" will also be established by virtue of the difference between "groundness" and "the nature of the absence of a jar."
Therefore, let it be that non-existence (abhāva) has the locus itself as its nature;

for even though the non-existence of sound, which is of the nature of the house, lacks the quality of being perceivable by the auditory organ in its form as "house-ness," [it is nonetheless perceived].
Its cognizability will occur by way of the form of being an absence of sound,
just as even in the system of the Naiyāyikas, there is the cognition of the absence of taste in a locus that is itself an absence of color.

Just as it is accepted that even though [the absence of color] has the nature of the absence of color, its status as an object of visual perception occurs precisely as the absence of color and not as the absence of taste, so too it is with the absences of sound and the rest.
And thus, regarding the absences of sound and so forth...
Nor is there any impossibility of its being perceived;
for although it is not perceived as a particular cognition or as a particular time, it is nevertheless perceived as the absence of this or that [object].
The perceptibility of specific cognitions and specific times is indeed possible;
therefore, even if non-existence (*abhāva*) is not something distinct [from existence], there is no fault whatsoever. To this, it is replied:
In the world, the relationship between locus and located (ādhārādheyabhāva) is generally well-known to exist only between distinct entities;
and this is easily established in the system of the Naiyāyikas, who maintain that absence is a category distinct from existence.
This is particularly evident in cases involving an absence that has another absence as its locus.

Even if the cognition of the relation between locus and located could be explained as figurative due to the absence of any other alternative, such an explanation would be inappropriate when another alternative exists;
therefore, the position that [the self] consists of the substratum is not tenable.
In the view that [time] consists of specific forms of cognition,
as well as in the view that it consists of specific forms of time, the defect of the impossibility of perceiving the absences of sound and so forth is difficult to avoid.

Regarding that which was stated— that although those two lack the status of being perceivable by the external senses in their forms as "cognition" and "time," their reality remains intact insofar as they are the absence of sound and so forth—
it is now replied:
Even in another form, it is not possible for those two to be the objects of such a perception.
For instance, in the cognition "there is no sound in the house," is the object the knowledge itself in its own nature, under the aspect of the non-existence of sound?
Or is it the cognition belonging to another person?

Not the first, because in perception the object is a causal factor, and since one's own cognition does not exist in the preceding moment, that which is non-existent in the preceding moment [cannot be its cause].
Because it is impossible for [the absence] to be the cause;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because in a single cognition of absence there are many [non-existents].
Because it would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*) to assume that the individual manifestations of knowledge belonging to other persons could be objects [of such a cognition],
likewise, even a specific time cannot possibly be the object of such a perception;
for the moment constituting the time of the arising of such knowledge lacks prior existence.
Furthermore, the time consisting of the preceding moment does not exist at that [present] time.

Nor can it be maintained that gross time, which persists through both the moment of the cognition's arising and its preceding moment, is the object of perception in such cases as "there is no sound in the house."

And thus it should be said that the aforementioned fault does not apply; nevertheless, they have demonstrated that even so, there is excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating that gross time— consisting of various entities persisting for two such moments— is the object of each individual such cognition.
[14] The examination of the meaning of verbal suffixes (*ākhyātārthavicāra*) and the process of word-comprehension (*śabdabodhaprakriyā*) are like a casket for the *Muktāvalī* in the *Dīpikā*.
And in the *Prakāśikā*, in the context of defining the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*), having established that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has the sense of "effort" (*kṛti*),
it is stated that the sentence "Devadatta cooks rice" means: "Devadatta is the possessor of an effort conducive to the cooking whose object is rice."
This reality has been described; now it is briefly investigated.
What is called verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is knowledge produced by words. As for "word" (*śabda*):
A sentence (*vākya*) consists of a collection of words that convey meanings mutually related to one another.
If one were to state merely that "a collection of words is a sentence," then [the definition would over-extend to] such expressions as "cow, horse, man, elephant."

Otherwise, even a collection of words whose meanings are not mutually connected would constitute a sentence; therefore, it is specified that "the meanings of the words must be mutually connected," as in the example:
*gaur gacchati* ("the cow goes").
Although "the horse" and "runs" are each individually a sentence, these two do not constitute a single unified sentence when combined,
because there is no mutual syntactic connection between the two sentence-meanings.
Therefore, it follows that a single sentence is defined as a word expressing the qualified object (the subject), which is distinguished by all those words— whether directly or indirectly—
that express the meanings serving as its qualifiers; this alone is [the definition].

"Furthermore, it has been stated in the Pūrvamīmāṃsā Sūtra (3.1.46): 'Now, because there is a single purpose, there is a single sentence, provided that if it were divided, there would be a mutual expectancy.
[This applies when] other [words] [have a single purpose]."
It was stated, "If there is expectancy when [the sentence] is divided," precisely to indicate that the connection occurs by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*).
In that regard, among many words...
When [words] are being employed, it must be investigated: which word-meaning has what qualifier; which is the subordinate qualificand; and which is the primary qualificand?
In this regard, the grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas), the Mīmāṃsakas, and the Naiyāyikas each rely upon their own distinct paths.
This is the view of the grammarians.

For instance, the grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas) consider it thus: because of the experience that "the factors of action (kārakas) are connected with the action," it is understood that, in a verbal form (kriyāpada), there is generally a connection with words ending in case-suffixes (subanta).

In the sentence "nīlotpalam ānayati" (he brings the blue lotus), the meaning of the compound—the lotus qualified by blueness—is construed with the object denoted by the second case, and that [object] is in turn construed with the action denoted by the verbal root, "bringing.
Thus, the resulting cognition is: "bringing that which has as its object a lotus qualified by blueness."

Even in the case of the expanded expression "bring the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam ānaya*), since one does not experience a separate cognition of "bringing having blue as its object" and "bringing having the lotus as its object," there is no manifestation of two distinct objects (karmatva); rather, this occurs by setting aside such a dual manifestation and [accepting] the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words "blue" and "lotus."

By accepting that [the word *nīlam*] has as its primary referent the single object which is the form of a lotus qualified by blueness, and by admitting its connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—namely, "bringing"—through the mediation of the objecthood (*karmatva*) expressed by the second case suffix, the resulting cognition is precisely: "bringing whose object is a lotus qualified by blueness. And thus...

Since even the Naiyāyikas and others accept that all kārakas— whether they possess qualifiers or are devoid of qualifiers, and whether they are distinct from the agent— are construed with the action denoted by the verbal root (dhātvartha), it is likewise appropriate for the agent-kāraka, which is the referent of the nominative case-ending, to be construed in the same manner.
This follows from the same logical principle.

Thus, in the sentence "Devadatta brings a blue lotus," the meaning of the accusative case is the object (*karman*); therein, the referent of the base (the stem), namely the lotus qualified by blueness, is construed with the object through the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*). Of the object...
The verbal root-meaning is the core meaning;
the agent is the meaning of the finite verb (tiṅ);
and there, [the agent] is connected to that [root-meaning] by way of the relation of identity (abhedasaṃbandha).
The referent of the word ending in the nominative case, Devadatta, is construed [with the verb];
the agent as well is construed with the meaning of the verbal root, "bringing. And thus:

The cognition has as its primary qualificandum the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), namely: "bringing which has as its object an *utpala* non-different from that qualified by blueness, and which has as its agent Devadatta non-different [from the agent].
The proof for this is as follows:
They state that the Nirukta statement, "A verb has being as its primary meaning," and the Mahābhāṣya statement, "A verb has action as its primary meaning," represent the Mīmāṃsaka view.
The Mīmāṃsakas, however, describe the cognition as having the bhāvanā (productive operation), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (tiṅ), as the primary qualificand. For instance,
words ending in the accusative case, such as "rice" (taṇḍulam) and so forth, [are incomplete] without a verb.
It is established by experience that [words] do not produce a cognition free from expectancy;
therefore, it is concluded that a word ending in a verbal suffix (tiṅanta) provides the substantive (viśeṣya).
In that case as well, by the force of the grammatical rule— "The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together, but of these two, the suffix is predominant"—
it must be stated that the meaning of the suffix alone is predominant; thus, the meaning of the *tiṅ* [suffix] is what is otherwise known as *bhāvanā*.
In verbal cognition, the action (*kṛti*) alone is the primary qualificand.
And thus, in the sentence "Caitra cooks rice," [the action is the primary qualificand].
The meaning of the second case is the state of being an object (*karmatva*). In that context, *taṇḍula* (rice) is construed with it through the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatā*).

The property of being an object (*karmatva*)— which, through the relation of being a determiner (*nirūpakatā*), results in [the meaning of] "being conducive to the meaning of the verbal root that determines itself"— is construed with the effort (*kṛti*) expressed by the *tiṅ* suffix.
The meaning of the verbal root, *pāka* (cooking), is construed with the effort (*kṛti*) by way of the relation of having the cooked rice as its object and being performed by its own instrument.
The referent of the nominative case following the word *caitra* is Caitra, which is the meaning of the nominal stem.

The word "Caitra" functions as the indicator of the intended meaning; [it is connected] to the primary referent, Caitra, by means of the relation of being the locus of inherence (*ādheyatā-sambandha*).
The verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is construed with *bhāvanā* (the efficient force). The time (*kāla*) and number (*saṃkhyā*) denoted by the verbal suffix are also construed with *bhāvanā* alone.
Number is construed through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), while time [is construed]...
The distinction is that there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by way of the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatā-sambandha*).
And thus, there is a single present productive activity (*bhāvanā*) residing in Caitra, which has rice as its object, cooking as its instrument, and cooked rice as its purpose.

Regarding "bodhaḥ": in the *Nirukta*, according to the rule "a verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its primary meaning," the word *ākhyāta* refers to that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). The word *bhāva*, derived from the root *bhū* with the causative suffix *ṇic* and the suffix *ac*, is formed as one ending in *ac*; thus, it denotes *bhāvanā* (the efficient force).
The three meanings are verbal suffixes (tiṅ), number, and time;
among these, the efficient force (bhāvanā) is the primary element.
The Naiyāyikas explain that the author of the Nirukti considers the cognition itself to have the primary qualificand (viśeṣya) as its object.
In the sentence "Caitra is wise," the cognition experienced is that "Caitra is non-different from the wise"; in that case,
due to the absence of a finite verb (tiṅanta) word, there is neither the meaning of the verbal root nor the bhāvanā (productive operation), which is the meaning of the finite suffix.
Appearance as the primary qualificand is not possible;
and thus, in certain cases, it must be accepted that there is a cognition in which the meaning of the nominative (prathamānta) term is the primary qualificand.
It is appropriate to describe the cognition in the same manner even in cases where [the verb] is explicitly mentioned alongside the object.

Nor should it be argued that in those cases as well, verbal comprehension occurs only through the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of a suitable action; for when a satisfactory explanation is possible without such supply, the supply of a word is improper. Furthermore:

In the *Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa*, Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa, stating that "a sentence generally consists of a collection of nominal and verbal endings," accepts even those sentences that lack a verbal ending (*tiṅanta*).
Likewise, on the occasion of refuting the nature of agency (*kartṛtva*) as being the substratum of the operation denoted by the verb (*ākhyātārtha-vyāpāra*), [he maintains this position].

In the *Bhūṣaṇasāra* as well, the acceptance of the validity of sentences devoid of finite verbal endings (*tiṅanta*) is evident from the statement: "Otherwise, in cases such as *devadattaḥ paktā* (Devadatta is a cooker), which are empty of a finite verb, Devadatta would result in not being the agent.
And thus, in instances where there is no co-utterance with a finite verbal ending, there arises a cognition having the meaning of the nominative case as its primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
Since it must be accepted [as the meaning], it is appropriate to describe the cognition in the same way even in cases such as "Caitra cooks.
Thus, in the sentence "Caitra cooks rice," the meaning of the accusative case-suffix following the word "rice" is the status of being the object (*karmatva*).
The rice, which is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), is construed with the objecthood (*karmatva*) by means of the relation of being located therein (*ādheyatā-sambandha*);
the objecthood, in turn, [is construed with the verbal root] by means of the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatā-sambandha*).
The verbal root-meaning is connected with "cooking";
the meaning of the finite verb is "effort" (kṛti),
which is related to that [root-meaning] by the relation of being conducive (anukūlatā).
The cooking, which is the meaning of the verbal root, is construed [with the agent];
and the effort (kṛti) is construed with Caitra, the referent of the nominative case, by means of the relation of substratum (āśrayatā).
The meaning of the verb, namely present time, is construed only with the action;
however, the singular number is not the meaning of the singular verbal suffix.

Since oneness is obtained by the singular number itself, the resulting cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvayabodha*) is as follows: Caitra, who is the substratum of oneness and possesses a present effort conducive to cooking that is the determiner of the objecthood residing in the rice.
Furthermore,

according to the maxim that "pronouns generally refer to the primary subject," it must be stated that the word *tat* refers only to that which is the primary subject within the meaning of the preceding sentence.

If one accepts a cognition in which either the meaning of the verbal root is the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*) or the effort denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the primary qualificand, then [the following would be required]: "A person goes;
salute his feet."
In this case, there is an inconsistency:
if, in the sentence "the person goes," the primary element— either the act of going or the effort— is referred to by that pronoun (tat).
Because there is no syntactic connection with the phrase "salute at the feet," whereas in the Nyāya system,
since the person alone is the primary referent, it is that person who is referred to by the pronoun *tat*.
The connection [of the word "pādayoḥ"] with the phrase "salute" (abhivādaya) is correct and appropriate.
Furthermore, in the case of direct perception,
a sentence is used to convey the relationship of a perceived object with that by which it is related, exactly as it is understood.
It is applied as follows:
through direct perception, it is understood that factors of action (kārakas) are connected only with an action (kriyā), and not with bhāvanā, which is synonymous with "what is to be done" (kṛtya).
Therefore, the Mīmāṃsaka position is not tenable, nor is the Vaiyākaraṇa position;
for [in the case] of perception, there is no [cognition of] dharma as a qualifier (prakāratā) of the qualificandum (dharmin).

Furthermore, since the state of being a substratum (*kṣiṣyatā*) is established through experience, it is more appropriate for the subject—the referent of the nominative case—to be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the element *dharmabhūtadhātu*. Even in that case, between the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), the meaning of the suffix is predominant; therefore, [it is the meaning] expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)...
Since the effort (*kṛti*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root, it is appropriate that its locus— such as Devadatta— is the qualificand;
for he is the instigator of all the factors of action (*kāraka*), such as the object (*karman*).
For the primacy of the agent of action over all else is indeed established by experience.
Moreover, Pāṇini,

by means of the sūtra beginning with "prātipadikārtha," states that the meaning of the nominative case is precisely the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha), thereby [denying] its status as having the sense of a kāraka.
It is not accepted; therefore, it is clear that the connection of the meaning of the nominative case-ending with the action is not approved by him. For, [if it were] in the sense of a *kāraka*...
The insistence on action being the primary element is rooted in the connection with action;
therefore, there arises a cognition in which the meaning of the nominative case is the qualificand.

In the absence of a subverting factor (bādhaka), this [the agent as the locus of the action] is appropriate; however, when a subverting factor exists— as in the case of verbal roots denoting existence, such as "caitreṇa supyate" ("Caitra sleeps")— it is not.

Furthermore, in cases such as "the deer runs," it is accepted that the cognition has the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) as its primary qualificand; this is the essence of the Naiyāyika doctrine.

The Compendium of Reasoning:
A Discourse on Auspiciousness. Having placed the Lord of the Universe in his heart and performed the salutation to the Guru—
This *Tarkasaṃgraha* is composed for the easy understanding of the ignorant.
Having prostrated with speech before the Lord of the Universe, the Guru of words, who is the form of Ambā and Śiva together, [I compose] the Dīpikā.
I compose this *Tarkasaṅgrahadīpikā*, a commentary beneficial for beginners.

For the sake of the unobstructed completion of the work he intends to compose, and for the purpose of instructing his disciples, [the author] places at the beginning of the book a maṅgala consisting of a salutation to the chosen deity— a rite whose necessity is indicated by the Veda as inferred from the practice of the learned.
While performing the benediction, he declares his intended undertaking with the words "having placed" (*nidhāya*).

Now, one might object: auspiciousness does not possess the quality of being a means for completing a work, because even when an auspicious rite is performed, completion is not observed in works such as the *Kiraṇāvalī*.

If it is argued that there is a deviation [of the rule] based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), since completion is observed even in the absence of auspicious verses in works such as the *Kādambarī*— we say no;
for [such completion is also seen] in works like the *Kiraṇāvalī*.
Due to the abundance of obstacles, there is a lack of completion; for instance, in works such as the *Kādambarī*, the auspicious invocation was performed outside the text itself. Therefore...
There is no deviation [from the rule].
If it is asked, "What is the proof for the necessity of performing an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*)?", we say: No.

Because the authority [of the practice] derives solely from the Vedic revelation inferred through the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). For instance: auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) has its duty to be performed (*kartavyatā*) revealed by the Veda.
Because it is the object of the extraordinary, unobjectionable conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*),
like the *darśa* and other sacrifices; as in the case of eating and so forth.

The term "extraordinary" (*alaukika*) is used to exclude deviation [from the rule] in cases such as nocturnal *śrāddha* rites. The term "uncontradicted" (*avigīta*) is used to exclude deviation in cases such as [the performance of] nocturnal *śrāddha* and so forth. The word "learned" (*śiṣṭa*) is for the sake of clarity.
"One should not perform fruitless action"—
because even such acts as striking water or beating a forest are thus prohibited.
They are "reasoned" (tarkyante), that is, they are "established" (pratipādyante).
The "categories" (tarka) are the categories of substance and so forth; their "compendium" (saṅgraha) means that their essential nature is being stated in brief.
For what purpose?
To this he says: "for easy understanding.
"Easily" means without effort; that which is the understanding.
The meaning is that [the purpose] is for him to attain knowledge of the true nature of categories (*padārthatattvajñāna*).
Now, one might ask: since many treatises on logic (*tarka*) already exist, for what purpose is this unprecedented work being composed?
Therefore, he says "of the ignorant" (*bālānām*). The meaning is that because these [teachings] are extremely extensive, understanding does not arise for the ignorant;
here, "the ignorant" refers to one who is capable of grasping and retaining [the teachings], and not merely an infant.
Having done what is it performed? To this he says: "having placed"—the Lord of All, the ruler of the world.
"Having placed in the heart"— meaning, having firmly established [the Lord] there; that is to say, becoming constantly intent upon meditation on Him.
"Of the gurus" means of the teachers of knowledge;
"having performed the salutation" means having offered obeisance— this is the meaning.
I pay homage to the illuminating Guru, the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti Śiva with Ambā.
By bowing to whom even a dull-witted person may attain equality with a guru.

In order to ensure the completion of his work, consisting of one hundred treatises (*prāripsitagrantha*), without obstacles, he composes a benediction (*maṅgala*) in the form of a salutation to the Lord; enshrining this for the instruction of his disciples, he declares his intention to compose the work with the words: "Viśveśvaram... (to the Lord of the Universe).
"The teacher of speech"— the instructor of all branches of knowledge;
this also serves as an epithet for Viśveśvara.
However, if the reading is *giraṃ gurum*, the meaning should be understood as "having prostrated before Sarasvatī and the teacher of knowledge.
He demonstrates that his own work does not duplicate the content of other works:
"Beneficial for children" means the *Tarkasaṃgrahadīpikā*,
which is an illumination of the meaning of the *Tarkasaṃgraha*.
He demonstrates the fruit of the auspicious practice (*maṅgala*) and its basis by means of the words "of that which is intended to be done" (*cikīrṣitasya*), and so forth.
Now, with respect to completion—

If auspiciousness were the cause [of success], then the practice of it would be appropriate; however, that very causality is not possible—this is what is being doubted with the words "But surely" (nanu).
[The reason given is] "because of deviation" (vyabhicārāt).

The intention is that because there exists an obstacle in the form of the cognition of deviation in positive and negative concomitance, there can be no ascertainment of causality due to the impossibility of ascertaining the necessary co-occurrence of positive and negative concomitance.
"Because there is an absence of completion"—
this connects with the phrase "therefore there is no deviation.
[This refers to] that which has fewer obstacles [than the required number].

The point is that there is no positive deviation (anvaya-vyabhicāra) because the absence of such an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) serves as a means for the completion [of a work] by way of dispelling obstacles for one who possesses a more powerful auspicious rite.
"Only externally" means "only in another birth"; therefore, in some cases...
Even if the author of the work were a nihilist (*nāstika*), there is no harm;

for the meaning is that since such an auspicious rite exists by way of destroying obstacles, there is no deviation in negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). And thus, the sense is that its status as a cause is established.
Others, however, have explained it thus: "Therefore, due to the two aforementioned reasons, there is no deviation— that is, no deviation in positive or negative concomitance."
Maṇikṛt, however, says: "The fruit of an auspicious rite (maṅgala) is solely the destruction of obstacles; completion, on the other hand, occurs by the power of its own causal complex.
This essential point should be investigated in our commentary on the *Cintāmaṇi*.
He raises an objection in order to establish that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) has a duty-status (*kartavyatā*) as taught by scripture: "But [it might be argued]... [and so on].
"[Only from an inferred scripture]" means...

The intention here is this: although the Veda possesses the nature of having its duty to be performed (kartavyatā) as taught by scripture— thereby falling within the category of the predicate (vidheya) to be described later— it is nevertheless accepted as being predicated (vidheya) by virtue of being included therein.

Because that [universal] is unestablished prior to the hearing [of the word] and the inference; for this reason, there is no such conventional usage as "the universal of fire-ness and so forth has been inferred" by taking as the object of the inference the property to be proven (sādhya), such as fire, which is the locus of the inference.

The doubt as to how the conventional usage of "inferred" (*anumitatva*) can apply to what is heard (*śruta*) is dispelled; for since it is accepted that [the object] is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) when heard, there is no obstacle to such usage.
The particle *eva* (only) has the sense of "also" (*api*).

Therefore, there is no harm even if another means of valid cognition in the form of an inference exists, such as: "The auspicious rite (maṅgala) must be performed because its fruit is completion. Others, however, hold that the probandum belongs to the Veda itself through the relation of "having its duty to be performed indicated by [the Veda]."
"The purport of the subsequent text is precisely this;
and thus, the inference of the Śruti is established," so they say.
"Non-worldly" (alaukika) means that which is distinct from what is obtained through passion and the like, even in the absence of an injunction.

"Uncontradicted" (avigītā) means not opposed to the treatises on Dharma. "By the learned" (śiṣṭā) means by those who, through knowledge of the reality taught in the Vedas, perform the actions prescribed by the Vedas.
The third case ending is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a Buddhist who practices non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth as prescribed in the Vedas.
This is because [the definition] has "being the object of conduct" (*ācāraviṣayatva*) as its qualifier.
Here, "conduct" (*ācāra*) means volitional action (*kṛti*); of that...

Since the status of being a cause by way of the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) that does not restrict the occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*) is the subject of dispute, he pursues the causality of that very objecthood.
He states the purpose of the qualifiers of the reason in their respective order:
By the phrase "at the beginning of eating," etc.,
let the state of being the object of extraordinary and undisputed conduct alone be the probans;
[this applies] to that which is the object of the conduct of those who are not disciplined (aśiṣṭa).
He dispels the objection— that because such a cause does not exist, there can be no deviation (vyabhicāra)—
by accepting the point with the words "the term 'learned' (śiṣṭa)":
[this applies] to cases such as striking water, which are objects of the conduct of the unlearned (aśiṣṭa).

He clarifies the non-existence of such a reason with the words "one should not perform. To exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding results such as heaven (*svarga*), he specifies "being the object of [Vedic] conduct" (*ācāraviṣayatva*).
In brief, [the term] signifies being the object of conduct by way of being something to be performed.
To dispel the misconception that the word *tarka* means "superimposition," he defines *tarka* as common to substances and so forth by stating: "they are reasoned out (*tarkyante*)."
Because it is impossible for [the object] to be included within derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), he says "in brief.
This is a statement of its essential nature (*svarūpa*); that is, a word conducive to the knowledge of its essential nature. By this much—
The categories such as substance and so forth are the subject matter;
the ascertainment of the true nature of these categories is the purpose;
and the relationship is that of the expounder and the expounded.

The four prerequisites (*anubandhacatuṣṭaya*)—namely, that the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is one who desires to ascertain the true nature of categories (*padārthatattva*)—have been indicated as the necessary conditions for the engagement of a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*).
To prevent the misconception that this is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, he says: "easily" (*sukhena*).

With the intention that the desire for a purpose in composing this work would not be appeased because the purpose— consisting of easy comprehension and the nature [of the subject]— is already established from other sources, he introduces [the text] with "Now then" (*nanu*).
"Of them" refers to the *Bhāṣya* and other such works.
To the mine of peerless and supreme excellent qualities, who is devoted to protecting his devotees, a treasure-house of compassion, and who is incessantly [served] by the eternal sages— Bālapriyā.
I shall praise and worship the Lord of the Bull-Mountain. // 1 //
To him whose luster is like a fresh pearl from the illustrious Śaila lineage,
who is a bee at the lotus feet of the lordly sage Vedāntalakṣmaṇa, and who is utterly exhausted by the systems of sound reasoning and the Upaniṣads;
I bow to the illustrious and most excellent teacher Nṛsiṃha,
whose fame shines clearly in all directions like a dancing peacock,
and whose intellect is firmly established in the scriptures.
I daily revere the venerable master Śrī Devanātha, who is accompanied by many disciples, purified by his conduct, and delightful with his faultless virtues. 3.
To my sinless father, who was learned in the Nyāya and other treatises, radiant with the qualities of the self, self-possessed, and an obstacle to [worldly] honor and the like;
to him, I bow.
I take refuge in my venerable father and preceptor, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is endowed with forgiveness.
[She] is radiant with the arrangement of words that are mature, profound, and concise.
This *Prakāśikā* on the *Dīpikā* has been composed by Nīlakaṇṭha for those [who study] the works of Gadādhara and others.
Their familiarity is firm; they are able to correctly know that hidden intention which is made manifest. 6.
For the benefit of the ignorant, according to my ability and according to my understanding,
[I have composed this] clear and straightforward [work].
I am composing this commentary, *Bālapriyā*,
because my intended purpose is considered to be merely the knowledge of the meaning of the root text.
Detailed elaboration and analysis were not observed here, as they were not required.
Now,
there was Nīlakaṇṭha Bhaṭṭācārya, who was preeminent in the mastery of rigorous logical investigation.

Desiring to illuminate the *Tarkasaṅgrahadīpikā* with his own commentary titled *Prakāśikā*, [the author], for the sake of the unimpeded completion of the commentary he intends to compose, [performs] that which is obtained through the tradition of the conduct of the learned...
He extends the auspiciousness [of the work] with the words: "I salute the Guru. Now, regarding the phrase "the *Tarkasaṃgrahadīpikā*":
The meaning is: "that which illuminates the work consisting of concise words that generate knowledge regarding the categories of reality (padārtha).
This is obtainable according to the literal reading.
In that regard, [it refers to] the work consisting of words, namely the *Dīpikā*.

It is not tenable that [the Dīpikā] is an elucidation of the *Tarkasaṅgraha* consisting of words alone, because the text of the *Dīpikā* illuminates only the meaning of the *Tarkasaṅgraha* text; therefore, he explains: "an elucidation of the meaning of the *Tarkasaṅgraha*."
Just as a lamp placed inside a room illuminates the objects situated within that room,
so too does that which is called the "lamp."

The sense is that this work also illuminates the meanings hidden within the *Tarkasaṅgraha*. Thus, the intended meaning is that in the title *Tarkasaṅgrahadīpikā*, the word *tarkasaṅgraha* refers to the subject matter expounded in the *Tarkasaṅgraha* treatise.

From the *Dīpikā* passage beginning with "of that which is intended to be composed," it follows that the purpose of the auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) is the completion of the work without obstacles,
while the purpose of its composition is the instruction of the disciples.
The term "purpose" (prayojana) is understood [here].

In the *Dīpikā*, it was raised as a doubt by the passage beginning with "Now, [regarding] auspiciousness (*maṅgala*)," on account of positive deviation (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) and negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*).
Regarding the doubt as to how such deviation serves as a determinant for the absence of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), he says:
In the *Prakāśikā*, the passage beginning with "anvaya-vyatireka" [means the following]: the point is that for the ascertainment of causality,
there is both the ascertainment of constant positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*) and the ascertainment of constant negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*).

The cause is as follows: 1) "Invariable positive concomitance" (niyatānvayasahacāra) means that the absence of the effect is pervaded by the absence of the cause. 2) "Invariable negative concomitance" (niyatavyatirekasahacāra) means that the presence of the effect is pervaded by the presence of the cause.
"Deviation in positive concomitance" (anvayavyabhicāra) means the absence of the effect even when the cause is present.
This means that the effect does not possess the property of being pervaded by its cause;
"deviation in negative concomitance" (vyatirekavyabhicāra) refers to the existence of the effect even in the absence of the cause.
This means that the absence of the effect is due to the absence of its cause, which is its non-pervader.
In this context, the knowledge of a deviation from the positive concomitance (anvaya-vyabhicāra) acts as an obstacle to the knowledge of the necessary co-occurrence (niyata-anvaya-sahacāra).
The cognition of a concomitance that is necessarily negative is an obstacle to the cognition of a deviation from the negative concomitance;
this applies to the present case regarding the cause in the form of an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*).
Since completion, which is the effect [of the rite], is not observed even in works such as the *Kiraṇāvalī*, it follows that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is not pervaded by completion. Oṃ // Śrīḥ //

There is no certainty regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) characterized by the absence of the completion of an intrinsic nature (*svābhāvavyāpakasamāptyabhāvakam*). And thus, due to the absence of the cause— which consists of the certainty of positive and negative concomitance (*niyatānvayavyatirekasahacāraniścaya*)— the cognition that "auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is the cause of completion" [does not arise] with respect to auspiciousness.
[The opponent argues: "There is no certain cognition (*niścaya*) that apprehends [the rite] as having causality defined by completion.

For, one might raise the objection that there is a deviation from positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*), since in works such as the *Kiraṇāvalī*, completion does not occur even though the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) was performed."

For the purpose of providing a rebuttal, the passage beginning with "In the *Kiraṇāvalī* and other works, there was a failure to reach completion due to an abundance of obstacles" was composed; however,
by that very passage, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) [of the reason with the probandum] is in fact further strengthened.

Having raised the objection that the absence of completion is established even when auspicious causes are present, he explains the intended meaning so that the avoidance of the deviation of positive concomitance (anvaya-vyabhicāra) may be obtained from that text:
Regarding the phrase "of one for whom obstacles are fewer [in number]":
auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is not the direct cause of completion, but rather [it is so] by way of the destruction of obstacles.
The destruction of obstacles occurs through auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) that are either fewer in number than the obstacles or more powerful than them;
thus, an auspicious rite that is either numerically inferior to the obstacles or superior in strength is the cause of completion.
Furthermore, because there were many obstacles in works such as the *Kiraṇāvalī*, no such auspicious invocation was present, and thus the effect in the form of completion did not occur.
Therefore, even when the cause is present...
The meaning is that there is no positive deviation (anvaya-vyabhicāra) consisting in the absence of the effect.

If it were stated that [the cause] must have "an equal number of obstacles," then the intended causal status of an auspicious rite (maṅgala) having a number greater than the obstacles would not be established; therefore, it is said—
Regarding the phrase "of that which has a smaller number than the obstacles":
even if an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) has a number fewer than the obstacles, if it is more powerful,
[it ensures] its completion.

"Because of existence": likewise, since completion—which is of the nature of the absence of the absence of completion—exists in that which lacks auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), the absence of completion is precisely the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of that [completion].
Thus, it possesses the nature of not being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in that which lacks auspiciousness.
The meaning is that the absence of completion does not possess the property of being pervaded by the absence of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). [Objection:
It is accepted that [auspiciousness] is the destroyer of obstacles (*vighna*). [Response:
Considering that if one were to say "of obstacles numbering other than one," there would be no inclusion of those [obstacles], it was stated as follows:
"—or [it belongs] to that which is more powerful.

Now, one might object: since completion is observed even in works such as the *Kādambarī* composed by atheists (*nāstika*), where there is an absence of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), there is a deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*).

Indeed, the passage in the *Dīpikā*—"For the purpose of removing this doubt, the auspicious invocation was performed outside the text in works such as the *Kādambarī*; therefore, there is no deviation"—was composed [to address this].
By that [statement], it is shown that [in those cases] the composition of the auspicious invocation was not made at the very beginning of the work, but rather outside of it.
The meaning is that while an auspicious rite was performed, it was not performed as a formal composition of an auspicious opening; rather, an auspicious rite was indeed performed [at the beginning].
It is indeed found; however, that [explanation] is not tenable,

because one might suspect that it is impossible for an atheist author of works such as the *Kādambarī* to perform auspicious rites (maṅgala) in the form of salutations to the Lord (Īśvara) and so forth.
He explains: "only externally.
This means "only in another birth.
And thus, even if such an author of the treatise were an atheist (*nāstika*) in this life—

The intention is that because of his being a believer (*āstika*) in another birth, the completion [of the work] in this life results from the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) performed at that time; therefore, even in the absence of the cause, it is difficult to assert a deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) regarding the effect.

But surely, since auspicious acts belonging to a previous birth have already perished at that very moment, how can that which is non-existent immediately prior to the completion of this present birth function as its cause?

Or how is the deviation from the negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra) avoided? Anticipating this objection, [the author] states that because auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is a cause by virtue of the relation of possessing the destruction of obstacles produced by itself,
even in the absence of auspiciousness, there exists the medium consisting of the destruction of obstacles produced by it.
The status of being a cause is established;

for example, even though the sacrifice has perished, because the intermediate factor in the form of the *apūrva* produced by it exists immediately prior to heaven, the sacrifice possesses the status of being the cause of heaven— it is with this intention [that the argument is made].
He provides the justification: "Because such auspiciousness is the means for the destruction of obstacles.
And in this way, its status as a cause is established.
Because, according to the manner previously stated,
positive and negative concomitance have been shown to be non-deviant,
there is an absence of the obstacle consisting in the ascertainment of such deviation in positive and negative concomitance.

The meaning is that because there exists a cause consisting of the ascertainment of an invariable concomitance (sahacāra) through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), there arises the ascertainment that auspiciousness (maṅgala) is the cause of completion.
Alternatively, and furthermore—
The point is this: since auspiciousness belonging to another birth exists by way of destroying obstacles,
the causal status of auspiciousness belonging to another birth— defined as its occurring immediately prior to the completion [of a work]— is established.
1. "In what sense is there causality?"—the meaning is that the definition of the term "causality" (kāraṇatva) is precisely the state of occurring at the moment immediately preceding the effect. 2.
"Immediately preceding the completion," and so forth.

And thus, although there is an absence of the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) prior to the completion [of the work] by way of a direct relation, namely inherence (*samavāya*), it nonetheless exists by way of the relation consisting in possessing the destruction of obstacles produced by itself; therefore,
the meaning is that it occurs at the moment immediately preceding the completion.
Regarding the phrase "due to the two aforementioned reasons," etc.: it means that in the *Kiraṇāvalī* and other works,
there was no completion because of an abundance of obstacles.
The meaning is that the auspicious invocation was performed outside the text of the *Kādambarī* and other works due to the two reasons previously stated in the earlier text;
[this occurs] by the power of its own specific causal complex (*svasāmagrī*).
"Of its own completion":
the collection of causes such as intelligence (*buddhi*), creative intuition (*pratibhā*), and so forth; "by virtue of that" means by dependence upon that.
For even when auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) are performed, the completion of the work is impossible in the absence of the collection of causes such as intelligence and creative intuition.

The author of the Maṇi holds the view that factors such as intellectual capacity and eloquence alone are the causes for completion, whereas auspicious rites (maṅgala) are the cause for the removal of obstacles that hinder completion.
Without the knowledge that "an auspicious rite (maṅgala) must be performed," no one would perform it;
[this is] with respect to the volitional effort directed toward that object.
This is because the cognition that something is to be accomplished by an effort having that [thing] as its object is the cause [of action];
and "to-be-done-ness" (kartavyatva) consists in being achievable through effort.

With the intention that "the knowledge that an auspicious rite (maṅgala) must be performed" arises from the Vedic injunction— "one desiring completion should perform an auspicious rite"— which is inferred from the practice of the learned (śiṣṭas) in performing auspicious rites at the beginning of their works, [the author] first...

"In the *Dīpikā*, it is stated: 'The auspicious rite consists of a salutation to one's chosen deity, whose necessity is enjoined by a Vedic text inferred from the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). From this, it is understood that regarding the necessity of performing the auspicious rite, the Vedic text inferred from the practice of the learned serves as the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."

Now, by means of the passage from the *Dīpikā* beginning with "But what is the proof for the necessity of performing the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*)?", he establishes that the performance of the auspicious rite is based on the authority of scripture (*śruti*), using the form of raising an objection and providing its resolution.
This very point is stated in the *Prakāśikā*: "In order to establish that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) has the status of being something that ought to be performed as taught by the Veda."

Now, if it is argued that the scriptural injunction "one desiring completion should perform an auspicious rite" (*maṅgalam ācaret*) is not a valid authority for the necessity of performing auspicious rites, because such a scripture is not observed anywhere in the currently recited Veda;

In response to this doubt, the *Dīpikā* employs the qualification "inferred from the conduct of the learned" (*śiṣṭācārānumitā*) for the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). Although such a revelation is not directly perceived, nevertheless, by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that is the conduct of the learned, a corresponding revelation is inferred.
And thus, the Vedic revelation inferred from traditional practice (*ācāra*) is the authoritative source for the necessity of performing auspicious rites (*maṅgala*). 1.
An effort directed toward that [auspicious rite].

Understanding: the point is that, for instance, with respect to the effort directed toward a sacrifice, the cause is a cognition having the form "the sacrifice is achievable by my effort," which has the sacrifice as its qualificandum (viśeṣya) and the property of being achievable by effort (kṛtisādhyatva) as its qualifier (prakāra).
That is his intention;
and the method of inference has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "Auspiciousness has a duty to be performed as enjoined by the Veda."
In that inference,
what is to be proven (sādhya) is indeed the state of having its duty enjoined by the Veda,
and not the Veda itself. For...
That which is to be established by inference— that is, that which is the object of inferential cognition— is called "inferred. In that case,

since the status of being something whose duty is enjoined by the Veda is inferred from the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) and not from the Veda itself, how can it be maintained that this [status] is "inferred from the conduct of the learned" on the basis of the Śruti?

In response to the objection that if one were to justify the linguistic usage "it has been inferred" by accepting that even the delimitor of the inferential predicate-ness (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) possesses the status of being an object of inference merely by virtue of being an object of inference, then the usage "the property of fire-ness (*vahnitva*) has been inferred" would also result as a valid usage.
He reveals his intention:
"In this regard, this is the intention," beginning with the words "taught by the Vedas," and so forth.

The meaning is: even though [the object] belongs to the category of that which is to be accomplished—the prescriptive content (vidheya) to be described hereafter, whose nature consists in having its duty (kartavyatā) revealed by the Veda—even though it is the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of that [duty]; the word "api" (even/also) [indicates this].

The contradiction consisting in the impossibility of that which delimits the predicatedness (vidheyatāvacchedaka) being itself the predicated (vidheya) is indicated. "By its inclusion"— that is, by the inclusion of the delimiter of the predicatedness.
Because of that scriptural authority—
namely, the scripture stating, "One desiring the completion [of a work] should perform an auspicious rite"—
and because [the effect] was unestablished prior to inference.
And thus, it is precisely the prior non-establishment [of the object] that is the determinant for the status of being the predicate of an inference; such is the case with auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).

Just as there is a status of being the object of prescription (*vidheyatā*) for that [action] because it was unestablished prior to the inference of its duty (*kartavyatā*), so too is there such a status for the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) which serves as the delimiting factor of the object of prescription, since it was also unestablished prior to the inference.

The objective relation known as "being that which is to be enjoined" (vidheyatā) is accepted; and since the Vedic revelation possesses the status of being that which is to be enjoined by inference, its character as an inferred entity is established.
Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the conventional usage that "the Veda is inferred from the conduct of the learned."
The state [of being]. Now, if it is admitted that even the delimitor of the predicatedness (*vidheyatā*) in an inference possesses the status of being the predicate (*vidheya*) in that inference,
then [consider] the delimitor of the predicatedness in the inference "The mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*).

Fire-ness (vahnitva) would also possess the status of being the predicate (vidheya) of such an inference; and thus, just as there is the conventional usage "fire is inferred from smoke," there would likewise be [the usage] "fire-ness..."

He resolves the objection that the conventional expression "inferred from smoke" would also have to be considered valid by means of the phrase "by this," [referring to] that which was previously unestablished for the act of inferring.

The meaning is: by accepting that the delimitor of the predicate (vidheyatāvacchedaka) is the predicate-ness of the inference (anumitividheyatva). And thus, since fire-ness (vahnitva) is already established prior to the inference, there is no contingency of it being the predicate of the inference; this is the point. [Regarding the phrase] "the objectivity of the inference" (anumitiviṣayatām):
The meaning is that it refers to the objectness (*viṣayatā*) in the form of the delimitorship of the predicate (*vidheyatāvacchedakatā*).

It is precisely the state of being an object of inference— whether as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) or as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*)— that constitutes the conventional usage of the term "inferred" (*anumitatva*).
The meaning is "by accepting [it] as the motivator" (*prayojaka*).
"By the admission of its being the object of injunction in the scripture" (*śruti*);
the ellipsis to be supplied is "because it was not previously established prior to the inference."
"Such usage" means the usage [expressed as] "the Veda is inferred. "Due to the absence of sublation" means because there is no evidence to the contrary.

The meaning is that, in the conventional usage "it is inferred," the fact that the inference is already established prior [to the act of inferring] constitutes a sublation; [the phrase "because of the absence thereof" means because of the absence of that sublation].

Now, in the statement "because of the authority of scripture alone" (*śrutereva pramāṇatvāt*), since the particle *eva* has the sense of excluding connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), it is understood that the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) is excluded for anything other than scripture.
That does not hold together,
because even in the case of the necessity of performing an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), there is the inference: "An auspicious rite must be performed because its fruit is completion."
Anticipating the objection that [the reason] is "because it is a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇatvāt), he says:
"The word *eva* has the sense of *api*.
That which has the sense of *api* is "having the sense of *api*" (*apyarthaka*).
The meaning is that the word "api" (also/even) has the sense of both "even" and "cumulative addition. Thus, the phrase "from scripture alone" (śruter eva) means "from scripture as well" (śruter api).
By the use of "api," the validity of inference (anumāna) [as a means of knowledge] is also indicated.
It is collected [from other sources]; therefore, the meaning is that there is no inconsistency. The fact that the scripture is inferred [is as follows]:...

The authors of the *Prakāśikā* have established that even when the delimitor of the property to be proved (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) in an inference was previously unestablished, its status as the property to be proved can still be accepted; thus,
they avoid the difficulty of [the Vedic text] being merely inferential.

He states the view of those who establish [the position], beginning with "others, however": regarding the proposition that "a rite of auspiciousness (maṅgala) has its duty to be performed (kartavyatāka) as enjoined by the Veda," [the term] "maṅgala" [is used].

The meaning is that [the Veda] is qualified by the Veda through the relation of having its duty (kartavyatā) awakened by itself. And thus, in such an inference, the Veda alone is the thing to be enjoined;
the point is that the fact of the Veda being inferred is established without effort.

There is no evidence for such a tradition being the relation that delimits the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha*), and the abandonment of the literal meaning of the root text is an undesirable consequence; this is indicated by the phrase "so they say. In the *Dīpikā*, it is stated: "Because it is the object of the non-worldly, unobjectionable conduct of the learned (*alaukikāvigītaśiṣṭācāraviṣayatvāt*)."
The conduct of the learned is "śiṣṭācāra";
the object of such conduct is "śiṣṭācāraviṣaya"; and this [object] is also "uncontradicted" (avigīta).
The object of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is that which is the object of the unobjectionable conduct of the learned;

and that which is both non-worldly (*alaukika*) and the object of the unobjectionable conduct of the learned is the "object of the non-worldly, unobjectionable conduct of the learned" (*alaukikāvigītaśiṣṭācāraviṣaya*); of that...
The meaning is reality (*tattva*).
The resulting conclusion is that the logical reason (*hetu*) is being the object of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), provided that it is not worldly and provided that it is not contradicted.
Worldliness (*laukikatva*) is the state of being cognizable by means of knowledge other than scriptural injunction (*vidhi*);
non-worldliness (*alaukikatva*) is the state of being distinct from that. If "non-worldliness" were not included as a qualification in the reason (*hetu*), [the definition would be over-extensive].

In the case of food and the like obtained through passion— wherein the probandum, namely "having a duty to perform as enjoined by the Veda," is absent, yet the reason, namely "being the object of the unobjectionable practice of the learned," is present— there would be a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra). To exclude that, the qualification "not being based on worldly motives" (alaukikatva) is included.

"Non-contradiction" (avigītatva) means not being prohibited by the treatises on Dharma (dharmaśāstra). If that were not included [in the definition], then in cases such as the *rātriśrāddha* (night funeral rites), where the probandum—defined as having its duty enjoined by the Veda—is absent, the reason—defined as being the object of the practice of cultured persons (*śiṣṭa*)—would nonetheless exist. Thus, the reason would be present in a locus lacking the probandum.
There would be an instance of deviation;
to prevent that, the quality of being "uncontradicted" (avigītatva) is included [in the definition],
as in the case of the *rātri-śrāddha* and similar rites.
Because it is prohibited by the *Dharmaśāstra* that "one should not perform a *śrāddha* at night," there is no deviation [from the rule] in that case;
as stated in the *Prakāśikā*: "in the absence of an injunction."
An injunction (*vidhi*) is a Vedic statement composed of the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), or gerundive (*tavya*) suffixes.
[The phrase] "by means of the knowledge of reality taught in the Veda" [is used].

The meaning of the third [instrumental case ending] is "being produced" (*janyatva*), which here relates to the *kṛti* (volitional effort) that is the meaning of the root *kṛ* in the word *karmakārī*.

The meaning is: one who is a *śiṣṭa* (cultured person) is the locus of that volitional effort directed toward Vedic-prescribed actions, which is itself produced by a cognition whose object is that reality (*tattva*) which is declared in the Vedas.
In some places, the reading is "vedotthatattvajñānena" (by the knowledge of reality arising from the Veda);
the meaning is: by that knowledge of reality which is produced by the Veda.

That very reading is superior; for if one were to state merely that "the cultured person (śiṣṭa) is one who performs the rites prescribed by the Veda," then even a Buddhist, who performs such Vedic-prescribed acts as non-violence (ahiṃsā) and so forth, would [be included].
[Otherwise] there would be the consequence of [the Buddha] being considered an authoritative teacher (*śiṣṭa*).
To prevent that, [the definition specifies] "by means of the knowledge of reality arising from the Veda.
The knowledge of reality such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) possessed by a Buddhist does not arise from the Veda.
There is no over-extension [of the definition].
Alternatively, the reading "by means of the knowledge of reality as declared in the Veda" (yad vā vedoktatattvajñānena) is more appropriate.
One who performs the action prescribed by the Veda with the prior knowledge that "this is declared in the Veda" is a refined person (śiṣṭa);
whereas a Buddhist [performs] actions such as non-violence (ahiṃsā) which are not prescribed by the Veda.

Even while performing this [action], one does not do so with the thought "this is prescribed by the Veda"; therefore, because he does not accept the authority of the Veda, he does not incur the status of being a *śiṣṭa* (cultured person).
Now, [it may be argued] that the conduct of the *śiṣṭas* alone...
Let there be causality;
why pursue causality all the way to its being the object of conduct? Furthermore, conduct is not volitional effort (*kṛti*), for that—
1. Regarding the term *alaukika* (non-worldly):

the meaning is that since the nocturnal *śrāddha* is understood solely through the injunction "one should perform the *śrāddha*," it possesses the quality of being non-worldly, which consists in its not being cognizable by any means of knowledge other than scriptural injunction.

2. [The opponent replies: "It is better. And thus, it follows that being a *śiṣṭa* (an authoritative person) consists in possessing an inclination toward ritual acts such as sacrifice, which is produced by a cognition whose mode is the fact of being stated in the Veda.

It should not be argued that [the performance of the rite] cannot function as a logical reason because, while it resides in the self, it does not reside in the subject (pakṣa) in the form of an auspiciousness;
