for it is possible for the action (kṛti) to serve as a reason through the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā).

Anticipating the objection that an action residing in the self may stand in the relation of being a cause for auspiciousness residing in the rite through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā-sambandha*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*), he says: "The practice" (*ācāraḥ*).

By the words "the product" (*kṛti*) and so forth: *vṛtti* (occurrence) is the state of being located (*ādheyatā*); the relation that regulates that is the "relation regulating occurrence," such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so on.
Objecthood (*viṣayatā*), however, is not a relation that determines occurrence (*vṛttiniyāmaka-sambandha*).
[For example,] by virtue of the relation of objecthood, the effort [to compose] resides in the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*).
Because it exists dependently;

and the relation that restricts occurrence (*vṛttiniyāmaka-sambandha*) alone is the relation that delimits causality (*hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha*), whereas relations such as objecthood (*viṣayatā*) which do not restrict occurrence are not.

And thus, since it is impossible for the act of doing (*kṛti*) to have causality as delimited by the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatāsambandha*), one pursues the causality of being the object of customary practice (*ācāraviṣayatva*).

The intention is that being the object (*viṣayatva*) [of a rule] is the probans by way of the relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*), and since the relation of identity is a regulator of occurrence (*vṛttiniyāmaka*), it is possible for being the object of conduct (*ācāraviṣayatva*) to function as the probans through that very relation.
Since the purpose of the term "being the object of conduct" (*ācāraviṣayatva*) was not stated in the root text, he himself states that purpose: "having heaven and so forth as its fruit.
And thus, in the case of the reason (*hetu*).

If the term "being the object of conduct" (*ācāraviṣayatva*) were not included, the reason would be "not being contradicted while being non-worldly. Since this [reason] exists even in the case of a fruit such as heaven,
there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because the probandum— in the form of "having its duty-to-be-done (*kartavyatā*) taught by the Veda"— is absent there.
To exclude that [possibility], the phrase "because it is the object of conduct" (ācāraviṣayatvāt) is employed;
however, as for heaven and so forth—

The point is that there is no deviation [in the definition], because there is no state of being an object of volitional effort (*kṛti*). Now, one might object: volitional effort has three objects—an end (*uddeśya*), a means to be enjoined (*vidheya*), and a material cause (*upādāna*).
For example, the sacrifice is the means to be enjoined, and heaven is the end.
The *uddeśya* (the intended object) is the collection of subsidiaries such as the *prayāja* offerings; the *upādāna* (the means of attainment) is heaven.

Anticipating the objection that there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even when taking "being an object of volition" (*kṛtiviṣayatva*) as the *upādāna*—since heaven possesses the objective status (*viṣayatā*) termed "intendedness" (*uddeśyatā*) as defined by volition—the author says: [the term] signifies being an object of practice (*ācāra*) by way of being something to be enjoined (*vidheyatayā*).

Thus, the meaning of the third [case-ending] is non-difference (*abheda*). The reason [for the application of the suffix] is the state of having an object that is non-different from that which is to be enjoined as prescribed by the conduct (*ācāra*). [This applies] to heaven and so forth.
The point is that there is no deviation [in the logical rule], because there is an absence of the objecthood known as "predicability" (vidheyatā) as defined by the agent of the action.
Now, [one might object]: "By means of the superimposition of the pervader..."
Hypothetical reasoning (*tarka*) is the attribution of the pervader (*vyāpaka*).

Thus, the meaning of the term *Tarkasaṅgraha* is a treatise that expounds upon hypothetical reasoning, which consists in the attribution of the pervader produced by the attribution of the pervaded (*vyāpya*).
That is not tenable,
because the *Tarkasaṃgraha* does not establish mere superimposition (*āropamātra*).

Anticipating the objection that other categories of objects are also expounded [in the treatise], he states— beginning with the words "of the word *tarka*," etc.— that in the *Dīpikā*, the word *tarka* is etymologically explained in such a way that all the categories of objects intended to be taught by the text may be understood through that term.
The meaning is: the delusion that it has the purpose of superimposing [the pervader];
that is to say, the delusion that its purpose is the superimposition of the pervader by means of the superimposition of the pervaded.
There is also the sense that the word *saṅgraha* means "inclusion" (*upādāna*).
That is not possible here;
for it is impossible for categories such as quality (guṇa) and so forth to have space (ākāśa) and the like as their material cause (upādāna), even among substances.
For *upādāna* (appropriation) is indeed a specific activity of the hands and instruments; therefore,
he says "in the form of appropriation" (*upādānarūpa*), explaining that the meaning described in the root text is a concise statement of the essential nature of the term *saṅgrahapada*.
Now, in the phrase "stating the essential nature" (*svarūpakathana*),
the word "stating" (*kathana*) has the meaning of "utterance" (*uccāraṇa*).
And what is called "utterance"?
The operation conducive to the contact between the palate and the lips [is the cause].

Since that [operation], which has sound alone as its object, cannot have the nature of categories such as substance as its object, it is a description of the essential nature [of sound]; thus, how is "sound" [defined]?
Anticipating the objection that this is redundant, he says: "The statement of the essential nature (svarūpa-kathana) is a word conducive to the knowledge of one who knows the essential nature.
And thus, in the present context, the meaning of the word "kathana" (statement) is not utterance, but rather—
The meaning of a word is that which is conducive to knowledge.

Since [the suffix] *anukūla* (conducive to) connects with the object (*viṣaya*) of the knowledge itself, the meaning of the word "definition" (*svarūpakathana*) is a word conducive to a knowledge whose object is the essential nature of the thing denoted by the word.
The meaning is that there is no lack of logical justification.
Regarding the engagement of discerning persons—who act with prior reflection—in the study of a treatise: therein...
The fourfold adjuncts (*anubandha*) are the constituent parts.
The subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), relationship (*sambandha*), and qualified student (*adhikārin*) are the four adjuncts.

They are called "concomitants" (*anubandha*) because they bind a person, impelling them toward the study of the treatise; [these are] the subject matter expounded by the treatise and [the purpose] of the study of the treatise.
The purpose, the relationship between the treatise and its subject matter,
and the qualification for the study of the treatise.
Without knowledge of these four, no one would engage in the study of this treatise. Thus,

fearing that the root text might be deficient due to the failure to state the four prerequisites (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*) which must necessarily be mentioned, [the author]— even though not explicitly stated in so many words— [establishes] that tetrad by implication.
He says "it has already been indicated" (sūcitameva),
meaning by means of the explanation of the term *tarkasaṅgraha*.

Regarding the expression "sukhabodhāya," if one accepts the analysis as a genitive tatpuruṣa compound— namely, *sukhasya bodhaḥ* (the cognition of happiness)— it would follow that the purpose of this treatise is a cognition having happiness as its object.
If that were the case, it would contradict the indication—given in the commentary on the term *tarkasaṃgraha*—that the work intends to convey the understanding of all categories (*padārtha*).
Therefore, [the word] is easily [explained as follows]: 1.
The phrase "of the categories such as quality" (guṇādipadārthānām) is construed with the phrase "due to the impossibility of [their] being the material cause" (upādānasyāsambhavāt).

He states that the term "cognition" (bodhaḥ) has been explained as a genitive tatpuruṣa compound—namely, "the cognition of..."—and not as a third-case tatpuruṣa compound; thus he says, "as a genitive tatpuruṣa. From another [source].
"By virtue of being established" means that it is established even by the fact of its being recited in other texts such as the Bhāṣya.
The Compendium of Reasoning:
A Classification of Categories.
AnTs 2: Substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence—these are the seven categories.
The *Dīpikā* analyzes the categories [of existence] as follows: "Substance," etc.
By the etymological derivation that "the meaning of a word is *padārtha*," being denotable (*abhidheyatva*) is the general definition of a *padārtha*.
Now, [one might object: since the number seven is already established through the very classification [of the categories], why is it stated again?
If it is argued that the mention of "seven steps" is redundant, we say no; for its purpose is to exclude a greater number. [Objection:
But has an additional category of entity been established?
Or [is it] not? Not the first, because it is impossible to negate that which has been cognized;
not the second;
If it is argued that negation is untenable without the cognition of a counter-positive, we say: no;
for the property of being a category (padārthatva) is pervaded by being one or another among the seven categories, such as substance and the rest.
Because it has the sense of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). Now, [one might object]:
"The state of being one of the seven (*saptānyatamatva*) is the state of being different from that which is different from the seven.
But since that which is different from the seven is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), how [can this be]?
If it is argued that there is a certainty regarding the pervasion of being one of the seven [categories], we say no;
for "being one of the seven other than substance and so forth" means the possession of the absence of the sevenfold difference from substance and so forth.
Therefore, because it is free from faults;
this should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.
The *Prakāśikā* states that the seven categories (*saptapadārtha*) are those whose nature consists of substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth.
The meaning is that "categories" (padārtha) are those things which possess any one of the seven limiting adjuncts (upādhi) that differentiate categories.
In this context, the number "seven" consists in being the object of a particular enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). The same applies to the subsequent text as well.
This is the conclusion to be noted. Now, one might object:

since the knowledge of a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) is the cause for the specific cognitions (*viśeṣavijñāna*), it would be more appropriate to provide the classification immediately after stating the general definition.
And thus, in order to remove the deficiency [in the objection] as to how there can be a division at the very beginning in the root text, he says: "of the word" (*padasya*).
This is because, according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the meaning of a word is its denotation (*abhidheya*).

Although the status of being the object of denotation related to a word is obtained, [the author] says "the state of being denotable" because the factor of being related to a word does not serve to exclude [unintended objects]. The words "the definition is obtained" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
And thus, the sense is that there is no deficiency [in the definition]. "Precisely because of the division" means by way of the subordinate properties of the categories (padārtha).
The meaning is: "precisely by means of establishing the substratum (dharmin).
[The phrase] "because it has the purpose of excluding a greater number" means that its result is the establishment of the negation of such a number.

With the intention that, in a context involving the relationship between the subject (uddeśya) and the predicate (vidheya), it is a general rule that the pervasion of the predicate by the delimiting property of the subject (uddeśyatāvacchedaka) is manifested, he says: "the state of being a word-meaning" (padārthatva).
"Because it has the sense of exclusion (vyavaccheda)" means:
because its purpose is that exclusion or determination which takes the form of "thus."

"Being different from the seven distinct [categories]" means that one must state its difference from that which is qualified by the aggregate of the distinctions among those seven categories, namely substance and the rest.
This refers to the state of possessing the absence of the sevenfold division beginning with substance (*dravya*).

Since each of these seven divisions—substance and so forth—is well-known to exist individually, yet their non-existence is established in some [locus], the absence delimited by that sevenfold division exists everywhere; therefore, there is no [fallacy].
This is the sense of the objection;
however, in reality, "the property of being a category (padārthatva) is pervaded by being one or another of the seven [categories], such as substance (dravya) and so forth."
The meaning is that being a category (padārthatva) is pervaded by the property of possessing any one of the seven adjuncts, such as substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth.
By this, in many cases...

It should be noted that there is no deficiency even if the passage beginning with “But [is it not] being one of the seven?”— which is devoted to raising the doubt regarding the lack of established recognition for being one of the seven and providing its resolution— is absent from the books; the same applies to what follows.
The meaning is that it is in this same manner [that the definition applies] in cases such as "substances" (dravyāṇi) and so forth.
Bālapriyā: Indeed, from the root text as heard, namely "the seven categories" (saptapadārthāḥ), it is understood that the categories possess the number seven.
That is not correct;
because substances, qualities, and so forth are each manifold,
there are actually more than seven categories (padārtha) in total among all things.
With the intention that it is impossible for the word "seven" (*sapta*) to effect the exclusion of a number exceeding seven,
he explains the root text by means of another method, beginning with the words "having the nature of substantiality, etc. (*dravyatvādirūpā*).
And thus, because the indication is primarily of the property (*bhāva*), words such as "substance" (*dravya*) refer to [the universal] "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth;
whereas the final word, "non-existence" (*abhāva*), [refers to the universal "non-existenceness"].
"Because it is an indication where the state (bhāva) is predominant.

A word is an "indication where the state is predominant" (bhāvapradhānanirdeśa) when its predominant [element]—that is, its primary object of intention—is a property (dharma) that has become a qualifier of the meaning of the verbal root (prakṛtyartha). And thus:
Because words such as *dravya* (substance) have as their intended meaning properties such as *dravyatva* (substanceness) which serve as qualifiers (*prakāra*) of their own referents,
they possess the quality of being "expressions where the state [of the property] is predominant" (*bhāvapradhānanirdeśa*).
[This applies] when [the word] refers to that which possesses any one of *dravyatva* and so forth.
Indication (*lakṣaṇā*). There is a co-occurrence of the number seven with [the categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*).

Those properties (*dharma*) which are of the nature of substantiality and so forth, which are pervaded by the category of "being an ontological category" (*padārthatva*), and which possess any one of those seven, are the "seven categories. Thus, there are seven.
From the sentence "the categories (padārthāḥ)," there arises an understanding.

Even though substances and the other categories are manifold, there is no inconsistency, because the properties that subdivide the categories— such as substanceness (dravyatva) and so forth— are exactly seven.

[Objection: But surely "seven-ness" is a quality (*guṇa*) in the form of a number; therefore, its being the substratum [of that quality] does not exist in [categories such as] substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that "number" (saṅkhyā) is a quality (guṇa) because it resides only in substances (dravya), he explains— stating "here,

the state of being seven"— that in the present context, the state of being seven is not a specific form of number, but rather the state of being the object of a particular enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi).
The cognition "this is one," "this is one"—that is *apekṣābuddhi* (relational cognition);
the meaning is that [the object] has that as its objective domain. This also applies to the subsequent passage.
The meaning is that this also applies to the text to be stated later, such as "the twenty-four qualities beginning with form" and "the five actions beginning with upward throwing."
One should understand that the final point here is this:
the intended meaning of [the number] twenty-four and so forth is simply that they are the objects of a particular enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).
The meaning is that it is to be ascertained.

The statement beginning with "substance, quality, and action" (*dravyaguṇakarma*) is the sentence that effects the classification of categories (*padārtha*). Classification (*vibhāga*) is defined as that which generates a cognition whose qualifiers are mutually non-co-inherent properties (*parasparāsamānādhikaraṇadharma*) that are subsumed under the property of being a category (*padārthatva*), and whose qualificandum is a category that serves as the objective referent (*viśeṣya*) for a cognition whose qualifiers are general properties (*sāmānyadharma*).
"Sound.

Furthermore, it is only when a student possesses a desire to know the specific attributes (*viśeṇadharma*)—namely, "In how many ways is the category (*padārtha*) consisting of such things as sound divided?"—that it is possible to state that [the category of sound] is of this kind; otherwise, it could not be done.

Because this would entail the fault of *arthāntara* (irrelevancy), consisting in the statement of a matter not intended to be inquired about; for, with respect to a desire to know a specific [property],
knowledge having a general property as its qualifier is the cause.

Since the general definition of a category (padārtha) was not stated at the outset prior to the classification, it is not the case that the student has not yet acquired knowledge characterized by the mode of a general property (sāmānyadharma).

He states that the passage from the *Dīpikā* beginning with "the meaning of a word" (*padasyārthaḥ*) is intended to resolve the doubt that "it is improper to provide a classification because there arises no desire for specific knowledge (*viśeṣajijñāsā*) consisting of a wish for a cognition whose qualifier is a property pervaded by the state of being a word-meaning (*padārthatva*). Thus he says: "But surely... (*nanu*).
Regarding the phrase "of the knowledge of general properties" (*sāmānyadharmajñānasya*),
it means "because of being the cause.
That is to say, when there is a desire to know the particulars (*viśeṣajijñāsā*) following the knowledge of generalities, [the latter] functions independently.

Alternatively, its status as a cause consists in its producing the cognition of the delimiting property (dharmitāvacchedaka) of the subject [of the inference], which is the cognition that [the action] is a means to achieve what is desired.
1. "Even though there is multiplicity" means:
The meaning is: "even though there is a number exceeding seven.

2. A general property (*sāmānyadharma*) is "the state of being a category" (*padārthatva*). A category (*padārtha*) is that which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of a cognition having that [property] as its qualifier (*tadprakārakajñāna*). That which has that [category] as its qualificand...

The meaning is: those properties such as substanceness (*dravyatva*), qualityness (*guṇatva*), and so forth, which are pervaded by the property of being a category (*padārthatva*) and are mutually non-co-occurrent; knowledge having these as its qualifiers is of the form "categories possess substanceness, qualityness, etc."; the word that generates such knowledge is [the definition].
3. Of general cognition— that is,
of a cognition whose qualifier is a general property—
with respect to the desire for specific knowledge— that is, with respect to the desire for a cognition whose qualifier is a specific property.
In the section on *savyabhicāra*, Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya states:
"When there is knowledge of a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), there is a desire to know the specific; in its absence, that [desire] is absent."
The causality of the general cognition [of the property] consists in its possessing independent positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Alternatively,

it is the cognition that "the knowledge qualified by the specific property is a means to the desired end" (*iṣṭasādhana*) with respect to the desire for a cognition whose object is qualified by the specific property, by way of the relation of having that [specific property] as its qualifier (*svaprakārakatva-sambandha*).

The cognition having as its qualificandum a knowledge characterized by a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*) and having as its qualifier the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) is the cause.

With respect to such a cognition of being a means to a desired end, the cognition having as its qualifier the specific property that serves as the delimiting condition of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is the cause. [This applies] to the qualified [object].

For it has been established in the *Rājapuruṣavāda* and other works that a cognition having as its qualifier the delimitor of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) is the cause of a cognition that apprehends a specific distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*).

Furthermore, Gadādhara’s intention is that since knowledge of a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) is the cause of knowledge regarding the modes of a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*), knowledge of a general property is indirectly the cause for the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) a specific property.
Thus, without knowledge of a general property, there can be no desire to know the specific.
The meaning is that it is not capable of arising.
"Immediately after stating the general definition" means that once the general definition of the categories (padārtha) has been stated.

The sense is that, from the knowledge of a general property (sāmānyadharma) consisting of such characteristics, there ought to arise an inquiry into specific properties (viśeṣadharma) as to how many kinds of categories (padārtha) there are.
[Regarding the phrase] "deficiency" (nyūnatām): [it refers to the fact that the definition would be incomplete].
Anticipating the objection that "the failure to state a meaning that must necessarily be stated" would follow,
and asking how "being denotable" (abhidheyatva) can be established so that the statement in the root text is consistent, he says: "In the sense of a word, [it is] denotable."
Although, from the perspective of the word, what is obtained is the state of being the object of denotation related to the word, nevertheless, this alone is not the complete definition,
because it is merely the state of being the object of denotation.
Because the aspect of "being related to a word" is redundant, given the possibility that it is the general definition (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of the meaning of a word (padārtha). [Note:

1. One's own specific property (*viśeṣadharma*) refers to categories such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) or quality-ness (*guṇatva*); that which is qualified by substantiality and so forth through the relation of having that as its qualifier (*tatprakārakatva*);]

Knowledge is the desire directed toward that [knowledge], having the form "May knowledge qualified by [the mode] 'substance-ness' and so forth arise for me"; the cause of that [desire] is the cognition having the form "Knowledge qualified by [the mode] 'substance-ness' and so forth is the means to my desired end."
With respect to such a cognition, the knowledge of the delimiters of the subject (dharmitāvacchedaka), such as substanceness (dravyatva) and so forth, is the cause;
[this occurs] when there is knowledge of substanceness and so forth.
The meaning is that the knowledge of the general property consisting in being an object (*padārthatva*) is the cause.

2. In the *Vyutpattivāda*, during the discussion on the meaning of the sentence "the king's servant" (*rājapuruṣa*) under the section on the first case-role (*prathamākāraka*), [it is stated]: "one who lacks the state of not being the king's own (*arājasvatvābhāvavān*)."

In the cognition "The man is handsome," which apprehends the qualification of handsomeness in a man characterized by the absence of ownership by the king, there occurs the cognition "The man possesses the absence of ownership by the king," which has as its qualifier the absence of ownership by the king that serves as the delimiting property of the qualificandum (viśeṣyatāvacchedaka).
The reason has been determined;
it is now applied here:
therefore, "being denotable" (abhidheyatva), which constitutes a portion of the meaning obtainable from the word "category" (padārtha), is itself the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
The intended meaning is as follows:
"Because it is non-excluding" means that it is devoid of any purpose such as the exclusion of under-extension (*avyāpti*), over-extension (*ativyāpti*), and so forth.
In this regard, the following must be considered:

the method for obtaining the general definition (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) through the term "word-meaning" (*padārtha*) as it occurs within the sentence defining "division" (*vibhāga*), as stated in the *Dīpikā*, is not tenable.
Immediately after stating the general definition (*sāmānyalakṇa*), when the student— through their knowledge of that general property—

desires to know the specific details regarding how many kinds of categories (*padārtha*) there are, the statement of classification (*vibhāgavākya*) proceeds; therefore, it is appropriate that the general property be indicated by a term that is not a constituent part of that statement of classification.

Because it would lack propriety— due to faults such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)— for a word forming part of the defining statement to produce the knowledge of a general property (*sāmānyadharma*) that generates a desire for specific knowledge regarding the subject matter of that defining statement;
therefore, by the word "reasoning" (*tarka*) in the auspicious verse, the general definition consisting of the state of being knowable (*jñeyatva*) [is indicated].

This has been indicated. Therefore, it is only logical to state that the sentence beginning with "substance, quality," and so forth, was introduced as a result of the desire to know the specific distinctions;
and this very point is established in the section on etymological definitions (*nirukti*) and the subsequent text.
This is because the substratum (dharmin) is presented by means of a subordinate property of "being a category" (padārthatva).

The meaning is: from words such as "substance" (dravya), which present the substrata—such as substance itself—as qualified by properties like "substanceness" (dravyatva) that are pervaded by "being a category."

If it is asked: "But even if substances and so forth qualified by substanceness (*dravyatva*) and the like are understood from the mere words 'substance,' 'quality,' and so on, how is the number seven understood in relation to them?"—to this they reply:
"From the very classification," as stated in the root text.
The meaning is: "precisely because of the plural number co-occurring with the *dvandva* compound beginning with 'substance' (*dravya*) and 'quality' (*guṇa')";
and thus, there is a rule that a plural number co-occurring with a *dvandva* compound denotes a number that is sufficient to pervade all the meanings conveyed by that *dvandva*.
This must necessarily be accepted;

otherwise, in the case of "Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna," there would be the undesirable consequence of understanding a number such as three through the use of the plural suffix, which would contradict actual experience. And thus:

In the present context, since it must necessarily be accepted that the plural suffix co-occurring with such a *dvandva* compound denotes a number that is fully instantiated in a collection ranging from the substances denoted by the members of the *dvandva* up to their final limit.
Such a number must be the number seven; this is established by the use of the plural number.
It should be understood that even the *Nīlakaṇṭhaprakāśikā* has its purport in this very point somehow, because [the plural] serves to exclude a greater number in the root text.
The meaning is: because its purpose (artha) or objective is the exclusion (vyavaccheda)—that is, the definitive negation—of a higher number, specifically the numbers seven or eight.
Thus he says: "such a number."
And thus, it follows that by means of the seventh term, the non-existence of an eighth category is understood;
[this concerns] the eighth category.

With the intention that a refutation is not tenable because its negation would be impossible if it were established through error, the author of the *Mūla* stated "cognized" (*jñāta*) instead of "known" (*pramita*). [The term used is] *pramita*.
The meaning is that this [object] is the object of valid cognition (*pramā*).
The intention is that one can state that because there is a necessary rule (*niyama*) regarding the existence of the object of valid cognition, its negation is impossible.
In that very context, [the phrase] "without the cognition of the counter-positive" is used;
for although in the cognition of an absence the knowledge of the counter-positive alone is the cause, not the valid cognition (*pramā*) of the counter-positive.

Because it is impossible for a valid cognition (pramā) having the sky and so forth as its qualificandum and the sky and so forth as its qualifier to be the cause of the cognition of the non-existence of the sky and so forth;
for since the sky and so forth are non-occurrent (avṛtti), there can be no [cognition] qualified by them such as "this possesses the sky."
Because a valid cognition (*pramā*) having such a form is impossible;
nevertheless, in the present context,
by the term "cognition of the counter-positive" (*pratiyogipramā*), what is intended is not a cognition whose qualifier is the counter-positive, but rather—
Only a valid cognition (pramā) that has the counter-positive as its qualificandum and the delimitor of counter-positiveness as its qualifier is intended.

Since a valid cognition of the form "This is ether" (idaṃ gaganaṃ), which has ether as its qualificandum and the property of being ether (gaganatva) as its qualifier, is well-established, [the argument proceeds] by virtue of that.
The cognition of the non-existence of space is possible;
however, the intention of the *Dīpikā* is that in the present context, since there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) for an entity exceeding the seven categories, its negation is not tenable.
By the sentence beginning with "dravyaguṇa" (substance, quality, etc.), having pointed out the categories (padārthas),
it is enjoined that they possess the property of being one or another among the seven [categories] beginning with substance.
And in a case where there is a relationship between the subject (uddeśya) and the predicate (vidheya),...
The general rule is that the property of being pervaded by the predicate (vidheya-vyāpyatva) appears in the delimiting factor of the subject (uddeśyatāvacchedaka).

For example, in the statement "the wealthy person is happy" (*dhanavān sukhī*), when happiness is predicated with respect to wealthiness as the subject, the state of being pervaded by happiness appears in wealth, which is the delimiting factor of the subject; that is, wherever there is wealth, [there is happiness].
Just as in the example "it is pleasure," so too in the present case, within the delimitor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), namely "being a category" (*padārthatva*),

there appears the property of being pervaded by "being one of the seven [categories] other than substance" (*dravya* etc.); that is, wherever there is "being a category," there is "being one of the seven [categories] other than substance."
And thus, the meaning is that there is no contradiction by way of proof or non-proof;
this is what he states in the words: "in the case of the relationship between the subject and the predicate."
"General rule" (autsargika) means established by the general principle (*sāmānyanyāya*).
This is because [the term] "for the purpose of excluding a higher number" appears in the preceding root-text (*mūlagrantha*).

Just as the word "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) has negation as its meaning, so too [the term in question] has exclusion as its meaning because it signifies "that which is pervaded by being one of the seven [categories]. And thus,
in the cognition of absence...

The meaning of the common dictum "the cognition of the counter-positive is the cause" is simply that the cognition having the counter-positive as its qualificandum and the delimiting property of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) as its mode is the cause; the intention is not that the cognition must have the counter-positive itself as its mode.

To ensure that one does not fall into the error of thinking that the word *vyavaccheda* (exclusion), even when its root is cut off [as in the compound], has negation as its meaning, he explains it with the words "of this form" (*etadrūpa*) and "because it has that as its meaning" (*tadarthakatvāt*).
The word "of the seven" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the compound].
Now, one might object: being "one of the seven" means being different from that which is different from the seven.

Since that which is distinct from the seven categories (*saptapadārtha*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), the state of being "one of those" (*anyatamatva*)—defined as being distinct from them—is likewise unestablished. Consequently, it is impossible to ascertain the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) by that [unestablished property] with respect to the categories; thus, [the definition] possesses the efficacy of resulting in such an ascertainment.
In the *Ādīpikā*, it was raised as an objection that the mention of "seven" is not tenable, beginning with the words, "But [is it not] being one of the seven? In that context,
the objection regarding lack of established convention (*aprasiddhi*) is not tenable, for those who...
The seven categories, beginning with substance, each possess the property of being distinct from that which is distinct from themselves;

for instance, in the case of substance, it possesses the state of being distinct from qualities (guṇa) and so forth— which are distinct from substance— and in the case of quality, it possesses the state of being distinct from substances and so forth— which are distinct from quality.

Anticipating the objection that "it exists" (sat-tattva) applies to all seven categories because each possesses the property of being non-different from that which is different from them, he explains: "Those seven [categories] beginning with substance.
Thus, it is qualified by the aggregate of the differences from those seven categories beginning with substance.
That which is qualified by the sevenfold division is "the state of being different from those," which is the state of being one or another of the seven.
In this regard, that which is qualified by the sevenfold division is unestablished (*aprasiddha*),

because although the sixfold division having substance as its counter-correlative exists in a quality (*guṇa*) and so forth, the division having substance itself as its counter-correlative does not exist there.
Because a collection consisting of those seven types of difference is impossible,
the same applies to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. Thus,

since that which is characterized by the sevenfold difference— that is, the "seven-different" (*saptabhinna*)— is unestablished, [the definition] consisting of being different from that [is likewise unestablished].

The sense is that the objector’s intention is that the state of being distinct from seven [individual] distinctions is unestablished. The meaning is as follows: the distinctions well-known individually—such as the distinction of quality in substance and the distinction of substance in quality—the absence delimited by the collection of those seven is here [what is meant by] "being one of the seven."
Wherever the property of being a category (padārthatva) exists, there exists the absence of such a collection; therefore, the ascertainment of pervasion (vyāpti) is easily accomplished.
He states this intention with the words "of the distinctions such as substance" (*dravyādibhedānām*).
Since the status of being one of the seven [categories] is not well-known in many treatises, the subsequent passage is intended to address that doubt and provide its resolution.

It is observed; therefore, the property of being a category (padārthatva) is pervaded by being one of the seven [categories] beginning with substance (dravya). To avoid any suspicion of non-establishment regarding the description of the meaning of the *Dīpikā*, he states the intended meaning as follows:
"In reality, however... (vastutastu).

The pervasion intended in the present context is as follows: wherever there is the property of being an object (padārthatva), there are the seven limiting adjuncts (upādhi) or properties, such as substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth; that is, the state of possessing any one of those [seven] is the pervading factor.

The property of being a category-member (padārthatva) exists in substance (dravya), because therein exists the state of possessing one of the seven fundamental categories such as substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth; thus,
there is pervasion (vyāpti) in the case of substance and the rest.
It is easily grasped. Furthermore, "being one of those" (anyatamatva) is simply the state of being non-different from what is different from them.

Regarding the seven properties such as substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth, those things different from them are potness (ghaṭatva) and the like; the state of being different from those [potness and the like] exists in substantiality and the other [seven properties].
The sense is that there is no room for the suspicion of non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*).
"In this manner" refers to *dravyatva* (substantiality).
The meaning is that the word "nine" is used in the sense of determining that [the object] is pervaded by being one or another of the [substances] beginning with earth.
The Compendium of Reasoning:
Classification of Substances (AnTs 3).
Among these, substances are exactly nine: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind.
The *Dīpikā* analyzes substance:
"therein" (*tatra*) means among [the categories] beginning with substance.
The logical connection is that there are exactly nine substances.
To the question "Which are they?", he says: "Earth," and so forth.
"Manifestation is the substance"; this is the singular number used for the sake of the genus.
Objection: Is it not the case that the passage from the *Dīpikā*, "Therein he divides the substance," is untenable?
For instance: the meaning of the singular number following a nominal stem (*dravyapada*) is oneness;
its grammatical relation (*anvaya*) is with the substance that is the referent of the base (*prakṛtyartha*).
In its role as the second object,
that [cow] is construed with the [action] by means of the relation of being the locus (ādheyatā);
and the state of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatā) is construed by means of the relation of being the determiner (nirūpakatā).
The syntactic connection [occurs] when there is knowledge of one part of the root-meaning.

The meaning of the verbal root *bhaj* preceded by the prefix *vi-* is a word that produces a cognition consisting of a valid knowledge (*pramā*) whose qualifiers (*prakāra*) are various mutually contradictory properties (*dharma*) that are subsumed under the category of substance-ness (*dravyatva*).
The verbal suffix's meaning, *kṛti* (volitional effort), is construed with that [effort] through the relation of favorability (*anukūlatā*),
and it is construed with Annambhaṭṭa through the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*).

From the sentence "He divides substances" (*dravyaṃ vibhajate*), the understanding is as follows: Annambhaṭṭa is the locus of the effort conducive to the word which generates a cognition consisting of a valid knowledge (*pramā*) whose qualificandum is a substance qualified by oneness, and whose qualifiers are multiple properties that are mutually non-coextensive and pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*).

In that case, a cognition of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*) which has a single substance as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and multiple properties such as "earthness" (which is pervaded by "substancehood") as its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) is not possible.

It should also be understood that if earth and the other elements were distinct substances from the single substance that is color-form (*rūpa*), there would be the conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of postulating infinite parts, prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*), and so forth; therefore, it is established that they must necessarily be of the nature of the absence of light (*tejo-'bhāva*).
"Darkness (tamas) is the tenth substance,
because, while not being included among the [previously] established substances, it possesses the nature of a substance"— this is established by the inference of elimination (pariśeṣānumāna).

The tenth substance-ness of darkness is what is intended to be proven. In that regard, in order to avoid the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the substantive (viśeṣya) in the reason—namely, its being a substance—it is stated: "Darkness is a substance..."
By means of the inference: "because of possessing form and because of possessing action."
The substantiality of darkness (tamas) is to be established;
even in that regard, one should not entertain the suspicion of the unestablished reason (hetvasiddhi),
for [it is observed that] "darkness is blue."
The possession of color and motion by darkness is established by the uncontradicted perceptual cognition in the form of "darkness moves.
Thus, it is stated in the *Dīpikā* with the words "darkness is blue," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by the force of cognition" (*pratītibalāt*):
the word ending in the fifth case (*balāt*) is construed with both "the substratum of form" and "the substratum of action.
It is specified as "unsublated" (*abādhitā*) because a cognition whose object is sublated does not establish its referent.
In this context, the word *pratīti*, which generally denotes cognition (*jñāna*), refers specifically to perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣātmakajñāna*),
because there is no justification for abandoning that which presents itself first.
This pertains to a situation where perception is impossible.
With the intention that this is because the word denoting cognition in general is dependent upon inference, [the author] says in the *Prakāśikā*: "by the force of perceptual cognition.
Now, [one might object]: "Darkness is a substance..."
The inference "because it is the locus of blue color and because it is the locus of action" is inconclusive,
[as it applies] to that which lacks substantiality (*dravyatva*).

Anticipating the objection that even in qualities produced by other causes (*janya-guṇa*), etc., there exists the state of being a locus of color and the state of being a locus of action by virtue of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*), he says: "The meaning is 'possessing the quality of blue color through inherence' (*samavāyena nīlarūpavattā*). And thus, it is the state of being a locus, as determined by the substratum-ness residing in blue color, which is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
And in this context, what is intended as the reason is the state of being a locus (adhikaraṇatva) as determined by the property of being the substrate (ādheyatā) residing in such an action;
[this applies] to produced qualities (*janyaguṇa*) and so forth, when delimited by the relation of time (*kālikasambandha*).

To prevent the misconception that the word "pratītibālāt" (by the force of perception), being in the ablative case, is syntactically connected with the phrase "the substantiality of darkness is established," it is stated that its connection is rather with "being the locus of color" and "being the locus of motion."
2. There is nothing whatsoever in eternal entities by way of a temporal relation, because of the non-connection with time in what is eternal.
This follows from our established tenet (*siddhānta*).

Accordingly, with the intention that it is impossible for eternal qualities (*nityaguṇa*) and so forth to be the locus of color (*rūpa*) by means of the relation of time (*kālikasambandha*), it was stated [in the text] "in produced qualities" (*janyaguṇādi*).

The intended meaning is that there is no deviation [from the rule], because the substratum-ness (ādhāratva) defined by the locus-ness (ādheyatā) residing in the completion of the action of taking form (rūpakriyā) indeed exists. "Of that" [refers] by way of the temporal relation (kālika-sambandha).

The meaning is: "of being the locus of the action of form (rūpa) as delimited by a temporal relation. Even if it is over-pervasive—that is, even if it subsists in things other than substances—there is no harm; that is, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra).
The same should be understood for what follows as well.

Regarding the statement, "Darkness (*tamas*) is not included within the pentad beginning with space because it possesses color (*rūpavattvāt*)," here too, the phrase "because it possesses color" means [possessing color] by way of inherence (*samavāyena*).
The intended meaning is that it should be understood as "because of possessing form";
the implication is that by this much [it is established that] darkness is the tenth substance.

In the *pariśeṣa* inference— "because it is a substance while not being included among the [other] enumerated substances"— the "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) that constitutes the reason has been established.
Now, as for the constituent of the reason...
In the *Dīpikā*, the fact that darkness is not included among the enumerated substances is established by the passage beginning with "tatra tamasaḥ" (among those, of darkness).

Now, one might object: since it is already established that darkness is not included within air by the very reason of its possessing color (*rūpavattva*), the further presentation of the absence of touch (*sparśābhāva*) as a means of proving that same point is redundant.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "With the intention of [distinguishing] different types of relations.
Possessing color (*rūpavattva*) is the reason by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*);
however, the absence of touch (*sparśābhāva*) is the reason by way of the relation of essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The meaning is that, having stated the reason by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*), he now states the reason by way of the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*).
If darkness were included within air...
It would not possess form, nor would it be devoid of touch;
since darkness possesses form and is devoid of touch, the implication is that it is therefore not included within wind.
Is it not the case that the following inference is established: "Darkness is distinct from air, because it lacks touch"? In that regard:

There is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because in air— which possesses the absence of the probandum (the specific form of air) defined by its distinction as air— there exists the absence of touch, which consists of an absence whose counter-positive-ness is delimited by the relation of conjunction residing in touch. Nor is it the case that...
An absence whose counter-positive is delimited by the relation of inherence-in-that-which-is-based-on-contact is intended as the probans;
and that [absence] does not exist in air.
In that case, it should be stated that because touch exists by way of inherence (*samavāya*), its absence is impossible;
[this refers to] the absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) resides in touch and is delimited by the relation of inherence.

Because [the probans] exists in air by way of a temporal relation (*kālikasambandha*), the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was. Nor should it be argued that there is no deviation because what is intended is the causality of the absence of touch (*sparśābhāva*)—delimited by inherence (*samavāya*)—in relation to its own nature (*svarūpasambandha*); for even so, [the fault persists].

In the air delimited by the time of its origination, there is an absence of touch, according to the principle that "a substance, once produced, remains for a moment without qualities and without activity. 1.
[The absence of] color residing [in it].
And the meaning of "the state of being a substratum" (ādhāratva) is that which is determined by the state of being the locus of an action (kriyāniṣṭhā-ādheyatā).

Anticipating the objection that [the definition] is subject to deviation because [existence] exists by way of the relation of essential identity (svarūpasambandha), he says: "And this [is the case] in the locus of destruction and prior non-existence."

And thus, since there is no absolute absence of touch in air delimited by the moment of its production—which still possesses the prior absence of touch—there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason according to the opinion of the ancients; such is the sense. "Otherwise" means:

The meaning is that, according to the view of the Navya-Naiyāyikas, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is admitted in the locus of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Even in the Navya view, he says "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) in order to avoid the charge of inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*);
and thus, there is an absolute non-existence of touch (*sparśa*) in air.

The point is that [the property] exists only through the relation of spatial qualification delimited by the time of its origination, and not through the relation of unqualified spatial qualification; thus, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra).

In the texts of Navya-nyāya, the term *daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā* is used to denote the relation of spatial inherence (*svarūpa-sambandha*), while the term *kālika-viśeṣaṇatā* denotes the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*).
[The phrase] "a reason with uneven pervasion" (*viṣama-vyāpta-hetu*)...
A reason (*hetu*) that possesses a pervasion (*vyāpti*) defined solely by the probandum (*sādhya*) is "unevenly pervaded" (*viṣamavyāpta*);
a reason that possesses a pervasion defined by the probandum as well as a pervasion defined by the reason itself is "evenly pervaded" (*samavyāpta*).
And thus it is said: "Darkness is distinct from air,
because it possesses color."

In this formulation of the inference, wherever there is possession of color (*rūpavattva*), there is a particular wind (*vāyubheda*); thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) defined by the particular wind exists in the probans (*hetu*), which is the possession of color.
Wherever there is a particular wind...
In each case, the pervasion (vyāpti) defined by the possession of form— that is, the state of having form— is not possible in the case of a particular wind,
because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra): since the possession of form is absent in space and other such things that possess particular winds.
Therefore, the property of possessing form (*rūpavattva*) is a reason that is inconsistently pervaded (*viṣamavyāpta*).
The same applies to the absence of touch (*sparśābhāva*).
Wherever...

Although there is a pervasion (vyāpti) such that "wherever there is a distinction of wind, there is an absence of touch," there is no pervasion in the form "wherever there is a distinction of wind, there is an absence of touch," because touch itself exists in things like pots which possess a distinction of wind.

In the argument "Darkness is not differentiated by air, because it lacks constant motion," the absence of constant motion is a co-extended (samavyāpta) reason; for wherever there is differentiation by air, there is an absence of constant motion.
The pervasion defined by the absence of constant motion (sadāgatimattvābhāva) in the case of a particular wind is as follows:
wherever there is an absence of constant motion, there is a particular wind.
And because the pervasion determined by the distinction of air exists even in the absence of constant motion;
"action of a different genus" means an action characterized as distinct that resides in air alone.
Nor is it in light;
that is, darkness is not included within light (it is distinct from light).
The inference— "because of the absence of radiant color and because of the absence of hot touch"—
is such that therein, the absence of radiant color is "invariably pervaded" (viṣamavyāpta).
The absence of hot touch is co-extensive [with darkness].
Likewise: "Darkness is distinct from water, because it lacks cold touch and because it possesses blue color."
Thus, in this inference, the absence of cold touch is co-extensive (samavyāpta),
whereas the possession of blue color is non-co-extensive (viṣamavyāpta).
In the statement, "Darkness is distinct from earth, because of the absence of odor and because of the absence of touch," the absence of odor is co-extensive [with the probandum].
It should be inferred that the absence of touch is pervaded unevenly;
darkness possesses the very nature of a substance.
It does not exist; how, then, could it possess the status of a tenth substance?
For it is held that darkness is included within the seventh category called non-existence (*abhāva*), since darkness is of the nature of the absence of light; thus it is stated in the *Dīpikā*.

In this regard, if by the term "absence of light" one intends the absence whose counter-correlative is light, then there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "this is darkness" even in a place possessing the light of the sun and so forth, because of the existence therein of an absence whose counter-correlative is some other light.
If one intends to express an absence whose counter-correlate is delimited by "lightness" (tejas-tva), then even in a place possessed of darkness,
because light-atoms and the like exist there, the general absence of light (tejaḥ-sāmānyābhāva) is non-existent; consequently, the cognition "this is darkness" would be untenable.

Even if the aforementioned defect is avoided by intending an absence whose counter-correlate is delimited by the essence of that light which is illuminating— since fire-atoms and the like lack the status of being illuminating— nevertheless...
In a location containing light— such as a triad of luminous atoms or a firefly— the perception of darkness would be impossible. Therefore,
what is intended to be expressed is the absence of that light which is both intense and illuminating, characterized by a counter-correlativity delimited by its own essence (*tattva*).
And "maturity" (*prauḍhatva*) consists in possessing an excellence of magnitude.
Since this kind of maturity is absent in the triad (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, there is no logical inconsistency in the perception of darkness even when that [triad] exists.
Having taken all this into consideration, he says: "prauḍhaprakāśaka" (possessing intense illumination).
He states the purpose of employing the word "prakāśaka" (illuminator) with the words "ataḥ" (hence):
darkness (*tamaḥ*) is the absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by the property of being light that possesses intense illumination.
If this is said, the term "illuminator" (prakāśaka) is redundant;
for the exclusion [of atoms] is already possible simply because atoms of light lack the maturity consisting of a superior degree of magnitude. Therefore...
To exclude the luster of gold and other such things, it should be stated that the term refers to "that which illuminates. Even so,
the perception of darkness would still be untenable in locations containing light from the eyes and other sources.
To exclude that [over-extension], the property of possessing manifested color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) must also be added as a qualification for light. Thus,

darkness (*tamas*) is the absence whose counter-positive is delimited by the nature of light (*tejastva*), which possesses a manifesting manifested color and a pre-eminent magnitude (*prakṛṣṭamahattvavat*).
Alternatively, "solidity" (*pauḍhatva*) means the state of possessing great power (*mahāprabhāvatva*).
Since it is by that very quality that the obstruction of atoms as well as gold and so forth is possible, the term "illuminator" (*prakāśaka*) need not be included.
The result is that darkness (*tamas*) is an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the state of possessing great luminosity (*mahāprabhāvattva*).
Having this in mind, he says: "In the direction," etc.
Now, as for darkness...

Having raised the objection— "Since substantiality (*dravyatva*) was previously established by means of possessing form (*rūpavattva*), how can [darkness] be of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāvarūpa*)?"— it is stated in the *Dīpikā*: "Darkness is not a substance possessing form," and so forth.
In this context, what is intended to be proven is the absence of possession of color and the absence of substantiality in darkness.
If darkness were to possess color or be a substance, then...
It would have to be perceived by the eye only when assisted by light;
since it is perceived by the eye even when not assisted by light, therefore darkness is neither possessed of color nor is it a substance.
Wherever there is the property of being perceivable by the eye assisted by light, there is the property of being distinct from matter (rūpa) and distinct from substance (dravya),
as in the case of the absence of light; thus, because of the existence of this pervasion (vyāpti) in the reason (hetu).

If the qualification "not assisted by light" were not employed, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra), because the reason— being perceptible by the eye— would exist in a substance possessing color, such as a jar, which lacks the property to be proven (sādhya).
Therefore, that qualification is included.
A jar and the like are perceptible by the eye when assisted by light, but not perceptible by the eye when not so assisted; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule].
This is what he says: "In the case of a jar and so forth."
Is it not the case that "being perceptible by the eye" means being the object of a perception produced by the eye?
[This applies] in the case of a perception having darkness as its object, which is produced by the eye when it is not assisted by light.
Since the jar also appears through the proximity of the character of cognition,
there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of jars and the like, which are objects of that perception.
In response to this doubt, he says: "The state of being perceptible by the eye means being the ordinary object of a cognition produced by the eye;
thus, darkness is visual."
The meaning is: "in a visual perception whose object is darkness. "By way of the upanaya" means:
"by means of the cognitive condition (*jñānalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*)."

In some manuscripts, the reading is seen as: “Therefore, even though there is no defect [in our theory], since by means of the method of *upanaya* (application), a jar or the like appears in visual perception as ‘the jar possesses darkness’ because of the darkness [present there].”
In that regard, the portion "the jar is possessed of darkness" is invalid,
because it contradicts the established doctrine that what is presented [to consciousness] appears only as a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) and not as a qualificandum (viśeṣya).

Therefore, the reading seen in some places as devoid of that portion is indeed correct; or else, it should be read by emending it to "aghaṭavattamaḥ" (darkness not possessing a jar). Now, since the general absence of light (*tejaḥsāmānyābhāva*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), [is there not a problem] regarding the absence of illumination (*ālokābhāva*) included therein?
The statement that [the subject] is an example is not tenable, because an example must be something distinct from the subject (pakṣa); therefore, he says: "due to the absence of any distinction."
The subject (pakṣa) is an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a general property;
the example (dṛṣṭānta) is an absence distinct from that, whose counter-positive is delimited by a specific property.
Therefore, the sense is that there is no logical inconsistency.

Now, regarding the doubt that the reason—namely, "being perceptible by the eye when not assisted by light"—might exist while the probandum, "the difference from substances possessing color," does not, which would render the argument inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), it is stated in the *Dīpikā*: "In the case of the visual valid cognition of a colored substance," and so forth.
If there were no distinction from material substance, then that which is apprehended by the eye unassisted by light would not exist;
that is to say, if it were a material substance.
In that case, the following reductio ad absurdum (tarka)— namely, "it would follow that it is perceivable by the eye aided by light"—
must be stated as a refutation of the objection regarding its lack of probative force;
and that reductio is as follows:

With the intention that it would follow [only] if there were a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) such that "light is the cause of a visual perception (*pratyakṣa*) consisting of valid cognition (*pramā*) which has a substance as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and possesses the mode (*prakāra*) of 'having color'," the causal relation has been demonstrated.
Regarding that, he states the purpose of the term "valid cognition" (*pramā*)— namely, "without light. Thus, if the term "valid cognition" were not employed, then even in the absence of light,
a perceptual error consisting of the cognition "this has color," which takes darkness as its qualificandum and possesses "having color" as its qualifier, would arise.
There would be the fallacy of deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*). The intention is that the word "valid" (*pramā*) is included to prevent this. "Otherwise" means:

The meaning is that there is an absence of light as a cause for the visual valid cognition (*cākṣuṣapramā*) of a material substance (*rūpidravya*). Now, one might object: "It is not possible for light to be a cause for the visual valid cognition of a material substance."
Because there is a deviation from the negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra), since visual perception of a luminous substance possessing color occurs even in the absence of light.

Nor should it be argued that light is a cause only for the visual valid cognition (*cākṣuṣapramā*) whose object is a material substance (*rūpidravya*) distinct from light itself; therefore, there is no deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*).

Having also added the qualification "distinct from darkness," just as there is the qualification "distinct from light," [it refers to] that substance which is distinct from darkness and distinct from light.

Since light is accepted as the cause only for the visual valid cognition (*cākṣuṣapramā*) directed toward that [object], it is possible for darkness to be visually perceived even without light. Thus, there is no deficiency in its being graspable by the eye even when not assisted by light; therefore, darkness is a substance distinct [from the other nine].
Since there is indeed no obstacle [to this], he says "the direction" (*dig*).

This is because, since the substance of fire (*tejo-dravya*) must necessarily be accepted as the substratum of the currently experienced hot touch, it is for the sake of accounting for its perception.

Even if "being different from light" were included within the scope of the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there would be no deficiency even if darkness were of the nature of an absence (*abhāva*); therefore, its inclusion as being "different from that" (i.e., different from light) is inappropriate.
And thus:

The sense is that it has been well stated that darkness is not a material substance possessing color (rūpin), because if darkness were a substance, it would be impossible for it to be perceived by the eye when not assisted by light.
The definition of substance is as follows:
the general definition of substance is either the possession of the genus "substance-ness" (dravyatva-jāti) or the possession of qualities (guṇavatva).

The *Prakāśikā* states "substantiality," etc., because the knowledge of the true nature of categories (*padārtha*), which serves as the means to liberation, is not possible without the knowledge of their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*).

The point is that the genus *dravyatva* (substantiality) is established as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the capacity to produce conjunction. Now, one might object that there is no difference between a definition and the delimitor of the definiendum; to this, he says: "the possession of qualities" (*guṇavattva*).
"The general characteristic of substance" [is stated];
thus, the intention is that there is no deficiency because the common properties have not been mentioned.
In the *Bālapriyā* commentary on the root text, it is stated that the definition of a substance (*dravya*) is the possession of the genus "substanceness" (*dravyatvajāti*).
In that regard, what [is the proof] concerning the genus "substanceness"?
Anticipating the objection that this might be mere conceit (*māna*), he says: "by virtue of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the production of conjunction.
By this, inference (*anumāna*) is stated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the universal *dravyatva* (substanceness). To explain:
since conjunction occurs only between two substances, substance is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to conjunction.
With respect to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), substance (*dravya*) is the cause by way of the relation of identity (*tādātmya-sambandha*).

A causal power delimited by the relation of identity exists in the substance, which is defined by an effect-ness residing in conjunction that is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*).

Taking that causality as the subject (*pakṣa*), one must prove that it is delimited by some property (*dharmāvacchinnatva*) by means of the reason (*hetu*) consisting in its being causality. [This refers to] the causality residing in substance, which is delimited by the relation of identity (*ādātmya-sambandha*) and is determined by the effect-ness (*kāryatā*) residing in conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is itself delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
[The subject] is delimited by some property, because it is a causal capacity;
whatever is a causal capacity is delimited by some property, just as the causal capacity residing in the staff, which is defined by the effect-ness residing in the jar.

The meaning is as follows: through the inference "that which is delimited by stickness possesses that [causality]," once it is established that the aforementioned causality residing in substances is delimited by some property such as substanceness (*dravyatva*), then— given that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in the case of that established property being a universal (*jāti*)— the universal called "substanceness" is established by means of the assistance of the cognition of parsimony.
In the root text, another definition of substance (*dravya*) as "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattva*) has been stated;
its underlying rationale is explained by saying that there is no difference between the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
When it is stated that "the definition of substance is substanceness," the definiendum is substance,
the delimitor of the state of being the definiendum is substanceness,
and the definition is likewise nothing other than substanceness.

There would be non-difference between the definition (lakṣaṇa) and the delimiting factor of the thing to be defined (lakṣyatāvacchedaka). If it is asked, "Let there indeed be non-difference between the two; what fault lies therein?"—listen.

For the purpose of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) with respect to the definiendum (*lakṣya*) is the inference of its difference from others. That is to say, a definition is that which generates an inference whose subject (*uddeśya*) is the definiendum and whose predicate (*vidheya*) is its difference from others; as, for example, [the definition] of a cow.
If having a dewlap is the defining characteristic, then by the inference "the cow is distinct from others because it possesses a dewlap," the cow's distinctness from others is established.

Likewise, in the present case as well, if "substance-ness" (dravyatva) is the defining characteristic of a substance, then [the inference would be]: "A non-substance is distinct from others, because it possesses substance-ness."
Thus the inference should be formulated;
therein, the resulting inferential cognition is: "Substance is distinct from others."

With respect to that [object], the cause is the reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*): "The substance possesses substanceness, which is co-located with the difference from others and is pervaded by that difference.

And pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probans (*hetu*), its pervader (*vyāpaka*), and the probandum (*sādhya*). Thus, [the judgment is]: "The substance possesses substanceness, which is co-located with the difference from others and is pervaded by that [difference]."
The form of the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) is established;
therein, as substance-ness appears in its co-referentiality with the exclusion of others (itarabheda), [the latter] is likewise cognized through the same act of cognition (tulyavittivedyatayā).

In the case of other distinctions, there also appears co-referentiality with substantiality (*dravyatva*). What is called "being cognized by the same cognition" (*tulyavittivedyatā*) means being the object of a single cognition.

And in inference, the co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the delimitor of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka), which consists in subsisting in the subject (pakṣavṛttitva), appears in the probandum (sādhya). And thus,
by means of the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) of the subsistence in substance— which is distinct from other things and is the object of the inference— [the conclusion is established].

Since the very object that is established by the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) as having been made its own objective domain is what is being proved by the inference, the fallacy known as *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) follows;
for [the object] is [already present] in the subject (*pakṣa*) prior to the inference.
If there is certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) occurs.
Therefore, if the definition of a substance (*dravya*) is "possessing the universal of substanceness" (*dravyatvajātimattva*), then the fault known as *siddhasādhana* would necessarily follow.
The sense is that, having reflected [on this], the pursuit of another definition was undertaken;
for since the cognition of specific properties does not arise without the knowledge of general properties, it is improper to provide a classification [without first establishing those generalities].
He states "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*) to show that the definition of substance in general was stated in the root text (*mūla*) in order to dispel doubt.
"Deficiency" (*nyūnatā*) means a deficiency consisting in the failure to state the definition.
The *Dīpikā* [explains] the definition of non-pervasion and so forth;
there are three [types] of definition.

Regarding fallacies: non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) is the failure of a definition to apply to even one part of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*); for example, "tawny color" as a definition of a cow. Over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) is the application of a definition to that which is not the object to be defined.

For example, the possession of horns [is not a non-existence] in a cow. Non-occurrence (*asambhava*) is the state of occurring only in that which is to be defined (*lakṣya*); for example, the possession of a single hoof in a cow.

Since it will be stated that a definition is indeed a property free from the three types of defects, the cognition of that [definition] is not possible without the cognition of its qualifier, namely, the state of being free from the three defects.
However, the knowledge that [the definition] is free from the three defects depends specifically upon the knowledge of those three defects;
for the cognition of a negation is dependent upon the knowledge of the counter-positive as qualified by the delimiting condition of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*).
With this intention, he demonstrates the three defects, beginning with: "non-existence in a portion of the definiendum" (*lakṣyaikadeśāvṛttitvam*).
The meaning is: non-existence in some locus of the definiendum (lakṣya) by means of the relation intended as the delimitor of the definition (lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka).
[The phrase] "only in the definiendum" [is used].
The word "mātra" (only) has the sense of "entirety" (kṛtsna);
it indicates the general absence of occurrence in the locus as delimited by a specific relation.

Regarding the definition "having a single hoof": it should not be argued that there is a confusion of definitions here because over-extension (*ativyāpti*)—in the form of the definition's applying to things that are not the intended subject—is also present;
for according to the maxim, "even when there is a confusion of faulty definitions, the faults themselves remain distinct."

After hearing the passage from the *Bālapriyā* titled "The Lamp on the Definition of the General Characteristic of Substance" (*dravyasāmānyalakṣaṇamitidīpikā*), one might ask: what is the meaning of the word "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*)?
What indeed is the definition of a definition?
Thus, a desire to know arises in the student;
for the sake of pacifying that [desire], the definition of the definition must be stated.
Since it would be irrelevant to state the definitions of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and so forth prior to that, he says: "By the three defects," and so on.
The definition of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is being a property (*dharma*) that is free from the three defects.

And freedom from the three defects consists in possessing the absence of the three defects. Thus, it is established that the definition of a definition is being a property qualified by the absence of the three defects. In this regard:

Since the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is the cause of the qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*), the cognition of the qualifier— which consists in the absence of the three defects— is the cause;
and such a cognition of the qualifier...
This is not possible without the knowledge of the three types of defects,
because the knowledge of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is a necessary cause for the cognition of non-existence.
Therefore, there are three defects [of the definition]. (Note:
"lakṣaṇasya trīṇi dūṣaṇāni" is the reading accepted by the Nṛsiṃhaprakāśikā.)

The intention is that, with the aim of making [the definition] easy to perceive by way of its characteristics, the definitions of the three defects— namely, non-pervasion (avyāpti) and so forth— are stated in the *Dīpikā*.
This is the underlying meaning.
"Specifically, it depends on the knowledge of the three defects.

The intention here is as follows: "The state of being devoid of the three defects" does not mean an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by the property of being one of the three defects. For if that were the case, [the following would occur:]

For, according to the principle that "even if one property such as being a Kapila exists, the triad [of definitions] does not exist," since the absence of the three defects would exist in a property like being a Kapila— which possesses at least one defect such as non-pervasion—
that property itself would incur the status of being a definition.

However, one must state that "the state of being free from the three defects" refers to the absence of the three defects— characterized by non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*), and impossibility (*asambhava*)— where these defects are specified as such and their absences possess a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by those very characteristics (*avyāptitva*, etc.). And thus:

A property qualified by these three: the absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by non-pervasion (*avyāptitva*), the absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by over-pervasion (*ativyāptitva*), and the absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by impossibility (*asambhavatva*).
This is the established conclusion regarding the definition.
In that regard, since the cognition of the counter-positive as qualified by the delimiting property of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is the cause of the cognition of absence,
the cognition of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) and so forth as qualified by the state of being non-pervasive (*avyāpitva*) and so forth is the cause [of the erroneous cognition of pervasion].
In order to produce such knowledge, [the author] first states the nature of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and other fallacies in the *Dīpikā*:
"Under-extension is non-occurrence in a portion of the locus (*lakṣya*). This means the absence of the property of being located (*ādheyatva*) as determined by some part of the locus.

The meaning is that the absence of occurrence (vṛttitvābhāva) in any locus whatsoever that is delimited by the delimitor of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedakādhikaraṇa) constitutes the nature of under-extension (avyāpti).
When it is stated that "tawny-ness (kapilatva) is the definition of a cow," [the following occurs] regarding the definiendum...

The cow is the subject; the delimitor of its being the subject (lakṣyatāvacchedaka) is cowness (gotva).
