Its locus is a white cow, and the absence of subsistence (vṛttitvābhāva) as determined by that [locus] exists in brownness (kapilatva); thus, the definition applies to the property that is under-defined (avyāpta).
Now, since the property of being brown exists in a white cow— the locus of cowness— by way of a temporal relation,
there is no absence of occurrence relative to the locus of the delimitor of the indicated (lakṣyatāvacchedaka); thus, [the definition] would be over-narrow with respect to such a property.

Anticipating the objection that the definition would be either over-extensive (*avyāpta*) or impossible (*asambhava*), he says: "by means of the relation intended as the delimitor of the definitionhood.
The meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*) is "delimitedness" (*avacchinnatva*), which is construed with "subsistence" (*vṛttitva*).

And thus, the absence of occurrence— qualified by the relation that delimits the definitionhood and determined by the locus of the delimitor of the definiendumness— is the definition of the under-pervaded (avyāpta), and it is the essential nature of under-pervasion.
The state of being tawny exists in a tawny cow by way of inherence;
thus, inherence is the relation that serves as the delimiting relation of the definition.
1. That by which [something] is defined is the definition.
The relation by which [the property] exists in the locus of definition (lakṣya) is the "relation that delimits the definition" (lakṣaṇatāvacchedakasambandha). For example,

although the state of being a resident delimited by a temporal relation (*kālikasambandha*) as determined by a white cow that is the locus of cowness (*gotva*) does indeed exist in a brown cow, there is an absence of the state of being a resident delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāyasambandha*) as determined by that same [white cow].

The co-presence of the definition in the subject (kapilatva) consists in being the locus of that which delimits the state of being the definiendum; and this being the locus of that which delimits the state of being the definiendum is the state of being a locus as determined by the subsistence residing in that which delimits the state of being the definiendum.

In that context, regarding the state of being the locus (*ādheyatā*), one must incorporate the property of being delimited by the relation that delimits the delimitor of the definition-locus (*lakṣyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka-sambandha*). Otherwise,
in the case of the definition of "existent" (*sat*) as "possessing a dewlap" (*sāsnāvattva*) and so forth, [there would be an over-extension] through the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*).
Because there exists an absence of subsistence in that which is the locus of *gotva* (cowness)— the delimitor of the definiendum— such as buffaloes and the like,
the definition characterized by non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) becomes over-pervasive (*ativyāpti*). Likewise, [this applies] when there is co-occurrence with the delimitor of the definiendum.
The term "existing" (sat) must also be added as a qualification to a definition that is under-extended;
otherwise, there would be over-extension of an under-extended definition to such [pseudo-properties] as "having a single hoof," which are themselves afflicted by the fallacy of impossibility.
Because the absence of subsistence as determined by the locus of cowness exists there [in the one-hoofed animal] as well;
however, when that qualification is applied, there is no over-extension to such things as "possessing one hoof," because that lacks the absence of subsistence in the locus of cowness.

And "co-occurrence with the delimitor of the locus of being the definiendum" (lakṣyatāvacchedakasamānādhikaraṇatva) means: subsistence as determined by a substratum that possesses a locationhood (adhikaraṇatā) which is itself determined by a locatedness (ādheyatā) residing in the delimitor of the locus of being the definiendum. In this regard, concerning the locatedness residing in the delimitor of the locus of being the definiendum...

The property of being delimited by the relation that delimits the delimitor of the definiendum-ness (*lakṣyatāvacchedakatāvacchedakasambandha*) must be included [in the definition]. Otherwise, since the possession of a single hoof exists in a horse— which is the locus of "cowness" (*gotva*), the delimitor of definiendum-ness— by way of the temporal relation (*kālikasambandha*), the definition would suffer from over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with respect to a property that is already afflicted by non-possibility (*asambhava*).
However, in that particular locus (the cow), the substratum of "cowness" (*gotva*) is indeed the cow itself by virtue of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*);
since the property of "possessing a single hoof" does not have its occurrence (*vṛttitva*) as determined by that [inherence], there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Thus, in the definition of "occurrence," it must be specified that it is delimited by the delimiting relation of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha*); otherwise—

Because the property of having a solid hoof (*ekaśaphavatva*) exists in a cow through the relation of temporal connection (*kālikasambandha*), the aforementioned defect would arise. Thus, [the definition] must satisfy the condition: being a presence delimited by the defining relation of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedakasambandha*), which is itself delimited by a locushood (*adhikaraṇatā*) that is determined by a substratumhood (*ādheyatā*) residing in the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), and this substratumhood is in turn delimited by the defining relation of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedakasambandha*).

The result is that the definition of the under-pervading (avyāpta) is: the absence of occurrence, as delimited by the defining relation of the definition (lakṣaṇatāvacchedakasambandha), which is in turn determined by a substratum-ness (adhikaraṇatā) that is qualified by a locus-ness (ādheyatā) residing in the delimitor of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedaka), itself being delimited by the relation that delimits the delimitor of the locus of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedakatāvacchedakasambandha). For further details...
This should be seen in the *Paṭṭābhirāma-ṭippaṇī* and other works.

1. The property that delimits the state of being the indicated (lakṣyatāvacchedaka-dharma): That relation by which [the property] exists in the indicated object is the "relation that delimits the delimitor of the state of being the indicated" (lakṣyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka-sambandha).
In the *Dīpikā*: "The occurrence of a definition where there is no object to be defined (*alakṣya*) is over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

The meaning of the term *alakṣya* is "that which possesses a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) resides in the object to be defined. [This is the sense] of the locative case [in *alakṣye*].

The referents "That" (tat) and "Thou" (tvam) have been defined. Their connection occurs with the meaning of the word "functioning" (vartana), specifically in its sense of being the locus of inherence (ādheyatva).

It has been stated that over-extension (ativyāpti) consists in the state of having a subsistence (vṛttitva) defined by a difference whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) resides in the object to be indicated (lakṣya).
It occurs as follows: if the possession of horns is stated as the definition of a cow, this definition is flawed by the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*),
[since it would apply to] the cow, which is the definiendum (*lakṣya*).

Because "hornedness" (śṛṅgitva) exists in buffaloes and the like, which possess a difference whose counterpositiveness is determined by that [property]; in this context, one must include the qualification of being delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood (lakṣyatāvacchedakāvacchinnatva) within the counterpositiveness residing in the subject of definition (lakṣyaniṣṭhapratiyogitā).

Otherwise, since even the difference from a white cow could be grasped by the expression "difference whose counter-positive resides in a cow," and since the property of being brown exists in that [white cow] when it is a brown cow, the definition— which is over-extensive regarding non-pervasive properties— would result in over-extension.
In that case,
however, the cow is the indicated object (lakṣya), and cowness (gotva) is the delimitor of the state of being the indicated object (lakṣyatāvacchedaka).
The difference residing in a cow delimited by that [universal], which has as its counter-positive the state of being a non-cow— as established by the cognition "a cow is not"—
is the difference from the universal cowness; a tawny cow does not possess that [difference], but rather [the difference resides] in buffaloes and the like alone.
Since that subsistence does not exist in the state of being Kapila, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Likewise, in the case of subsistence (*vṛttitā*),
it must be specified as being delimited by the relation that serves as the delimiter of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha*).

Otherwise, since the property of being tawny (*kapilatva*) exists even in non-cows such as buffaloes by virtue of the relation of temporal coexistence (*kālika-sambandha*), the aforementioned logical fault would ensue.

Regarding its inclusion [in the definition], the relation by which the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) exists in the object to be defined (lakṣya) is precisely that relation termed the "delimiting relation of the defining characteristic" (lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha); thus, in the present context,
it is inherence (samavāya) alone that possesses such a status.

Since the occurrence of "tawny-ness" (*kapilatva*), as delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) specified by a buffalo (*mahiṣa*) and so forth, is absent there, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case.
Even so, [the definition] remains afflicted by the fault of being impossible (*asambhava*).

Since the property of "having solid hoofs" (ekaśaphavatva) and the like exists in horses— which are distinct from the definiendum (the cow) yet reside in it— the definition would suffer from over-extension (ativyāpti). To avoid this,
the qualification "while being co-locatable with the delimitor of the definiendum" (lakṣyatāvacchedakasamānādhikaraṇatve sati) must also be applied here.
There is no fault, because the property of having a solid hoof (ekaśaphavatva) does not reside in the locus of cowness (gotva), which is the delimitor of the definiendumhood (lakṣyatāvacchedaka).
And thus,

[the definition] is that which is related to the locus of the definiendum by a relation delimited by the delimitor of the definiendumhood, and which is further related to it by a relation delimited by the relation that delimits the definiendumhood.

The over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) consists in being a locus of the delimitor of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka*), while being related by the relation that delimits the definition as determined by the substratum [of the over-pervasion],

and simultaneously being a locus of the delimitor of the definition as determined by a difference residing in the definiendum (*lakṣya*)— which difference has as its counter-positive (*pratiyogitā*) that which is delimited by the delimitor of the state of being a definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
The definition is thus established:
"non-occurrence in the mere definiendum" constitutes the fallacy of impossibility (*asambhava*).
Non-occurrence in every instance of the definiendum is what is meant by impossibility.

It has been stated that "it exists everywhere" because non-occurrence in some instances of the subject occurs even in cases where the property is not pervading. If "having a single hoof" were stated as the definition of a cow, it would not exist in all individual cows;
thus, it would be vitiated by the fault of impossibility (*asambhava*).

What is intended here is an absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by the property of "being a subsistence as determined by the definiendum" (lakṣyanirūpitavṛttitvatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākābhāvaḥ), and not an absence whose counterpositiveness is the subsistence in the definiendum itself (na tu lakṣyavṛttitvapratiyogiko 'bhāvaḥ).
This applies even to properties such as "tawny-ness" (kapilatva) that do not pervade [the definiendum].

Because there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), as the absence of "subsisting in white cows" (which is the definiendum) exists in the definiendum itself— since that absence has "subsisting in the definiendum" as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
However, if that [absence] is intended [as the definition], then "subsisting in cows" does not exist [in the definiendum].

The word "all" (kṛtsna) is used to indicate that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because the absence of the universal of "subsisting-in-a-cow," which is established by common cognition, has as its counter-positive-ness that which is delimited by "the state of being a subsistence in what is defined as the definiendum"; and since this [absence] is absent in the case of Kapila— that is, in the subsistence in a brown cow— there is no over-extension.

The word "only" (*mātra*): likewise, when [the relation] is determined by the definiendum, it must also be specified as being delimited by the relation that serves as the delimitor of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha*). Otherwise, [the definition would be over-extensive].

Since even properties such as "having a solid hoof" (ekaśaphavatva) reside in a cow through the relation of temporal connection (kālika-sambandha), there would be no absence of their residing therein;

consequently, the definition would suffer from the fault of being impossible (asambhava). Therefore, [the required absence] is an absence whose counter-positive-ness is delimited by the property of "residing-ness" (vṛttitvatva) as qualified by the relation that delimits the character of being a definition (lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha) relative to the definiendum (lakṣya).
The result is that [the object] is impossible.
Having intended all of this, the *Prakāśikā* states: "The word *mātra* has the sense of 'entirety' (*kṛtsna*)."

"Specific relation" means the relation that delimits the definition (lakṣaṇatāvacchedakasambandha). "The general absence of existence in the locus of the definiendum" (lakṣyavṛttitvasāmānyābhāva) [is the meaning].
The meaning is: an absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by the property of being the state of occurring in non-lakṣyas.

[Objection: But surely, since the state of having a single hoof is afflicted by impossibility (as it does not occur in non-lakṣyas such as horses), the defect known as over-extension (ativyāpti) is also present.
He raises an objection, stating that "the commingling of multiple defects would result in one place," with the words beginning "And not here" (*na cātra*).
This objection is intended with reference to the definition of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) as it stands literally;
for [the definition] is qualified by the condition "while being co-locative with the delimitor of the definiendum" (*lakṣyatāvacchedakasamānādhikaraṇatve sati*).
Because the nature of the over-extension (ativyāpti) previously described is absent in the case of having a single hoof;
for there must be a distinction among the defects according to the difference in the faulty cases— this is the intention of the objector.
He provides the resolution: "Even in the case of a corrupt mixture.
The meaning is that even if the corrupt [element] is one, it does not follow that the fault is one.

The intention of the respondent is that, because multiple defects can coexist in a single locus, the distinction between the defects does not entail a distinction between the defective loci that serve as their substrata; for it is said:
"Even when there is a confusion of the things to be qualified (the substrata), there is no confusion of the qualifiers (the defects)."
This is precisely the meaning of the Maṇikāra’s statement as well:
the *Dīpikā* is an investigation into the definition of definitions.
A characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is a property that is free from these three defects;
for example, the possession of a dewlap and so forth in the case of a cow.
That very same thing is called the "uncommon property" (*asādhāraṇadharma*).

Uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*) consists in being co-extensive with the delimiting factor of the object of definition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). If a definition were merely that which distinguishes [the object], there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such things as "being denotable" (*abhidheyatva*), which also serve to distinguish [the object] from others; therefore, to exclude these, the condition of being "different from that" (*tadbhinnatva*) is added.
The qualification of the property (dharma) must be stated;
however, it need not be stated if both the definition and the purpose pertain to the conventional usage (vyavahāra),
because exclusion (vyāvṛtti) also serves as a means for establishing conventional usage.
The *Prakāśikā* states that [the definition] is free from these three defects; that is,
it is characterized by the absence of the three aforementioned defects.

This is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Is it not a settled principle that a definition (lakṣaṇa) is an uncommon property (asādhāraṇadharma)? Therefore, for what reason is a property devoid of the three defects said to be a definition? To this, he says: "That very [property]... and so on, concluding with "...is so called."

The word "by those who are proficient" (*abhiyuktaiḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Now, since being common (*sādhāraṇya*) consists in occurring in both the similar and dissimilar instances, its opposite—uncommonness (*asādhāraṇya*)—exists even in a property that is afflicted by defects such as under-extension (*avyāpti*); how then [can it serve as a definition]?

Desiring to dispel the doubt that a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) might simply be one devoid of the three defects, he defines uniqueness in a different way—as "being co-extensive with the delimiting factor of the object to be defined" (*lakṣyatāvacchedakasamaniyatatva*). This means:
while being a pervader of the delimiting factor of the object to be defined...
The meaning is "the state of being pervaded by the delimiting condition of the locus" (*lakṣyatāvacchedakavyāpyatva*).

The term "existent" (*sat*) is included to exclude those [definitions] that are afflicted by under-extension (*avyāpti*) or impossibility (*asambhava*). The qualifying term (*viśeṣya*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

The meaning is that the *dharmapada* (the word expressing the property) serves as an indicator of the intended sense— such as pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*)— by means of the relation that constitutes its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatāghaṭakasambandha*).
Here, this should be understood:
These defects are the subverters of the property of being uncommon (asādhāraṇatva),

because in the case of over-extension (ativyāpti) there is a failure of the property of being pervaded (vyāpyatva), and in the other two cases, a failure of the property of being the pervader (vyāpakatva).

The seed of their fallaciousness, according to each respective definition, is as follows: in the case of proving the difference from others, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) due to over-extension (*ativyāpti*);
and in the case of the other two, there are the fallacies of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*) and essential unestablishedness (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Now, one might object:

Regarding the objection that if "being co-extensive with the delimitor of the locus of definition" (*lakṣyatāvacchedakasamaniyatatva*) is the definition of a definition (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇa*), then since— according to the view that the sole purpose of a definition is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)— only that which effects exclusion would be the object of the definition of a definition,
there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to exclusion and the like; he refutes this objection in accordance with that very view:
"Of that which is indeed a differentiator" means: of that which alone generates an inference whose probandum is the difference from others;
that is, [of that which] generates an inference having the difference from others as its predicate (vidheya).
This means: "only that which is the substratum of a specific objective determination (viṣayatā) delimited by that [definition]. By this, the conventional (vyāvahārika) is excluded.

Regarding the state of being a definition (*lakṣaṇatva*)—such as the definition of a cow and so forth—it means the state of being the definiendum (*lakṣyatva*) according to the definition of a definition stated above.
Even if the reading is *lakṣyatve*, this same meaning is to be understood.
Regarding the phrase *vyāvṛttau*:

it refers to the state of being co-extensive (*samanaiyatyam*) with the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), such as "cowness" (*gotva*), in the case of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from what is other than cows and so forth.

The meaning is that, because properties such as "being denotable" (*abhidheyatva*) and "being cognizable" (*prameyatva*) are co-extensive with "being a category" (*padārthatva*), one must include "being distinct from exclusion" (*vyāvṛttibhinnatva*) and "being distinct from being denotable, etc. (*abhidheyatvādibhinnatva*) in the definition of a definition (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇa*) in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Although it might seem inappropriate to mention exclusion separately— since all things can be subsumed under that very form of "conventional reality" (vyāvahārikatva), as will be explained later regarding the conventional nature of exclusion itself— nevertheless:

If the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) were identical, then at the time of the ascertainment of the possession of the reason (*hetumattāniścaya*), the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*)— which consists in doubt regarding the probandum— would be absent; consequently, that inference would not occur.

According to the view of the ancients, since the difference from others lacks the quality of being a differentiator (*vyāvartakatva*), there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case. However, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—which holds that "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*) is the absence of proof qualified by the absence of the desire to prove—the difference itself is indeed a differentiator; therefore, as it is the very object to be defined (*lakṣya*), [the definition applies] therein.
It should be understood that the separate statement is intended to show that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), since the application of the definition is accepted [in those cases].
Now, what indeed is this?

The delimitor of the state of being the characterized (lakṣya) for the definition of the definition (lakṣaṇalakṣaṇa) is the quality of being a differentiator. It is not, first of all, the quality of being an inferential indicator of difference in general.

Furthermore, since even properties such as "being denotable by exclusion" (vyāvṛttyabhidheyatva) imply a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by some instance of "duality" (ubhayatva), it would be inconsistent to state that there is an over-extension (ativyāpti) in those cases.

Furthermore, for all properties that are distinct [from the subject], since they would exclude only some [of the instances], there would follow the futility of properties such as pervasiveness (vyāpakatva) which constitute the definition of the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) fallacy.

Nor does it possess the capacity to specifically infer the exclusion of others as delimited by this or that particular property; for if that were the case, then the possession of a dewlap and so forth— which infers the exclusion of others as delimited by cowness— [would likewise have to be the probans].

Since the definition must be stated specifically for each individual case in the manner that "the state of being invariably concomitant with cowness (*gotva*) is the definition," there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*ativyāpti*); for the state of being invariably concomitant with those respective properties— which serve as the delimiters of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) such as cowness— is present in the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) consisting of the difference from others not delimited by cowness.

If it is argued that even if [the definition] were possible, it would result in the fallacies of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and non-occurrence (*alagnakatā*) in respect to "denotability" (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth— since the co-presence (*samanaiyatyam*) with "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like does not exist there—
that is not so; for:

Taking "the possession of a dewlap and so forth" as the subject (*pakṣa*), when the probandum (*sādhya*) is the inference of the difference from everything other than that which is delimited by "cowness," one proceeds by way of a general pervasion (*sāmānyamukha-vyāpti*)—

since a positive instance (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*) is unavailable for the specific pervasion— according to the principle: "Whatever is co-extensive with a particular property is the differentiator of that which is delimited by it."

Since pervasion must be admitted, there exists— either in that [subject] or in something similar to it— the reason under discussion, which consists in the necessary concomitance (*samanaiyatyam*) with those respective properties, or another reason of the same kind, because of the presence therein of both "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) and "denotability" (*abhidheyatva*), which cannot be excluded from the subject due to the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or lack of proof (*aprasiddhi*).
There would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the non-existence of the subject under discussion (*prakṛta-sādhya*) or a similar subject;
therefore, in order to avoid that fault,

[the definition] must be distinct from the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) consisting of the difference from others as delimited by those respective properties (*tattaddharmāvacchinnetarabheda*), and distinct from [the property of] being nameable (*abhidheyatva*), and so forth.
And since this treatise intends that [the definition] should be applied to such a characteristic, there is no occasion for the previously mentioned fault; however,
further investigation should be pursued elsewhere.
But is it not the case that practical usage is also a purpose of a definition?
For without the knowledge of the object to be designated in its specific form, there can be no such usage.

Because it is impossible for there to be linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) consisting of words that convey [an object] as delimited by that [nature], and because even a conventionally defined (*vyāvahārika*) definition is itself something to be defined, the qualification "being different from that" need not be supplied; thus he says: "and also of linguistic usage."
Is it not the case that, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), its being distinct from that [the object] is necessary?
[This is said] because of the delusion that exclusion lacks conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*).
He refutes [the objection] with the words "even of exclusion" (*vyāvṛtterapi*).
By the word "even" (*api*), [terms such as] "denotability" (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth are included for the sake of obtaining an illustrative example.
Bālapriyā:

Is it not the case that "a property devoid of these three defects" means a property characterized by the absence of the three defects consisting of under-extension (avyāpti), over-extension (ativyāpti), and impossibility (asambhava)?
The meaning is "the definition. Thus,

having raised the objection that even in cases such as being tawny (*kapila*), which possesses only one defect, the three defects are not present— and therefore it would follow that this [single defect] is a valid definition— he explains as follows:

The phrase "qualified by the three absences of the aforementioned defects" means that the number three is not intended to apply to the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), but rather to the absences themselves; this is the sense.

It should be understood that even when there is the presence of two absences of defects— namely, the absence of the other defects while one defect exists— the three absences of defects are not present; thus, the aforementioned logical consequence does not apply.
1. "Even when possessing a single defect" means even when characterized by a single defect in the form of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*). 2. "The consequence of becoming a definition" (*lakṣaṇatvāpatti*).
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [properties such as] "being a cow" being the definition of a cow.
3. "The aforementioned consequence" means that there would be the consequence of [properties such as] "being a Kapila" being the definition of a cow.
But surely, since "asādhāraṇa" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "not common," the word "asādhāraṇa" has the sense of "different from the common."
And the meaning of "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) is: that which, while occurring in the subject (*lakṣya*), also occurs in what is not the subject (*alakṣya*);
that is, that which possesses the property of occurring in the non-subject while being qualified by the property of occurring in the subject.
Up to this point: the meaning of "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) is that which possesses the absence of occurrence in non-lakṣyas, qualified by occurrence in the lakṣya.
[This applies] when [the definition] is afflicted by under-extension (*avyāpti*).

In the case of being tawny (*kapilatva*) and so forth, there exists an absence of the qualified (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) due to the absence of the qualificand, namely, the property of residing in the non-definendum (*alakṣyavṛttitva*).

Being one-hoofed (*ekaśaphavattva*) and so forth is seized by impossibility (*asambhavagrasta*), as it possesses the absence of the qualified due to the absence of the qualifier, namely, the property of residing in the definendum (*lakṣyavṛttitva*).
Furthermore, one might object that both [the presence and absence of defects] would then result in being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) characteristics,
and that it would be inconsistent to claim that only that which is free from the three defects is "uncommon," since even that which possesses defects is uncommon.
Anticipating this, the meaning of the term *asādhāraṇa* is [as follows]:

It is stated in another way in the *Dīpikā*, as he says: "Now, regarding 'commonality' (*sādhāraṇya*)," and "of a different kind," because it lacks the absence of occurrence in non-exemplars qualified by occurrence in exemplars.
The meaning is "of any other kind.
Regarding the phrase "while being a pervader of the delimitor of the state of being the definiendum" (*lakṣyatāvacchedakavyāpakatve sati*): the *lakṣyatāvacchedaka*...

Wherever it exists, its existence in all those places constitutes pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) of the delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). Its non-existence wherever the delimiting factor of the definiendum does not exist constitutes subservience (*vyāpyatva*) to the delimiting factor of the definiendum.
The cow is the object to be defined (*lakṣya*); the delimitor of the state of being the object to be defined (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is "cowness" (*gotva*).
In this regard, wherever it exists—in every individual cow—it is accompanied by the possession of a dewlap and so forth; such is cowness.
Since the possession of a dewlap and so forth does not exist where a buffalo and the like do not exist,

and because it is pervaded by the delimitor of the definiendum while being itself pervaded by that delimitor of the definiendum, the possession of a dewlap and so forth is an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*).
It exists; therefore, the intention is that this is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of a cow.

Thus, it is stated that the definition of a definition is: being pervaded by the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), while simultaneously being co-extensive with the delimitor of the definiendum.
He states the purpose of its inclusion: "for the sake of excluding [theories] that are afflicted by under-extension (*avyāpti*) or impossibility (*asambhava*).
Regarding Kapila’s doctrine, which is afflicted by under-extension:

In a case where the definition is distinct from the definiendum—such as a buffalo, which lacks "cowness" (gotva) as the delimitor of the definiendum—the definition possesses the property of being pervaded by the delimitor of the definiendum, namely, the state of not occurring in non-cows.
Consequently, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition's own definition in that case;
therefore, the phrase "while being a pervader of the delimitor of the definiendum" was stated [as a necessary condition]. This applies to that which possesses cowness.

Because the state of being a white cow or a pilu tree is absent [in those cases], the property of being a pervader of the delimitant of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedakavyāpakatva) does not exist there;
thus, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).
Now, according to the aforementioned method...

Even though a purpose consisting in the exclusion of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) may be possible when [a definition] is afflicted by under-extension (*avyāpti*), a purpose consisting in the exclusion of that [over-extension] is not possible when it is afflicted by impossibility (*asambhava*).
This is the case with such [definitions] as "having a single hoof" (*ekaśaphavattva*), which are afflicted by impossibility.

If it is argued that there is no possibility of over-extension (ativyāpti) because the property of being pervaded by the delimitor of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedaka-vyāpyatva) is absent— since [the property] resides in horses which are devoid of cowness (gotva), the delimitor of the definiendum—
then here they say: in this context, the term "seized by impossibility" (asambhavagrasta) refers to the sky (gagana), which is seized by impossibility, as the intended meaning.

If it is said that "the sky" is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) intended to indicate a cow, that is impossible; for since the sky is a non-occurrent entity (*avṛttipadārtha*), it does not exist anywhere in a cow.
Thus, the sky is seized by the fault of impossibility (*asambhava*).

Since it is precisely because [the term] does not denote non-occurrent entities that it also possesses the property of not occurring in non-cows such as buffaloes— which are devoid of "cowness" (gotva), the delimitor of the definiendum—
if one were to state merely that [the definition] is pervaded by the delimitor of the definiendum, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case.
To exclude that [over-extension], it is stated: "while being a pervader of the delimiting property of the definiendum" (*lakṣyatāvacchedakavyāpakatve sati*).
To exclude over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*), the qualifier (*viśeṣya*) is provided.

In the absence of the qualifying element consisting of "being pervaded by the delimitor of the definiendum-ness," the definition of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇa*) would be "pervasion of the delimitor of the definiendum-ness. If that were the case, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the instance of that which is defective.

In order to indicate this existing distinction between exclusion (vyāvṛtti) and denotability (abhidheyatva), [the author],
instead of saying "there is over-extension in conventional exclusion," says "in exclusion, [such as] denotability, etc."
"It is stated in the *Dīpikā* that [the definition] suffers from over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Now, as for the question "What is this? and so forth: the meaning of this section is as follows—that the definition must indeed exclude [what is not the object].
Since it was stated previously that a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which is co-extensive (*samaniyata*) with the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*),
it follows that "exclusionary character" (*vyāvartakatva*) is the delimitor of the definiendum for the definition of a definition. In this regard, what indeed is this exclusionary character?
To begin with, there is no capacity to generate an inference having difference as its predicate by way of the form of a universal,
because [the property] "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), "denotability," and so forth would also [be such].

Because it would result in the definition being over-extended (*ativyāpti*) there—since [the universal "cowness"] would become the definiendum by virtue of being a differentiator that generates an inferential cognition of difference—the statement [of such an over-extension] would be inconsistent.
[For example: "A cow is distinct from both a cow and a pot."
Because of its difference from non-cows,
the object [of the word "cow"] is distinct from both the pot and the cloth, because it is denotable; thus,
[the reason possesses] the property of being a generator of an inference whose probandum is the difference from some pair whatsoever that is subsumed under the category of "difference."
Because [the property of] being denotable by exclusion (vyāvṛtti) and so forth also exists [in the subject];
furthermore, because all properties that are absolute absences (atyantābhāva) possess counter-correlates (pratiyogin).

Because they indicate some form of difference, even properties such as "tawny-ness" (kapilatva), which are themselves subject to the flaw of being over-pervasive (avyāpti), function as differentiators by generating an inference where the predicate is difference— such as "a tawny cow is distinct from a white cow because it is tawny"— and thus they are to be considered objects of definition (lakṣya).

2. In that case, since there is no possibility of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), [the definition] serves to exclude that— [referring to] "of the negative-only (*vyatirekin*) [inferences]" such as "this is different from a cloth,
because it possesses potness" (*ghaṭatva*), and so forth.
The intended meaning is that [existence] is an inferential mark for difference because it brings about the inference of difference.
Furthermore, even in the case of purely positive (kevalānvayin) properties,
with respect to whatever difference one wishes to establish, existence serves as the inferential mark for that difference.

With the intention that it might even be possible to say "it does not exist," the term "of the negative instances" (*vyatirekiṇām*) was stated. Thus, the meaning is that since qualities such as being tawny (*kapilatva*) are also negative instances, they ought to be capable of inferring a distinction. 2.
Regarding the phrase "by way of over-extension and non-application":
over-extension (*ativyāpti*) consists in the presence of a definition in that which is not the subject of the definition (*alakṣya*), but not in the subject of the definition (*lakṣya*).
This is the intended meaning.
[The point is that] the qualifier "pervasion" (vyāpakatva), which constitutes the element of necessary concomitance (samanaiyatyam),
is over-extensive (ativyāpta).

Because [the definition] would over-apply to "hornsiness" (śṛṅgitva) and the like— since these generate an inference of some arbitrary difference, such as "a cow is different from a jar because it has horns"— and since they are thus included within the scope of the definition (lakṣya), there would be no possibility of over-extension (ativyāpti) in those cases; consequently, the qualification "pervadedness" (vyāpyatva), intended to exclude them, would be rendered redundant.
And it is not by taking up the differences individually as the difference from what is delimited by each respective property that serves as the delimitor of the locus of those various definitions.

In this context, what is intended by "differentiating" (vyāvartakatva) is precisely the capacity to produce an inference whose subject is that which is qualified by it and whose object is the exclusion [of others].
This is because the difference from both [the cow and the non-cow] lacks the nature of being a difference from everything other than that which is delimited by cowness (gotva).

By taking as the basis the capacity to produce an inference whose object is that [property], there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the status of being a differentiator (*vyāvartakatva*) to such things as "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), "denotability" (*abhidheyatva*), and so forth,
nor to "tawny-ness" (*kapilatva*) and the like.

It does not possess the property of being a generator of an inference whose subject is delimited by cowness (*gotva*) and whose predicate is the exclusion of what is other than what is delimited by cowness; for in the inference "a cow is distinct from non-cows because it is brown," there is the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*).
It should not be argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the inference "A cow is distinct from non-cows because it possesses horns"; for if that were the case,

then the possession of a dewlap (*sāsnādimattva*), which generates the inferential cognition of the difference of [the subject] from others as delimited by cowness (*gotvāvacchinnetarabheda*), [would likewise be subject to such deviation].
Since the definition must be stated specifically for each individual definition as "the state of being invariably concomitant with cowness" (*gotvasamaniyatatva*),

there is the possibility of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) consisting of the difference from non-cows; for this is because the state of being invariably concomitant with cowness— which is itself the definition consisting in the possession of a dewlap and so forth— is present therein.
Because there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) or impossibility (*asambhava*) regarding the property of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth;
for [the reason] "being denotable" exists in buffaloes and the like, which are devoid of cowness (*gotva*).

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: since there is an absence of the property of being co-extensive with "cowness" (*gotva-samaniyatatva*), due to the absence of the state of being pervaded by "cowness"— which consists in not occurring in what is empty of "cowness"— therefore, the statement regarding the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to such properties as "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*) is inconsistent.
1. There is no consequence of [the definition] becoming a differentiator; for when specified [as such], "a non-cow is that which is distinct from what is other than a cow."
The formulation of the inference should be stated as: "The referent of a word is distinct from what is other than itself, because it is denotable.
In that case, regarding the first [formulation], there is an identity between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*).
Such an inference does not occur;
in the second case, since that which is other than the word-meanings is unestablished,
such an inference is impossible.
Therefore, because [the property] such as being denotable by exclusion (vyāvṛttyabhidheyatva) lacks the capacity for exclusion, it does not follow that it would become an excluder;
thus, it is appropriate to state that there is over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case due to its not being a subject of definition (alakṣya).
Thus, the intention of the speaker is that "exclusion" (*vyāvartakatva*) consists in being the inferential indicator of a specific difference.

[The phrase] "it does not exist" is used; and so, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) therein due to its not being the subject of the definition (*alakṣyatayā*), [the qualification is added].
The intended meaning is that the components such as "being a constituent of the same certainty" (*samanaiyatyaghaṭaka*) and "pervasion" (*vyāpakatva*) serve a purposeful function.
As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): just as the difference from others (*itarabheda*) in the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) is inferred by means of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), so too...
The delimiting property of the subject (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is also inferred;

for example, in the inference "The jar is earth because it possesses odor," the nature of being earth (*pṛthivītva*) [is inferred] in the jar by means of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of possessing odor.

The delimitor of the object of indication (lakṣyatāvacchedaka) is inferred. In the present case, "possessing a dewlap and so forth" is the object of indication, while "being co-extensive with cowness" is the definition (lakṣaṇa).

The defining characteristic (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is the state of being a differentiator (*vyāvartakatva*), which consists in the capacity to infer the exclusion of others not delimited by "cowness" (*gotva*);
it is in that very form that the possession of a dewlap and so forth [serves as the definition].

Because it is that which is characterized by the definition of definitions; and thus, having taken "the possession of a dewlap and so forth" as the subject (*pakṣa*), [it is established] therein by way of its co-extensiveness with "cowness" (*gotva*).
The point to be proven is that the possession of a dewlap and so forth is an inferential indicator of the exclusion of what is other than a cow, because it is co-extensive with cowness;
that is: "The possession of a dewlap and so forth is an inferential indicator of the exclusion of what is other than a cow, because it is co-extensive with cowness."

Furthermore, in that inference, it is impossible to state a specific pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form "wherever there is co-extensiveness with cowness, there is the capacity to infer the difference from non-cows," because the probandum and the reason reside only in the subject (*pakṣa*), and thus there is no example (*dṛṣṭānta*) distinct from the subject.
Due to scarcity [of examples].

Therefore, in general form: wherever there is the state of being invariably concomitant with a given property (dharmasamaniyatatva), there is the capacity to generate an inference of the exclusion of others not delimited by that property (taddharmāvacchinnetarabhedānumitijanakatva).
The pervasion (vyāpti) must be stated:

the possession of odor (gandhavattva), which is co-extensive with earthness (pṛthivītva) and which leads to the inference of the difference from that which is other than what is delimited by earthness, serves as the example (dṛṣṭānta).
Furthermore, in the case of a universal-positive pervasion (*sāmānyamukhavyāpti*), if the reason under discussion— or a reason equivalent to the reason under discussion—

is present, while the probandum under discussion— or a probandum equivalent to the probandum under discussion— is absent, this constitutes the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). And thus, in the case of [the exclusion] consisting of the differentiation from non-cowhood...
There is no capacity to produce an inference of the exclusion of non-cows, because, due to the identity of the probandum and the reason,
there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) according to the manner previously stated. And thus:

The probandum (sādhya), which consists in being the inferential indicator of the exclusion of others delimited by "cowness" (gotva), is absent there; yet the reason (hetu), which consists in being co-extensive with "cowness," is present. Thus, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra).
In the case of "nameability" (abhidheyatva) and so forth, [there is] a property co-extensive with "being an object" (padārthatva), which is equivalent to the reason under discussion.

There is a reason; likewise, the delimiting factor of the object of definition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is also inferred as being equivalent to the subject of the thesis under discussion (*prakṛtasādhya*).

In the *Prakāśikā*, how is it consistent to take "the possession of a dewlap and so forth" as the subject (*pakṣa*) and establish the probandum (*sādhya*) as its being the inferential indicator of the difference from others as delimited by cowness (*gotvāvacchinnetarabheda*)?

This was stated with the following doubt in mind: that by means of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), the difference from others is established, but not the status of being an inferential mark (*anumāpaka*) for that difference from others.
Alternatively, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is as follows:

It must indeed be explained that, by means of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), the exclusion of others (*itarabheda*)— that is, the difference from whatever is not delimited by the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*)—
is to be established in the definiendum (*lakṣya*). In the present case, this concerns the definition of "definition" itself, which consists in being co-extensive with "cowness" (*gotva*).
The delimitor of the locus (lakṣyatāvacchedaka) is the capacity to infer the difference from what is delimited by "cowness" (gotva).

That difference from others delimited by that [cowness] is to be established in the subject characterized by the dewlap and so forth (sāsnādimattva), using as the reason its being co-extensive with cowness.

And the exclusion of others delimited by that [the cow] is the exclusion of what is different from that which causes the inference of the exclusion of non-cows; this results in [the cow's] being the cause of the inference of the exclusion of non-cows—
this is the intention [expressed] in the *Prakāśikā*.
It has been stated that the probandum (*sādhya*) consists in being the inferential indicator of the exclusion of others qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*).
[Otherwise], since there is no such probandum in the form of being the inferential indicator of the exclusion of others qualified by "being a category" (*padārthatva*),
because "other than a category" (*padārthetara*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
To exclude that [fallacy],

the qualification "being different from exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti-bhinnatve sati*) and "being different from 'nameability' (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth" must be added to the reason, which consists in the state of being co-extensive with the property in question (*taddharma-samaniyatatva*). By means of that, where—

The intended meaning is that the universal form of pervasion (sāmānyamukhī vyāpti) results as follows: given that there is a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and a difference in being denotable (*abhidheyatva*), whatever constitutes the state of being co-extensive with a certain property, in that case there arises the capacity to generate an inference of the difference from what is other than that which is delimited by that property; and in this regard, there is no defect whatsoever.
Regarding the word "of the Dīpikā text": now, the meaning of the lines is stated in succession.

It cannot be said that "being a differentiator" consists in being the cause of an inference whose predicate is mere difference (*bheda*) in general— without specifying a particular counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)— by introducing difference as such.
The meaning is that it is possible [to prove].

This applies even to such properties as being denotable by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-abhidheyatva*) and so forth; for instance: "A cow is distinct from both a cow and a jar, because it is different from what is other than a cow."
In the intended inference, "A category (padārtha) is distinct from both a pot and a cloth, because it is nameable," there would be no logical consistency in stating an over-extension (ativyāpti).
The intended meaning is that the presence of the definition in the locus is accepted.
Regarding the phrase "of negative properties":
this refers to purely positive properties such as "being denotable" (abhidheyatva) and so forth.

The capacity to infer difference from others is not possible, because there is no "other" that is devoid of nameability; thus, even the inference "the pot is different from others, because it is nameable" [is untenable].

The meaning is that it cannot be employed because anything other than the word-meaning itself is simply not established. [The term] "asādhāraṇyaghaṭaka" means "that which constitutes the factor of uniqueness."

The meaning is that there would follow the consequence of the uselessness (*vaiyarthyaprasaṅga*) of both the pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) and the pervaded-ness (*vyāpyatva*) which constitute the "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*) defined as being co-extensive with the delimiting property of the subject (*lakṣyatāvacchedakasamaniyatatva*).
Nor [can it be said] "by way of qualification" (*viśiṣya*).

The word "viśiṣya" (distinguishingly) is construed with "bhede" (in the difference). Here, having supplied the phrase "in that which is delimited by the delimitor of the definiendum, such as cowness (*gotva*) and so forth," [the meaning is]:

"the state of being a generator of an inference in which the distinction from what is other than that which is delimited by cowness and so forth is the probandum (*vidheya*), while that which is delimited by cowness and so forth is the subject (*uddeśya*)."
This must be explained;

otherwise, since the inference "a brown cow is distinct from non-cows because it is brown" would be possible, the aforementioned defect would exist, and it would be untenable for this to be a different alternative.
"It should be included within such a definition" means that it should be included within the reason (hetu) which consists of such a definition.
Now, as for the objection beginning with "Is not the purpose of a definition also linguistic usage? and so forth:
just as the purpose of a definition is the inference of the object's difference from others, [so too is linguistic usage].
Likewise, linguistic usage in the form of the employment of words is also a purpose [of the definition].
If one asks how, it is as follows:
with respect to the individual cow standing before one, [one thinks] "this is a cow."

With respect to the employment of a word that denotes [an object] as delimited by the universal *gotva* (cowness) in the form "this is a cow," the cause is a cognition that has *gotva* as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and the cow as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
This applies with respect to the linguistic usage consisting in the employment of a word that brings about a cognition delimited by that property (*taddharma*).

Because a cognition having that property as its qualifier and the object of practical activity (*vyavahartavya*) as its qualificand is the cause [of such activity], and because a cognition in the form "this is a cow" is not possible without a cognition of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) that delimits cowness,
the definition [serves] by means of a cognition whose object is the object of practical activity produced by the cognition of itself.
The purpose is practical application (*vyavahāra*). Thus, since a definition can also be practical (*vyāvahārika*),
the definition of a practical definition is that it must be co-extensive with the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka-samaniyatatva*).

The point is that even conventional objects are the "defined" (lakṣya), since properties such as being excluded from others (vyāvṛtti) and being denotable (abhidheyatva) are also among those defined; because it is accepted that the definition exists in those cases, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti), and thus the qualification "being different from that [definition]" need not be provided.
"Knowledge of that which is to be designated by that form" means knowledge having that property as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and that which is to be designated as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
It is knowledge having "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth as its qualifier and "cow" (*go*) and so forth as its qualificand.
Up to:
"even of a conventional characteristic"—
that is, even of a characteristic consisting in such forms as exclusion, denotability, and so forth, which serve the purpose of conventional usage.
Because it is the object of definition— that is, because it is the object of definition by means of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—
it is distinct from that [characteristic].
"Differentiation from denotability and so forth" means that it is distinct [from those].
"In order to obtain an example" means that just as denotability and the like produce linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), so too does exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) produce linguistic usage.
The meaning is that this is for the sake of making it known.
The Lamp:
An Establishment of the Possession of Qualities as the Definition of Substance.
Is it not the case that possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*) is not the definition of a substance (*dravya*),
because it fails to apply (*avyāpti*) to a substance delimited by its first moment and to a substance that has been produced and then immediately destroyed?
If it is argued: "No, because what is intended is the possession of a genus that is distinct from existence (*sattā*) and co-locus with quality (*guṇa*).
If it is further objected: "Even so, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to color and the like, because of the conventional usage: 'One color is distinct from taste.'"
No; for since such conventional usage is established by the very fact of inherence in the same object, one does not admit a quality in a quality.
[The *Prakāśikā* says: "But surely..."
Even though the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) is absent in a substance delimited by its first moment, its presence in that same substance as delimited by another time remains unimpaired.
And thus, the definition [of substance] as "that which is the substratum of qualities" is valid; to this, he says:
Regarding the term "arisen and destroyed":

it refers to a substance for which, in the third moment following the production of the action that generates the conjunction initiating its composition, an action has arisen in another part that destroys such a conjunction. Such a substance—

This is the meaning. The moderns, however, relying on the causal efficiency of a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) through its coexistence with the effect, do not accept [the category of] "perished upon arising" (*utpannavinaṣṭa*).
The qualifier "co-locating with quality" (*guṇasamānādhikaraṇa*) is applied to the genus (*jāti*) in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to qualities and so forth.
The term "distinct from existence" (*sattābhinnā*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by taking "existence" (*sattā*) itself as the locus.
The term "universal" (*jāti*) is used to exclude over-extension by taking "the state of being either substance or quality" (*dravyaguṇānyataratva*) as the locus.
[This is] by way of inherence (*samavāyena*).
The intention is that this serves as a grasper of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) regarding the possession of such a property;
therefore, the sense is that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by taking possession [of the property] through relations such as temporal connection (*kālika-sambandha*).

"Even so" means: even though the charge of under-extension (*avyāpti*) has been avoided by the intended meaning already stated, [the reason remains] "only because of inherence in a single object" (*ekārthasamavāyāt*), that is,
by way of inherence (*samavāyena*) in one and the same object.
The meaning is "precisely because of existence.
[This is] because qualities are not admitted;
and thus, by what has been established...

The point is this: since the conventional usage of "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattā*) can be accounted for simply through a co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) mediated by inherence (*samavāya*), it is not possible to postulate an unestablished "possession of qualities" in that [substratum], because such a postulation would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). *Bālapriyā*.
It was stated previously that the definition of substance (*dravya*) is either the possession of the genus "substance-ness" (*dravyatvajāti*) or the possession of qualities (*guṇavat*).
Among these, the possession of qualities is not the [correct] definition.

This cannot be so, because there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) due to the absence of possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) in a jar delimited by its moment of origination, according to the principle: "A substance that has just arisen remains for a moment without qualities and without action."

Thus, in the case of a jar that has arisen in the first moment and perished in the second moment, there is no quality [in it] during the first moment, according to the principle: "A substance that has just arisen is for one moment devoid of qualities."
Furthermore, since the substratum—the jar—is destroyed in the second moment, the quality [no longer exists];
thus, there is the objection raised in the *Dīpikā*: "But surely, [the definition] would lack pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a jar that has been produced and then destroyed."
By the statement beginning with "Possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*) is not the definition of substance (*dravya*)," etc.,
he states the reason for pursuing the second position there: "But [is it not the case that] substance [exists] as delimited by the first moment?"
"Delimited by another time" means delimited by the second moment and so forth. In that context,
"the existence of that" refers to the existence of substance and quality.
"Being the locus of qualities" means being the substratum of qualities; [it refers to] a quality by way of inherence (*samavāya*).

The point is that although there is over-extension (*avyāpti*) when "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) is stated alone, there is no over-extension when "the state of being the substratum of qualities" (*guṇāśrayatva*) is stated.
"Of the same kind as the substance-initiator," and so forth:
[there is] action; from action, disjunction; from disjunction, the destruction of the prior spatial conjunction.
Then there is conjunction with the northern direction, and then the production of the substance; such is the sequence.
Herein, there is both disjunction and conjunction of the parts.
And regarding the eastern and northern locations:

that conjunction with the northern location which arises in the fourth moment is the producer of the jar; the action that produces it arises in the first moment, and its third moment [is the one under consideration].

At the moment of the destruction of the conjunction with the eastern region, if an action arises that produces the destruction of the originating conjunction, then the substance undergoes destruction in the moment immediately following its production;
and such is the sequence.
In the first moment, the action that produces the jar; in the second moment, disjunction;
in the third moment—
In the third moment, there is the destruction of the conjunction with the previous location and the action that causes the destruction of the conjunction with the subsequent location;
in the fourth moment,
there is the conjunction with the subsequent location and disjunction.
In the fifth moment, there is the production of the jar and its conjunction with the preceding location;
in the sixth moment, there is the destruction of the jar and its conjunction with the succeeding location.
This is the state of affairs.
"But the new [theorists]," however,
[hold that] according to this view, in the very fourth moment, the jar also [is destroyed] by means of its conjunction with a subsequent location.

It arises together with its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Furthermore, since the destruction of the jar occurs at the very third moment [after its production], there is no destruction of the jar during the second moment of its production; therefore, a jar that is produced and then immediately destroyed is not established by valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇika*).
Such is the meaning.
In the *Dīpikā*, it says:
"co-extensive with quality (*guṇa*)."

The definition of substance (*dravya*) is the possession of that *jāti* (universal) which is co-located with qualities (*guṇa*), resides in the locus of qualities, and is distinct from *sattā* (existence). For there exists such a *jāti* in the form of "substanceness" (*dravyatva*).

If it is argued that "possessing qualities" applies to substance by taking as the basis the existence of qualities in earth and other substances— which are substrata of qualities— and which is distinct from "Being" (sattā),
[we reply: even though qualities are absent in a jar delimited by its first moment of existence and in a jar that has perished immediately after arising, [the definition still holds].

There is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti), because the genus "substance-ness" (dravyatva-jāti) exists in the same locus as that [quality]. If the qualification "co-locating with a quality" were not applied to the genus,

there would be over-pervasion (ativyāpti) in respect to a quality, since the property of possessing the genus "quality-ness" (guṇatva-jāti)— which is distinct from existence (sattā)— exists in a quality.

However, when the qualification "co-inherent with qualities" (*guṇasamānādhikaraṇa*) is employed, since a quality is not admitted to possess further qualities, that which is the substratum of a quality is not a quality itself,
but rather substance alone; thus, the property of residing therein does not exist in the category of quality (*guṇatva*), and for this reason, the word "universal" (*jāti*) is used.

There is no over-extension [of the definition] because it is impossible to apprehend "being a quality" [in a quality]. However, there would be over-extension because the genus "existence" (sattājāti), which resides in substances that are substrata of qualities, also exists in a quality.

To exclude that [over-extension], the qualification "non-different from existence" (*sattābhinnā*) is applied to the genus (*jāti*); in place of the word "genus," the word "property" (*dharma*) may be used.

If it is stated that the definition of substance (*dravya*) is "the possession of a property that is distinct from existence (*sattā*) and co-locates with qualities (*guṇa*)," then the property consisting of being either a substance or a quality (*dravyaguṇānyataratva*) would also reside in a substance, which is the locus of qualities.
Furthermore, because "possessing that" (tadvattva) exists in quality (guṇa) as well— since it is non-different from existence (sattā)— there would be over-extension (ativyāpti).
To exclude that,
the word "universal" (jāti) was stated.
However, being one or the other (*anyataratva*) is not a genus (*jāti*).

[Objection: But even when the word "genus" is employed, since the possession of such a genus as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*)—in the form of a temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*)—also exists in a quality (*guṇa*), [how can it be excluded?]
There is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with respect to existence (*sattva*).
However, if one intends to specify the possession of such a genus (*jāti*) by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), then the word "genus" (*jāti*) is redundant.

This is because the definition is perfectly adequate by stating simply: "the state of possessing a property that is distinct from existence (sattā) and is co-locus with quality (guṇa) through the relation of inherence (samavāya)."

If it is argued that, because the property consisting of being either a substance or a quality has its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) as the relation, the possession of that [property] by a quality is absent through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), we say: no; [this is not so] with respect to the relation of inherence.
The inclusion of the term "jāti" (genus) is precisely for the purpose of indicating that what is intended here is the possession of such a property (*tādṛśadharmavattva*).
Thus, it is stated in the *Prakāśikā*: "In order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth," and so on.
In the *Dīpikā*—
"But even so," [it is argued]:
from the conventional usage "one form," it is understood that there exists in form a quality consisting of the number one.

From the conventional usage "form is distinct from taste," it is understood that the quality of distinctness (*pṛthaktvaguṇa*) exists in form. Thus, form is the substratum of qualities; and the universal (*jāti*), which resides therein, is distinct from existence (*sattā*)—namely, the quality-ness (*guṇatva*)—the possession of which [is established].
The intention of the objector is that because a quality exists [in a substance], the definition of a substance over-extends (ativyāpti) to it.
He provides the resolution: "Because of inherence in a single object" (ekārthasamavāyāt).
This means: because of inherence in one and the same object.

Because unity and diversity reside in a single object such as a jar through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), the linguistic usages "one color" and "color is distinct from taste" are justified. The phrase "one color" means that color possesses unity by virtue of the relation of inherence in its own substratum; however, it does not mean...
"Because it possesses oneness through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

And thus, since such linguistic usage regarding a quality is justified precisely by its having oneness and separateness as its objects through the aforementioned indirect relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) with respect to color (*rūpa*), [the objection is resolved].
A quality (*guṇa*) is not admitted [to exist] by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

Furthermore, in the definition beginning with "co-referential with a quality" (*guṇasamānādhikaraṇa*), the state of being the locus of a quality is intended to be understood by way of the relation of inherence.
The point is that, therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to color and so forth.
In the *Prakāśikā*, it says: "by way of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as constituted by inherence (*samavāya*)."
This means "by way of inherence in its own substratum.

Co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya), as constituted by the relation of inherence, consists in the state of being located (ādheyatva) as delimited by the relation of inherence, which is itself defined by the locus-hood (adhikaraṇatā) that is defined by the state of being located as delimited by the relation of inherence residing in itself.
In its purification,
it results simply in the inherence [of the quality] in its own substratum;
that is, the postulation of a possession of qualities not previously established.
The meaning is: the postulation of the possession of qualities (*guṇavattva*) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), where [that possession] has not yet been established.
This concludes the *Tarkasaṃgraha*, the classification of qualities.

The twenty-four qualities (guṇas) are: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, sound, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression.

Form, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, sound, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression— these are the twenty-four qualities.
The *Dīpikā* analyzes the qualities (*guṇa*),
beginning with "rūpa": a quality is that which possesses generality (*sāmānya*) while being distinct from substance (*dravya*) and action (*karman*).
Or [it is] that which possesses the universal (jāti) of "quality-ness" (guṇatva). If it is asked:
"But since lightness, hardness, softness, and so forth exist, how can there be only twenty-four qualities?"—[the answer is]: no.
Because lightness consists in the absence of heaviness, whereas softness and hardness consist in specific types of conjunctions of parts.
— *Prakāśikā*
"Possessing a universal" (sāmānyavān): by this it is understood that the possession of a universal is through the relation of inherence (samavāya).
Therefore, [the term does not apply] to that which possesses it through relations such as temporal connection (kālika-sambandha) and the like.
There is no over-extension to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).
"Quality" (*guṇa*) is the indication of the definiendum. He states it thus for the sake of brevity:
It follows that [the definition] possesses the universal *guṇatva* (quality-ness).
Although there is non-difference between the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), nevertheless,
when the difference from others is to be proven by means of the definition, even if the co-presence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum with the reason is ascertained—

In brief, this definition is intended with the view that the certainty regarding the probandum (sādhya), which has the delimiting property of the reason (hetu-dharmitāvacchedaka) as its locus, is not invariably fixed;
this should be understood as applying to what follows as well.

The Bhaṭṭācāryas, in their *Guṇadīdhiti*, maintain that the establishment of the universal *guṇatva* (the quality-ness) is by virtue of its being the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "quality" (*guṇa*). And it is not the case that, in this same manner,
there is a universal *vibhutva* (all-pervasive-ness) by virtue of its being the delimitor of the denotative capacity of the word "all-pervasive" (*vibhu*).
It cannot be said that [the property] would be established;
for since there exists the subverting factor of the commingling (*saṅkara*) of "being an entity" (*bhūtatva*), it is impossible for that [commingling] to be a universal (*jāti*),
because it is precisely the commingling of what is intended to be a universal that constitutes the subversion of its being a universal.
And so it has been stated by the teacher Udayana in the *Dravyakiraṇāvalī*:
"The non-difference or equality of the individual [instances]..."
"Confusion, lack of stability, loss of form, lack of connection,
and the summary of the subverters of genus."

Thus: the non-difference of the individual (vyakti)—that is, the identity of the individual which is its own substratum—is a subverting argument against the generic nature (jāti) of "space-ness" and the like. [Likewise is] the sameness of the individual.

The state of having neither fewer nor more individual instances constitutes the identity of the universals *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) and *kalaśatva* (jar-ness), even though they are distinct universals. *Saṅkara* (confusion) is the coexistence in a single locus of two properties that are each co-present with the absolute non-existence of the other.
If being an entity (*bhūtatva*) and being corporeal (*mūrtatva*), and so forth, were universals (*jāti*),
there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*); that is, an absence of finality (*anāvasthā*) if a universal itself possessed another universal.
The loss of its own nature consists in the loss of the specific form that constitutes its exclusion from what is not itself, given that it possesses a universal (*jāti*).
Non-connection consists in not being inherent (*asamavetatva*), given that non-existence (*abhāva*) and the like possess a universal.
In brief:
although qualities such as lightness are established by authoritative means of knowledge, it is logical that they be included within those [qualities] already enumerated.
He explains [this] with the words "of lightness.
[The term] *dhvaṃsa* [refers to] destruction in that which possesses it (*tadvati*). *Bālapriyā*.
Thus, because universals (sāmānya), particulars (viśeṣa), inherence (samavāya),

prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), and absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) are unproduced, and since only that which is produced serves as a temporal adjunct (kālopādhi), in those [latter cases...]

Considering that it is impossible for there to be possession of a universal (*sāmānyavattva*) by way of a temporal relation (*kālikasambandha*), and thus over-extension (*ativyāpti*) cannot be asserted [in that case], the over-extension in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) was stated. This is because,
although there is non-difference between the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the delimitors of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).

If the definition of a quality is "the possession of the universal of quality-ness" (guṇatvajāti), then quality-ness itself is the definition, and that very same thing is also the delimitor of the definiendum.
There would be no difference between the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—it is replied:
For a definition is that which distinguishes [the object from others].

It is that which generates an inference having as its qualificandum the subject (*lakṣya*) and as its predicate the difference from what is other than the subject (*lakṣyetara-bheda*). Thus, if "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) is the definition of a quality, the formulation of the inference must be: "That which is not a quality is distinct from others, because it possesses quality-ness. In that case...

The inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) must be stated as: "A quality (*guṇa*) possesses the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) which is co-located with the exclusion of others (*itarabheda*), [the latter] being pervaded by the property of being a quality.
In that [consideration], regarding the property of being a quality, there is its co-location with the exclusion of others.

When [the quality] is appearing, because it is cognized by the same cognition (*tulyavittivedyatā*), it is possible for the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the universal of qualityness (*guṇatva*) to appear at some time as being distinct from other things.

And thus, there is a co-occurrence of the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), which is the nature of qualityness, with the probandum (*sādhya*), which is the difference from other things.

The intention of the objector is that, because the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) with the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*)— which is the object of the inference— is already apprehended by the *parāmarśa* itself through its very cognition, the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) would necessarily follow.
He responds with "even so" (tathāpi).

When the co-occurrence of the probandum with the reason (*hetu-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is manifest within the reason, it is not possible for the co-occurrence of the reason with the probandum (*sādhya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) to necessarily manifest within the probandum.
Therefore, there is no consequence of proving what is already established;
the point is that possessing the universal (jāti) of "quality-ness" (guṇatva) is fit to be the definition of a quality (guṇa).
[This is stated] because it serves as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (śakyatāvacchedaka) of the word "quality."
