The intention is that the universal "quality-ness" (*guṇatvajāti*) is established by the following inference: "The denotative capacity residing in quality, which is the state of being the denotation of the word 'quality' as delimited by some property, is [itself] delimited by some property, because it is a denotative capacity, like the denotative capacity of the word 'jar' residing in a jar."
"Of the commingling of the state of being an element" (*bhūtatva-saṅkarasya*) means:

of its coexistence in a single locus with [the property of] being an element (*bhūtatva*). Now, since even the state of being an element lacks the status of a universal (*jāti*), how can there be such a commingling? [This would be impossible] if the state of being all-pervasive (*vibhutva*) were a universal.

Anticipating the objection that there is a contradiction [to the definition of a genus], [the author] states: "There is no confusion of genera (*jāti-saṅkara*) that contradicts the status of being a genus; rather, it is precisely the confusion of properties that are intended to be genera which is so [contradictory].
This is even the case when 'being an element' (*bhūtatva*), though not a genus, [is confused]."
He provides the resolution: "Because there is the state of being the object of the conceit of being a genus, the confusion of those [classes] is a sublater of genus-status"—
meaning that the identity or equality of the individual instances [is what constitutes the sublation].
Furthermore, if [the universal] were to possess another universal, there would be contradictions:
infinite regress, loss of its specific form, and lack of connection are the contradictions against [its being] a universal.

The meaning of the phrase *jātibādhakasaṅgraha* is: a concise term whose object is the object of a cognition that obstructs a cognition having as its content either "being a universal" (*jātitva*) or "possessing a universal" (*jātimattva*).
The meaning of "non-difference from the individual" (vyakterabhedaḥ) is that [the property] has only one individual as its own locus;
this is determined by the two relations of "subsisting in the same as its own counter-correlative" and "subsisting in the same as its own sub-stratum."

This means "otherness qualified by difference. That whose individual instances (vyakti) serve as its substrata becomes qualified by difference through the aforementioned twofold relation, just as, for example, potness [is].
[The object] is qualified by the exclusion of a blue pot;
its own [exclusion] is the exclusion of a blue pot,
and its own counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is the blue pot.
The subsistence of that [blue-ness] resides in pot-ness;
thus, "self" refers to the difference from the blue pot. (1. By way of being cognized by the same cognition.)

The meaning is "by virtue of being the object of a single cognition. A red jar is the correlate of that [cognition], and the property of residing in it belongs to jar-ness; thus, jar-ness [is related] by means of the aforementioned two relations.
The nature of space (ākāśatva), however, is not qualified by the exclusion of a blue pot in that manner; this is because of the term "exclusion" (bheda).
When space is taken as the locus of division, space itself is its own counter-correlative;
although the property of residing in that [space] indeed exists in space, [the definition fails].
Likewise, there is no subsistence in a jar or the like, which is the counter-correlate (anuyogin) of the difference from space.

Although, when the difference from a jar is taken as the basis, there is indeed subsistence in space—which is its own counter-correlate—within the nature of space, nevertheless, there is no subsistence in a jar, which is the specific counter-correlate of that [space]. And thus:

That which is "other than what is distinguished by difference" through the relation of being both [space and] what has been called "spatiality" (ākāśatva) possesses only one individual instance as its own substratum;
therefore, it is not a universal (jāti).
For being a universal (jātitva) consists in being inherent in many while being eternal;
and being inherent in many [is established] by means of the aforementioned two relations.
The state of being qualified by difference;
and here, "space-ness" is the universal (qualified by difference through the aforementioned two relations).

Thus, with respect to the cognition [of ether], the state of being ether— which consists of a single individuality as its own substratum (being distinct from that which is qualified by difference through the two aforementioned relations)—
is the cause of the cognition of possessing that [ether-ness].

It should be noted that because the cognition of the absence of that [universal] acts as an inhibitor according to the principle that "the cognition of the absence of X is an inhibitor," and because the property of being the object of a cognition that inhibits the cognition whose object is the universal-ness (jātitva) exists in the individual (vyakti) given its non-difference from it, this constitutes a sublation of the universal.
The equality of manifestation (vyakti) means having neither fewer nor more instances of manifestation;
that is to say, it means having a basis that is neither less nor greater.
Since such equality exists between "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "pot-ness" (*kalaśatva*), these two do not constitute distinct universals (*jāti*).
In reality, however,

[two universals are distinct] if they reside in individuals that possess a number of instances neither less nor greater than the number of instances residing in individuals that serve as the substrata for a universal distinct from themselves.

The meaning is that "equality" consists in the property of being a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of a mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) co-present with one's own self, which is co-present with a genus distinct from itself, while simultaneously being a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of a mutual absence co-present with that same genus.
This is the subverting argument against the status of "possessing a shell-like neck" (*kambugrīvādimattva*) as a universal (*jāti*): its own self— namely, "possessing a shell-like neck"—
is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) that is co-located with it, which is a universal distinct from itself.

The universal "pot-ness" (ghaṭatvajāti) exists in the possession of a conch-like neck and other features, characterized by the non-restriction of the counter-correlativity of mutual absence (anyonyābhāvapratiyogitānavacchedakatva) that is co-located with it.

Where such equality exists, there is no generic nature (*jātitva*). Thus, the cognition of such equality acts as an obstacle to the cognition of generic nature by way of being a cognition of the presence of a property that is pervaded by the absence of generic nature.

1. In that case, there is no "genus-ness" (*jātitva*), just as there is none in the state of being any one among [the categories] from earth up to mind. Its own state of being any one among [the categories] from earth up to mind—
A genus distinct from that [substance-ness] is "substanceness" (*dravyatva*);
since the state of being co-extensive with it exists in the state of being any one among the nine categories beginning with earth and ending with mind, that [latter] is not a genus.
Thus, equality consists in being co-extensive with a genus other than itself.

The meaning is that "the state of being invariably concomitant with a genus distinct from itself" consists in the property of not being a delimitant of the counter-correlativity of a mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) that is co-located with itself, and also not being a delimitant of the counter-correlativity of a mutual absence that is co-located with a genus distinct from itself.
Confusion (*saṅkara*) is the occurrence, in a single locus, of two properties that exist by mutually excluding one another;
[that is,] the co-occurrence in a single locus of two properties whose loci are identical with the absolute non-existence of each other.
This is the sense: this is the subverting argument against *bhūtatva* (elementality) and *mūrtatva* (corporeality) being universals (*jāti*), namely that *mūrtatva* exists apart from *bhūtatva*.

In the case of *manas*, having abandoned corporeality (*mūrtatva*), there is the property of being an element (*bhūtatva*) in space (*ākāśa*); since both [properties] coexist in the four elements beginning with earth, they are not true universals (*jāti*) due to this mutual overlap (*saṅkara*). [The definition of a universal requires: existing in its own locus and existing in that which possesses the absence of itself.

It follows that *saṅkara* (intermixture) consists in being qualified by some property through these three relations: [1] being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in its own locus; [2] being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the locus of the first relation; and [3] being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the locus of the second relation.
Of such an intermixture...
If it is asked how it constitutes a sublation of its being a genus (jāti), it is said:
its status as a sublation of its being a genus is precisely by way of [its functioning as] a logical mark (liṅga).

For instance—the state of being an element (*bhūtatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*), because it possesses corporeality (*mūrtatva*) through its connection with the aforementioned triad; whatever possesses corporeality through its connection with the aforementioned triad is not a genus, as in the case of the conjunction of space and mind (*ākāśa-manassaṃyoga*). Thus, by this inference, the absence of the status of a genus in "being an element" is established.

Since the aforementioned *sāṅkarya* (overlapping) is the object (*viṣaya*) of the knowledge of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth that produces the aforementioned inference— which is itself an obstacle to the knowledge of *jātitva* by way of being a subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*)—
it is [an obstacle] just like the object of a cognition that is a direct obstacle.

1. "svādhikaraṇa" and so forth: its own [property] is "being an entity" (bhūtatva); its locus (svādhikaraṇa) is the fourfold [group] beginning with earth; the state of residing therein exists in corporeality (mūrtatva).
Thus, its own reality (bhūtatva) is its intrinsic nature (svābhāva); the absence of that reality is likewise present in the mind and in its modifications when they possess corporeality (mūrtatva).
In this way, its own reality has space as its locus.
The absolute absence that resides in that [earth] is the absence of corporeality; the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of that [absence] exists in corporeality.

Thus, the meaning is that the very fact of corporeality being qualified by "element-hood" (*bhūtatva*) through the aforementioned threefold relation is precisely what constitutes "confusion" (*saṃkara*).
2. Regarding the "conjunction of the sky and the mind":

because the conjunction of the sky and the mind resides in the mind, which is the locus of corporeality (*mūrtatva*), and because it resides in the sky, which is the locus of the absence of corporeality.

The reason exists because there is the absence of the conjunction between ether and mind, which resides in the four elements—earth and the others—which are the substrata of corporeality; and by virtue of being the counter-positive of that [absence], there is the possession of corporeality through the aforementioned threefold relation. Furthermore, the probandum, which consists in the absence of being a genus (jātitva), also exists.
The conjunction of the sky and the mind serves as an example [of a non-entity].

This is because even that which is the object of a cognition producing an obstructing cognition is not excluded from being a category-subverting entity (*jātibādhaka-padārtha*), since its inclusion within the category of "mixed" (*sāṅkarya*) remains unimpaired. Alternatively:

Because the consideration (*parāmarśa*) of corporeality (*mūrtatva*), by virtue of its being a certainty regarding the possession of the pervader of the absence of that [genus-ness]— namely, the consideration of the absence of genus-ness which generates the inference of the absence of genus-ness through the aforementioned threefold relation—

acts as an inhibitor of knowledge having "genus-ness" as its qualifier by way of being a certainty regarding the possession of the pervader of its absence; and because the aforementioned commingling (*sāṅkarya*) has that [absence of genus-ness] as its object.
They say that the state of being the object of a cognition which directly obstructs the cognition of "jātitva" (the nature of being a genus) remains unimpaired.
Infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is the absence of a resting point due to the postulation of an endless series of further [entities] lacking empirical justification; this [applies] to *jāti*.
It is a sublater with respect to mere generic existence;
its status as a sublater is by way of reasoning (*tarka*);
[it constitutes] the loss of essential nature (*rūpahāni*).

The refutation of the definition consisting in being self-distinguishing: this serves as a sublation of the view that the ultimate particular (*viśeṣa*) possesses a genus (*jāti*). For the ultimate particular is indeed defined by its nature of being self-distinguishing.

If the particular were possessed of a genus, then since the genus itself could serve as the cause for the exclusion of that particular from others, [the particular] would possess the nature of being self-excluding.
The defining characteristic would be destroyed;
therefore, there is no distinction based on genus. And thus, even the loss of form occurs only through the method of logical reasoning.
The sublater of the property of possessing a genus is non-relation—
namely, the absence of inherence by way of either the relation of counter-correlativity or the relation of substratum-hood. And this...
There is a subverting argument against the possession of a genus (*jātimattva*) by both inherence (*samavāya*) and non-existence (*abhāva*).
Wherever the possession of a genus exists, there inherence must exist, related either as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) or as a substratum (*anuyogitva*). [In the case of] inherence...
Regarding "of that" (*tasya*):
it means of the state of being the object of the cognition that produces the obstructing cognition. 2.

Regarding the phrase "the inference of the absence of being a genus" (*jātitvābhāvānumiti*): it refers to that inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) which produces the inference of the absence of being a genus, namely, [the cognition] that "being past" (*bhūtatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*). "Being past" [is the subject].

The meaning is that [the cognition] has the form "possessing incorporeality, which is pervaded by the absence of being a genus" (*jātitva*). Thus, by means of the aforementioned threefold relation, the state of possessing corporeality— which constitutes a *saṃkara* (overlapping)—
serves as the object of the *parāmarśa* (inferential consideration) that obstructs the inference of being a genus.
The intended meaning is that the sublation of a universal (*jātibādhakatva*) consists in being the object of a cognition that obstructs a cognition whose object is the state of being a universal.
3. "By way of a *tarka* (reductio argument)": if...

In this context, the intended reasoning (*tarka*) is as follows: if the universal (*jāti*) were itself possessed of a universal (*jātimatī*), then there would be no cessation for the postulation of successive universals.
Furthermore, [the universal possesses] the quality of being self-excluding (*svatovyāvartakatva*).
The state of not being the object of an inference of the difference from others of its own class, which has a gender different from itself as its qualificand.
For example: "Inherence exists," just as "the possession of a universal exists in a jar."

In that regard, the inherence of the pot exists in the potsherd by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*), because the pot is the counter-correlative of that inherence of the pot;
likewise, the inherence of potness exists in the pot by way of the relation of sub-correlativity (*anuyogitā*).
The inherence of potness [resides] in the pot because the pot is its relatum;
and because that [inherence] does not exist in those two [the universal and the particular], they do not possess that genus.
By means of the aforementioned relation, the absence of inherence (samavāya) is pervaded by the absence of possessing a genus (jātimattva);
therefore, there is the cognition of non-relation.

The *Tarkasaṃgraha*, in its section on the classification of action (*karmavibhāga*), states that the cognition of possessing a genus (*jātimattvajñāna*) is obstructed by way of the cognition of possessing that which is pervaded by the absence of that [genus].
The five types of action (karman) are upward movement, downward movement, contraction, expansion, and locomotion.
The five types of action are: throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion.
— *Dīpikā*
He analyzes action [as follows]:
"Throwing upward," etc. Action is that which, while being distinct from conjunction, is the inherent cause of conjunction.
Or [it is] that which possesses the genus *karmatva*.
If it is objected that the number "five" is untenable because there exist other actions such as whirling (*bhramaṇa*) and so forth, we say: no.
Since activities such as wandering are also included within "going," there is no contradiction with the number five.
— *Prakāśikā*

The phrase "being distinct from conjunction" (*saṃyogabhinnatve sati*) is included in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is both a cause of conjunction and its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
[Conjunction] is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of conjunction.
The term "non-inherent" (*asamavāyin*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to substances (*dravya*).
By the phrase "of whirling, etc.," there is an inclusion of throwing upward (*recana*), flowing (*syandana*), upward flaming (*ūrdhvajvalana*), and horizontal motion (*tiryaggamana*).
"Because it is included within going.
Nor should it be suspected that upward motion and the others might likewise be included within going.
The meaning is that this is because the Sage, who acts according to his own independent will and is beyond the scope of injunctions or questioning, is so regarded.
1. "Because of its absence" means:
Inherence or absence does not exist elsewhere by way of the relation of inherence;
therefore, neither inherence nor absence possesses inherence by way of the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*).
Likewise, nothing else whatsoever exists in inherence or in absence by way of the relation of inherence; therefore—

The meaning is that, by virtue of the relation of *anuyogitā* (substratumness), those two do not possess inherence (*samavāya*). [In the phrase] "being distinct from conjunction" (*saṃyogabhinnatve*), [the following applies].
It has been stated that "action is that which, when existing, is the non-inherent cause of conjunction";
for if the phrase "while being distinct from conjunction" were not included, then conjunction itself would also be a non-inherent cause of conjunction.

Because, with respect to the conjunction between the body and the book, the conjunction between the hand and the book serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); therefore, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to conjunction.
To exclude that [over-extension], it is stated that [the cause] must be "distinct from conjunction.
If one were to state merely that it is "the cause of conjunction," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a substance (*dravya*) which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of conjunction.
To exclude that [possibility], the qualification "non-inherent" (*asamavāyin*) is applied to the cause. Thus it says: "the non-inherent cause of conjunction.
[The phrase] "of one who acts according to his own independent will" [is used].
The meaning is that the Sage, who acts according to his own will, is universally agreed to be beyond both command and questioning; "command" (niyoga) means an order,
and "questioning" (paryanuyoga) means an inquiry.
The Compendium of Reasoning:
Classification of Universals.
Universals are of two kinds: the higher and the lower.
Generality is of two kinds: the higher and the lower.
The *Dīpikā* analyzes generality as follows:
— "Supreme" (param) means existing in a greater number of locations; "inferior" (aparam) means existing in a smaller number of locations.
The universal (jāti) does not exist within the fourfold category beginning with generality (sāmānya).
Regarding the passage beginning with "the supreme illuminator" (*prakāśikā param*),
it should be understood that there is no deficiency [in the text], because the author of the root treatise himself will explain the general definition later on.
Existence (*sattā*) is indeed "higher" (*para*) because it subsists in a greater number of loci relative to substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like;
whereas potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like are "lower" (*apara*) because they subsist in fewer loci.
This is also the case for substantiality and the like [relative to existence].
Existence (*sattā*) is "lower" (*aparatva*) than [the universals] such as potness (*ghaṭatva*), while potness is "higher" (*paratva*); this is the distinction.
This concludes the section on the classification of particulars (*viśeṣavibhāga*) from the *Tarkasaṅgraha*.
The ultimate particulars (viśeṣas), however, which reside in eternal substances, are indeed infinite.
The *Dīpikā* analyzes the distinction [of eternal substances] as follows:
"eternal" refers to the atoms of the four elements beginning with earth, as well as the five beginning with space (*ākāśa*).
Eternal substances. [From] the Tarkasaṃgraha: the definition of inherence.
Inherence, however, is only one.
He states that there is no difference in inherence by saying: "But inherence... (samavāyastu).

The *Prakāśikā* states that there is no difference in inherence (*samavāya*). And since there is no difference in inherence, [the quality of touch] would exist in air, which possesses the inherence of touch.
It might be suspected that there would be a cognition of possessing color;
however, even when the inherence of color exists, such a cognition does not occur because of the absence of color— this is the general direction of the argument.
The objection that there would be the perception of color even for a blind person arises because,
given the existence of the inherence of touch, the inherence of color— which is non-different from it— must also exist.
The meaning is that it is precisely the inherence of color (*rūpasamavāya*) that is the determinant for the cognition of "possessing color" (*rūpavattā*).
It is not the inherence of color itself that determines the cognition of possessing color;
rather, it is [the quality] through its relation of inherence (*samavāyasambandhena*).

Regarding form: since there is no form in wind, he offers a resolution with the intention that there is consequently no undesirable consequence of perceiving it as possessing form—namely: "rūpam/ vāyau tu na rūpamasti, ato na rūpavattāpratītiprasaṅgaḥ."
"Even though the inherence of color exists [in air]"—

having raised the objection that one cannot say "color does not exist in air" even if the inherence of color exists there, because the existence of a relation necessarily entails the existence of the relata, he says:

"—the word 'diṅ' (direction). This is the intended meaning: inherence (samavāya), as qualified by having air as its relatum and as qualified by having color as its counter-correlative, is the regulator of the cognition that air possesses color."

Since the absence of air-as-counterpositive-ness in the inherence qualified by air-as-relatum-ness exists, the cognition "air possesses color" cannot be induced. For further details, one should consult the Muktāvalīmañjūṣā and other such works.
Tarkasaṅgraha:
Classification of Absence (AnTs 9). Absence is of four kinds.
These are antecedent non-existence, non-existence through destruction, absolute non-existence, and mutual non-existence.
Non-existence is of four kinds: antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva), non-existence through destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva), absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva), and...
"And mutual non-existence.
The *Dīpikā* analyzes non-existence:
"Non-existence" [is thus defined]. This concludes the examination of earth from the *Tarkasaṃgraha*.
The earth possesses fragrance;
it is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.
That which is eternal exists in the form of atoms.
It is impermanent and of the nature of an effect;
furthermore, it is threefold due to the distinction between body, sense-faculties, and objects.
The body belongs to those such as ourselves.
The faculty that perceives odor is the nose, which resides at the tip of the nostrils;
its object consists of earth, stone, and so forth.
In this context, "gandhavatī" refers to earth.

Following the sequence of the topical outline (*uddeśakrama*), he first states the definition of earth with the word "tatra": "In that [context], earth is that which possesses odor."* *Note: The original Sanskrit for the definition provided here is "tatra gandhavatī pṛthivī," which is translated as "In that [context], earth is that which possesses odor."*
Enumeration (*uddeśa*) is the mention of the names of categories (*padārtha*). And in the order of enumeration, desire alone is the regulating factor everywhere. Now, one might object:
There would be an under-extension [of the definition] because fragrance is not produced in a substance composed of both fragrant and non-fragrant parts due to their mutual opposition;
nor should it be argued that the perception of fragrance is impossible in such a case.

Because only the odor of the constituent parts can be perceived there, a variegated odor is not admitted [as existing]. Furthermore, if it is argued that there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of a jar that has been produced and then destroyed, we say no; for what is intended is the possession of a subordinate genus of substantiality (*dravyatvāparajāti*) that is co-located with odor.

If it is objected that there is over-extension [of the definition] because odor is also perceived in water and so forth— no; this is not so, because [the status of being an earth element] is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Because it is accepted that only the odor of earth manifests there [in the lotus].
Now, if it is argued that even so, since time is the substratum of all things, the definition over-extends (ativyāpti) to time—[we reply]: no.
This is because the definition [of earth] is intended to be related by a relation distinct from the relation that serves as the basis for its being the substratum of all [qualities],
according to the *Prakāśikā*.
He states the reason for its being mentioned first:
"Therein" means among earth and the other [elements].
The universal *pṛthivītva* (earthness) is established as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the status of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of odor.
The object to be awakened; "by name" indicates that the meaning of the instrumental case is non-difference [of the name] with respect to the referent of the word "proclamation."
It connects with the word that conveys [the object];
thus, the definition results in this: an *uddeśa* is merely a name that conveys a real entity (*vastu*).

In this context, the term "entity" (*vastu*) is intended to refer to the entity that is to be defined (the definiendum), such as earth and so forth, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*).
This is because the definiendum, such as earth, exists only in a general sense.

In order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) onto the term "object of cognition" (*prameya*) within the word "proponent" (*pratipādaka*), the word "name" (*nāma*) refers to that which is delimited by the delimitor of the state of being the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedakāvacchinna*);
for the word "name" is present in the definition-statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*).
It should be understood that the word "only" (*mātra*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Regarding the term "begun" (*ārabdhe*), it means "produced" (*janye*).
[The phrase] "due to mutual contradiction" (*parasparavirodhena*)...
The meaning is that there is an obstruction of the foul odor with respect to the fragrant odor, and of the fragrant odor with respect to the foul odor. Thus, there is an impossibility of perception.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that only the variegated odor (*citragandha*) itself must be accepted as unobstructed. Regarding the phrase "of the odor of the parts" (*avayavagandhasyaiva*),
it means by way of the relation of inherence in its own substratum (*svāśrayasamavetatva-sambandhena*), and so forth.

Accepting the maxim "let the wicked man be satisfied," he says "And what more? To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by taking [the property of] being water (*jalatva*) and so forth as the basis, he adds "co-existing with odor" (*gandhasamānādhikaraṇa*).
To exclude existence (*sattā*), he adds "subordinate to substantiality" (*dravyatvāparā*), which means "subsisting in a narrower domain than substantiality" (*dravyatvanyūnavṛtti*). Thus...
The exclusion of [the property of] substantiality [is established] because of the cognition of fragrance; that is to say, because of cognitions such as "the water is fragrant."
"Of the odor of earth alone" means by way of the relation of being conjoined with its own substratum, and so forth;
"therein" refers to water and the like.
One who grasps [the teaching] exactly as it was heard raises a doubt with the words "nanu" (but surely).
He avoids over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to time and so forth by introducing the relations that constitute the definition through a common form (*anugatarūpeṇa*).
Regarding the term "universal substratum" (*sarvādhāra*):
according to the Vaiśeṣika school, since inherence and the like function as relations precisely by virtue of their nature as inherence and so forth,
it is in that very form that each respective relation constitutes the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of its corresponding [definition].

To be understood: [the term] "bodhya" refers to [the property of] being the delimiting condition for the status of being an inherent cause of odor (*gandha-samavāyikāraṇatāvacchedakatā*). Thus says the *Bālapriyā*.

The intended formal inference (*anumāna*) here is as follows: "The causal capacity residing in earth, which is delimited by the relation of identity and is the counter-correlate of the effect-ness residing in smell— which is itself delimited by the property of smellness and delimited by the relation of inherence— is delimited by some property, because it is a causal capacity, like the causal capacity for a jar residing in its potsherds."
The root text states: "Enumeration (uddeśa) is the mention of the categories by name. The phrase "mention of the categories" (*padārthasaṅkīrtanam*) means the enumeration of the categories.
The word *saṅkīrtana* signifies a term that makes something known.
The word "padārthaviṣayakajñānaka" means that which possesses knowledge having the category-meaning (padārtha) as its object; that is to say, it is the mention of the category-meaning.
The word "padārtha" here refers to a real entity (vastu).
By the word "nāmnā," the sense of non-difference, which is the meaning of the instrumental case, [is expressed].

Because it follows [the object] in the word, it results that an *uddeśa* (enunciation) is a word that generates knowledge whose object is a real entity (*vastu*) and which is non-different from its name.
This is because, in the statement "earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self,
and mind," words such as "earth" and so forth convey real entities like earth and are thus names.
Regarding the definition of *uddeśa* (naming):
since the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) also conveys a real entity and possesses the nature of a name, the definition of *uddeśa* would be over-extended (*ativyāpti*) to it as well.
To exclude that [undesired consequence], the term "entity" (*vastu*) must be stated as referring to the entity that is the object of definition;
and a word such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*) is not of such a nature.
There is no over-extension [of the definition].
Even the term "knowable" (prameya) conveys the earth and so forth, which are the objects to be defined; therefore, there would be over-extension in that case.
To exclude that [over-extension], the term "entity" (vastu) must be stated as referring to an entity delimited by the delimitor of the definiendum;
this applies to the word "knowable" (prameya).

Even though the word "earth" (pṛthivī) in such definitions conveys earth as delimited by knowability (*prameyatva*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because it lacks the capacity to convey earth as delimited by the specific delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), namely earthness (*pṛthivītva*). This applies even to the word "earth" within a definitional sentence such as "Earth is that which possesses odor."
Because it conveys the cognition of that which is delimited by "earthness" (pṛthivītva) and because it is a name (nāman), it would follow that it is a subject of enunciation (uddeśa).
To prevent this, it must also be stated that it is "merely a name" (nāmamātra); by the word "merely" (mātra),...
It is stated that [the subject] consists in not being co-occurrent with words expressive of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth. Thus,

a word that is non-different from a noun (*nāman*) which generates a cognition having the definiendum as its qualificandum and the delimitor of definability (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) as its mode, while not being co-occurrent with words expressive of the definition and so forth, is the "subject" (*uddeśa*).
This is the conclusion. Thus he says: "The meaning of the third case is non-difference," and so forth.
The explanation of the term *saṅkīrtane* is "in the word that expresses [it]."
"In general" means by way of the common property consisting in the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*).
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is connected with the act of comprehension (*pratipatti*).
The meaning is "being a mode" (prakāratva).
[This refers to] the case where having fragrance is the definition of earth.

In a substance produced from parts possessing fragrant odors and parts possessing non-fragrant odors, there is no production of any odor whatsoever; thus, the definition is under-extended (avyāpti). Nor can it be argued that an odor must arise because the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) consisting of the odor residing in the parts exists.
It should not be suspected that [an odor] does not arise;
for since a fragrant odor acts as an obstacle to a non-fragrant odor, and a non-fragrant odor acts as an obstacle to a fragrant odor, [this applies] to any odor whatsoever.
Because production is impossible there;
and if no odor is produced there, then how [could it exist] there?
The odor would be perceived;
therefore, in that case, there is a mutual obstruction.
1. The nature of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*).
Thus,

the meaning is as follows: in the case of the word "knowable" (*prameya*), which generates a cognition having as its qualificandum (viśeṣya) earth and so forth, and as its mode (prakāra) the general property (*sāmānyadharma*) consisting in knowability (*prameyatva*).
Let neither a fragrant odor nor a foul odor arise;
let a variegated odor arise by means of that.
It should not be said that the cognition of fragrance arises [in the whole] because the possession of fragrance is absent [there], nor that there is no pervasion;
for it is precisely the fragrance residing in the parts that exists in the whole through the relation of inherence in its own substratum.

Because a variegated fragrance is not admitted to be possible through cognition, the defect of under-extension (*avyāpti*) remains as it was. Furthermore, consider a jar that has arisen in the first moment; then...
In the second moment, [the definition] would be under-extended (*avyāpti*) with respect to that jar,
because according to the principle "a substance produced in the first moment is devoid of qualities," it is at that time lacking fragrance.
With the intention that the substratum itself perishes in the second moment, he raises an objection in the *Dīpikā*: "Now, [regarding] the fragrant and the non-fragrant... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "co-inherent with smell":
the definition of earth is the possession of that genus which resides in the substratum of smell and is pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*).

The basis for fragrance (*gandhādhikaraṇa*) is flowers and so forth, which are its instances; the universal (*jāti*) pervaded by the category of substance (*dravyatva*) is the universal of earthness (*pṛthivītva*);
and the possession of that [universal] exists in a substance composed of fragrant and non-fragrant parts, as well as in a jar that has been produced and subsequently destroyed.

There is no lack of pervasion [in the definition]. If one were to state merely "the possession of a genus that is pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvavyāpyajātimattva*), there would be over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) with respect to water, because the genus "waterness" (*jalatva*), which is pervaded by substanceness, exists in water. Therefore, the term "co-located with odor" (*gandhasamānādhikaraṇa*) is included.

There is no fault, because the property of being water (*jalatva*) does not reside in that which has odor as its locus (*gandhādhikaraṇavṛttitva*). If one were to state merely "possessing a genus that is co-locus with odor" (*gandhasamānādhikaraṇajātimattva*), then since the genus "existence" (*sattājāti*) resides in earth— which is the locus of odor— this [definition] would apply to water and other substances as well.
There is over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
To exclude that, the qualifier "pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvavyāpya*) is added to the genus (*jāti*). Now, even when the qualifier "pervaded by substanceness" has been provided—
If it is argued that, by taking the genus *dravyatva* (substance-ness) as the defining characteristic, over-extension (*ativyāpti*) into water and other substances is unavoidable—
since *dravyatva* resides in earth, which is the locus of odor, and yet it also resides in things devoid of *dravyatva*— then [the response follows].

No; in the present context, being pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatvavyāpyatva*) does not mean non-occurrence in that which is devoid of substantiality, but rather consists in having a locus smaller than that of substantiality (*dravyatvanyūnavṛttitva*). And substantiality itself does not have a locus smaller than that of substantiality.

This is because of such an intention. Furthermore, "subsisting in a locus smaller than that of substanceness" means being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference (*bheda*) that is co-located with substanceness.
This is stated in the *Prakāśikā*: "taking water-ness (*jalatva*), etc. and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "co-occurrent with substantiality" (*dravyatvasamānādhikaraṇa*): water is the locus of substantiality; the exclusion (*bheda*) residing therein is the exclusion of earth. Since earthness is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of that [exclusion], [earthness is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the absence of earth].
[The definition is] having a substratum that is narrower than substance-ness (*dravyatva*).

Substance-ness, however, is not the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in the locus of substance-ness, because [there is no such thing as] a difference from substance.
The meaning is that, because it does not reside in the locus of substanceness (*dravyatva*), substanceness does not subsist in a manner subordinate to [the category of] substanceness.
In the *Dīpikā*: "But surely, since fragrance is perceived even in water and so forth..."
And thus, the point is that the definition of earth as "possessing odor" would be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) in the case of water and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by means of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatirekābhyām*), [this refers to] in water and so forth.

The meaning is that, according to the *Prakāśikā*, the perception of odor occurs when there is the existence of a conjunction with odor-bearing earth, and its absence occurs when that [conjunction] is absent; this is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
"By way of the relation of being conjoined with its own substratum":
"its own" refers to the earth-odor;
"its own substratum" is the earth.
The state of being conjoined with that [earth] exists in water and so forth.
One who grasps according to the literal expression is one who maintains the conceit that the definition is simply "possessing odor," without being delimited by a specific relation.
The meaning is: "by way of a relation distinct from those relations that serve as the basis for being the substratum of all.

Temporal and other such relations are the ones that serve as the basis for being the substratum of all; therefore, the property of being a relation distinct from those exists in inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth.
From the relations that constitute the nature of being a definition, [he means] the relations that delimit the nature of being a definition,
such as inherence (samavāya) and so forth;
[this implies] that inherence and the others function as relations precisely in their capacity as inherence-ness (samavāyatva) and so on.
This is clear in the *Vyadhikaraṇagādādharī*; [it is also found in] the *Tarkasaṅgraha*,
the section on the classification of earth (*pṛthivīvibhāga*).
That [matter] is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal is in the form of atoms;
the non-eternal is in the form of effects.
Furthermore, it is threefold, distinguished by way of body, sense faculty, and object.
The body is that of ourselves and others.
The sense faculty is the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*), which perceives odors and is located at the tip of the nose.
The object consists of earth, stone, and so forth.
It is of two kinds:
eternal and non-eternal. The eternal is that which has the nature of atoms.
It is impermanent and of the nature of an effect;
furthermore, it is threefold, distinguished as body, sense-faculty, and object. The body belongs to those such as ourselves.
The sense faculty that perceives odor is the nose, and it is located at the tip of the nose. Its object consists of earth, stone, and so forth.
The Dīpikā analyzes the earth:
"It is of two kinds."
Eternality is the state of not being the counter-positive of destruction;
non-eternality is the state of being the counter-positive of destruction.
He divides [the categories] again by another method, starting with "furthermore": the body is the locus of experience for the self;
it is that delimited by which experience arises within the self.
That is the locus of experience.

Experience (*bhoga*) is the direct perception of either pleasure or pain. [The definition of the self is: that which, while not being the substratum of manifested specific qualities other than sound, [is the locus of experience].
The nature of a sense organ (*indriyatva*) is being the substratum of the mental contact that is the cause of cognition.
An object (*viṣaya*) is that which is distinct from the body and the sense organs. And thus, a body possessing odor is an earthy body.
The sense organ possessing odor is the earthy sense organ; the object possessing odor is the earthy object— such is their respective definition.
He shows the body composed of earth as "the body";
he shows the sense-faculty composed of earth as "the sense-faculty."
"Grasper of odors" is the statement of its function;
"nose" is its designation; "at the tip of the nose" is the description of its physical basis.
The same should be understood for what follows.
He shows the domain of the earth element with the words "clay, stone, and so forth."— *Prakāśikā*.
It demonstrates that permanence and so forth reside within the characteristics of form, such as eternal earth-ness and so on—
by means of the phrase "permanence" and "in another way."

The word "earth" (pṛthivī) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. Here, eternal earth possesses the status of being included among objects (*viṣaya*), as it is characterized by the definition of an object—namely, being distinct from the body and the sense organs. Thus, earth is of three kinds.
Therefore, it should be understood that the statement "again, threefold" in the root text is consistent for this very reason.
However, some [hold]—
They describe the threefold nature of impermanent earth alone.
Following the order of the enumeration, he first states the definition of the body with the words "of the self" (ātmanaḥ).
The *āyatana* is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). Thus, he states the definition as it is constituted when combined: "that which is delimited by...
This means: that which is the delimiting factor for the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of either pleasure or pain. In this context...
The qualification "being the ultimate whole" must be added;
by this, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to the feet and so forth, even though they possess the status of being delimiters.

With the intention that "sensed-organ-ness" (*indriyatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*), just as "body-ness" (*śarīratva*) is not a genus because it would involve a cross-classification (*saṅkara*) with "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, he says: "arisen from something other than sound" (*śabdetarodbhūta*).
The term "existent" (sat) is included to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) to the self (ātman) and so forth;
"other than sound" (śabdetara) is included to exclude under-extension (avyāpti) in the case of the auditory organ (śrotra).

The term "manifest" (*udbhūta*) is included in order to exclude the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) that would otherwise arise because of the existence of non-manifest color-form (*anudbhūtarūpa*) and other specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) in the eye and other sense organs.
Manifestness (*udbhūtatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*).
Because there would be a confusion [of categories] due to [the property of] whiteness and so forth;
nor should it be argued that there are multiple instances of manifestedness (udbhūtatva) pervaded by whiteness and so forth.
Because it is untenable for [color] to be a cause in visual perception and so forth by virtue of having manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) and the like;
rather, non-manifestation (*anudbhūtatva*) is manifold, being pervaded by [qualities such as] whiteness and so forth.
Manifestness (*udbhūtatva*) consists in possessing the aggregate of the absence of that [non-manifestness].

And this [manifestness] exists even in conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth. Thus, in order to avoid the impossibility [of the definition] by taking conjunction—which is a quality other than sound yet is manifest—the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is included.

In the view of the ancients, the term "qualified" (viśeṣya) is included to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) to time and so forth; the phrase "cause of knowledge" (jñānakāraṇa) is included to exclude over-extension to that very same [time].

Since the conjunction of the parts of the object and the parts of the sense organ is the cause of perception, [the definition applies] to that part of the sense organ which is its substratum; furthermore,
according to the view of the Neo-Logicians (Navīna), it applies in the case of the perception of the absence of color in time and so forth.

The term "mind" (*manas*) is included to exclude time (*kāla*) and space (*deśa*), which are substrata of the eye-contact that serves as a cause by being a constituent of the sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*).
Nor [is it redundant] because [the definition already excludes them] by the phrase "provided it is other than the self" (*ātmānyatve sati*), since [time and space are not the self].

It must be asked: since it is possible to avoid over-extension [of the definition], what is the purpose of the cumbersome qualification "produced by something other than sound" and so forth? For if that were the case, then according to the view that the contact between the skin and the mind is a cause for all cognition whatsoever—
In that case, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*); enough with this elaboration.
"And thus" refers to each respective object.
The meaning is: "and in the case of [the definition] being a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) such as the body.

Now, an objection: since that definition is perfectly adequate by the inclusion of "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*) alone, it is improper to include "the state of being the perceiver of odor" (*gandhagrāhakatva*). And thus...

Desiring to dispel the suspicion that the statement "the sense-faculty is the grasper of odor" is fundamentally inappropriate, he explains its basis by focusing on the statement of its purpose: "it is the grasper of odor."
Later on, in such passages as "the sense-organ is the grasper of taste," and so forth. [Objection: But surely... [Bālapriyā]... again.

Regarding the passage "It is threefold due to the distinction between body, sense organ, and object," does this state a threefold division of the universal *pṛthivītva* (earthness), or rather of impermanent earth? It cannot be the first,
for if this division were of the universal *pṛthivītva*, then it would also apply to eternal earth.
It must be stated that [eternal earth] would have to be included within either the body, the sense organs, or the objects;
yet that is not possible.
For instance, first of all, its inclusion within the body is not possible, nor is it possible for eternal earth to be included in the sense organs.
Nor [is it] in the sense-faculties, because both of those are impermanent; nor [is it] in the object.
Because an object consisting of earth, stone, and so forth lacks permanence;
nor is it the second [alternative].

Anticipating the objection that the word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates that a further classification is being made of that which was already previously divided, he says: "In this context, of eternal earth," and so forth. And thus:
Furthermore, the category of earth itself is divided into three types;
since eternal earth is distinct from bodies and sense organs, it is included within the objects [of perception], and thus there is no logical inconsistency.
[This is] the state of affairs.
[Objection: Even if it can be somehow resolved here, the statement "it is threefold" again within the section on fire (*tejas*) does not cohere.
Because eternal light, which exists in the form of atoms, cannot be included within the four types of objects— terrestrial, celestial, digestive (gastric), and mineral—
since the property of being terrestrial and so forth is defined by being produced (*janya*).
Because the disjunction of an eternal [substance] is impossible,
this disjunction belongs only to non-eternal earth;
and since the word "again" (punar) serves as a rhetorical ornament of the sentence, there is no inconsistency— this is the intention of those who hold this view.
He states the opinion: "But some...
The phrase "some" indicates a lack of full conviction (*asvārasya*).
The reason for this is that because of the lack of conviction in the word "again" (*punar*), this division does not apply to impermanent earth; nor is it...

It should be stated that it is a "sentence ornament" (*vākyālaṅkāra*); for the status of the word *punaḥ* as a sentence ornament when employed at the beginning of a sentence has never been observed anywhere.
For it is observed in various places that the word *punaḥ*, when employed immediately after any given word, serves as a mere embellishment of the sentence;
furthermore, as for the word *punaḥ*...
Annambhaṭṭa’s own intention is also clearly that [the text] intends another classification, as evidenced by his introductory remark:
"He divides [them] again according to another method—'furthermore, they are of three kinds. Nor is it the case that...

Even if it could somehow be established that there is a division of the generality of earth (*pṛthivīsāmānya*) here, it must be stated that this is untenable within the section on fire (*tejaḥprakaraṇa*),
because in that context the terms "terrestrial" (*bhauma*) and so forth [do not apply].
The meaning is simply "connected with the earth" and so forth,
and not "produced by the earth"; and thus, since even the color of fire-atoms possesses the quality of being connected with the earth and so on, [the definition remains intact].
It is logical that [the body] is included within the objects [of experience].
The definition of the body is: that which is the locus of experience for the self.
The meaning of the genitive case following the word *ātman* (self) is inherence (*samavetatva*). This [inherence] is construed with enjoyment (*bhoga*).
Enjoyment, by name, is the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of either pleasure or pain.

The locus (*āyatana*) is that which serves as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). Thus, it is stated that the body is the delimiting factor for the direct perception of either pleasure or pain inherent in the self.
This definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*), as it applies to parts of the body such as the hands and feet.
Because even through the amputation of hands, feet, and so forth, there arises in the self the direct perception of either pleasure or pain;
therefore, [the definition] includes the qualification "being a final whole."
A qualification must be added:
"being a final whole" (antyāvayavitva) means being a composite substance (avayavitva) while not being the originator of another substance (dravyānārambhakatve sati).
Since hands and other such parts do not possess an ultimate absence (atyantābhāva) of being initiators of the body, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
Thus it is said: "that which delimits the direct perception of either pleasure or pain."
By the phrase "as far as... and so forth, [it is meant] because of the confusion [of categories] with respect to earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so on;
for, leaving aside the property of being a body (*śarīratva*), earth-ness exists in jars and the like.

The meaning is that there would be a confusion (saṅkara) because earth-ness (pṛthivītva) is absent from bodies composed of water and so forth, while body-ness (śarīratva) is present in them; yet both are co-present in an earthly body. Likewise, sense-faculty-ness (indriyatva) is not a genus (jāti).

Earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is excluded from the sense organ of taste (*rasana*) and others, while the nature of being a sense organ (*indriyatva*) is excluded from jars (*ghaṭa*) and the like; yet both coexist in the olfactory sense organ (*ghrāṇendriya*). Thus, there is a confusion (*saṅkara*) due to [the overlapping of] earth-ness and the other properties.
The point is that being a sense-faculty (*indriyatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*).
The term "existent" (*sat*) is included in the definition to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such things as the self (*ātman*).
If one were to state only this much— that the nature of a sense organ (*indriyatva*) consists in being the substratum of the mental contact that is the cause of cognition—

then there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because the self (*ātman*) also possesses the quality of being the substratum of that mental contact which serves as the cause of cognition, namely, the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanassaṃyoga*).
To exclude that [over-extension], the "real" (sat) clause is included.

And when that is inserted, there is no over-extension, because the property of being the substratum of those things other than sound which possess manifested specific qualities—such as cognition, pleasure, and so forth—exists only in the self (ātman). This is the meaning.

If the qualification "other than sound" were not included in the phrase "having a manifested specific quality," then the auditory organ would possess only the state of being the substratum of that which is a manifested specific quality in the form of sound,
and not the state of not being its substratum; thus, there would be the fallacy of under-extension (avyāpti).
It might [be so];

to exclude that, the qualification "other than sound" (*śabdetara*) is added. If the qualification "manifested" (*udbhūta*) were not applied to the specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), [the definition would over-apply] to the eye and other [senses].
Since there exists only the state of being the substratum for those specific qualities other than sound— such as unmanifest color and so forth— there would be a lack of pervasion (avyāpti).
To exclude that, the term "manifest" (udbhūta) is used.
Regarding the qualification:
if one were to state only "not being the substratum of qualities produced other than sound," without employing the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*),
it would fail because [sound] is indeed the substratum of the general quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*) called conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is other than sound.
There would be the possibility [of contact] existing in the sense organs, such as the eye;
to exclude that, the word "specific" (viśeṣa) is used. But surely, even if the word "specific" were not employed, conjunction could not be admitted [as the cause].

Anticipating the objection that since manifestness (*udbhūtatva*) does not exist [as a real entity], it is already excluded by the very word "manifest" (*udbhūta*), he says: "Manifestness is not a universal (*jāti*)," and so forth. Manifestness...
In the case of non-manifest white,
having abandoned whiteness; in the case of manifest blue, having abandoned manifestation.

Because there is an overlap (*sāṃkarya*)— namely, that both manifestedness (*udbhūtatva*) and whiteness (*śuklatva*) coexist in what is both manifested and white— manifestedness is not a universal (*jāti*),
nor is it subsumed under whiteness.

Manifestness (*udbhūtatva*) is one thing, while manifestness as pervaded by blueness (*nīlatvavyāpya-udbhūtatva*) is another; thus, manifestness as pervaded by whiteness (*śuklatvavyāpya-udbhūtatva*) and so forth is indeed manifold.
And so, having set aside whiteness...
It should not be said that there is no confusion [of categories] because manifestedness (*udbhūtatva*) does not exist;
for if manifestedness were manifold, then with respect to visual perception and the like—

Because it would follow that the uniform relationship between cause and effect— namely, that "the cause is that which possesses manifested color"— would be undermined; therefore, non-manifestation, as it subsists in those [substances] through the distinctions of white and so forth, is manifold.
Manifestness (*udbhūtatva*) consists precisely in possessing a collection of absences of non-manifestness;
and that alone has been included in the definition. Furthermore, that [manifestness] exists even in conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
For conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is indeed not non-manifest; since the state of possessing a collection of absences of non-manifestness exists therein,

and since the state of being the substratum of a conjunction whose substratum is that which possesses the aforementioned manifestness exists in the sense-faculties, [the definition] must include [this qualification] in order to avoid the fault of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*).
The intended meaning is that it is a "distinctive term" (*viśeṣapada*).

The "subject portion" (*viśeṣyadala*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to time (*kāla*) and other such factors. If the subject portion—defined as "being the substratum of the mental conjunction (*manassaṃyoga*) which is the cause of cognition"—were not employed, then [the definition would apply] to time.

Because there is an absence of any specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) whatsoever, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti), as [the definition] would apply to that which is not the substratum of manifested specific qualities other than sound.
However, when the qualifying portion (viśeṣya-dala) is included, [it refers to] that conjunction with the mind (manassaṃyoga) which serves as the cause of cognition.

The point is that since the conjunction of the self and the mind, or the conjunction of the mind and a sense organ, does not exist in time as their substratum, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
Regarding the conjunction with the mind, it is the cause of cognition.
The purpose of the qualification is stated as "in that very [time].

Since time is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), and pervasiveness consists in being conjoined with all corporeal substances, time possesses the status of being the substratum of conjunction with the mind. Thus, in time...
The term "cause of cognition" (jñānakāraṇa) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti).
The point is that there is no over-extension because mental contact (manassaṃyoga) related to time (kālānuyogika) lacks the status of being a cause of cognition.
He states the purpose of the term "mind" according to different opinions, beginning with "according to the opinion of the ancients," without employing the word "mind."

If it were stated merely that [the definition] is "being the substratum of the conjunction that is the cause of cognition," then, according to the view of the ancients, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the parts of the sense organ; for since the conjunction between the object and the part of the sense organ is also a cause of cognition, the status of being its substratum exists in those parts as well.
In the view of the Neo-Nyāya school, since the conjunction of the object and the sense organ alone is the cause of cognition,
it might be argued that over-extension (ativyāpti) to the parts of the sense organ is not possible.
Nevertheless, in the perceptual cognition "there is no color at this time," which has the absence of color as its qualificandum and the specific time as its qualifier,
the subjectness (viśeṣyatā) determined by the time conjoined with the eye functions as a means of contact (saṃnikarṣa).
Because it is a cause,

the visual contact that constitutes it is also a cause; thus, since the property of being the locus of that visual contact which serves as a cause of cognition exists in time, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
To exclude that [undesired consequence], the word "mind" (manaḥ) is included;
for if that were the case, there would be [the undesirable result] of the conjunction between the object, the sense organ, and a part [of the body].
The sense is that since the conjunction of the eye with kāla (time) does not possess the nature of a mental conjunction (*manassaṃyoga*),

there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the aforementioned definition by taking that [conjunction] as an instance; for previously, when the "existence" (*satyam*) clause was not included, [the definition would apply] to the self (*ātman*).

It was stated that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*). And that [over-extension] consists in possessing a collection (*kūṭa*) of absences of non-manifestness (*anudbhūtatva*), as defined by the aforementioned "manifestness" (*udbhūtatva*).
The meaning is that "manifestness" (udbhūtatva) is its substratum.

Even if one were to add the qualification "provided it is other than the self" (ātmānyatve sati) in order to avoid over-extension (ativyāpti), it would still be possible to exclude [the objection]; why then [is this necessary]?
He raises the objection that the qualification beginning with "other than sound" (*śabdetara*) and so forth is overly cumbersome by saying, "If not," and he provides the resolution by saying,
"That being the case."

If it is stated that [the definition of the self] is "being the substratum of the mind-contact which is the cause of cognition, while being distinct from the self," then because the skin is distinct from the self and is also the substratum of the skin-mind contact which serves as a cause of cognition, [it would follow that the skin is the self].
There would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to leather;
the meaning is that to prevent this, one must provide the more cumbersome qualification beginning with "other than sound" (śabdetara).
The Compendium of Reasoning:
Definition of Water (AnTs 11). Water is that which possesses cold touch.
They are of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal ones are in the form of atoms;
the non-eternal ones are in the form of effects.
Furthermore, they are of three kinds, distinguished by way of body, sense organ, and object.
The body [of water] is in the world of Varuṇa;
the sense organ is the gustatory organ (*rasana*) which perceives taste and is located at the tip of the tongue.
The object consists of rivers, oceans, and so forth.
Water is that which possesses the quality of cold touch; it is of two kinds:
eternal and non-eternal.
They are eternal in the form of atoms;
they are non-eternal in the form of effects.
Furthermore, they are of three kinds, distinguished as body, sense organ, and object.
The body resides in the world of Varuṇa;
the sense organ that perceives taste is the tongue, and it is located at the tip of the tongue.
The object consists of rivers, oceans, and so forth.
The *Dīpikā* states the definition of water:

Regarding the term "cold" (*śīta*): in order to avoid the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of water that has arisen and then perished, what is intended is the possession of a sub-genus of substantiality (*dravyatvāparajāti*) that is co-located with the quality of cold touch (*śītasparśa*). In instances such as "the stone slab is cold," the manifestation of the cold touch occurs precisely through connection with water.
There is no over-extension [of the definition].
Everything else is to be explained according to the previous method. — *Prakāśikā*
Regarding the phrase "co-inherent with cold touch," the purpose of the qualification therein is to be inferred according to the manner previously stated.
It should be understood that the establishment of the genus *jalatva* (the nature of water) is by virtue of its being the delimitor of the generality of being a producer of viscidity (*sneha*);
everything else follows the previously stated method.

The meaning is that, following the method described in the definition of earth, one should substitute "possessing cold touch" for "possessing odor" [in the definition of water], while retaining "eternality" and so forth as well as the characteristics of having a body and so on;
the same should be inferred for what follows as well.

It should be inferred according to the manner previously stated. This is because if one were to state merely "the possession of a genus that is pervaded by substantiality" (*dravyatvavyāpyajātimattva*), [the definition would be too narrow].
There would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to earth, which possesses the genus "earthness" (pṛthivītva) that is pervaded by "substance-ness" (dravyatva).
To exclude this, the qualifier "co-existent with cold touch" (śītasparśasamānādhikaraṇa) is applied to the genus.

By including the term "pervaded by substance-ness" (*dravyatvavyāpya*), the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to earth and the other substances is avoided, based on the genus of existence (*sattājāti*) which resides in water and possesses the touch of cold.
Furthermore, being pervaded by substance-ness means having a distribution that is narrower than that of substance-ness, and not—
The meaning is that it is the state of not occurring in that [quality] which is empty [of substancehood];

therefore, by taking the genus *dravyatva* (substancehood), the aforementioned fault does not arise. [Regarding the phrase: "by way of being the delimiting factor for the production of viscidity (*sneha*)."

The meaning is that the universal *jalatva* (water-ness) is established by the following inference: "The causality residing in water— which is delimited by the relation of identity and is the counter-correlative of the effect-ness residing in viscidity (sneha), which is itself delimited by the relation of inherence— is delimited by some property, because it is causality."
The Compendium of Reasoning:
Definition of Fire (Tejas).
AnTs 12: Fire is that which possesses hot touch.
That is of two kinds: eternal and impermanent. The eternal is the form of the atom;
the impermanent is the form of the effect.
Furthermore, it is threefold, distinguished by body, sense organ, and object.
The body is in the world of the sun;
the sense organ is the eye, which perceives form and resides at the tip of the black pupil.
The object is of four kinds, distinguished as terrestrial, celestial, alimentary, and mineral. Terrestrial refers to fire and so forth.
Celestial fuel consists of lightning and the like;
the digestive fire of the stomach is the cause of the transformation of what has been eaten; and that produced from mines consists of gold and so forth.
Fire has the quality of hot touch. It is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. That which is eternal is in the form of atoms.
The impermanent is that which has the nature of an effect;
furthermore, it is of three kinds, distinguished as body, sense-faculty, and object.
The body is in the world of the sun;
the sense faculty that perceives form is the eye,
and it resides at the tip of the black pupil.
The object is of four kinds, distinguished as terrestrial, celestial, digestive, and mineral. Terrestrial consists of fire and so forth.
Celestial fuel consists of lightning and the like; that which causes the digestion of what has been eaten is the digestive fire within the stomach;
and that produced from mines consists of gold and other such minerals.
The *Dīpikā* states that heat is the defining characteristic of fire: "possessing hot touch.
This is because the cognition "the water is hot" and similar instances are dependent upon conjunction with fire.
There is no over-extension [of the definition].
He divides the objects [of perception]—namely, "terrestrial" and so forth. This is the doctrine that gold is composed of light (*taijasa*).
If it is argued that gold is composed of earth (pārthiva) because it is yellow and heavy, like turmeric— no;
for we observe that when there is contact with intense fire, the fluidity in substances such as clarified butter is destroyed.
And because the destruction of fluidity in substances such as ghee situated in water is not observed, it is determined that, in the absence of an obstructing factor,

there is a causal relationship between the conjunction with fire and the destruction of the fluidity of earthy substances; therefore, gold— by virtue of being the substratum of a fluidity that is not destroyed even when in contact with intense fire [is established as non-earthly].

Since it cannot be established as being earthen, and since another liquid substance is proven by its acting as an obstacle to the destruction of the liquidity of the yellow substance, and since it cannot be water because it is the substratum of adventitious liquidity, and since it is not included among wind and the other elements due to its possession of color, its status as luminous (taijasa) is established.
The non-perception of its hot touch and luminous form is due to their being obstructed by the color and touch of the supporting earthly substrate;
therefore, it is established that gold is fiery in nature.
In the root text,
"without fuel" (*abindhanam*) means that which has water (*adbhiḥ*) as its fuel (*indhana*), that is, its means of ignition (*dīpana*).
Regarding the phrase "of what has been eaten": it means that the transformation (*pariṇāma*) or digestion (*paripāka*) of the food, such as boiled rice and so forth, is the cause in that regard.
"Produced from a mine": a mine (*ākara*) is an excavation; the meaning is that it is born there.
This establishes the luminous nature (*taijasatva*) of gold.
He raises a doubt in order to establish [the point], saying "nanu" (but surely) in the *Dīpikā*.

Having stated the reason of yellowness (*pītatva*) as proving its being earthen (*pārthivatva*), he states the reason proving the absence of luminosity (*taijasatva*), saying "due to weight" (*gurutvāt*).
By this, a heterogeneous yellow color is admitted in gold, which is of the nature of fire (taijasa), on the strength of the uncontradicted perceptual cognition: "Gold is yellow.
And thus, regarding its being of the nature of fire...
The misconception of some who claim that "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) is not established due to its being non-obstructive is refuted;
for it is impossible to state such a thing because weight (gurutva) is imperceptible. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Regarding gold...
In order to establish that [the substance] is distinct by virtue of being the substratum of yellow color and heaviness,
and to eliminate the suspicion of the reason being irrelevant (*aprayojaka*) within the inference, he establishes the supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*) based on the causal relationship:
"because it is not absolutely non-luminous," and so forth.
"Of gold," and so forth.
The formulation of the inference is to be understood as follows: Gold is not composed of earth, provided there is no obstructing factor.
Because it is a substratum of fluidity that is not destroyed when in contact with intense fire; for whatever is not thus [is] not thus, like earth.
[The term] "asati" is included to prevent a deviation in the case of ghee and the like situated in water.
Regarding the term "obstructing factor" (*pratibandhaka*):

the phrase "when there is contact with intense fire" is included to prevent a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), which possesses fluidity that does not coexist with the conjunction of fire [at lower temperatures].

Regarding the phrase "upon the establishment of another liquid substance": [the argument is that] a yellow substrate in contact with intense fire is conjoined with another liquid substance which prevents the destruction of its liquidity, even when there is contact with intense fire.

Its establishment should be understood through the following inference: "It is [fire], because, while being the substratum of non-interrupted fluidity, it possesses weight, like ghee and the like situated in water.
He prevents the inference from terminating by taking water and other such substances as the subject, stating: "accidental" (*naimittika*). Now, [an objection]:
Since the fiery nature of gold is untenable due to the non-perception of its hot touch and luminous form, he says "of that" (*tasya*) and "due to obstruction" (*pratibandhāt*).
"By way of defects," and so forth; "gold is made of earth" (bālapriyā).
In the root text, the proponent [of the prima facie view] asserts the earth-nature (*pārthivatva*) of gold by means of two reasons: its yellowness and its heaviness, just like turmeric.

It has been established. In that regard, one might object that since the proof of earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is possible through the single reason of yellowness (*pītatva*), the presentation of a second reason in the form of heaviness (*gurutva*) is redundant;
anticipating this, he says: "the proof of earth-ness."
And likewise, yellowness is a prover of being earthen,
whereas heaviness is a prover of being distinct from fire; and it is not the case that...
It should not be said that the second inference is redundant;
for since one's own established doctrine must be stated after first refuting the views of others, this [inference] serves to refute the opponent's assertion that [the eyes] are composed of fire.
The sense is that a second inference is necessary.
[Objection: But surely, by the very proof of gold's being earthen, its lack of luminosity (taijasatva) is determined by implication.

If it is argued that there is the futility of formulating another inference because it is possible to establish both the distinctness from the earthen and the distinctness from the luminous by the single reason of yellowness alone— on this point, they say:
In the inference "gold is earthy" (*suvarṇaṃ pārthivam*), the property of being gold (*suvarṇatva*) is not the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

For if it were so, silver— since it is not encompassed by the delimiting factor of the subject— would result in the fallacy of the unestablished probans (*asiddhi*) with respect to earthiness (*pārthivatva*) therein.
Furthermore, it would involve the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) in formulating a separate inference for that purpose.

Nor can "gold-ness" (*hiraṇyatva*), which is common to silver, serve as the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). For if that were the case, the reason (*hetu*)—the property of yellowness (*pītatva*)—would be absent from silver, which is the substratum of the subject-delimiting condition.
Because it would follow that there is the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*). Therefore, one must follow the reason of gravity (*gurutva*); for gravity, however—
"Since it also exists in silver, there is no fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*).
In reality, however, the proponent here has no primary concern with proving that gold is composed of earth (*pārthivatva*). Regarding gold...

Since it has not been stated by anyone that there is an absence of earth-ness (*pārthivatva*), the prima facie objection—that earth-ness itself must simply be the absence of that [absence]—does not arise;
as the author of the text states: "Gold and so forth are produced from mines."
Since it was stated that the preceding gold possesses luminosity (*tejas*), the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) alone is logical—that gold above that [silver] is not luminous.
For this very reason, it is said: "Therefore, gold is composed of light (*taijasa*)."
In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), even the summary (*upasaṃhāra*) is consistent;
and thus, it is also the opponent's intended thesis here that gold is distinct from fire.
However, it cannot be established by the reason of yellowness that gold is distinct from fire,
because even though gold is indeed fire, this is due to the force of uncontradicted perception in the form "gold is yellow."
In that case, because yellowness is possible [therein],
the second reason is presented as "because of weight" (*gurutvāt*). Even though gold is of the nature of fire (*tejas*), there is an absence of the perception that "gold is heavy."
It is impossible to say that weight is established [as a separate quality];
therefore, the intended meaning here is understood to be that weight is capable of proving its difference from fire.
And this point has been clarified by the passage beginning with "etena" and so forth,
as stated in the Dīpikā:
