"In the case of contact with extreme fire," and so forth.
This is the meaning: when there is contact with extreme fire, the fluidity that exists in earth such as ghee and the like undergoes destruction. By this...
The causal relation is established that intense contact with fire (*atyantāgni-saṃyoga*) is the cause for the destruction of the fluidity residing in earth;
however, this concerns the fluidity of ghee situated in the middle of a balance scale.

To exclude the suspicion of a deviation from the positive concomitance (anvaya-vyabhicāra)— namely, that destruction does not occur even when there is contact with fire for an extremely long duration— the qualification "provided no obstacle exists" must be added to the stated causal relationship. By means of this:

The causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) results as follows: intense contact with fire occurring at a time when there is no presence of an obstructing factor is the cause for the destruction of the fluidity of earthy substances;
however, in the case of ghee situated in water, it is the [fluidity] of the water [that is destroyed].

Because there is an obstructing factor, there is no destruction of fluidity. Thus, due to the absence of the cause—namely, contact with fire unaccompanied by an obstructing factor—there is an absence of the effect, which is the destruction of fluidity; therefore, there is no deviation from the previously stated positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of gold.
However, even when there is contact with extreme fire, the liquidity of the earthly portion existing therein is not destroyed;
therefore, there must be something that acts as an obstacle to the destruction of that liquidity.
It should be said that substance exists in gold;
that very [substance] is fire.
And thus, in gold...

One must accept two constituent parts: the earthy portion, which is the substratum of the yellow color and heaviness uniquely experienced in earth, and the fiery portion, which acts as the impediment to the fluidity residing in that [earthy portion].
Likewise, if this were not accepted, then since all gold would be composed of earth (*pārthiva*), its fluidity would perish;
and thus, upon contact with intense fire, [the gold would no longer exist as such].
The part consisting of the substratum of liquidity [is] conjoined with another liquid substance that prevents the destruction of its own liquidity,
because even when there is contact with an intense fire, it possesses a liquidity that is not destroyed,
like ghee situated in the midst of water; thus, by this inference, another liquid substance acting as a preventer is established.

"By the inference: 'That substance is not earthen, because, in the absence of an obstructing factor, it possesses fluidity that is not destroyed even when there is intense contact with fire; for whatever is not thus is not thus, like earth,' the distinctness from earth of such another substance is established. Regarding that...
When, by the inference "that other substance is not water,
because it possesses fluidity caused by heat," the absence of water-ness (*jalatva*) is established,
and when, by the inference "that other substance is not air and so forth, because it possesses color," the absence of being air and so forth is established, that substance is fiery (*taijasa*).

Its nature as consisting of light (*taijasatva*) is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*), namely: "because it is a substance while being distinct from the eight [substances] beginning with earth.
Nor is it unestablished that such a substance possesses color; how then...
Therefore, it must be stated that the distinction between air and the other elements is what is to be proven;

for if air were devoid of color, it would— just like air itself— be impossible for it to possess the properties of being a cause for the destruction of fluidity or for acting as an obstacle [to it], and thus one must accept that it possesses color.
This is because [the author] intends [to show] that [this property] is necessary;
in fact, by the very reason of possessing occasional fluidity (*naimittikadravatvavattva*), the distinction from air and other elements can also be established.

And thus it is established that gold— which is determined to be a substance by virtue of its being fire (tejas)— is designated by both specific terms such as *suvarṇa* and *hiraṇya*, as well as by general terms, [precisely because it is] an obstructing substance.
The truth here is this:
intense contact with fire, qualified by the absence of an obstructing factor, is the cause for the destruction of the fluidity of earthy substances.
The causal relationship is necessary; in this case, the absence of the effect— namely, the destruction of the fluidity residing in the earthly portion within the gold—
is necessitated by the absence of the cause, which is the intense contact with fire qualified by the absence of an obstructing factor.
There is no dispute on this point: in that case, the absence of the cause, which consists in the absence of such a qualified entity,
does not arise from the absence of the qualificand.

Since the substantive (viśeṣya), consisting of contact with an intense fire, exists there, it must be stated that [the absence of melting] is due solely to the absence of the qualifier (viśe�ṣaṇa), which consists of the non-existence of an obstructer. Therefore, it must be stated that some other liquid substance acts as an obstructer in that case; for that too—

If there were another substance acting as an obstacle to the destruction of that fluidity within earthiness, and yet another for that [substance] as well, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would result;
therefore, [this occurs] without any further obstacle.
"Because its fluidity is non-perishing, it is not earth"—
this passage from the *Dīpikā* accepts that there is fluidity in the earthy portion as well as fluidity in the fiery portion.
It is understood that [the process] has commenced, due to the natural force of the two phrases "destruction of the liquidity of the yellow substance" and "another liquid substance.
However, in the *Muktāvalī*, it is said: "like a powder of ink situated in the midst of water..."
By the passage beginning with "because of its non-fluidity" (*tasyādrutatvāt*), the very absence of fluidity in the earthy portion is established;
according to that view, the inference proving the luminous nature (*taijasatva*) of gold is indeed different.
In the *Prakāśikā*: "Gold is something distinct from the substratum of its yellowness and weight";
that is, [distinct] from what is denoted by the word "gold."
The meaning is that the specific portion [of gold] is distinct from the portion that is earth;
this is for the purpose of removing the suspicion of the argument being "unproving" (aprayojaka) in the inference regarding that which is denoted by the word "gold."

In the inference "gold is non-earthy because, when there is intense contact with fire, it is the locus of a liquidity that is not destroyed," which establishes the distinctness of a specific portion [of earth] from earth,
[the condition is] "when there is intense contact with fire."

In response to the doubt that the reason— consisting in being the substratum of a fluidity that is not subject to destruction— might exist while the probandum— consisting in non-earthiness— does not, which would render the argument inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), [the author] provides this to ward it off: "If gold were earthy, then, upon contact with intense fire..."
It would be nothing other than the substratum of fluidity in the process of being destroyed;
for absolute conjunction with fire is the cause for the destruction of terrestrial fluidity.
The meaning is that he states such a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*).
The phrase "when there is no impediment" (*asati pratibandhake*) means "qualified by the absence of an impediment" (*pratibandhakābhāvaviśiṣṭam*).
Its positive concomitance (anvaya) with liquidity [is established];

and its qualification (vaiśiṣṭya) is by way of the relation of co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), which consists in subsisting in the same locus at the same time, as constituted by conjunction (saṃyoga) and inherence (samavāya).

The phrase "when there is contact with extreme fire" also means "qualified by contact with extreme fire" through the aforementioned relation of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) as constituted by inherence (samavāya).
And its positive concomitance (anvaya) exists only with respect to liquidity;
this is for the purpose of avoiding a deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases such as ghee situated in the midst of water,
where the probandum— being non-earthen— is absent.
The meaning is that this is because of the existence of the reason consisting in the nature of liquidity which is not being cut off.
"In ghee and the like, which possess liquidity not co-located with fire-contact" means in ghee and so forth situated on a scale.
Regarding the passage beginning with "that which is in contact with an eternal fire," etc.:

if the mere state of being a substratum of yellowness (*pītimāśrayatva*) constitutes the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), and if the inference is intended to be established as delimited by that very condition;
Since even a substrate of yellowness that lacks contact with fire is included within the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*),
the reason— which consists of contact with fire— would be unestablished in part (*bhāgāsiddhi*) therein; therefore,
the qualification "in constant contact with fire" is added to the subject to exclude that possibility.

Since the fiery portion in contact with an eternal fire would be devoid of the property to be proven (the probandum), there would be a contradiction (bādha); therefore, the phrase "substratum of yellowness" is included to prevent that.
This is because another liquid substance would not act as an impediment.
Even if that [property] were postulated, it would be of no use in the present context; thus, to indicate this, the qualification of the probandum is "obstructing the destruction of fluidity.
This applies to cases such as ghee situated in the midst of water.

The qualification "liquid" (drava) is employed with the intention that, since it is observed that only a liquid substance acts as an impediment to the destruction of the liquidity of an earthy substance, the impeding substance in the present case must likewise be liquid. This concludes the inference.
The meaning is that this is intended to exclude an *arthāntara* (an irrelevant conclusion) consisting in the establishment of a matter not sought to be known.
Now, if gold were composed of fire (*taijasa*), then [the qualities of fire], namely the hot touch and the bright white color, which are the two qualities of fire—
There would be perception [of heat] in gold;

since there is no perception of those two in gold, the purpose of the passage beginning with "tasya" (of that) is to dispel the doubt that gold is not composed of fire (*taijasa*). Thus he says: "But surely..."
Regarding the phrase "hot touch":
although hot touch and white color actually exist in gold, they act as obstructions to perception with respect to the touch and color belonging to the earthy [substratum].

It is stated in the *Dīpikā*: "And that status as an impediment is by way of being a defect (*doṣa*), and not by way of being a cognition of the absence of that [property] with respect to the cognition of its possession; intending this, he says—"
"By way of the faults," and so forth;
this is the *Tarkasaṃgraha*,
the definition of air (*vāyu*).
Wind is that which is devoid of form and possesses tangibility.
It is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. The eternal is in the form of atoms.
It is impermanent and of the nature of an effect.
Furthermore, it is threefold, distinguished as body, sense-faculty, and object.
The body exists in the world of wind.
The faculty is the skin, which perceives touch and resides throughout the entire body;
its object is the cause of the trembling of trees and so forth.
The wind that moves within the body is the *prāṇa*.
Although it is one, it receives the designations of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth due to the distinction of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Wind is that which is devoid of color and possesses tangibility;
it is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.
Thus: eternal in the form of atoms;
non-eternal in the form of effects;
furthermore, it is of three kinds—
Due to the distinction between body, sense faculty, and object:
the body is in the world of wind; the sense faculty is the skin, which perceives touch.
The function of all bodies is as follows:
wind (vāyu) is the object that causes the shaking of trees and other things;
wind moving within the body is the vital breath (prāṇa).
And although it is one, it receives the designations of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth due to the difference in its limiting adjuncts (upādhi). —
Dīpikā.
He defines air as "that which is devoid of color";
the phrase "possessing touch" is included to exclude over-extension to space and other such entities.
The term "devoid of color" (*rūparahita*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to earth and the other elements.
To the question of where the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is included, he says: "in the body" (*śarīre*).
"And that" means that there is only one single vital breath (prāṇa) which, due to the difference in its locations, is designated by such terms as "prāṇa," "apāna," and so forth.
Air is to be inferred from touch.
For instance: this non-hot-and-cold touch which is perceived when air is blowing must be supported by something, because it is a quality, just like color.
Nor is its substratum earth,
because it is a rule that what is derived from earth possesses manifest color, just as it possesses manifest touch;
nor is it water or fire.
Because it possesses a touch that is neither hot nor cold;
nor is it the fourfold all-pervading [elements], for that would entail the consequence of being perceived everywhere.
It is not the mind, because the touch of an atom is beyond the senses.
Therefore, that which is the substrate of the perceived touch is indeed air (*vāyu*).
But is it not the case that air is perceptible?
If it is argued that [air] is [a substance] because it is the substratum of perceptible touch, like a jar—no;
for "possessing manifest color" (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*). [For wherever there is perceptible touch, there is manifest color, provided that it is a substance.]
The state of being a perception produced by an external sense organ,
wherein there is the possession of manifested color-form (*udbhūtarūpavattva*),
constitutes the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*).

In the case [of air], there is the non-pervasion of the probans. Nor does it follow that fire situated in heated water would likewise be imperceptible, for that is accepted [as a possibility]. Therefore, because it is devoid of color, air is imperceptible.
"The body is the illuminator"— such is the meaning; and thus, the intention is that [the self] is included within the domain of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
"Due to the difference in location" means due to the difference in locations stated in the *Kośa*, such as "Prāṇa is in the heart. [The breath] [proceeds] through the mouth and the nose.
It is called *prāṇa* because of its exiting and entering;
*apāna* because it leads waste products and so forth downward;
and *samāna* because it equalizes the fire for the purpose of digesting food.
It is called *udāna* because it leads [the breath] upward;
it is called *vyāna* because it extends through the openings of the channels.
He sets forth his own view: "It is to be inferred by touch."
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Earth is not the substratum of this [earth] which possesses a perceptible touch.
Regarding the term "tetrad":
this is intended to establish the distinctness of each [element], beginning with space (*ākāśa*).
"Because it would follow that [the object] would be perceived everywhere"—
this refers to the passage beginning with "of touch," etc.,
regarding space and so forth.
The intended meaning is "due to its pervasiveness.
"Perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) means being an object of perception produced by the external sense organs.

The term "perceptible" is included to exclude the possibility of a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*), which has as its substratum a touch that is not manifested (*anudbhūta*).

"Because it is a limiting condition (upādhi). The meaning is that, since it is possible to infer the deviation from the probandum (sādhya) based on the deviation from the probandum-possessor (hetu) due to the presence of a limiting condition, the establishment of [the property of] being perceptible (pratyakṣatva) does not occur. Now, [one might object]:

Since such perceptibility exists even in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, and since manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is absent there, [manifested color] does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*); how then can it be a limiting condition (*upādhi*)? To this he says: "Where... The sense is that this limiting condition pervades the probandum as delimited by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Thus, even though it is the locus of a perceptible touch, if its own perceptibility is not admitted due to the absence of manifest color (*udbhūta-rūpa*), it would follow that it is imperceptible;
this is the meaning of the phrase "due to the absence of manifest color."
The meaning of "the fourfold lordship does not exist" is not that [the subject] possesses a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the property of being the fourfold lordship.
Even if one were to analyze each [of the categories], the desired conclusion would not be established because of the possibility of various subdivisions within those four.
Rather, the intended meaning is that the substratum of the perceived touch is distinct from any one among the others, beginning with space and ending with the self; with this intention, he says:
This is intended as a proof for each individual distinction, such as space and so forth;
and likewise regarding the reason:
"being the substratum of perceptible touch."

The argument intended here is: "Being perceptible is deviant [with respect to being produced by effort], because it is deviant with respect to manifested color (udbhūtarūpa), which is the pervader of being perceptible; for whatever is deviant with respect to the pervader of X is itself deviant with respect to X."

Now, in the inference "Air is the object of perception produced by an external sense-organ, because it is the substratum of perceptible touch," it is argued that *udbhūtarūpa* (manifested color) cannot serve as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

He raises an objection, beginning with "But [regarding] such perceptibility," on the grounds that the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) lacks pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*), because manifested color is absent in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, which are objects of perception produced by external sense organs.
The meaning is: "of being the object of a perception produced by an external sense-organ. And likewise:
the subject (*pakṣa*) is air (*vāyu*).

The meaning is as follows: "dharma residing therein" is substantiality (*dravyatva*); that which is delimited by it, qualified by it through the relation of co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), is the probandum (*sādhya*). "Being the object of perception produced by external sense organs" is its pervader (*vyāpaka*).
And thus, [the probandum] is "being the object of perception produced by external sense organs as qualified by substantiality."
It does not exist in qualities and so forth, because there is an absence of the qualifying attribute "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) therein;
rather, it exists only in substances such as a jar and the like.

And in that case, since manifest color exists, it is logical for manifest color to function as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because it pervades the probandum as delimited by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). For a limiting condition is that which pervades the probandum alone.

It is of three kinds: that which pervades the probandum as delimited by the property of the subject (pakṣadharma), and that which pervades the probandum as delimited by the probans (sādhana). The point is that this [present case] is the middle variety of such a limiting condition (upādhi).
The word "thus" (*evam*) is to be explained as follows:
its explanation is that even though it is the locus of a perceptible touch, it is not admitted to be perceptible due to the absence of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*).

The meaning is that the absence of perceptibility is established by the principle that "the absence of the pervader entails the absence of the pervaded," because of the absence of manifested color— which is a pervader of the probandum— in air.
Now, the *Dīpikā*, the procedure for emanation and reabsorption.

The sequence of the arising and destruction of the four elements—earth and the others—in their state as effects is now described. By the power of the Lord’s desire to create, motion arises in the atoms. Thereupon—
When there is a conjunction of two atoms, a dyad is produced;
by three dyads alone, a triad is produced.
In this manner, through the sequence beginning with the tetrad (caturaṇuka), the great earth, the great waters, the great fire, and the great wind arise.
Thus, when the effect-substance has arisen,
through the force of the desire to withdraw [the world], the disjunction of two atoms occurs by means of motion, resulting in the destruction of the dyad;
in this manner, the destruction of earth and the other elements occurs.
The traditional doctrine holds that the destruction of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) results from the destruction of its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*),
whereas the destruction of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) results from the destruction of its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
The moderns, however, maintain that in all cases, the destruction of a substance results from the destruction of its non-inherent cause.
But what is the proof for the actual existence of atoms?
It is said: [it is seen] everywhere in the rays of the sun passing through a lattice window.

Whatever substance is perceived as most subtle possesses parts, because it is a visible substance, like a jar. Even the constituent part of a triad (tryaṇuka) possesses parts, because it is the originator of something large, like a potsherd.
That which is the constituent part of a dyad (dvyaṇuka) is itself the atom (paramāṇu).
And that [cause] must be eternal, because if it too were an effect, it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress.
Regarding the reality of creation and dissolution, the very scripture stating, "As before, the Creator fashioned [the world] again," is the authoritative proof.
Furthermore, the destruction of all effect-substances constitutes an intermediate dissolution (*avāntara-pralaya*).
"The destruction of all entities and their effects is the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); this is the distinction," says the *Prakāśikā*.

One might raise the objection: "Since objects such as jars are merely aggregates of atoms and no distinct whole (avayavin) exists, the classification of the four elements—earth and the rest—as either eternal or non-eternal is untenable. To address this doubt:

He precludes [the objection] with the words "now" (*idānīm*), meaning immediately after the description of the four elements beginning with earth. Regarding the phrase "destruction of the dyad" (*vyaṇukanāśa*), the full expression is "due to the destruction of the conjunction of two atoms" (*paramāṇudvayasaṃyoganāśāt*), and so forth.
"In all cases" means in the case of produced substances and universals; in all such cases, a single uniform method is appropriate.
This is the intended meaning.
"Because it is a substance that is visible" means:
because it is a substance while possessing visibility.
The qualifiers and the qualified are included in order to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as with respect to the self (*ātman*);
nor is this [reason] unproven (*aprayojaka*).

This is to be suspected: since magnitude (*mahattva*), which is a cause for visual perception, must depend upon a *truṭi* (the smallest atom), it is impossible to accept that [magnitude] as being produced by the number of parts (*avayava-saṅkhyā*) without [the atom] possessing parts (*sāvayavatva*).
This is the summary. [The word] "all" is used because the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of any produced substance (*janyadravya*) exists even now.
It is "an effect" (*kārya*) because destruction is impossible for eternal substances;
it is "substance" (*dravya*) because qualities such as color residing in atoms exist even at that time.

Since destructions cannot themselves be destroyed, they persist even during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya); thus, [the category] exists as a positive entity—this is the general direction of the argument.
— *Bālapriyā* (The Child’s Delight)
"Of the mere heap of atoms" means "of the collection of atoms alone. "Of a separate whole" [means...]

The meaning is that of a whole (avayavin) distinct from atoms; [the opponent claims] the statement regarding division is untenable because of the absence of the four [elements] beginning with earth, which are non-eternal.
Such is the meaning. In the root text, "by the force of the desire to act" means "by the force of the desire to create.
"By three dyads alone," [is the intended sense].
The production of a triad (tryaṇuka) from two dyads (dvyaṇuka) does not occur,
because the term "triad" would be untenable; for that term is applied on the basis of having three atoms as its constituent parts.
Having understood it as stated thus:
"By virtue of the desire to withdraw the effect-substance. This means:
by virtue of the Lord's desire for withdrawal directed toward the effect-substance.
"Due to the destruction of the non-inherent cause":
that which is the non-inherent cause of the dyad is the conjunction of two atoms.
The meaning is that from its destruction, there is the destruction of the dyad;
that is, from the destruction of the inherent cause,
there is the destruction of the triad— referring to the dyad which is the inherent cause of that triad.
The meaning is that the destruction of the triad (tryaṇuka) results from [the destruction of its parts].
However, it cannot be said that the destruction of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) results from the destruction of its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa).
The meaning is that the destruction of the atom, which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), is impossible.
[This refers to the passage beginning with] "the sunbeam through a lattice," and so forth.
The distinction is that the first inference establishes the dyad (dvyaṇuka), while the second inference establishes the atom (paramāṇu).
Regarding the compound *cākṣuṣadravyatvāt* (because of being a visible substance),
it is analyzed as "that which is both visible (*cākṣuṣa*) and a substance-ness (*dravyatva*).

Since this very [property of] visible substance-ness exists in the self (*ātman*), the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to that [self], which lacks the absence of having parts (*sāvayavatvābhāva*).
It may be so. Therefore, that which is both visual (*cākṣuṣa*) and a substance (*dravya*) is a "visual substance" (*cākṣuṣadravya*); its state [is what is meant]. 1.
Regarding the term *tritvasaṃkhyāka*: the analysis (*vigraha*) is "that which has three atoms is a triad (*tryaṇuka*). And thus...
The ground for the application of the term *tryaṇuka* (triad) is its having atoms qualified by the number three as their constituent parts.
The point is that this [ground] is consistent only when a triad is produced from three dyads (*dvyaṇuka*).
[This is] its visual substance.
The compound "bhāvaḥ" (existence) is intended here as a tatpuruṣa;
by this, it results that the reason is "substantiality qualified by visibility."

And the qualification [of the reason] is by way of the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Since the qualifying attribute of "being visible" (*akṣuṣatva*) is absent in the self (*ātman*), the reason consisting of "qualified substantiality" (*viśiṣṭadravyatva*) does not exist there; thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
With this intention, he says:
"The meaning is 'because of being a substance while possessing visibility'"; for if only "visibility" were stated...

Since "visibility" (cākṣuṣatva) exists in color-form (rūpa) and so forth—which possess the absence of the probandum (sādhya), namely "having parts"—there is a deviation (vyabhicāra). To exclude this, the term "substance-ness" (dravyatva) is included.
If only "substance-ness" were stated, [the deviation would occur] in the self (ātman).
The term "deviation" (vyabhicāra) refers to the occurrence [of the reason] in the absence of the probandum; to exclude that, "substancehood" (dravyatva) is introduced.
If only "substancehood" were stated, there would be deviation with respect to the self (ātman); therefore, to exclude that, [the qualification is added].
The inclusion of "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*) consists in being the object of a perception produced by the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
Regarding the terms "the qualified" (*viśeṣya*) and "the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*): the qualified is substantiality (*dravyatva*), and the qualifier is...
And visibility [is the reason];
nor is this [reason] irrelevant;
let the reason consisting of being a visible substance be accepted.

[the sequence is]: "he knows," "he desires," "he exerts effort," and "he acts."

In order to demonstrate that, in sequence, effort is the cause with respect to the general effect, the desire to act (cikīrṣā) is the cause of effort, and knowledge is the cause of the desire to act, the triad was stated in the *Dīpikā*.
The intended meaning is that the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is simply "being produced by volitional effort" (*kṛtijanyatvam*).

Now, one might object: since the term *sarvavit* (all-knowing) has the same meaning as the term *sarvajña* (all-knowing) in the scriptural passage, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," [the two terms must refer to the same thing].
Anticipating the objection that this is a tautology, he says: "The meaning of the root *vidhā*.
Thus, by the word "omniscient" (*sarvajña*), knowledge having all things as its object is expressed in a general sense, such as through the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*).
By the term "all-knowing" (sarvavit),
knowledge having all things as its object is expressed through specific forms such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and "cloth-ness" (paṭatva). Therefore,
the intention is that there is no tautology.

Now, an objection: since the root text states, "The individual soul (jīva) is distinct in each body," it is the very difference of the soul in every body that is being expressed, not its definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Consequently, the introduction to that verse, "He states the definition of the soul," would be inappropriate.
To show that this is logical, he says: "the meaning is that it expresses its own essential nature.
He raises an objection: "If not," because a difference [in the body] is necessarily entailed by the accumulation and loss of the parts of Caitra's body.

In relation to the body of a child in the month of Caitra, a difference must be stated regarding his bodies as a youth, an old man, and so forth. And thus, even though there is a difference between the bodies of a child, a youth, and so on, the self delimited by them is one and the same.
In this way, although the selves of Saubhari and others are many, [the self remains one].

The meaning of the objection is as follows: since [the opponent] accepts that the body is a collection [of parts], and since there is no difference in the individual soul (*jīva*) for each respective body, how can it be consistent to say that "the soul is distinct for each body"?
This refers to the context of the "multiplication of bodies" (*kāyavyūha*).
The meaning is: the state of a single soul presiding over multiple bodies.
He provides the resolution:
Regarding the term "simultaneous":

what is intended in the root text is that where there is a difference among bodies existing at the same time— which are not produced by the dharma born of yoga— there is a difference in the individual souls (*jīva*).
Because the bodies of a child, a youth, and so forth belonging to Caitra do not exist simultaneously,
[this does not apply] to the bodies presided over at one time by Saubhari and others.

Since there is an absence of non-production [of those bodies] by that [dharma], because they are produced by dharma born of yoga (*yogajadharma*), the distinction between such bodies is not intended by the root text as being pervaded by a distinction between selves; thus, there is no inconsistency. And so, the individual soul (*jīva*) is the counter-positive of a difference that pervades the distinction between bodies not produced by dharma born of yoga at the same time.

Thus, the fundamental meaning is that "the soul (jīva), however, is distinct in each body. The sense is that such a distinction of bodies—as in the bodies of Caitra, Maitra, and others—implies a corresponding distinction of selves (ātman) therein.
And so on, beginning with "In this way," etc.

The logical reason (*hetu*) must be completed as: "because of possessing a body distinct from that [specific] body by way of the relation of being delimited (*avacchedyatā-sambandha*). Regarding the phrase "otherwise," etc.:
[it would follow] that in the self (*ātman*), which is the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*), [there would be the cognition] "I am a human," and so forth.
Properties such as humanity appear as qualifiers;
humanity and the like reside in the body itself. Therefore:

This cognition, which has the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) as its substantive subject and human-ness and other bodily attributes as its qualifiers, leads to the understanding that the body alone is the self (*ātman*).
However, if the self were distinct from the body, then...

The point is that this cognition, which takes the form of "human-ness" and so forth with respect to a self devoid of human-ness and the like, would be of the nature of an error and not of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*). Otherwise— that is, if the self, distinct from the body, were the referent of the "I"-notion— [the aforementioned consequence would follow].
The meaning is that there is no connection with the condition itself; thus, the status of the cognition as valid knowledge is untenable. [This applies] to the word "man" (manuṣya).
The cognition "I am a human being" implies that the object of the "I" (ahamartha) is delimited by a human body; therefore,
this cognition serves as a proof for the identity of the body and the self.
With the tenet in mind that "this is not a valid cognition," it was stated, "it is a conceit.
[The term] "belonging to the past" means:
From the cognition, "I who saw [it] am now touching [it]," the identity between the locus of the past visual perception and the locus of the present tactile perception is understood.
In the theory that the sense organs are the self (*indriyātmavāda*), the locus of visual perception is the eye, and the locus of tactile perception is the skin.

The point is that because of the difference between those two, the cognition of recognition—which apprehends their identity—is not possible. In the *Dīpikā*, it says "experienced by another. [Objection:
But surely, because of the difference between the eye and the skin, a cognition of recognition that apprehends their non-difference is not tenable.
This is exactly what must be said. If it is asked, "But since it is not so, how is this passage to be interpreted?"— listen.
Just as the aforementioned recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) apprehends the identity between the substrata of visual and tactile perception,
so too does it apprehend that the very object of visual perception is also the object of tactile perception. In that regard:

Since it is impossible for a jar, which is the object of a visual perception produced by the agent that is the eye, to be the object of a recollection produced by the agent that is the skin, there could be no tactile recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)— produced by the agent that is the skin— which, preceded by that recollection, apprehends the jar as being the object of a tactile perception. Therefore...
One must accept a single substratum for both visual and tactile perception that is distinct from the sense organs;
and that [substratum] is one's own self.
With the intention that [the author] ought to connect the object experienced by himself without distinction, the *Dīpikā* proceeds; thus,
in the *Prakāśikā*, it is stated that "abandonment" (*hāna*) means destruction (*nāśa*).
The destruction of all karma means its fruitlessness;
for it is destroyed without the agent experiencing its result.
Regarding "the arrival of what was not done": even when an action has not been performed, there is an "arrival," which is the attainment of its fruit;
[thus] the experiencer of the fruit would be someone other than the doer of the action.
The meaning is that "thus" [it occurs] because the attainment of that fruit happens for him even without the performance of ritual action. He states this with the words:
"by the agent's mind," because it is accepted that light radiates forth.
The meaning is that this is because it is accepted that the radiance of the nature of gnosis pervades the entire body.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the array of bodies" (kāyavyūha):

In the case of multiple bodies simultaneously presided over by a single soul, since the atom-sized soul resides in one particular body, although there is an expansion of the soul’s light— namely, knowledge— in that body,
there is no such expansion in other bodies; consequently, the self lacks the recollection of pleasure and other experiences delimited by those other bodies.
The intended meaning is that [the light] would not exist [there]. Now, one might object:
even in the case of the array of bodies (*kāyavyūha*), it is accepted that the radiance of that [light] extends as far as all the bodies are presided over by the living soul (*jīva*).
Therefore, suspecting that the non-perception [of the light] would not be possible, he says "direction" (diś).
Just as the radiance of a lamp placed inside a single room...
The meaning is that just as light does not spread into another house, so too the radiance of a living being residing within one body would not spread into another body.
Tarkasaṅgraha:
Definition of the Mind (manas). Tarkasaṅgraha 18: The mind is the sense organ that is the means for the apprehension of pleasure and so forth.
And that atomic form is infinite because it is restricted to each individual self, and it is eternal.

The sense organ that is the means for the apprehension of pleasure and so forth is the mind (*manas*). And because it is restricted to each individual self, it is infinite, atomic in form, and eternal.
— *Dīpikā*
He states the definition of the mind (manas) as "pleasure," etc.
The definition of the mind is its being dependent on action while being devoid of contact (sparśa).
He analyzes that [definition].
Regarding the phrase "and that": since each individual self requires a single mind, the meaning is that because there is a plurality of selves, there is also a plurality of minds.
As for the phrase "in the form of atoms": [it means that the mind exists in the form of atomic particles].
The meaning is that if it possessed a medium dimension, it would follow that it is impermanent.
[Objection: But surely the mind is all-pervading (vibhu), because, while being devoid of touch, it is a substance.
If it is argued that [the mind] is like space and so forth— no;

for if the mind were all-pervasive, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of cognition due to the absence of the contact between the self and the mind, which is the non-inherent cause [of cognition].
Nor should it be said that there is a conjunction of two all-pervading entities;
for since such a conjunction would be eternal, it would follow that deep sleep could never occur,
as the conjunction of the self and the mind would exist at all times in locations other than the pericardium (purītat).
As for its atomicity: when the mind enters the pericardium (purītat), then deep sleep occurs;
when it emerges, then the arising of cognition occurs—thus is the proof of its atomicity. (The *Prakāśikā*)

He states a concise definition— namely, "being devoid of touch"— which excludes over-extension (ativyāpti) caused by the mind's conjunction and so forth, as compared to the previously stated definition which includes the sense-organ (indriya) as a constituent.
"Each one is a mind" [is the conclusion].
If one accepts that there is only a single mind for all souls, it would be impossible for another [mind] to exist at the time when that one is in a state of cognition;
this is because, being atomic in size, it cannot simultaneously come into contact with all the sense organs.

The meaning is as follows: [it is] "vibhu" (all-pervading). And thus, because it possesses supreme magnitude (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*), there is no room for the previously mentioned defects; this is the intended meaning.
"Because of non-existence":
the meaning is that the conjunction of two all-pervading [substances] is not admitted.
"All-pervading" [refers to this].
And thus, because it possesses the dimension of supreme magnitude (*paramamahatparimāṇa*), the previously mentioned defects find no footing; this is the intended meaning.
[The phrase] "due to non-existence" [is explained as follows].
The meaning is that this is because the conjunction of two all-pervading substances is not admitted.
Regarding the phrase "non-arising of cognition":
it is because there is a rule that an effect which is a positive entity must be produced by a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

The meaning is: "Let there be a conjunction of two all-pervading substances. The point is that because such a conjunction is eternal, there is no deficiency even in the absence of an efficient cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), such as motion.
In the *Bālapriyā*,
having set aside the definition of the mind (*manas*) as stated in the *Tarkasaṅgraha*, another definition of the mind is provided in the *Dīpikā*.
He states the seed [of the definition]: "from the conjunction with the mind," etc.

If one were to state only this much—that "the definition of the mind is its being the instrument for the direct realization of pleasure and so forth"—there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the conjunction of the self and the mind.
Since that [mind] is also a means for the direct realization of pleasure and so forth,

the property of being a sense faculty (*indriyatva*) has been introduced to exclude it. And since the property of being a sense faculty consists in the form "that which is other than sound," etc., it is defined as being composed of those [elements].
The sense is that, having reflected that the definition of the mind (*manas*) is too cumbersome, the definition of the light [element] was stated in the *Dīpikā*.
The meaning of the term "means" (*sādhana*) here is "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

"Nṛsiṃha Śāstrin, however, has said: 'The term *indriya* (faculty) is employed solely for the sake of this attainment; there is no entry [into the state] by way of that form, because it would involve unnecessary complexity. Regarding them:

Since there would be the defect of incompleteness (*nyūnatā*) if another definition that is possible for one position were not stated, it is precisely to avoid that that another definition is provided in the *Dīpikā*.
And they themselves have said: "In order to avoid the charge of incompleteness, he himself states the definition of the mind."
But how can there be a conjunction of two distinct entities,
given that both action and conjunction are causes for conjunction?
Furthermore, because the two all-pervading entities are devoid of action,
a conjunction produced by action is not possible;
this is also due to their being devoid of constituent parts.

Regarding the claim that even "conjunction produced by conjunction" (saṃyogaja-saṃyoga) is impossible—just as the conjunction of a body with a book is not possible through the conjunction of the hands with the book—it is said here: "Because of its permanence.
In the phrase "action, etc.," the word "etc. includes conjunction.

And thus, the meaning is that action and so forth are causes only with respect to a produced conjunction (*saṃyoga*), but not with respect to a non-conjunction, because that would contradict its being unproduced (*ajatva*).
— *Tarkasaṅgraha*.
The Determination of Form (Rūpanirūpaṇa):
Form is a quality perceivable by the eye alone.
It is of seven types—white, blue, yellow, red, green, brown, and variegated—and it resides in earth, water, and fire.
In that regard, there are seven kinds [of white] on earth;
non-luminous white in water;
and luminous white in fire.
Color (*rūpa*) is a quality (*guṇa*) perceivable by the eye alone; it is of seven types, distinguished as white, blue, yellow, red, green, brown, and variegated (*citra*).
It functions within earth, water, and fire.
Among these, it is of seven kinds in earth.
Non-luminous white [light] is in water;
luminous white [light] is in fire; this is the lamp.
He defines *rūpa* (color/form):

"the eye" [is its perceiver]. The word "only" (*mātra*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to number and other categories. The word "quality" (*guṇa*) is used to exclude over-extension to the universal *rūpatva* (the property of being color/form).
He analyzes color—namely, "that" (tacceti).

If it is argued that a variegated color (*citrarūpa*) is simply a collection of non-pervasive colors such as blue and so forth, we say no; for there is a rule that color must necessarily be pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*).
If it is argued that on a variegated cloth there should be the perception of only the form of the parts— no,
because [the whole] is devoid of [such] form.
Otherwise, it would follow that the cloth itself is imperceptible.
Furthermore, inherence in something possessing color (*rūpavat*) is not the cause of perceptibility, because that [definition] is unnecessarily cumbersome (*gaurava*).
Therefore, since the perceptibility of the cloth would otherwise be untenable, the existence of a variegated color (*citrarūpa*) is established.
He states the substratum of that color: "earth."
He shows the analysis of the basis with the words "therein" (*tatra*).—
*Prakāśikā* (The Elucidator).

Regarding the phrase "the word 'only'": although being perceivable by the eye alone means being perceivable by the eye while not being perceivable by anything other than the eye, and this [condition] does not apply to visible form (*rūpa*);
Nevertheless, it should be understood that its nature is being perceptible by the eye while being imperceptible by the sense of touch.
This refers to the term "quality."
Nor should it be argued that even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the contact between light and a wall;
for since the definition ultimately resolves to "possessing a property that distinguishes qualities perceptible by the eye but not by the sense of touch," there is no fault. Therefore...
Thus, it should be understood that there is no pervasion by parts in the case of the color-form of an atom and so forth;
[the phrase] "only in the aggregate" uses the particle *eva* to exclude a distinct, variegated color-form (*citrarūpa*) that would be something additional.
"Or as pervasively occurring" means "as spatially pervasively occurring.
This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).

There is prolixity (gaurava) because one must postulate multiple forms in each instance of a single variegated form, and multiple prior absences (prāgabhāva) and so forth in each instance of their respective individual prior absences and so forth, as well as postulate that multiple forms are the objects of the cognition "this is variegated."
"By way of being devoid of form" means "by way of inherence," and so forth. "As a consequence" means: [as follows].
The meaning is that color (*rūpa*) is the cause of the visual perception of a substance by way of inherence (*samavāya*). Thus,
it is "inherence in that which possesses color."
"Color is the cause of perceptibility by virtue of its inherence in its own substratum"—
this means that it should be the cause of being an object of perception.

"Because it is more cumbersome (gauravāt)": this means because it is more cumbersome than [positing] causality through a direct relationship. This is said in accordance with the fact that a cloth produced by potsherds which themselves possess variegated parts must be visible to the eye.
It must be admitted that color is the cause of that [perception] by virtue of the relation of "inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-what-is-inherent-in-itself";
and in this way, the impossibility of the visual perception of an atom (*truṭi*) is also resolved.
It is to be seen that [a single taste] cannot be established because direct perception is impossible;
by this, the doubt that a variegated taste might be established just like a variegated color is refuted.

In brief, since the aesthetic relish (*rasana*) of a composite flavor (*davaya-rasa*) is not established, and thus there is no impossibility [of its existence], one does not accept a "painted" or variegated flavor (*citrarasa*). This is the summary.
[Objection: But surely... [the text continues with *bālapriyā nanu*].
The property of being perceptible by the eye alone is impossible in the case of visible form (*rūpa*).
For "perceptibility by the eye alone" means being perceptible by the eye while not being perceptible by any sense-faculty other than the eye.

He raises an objection with the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*), on the grounds that since the mind is a cause for cognition in general, the property of being an object of perception produced by the mind other than the eye exists in color (*rūpa*); thus, the property of not being graspable by anything other than the eye is absent in color.
"Not being graspable by anything other than the eye" means not being an object of perception produced by anything other than the eye.
"Being graspable by the eye" means being an object of perception produced by the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
He provides the solution: "Even so" (*tathāpi*).

By the word "other" (*itara*), the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*) is intended. Thus, [the definition] is: being an object of visual perception produced by the visual sense-organ, while not being an object of tactile perception produced by the tactile sense-organ.
The meaning is that since there is the property of being perceivable by the eye alone in the case of visible form (*rūpa*), there is no impossibility [of the definition].
If the term "real" (*satya*) were not included, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to numbers such as unity and so forth, because those too...

Because it is the object of a perception produced by the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*). However, if that [visual faculty] were included, then since number is also graspable by the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*), it would not be the case that it is not the object of a perception produced by the tactile faculty.
There is no over-extension [of the definition].
The qualifier is included to exclude over-extension to supersensuous entities such as *dharma* and the like. Nor is there [over-extension] even in this case.
The point is that the conjunction with a luminous wall is not perceivable by the sense of touch,
but is perceivable by the eye. Thus, it is said to be "ungraspable by the sense of touch."

The definition of color (*rūpa*) is the possession of that property which is a differentiator of qualities (*guṇavibhājakadharma*), being an object of visual perception produced by the sense organ of sight (*cakṣurindriya*) while not being an object of tactile perception produced by the sense organ of touch (*tvagindriya*). The differentiator of qualities is the universal (*jāti*) "color-ness" (*rūpatva*).
And that [color] is not apprehended by the sense of touch but is apprehended by the eye;

for according to the logical principle that whatever quality is apprehended by a particular sense organ, both the universal residing in that quality and the absence of that quality are apprehended by that same sense organ.
And since the state of possessing "form-ness" exists in form, there is a congruence of the definition;
this being present in the conjunction of light and the wall.
The property that distinguishes conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the nature of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*);
and this is not imperceptible to the sense of touch, as is the case with the conjunction between a jar and a cloth, and so forth.
The meaning is that because the nature of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*) is perceived by the sense of touch, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the conjunction between light and a wall.

He says "for this very reason" with the intention that, by formulating a definition composed of such a genus (jāti), the purpose is to avoid the defect of under-extension (avyāpti) in the case of the color of an atom (paramāṇu-rūpa), just as one avoids over-extension (ativyāpti) in the case of the conjunction of light and a wall.
Because the form residing in an atom is beyond the senses, it lacks the quality of being graspable by the eye;

thus, there is an over-narrow definition (avyāpti) if the definition is taken literally. However, if the definition is formulated as consisting of the aforementioned genus, it exists within the form of an atom.
The property that differentiates qualities is "form-ness" (*rūpatva*).
This, however, is indeed perceptible by the eye in the case of the form of a jar.
Thus, because the definition is present in the form of an atom by virtue of its possessing form-ness that is perceptible by the eye, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
[The opponent states: "But surely, since there is an absence of color in a jar and the like at the moment of its production, color has a non-pervasive temporal occurrence (*kālikāvyāpyavṛttitva*);

therefore, [the claim] that 'there is a rule that what lacks color must have pervasive occurrence (*vyāpyavṛttitva*)' is inconsistent. To this, he replies: "Regarding spatial pervasive occurrence (*daiśikavyāpyavṛttitva*). But surely...
Since threads possess color through the relation of inherence in their own substratum, the claim that [the cloth] is "devoid of color" is inconsistent; therefore, he says: "by way of inherence," etc.
This is because, with respect to perception, color is a causal factor through the relation of inherence, while the object itself is related through the relation of objectivity (*viṣayatā*).
The point is that if color does not exist in the cloth by way of inherence (*samavāya*), then the cloth would not be an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Now, perceptibility resides in perceptual cognition; and in perceptual cognition...

Anticipating the objection that the statement "inherence in that which possesses color (*rūpavatsamavetatva*) is the cause of perceptibility" is inconsistent because [the universal] lacks inherence in that which possesses color, he says:
"it is the cause of being an object of perception."
The intended meaning here is that the term "being perceptible" (*pratyakṣatva*) signifies being an object of perception (*pratyakṣaviṣayatva*).
[This is stated] with respect to the perception of a substance (*dravyapratyakṣa*) by way of the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*).
Color is the cause by way of the relation of inherence in its own substratum (*svāśrayasamavetatva*).

Even though color is absent from the cloth by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), the color of the threads exists therein by way of the relation of inherence in its own substratum. Therefore...
It becomes an object of direct perception;
therefore, the intention is that there should be no such thing as a variegated color (*citrarūpa*).
[This occurs] by way of the relation of being inherent in that which is inherent in that which is inherent in itself (*svasamavāyisamavetasamavetatvasambandha*).
Its own variegated form [is that which] inheres in those parts which are its own inherent constituents, namely, the parts of the potsherds and their further parts.

The parts of the potsherd, the inherence in those [parts], the inherence in the potsherd, and the inherence in the jar; thus, there is the impossibility of the atom (*truṭi*) being perceived by the eye.

Although the color residing in an atom exists in a triad (tryaṇuka) by way of the relation of being inherent in a dyad (dvyaṇuka) which is itself inherent in the atoms that are its own inherent substrates,
it does not exist [in that triad] by way of the relation of being inherent in that which is inherent in what is inherent in its own inherent substrate.
The point is this: since color exists in a triad (tryaṇuka) by means of the aforementioned relation only if it exists in the parts of the atom,
it follows that if color were absent from the triad by way of that same relation, the triad could not be an object of visual perception.
Now, it might be argued that the existence of a distinct "variegated flavor" (*citrarasa*) is established by the cognition "the flavor is variegated"; to this he says: "In brief.
This is because such a cognition is accounted for by the various flavors residing in the individual parts.

The sense is that it is due to the complexity [gaurava] involved in postulating the prior non-existence, destruction, and so forth of each of the many distinct aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*). This concludes the definition of taste (*rasa*) in the *Tarkasaṅgraha*.
Taste is a quality apprehended by the tongue.
It is of six kinds, distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, astringent, and bitter.
All six kinds exist in earth.
In water, it is indeed sweet.
Taste is the quality apprehended by the gustatory organ. It is of six kinds, distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, astringent, and bitter. It resides in earth and water.
Among those, on earth there are six kinds;
in water, there is only the sweet.

1. *Svāśraya* means: its own [form] is the nature of the thread (*tantu-rūpa`); the substratum (*āśraya*) of that is the thread; the cloth's inherence (*samavetatva*) therein [is what is meant]. *Dīpikā* (Commentary): *Sva* refers to the form of the thread (*tantu-rūpa`); its substratum (*āśraya`) is the thread. The cloth's state of being inherent (*samavetatva`) in that [thread] is what is intended.

He defines *rasa* (taste) with the words "by the sense of taste" (*rasanena*). The term "quality" (*guṇa*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to *rasatva* (the generic property of being taste).
He states the substratum (*āśraya*) of *rasa*:
"Earth. He demonstrates the analysis of its basis with the word "therein.
"The illuminator is tastiness."
The intended meaning is [the possession of] a delimitor that distinguishes the quality perceivable by the gustatory organ;
the same applies to the definition of odor as well.
— *Bālapriyā*

An objection is raised: "Even if it is stated that the definition of taste (*rasa*) is 'being a quality while being perceptible by the gustatory organ' (*rasanāgrāhyatve sati guṇatvam*), this definition lacks applicability (*avyāpti*) to the taste of an atom (*paramāṇurasa*), because that [taste] is not an object of perception produced by the gustatory sense-organ. Anticipating this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "perceptible by the gustatory organ" (*rasanagrāhya*):

the definition of taste (*rasa*) is the possession of that property which is a sub-classifier of qualities (*guṇavibhājaka-dharma*) and is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) produced by the gustatory sense-organ (*rasanendriya*).

In the taste of fruits and the like, the universal *rasatva* (tasteness) becomes the object of sensory perception produced by the gustatory organ (*rasanendriya*), according to the logical principle "whatever is a quality [is perceptible by a sense organ].
Since the possession of such a universal *rasatva* exists even in the taste of atoms (*paramāṇu*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
The meaning is as follows: the same applies to the definition of odor (*gandha*).
The meaning is that the definition of odor is "possessing the qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) which distinguishes it as a quality perceivable by the olfactory organ."
The Compendium of Reasoning (Tarkasaṅgraha):
Definition of Odor (Gandhanirūpaṇa). Section 21: Odor is a quality perceivable by the sense of smell.
And that [smell] is of two kinds: fragrant and non-fragrant.
It resides only in earth;
it is a quality perceivable by the sense of smell.
Odor. It is of two kinds: fragrant and non-fragrant. It subsists in earth alone. [This is] the Lamp.
One perceives odor by means of the nose; the word "quality" is included to exclude over-extension to the universal *gandhatva* (odor-ness). — Tarkasaṅgraha.
The Definition of Tangibility: Tangibility is a quality apprehended solely by the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*).
It is of three kinds, distinguished as cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold.
It functions within earth, water, fire, and air;
therein, it is cold in water and hot in fire.
It is neither hot nor cold, like earth and wind.
Tactile sensation (sparśa) is a quality perceivable by the sense organ of touch alone.
It is of three kinds, distinguished as cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold.
It functions within earth, water, fire, and air.
Among these, it is cool in water and hot in fire.
Neither hot nor cold, like earth and air;
the lamp illustrates the characteristic of touch.
"Skin" (tvak). The word "quality" (guṇa) is included to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) to the nature of touch (sparśatva).
The word "only" (mātra) is included to exclude over-extension to conjunction (saṃyoga) and so forth.
— *Prakāśikā*
Regarding the phrase "the word *mātra*":

the resulting meaning is "the state of possessing a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) that distinguishes qualities (*guṇa*) which are not perceptible by the eye but are perceptible by the sense-organ of touch.
[The commentator] Bālapriyā asks: "But surely..."

Even if it is stated that the definition of touch is "being a quality while being perceivable by the tactile sense alone," there is still the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding the touch residing in atoms (*paramāṇu*),
because that [atomic touch] is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).
Anticipating the objection that [touch] lacks the property of being perceivable by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*), he says: "not perceivable by the eye" (*cakṣuragrāhya*).

The definition of touch (*sparśa*) is the possession of that quality which serves as the differentiator of qualities (*guṇavibhājaka-dharma*) and is the object of perception produced by the sense of touch, while not being the object of perception produced by the visual sense (*cakṣurindriya*).
The genus "tangibility" (sparśatva) exists in the tangibles of jars and other objects; it is imperceptible by the eye but perceptible by the skin.
Since this [property] is present in the tangibility residing in atoms as well, there is a logical consistency (samanvaya).

The term "not perceptible by the eye" (*cakṣuragrāhya*) is stated in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to number (*saṅkhyā*), which is perceptible by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya-grāhya*) when taking its property of "number-ness" (*saṅkhyātva*) as the basis; for [number-ness] would otherwise be included among those things not perceptible by the eye. Furthermore, it is stated to exclude such supersensible (*atīndriya*) properties as "dharma-ness" (*dharmatva*) or "adharma-ness" (*adharmatva*).
The phrase "perceptible by the sense of touch" (tvagindriyagrāhya) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) to dharma, adharma, and so forth.

Since the property of being a quality (guṇatva), when apprehended as residing in touch, is not perceptible by the eye but is perceptible by the sense of touch, [the definition] would otherwise over-extend to number (saṅkhyā) and other categories by virtue of possessing that [property of being perceptible by touch]; therefore, [the term "touch"] is included to prevent such over-extension.
The term "guṇavibhājaka" (qualifier that differentiates qualities) is an adjective modifying "upādhi" (limiting condition).
The intended meaning is that "guṇatva" (the nature of being a quality) is not, however, a differentiator of qualities.
The Compendium of Reasoning:
An Exposition on the Process of Maturation (Pākaprakriyānirūpaṇam).
In earth, the four qualities beginning with color are produced by maturation and are impermanent.
Elsewhere, that which is not produced by maturation (apākaja) is eternal, as is the ultimate [atom].
That which resides in what is eternal is eternal;
that which resides in what is non-eternal is non-eternal.
The four beginning with form (rūpa) produced by heating (pākaja) in earth are impermanent; elsewhere, they are both non-produced by heating (apākaja), permanent, and impermanent.
That which belongs to the eternal is eternal;
that which belongs to the non-eternal is non-eternal.
This is the lamp.
Regarding the term *pākaja*: *pāka* is conjunction with fire (*tejaḥ*).
By means of this, the previous [quality] perishes and another form (*rūpa*) arises; such is the meaning.
In that regard, the baking occurs only in the atoms, not in the dyads and so forth.

When a pot placed on the kiln undergoes the production of a different color in its atoms, the black pot is destroyed; then, once again, through the sequence of dyads and so forth [the pot is reconstituted].
The production of a red jar:
therein, the atoms are the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa),
and the conjunction with fire is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa).
The non-inherent cause is [the conjunction].
The unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth are the efficient causes,
with respect to the form of dyads and the like.
The Vaiśeṣikas who maintain the theory of baking in the atoms (pīlupākavādins) hold that the causal form is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) of the previous jar.

The Naiyāyikas, proponents of the theory of baking in the pot (*piṭharapākavāda*), maintain that without the destruction [of the whole], a simultaneous production of different colors occurs in the parts and in the whole, down to the level of the atoms. For this very reason,
the meaning is that the color and other qualities of the earth-atoms are impermanent.
"In another place" means in water and so forth. "Inhering in the eternal" means...
The meaning is "residing in atoms. The meaning of "residing in the impermanent" is "residing in dyads and so forth."
The fourfold group beginning with visible form (*rūpa*) is perceptible when manifested (*udbhūta*),
and imperceptible when unmanifested (*anudbhūta*).
Manifestation is the property that serves as the cause for perceptibility.
The absence of that [manifestation] is non-manifestation (*anudbhūtatva*). The process of heating (*pāka*) occurs only in the atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Thus, the meaning is that the conjunction of fire which produces the transformation of the previous color and so forth occurs in the atoms themselves. He clarifies what is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*)— it does not [occur elsewhere].
"In the case of dyads and so forth" means:
when a jar has been placed upon a cloth;
that is, when the jar is situated on the cloth.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when the dark-colored pot is destroyed, a different color arises in the atoms.
Regarding that color of the atoms, he says "the color of the cause" because he does not accept the ripening (*pāka*) of a composite whole (*avayavin*).
The intention of the Vaiśeṣikas, who maintain that cooking occurs in the atoms themselves, is as follows:
when there is a conjunction through impact between the atoms and fire possessing an excess of velocity, an action necessarily arises within them.
From that [division] comes separation; from that, when the originating conjunction is destroyed, the destruction of the whole necessarily follows; thereafter, [the state exists] in independent atoms.

Furthermore, upon the production of another form, by the power of a causal complex consisting of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors, there occurs— through the sequence of action, disjunction, and so forth within the atoms— the production of [the whole] as it was previously situated, up to the limit of the non-composite (*aparāvayavin*).

As for the Naiyāyikas who maintain that cooking occurs even in the composite whole (*avayavin*), their underlying intention is this: even when there is a conjunction through impact with fire at the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), it necessarily [occurs]...
Since there is no evidence for the existence of an action that produces a disjunction which is the counter-agent to the conjunction that initiates [the whole],
it is appropriate to accept that cooking occurs even in the composite whole (*avayavin*).
For this very reason, one can say, "This is that same jar."
Recognition also becomes consistent;
furthermore, there is parsimony by not postulating the destruction of infinite composite wholes.
Nor is there [causality] of the form of the parts toward the form of the whole.
It should not be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the causality of the destruction of the substratum with respect to the destruction of that [effect],
because [the restriction] is within the scope of the delimiting condition of being an effect (kāryatāvacchedaka).
Because it is possible to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by specifying that [the property] must belong to a different genus (*vaijātya*). "Elsewhere" means in water and so forth;
for although the fourfold set beginning with color (*rūpa*) is sublated in water and the like.
Nevertheless, the intended meaning (tātparya) regarding the positive concomitance (anvaya) is according to what is appropriate;
that is, "manifestness" (udbhūtatva). As for this manifestness:
It is a genus (*jāti*), and there is no confusion (*sāṅkarya*) with whiteness and so forth.
This text is intended according to the view of the moderns (*navīna*), who hold that confusion among qualities (*guṇa*) is not a fault; therefore, there is no defect.
Some, however,
hold that non-manifestness (*anudbhūtatva*)— which is subsumed by whiteness and so forth— is manifold;
[the state of being white] consists precisely in possessing the collection (*kūṭa*) of the absences of those [various instances of non-manifestness].
They say it is "manifestness" (udbhūtatva). [The commentary] says:
"by the transformation of the prior form," and so forth.
*Parāvṛttiḥ* means destruction; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the arising of another form is included.
The word *tatra* is the term to be explained.
Its explanation is "in the form of an atom" (paramāṇurūpa);
the meaning is "in the color residing in an atom. Now, [one might object]:...

Anticipating the objection that— since in the color belonging to dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, it is only maturation (*pāka*), consisting of contact with heterogeneous fire, that can possibly serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and thus it is incorrect to say that "the color of the cause is the non-inherent cause"— he says: "In the case of the whole (*avayavin*)."
"Because the baking [of the whole] is not admitted":

this is because, in the Vaiśeṣika system of those who maintain the theory of the baking of the *pīlu* fruit, it is not admitted that the transformation of the previous color and other qualities and the production of different qualities in the composite whole (*avayavin*) occur by virtue of the baking of its parts.
The point here is that it is impossible for maturation to serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to another form.
"Until the destruction of the whole" means that the destruction extends up to the final constituent part.

"By the conjunction that initiates [the effect]," and so forth: that disjunction which is the opposite of the atomic conjunction that initiates the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and other such effects— that is, the disjunction which is the destroyer of that conjunction— is that which produces [it].
"Action" means the state of being its producer.
Regarding the phrase "by introducing a specific universal" (*vaijātyaniveśanena*):
it refers to that which is delimited by a specific universal (*vaijātya*) that does not reside in the color produced by cooking (*pākaja-rūpa*) nor in its destruction.

The meaning is that the cause consists of the form of the constituent parts and the destruction of the substratum. "In other cases, that which is not produced by heat is eternal and non-eternal" is the root text.

The meaning of "elsewhere" (anyatra) is "in water and so forth. Since the phrase "the fourfold [set] beginning with color" (rūpādicatuṣṭaya) is carried over from the preceding sentence, it is likewise [to be understood].
And the meaning obtained is that the fourfold [qualities] beginning with color existing in water and so forth are not produced by heat (*apākaja*).
This is inconsistent, because the fourfold [qualities] beginning with color do not exist in water. In water...

Because only the triad beginning with form exists in fire when devoid of odor, because only the dyad of form and touch exists in wind when devoid of odor and taste, and because only touch exists in wind, he says:
By the words "even though" and so forth,
the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is stated according to what is appropriate;
this refers to the phrase "the fourfold [group] beginning with form."
The meaning is that it consists of the fourfold group beginning with form (*rūpa*).
And since that which constitutes it may be a triad, a dyad, or a single unit, there is no logical inconsistency; this is the intended sense.
Tarkasaṅgraha:
Definition of Number (AnTs 24).
Number is the cause of the conventional usage of "oneness" and so forth.
Number resides in nine substances and ranges from unity up to the highest numeral (parārdha).
Unity is both eternal and non-eternal;
that which resides in eternal things is eternal, and that which resides in non-eternal things is non-eternal.
But duality and so forth are invariably impermanent in all cases.
Number is the cause for the conventional usage of "oneness" and so forth;
it resides in the nine substances;
and it ranges from oneness up to the highest number (parārdha).
Unity residing in eternal things is eternal;
that residing in non-eternal things is non-eternal;
but duality and so forth are invariably non-eternal in all cases.
The *Dīpikā* defines the number [of verses] as follows: "One," etc.
In the *Prakāśikā*, however, it is stated that duality and so forth are invariably non-eternal in all cases.
The meaning is that the destruction of duality and so forth occurs through the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) which serves as its cause.
— *Tarkasaṅgraha*
The Definition of Dimension:
Dimension is the cause of the conventional usage of measurement;
it resides in nine substances.
That is of four kinds:
minute, large, long, and short.
Dimension is the unique cause of human conventional usage;
it resides in nine substances.
It is of four kinds: atomic, large, long, and short.
The *Dīpikā* defines dimension (*parimāṇa*) with the words "measure" (*māna*), and analyzes it with the words "and that" (*tac ca*).
This is an indication where the abstract quality is predominant;
the meaning is "atomicity," "largeness," "length," and "shortness.
— *Prakāśikā*
It is inconsistent to divide measurement by means of words that denote the possessor of the quality;
therefore, it is said in the *Dīpikā* that "the emphasis is on the state" (*bhāvapradhāna*).

Now, since dimension (parimāṇa) is a quality, its classification must also be expressed by words denoting qualities, such as "atomicity" (aṇutva), "largeness" (mahattva), and so forth. This is the objection raised by the Bālapriyā.

In response to the doubt that [the term] should not be used with words such as *aṇu* (minute) or *mahat* (great), which denote qualities characterized by specific dimensions, the resolution has been stated in the *Dīpikā*:
"The designation is one in which the state (*bhāva*) is primary."
Words such as "minute" (aṇu), "large" (mahat), and so forth, primarily denote qualities (dharma) in their original sense;
and thus, the minuteness (aṇutva) of those [entities] is expressed by those words.

There is no inconsistency in the fact that the meaning [of the term] consists solely of qualities such as dimension (*parimāṇa*), beginning with "greatness" (*mahattva*). Thus he says: "Of dimension," etc.—*Tarkasaṅgraha*.
The Definition of Separateness (pṛthaktva): Separateness is the cause of the conventional usage of "distinct.
It resides in all substances.
Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is the uncommon cause for distinct usage;
it resides in all substances.
— *Dīpikā*
He defines separateness (*pṛthaktva*)—the term "separate" (*pṛthak*).
The meaning is that separateness is the cause for the conventional usage: "This is separate from that."
The Compendium of Reasoning (Tarkasaṅgraha):
Definition of Conjunction (Saṃyoga). Conjunction is the cause for the conventional usage of the term "conjoined."
It exists in all substances.
Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the cause for the conventional usage of "conjoined. It resides in all substances.
[This is from] the *Dīpikā*.
He defines conjunction (saṃyoga) with the words "that which is conjoined" (saṃyukta).
The meaning is that it is the cause for the conventional usage: "these two are conjoined."
In all definitions of number and so forth,
the qualification "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) must be added in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to space, time, and the like.
Conjunction is of two kinds: that produced by action and that produced by conjunction. The first is, for example, the conjunction between a hand and a book resulting from the movement of the hand.
The second [type of conjunction] is the conjunction of the body with the book resulting from the conjunction of the hand with the book.
Conjunction is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*). Non-pervasiveness consists in having a common locus with its own absolute non-existence (*svātyantābhāvasamānādhikaraṇatva*).
The phrase "the illuminator is uncommon" means that since time and so forth are common causes, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to them; this is the intended sense.
Regarding "its own absolute absence":
the refined meaning is the state of possessing an absence through the two relations of having itself as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and being co-located with itself (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
In the expression "bālapriyā svapratiyogitve," *sva* refers to the absence of conjunction with a monkey (*kapisaṃyogābhāva*).
