The counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of that [absence] resides in the conjunction with the monkey; likewise, "self" (*sva*) refers to the absence of conjunction with the monkey.
And the state of residing in the tree which is the locus of that [disjunction] exists in the monkey-conjunction; thus,
by way of both relations— namely, having itself as the counter-positive and residing in its own locus.
The state of being qualified by the absence of conjunction with a monkey exists in the conjunction with a monkey; thus, that [conjunction] is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti).
[This is so] because it is qualified by the absence of a jar through the relation of having itself as its counter-positive.

The inclusion of "co-occurrence in the same locus" (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) is for the purpose of precluding the case of a jar's non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*). Since a jar does not possess co-occurrence in the same locus with the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar, there is no fault. [This refers to] that which is qualified by the absolute absence of a jar through the relation of "subsisting in its own locus."
The inclusion of "being its own counter-positive" (*svapratiyogitva*) is for the purpose of precluding the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) of the cloth;
since the cloth is the counter-positive of the absence of the jar, there is no fault.
— *Tarkasaṅgraha*
The definition of disjunction (vibhāga): Disjunction is the quality that causes the destruction of conjunction;
it resides in all substances.
Disjunction is the quality that destroys conjunction;
it resides in all substances.
The *Dīpikā* defines division (*vibhāga*) as follows:

"Conjunction... [and so on]. The term "quality" (*guṇa*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to time (*kāla*) and other such entities. [The term "disjunction"] is included to exclude over-extension to color (*rūpa*) and other such qualities.
The term "destruction of conjunction" is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Disjunction (*vibhāga*) is of two kinds: that produced by action (*karmaja*) and that produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja*).
The first is the state of manual activity, which is the inseparability of the hand and the book;
the second is the inseparability of the body and the book, resulting from the inseparability of the hand and the book.
This is the illuminator.
Regarding the phrase "the destroyer of conjunction": even so, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to conjunction itself,
because [conjunction] functions as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
It should not be said that [the definition] fails because [the pot] is a cause of destruction;

for some maintain that there is no fault, since the intended meaning is the causality characterized by a generativity residing in destruction, where that generativity is not delimited by the relation of counter-positive-ness (*pratiyogitā*).
Others,

however, maintain that the precise definition is: the causality delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya-sambandha), as characterized by the effectness delimited by the property of being the destruction of conjunction (saṃyoga-nāśatva).
They say that this term "quality" (guṇa) is intended to include all these [categories].
Regarding "disjunction" (vibhāga):
it should be understood that this, too, is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti).
Regarding the term "first" (*ādya*):
here, being "first" means not being simultaneous with a destruction whose counter-positive is a falling that has the same locus as itself.
The meaning is that [the definition] excludes the second fall and so forth, because they are simultaneous with the destruction of the first fall. —
*Bālapriyā*
And yet, it is not a conjunction;
for the state of being a destroyer of conjunction is the state of being a producer of the destruction of conjunction. [Regarding] destruction...
The meaning is that because each counter-positive is a cause [of its own destruction], conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is also a cause with respect to the destruction of a conjunction; thus,
since the quality of being a generator of the destruction of a conjunction exists in a conjunction itself,
there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
"By way of being a counter-correlate" means "as a counter-correlate.
[The phrase] "not delimited by the relation of counter-correlativity" [is used].
Due to the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) wherein, with respect to destruction (nāśa), the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is the cause by way of the relation of identity (tādātmya),
there exists a state of being an effect (kāryatā) residing in the destruction of conjunction (saṃyoganāśa), which is delimited by the relation of counter-positiveness (pratiyogitāsambandha).

The point is that although the causality delimited by the relation of identity (tādātmya) as determined by that [conjunction] exists in the conjunction, there is no generativity (janakatā) corresponding to a producedness (janyatā) residing in the destruction of the conjunction that is not delimited by the relation of counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā); therefore, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) to the conjunction.
"But others," [they say],

because of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) that "with respect to the destruction of conjunction, disjunction is the cause by means of the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*)," and following from that, [the effect] is delimited by the relation of essential nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

The definition of disjunction intended here is the causality, delimited by the relation of inherence, which is characterized by an effectness delimited by the state of being the destruction of conjunction. As for conjunction, however...

The meaning is that even though there exists a causality delimited by the relation of identity (tādātmya) which is itself defined by an effectness delimited by the relation of counter-positiveness residing in the destruction of conjunction, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti), because the aforementioned type of causality is absent [in that case].
This is what captures the intended sense (tātparya).
The meaning is that it indicates the intention [of the author] regarding causality as delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
Regarding "primordiality here":
whatever is simultaneous with a destruction whose counter-positive is a falling motion co-located with itself...
The meaning is that being different from that [subsequent action] constitutes "primacy" (*ādyatva*).

One's own [action], such as a second falling and so forth, has a co-occurrence (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a primary falling; that [primary falling] exists precisely at the same time as the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of that [second falling].
Since the second falling and so forth, as well as their distinctness from it, exist in the first falling, the definition is thus consistent.
This concludes the *Tarkasaṅgraha*,
the exposition of priority and posteriority.
Remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are the uncommon causes for the conventional designations of "far" and "near.
They reside in the four elements beginning with earth, as well as in the mind (*manas*).
These two are of two kinds: produced by space (*dikkṛta*) and produced by time (*kālakṛta*).
Remoteness caused by direction exists in that which is situated at a distance; proximity caused by direction exists in that which is situated nearby;
and remoteness caused by time exists in that which is older.
In the case of the youngest, inferiority is determined by time.
Remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are the uncommon causes for the conventional designations of "remote" and "proximate.
They are of two kinds:
those produced by space (*dikkṛta*) and those produced by time (*kālakṛta*).
Remoteness caused by direction occurs when [an object] is situated at a distance; proximity caused by direction occurs when [an object] is situated nearby.
In the case of the elder, priority is produced by time;
in the case of the younger, posteriority is produced by time.
The *Dīpikā* states the definition of priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) as follows: "Priority and posteriority... etc.
The meaning is that "remoteness" (*paratva*) is the unique cause for the conventional usage of "remote," and "nearness" (*aparatva*) is the unique cause for the conventional usage of "near.
He distinguishes these two as follows:
"These two are of two kinds. He provides an example of those produced by direction: "one standing at a distance.
He provides an example of those produced by time: "the elder."
The Compendium of Reasoning (Tarkasaṅgraha):
Definition of Gravity (Gurutvanirūpaṇam). Gravity is the non-inherent cause of the first instance of falling.
It functions through earth and water.
Gravity is the non-inherent cause of the first fall; it resides in earth and water. [Now follows] the definition of fluidity.
Fluidity (*dravatva*), which is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the first [type of] motion (*ādyasyandana*), resides in earth, water, and fire.
It is of two kinds: natural (*sāṃsiddhika*) and incidental (*naimittika*). Natural fluidity exists in water; incidental fluidity exists in earth and fire.
In earth, such as in ghee and the like, there is fluidity produced by conjunction with fire; in fire, such as in gold and the like, it is natural.
Fluidity (*dravatva*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of initial flow (*ādyasyandana*).
It resides in earth, water, and fire.
It is of two kinds: natural (*sāṃsiddhika*) and incidental (*naimittika*).
Conjunction in water is *sāṃsiddhika* (natural);
it is not [natural] in earth and fire;
in earth, as in ghee and the like, it is produced by conjunction with fire (*agnisaṃyogaja*).
Fluidity [is found] in fire, such as gold and the like. Regarding the definition of viscidity (*sneha*):
viscidity is the quality that is the cause of the aggregation of powders and other substances into a mass.
Subsisting on water alone.
Stickiness (*sneha*) is the quality that causes powders and the like to form into a mass;
it resides exclusively in water.
— *Dīpikā*
He defines heaviness (*gurutva*) with the word "first" (*ādya*). Since velocity (*vega*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the second and subsequent falls,
the term "first" is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to velocity.
He defines fluidity (*dravatva*) with the word "ādyeti": *syandana* means flowing. That which is produced by contact with fire is occasional (*naimittika*).
That which is distinct from that is the innate (*sāṃsiddhika*).
He illustrates the occasional (*naimittika*) [buoyancy] in earth with the example "in ghee and so forth."

Regarding fire, he says: "In gold and so forth. He defines viscidity (*sneha*) as "powder" and so on. The word "quality" (*guṇa*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to time (*kāla*) and other such entities.
In order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to form (*rūpa*) and so forth, [the definition] specifies "the state of becoming a mass from powder and so on.
The *Prakāśikā* states this as follows:
The meaning is that he states the occasional cause (*naimittika*).
Regarding the term "state of being a mass" (*piṇḍībhāva*):
"state of being a mass" refers to a particular kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*).
The Compendium of Reasoning:
Definition of Sound (AnTs 33). Sound is a quality apprehended by the sense of hearing.
It exists only in space.
It is of two kinds: consisting of substance and consisting of color. That which consists of substance is found in drums and the like.
That which consists of phonemes (varṇa) takes the form of the Sanskrit language and so forth.
Sound is the quality apprehended by the auditory organ; it subsists solely in space (*ākāśa*). It is of two kinds: consisting of noise (*dhvani*) and consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*).
That which consists of resonance is found in drums and the like;
that which consists of phonemes takes the form of the Sanskrit language and so forth.
*Dīpikā*.

He defines sound (śabda) as "that which is perceived by the auditory organ" (śrotra). The term "quality" (guṇa) is included to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) to the universal "soundness" (śabdatva).
The term "perceived by the auditory organ" is included to exclude over-extension to color-form (rūpa) and other qualities.
Sound is of three kinds: produced by conjunction, produced by disjunction, and produced by sound.
Among these, the first is generated by the conjunction of a drum and a stick; the second—
When a bamboo staff is being split, there arises the "caṭacaṭa" sound produced by the separation of the two halves.
Starting from the location of the drum and extending to the location of the ear, the second and subsequent sounds are born of sound (*śabdaja*).
— *Prakāśikā*
Regarding the phrase "produced by the conjunction of the drum and the stick":
in the first case, the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) is the conjunction between the drum and space (ākāśa).

The conjunction of the drum and the drumstick is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). In the second [case], the disjunction between the bamboo split and space is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), as is the disjunction between the two halves of the bamboo.
The instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa) is [the wind];
however, in the third case, the term "prior conjunction" (pūrvaparvaśabda) is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa),
while the wind and so forth are the instrumental causes— this is the distinction.
Tarkasaṅgraha:
Definition of Intellect (buddhi). Tarkasaṅgraha 34: Intellect is knowledge; it is the cause of all worldly transactions.
That [cognition] is of two kinds: memory and experience.
Memory is knowledge produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Knowledge distinct from that is experience.
The quality that is the cause of all worldly transactions is knowledge, which is the intellect (*buddhi*). This is the classification of the intellect.
It is of two kinds: memory (smṛti) and experience (anubhava).
Knowledge produced solely by mental impressions (saṃskāra) is memory.
Cognition distinct from that [object] is experience (*anubhava*).
It is of two kinds: valid (*yathārtha*) and invalid (*ayathārtha*).
It is of two kinds— veridical and non-veridical—
the *Dīpikā* states the definition of cognition (*buddhi*).

The term "all conventional usage" (*sarvavyavahāra*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to time and so forth; the term "quality" (*guṇa*) is used to exclude over-extension to color and so forth; and the term "all conventional usage" is used to exclude over-extension to [the cognition] "I know."
The sense is that the definition [of cognition] is simply "cognitiveness" (jñānatva), which is apprehended by the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya).
He divides cognition with the words "It is... (seti). He states the definition of memory with the words "by means of a latent impression" (saṃskāreti).
It is a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) known as cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the destruction of a mental impression. The phrase "produced by a mental impression" (*saṃskārajanya*) is included to exclude over-extension to direct experience (*anubhava*).
The word "only" (*mātra*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to recognition (*pratyabhijñā*);
it thus defines direct experience (*anubhava*).
"Different from that" means that knowledge distinct from memory is experience (*anubhava*). He divides experience: "It is of two kinds."
"Manifestation is that which thinks 'I know'";
thus, the mere nature of cognition is the defining characteristic.

The phrase "I know" indicates that the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) is accessible through after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), thereby demonstrating its establishment by means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇasiddhatva*).
For instance: "I know the jar."

Since the aforementioned uniform after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) would be inexplicable without a uniform property (*anugata-dharma*), that property must be accepted; and because this is the simpler explanation (*lāghava*), its status as a universal (*jāti*) is established.
And thus, in the root text:
The meaning is that "the cause of all conventional usage" is a statement regarding the essential nature of cognition (*buddhi*).
Since mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are of three kinds, he says: "called cultivation (*bhāvanā*)."
Regarding the objection that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of recognition:

in the recognition "This is that Devadatta," there exists the quality of being produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of "thatness" (*tattā*), which consists in the state of existing in that particular place and time.
The meaning here is that there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Regarding the phrase "by the mother alone" (*mātrīti*):
although [the definition] consists in being produced solely by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*),...
It is the state of being produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) while not being produced by anything other than a mental impression.
This [definition] is impossible in the case of memory (*smṛti*),
because in that case there exists the state of being produced by something other than a mental impression, such as the self (*ātman*).
Nevertheless, the intended meaning should be understood as being that [the cognition] is not produced by the eye and other [senses], while being produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
[Objection: But surely, *Bālapriyā*—?

Raising the objection: "If being the possessor of the universal property *jñānatva* (cognitiveness) alone constitutes the definition of cognition, then why is the definition of the Guru stated in the root text as 'the cause of all worldly transactions'?"— it is replied that the root text does not intend to provide a formal definition (*lakṣaṇa*),
but rather intends to describe the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Therefore, he says "and thus" (*itthaṃ ca*) to show that there is no inconsistency;
the meaning is that the very nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) constitutes the definition of cognition.
Regarding the phrase "existence at that place and time":

the meaning is [the definition of memory as] being produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose object is that "thatness" (*tattā*) which consists in existence at that particular place and time.
Nevertheless, it is not produced by the eye or other [sense organs].

The point is that recognition (pratyabhijñā), however, is produced by the eye and other sense organs assisted by mental impressions (saṃskāra); therefore, because it lacks the property of "not being produced by the eye and other [senses]," there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition to it.
The Compendium of Reasoning (Tarkasaṅgraha):
The definition of valid experience (yathārthānubhava). [AnTs 35(2)] An experience that possesses a qualifier in that which actually bears that qualifier is valid.
For example, the cognition "this is silver" with respect to silver is called valid knowledge (*pramā*),
because it occurs in relation to that which possesses the object.
An experience that possesses that specific mode [of the object] is "corresponding to reality" (yathārtha). That alone is called valid cognition (pramā).
— *Dīpikā*
He states the definition of valid experience (*yathārthānubhava*) as "tadvati... [and so forth].
Now, an objection is raised: is there not an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in the case of the valid cognition "there is potness in the pot"?
If it is argued that [the universal] "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) does not exist in a pot—[we reply: no;
for the meaning is that wherever there is a relation with something, there is the experience of that relation; thus, the relation with the pot exists in pot-ness.
There is no lack of pervasion. "That very thing" means that in the treatise, only a cognition that accords with reality is called valid knowledge (*pramā*).

In the *Prakāśikā*, it is stated in the root text that [valid cognition] is an experience (*anubhava*) which possesses a qualifier (*tatprakāraka*) with respect to that which possesses it (*tadvati*).
The meaning of the locative case is the state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*),
which is connected with the experience (*anubhava*) by way of the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatā*).
And thus, [the cognition] has that [object] as its qualificandum—

The definition of a veridical experience (*yathārthānubhava*) is the state of being an experience possessing that [object] as its qualifier (*tatprakāraka*). The referent of the term "that" (*tat*) is the qualifier (*prakāra*);
and its possession (*tadvattva*) is to be understood by means of the relation that delimits the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratāvacchedaka-sambandha*).
Therefore, even though silver-ness exists in mother-of-pearl and the like through the relation of temporal connection, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to the error "this is silver."
And yet, there is no [cognition] such as "these are both vermilion and silver" that apprehends vermilion as being silver, or apprehends silver as being vermilion.

It should not be argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to a collective delusion (*samūhālambana-bhrama*) of the form "this is silver and this is a piece of cloth," because in that case both the state of having "piece of cloth" as the qualificandum and "clothness" as the qualifier,
as well as the state of having "silver" as the qualificandum and "silverness" as the qualifier, are present.

Likewise, there is no fault because one intends to express the meaning as "the nature of experience qualified by having that [object] as its qualifier, delimited by having that [object] as its qualificandum. For it is an established tenet that when two objective relations stand in the relation of the defined and the definer (*nirūpya-nirūpakabhāva*), their corresponding objective presences (*viṣayitā*) stand in the relation of the delimited and the delimiting (*avacchedya-avacchedakabhāva*).

Due to the absence of the property of being qualified by the qualificandumness of *raṅga* (the red-ochre) in the modehood of *raṅga*, as manifested by the error, and the absence of the property of being qualified by the qualificandumness of silver in the modehood of silverness,
[there is] the state of having *raṅga*-ness as its mode, delimited by having *raṅga* as its qualificandum—

And because the property of having silverness as its qualifier (prakārakatva) delimited by the property of having silver as its qualificand (viśeṣyakatva) does not exist [in that erroneous cognition],
there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).
The inclusion of the property of being an experience (anubhavatva) is for the purpose of excluding memory (smṛti).
This result will become clear immediately hereafter.
Now, as for the term "tadvati" (in that which possesses it):
Since the term "adhikaraṇe" (in the locus) signifies the sense of [the relation of] being a locus, there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*) in the valid cognition "potness is in the pot.

With the intention that the relation of being a locus (*ādheyatā*) is not a determinant of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*), and thus the locus of the qualifier "pot-ness" in relation to that connection is unestablished, he raises the objection: "But in the pot..."
Regarding "ghaṭatvāmiti":
the meaning of the term "tadvati" is "that which is related to that."
And thus, since potness also stands in a relation to the pot,

it exists in such a valid cognition as the locus (ādheya) in relation to the pot; therefore, the property of having "pot" as its qualifier, delimited by having "potness"— which is related to the pot— as its qualificandum, is present [in that cognition].
He resolves the objection that there would be no over-extension (avyāpti) with the words "yatreti" (where...).
[The definition is] "only valid experience of an object as it is" (yathārthānubhava eva). By the use of the restrictive particle "eva," there is the exclusion of valid memory (yathārthasmṛti).

The point is that if mere knowledge of an object as it is were to constitute valid cognition (*pramā*), then the instrument of memory would result in being a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). This is the intended meaning. *Bālapriyā*.
The meaning of the locative case is "being the qualificand.
In the expression "tadvati" (in that which possesses it), the word "tat" (that) refers to the property functioning as the qualifier (*prakāra*).
The meaning of the locative case is the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyitva*).
In that context, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*)— that is, the referent of the word [ending in the locative]—
is construed with [the action] by means of the relation of being determined (*nirūpitatva*).
The property of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyitva*) is construed with the experience (*anubhava*) by means of the relation of substratumhood (*āśrayatā*).
Thus, [the definition] is: that which is the substratum of the property of being the qualificandum as determined by that [qualifier].
A valid cognition (*yathārtha-anubhava*) is an experience that has a qualifier-nature (*prakāratā*) residing in that [object].

The definition of a valid experience is: being an experience, while having a qualificand-nature (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in that which possesses that [qualifier], and while having a qualifier-nature residing in that [qualifier].

In the valid cognition "this is a pot," there exists the state of being the determiner of a qualificandum-ness residing in the pot which possesses pot-ness, the state of being the determiner of a qualifier-ness residing in pot-ness, and the state of being an experience.
The definition consists in being endowed with the [required] characteristics.
The inclusion of "being an experience" (*anubhavatva*) is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to memory (*smṛti*).

[This is because] in the error of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, although there is the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) residing in "silverness," which is the object of cognition, it lacks the nature of being an experience.

Since there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) due to the existence [of the property] in the subject (*sattva*), the inclusion of the condition "being the determiner of a qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in that which possesses it" is made in order to exclude that.

In the case of the error of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, however, there is the inclusion of the condition that the qualificandum-residence (viśeṣyatā) resides in the mother-of-pearl shell as being qualified by the absence of silverness.

In the error of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there exists precisely the state of having a qualificandum-residence residing in the mother-of-pearl shell as being qualified by the absence of silverness;
it does not, however, have silver—as qualified by silverness—as its qualificandum. Thus, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).

Similarly, if one were to state only "the nature of being an experience" while [defining valid knowledge] as having that [object] as its qualificandum, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the erroneous experience "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl;
for in that case, the requirement of "having that as its qualifier" (*tatprakārakatva*) is absent, and thus the word "that" (*tat*) [in the definition] does not apply.
Since there is no restrictive rule that only the mode (prakāra) is to be grasped, when "shell-ness" (śuktitva) is grasped by that word,
both the state of having shell-ness as its qualificandum and the state of being an experience would exist therein; therefore,
in order to exclude that [undesired consequence]:
The term "having that mode" (tatprakārakatva) is used;
and upon its inclusion, by the rule that two instances of the word *tat* uttered in the same context denote a single object, it refers specifically to the meaning of the first-encountered *tat*-word.

Some maintain that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the property of having "being silverness" as its qualifier— which was grasped by the first *tatpada*— is absent from the aforementioned experience, even with respect to being the object of apprehension (*grāhyatayā*) by the second *tatpada*.
However, in reality:
In the cognition "this is indeed silver," there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it possesses the status of a valid cognition (*pramātva*) regarding silverness;
therefore, the inclusion of the condition "having that as its qualifier" (*tatprakārakatva*) is necessary, as is clear from the *Dinakaryā* and other works.
Now, [one might object] even in the case of mother-of-pearl...

Since the possession of silverness by way of the relation of temporal succession (kālika-sambandha) exists even in the erroneous cognition "this is silver"—because the state of having silverness as its qualificandum and silverness as its qualifier exists therein—there would be over-extension (ativyāpti). Therefore, he says: "the possession thereof" (tadvattvam).
"It is to be grasped by means of the relation that delimits the modehood. In the present context, the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation that delimits the modehood.
The point is that, by virtue of that relation, it is silver itself— possessing the property of silver-ness—
and not mother-of-pearl; furthermore, since the state of having silver as its qualificandum does not exist in the error regarding silver,
there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
1. "The consequence of [the cognition] being a valid cognition (*pramā*) of silver-ness" means that its qualificandum possesses silver-ness; this is the intended sense.
And yet, as expressed by the words "not even so," and so forth:
while silver and turmeric are present before one and in contact with the sense faculties,
one perceives turmeric-ness in the silver and silver-ness in the turmeric, thinking, "These..."

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a collective delusion (*samūhālambana-bhrama*) characterized as "this is yellow and silver," because in that delusion both yellow and silver are the qualificands (*viśeṣya*),
while yellowness and silverness [are the qualifiers].

And both are the modes (prakāra). Likewise, there is the state of having "being a bracelet" as the qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*), the state of having "silverness-possessing silver" as the qualificand, and the state of having "braceletness" as the mode.
"And because there is the presence of the state of having 'silverness' as its qualifier"—this is the intention of the objector.
A cognition that has multiple primary qualificanda is called a "collective apprehension" (*samūhālambana*). He provides the resolution:
This is expressed by the phrase "delimited by having that as its qualificandum" (*tadvad-viśeṣyakatvāvacchinna*), and so forth.

Correct experience (*yathārthānubhava*) is the state of being an experience whose locus is that which has the property of having that [object] as its qualifier (*tat-prakārakatva*), as delimited by the state of having that [object] as its qualificandum (*tadvad-viśeṣyakatva*).

The relationship of the delimited (*avacchedya*) and the delimiter (*avacchedaka*) between the state of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyitva*) and the state of being a qualifier (*prakāritva*) occurs only when there is a relationship of the determined (*nirūpya*) and the determiner (*nirūpaka*) between the state of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) and the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*).
Even though in the aforementioned error of collective apprehension (*samūhālambana-bhrama*), both "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) and "brass-ness" (*raṅgatva*) are qualifiers, nevertheless...

The property of being brass (*raṅgatva*) is the qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the brass portion, and the property of being silver (*rajatatva*) is the qualifier with respect to the silver portion; thus, the qualifierhood residing in the property of being brass is determined by the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the silver, and not by the qualificandhood residing in the brass which possesses the property of being brass.

Thus, the qualifierhood (prakāratā) residing in silverness is determined by the qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) residing in the mother-of-pearl shell, but it is not determined by the qualificandhood residing in silver as qualified by silverness. And so it is.
Because there is no relation of the determined and the determiner between the subjectness residing in the wave and the qualificandness residing in the wave,
and because there is likewise an absence of that relation between the subjectness residing in silverness and the qualificandness residing in the silver.

Because there is no relationship of the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) between the state of being a qualifier (*prakāritva*) as determined by redness and the state of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyitva*) as determined by redness, nor between the state of being a qualifier as determined by silverness and the state of being a qualificand as determined by silverness.

The point is that there is no over-extension [of the definition] because the property of having "cloth" as the qualificandum (viśeṣyakatva) delimited by the mode (prakārakatva) of "cloth-ness," and the property of having "silver" as the qualificandum delimited by the mode of "silver-ness," are both absent in the aforementioned error of collective apprehension (samūhālambana-bhrama).

The meaning is: "It will become clear immediately [later on]," specifically at the occasion of explaining the passage from the *Dīpikā* which states, "In the treatise, only the experience of an object as it truly is is called valid cognition (*pramā*)."
By virtue of having the sense of "in the locus" (adhikaraṇe);
and thus, by means of the relation that delimits the modehood (prakāratā).
It is thus established that an experience whose qualificandum is a particular locus of a mode is "corresponding to reality" (yathārtha).
In the valid cognition (pramā) "potness is in the pot," potness is the qualificandum.
In that case, the pot is the qualifier by way of the relation of being located;
the relation that delimits the state of being a qualifier is the relation of being located.
The state of being the locus (*ādheyatva*) does not restrict occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*);
therefore, [the relation] by way of the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatāsambandhena*).

The intention of the objector is that, because a locus for a jar— which serves as the qualifier— is unestablished, the definition of valid cognition (pramā) suffers from the fault of non-pervasion (avyāpti) with respect to such a valid cognition.
[This applies to] the term "tadvati" (in that which possesses it).
The meaning is "related to that.

The intention is that [the locus] is the relatum (anuyogin) of the relation which serves as the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) for the mode (prakāratā) having that [property] as its counter-correlative (pratiyogika).
And thus, if [the phrase] "tadvati" [is interpreted as]:

The meaning would be "that which possesses a locus-hood (adhikaraṇatā) as determined by a substratum-ness (ādheyatā) qualified by a relation that delimits the modehood (prakāratā) residing therein"; however, since substratum-ness is not a determinant of occurrence (vṛttyaniyāmaka),
there is no established locus-hood determined by a substratum-ness qualified by a relation delimited by a substratum-ness residing in a jar.
There would be an under-extension;
however, that meaning is not intended in the present context,
[namely] by way of the relation of being located in (*ādheyatā*).

The intention of the respondent is that there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti), because the property of having "potness" as its qualifier— delimited by having "that which is related to a pot" as its qualificandum— is present in the valid cognition (*pramā*) "potness is in the pot," since this cognition has "potness related to a pot" as its qualificandum and "pot" as its qualifier.
Regarding the claim that "validity consists merely in being a cognition that accords with reality":
if validity were simply the state of being a cognition that accords with reality, without including the property of being an experience (*anubhavatva*), [then the following would occur].

If that is so, then it follows that memory (smṛti) would also be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it is a cognition of an object as it truly is; yet this is not an acceptable consequence, since memory is a distinct instrument of knowledge characterized by its nature as recollection, which differs from the cognitions produced by perception and other means of valid knowledge.

The point is that since a fifth distinct means of valid cognition would be necessary, it would result in an inconsistency with the author of the Sūtras’ statement that "the means of valid cognition are four.
— *Tarkasaṅgraha*
The definition of erroneous experience (ayathārthānubhava) is as follows: [AnTs 35] An experience that has a particular qualifier (prakāra) where that qualifier is absent is erroneous;
for example, the cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl.
An experience that has a particular qualifier in a locus where that qualifier is absent is "non-correspondent" (ayathārtha).
That very [experience] is called invalid cognition (apramā) (and that very [experience] is called error).
The *Dīpikā* defines erroneous experience (*ayathārthānubhava*) as "that which possesses the absence of that [object].
If it is objected that this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*), applying even to the valid cognition (*pramā*) "this possesses conjunction," we say: no.
Because what is intended is the knowledge of that relation with respect to the same delimiting factor by which the absence of that relation [is known];
for example, the knowledge of conjunction with respect to the delimiting factor that is the absence of conjunction.
1. "Related to the jar" means that which is the locus (*anuyogin*) of the relation of being contained (*ādheyatā*), of which the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the jar. *Prakāśikā:*

"Over-extension" (ativyāpti) means that the property of having "conjunction" as its qualifier exists even in that which lacks conjunction; this is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase "by whatever delimitation":

The meaning is that what is intended is an experience having that [property] as its qualifier, by means of that delimitation and through that relation, wherein there is the absence of that [property] which has a counter-positive delimited by that [relation] and delimited by that [delimitation].
"By way of delimitation through the absence of conjunction" means "by way of delimitation by that which delimits the absence of conjunction.
[The phrase] "by way of conjunction" [is used].
The meaning is "by way of delimitation through the delimitant of the conjunction.
Regarding the phrase "of the relation of conjunction," the meaning is "of the conjunction by way of the relation of inherence (samavāya)."
In this regard, the following should be noted:

this [definition] is formulated in accordance with erroneous cognitions (*bhrama*) that have as their qualifier conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like, which are non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*). However, the definition of erroneous cognition having as its qualifier silverness (*rajatatva*) and the like, which are pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), is as follows:

It is the nature of experience qualified by having that [object] as its qualificandum and being characterized by having that [object] as its qualifier, under the relation [in question], with respect to that absence which has a counter-correlativity delimited by that very relation.

Because the relation delimited by the delimiting factor of the qualifier (prakāratāvacchedaka-sambandha) is included in the definition of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā), even though in the valid cognition "The mountain possesses fire" there exists the state of having as its qualificandum a mountain possessing the absence of fire delimited by inherence (samavāya).
There is no over-extension [of the definition],

because one intends to express a relationship of the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) between the state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) and the state of being the qualifier (*prakāritva*); thus, in the case of the valid cognition (*pramā*) "these are silver and cloth," [the definition does not apply].

Even though there exist [cognitions] having silver and the like as their qualificandum (viśeṣya) and having "silver-ness" and the like as their qualifier (prakāra), provided they lack "shell-ness" and so forth, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti); thus, enough with this excessive detail.
"Bālapriyā is devoid of conjunction," because conjunction is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti).
The point is this: since the absence of conjunction exists even where conjunction is present,

there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of error— namely, "being a cognition that has a qualifier in a locus where that qualifier is absent"— to the valid cognition "this is conjoined," because such a cognition possesses the property of having conjunction as its qualifier in a locus where conjunction is actually absent.
Regarding the phrase "by way of which delimitation" and so forth:
the absence of monkey-contact, as delimited by the root and related to the tree by the relation of inherence, exists in the tree;
and if there occurs a cognition apprehending monkey-contact with respect to that same delimitation, then—
That cognition is an error;
however, the cognition of conjunction with a monkey delimited by the top [of the tree] is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*),
because there is no absence of conjunction with a monkey delimited by that [top].
In the case of a tree possessing conjunction with a monkey at its tip (*agra*), there exists at that very same location (the tip) an absence of conjunction with a monkey as delimited by that [tip],
where the absence is qualified by a relation other than inherence (*samavāya*). At the tip...
There would be the undesirable consequence of regarding the valid cognition "the tree is in contact with the monkey" as an error;
to prevent this, the phrase "delimited by that relation" is included.

The phrase "by that relation" (*tatsambandhena*) is stated in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of a true cognition (*pramā*) which has "connection with a monkey" (*kapisaṃyoga*) as its qualifier, occurring in a tree at the root— which lacks connection with a monkey by way of the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*)— but possesses it by way of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*).
Is it not the case that the statement in the *Dīpikā*, "of the cognition of conjunction as delimited by the absence of conjunction," is incorrect;
for [it would apply to] the erroneous cognition, "The tree at the root is conjoined with the monkey"?
Even though there is a cognition of conjunction delimited by the root, there is no cognition of conjunction delimited by the absence of conjunction;
for it is not the case that [conjunction... of conjunction.
Since the absence of conjunction (*saṃyogābhāva*) is not perceived as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) in that manner, he explains:
"The meaning is 'by way of being delimited by the delimiter of the absence of conjunction'."
The meaning is: "by way of delimitation by that which is the delimitant (*avacchedaka*) of the absence of conjunction," such as the root and so forth;
[this is expressed as] "by way of delimitation by the delimitant of the conjunction.
That which is the delimitant of the conjunction is the tip and so forth.

The meaning is: "by way of that delimitation. Now, one might object: although an error whose qualificandum is a non-pervasive entity has a delimited object, an error whose qualifier is a pervasive property such as "silver-ness" lacks that [delimited object].
Since the definition of error stated in the passage beginning with "yadavacchedena" (by the delimitation of which... does not apply to all errors, he says:
"In this regard, the following should be noted," namely, "delimited by that relation," and so forth. [This refers to] the mother-of-pearl.
In the case of the error "this is silver" regarding an object in contact with the senses, the following subsumption is established:
the object present before one, which is the mother-of-pearl, possesses the absence of silverhood, where the counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
The state of having "silverness" as the qualifier while having that [object] as the qualificandum exists in the aforementioned error;
however, if the property of being delimited by the relation that serves as the delimitor of the qualifierhood is not included within the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā), then—

If the definition of error were "an experience qualified by having that [object] as its qualifier and being delimited by having that [subject] as its qualificandum, where that subject possesses the absence of whatever has a counter-correlativity delimited by some relation," then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the valid cognition "the mountain possesses fire."

For instance— if by the word "that" (tat) the qualifier *vahni* (fire) is grasped, then even though it exists on the mountain (*parvata*) by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it does not exist there by way of inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore,
[the locus] is that which possesses the absence of fire as delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandhāvacchinna-vahnyabhāvavān*).
1. "Because it is not so perceived":
the meaning is that the absence of conjunction is not perceived as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the conjunction.
[In the case of] "the mountain," regarding its being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
The property of having "fire" as its qualifier (*vahniprakārakatva*) exists in the valid cognition (*pramā*) "the mountain possesses fire. However,

if one introduces the requirement that [the absence] be delimited by the relation that serves as the delimiting condition for the qualifier (*prakāratāvacchedakasambandhāvacchinnatva*), then— since the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) alone is the delimiting condition for the qualifier— the [subject] would possess an absence of fire whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by that very [conjunction].

Since the qualificandum [of the cognition] "the mountain is not [existent]" does not possess the state of having as its qualificandum that which lacks the counter-positive of the absence of that [mountain], where the counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation delimiting the modehood— as is the case with the valid cognition "the mountain possesses fire"— there is no over-extension.
The state [is as follows]:

regarding the states of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) and the mode (*prakāritva*). And thus, when there is no intention to express a relationship of the delimited (*avacchedya*) and the delimiter (*avacchedaka*) between the states of being the qualificandum and the mode...
If one were to state only this much— that an error is an experience that has as its qualificandum something in which the [supposed] property is absent, yet takes that property as its mode—

then in the case of the valid experience "these are brass and silver," which apprehends brassness in the brass and silverness in the silver, both the brass and the silver [would have to be considered erroneous].

The qualificandum (viśeṣya) is [the object], while "being a shell" (raṅgatva) and "being silver" (rajatatva) are the qualifiers (prakāra). When the term "that" (tatpada) grasps "being a shell," then silver—which lacks that [quality of being a shell]—becomes the qualificandum in the aforementioned cognition, and "being a shell" becomes the qualifier; thus, there is the property of having as its qualificandum silver that lacks "being a shell."
Furthermore, there exists the property of having "shell-ness" as its qualifier;

likewise, there exists the property of having a shell devoid of "silver-ness" as its qualificand and "silver-ness" as its qualifier. Consequently, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Therefore, of these two...
There is an intention to express the absence of both the delimited (avacchedya) and the delimiter (avacchedaka).

Thus, the definition of error (bhrama) becomes: an experience qualified by that "having that as its qualifier" (tatprakārakatva), which is itself delimited by "having as its objective locus that which possesses the absence of that" (tadabhāvavad-viśeṣyakatvāvacchinna).
In the aforementioned collective cognition (*samūhālambana-pramā*),
the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in "being silver" is determined by the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the silver [which is actually a piece of cloth],
and not by the qualificandhood residing in the silver [which is actually] that which lacks the property of being silver. Regarding the silver [in the erroneous cognition]:

Because "being silver" (*raṅgatva*) is not a qualifying attribute (*prakāra*). And thus, there is an absence of the relationship of the determined and the determiner (*nirūpya-nirūpakabhāva*) between the qualifier-ness residing in "being silver" and the qualificand-ness residing in "silver"; likewise [there is an absence] between the state of having "being silver" as a qualifier and the state of having "silver that lacks being silver" as a qualificand.
There is no relation of delimited and delimiter [between two objects],

because of the rule that the relation of delimited and delimiter exists only between those two objective contents (*viṣayatā*) which themselves stand in a relation of the defined and the definer (*nirūpya-nirūpaka-bhāva*).

The point is that there is no over-extension [of the definition], because the property of having "silverness" as its qualifier delimited by having a substrate that lacks silverness, and the property of having "rajata-ness" (silverness) as its qualifier delimited by having a substrate that lacks rajata-ness, are both absent in the aforementioned collective valid cognition (*samūhālambana-pramā*).
The definition of error (*bhrama*) is: being an experience (*anubhavatva*) while being the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of a qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) that is qualified by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*).

And the qualification of the qualificandumness by the mode-ness [is established] by way of both relations: (1) residing in a locus of the absence of its own substratum, where the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by its own delimiting relation (*svāvacchedakasambandha*), and (2) being determined by itself (*svanirūpitatva*).
The summary:
the classification of valid experience according to the *Tarkasaṃgraha*.
Valid experience of reality is fourfold, distinguished as perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony;
its instruments are also fourfold, distinguished as perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony.
Valid experience of reality (yathārthānubhava) is fourfold, distinguished as perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumiti), comparison (upamiti), and verbal testimony (śabda);
its instrument (tatkaraṇam) is likewise [fourfold].
It is fourfold, distinguished as perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), comparison (upamāna), and verbal testimony (śabda).
A lamp is that which provides experience of objects as they truly are (yathārthānubhava).
He analyzes [the term] as "according to the object.
Incidentally, he analyzes the instrument of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with the words:
"that which is its instrument" (tatkaraṇam api).
The meaning is "the instrument of valid cognition" (*pramākaraṇam*).
"The instrument of valid cognition is a means of knowledge" (*pramāyāḥ karaṇaṃ pramāṇam*) is the general definition of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
"By way of occasion" (*prasaṅgāt*) means "because of the occasion," that is, because that which has been brought to mind is not fit to be neglected.

Since it is only that which has been understood in a general way that can be established in its specific form, he clarifies the general definition [of valid cognition] as follows: "The instrument of valid cognition (pramā) is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). — *Bālapriyā* The general definition is clarified by stating: "The instrument of valid cognition is the means of valid cognition. This is because it is only that which has been apprehended in a general manner that can subsequently be presented in its specific form. *Bālapriyā* (the "Beloved of the Child") is the name of a commentary.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is remembered" (*smṛtasya*): the meaning is that once the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*) has been stated, its instrument (*karaṇa*) becomes known by implication; therefore, it is not appropriate to disregard it.
1. Regarding the term *svāvacchedaka*:
in the error "this is silver" (*śuktau idaṃ rajatam*) with respect to mother-of-pearl, the application is as follows—*sva* is the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in silverness;

the relation that delimits it (*tadavacchedakasambandha*) is the relation of inherence (*samavāyasambandha*); [the absence] has a counter-correlativity delimited by that [relation] (*tadavacchinnapratiyogitāka*).
The absence of silverness— which is the locus of its own substratum and the locus of the qualifier-ness— is its residing in the mother-of-pearl as the qualificandum; likewise,
"itself" refers to the qualifier-ness residing in silverness, and [the absence] consists in being determined by that.
In the qualificandumness residing in the mother-of-pearl;
and thus, there is that qualificandumness residing in the mother-of-pearl which is qualified by the qualifierhood residing in silverness through the aforementioned two relations.
The definition of an instrument (*karaṇa*) according to the *Tarkasaṅgraha* is: being an experience while having that [object] as its qualifier; this exists in the error "this is silver."
An instrument (*karaṇa*) is an uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*), [that is,] it is that which possesses an operation (*vyāpāravat*).
An instrument is an uncommon cause.
The *Dīpikā* states the definition of the instrument (*karaṇa*) as follows: "That which is uncommon... and so forth.
The term "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to common causes such as space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*).
— *Prakāśikā*

Regarding the phrase "asādhāraṇa" (uncommon): since space, time, unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth, are causes only with respect to that which is delimited by the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) in general, they lack the status of an uncommon cause— defined as causality relative to an effectness that resides in valid cognition (*pramā*) as delimited by a property pervaded by the nature of experience (*anubhavatva*).
In that case, because [the definition] does not exist there, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
However, the earlier [teachers] maintain that one must also state: "provided that it possesses activity" (*vyāpāravattve sati*).
Therefore, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to the contact of the eye and so forth;
for the contact of the ear and mind, or sound itself, can indeed be the instrumental operation (*vyāpāra*).
They say that there is no lack of pervasion by the definition of an instrument (*karaṇa*) regarding the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*),

because that which causes the non-production of a specific effect due to its delay is itself the nature of being an uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇatva*) of causality, [and this applies] to time (*kāla*) and so forth.

Because such causality is absent, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. Only that which is intended as an operation, such as the contact of the sense organ and so forth, is the instrument (*karaṇa*). This will become clear in the root text itself in the statement: "Inference is precisely the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*). Therefore...

Thus it has been stated by the authors of the Maṇi in the passage beginning with "And that is the consideration of the middle term (liṅgaparāmarśa)"; such is the view of the moderns. Further details should be sought in our Cintāmaṇiprabhā.
[End of] Bālapriyā.
Regarding the phrase "from space, time, unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), and so forth":
the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is being the uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*) as determined by valid cognition (*pramā*).

The meaning is: the state of being a cause (kāraṇatva) as defined by that which is the effect-ness (kāryatā) delimited by a property pervaded by the nature of experience (anubhavatva), which resides in valid cognition (pramā).
A property pervaded by the nature of experience—

Regarding validity (*pramātva*): if, in the definition of being an effect (*kāryatā*), one does not include the qualification of being delimited by a property pervaded by the nature of experience (*anubhavatva*), then since space, time, unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth are causes for effects in general, they would also be causes for valid cognition (*pramā*).
The definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be over-extended to space, time, and so forth; however,
if that [qualification] is included,
then the causal efficacy (*kāraṇatā*)— which is defined by the effect-nature (*kāryatā*) delimited by being an effect residing in light— is not present in space, time, and so forth.
Even though [the sense organ] exists, there is no causality characterized by the effect-ness delimited by the nature of being a valid cognition (prāmāṇya) established in a valid cognition;
thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
This applies to the contact with that [object], just as it does to the eye and so forth.

Since the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in being the cause of valid perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣapramā*), in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to operations such as sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*) and the like, causality mediated by an operation must be included in the definition. And it is not the case that...
There is non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding the auditory faculty (śrotrendriya),
because the contact consisting of inherence in the ear (śrotrasamavāya-rūpa-saṃnikarṣa) is eternal; thus,
the definition of an operation (vyāpāra) as being constituted by that which is produced [by the contact] is absent, since the nature of being a cause through the medium of an operation is [required].
It should not be said that the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is absent in the auditory faculty (*śrotra*),

because either the conjunction of the ear and the mind or the sound itself constitutes the operation of the ear; thus, the status of being a cause of perception through that medium exists in the ear as well.
"Because of existence"— this is the view of the ancients.
He states the view of the moderns with the words beginning "yadvilambāt" (due to which delay).
Being a cause characterized by activity is not what constitutes being an uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*).

Rather, it is the state of that [cause] whose delay results in the non-production of the effect in question. Since time and other such factors lack this kind of uncommon causality, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to them.
As the very nature of operation (vyāpāra),
it resides precisely in those [factors] such as contact (saṃnikarṣa) and so forth, which were previously accepted [as such].

The view of the moderns (*navīna*) is that since such causality exists, only the contact (*sannikarṣa*), the reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*), and so forth possess the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
— *Tarkasaṅgraha*
The definition of a cause:
A cause is that which invariably precedes its effect (while being not otherwise established).
The cause is that which necessarily precedes its effect.
The *Dīpikā* states the definition of a cause as follows: "the effect," etc.
If it were stated that "the cause is that which exists prior [to the effect]," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such things as a donkey;
therefore, the term "invariable" (*niyata*) is added.
If only that much were done, there would be over-extension; therefore, it is specified as "occurring prior.
— *Prakāśikā*
"Fixed" (niyata): for "fixedness" is indeed pervasiveness (vyāpakatva).
And since that is not possible in the case of a donkey and so forth, it does not apply there.
The sense is that there would be the over-extension [of the definition] to the cause of a jar.
Regarding the term "previously occurring" (*pūrvavṛtti*):
it refers to its own pervasion (*svavyāpakatva*).
The intention is that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) because, although [the effect] exists in its own locus, it does not exist at a time prior to that [moment].
[This applies] to the locus of the effect, with respect to the relation that delimits its status as an effect,
delimited by the moment immediately preceding the effect.

The collective meaning to be understood is that causality in that form consists in possessing a property (taddharma) which is not a delimitor (anavacchedaka) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) that is actually present. *Bālapriyā* [Commentary].
The definition of a cause is its being invariably antecedent to the effect, provided that it is necessarily related to that effect.
And this "invariable relation to the effect" is as follows:
[The definition of a cause is] being a pervader of the effect. If one were to state merely that [a cause] must precede the effect,
then since even a donkey or similar entity sometimes exists prior to a jar, it would follow that such things are also causes of the jar.
To exclude that [over-extension], the property of being a pervader of the effect (*kāryavyāpakatva*) is introduced.
Since the effect itself is also a pervader of the effect,
the property of occurring prior to the effect (*kāryapūrvavartitva*) is introduced to exclude over-extension in that case as well.

He says this with the words beginning "for [the nature of] necessity," and so forth. He refines the definition by incorporating the state of being antecedent to the effect within the very body of the definition of being a pervader of the effect, using the phrase "by the relation that delimits the state of being an effect," and so on.

By the relation that delimits the state of being an effect— namely, conjunction— the absence that exists in the locus of the effect, such as the locus of a jar, at the spatial point delimited by the moment immediately preceding the jar, is not the absence of the staff, the wheel, or other such factors.

Rather, the absence of a donkey and so forth has as its counter-positive-ness-delimiter (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) "donkey-ness" and the like, while "staff-ness" and the like are not the counter-positive-ness-delimiters;
[the definition consists in] possessing that [non-counter-positive-ness-delimiter].
The application of the definition [of locus] exists in the case of *taṇḍula* (rice) and so forth.

If the phrase "by means of the relation that delimits the state of being an effect" (*kāryatāvacchedaka-sambandhena*) were not stated, then even a location where a jar has not yet arisen— such as a place that is the locus of a jar by way of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*)— would [erroneously] qualify as such.
The absence that constitutes its occurrence is the absence of the staff and so forth;

since the staff and such possess precisely the property that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma*) of that absence, and do not possess a property that does not delimit it, there would be the fallacy of impossibility (*asambhava*).

To exclude that [over-extension], it is specified as "by the relation that delimits the effect-ness" (*kāryatāvacchedakasambandhena*). If one were to state merely "the non-opposition to an absence residing in the locus of the effect," then there would be the absence of both the staff and the thread, which resides in the locus of a jar by way of the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
In that case, by taking both absences in the manner that "the state of being the counter-positive of that [absence] exists in the staff," an impossibility (asaṃbhava) would arise.
To avoid this, the inclusion of the property of "possessing a property that is not a delimitant of counter-positiveness" is made;
that is, with respect to that property under whose aspect the causality is intended.
What is intended is the state of not being a delimiting factor of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitānavacchedakatva*).
What is intended is that the stick, the wheel, and so forth possess causality by way of their respective universals, such as "stickness" (*daṇḍatva*) and "wheelness" (*cakratva*).
However, since "stickness" (daṇḍatva) and so forth indeed possess the status of not being a delimiting factor for such a counter-correlativity, the definition is properly applied. Consequently,
there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) to a donkey or similar objects by taking "knowability" (prameyatva) as the [delimiting] property.
The Lamp:
An Exposition on Otherwise-Established Causes.
Now, is not even the color of the thread [an otherwise-established cause]?

If it is argued that [the color] must be the cause with respect to the cloth— no, because of the qualification "provided it is not otherwise established" (*ananyathāsiddhatve sati*). "Not otherwise established" means being devoid of any other way of being established.

*Anyathāsiddhi* (redundant causality) is threefold: that which is *anyathāsiddha* with respect to a given effect by means of another thing, when its antecedence to that effect is understood only in conjunction with that other thing;
for example, [the antecedence of] the yarn [to a cloth is understood only in conjunction with the shuttle].
The form of the yarn and the state of being yarn [are antecedent conditions] with respect to the cloth.
That which is known to have antecedence with respect to something else is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) with respect to that [other thing]. For example:
Just as the prior existence of space with respect to a cloth is known only when its prior existence with respect to sound is already known; so too,
when an effect can be accounted for by something else that has been established as a necessary antecedent elsewhere, that which merely co-exists with it is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha).

Just as, in the case of a product of baking (*pākaja*), the prior non-existence of color (*rūpa-prāgabhāva*) is [the cause] with respect to odor; and thus, causality consists in being invariably antecedent while not being otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha-niyatapūrvavṛttitva*).
— *Prakāśikā*
"It would be the cause"—
the sense is that this is because it invariably precedes [the effect].
In other treatises, [this is excluded] by way of "established otherwise" (anyathāsiddhi).
Although there are five types [of causes], he says "threefold" according to the intention of the master Maṇika:
"together with which," and so forth.
Together with whichever thread (*tantu*), of whichever that form (*tatturūpa*) and thread-ness (*tantutva*) [are present], and whichever...

The meaning is that, with respect to the cloth, the state of having existed previously is understood; however, with respect to that same cloth, the form of the thread and the generic property of being a thread (*tantutva*) are rendered superfluous (*anyathāsiddha*) by that very thread.
In this context, there is concomitance (*sahitatva*).
It should be understood that they share the status of being the object of a single cognition.
When there is a cognition of the thread's color as existing prior to the cloth, its objecthood must be stated precisely as "the form of the thread," in order to avoid over-extension.
And likewise, the nature of the thread is established as otherwise-accomplished;
in this way, even the cognition of the prior existence of the state of being a thread [is otherwise-accomplished].
The sense is that even the claim that [the cause] pertains exclusively to the domain of the yarn is established otherwise;
here, for the word "yena" (by which),
[the gloss is] "possessing independent positive and negative concomitance," and for the word "yasya" (of which)...
The qualification "devoid of independent positive and negative concomitance" (svatantrānvayavyatirekaśūnya) should be understood. By this,

there is no "otherwise-established" status (anyathāsiddhi) of the thread by way of its being a thread— which is not such [i.e., lacks independent concomitance]— nor is there such a status for the conjunction of the threads.
The summary is that [the thread] is established as otherwise-superfluous (*anyathāsiddhi*) by means of the yarn.
However, others maintain that whatever possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) necessitated by the positive and negative concomitance of another is "otherwise-superfluous."
Regarding the cognition "sound": for the nature of space (*ākāśatva*) consists in being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of sound;
thus, without having grasped its status as the cause of sound, [one cannot grasp its nature].
The meaning is that because space cannot be apprehended as existing prior to the jar by virtue of its nature as space, space is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha).
Regarding the phrase "established elsewhere": [it refers to being established in relation to something other than the effect].

The meaning is this: since the prior absence of odor (*gandhaprāgabhāva*), which is established as a necessary antecedent in cases where [substances] are not produced by heating (*apākaja*), can account for the presence of odor even in cases produced by heating (*pākaja*), the prior absence of color (*rūpapragabhāva*) is superfluous (*anyathāsiddha*). For this very reason, the word "necessary" (*niyata*) is redundant.

If it is argued that [the definition] is unnecessary because the third type of "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*)— namely, that which is otherwise established by being a common property (*sāmānya*) such as the "unrestricted" (*aniyata*)— can be excluded by the very phrase "only that which exists" (*satyantenaiva*)— we say no; for with respect to the general category of pot (*ghaṭasāmānya*),...

The Compendium of Reasoning:
Division of Causes (AnTs 40). Cause is of three kinds, distinguished as inherent (samavāyin), non-inherent (asamavāyin), and instrumental (nimitta).
That which, being inherent, produces an effect is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
For example, threads are the inherent cause of cloth, and cloth is the inherent cause of the color and other qualities residing in the sky.
That cause which exists in a single substrate together with either the effect or another cause is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Just as the conjunction of threads is the cause of cloth, and the form of the threads is the cause of the form of the cloth, so too a cause distinct from both of these is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), such as the shuttle, loom, and so forth,
which are the causes of cloth.
The cause is threefold, distinguished as inherent (samavāyi), non-inherent (asamavāyi), and instrumental (nimitta).
That in which the effect is produced as inherent is the inherent cause.
That is its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). For example, threads are the inherent cause of cloth, and cloth is the inherent cause of the color and other qualities residing within itself.
An *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) is a cause that is inherent in the same object as either the effect or the cause;
for example, the conjunction of threads is the non-inherent cause of a cloth.
The form of the threads and the form residing in the cloth—
distinct from both of these is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa), as for example:
The shuttle, loom, and so forth belong to the cloth.
Among these three kinds of causes, that which is the uncommon cause is alone the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Among these three types of causes, that which is the uncommon cause is alone the [true] cause.

The cause of perceptual knowledge is the contact between the sense organ and its object, which is of six kinds:

In the production of the perception of a jar by means of the eye, conjunction is the contact.

In the case of sound and the auditory organ, since sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), and because there is inherence between a quality and its possessor, [the contact is *samavāya*].
In the direct perception of "soundness" (*śabdatva*), the contact is inherence-in-the-inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), because soundness inheres in the sound that is inherent in the auditory organ.

rather than that, it would be better to postulate non-apprehension itself as the instrument. Anticipating this objection:
Since the sense organ must necessarily be relied upon for the perception of the locus, such as the ground, which is the substratum of the absence,

it is improper to postulate that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the instrument for a distinct type of valid cognition (*pramiti*), given that the perception of absence is already established by the very fact of the sense organ being the instrument; thus he says:
Regarding the term "adhikaraṇa":

[the opponent objects] that you must postulate a distinct relation called the "relation between qualifier and qualified" (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva). To this, he replies: "The relation between qualifier and qualified."
In this regard, the following should be understood: perception is of two kinds, namely, worldly (laukika) and non-worldly (alaukika).
And as for the state of being worldly...
It is a specific type of subjecthood (*viṣayitā*).

In the case of ordinary perception, the sixfold sensory contact (*ṣoḍhā sannikarṣa*) is the cause; however, in the case of extraordinary perception, it is the "characteristic of the universal" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*).
Proximity (pratyāsatti) is threefold: the characteristic of knowledge (jñānalakṣaṇā), the dharma produced by yoga (yogajadharma), and [the relation of conjunction].
Among these, the "characteristic of generality" (sāmānyalakṣaṇā) consists of the form of "smokeness" (dhūmatva) and so forth, or the form of the cognition thereof.
This is because of the etymological derivation: "that which has a universal as its characteristic, its own nature, or its object.
And that [cognition] belongs to its substrata...
It is employed for the extraordinary perception (*alaukikapratyakṣa*) of all smoke and so forth,

because in the case of past and future smoke and the like, the conjunction of the eye and so on is impossible, and because the sense organs do not produce perception when they are not in contact with their objects.

Cognition characterized by knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇā*), however, occurs in the case of visual presentation where fragrance is brought to mind— as in the thought "the sandalwood is fragrant"— because there is no suitable sense-object contact for the eye with respect to that fragrance. Likewise, in the case of yogis perceiving objects remote in space or time, the proximity is the dharma born of yoga (*yogajadharma*).
This is the summary: [it is] the cause.
Thus ends the chapter on direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pariccheda*) in the *Prakāśikā*,
[a commentary] dear to beginners (*bālapriyā*).

Now, regarding the passage beginning with "from non-apprehension" (*anupalabdheḥ*): non-apprehension is defined as the absence of a perceptual cognition whose object is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
The non-apprehension of a jar is the cause of the valid cognition (pramā) whose content is the absence of a jar, such as the cognition "the ground possesses the absence of a jar.
This is because, at the time when a jar is perceived— as in the cognition "the ground possesses a jar"— there arises no valid cognition of the absence of a jar.

If non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) were not the cause for the valid cognition of absence (*abhāvapramā*), then it would follow that the valid cognition of the absence of a jar or the like would occur even at the time when that very jar or other counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is being apprehended; therefore, the Bhaṭṭas maintain that non-apprehension is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being the cause of the valid cognition of absence.
The Naiyāyikas, however,

maintain that since the perception and inference directed toward non-existence are accounted for by the sense organs and logical marks (liṅga) alone when assisted by non-apprehension (anupalabdhi), there is no separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) directed toward non-existence.
The valid cognition resulting from perception and so forth is distinct [from ordinary cognition],
and likewise, its means of accomplishment is also not distinct from the instruments of valid cognition such as perception.

Rather, they maintain that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is merely a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) for the sense faculties and so forth that produce the valid cognition of non-existence (*abhāvapramā*).
This refers to the passage beginning with "of reasoning" (*tarkasya*), etc.
"Pervasion, non-frustration by a counter-argument, an undesirable consequence in the opposite case, and consistency with what is not undesired— these are the five limbs of a *tarka*."
According to the manner thus stated, five factors are required for a *tarka*:
pervasion (*vyāpti*), the probans (*āpādaka*) such as the absence of fire, and the probandum (*āpādya*).
The relationship of pervaded and pervader exists between the absence of smoke and [the absence of fire].
Non-contradiction by reasoning (*tarkāpratihati*) means the absence of a counter-reasoning (*pratikūlatarka*).

The conclusion by way of contraposition (*viparyaye paryavasānam*): for the reductio ad absurdum (*āpādana*)—namely, "if there were an absence of fire, then there would be an absence of smoke"—results in its contrapositive conclusion: "because smoke exists, fire alone is logical.
This is what constitutes the conclusion by way of contraposition.
Unwantedness (*aniṣṭatva*)— the unwantedness of the consequence to be established, such as the absence of smoke, for the questioner; that is,
its being unfavorable.
The absence of being a prover for the opponent's position;
having refined that, he states the conclusion regarding its contrapositive:
"In the absence of the subsumer," and so forth.

The reductio-implicans (*āpādaka*) is the absence of fire; its absence is the absence of the absence of fire, which is fire itself. That which establishes this is the contrapositive (*viparyaya*). The absence of smoke, which is the smoke-absence, is the absence of the probandum (*āpādya*);
its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is smoke. The nature of that *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) is that for which smoke-absence is the probandum.
