The meaning is that [the tarka] culminates in the opposite [of the antecedent]. In the present context, regarding the form of the tarka, "If a jar were here, then the jar would be seen, just like the ground," the jar is the *āpādaka* (the hypothetical antecedent).

The absence of that [perception] is the absence of the jar; the counter-positive (viparyaya) that establishes it is the absence of perception; and the counter-positive of that [absence of perception] is perception itself, which is what must be established as the consequence (āpādya). Thus, the nature of *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) consists in having as its consequence that which is the counter-positive of the counter-positive (viparyaya-pratiyogin) of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) of the subverting factor (āpādaka) that establishes the absence of the [consequence]. And so:

Because it is not observed that in a case where, within a particular reductio (*tarka*), the thing to be established (*āpādya*) is the counter-positive of the absence of the prover (*sādhaka*) which establishes the absence of the reductio-implicans (*āpādaka*), there is a final conclusion regarding the absence of the reductio-implicans itself by means of the absence of the thing to be established as the reason.
By this, it is shown that "because of the absence of perception" means "because of the absence of the perception of the jar," [which implies] "it does not exist."

The meaning is "the absence of a jar. For if mere non-perception were the cause for the direct perception of absence, then since the non-perception of a jar exists during a state when light-contact and other factors are absent, [the absence of the jar would be perceived].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the perception of the absence of a jar [even when it is present].
Therefore, it must be stated that the cause is non-apprehension qualified by capability (*yogyatā*). And this capability is...
The meaning is that [the non-apprehension] consists in being the counter-positive of an apprehension that contradicts the existence of the counter-positive as conceived by reasoning;
the fact that the reasoning constituting this [non-apprehension] culminates in its contrapositive is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "If here... and so forth.

He explains the root text beginning with "tarkitā" (conceived) and so forth by means of the passage beginning with "āpāditā" (brought about) and so forth. According to the literal sense [of the text], the perception of the counter-positive consists in the existence of the counter-positive.
It is understood [by some] that it is contradictory; however,
that is incorrect, because the perception of a jar does not contradict the existence of the jar.

Therefore, it has been explained that because of the possibility of the existence of a real entity (*sattva*), there is the possibility (*prasakti*) of attributing existence to a jar; this possibility is what contradicts the perception of the jar. For indeed—
The sense is that while a jar is being perceived, someone might hypothetically raise the possibility of the jar's existence by thinking, "If there were a jar here.
This is for the purpose of indicating that [the cognition] is not an artificial imposition (*anāhārya*).
The sense is that it is precisely because of the incompatibility with non-removable knowledge (*anāhāryajñāna*).
This remains true even when explaining it as "the consequence of existence [leading] to existence."

The state of being inferred (*tarkitatva*) consists in the fact that the existence of the counter-positive has been brought about (*āpādita*), and not merely in its possibility (*prasakti*). Furthermore, it is observed that the conclusion of the contrapositive (*viparyaya-paryavasāna*) occurs only in those cases where both the probans (*āpādaka*) and the probandum (*āpādya*) are equally applicable.

From the root [text], however, it is obtained that only the subsumer (prasañjita)— which has the nature of bringing about the existence of the counter-correlate— is [the object], and not the apprehension (upalabdhi) which is the subsumed (āpādya).
Therefore, he states the intended meaning:
"by bringing about the existence of the counter-positive," that is,
by bringing about the existence of the counter-positive such as a jar.

That non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) which has as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) an apprehension that has been brought about through a reductio (*prasañjana*)— in the form "If there were a jar here" and whose object of the reductio is an apprehension in the form "then it would be perceived"— is qualified by the capacity for that [apprehension].
The meaning is "non-apprehension.
He states the purpose of the qualification "yogyatā" (suitability) as follows: "in connection with light," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of bringing about [the object]": likewise,
because there is an absence of the fitness consisting in having a counter-positive that is implied by the implication of the existence of that counter-positive,
there is no "fitness-unperception" (*yogyānupalabdhi*) in that case for the non-perception [of the object].

Therefore, the point is that there is no perception of the absence of a jar. Now, one might object: "In a case where, even without the application of the existence or the perception of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there arises immediately after the contact of the sense-organ with the locus the perception 'the jar is not,' [how is this explained?]"

Anticipating the objection that the perception of that [non-existence] is untenable because it lacks the capacity (yogyatā) constituted by the actualization of its counter-positive, he says: "In brief.
And [this refers to] the state of being brought about by the actualization of the existence of the counter-positive.
The meaning is that there is no logical inconsistency, because [the object] possesses the fitness for the contingency that would entail the existence of its counter-correlate.
For this very reason, it is said, "in darkness."
The absence of the perception of a jar in darkness is not caused by the absence of the jar's existence,
but rather is caused by the absence of another cause, namely the conjunction with light; and thus,
there is no "non-perception of the capable" (yogyānupalabdhi), which consists in the absence of perception caused by the absence of the existence of the counter-positive.
The point is that because [the absence] does not exist there, there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the absence of a jar.
Regarding the phrase "in the form of smokiness" and so forth:
at the beginning, the word *lakṣaṇa* signifies the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
In the second [view], however, it is the indicator of the object.

In the first position, even for one who does not know "smokeness" (dhūmatva) and so forth, there would be [the cognition] "these are smokes" through the proximity of the existent *svarūpa* of smokeness.

The pursuit of the second alternative is due to the lack of internal consistency [in the first], namely that it would lead to the undesirable consequence (apatti) of smoke being an object of direct perception (dhūma-pratyakṣa).
Regarding the phrase "in the case of a presence brought forward by visual perception" (cākṣuṣopanītabhāve):
this refers to that which is visual and has as its object a fragrance remembered [at the time of smelling].
The meaning is "knowledge. Thus [ends] the Bālapriyā commentary on the Tarkasaṅgrahadīpikāprakāśikā.
The Chapter on Direct Perception,
the Chapter on Inference, and the Compendium of Reasoning.
The definition of inference (anumāna):
Inference is the instrument of inferential cognition (anumiti).
Inferential cognition is a knowledge produced by a subsumptive reflection (parāmarśa).
The cognition of the subject's possession of the property qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*) is *parāmarśa*.
For example, the cognition "this mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire" is *parāmarśa*.
The cognition produced by that, namely "the mountain possesses fire," is inference (*anumiti*).
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the rule of concomitance that wherever there is smoke, there is fire;
the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) in a locus such as a mountain is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Inference is the instrument of inferential cognition. —
Dīpikā.
He defines inference as "the instrument of inferential cognition," [as stated in] the *Prakāśikā*.
"It defines inference" means that it describes inference by way of its connection as being dependent upon perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"By way of connection with that which subsists upon perception" means by way of the connection consisting in being an effect of perception.
This is the meaning. Inference arises precisely from the perception of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the kitchen or similar locations by means of the sense organ;
for the perception of pervasion functions as a cause—by way of being a direct experience (*anubhava*)—toward the inference that consists in the recollection of pervasion.
And thus, the intention is that the definition of inference follows immediately after perception due to the logical connection (*saṅgati*) consisting of the relationship between cause and effect.
By this [connection], of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)...

The relationship of cause and effect has been stated. Since the cognition consisting of inference is the effect of the mental perception consisting of the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection), there exists a causal relationship between these two cognitions.
It is to be known.
Tarkasaṅgraha:
The definition of inference is that which is produced by subsumptive reflection (parāmarśa).
Knowledge is inference (*anumiti*).
The *Dīpikā* defines inference as "the [result of] the final consideration" (*parāmarśa*). Now, one might object:

There is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to the case of perceptual cognition following doubt; for when, immediately after the doubt "Is this a post or a person," there occurs the subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) "This possesses hands and so forth, which are pervaded by personhood," the perception "It is indeed a person" arises.

And it should not be argued that "in that case, there is only an inference," because that would contradict the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form, "I perceive the person directly. [To this we reply:
No, for what is intended is that [the cognition] is produced by a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) assisted by the state of being the subject (*pakṣatā*).

The *Prakāśikā* states that it is "due to reflection" (*parāmarśa*). Thus, because inference possesses a distinct nature of valid cognition (*pramā*) in comparison to perceptual valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramiti*), [it is established as a separate means of knowledge].
The intention is that it is established as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

He raises an objection by relying on the view of those who accept that the perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) is the cause of the subsequent perception that follows a contrary cognition (*viparītajñāna*):
Regarding the word "nanu": the phrase "the doubt between a post and a person" is used by accepting a doubt that has two mutually contradictory alternatives as its objects.
However, others [interpret] it as "the [doubt] regarding a post and a person."

They say that this means [the cognition] has as its alternatives (koṭi) the states of being a post and the absence thereof, and the states of being a person and the absence thereof. The phrase "it is indeed a person" is used to indicate the final ascertainment (nirṇaya).
In that context—namely, in a case where perception occurs subsequent to doubt.
"Because of the contradiction with the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya).

This is an elliptical indication; one should also understand that [the argument] "because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), as there is an absence of the subsequent reflective awareness in the form 'I infer the person'" applies as well.

He states that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because, since there is no purpose for the condition of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) to act as an auxiliary to the subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) when producing a perceptual cognition that follows upon doubt, he intends to define [the definition] as "being produced by a subsumptive reflection assisted by the condition of being a subject."

Regarding the term *pakṣatā*: by this [it is meant that] "this place possesses a mountain possessing smoke pervaded by fire" is [the state of being a subject], insofar as it functions as a certainty (*nirṇaya*) having the delimiting property of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*) as its mode (*prakāra*), with respect to a cognition that apprehends the qualifiedness of the qualified (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhibuddhi*). "Possessing smoke pervaded by fire" [is the required certainty].

Even though the reflective awareness "this is a mountain" (*parvataḥ*) serves as a cause [of inference], there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case; for since it is not produced by a reflective awareness conjoined with the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), there is an absence of over-extension—
this is the summary.
"Bālapriyā" [comments]:
"Because it is a means of knowledge (pramā) distinct from others.
That which is the instrument (karaṇa) for the perception (pratyakṣa) of a known object is the sense organ (indriya).

The point is that because inference is produced by a cause consisting of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) which is distinct from that [perception], it possesses a distinct nature of valid cognition (*pramātva*). Thus, it constitutes a separate means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).
The meaning is that it possesses the status of a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in comparison to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In the *Dīpikā*, by the passage beginning with "Now, [one might object]... (*nanu*), it is shown that when, after seeing a tall object from a distance, one thinks, "Is it a post or a person?"...

Thus there arises doubt; from that, the "consideration" (*parāmarśa*)—in the form of a cognition of the possession of a pervaded property, namely, "this possesses hands and so forth, which are pervaded by being a person"; from that, the perception "this is a person," and within that perception...

The objection was raised that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of inference—characterized as being a cognition qualified by being produced from a *parāmarśa*—to [the case of doubt]. This, however, is not tenable;
for immediately after a doubtful or erroneous cognition...
This is because the very perception "this is a person" is impossible;
for even if there were such a perception, the cognition of the absence of that [quality] acts as an obstacle to the cognition of its presence. This is the objection being raised.

If there were a perception of the specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) regarding a mistaken cognition, then that perception of the specific feature would become the producer of a perceptual cognition; thus, "of the perception of the specific feature" means "of the perception of the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*)."
In the present context, the intended *parāmarśa* (inferential consideration) is: "This [subject] possesses hands and so forth, which are pervaded by non-humanity.
The phrase "having two positive alternatives" (*bhāvadvayakoṭika*) means as follows:
The meaning is: a doubt whose mode (prakāra) consists of two properties in the form of positive entities, namely "being a post" and "being a person.
[Regarding the phrase] "being a post and its absence": [it refers to the doubt concerning these two].
The meaning is that there is a fourfold doubt consisting of: (1) the state of being a post, (2) the absence thereof, (3) the state of being a person, and (4) the absence thereof;
[as in the case of] "Is it a post or not?"
The form of the doubt is "Is it a post or a person, or is it neither?
Alternatively, two types of binary (dvikoṭika) doubt are intended here.
"Because there is an absence of valid means of knowledge" (pramāṇābhāvāt).
The meaning is that there is an absence of a valid means of knowledge for the claim that an inference alone arises in that case.

And likewise, if the certainty "this is a person" were an inference, then the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya) which apprehends it as a direct perception— namely, "I perceive the person directly"— would be untenable.
The subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) would indeed take the form "I infer the person," which implies the apprehension of the property of being an inference (*anumititva*). Therefore,
that cognition does not possess the nature of an inference.

Rather, it is indeed perception; the point is that because the definition exists in that which is not the object of definition (the *alakṣya*), there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of inference. In the *Dīpikā*, the phrase "accompanied by *pakṣatā*" [is used].
And thus, being merely produced by a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) is not the definition of inference;
rather, it is being produced by that subsumptive reflection which is assisted by the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*).
In the case of perception following doubt, however, although the subsumptive reflection is indeed a producer [of the cognition], [it lacks the required assistance].
1. By this, it is shown that there is also another opinion;
for instance, [it applies] to every direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) following a doubt.
The perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) is not the cause [of perceptual certainty],
because even in the absence of such a perception, the subsequent perception following a doubt about a jar in the dark is established merely through the presence of light. Nevertheless...

In a case where doubt arises due to defects such as the non-perception of specific differences (*viśeṣādarśana*), that [non-perception] serves as the cause for the subsequent perception. And in the aforementioned instance, the doubt is dependent on the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). For further detail, see the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, in the section on the "Arising of Validity" (*prāmāṇyotpatti*), and its commentary, the *Prakāśa*.
It should be observed:
"The two-angled" refers to one type of doubt, such as the form "Is it a post or not?"
The meaning is that there are two types of doubt: one characterized by the form "Is it a person? and another [doubt]; thus, there are two doubts.
[This concludes the section on] the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*).
There is no utility [in this], because there is a lack of valid evidence; even if its existence were established, [it would still be useless].
Furthermore, because it is impossible for the absence of proof—constituting *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject)—to serve as a cause for the arising of a continuous stream of perception;
and thus, since there is an absence of being produced by a *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) assisted by *pakṣatā*, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This is the intended meaning.
Thus it is said in the *Prakāśikā*: "In order to produce a perception that follows doubt.
[The phrase] "due to the absence of a purpose" refers to the case where one does not accept that *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject of inquiry) acts as a cooperative factor.
The meaning is "by way of the absence of non-occurrence.
By this means refers to the reason that will be stated hereafter. If...
If being merely produced by a *parāmarśa* were the definition of inference,

then [the definition would over-extend] to a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*) of the form "this place possesses a mountain which has smoke pervaded by fire," which apprehends the qualification of the mountain as qualified by smoke pervaded by fire.

Since the cognition "this mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire"— which takes the form of a *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection)— is a cause by virtue of being a certainty (*niścaya*) whose qualifier is smoke,

[the property of] being produced by such a *parāmarśa* exists even in the case of a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*) that apprehends a qualified object as possessing a further qualifier (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhin*).
Since the definition of inference (anumiti) exists [in other cases], over-extension (ativyāpti) would follow; however,
the intention is that this can be avoided by taking the definition of inference to be "being produced by a subsumptive reflection (parāmarśa) assisted by the state of being a subject (pakṣatā)."
Because such a perception lacks being produced by *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject).
[This concludes] the *Dīpikā* on the definition of *pakṣatā*.
Pakṣatā (the state of being a subject) is the absence of proof qualified by the absence of the desire to prove.
The establishment of the probandum is an obstacle to inference.

Since an inference is observed even when the object is already established, provided there is the desire "may I infer," the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) acts as an excitant (*uttejikā*). Consequently,
the absence of the jewel (*maṇi*), qualified by the absence of such an excitant, [is the cause of the non-production of the effect].

1. Although it has been stated that the definition of inference (*anumiti*) is "the state of being a cognition possessing a producedness (*janyatā*) determined by a generative capacity (*janakatā*) delimited by the nature of *parāmarśa*— which consists in being a cognition that apprehends the qualification of both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the probandum (*sādhya*)— nevertheless..."
It is possible to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the perception that apprehends the qualifiedness (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of what has been stated,

because in such a cognition, the consideration (*parāmarśa*) functions as a cause only by way of being a determination (*nirṇaya*) whose mode (*prakāra*) is the delimiting adjunct of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*), and not by way of being the aforementioned consideration itself. Nevertheless...

In the case of a perceptual cognition that follows a doubt, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because such a cognition possesses the property of being produced by the observation of the pervader (*vyāpyadarśana*)—namely, its being a knowledge that apprehends the qualified relation between the pervader and the subject (*pakṣavaiśiṣṭya*).

This [over-extension] must be excluded solely by specifying that [the definition] consists in being produced by a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) aided by "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*). It is excluded by that alone.

The point is that since it is possible to exclude a perception that apprehends a qualified entity as being qualified (viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhipratyakṣa), the generative capacity (janakatā) delimited by the aforementioned nature of *parāmarśa* need not be included [in the definition].
This is like [the case of] being the cause of burning (*dāhakāraṇatva*).
The absence of proof, qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (*sisādhayiṣā*), is also a cause of inference.

Although it is possible to prevent inference at the time of the ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*) even if doubt regarding the probandum constitutes the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), nevertheless...
There is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the inference of a cloud from the sound of thunder;
therefore, he states a different kind of "subjectness" (pakṣatā),
namely, the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā).

The meaning is: the absence, by way of inherence (*samavāya*), of a *siddhi* (established knowledge) which is qualified by the absence— through the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as constituted by the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and inherence— of the desire for the inference of the probandum (*sādhya*), which is itself the desire of the sage (*ṛṣi*) to establish [the probandum].
The establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) is a certainty (*niścaya*) that apprehends the qualified probandum—

characterized by the delimitors of the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*)— as residing in the subject as characterized by the delimitors of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). [This occurs] when there is no [prior] establishment (*siddhi*).
He demonstrates the purpose of including the qualification "the absence of the desire to prove" by stating:
"even when there is proof."

In this context, the "accomplishment" (siddhi) consists of a collective cognition (samūhālambana) in the form: "The mountain possesses fire, and it possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire. Therefore, it should be understood that the requirement for the "reflective judgment" (parāmarśa) is fulfilled.

He states the reason for disregarding the statement of the ancients— that "the state of being a subject (pakṣatā) consists in a doubt regarding what is not established"— with the words beginning "Even though," and so forth.
Indeed, the purpose of accepting that "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*) is a cause of inference is to prevent inference at the time when the proof takes the form of a certainty regarding the probandum;
and that [prevention] occurs through doubt regarding the probandum.
Even if *pakṣatā* (the state of being the subject of inference) is [defined as] such, it remains consistent;

for in this manner, the prevention of inference is possible precisely because at the time of the ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*), there is an absence of *pakṣatā* in the form of doubt regarding the probandum. Thus it is.

The intention of the objector is that "let the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) be simply the doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhyasaṃśaya*). To this he replies: "Nevertheless," [the state of being a subject] consisting of doubt regarding the probandum is not the cause of inference;
for even without doubt regarding the probandum, [inference occurs].
The intention of the respondent is that there is a deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) because clouds are inferred from hearing a deep thundering; thus,
there is "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*).
What is intended here is the deviation from negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra), which consists in the arising of an effect even in the absence of its cause.
"Of a different kind" means of a nature other than that which arises from doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
The intended inference here is: "This [place] possesses clouds, because it has the roar of thunder.
In the *Dīpikā*, the phrase beginning with "qualified by the absence of the desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣāvirahaviśiṣṭa*) and so forth is used.

Even where there is proof (*siddhi*) in the form of a certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), if there exists a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) characterized by the thought, "I shall infer the probandum in the subject (*pakṣa*)," then inference occurs.
If mere absence of proof were the nature of the subject (*pakṣatā*), that [subjecthood] would not exist there, because proof itself exists in that case; therefore, in that instance...

To ensure the fulfillment of the conditions for being a subject (*pakṣatā*), the qualification "qualified by the absence of the desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣāvirahaviśiṣṭa*) is applied to the "established conclusion" (*siddhi*).
This is because in the aforementioned instance, due to the presence of the desire to prove,
the qualifying factor— the absence of the desire to prove— is lacking.
Since the absence of proof qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) remains intact, the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) is established.
Thus, it follows that the desire to prove acts as an "excitant" (*uttejikā*). And as for this excitatory nature:
The nature of an *uttejaka* (excitant) is the state of being a causal factor for the production of an effect at a time when an obstructing condition (*pratibandhaka*) is present.

It is called an excitant because, even at a time when an obstruction in the form of established knowledge (*siddhi*) exists, the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) serves as the causal factor for the production of the effect in the form of an inference (*anumiti*), just as follows:
The status of being an "excitant" (uttejakatva) consists in being the cause for the production of burning even during the time when a jewel acts as an obstacle,
just as mantras and the like possess the status of being excitants because they are the causes for the production of burning during the time when a jewel acts as an obstacle.
Because the absence of the obstructer, qualified by the absence of an inciter, is the cause for the production of the effect;
and because the absence of established knowledge, qualified by the absence of the desire to prove, is the cause of inference.
The term *bhāva* refers to the following: "desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣā*) is a desire whose object is the inferential cognition of the probandum (*sādhyānumiti*).
The "absence of the desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣāviraha*) is an absence characterized by a counter-correlativity residing in that desire to prove.
In that context, the property of being delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya) must be included within the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā);
otherwise, [the definition would fail] where there is establishment (siddhi).
Furthermore, there is no desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) in that case; because of the absence of the desire to prove through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*),

there would be no "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*), which consists in the absence of such a proof, since the proof itself exists as qualified by an absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the relation of conjunction residing in the desire to prove.
And because, in that house, there exists a desire to prove [the probandum] through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*),
there is an absence of the qualification consisting in the non-existence whose counter-positive is the desire to prove as delimited by that very relation.

Thus, *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject) is established as having the nature of a qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*). In this way, the qualification by the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) [is present] in the presence of proof (*siddhi*) through the relation of co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Otherwise, if the qualification by the absence of the desire to prove were introduced through the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*), [the definition would fail].

Even when there is a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), since the absence of that desire exists in relation to the proof by way of its own nature (*svarūpasambandha*), the probans (*sādhana*) remains qualified by the absence of the desire to prove; consequently, the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), which consists in the absence of such [qualified] proof, would be untenable. Therefore, [the qualification must be understood] by way of the relation of co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
The specific distinction (vaiśiṣṭya) must be introduced;
and co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) consists in residing in the same locus (svādhikaraṇavṛttitva).
Being the locus of x (svādhikaraṇatva) is [defined] by means of the relation of identity (svarūpasaṃbandha).
The occurrence [of the property] is defined with respect to its own locus by means of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). And thus,

[the relation is] by way of the relation of occurrence delimited by inherence, which is in turn defined with respect to a locus that is the counter-correlative of a substratumness (*ādheyatā*) delimited by the essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) residing in itself.

Pakṣatā (the state of being a subject of inquiry) is the absence of that "establishment" (siddhi) which is qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*). "Its own" (*sva*) refers to the absence of the desire to prove; its locus (*adhikaraṇa*) through the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) is the self (*ātman*); therein, "that establishment" is that which exists through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*), and the absence of that is what is meant. In this regard:
If the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*) were not introduced, then even at the time when there is a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*),

the property of subsistence by way of inherence (*samavāya*) would exist in the self— which is the locus of the absence of the desire to prove— by means of the relation of being the object of a single cognition; thus, [the definition would fail] because of such subsistence by that relation.
Since there would be the existence of a "proof" (siddhi) qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā), the status of being a subject (pakṣatā) would not be established.

However, if an essential relation (svarūpasambandha) is posited, then by that [relation], the self— which is the locus of the absence of the desire to prove— does not become one who possesses the desire to prove.
However, since there is no other self whose subsistence in that [object] has been established as residing in this self,
[the relation is] by way of the relation of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which consists in such subsistence.
Since the absence of "establishment" (siddhi)— qualified by the non-existence of the desire to prove— is present, there is no inconsistency regarding the status of the subject (pakṣatā).
Likewise, this holds true when "subsistence" (vṛttitva) is not qualified by being delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya-sambandha).
Even though proof exists in the self— which is the locus of the absence of the desire to prove— by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*),
it does not exist by way of relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*); therefore,
co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in having a mode of subsistence delimited by a relation other than inherence.
Otherwise, it would follow that "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*)— which consists in the absence of a specific property— would be non-existent in the case of a proven instance (*siddhi*). Therefore,
the qualification of being delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*) is introduced into the "subsistence" (*vṛtti*) that constitutes the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Thus, the absence of proof (*siddhyabhāva*) is an absence that characterizes a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) residing in proof. In this context, the property of being delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāyasambandhāvacchinnatva*) must be included within that counter-correlativity; otherwise, even at the time when proof exists, the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) would arise by taking into account an absence of proof delimited by some other relation.
This would follow as a logical consequence.
Having intended all of this, he says in the *Prakāśikā*: "of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), that is, the desire for the inference of the probandum," and so forth.
It is constituted by both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and inherence (*samavāya*).
Within the locus-hood (*adhikaraṇatā*) that constitutes co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
there is the property of being delimited by the relation of essential nature (*svarūpasambandha*).

The point is that, in the case of subsistence (*vṛttitā*), one must also include the property of being delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). This is because [otherwise] there would be the non-existence [of the probans] in respect to inherence.
The meaning is: an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) as restricted to that which culminates in the attainment of perfection (*siddhiniṣṭha*).

"Qualified by the delimitor of the subject" (*pakṣatāvacchedakaviśiṣṭa*), etc., refers to a certainty (*niścaya*) possessing a qualificative mode (*prakāratā*) residing in the probandum (*sādhya*)—which is delimited by the delimitor of the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*)—as determined by a qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the subject (*pakṣa*) which is delimited by the delimitor of the subjectness (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

This is the meaning: because the inference "the mountain possesses fire" arises at the time of a certainty in the form "it is a substance that possesses fire," which has the mountain as its object under the aspect of substantiality (*dravyatva*), [the certainty] "it is a substance that possesses fire" [is not a sublater].

The inclusion of the condition "being delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood" (pakṣatāvacchedakāvacchinnatva) within the objective determination residing in the subject (pakṣaniṣṭhaviśeṣyatā) is for the purpose of avoiding the over-extension [of the definition] to the counteracting factor of the inference "the mountain possesses fire."

Thus, in order to exclude the certainty in the form "the mountain possesses substance" from being a sublater of such an inference, the qualification of being delimited by the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedakāvacchinnatva) is introduced into the property-locusness (prakāratā).

In this way, within the nature of the mode (*prakāratā*), the property of being delimited by the relation that delimits the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) must also be included; otherwise, [the following would be a fallacy]: "The mountain..."

For there would also follow the undesirable consequence that even the certain cognition "it possesses fire by way of inherence" would obstruct the inferential cognition "the mountain possesses fire by way of conjunction."
Now, if there is a desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā) at the time when proof (siddhi) has already occurred, then even in that case, for the sake of establishing inference,
the qualification "characterized by the absence of the desire to prove" (siṣādhayiṣāvirahaviśiṣṭa) is indeed provided [in the definition of the probans].
And that [inference] becomes meaningful only if there is a simultaneous convergence of the proof (siddhi), the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā), and the consideration (parāmarśa).
And that is difficult to establish;
for instance: where first there is the establishment [of the reason], immediately after which there is the desire to prove [the conclusion], and from that, the reflective consideration (parāmarśa).
Consequently, inference [occurs];

for at that moment of the *parāmarśa*, since the absence of the obstructing factor [is present] due to the very destruction of the *siddhi* (the already-established cognition), the occurrence of the inference is established, and thus [the postulation of a separate *anumitihetu*] is redundant.
The qualification "being characterized by the absence of the desire to prove" [is added].
In a case where there is a sequence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), the proof (*siddhi*), and the consideration (*parāmarśa*), at the moment of the consideration, [the desire to prove]...
Because the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*)— qualified by the absence of proof (*siddhi*)— is indeed present due to the destruction [of the former],

the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) is not established even when the qualification "being qualified by the absence of the desire to prove" is introduced. However, in a case where the consideration (*parāmarśa*),
the proof, and the desire to prove occur in succession, at the moment of the desire to prove...
Due to the destruction of the consideration (*parāmarśa*), that is, due to the deficiency of the cause in the form of consideration, there is no inference.
Furthermore, it is not accepted that two cognitions—or a cognition and a desire—arise simultaneously in a single moment.
And thus, how could [the absence of] the qualification "being devoid of the desire to prove" [apply]?
Anticipating the objection that [the term] would be meaningless, he says: "And here, 'accomplishment' (siddhi), etc.

The accomplishment that constitutes a factor of the state of being a subject (pakṣatā) is of the nature of a collective apprehension (samūhālambana), encompassing both fire and smoke which is pervaded by fire.

The intended form is: "The mountain possesses fire, and it possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire. This very [cognition] is designated as the *parāmarśa* consisting of proof (*siddhyātmaka-parāmarśa*), because it takes the form of a certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) and takes the form of a certainty regarding that which is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpya*).

And likewise, in a case where first there is the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) consisting of proof in the aforementioned form, then the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā), and then the inference (anumiti),
there is no "subjectness" (pakṣatā) because, since proof exists in the second moment, subjectness— which consists merely in the absence of proof— is absent.

It functions [as required]. Therefore, the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) is a qualification of the "established" (*siddhi*). In that case, however, because the desire to prove is present, the qualification consisting of the absence of the desire to prove is non-existent;
thus, the "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*), which consists in the absence of that qualified [state], is established. Such is the function of that qualification.
The sense is that its purposefulness must be established;
hence, there is the attainment of the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection).

This refers to the state where, in the moment immediately preceding the inferential cognition (*anumiti*), there is neither the certainty of the conclusion (*siddhi*) nor the desire to prove it (*siṣādhayiṣā*), but rather the *parāmarśa*.
The meaning is "conjunction."
The Compendium of Reasoning:
The definition of *parāmarśa*.
*Parāmarśa* is the cognition of the presence of the middle term in the subject as qualified by its invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*). For example:
The cognition "this mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire" is *parāmarśa*. The cognition "the mountain possesses fire," produced by that, is *anumiti*.
— *Dīpikā*

He defines *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) with the words "vyāpti... [etc.]. The meaning is that *parāmarśa* is that cognition of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*) which has pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its object.
He demonstrates *parāmarśa* by way of illustration with the words "yathā" [etc.].
He demonstrates inference by means of a dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*), saying "produced by that";
the meaning is "produced by the consideration (*parāmarśa*)."

In the passage "the knowledge of the subject-attribute-hood qualified by pervasion" (*prakāśikā*), *vyāptiviśiṣṭapakṣadharmatā* means the subject-attribute-hood (*pakṣadharmatā*) as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*); [the compound thus refers to] the knowledge of that.

If a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound were accepted [in the definition], there would be an under-extension (*avyāpti*) because an inference based on a deviant middle term (*vyabhicāriliṅga*) lacks the quality of being produced by the knowledge of the presence of the middle term in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*); therefore,
regarding the phrase "qualified by pervasion" (*vyāptiviśiṣṭa*),...
Relying on the meaning "having pervasion as its object," he accepts a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word ending in *jñāna*, stating: "having pervasion as its object" (*vyāptiviṣayaka*).
[This refers to] that which is qualified by a modehood delimited by pervasion (*vyāptyavacchinnaprakāratānirūpita*).
The distilled meaning is: "Parāmarśa is a certainty possessing a qualificandum-ness delimited by the delimitor of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka).
"Abhinīya" means having uttered the expressive word.
Regarding the phrase "the knowledge of the property of the subject qualified by pervasion" (*vyāptiviśiṣṭapakṣadharmatājñāna*) and so forth:
where there is a mark (*liṅga*), [it is as follows].

In that case as well, there occurs an inference of the form "the mountain possesses smoke," arising from the erroneous *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) "this mountain possesses fire which is pervaded by smoke," even though [the reason] is deviant with respect to the probandum (*sādhyavyabhicārin*).

If, however, *parāmarśa* is defined as a cognition that, in reality, apprehends the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*), and if being produced by that [cognition] were stated to be the definition of inference,
then [the problem arises] because the aforementioned *parāmarśa* lacks the apprehension of that [reason] as qualified by pervasion.

Because it lacks the nature of *parāmarśa*, the cognition produced by it would not be an inference (*anumiti*). Therefore, *parāmarśa* is that cognition which has pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its object and apprehends the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).
Since the aforementioned erroneous cognition possesses the property of having pervasion as its object, it retains the character of *parāmarśa*. Thus...

The point is that, since the knowledge produced by that [inferential indicator] is pervaded by the definition of inference— namely, being produced by a *parāmarśa* (reflective judgment)— its status as an inference is also established.
Now, even when defining *parāmarśa* as "a cognition that has pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its object and which apprehends the connection with the subject (*pakṣa*)," [the following objection arises]:
"Smoke is pervaded by fire, and the mountain possesses smoke."

Since even a collective cognition (*samūhālambana-jñāna*) having such a form would result in being a *parāmarśa*— because it has pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its object and because it has the relation to the subject (*pakṣasambandha*) as its object— the author says:
"delimited by pervasion" (*vyāptyavacchinna*).

The meaning is that *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) is a certain cognition which is the determinate qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in the reason, as delimited by pervasion (*vyāpti*), and which determines the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the subject (*pakṣa*), as delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). And such [a cognition] indeed exists.

The certainty "the mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire" is of such a nature; for the qualifierhood residing in smoke, as determined by the qualificandhood residing in the mountain, is delimited by pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And "being delimited by pervasion" means being determined by a qualificative-ness residing in pervasion, which is itself determined by a qualificative-ness residing in the probandum (*sādhya*).
By this, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the cognition "the mountain possesses smoke that is non-pervasive. [In the case of] "smoke..."

In the objective universal (prakāratā) residing in smoke within a collective cognition such as "The mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire," there is no being qualified by the objective universal residing in pervasion.

The meaning is that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not appear as a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the portion consisting of smoke. And thus:

The refined definition is as follows: *parāmarśa* (reflective judgment) is a certainty characterized by a subject-locusness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the pakṣa (the subject), which is delimited by the delimitor of pakṣatā, and which is itself determined by a property-locusness (*prakāratā*) residing in the hetu (the reason), which is delimited by the delimitor of hetutā; this [reason-property-locusness] is in turn determined by a property-locusness residing in vyāpti (pervasion), which is determined by a property-locusness residing in the sādhya (the probandum), which is delimited by the delimitor of sādhyatā. This is the essential conclusion.

Therefore, from such certainties as "the mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by substance," "the mountain possesses a substance which is pervaded by fire," and "there is a substance possessing smoke which is pervaded by fire," [the inference] "the mountain possesses fire" [arises].
It should be noted that, in this way, the status of being a *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) which serves as the cause of inference does not [inherently] follow.
"Nirgalitārtha" means "extracted meaning" (*niṣkṛṣṭārtha*).
"Having uttered the expressive word" means having uttered the word that indicates the form [of the object],
because a physical gesture in the form of bodily movement is impossible here.
The Compendium of Reasoning:
The Definition of Pervasion.
Wherever there is smoke, there is fire.
"Agni" refers to the rule of concomitance, which is pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The *Dīpikā* states the definition of pervasion:
Regarding "where...": "Where there is smoke, there is fire" is the demonstration (*abhinaya*) of pervasion (*vyāpti*);
"the restriction of concomitance" (*sāhacaryaniyama*) is its definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

Co-occurrence (*sāhacarya*) is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); its restriction is "the co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhya*) of that which is not the counter-positive of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is coreferential with the probans (*hetu*)."
The meaning is "pervasion" (vyāpti).

It is not the case that it is restricted co-occurrence (niyatasāmānādhikaraṇya), which takes the form of "not occurring in that which possesses the absence of the probandum" (sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitva) and so forth.
[The definition] is possible;

however, [the author] says "co-present with the reason" (hetusamānādhikaraṇa), having considered that [the definition] would be over-narrow (avyāpti) in cases such as "this is expressible because it is knowable," since the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) is not established there.

In such cases as "there is fire because of smoke," fire is the non-counterpositive of that absolute absence— namely, the absolute absence of a jar— which coexists with the smoke; the coexistence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of that [fire] with the smoke [is the definition of pervasion].
"Existence" (asti) refers to the possession of the definition [of the probandum].

However, in cases such as "possessing smoke because of fire," since even the general absence of smoke is co-located with the reason, it is precisely the counter-positive of that [absence] which [is the object of the inference].
Thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to "smoke.

Nor is there [over-extension] in cases such as "this [mountain] possesses fire because of smoke," since the absence of each respective fire coexists with smoke according to the logic of the winnowing-basket (*cālinī-nyāya*).
It should not be argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because no fire whatsoever possesses the property of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of such an absence;

for the phrase "having a probandum that is a non-counter-positive" intends the meaning "having a probandum delimited by a delimitor of probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) that is not a delimitor of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitānavacchedaka*)," and thus there is no fault.
In the definition of counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*), the property of being delimited by the delimiting relation of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) must be included.

Consequently, in cases such as "This [mountain] possesses fire because of smoke," even though there exists an absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by the nature of fire (*vahnitva*) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) and which is co-located with smoke, [this does not constitute a fallacy].
[There is] no deficiency. The term "cause" (hetu) refers to that which is delimited by the delimitor of causality (hetutāvacchedaka).
Therefore, in cases such as "substance [is] because of qualified existence" (*viśiṣṭasattvāt*), since the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) is not distinct from the pure (*śuddha*),...
Even though the absence of substanceness (dravyatvābhāva) resides in qualities and so forth that are substrata of the reason, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti).
The status of being the locus of the reason (hetvadhikaraṇatā) must be understood as being delimited by the relation that delimits the nature of the reason (hetutāvacchedakasambandha).

Therefore, in cases such as "this [mountain] possesses fire because of smoke," there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti), even though the absence of fire in general resides in that which is inherent in smoke. Nor does this same problem arise in cases such as "this possesses conjunction with a monkey because it is a tree."

It should not be argued that there is non-pervasion (avyāpti) because the probandum (sādhya) is delimited by the delimiter of the counter-positiveness (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) of an absolute absence (atyantābhāva) that is co-located with the reason (hetu); for [in our view], the condition of "non-co-location with the counter-positive" (pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya) applies to the absolute absence co-located with the reason.
Because it must be included [in the definition];
for in the case of a probandum that is purely positive (*kevalānvayi*), such things as the absence of a jar are well-established, and thus there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
The more extensive [explanations] should be investigated by those skilled in intellect from our commentary, Maṇidīdhiti; thus says Bālapriyā.
"Because the absence of the probandum is unestablished":
since the probandum, namely "being denotable," is a purely positive (kevalānvayi) property existing everywhere, its absence is unestablished.

The meaning is that there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a valid reason (*saddhetu*) whose probandum (*sādhya*) is purely positive (*kevalānvayi*). This is because [the definition] suffers from this defect due to its intended meaning. And thus, [the definition consists in] the non-limitation of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*), by the delimitor of the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*).
Pervasion (vyāpti) is the co-presence with the probandum (sādhya) as delimited by the absence of the probandum.
In such cases as "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke," the reason (hetu) is smoke.

The locus of that [absence] is the mountain; the absolute absence residing therein consists of the absence of jars and the like, as well as the absence of fire belonging to the kitchen; the delimitors of the counterpositiveness (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) of those [absences] are...
The nature of pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), the nature of fire in the kitchen (*mahānasīyavahnitva*), and so forth,
are not the delimiters of that counter-correlativity (*tatpratiyogitānavacchedaka*);
rather, it is the nature of fire (*vahnitva*) which serves as the delimiter of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*).

Since the co-presence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) delimited by that [smoke]— which consists in its subsisting in a locus such as Mount Meru that is the substratum of such fire— exists in smoke, the definition is fully applicable.

In the case of "The mountain possesses smoke because of fire," the reason (*hetu*) is fire; its locus is the non-joined pillar (*ayogolaka*); the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) residing therein is the absence of smoke;
and the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of that [absence] is precisely the nature of "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*).

1. The meaning is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the essential nature, while the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is its defining characteristic. — [The term] "the delimiting factor of the probandum" (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*)...

The point is that there is no over-extension (ativyāpti), because the delimitor of the probandum-ness lacks the property of being a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence that is co-located with the reason.
In the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*),

one must include the property of being delimited by the relation that delimits the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandhāvacchinnatva*), and so forth. In the case of "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke" (*parvato vahnimān dhūmāt*), [the absence] exists on the mountain, which is the locus of the smoke.

That which is absolute non-existence is the absence established by the cognition "fire does not exist through the relation of inherence," which has as its counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā) delimited by the property of firehood (vahnitva) and delimited by the relation of inherence.
Since firehood itself is the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of that counter-positiveness, there would be the fallacy of under-extension (avyāpti).

To prevent that [over-extension], one must include "being delimited by the relation that delimits the probandumhood" (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandhāvacchinnatva*) within the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*) belonging to the absence that resides in the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*). And when this is included,
regarding the phrase "the absence residing in the locus of the reason," whichever absence is taken as the instance—
That very absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation of conjunction (saṃyoga)— which serves as the delimiting relation for the probandum (sādhya)—
is what should be accepted; thus, it is only the absence of a jar and the like through the relation of conjunction that is such,
and not the absence of fire through the relation of inherence (samavāya), because its counter-positiveness [is not so delimited].
This is because it is impossible for [fireness] to be delimited by the relation of conjunction (saṃyoga).

Thus, the meaning is that since potness and the like are the delimiters of the counter-positiveness delimited by the relation of conjunction belonging to the absence of a pot etc., which resides in the locus of the reason (the mountain), while fireness is not such a delimiter, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti). Not so.

"Kṣati" means there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti). Thus, it is the co-existence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the probandum (sādhya), which is delimited by the delimitor of the probandum-ness (sādhyatāvacchedaka) that is not the non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) residing in the locus of the reason (hetu), as determined by the relation delimiting the probandum-ness.

By this much, "pervasion" (vyāpti) is established. The term "reason" (hetu) refers to that which is delimited by the delimitor of the reasonhood (hetutāvacchedaka), and so forth. [For example: "A pot is a substance."
In the valid reason "because of existence qualified by the difference from quality and action," the reason— namely, pure existence— is also present [in the subject],
because there is no difference between the qualified and the pure. Furthermore, qualities and actions are also substrata where the reason does not reside.
In that case, the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) that exists there is the absence of substanceness (dravyatvābhāva);

since the delimitor of its counterpositiveness (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) is indeed the nature of substanceness (dravyatvatva), there is no non-delimitation of counterpositiveness with respect to the nature of substanceness as the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka). Consequently, there is an over-narrowness (avyāpti) [of the definition].
To prevent that [fallacy],

one must introduce the condition of being the locus of the reason as delimited by the delimitor of the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedakāvacchinnahetvadhikaraṇatva*). This is because, although the state of being the locus of existence (*sattādhikaraṇatva*) delimited by the property of existence (*sattātva*) does indeed exist in qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), [the definition would otherwise over-extend].
The state of being the locus of that which is delimited by the causal determinant— the property of existence (sattātva) qualified by the difference from quality and action— is not possible,
because [the locus] would be either a quality or an action.
Because there is no such cognition as "possessing existence qualified by being other than quality and action," therefore,
the locus delimited by the property of "existence qualified by being other than quality and action" is substance alone;
the absence that resides therein is not the absence of substanceness, but rather the absence of qualityness and so forth.

The point is that the delimitors of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*)—such as *guṇatvatva* (the property of being a quality)—are not non-delimitors of the counter-correlativity of the absolute absence residing in the locus of the reason as delimited by the delimitor of the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedaka*), namely *dravyatvatva* (the property of being a substance);
thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). And so, [the definition is]:

that which is not a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity—delimited by the relation that delimits the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha*)—of the absolute absence residing in the locus of the reason as delimited by the delimitor of the reasonhood.
Pervasion (vyāpti) is the co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the probandum as delimited by the delimitor of the property to be proven (sādhyatāvacchedaka).
It should be understood that the locus-hood of the reason (hetvadhikaraṇatā) is delimited by the relation that delimits the nature of the reason (hetutāvacchedakasambandha).

In the inference "This [mountain] possesses fire because of smoke," the locus of the reason, smoke, by means of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), is the constituent part of the smoke; the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) residing therein is the absence of fire by means of the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Since the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of that [absence] is precisely fire-ness (*vahnitva*), which is the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*).

To avoid this, it must be stipulated that the locus-membership (*ādheyatā*) residing in the reason is delimited by the relation that delimits the status of being the reason (*hetutāvacchedakasambandha*). And in the present case...
The relation delimiting the causal state is conjunction;
the locus characterized by the substratum-ness (ādhikaraṇatā) as determined by the locus-ness (ādheyatā) residing in smoke delimited by that [conjunction] is not a constituent part of smoke.

Because the locus-hood (adhikaraṇatā), which is the counter-correlative of the substratum-hood (ādheyatā) residing in smoke as delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya-sambandha), exists only there [in the mountain];
rather, it is the mountain and so forth itself.

The meaning is that the absence residing in that [locus] is not the absence of fire, but rather the absence of a jar or the like; since "fire-ness" (vahnitva) is the delimiting property of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) for that absence, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti).
Of the absence of the generality of fire— that is, of the absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by fire-ness—
even though it resides in that which possesses smoke-inherence—

Even though [the absence] resides in the parts of the smoke that are the locus of the smoke shaken by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), it is nevertheless the case that the probandum is that whose non-restrictor of the counter-correlativity— restricted by the relation that restricts the state of being the probandum— is the absolute absence residing in that which possesses the locus-hood (substratum-hood) determined by the superstratum-hood (residuum-hood) residing in the probans, which is itself restricted by the property that restricts the state of being the probans and restricted by the relation that restricts the state of being the probans.
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by its own delimiting factor (*tāvacchedaka*). 1.

The phrase "the locus of the reason as delimited by the delimitor of the reasonhood" (*hetutāvacchedakāvacchinnahetvadhikaraṇa*) means that which possesses a substratum-hood (*ādhikaraṇatā*) determined by a locationality (*ādheyatā*) residing in the reason as delimited by the delimitor of the reasonhood.
2. By means of the particle *eva*,
the substratumhood (*adhikaraṇatā*)— which is the counter-correlative of the locusness (*ādheyatā*) residing in smoke and delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—
is excluded.
And even so, there is no fallacy.

In the case of "This tree is in contact with a monkey, because it is this particular tree," the reason—being this particular tree—subsists in its locus, which is this very tree; and in that [locus], there also exists the absence of contact with a monkey.
For even though monkey-contact exists in that tree as delimited by its upper part,
monkey-contact is absent as delimited by its root part; and thus,
the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of the absence of monkey-contact— which resides in the locus of the reason— is indeed [the property of being delimited by the upper part].
The sense is that there is an over-narrowness (avyāpti) because the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka) is the nature of being in conjunction with a monkey;
this is because the condition of "residing in a different locus from the counter-positive" (pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya) must be introduced.
And thus, [the absence] residing in the tree...

The absence of conjunction with a monkey (*kapisaṃyogābhāva*) exists in the tree, which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), namely the conjunction with a monkey; therefore, it is co-locus with its counter-positive (*pratiyogisamānādhikaraṇa*) and not non-co-locus with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*).

Only the absence of a jar (*ghaṭādyabhāva*) and the like are such [i.e., non-co-locus with their counter-positives], because the property of being a conjunction with a monkey (*kapisaṃyogatva*) is not the delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) of the counter-positivehood (*pratiyogitā*) of that [absence].
The intention is that there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) because [the definition] applies.
If pervasion were defined as "not occurring in that which lacks the probandum" (sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitva),
then the lack of pervasion mentioned in the case of the argument "this is expressible, because it is knowable" would arise.

He states that [the definition] does not over-apply to the definition of pervasion (vyāpti) as established in the present context: "that which has a purely positive probandum" (*kevalānvayisādhyaka*).

Thus, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the reason (*hetu*), namely knowability (*jñeyatva*), is the ground (*bhūtala*) and so forth; the absence (*abhāva*) residing therein is the absence of a jar (*ghaṭādyabhāva*); and the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of that [absence] is "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth.

The meaning is that the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), which is the nature of "being denotable" (*vācyatvatva*)—being non-delimiting—is present in "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) as co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum, namely "denotability" as delimited by that [nature];
thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). In this way...

The property of being non-occurrent in the locus of the counter-positive (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇatva) means occurring in a locus that is not the locus of the counter-positive; it does not mean non-occurring in the locus of the counter-positive, as in the case of "this [mountain] possesses conjunction because it possesses existence."
Because, in this case, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
① "Such" means "non-co-referential with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*). ② [End of note].
Because it would entail the fallacy of over-extension (*ativyāpti*):
since existence (*sattā*) resides in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth which lack conjunction (*saṃyoga*), this reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).
In this context, the substratum of the reason (*hetu*) is the substratum of existence (*sattā*), such as quality (*guṇa*) and so forth;

the absence residing therein is the absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga-abhāva*). The delimiting factor of its counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-avacchedaka*)—namely, the nature of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*)—is indeed the delimiting factor of the probandum (*sādhyatā-avacchedaka*). Thus, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) must be avoided. However...

If "non-occurrence in the locus of the counter-positive" (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇatva) means "not occurring in the locus of the counter-positive," then, because the absence of conjunction (saṃyogābhāva) is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), it exists in substances that are loci of conjunction; therefore, the absence of conjunction would not be "non-occurrent in the locus of the counter-positive. Rather, [it is defined as]...

However, since it is precisely the absence of a jar and the like that [is the counter-positive], the property of being a non-delimiter of its counter-positiveness exists in "conjunctionness" (saṃyogatva), and thus the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti) follows.

However, if it is stated that "having a different locus from the counter-positive" means "subsisting in a locus other than that of the counter-positive," then even the absence of conjunction would fall within the definition,
since it subsists in qualities (guṇas), which are loci other than those of conjunction.

The point is that since the property of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) exists in "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). [This refers to] the definition beginning with "the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in the locus of the reason (*hetu*), which is not the locus of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)," and so forth.
This is what is intended to be expressed:
"not having the counter-positive as its locus" means "not having as its locus that which is delimited by the delimitors of the counter-positivehood."
For instance, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the [inferential] cognition "this non-pot possesses existence qualified by being other than quality and action,
because of its genus," since the genus exists in both quality and action, which are the loci where the absence of "existence qualified by being other than quality and action" resides.

This is a deviant reason (*vyabhicārī hetu*). Here, in the locus of the universal (*jāti*), there exists the absence of existence (*sattā*) qualified by its being distinct from quality and action, which resides in a quality.

Because there is an absence of the property of subsisting in a locus of the reason that is not a locus of the counter-positive— given that [the property] subsists in a quality which is the locus of the reason and the locus of a pure existence (sattā) that is distinct from the counter-positive—
therefore, by taking such another absence as the absence of a jar, the state of being the non-delimiter of the counter-positivehood [of that absence] resides in qualified existence (viśiṣṭasattātva).
Because [the property] exists, the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti) follows;
however, if "delimited by the delimitor of counter-correlativity" (pratiyogitāvacchedakāvacchinna) is inserted [into the definition], then...

The quality (*guṇa*) is a locus that is not occupied by that which is delimited by the delimitor of the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) consisting of the nature of qualified existence (*viśiṣṭasattātva*). Since it resides therein, the absence of qualified existence (*viśiṣṭasattābhāva*) is also a constituent of the definition;
the delimitor of its counterpositiveness is precisely the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), namely, the nature of qualified existence (*viśiṣṭasattātva*).
There is no over-extension.
Likewise, it must also be stated that [the locus] is one in which the counter-positive does not reside by way of the relation that delimits the counter-positive-ness.
Otherwise, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of "The self possesses knowledge because it is a substance," since this would apply to jars and the like, which lack knowledge.

This [reason] is inconclusive because of its existence as a substance (*dravyatva-sattvāt*). Here, the locus of the reason "substance-ness" is a jar or the like, and there exists an absence residing therein.
Although there is an absence of knowledge, nevertheless,
it does not reside in the locus of the reason (hetu) which is non-locus of its counter-positive (pratiyogin).
The locus of cognition—by way of the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*)—is precisely that which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the absence of cognition. 1.

Now, an objection: Is "being non-locus of the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇatvam*) to be understood as "subsisting in a locus that is not a locus of the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogy-anadhikaraṇa-vṛttitvam*)?

Even when a valid reason (*saddhetu*) is intended to be expressed, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "This [tree] possesses conjunction with a monkey, because it is a tree-ness," and so forth.
For the absence of conjunction with a monkey, due to being non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), exists in the tree, which is the locus of the reason.

Just as it exists [in the tree], so too does it exist in a quality (*guṇa*), which is a locus that is not the substratum (*anadhikaraṇa*) of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), namely the conjunction with a monkey (*kapisaṃyoga*); thus, the absence— which is the absence of conjunction with a monkey— that resides in the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇavṛtti*) and is non-occurrent in the same locus as its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*), has precisely that [conjunction] as its counter-positive-ness-delimiter (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*), which is the delimitor of the probandum-ness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*).
Since it exists in the state of conjunction with a monkey, he states the extracted meaning: "not having as its locus the counter-positive.
This refers to the portion ending with "residing in the locus of the reason which is non-locus of the counter-positive."

The meaning is: "subsisting in the locus of the reason (hetu) which is not the locus of the counter-positive (pratiyogin). In the case of "it possesses conjunction (saṃyogī), because of existence (sattvāt)," the locus of the reason, existence, which is not the locus of the counter-positive, conjunction, is a quality (guṇa); the absence that subsists in that [quality] is the absence of conjunction.
Since the delimiting factor of that counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is precisely "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

In the case of "This [tree] possesses conjunction with a monkey because it is this tree," the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the reason— the tree— is indeed the very locus of the conjunction, which is the counter-correlative.

The meaning is as follows: the absence that resides in the locus of the reason (hetu), which is not the locus of the counter-positive (pratiyogin), is not the absence of monkey-connection (*kapisaṃyoga*), but rather the absence of a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth. Since the state of not being the delimiting factor (*anavacchedakatva*) of the counter-positive-ness (*pratiyogitā*) exists in "monkey-connection-ness" (*kapisaṃyogatva*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

[The example is] "such as a pot" and so forth. Therefore, the absence that resides in the locus of the reason (hetu) which is not the locus of the counter-positive (pratiyogin)—namely, the absence of a cloth and so on—is precisely that [absence];
and the state of being a non-delimiter of the counter-positiveness (pratiyogitānavacchedakatva) resides in the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka).
If [the definition] were simply "existence in knowledge," the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) would result;
however, when the relation that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is introduced,
it is only the absence of knowledge delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) that exists in the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*).

The relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*) itself is the delimiting relation of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha*). By means of that relation, a jar and the like are non-loci of cognition; the absence of cognition residing therein has precisely "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*) as its delimiting counter-positiveness. Thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). And so it is.

The locus-hood (ādhikaraṇatā) qualified by the substratum-hood (ādheyatā) residing in the probans (hetu), which is delimited by the delimitor of the probans-hood (hetutāvacchedaka-dharma) and delimited by the relation that delimits the probans-hood (hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha), and which is distinct from the locus-hood (ādhikaraṇatā) qualified by the substratum-hood (ādheyatā) residing in the counter-positive (pratiyogin),

which is delimited by the delimitor of the counter-positive-hood (pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma) and delimited by the relation that delimits the counter-positive-hood (pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha).

The result is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in the coexistence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*)—as delimited by the delimitor of the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) which is not the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), as determined by the delimitor of the probandumness.
Having this in mind, he says: "More [is to be found] in our commentary on the *Maṇidīdhiti*."
The Tarkasaṅgraha: the determination of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) of the pervaded (vyāpya).
The property of residing in the mountain and so forth is the "property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatā).
Regarding the classification of inference:
inference is of two kinds, for oneself (svārtha) and for others (parārtha).

In that context, the inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is the cause of one's own inferential cognition. For instance, having personally grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, "wherever there is smoke, there is fire"—in the kitchen and other such places through repeated observation, one approaches a mountain; while doubting whether fire exists on that mountain, one perceives smoke on the mountain and [recollects] the pervasion.

When one recalls that "where there is smoke, there is fire," immediately thereafter the cognition arises: "this mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire. This very [cognition] is called the *liṅgaparāmarśa* (consideration of the mark).
