Therefore, the cognition "the mountain possesses fire" arises as an inference;
this is inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
However, when one, having personally inferred fire from smoke, employs a five-membered syllogism for the sake of communicating it to another, that is inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
For example: "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke;
whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as in the case of a kitchen; and so does this [mountain]."
Therefore, it is said "so it is.
By means of this, another person also understands fire from the sign (liṅga) that has been demonstrated.
Inference is of two kinds: for oneself and for others.

Furthermore, it is that which is distinct from the locus (adhikaraṇa) as defined by the substratum-ness (ādheyatā) residing in the counter-positive (pratiyogin), where that substratum-ness is delimited by both the counter-positive-ness-delimiting relation (pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha) and the counter-positive-ness-delimiting attribute (pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma).

That which possesses the locus-ness (ādhikaraṇatā) determined by that which is the locus-ness (ādheyatā) residing in the probans (hetu), which is itself delimited by the relation that delimits the probans-ness (hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha) and delimited by the property that delimits the probans-ness (hetutāvacchedaka-dharma);

and that which is the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) residing in that [locus], which is determined by [a locus-ness] delimited by the relation that delimits the probandum-ness (sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha).

The meaning is that pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in the subsistence, in the locus of the probandum (*sādhya*), of that probandum which is delimited by a delimitor of the probandum-ness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) that is not a non-delimiter (*anavacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) [of the absence]. *Dīpikā:* [This is the commentary on the above definition.]
He states the essential nature of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) with the words "of the pervaded" (*vyāpyasya*).
He divides inference (*anumāna*) with the words "inference" (*anumānam*). 000
The Compendium of Reasoning:
Definition of Inference for One’s Own Sake.
Inference for one's own sake is the cause of one's own inferential cognition. To explain:
Having personally grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire"— through repeated observation in such places as a kitchen, he goes near a mountain;
and seeing smoke on that mountain, [he infers] fire.
Being in doubt, one recalls the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire.
Immediately thereafter, the cognition arises: "This mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire. This very [cognition] is...
This is called the consideration of the logical mark (liṅgaparāmarśa).
Therefore, [the inference is]: "The mountain possesses fire."
Thus, this inference arises;
this is inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
— *Dīpikā*

He demonstrates inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) with the words "one's own" (*svam eva*). Now, [the following] is the determination of the means for grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*): [The opponent objects: "But surely..."

If it is asked: "How can pervasion (vyāpti) be grasped through repeated observation, given that even when co-occurrence has been seen hundreds of times in cases such as 'being earthen' and 'being scratchable by iron,' a deviation is observed in the case of the diamond-gem (vajramaṇi)?"—we say:
No. This is because the cognition of co-occurrence, when assisted by the absence of the cognition of deviation, is what grasps pervasion.
The cognition of deviation consists of both certainty and doubt;
its absence occurs in some cases through *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) and in others as something established by itself (*svataḥsiddha*).

In the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between smoke and fire, reasoning (*tarka*)—characterized by the undesirable consequence of breaking the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—is that which removes the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). If it is asked:
"But how can there be an apprehension of pervasion when there is no sensory contact with all fires and all smokes?"—it is not so.

Because it is possible to have knowledge of all fires and all smokes through the universal proximity (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) consisting of the universals "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*) and "smoke-ness" (*dhūmatva*).
"Therefore" means: from the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*).
— *Prakāśikā*

Regarding the term *svārthānumāna* (inference for oneself): it is so called by way of etymology, as that from which one's own purpose— the cessation of doubt concerning the probandum (*sādhya*)— arises.
The meaning is: an inference that serves as the cause for the removal of one's own doubt. Regarding the word "seeing" (*paśyan*):
the meaning is that seeing is the cause of recollection according to the principle that "the cognition of one related member brings about the recollection of the other related member."
"How is the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) possible?"— the sense is that since no one accepts a certainty regarding pervasion when there is a cognition of deviation (vyabhicāra),
it is impossible for repeated observation (bhūyodarśana) to be the cause of the certainty of pervasion.
This is an illustration: "observation of many" (*bhūyodarśana*) means either (1) a collection of many observations, or (2) the observation of many [instances of] the probandum and the reason,
or (3) [observation] in many [places].
Or, the meaning might be that "observation" refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) would result from a continuous stream of observations of concomitance in only a single location.
The second and third [conditions] do not hold,
because in cases such as "this possesses that color because of its taste," there is an absence of multiplicity (bhūyastva) both in the locus of the probandum and the locus of the reason.
It should also be understood that [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of the pervasion (vyāpti) not being ascertained.
Relying on the established doctrine (siddhānta) of Maṇikāra, he says:
"In the absence of the cognition of deviation (vyabhicāra)."

"Because it is the grasper of pervasion (*vyāpti*). And pervasion is precisely the nature of the delimiting property of the reason (*hetutāvacchedaka*), as qualified by its subsistence in the locus of the probandum (*sādhya*)— which is delimited by the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) that is not a delimiter of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) co-located with the reason.
Because the end of the term "co-referentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is common to donkeys and other such things;

[whereas] smoke-ness and the like possess the status of being the delimitor of pervasion (vyāpyatāvacchedakatva) by their own nature, and [they possess it] in the form of "smoke-ness-ness" and so forth.
There is no deficiency even if the pervader-ness (*vyāptitva*) consists in the identity of the delimited (*avacchedya*) and the delimiting (*avacchedaka*); and thus,

in the case of the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), there is an absence of the apprehension of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the form of being the delimitor of such a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*).
The reason functions by way of the absence of a contrary apprehension; however,
when there is an apprehension of the delimiting factor of the reason as residing in a locus co-located with the probandum,
the knowledge of co-location functions as a reason by way of being a knowledge of a qualifier— according to this principle.
It should be understood that the absence of the cognition of deviation and the cognition of co-occurrence are both causes for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
However, in reality:

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is simply the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the reason and the pervader with the probandum. Nor [is there a problem] because, since pervasion is common to donkeys and so forth, there could arise from a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) based on the donkey as a valid reason...

There would be the undesirable consequence of an erroneous inference of fire, because [the required] parāmarśa would not be of the nature of valid cognition due to the absence of a majority [of confirmatory instances]. 1.
"Due to the absence of a majority... means:

The meaning is that, because the probandum (*sādhya*), the probans (*hetu*), and their locus (*tadadhikaraṇa*) each consist of a single individual (*ekavyakti*), there is an absence of "plurality" (*bhūyastva*), which consists of a multiplicity (*anekatva*) of many instances.
This is because there exists a rule that [such a case] does not produce an erroneous inference of fire (*bhramātmakavahnyanumiti*).
It must be stated that the acceptance of such a consequence is untenable;
for it is the state of being a pervader (vyāpakatva) of that which is delimited by a particular property (dharmāvacchinna) which constitutes the element of pervasion (vyāpti).

There is no fault, because it is accepted that only a certainty (*niścaya*) whose qualifier is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and whose subject-locus is the delimitor of that [subject] is the cause of inference;
for this very reason, in the body of the definition of pervasion...
There is brevity because smoke-ness is not included; this is the general direction. And "doubt" refers to doubt regarding deviation as well.

The core point is that, because it is experienced as an obstacle to the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the absence of that which is delimited by the nature of the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—which is common to both [types of deviation]—is the probans (*hetu*).
"Its absence" means the absence of doubt regarding deviation. "In some cases" refers to...
The meaning is: in a situation where all other causes, excluding the absence of reasoning (*tarka*), are present. "In some cases, it is established by itself" means:
in a situation where other causes are absent.
The meaning is that it is indeed necessitated by the absence of such a cause;
thus, the implication is that there is no requirement for *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) in that case.
Regarding the phrase "of smoke and fire":
when the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between smoke and fire is about to arise,
the *tarka* (reductio argument) characterized by the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of the causal relationship serves to eliminate the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
This is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
That *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) should be understood as having the form: "If smoke were to deviate from fire, then it would not be produced by fire. Now, one might object:
Even though the concomitance between the fire and smoke of the kitchen is grasped due to their proximity, because other fires and smokes are not in contact,
it is impossible to perceive their concomitance; thus, there can be no perception of pervasion (vyāpti) with respect to all instances of smoke.
And thus,

since it is impossible to remember the pervasion upon seeing smoke on a mountain, the subsequent reflection (parāmarśa) would be untenable; with this intention, he raises an objection, beginning with "But surely" (nanu).

Because, even in the absence of ordinary sense-contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*) regarding all fires and smokes, there exists extraordinary sense-contact (*alaukika-sannikarṣa*) consisting of the "perception through the universal-characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*),
by way of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) delimited by the universal of firehood (*vahnitva*).
Since it is possible to perceive the concomitance (*sahacāra*) between all fires and smoke, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is possible with respect to all instances of smoke.
And thus, since the pervasion has already been grasped even in the case of the smoke on the mountain, by the sight of that smoke—
He provides the resolution—that there is no impossibility of the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) because the recollection of pervasion is possible—with the words:
"vahnitva-dhūmatva... (*Bālapriyā*).

Although in many treatises it is stated that *svārthānumāna* (inference for oneself) is so called because its purpose (*prayojana*) consists of inference itself— which is for one's own sake— nevertheless, even for inference, the purpose is the cessation of doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
Having considered this, he explains: "its own object" and "the cognition of one related member.
Regarding the relation called pervasion (*vyāpti*), there are two related members: the probans (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*).
The cognition consisting of the perception of the probans (hetu), which is related to one of the two [terms], produces the recollection of the probandum (sādhya), which is related to the other.

The sense is that when the probandum is remembered, the pervasion between the probandum and the reason is also remembered. In reality, however, the perception of smoke produces the memory of pervasion only by means of awakening the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of the memory of pervasion.
However, it should be understood that this does not mean the cognition of one related term is the means [of grasping pervasion].
In order to establish that the cognition of concomitance (*sahacārajñāna*), assisted by the absence of the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicārajñānābhāva*),
is the cause for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), [the author first] explains pervasion...

He elaborates [on this] with the words "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) and so forth. Although previously it was stated that pervasion consists in the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum—qualified by its own delimitor (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), which is not a delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that resides in the same locus as the probans (*hetu*)— [The text continues: ...[the author] refutes [that definition] by means of the following two verses. For, even if one were to accept that definition, it would still be necessary to state the following: "In the case of an inference such as 'this mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke,' the co-occurrence of the probandum (fire) with the probans (smoke)—where the probandum is qualified by its own delimitor (fireness), which is not a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the absolute absence residing in the same locus as the probans—is indeed present. Since this is the case, how could there be a fallacy of over-extension (*ativyāpti*)? Therefore, he states the following verse to refute [that definition]. It has been stated that this is "pervasion" (vyāpti);
nevertheless, if only that much were stated, then in the case of the inference "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," even a donkey [would be considered pervaded].

Otherwise, because it exists on the mountain—the locus of fire which pervades smoke—it would follow that [smoke] possesses the state of being pervaded by fire due to being encompassed by such co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Therefore, [the definition of pervasion is:

the state of being delimited by the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), which is not a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is co-located with the reason (*hetu*).

The definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) should be refined as: "the state of possessing the delimitor of the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedaka*), as qualified by co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*).
This is so even though co-occurrence with fire exists in a donkey.

There is no over-extension (ativyāpti), because of the absence of the property of possessing "smokiness" (dhūmatva) as the delimiting factor of the cause. Nor is it the case that if pervasion (vyāpti) extends up to smokiness itself, then the linguistic usage—that "smokiness is the delimiting factor of pervasion"—is untenable; for in that case, since the pervasion to be delimited is of the very nature of smokiness, [the relation holds] within smokiness itself.
It should not be argued that this is because it is impossible for "smokeness" (dhūmatva) to be a delimiting factor (avacchedaka),
since the relationship between the delimited (avacchedya) and the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) is necessarily dependent upon difference (bheda).

There is no fault here, because smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*) as delimited by the form of "smoke-ness-ness" (*dhūmatvatva*) is the pervasion (*vyāpti*), whereas smoke-ness in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) is the delimiting factor of that pervasion (*vyāptyavacchedaka*).
In such a cognition of pervasion...
If it is asked, "How can the absence of knowledge of deviation be a cause,
and how can the knowledge of concomitance be a cause?"—
listen.
The phrase "the delimiting condition of the probans as qualified by co-referentiality" means "the delimiting condition of the probans that subsists in a common locus. Thus— [Note:
1. *Adoṣāt* (because it is not a fault): although...]

Smoke-ness itself is both the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the pervaded; thus, there is identity between the delimited (*avacchedya*) and the delimiting (*avacchedaka*).
Nevertheless, the state of being delimited (*avacchedyatā*) resides in smoke-ness.

The property being delimited by "smokeness" (dhūmatvatvāvacchinnā) has an undelimited delimitation (niravacchinnāvacchedakatā); thus, because there is a distinction between the delimitation of the delimitedness (avacchedyatāvacchedakatā) and the delimitation itself, the relationship of the delimited and the delimiting (avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva) is established for a single entity.

The meaning is "thus. Furthermore, there is the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form: "Smoke possesses the property of smokeness, which resides in smoke that occurs in the locus of fire, and is delimited by the property of fireness—which is not the delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of the absolute absence residing in a locus other than that which possesses smoke."
The form [of the cognition] is as follows:

"Smoke possesses the property of smokeness, which resides in smoke and is co-located with that which is delimited by the firehood that delimits the counter-correlativity of the absolute absence co-located with smoke"— this is the form of the cognition of deviation (vyabhicāra).

In the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the absence of being a delimitant of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitānavacchedakatva*) with respect to the delimitant of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) appears; however, this is not the case in the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
In the [cognition of] the probandum, the non-delimitation of the counterpositiveness occurs with respect to the delimitant of the probandum-ness;
however, in the cognition of deviation, [the situation is different].

The property of being a delimitant of counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) appears in the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*). In that context, with respect to the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) which apprehends the non-delimitation of counterpositiveness, there exists the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) which apprehends the delimitation of counterpositiveness; this [acts as an obstacle] toward the cognition of the locus of that [delimitor].

Since the cognition of the absence of that [invariable concomitance] acts as an inhibitor by way of being a cognition of the presence of deviation, the absence of the cognition of deviation acts as an inhibitor by way of being an absence of an inhibitor; thus, the absence of the cognition of deviation is the cause for the cognition of pervasion by way of being an absence of an inhibitor.

The aspect "the delimitor of the reasonhood (hetutāvacchedaka) residing in the reason as qualified by co-inherence with the probandum (sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya)" also appears in the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti); indeed,
it is precisely the apprehension of co-inherence with the probandum [that constitutes it].

This is called the apprehension of concomitance (*sahacāragraha*). Such an apprehension of concomitance functions by way of the principle that "the knowledge of the qualifier is the cause of the qualified cognition," with respect to the knowledge that "the reason is characterized by co-occurrence in the same locus (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*) [with the probandum]."

Regarding the term "hetu" (reason): this should be consulted in our commentary on the *Pañcalakṣaṇī*, the *Bālabodhinī*. [The phrase] "qualified by subsistence in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyādhikaraṇavṛttitāviśiṣṭa*)" [is explained as follows].
And the qualification of the locus-of-the-probandum-residence in the delimiting factor of the causehood [of smoke] is by way of the relation of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
as in the case of "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*).
And because the property of "subsisting in the locus of fire" exists in one instance of smoke;
the resultant meaning, however, is: "the nature that delimits the causality residing in the reason, which subsists in the locus of the probandum."
"By way of the absence of erroneous apprehension" means by way of the absence of the cognition that [the object] possesses that [erroneous property].
Here, there is the cognition that [the object] possesses that [property].

The cognition that "the delimitor of the probandum-ness (sādhyatāvacchedaka) is like [that which is] not a delimitor of counter-correlativity" leads to the cognition that "the delimitor of the probandum-ness is the counter-correlator," in the sense that it is the absence of the absence of being a non-delimitor of counter-correlativity— that is, the absence of non-counter-correlativity.

1. Now, since in a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) the knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) alone is the cause, the knowledge of the co-presence with the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*) is itself the cause for the cognition that "the reason is qualified by co-presence with the probandum," and not—

Even the knowledge of concomitance (*sahacārajñāna*) in the form "the reason is qualified by co-presence with the probandum" is [not required], because the status of having the reason as its object does not enter into the defining condition (*avacchedaka*) of the causality for a qualified cognition;
therefore, he says: "moreover."

The point is this: the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), which takes the form "the delimiting factor of the probans (*hetutāvacchedaka*) is qualified by the probans as qualified by co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*)," [resides] in the delimiting factor of the probans.
And the excellence of the reason [is established] by way of the relation of being superposed (ādheyatā).

Such knowledge of pervasion [arises] by way of a cognition apprehending qualified-qualificative relation (viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhibuddhi), specifically as the knowledge of the qualifier in its role as the delimitor of the qualifierhood (viśeṣaṇatāvacchedakaprakārakajñāna).
The apprehension of concomitance in the form of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the cause [of inference].

With the intention that there be no contradiction with the root text—which defines pervasion (*vyāpti*) as "coexistence with the probandum" (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*)—he says: "But in reality... and "Nor is it...".

Since the pervasion, which consists in the co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of smoke with its pervader fire, also exists in a donkey, the reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*) in the form "the mountain possesses a donkey that co-inheres with fire, which is the pervader of smoke" would be a valid cognition (*pramā*); therefore, from that [cognition] as well—
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of an inference of fire from a donkey-liṅga which is of the nature of an error (bhrama).
Although the inference "the mountain possesses fire" is valid (pramā), how can the resulting inference [of the opponent] be characterized as erroneous?
Although such a doubt may arise,

it should be understood that this was stated with the intention that only an inference based on a pervaded (vyāpya) logical mark possesses validity, whereas an inference based on a non-pervaded (avyāpya) logical mark does not.
Regarding the phrase "delimited by that property" (*yaddharmāvacchinna*):
pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in being the pervader as delimited by the property of smokiness (*dhūmatva*).

Therefore, it is a certain cognition (*niścaya*) whose delimiting factor for the subject-locus (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is the property of smokiness, and which has pervasion as its qualifier (*prakāra*).

The certainty that "the mountain possesses smoke which is co-located with smoke that is pervaded by fire" is itself the cause of the inference that "the mountain possesses fire"; however, the consideration (parāmarśa) that "the mountain possesses an ass which is co-located with smoke that is pervaded by fire" [is not].

The point is that [a cognition] whose delimiting factor of the subjecthood (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is "donkey-ness" (*rāsabhatva*) and which has "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) as its qualifier cannot be a cause of inference. "For this very reason" means that a certainty (*niścaya*) which has as its qualifier a co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) whose delimiting factor of the subjecthood is the same as the delimiting factor of the causal state (*hetutāvacchedaka*) that enters into the pervading state (*vyāpakatā*) is the cause of inference.

The meaning is: even though pervasion (*vyāpti*) is common to donkeys and other such things, there is no deficiency [in our position], because by accepting that an inference of fire—which is of the nature of an error—arises from a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) whose probans is a donkey and which is of the nature of valid cognition, the [undesired] consequence is avoided.
This refers to the passage beginning with "sāmānyalakṣaṇā" and so forth.

That whose general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is "proximity by general characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā pratyāsatti*), which is a type of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*). [This occurs] through the contact consisting of the universals of fire-ness (*vahnitva*) and smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*).

For when there is perception of all fires and all smokes that serve as its substrata, there is also the apprehension of all instances of co-occurrence with fire residing in all instances of smoke, by way of the form of co-occurrence as determined by the property of fireness (*vanhitva*).
The coexistence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of mountain-dwelling smoke with mountain-dwelling fire was also previously perceived through direct perception;
therefore, by the sight of smoke...

The intention is that there ought to be a recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of mountain-fire with mountain-smoke. By this, [it is established that] the state of having the pervaded as its logical mark (*vyāpyaliṅgakatva*)— ①...
Furthermore, the inferential cognition (*anumiti*) would be erroneous because it is produced by a cognition whose object is a mark (*liṅga*) that is pervaded [by the probandum]—
[in this case] the cognition of pervasion being erroneous due to the pervasion being common to donkeys as well. And [this is so] when the pervasion is shared with a donkey.

The point is that since the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti) having a donkey as its subject is a valid cognition (pramā), the inferential knowledge of fire produced by it must also be a valid cognition and not an error (bhrama).

Even though all fires and all smokes are presented through the universal-characterized (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) perception of the forms "fire-ness" and "smoke-ness," the pervasion— consisting of the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of fire and smoke— resides individually [in each instance], as was previously observed in the kitchen.

The objection— namely, that even though the co-presence residing in the smoke of the kitchen has been apprehended, the co-presidence residing in the smoke of the mountain has not been apprehended, so how can there be a recollection of it— is thereby refuted.

Because it is possible to apprehend even the co-presence residing in the smoke on the mountain through the general-character mediation (*sāmānyalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*), which consists in the state of being co-present as delimited by the property of fire-ness.
The *Tarkasaṃgraha*: the exposition of inference for the sake of others; that which [is performed] by oneself alone.
Having inferred fire from smoke, one employs a five-membered syllogism for the sake of communicating it to another; that is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
— *Dīpikā*
He states the inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) with the words "yattu" ("as for that which").
The word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "that is the inference for others" connects with the word "which" (*yat*).
Although the term *parārthānumāna* has as its object (*artha*)— that is, its purpose (*prayojana*)— the other person, namely the neutral mediator (*madhyastha*), it is an illuminator (*prakāśikā*).

By the etymological derivation *yasmāt* [it arises] as an inference whose nature is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), the meaning is the consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) which is the instrument for an inference inherent in another. For this very reason, it is said: "In both inference for oneself and inference for others, the consideration of the mark alone is the instrument."
Thus, the subsequent root text beginning with "ityādi" is properly consistent;
nevertheless, in the five-membered statement that prompts an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the term *parārthānumāna* is used in a figurative sense (*aupacārika*).
Having kept the root [text] in mind, he introduces it, saying: "He states the inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). [The commentary *Bālapriyā* explains: "For another..."
Regarding the term "of the neutral" (madhyasthasya):
although the word *para* means "other," the literal meaning of the term *parārthānumāna* is, by its own natural force, "an instrument of inference residing in another."

Nevertheless, since inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), which consists of formal reasoning, is generally employed only in debates and the like, and since the word "other" (*para*) in that context refers to another opponent, an inference free from the suspicion of invalidity does not arise from the reasoning stated by the proponent, because the cognition of a sublation (*bādhajñāna*) exists [in the mind of that other].
This explanation was made with the intention that an inference ought to occur for a neutral person who is free from attachment to either side.

"An impeller of inference for the sake of others" means [the impeller] of the inferential consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), which is the instrument of inference residing in another person— that is, inference for the sake of others.
The term "prayojaka" (instigator) is used figuratively for the *nyāya*— the great five-membered syllogism— which serves as the indirect cause.
It is technical (lākṣaṇika);
that is to say, it is a metaphorical designation of the cause by the name of the effect, referring to the term "inference for others" (parārthānumāna).
If it is asked: how can the *nyāya* (logical argument) be the instigator of inference for others, which consists in the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*)?

In this manner, first, the comprehension of the meaning of each individual sentence arises through the five sentences beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*). Thereafter, through these five sentences forming a single syntactic unity, the comprehension of the meaning of one great sentence (*mahāvākya*) arises.
Then, by means of the mind assisted by that [perception], the consideration of the middle term (liṅgaparāmarśa) arises, and from that, the inference; thus it is.

The five-membered syllogism (*nyāya*), consisting of a statement of five members, functions as the instigator of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) by virtue of generating the comprehension of the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*), which in turn generates the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) that produces inferential cognition (*anumiti*).
As for the form of this comprehension of the meaning of the great sentence:

The mountain is non-different from that which possesses smoke pervaded by fire, which is non-different from that which possesses fire pervading smoke, which is non-different from that which possesses smoke, which is non-different from the mountain possessing fire as known by the cognition of smoke;
[and it is] non-different from the mountain possessing fire as known by the cognition of smoke, which is uncontradicted and unopposed.
1. The cause is the logical method (nyāya), and the effect is the consideration of the mark (liṅgaparāmarśa). [This refers to] that which expresses the consideration of the mark, which is the effect.
The meaning is that the term *parārthānumāna* (inference for others) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to refer to its effect, namely the consideration of the mark-bearer (*liṅgiparāmarśa*).
2. "The mountain..."

Five cognitions arise, each having as its object the meaning of one of the individual constituent sentences— such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth— having the forms "non-different from that which possesses fire" and "the state of being an indicator residing in smoke," and so on;
[the third being] "that which is made known by the cognition of smoke," and so forth.

Because the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā), which is conjoined with the meaning of the reason (hetu), and the meaning of the example (udāharaṇa) function as the delimiters of the object to be indicated (uddeśyatāvacchedaka) for the purpose of the application (upanaya), while the meaning of the conclusion (nigamana) functions as that which is to be predicated (vidheya) in its connection [with them].
Since it is accepted that the demonstrative pronouns *yad* and *tad* contained within the illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*), as well as the indicator of the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*),
function to apprehend the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the aforementioned comprehension of the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) [arises].
It is obtained as follows: the meaning of the word ending in the fifth case, "from smoke" (*dhūmāt*), is "the state of being made known" (*jñāpyatva*) as determined by the cognition of smoke;
this [state] exists through the relation of locus (*āśrayatā*).
The word "fire" (vahni) within the thesis (pratijñā) has its connection [with the probandum] in the object fire;

the object denoted by the term "fire-possessing" (vahnimat) has its connection with the object denoted by the term "mountain" (parvata) through identity (abheda), and it has its connection with the mountain— the object denoted by the word "idam" (this) within the application (upanaya)— through the relation of identity.
In the example, there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "fire" in the sense of fire as that which pervades smoke;
the words "that," "this," and "kitchen" function to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*),
[showing] the non-difference of [the subject] from that which possesses smoke.
There is a positive concomitance (anvaya) with smoke in that which possesses fire as its pervader;
and that [concomitance] is subsumed non-differently into the referent of the word "this" (idam) in the application (upanaya).
The meaning of the conclusion (*nigamana*) is "the mountain possesses fire as known by the cognition of smoke that is uncontradicted and lacks a counter-argument";
this [meaning] is related [to the rest of the syllogism] by way of the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*).
The word *idam* (this) has its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the object denoted by the *upanaya*.

The meaning of the *upanaya* sentence, however, is: "The mountain is non-different from that which possesses smoke pervaded by fire," because the word *tathā* signifies "that which possesses smoke pervaded by fire," while the word *idam* [signifies the mountain].
The intention is that [the word "parvata"] signifies the mountain.
This concludes the *Tarkasaṅgraha*,
which is a definition of the members of a syllogism (*nyāyāvayava*).
Just as: "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke;
whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, as for example [a kitchen hearth]."
"The kitchen is such, and this [person] is likewise;
therefore, he is so"—
by means of this statement.
From the probans (liṅga) that has been presented, even another person understands the fire.
The five members [of a syllogism] are the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion.
"The mountain possesses fire" is the proposition.

"Because of possessing smoke" is the reason (*hetu*). "Whatever possesses smoke, that possesses fire, just as a kitchen" is the example (*udāharaṇa*). "And so is this [mountain]" is the application (*upanaya*).
Therefore, "thus" constitutes the conclusion.
The five members [of a syllogism] are the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion. "The mountain possesses fire" is the proposition.
"Because it possesses smoke" is the reason. Whichever...
"Having smoke, that [mountain] possesses fire, just like a kitchen"— this is the example (*udāharaṇa*).
"And this [mountain] is likewise"— this is the application (*upanaya*).
Therefore, "thus" (*tathā*) constitutes the conclusion (*nigamana*).
The *Dīpikā* provides an example of the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayavavākya*), beginning with "as follows" (*yathā*).
He states the nature of the members [of the syllogism]:
"the proposition" (*pratijñā*). He explains the division of the proposition and so forth within the cited statement: "the mountain..."
"Fire-possessing":
the statement of the subject as possessing the property to be proven is the proposition (*pratijñā*);
it ends in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*).
The reason (hetu) is that which establishes the logical mark (liṅga).
The example (udāharaṇa) is that which establishes the pervasion (vyāpti). The application (upanaya) is the statement that establishes the logical mark as qualified by the pervasion.
The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the statement that establishes the subject (*pakṣa*) as possessing the probans and the probandum;
it [also] consists of [the demonstration of] its being uncontradicted (*abādhitatva*) and so forth.
The purpose of the conclusion:
the *prakāśikā* [states that] the five-membered syllogism.

By this [statement], through the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that sentence which possesses five members," the definition of *nyāya* (the formal argument) should be understood as being the collection of the five members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*).
This [definition] follows from the root text's phrase "from the inferential mark (*liṅga*) established by this."

The meaning is: [the cognition] produced by the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*), which is brought about by the employment of the collection of the five members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*).
"The statement of the subject as possessing the probandum" means:

a sentence that generates a cognition in which the subject is qualified by the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) and the probandum is qualified by the delimitor of the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*).

From the example (udāharaṇa), there arises the cognition of the qualified relation with the property delimiting the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka) as qualified by the reason (hetu); it does not arise [in that way] regarding what is qualified by the property delimiting the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka). And from the application (upanaya), [it arises] regarding what is qualified by the property delimiting the subject.

The exclusion of those two [types of cognition] is because it is a cognition of the qualified by that which delimits the state of being a cause (*hetutāvaccheka*), and not a cognition that apprehends the qualified by that which delimits the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*).
Furthermore, the term "sentence" (*vākya*) refers to a sentence that is a member of a formal inference (*nyāyāvayava*), thereby excluding sentences that fall outside of such a formal inference.
The same applies to what follows.

In order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*)— since the property of having an ablative ending exists in the proposition (*pratijñā*) such as "This [substance] is not from a stick, because it is a substance not produced by conjunction with that stick"— [the definition must be qualified].
"Establishing the *liṅga*" means establishing the logical reason (*hetu*).
"Establishing the pervasion (*vyāpti*)" means... [the rest of the sentence].
The meaning is: a statement that makes known the probandum (sādhya), which is the pervader of the relevant reason, within the context of the relevant reason.
How [does this apply] to the example?

If it is argued that [the word "sādhya"] conveys pervasion— then it is so, because the term "sādhya" possesses a conventional metaphorical indication (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā) for the probandum as qualified by being the pervader of the reason.
Nor should it be suspected that the repetition of the word *yat* is purposeless, for it serves a purpose by indicating such an intended meaning (*tātparya*). Alternatively:

In the first referent of the word *yat*, namely the kitchen (*mahānasa*), there is the property of possessing the subject-locus (*prakṛtahetumatva*) in the second referent of the word *yat*, namely something other than the kitchen; and in the first referent of the word *tat*, namely the kitchen, [there is that same property] in the second referent of the word *tat*.
When the verbal cognition of the probandum arises in another [person] from the kitchen [example],
the subsequent cognition of pervasion is mental; thus,
the function of the example as the means for the apprehension of pervasion remains intact, and there is no fault whatsoever.
"Direction" (*dik*) means that which expresses the logical mark (*liṅga*) as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The meaning is: a sentence that generates a cognition having as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) that which is qualified by the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), and having as its qualifier (*prakāra*) the reason (*hetu*) which is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*) under discussion.

However, in the reading "The application (*upanaya*) is for the sake of the knowledge of the presence of the reason in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatājñānārtham upanayaḥ*), the word "is employed" (*prayujyate*) [is understood].
The meaning already demonstrated by completing the remainder [of the definition] should be connected in some way or another:
"A statement that indicates the subject as possessing both the reason and the probandum.

This means: a sentence that generates a cognition whose object is the subject as qualified by being the locus of the probandum, which is itself characterized by being made known by the cognition of the reason.
The mental cognition whose object is the state of being uncontradicted and not having a counter-argument at a subsequent time is to be understood [as the definition of a thesis].
This is the definition of the thesis (*pratijñā*).
He states the refinement: "delimited by the delimitor of the probandum," and so forth.
[This refers to] the cognition in the form "the mountain possesses fire."
Because it has as its qualificandum a mountain delimited by "mountain-ness," which serves as the delimiting property of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka),

and because it has as its qualifier fire delimited by "fire-ness," which serves as the delimiting property of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka), the definition applies to the sentence "The mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*), which generates such a cognition.

If the property of having as its qualificandum that which is delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) were not included [in the definition], then from the portion "he is fire-possessing" (*so 'gnimān*) within the example "whatever is smoke-possessing is fire-possessing," there would arise a cognition in the form "the smoke-possessor is fire-possessing" (*dhūmavān vahnimān*); therefore, of that...
There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the example sentence (*udāharaṇavākya*), which generates such a cognition by having "being fire" (*vahnitva*) as its delimiting qualifier; however,
if one includes the condition that the subject must have the delimitor of the pakṣa (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) as its qualificandum, then [this does not apply] to the aforementioned cognition.
Even though there is the state of having "possessing smoke" (dhūmavattva) as the delimiting property of the qualificandum,
there is no fault because there is an absence of the state of having "being a mountain" (parvatatva) as the delimiting property of the qualificandum;
this is so provided that one does not include the state of having [the property] delimited by the delimitor of the probandum-ness as the mode.

If one were to state merely that [the definition] is "the capacity to produce a cognition whose qualificandum is delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*)," there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the statement of the application (*upanaya*), namely "and so this [is]," because [that statement] produces such [a cognition].
This is because the cognition ‘the mountain possesses smoke pervaded by fire’ has as its qualificandum the mountain as delimited by the property of being a mountain (*parvatatva*).
However, if one includes the condition of having a qualifier delimited by the delimitor of the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), then for that [cognition]...
There is no fault, because there is an absence of the property of having fireness as its delimited qualifier when there is the property of having smokeness as its delimited qualifier. Likewise,
if one were to state merely that [the cognition] has the subject as its qualificandum, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the sentence "The substance possesses fire."

To exclude that [over-extension], the qualification of "having as its qualificandum that which is delimited by the delimitor of the subject" (*pakṣatāvacchedakāvacchinnaviśeṣyakatva*) is introduced. Furthermore, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the sentence "The mountain possesses substance" (*parvato dravyavān*), the phrase "having as its qualificandum the probandum" (*sādhyaviśeṣyakatva*) is not mentioned.
It was stated that [the object] has as its qualificandum that which is delimited by the delimitor of the property to be proved (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*).
This is because even a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) produced by the sentence "The mountain possesses substance; substance possesses fire" [would otherwise be excluded].

In order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such a sentence— because it has as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) that which is delimited by mountain-ness (*parvatatva*) and as its qualifier (*prakāra*) that which is delimited by fire-ness (*vahnitva*)—
one must incorporate the relationship of the defined and the definer (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*) between the roles of qualificandum and qualifier.

It should be stated that a *pratijñā* (the thesis) is a sentence that generates a cognition characterized by a subject-locus (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by the delimitor of the pakṣa (the locus of inference), which is itself determined by a qualifier-locus (*prakāratā*) residing in the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by the delimitor of the probandum.

The phrase "lying outside the logical method" (nyāyabahirbhūtā) excludes a neutral statement such as "the mountain possesses fire," which does not fall within the framework of the five-membered syllogism.

The same applies to what follows: the phrase "the constituent words of a sentence" (ghaṭakavākyapada) referring to the characteristics of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, refers here to sentences in the form of members of a syllogism (*nyāyāvayava*), and thus [the definition] does not apply to those outside the syllogism.
The meaning is that it should be understood that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a sentence that has the same form as a sentence containing "the reason" (*hetu*) and so forth.
According to the *Dīpikā*, the reason (*hetu*) is that which conveys the logical mark (*liṅga*) and ends in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*).
Provided that it ends in the fifth case...

The meaning of that [definition] is: "being a sentence while possessing the capacity to generate a cognition whose object is a *liṅga* (probans). And since the portion "from smoke" (*dhūmāt*) possesses that quality, the application of the definition is established. This is so because it ends in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*).
If [the definition] were simply "being," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the three [factors] beginning with the example (*udāharaṇa*),
because these too indicate the logical mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, it is stated that [the indicator must] be "ending in the fifth case" (*pañcamyantatve sati*).

In such cases as "This [substance] is not from the staff, because it is a substance not produced by conjunction with that staff," even though the proposition (*pratijñā*) "This is not from the staff" contains a word ending in the ablative case, this [definition] avoids over-extension (*ativyāpti*) there.
It was stated that [the definition] must be "while being indicative of a *liṅga*.
Its meaning is "being indicative of a *liṅga* that serves as the cause for the inference of the *sādhya* under discussion"; thus, there is no fault.

This is because the term "sentence" (*vākya*) refers to a member (*avayava*) of a formal argument (*nyāya*), and therefore it does not apply to the portion "therefore" (*tasmāt*) within the member of conclusion (*nigamana*).
There is no over-extension [of the definition],
because that part, although it is a member of the conclusion (*nigamana*) within the members of a formal argument (*nyāya*), is not accepted as being a member of the formal argument itself.
And this being the case, although the portion "from the staff" contained within the proposition "this is not from the staff" is indeed a member of the proposition,

there is no over-extension [of the definition] precisely because it lacks the status of being a member of the *nyāya* (the formal syllogism); thus, [the definition] refers to that which expresses the *liṅga* (the logical mark).
It should not be said that the qualification is redundant;
for in that case, since the member *pratijñā* (the proposition) is also a member of a syllogism (*nyāya*), there would follow the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
And it should not be argued that, in that case, there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the part "therefore" (*tasmāt*) within the member of conclusion (*nigamana*);
for [this is excluded] by the phrase "the state of having the fifth case-ending."

This is because the intended meaning is that there is no fault, since what is intended [by the definition] is the state of being a word ending in the fifth case (ablative) which expresses its own meaning as connected with the probandum (sādhya) that has become a qualifier of the subject under discussion (prakṛtapakṣaviśeṣaṇa). Now, one might object:
"The example is that which demonstrates pervasion (vyāpti)," according to the *Dīpikā*.

It is understood that the definition of an example (*udāharaṇa*) is "being a statement that produces a cognition whose object is pervasion" (*vyāpti*). However, this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) with respect to the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*), because these two also convey pervasion.

Anticipating the objection that the word *tathā* contained within the application (*upanaya*) has the meaning "possessing smoke pervaded by fire," and that the word *tasmāt* contained within the conclusion (*nigamana*) has the meaning "because of possessing smoke pervaded by fire," he explains as follows:
Regarding the phrase "possessing the reason under discussion":
in the example "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire," there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "fire" as referring to fire that pervades smoke.
The repeated word *yat* and the word *tat* serve as indicators of the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Thus, [the inference is]: "that which possesses smoke."

The meaning is: "possessing fire, which is the pervader of smoke. By this, it is established that the definition of an *udāharaṇa* (example) is: a sentence that generates a cognition whose qualificand is the subject of the current reason and whose qualifier is the probandum that is the pervader of that reason.
The point is that there is no over-extension [of the definition] because such characteristics are absent in the *upanaya* (application) and *nigamana* (conclusion).
Now, even so, [in the case of] "that which possesses smoke..."

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even sentences such as "the mountain possesses fire, which is pervaded by smoke" would qualify as *udāharaṇa* (the third member of a syllogism).
This is not an acceptable conclusion, because it contradicts the established tradition of logicians (*kathaka-sampradāya*). Therefore, he says "dig" (and so forth).

The intended definition of an *udāharaṇa* (exemplification) is the status of being a collection of words consisting of: a word denoting the reason (*hetu*) qualified by the delimitor of the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedaka*) following a repeated [word], and a collection of words denoting the probandum (*sādhya*) qualified by the delimitor of the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) following that [word].
The sense is that, therefore, there is no fault;
the further details are elsewhere,
beginning with "qualified by the delimiting condition of the subject" (*pakṣatāvacchedakaviśiṣṭa*), and so forth.

The inclusion of the condition "having as its qualificandum that which is qualified by the delimitor of the subject" (*pakṣatāvacchedakaviśiṣṭaviśeṣyakatva*) is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the sentence "that which possesses smoke pervaded by fire.
It is also for the purpose of avoiding over-extension in the sentence "the mountain possesses smoke."

The inclusion of "being pervaded by the probandum under discussion" (prakṛtasādhyavyāpyatva) means: a sentence that generates a cognition possessing a subject-locus property (prakāratā) residing in the reason, which is itself determined by a property-locus (prakāratā) residing in pervasion, which is in turn determined by a property-locus residing in the probandum under discussion. By this, even a sentence such as "the mountain possesses smoke," which [in fact] possesses [the property of] being pervaded by fire...
There is no occasion for the doubt that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because [the definition] consists in having "that which is smoke" as its qualifier;

for from the *Dīpikā* passage stating that "it is that which presents the subject (*pakṣa*) as possessing the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of the reason (*hetu*"), it is understood that the definition of the conclusion (*nigamana*) is the property of presenting the subject as possessing the reason and as possessing the probandum. Thus...
If there were a conclusion (*nigamana*), it would be impossible;

for although the concluding statement "therefore, thus" makes known the subject (*pakṣa*) as possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyavat*), it lacks the capacity to make known the subject as possessing the reason (*hetumat*).
Because the meaning of the fifth case (the ablative) does not connect with the subject (*pakṣa*) when it is connected with the probandum (*sādhya*),
there would likewise be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in a sentence such as "The mountain possesses smoke and possesses fire."
Therefore, he explains:
"by the knowledge of the cause.
The meaning of the ablative case here is "being made known by knowledge. Regarding "knowledge":
The cause, which is the meaning of the base (prakṛti), is construed with the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā).
The word "tathā" means "possessing the probandum" (sādhyavat). [This applies] to the probandum (sādhya).

The meaning of the fifth case (the ablative), namely "being made known by a cognition," is construed as the locus [of the probandum]. Thus, the cognition produced by the conclusion (*nigamana*) takes the form: "The subject (*pakṣa*) possesses the probandum (*sādhya*), which is the locus of being made known by a cognition whose object is the reason (*hetu*). In this way, the definition is fully applicable to the sentence of the conclusion.
How can it be said that the purpose of the conclusion (*nigamana*) is [the demonstration of] non-sublation and so forth?
Anticipating the objection that non-sublation and non-contradiction by a counter-argument are not understood from the sentence of the conclusion, he says:
"At a later time" means that,
in the manner previously described, after the verbal comprehension [of the inference],
a mental cognition arises to the effect that "this reason is uncontradicted and not counterbalanced. This is the intended meaning.
Tarkasaṅgraha:
In both inference for oneself (svārthānumiti) and inference for others (parārthānumiti), the consideration of the mark (liṅgaparāmarśa) alone is the instrument.
Therefore, inference is the consideration of the mark.
In both inference for oneself (*svārthānumiti*) and inference for others (*parārthānumiti*), the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) alone is the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Therefore, the consideration of the logical mark is inference.
— *Dīpikā*
He states the instrument of inference (*anumitikaraṇa*)—
namely, "for one's own sake" (*svārtha*).
This is indeed the establishment of the fact that the qualified reflective awareness (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) is the cause of inference.

If it is asked: "Since inference can occur through the mere cognition of the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), for what purpose should a 'qualified consideration' (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) be admitted?"—the answer is: no, because [one must first know] "this [subject] possesses that which is pervaded by fire."

Thus, since the consideration (*parāmarśa*) is necessary in cases of verbal consideration (*śābdaparāmarśa*), and because, by parsimony (*lāghava*), the consideration alone is the cause in all instances,
the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is not the instrument (*karaṇa*), especially in the case of past objects and the like.
Because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

According to the view that "an instrument (*karaṇa*) is a cause possessing an operation," the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti-jñāna*) is the instrument by means of the intermediate step of the reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*).
An operation (*vyāpāra*) is that which, while being produced by something, produces what is produced by that same thing. He concludes the inference with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
[The *Prakāśikā* says: But surely...

If a parāmarśa (inferential cognition) that apprehends a qualified-qualifier relation (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*) is held to be the cause of inference, there is the complexity (*gaurava*) of having to postulate both "non-superfluousness" (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) and "invariable antecedence" (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*) in that case. [For example:
"Smoke is pervaded by fire..."

The Prābhākara raises an objection, arguing that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in your view because, since the two cognitions "the mountain possesses smoke" and "there is fire on the mountain" are postulated as causes for the qualified reflective cognition (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*), one need only postulate their status as instruments (*karaṇatva*) by virtue of their being non-otherwise-established (*ananyathāsiddhatva*). Thus he objects:

The word "nanu" [introduces an objection]. The point is this: in the cognition "this possesses the pervader of fire," it is impossible for two cognitions to be the cause, because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the absence of the cause you have proposed.

The term "verbal" (*śābda*) is used to indicate that, in any way whatsoever, the manifestation of the delimitors of pervasion— such as "smokiness" (*dhūmatva*)— is not possible within the act of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). The phrase "by way of parsimony" (*lāghavena*) is used [to justify this].
The meaning is "by way of parsimony of conceptualization" (*kalpanālāghavena*).

For instance, this is because [the latter] is preferable to the conceptualization of both non-otherwise-establishedness (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) and invariable antecedence (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*) in relation to two cognitions.
In the case of a qualified *parāmarśa*, the postulation of that [qualified cognition] itself is more parsimonious (*laghīyas*).
In reality, however,

[the cause of inference is] a subject characterized by the delimiting property of the pakṣa (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), which is qualified by a certainty (*niścaya*) having as its qualifier the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and having as its qualificandum that which is delimited by that same property.

In that [Buddhist] view, it should be understood that the status of being the delimiting condition (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatva*) belongs exclusively to a certainty whose qualificandum is new, and not to something common to both cognitions.
However, in the Naiyāyika view—

It should be noted that there is parsimony regarding the determinant of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), namely that the determinant of causality is the nature of a certainty (*niścayatva*) which apprehends the qualified presence of the pervasion (*vyāpti-viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya*).
This is so because there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanā-viraha*) [to prefer any other alternative].
He refutes the opinion of those teachers who maintain that the mark (liṅga) is an instrument (karaṇa) even in its capacity as a sign of knowledge, stating: "The mark is not an instrument,
because of deviation."

The point is that even in that case, since inference is established by experience, smoke and other factors—whether past or future—that exist immediately prior to it are non-existent. Regarding the phrase "in the view":

according to the view that "the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the cause (*kāraṇa*) delimited by the non-connection with the result," it is the *parāmarśa* (reflective judgment) itself [that is the instrument].
It should be understood that [the definition] is "the instrument" (*karaṇa*).
To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the instrument itself, the phrase "provided it is produced by that" (*tajjanyatve sati*) is included.
— *Bālapriyā*
Even for the Naiyāyika, first there is the perception of smoke,
then the recollection of the pervasion (vyāpti), and then...

Since the sequence— namely, that there must first be the qualified reflective awareness (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) "this [mountain] possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire," and from that, inference arises— must be accepted, [inference] follows from the perception of smoke and the recollection of pervasion alone.

The Prābhākara has raised the objection: "Since inference is possible [directly from the knowledge of the mark], for what purpose is a qualified intermediate consideration (viśiṣṭaparāmarśa) required? This objection is not tenable;
[for inference arises] precisely from the qualified consideration.
Since the Naiyāyika could argue that when an inference is possible, two cognitions cannot be the cause of that inference because they are otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*),
[the author] clarifies the intention of the objector: "But surely..."
By the phrase "viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya" and so forth;

thus, both the non-otherwise-establishment (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) and the necessary antecedent occurrence (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*) of the qualified reflective cognition (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) must be postulated.
For the two cognitions, however, both their non-otherwise-establishment (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) and their necessary antecedence (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*) must be postulated;
whereas for the two cognitions, only their non-otherwise-establishment needs to be postulated, and not [their necessary antecedence].
Since its status as an invariably antecedent factor is already established,
the Prābhākara maintains that, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), two cognitions alone are the cause of inference, and not a qualified reflective awareness (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*).

The term "bhāva" means intention (āśaya). In this context, it refers to the qualified reflective awareness (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) consisting of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), which arises from hearing the statement "this possesses the pervader of fire," namely, "this possesses the pervader of fire."
Since an inference arises at the very next moment after that [perception] has been produced, there is a positive deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) between the two cognitions; thus,
because [perception] cannot be the cause of inference, it follows by this reasoning that it must be the cause in every instance [of knowledge].
The Prābhākara view has been refuted in the *Dīpikā*.
Now, in the Prābhākara system,
both types of cognition possess the nature of the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the nature of the cognition of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Causality is accepted [for this as well],

because even the verbal reflection "this possesses that which is pervaded by fire" is encompassed by the delimiters of causality, namely, the nature of being a cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the nature of being a cognition of the property's presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Anticipating the objection that "causality is indeed accepted [in this case], so there is no deviation," he says:
"in any way whatsoever.
The meaning is as follows: [this applies] to the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the knowledge of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

If causality were accepted on the grounds of being a cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and a cognition of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the inference "the mountain possesses fire" would arise even from the two cognitions: "light is pervaded by fire" and "the mountain possesses smoke."

Therefore, the causality [of the inferential cognition] must be stated as residing in a cognition that apprehends the presence of the reason in the subject (pakṣadharmatā) with respect to that which is delimited by a property grasped as the delimitor of pervasion (vyāpyatāvacchedaka).
And thus, in the cognition "this possesses what is pervaded by fire" (vahnivyāpyavān ayam),...
Since the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*), such as "smokiness" (*dhūmatva*), does not appear [in the cognition],

it is not subsumed under the aforementioned delimitors of causality; consequently, because the effect arises even in the absence of that which is delimited by the delimitors of causality, the fallacy of negative deviation (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*) is unavoidable in the Prābhākara school's view.
"For the sake of manifestation" means that there is an absence of any word that brings about the presence of "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*).
This is explained by the passage beginning with "for instance," and so forth.

In cases where inference arises from verbal apprehension (*śābdaparāmarśa*), since the occurrence of inference is established by experience even without two [separate] cognitions, if one were to postulate that inference arises there too from only two cognitions,
then the non-redundancy (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) of those two cognitions [would have to be established].
Both [the conditions] must be postulated: being invariably antecedent and being otherwise unestablished.

Among these, since the fact that the qualified reflective awareness (viśiṣṭaparāmarśa) is invariably antecedent is already established, only its "otherwise unestablished" status needs to be postulated.
The sense is that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in the Naiyāyika position. Now, one might object:

even if there is parsimony in the Naiyāyika position regarding cases of verbal *parāmarśa*, in cases where inference arises from two cognitions alone, there is parsimony in the Prābhākara position according to the method previously stated.

Anticipating the objection that this [definition] is too broad, he says: "In reality, however... A certainty whose qualificandum is delimited by *dhūmatva* (smokeness) and whose qualifier is pervasion (*vyāpti*)—having the form "smoke is pervaded by fire"—is qualified by that [pervasion] through the relation of subsisting in one and the same self at one and the same time.
The certainty whose qualificandum is delimited by mountain-ness and whose qualifier is delimited by smoke-ness has the form "the mountain possesses smoke. Thus,
the state of being such a certainty— qualified by the aforementioned certainty— is [the definition].
In the Prābhākara view, the delimitor of the causality of inference is [the cognition of the qualifier-possessor as qualified by the qualifier];
however, in the Naiyāyika view,
it is the state of apprehending the qualifiedness of that which is qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*).
That [cognition], however, exists even in the case of a verbal parāmarśa such as "this possesses that which is pervaded by fire," which does not involve the apprehension of "smoke-ness. Therefore,
the meaning is that the view of the Naiyāyikas alone is correct due to the parsimony (lāghava) of the delimiting condition of causality.
"Due to the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraheṇa*)," [means: between the two positions—

namely, that the inferential mark (*liṅga*) as it is being cognized is the instrument (*karaṇa*), or else that the cognition whose object is the inferential mark is the instrument— there is no factor for deciding in favor of one over the other.
The meaning is: "due to the absence of reasoning that establishes its validity.
If the inferential mark (*liṅga*) were the instrument of inference, then inference could not occur on the basis of past or future marks that are currently unknown.

Because it is impossible for those two, being non-existent immediately prior to the inference, to possess the status of an instrument (karaṇatva) defined by their existence immediately preceding [the effect],
[namely] the cognition of the mark (liṅga).
But if it is the instrument (karaṇa), then even though the past and future marks (liṅga) are non-existent, inference is established because the cognition having them as its object exists.
Thus he says: "In that case too, because of inference..."

"Exclusion of non-conjunction with the effect" (*phalāyogavyavacchinna*) refers to the view that an instrument (*karaṇa*) is a cause characterized by its occurrence immediately prior to the effect (*kāryāvyavahitapūrvavṛttitva-viśiṣṭa-kāraṇa*).
The point is that because the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) occurs immediately prior to the inference, it alone is the instrument (*karaṇa*);
whereas the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti-jñāna*) is not the instrument, as it is separated from the inference by the *parāmarśa*. — *Tarkasaṅgraha*.
The classification of reasons: the logical mark (liṅga) is of three kinds—
positive-and-negative concomitant (anvayavyatirekin), purely positive (kevalānvayin), and purely negative (kevalavyatirekin).
That which possesses pervasion (*vyāpti*) by way of both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the *anvayavyatirekin*.
For example, when fire is the probandum (*sādhya*), the state of possessing smoke [is such a reason].
"Wherever there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen"—this is positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*).

Where there is no fire, there is also no smoke, as in the case of a great lake; this is negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*). That which possesses only positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the purely positive inference (*kevalānvayi*), such as: "A jar is nameable because it is cognizable, like a cloth. In this case, there is no negative concomitance between cognizability and nameability, because everything is both cognizable and nameable.
A *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative) inference is one whose pervasion consists solely of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), such as: "Earth is distinct from the others because it possesses odor;
whatever is not distinct from the others does not possess odor, as for example, water."
And this [earth] is not like that;

therefore, in the statement "it is not like that," there is no positive example (anvaya-dṛṣṭānta) such as "that which possesses odor is distinct from others," because the subject (pakṣa) consists of earth alone.
The logical mark (liṅga) is of three kinds: positive-and-negative (anvayavyatirekin), purely positive (kevalānvayin), and [purely negative].
And there is the purely negative [inference].
The definition of the positive-negative [inference] is by way of positive concomitance (anvaya).
And that which possesses pervasion through both positive and negative concomitance is the *anvaya-vyatirekin* (positive-negative);
for example, the possession of smoke when fire is the probandum (*sādhya*).

"Where there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen"— this is positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*). "Where there is no fire, there is also no smoke, as in a great lake"— this is negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*).
Negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti).
The *Dīpikā* analyzes the inferential mark (*liṅga*).
Regarding the term "liṅga" (the logical mark):
he defines that which possesses both positive and negative concomitance by means of the phrase "by way of positive concomitance."
The pervasion between the reason and the probandum is positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti);
the pervasion between their absences is negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti).
— *Prakāśikā*

Although the classification of inference alone was appropriate since that was what was promised to be defined, nevertheless, bearing in mind that once the threefold nature of the mark (liṅga) is demonstrated, the threefold nature of the knowledge thereof follows as a consequence, he says: "He classifies the mark."

Having kept in mind the meaning of the root text, "possessing pervasion through both positive and negative concomitance," as being: "that which possesses a pervasion graspable by the apprehension of positive concomitance, while simultaneously possessing a pervasion graspable by the apprehension of negative concomitance."
It elucidates those two types of pervasion [by stating] "of the reason and the probandum" (*hetusādhyayoḥ*). [The commentary] *Bālapriyā* [explains]: "by way of positive concomitance" (*anvayena*).
And from the root text as it stands— "and [it is] possessed of pervasion by way of negative concomitance"—

it is understood that the definition of an *anvaya-vyatirekin* (probans with both positive and negative concomitance) is: being possessed of positive pervasion while being possessed of negative pervasion.

If that were the case, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) inference, because even there, positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) exists in reality; therefore, he explains:
"to be grasped by the apprehension of positive co-occurrence" (*anvayasahacāragrahagrāhya*).

The co-occurrence of the probandum and the reason in the same locus is positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*). Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that which becomes the object of a cognition produced by the knowledge of that [concomitance];
it takes the form of the co-occurrence of the probandum—which is the pervader—with the reason, and is thus called positive pervasion (*anvaya-vyāpti*).
The co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) and the absence of the reason (*hetvabhāva*) is negative concomitance (*vyatirekasahacāra*).

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) that becomes the object of the cognition produced by the knowledge of that [concomitance] is negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*), which consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an absence that pervades the absence of the probandum.

In the expression "by way of positive concomitance" (*anvayena*), the meaning of the instrumental case is "being made known by cognition," and the word *anvaya* refers to positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*).
The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of "being cognizable by cognition" resides in pervasion;

thus, it is understood from the root text that pervasion is "cognizable by cognition through the knowledge of positive concomitance. Similarly, the word "negative" (*vyatireka*) refers to negative concomitance (*vyatirekasahacāra*).
The meaning of the third case (tṛtīyārtha) is "being made known by a cognition" (jñānajñāpyatva);
the sense is that by this, one obtains [the definition]: "non-pervasion is that which is made known by a cognition of negative concomitance" (vyatirekasahacārajñānajñāpyāvyāptiḥ).
The *Tarkasaṅgraha*:
Definition of the Kevalānvayin [Reason]. A *kevalānvayin* is that which possesses a pervasion consisting solely of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
For example: "A pot is denotable because it is cognizable, like a cloth.
Here, regarding the two properties of being cognizable and being denotable:
There is no negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti),
because everything is both knowable (prameya) and nameable (abhidheya). —
Dīpikā.
He states the definition of the purely positive (kevalānvayin) [reason] with the words "anvaya" etc.: a reason whose probandum is purely positive is a purely positive reason.
Kevalānvayi (pure positive concomitance) is the state of not being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) that possesses an occurrence [in the locus].
It is also the state of being the object of God’s cognition and the state of being denotable by all words.

"Existence everywhere" means the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). In the definition of a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) reason— characterized by having only positive concomitance (*anvaya*)— the word "only" (*mātra*) [excludes negative concomitance].
