Considering that there would be a contradiction based on whether the exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is established or not, he reformulates [the definition] in another way: "that which has a purely positive probandum" (*kevalānvayisādhyaka*).
[This refers to] a negative reason (*vyatirekihetau*) whose probandum is purely positive.

1. And likewise, the definition of an *anvaya-vyatirekin* [reason] is: being possessed of a pervasion that is the object of a cognition produced by the knowledge of positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*), while simultaneously being possessed of a pervasion that is the object of a cognition produced by the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*).
Regarding the definition: in that context, if the term "only" (*eva*) is not included, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*).

If the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is not included, there is over-extension to the purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*), according to the view that even through negative concomitance (*vyatirekasahacāra*), it is only positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*) that is apprehended.

The definition of an *anvayavyatirekin* (inference based on both positive and negative concomitance) is the possession of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that is the object of a cognition produced by both the cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra-jñāna*) and the cognition of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra-jñāna*).
[This is stated] for the sake of inclusion regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
The property of being purely positive (kevalānvayitva) has been introduced.
He explains that very point with the words "absolute absence" (atyantābhāva): the meaning is "an absolute absence whose occurrence is unconditioned" (niravacchinnavṛttimat). By this—
This includes reasons that have as their probandum (sādhya) the absence of the nature of space, the absence of conjunction, and so forth.
Since the state of being denotable by the word "pot" cannot exist in everything—because it is absent in things such as cloth—he says: "the state of being denotable by the word 'all'."
Bālapriyā: Is it not the case that,

according to the root text, "a purely positive [inference] (kevalānvayin) is that which possesses only positive concomitance," a purely positive inference is defined as having positive concomitance while being devoid of negative concomitance?
It is understood as a definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
That being the case, since the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is well-established in the case of a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*), its absence there is not possible.
With the intention that if that [subject] were unestablished, its emptiness would be even more unestablished— and thus this definition would be untenable—
it is stated in the *Dīpikā* that "that which has a purely positive probandum is purely positive. He says:
"Merely positive concomitance" (anvayamātra) means:

a reason whose probandum is exclusively positively concomitant is a purely positive reason (*kevalānvayin*), such as "this is expressible because it is knowable," which is [an example of] a purely positive [reason].

Likewise, even a negative reason (vyatirekin) whose probandum is purely positive (kevalānvayi), such as "this is expressible because it possesses the nature of a jar" (idaṃ vācyaṃ ghaṭatvāt), is itself purely positive.
And likewise, in order to include both types,

the definition of a purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason is formulated as "the state of being a reason whose probandum is purely positive," without introducing the property of being purely positive into the reason itself.
He states what was said:
"having a probandum that is purely positive" (*kevalānvayisādhyaka*). A negative reason (*vyatirekihetau*) is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

The reason is this: "that very thing" means precisely the state of being purely positive (kevalānvayitva). Now, one might object that being purely positive consists in not being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence.

If it were stated that "the state of being a reason whose probandum is that [absence]" constitutes the nature of a purely positive (kevalānvayi) mark, then there would be no inclusion of reasons such as "pot-ness" when the probandum is the absence of space (*ākāśābhāva*), because the absence of space...
Because [ether] is the counter-positive of the absolute non-existence of the absence of ether,
it lacks the property of not being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence. The same applies to the reason that establishes the absence of conjunction as the probandum.

Inclusion would not be possible for the absence of conjunction (*saṃyogābhāva*), because it is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) whose nature is conjunction; therefore,
he says "unconditioned" (*niravacchinna*), and so forth.
1. "Having the nature of space" means by way of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the absence of space;
for there is no non-existence of a non-existence.
The sense is that it is because [the absence] has the nature of its own counter-positive (*pratiyogi*).
2. It means that it is because [the absence] is the counter-positive of that absolute absence of conjunction which consists in the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) has a non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitā*), it possesses a delimited occurrence (*sāvacchinnavṛttikatva*); therefore, an absence that possesses an undelimited occurrence cannot be of the nature of conjunction, but must rather be the absence of a jar or the like. Since the state of not having that [conjunction] as its counter-positive (*tadapratiyogitva*) exists in the absence of conjunction, [the definition applies] to that.
The establishment of being purely positive (kevalānvayitva) is as follows:
however, an absence whose nature is like space (gagana) is not possessed of occurrence, because it is non-occurrent.

The meaning is this: rather, the absence of a jar or the like possesses an occurrence (vṛtti), and since the state of not being its counter-positive exists in the absence of space, it too is logically established as a purely positive (kevalānvayi) entity. And thus, that which exists everywhere—
Since its absence is nowhere to be found, it is established as being purely positive (*kevalānvayin*). But how can "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*) be purely positive?
For nameability—
The state of possessing word-potency (*padaśaktimattva*);

and since that [potency] differs according to the distinction between words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and "cloth" (*paṭa*), it follows that [the property] of being denoted by the word "jar" (*ghaṭapadābhidheyatva*)...
He raises the objection: "Because it is the counter-positive of the absolute non-existence residing in cloth and so forth"—this refers to the phrase "by the word 'jar'.
"Denotability by all words" means being denotable by that word which is "all."

"Existing everywhere" means being denotable by all words; this is a purely positive (kevalānvayin) [reason]. Thus, in the formal argument "A jar is denotable because it is knowable," being denotable by all words is the property to be proven (sādhya).
The sense is that the state of being a purely positive concomitant (kevalānvayitva) is thus established.
The *Tarkasaṅgraha*:
Definition of the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*). A purely negative inference is that which possesses a pervasion consisting solely of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Just as earth is distinguished from other things because it possesses odor;
that which is not distinguished from others does not [possess odor].
Just as water possesses fragrance, but this [earth] is not like that; therefore, it is "not like that. In this regard, that which...
There is no positive example (anvayadṛṣṭānta) for the statement "that which possesses fragrance is distinct from others," because the entire category of earth constitutes the subject (pakṣa).
— *Dīpikā*

He states the definition of that which possesses a negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*)—namely, "vyatireka..."—and illustrates it with "yathā...". Now, one might ask: is the difference from others (*itarabheda*) already established or not?
In the first case, where [the property] is well-known, if the reason is present there, it is positive concomitance (anvaya);
if it is absent, it is the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) fallacy. In the second case...
Since there is an absence of knowledge of the probandum (*sādhya*), how can there be an inference qualified by it?

For, in the absence of knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) does not arise; this is because of the absence of knowledge of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

If it is argued that even the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) would not be possible—[we reply]: no. The conjunction of the thirteen mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*) of water and the other [twelve categories], each of which is well-established in its own respective locus, is what is established in earth. In that case:

Because the probandum, which consists of the exclusion of what is delimited by the state of being thirteen, does not reside in a single locus, there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor the fallacy of the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇya*);
for [the probandum] is established in each individual locus.
[The definitions are] inference qualified by the probandum and the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*).
In the *Prakāśikā*, the root text states: "that which possesses only negative concomitance."
The meaning is that it possesses a pervasion consisting solely of an ascertained negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Consequently, in cases such as "Earth is distinct from others because it possesses odor," there is no lack of consistency with the definition, even though positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*) exists.
The difference from this is: a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "otherness than earth.
This is what is meant by "being the correlate" (anvayitva).
The meaning is that it would possess a pervasion (vyāpti) graspable by the apprehension of positive concomitance (anvaya-sahacāra).
"Asādhāraṇya" [means] because it is subject to the definition of the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) reason, which consists in its exclusion from the similar instances (sapakṣa); this is the intended sense.
Even in the case where the probandum is not previously established, he says "the probandum," etc., with the intention that there is indeed an inference qualified by the probandum.
[He refers to] "negative pervasion" (vyatirekavyāpti).
The meaning is that [the probans] consists in being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of the probandum.
It is not the difference from the generality of "other than earth" that is being proved, but rather the difference consisting of water and so forth.
It is established as follows; and thus, since there is no occasion for the aforementioned fault, he says "of water and so forth.
The meaning is that the aggregate (*kūṭa*) of the thirteen mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*) of water and the other [categories] is what is being proved.
Because it is impossible for the collection [of the whole] to be established, he says: "each individually" and "delimited by the number thirteen."

The collective meaning is as follows: since prior to the inference, the very subject (dharmin) possessing the property delimited by the ascertained delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka) is unestablished, there can be no positive concomitance (anvaya) or the "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇya) of the reason based on its presence or absence therein.
When each [member] is individually established, there can arise a cognition qualified by "collection-ness," which consists in being the object of a specific enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*);
and thus, because there exists a determinate judgment (*nirṇaya*) whose qualifier is the delimitor of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*).

He states— beginning with the words "in each locus" (*pratyekādhikaraṇa*)— that an inference which apprehends the qualified relation of that which is delimited by the property to be proven (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya-avagāhin anumiti*) and the cognition of negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāpti-jñāna*) are both possible.
Although [it might be argued that] the fourteen mutual absences (anyonyābhāva) of water and so forth are each well-established within those same fourteen [categories].

Although it would have been more appropriate to speak in that manner, [the author] nevertheless proceeds in this way in order to challenge the Prābhākara, who maintains that presumption (*arthāpatti*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Since it is necessary to demonstrate that negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is a constituent factor of inference,
the statement beginning with "the thirteen [categories] such as water" is made in order to show that negative concomitance is common to all those systems of thought.
Furthermore, it should be noted that in his view, fourteen types of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) are not established,
because he accepts that non-existence is of the nature of its locus (*adhikaraṇātmaka*).
Some, however, explain it by the analysis "those for whom water is the first among thirteen," meaning the fourteen [categories] having water as their counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
"In thirteen" refers to water and so forth,
according to the previously stated analysis of the compound.
The meaning is "in fourteen. They say that this should be understood similarly in what follows as well. [The commentator] Bālapriyā says: "But surely..."

The meaning of the term *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative inference) is that which possesses only negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*). Its definition is: being possessed of negative concomitance while being devoid of positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*). Thus, in the case of the argument: "Earth is distinct from others because it possesses odor," [this is a purely negative inference].
Since, in the case of a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), there is in reality also a positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*), [the definition] would be impossible;
therefore, he explains [it] as "where the negative concomitance is ascertained.
And thus, in the aforementioned instance, in reality...
Even though positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) exists, because the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished (due to ignorance),

there is no ascertainment of positive concomitance— defined as the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum with the pervader of the reason; however, since there is ascertainment of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), this constitutes the state of having a concomitance consisting solely of ascertained negative concomitance.
The sense is that its status as a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason is established because of [the property's] existence [in the subject].
Since the difference from anything else is well-known, there is no occasion for the dilemma of whether it is "well-known" or "not well-known"; therefore, he explains:
"A difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by being other than earth" means the difference of all things from those other than earth.
And likewise, if the difference of earth from all other things were known in some instance, such as a jar, then, since the reason (hetu) is present there,
one would apprehend the positive concomitance (anvaya-sahacāra) between the probandum and the reason in that very instance.

Since the state of possessing positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) with respect to that which is to be grasped exists, this must be a case of inference based on both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireki-anumāna*), not a purely negative one (*kevala-vyatirekin*). If the reason (*hetu*) were absent there, then, because the reason would not occur in any instance where the probandum (*sādhya*) is ascertained, [the definition of a valid reason would fail].

Since the reason would be pervaded by the definition of the fallacious reason known as the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), which consists in its exclusion from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), the reason would consequently become uncommon.
This is provided that the probandum— in the form of a difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by "otherness than earth"— is not cognized.

Due to the absence of the cognition of the qualifier that is the probandum (*sādhya*), there would be no inference in the form of the cognition of the subject (*pakṣa*) as qualified by the probandum, because the cognition of the qualifier is a necessary cause for a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*). Likewise, if the probandum were unknown, there could also be no cognition of the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), which is constituted by the absence of the probandum.

The meaning of the passage in the *Dīpikā* expressing the doubt is as follows: "Because the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogijñāna*) is the cause for the cognition of non-existence. Now, one might object:

in cases where the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), there can be no inferential cognition in the form "the subject possesses the probandum" which has the probandum as its qualifier.
One might object: "Let there be no inference [of the form 'Earth is different from others'] due to the absence of the cause consisting in the cognition of the qualifier;

however, an inference having the probandum as its qualificand, in the form 'the difference of earth from others,' ought certainly to occur. Anticipating this, he says: "Even in the case where the probandum is unestablished (*aprasiddhasādhyaka*)."
[The opponent claims: "It is only an inference qualified by the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇakānumiti*) that arises.

[The author replies: On the position that it is only an inference qualified by the probandum that arises, such an inference is not possible in the present case because of the absence of knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*).

The refutation is as follows: it must be explained that the intended inference— wherein the probandum is the qualificand— is impossible because, in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*), there is an absence of knowledge of the counter-positive, and consequently, an absence of the cause consisting in the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*).
"Jalādibhedakūṭam" means a collection of the fourteen subdivisions for each of the fourteen elements beginning with water, excluding earth.
Regarding the thirteen mutual absences (anyonyābhāva) of water and the other categories:
[it may be objected] that the distinction between the eight substances beginning with water and the six categories beginning with quality must be established in relation to earth.
And if it is argued that, since one ought to speak of "fourteen mutual absences" such as water and so forth, the mention of "thirteen" is improper—
here some [respond] that this is because the Mīmāṃsakas accept that absence is of the nature of its locus (*adhikaraṇātmatva*).

This was stated in accordance with their own doctrine, because they do not accept that there are more than six categories of existence; thus, it refers to the "mutual absence" (*anyonyābhāva*) as the thirteenth category.
This is said specifically in response to those who do accept that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
They say that this is because the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekyanumāna*) must be demonstrated; however, that is not correct.

For, according to their own view, since each of those thirteen mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*)—which are well-established in water and so forth—is of the nature of water and the rest, there is no absence of the thirteen distinctions from water and so forth in earth.
Because it is impossible to establish that [property] by means of the mark of possessing odor;
for such a thirteenfold division residing in earth, being of the nature of earth itself, does not exist in water and the other elements individually.

Because there is no established [instance], and due to the impossibility of knowing the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) by the aforementioned method— since that proof is impossible due to its non-establishment—
the phrase "of the thirteen mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*) such as water and so forth" [is used].
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those for which water is the first" are "water and so forth";
"water and so forth" refers to the thirteen [categories] beginning with water; "the mutual non-existences of those" is the full analytical explanation.
In the phrase "jalādi," this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the type where the qualities of the members do not apply to the referent (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). Therefore...
It should be explained that this is the acquisition of the fourteen mutual absences (anyonyābhāva) belonging to the fourteen [categories] beginning with water;
all of this will become clear in the *Prakāśikā* above.
In reality, however, those fourteen divisions of the fourteen elements beginning with water are not all well-known within the categories of water and so forth. For instance,
there is the division of water.
It is well known among thirteen things beginning with fire, but not in fire alone;
thus, that which is well known among these thirteen—
The combination of each one of their divisions is established on earth; that is to say,
the aggregate of fourteen divisions is established on earth, delimited by the state of being thirteen.
The meaning is that the aggregate consisting of fourteen parts, which is composed of each of those well-known individual differences, is what is to be proven in relation to the earth.
And thus, [the probandum is] the difference qualified by the state of being fourteen.
Because it is not established anywhere [as a locus], there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor the fallacy of being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*).

Since the single absence that constitutes the probandum (*sādhya*) is well-established by way of the delimitation of the thirteen [locuses], the cognition of the qualifier in the form of the probandum exists; thus, an inference qualified by the probandum is logically justified. In this same manner...

Nṛsiṃha Śāstrin states that when there is the cognition of the counter-positive consisting of the probandum (*sādhya*), the cognition of the absence of the probandum is possible; thus, the cognition of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is also easily obtained.
[The phrase] "where the delimiting property of the probandum is ascertained" [is used].

The meaning is as follows: the delimiters of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka) are either thirteen-ness or fourteen-ness; the differences delimited by those [numbers] belong to that which possesses them. Regarding the phrase "in each case being well-known": [it means that these are established individually].

Since the distinctions among water and so forth are well-known, there arises the cognition of that which consists in being the object of a particular enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), namely the state of being fourteen;
by means of that, [there arises a cognition] having as its qualifier that which is the delimitor of the qualifier-ness (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*), characterized by the mode of being fourteen.
The determination arises in the form "these differences are fourteen"; from that,
the inferential cognition (anumiti) characterized by the apprehension of a qualified entity— namely, "the earth possesses fourteen differences"— is easily obtained.

The point is that the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)— namely, "the possession of odor is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of any particularity qualified by being one of fourteen"— is easily obtained.
However, in reality...
In the case of purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekyanumāna*), the resulting inferential cognition has the probandum as its predicate;
therefore, there is no defect even if the probandum was previously unestablished.

Thus, the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)— in its form as the non-existence of a distinction from other earths— does not enter into the composition of the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*),
such that there would be a lack of knowledge of the negative concomitance due to the non-establishment of the absence because of the non-establishment of its counter-positive (*pratiyogi*).
[Otherwise] there would be an impossibility;
rather, the subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) is simply this: "Earth possesses odor, which is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the state of being other than earth."
Therefore, they say that the effort undertaken in the *Dīpikā* is fruitless;
this is clear from the *Pakṣatā* section of the *Dīdhiti* and other works.
The Compendium of Reasoning (Tarkasaṅgraha): The definition of the subject (pakṣa). The subject is that which possesses the probandum (sādhya) as something doubted.
For example, when "possessing smoke" is the reason, [the subject is] the mountain.
The subject (*pakṣa*) is that which possesses the probandum (*sādhya*) in a state of doubt;
for example, a mountain when "possessing smoke" is the reason (*hetu*).
— *Dīpikā*
He states the definition of a thesis (*pakṣa*) as "doubtful," etc.
[Objection: But is there not a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of reflection (*manana*), which occurs immediately after hearing (*śravaṇa*)? In that case...
Because there is an absence of doubt due to the certainty regarding the self derived from Vedic statements.
Furthermore, if it is argued that there is an over-extension (avyāpti) in cases where, even when fire is perceived, an inference occurs by choice— that is not so.
Because the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*) consists in being the locus of the stated property of being a subject;
as it says in the *Mūla*: "that which possesses the probandum (*sādhya*) as something doubted."
The meaning is: "qualified by a doubt whose qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) is related [to the subject] through the relation of being the object of the predicate (*sādhyaprakāraka*).
The definition of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and so forth should also be understood in this way.
It must be refined.
[The author] raises the objection that the definition of a *pakṣa* (the subject) is too narrow—stating "nanu" (but surely) in the *Dīpikā*.
Having stated the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of verbal cognition that dispels doubt, he states it in the case of perception as well:
"What does it mean? [It means] "it has been stated.
The meaning is that the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*) consists in being the locus of the absence of proof (*siddhi*) qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*).
"By way of the relation of being the qualificand," as in:
"Is the mountain fiery or not?"
In a doubt of this form, "Is there fire? fire is the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the mountain is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
For this very reason, in cases where the probandum is already well-known, the resulting inference is experienced as having the subject (*pakṣa*) as its qualificand.
Regarding the *pakṣatā* (the state of being the subject), there is the following passage from the *Dīdhiti*:

"In this context, since it is stated that in cases where the probandum (*sādhya*) is well-known, the inference has the subject (*pakṣa*) as its primary qualificand, [it follows that] in cases where the probandum is not well-known..."

It is indicated that the inference has the probandum as its qualificand (*sādhyaviśeṣyikānumiti*). In this regard, Gadādhara’s commentary states: "However, in cases where the probandum is unestablished (*aprasiddhasādhya*), due to the absence of the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) and so forth..."

It should be understood that it has been stated [by others] that, because an inference having the property to be proven (*sādhya*) as its qualifier is untenable, an inference having the property to be proven as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) is accepted;
and that such a doubt, which has the property to be proven as its mode (*prakāra*), exists in the mountain by way of the relation of qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*).

The mountain possesses the status of being the subject (*pakṣatā*) because such a doubt exists with respect to fire through the relation of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*). To exclude fire from having the status of the subject, it is stated that [the doubt must exist] through the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*).
The definition of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and so forth should also be refined in this manner:
the similar instance is that which is qualified by a certainty (*nirṇaya*) having the probandum (*sādhya*) as its qualifier, through the relation of qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*).

The counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is that which is qualified by a certainty (*nirṇaya*) whose qualifier is the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), related through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*). This is the method [of definition].
The meaning is that it must be refined.
Regarding the phrase "dispelling doubt": it refers to that which acts as an obstacle to the doubt as to whether the self is distinct from the body, the senses, and so forth.

The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by the Vedic statement would have the form "the Self is distinct from the body, senses, and so forth. In that case, following such hearing (*śravaṇa*) consisting of that verbal cognition, there could not occur reflection (*manana*) in the form of an inference (*anumiti*) having the content "the Self is distinct from the body, senses, and so forth."

The meaning is that, for oneself, there is an absence of "pakṣatva" (the state of being a subject of inquiry), which consists in possessing a doubt whose qualificandum is the self and whose qualifier is the probandum, by virtue of the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā-saṃbandha*).
— *Tarkasaṅgraha*.
The definition of the similar instance (sapakṣa): A similar instance is that which possesses the property to be proven (sādhya) as something ascertained;
for example, in that very same case, the kitchen.
The similar instance (sapakṣa) is that which possesses the probandum ascertained; for example, in that very same case, the kitchen.
The definition of the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa):
The *vipakṣa* (the dissimilar instance) is that which definitely possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*);
for example, in that same context, a great lake.
The dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is that which definitely possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*),
such as the great lake in that very same case.
[This concludes] the examination of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

AnTs_52: The five fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are the erratic (savyabhicāra), the contradictory (viruddha), the one whose locus is doubtful (satpakṣa), the unestablished (asiddha), and the sublated (bādhita).
The five fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) are: the erratic (savyabhicāra), the contradictory (viruddha), the counter-balanced (satpratipakṣa), the unestablished (asiddha), and the sublated (bādhita).
— *Dīpikā*
He states the definition of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)—
namely, "ascertained"—
and he states the definition of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
"Certainty" (niścita):
having thus examined the valid reasons (*saddhetu*), he analyzes the fallacious reasons (*asaddhetu*) by classifying them as "inconclusive" (*savyabhicāra*).
The definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is being the object of a true cognition that obstructs inference. Having thus defined valid reasons, the *Prakāśikā* states:
The meaning is: "having examined the reasons characterized by pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth.

The intention is that the examination of fallacious reasons (*asaddhetu*) follows by way of *prasaṅga-saṅgati* (the connection of incidental relevance), since one remembers the fallacious reasons while examining the valid reasons (*saddhetu*). [End of] the root text.
Regarding "fallacious reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*):
they are called *hetvābhāsa* because they appear like valid reasons (*hetuvat ābhāsante*). The meaning is that defective reasons are being examined. Now, one might object: [is this not so?]

Desiring to dispel the objection that the classification [of fallacies] as "savyabhicāra" and so forth is improper because the desire to know specific details does not arise without a prior cognition of the general property (*sāmānyadharma*),

[the author notes that] once the definition of a *doṣa* (fallacy) has been stated, the acquisition of the definition of a "defective" (*duṣṭa*)— consisting in the possession of such a *doṣa*— is extremely clear.
With the intention that "it exists," he states the general definition of a fallacy: "anumiti" and "hetvābhāsatvam.
"Hetvābhāsāḥ" means the semblances of reasons; they are the defects residing in the reason (*hetu*).
The state of those [properties] is their "tattva" (reality); this is the meaning.
With respect to an inference such as "the lake possesses fire," the certain cognition of a sublation—such as "the lake is devoid of fire"—is an obstacle.

The property of being the object of such a certainty whose nature is valid cognition (pramā) is unimpaired in cases such as a lake possessing the absence of fire; thus, the definition is fully applicable.
Here, the word "inference" (*anumiti*) is used in a non-exclusive metaphorical sense (*ajahallakṣaṇā*).
This refers to either the inference or its instrument.

Therefore, since the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth is accounted for solely by its being an obstacle to the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection), it does not constitute an obstacle to the inference itself.
There is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of fallacies such as the inconclusive (vyabhicāra),
because the erroneous sublation-cognition (bādhabhrama), "The mountain is without fire," acts as an impediment to the inferential cognition, "The mountain possesses fire."
There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the absence of fire and so forth in that same object; therefore, it says "as it truly is" (*yathārtha*).
This means "not different from error" (*bhramābhinna*).
Now, even if this were the case...
If it is argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the absence of fire (*vahnayabhāva*), which is a part of the sublation (*bādha*) consisting of the lake devoid of fire—
since the property of being the object of a cognition whose content is contrary to reality, namely "the lake possesses the absence of fire," exists therein— the answer is no.

This is not a flaw, because the meaning culminates in the following: "The state of being a defect consists in being delimited by that property which delimits the object of a cognition in general that acts as an obstacle to inference."

Although the cognition ‘the lake possesses the absence of fire’— which has as its object that which is delimited by the property of being the absence of fire— is an impediment to inference, the cognition in the form ‘absence of fire,’ which is included within the general class of such cognitions, is not an impediment; therefore, [the property of] being the absence of fire, etc.,...
Because it is impossible to include [such cases] by means of the term "of that form" (*yadrūpa*).

Nor, then, is the term "as the object exists" (*yathārtha*) redundant; for there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the absence of fire and so forth even in the case of an error such as "the mountain is fireless."
It should not be said that [the definition] is excluded by the very manner already stated;
for the word "knowledge" (jñāna) serves to indicate the intended meaning of a specific type of knowledge, thereby making the word "as it is" (yathārtha) purposeful. And thus:

The final meaning is this: *doṣatva* (the nature of being a fallacy) consists in being delimited by that specific form (*rūpa*) such that the general class of non-exceptional, non-invalidating cognitions (*niścaya*)— which have as their object what is delimited by that form and which are not overridden by a cognition of invalidity— is an obstacle to the inference under consideration (*prakṛtānumiti*).
Therefore, even though a non-spontaneous (āhārya) doubt regarding a lake possessing the absence of fire— which is characterized by the cognition of invalidity— is not an obstacle to inference,
there is no impossibility [in our position]; enough with this prolixity.
Others, however, say: "This is indeed the definition of fallacious [reasons];
but [it applies] to those whose deviation (vyabhicāra) and so forth are known."
Having accepted the status of being an obstructer;

its meaning, however, is that those [fallacies] such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*) which are obstructers of inference, [are so] by virtue of the relation of "possessing the delimitor of the reasonhood of the subject under discussion, which is the object of a single cognition."
It is the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) of a true cognition possessing that specific mode.
In cases such as "smoke-possessing [locus] because of fire," the fire qualified by subsisting in what lacks smoke is the *vyabhicāra* (inconstancy).

By the aforementioned relation, there exists the state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) of a true cognition in the form "the fire possesses that" (*tadvān vahnih*); thus, the definition is consistent.
Since the term "inference" (*anumiti*) refers here to the inference under discussion, [the definition applies] to a valid reason (*saddhetu*).

There is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because [the definition] does not apply to errors such as *vyabhicāra* (inconstancy), which serve as obstacles to inference, since these are unestablished (*aprasiddha*).

If the term "corresponding to reality" (*yathārtha*) were not included, there would be over-extension, because even in the case of a valid reason (*saddhetu*), the property of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) of an erroneous cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is *vyabhicāra*— by way of the aforementioned relation— is present.
They say that the inclusion of the word "syāt" (might be) is for the purpose of [indicating] reasons qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth. This is the *Bālapriyā* commentary.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is included.
Thus, the meaning is that the definition of a valid reason (*saddhetu*) is the state of being a reason qualified by both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of being a feature of the subject.
They "appear like reasons" (*hetuvadābhāsante*).

The meaning is: those which are the objects of an error (bhrama) whose mode (prakāra) is "being a reason" (hetutva). And "being a reason" consists in being qualified by both pervasion (vyāpti) and subsistence-in-the-subject (pakṣadharmatā). Thus, the state of being a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsatva) is the state of being the object of an error whose mode is "being qualified by pervasion and subsistence-in-the-subject."
The meaning is that this [invalidity] occurs only in the case of fallacious reasons (*duṣṭahetu*), because valid reasons (*saddhetu*) are the objects of such valid cognition;
thus, the term *hetvābhāsa* refers to fallacious reasons.
Regarding the phrase "endowment with the definition" (*lakṣaṇasamanvaya*):
likewise, in the case of "the lake possesses fire because of smoke," the defect (*doṣa*) consisting of sublation (*bādha*) is that which has the nature of a lake possessing the absence of fire.

And such possession of a defect in the reason—smoke—exists by virtue of the relation of "possessing the delimitor of the nature of the subject-reason which is the object of a single cognition"; thus, there is "defectiveness.

This is because both the sublation (*bādha*) regarding the lake devoid of fire and the property of smokeness (*dhūmatva*) reside in the single cognition: "'The lake devoid of fire' and 'the property of smokeness'."
The phrase "because it is an object" (*viṣayatvāt*) and so forth should be inferred accordingly.

Now, if the definition of a defect (*doṣa*) is "being the object of a true cognition that obstructs an inference," then this definition would apply only to sublation (*bādha*) and the counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*).

Regarding the cognition of the presence of that [property] (*tadvattābuddhi*), there are the ascertainment of sublation (*bādhaniścaya*)— in the form "the lake possesses the absence of fire"— and the ascertainment of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣaniścaya*)— in the form "the lake possesses moss which is pervaded by the absence of fire."

This is because [the cognition] acts as an inhibitor by way of being a certainty regarding the possession of that absence, and by way of being a certainty regarding the possession of that which is pervaded by that absence; thus,
the definition consisting in "having that as its object" is present.
This definition does not apply to cases such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*), contradiction (*virodha*), and lack of essential property (*svarūpāsiddhi*),
because the cognitions of these do not constitute obstacles to inference;
rather, it is only the cognition of deviation and so forth that constitutes an obstacle to the *parāmarśa*, which is the instrument of inference.
Because [the definition] would over-apply to real entities (*sattva*), he says: "In this context, the term is 'inferential cognition' (*anumiti*).

And thus, the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is: being the object of a true cognition that constitutes an obstacle to either the inferential cognition itself or its instrument (the logical mark).
"By way of being an obstacle to the *parāmarśa* [inferential cognition] itself.
That is, the knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is an obstacle to the aspect of the manifestation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) within the *parāmarśa*.
The cognition of contradiction is an obstacle to the manifestation of the aspect of co-occurrence with the probandum;
so too is the cognition of the lack of essential property (svarūpāsiddhi).

The meaning is that there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti), because for everyone, the manifestation of the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) acts as an obstacle; thus, the obstacle to the inferential instrument—the reflective cognition (parāmarśa)—is present.
This is because [the definition] is successfully established (nirvāhāt).
The meaning is "because of the occurrence of the defining characteristics.
He states the purpose of the word *yathārtha* (as it truly is) as follows: "the mountain is without fire."

And likewise, since a misconception in the form "the mountain possesses the absence of fire" prevents the inference "the mountain possesses fire" when non-corresponding (yathārtha) terms are not employed,
such a misconception has as its object the absence of fire.
It would constitute a defect. To prevent that, the term "as it is" (yathārtha) is used [to exclude] the aforementioned error.
The intention is that there is no over-extension because of the absence of correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*). [Objection:
Even if the term "corresponding to reality" (*yathārtha*) is included, it is impossible to exclude the erroneous cognition "the mountain possesses the absence of fire."

Since that [cognition] also possesses truthfulness— because it is characterized by "having a qualifier in a locus possessing that [qualifier]" (e.g., having the qualifier *parvatatva* in a locus possessing *parvatatva*) and "having a qualifier in a locus possessing that [qualifier]" (e.g.,

having the qualifier *vahnayabhāvatva* in a locus possessing *vahnayabhāvatva*), it falls under the definition of truth as "having a qualifier in a locus possessing that [qualifier]"; therefore, he says:
The meaning is "distinct from error.

Thus, the term *yathārtha* (corresponding to reality), which is a constituent of the definition under discussion, signifies that which is distinct from [a cognition] having a particular qualifier in that which lacks that qualifier.

The cognition "the mountain possesses the absence of fire," however, is erroneous because it takes "absence of fire" as its qualifier with respect to that which lacks the absence of fire (i.e., the presence of fire);
since it is not different from that [erroneous cognition], there is no fault— this is the sense.
The state of being free from error is said to be the nature of valid cognition (*pramātva*) in all its aspects;
and that [nature] consists in whatever [cognition] is delimited by a qualifier residing in a locus other than itself (*svavyadhikaraṇaprakārāvacchinna*).
The state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) consists in not being the determiner (*anirūpaka*) of this or that [property].
1. Regarding the term *svavyadhikaraṇa*:
the meaning of *svavyadhikaraṇa* is "not occurring in its own locus" (*svādhikaraṇāvṛtti*).

In the erroneous cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl, when the subjectness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the mother-of-pearl is denoted by its own term (*svapada*), [it is as follows]: the locus of that [subjectness] is the mother-of-pearl;
the qualifier (*prakāra*) which does not reside therein is "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*); and the subjectness that is delimited by that [qualifier]—[is what is meant].

The application of the definition is as follows: the qualificand-ness residing in the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) is that which is defined by it (*tannirūpakatva*); this is present in the error "this is silver.
In the valid cognition (*pramā*) "this is silver," there is the absence of being so defined.
[This is established] through the relation consisting of both: (1) not being defined by itself (*svānirūpitatva*), and (2) subsisting in that which lacks its own locus (*svāśrayābhāvavadvṛttitva*).
That is to say, it is the state of not being the determiner (*anirūpaka*) of that which is the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) as qualified by the mode-ness (*prakāratā*).
For more detail, see the original texts.
He raises an objection:

"Now, even thus" means: even when the term "yathārtha" (corresponding to reality) is included as something distinct from error. In the case of [the inference] "The lake possesses fire because of smoke," there is the certainty "The lake possesses the absence of fire."

The meaning is as follows: because it acts as an obstacle [to inference], the property of being its object exists in the absence of fire (*vahnayabhāva*) just as it does in the place [e.g., a lake] possessing that absence of fire;

thus, there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)—which consists in being the object of a true cognition that obstructs inference—to the absence of fire, which is not itself a sublation (*bādha*).
He explains: "delimited by whatever form" (*yadrūpāvacchinna*).

Thus, when the property of being the absence of fire (*vahnayabhāvatva*) is taken as the term "whatever form," then [the cognition] having that delimited as its object is "[the cognition] that possesses the absence of fire."
Even though the cognition "this is a lake" acts as an obstacle to inference,
it is included within the general class of cognitions whose object is delimited by the property of being the absence of fire, such as the cognition "absence of fire."
A cognition of the form "the lake possesses fire" does not possess the capacity to obstruct an inference of the form "the lake is fireless"; therefore,
the property of being a lake that possesses the absence of fire (*vahnyabhāvavaddhradatva*) alone must be taken as the term *yadrūpa*.
The meaning is that since any cognition whatsoever whose object is delimited by that [absence] acts as an obstacle to inference,
and since being delimited by that form exists only in "the lake possessing the absence of fire" and not in "the absence of fire" itself,
there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
"And not then" means:

for the term "corresponding to reality" (*yathārtha*) has been employed in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the absence of fire, which is the object of the erroneous cognition "the mountain possesses the absence of fire."
However, in the context of the *nirukta-pariṣkāra*, it is not possible to take "absence of fire" (*vanhyabhāvatva*) as the defining property (*rūpa*) by means of the word;
for this reason, the cognition "absence of fire"— which is included within the general class of cognitions whose objects are delimited by that [property]— is [excluded].

Because there is an absence of being a sublater (*pratibandhakatva*) of the inferential cognition "the mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vanhimān*), and thus, since over-extension (*ativyāpti*) does not occur in the case of the absence of fire, the term "consistent with reality" (*yathārtha*) is redundant; this is the intended meaning. [The phrase] "as that which grasps the purport of the specific cognition" means...
Now, by the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*), what is meant here is a cognition that is non-derivative—that is, not sublated by a cognition of invalidity—and which is of the nature of a certainty.
[Note: Regarding the phrase *svanirūpitatva*: [This refers to] the state of being defined by itself.

In the error "this is my own silver," the property of being a qualifier (prakāratā) residing in silverhood exists within the property of being a qualificand (viśeṣyatā) residing in the mother-of-pearl, as defined by that [silverhood].
Thus, one's own...

The property of being silver (rajatatva) resides as the qualifier (prakāratā), its locus is silverness, and its occurrence in the locus of the absence of that [silverness]— namely, the shell— is present in the qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā).
Such a state of being the determiner of such a qualificandumness exists in error, whereas the state of not being its determiner [exists in valid cognition].
The connection [of the term] "in valid cognition" (pramāyām) should be understood as follows:
the intention is that the word "as it is" (yathārtha) is used to indicate what is intended to be expressed (vivakṣita).
Incorrigibility (*anāhāryatva*) consists in the absence of being produced by a desire existing at the time of sublation.
If that [incorrigibility] were not included [in the definition], then in the case of "the lake possesses fire," [the cognition would be considered a valid inference].

Thus, at the time of the subverting cognition, even the cognition "the lake possesses the absence of fire," which arises by the desire "let there be the cognition of the absence of fire in the lake," is included within the general class of cognitions whose object is delimited by being a lake possessing the absence of fire; therefore, of that [cognition]...
Furthermore, since there is an absence of being a sublater of inferential cognition (*anumiti-pratibandhakatva*) in the case of sublation (*bādha*), there would be an over-extension (*avyāpti*);
to exclude that, the property of being non-artificial (*anāhāryatva*) must be introduced into the definition of the obstructing cognition. Thus...

"Unassailed by the cognition of invalidity" means being qualified by the absence of the cognition of invalidity through the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). If that [qualification] were not included, then in the case where "the lake possesses the absence of fire," [the following would occur].

Thus, immediately after a cognition, there arises the cognition "this cognition is invalid"; since the cognition of sublation (*bādhajñāna*) does not act as an obstacle to inference in that case, there would be an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) regarding sublation.
Therefore, that [definition] must be included.

Thus, if the requirement of being of the nature of certainty (*niścayātmakatva*) were not included, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*), because a doubt (*saṃśaya*) such as "Is this lake fiery or not?"—which is included within the general category of cognition (*jñāna*)—would not function as an inhibitor [of inferential knowledge].
Therefore, that [requirement] must be included. And so:

The final definition of a fallacy (hetudoṣa) is this: it is the state of being delimited by that property (dharma) which, when its object is determined by a general certainty that is non-artificial (anāhārya), not infected by the cognition of invalidity (aprāmāṇyajñānānāskandita), and constitutes an obstacle to the inference in question.
"But others," and so forth.
In the previous [view], "yathārthajñāna" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "a cognition that is consistent with reality," which serves as an obstacle to inference.
In this context, the compound *anumitipratibandhakānāṃ yathārthajñānam* is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound) meaning "the true cognition of those things which obstruct inference.
For example, in the case of the [inferential] cognition "The lake possesses fire because of smoke," [the obstruction is the cognition] "The lake possesses fire..."
Thus, sublation (*bādha*), which consists of a lake possessing the absence of fire, is an obstacle to inference;

it is a true cognition having that [absence] as its qualifier, by virtue of the relation of "possessing the delimiting property of the reason under consideration, which is the object of a single cognition."
In the case of the cognition ‘dhūmaḥ (smoke) has a lake possessing the absence of fire,’ that which constitutes its being the qualificandum exists in the smoke; thus, the smoke is defective.
This is not the case in the instance: ‘The mountain possesses smoke because of fire.’

In the case of an erratic reason (*vyabhicārin*), the erraticity (*vyabhicāra*)— which consists of fire qualified by its subsistence in that which lacks smoke— is an obstacle to inference; the true knowledge having that [erraticity] as its object is a true cognition characterized by that mode, and fire possesses such erraticity through the aforementioned relation.
It has such a form;

since that state of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatva) exists in the fire, the definition is consistent. Now, an objection: is there not over-extension (ativyāpti) in the case of "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke"?
By the term "inference" (*anumiti*),
having taken the inference "the mountain possesses smoke," that which obstructs it is the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), consisting of fire qualified by its subsistence in what lacks smoke.

Because the property of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*)— of that true cognition which has as its qualifier [the property] "possessing such fire" (in the form "smoke possesses such fire"), by way of the relation "being the delimiting condition of the cause under discussion which is the object of a single cognition"—
exists in smoke, [the author] says: [the purpose of] the word "inference" (*anumiti*).
"By way of being intent upon the inference under discussion" means:

by way of being intent upon an inference whose subject is delimited by the delimiting factor of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka) currently under discussion, and whose predicate is delimited by the delimiting factor of the probandumhood (sādhyatāvacchedaka) currently under discussion.
And thus, the inference "The mountain possesses fire" alone is what is to be accepted.
The sense is that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the defect that would obstruct that [definition] is not established.

"By the aforementioned relation" means by the relation of possessing the nature of being the subject-locus of the reason (*prakṛtahetu*) as delimited by its own determinant (*avacchedaka*), which is the object of a single cognition.
The Compendium of Reasoning (Tarkasaṃgraha):
Definition of the Inconclusive (Savyabhicāra). Tarkasaṃgraha 53: The inconclusive (savyabhicāra) is that which is non-concomitant (anaikāntika).
It is of three kinds,
distinguished as common (*sādhāraṇa*), uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), and inconclusive (*anupasaṃhārī*).
Among these, the common inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) is that which occurs in a locus where the probandum is absent.
For example, in the argument "the mountain possesses fire because it is knowable," the property of knowability exists in a lake, which lacks fire.
An uncommon [reason] is one that is excluded from all similar instances (sapakṣa) and dissimilar instances (vipakṣa);
for example, "sound is eternal because it is sound-ness."
The property of being sound (*śabdatva*) is excluded from all eternal things and from ultimate particulars (*antyabhāva*), and it subsists only in sound.
A reason that lacks both positive and negative concomitance and examples is "inconclusive" (*anupasaṃhārī*), such as: "Everything is impermanent, because it is knowable."
In this case, since everything is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The deviant reason (*savyabhicāra*) is the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

It is of three kinds, distinguished as common (*sādhāraṇa*), uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), and non-conclusive (*anupasaṃhārī*). Among these, that which occurs in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*) is the common [inconclusive].
It is common [to both the similar and dissimilar instances]. For example: "The mountain possesses fire because it is knowable.
Here, [the reason] "knowability" [is common].
Because it exists in a lake which lacks fire (i.e., lacks the probandum),
the [reason] that is excluded from all similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).
For example: "Sound is eternal because it possesses the nature of sound. Here, the nature of sound is excluded from all eternal and non-eternal things and subsists in sound alone.
The "non-conclusive" (anupasaṃhārī) [fallacy] is that which lacks both positive and negative examples;
for example: "Everything is impermanent, because it is knowable."
In this case, because everything is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*);
[the term] *dīpikā* indicates the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*savyabhicāra*).
He analyzes it by stating, "It is of three kinds.
He defines the common [type] with the words, "In that case..."
He provides an illustration with "yathā" (for example).
He defines the uncommon [reason] with "sarva" (all).
He states the definition of the non-conclusive (*anupasaṃhārī*) reason: "Anvaya... [as follows]. (Prakāśikā)
"It is of three kinds" means that its general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)— namely, being any one of the common [factors] and so forth— is clear. Regarding "therein" in the root text:

The meaning is "in the middle of the common [reason] and so forth. "Residing in that which possesses the absence of the probandum" means: possessing a substratum-ness (ādheyatā) delimited by a relation that delimits the state of being a reason (hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha), as determined by an absence whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by a relation that delimits the state of being the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka-dharma).

Therefore, in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," although the absence of the respective probandum (sādhya) and the absence of the probandum in general— delimited by other relations— exist in the locus of the reason (hetumat), such as the mountain, [the definition does not fail] because [the reason, smoke,] exists in the parts of the smoke by means of inherence (samavāya) and so forth in that which possesses the absence of the probandum.
Furthermore, even though smoke and the like do occur [in such places], there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

And here, if one does not include the qualification of being "delimited by a specific relation" (*sambandhaviśeṣāvacchinnatva*) regarding the state of possessing the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavattā*), then in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," [the definition would fail].
There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the absence of fire and so forth exists on a mountain and other such loci by way of the relation of temporal connection (*kālika-sambandha*).
If, however, one introduces the qualification of being delimited by a specific spatial qualifier-ship (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā-viśeṣa*),

then in the case of a fallacious reason (*vyabhicārin*) where the probandum is the absence of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva-abhāva*), the absence of the probandum— namely "pot-ness" and the like— [would not be included].
There is non-pervasion (avyāpti) because the locus of the qualifier—the locus of the qualification—is unestablished.

Therefore, for the apprehension of the locus as possessing the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of the relation that delimits its probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*), the certainty of the absence of the probandum by way of some other relation is the sublator (*pratibandhaka*). Consequently, it is the state of possessing the absence of the probandum by way of that [other] relation [which constitutes the counter-positive].
This is what is intended to be said:
when fire and the like are the probandum (*sādhya*), such a relation is spatial non-delimitation (*daiśikāviśeṣaṇatā*);
and when the absence of potness and the like are the probandum, it is inherence (*samavāya*). Thus, there is no fault.

In such cases as "this [tree] is conjoined with a monkey because it is this kind of tree," that kind of relation is *niravacchinnadeśika-viśeṣaṇatā* (unconditioned spatial qualification); such is the direction of the argument.
Nor should it be mistakenly thought that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of contradictory [properties],
because of the principle that "even when the substrata (*upadheya*) are mixed, the defining attributes (*upādhi*) remain unmixed. This is its [the definition's] nature.
Even in the case of a contradictory commonality (*viruddhasādhāraṇya*), there is no deficiency;

for the root [text] states "excluded from all similar instances" (*sarvasapakṣavyāvṛtta*), which means possessing the general absence of occurrence in similar instances (*sapakṣavṛttitvasāmānyābhāvavat*).

The term "all" (*sarva*) indicates the inclusion of the absence of the general property of occurring in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*); this is the function of the term "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*).

The masters of the tradition maintain that [the definition] "meaningful because it possesses a determined object similar to the probandum" is intended; for even in the case of a valid reason such as "being a word" which proves the impermanence of sound, the status of being "uniquely inconclusive" (asādhāraṇya) is accepted when there is a state of doubt regarding the probandum in the subject (pakṣa).
The moderns,

however, [hold that] even in the case of a valid reason (*saddhetu*), there is "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*) during the state of doubt regarding the probandum in the subject (*pakṣa*), and there is a "counter-balanced opposition" (*satpratipakṣa*) during the state of a conflicting consideration (*viruddhaparāmarśa*) at the time of the relevant inferential cognition (*prakṛtaparāmarśa*).
For if [the cognition] were accepted as valid, it would follow that even the sublation itself must be accepted during a state of delusive sublation;
indeed, we see no reason for such a distinction.

Thus, they say that here the term "sapakṣa" (similar instance) refers exclusively to that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*); since only a reason that does not occur in that which possesses the probandum— such as "sound is eternal because it is sound-ness"— is the object of the definition, there is no fault whatsoever.
Regarding the term "anvaya":

being devoid of positive and negative examples (*anvayavyatirekadṛṣṭānta*) consists in having as its probandum (*sādhya*) something that is not the object of a certain cognition (*niścaya*) whose qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is some particular [property].
It is the state of having an absence of the probandum (sādhya) that is not the object of a certain cognition whose qualificandum is something specific.

However, according to the modern view, non-conclusiveness (anupasamhāritva) consists precisely in having as its nature a probandum and so forth qualified by the state of not being the counter-positive of an absolute absence (atyantābhāva).

The definition of generality (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) is the state of being an obstacle to the knowledge of the negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) of that [knowledge]. Bālapriyā: [This is] the general definition.
"Tviti" means "as for the general definition of the *savyabhicāra* (the erratic).
"Sādhyatāvacchedakasambandhetyādi" [refers to] the counter-correlativity residing in the probandum (*sādhya*).

If the property of being delimited by the delimiting factor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakadharma*) were not included [in the definition], then in the case of "The mountain possesses fire, because of smoke," even smoke would incur the status of a common fallacious reason (*sādhāraṇahetvābhāsa*). To explain: the probandum is fire; the absence (*abhāva*) that has its counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) residing in that [fire] is as follows:

Even the absence of fire belonging to the kitchen (mahānasīyavanhayabhāva) exists in that [locus], namely the mountain; for the property of being a subsistent (vṛttitva) as determined by that [absence] exists in smoke.
Thus, [the definition applies] because the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by the property that delimits the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedakadharma).
However, in the case of the kitchen, the absence of kitchen-fire cannot be apprehended;

for although that absence has a counter-positivity delimited by both "kitchen-ness" and "fire-ness," it lacks a counter-positivity delimited by "fire-ness" alone. Rather, [it is the absence of fire in general that is apprehended].
The absence of fire as established by the cognition "there is no fire" is precisely the general absence of fire (vanhisāmānyābhāva),

which has fireness (vanhitva) as its delimiting property of the counter-correlate (pratiyogitāvacchedaka). A lake or similar locus possesses that [absence], and since the relation of being located-in (ādheyatva) as determined by that [absence] does not exist in smoke, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).

Thus, if the property of being delimited by the delimiting relation of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha) were not included within the counterpositiveness residing in the probandum, then in the very case of "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke," [there would be a fallacy] regarding that which is established by the cognition "Fire does not exist [on the mountain] by way of inherence" (samavāyena).

Since even the absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by "fireness" (vanhitva) and whose relation is delimited by inherence (samavāya) is included within the definition, the mountain (parvata), which possesses that [absence], is also [a locus of the absence] there, because fire is absent by way of inherence even though fire exists there by way of conjunction (saṃyoga).
Furthermore, because the property of being located on a mountain (parvatavṛttitva) exists in smoke, there is over-extension (ativyāpti).
However, if the qualification of "being delimited by the relation that delimits the probandum-ness" (sādhyatāvacchedakasambandhāvacchinnatva) is introduced [into the definition], then...

Since only the absence of fire as delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is what is to be apprehended, the lake and so forth—which possess that [absence]—do not have the "locusness" (*ādheyatva*) restricted by it in the smoke; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Regarding locusness...

If the qualification of being delimited by the relation that delimits the state of being a cause (*hetutāvacchedakasambandha*) were not introduced, then even a part of smoke— which possesses the absence of fire delimited by the relation of conjunction— would [falsely] possess the state of being located (*ādheyatva*) as determined by that [absence], and thus there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

However, in that case (the house), although there exists in the smoke the property of being located (*ādheyatva*) as delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) as determined by the parts of smoke,
there does not exist the property of being located as delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*); thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the locus of the probans (*hetumat*).
Regarding the phrase "on a mountain, etc.":
this is stated to indicate that the reason indeed possesses the property of being located (ādheyatva) as determined by that which lacks the probandum (sādhyābhāvavat).
"Of that respective absence of the probandum" means "of the absence of the mountain-fire and so forth.
"Of the general absence of the probandum as delimited by another relation" [is the meaning].

The meaning is: [the absence] of fireness delimited by a counter-correlativity restricted by the relation of inherence (samavāya), which is distinct from the relation of conjunction (saṃyoga) that delimits the state of being the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka).
And in that regard, [the phrase] "in the state of possessing the absence of the probandum" and so forth [is used].
If, in the possession of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavattā*),

the qualification of being delimited by a specific relation is not introduced, then [there would be the problem of] the absence whose counter-positivehood is delimited by the property of fireness (*vanhitva*) and delimited by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Since even a mountain (*parvata*) is a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) by virtue of a temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*), the property of being a substratum (*ādheyatva*) as determined by that [relation] exists in smoke; thus, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a valid reason (*saddhetu*). [The definition must therefore be:

the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) as determined by a substratum-ness (*ādheyatā*) that is delimited by the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) and resides in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).

And if one intends to define it as "the state of possessing the absence of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvavattva*), although the locus of the absence of fire (*vahnyabhāva*) by way of its own nature (*svarūpasambandha*) is not the mountain (*parvata*),
but rather the lake (*hrada*) and so forth;

Although over-extension (*ativyāpti*) can be avoided by [defining the definition as] "the state of being a locus (*ādheyatva*) as determined by that [the probandum] does not exist in the smoke," nevertheless,
there remains over-extension in the case of the fallacious inference: "The cloth possesses the absence of potness, because it is a substance."

For instance: since "substance-ness" (dravyatva) exists in a jar— which possesses "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva), which is the absence of the absence of "jar-ness," and which is the locus of the absence of the probandum—
this reason is a common inconclusive (sādhāraṇa-vyabhicārī) one.

In this case, the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)—namely, the absence of the absence of potness, which is identical to potness itself—has no locus (*adhikaraṇa*) established by way of the relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*), because positive entities do not subsist anywhere by way of the relation of identity. Thus, there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*). Therefore:

The state of possessing the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavattva*) should be intended as being determined by a relation that restricts its opposition to the apprehension of the locus as possessing the probandum (*sādhyavattāgraha*).

[This is] qualified by the subjecthood (*prakāratā*) residing in the probandum, which is delimited by the property delimiting the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-dharma*) and delimited by the relation delimiting the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*).

The relation by virtue of which a certainty possessing a qualifierhood (prakāratā) residing in the absence of the probandum (sādhya), delimited by that [specific] relation, acts as an obstacle to a cognition characterized by having a subjecthood (viśeṣyatā) residing in the subject (pakṣa) as delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka),
is called the "determiner of opposition" to the apprehension of the possession of the probandum. For example, in the case of "the mountain..."

In the case of "the mountain possesses smoke because of fire," with respect to the cognition "the mountain possesses smoke by way of conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), the certainty that "the mountain lacks smoke by way of its own nature" (*svarūpa-sambandha*) acts as an impediment; therefore, it is indeed *svarūpa-sambandha* [that constitutes the counter-positive relation].

The restrictor of the opposition to the apprehension of the locus as possessing the probandum (*sādhyavattāgrahavirodhitāniyāmaka*) is that relation; by that relation, the iron ball (*ayogolaka*) possesses the absence of smoke, and the state of being located (*ādheyatva*) in it is present in fire—thus the definition is satisfied. In the case of "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke," [the locus] "mountain" [is related to the probandum] by the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

With respect to the cognition "there is fire," the very certainty that the mountain is the locus of the absence of fire by way of the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*) is the sublater,
and not [the certainty] by way of the temporal relation (*kālikasambandha*).

Even when there is the certain cognition that "the mountain is the locus of the absence of fire," the cognition "the mountain possesses fire by way of conjunction" still arises despite the presence of such a certainty; thus,
it is only the relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*) [that is required].

Since it is that which determines the contradiction with the apprehension of the locus as possessing the probandum (*sādhyavattā*), by that very relation the locus of the absence of fire is the lake and so forth; the property of being located (*ādheyatva*) relative to that locus does not exist in smoke.
Thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

In the case of "that which possesses the absence of potness [is such] because it is a substance," the cloth is [the counter-positive] with respect to the cognition of the presence of the probandum, namely, "the cloth possesses the absence of potness."
The cognition in the form "that which possesses the absence of the absence of potness" (i.e.,
that which possesses potness by way of inherence) is the subverting factor; thus, [the relation] is inherence (*samavāya*).

The relation that determines the opposition to the apprehension of the locus as possessing the probandum (*sādhyavattā*) is the [inherence] relation. By means of that relation, the substratum of the absence of the probandum is the pot; since the property of being located (*ādheyatva*) relative to that [pot] exists in substanceness (*dravyatva*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). In the case of "This tree possesses contact with a monkey, because it is this-tree-ness," [the substratum of the absence of the probandum is] the tree...

Regarding the cognition "connected with a monkey," [the counter-argument is] that "the tree possesses the absence of connection with a monkey" by way of the relation of unconditioned spatial qualification (*niravacchinnadaiśikaviśeṣaṇatā*).

The relation by which a certainty having the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) as its qualifier acts as an obstacle to a cognition having the probandum as its qualifier— by way of both the relation that delimits the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) and the property that delimits the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-dharma*)— is called the "determiner of opposition" (*virodhitā-niyāmaka*) to the apprehension of the locus as possessing the probandum (*sādhyavattā-graha*).
Refining that very point, he says: "delimited by the relation that delimits the probandumness" (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandhāvacchinna*), and so forth.

[The objection is: "It is only the certainty (*niścaya*) [of the absence] that is the sublater (*pratibandhaka*), and not [the mere cognition] 'possessing the absence of monkey-connection' by way of the relation of delimited qualification (*sāvacchinnaviśeṣaṇatāsambandha*)."

Even when there is the certainty that "the tree, as delimited by its root, possesses the absence of conjunction with a monkey," the cognition arises that "the tree [as a whole] has conjunction with a monkey at its top. Thus,

by means of the relation of unqualified qualification (*niravacchinna-viśeṣaṇatā*), which is the regulator of the opposition to the apprehension of the locus as possessing the probandum (*sādhyavattā-graha*).

That which possesses the absence of conjunction with a monkey is precisely a quality (*guṇa*) and so forth; the state of being a locus (*ādheyatva*) as defined by that [conjunction] does not exist in this tree-ness (*etadvṛkṣatva*).
Thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). And so it is.

The "common" (sādhāraṇa) [inconclusive reason] is that which possesses a substratum-ness (ādhikaraṇatā) determined by a locus-ness (ādheyatā) delimited by the relation delimiting the probans-hood, which in turn is determined by a locus-ness (ādheyatā) delimited by a relation delimiting the probandum-hood, which is delimited by a relation delimiting the probandum-hood, which is delimited by the delimitor of the probandum-hood, and which is the counter-correlativity residing in the probandum as delimited by that same delimitor of the probandum-hood; this counter-correlativity resides in an absence that is the subverter of the apprehension of the presence of the probandum, and this subversion is mediated by a relation that determines the subverting power.
This is the result:

even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a valid reason (*saddhetu*), such as "The pot is a substance, because it possesses existence qualified by being other than quality and action."
Since existence (*sattā*) resides in a quality (*guṇa*), which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the form of "substantiality" (*dravyatva*),

and because there is no difference between the qualified and the pure [existence], the locusness (*ādhāratā*) relative to that which possesses the absence of the probandum exists even in "existence qualified by being other than quality and action" (*guṇakarmānyatvaviśiṣṭasattā*); therefore, he says, "the direction [is as follows]."
