What is intended by "commonality" (sādhāraṇatva) is the possession of the delimiting property of the probans-hood (hetutāvacchedaka), which serves as the delimitor of the locus-ness (ādheyatāvacchedaka) as determined by that which possesses the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvavat).
This applies to *viśiṣṭasattā* only in its form as *sattā*.

The point is that, because it functions as a quality (guṇa), the delimitor of the locus-ness (ādheyatāvacchedaka) relative to qualities possessing the absence of the probandum is simply "existence-ness" (sattātva) itself, and not the delimitor of the reason (hetutāvacchedaka)— which is "existence-ness qualified by being other than quality and action. Therefore, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).

But is it not the case that even in the contradictory [reason], "Sound is eternal because it is produced," the property of subsisting in a jar— which possesses the absence of the probandum (eternality)— exists in "being produced"?

He raises the objection that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the common characteristic (*sādhāraṇalakṣaṇa*) by stating, "Nor is it contradictory," and "even when there is a confusion of the substrata (*upadheya-saṅkara*). The sense is that multiple defects can occur in a single instance.

Even when there is a confusion of the superimposed (upadheya), that is, even when the defect (doṣa) is one, there is no confusion of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi); that is, the defects remain distinct. [Note:
1. It is not the case that it is merely a quality (guṇa) and so forth.]

However, in the case of a tree, since the absence of conjunction with a monkey exists there precisely through the relation of delimiting qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*) by the root and so forth, this is the intended meaning [in the definition of the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*)].
The term *sapakṣa* means "that which possesses the probandum (*sādhya*) ascertained";
that is to say, it is that which possesses an ascertainment whose qualifier is the probandum by way of the relation of qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*).

The result is that "the uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) is that which possesses the absence of the general property of subsisting in the similar instances (sapakṣa), that is, it possesses the absence whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by the property of subsisting in the similar instances. This is because even a valid reason (saddhetu) possesses the absence of subsistence in some [particular] similar instance.
There is no occasion for the objection that [the reason] would be uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).

In the case of the valid reason "Sound is impermanent because it possesses soundness" (*śabdo 'nityaḥ śabdatvāt*), at the stage when there is doubt regarding the probandum— in the form of impermanence— within the subject, namely sound;
That which possesses a certainty regarding the property to be proven (sādhya) is not sound, but rather a jar or the like;

since the absence of that [property] exists in "soundness" (śabdatva), soundness is the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reason. However, when there is a certainty of impermanence with respect to sound, then sound itself [is the subject].

The similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is that which possesses a certainty whose qualifier is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). Since the absence of [the reason] from that [similar instance] does not exist in the case of "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), there is no "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*).
Thus, the ancients held that uniqueness is an impermanent defect.

The moderns, however, do not accept that a valid reason can have an occasional lack of concomitance (*asādhāraṇya*). In their view, the term "sapakṣa" refers merely to that which possesses the probandum;
thus, it is the general absence of occurrence in that which possesses the probandum [that constitutes the definition of the uncommon inconclusive reason].
Uniqueness (*asādhāraṇya*):

Even during the state of doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) when the reason is valid, the subject possesses the probandum; therefore, [the reason] does not reside in that [subject].
Since it does not exist in the reason (*hetu*), there is no lack of commonality (*asādhāraṇya*).
Regarding the phrase "having something as its qualificandum" (*kiñcid-viśeṣyaka*):

if the probandum (*sādhya*) is ascertained anywhere at all, then [the reason] is that which serves as the qualifier (*prakārībhūta*) in an ascertainment having that very thing as its qualificandum (*tad-viśeṣyaka-niścaya*).
It would be a [valid] probandum.
However, in the case of "everything is denotable because it is knowable," since everything constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*), denotability is not ascertained anywhere; therefore—
The probandum (*sādhya*) is that which is not a qualifier of any certain cognition (*niścaya*) having a particular subject as its object, and the reason (*hetu*) has such a probandum;
however, in this case, because the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
The condition "the state of having an absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) that is not the object of a certainty whose qualificandum is something specific" does not fit [in this case].

Therefore, the moderns say that "non-conclusiveness" (*anupasamhāritva*) consists in the probandum and so forth not being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Now, consider the following: "A pot is nameable, because it is knowable. In this instance...
Regarding "even in the case of a valid reason" (*saddhetāv api*):

in the argument "sound is impermanent because it possesses the nature of sound" (*śabdo 'nityaḥ śabdatvāt*), there is an absence of occurrence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as a jar, within the property of being sound (*śabdatve*).
The meaning is "because of existence.
This is because it is a valid reason (*saddhetu*) at the stage when the impermanence of sound is ascertained;

for, taking a pot or the like—which possesses the property to be proven—as the referent of the phrase "that which possesses some ascertained locus of the probandum," [the reason] exists as not occurring in that [pot].
An over-extension (ativyāpti) would result; furthermore, if the absence of the universal (sāmānyābhāva) were introduced,

then because the property of subsisting in sound— which serves as a similar instance (sapakṣa)— is present, the absence delimited by the state of subsisting in a similar instance (sapakṣavṛttitvatvāvacchinnābhāva) does not exist.

The intention is that there is no over-extension (*atibyāpti*). If it is argued that because the property of having a probandum (*sādhya*) that is not the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) exists [in such cases], it would follow that they are non-conclusive (*anupasamhārin*)— we say no, because that is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

In that case, because the knowledge of the negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) is obstructed by the knowledge of the non-occurrence of the reason in the subject (anupasaṃhāritva), the inference caused by the knowledge of the negative concomitance does not arise.
Inference, however, which is rooted in the knowledge of positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*), remains entirely unimpeded.

If it is asked how the knowledge of the state of being "non-conclusive" (*anupasaṃhāritva*) can act as an obstacle to the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), the answer is as follows: at the time of the cognition that "the probandum (*sādhya*) is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence," [the obstacle arises].
Just as the cognition "the probandum (sādhya) is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence" does not arise,
so too the cognition "there is an absolute non-existence whose counter-positive is the probandum" does not arise; and consequently,
even the cognition of negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti), which is constituted by such an absolute non-existence having the probandum as its counter-positive, does not occur.
It is as follows:
the *Tarkasaṅgraha* is an exposition of contradictions.
A contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is one that is pervaded by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāpta*). For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced.
For the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is indeed pervaded by non-eternality, which is the absence of eternality.
A contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is one that is pervaded by the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyābhāvavyāpta*).
For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is a product" (or "because it is created"), like a pot.
(Here, indeed, being produced is pervaded by impermanence, which is the absence of permanence.
The definition of the counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*): That [reason] for which there exists another reason that establishes the opposite of the probandum is a counter-balanced reason.
For example: "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (śabdatva)";
and "Sound is non-eternal because it is a product, like a jar."
That [reason] for which there exists another reason that establishes the absence of the probandum is "counterbalanced" (*satpratipakṣa*).
For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is audible."
Sound is impermanent because it is a product, like a pot.
[This is] the definition of the unestablished (asiddha). The unestablished is of three kinds.
There are three types: the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), the unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), and the unestablished in its pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*).
An example of the unestablished locus is: "A sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus, like a pond-lotus.
Here, the sky-lotus is the locus.
And that [reason] does not exist at all;
it is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), as in the case: "Sound is a quality because it is visible.
Here, visibility does not exist in sound, because sound is audible.

The fallacy of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*) is that which is accompanied by a limiting condition (*sopādhika*). A limiting condition (*upādhi*) is that which, while being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*), is not a pervader of the probans (*sādhana*).
Being a pervader of the probandum consists in not being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is co-located with the probandum.

The state of being the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence that is co-extensive with the probandum (sādhya) while not being co-extensive with the probans (sādhana) is "over-pervasion" (sādhāraṇāvyāpakatva).
For example, in the inference "The mountain possesses smoke because it possesses fire," the conjunction with wet fuel (*ārdrandhana-saṃyoga*) is an *upādhi*. To explain:
Where there is smoke, there is contact with wet fuel; thus, [contact with wet fuel] pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatā*).
Where there is fire, there is an absence of contact with wet fuel; thus, it does not pervade the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatā*).
Therefore, since it pervades the probandum while not pervading the probans, contact with wet fuel is an *upādhi* (limiting condition).
Because it possesses an adventitious condition (upādhi), the state of possessing fire is unestablished as a pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddha).

The unestablished (asiddha) is of three kinds: the unestablished in respect of its locus (āśrayāsiddha), the unestablished in respect of its own nature (svarūpāsiddha), and the unestablished in respect of its pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddha).
An example of the unestablished in respect of its locus is as follows:
"The sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus, like a lotus in a lake. Here,
the "sky-lotus" is the locus (*āśraya*),
and that simply does not exist.
An example of the unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) is: "Sound is a quality, because it is visible.
Here, visibility does not exist in sound, for sound...
Because it is audible;
this [reason] is fallacious due to a limiting condition (sopādhika) and is unestablished as to its pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddha).
The *Dīpikā* defines the contradictory (*viruddha*) [reason] as follows:
"sādhyeti."
He defines the "counter-balanced" (satpratipakṣa) with the words "of which," and analyzes the "unestablished" (asiddha):
Regarding "unestablished" (asiddha):
he provides an example of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) with the words "the sky," etc.
He provides an example of the unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*)— beginning with "for instance"—
and [now addresses] the unestablished in its pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*).
He states the definition: "that which has an adjunct" (*sopādhika*).
The *prakāśikā* explains it as that which is pervaded by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāpta*).
Thus, the pervasion by the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvavyāpti) consists in not occurring in that which possesses the probandum (sādhyavadavṛttitva).
However, there is no identity [between this and] the "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇya), because the latter consists in the certain non-occurrence in that which possesses the probandum.
In the view of the new school (Navīna), however,
the negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) of the absence of the probandum consists in being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the probandum; thus,
there is no identity with the "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*) [fallacy].
It should be understood that the knowledge of the presence of a reason characterized by such pervasion is a direct impediment to inference.
Of whom...
"Absence of the probandum," and so forth.

The meaning is: when there exists in the subject (pakṣa) the cognition of another reason which is pervaded by the absence of that probandum which is related to [the first] reason, that is a "counter-balanced" (satpratipakṣa) fallacy.

This is for the purpose of indicating that a reason is a *satpratipakṣa* (counter-balanced) only at the time when there is a cognition of the pervasion of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāpyatva*) in a reason other than the present reason— which is itself cognized as being pervaded by the probandum under consideration.
"The ancients [define it as] 'another reason' (hetvantara).
The moderns, however, describe it thus:
that which consists in the presence in the subject (pakṣa) of another reason that is pervaded by the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) related to that [subject]."
"Such is the meaning. Regarding "for example, [the fallacy of] unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddha)":
the unestablished locus consists in the absence of the delimiting property of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) in the subject (pakṣa).
Or else, the subject (pakṣa) is that which lacks the delimiting property of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka);
and such [a subject] simply does not exist.
Since the lotus (*aravinda*) is well-known [as existing], by the maxim "when there is a qualification," the resulting meaning is that the state of being sky-like does not exist in the lotus;
furthermore, there is a lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) in the subject (*pakṣa*).
Either the absence of a reason (*hetvabhāva*) or the subject (*pakṣa*) possessing the absence of a reason.
Now, one might ask: since there exist additional fallacies that possess a limiting condition (*upādhi*), how can there be only five types of fallacious reasons? To this, he says:
Regarding the term *sopādhika*:
it refers to the lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is the fallacy of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*).

Since this [lack of pervasion] necessarily exists in a reason that possesses an adventitious condition (*upādhi*), a *sopādhika* reason is indeed nothing other than one characterized by unestablished pervasion.

The sense is that a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is something distinct from you [the probans]. That the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) constitutes a defect will become clear later in the *Dīpikā*.
In this regard, the following should be noted:

the absence of the delimitor of the probandum-ness in the probandum is the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*); the absence of the delimitor of the reason-ness in the reason is the non-establishment of the means of proof (*sādhanāprasiddhi*).
As in the case of "there is a mountain consisting of gold because there is smoke consisting of gold," and so forth; at the time of grasping that [inference].

The result is the obstruction of the apprehension of pervasion qualified by the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka) with respect to that which is qualified by the delimitor of the reason (hetutāvacchedaka).
Since these two are included within the "unestablishedness of pervasion" (vyāpyatvāsiddhi), there is no excess in the number of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
The pervasion by the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvavyāpti) consists in not occurring in that which possesses the probandum (sādhyavadavṛttitva).
Pervasion by the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvavyāpti) is the state of not occurring in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvābhāvavadavṛttitvam).
And this is precisely the state of not occurring in that which possesses the probandum (sādhyavadavṛttitvam).
The meaning is that the absence of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvābhāva) is identical with the probandum itself.
"Uniqueness" (asādhāraṇya) consists in not occurring in any locus where the probandum is definitely known to exist.

The meaning is that there is a distinction between the two because "contradictoriness" (*viruddhatva*) consists in not occurring in that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*). According to the view of the New School (*navīna*), it is precisely this non-occurrence in that which possesses the probandum.

Because it is uncommon, he states the meaning of the term "contradiction" (virodha) as distinct from that [uncommon] view, according to his own opinion, by saying: "In the new school's view, however..."
The negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) of the absence of the probandum consists in being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of the absence of the probandum;
this is ultimately equivalent to being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the probandum.
In the argument "Sound is eternal because it is produced," the probandum is eternity;
its pervader is non-existence.

The absence of being produced (*kṛtakatvābhāva*) exists in "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*); thus, the definition is satisfied. [This refers to] that which directly obstructs inference;
with respect to the cognition of possessing that [property].

Because the cognition of the presence of that which is pervaded by the absence of [the probandum] acts as an inhibitor, there is an inhibition of the inferential cognition "sound is eternal" by the cognition of the presence of a reason possessing negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti) characterized by the absence of eternity.

The point is that the cognition of contradiction— namely, "Sound possesses the property of being produced, which is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades eternality"— functions as an inhibitor because it takes the form of a cognition of the presence of something (producedness) that is pervaded by the absence of that [eternality].
The ancients maintain that *satpratipakṣatva* (counter-balanced opposition) occurs precisely at the time when two contradictory subsumptive cognitions (*parāmarśa*) exist.

However, even at a time when such subsumptive cognitions are absent, if there exists in the subject another reason that is pervaded by the absence of the probandum of the original reason, *satpratipakṣatva* certainly does occur.
The moderns [hold this view]. Thus he says: "that which is related to that," "that which is to be proven," and so forth.
The meaning of the phrase "that which is related to that" is "that which is related to the reason (hetu)."

And thus, when there exists in the subject (pakṣa) the cognition of another reason which is pervaded by the absence of that probandum which is related to the [original] reason, that is a counter-balanced reason (satpratipakṣa). For example,
in the case of "Sound is non-eternal because it is produced," the probandum in the form of non-eternality is related to the reason "being produced."

The probandum (*sādhya*) is such that there exists in the subject (*pakṣa*), which is sound, the cognition of another reason—namely, audibility—which is pervaded by the absence of that very impermanence [one seeks to prove]. Thus, that reason of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is one that has a counter-reason (*satpratipakṣa*).
It is the object of a cognition of another reason that is pervaded by the absence of the property intended as the probandum of a given reason.

A "counter-thesis" (satpratipakṣa) is a reason of that kind; that is to say, it is a reason which, at the time of a cognition having as its qualifier the state of being pervaded by the absence of the probandum under discussion and having another reason as its qualificand, becomes the qualificand of a cognition having as its qualifier the state of being pervaded by the probandum under discussion. This is the established meaning.
Regarding the passage beginning with "yatsambandhisādhya":
when there exists in the subject (pakṣa) another reason that is pervaded by the absence of whatever probandum (sādhya) is related to a given reason,
such a reason is a "counter-balanced" (satpratipakṣa) reason.
Eternality is the absence of that impermanence which is related to being produced;
audibility is another reason (hetu) pervaded by that [eternality]; since this [audibility] does not exist in the subject, sound, being produced constitutes a counter-balanced reason (satpratipakṣa).
And "unestablished locus" (āśrayāsiddhi) consists in the absence of the delimiting property of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) in the subject;
as in the case of [the argument] "a sky-lotus is fragrant."
The subject (*pakṣa*) is a lotus qualified by sky-ness (*gaganīyatva*).
Since sky-ness, which is the delimiting condition of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), does not exist in that subject— the lotus— there is either the absence of sky-ness residing in the lotus.
The meaning is that the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) consists in a lotus qualified by the absence of being sky-like.
This is according to the maxim: "For when there is a qualification, [the affirmation or negation applies] to that which possesses the qualification.
(In other words, when a rule or prohibition concerns something qualified, it applies to the thing as qualified.)

This is the maxim: "When there is an obstruction regarding the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), [the operation] shifts to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). That is to say, when an injunction or a prohibition is being applied to that which is qualified by a qualifier, if there is an obstruction to that injunction or prohibition with respect to the qualified object, then the injunction or prohibition applies to the qualifier.
The meaning of the principle is that [the property] "transfers" [to the substratum].

For example, in the expression "the crested one is destroyed," the destruction predicated of the person qualified by the crest cannot reside in the person itself because it is precluded [from the person].

Just as from the sentence "the crested one (śikhī) is destroyed," because he is one who possesses a crest (śikhā) that serves as a qualifier, the state of being destroyed ultimately pertains to the crest;
so too when it is said, "a sky-lotus does not exist."
The meaning is that negation, being of the nature of non-existence, because it is sublated in the case of the lotus,
resorts to the qualifier "being sky-like," and thus results in the absence of being sky-like.

Now, in the case of a reason that possesses an adventitious condition (*upādhi*), let the fault belong to the condition itself; what is the use of [speaking of] the "unestablished nature of the pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*)?
Regarding the phrase "as a defect," he says: "It is impossible for a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) to be a defect.
This will become clear [later], as it is said:
"The limiting adjunct, however, is an obstacle to the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by way of producing the knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)."
The word "by the text" (*granthena*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Now, one might object:

since the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) and the non-establishment of the reason (*sādhanāprasiddhi*) are also fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), their omission constitutes a deficiency (*nyūnatā*).
Anticipating this objection, he states that these two are included within the "unestablished due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*): "In this regard... (*atre*)...
This is what must be noted:
at the time of knowing the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) in the form "fire is that which possesses the absence of being composed of gold,"...
Because a cognition of fire qualified by being made of gold is impossible,

the cognition of the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) acts as an obstacle toward the manifestation of fire qualified by being made of gold within the *parāmarśa* (inferential reflection) "that which possesses smoke pervaded by fire qualified by being made of gold."
An obstacle: likewise,

at the time of knowing the non-establishment of the probans (*sādhanāprasiddhi*) in the form "smoke is devoid of being made of gold," the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*)— "the mountain possesses smoke that is made of gold and is pervaded by fire"— does not arise.
It is possible [to say this],

because a cognition having smoke as its qualificandum and the property of being made of gold as its qualifier is obstructed by a cognition having smoke as its qualificandum and the absence of the property of being made of gold as its qualifier.

And thus, by virtue of being the objects of a cognition that obstructs the *parāmarśa* which generates an inference, the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) and the non-establishment of the probans (*sādhanāprasiddhi*) constitute fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). If it is asked how these two are included within the "unestablishedness of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), listen:

For pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed the coexistence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum as qualified by the delimitor of its probandumness with the probans as qualified by the delimitor of its probansness; however, in a case where the probans is unestablished (*sādhanāprasiddhi*),
there is an absence of the probans as qualified by the delimitor of its probansness.
Vyāpyatvāsiddhi (the unestablished nature of the pervasion) consists in the absence of a pervasion constituted by such a reason;
in cases where the probandum is unestablished (*sādhyāprasiddhi*), it arises from the absence of the probandum as qualified by its delimitor of probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*).
Because there is an absence of pervasion (vyāpti) characterized by such a probandum (sādhya), there is "unestablished pervasion" (vyāpyatvāsiddhi);
thus, these two are included within unestablished pervasion.
[Note: 1. Regarding the absence of being a property of the sky (gaganīyatvābhāve).]
[The argument] concludes as follows:
by this, the statement in the primary root-text— "The locus is a sky-lotus, and that [locus] does not exist"— is shown to be incoherent.
For the meaning of "sky-lotus" (*gaganāravinda*) is a lotus qualified by being situated in the sky;
since a lotus exists there [in that context], it follows that...

The doubt— namely, that [the statement] would be contradicted by non-existence— is thus dispelled; the final meaning of the sentence "And that does not exist at all" is simply that there is an absence of being in the sky in the lotus.
And in that case, because there is no impossibility [of its occurrence]. *Tarkasaṃgraha*:
Definition of the Condition (*upādhi*).
The nature of an *upādhi* (limiting condition) is the state of being a non-pervader of the probans while being a pervader of the probandum.
Pervasion of the probandum consists in not being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is co-located with the probandum.

The state of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that resides in the locus of the probans (*sādhanavanniṣṭhātyantābhāvapratiyogitva*) constitutes non-pervasion of the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*). (For example,) in the argument "The mountain possesses smoke because of fire," the conjunction with wet fuel (*ārdrendhanasaṃyoga*) is the *upādhi*. This is because it pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatayā*), such that: "Wherever there is smoke, there is conjunction with wet fuel."
It is not the case that wherever there is fire, there is contact with moist fuel; for in the case of a red-hot iron ball, there is an absence of contact with moist fuel.
Thus, because it pervades the probandum while not pervading the probans, contact with moist fuel is an *upādhi*;
[the argument] is fallacious due to being *sopādhika*.
The state of possessing fire (*vahnimattva*) is unestablished due to lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*).
The *Dīpikā* states the definition of a limiting condition (*upādhi*):

Regarding the term "sādhya": the *upādhi* (limiting condition) is of four kinds: that which pervades the *sādhya* alone, that which pervades the *sādhya* as delimited by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), that which pervades the *sādhya* as delimited by the probans (*sādhana*), and...
And [the second type] is that which pervades the probandum as delimited by the property of being neutral (*udāsīna*).
The first is the conjunction with moist fuel (*ārdrendhana-saṃyoga*).
As for the second, for example, in the case: "Air is perceptible because it is the substratum of perceptible touch."

The possession of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) pervades perceptibility as delimited by being an external substance. An example of the third [type of pervasion] is as follows: in the inference "prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is perishable because it is produced," the state of being an entity (*bhāvatva*) pervades impermanence as delimited by being produced.

The fourth [type of fallacy] is as follows: in the argument "prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is perishable because it is an object of cognition," being an entity (bhāvatva) pervades impermanence as delimited by the property of being produced.

The *Prakāśikā* states: "Regarding 'pervading the probandum' (*sādhyavyāpakatva*)," this means that [the negative concomitance] possesses both the property of pervading the probandum and the property of not pervading the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*) by a single form and through a single relation.

Regarding the object of apprehension (*grāhya*): therefore, in cases such as "this possesses fire because of smoke," although there exists the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) by way of that specific fire-ness in each respective fire, and the non-pervasion of the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*) by way of that specific fire-ness,
there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Nor is there over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case, even though fire— which pervades the probandum (sādhya) by way of conjunction— is not a non-pervader of the probans (sādhana) by way of inherence;
[this addresses] the under-extension (avyāpti) in the definition of the "upādhi" stated in the root text.

To exclude [invalid cases], he demonstrates the distinction between the definition by means of the distinction of the object to be defined: "The adjunct (upādhi) is of four kinds. In the definition, one must include the property that it pervades the probandum as qualified by a certain attribute, while not pervading the probans as qualified by that same attribute. Otherwise—

It should be noted that there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because some property that pervades the probandum as delimited by the mountain-ness (*parvatatva*)—which is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)—does not pervade [the probandum] as delimited by smokiness (*dhūmatva*).
Regarding the term "indifferent" (*udāsīna*): it means distinct from both the property of the subject and the property of the probans.
Being an external substance— meaning being a substance other than the self—
is stated here in accordance with the fact that only pure perceptibility (*kevalapratyakṣatva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).
"Prior non-existence is perishable because it is produced"—
in this case, "being produced" is not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); therefore, the definition [of the fallacy] consists in being a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the probans.
"Being the pervader of impermanence" means being the pervader of perishability. This is stated in order to establish that "being produced" is irrelevant [to the argument].
"Because it is an object of valid cognition" (*prameyatvāt*). Now, one might ask:
is not the definition of a *upādhi* stated in the root-text the form "that which, while being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*), is not a pervader of the probans (*sādhana*)"?
In a valid reason such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with respect to each respective fire (such as the kitchen fire and so forth).

This is because the fire of the kitchen, in its form as fire (*vahnitva*), is a pervader of the probandum in the form of fire in general, yet it is not a pervader of the probans in its specific form as the fire of the kitchen.
In that which possesses the probans (sādhana) and possesses smoke,
[the absence of] kitchen-fire exists in the form of kitchen-fire, because of the absence of kitchen-fire [as a specific instance];
likewise, in that very same place.

Light would incur the status of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because light exists everywhere in that which possesses fire through the relation of conjunction; thus, by the relation of conjunction, it pervades the probandum (*sādhya*). In this way...

Anticipating the objection that light does not exist on the smoke-bearing mountain by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), and therefore it is not a pervader of the probans (*sādhana*) by way of the relation of inherence, he says:
"The state of being a pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the state of not being a pervader of the probans."

And likewise, by whichever relation and in whatever form the adjunct (upādhi) possesses pervasion of the probandum (sādhyavyāpakatva), it [must be shown] by that very relation and in that very form [to be absent from the locus of the reason].

And its non-pervasion of the probans (sādhana) is intended; therefore, [the absence] of the fire of the kitchen and so forth— which is pervaded by fire in its nature as fire— is [intended] by way of its being the fire of the kitchen.
Even though [fire] does not pervade smoke, it does not fail to pervade smoke by virtue of being fire; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Likewise, although light, which is a pervader of fire by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), is not so by way of inherence (*samavāya*)...

The point is that even though [the property of being produced by wet fuel] is non-pervasive with respect to smoke, it is not non-pervasive with respect to smoke by means of that very relation of conjunction; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
This refers to the pervasiveness of the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*).

The meaning is: "the state of possessing the property of fire-ness (vahnitva), which is not a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence residing in that which possesses the probandum (sādhyavat). [And] "the state of being a non-pervader of the probans (sādhanāvyāpaka) by virtue of this or that specific fire-ness" means: "the state of possessing this or that specific fire-ness, which is a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence residing in that which possesses the probans (sādhanavat)."

Thus, pervasion by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) consists in possessing a property that is not the delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by the relation of conjunction, as determined by an absolute absence residing in that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*).
Pervasion by inherence (*samavāya*) consists in [the reason] not being a pervader of the probans (*sādhana*).

It should be understood that [the definition] consists in possessing a property that serves as the delimiting condition (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), which is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) as determined by an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in the locus of the probans (*sādhanavanniṣṭha*). This is stated "in order to avoid under-extension" (*avyāpti*);
for example, [the argument] "Air is perceptible... [is intended to be avoided].

In the argument "because it is the substratum of perceptible touch," the presence of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) is the *upādhi*. In that case, the definition stated in the root text—which consists of being pervaded by the probandum—is absent;
for [manifested color] exists in that which possesses the probandum in the form of perceptibility.

Because visible form (*rūpa*) does not arise within the self (*ātman*), the definition would result in being over-narrow (*avyāpti*). To prevent this, it must be stated that the definition varies according to the distinction between the objects to be defined (*lakṣya*); thus, the limiting condition (*upādhi*) is fourfold.
Such is the intended meaning of the *Dīpikā*; this is the underlying point.

And thus, the definition of a condition (*upādhi*) that is a pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*) alone is: being a pervader of the probandum alone while not being a pervader of the probans (*sādhana*).
The definition of a qualifying condition (*upādhi*) that pervades the probandum as delimited by a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is:

being a pervader of the probandum as delimited by a property of the subject while not being a pervader of the probans as so delimited. [This applies] to a qualifying condition that pervades the probandum as delimited by the probans (*sādhana*).
The definition [of a *upādhi*] is: being a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the probans, while not being a pervader of that same probans.
For an *upādhi* that is a pervader of the probandum as delimited by an indifferent property (*udāsīnadharma*), [the definition is]:
being a pervader of the probandum as delimited by that indifferent property, while not being a pervader of the probans as delimited by that same indifferent property.

The intention is that a distinction between definitions is intended by way of the phrase "the definition" (*lakṣaṇam*). Thus he says: "that which is qualified by a property [serving as] the probandum," and so forth.
[This refers to] qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*).

By way of the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). He states the purpose of the intended identity of the property (*dharmaikyavivakṣā*) with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*): [for example], in the case of "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke," [the reason would fail] regarding the fire belonging to the mountain...
That which is the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) consisting of mountain-ness possesses pervasion by fire qualified by that [mountain-ness], and it also lacks pervasion by the probans;
for in a kitchen possessing smoke, there is an absence of fire belonging to the mountain.
Thus, the fire on the mountain would be the limiting adjunct (upādhi).

However, if one intends to express the identity of the property (dharmaikya), then the fire on the mountain— which is the pervader of the fire qualified by mountain-ness— is [the pervader] of that which is qualified by mountain-ness.
There is no non-pervasion with smoke,
because the fire belonging to the mountain exists on the mountain which is qualified by being a mountain and possessing smoke.
The point is that, therefore, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
In the *Dīpikā*, the first [cause] is stated to be contact with moist fuel (*ārdrendhana-saṃyoga*).
In the case of "The mountain possesses smoke because of fire," the conjunction with wet fuel (*ādrendhana-saṃyoga*) is the *upādhi*;
and it is a pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*), which is smoke.
The meaning is that this is an *upādhi* which pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) alone, while not pervading the means of proof (*sādhana*) in the form of fire.
Regarding the second [type], "for example":
the meaning is that an *upādhi* is that which pervades the probandum as delimited by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

In the argument "Air is an object of perception because it is the substratum of a touch that is an object of perception," the presence of manifest color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) is the *upādhi* (limiting condition);
furthermore, this [condition] does not pervade the mere probandum (*kevalasādhyavyāpaka*).

Because the self, which possesses the probandum in the form of being an object of perception, lacks the quality of possessing manifest color; therefore, this is an *upādhi* (limiting condition) that pervades the probandum as delimited by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
"Property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*) means the property of the subject (*pakṣa*).
That which is delimited by that [property], qualified by that, and co-located with that—namely, the probandum—is its pervader.

In the present case, the subject (*pakṣa*) is air (*vāyu*); the property residing therein (*tadvṛttidharma*) is being an external substance (*bahir-dravyatva*). That which is qualified by this [property] is perceptibility (*pratyakṣaviṣayatva*), and that does not exist in the self (*ātman*), because the self...

Because of the absence of the qualifying attribute "being an external substance," wherever there is the state of being an object of perception qualified by being an external substance— as in the case of earth and so forth— there exists the possession of manifested color; therefore,
the possession of manifested color [is established].
It is a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the property of being a subject-attribute (*pakṣadharma*). Likewise,

it exists in the case of air (*vāyu*), where there is the means of proof (*sādhana*) consisting of being the locus of perceptible touch qualified by being an external substance, which is itself delimited by the property of being a subject-attribute.

In that case, since there is no manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*), the property of possessing manifested color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) does not pervade the probans as delimited by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); thus, the definition [of the fallacy] is satisfied.
The third [type] is "yathā" (as for example).
The meaning is that an *upādhi* is that which pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by the probans (*sādhana*).
Regarding the state of being delimited by the probans (*sādhanāvacchinnatva*):
And [the property of being qualified by the probans] occurs through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
In the case of "Prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is perishable because it is produced," the property of being an entity (*bhāvatva*) is accepted as the limiting condition (*upādhi*). That...

It does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) alone, because "existence" (*bhāvatva*) is absent in antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which possesses the probandum in the form of perishability (*vināśitva*). Therefore,
this is an adjunct (*upādhi*) that pervades the probandum as delimited by the probans (*sādhanāvacchinna-sādhyavyāpaka*).

The meaning is that perishability, as qualified by the probans in the form of being produced, exists wherever it is found— such as in a jar— and in those cases, the nature of being an entity (bhāvatva) is present.
As for the fourth [example], it is as follows:
The meaning is: that which pervades the probandum as delimited by a neutral property (*udāsīnadharmāvacchinna*).

In the argument "Prior non-existence is perishable because it is knowable," "possession of being" (*bhāvatva*) is the extraneous condition (*upādhi*). A neutral property is a property other than both the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*).
For the property of being produced does not exist in the subject, namely prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), and thus it is not a property of the subject (pakṣadharma).
Thus, because it is distinct from both the probans (*sādhana*) and the object of cognition (*prameyatva*), it is a neutral property (*udāsīnadharma*).

Wherever there is perishability qualified by being produced (*janyatva*) as delimited by that [neutral property], such as in the case of a jar and so forth, existence (*bhāvatva*) is present; therefore, in prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which possesses objectivity (*prameyatva*) qualified by being produced, [existence is likewise absent].

The meaning is that because existence (bhāvatva) is absent [in the counter-example], existence is an *upādhi*— that is, it pervades the probandum as delimited by an indifferent property (udāsīnadharmāvacchinna), yet it does not pervade the probans as delimited by an indifferent property.
In the *Prakāśikā*, this is expressed as "by means of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and the property of the probans (sādhanadharma)."

A property that subsists in the subject (*pakṣa*) is a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*). A property that has the form of a means of proof (*sādhana*) is a "property of the means of proof" (*sādhanadharma*).
This is the explanation of the term "being an external substance."
Regarding the statement "the self possesses a substance other [than itself]":

if the meaning of the term *pratyakṣa* in the proposition "air is perceptible" (*vāyuḥ pratyakṣaḥ*) is "an object of perception produced by an external sense-organ," then [the definition of air as] possessing manifested color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) [would apply].
An upādhi is indeed that which pervades only the probandum (sādhya) in its entirety.

However, when the probandum is merely "being an object of perception," then [the upādhi] is that which pervades the probandum as delimited by the property of the subject (pakṣadharma); with this intention, he says: "This..."
The phrase "of mere perceptibility alone" means of the state of being an object of perception in general, without being constituted by the property of being produced by an external sense organ.
This is its indifference (*udāsīnatva*).
"To establish" means:

if "being produced" (*janyatva*) alone were the reason (*hetu*), then the adjunct (*upādhi*) would indeed be a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the probans (*sādhanāvacchinna-sādhyavyāpaka*).
There is no pervasion of the probandum as delimited by the property of being neutral (*udāsīna*),
because the meaning of the word "neutral" refers exclusively to that which is other than the probans. Therefore, [this does not apply] to knowability (*prameyatva*).
The pursuit was based on [the reason's] being a cause;

however, now, since "being produced" (janyatva) is distinct from "knowability" (prameyatva) as the means of proof, the intended meaning is that the probandum (sādhya)— namely, perishability qualified by being produced— is delimited by an indifferent property (udāsīnadharmāvacchinna).
*Tarkasaṃgraha*:

Definition of the Sublated (*bādhita*). (AnTs 57) That [reason] for which the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is ascertained by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is the sublated.

For example: "Fire is not hot because it is a substance. Here, non-hotness is the property to be proven (sādhya); its absence, namely hotness, is apprehended through tactile perception. Thus, the reason is sublated (bādhitatva).
That [reason] for which the absence of the probandum is ascertained by another means of valid cognition is "sublated" (*bādhita*);
for example, "fire is not hot."
Because it is an object (padārtha).
Here, "non-heat" is the property to be proven (sādhya),
while its absence, namely "heat," is established by tactile perception (tvācapratyakṣa).
It should be understood that [the object] is apprehended. Inference has been explained.
Thus ends the Tarkasaṅgraha.
The Chapter on Inference (Anumānapariccheda) 1. "Pervading only the probandum" (*kevalasādhyavyāpaka*) means:
wherever there is the state of being an object of perception produced by an external sense organ, as in the case of a jar and so forth, [there is the probans].
The meaning is that this is because of the existence of the possession of manifested form (*udbhūtarūpavattva*).
2. "At that very time, it is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*): wherever there is the state of being an object of perception, even in the case of the self (*ātman*), [it is so].
In that case, because of the absence of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*),
it is not possible for manifested color alone to be a pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*); therefore,

the condition (*upādhi*) must be a pervader of the probandum in the form of being an object of perception qualified by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), namely, the state of being an external substance (*bahir-dravyatva*).
The sense is that it must be established for that which has manifested form. [Dīpikā: Of that which is sublated...
He states the definition with the words "of which" (*yasya*).
Here, the analysis of the manner in which defects (*doṣa*) act as obstructions to inference pertains to sublation (*bādha*).

The counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*) possesses direct obstructiveness toward inference by virtue of being a cognition of an opposing factor, specifically through its nature as the ascertainment of the non-existence of the object to be apprehended (*grāhya*).
But for the others,
there is the status of being an obstacle to the consideration [of the subject].
Even among those, the common [inconclusive reason] functions as such by way of the absence of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*).
Because the contradictory [reason] lacks co-referentiality,
and because the unestablished due to lack of pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddha) lacks qualified pervasion.

The uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) and the non-conclusive (*anupasaṃhārī*) [reasons] function as obstacles to the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by engendering doubt regarding that pervasion. The unestablished due to the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and the unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) function as obstacles to the cognition of the reason's presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
The ancients, however, maintain that a limiting condition (upādhi) obstructs the knowledge of pervasion by means of producing a cognition of deviation,
whereas "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana) is included within the fallacy of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddha) because it destroys the status of the subject (pakṣatā).
The moderns [hold] that there is another point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Thus ends the section on inference (*anumāna*) in the *Dīpikā*, the *Prakāśikā*.
Of the sublation (*bādha*),
which is the ascertainment of the presence of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavattāniścaya*);
[it acts] by way of being an ascertainment of the absence of the apprehended object (*grāhyābhāvaniścayatvena*).
This connects with the phrase "the state of being an obstacle to inference. "By way of being the causal complex for a contradictory cognition" refers to the view of the ancients.

In reality, however, it should be noted that the counter-inference (parāmarśa) of the contradictory [reason] functions as an inhibitor precisely by virtue of being a certainty regarding the possession of the pervader of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvavyāpyavattvaniścaya), on account of parsimony (lāghava).
Of others— that is,
of the apprehensions of deviation and so forth.
Even there— that is, even among those apprehensions of deviation and so forth.
Regarding the term "of the common" (*sādhāraṇasya*): because it is an indication where the state (*bhāva*) is primary, it means "of the commonality" (*sādhāraṇyasya*).
This is because [the common] consists in the absence of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*).

The word "of that apprehension" (*tadgrahasya*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. It connects with the phrase "the state of being an obstacle to the knowledge of pervasion" (*vyāptijñānapratibandhakatvam*). The same applies further on as well. Regarding the reason (*hetu*):

Just as the subsistence in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadvṛttitva*) constitutes deviation (*vyabhicāra*), so too does the state of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence co-located with the reason (*hetusamānādhikaraṇātyantābhāvapratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) within the delimiting factor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) constitute deviation; therefore, the apprehension of that [latter]— [...is what is meant by the term "deviation"].

The meaning is that [the definition of fallacy] consists in being an obstacle to the apprehension of non-deviation, which is of the nature of the absence of the property of being a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence that is co-referential with the reason. However, regarding the reason,
the apprehension of it as having the occurrence of the absence of the probandum as its qualifier is an obstacle to the apprehension of pervasion.
By way of the analogy of the "jewel and the mantra" and so forth, because there is an absence of a qualified pervasion—

that is, because it consists in the absence of co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between that which is delimited by the delimitors of the pervader of the reason and that which is delimited by the delimitors of the probandum—
and because it engenders doubt regarding pervasion.

In the state of knowing the reason (*hetu*) as being uncommon (*asādhāraṇya*) and so forth, because it is impossible to ascertain the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the reason and the probandum (*sādhya*), and because doubt regarding the probandum exists by virtue of the subject (*pakṣa*) being included therein, doubt regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) arises; thus, there is no determination of pervasion.
This is stated with reference to the view of the ancients:

that [the definition of a fallacy] consists in being a sublater of the cognition of the property of being a reason (pakṣadharmatā). This refers to the state of certainty regarding the absence of the property delimiting the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) and the absence of the reason (hetu) in the subject (pakṣa), while the reason [is otherwise present].

The meaning is that it is impossible to apprehend the subsistence [of the reason] in the subject as qualified by the delimiting property of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). Now, an objection: the mention of "fivefoldness" is inconsistent, even at the time when a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is apprehended in the reason.

Since it must necessarily be stated that the knowledge of a *upādhi* (limiting condition) acts as an obstacle to the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) due to the impossibility of ascertaining such pervasion, and since the *upādhi* itself is thus covered by the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), he says:
"But the *upādhi*..."
"By way of the cognition of deviation":

thus, since in the definition of a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) one must include precisely the state of being an obstacle to either the inference itself or its instrument (the means of knowledge), directly.
The point is that a condition (*upādhi*) which depends on the observation of another's face does not constitute a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

Now, even so, since inference does not arise when there is already established knowledge (*siddhi*), the subject (*pakṣa*)— which is the locus of the object of that [inference] and possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*)— is likewise [not a cause].

Anticipating the objection that the status of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is necessarily required, he refutes it by accepting the point as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), following the view of the older Naiyāyikas: "But [the case of] proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)...
and "...by way of destroying the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*)."

The point is that, according to that view, since the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) consists in doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), the certainty of the probandum remains unimpeded as it subverts that [doubt].
Regarding the phrase "is included": and thus...
The sense is that there is no contradiction regarding the distinction [between the two].

Having observed that the presented view is extremely weak, he says "nigraha" (refutation). Furthermore, in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since the cognition of the probandum (*siddhi*) acts as an obstacle to inference...
It must be explained how the object of that [cognition] does not constitute a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
This is because, in the case of the counteracting force residing in the proof (*siddhi*) of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), it acts as an intensifier (*uttejaka*) for the mere...

Because there is an absence of being a subverting factor (pratibandhakatva) toward the establishment [of the probandum] when accompanied by the desire to prove it, the definition of the aforementioned fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) does not apply to that object; for further detail,
see our commentary on the *Abhinavadīdhiti*.
This should be investigated by those preeminent in the skill of investigating with the rigor of logic.
Thus ends the section on inference in the *Prakāśikā*,
the *Bālapriyā*.

"By way of being a certainty regarding the non-existence of the apprehended object" means: by way of being a certainty whose qualifier is the non-existence of that which is to be proven (sādhya), which is the object to be apprehended by inference.
That is to say, it functions as a certainty regarding the absence of that [property] with respect to the cognition of its presence.
This refers to the case of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*).
[The sublation consists] in the cognition that "the subject possesses a counter-reason pervaded by the absence of the probandum";

this is because it is a causal complex for a contradictory cognition— that is, by virtue of its being the producer of the cognition that the subject possesses the absence of the probandum, which contradicts the cognition that the subject possesses the probandum.

And thus, the cognition of a counter-balanced reason (satpratipakṣa) generates a cognition of the presence of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvavattājñāna), which in turn obstructs the inference of the probandum; therefore, [the counter-balanced reason is a fallacy] by virtue of producing a cognition that acts as an obstacle to inference.

The ancients maintain that the counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*) possesses the capacity to obstruct inferential cognition (*anumiti*). The moderns, however, hold that the cognition of a counter-balanced reason takes the form: "The subject (*pakṣa*) possesses a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) which is pervaded by the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)."

In this manner, the cognition of the presence of that which is pervaded by the absence of the probandum (tadabhāvavyāpyavattājñāna) obstructs the inference by acting as a direct counter-agent (*pratibandhaka*) to the cognition of the presence of the probandum (*tadvattājñāna*),
rather than obstructing it indirectly by producing a cognition that itself obstructs the inference.
They say that [the opponent's view] is rejected because of its complexity (*gaurava*), given the possibility of [another] obstructive factor (*pratibandhakatva*).
Regarding the phrase "of the others," etc.:

in the reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*) whose form is "the subject (*pakṣa*) possesses the reason which is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*)," within the aspect consisting of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti-graha*),...
The cognitions of commonality (*sādhāraṇya*), contradiction (*virodha*), unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), uncommonness (*asādhāraṇya*),

and non-conclusiveness (*anupasaṃhāritva*) function as cognitive obstructions with respect to the aspect of the knowledge of the property's presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), namely, the cognition that "the subject possesses the reason."
The non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and the non-establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) function as cognitive obstructions. To explain:

according to the view that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason consists in its not occurring in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*), the occurrence of the reason in that which possesses the absence of the probandum within the subject (*pakṣa*) constitutes the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

And likewise, in the case of "The mountain possesses smoke because of fire," there is the non-cognition of the fallacy of commonality (sādhāraṇya-rūpa-vyabhicāra) in the form "Fire resides in that which lacks smoke," and [the cognition] "The mountain possesses fire which does not reside in that which lacks smoke."

In the reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*) of this form, regarding the aspect of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, "fire does not subsist in that which possesses the absence of smoke"—the certainty of the presence of that [absence] acts as an inhibitor with respect to the cognition of its presence (*tadvattābuddhi*), by way of being a certainty of the absence of that [pervasion].

[The definition of pervasion is: the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum, as delimited by the delimitor of the probandumhood, with that which is not the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of the absolute absence subsisting in the locus of the reason.
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists, in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*),

in the property of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence residing in the locus of the reason (*hetu*), with respect to that which delimits the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*).
The cognition of deviation, namely "smokiness is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence residing in a locus of fire," [leads to the inference]:

"that which possesses fire co-located with smoke, where that smoke is delimited by smokiness which is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of an absolute absence residing in a locus of fire."

With respect to the manifestation of the component "the property of being smoke is non-delimiting of counterpositiveness" within the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) in the form "This is a mountain [possessing smoke]."
An obstacle [is presented] to the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) concerning the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of such a thesis,
namely the knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the form: "The probans (*hetu*) subsists in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*)."
Because it does not apprehend the absence of the object to be grasped (*grāhya*), it possesses no obstructive power.
If, even at the time of such knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*),
the non-arising of the knowledge of the established pervasion (*siddhāntavyāpti*) is established by experience, then [the objection] regarding that...
The nature of the sublation (pratibandhakatā) must be stated according to the very principle of the "jewel and mantra" (maṇimantra) and so forth.
In the case of the argument "Sound is eternal because it is produced," [the sublation consists in] "producedness being non-co-instantaneous with eternality."

[This] knowledge of contradiction, consisting in the non-coexistence with the probandum (sādhyāsāmānādhikaraṇya) and having the form "thus characterized," [acts as an obstacle] toward the cognition that apprehends coexistence with the probandum— which is a constituent of pervasion (vyāpti)— and which has the form "producedness (kṛtakatva) coexists with impermanence (anityatva)."

The nature of being an impediment [belongs] to the cognition of the "unestablishedness of pervasion" (vyāpyatvāsiddhi) in the form "the reason is that which lacks the state of being pervaded by the probandum," with respect to the [cognition] "the subject possesses the reason which is pervaded by the probandum."

Thus, in the case of such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), there is an obstructive factor regarding the component consisting of the knowledge that the reason is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpyatva*). At the time of the cognition that "this reason is *asādhāraṇa*" (uncommon) or "it is *anupasaṃhārī*" (non-conclusive),

the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*) does not occur, because it is impossible to apprehend the co-presence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum and the reason outside of the subject (*pakṣa*).
It is possible;

for, since there is doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), there would only be doubt regarding the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum with the reason (*hetu*), and not certainty— according to this principle.
The cognition of the uncommon (asādhāraṇya) and the inconclusive (anupasamhāritva) reasons acts as an obstacle to the ascertainment of pervasion; likewise,

in the case of "A sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus," the cognition of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi)— namely, that "the lotus lacks the property of being located in the sky"— acts as such an obstacle.

In the case of the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) in the form: "The sky-lotus possesses lotus-ness, which is pervaded by fragrance," regarding the cognitive element that has as its qualificandum the lotus and as its qualifier the property of being a sky-entity (the delimitor of the subject, *pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
Obstructiveness [is the definition].
Likewise, in the case of "The lake possesses fire because of smoke," there is the cognition of a svarūpāsiddhi (unestablishedness in essence) in the form: "The lake is devoid of smoke."

In the case of the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) "the lake possesses smoke pervaded by fire," there is an obstructive effect regarding the aspect of the manifestation of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), namely "the lake possesses smoke.
Having taken all of this into account, he says:

In the *Prakāśikā*, [this is stated] by the passage beginning with "of the occurrence in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadvṛttitva*) in the reason (*hetau*)," and so forth.
Now, one might object: is it not improper to say that there are only five fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)?

Because, at the time of cognizing a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in the reason (*hetu*), there is an absence of certainty regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*) due to the ascertainment of deviation (*vyabhicāra*),
the limiting condition is also [to be excluded], since it is the object of a cognition that obstructs the certainty of pervasion— the instrument of inferential knowledge (*anumiti*).

He raises an objection: "Since it must be stated that there are six fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) because they are characterized by the definition of a fallacious reason, the statement that there are five is incorrect"—
or rather, [this objection applies] to inference.

Alternatively, that which possesses the status of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is precisely that whose cognition, regarding its own object, is directly an impediment to [the inference]. However, the cognition of a *upādhi* functions only by way of producing a cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

It obstructs the [wrong] apprehension (*parāmarśa*) but not directly; therefore, it does not constitute a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Consequently, there is no contradiction with the statement that [fallacies] are fivefold.
Thus he says: "And so..."
Regarding the phrase "the definition of a fallacious reason" (*hetvābhāsalakṣaṇa*):
the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is construed with "being an obstacle" (*pratibandhakatve*).
As for the phrase "of one who looks to another's face": [it refers to that which depends on the perspective of another].
The meaning is: "of one who is observing the ignorance of deviation (vyabhicāra), which is the obstacle to the final ascertainment (parāmarśa).
By this, it is shown that the knowledge of the limiting condition (upādhi) does not function as a direct obstacle.

It is indicated as follows: Now, just as in cases such as "the lake possesses fire because of smoke," the sublation consisting of the form "the lake possesses the absence of fire"— namely, "the lake possesses the absence of fire"—
is that which obstructs the inference "the lake possesses fire."
Knowledge of such a form [e.g., "the mountain possesses fire"] constitutes the fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) by virtue of having that [unreal object] as its object;
likewise, in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," [the cognition] "the mountain possesses fire" [is a fallacy].

At the stage when there is a certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the form "it is thus," since a doubt regarding the probandum— such as "Is the mountain fiery or not?"— does not arise, there is an absence of *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject of inquiry) consisting of such doubt; consequently, because the inference "The mountain is fiery" does not arise, [the object] which is the content of the *siddhi* (established knowledge) that acts as an obstacle to inference [is the subject].

One might raise the objection: "Even a mountain possessing fire would be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), because it is subject to the definition of a fallacious reason. To this, he says: "In that view... and so forth; likewise.
Furthermore, according to the view of the ancients, since the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) consists in doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhyasaṃśaya*),

a subject that possesses the probandum (*sādhyavatpakṣa*) is indeed accepted as a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), because it is the object of a cognition that obstructs the state of being a subject which generates an inference. Not [otherwise].
Nor should it be said that there is a "contradiction through fivefold division," because it is included within the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
If it is asked how it is included— [it is] as follows.

The unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is of two kinds: the non-establishment of the essential nature of the subject (*dharmisvarūpāprasiddhi*) and the non-establishment of its status as the thesis-locus (*pakṣatvāprasiddhi*). Among these, regarding the non-establishment of its status as the thesis-locus:
This is the inclusion of *siddhasādhana* [within the definition of a fallacy].

As it has been stated in the *Kusumāñjali*: "The middle [type of fallacy] is also twofold: due to the non-apprehension of the nature of the locus (*āśrayasvarūpa*), and due to the non-apprehension of the subjecthood (*pakṣatva*) consisting in its being qualified by that [locus]. Of these, the latter is designated as *siddhasādhana*."
"Because the status of being a subject (*pakṣatva*) is directly undermined when pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established"— thus,
the presented view is extremely weak.
Since the subjectness (*pakṣatā*)— as existing in its own right— is a distinct cause [of inference],

even though established knowledge (*siddhi*) acts as an inhibitor of it, there is neither the subversion of the *parāmarśa* (the consideration which is the instrument of inference) nor the subversion of the inference itself in cases of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established). Thus, it is not so.
A reason accompanied by a valid proof is a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*);
because of the absence of the reason in the form of the state of being the subject (*pakṣatā*), no inference can arise.

Therefore, the point is that in a case of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established), there is no pointing out of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), but rather merely the defeat (*nigraha*) of the proponent.
Now, [one might object]: even in the view of the Neo-logicians (*navīna*),...
Since no inference arises at the stage when the probandum is already ascertained, it must be stated— following the analogy of the jewel, the mantra, and so forth—

that "establishment" (*siddhi*) acts as an inhibitor of inference. And if that is so, why would there not be [inference] from a subject (*pakṣa*) possessing the probandum, which is the object of such an established cognition that inhibits inference?
He raises the objection that this constitutes a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) with the words "And not in the established doctrine" (*na ca siddhānte*).
[This refers to the case where] something does not necessarily arise when another thing is present.
And when something arises in the absence of another, that [absence] alone possesses the nature of an obstacle;
for even if the proof exists, if that proof is accompanied by a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*).
In that case, since an inference arises, there is no proof [of the probandum] that would constitute an obstacle to the inference;

therefore, the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)—consisting in being the object of a cognition that obstructs inference—is not present in the case where the subject possesses the probandum. He provides this resolution with the words "siṣādhayiṣāyāḥ" and so forth.

But even so, since the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) qualified by the presence of proof (*siddhi*) is an obstacle to inference, it would be difficult to avoid the conclusion that its object is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*); therefore, he says: "moreover" (*adhikam*).
The meaning is this: even when there is sensory contact with an object already perceived, as in the case of a continuous stream of perceptions (*dhārāvāhika-pratyakṣa*),
and even upon hearing a word whose referent has already been cognized.
Furthermore, since awareness (*bodha*) is accepted [as a cause], just as in that case,
when there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) regarding an object already established,
there is no obstacle whatsoever to the arising of an inference; therefore, [the objection does not hold].
Established knowledge (siddhi) does not act as an impediment to inference. Likewise,
since inference arises even in the absence of doubt regarding the probandum (sādhya), the state of being a subject (pakṣatā) consisting of doubt about the probandum is not a cause of inference.

And thus, since there is no status as an inhibitor with respect to the accomplishment [of the inference], or with respect to the inference itself, or with respect to the cause of the inference, the subject (pakṣa) which possesses the property to be proven (sādhya)— being the object of the accomplishment— does not fall under the definition of a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa). Thus it is said.
The Section on Inference in the *Bālapriyā*, a commentary on the *Tarkasaṅgrahadīpikāprakāśikā* // [End] //
The Section on Analogy,
from the *Tarkasaṃgraha*:
Analogy is the instrument of analogical cognition.
Comparison (*upamiti*) is the knowledge of the relationship between a name and the object named;
its instrument (*karaṇa*) is the knowledge of similarity;
and the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) is its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).

For instance, someone who does not know the referent of the word "gavaya" hears from a forest-dweller that "a gavaya is like a cow. Having gone to the forest and recollecting the meaning of that statement, he sees an individual object resembling a cow.
Immediately thereafter, the analogical cognition arises: "This is what is denoted by the word 'gavaya'."
Comparison (*upamāna*) is the instrument for analogical cognition (*upamiti*). Analogical cognition is the knowledge of the relationship between a name and the object named;
its instrument is the knowledge of similarity.

For instance, someone who does not know the meaning of the word "gavaya" hears from a forest-dweller that a gavaya is like a cow; having gone to the forest and recollecting the meaning of that statement, he perceives an individual object that resembles a cow.
Immediately after that, the analogical cognition arises: "This is what is denoted by the word *gavaya*.
Thus, analogy has been explained.
Thus ends the section on comparison in the Tarkasaṅgraha-dīpikā.
He defines comparison (*upamāna*) as "the instrument of analogical cognition," according to the *Dīpikā*.
The section on analogy:
the elucidation of analogy.
"Lakṣayati" means that he defines analogy (upamāna) by way of the logical connection of the occasion (*avasara-saṅgati*).
He explains the nature of analogical cognition (*upamiti*) [in the verse] with the words "the name" (*saṃjñā*) in the root text.
The name is the word "gavaya";
the named object is the *gavaya*;
the relationship between the two is the expressive power (*śakti*).
The meaning is that this is the knowledge [resulting from comparison].
As for its definition, it is simply the state of being a comparative cognition (upamiti) as apprehended by the reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya): "I am comparing."
Recalling the meaning of the sentence,
one perceives an object that resembles a cow;
this recollection is produced by the perception of similarity.
Or [it may be] produced by another excitant;
both types are assisted by the perception of similarity,
but it is indicated that recollection itself— rather than being produced solely by the perception of similarity— is the auxiliary factor.
But the predecessors [hold that] in the phrase "remembering the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārthaṃ smaran*), the suffix denotes proximity to the present;
[that is, one remembers] the meaning of the sentence...
The meaning is "remembering.
And thus, by obtaining that the remembrance of the sentence-meaning is produced by the perception of similarity, they say that its status as an operation (vyāpāra) is obtained.
"Immediately after that," and so forth.

The meaning is that immediately after perceiving the similarity, there arises an analogical cognition (*upamiti*) in the form "the *gavaya* is denotable by the word *gavaya*," wherein the limited property (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is the light category (*laghudharma*) of *gavayatva*.
This is an elliptical indication; it should be understood that there is also an analogy based on the observation of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

The Vaiśeṣikas, however, maintain that from the consideration of similarity and so forth—which are pervaded by being denotable by a word—there is indeed an inference (*anumiti*) of being denotable by a word.
