Therefore, they say that analogy (*upamāna*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This, however, is to be considered: for even without the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is the experience of the cognition of the denotability of a word.
Thus ends the detailed exposition here;
this concludes the section on Analogy (*upamāna*) in the *Prakāśikā*, [titled] *Bālapriyā*.
Regarding "connection by way of occasion" (*avasarasaṅgati*): *occasion* (*avasaras*) is the necessity of speaking [something] once the desire to know the obstructing factor has been resolved;
this refers to inference (*anumāna*).
Because it is accepted by many proponents and because the disagreements of those with few proponents are easily refuted,
the desire to understand first arises in the seeker of knowledge regarding inference itself, and not regarding comparison.
Because it is accepted by few speakers, it is subject to many conflicting interpretations from those who would refute it;
and thus, in the case of inference:

The meaning is that, once the initial desire to know— which acted as an obstacle to the investigation [of inference]— has been satisfied by its definition, the investigation of comparison (*upamāna*) follows immediately after inference due to the logical connection (*saṃgati*) known as "occasion" (*avasara*), which consists in the necessity of what must necessarily be stated next.
The name (*saṃjñā*) is the expressive word,
such as the term "gavaya" and so forth;
the named (*saṃjñin*) is the expressed object, such as the gavaya and so forth.
The cognition having as its object that relation between the two called "power" (śakti)— in the form, for example,
"the gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'"— is analogical knowledge (upamiti).
The knowledge of capacity (*śaktijñāna*) is what is meant by "analogy" (*upamiti*).

This is because other texts state that analogy is a cognition whose instrument is the knowledge of similarity; thus, [the definition] consists in having the knowledge of similarity as its instrument (*sādṛśyajñānakaraṇakatva*).

Intending to show that, although the definition could be formulated as "the state of having the nature of an analogy," it is more appropriate to define it as "possessing the universal (jāti) of being an analogy" due to its relative simplicity, he says: "But the definition...
[1. *pratibandhakībhūteti*]
The phrase "in the examination of analogy" (*upamānanirūpaṇe*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Now, [an objection]: from the root text, it follows that "one perceives the object (*piṇḍa*) similar to a cow while recollecting the meaning of the sentence"—thus, at the outset...

The sequence— first the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), and then the perception of the object (*piṇḍa*) similar to a cow— is thus obtained; however, that is incorrect,
because [recognition occurs] immediately after the perception of the object similar to a cow.

Anticipating the objection that [the cognition arises] from the recollection of the meaning of the extended injunction (*atideśavākya*), he says: "By this," and "in the vicinity of the present" (*vartamānasāmīpye*). [This refers to the rule: "In the vicinity of the present, one may optionally treat [the action] as if it were present."
By this grammatical instruction, the form *smaran* is derived from the present tense (*laṭ*) with the suffix *śatṛ*;
the meaning of *smaran* is "about to remember" (*smariṣyan*).
Thus, since the very sequence is established from the outset— first the perception of the individual gavaya qualified by similarity,

then the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), and finally the analogical cognition (*upamiti*)— the perception of similarity, which has the recollection of the meaning of the statement as its mediating operation, is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of analogical cognition.
The sense is that this is logical.
Now, one might object: let the nature of the resulting cognition (upamiti) be simply "the gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya' because it is similar to a cow."

This is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would entail the failure to establish that "gavaya-ness" is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "gavaya"; to this, he replies:
"[The cognition] has the form 'the gavaya is denotable by the word gavaya'."

If the nature of comparison (*upamiti*) consists in the form "that which is similar to a cow is denotable by the word *gavaya*," then similarity to a cow must be stated as the delimiting property of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*).
This is because, at the stage of the cognition that "similarity to a cow is more complex than *gavayatva*," [the former would not serve as the subject-delimiter].
The point is that a cognition of "being denotable by the word *gavaya*" delimited by similarity to a cow cannot arise;
therefore, it is logical that the nature of the resulting analogical knowledge (*upamiti*) is precisely the form: "A *gavaya* is denotable by the word *gavaya*.
This [point] is also illustrative.

Since the cognition of a word's power (śakti) with respect to a specific delimitor is the cause for a verbal comprehension that has that as its qualifier, from the word "gavaya" there would arise only a cognition of the gavaya qualified by similarity to a cow, and not one qualified by the property of being a gavaya (gavayatva).
And it is experienced that from the word "gavaya," there arises a verbal cognition having precisely "gavaya-ness" as its qualifier;
therefore, [the cognition] "the gavaya... which apprehends the state of being denotable by the word "gavaya" as delimited by gavaya-ness...
It should also be understood that the very cognition "the word *gavaya* denotes this [animal]" is itself the result of comparison (*upamiti*).

Furthermore, comparison arises even through the observation of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); for instance, when by someone the horse is perceived as possessing properties different from those of a cow.

Having heard this, someone at some time and somewhere sees a horse that possesses the properties of a cow; in that case, the perception of an individual object characterized by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is the instrument,
[and] the horse possesses the properties of a cow.
1. Regarding the term *atideśavākya*: a sentence such as "this is like that" is an *atideśavākya*. In the present context, it is the sentence "a *gavaya* is similar to a cow."
The sentence is the sentence of extended application (*atideśavākya*).
Regarding "a mass (*piṇḍa*) similar to a cow": the word *piṇḍa* refers to an individual (*vyakti*) qualified by its form (*ākṛti*).

The meaning is: "the perception of an individual gavaya that has a form similar to a cow. In this context, the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), and the resulting cognition—that "a horse is denotable by the word 'horse'"—is the analogy (*upamiti*); such is the intended sense.
As for the Vaiśeṣikas, they say:
"The gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya' because of its similarity to a cow."
Whatever is not denotable by the word "gavaya" is not similar to a cow;
and this [animal] is similar to a cow.

Therefore, the intended application of inference here is: "This is denotable by the word *gavaya*. And thus, from the *parāmarśa* (reflective judgment) "This possesses similarity to a cow, which is pervaded by being denotable by the word *gavaya*," [the resulting cognition arises].

The cognition "the gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'" is merely an inference (*anumiti*) and not something distinct from it; therefore, comparison (*upamāna*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is the intention of the Vaiśeṣikas.
He refutes that view as follows:
"Even without the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti)" means "in other [works]," that is to say,
in treatises such as the *Kusumāñjali*.
Thus ends the *Bālapriyā*, a commentary on the *Tarkasaṅgrahadīpikāprakāśikā*.
The Chapter on Analogy ///dṛ///
The determination of verbal testimony;
the compendium of logic;
the definition of verbal testimony.
Verbal testimony (śabda) is the statement of a reliable person (āptavākya). A reliable person, moreover, is one who speaks in accordance with reality.
A statement (vākya) is a collection of words (padasamūha).

For example, in the command "Bring the cow," the word "cow" possesses a capacity (*śakti*). This capacity is the divine convention (*īśvara-saṃketa*) by which one understands that this specific meaning is to be derived from this specific word.
Verbal testimony (śabda) is the statement of a reliable person (āpta). A reliable person, however, is one who speaks in accordance with reality.
— Dīpikā.
He defines verbal testimony (*śabda*) with the words "āpta" (reliable). He defines a reliable person (*āpta*) with the words "āptas tu" (but a reliable person...).
[This is from] the *Prakāśikā*.

"It characterizes verbal testimony" means that it determines verbal testimony by way of the logical connection between the dependent and the basis of dependence (*upajīvya-upajīvakatva*). In this context,
since the word being known constitutes the verbal authority (*śabdapramāṇa*), there is no dependence on comparison (*upamāna*) with respect to the word itself.
The connection between the two results— namely, analogy (*upamiti*) and verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*)— should be understood as follows:

for analogy consists precisely in the determination of linguistic capacity (*śakti*), and since this [determination] is that upon which verbal comprehension depends, [the former is the cause of the latter].
The possibility of the relationship between the two results as that of the supported and the supporter exists;
and although such a connection resides in the results themselves, it occurs through a mediated relation consisting in the instrumentality (karaṇatva) whose locus is itself.
Because it rests upon the instruments [of knowledge], the two instruments possess the quality of being the immediate antecedents for the subsequent designation.

However, in the view of the moderns who accept that verbal cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since analogical cognition (*upamiti*) has as its object a word endowed with expressive power (*śaktapada*), [it follows that]...

It should be understood that since verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in that context, and since the status of being produced by analogy (*upamāna*) remains unimpaired there, a connection between the two essential natures (*svarūpa*) is also established.
In the root text, "verbal testimony" (*śabda*) refers to the statement of a reliable person (*āptavākya*).
Thus: "word" (*śabda*) is the indication of the definiendum; "the word as a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa-śabda*) is its meaning;
and "the statement of a reliable person" (*āpta-vākya*) is the definition.
For the expression "one sprinkles with milk" and so forth is a statement uttered by a reliable person (āpta),
but not [the expression] "with fire."

The word "siñcati" (he sprinkles) and so forth lacks the status of being an authoritative source (*āptatva*)— defined as the speaker's quality of speaking in accordance with reality— for the person who utters it.

The refined definition is: a sentence that produces a true cognition whose object is the meaning of the sentence currently under discussion is a word of authority (*pramāṇa-śabda*). Since the knowledge of the sentence-meaning is the cause for the employment of a sentence, the definition is consistent.
This is clear in the *Śabdamaṇi*.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the relationship between the supported and the supporter" in the *Bālapriyā*:
the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is that which is supported.
The word is the cause, and comparison is the effect that depends upon it;
thus, because there exists a causal relationship between the word and comparison, they are connected by way of this causal relation.
The intention is that the definition of verbal testimony (śabda) follows immediately after that of analogy (upamāna).

He establishes this very relationship of the supported and the supporter (upajīvya-upajīvaka-bhāva) with the words beginning "here" (atretyādi). The meaning is as follows: in this context, it is difficult to state a relationship of supported and supporter between two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For the means of valid cognition known as verbal testimony is a word consisting of a sentence that is being cognized; whereas the means of valid cognition known as analogy is the perception of similarity.
However, since the state of being its effect does not exist in the word,
the relationship of cause and effect between the two means of valid cognition consisting of verbal testimony and comparison is not possible.
In this context, the causal relationship exists only between the two cognitions produced by verbal testimony and comparison.
A cognition produced by verbal testimony is *śābdabodha* (verbal comprehension).
The valid cognition produced by comparison (*upamāna*) is the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śakti*), taking such forms as "this is the referent of the word *gavaya*.
Furthermore, the property of being produced by the apprehension of that power resides in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

Thus, it should not be argued that because the relationship consisting of the nature of cause and effect resides in two cognitions (*pramiti*) rather than in two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such a connection is of no use for the presentation of verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*) immediately following the presentation of comparison (*upamāna-pramāṇa*).

This is because the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) residing in the two types of valid cognition consisting of comparison (upamiti) and verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) resides in the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) by virtue of the relation of being the generator of its own locus; here,
"its own" (sva) refers to the causal relation.
The analogical cognition (*upamiti*) and verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) have their own respective substrata;
the instruments of analogy (*upamāna*) and word (*śabda*) possess the quality of being the generators of those cognitions.
Thus, by virtue of the relation of "being the generator of its own substratum," there exists a connection (*saṅgati*) consisting of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

Because it is established upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the investigation of verbal testimony (*śabda*) is logically connected immediately after analogy (*upamāna*); this is according to the opinion of the ancients. However, according to the view of the moderns:

Verbal cognition alone is the verbal means of valid knowledge (*śabda-pramāṇa*). Analogical cognition (*upamiti*) as well—having the form "the *gavaya* is denotable by the word 'gavaya'"—has the *gavaya* as its subject (*dharmin*) and the property of being denotable by the word 'gavaya' as its qualifier (*prakāra*). The word 'gavaya'...

The cognition having the form "the word *gavaya* denotes a *gavaya*," which has the word *gavaya* as its subject (*dharmin*) and the property of denoting a *gavaya* as its qualifier (*prakāra*), is indeed of the nature of verbal knowledge because it has a [proposed] thesis as its object. Furthermore, that [cognition] is produced by the means of valid knowledge known as comparison (*upamāna*), which consists of the cognition of similarity. And thus...

Since comparison (*upamiti*), which consists of the verbal cognition whose form is the means of valid knowledge (*śabda-pramāṇa*), is produced by the means of valid knowledge of comparison (*upamāna-pramāṇa*), which consists of the cognition of similarity, there exists a connection between these two means of valid knowledge in the form of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
"Because of the absence of dependence on comparison" means because of the absence of being produced by the means of valid cognition known as comparison (upamāna).
"The determination of capacity" [is the meaning].
The meaning is "knowledge regarding capacity.
And of that— of the determination of capacity—
it is by way of being the basis for verbal cognition— that is, by way of generating verbal cognition.
The state of being the motivator for the immediate mention of the two instruments (*karaṇa*).

That is to say, regarding the immediate mention of the two instruments— the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— the state of being its motivator is the state of being its cause, [namely, the cause] of that sequential mention.
The meaning is "due to connection.
Regarding the phrase "the statement uttered by a reliable person" (*āptoktavākya*): it refers to that which is the object of an utterance performed by a reliable person (*āpta*).
The meaning is "a statement";
for, according to the root text, an authoritative person (āpta) is one who speaks in accordance with reality.
The meaning obtained is: "one who employs words that produce a cognition whose object is an uncontradicted reality.

This is because of the analysis [of the compound] as "the speaker (vaktā) of that which is real (yathārtha)," where "that which is real" refers to an uncontradicted object exactly as it is. Thus, he is the speaker.
The author of the utterance of a word that produces knowledge having that [object] as its content;

and from the root text, "Verbal testimony (śabda) is the word of a reliable person (āpta)," it follows that [verbal testimony] is the state of being a word which is the object of an utterance by one who is the author of the use of a word that produces knowledge having an uncontradicted object as its content.
It is understood that this is the definition of verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*),
because it is more concise (*lāghava*) in comparison to that [other definition].

With the intention that the definition of a word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-śabda*) must be precisely "being a sentence produced by a cognition whose object is an uncontradicted meaning," he says: "the meaning of the sentence under discussion" (*prakṛta-vākyārtha*).
[Having understood the meaning... *arthaṃ buddhvā*...

According to the maxim "the arrangement of words [precedes]," a word in the form of a sentence is produced precisely by a speaker’s true cognition whose object is the meaning of that sentence; thus the definition is consistent.
Regarding this, he says: "the employment of a sentence.
This is clear in the *Śabdamani*.
In the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*, in the section on verbal testimony (*śabdakhaṇḍa*),

the statement of Gaṅgeśa intended here is: "Verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which is produced by a knowledge of the reality of the object that serves as the cause for its employment."
The Tarkasaṅgraha states:
A sentence (vākya), however, is a collection of words.
Power (*śakti*) is the capacity of a word; it is the convention established by God that "from this word, this meaning is to be understood."
The *Dīpikā* states the definition of a sentence as "vākya" (sentence); it states the definition of a word as "śakta" (significant).
The definition of *śakti*:

*Śakti* is the relationship between a word and its referent that is conducive to the recollection of the meaning. And the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that this [relationship] is a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*).
To refute that [objection], he says: "from this" (*asmāt*).

The meaning is that, just as in the case of names such as *Ḍittha*, in the case of objects such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) as well, it is convention (*saṅketa*) alone that constitutes the expressive power (*śakti*), and not some other distinct entity.
The *Prakāśikā*, in order to introduce the subsequent root-text by way of refuting the Mīmāṃsaka position, states the category of *śakti* (potency) as it is common to that school's view:
"Conducive to the recollection of the meaning":

the meaning is that *śakti* (potency) is the relationship between a word such as "ghaṭa" and its referent, such as the object "jar," which is conducive to the recollection of the meaning that generates verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
Conformity;

here it means being the motivator (prayojaka). And that [status] remains intact even in the case of a relation between a word and its meaning which serves as the delimitor of causality (kāraṇatāvacchedaka).
To exclude other relations between words such as "jar" and their referents, the term "anukūla" (conducive) is intended to specify the desired meaning;
for even though the cognition of another relation may produce the recollection of the object, [it does not constitute the specific causal link required].
This is because [the definition] lacks the property of being a producer of the recollection that generates verbal cognition. Furthermore,
it should be understood that the qualifier "conducive to the recollection of the meaning" is included to exclude things such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), which are common to other factors.

"Another category of entity" (padārthāntara) means: that which possesses the collection of absences of the respective delimiters of those categories of entities. By this, [the property of] being an additional category of entity—
Even if it is not established by another's opinion, there is no contradiction;
for the root [intention] is "this meaning is to be understood from this word," which means "this meaning is the object of the cognition produced by this word."
The meaning is that power (*śakti*) is the will of the Lord (*īśvara*) having such a form;
it is not, however,
a separate category of entity (*padārthāntara*).

Nor should it be argued that power (*śakti*) is something distinct [from God], because there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) to conclude that the nature of God’s knowledge, will, or effort is not itself power;
for since a modern convention is of the nature of a will, if power were also of the nature of a will, [the two would be identical].
The universal relation of cause and effect is possible for the knowledge of conventions and not otherwise; thus, because such a determining factor exists,
it is accepted that intention alone constitutes the expressive power (śakti).
And it is not the case that— by accepting the Lord’s will, which has everything as its object, as being a capacity (śakti)—
the desire to be understood by the word "pot," which has [being] the qualifier [of the pot], exists even in the case of a cloth.

It should not be argued that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the denotability of the word "jar," and that since the desire whose qualifier is being the object of the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā" exists even with respect to the bank (*tīra*), the cognition of it could occur through primary denotation (*śakti*) alone, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the abolition of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is because:

Being the denotation of a particular word consists in possessing a subjecthood (viśeṣyatā) that is determined by a modehood (prakāratā) residing in the cognition produced by that particular word, as intended by the Lord;
or alternatively, it consists in possessing that intention (tadicchā) through the relation of subjecthood determined by such a modehood. And thus:

Since such denotability by the word "pot" does not exist in a cloth, there is no over-extension [of the term]. [Likewise,] the property of being produced by words such as "Gaṅgā" resides in the aspect of the cognition, while the property of being the object of that cognition resides in the aspect of the bank.
The independent manifestation [of the meaning] is accepted as being due to the will of the Lord (Īśvara). And thus,

in a case where there is a fragmented manifestation, since there is an absence of a subject-object relationship (*viṣayatā*) characterized by the relation of the defined and the defining (*nirūpya-nirūpaka-bhāva*), [the cognition occurs] through the relation of the qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) of being the object of cognition, which is itself determined by the qualifier-ness of being produced by the word "Gaṅgā."
The summary is that there is no flaw, because the property of being desired does not exist on the bank.
[This refers to] "that which generates verbal cognition" (*śābdabodhajanaka*). *Bālapriyā*.
Verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is a cognition that apprehends the relation between multiple word-meanings;
its producer is the recollection of those word-meanings.
The relation between words and word-meanings that is conducive to that [cognition] is *śakti* (potency). And being conducive to that consists in being the object of the cognition that generates it.

And thus, for one who possesses knowledge of the relationship between a word and its referent, it is precisely that person who, through the cognition of the words constituting a sentence, comes to have the recollection of their respective referents;
for the cognition of a word [is the cause].

In accordance with the principle that "the cognition of one related member causes the recollection of the other related member," it generates the recollection of the word-meaning; for example, just as between an elephant and its keeper— who were previously perceived as being related—
there subsequently occurs, upon the sight of one related member (the keeper), the recollection of the other (the elephant).

Just as there occurs a recollection of that which is related to the form of an elephant, so too, one who previously knows the relationship between a word and its referent is able to recall the other related entity in the form of the referent when there is knowledge of one related entity in the form of the word. And thus:

The sequence intended here is this: from the knowledge of a word, assisted by the knowledge of its relation [to its meaning], there arises the recollection of the word-meaning; from that, verbal cognition (śābdabodha) follows. Now, one might object:

In the sentence from the *Dīpikā*, "Power (*śakti*) is the relationship between a word and its referent that is conducive to the recollection of meaning," if the word "conducive" (*anukūla*) means "cause," then even though the cognition of the relationship between a word and its referent is the generator of the recollection of meaning;
Since the relationship between a word and its meaning lacks the capacity to produce the recollection of the meaning, it would be impossible [for it to be the cause]; therefore, he says:
"In this context, being conducive constitutes causality. And this causality is common to both the direct cause and that which delimits the status of a cause.
The phrase "knowledge of the relationship between word and meaning" means a cognition qualified by a relation through the relation of objectivity (*viṣayitā*).
Thus, it is the cause of the recollection of meaning.
[It is] the cognition qualified by a relation.

In that case, since it exists by way of the relation of being the object (*viṣayitā*), the status of the word-meaning relation as the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatva*) remains unimpaired. Regarding the cause...
Because only that which already exists can serve as a delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for causality;

thus, since the relationship between a word and its referent (*padapadārthasambandha*) is the cause of the recollection of the meaning, it is possible for it to be conducive to that [recollection]—this is the intended sense. And so:

The definition of *śakti* (denotative power) is established as: being a relation between a word and its meaning, which serves as the cause for the recollection of the meaning that generates verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), while satisfying the condition of being the basis for such recollection.
In this regard, if the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) were not included [in the definition],...
There is over-extension [of the definition] to the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth,
because they, being causes with respect to general effects, are also causes with respect to the recollection of an object.
To exclude that [over-extension], the qualificandum (viśeṣya) is included.
Since there is no relation between words and word-meanings in the case of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) and so forth, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).
If the qualifier were not included, [the definition would apply] to the word "jar" and its meaning, which consists of the object possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth.
There would be over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case regarding the temporal (kālika) relation and so forth;
therefore, a qualification is added to exclude that.
For although the temporal relation between the word "jar" and its referent somehow serves as a condition conducive to the recollection of the meaning, [it is not the intended relation].
That recollection does not possess the capacity to produce verbal cognition; therefore,
because the property of being conducive to the recollection of an object that produces verbal cognition is absent in relation to the temporal connection (*kālika-sambandha*),
there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
This is stated by the passage beginning with "the word 'pot' and so forth.
The phrase "conducive to the intended meaning" means that it is conducive to the recollection that generates verbal cognition.

From the *Dīpikā*, which states "and that [power] is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*)," the meaning obtained is that power is a category distinct from the seven established categories; if this were the case, there would be a contradiction with the Nyāya school's doctrine.
Because the state of being something over and above the established categories is unestablished;
and thus, when a Mīmāṃsaka attempts to prove that [the self] to a Naiyāyika.
Considering that the Naiyāyika might raise the objection of *aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva* (the fault of having an unestablished qualification), [the author] explains:

"The meaning is 'possessing the collection of absences of the respective delimiters of the categories'. This refers to that which possesses the aggregate composed of those absences of substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth, each of which is established individually in substances and the other categories.
The meaning is "power" (śakti). "Even though it is not established in other systems" means even though it is not established in the system of the Naiyāyikas.
This is the meaning. There is no contradiction—that is, no inconsistency.
In the phrase "from this word" (*asmāt padāt*), the meaning of the ablative case is "being produced" (*janyatvam*).
Its connection [is] with the understanding of the meaning of the element *budha*;
the meaning of the suffix *ṇyat* is the state of being fit for slaughter (*vaṣīyatva*).

And thus, it is understood that "this is the meaning which is the object of the cognition produced by this word. This is what [the author] states with the words "of the root" and "of the modern convention," and so forth.

One must accept that from words such as "Dittha," there arises the cognition of a specific individual, due to the apprehension of a convention in the form of a modern intention, characterized by the thought: "By this word 'Dittha' and so forth, this particular meaning is to be understood."

It must be stated that from words such as "pot," the cognition of the pot and so forth arises through the apprehension of a convention in the form of the Lord’s will, characterized by the thought: "This meaning is to be understood from this word."

And the property of being a convention (*saṅketatva*) is a common characteristic of both a contemporary desire and the desire of God, consisting in the mode of "being that which is to be understood by this or that word.
Thus, if the desire of God constitutes *śakti* (denotative power),...

With respect to verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), there is only one kind of causal efficacy (*kāraṇatva*), namely, by way of being a cognition whose object is delimited by the convention common to both [the speaker and the hearer].
This applies to that which has as its qualifier the state of being the object of a cognition produced by this or that word.

If, however, the power (śakti) resides in God’s knowledge or God’s effort, then in the case of words such as "Ḍittha," verbal comprehension arises from the knowledge of the convention in the form of a desire; whereas in the case of words such as "jar" (ghaṭa),
it arises from the knowledge of that power which consists of God’s knowledge or God’s effort.

Since many causal relations (kāryakāraṇabhāva) would have to be postulated in this way regarding verbal cognition (śābdabodha), there is complexity (gaurava). Therefore, the meaning is that the power (śakti) is simply the will of God (īśvarecchā).
This is the deciding factor (vinigamaka); [it is] the principle of exclusion (vinigamanā).
This means that the reasoning provided for either of the two positions regarding the two terms [is as follows]:
"And not because of the Lord's will," and so forth. It is accepted that the will of the Lord has all things as its object and is unitary.
If that were the capacity (śakti), then it would follow that even cloth and other such things possess the status of being denotable by the word "pot" and so forth. To explain:

the denotability of the word "pot" consists in its possessing the divine will which has as its qualifier the state of being the object of a cognition produced by the word "pot," related [to that cognition] by the relation of qualificandness (viśeṣyatā).

It must be stated: in the divine will (*īśvarecchā*) whose form is "Let the pot be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'pot'," the pot is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and being the object of the cognition produced by the word 'pot' is the qualifier (*prakāra*).
[This refers to] the divine will which has as its qualifier the state of being the object of the cognition produced by the word 'pot'.

Because existence [of the denotation] resides in the jar through the relation of the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) as specified by itself, the jar possesses the status of being the denotatum (śakyatva) of the word "jar.
And because the will of God is unitary, it [is established] by that [will].

One must also accept that [the mental resolution] takes such forms as, "Let the cloth be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'cloth'," and "Let the wall be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'wall,'" and so forth. Likewise...

Since even a cloth or the like would be the qualificandum (viśeṣya) with respect to God’s will, and since God’s will— characterized by having the state of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "jar" as its qualifier— exists in a cloth or the like through the relation of qualificandum-ness (viśeṣyatā-sambandha),
it would follow that a cloth or the like is also denotable by the word "jar. Thus...

Since it must also be stated that God’s will has the form: "Let the stream be the object of the cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā*," and "Let the bank be the object of the cognition produced by the word *tīra*," [the property of] being the object of the cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā* exists there [in the stream].

The mode (*prakāra*) is "bank" (*tīra*), which is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*). Since the divine will— which has as its object the state of being the content of the cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā*— exists in the bank as well, by virtue of the relation of "qualificandum-ness" (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*), the bank too is denotable (*vācya*) by the word *gaṅgā*.

The intention of the objection is that since the understanding of the bank can arise from the word *gaṅgā* through its primary power (*śakti*) alone, the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *gaṅgā* for the bank would not be necessary, and thus the very possibility of secondary indication would be undermined.
"Of that desire which has as its qualifier the state of being the object of a cognition produced by the word 'jar'";
this means "of the desire of God which has as its qualifier the state of being the object of a cognition generated by the word 'jar'.
This is because [the definition] begins with "the state of being denotable by that word," and so forth.

The denotability (*vācyatva*) of a word is not the state of possessing a divine will (*īśvarecchā*) that has as its qualifier the status of being an object of a cognition produced by that word, related [to that cognition] through the relation of qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*),
such that the two aforementioned defects would arise; rather, it is as follows:

It is either the possession of that objective predication (viśeṣyatā) which is determined by the subject-predication (prakāratā) residing in the state of being the object of the cognition produced by that word, and which is itself determined by the will of God;

or it is the possession of the will of God through the relation of objective predication as determined by the subject-predication residing in the state of being the object of the cognition produced by that word.
The state of being the denotation of that word [is as follows]:
since the will of God (īśvarecchā) is unitary, when everything is both the qualificand and the qualifier within it,
there exists a subjecthood (viśeṣyatā) residing in each respective object, belonging to the will of God.
It becomes distinct and different according to the difference in its modes;
and thus, "let the pot be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'pot'."

The very state of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatā) residing in the pot, which is determined by the will of the Lord in the form "Let the pot be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'paṭa'," is itself determined by the modehood (prakāratā) residing in the state of being the object of the cognition produced by the word 'ghaṭa'.

The qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) does not terminate in the cloth, because the Lord’s will does not encompass the state of being the object of a cognition produced by the word "pot" with respect to the portion that is the cloth. Therefore...

Since the Lord's intention (*īśvarecchā*)— as characterized by the relation of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by the mode (*prakāratā*) residing in "being the object of the cognition produced by the word *ghaṭa*"— exists only with respect to the jar (*ghaṭa*), only the jar possesses the status of being denoted by the word *ghaṭa*, and not cloth (*paṭa*) or other things. Likewise, in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the intention is] "let there be a cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā* [with respect to the bank]."
It is precisely the nature of God’s will that is accepted as having the form: "Let the bank be the object of the word *bodha* (i.e., the meaning of the word *gaṅgā*).

[This is] qualified by the qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the bank, which is itself determined by the mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the property of being produced by the word *gaṅgā*.

The denotability (vācyatva) of the word "Gaṅgā" consists precisely in its being possessed by the will of God (īśvarecchā), through the relation of being the qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) as determined by the objectness (viṣayatva) which is itself determined by the modehood (prakāratā) residing in the ultimate object (bodhaniṣṭha).
In the divine will (*īśvarecchā*), which consists of the previously demonstrated state of being disjoined (*viśakalitabhāna*),

there is no property of being qualified by the modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in the state of being produced by the word "Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāpadajanyatva*), with respect to the modehood residing in the cognition (*bodha*).

The intended meaning is that, because the possession of God’s will— connected [to the word] as previously stated— is absent in the bank, the bank does not possess the status of being the denotation (*vācyatva*) of the word "Ganges"; therefore,
one must accept figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "Ganges" with respect to the bank, and thus there is no consequence of the total abolition of figurative indication.
"Of such a thing being the denotation of the word 'jar'" means:

of the state of being the denotation of the word 'jar', which consists in the possession by God's will of a qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) determined by a mode-ness (prakāratā) residing in the state of being the object of the cognition produced by the word 'jar'.
There is no over-extension—that is, there is no contingency of a cloth being denotable by the word "pot. [Objection:
But surely, where [there is a relation] by virtue of *śakti*...
The comprehension of word-meanings occurs only where there is the will of God;
however, where comprehension arises through indication (lakṣaṇā), the will of God is not necessary.

Because it is only the mere possibility of a relation that is required; and thus, [one may intend]: "Let there be a cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā*, and let the bank be the object of that cognition."

Thus, the postulation of a desire characterized by such a form [of cognition] is futile. Furthermore, the claim that the riverbank (*tīra*) is the denoted meaning (*vācyatva*) of the word "Ganges" is refuted precisely by the method previously stated;
for it is established that the riverbank is the indicated meaning (*lakṣyatva*) of the word "Ganges" solely through its connection with the flow, which is the primary denoted meaning. Therefore...
He said: "In brief.
Because the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) is the cause with respect to the general effect, the will of God [is also the cause] for the cognition directed toward the riverbank from the word "Gaṅgā."
It must be stated that this is the cause.

In that regard, when the inquiry arises as to what form the will of God takes as the cause, [it is seen that] because the conventional usage of the word "Gaṅgā" to denote a riverbank and the like does not exist, [the will of God is the cause].

The meaning is that, as has been stated, since it must necessarily be asserted that the very will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*) is the cause of the diverse manifestations [of phenomena], [this is the case].
— *Dīpikā*

Regarding the establishment of a specific capacity: is it not the case that the word-potency (*śakti*) of words such as "cow" resides in the universal (*jāti*) alone, since the universal functions as the qualifier?
Because the individual is what presents itself first;

as for the acquisition of the individual, some say it occurs through implication (*ākṣepa*). That is not correct—for in all cases such as "Bring the cow," in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), the bringing and so forth apply only to the individual.
Because,
according to the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the capacity [of a word] is postulated only for an individual qualified by its genus (*jāti*).
In order to establish that the expressive power resides in the qualified [object], he introduces and refutes the Mīmāṃsaka position with the words "gavādi" (cow,
etc.). Since it is impossible to apprehend a qualified object without first apprehending the genus (*jāti*) which serves as its qualifier, [the power must reside] in the qualified.
The postulation of a linguistic capacity (śakti) for the individual is not possible;

therefore, since the apprehension of the universal (jāti) is required first, it is more appropriate to postulate the capacity for the universal alone due to parsimony (lāghava). Thus he says: "by way of being a qualifier" (viśeṣaṇatayā).
"Because it is presented first" means because it is understood prior to the apprehension of the qualified [object].
To the question, "How then is the individual (vyakti) obtained?", he says: "The individual... and so forth.
"By implication" means by the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
"Only in the case of the manifest" means that it is possible only there.

It should also be understood that even in the state of emptiness regarding non-arising and reconnection (*anupapatti-pratisandhāna-śūnyatā*), the manifestation of the individual (*vyakti*) is established by experience.
Regarding the phrase "only in the qualified individual" (*viśiṣṭavyaktāveva*), the word "only" (*eva*) [excludes other possibilities].
This is the exclusion of the hypothesis of a universal alone.
Here, this should be understood: a capacity must be postulated for all three—the universal, its specific relation (vaiśiṣṭya), and its substratum.

This is because the relation between two word-meanings alone is obtainable through the co-occurrence of two words; therefore, it is impossible for anything else that cannot be so established to appear in verbal cognition.
However, the Neo-Naiyāyikas [hold as follows]:
Just as the delimitor of the indicated (lakṣyatāvacchedaka) appears in verbal cognition merely through the apprehension of its being the delimitor of the indicated,

so too the delimitor of the denotable (śakyatāvacchedaka) can appear in verbal cognition merely through the apprehension of its being the delimitor of the denotable; therefore, there is no [separate] power (śakti) residing in the delimitor of the denotable.
They say it must be postulated; [the author of the *Bālapriyā*] [asserts] that the power resides in the qualified [object].
"To establish" means to determine the expressive power (*śakti*) of words such as "cow" with respect to individuals qualified by universals such as "cowness."
Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of apprehending the qualified":

since knowledge of the qualifier is a cause for a cognition whose object is a qualified entity, it is necessary that there be prior knowledge of the qualifier— in this case, the nature of "cowness"— before there can be knowledge of an individual qualified by cowness.

And thus, because it is the first to present itself and for the sake of parsimony, it is appropriate to postulate the expressive power (śakti) in the genus alone, and not in the individual qualified by that genus; this is the intended meaning.
"In the genus alone":
by the particle *eva*, the capacity [of the word] is excluded from individuals.
"Because of parsimony" (*lāghavāt*): [this refers to the principle that the postulation of fewer entities is preferable].
The sense is that this is because individuals are infinite while the genus is unitary.
Now, if it is granted that the word-potency resides in the genus, [then] from words such as "cow" (*gavādi*),...

There would be cognition of the genus *gotva* (cowness) alone, and not of the individual, because that is what is denoted by the word "cow" (*go*). If one were to admit that even that which is not denoted by the word "cow" is cognized from it, then [the word] "cow"...
With the intention that there would be cognition even of a jar and so forth, he raises an objection: "How then?
This means [the answer is] "by means of the pramāṇa of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
[This refers to] the knowledge whose object is the universal (jāti).

The meaning is this: because of the rule that [a word] must have an individual as its object, the manifestation of a universal without the manifestation of an individual is untenable; thus, through the presentation of the individual—which is produced by the means of knowledge known as *arthāpatti* (presumption) consisting in the recognition of such untenability—the individual manifests in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) generated by the word "cow."
This is an illustration.

Even though the word *go* lacks primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the individual cow (*govyakti*), metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted [in its case]. Therefore, it should also be understood that the manifestation of the individual occurs in verbal cognition through metaphorical indication. By this—

Even in the absence of a word denoting a specific individual cow, if one accepts that the specific cow presented by the means of valid cognition *arthāpatti* (presumption) appears in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*),
then [by parity of reasoning] a jar or other object— though not presented by a word and even if presented by perception or other means— would also appear in verbal cognition.
The claim that there is an appearance [of universals] is rejected;
for there is no connection with a non-occurrent [universal],
since there is no manifestation of the individual.

Since the manifestation of the individual (vyakti) is established by experience even at a time devoid of the recollection of the impossibility of its manifestation in the form "the manifestation of the genus is untenable," the manifestation of the individual does not arise from the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
This is because the manifestation of the individual is established by experience even at a time devoid of the recollection of the impossibility of its logical concomitance (anvaya).
The meaning is that there is no manifestation of the individual through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
"The exclusion of the assumption of a mere universal" means the exclusion of the assumption of a linguistic potency (*śakti*) in a mere universal. Now, [one might object]:
If the expressive power (śakti) is postulated for the individual as qualified by the universal,

then since there is no expressive power either in the universal itself or in the relation— which is of the nature of inherence (samavāya)— between the universal and the individual, how could there be a cognition produced by the word "cow"?
The manifestation of the genus "cowness" and the inherence of cowness is possible;
for although the manifestation of cowness occurs in some way because it is the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*), [it is still possible].
How can there be a manifestation of inherence (*samavāya*), which is not a delimitor of possibility?
Nor should it be said that its manifestation occurs through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), for [expectancy] belongs to both.
Because the relation between the two meanings presented by the two words— or rather, the relation between the two meanings presented by the two powers—
is manifested by the expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) consisting of co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra), [this applies] to the word-meanings and their respective delimiters.
Anticipating the objection that it is untenable for the relation to be manifested by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), he says: "In this regard, the following should be understood," and so forth.
And thus, the word "pot" has a single [denotative] power with respect to the three—potness, inherence, and the pot.
The meaning is that there is such a capacity; thus, because it is possible [to denote them], the manifestation of all three in the cognition produced by the word "pot" is feasible.
[This refers to] "only the relation between two word-meanings."

What is intended by the term "relation between two word-meanings" (padārthadvayasambandha) is either the relation between two meanings presented by two words, or the relation between two meanings presented by a single word through two distinct functions (vṛtti).
By the particle *eva*, the relation between the capacity [to denote] and the delimitor of that capacity is excluded;
this is because [the relation] is obtainable through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the two words.
The meaning is: "by way of being expressed through expectancy.
Regarding the phrase "of another that is impossible":
it means [that which is] unobtainable through expectancy.

The meaning is that of the relation, which is devoid of being a denotable object (*śakyatva*), and of the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), such as the universal "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth.
"The moderns, however," means as follows:
In cases such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," even though the word *gaṅgā* is accepted as having secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the bank,
and even though there is no secondary signification with respect to "bank-ness" (*tīratva*), because "bank-ness" is the delimitor of the object of secondary signification (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*),

[the required cognition] arises merely from a cognition whose qualifier is the state of being the delimitor of the object of secondary signification, in the form: "bank-ness is the delimitor of the object of secondary signification."
Just as the state of being a "bank" (tīratva), even though it is not directly denotable, appears in verbal cognition,
so too does "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) appear [in the cognition of a pot], despite the absence of a direct denotative power (śakti) for it.

The point is that since the manifestation of "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) from the word "pot" is possible through the mere knowledge characterized by the mode of "being the delimitor of denotability" (*śakyatāvacchedakatva-prakāraka-jñāna*), it is unnecessary to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in the delimitor of denotability, such as the pot itself.

In this regard, some [object]: "If one does not accept a primary denotative power (śakti) in the delimitor of denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka), then from the word 'earth' (pṛthivī), at one time there would be comprehension by way of being a substance distinct from the eight substances, at another time by way of possessing odor, and at yet another time by way of being earth-ness."

And there would be the undesirable consequence of a verbal cognition [of the following]: "Earth is a substance other than the eight substances," just as one might have the cognition "Earth is the denotatum of the word 'earth'."

Because it is possible to grasp the word-potency (*śakti*) in the form "the earth-word [denotes] that which possesses fragrance," [this applies] to that which is delimited by the property of being a river-bank (*tīratva*).

Just as the cognition of the bank as "bank-ness" arises from the knowledge of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) consisting in the relation that is the capacity of the word *gaṅgā*, and the cognition of the bank as "Gaṅgā-bank-ness" arises from the knowledge of indication of the word *gaṅgā* with respect to that which is delimited by Gaṅgā-bank-ness.

And likewise, just as there is no such rule that verbal cognition must have as its object only that which is delimited by some single property through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), so too [is it here].

Even if there were an understanding of the denotable object (*śakyārtha*), there would be no restriction [regarding the specific mode of cognition]. However, if one accepts that the power (*śakti*) resides in the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*),
then the restriction— that from the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*) there arises a verbal cognition precisely as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*)— is logically established.

Therefore, they say that the denotative power (śakti) must also be admitted in the delimitor of capability (śakyatāvacchedaka). This is to be considered; for [the question remains] regarding the specific property under which a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) is desired to occur.

Only the knowledge of the word's power (śakti) as having as its qualifier the property of being the delimiting factor of the capacity for that specific property-bearer is the cause of such verbal cognition;
and the delimiting factor of the capacity is, in all cases, [the universal].
A property that is possible, neither too narrow nor too broad, is indeed the simpler one;
for when a simpler property is possible as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), a more complex property is not.

This is because the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) is not accepted. Consequently, since the property of being a substance distinct from the eight [other] substances is more complex than the property of earthness (*pṛthivītva*), it cannot serve as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

Therefore, in that case, the cognition of the delimitor of capability cannot be of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*); thus, it does not serve as the cause for a verbal cognition that is itself valid.
However, in the case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), [the situation is different].

Since the cognition of indication (*lakṣaṇājñāna*) in the form "the bank of the Gaṅgā possesses a connection with the current"— just like the cognition in the form "the bank possesses a connection with the current"— is established by experience,
there must also be, even in the case of the Guru, a cognition of the delimitor of the indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedakatva*) in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*).
It is accepted as the cause of verbal cognition.

And thus, in the case of denotation (*śakti*), from the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*), the cognition of earth occurs by means of the denotative power precisely through the universal of earthness (*pṛthivītva*).

However, there is no such rule that [the cognition] must be by way of the property of being a substance distinct from the eight substances; and since it is established that in cases of indication (lakṣaṇā), there is no fixed rule— where at one time there is cognition by way of "bankness" (tīratva) and at another time by way of "being the bank of the Gaṅgā" (gaṅgātīratva)— it follows that there is no indication with respect to the delimitor of the indicated (lakṣyatāvacchedaka).
Likewise, the intention of the moderns is that there is no denotative power (śakti) even in the delimitor of denotability (śakyatāvacchedaka).

All of this [is explained] by the mere apprehension of being the delimitor of the denotable (lakṣyatāvacchedakatva) and the mere apprehension of being the delimitor of denotability (śakyatāvacchedakatva).
It should be understood that this is indicated by the two words;
the *Dīpikā* is the exposition of the means for grasping the word-potency (*śakti*).
And the apprehension of the word's power [to denote its meaning] occurs through the linguistic usage of elders; for instance,
a child desiring to acquire proficiency [hears the command] "Bring the cow."

Immediately after hearing the words of the senior elder, having observed the activity of the middle-aged elder and seen the bringing of the cow, and having determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the cognition producing the activity of the middle-aged elder was generated by the sentence, [the child understands] "Bring the horse,"...

Through the process of insertion and deletion in other sentences such as "Bind the cow" (gāṃ badhāna), the word *go* has its expressive power (*śakti*) residing in that which is qualified by cowness (*gotva*), and the word *aśva* [has its expressive power residing in that which is qualified by horseness].

The linguistic convention is acquired such that the expressive power resides in that which is qualified by horsehood; and this is the apprehension of the expressive power as explained in the *Prakāśikā*.
"By means of the linguistic usage of elders" (vṛddhavyavahāreṇa):
the meaning is that the apprehension of the word's expressive power (śaktigraha) is possible through the linguistic usage of elders and so forth;
by "and so forth" (ādi), grammar and other such means are included. For this very reason...
The apprehension of the expressive power of a sentence [is derived] from grammar, comparison, lexicons, the statements of authoritative persons,
and linguistic usage.
The elders say that [the meaning] is understood from the remainder through the proximity of the established word.
Thus, the statement of the learned is consistent:
the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of bases (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and so forth, arises from grammar; [and] from analogy (*upamāna*).
The apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*), however, has been shown below.

From the lexicon [entry]: "Also *ekadanta*, *heramba*, *lambodara*, and *gajānana*," it follows that words such as *ekadanta* and others have the meaning that they possess the power (*śakta*) with respect to the entity qualified by the nature of Gaṇeśa.
The apprehension of the denotative power (śaktigraha) resides in that which is qualified by the state of being Gaṇeśa.
In that case, since words such as "Ekadanta" and so forth constitute the referents of the words, their distinctness allows for the formation of a *dvandva* compound.
The apprehension of the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *pika* with respect to the cuckoo occurs through the authoritative statement (*āptavākya*): "The *kokila* is denoted by the word *pika*.
Regarding the apprehension of power through usage (*vyavahāra*):
He provides the justification: "one who desires to learn" (*vyutpitsuḥ*);
this means one who possesses the desire to grasp the word-potency (*śakti*). "From the elder" (*uttamavṛddhāt*)—[and so forth].
"By the instigating elder" means [the elder who prompts the action];
"of the middle-aged elder" means [the elder who is the object] of the instigation.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "having seen the bringing of the cow and having perceived [the cause] by means of inference" (*upalabhya*).
The meaning of *upalabhya* here is "having inferred. [The inference is:
"This action is preceded by an effort."
The application of the inference should be understood as follows: "Because it possesses a distinct action, like its own [inherent] action.

Regarding the cognition that generates activity—that is, the cognition of bringing the cow which generates the effort directed toward bringing the cow—the capacity of the sentence for a specific meaning need not be postulated.
Because such a meaning is obtainable through syntactic co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra),
for it is said that "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained by other means."
He states his intention regarding the logical principle with the words "Bring the horse," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "by means of insertion and deletion" (*āvāpodvāpābhyām*): *āvāpa* means inclusion (*saṅgraha*).
Udvāpa means abandonment;
it is that which is derived [from a root], thus it is the basis of derivation (vyutpatti).
The meaning is that [it] exists.

This is because of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*); for example, in the case of "the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) consists of barley," the word "barley" [is understood] from the usage of the Āryas.
When there is doubt as to whether [the word] denotes something distinguished by long awns or denotes the *priyaṅgu* plant due to the usage of the Mlecchas—
In spring, the shedding of leaves occurs for all crops,
yet they remain rejoicing.
From the completion of the sentence, "barley [is] characterized by its awns," the determination of the word's denotation is established as being qualified by long awns.
In the case of *priyaṅgu*, however, the usage arises from a confusion with the root *śak* (to be able).
As stated in the *Vivaraṇa*:
"In the expression ‘it cooks’ (*pacati*), which means ‘it performs cooking’ (*pākaṃ karoti*), [the action is expressed] by the verb *karoti*, which has the sense of effort (*yatna*)."
From the explanation of all verbal roots, the apprehension of the expressive power (śakti) of a verbal root resides in that which is qualified by effort (yatna).

The apprehension of the word's power (śakti), however, through the proximity of well-known words, will become clear from the subsequent passage beginning with "the bee [is on] the blossomed lotus"; therefore, enough of this prolixity.
— *Bālapriyā*

Regarding the phrase "by means of the usage of elders" (*vṛddhavyavahāreṇa*): the usage (*vyavahāra*) of two elders— meaning their activity (*pravṛtti*) and the employment of words (*śabdaprayoga*)— is what constitutes the "usage of elders."

Regarding the phrase "of roots, suffixes, and so forth": through grammatical rules such as "√bhū [is used] in the sense of existence" (*bhū sattāyām*), one acquires the grasp of the expressive power (*śakti*) of roots like *bhū* with respect to meanings such as existence.

The apprehension of the specific meaning of an affix— such as that [the *l*-suffixes denote] both the object and, in the case of intransitive verbs, the state (*bhāva*)— is derived from grammar, as in the rule "laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ," and so forth;
this has been shown below.
Thus [it is said]. Previously, the section on analogy (*upamāna*) was presented.
Now, one might object: in lexicons such as "Even Ekadanta and Heramba," words like *ekadanta* and *heramba* appear as synonyms.
How can there be a *dvandva* compound when [the members] express a single meaning?

Since it is accepted that a *dvandva* compound occurs only when there is a difference in the referents of the words (*padārtha*), he says in response: "In that case, *ekadanta* and so forth. These words...
For a lexicon (kośa) exists indeed to make known that these words convey such meanings;
the point is that therein words such as *ekadanta* and others denote precisely those objects whose sequence of phonemes corresponds to them.
In the *Dīpikā*,
[it says] "a child desiring to acquire proficiency," and so forth.
A certain child [wonders] regarding which object the words "cow" and so on [denote].
He desires to know what "capacity" (śakti) is. Once, when a certain instigator, such as a teacher,
says to a disciple, "Bring the cow," the disciple hears that sentence and [performs] the bringing of the cow.
He perceives [the cow]; from that, he infers the effort which is the cause of the action consisting of bringing the cow;
thereafter, [he infers] the effort directed toward some specific action.

Because the knowledge regarding that action is the cause [of the action], one determines through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the sentence uttered by the prompting elder is itself the cause of such knowledge; and thus,
the prompting elder's knowledge has as its object the bringing of the cow as its object.
One determines that [the cognition] is produced by the sentence "Bring the cow," because in that case,

without the word *go* having a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to that which is qualified by cowness (*gotva*), it would be impossible for the meaning of the word *go* to be construed as the object (*karmatva*).

The point is that the term *vyavahāra* (linguistic usage) serves as the means for grasping word-meaning (*śakti*) by way of determining that "the word *go* has its denotative power (*śakti*) in that which is qualified by cowness (*gotva*).
The word *pravṛtti* refers to volitional effort (*prayatna*).

To the objection that— since the knowledge regarding the bringing of a cow, which generates activity, is produced by the sentence, the capacity for the bringing of the cow as its object should be attributed to the sentence itself— the author replies with the words "of the sentence" (*vākyasya*) in the *Prakāśikā*.
"In a qualified object" means in the sentence-meaning consisting of the act of bringing qualified by the state of having "cow" as its object. And thus,
[it refers to] the sentence-meaning in the form of a relation among the meanings presented by the powers of the individual words.

The point is that since the manifestation [of meaning] is established through the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consisting in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) alone, there is no expressive power (*śakti*) in the sentence-meaning.

Furthermore, if one were to accept that the word *go* has its expressive power in a cow as connected with "bringing" (*ānayana*), then the understanding of such a cow would also be established in the case of the sentence "Bind the cow" (*gāṃ badhāna*).

If the word *ānaya* (bring) were thus accepted as having the power to denote the act of bringing with "cow" as its object, then there would be the undesirable consequence of that same meaning being understood even in the sentence "Bring the horse" (*aśvam ānaya*).
Therefore, [the denotation of] the word *go*...

Through the processes of insertion and deletion (āvāpodvāpa), it is firmly established that the word "bring" has a denotative power (śakti) with respect to that which is qualified by "cowness," and [the verb] has a power with respect to that which is qualified by "bringing-ness";
furthermore, the mutual connection between the action and its factors (kriyākāraka) is obtainable through co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra).
The intended meaning is precisely this: the purpose of presenting the insertion and deletion [of words] is that it becomes a basis for linguistic proficiency;
that is to say, it results in the ascertainment of the expressive power [of words].

Regarding "as in the case of *vivaraṇa*": *vivaraṇa* (explanation) is the statement of a meaning by means of another word having that same meaning. [For example: "The apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigrahaṃ*)..."

Having considered that even the use of words preceded by the pointing of a finger and so forth— which were not mentioned in the verses beginning with "grammar and comparison"— also serve to apprehend linguistic capacity (*śakti*), he said: "Enough of this prolixity."
The exposition that words also possess the capacity to denote established entities (*siddha*).

If it is argued that, because linguistic usage everywhere pertains to what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), the acquisition of meaning (*vyutpatti*) occurs only with respect to sentences whose purport is what is to be accomplished and not with respect to those whose purport is an established fact (*siddha*)— we say no. This is because [such understanding occurs] even in cases such as, "In Kāśī, the king Tribhuvanatilaka resides."

Even when [the meaning] is already established, we observe the acquisition of the word-meaning for "bee" and so forth through common usage— as in the expression "the bee sits upon the blooming lotus"— and through the co-occurrence with well-known words, even when [the referent] is already established.
(Prakāśikā)
The construction is: "because conventional usage is intent upon the effect.
And as for this being intent upon the effect:
The meaning is the intentionality toward an action such as bringing [an object], which is to be accomplished through effort (*kṛti*).
"Vyutpatti" refers to the apprehension of linguistic capacity (*śaktigraha*).
He clarifies what is excluded by stating, "not established" (*na siddha*).

"Even when [the meaning] is established, [it is known] from linguistic usage. Thus, even when the [meaning] is established, the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śakti*) is necessarily required;
otherwise, the verbal cognition established by experience therein [could not occur].
The sense is that this would lead to the consequence of denial (*apalāpa*). Even though [the meaning] is established, the apprehension of the word's expressive power (*śaktigraha*) [is required].
In this context, the word *siddha* refers to that which is distinct from action. [This concludes] the *Dīpikā*:
the definition of *lakṣaṇa*.
Indication (lakṣaṇā) is also a function of words;
indication is the relationship with that which is directly denotable (śakya).

In the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," since the bank is apprehended through the very relationship with the flow that is denoted by the word *gaṅgā*, a primary denotative power (*śakti*) is not postulated for the bank as well; this is because, in cases such as *saindhava*, there is no mutual relationship between salt and horse.
The postulation of various powers.
Indication (lakṣaṇā) is threefold: indicative exclusion (jahallakṣaṇā), [ajahallakṣaṇā, and jahadajahallakṣaṇā].
[Indication] is of two kinds: non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) and abandoning-and-non-abandoning indication (*jahadajahallakṣaṇā*).
Where there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the primary meaning (*vācyārtha*), there is abandoning indication (*jahallakṣaṇā*).
As in the expression "the beds cry out," where the literal meaning is also included, there is the *ajahat* [lakṣaṇā];
as in "those with umbrellas are going," where...

When there is a connection with one part [of the referent] by means of abandoning one part of the expressed meaning, that is the "partially abandoning and partially not abandoning" (jahadajahat) [mode].
For example: "That thou art" (tattvamasi).
Even on the shore of the Prakāśikā, potency is not to be postulated.
The words "of the word *gaṅgā*" are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Now, one might object: in that case, the polysemy of words such as *saindhava* would be untenable.
Since it could be maintained that there is primary denotation (*śakti*) in one case and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in another, he says: "In the case of *saindhava* and so forth.
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), words such as *hari* are included.
"Because of the absence of a relation" means because of the absence of a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.
This is an elliptical indication [of the following point]: regarding two well-known objects, in what [context] would there be a definition?
Since there is no decisive factor [to prefer one over the other], it is necessary to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*) for both; thus,
in the case of "the platforms" (*mañcāḥ*), the word "platform" (*mañca*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote the person standing on the platform.
The meaning is that there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the act of shouting.
Regarding the phrase "of the expressed meaning also" (*vācyārthasyāpi*), the word "also" (*api*)...
The Compendium of Objects of Reference:
"Those with umbrellas" refers to both those with umbrellas and those without umbrellas by virtue of their traveling as a single caravan.
There is the syntactic connection with the agency of going.

The very impossibility of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*) is the seed of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor [is there a problem] because the word *chatrī*, which ends in the suffix *ini* expressing the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*, is a collection of words.

It should not be asked how this can be an example, given that there is an absence of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)— which consists in a relation to that [meaning]— due to the non-establishment of that [meaning].
For indication is precisely the relation to what is to be conveyed (*pratipādya*).
This is because that example was given with this very intention;
otherwise, examples such as "Let the curd be protected from crows" would have been cited instead.

In that context, the term *kākapada* (crow’s foot) refers to that which is delimited by the state of being a common substratum for both the crow and something other than it, such as curd or a parasol;
however, some maintain that the term *chatra* (parasol)—
The secondary derivative (*lakṣaṇā*) [is applied] to "one caravan";
the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is the relation;
and thus, [it refers to] those who are related to one caravan.
They say that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is understood as "they go.
Regarding the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*):
in the referent of the word "That" (*tat*), which is qualified by omniscience and other attributes...

Because it is logically untenable for that which is denoted by the term *tvaṃ*— as qualified by the internal organ and so forth— to enter into a relation of identity [with the denotation of *tat*], the qualifying portions in both cases must be discarded.
Thus, there is [identity] between the pure reality indicated by the term *tat* and that indicated by the term *tvaṃ*.
The intention is that the occurrence of non-difference is established simultaneously.
This example, however,
is according to the view of the Brahmavādins who assert the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.
Because that [identity] is not accepted in the Nyāya school;
however, according to the Nyāya system, "This is Devadatta."

In such cases, they describe this as "indirect indication with both abandonment and non-abandonment" (*jahadajahallakṣaṇā*), because the aspect of "thatness" (*tattva*) is abandoned due to its impossibility at present, while the aspect of "thisness" (*idantva*) is not abandoned because it is possible.

Others, however, argue: "In cases such as 'the jar is eternal,' just as the property of jar-ness (ghaṭatva) appears as a qualifier, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the appearance of the aspect of 'that-ness' (tattā) as a mere indicator (upalakṣaṇa) in cases such as 'this is that Devadatta'; so what [is the problem]?"
They say it is by means of "indication with partial exclusion" (*jahadajahallakṣaṇā*).
[The opponent objects: "Because there is an absence of a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth. And thus:
The meaning is that, because a definition based on a possible relation is impossible, the word *saindhava* has its primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to both salt and horse.
As for the example "the person on the bed":
They say that it is appropriate [to say] "the child on the bed," because the agency of crying and so forth, which constitutes the act of wailing, belongs naturally to that [child] alone.
Regarding the phrase "of the expressed meaning":

because the couch, which is the primary referent (śakyārtha) of the word "couch," lacks the syntactic connection (anvaya) with the status of being the agent of crying, which is the meaning of the co-occurring word "cries."

Because the seed of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists in the impossibility of the literal connection (*anvayānupapatti*), exists— the sense is that the word "bed" indicates the person situated on the bed.
And thus, in whatever kind of word...

When it is impossible for a word to generate a verbal cognition whose object is the relation of other word-meanings with the denoted meaning as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), there is *jahat-svārthā-lakṣaṇā* (indication that abandons the denoted meaning) in that word;
that is, the indication which abandons the denoted meaning.
It is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is *jahat* (abandoning) and is also *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function).
Alternatively, [it refers to] the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*).

The term *jahallakṣaṇā* is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of that which is being abandoned (*jahataḥ*), i.e., relinquished. Where the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) is not discarded, and the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is understood without the abandonment of the primary meaning, there is *ajahallakṣaṇā*.
In the expression "those with umbrellas are going" (*yathā chatriṇo gacchanti*),
there is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *chattrin* (umbrella-bearer) applied to a collective group consisting of both those who possess umbrellas and those who do not.
"By way of being a single caravan-leader" means by way of being a constituent of a single aggregate.
The meaning of the instrumental case [suffix] is "qualification" (vaiśiṣṭya). Of that...
The meaning is that there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the umbrella-bearer and the non-umbrella-bearer;
