that is, within those who are indicated by the word "umbrella-bearer" (i.e., those characterized as being members of a single group), there is a connection with the status of being the agent of the act of going for both the umbrella-bearer and the non-umbrella-bearer.
Now, surely the non-occurrence of the literal connection (*anvayānupapatti*) is not the sole seed of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*);
for in examples such as "Bring in the sticks" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), [the connection fails] with respect to those things denoted by the word "sticks."

Since it is possible for even the sticks (*yaṣṭi*) to possess the property of being the object of the action of entering, there is no lack of logical connection (*anvayānupapatti*)— which serves as the seed [for metaphorical usage]— and therefore the application of the word *yaṣṭi* to the stick-bearer through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is inappropriate; to this, he says:

The failure of the intended meaning (*tātparya-anupapatti*) alone is the seed of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For if one does not accept metaphorical indication, the sentence "Bring in the staffs" would have been uttered with the intention of referring only to those holding staffs.
The sense is that even there, the seed of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) exists, because such an intention (*tātparya*) would otherwise be untenable.
By the word "only" (*eva*), the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) is excluded.

Now, according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), since a word is defined as that which possesses expressive power (*śakti*), the expression "one with an umbrella" (*chatrin*) is indeed a sentence; for the word "umbrella" (*chattrapada*) [possesses power] only with respect to the umbrella.

Because the suffix *ini* has the capacity [to denote] a relationship, and because the word *chattrin* consists of a collection of two words in the form of a base and a suffix, whereas a sentence lacks such capacity— since the meaning capable of being denoted by a sentence is not established— the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists in a relationship with what is denoted, does not apply to it.

And thus, he raises the objection that it is not possible for "chatrī" (the umbrella-bearer) to be an example of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (indication without abandoning the primary meaning), stating: "na ca chatrītyasya... (Nor [is it possible] for "chatrī"...).
"Having the sense of the matup suffix" means having the sense of a relationship;
[it refers to] "the relationship to be established."
The meaning is that there is a connection with the object of awakening (*bodhyārtha*). And thus,
even though the denotable meaning (*vācya-artha*) of the sentence "O umbrella-bearer" (*chatrin*) is not established [in this context], it is the object of the cognition produced by such a sentence.
The meaning is that because the connection with the umbrella exists in the aggregate [of the parts], the definition applies to the sentence as well; such is the intention.
"Otherwise" means:
The meaning is that one accepts that the definition (*lakṣaṇā*) consists precisely in a possible relationship (*śakyasambandha*).
[This is illustrated by] the example "the crow and others."

The meaning is that the word "crow" has a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) with respect to that which is delimited by the property of being a destroyer of curd— a property common to crows, others, cats, and so forth.
Because the crow is also understood by way of its form as a "destroyer of curd," this is a case of non-abandoning secondary indication (ajahallakṣaṇā).
He states the view of those who claim that the purpose is accomplished through the primary meaning of the words alone, beginning with "But some...
and "A single caravan... etc.
The meaning is "being a single collective. The phrase "the umbrella-bearers are going" means "those who possess the state of being a single collective are going."
And "being a collection" (samudāyatva) consists in being the object of a specific enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). Alternatively,
the meaning of the word *chattrin* is a single collection, [the suffix] *ini* [denoting that].
The meaning is qualified by the relation consisting of being a constituent part (*ghaṭakatva*).
The phrase "they say" indicates a lack of full satisfaction (*asvarasa*).
The reason for this is that if the word *chatra* were to mean a collection constituted by an umbrella-bearer (*chatrin*), [the following would occur].

In the verbal cognition produced by the word *chatra* (umbrella-bearer), since the primary meaning of the word *chatra*, namely the umbrella (*chatra*), does not appear as the primary qualificand (*mukhyaviśeṣya*), it is untenable for the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here to be of the "non-abandoning of its own meaning" (*ajahatsvārtha*) type.
In this regard, that which is denoted by that word...
And so forth. In the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the denoted meaning of the word *tat* (That) is consciousness qualified by omniscience and other such attributes;
the denoted meaning of the word *tvam* (thou) is consciousness qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The meaning of non-difference belongs to words in the same case-ending;

however, that [non-difference] is sublated when applied to two qualified entities. Therefore, by abandoning the two qualifiers—omniscience and the nature of the internal organ—which are parts of the expressed meanings, [the identity remains].
Pure consciousness is indicated by two words,
as in such expressions as "this is that Devadatta."
The meaning of the word *tat* (that) is an object qualified by existence in that place and at that time;
the meaning of the word *idam* (this) is an object qualified by this place and this time; and there is identity between these two qualified objects.

This is contradicted; therefore, by abandoning the qualifier consisting of the existence of that specific object in a particular place and at a particular time— which qualifies a part of the denoted meaning of that word— there is a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) of that word upon the substantive, Devadatta.

And thus, it is said that where there is a cognition of a portion of the denotable meaning of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) through the abandonment of a portion of the denotable meaning of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), that is *jahadajahallakṣaṇā*.
As for the phrase "others, however," it is as follows:
In the statement "the pot is impermanent," a non-difference qualified by impermanence cannot exist in that which is qualified by potness,
because impermanence is absent in potness.
The explanation is established by accepting the inherence of impermanence in that which is characterized as "pot-ness";
likewise, in cases such as "This is that Devadatta," the explanation is established through the inherence of "this-ness" in that which is characterized as "that-ness."

The intention is that there should be no *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication involving both abandonment and non-abandonment). This concludes the refutation of the view that *gauṇī* (secondary) and *vyañjanā* (suggestion) are distinct modes of operation (*vṛtti*).
Even the secondary (gauṇī) [function] is indeed indication (lakṣaṇā),
for its nature consists in the connection with the quality being indicated;
as in the example, "The boy is fire."
Suggestion (vyañjanā) is also included within the characteristics of power (śakti),
as it is rooted in the power of words.
And that which is rooted in the power of the meaning is established otherwise through inference and so forth;
it is the illuminator.
He refutes the claim that *gauṇī* is a distinct mode of operation by stating: "Even *gauṇī*...
[Objection: But in the case of "The hamlet is on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*)...

In this regard, just as in the case of the bank [of a river], there is no direct connection possible between the boy and the fire—the denotable meaning of the word—as there is between the stream and the bank; therefore, how can the matter be resolved through indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? To this, he says: "the indicated" (*lakṣyamāṇa*).
The meaning is that [the relation] consists in the connection with those qualities such as purity and so forth which are being perceived.
This is the intended sense: the relation is one that is possible [to exist].

For [indication] is indeed [based on] a relation; and that is, in some cases, a direct relation and, in other cases, an indirect relation. Thus, in this way, indication is precisely the relation of the denoted fire with its own inherent possession of purity.
The rhetoricians, however, say this: "When the expression of the word 'a hamlet on the bank' is within one's own control,
the statement 'a hamlet in the Ganges' is an instance of expressing what is logically unconnected."
This is for the purpose of conveying qualities such as coolness and purity;
nor is that cognition established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
since the inconsistency of the syntactical connection (*anvayānupapatti*) is already resolved by the indication of the bank alone.

Because there is no evidence for a definition characterized by qualities such as coolness or purity [in the case of the word "river"], one must therefore accept the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*). He refutes that view:
"Even the secondary meaning (vyañjanā) is included within the characteristic of capacity (śakti). This is the intended meaning:
in a case where there are multiple meanings, [the word] refers to mountains situated nearby.
In examples such as "ramyāḥ" (delightful), the cognition of kings— just as that of mountains— is possible through the primary power (*śakti*) of the word *bhūdhara* (mountain) itself.
However, in cases such as "gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ" (a hamlet on the Ganges), [the cognition of the bank is not possible through primary power].

Even the cognition of the bank as qualified by coolness, purity, and so forth, arises solely through the sovereign power of indication (lakṣaṇā); since the very non-occurrence of the intended meaning (tātparyānupapatti) exists there as the basis for postulating indication, what need is there for suggestion (vyañjanā)?

Now, it might be argued that although suggestion rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla-vyañjanā*) may be established otherwise, there is no such alternative establishment for that which is rooted in the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*).
To explain:
“Go, if you must go, my beloved; may your paths be auspicious. May my rebirth also be in that very same place.”
"May you go where you have gone," and so forth; here [the meaning is]: "O beloved, after your departure, the destruction of my life will occur."
Therefore, the meaning "one must not go" and so forth is suggested;
for in this case, the purpose cannot be accomplished through either primary denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And thus:
Because the necessity of *vyañjanā* [suggestion] has been established, he says: "and that which is rooted in the power of the meaning" (*arthaśaktimūlā*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "but" (*tu*).
[The phrase] "by means of inference and so forth" (*anumānādinā*)...
The formulation of the inference, however, takes such a form as:
"This woman, who experienced the departure of her life-breath subsequent to my departure, was one who uttered a distinctive sound," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [concepts such as] possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) and so forth are included.
Possibility is a doubt whose one alternative is predominant (*utkaṭa*). And this predominance is a specific kind of objective determination (*viṣayatā*).
If, however, there is an empirical experience common to people— a spontaneous flow consisting of the experience "I understand this meaning from the word"—
then even the Teacher of the Gods (Brahmā) would be unable to prevent this manifestation-based comprehension; thus, the establishment of *vyañjanā* is indeed beyond dispute.
It should be understood:
that which is being observed by the Bālapriyā.

"Quality," and so forth. The meaning is that *gauṇī* (secondary) function consists in possessing qualities of the same genus as the quality that is being indicated and which resides in the literal sense.

In the expression "The boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*), the cognition is that the boy possesses a purity similar to the purity— a quality residing in the fire— which is the meaning denoted by the word "fire."
To the question, "How can such a secondary function (gauṇī vṛtti) be included within indication (lakṣaṇā), which consists of a possible relationship? he says:
"The intention here is as follows."
Indication (lakṣaṇā) is a relation whose counter-correlate is the denoted meaning (śakyārtha).
And this relation is common to both direct and indirect [connections].
In expressions such as "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," there exists a direct relationship in the form of conjunction between the denoted meaning of the word *gaṅgā* and the riverbank.
However, in the case of "the boy is fire," [there is no such relation] with the denoted meaning, fire.
The indirect relation (paramparā-sambandha), consisting in the possession of a quality of the same class as the quality residing in its own substratum, exists in the boy (māṇavaka).
The point is that both types of relations are indeed instances of indication (lakṣaṇā).
[This excludes] that which is called manifestation (vyañjanā) as something distinct.
He restates the opinion of the Alaṅkārikas who speak of *vṛtti* (function): "The Alaṅkārikas, however...
If, in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the intended cognition is of the form "the hamlet has the riverbank as its locus" (*tīravṛttir ghoṣaḥ*), [then...]
In that case, one should employ only the word denoting the bank itself,
such as "the hamlet is on the bank," and one should also employ the word "Ganges," which denotes an object not actually connected with the hamlet.
Therefore, in this case, the meaning consisting of the coolness, purity, and so forth associated with the literal sense is also intended to apply to the *ghoṣa* (the hamlet);
and that [meaning] would not be understood from the expression "the hamlet is on the bank" (*tīre ghoṣaḥ*). However, when the word *gaṅgā* is employed, [it is understood].

It can be said that by its power (sāmarthya), qualities such as coolness and purity residing in the flow of the Gaṅgā are manifested. Nor, however, should it be argued that the word "Gaṅgā" itself possesses a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) for the bank as qualified by coolness, purity, and so forth.
And thus, since the cognition of qualities such as coolness and purifying power is established through indication (lakṣaṇā) alone,
there is no need for suggestion (vyañjanā);
for the impossibility of the literal connection (anvayānupapatti) is indeed the seed of indication.
And since that [meaning] can be avoided by means of the definition of "bank" alone— given the absence of evidence for a definition characterized by coolness, purity, and so forth—
it follows that a distinct function called *vyañjanā* (suggestion) must be accepted.
The view of the Alaṃkārikas is that [suggestion] conveys a meaning that cannot be understood through either direct denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
This is the sense of the passage beginning with "This is the sense," and so forth.
In the phrase "The beautiful mountain stands afar," the primary meaning (*prakṛtārtha*) is the loveliness of the mountain denoted by the word *bhūdhara* (earth-bearer) situated at a distance;
[this applies] even to kings because of their unsteady minds.
In this case, even a non-contextual meaning is perceived, namely that "those situated at a distance alone are beautiful.
And that perception is rooted in the power (*śakti*) of the word *bhūdhara*.

And thus, the theorists of poetics (ālaṅkārikas) maintain that *avyañjanā* rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūlā*) is that function by virtue of which there occurs the cognition of a non-contextual meaning— which, in a case of multiple meanings, has been set aside by the context of the subject matter and other factors.

In that context, since the cognition of kings— just as that of mountains— is possible through the power of the word itself by means of the term "supporter of the earth" (*bhūdhara*), there is no need for suggestion (*vyañjanā*).
The Naiyāyikas maintain that [the meaning] is necessary;
likewise, in such cases as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the word *gaṅgā* [possesses a primary meaning].
The cognition of coolness and so forth is established precisely by accepting figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) for the bank as qualified by coolness, purity, and other such attributes;
even though there is no failure of syntactic connection (anvayānupapatti) here, nevertheless...
There is an incompatibility with the intended meaning (tātparya),

because the word "Gaṅgā" is employed in place of the word "bank" precisely with the intention of conveying qualities such as coolness and purity; therefore, that intended meaning [is established] through indication (lakṣaṇā).
Because [the literal meaning] is untenable without [a figurative one].

It has already been stated, and will be stated again in the *Dīpikā*, that the seed of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is precisely the unaccountability of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), not the unaccountability of syntactic connection (*anvaya*). And thus:
The meaning is that it has been accomplished by means of indication (*vyañjanā*).
He raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*):
even if it is established otherwise—that is, even if its purpose is already served through either primary denotation (*śakti*) or secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
When another meaning is understood through the power of the sense (arthasāmarthya), there is suggestion (vyañjanā) rooted in the capacity of that sense.
For example: "Go, you are going."

In the phrase "cet" (if), by stating that the heroine was born in the very place where her husband goes, and since birth occurs at a time subsequent to death, the meaning of death occurring after his departure on a journey is manifested through the inherent power (*padārthasāmarthya*) of the object that is birth.

And by that, the absence of going is manifested. The intention of the objector is that since this meaning cannot be understood through the function of the word (*padavṛtti*)— whether by primary denotation (*śakti*) or by indication (*lakṣaṇā*)— the function called suggestion (*vyañjanā*) must be accepted.
The remainder is clear. This concludes the *Dīpikā*,
the definition and analysis of the seeds of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The failure of the intended meaning (tātparya) to be established is the seed of indication (lakṣaṇā). Intended meaning is the state of being uttered with the desire for that [specific] cognition to arise.
And the knowledge of the intended meaning (tātparya) is the cause for the knowledge of the sentence-meaning, because of the necessity of accounting for multiple meanings;
[this is determined] by context and so forth.
The *prakāśikā* [is] the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) due to the impossibility of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).

Regarding the status of [the word] as a seed for indication (*lakṣaṇā*), in cases such as "bring the staff-bearers" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), indication would be untenable. However, since the failure of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is the basis for indication, and since that [failure] exists there as well, the intention is that indication of the word "staff" (*yaṣṭi*) for the "staff-bearer" is possible; with this in mind, he says: "because of the failure of the intended meaning."
"Tatpratīti" means the cognition of an object whose form is a bank or the like.
"Nānārtha" [means] manifold objects.

In cases involving words with multiple meanings, such as "Bring the *saindhava*," since the word *saindhava* possesses an equal expressive power (*śakti*) for both a horse and salt, there can be no justification for the occurrence of specific cognitions at specific times without the comprehension of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) being a cause for verbal cognition. Therefore, in that regard:

The point is that since its status as a cause is necessary, it must be present everywhere in accordance with that necessity. Nor is there an impossibility of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) in cases such as the verses of the silent sage (*mauniśloka*); for in those instances, the aforementioned intention (*tātparya*) [is present].
Or rather, it should be stated that [the fault does not apply] because of the absence [of such intention];
for since the nature of intention (tātparya) ultimately consists in the desire for that cognition to arise, there is no fault here, as such an intention exists in that case.

Nor is it the case that the difficulty remains unsolved because verbal cognition is experienced even from sentences uttered by parrots and the like, which lack the speaker's desire for such comprehension; for [the theory of] the intention to communicate (*vivakṣā*) can still account for that instance.

This is to be suspected: that since the impossibility [of the objection] can be resolved by simply taking the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*) into account, such a suspicion is groundless; for since the resolution is possible by resorting precisely to the will of the Lord, enough of this excessive prattle.
Regarding the phrase "context and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi),

there is the inclusion of qualifiers such as "possessing a conch and a discus," which determine the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the word "Hari" as referring to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*) in statements such as "Hari, possessing a conch and a discus, is to be worshipped."

If it is asked how context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth function as indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the answer is as follows: grasp it in this manner: "This word *saindhava* is uttered with the intention of conveying salt, because it is spoken within the context of a meal. Thus you should understand it.
Regarding the phrase "at fixed times" (*niyatakāla*):
sometimes it concerns salt, and sometimes it concerns horses; thus [it is so].
The meaning is "the determination of time. "In accordance with that" means in the case of a word having multiple meanings, within the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).
The meaning is: "in accordance with the [established] causality of the knowledge of the speaker's intention (tātparya-jñāna).
"Its necessity" means the necessity of the knowledge of the speaker's intention. Now, an objection:

If one accepts that the knowledge of *tātparya*— defined as the state of being uttered with the intention of communicating that [meaning]— is a cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), then in cases where verbal cognition occurs through means such as written script which conveys a sentence produced by a mute person, there would be no *tātparya* in the form of being uttered with the intention of communicating that [meaning], because such a person lacks the capacity for speech.
He raises the objection that knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is impossible, stating: "Nor [is it possible] in the case of the verses of sages (*mauniśloka*) and so forth. This means:
in the case of inscriptions and the like which indicate a statement composed by a silent sage (*maunika*). Regarding the aforementioned intended meaning—
The intention (*tātparya*) consists in being uttered with the desire for that [specific] cognition;
intention is merely the desire for that cognition.
Moreover, even silent persons possess such intention.

With the intention that verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is possible from scripts and so forth through the knowledge of that [intention], he provides the resolution: "of the *tātparya*. Now, one might object: even the desire for that [verbal] cognition is not *tātparya*.

He raises the following objection: "And even so... [na ca tathāpīti], because it is established by experience that verbal cognition arises from a sentence uttered by a parrot and the like, even though such a speaker lacks the aforementioned intention.

Regarding "the will of God" (īśvarecchā): the intention (tātparya) in that case is precisely the will of God in the form, "Let there arise from this sentence uttered by Śuka an understanding of such a meaning."
The meaning is that verbal cognition arises from the knowledge of that [intention]. Now, one might object:

although the intention of God’s will exists even in the case of the words of a parrot—which produce valid knowledge—such intention does not exist in the case of a parrot’s words that produce error, such as "he sprinkles with fire."
It is possible;
however, since [otherwise] the will of the Lord would result in being unreliable (*visaṃvāditva*), he says:
"Enough with further talk."
The point is that in the case of a parrot’s statement that is non-conformative to reality, the intention (*tātparya*) belongs solely to the trainer; therefore, there is no fault.
This applies where verbal comprehension arises from a sentence composed of words denoting a single referent.

Even if the knowledge of speaker’s intention (*tātparya-jñāna*) were of no utility, the regularity— namely, that from a sentence such as "bring the *saindhava*," which contains a polysemous term like *saindhava*,
there is sometimes the cognition of bringing a horse and sometimes the cognition of bringing salt— is established by the knowledge of speaker’s intention alone.
Because it must be accounted for, it is necessary that the knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) be a cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
Furthermore, the knowledge that "the word *saindhava* has this meaning as its intended referent" arises through context and other such factors; thus it is stated in the *Dīpikā*.
It has been stated.
Regarding that, he states what is to be understood by the term "and so forth" (*ādinā*):
"the treatise" (*prakaraṇa*).
The phrase "the occasion of eating, walking, and so forth" includes,
by means of the word "and so forth," such states as being face-to-face and the like.

"Because it was stated in the section on food (bhojanaprakaraṇa). The remainder of the argument must be supplied as follows: "That which is not thus is not thus, just like the word 'saindhava' when employed in the section on means of valid cognition (pramāṇaprakaraṇa). Thus.
"By way of" (rītyā) means "by way of inference" (anumānavidhayā). This concludes the *Dīpikā*’s refutation of the theory of supplying missing words based on implied meaning (*arthādhyāhārakhaṇḍana*).
In the phrase "the door" and so forth, there is an ellipsis of the word "close.
Now, one might object that [this is unnecessary] because [the purpose of the text] is the comprehension of the meaning.

If it is argued that since the insertion of a word (śabdādhyāhāra) is impossible without knowing the meaning of a word, the insertion of a meaning (arthādhyāhāra) alone is appropriate— this is not so;
for the recollection of a word-meaning produced by a specific word is the cause of verbal cognition (śābdajñāna).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even in the case of "The pot, the objectness, the bringing, the effort," there would arise verbal cognition [despite the absence of a syntactic relation].
(Prakāśikā)
Intending to refute the Prābhākara position, he sets forth his own established doctrine with the words: "The door," because the word exists for the purpose of making the object known.
The meaning is that the cognition of a word has the cognition of its referent as its fruit.
By this much, it is indicated that there is economy (lāghava) if one first reflects upon the referent. Furthermore, "the referent... [the text continues].

Having understood that, according to the maxim "one understands the composition of words," since the mental supply of words (śabdādhyāhāra)— which consists of reflecting upon words possessing expectancy and so forth— is impossible without prior knowledge of the meaning, he states "without knowing the meaning" to show that the mental supply of the meaning (arthādhyāhāra) is necessarily required first.
Since verbal cognition does not arise from objects presented in any arbitrary manner,

it is necessary that the condition of being produced by a word (*padajanyatva*) be applied as a qualifier to the presentation; therefore, in order to achieve such a presentation, one must, as a last resort, resort to the mental supply of words (*śabdādhyāhāra*).
Thus he says: "by means of a specific word.
In order to demonstrate the purpose of the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) as well, there is the pursuit of examples such as "the pot is the objectness" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*). In that regard:

The point is that even though there exists the mental presence (*upasthiti*) of "objectness" (*karmatva*) and so forth produced by words such as "objectness," there is no undesirable consequence of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the mental presence of "objectness" and so forth produced by the word *am* following the word *ghaṭa* does not exist.
In the phrase "produced by specific words," it should also be understood as "produced by specific words through their function (vṛtti).
Therefore, in cases such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), etc.,...

Even though space and so forth are presented by words such as "jar," there is no verbal cognition; this is the general direction [of the argument]. [The phrase] "because it has the knowledge of the meaning as its fruit" means... [end of fragment].
The meaning is: "because it is the cause of the knowledge of the object consisting of verbal comprehension.
Regarding the phrase "by this logic": just as the knowledge of the object is the cause for the composition of words consisting of the employment of speech, so too...

Even for the mental supply of a word (śabdādhyāhāra) consisting of the recollection of a word, the knowledge of its meaning is the cause. Therefore, since the verbal comprehension can be accomplished by the mental supply of the meaning alone—which consists of the knowledge of the meaning and which precedes the mental supply of the word—what is the purpose of the mental supply of the word? This is the underlying point.
"In whatever manner" means:
recollection of word-meanings (*padārthasmaraṇa*) is the cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Regarding the recollection of word-meanings...
The qualification "being produced by the cognition of a word" must be added;
otherwise, in cases where there is no recollection of the word-meaning from the word, [the definition would fail].
Rather, it is by means of an excitant (*udbodhaka*) and so forth;

for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the recollection of a word-meaning produced by an excitant and the like would itself become a cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
And thus, in cases such as "the door," in order to achieve the presentation (*upasthiti*) of the act of closing generated by the cognition of the word, [an excitant is required].
The sense is that the mental supply (*adhyāhāra*) of a word in the form of the cognition of that word is indeed indispensable.
The meaning of the phrase "in some way or other" (*yathākathaṃcit*) is: by means of an expedient such as an awakener (*udbodhaka*), distinct from the mere cognition of the word.
"For the attainment of such a presentation" means for the accomplishment of the presentation of word-meanings generated by the words;
"anāyatya" means "due to lack of recourse," that is, "because there is no other way."
Regarding the phrase "from words such as 'jar'":
since the word-form "jar" and so forth exists in space through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), [the cognition arises] from that inherence.
The word "jar" and "space" are two related entities;
therein, from the cognition of one— the word "jar"— there arises the recollection of the other— space.

According to the principle that "the cognition of one related member causes the recollection of the other related member," it must be stated that the recollection of a word-meaning produced by the cognition of a word through its *vṛtti* (semantic function) is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), in order to exclude from such verbal cognition space (*ākāśa*), which is the object of such a recollection [triggered by hearing the word 'space' but not connected to the sentence meaning]. And *vṛtti* is...
The relation [between a word and its meaning] consists in either the form of denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Since the recollection of "space" (*ākāśa*) from the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is not brought about by a function residing in the word "jar," that recollection does not serve as a cause for verbal cognition.

The state [of being so produced] consists in being produced by the knowledge of a word through its *vṛtti* (linguistic function); and this means being produced by the knowledge of a word aided by the knowledge of its *vṛtti*.
This is the analysis of the words in the *Dīpikā*.
In words such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), there is both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
Etymology (*yoga*) refers to the power residing in the individual components [of a compound].
Conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) consists in the power of the whole [word].
The power of the whole is for the sake of producing the certain cognition that [the word] refers to a lotus and so forth;
otherwise, it would [apply] even to a humpbacked person.
Because it would entail the consequence of [unnecessary] application; although it is indeed an illuminator, it is not a word.
First, it is fourfold: etymological (yaugika), conventional (rūḍha), and based on both etymology and convention (yogarūḍha).
And [the word] is both etymological and conventional (*yaugikarūḍha*). "Etymology" (*yoga*) refers to the power of the individual parts;
that which conveys a meaning by means of that alone is the first type. For example:
A word such as "cook" (pācaka) is a conventional term; it is a conventional power (rūḍhi), which is a collective power (samudāya-śakti),
and it conveys its meaning by that alone.
The second [type] is, for example, the word "cow" (*gavādi*) and so forth;
the third [type] conveys its meaning through both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), acting as mutual auxiliaries.

The fourth [type of word] conveys distinct meanings through the mutual assistance of both etymological power (*yoga-śakti*) and conventional power (*samudāya-śakti*); for example, the word *paṅkaja*. Similarly, the word *udbhid* conveys [a meaning] through etymology as "a tree, shrub, and so forth," but through convention—
And it is the denoter of a specific sacrifice; nevertheless, having demonstrated that it is both etymological and conventional (yogarūḍha) therein—

With the intention that by demonstrating the nature of *yoga* (etymological derivation) and *rūḍhi* (conventional usage), one may understand other cases in the same manner, he demonstrates the *yogarūḍhi* (combined etymological-conventional meaning) in words such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus")—
namely, "in *paṅkaja*, etc. [as follows].
"Etymological-lexical derivation" (yogarūḍhi) means lexical convention accompanied by etymological derivation.
One might object: "In words such as *paṅkaja* (mud-born) as well, let there be only etymological derivation (*yoga*), for that alone suffices for the explanation.

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that it is established by experience that the word *paṅkaja* necessarily brings to mind the property of being a lotus (*padmatva*) unless there is a function (*vṛtti*) directed toward that which is delimited by the property of being a lotus.

He states that the conventional meaning (rūḍhi) restricted to that which is delimited by the property of being a lotus is necessary, because [the word] "nirvahati" [is used in this sense]: "niyateti."

He addresses one who is in disagreement with the experience of the manifestation of [the object] as delimited by the specific property of being a lotus (*niyatapadmatvāvacchinnabhāna*) by saying "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
This refers to the non-acceptance of the collective power (*samudāyaśakti*) which is necessary for the manifestation of [the object] as delimited by the specific property of being a lotus.
This is the meaning. Regarding "in usage" (*prayoge*):
it means in the usage of the word *paṅkaja*.
— *Bālapriyā* [Commentary]
"Yoga is the power of the constituent parts," and so forth.
A word that conveys meaning solely through the power of its constituent parts is *yaugika* (derivative). In the word *pācaka*, there are two constituent parts: *pac* and *aka*.
In that context, the root *pac* has the meaning of "cooking," and the suffix *aka* has the meaning of "agent. By the word *pācaka*, the agent of cooking is understood.
The word *pācaka* (cook) is etymological (*yaugika*) because it conveys only the meaning of its constituent parts;
by the word "only" (*mātra*), there is an exclusion of words that are both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*).
A word is *rūḍha* (conventional) when it conveys its meaning solely through the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*).

By the use of the word "solely" (*mātra*), there is an exclusion of words that are both etymological and conventional (*yoga-rūḍha*) by way of excluding the power of the individual parts (*avayava-śakti*). For example, in a word such as *go* ("cow"), only the power residing in the whole exists.

Etymological (yaugika) status consists in being the relatum of a denotative power (*śakti*), while being composed of meaningful words (*śakta-pada*) and being distinct from a compound (*samāsa-bhinna*).
For example, as in the word *pācaka*.

The syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) is as follows: [the term *pācaka*] possesses a single denotative power (*śakti*) delimited by the single property of being the agent of cooking, while being composed of words that possess individual denotative powers (*śakta*) such as "cooking" (*pāka*), "power" (*śakti*), "agent" (*kartṛ*), and "suffix" (*ap*).
The phrase "being composed of words possessing individual denotative powers" is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to conventional terms (*rūḍhi*).
The phrase "provided it is distinct from a compound" (*samāsabhinnatve sati*) is included in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to compounds.

Although even with this qualification, an over-extension still occurs in the case of words that possess both etymological and conventional meanings (*yogarūḍha*), such as *paṅkaja* ("lotus"), nevertheless...
The state of having a denotative power delimited by a property constituted by the meanings of the constituent parts [is the definition];
this is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to compounds (*samāsa*).
Nor can it be argued that there is no admission of denotative power in a compound.
It should not be asked how there could be the possibility of over-extension (ativyāpti) given the absence of a capacity-determining factor;
for just as the word *pācaka* has a capacity delimited by a single property consisting of being the agent of cooking, so too does a compound such as *rājapuruṣa*.
The intention is that there exists a capacity delimited by a single property consisting of being a person distinguished from a king;
this is what is intended by the term "the state of being the determiner of the capacity.
Because the word *pācaka* (cook) possesses a capacity delimited by such a property as being an agent of cooking (*pākakartṛtva*), it is appropriately applied [to the king].

The word *paṅkaja*, however, has a denotative power (*śakti*) delimited by lotus-ness that is not constituted by the meanings of its constituent parts; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in its case.
Conventional status (*rūḍhatva*), moreover, consists in being a denotator of a power while not being composed of [other] words.
In the case of a word such as *gavādi* ("cow, etc."), there is the property of "not being composed of other words" because the word is not a constituent part of itself;
and because it possesses a power delimited by *gotva* (cowness), it also possesses the property of being the "determiner of power. Thus, the definition is consistent.
The first part of the definition (the "satyanta") is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to derivative (*yaugika*) words.

The qualificand [in the definition] is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Apabhraṃśa. Etymological-conventional (*yogarūḍha*) status consists in having a power delimited by a property that is not constituted by the meanings of its constituent parts, while being composed of words possessing expressive power (*śakti*).

In the word *paṅkaja*, there is the composition of two meaningful constituent parts, namely *apaṅka* and *ja*; and there is also the state of having a denotative power (*śakti*) delimited by lotus-ness (*padmatva*), which is not constituted by the meanings of those constituent parts— thus is the coordination [of the definition].

Yaugika-rūḍhatva (the state of being both etymological and conventional) consists in being a member of a collection that contains a word possessing a power delimited by a property that is non-co-referential with the delimitor of the conventional meaning-determining factor of the conventional sense.
This applies to words such as *udbhid*.

In the case of a word with a derivative (yaugika) meaning, there is coherence because it possesses that property of being the collective nature (*samudāyatva*) of the term *udbhid*, which serves as the delimitor of the relatum of the conventional denotation (*rūḍhi-nirūpakatāvacchedaka*) as defined by the sacrifice, and which is composed of the verbal root *bhid* whose power is delimited by the property of "upward-splitting" (*ūrdhva-bhedanatva*) that does not co-occur with the property of "sacrificeness" (*yāgatva*), which is the delimitor of the object of the conventional denotation.

To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words such as *pācaka* (cook), the definition includes the qualification that the delimitor of the denotative function (*nirūpakatāvacchedaka*) of the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) must reside in the status of being a composite whole (*samudāyatva*).

To exclude over-extension to conventionally fixed words such as *go* (cow), the inclusion of the condition "being composed of meaningful word-units" (*śaktapadaghaṭitatva*) is necessary. [This applies] to words with both etymological and conventional meanings (*yogarūḍha*).

The path shown by Nṛsiṃha Śāstrī is that, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born"), the definition of a word must include the qualification that it possesses a power (*śaktatva*) not delimited by a property that is non-co-referential with the delimitor of the conventional meaning (*rūḍhyarthatāvacchedaka*).
By means of both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), acting in mutual cooperation:
by the power of etymology, it denotes the agent of producing mud; by conventional usage, [it denotes a lotus].
It is called a lotus;
by the mutual cooperation of those two, that which is born from the mud is called a lotus.
The *Dīpikā*: Refutation of the Theory of Power (*śakti*) as Related to Another (*itarānvita*).
The Prābhākaras maintain that there is a [separate] power (*śakti*) [for each word].

The followers of Gautama (the Naiyāyikas) hold that since the relational connection (*anvaya*) can be manifested as the sentence-meaning, it is unnecessary to postulate a power even for the aspect of that connection.

The term "delimiting factor of the denotation of the conventional meaning" (*rūḍhinirūpakatāvacchedaka*) connects with [the word] "in the state of being a composite whole" (*samudāyatve*). The phrase "not co-locating with the delimiting factor of the conventional meaning" (*rūḍhyarthatāvacchedakāsamānādhikaraṇa*) is a qualification of the property (*dharma*). *Prakāśikā:* [This is the commentary on the above.]
Although the Prābhākara position is that "the expressive power [of a word] resides in that which is connected with an action to be accomplished" (kāryānvite śaktiḥ),
nevertheless, in the case of a sentence whose purport is an already established fact (siddhārtha),...
Having refined that view for the sake of its consistency with the established nature of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*), he demonstrates it as follows: "related to another" (*itarānvita*).
The essential point, however, is that "the expressive power (*śakti*) resides in what is related."
The intention is this:
in order to prevent the verbal cognition of objects that have somehow presented themselves, [a condition] must be established with respect to the verbal cognition having those objects as its content.

Since it must be postulated that the causality [of the word] consists in the presentation of the object produced by the knowledge of its usage (*vṛtti*), a denotative power (*śakti*) is required even for the positive concomitant aspect (*anvaya*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of violating such a general causal relationship. Nor is it the case that...

Let it be held that, with respect to a verbal cognition possessing various distinct object-nesses (viṣayatā) other than the object-ness of the relation [of co-reference], the cause is the respective presentation (upasthiti) dependent upon the knowledge of the word's denotative function (vṛtti); and thus,
regarding the aspect of the relation [of syntactic connection]...

It should not be argued that there is no harm even if *śakti* (denotative power) is not admitted; for if that were the case, it would result in the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).
And thus, [the view is that] "a jar associated with [its constituents] is the denotation of the word 'jar'."
Thus, it is the knowledge of the word's power (*śakti*) in this very form that is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
However, some maintain that the statement "the power [resides] in what is connected to another" means "the power resides in what is connected to an action (*kārya*). This is supported by reasoning.
He presents the Naiyāyika position with the words "of the positive concomitance" (anvayasya):
because the relation between word-meanings can appear in verbal cognition solely by virtue of the co-occurrence of the words.
The summary of the overall meaning is that even with respect to the element of such a relation (*saṃsarga*), a separate expressive power (*śakti*) need not be postulated.

This is the underlying intention: there is no single, uniform causal relationship (*anugata-kāryakāraṇabhāva*) whereby the verbal cognition regarding each respective object depends upon the presentation (*upasthiti*) of that object as being governed by the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*).
This is possible, because it is difficult to state a property of occurrence (*vṛttitva*) that is common to both [the word] characterized by capacity and [the object] itself; rather,
there is a single causal relation consisting in the presentation of that [object] produced by the cognition of a word capable of denoting it.

Furthermore, another causal capacity must be admitted, namely: [the capacity] by way of the presentation of that [object] produced by the knowledge of a word possessing its specific characteristic (tallakṣaṇika).
This is for the purpose of avoiding deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of verbal cognition produced by various mutual presentations of those [objects].
And the state of being immediately followed by each respective cause must be included within the scope of the delimitors of the effectness of each respective effect;
and thus, even for the relation between two word-meanings that is not presented by a verbal function (*vṛtti*), [the cognition arises].

Since the two-fold causal relationship shown remains unassailable when verbal comprehension is accepted— given that any deviation [of meaning from the word] would otherwise result— what is the use of postulating a power (śakti) with respect to the positive concomitance (anvaya)?
Bālapriyā: Is it not improper to say, "The Prābhākaras hold that the word-potency resides in what is associated with another [meaning]"?
[For they hold] "in what is associated with an action (kārya)."

Anticipating the objection that "this is established by the very principle that [the word] denotes capacity (*śakti*)," he says: "Even though [it is understood as] connected with the effect," and "nevertheless": "In Kāśī, there dwells a king who is the ornament of the three worlds."

Since it has already been established previously that words possess expressive power (śakti) even with respect to an accomplished object (siddha-artha), because words are employed even when such an object is already known, it is not tenable to maintain that the expressive power [of words] resides only in connection with an action to be accomplished by volitional effort (kṛtisādhya-kriyānvita). Considering this,
certain followers of the Prabhākara school hold the view that "the expressive power [of words] resides in connection with something other [than an action]" (itarānvite śaktiḥ).
The sense is that their opinion—that [the word] has been refined—is being restated.

Even in a sentence where the referent is already established, the meaning of a word possesses the quality of being connected to others; thus, when it is stated that the expressive power (śakti) resides in that which is connected to others...

"Arising everywhere" means that the other [word] has its power (śakti) in the object denoted by the word with which it is uttered together (samabhivyāhṛta), as well as in what is associated with that [object]; and the object denoted by the co-uttered word is either of the nature of an action (kārya) or of the nature of an accomplished entity (siddha).
With the intention that the other component is also obtained through another word, and thus the capacity resides in the related meaning (*anvita*) alone, he says:
"The capacity resides in the related meaning."

Now, one might object that since the aspect of syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is obtainable through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in the form of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), it is improper to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for that aspect;
therefore, he reveals the intention of the Prābhākaras who maintain that there is such power in the aspect of relation: "This is the intended meaning."
Thus: "of those [meanings] presented by some means" means:
of those objects of presentation produced by causes other than the knowledge of the word-constituent (*padavṛtti*).
The syntactic relation (*anvaya*) of the word-meanings manifests in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

The point is that if the capacity (śakti) for the relational component (anvaya) is not admitted, then, due to the absence of the cause— which is the knowledge of the word's capacity regarding the relation— there would be no verbal cognition (śābdabodha) having the relation as its object.
"Not so" [means]:
in the case of "Bring the jar," there is a verbal cognition possessing that objective relation residing in the jar which is distinct from the objective relation termed *saṃsargatā*.

The cause for the verbal cognition [of a pot] is the presentation of the pot (*ghaṭa*) produced by a knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*) in the form "the pot is denotable by the word 'pot'. However, for a verbal cognition characterized by a relationhood (*saṃsargatā*) residing in the syntactic connection (*anvaya*), the presentation of the connection produced by a knowledge of the denotative power (*śakti*) is not required.

The meaning is that the verbal cognition regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not subsumed under the delimitor of the effect-nature (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), which consists in being a verbal cognition possessing a subject-object relation (*viṣayatā*) that is non-different from the relation-nature (*saṃsargatā*). This is because it would result in an undue complexity (*gaurava*) in the delimitor of the effect-nature.

The point is that the property of being a verbal cognition possessing a subject-object relation distinct from the relationhood (*saṃsargatā*) is more cumbersome than the property of being a verbal cognition having that [relation] as its object.
Regarding this view, he states the form of the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) with the words "And thus" (*evañca*).

And likewise, in the case of "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the relation between the jar and its objecthood, between objecthood and bringing, and between bringing and the meaning of the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) appears in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).
This is because of the verbal cognition: "The action of bringing, which has as its object that which resides in the pot, is to be performed.
In this context, if one accepts that the word "pot" (ghaṭa) possesses denotative power (*śakti*) only with respect to the meaning that is the pot itself...

Since there is no word expressive of the relation between the pot and the objecthood— which consists in the nature of being the locus (ādheyatva)— that [relation] would not appear in the verbal cognition;
therefore, of the word "pot" (ghaṭa)...

The word "ghaṭa" (pot) has its denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to a pot qualified by a relation consisting of the property of being located (*ādheyatva*), where this relation has as its correlate the objecthood (*karmatva*) that is co-uttered with the word itself. Furthermore, the qualification of the pot by this relation consists in the pot's being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that relation.

In this context, since the other term of the relation—namely, objecthood—is already obtained through the suffix *am* alone, it is the [relation] not obtainable by any other means [that constitutes the denotation].

Since it is the meaning of the word, the word *ghaṭa* does not possess denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the aspect of "objectness" (*karmatva*). Likewise, the word *am* also does not possess denotative power with respect to "objectness" as qualified by a relation characterized by having the jar as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

And thus, the relation between the pot and the objecthood is obtained through the word-potentialities (*śakti*) of the words "pot" and "accusative suffix" (*am*); therefore, this aspect of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is manifested by the word-potentialities alone.
The same applies to the relation between the objecthood denoted by the accusative suffix and the action of bringing denoted by the verbal root.
The intention of the Prābhākaras is that even the relation [between word-meanings] is obtainable through the power (*śakti*) of the two words.
He reveals the intention of the Naiyāyikas with the words "of the relation of word-meanings," and so forth.
Even in the Prābhākara view, in order to prevent verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) from arising from the expression "am ghaṭaḥ" (this pot),...

It must necessarily be stated that the cognition of the word "ampada" occurring immediately after the word "ghaṭa" is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). And thus, since the relation-component can appear in the verbal comprehension by the force of such a cause alone, it is not appropriate to postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for the relation.
The sense is that the meaning of a word is precisely that which cannot be obtained from anything else. "Co-occurrence of words" (padasamabhivyāhāra) [is the means].
The co-utterance of words (*padasamabhivyāhāra*) consists in a word being qualified by another word through the relation of "immediately following" (*avyavahitottaratva*). Now,

with respect to the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having that [word-meaning] as its object, there is the requirement of an apprehension (*upasthiti*) of that object produced by the knowledge of the linguistic function (*vṛtti*).

Since the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) must be accepted as the cause for preventing the appearance— however they may otherwise present themselves— of all objects in verbal cognition, how can a relation that is not presented through a linguistic function (vṛtti) appear in verbal cognition?

This being the case, since there would follow the fallacy of deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) regarding the aforementioned relationship between cause and effect, he clarifies the position of the Naiyāyikas with the words "this is the intention," and so forth.
And thus, the previously mentioned general relation of cause and effect is not possible,
because [the definition] common to both characterized by "capacity" (śakti) and "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) [is untenable].
Because it is difficult to define the nature of "functionality" (vṛttitva),

the cause for the verbal cognition of a given meaning is the mental presentation (upasthiti) of that meaning, which is produced by the knowledge of the expressive power (śakti) directed toward that meaning.

The causal relation must be postulated as follows: the mental presentation (upasthiti) of that meaning, which is produced by the knowledge of the secondary function (lakṣaṇā) directed toward that meaning, is the cause for the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) whose object is that meaning; thus, two pairs of cause and effect are to be assumed.

Even so, in a case where there is a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) regarding a jar produced by the presentation of the jar— which itself is produced by a knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) residing in the word for the jar—
there would be an absence of the cause, namely, the presentation of the jar produced by a knowledge of the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the jar; [this being so] in that case...

Since verbal cognition arises from the presentation of a jar produced by the knowledge of its secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and since in that case there is an absence of the cause— which consists in the presentation of the object produced by the knowledge of its primary denotative power (*śakti*)— there occurs a positive deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), wherein the effect arises despite the absence of the cause. Therefore, [the definition must be modified] in order to exclude such a case.

By incorporating "immediate succession" (*avyavahitottaratva*) into the scope of the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedakakoṭau*), [one establishes that] with respect to the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) immediately following the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) of that [object] which is produced by the knowledge of the power (*śaktijñāna*) having that as its object— [The causal relation is established.]
The causal relation must be stated as follows: the cause is the mental presentation (upasthiti) of that [object] produced by the knowledge of the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding it;

for a verbal cognition dependent on the knowledge of secondary signification is not subsumed under the delimitor of the effecthood (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), which consists in being immediately subsequent to a presentation produced by the knowledge of primary denotation (*śakti*).
In that case, even in the absence of an apprehension produced by the knowledge of the capacity (*śakti*), there is no fallacy of negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*);
for the fault of negative deviation occurs only when the effect characterized by its specific defining property (*tatkāryatāvacchedaka*) arises despite the absence of its cause.

And thus, since verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) regarding positive concomitance (anvaya) does not follow upon an apprehension (upasthiti) produced by knowledge of either primary denotation (śakti) or secondary indication (lakṣaṇā),
it is not subsumed under the two types of delimited causal capacities; therefore, even though the two types of causes are absent there, [the result does not fail to arise].
There would be the consequence of deviation in negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*).

Therefore, the meaning is that, for fear of such deviation in the relationship of cause and effect, one should not postulate a causal capacity (*śakti*) in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) aspect.
Because it is difficult to define what constitutes "mode of operation" (*vṛttitva*);
nor can it be easily stated that "mode of operation" is simply being either primary denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

This must be stated: for "either-or-ness" (anyataratva) is indeed the state of being different from that which is different from it. And thus, it consists in possessing a difference delimited by two differences.
Furthermore, the state of being two differences is...
It is the state of being another particular qualified by one particular;
and thus, since there is no decisive reason for determining the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two particulars.
Alternatively, it is the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the non-difference of the definitions as qualified by the difference of powers;

or else, it is the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlation is delimited by the difference of powers as qualified by the non-difference of the definitions; or else, it is the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlation is delimited by the difference of powers as qualified by the non-difference of the definitions.

Regarding the term *anyataratva* (one or the other), since there is no decisive factor (*vinigamanā*) [to prefer one over the other], one would have to postulate two separate causal capacities for a cognition whose occurrence is delimited by both; thus, a single cause-and-effect relationship is not possible—this is the underlying intention.
Consequently, it is established that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) portion is obtainable solely through syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
*Tarkasaṅgraha*:
Definition of Expectancy and Other Factors. (AnTs_60) Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and contiguity (*saṃnidhi*) are the causes for the cognition of the meaning of a sentence.

Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is a word’s incapacity to convey a syntactic connection when another word is absent. Compatibility (*yogyatā*) is the non-sublation of the meaning. Contiguity (*saṃnidhi*) is the non-delayed utterance of the words.
A sentence devoid of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the other [factors] is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
For example, "cow, horse, man, elephant" is not a means of valid cognition because it lacks expectancy.
"One should sprinkle with fire" is not a means of valid cognition because it lacks compatibility (*yogyatā*).
Words such as "bring the cow," uttered at every single moment, are not a means of valid cognition due to the absence of proximity (saṃnidhi).
Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*),

and proximity (*sannidhi*) are the causes for the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence. Expectancy is the state of a word not bringing about the experience of a syntactic connection with another word when that connection is absent.

Non-sublation of the meaning is semantic competency (*yogyatā*). The non-delayed utterance of words is proximity (*sannidhi*). [A sentence] devoid of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth [is not a valid sentence].
A sentence is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For example, the sentence "cow, horse, man, elephant" is not a means of valid cognition because it lacks syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

The sentence "He sprinkles with fire" is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks semantic competency (*yogyatā*). [For example,] the words "Bring the cow," uttered at every single hour, [do not constitute a valid sentence].
Words such as "ityādi" (and so forth) are not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because of the absence of proximity (*sānnidhya*).
"Dīpikā" (the lamp) refers to expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
The meaning is "the cognition of expectancy and so forth.
Otherwise, due to an error regarding expectancy and the rest, there would be no erroneous verbal cognition (*śābdabhrama*). He defines expectancy with the words "of the word" (*padasya*).
He states the definition of *yogyatā* (semantic competency) with the words "artha... [meaning: the mutual compatibility of word-meanings].
He states the definition of *sannidhi* (proximity) with the words "padānām... [meaning: the non-delayed presentation of word-meanings]. This constitutes the proximity of word-meanings.

Proximity (*sannidhi*) is mentioned because it is useful for that [syntactic expectancy]. Examples such as "cow, horse" (*gauraśva*) and "jar, objectness" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*) should also be understood as illustrations of the absence of expectancy (*anākāṅkṣā*).

In the *Prakāśikā*, in order to exclude verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) arising from a collection of words that lack expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other such factors, the author of the root text has stated that expectancy and the rest are causes of verbal cognition. And that [is as follows]:
Since [the required cognition] is not possible according to the new school (navīna-mata), he states that the knowledge of that [sentence] is the cause:
"the knowledge of expectancy and so forth" (ākāṅkṣādijñāna). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of compatibility (yogyatā) is intended; otherwise...
Regarding the fact that expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth are causes of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), [the author] states in the root text: "In the case of 'madasya' (of the rut-fluid), etc."

The meaning is that *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) consists in the fact that a given word, when co-uttered with another word, possesses the property of not generating a cognition of syntactic connection (*anvayabodha*) due to the absence of that other word.
And being "employed" (*prayuktatva*) is a specific kind of essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) attested by the cognition "in the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect";
the phrase ending with "non-productivity" (*ajanakatva*) is merely a subordinate description.

According to the view that semantic competency (*yogyatā*) consists in one word-meaning possessing another word-meaning, the cause of verbal cognition is that specific cognition delimited by its own nature (*tattajjñānatva*), which is common to both doubt and certainty.
However, according to the modern view, where semantic competency is the absence of a certainty regarding sublation (*bādhaniścayābhāva*), competency exists as a real entity (*svarūpasat*) itself.
"That is its cause" is the general direction; furthermore,
that [cause] is not possible according to the modern view.

If expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) were the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), then in a case where there is no actual expectancy, but rather a delusion that expectancy exists, the desired verbal cognition would not occur.
However, if the cognition of expectancy is the cause, then even in the absence of actual expectancy...
The point is that verbal cognition is possible from a cognition consisting of an error regarding that object. Likewise,
if fitness (*yogyatā*) were the cause of verbal cognition, then even in the absence of fitness, verbal cognition would not occur due to an error regarding fitness.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that one must state that the cognition of co-occurrence (*yaugapadya*) is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
Regarding the phrase "of which word" (*yatpadasya*):

The [inexpressibility] of the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) consists in its lack of capacity to produce a verbal cognition of the form: "the objecthood residing in the pot, which is caused by the absence of the word 'am' (accusative case-ending). This is the [definition] of the word "pot."
*Ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) is the state of being uttered together with a word-form (*ampada*).

"Due to the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect" means that due to the absence of the cause, which is the word-form (*ampada*), there is the absence of the effect, which is verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
The phrase "non-productivity" serves as a delimiter. Thus, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consists precisely in the co-occurrence of a given word with another word.
When the inquiry arises as to what kind of word co-occurs with what kind of word, [it is defined] as that which, in the absence of a certain word...

The term "non-productive" (*ajanaka*) was stated in order to indicate that [the word] whose co-utterance with another word does not produce cognition [of its own meaning]; however, even that [term] is not a constituent part of the definition itself.

The meaning is that it is due to the absence of a purpose. Furthermore, being a "distinguisher" (paricāyaka) consists in making known the objects included within a definition, while itself not being a constituent part of that definition.

"Regarding the phrase *ekapadārtha* and so forth: semantic competency (*yogyatā*) consists in the capacity of one word to convey a meaning qualified by the meaning conveyed by another word within its own constituents.
In the sentence *payasā siñcati* ("he sprinkles with water"), the word *sva* refers to that sentence; the word *tadghaṭakamekapadaṃ* refers to the single word *payasā* contained therein."
The meaning to be conveyed by that [word] is "having milk as the instrument"; the other word-meaning qualified by that is "sprinkling.

Since the state of being a conveyor of that [meaning] exists in the sentence "he sprinkles with milk," such a sentence possesses semantic competency (*yogyatā*). This [competency] is the object of a cognition that may be either of the nature of doubt or of the nature of certainty.
Knowledge is the cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
Compatibility (*yogyatā*) is the absence of a certainty regarding the object of sublation (*bādha*), which consists in the non-existence of another word-meaning in a given word-meaning.

According to the Navya-Nyāya school, however, the meaning is that fitness (*yogyatā*), which consists in the absence of a certainty of sublation, is a cause by way of being an absence of an impediment (*pratibandhakābhāva*) as a positive entity in its own right (*svarūpataḥ satī*); it is not the cognition of such fitness that is the cause.
[Objection: But on the view that fitness is the existence of one word-meaning in another word-meaning, where...
The meaning of a sentence is something unprecedented (*apūrva*); therefore, in that case, it is impossible for such a prior cognition of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) to exist.
According to the view that semantic competency is simply the absence of a certain sublation (*bādhaniścaya*), the postulation of its status as a cause for verbal cognition is unnecessary.

Since this can be accounted for simply through a general relationship of the sublated and the sublator— namely, that the certainty of the absence of a property is an inhibitor with respect to the cognition of its presence—
it says "and so forth" (dig).

When there is recollection of the respective word-meanings constituting that sentence, a cognition of semantic competency (yogyatājñāna)— either in the form of a certainty or a doubt— becomes possible;
as in the case of the verbal comprehension arising after the perceptual certainty "there is a jar on the ground."
In cases where the sentence-meaning is already known, the cause is a cognition of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) consisting of a perceptual certainty; however,
where the sentence-meaning is new— as in "There are five fruits on the riverbank"—
the cause is a cognition of semantic competency consisting of doubt.
Therefore, there is no fault in the first position;

for it is not possible for there to be a general obstructive capacity (pratibandhakatā) at the level of all cognitions of possession of that [property], based on the status of being a certainty regarding its absence.

Even after the certain cognition that "the ground is devoid of a jar," a visual cognition of the form "the ground possesses a jar" arises through the force of the desire, "Let there arise in me a visual cognition having a jar as its qualifier and the ground as its qualificandum."
Because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*).

Rather, the relationship between the sublated (*pratibadhya*) and the sublator (*pratibandhaka*) must be stated specifically as: "the certainty of the absence of that [object], qualified by the absence of a desire for visual perception of it."

Since induced inference (*āhāryānumiti*) is not admitted, the absence of desire (*icchāviraha*) is not included among the factors that obstruct the certainty of its absence with respect to inference; therefore,
[this applies] to inference having that as its qualifier.
Since the absence of desire is not included among the factors that obstruct the certainty of the non-existence of that [object],
there is a distinct state of being an obstructor for an inference having that [object] as its qualifier, by virtue of being a certainty having the non-existence of that [object] as its qualifier.

In the same way, even in the case of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), a distinct status as a counter-agent (*pratibandhakatva*) must be postulated; thus, it is necessary to postulate that fitness (*yogyatā*), in the form of the absence of a certainty regarding sublation (*bādhaniścaya*), is a cause of verbal cognition.
The meaning is that there is no fault even in the second alternative; thus ends the *Tarkasaṅgraha*.
Speech is of two kinds:
Vedic and worldly.
Because it was spoken by the Lord, all that is Vedic is indeed authoritative.
However, in the worldly context, that which is spoken by a reliable person (āpta) is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); anything else is not a means of valid cognition.
The knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is the knowledge of the word;
the word is the instrument for that [knowledge].
Speech is of two kinds: Vedic and worldly.
All that is Vedic is [considered authoritative] because it was spoken by the Lord.
Valid cognition: worldly valid cognition consists of the word of a reliable person; anything else is not valid. The knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is verbal knowledge.
Sound is the instrument for that [perception].
Thus has valid experience (yathārthānubhava) been defined.
Thus ends the section on verbal testimony in the Tarkasaṅgraha-dīpikā.
He analyzes the term "sentence" (vākya):
"sentence" [is defined as follows]. He states the distinction of the Vedic [sentence]: "The Vedic [sentence] is such because it was spoken by God.
This refers to the non-human authorship of the Vedas.
If it is objected: "But since the Veda is beginningless, how can it be said to have been spoken by God?"—we reply: No;
[for] the Veda is of human origin.
Because its status as a human composition is established by the inference: "It is a human composition because it is a collection of sentences, like the *Mahābhārata* and other such works.
Nor is "having a remembered author" a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because [the authorship] of [works such as the *Nyāyasūtra*] was transmitted by Gautama and others through a lineage of disciples.
Because the Veda itself records that it has an author, which pervades the probandum;
and because of the Vedic revelation (śruti): "From Him, through intense heat (tepāna), the three Vedas were born.
[Objection: But surely the phonemes (varṇa) are eternal... sa...
If it is argued that the Veda is eternal because of the power of recognition— namely, the cognition "this is the very same letter *ga*"— then we say: no.
Because phonemes are impermanent, as evidenced by such cognitions as "the sound *ga* has arisen" and "the sound *ga* has perished."
This is because the recognition "this is that same letter *ga*" has as its basis a similarity [of the individual instances], just like the [recognition] "this is that same lamp-flame";
and furthermore, even if the phonemes (*varṇa*) were eternal, a sentence characterized by a specific sequence would still be non-eternal. Therefore:
The Vedas were spoken by Īśvara.
The Mīmāṃsaka, acting as an elucidator, raises an objection: "But surely," he says, regarding the Veda.
He establishes the fact that [the Veda] was spoken by God through inference—[stating] "the Veda. Now, one might object:
by the force of such authoritative evidence as "the son of Satyavatī is the author of the eighteen Purāṇas," an author is indeed perceived in the Mahābhārata and other works.
For it is not so in the case of the Veda; and thus,

since having a remembered author (smaryamāṇakartṛkatva) is an *upādhi*— because it pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) in cases such as the *Mahābhārata* and the like, yet does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) [the Veda]— how can this inference be valid?
He raises the objection that it might be effective, saying "If not," [referring to] the Veda through the lineage of disciples beginning with Gautama.
He says "tasmāt" (therefore) in response to one who disputes the identity of the agent of production:
"This very same *ga*-sound [is that]. Here, the non-difference from the previously occurring *ga*-sound appears in this currently occurring *ga*-sound; and that...
The meaning is that [the perception of identity] is not possible if phonemes were impermanent.
Regarding the phrase "because of impermanence," one might then object that this contradicts recognition; therefore, he says: "It is this very same [phoneme]."

The underlying point is that there is parsimony (lāghava) in assuming that the cognition [of the word] is of such a nature, rather than assuming that the cognitions of its production and destruction have different objects.
In cases such as "agnim īḷe," [this refers to] the sequential order (ānupūrvī).
—It consists of forms such as having the letter *ā* as a subsequent [element] or having the letter *ka* as a subsequent [element].
In that context, "subsequent-ness" (*uttaratva*) should be understood as occurring in the immediately succeeding moment.
And thus, regarding phonemes...

Even if one does not accept the eternity [of phonemes], since the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) composed of impermanent moments is itself impermanent, the impermanence of the Veda—which you maintain to consist of a collection of sentences qualified by that sequence—cannot be established; therefore, it is more appropriate that the phonemes themselves are impermanent. Thus he says: "Of the phonemes... (*varṇānām iti*).
"Bālapriya Mīmāṃsaka" means one who asserts that the Vedas are not of human origin; this is the implied meaning.
"Establishes" means "proves.
This is because [the author] establishes the fact of being of human origin in the *Dīpikā*.
And thus, since the non-eternality of the Vedas is unestablished by the proof of their being composed by a person through the aforementioned inference,
[the argument] fails because of this lack of non-eternality.
The sense is that there is no occasion for the doubt as to how [the Veda] could have been spoken by Īśvara. "Because it is a limiting condition (upādhi)" means:
