wherever there is authorship by a person, as in the case of the *Mahābhārata* and so forth, there...

Since there is the property of having an author who is remembered, the property of having an author who is remembered is a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the probandum (*sādhya*), which consists in being of human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*). This is because where the probans (*sādhana*)—namely, being a collection of sentences—exists in the subject (*pakṣa*), the Veda, the property of having an author who is remembered does not exist; therefore, [the probans] is not a pervader of that [probandum].
The meaning is as follows: [the probans] does not pervade the locus of the sādhya.

Therefore, since "being composed by an author who is remembered" is a limiting adjunct (upādhi), the aforementioned inference is flawed due to being sopādhika; how then can it prove that [the Veda] is of human origin?
Regarding the phrase "by Gotama and others": Gotama taught his own disciple that the Vedas have an author.

He, in turn, taught it in that same manner to his own disciple; thus, through this lineage of disciples, the followers of Gautama (the Mīmāṃsakas) remember the Vedas as having an author. And so, since the state of having a remembered author resides in the subject [of the inference], there is no lack of pervasion by the probans (*sādhana*).

The meaning of the objection is this: "The statement in the *Dīpikā* that [the self] is not an *upādhi* is inconsistent; for there is no evidence that Gautama and the others taught it in such a manner."
"Therefore, thus": the meaning of the Vedic scripture is that from that Lord who was performing austerity, the three Vedas were born.
And thus, since the human origin of the Vedas— in the form of their being created by God— is established by this very scripture, the implication is that there is no need for inference.
It is not possible [for them] to exist in a state of impermanence;
for if phonemes were subject to arising and destruction, then...

The point is that because the *ga*-sound of the previous time has perished, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) which apprehends non-difference from that [previous sound] with respect to the *ga*-sound of the present time would not be tenable. Now, if it is argued that the letters possess origination and destruction since their possession of these is established by the force of the cognition apprehending the origination and destruction of the letters...
Since it is impossible for the *ga*-sounds occurring at earlier and later times to be identical, the recognition "this is that same *ga*-sound" does not apprehend identity;
rather, it apprehends membership in the same class (*tajjātīyatva*).

The statement in the *Dīpikā* that "the meaning of the proposition is: 'This present *ga*-sound possesses the universal *gatva* residing in the *ga*-sound belonging to a previous time'" is not tenable;
for [the cognition is] "this is that very *ga*-sound."

Once the non-difference between two instances of the letter *ga* is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the cognitions "the letter *ga* has arisen" and "the letter *ga* has perished"— due to their contradiction with that [recognition]— do not apprehend arising or destruction in the letter *ga* itself;
rather, they apprehend [arising and destruction] as belonging to the particular conjunctions of the air (*vāyu*) that manifest the phoneme.
For it can also be said that the description of arising and destruction is merely a superimposition; or alternatively,
it can be said that the meaning of "arisen" is "manifested" and the meaning of "destroyed" is "unmanifested."
And thus, suspecting that the eternity of phonemes would remain unrefuted, he says: "Of the two cognitions of arising and destruction.
This means: of the two perceptions, "the letter *ga* has arisen" and "the letter *ga* has perished."
"Assuming another meaning" means assuming meanings such as manifestation (*abhivyakti*) and so forth; this is the sense.
— *Dīpikā*
The authority of tradition and conduct refers to the *smṛtis* of Manu and others.
The authority of the *ācāras* (traditional practices) is derived from their being rooted in the Veda.

Since the original Vedic statements that serve as the basis for the *smṛtis* (traditions) are no longer studied today, it is inferred that some particular Vedic branch (*śākhā*) which formed their foundation has become extinct.

If it is argued that, since it is impossible to postulate the destruction of Vedic sentences currently being recited, the theory of scattered [Vedic texts] is untenable, and therefore the eternally inferable Veda must be the source—[we reply:
no; for if that were the case, there would never be knowledge of the sequence of phonemes, and thus the capacity to convey meaning would be impossible.

The *Prakāśikā* states: "Although the validity of the *Smṛtis* and other texts is established precisely because they were spoken by authoritative persons (*āpta*), since their authors, such as Manu and others, are authoritative,"
Nevertheless, he says "Manu and others" with respect to those who disagree regarding their authority;
"of the practices" means "of the words of the learned (śiṣṭa) that set forth those practices. By this—
The doubt regarding the contradiction of the classification of the means of valid cognition has been dispelled;
for Manu and others composed their Smṛtis and other works concerning that subject only after having understood the meaning of the Veda.
Therefore, having in mind that their authority is derived from this, he says: "by being rooted in the Veda.
[Objection: But then, why is that Veda not perceived?
To this he says: "having its root in tradition" (*smṛtimūla*), and so forth.
It is inferred that some branch, which served as the root for the tradition and other sources, has been lost from the recitation.
This is the meaning. Regarding "the destruction of sentences"—that is, the annihilation of sentences—[one might object]:

since the recitation of the Veda with its identical sequence of phonemes is established by tradition (*saṃpradāya*), and since it is impossible to postulate the destruction of even a few sentences within such a Veda, [the objection holds] even while the Veda is being recited.
He says "because they are scattered" (*viprakīrṇa*) to show that there is no basis in the Smṛti for those statements that exist only in a fragmented state;
this is because it would be illogical [otherwise].
The meaning is that sentences having the same sense as "smṛti" and so forth are not found in the recited Veda; thus,
it is "to be inferred eternally."

The meaning is that [the word] is eternal and of the nature of an object of inference. [The phrase] "due to the absence of knowledge of the sequence of phonemes" is used because even such knowledge is a cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
The point is that otherwise, there would be no possibility of cognizing specific meanings through words such as "river" or "well.
(Bālapriyā)

Now, if it is granted that conduct (*ācāra*) is authoritative because it is rooted in the Veda, then since conduct in the form of action is not included among the four distinct means of valid cognition— perception and the others— it would follow that it is an additional, independent means of valid cognition.
The fourfold division of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is therefore untenable; for this reason, he explains [it] as "that which teaches conduct" (*ācāra-pratipādaka*).
Those [scriptures] which are the indicators of conduct—that is, of practice—[are the *smṛtis*].

"Of the learned" (śiṣṭānām) means "of their [words]. "By this" (etena) means "by the explanation that the word *ācāra* refers to the aforementioned statements. "Only after knowing the meaning of the Veda" (vedārthaṃ jñātvaiva).
And thus, it is stated that being rooted in the Veda means either being composed preceded by knowledge of the meaning of the Veda, or being produced by knowledge of the meaning of the Veda. —
Dīpikā.
Refutation of the inclusion of verbal testimony within inference:
Now, [it may be argued that] "these words possess a connection between the meanings they cause to be remembered, because they constitute a collection of words possessing expectancy and so forth."

If it is argued that verbal testimony is not a separate means of valid cognition because the knowledge of a relation can arise from inference alone— just as in the case of my own statement, "Bring the cow with a stick"—
we say no; for verbal cognition, which is distinct from inferential cognition, is experienced as "I understand through words."
This is because [the existence of the illuminator] is universally accepted as being evidenced by subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*); thus,
the illuminator of the word is distinct.
He introduces the critique of the Vaiśeṣika position, which does not accept the status of [words] as a means of valid cognition, with the words "But these... and so forth.
These words refer to expressions such as "Bring the jar" and the like.

"Possessing a connection between the objects recalled" means that they are preceded by a cognition of the connection between the objects recalled. In this context, "being the object of the speaker's intention" (tātparyaviṣayatva) should be included as qualifying the connection.
Therefore, by taking another instance of association, there is no shift in the subject matter (*arthāntaratā*).
By the phrase "expectancy and so forth," both semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and contiguity (*āsatti*) are included.
The term "expectancy and so forth" (*ākāṅkṣādi*) is used to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a collection of words devoid of expectancy and the rest.
This is because [these conditions] are universally accepted. Thus, in accordance with the distinctness of the effects, the word...

The meaning is that they are preceded by a cognition of the connection between objects already recalled; such is the sense of "another means of valid cognition" (pramāṇāntaram). This is the intention of the *Bālapriyā*.

The meaning is that [the utterances] are preceded by a cognition whose object is the relation (*saṃsarga*) among those word-meanings which are recalled by words such as "pot" contained in sentences like "bring the pot," and which thus constitute the objects of the recollection produced by such words.
And thus, what is to be proven (sādhya) is the state of being preceded by the knowledge of an object already recalled.

That "knowledge" which constitutes the probandum is the speaker's knowledge— which serves as the cause for the composition of words— established by the principle that "the formulation of words occurs after having cognized the object."

The state of being preceded by that [cognition], which consists in being produced by it, resides in the words constituting a sentence such as "Bring the jar. Even so, although the cognition of the sentence-meaning or the cognition of the sentence-meaning itself might be the probandum (*sādhya*), the sentence-meaning in the form of a relation is not the probandum; therefore, [the cognition] of the sentence-meaning...
It must be explained how it possesses the nature of an inference,
and in its absence, how the sentence that produces it can be a means of valid cognition by way of inference.
Because the relation, which enters into the category of the predicate as part of the knowledge qualified by having that relation as its object, is itself the probandum (sādhya);
[this is said] with reference to taking up a different relation.

In cases such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), there arises the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*), which is caused by the establishment of the fact that [the cognition] is preceded by a knowledge of an unreal relation— such as between the jar and the objecthood (*karmatva*), or between the objecthood and the act of bringing— which is not the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*).

The intention is that, in order to exclude [inappropriate] association, the property of being the intended object of the speaker's purport (*tātparya*) is added as a qualification. This purpose of the qualification "being that which is recalled" (*smāritatva*) with respect to the word-meaning has been stated thus in the *Muktāvalīprabhā*: "In the view of the Naiyāyikas..."

In the case of the verbal cognition produced by the sentence "ghaṭam" (the pot), which has the pot as its qualifier, the relation of superstratum-ness (*ādheyatā*), and the objecthood (*karmatva*) as its qualificandum, [this cognition arises] from the desire for a communication that intends a representation having the word-meaning "pot" as its qualifier, the relation of superstratum-ness as its connective relation, and the meaning of the item "am" as its qualificandum.
The cause is precisely the knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparya-jñāna*) which apprehends the object as having the form "it has been uttered" as its referent. And thus,

there is also [the requirement for] a cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of the word *am* (i.e., the locus), whose relation is that of location (*ādheyatā*), and whose qualifier is the meaning of the word *ghaṭa*.

There is the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), because [the probandum] consists in the cognition of the relation between the word-meanings that constitute the intended object (*tātparya-viṣaya-padārtha-saṃsarga-jñāna-rūpatayā*), thereby implying that it is preceded by such a cognition.
This is the nature of the action.

Because it is intended that "qualified by a jar through the relation of being located" refers specifically to a cognition whose relation is location, characterized by the property of belonging to a jar as delimited by jar-ness;
therefore, "being remembered" is a qualifier of the word-meaning.

The meaning is: delimited by a property characterized by being the delimitor of the objecthood of an apprehension produced by a knowledge of the relation expressed by the word (*pada*). And thus, the referent of the word *am* [is delimited] by the relation of being located-in (*ādheyatva*).

Although the cognition "qualified by the object pot" (ghaṭapadārthaviśiṣṭa) involves the apprehension of a relation of being-located (ādheyatā) by virtue of its being qualified by the state of being the object of the word "pot," it nonetheless [relates] by virtue of its being qualified by potness (ghaṭatva) as characterized by the aforementioned delimitation of the objective content (viṣayatāvacchedakatva).
“There is no risk of [the definition] lapsing into a different meaning because it does not involve the [cognition’s] non-comprehension of the property of being the locus.

Likewise, in the *Dinakaryā*: “In the case of the cognition of the intended meaning (*tātparya-jñāna*), because the object of one word enters [into the cognition] as the object of the other word, the relation of that which is remembered as ‘pot-ness’ and so on would not be established; therefore, [it must be said to be] ‘recalled’ (*smārita*).”
What is to be understood here has been stated in brief:
[it concerns] a collection of words devoid of expectancy and so forth,
such as "pot," "objectness," "bringing," and "effort."

"In accordance with the diversity of the effects" means that here the effect is reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), whereas in the case of inference it takes the form "I infer," and in the case of verbal cognition it takes the form of the resulting understanding (*śābdabodha*).
"I understand from the word" is a cognition with a single factor.
Alternatively, inference and verbal comprehension are both effects.
The meaning is: "in accordance with the distinct characteristics of those two.
[This refers to] the *Dīpikā* [commentary] on presumption (*arthāpatti*) and the other means of knowledge.
Refutation of [Arthāpatti] as a Separate Means of Valid Cognition:
Now, it may be argued that arthāpatti (presumption) is also a separate means of valid cognition.

If it is argued that, when one has seen or heard the statement "Devadatta is fat and does not eat during the day," nocturnal eating is postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) because his fatness would otherwise be inexplicable—[we reply:
no; [for this is already established by inference as follows: "Devadatta eats at night, because, while not eating during the day, he is fat."
Since the eating at night is established by the inference itself— "because of his corpulence"—
and since "fifty out of a hundred" is a probability (*sambhava*) that is also a form of inference, [so too is] the statement,
"A yakṣa dwells here in this banyan tree."
Thus, even *aitihya* (tradition) is simply a verbal testimony whose original source and speaker are unknown.

Furthermore, even bodily gestures (*ceṣṭā*) are causes for practical activity only by way of verbal testimony or inference; therefore, they are not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently:
Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony— these alone are the four means of valid cognition.
Thus ends the section on verbal testimony in the Dīpikā.
The commentator, a Mīmāṃsaka, raises an objection: "Now, [it might be argued]... (nanu).
When the meaning "he does not eat during the day" is seen— known through direct perception— or heard— understood from verbal testimony;
by this, presumptive testimony based on what is perceived (dṛṣṭārthāpatti) is established.
Thus, the two-fold nature of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)— namely, that based on what is heard (*śruta-arthāpatti*) and that based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭa-arthāpatti*)— is indicated.
By the phrase "because corpulence would otherwise be inexplicable," it is shown that eating at night is the [presumed cause] of corpulence.
The meaning is "without which it would be impossible.
Here, this should be noted: that which is impossible without something else is the subsumer (*upapādaka*) of that thing; thus, eating at night is the subsumer.
Fatness is the object to be established;
the knowledge of the establishing factor is the result; and the knowledge of the object to be established is the instrument.
The term *arthāpatti* applies to both the result (*phala*) and the means (*karaṇa*),
based on the etymological derivation: "the attainment (*āpatti*) or postulation (*kalpanā*) of a purpose (*artha*)" in the case of the result.

But as for its being an instrument [of knowledge], it is because of the etymology: "it is the postulation (*kalpanā*) of an object (*artha*) since [without it] there would be an impossibility (*āpatti*).
For the purpose of *arthāpatti* is already encompassed by negative inference (*vyatirekī-anumāna*) alone.

He provides a resolution [to the objection] that it would be improper for this to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) by saying "Devadatta. The positive member (*satyanta*) of the definition is for the purpose of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of one who eats only during the day while being fat; the negative member (*viśeṣya*) is for the purpose of excluding deviation in the case of one who does not eat at all during the day and night while being fat. And that...
It refers to fatness not produced by anything other than yoga;
therefore, there is no deviation [of the reason] in the case of a fat yogi who is devoid of eating.

He refutes the view of the Paurāṇikas, who assert that probability (*sambhava*) and tradition (*aitihya*) are means of valid cognition distinct from the others, with the words "fifty in a hundred" and so forth,
stating that [these are] merely inference (*anumāna*).
The meaning is that this is merely inference (*anumāna*) and not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
For instance, when it is said, "He has a hundred," the knowledge that "he has fifty" [is inferential].
It is possible [to establish it] by means of inference alone, because fifty is pervaded by a hundred; this is the sense.
"With an unknown root" (ajñātamūla).
The meaning is that a word whose original speaker is uncertain is distinguished [from other means of knowledge], yet it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If such a word is true to reality, it is included within the category of verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*); otherwise, however, its essence is that it is simply not a valid cognition.

He refutes the one who argues that "since this object must be understood through this gesture, and since a cognition of a different class is produced by a gesture whose convention has been established, gesture (ceṣṭā) is also a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)"—by stating: "Gesture, too... (ceṣṭāpi).
"By way of verbal testimony and inference" means either by way of verbal testimony or by way of inference, but not independently.
Because it is cumbersome to accept that a word constructed through behavioral indication (ceṣṭā) is a means of valid cognition,
one follows inference.
[This is expressed by the phrase] "in practice" (vyavahāra).
The meaning is "knowledge whose nature is valid cognition.
He concludes with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
Thus ends the section on words in the *Prakāśikā*, titled *Bālapriyā*.
The meaning is as follows: "in the sense of" means in the sense of the absence of eating during the day. This is "presumption based on what is perceived" (dṛṣṭārthāpatti).

When fatness, which is known through direct perception and is established as being non-existent during the day, is logically untenable without a certain fact— namely, that which is called eating at night— the postulation of that fact called eating at night is *dṛṣṭārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is perceived).

The object without which there would be an inconsistency (*anupapatti*) regarding the fatness understood from the heard sentence, such as "Devadatta does not eat during the day," [is that which is inferred].

The postulation of eating at night is an *arthāpatti* based on what has been heard. Now, what is the definition of knowledge through *arthāpatti* and of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as *arthāpatti*?
For indeed, without knowing its definition, it is impossible to investigate whether it constitutes a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); therefore, he says:
"In this regard, the following should be noted," and so forth.
That which is impossible without nocturnal eating— that is, the fatness which is impossible [without it]—
is that nocturnal eating; it is the establisher of that [fatness].
The subsumer is that which accounts for the subsumed.

Knowledge of the subsumer, arising from knowledge of the subsumed, is a valid cognition in the form of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). From the knowledge of the subsumed—namely, corpulence—there arises [knowledge] of the subsumer: eating at night.

The syntactical connection is: "knowledge arises. Furthermore, there is no subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) whose object is the knowledge of the thing to be proven, such as having the form "I know fatness."

It should not be argued that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case as well, because there is a subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) having as its object the cognition of the probandum— namely, the form "I know fatness"— and since this too is produced by the cognition of the probandum,
it would fall under the definition; for what is intended is production by the cognition of the probandum *qua* being the cognition of the probandum.

Although mental perception consisting of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) is produced by a knowledge of the object to be established (*upapādya*) by way of being its objective content, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because it is not produced by that [object] in its capacity as a knowledge of the object to be established. Thus, the definition of valid inferential cognition (*arthāpatti-pramā*) is: a cognition possessing a state of being produced (*janyatā*) as determined by a generative capacity (*janakatā*) delimited by the property of being a cognition whose object is the thing to be established.

Thus, the definition has been stated: the definition of the means of valid cognition known as presumption (*arthāpatti*) is its being the instrument for such a cognition. This refers to [the distinction between] the result and the instrument.
The meaning is: "in the result of valid cognition" (*pramiti*) and "in the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*).
"By means of negative inference alone" (*vyatirekyanumānenaiva*): [as in the case where one argues] "Devadatta eats at night, because he is fat despite not eating during the day..."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: "Because he is fat while not eating [during the day], whoever does not eat at night is not fat while not eating during the day—just like the emaciated great sage who eats neither at night nor by day; but this person is not like that, therefore he is not like that."
This is what is intended to be expressed.
Some, however, [formulate it as]: "He who is fat while not eating during the day eats at night, just like Yajñadatta, who eats only at night."

Thus, they say that even by means of positive inference (*anvayyanumāna*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has the capacity to lead to the understanding [of the object]. Regarding the phrase "ending with 'satyam'": if "satyam" were not included, then in a case where the probandum—in the form of eating at night—is absent, [the reason would still appear to be present].
In the case of Yajñadatta, who is fat and eats only during the day, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because the reason—the state of being fat—is present.
To exclude this, the qualification "provided that he does not eat during the day" is added. During the day...
Since the state of eating exists in Yajñadatta himself, there is no deviation [from the rule].
Regarding the phrase "not eating for a day and night":
likewise, if the qualifier "because of fatness" were not employed, it would follow that Devadatta eats at night.
The reason would simply be "because he does not eat during the day.
If that were the case, then it would apply even to an ascetic who eats neither by day nor by night and is emaciated for that very reason.

There would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) [of the reason] in the case of one who does not eat during the day, because while they lack the absence of the cause consisting in the consumption of food at night, they nonetheless possess the reason consisting in not eating during the day;
therefore, "because of corpulence" (pīnatvāt) is stated to exclude that.
And since that ascetic lacks corpulence, there is no deviation [from the rule].
But even so, what of the yogi who does not eat?

Furthermore, one might raise the objection that even if a person becomes fat through the power of yoga, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—since in that case, while the probandum (the state of being a night-eater) is absent, the reason (being fat while not eating during the day) is present. Anticipating this, he says: "And that..."

The meaning is that [the example] refers to fatness not produced by yoga; thus, since the fatness found in a yogi is produced by yoga, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the absence of fatness produced by yoga.
It was stated, "he possesses hundreds."
And so forth. In the section concerning a group of one hundred Brahmins, after the doubt arises as to whether there are fifty Brahmins present in the assembly or not,
[it is concluded that] because the group possessing the number one hundred is composed of parts possessing the number fifty...

Some maintain that "possibility" (*sambhava*) is also a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because from the cognition in the form "given one hundred items, fifty items are possible," there arises a determinate knowledge consisting of the realization: "There are fifty Brahmins here. This is not correct.
This residence possesses fifty Brahmins because it possesses one hundred Brahmins;
for whatever possesses a quantity of one hundred things must possess a quantity of fifty things, just as a floor that is the locus of one hundred jars possesses fifty jars.

The meaning is that the cognition consisting of possibility (*sambhava*) is nothing other than an inference (*anumiti*) produced by the consideration of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) in its general form; therefore, possibility is not a separate means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is because fifty is pervaded by a hundred.
Where there are fifty items, there are one hundred items; this is the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
"By means of words" (*śabdadvāra*) means as follows:

The perception of a word (lipidarśana), although it is a cause in an indirect sense by producing the recollection of the word (śabdasmṛti) which in turn brings about verbal cognition (śābdabodha), is not a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) because it lacks the status of an instrument (karaṇatva);
the same applies to bodily gesture (iṣṭā) as well.

The sense is that [the sense organ] is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it does not produce the cognition of duality and so forth by way of recollecting the word that denotes duality; rather, it functions through the medium of inference.
Regarding the phrase "by way of inference": [it means as follows].
The meaning is: "by means of inferring a specific intention of one who is acting.

The form of the inference is as follows: "This person possesses the intention to convey duality, because they possess a distinctive action that is invariably concomitant with the conveying of duality."
This is what is intended.

Now, regarding the phrase "the cause of linguistic usage" (*vyavahārahetu*), if the word *vyavahāra* is taken to mean "activity," then the status of being its cause exists only in the cognition of duality and so forth, and not through a mediated succession.
Anticipating the objection that [the term] refers to an activity that produces knowledge, he explains the term *vyavahāra* as being intended in the sense of "valid cognition" (*pramā*), stating:
"The meaning is 'knowledge consisting of valid cognition'.
This is based on the etymological derivation: that by which one acts (*vyavahriyate*) is *vyavahāra*.

The meaning is that, in the present context, the term *vyavahārapada* signifies knowledge whose nature is valid (*pramātmaka*). Thus ends the section on verbal testimony (*śabda*) in the *Bālapriyā*, a commentary on the *Tarkasaṅgrahadīpikāprakāśikā*.
...seen...
The Theory of Validity:
A Commentary on the *Dīpikā* [of the *Nyāyasiddhāntadīpa*]
In that regard,
there is the demonstration of error concerning cognitions with respect to that which possesses those [qualifiers].
It is now investigated whether the possession of that specific mode (tatprakārakatva) is apprehended intrinsically (svataḥ) or extrinsically (parataḥ). Regarding this, there is a disagreement:
is the validity of a cognition apprehended by the entire causal complex that apprehends the cognition itself, provided that complex does not apprehend its invalidity, or is it not?
Thus: here, the positive alternative (*vidhikoṭi*) is self-validity (*svatastva*), and the negative alternative (*niṣedhakoṭi*) is extrinsic validity (*paratastva*).
This is clarified because of the context of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Wishing to establish that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is apprehended extrinsically (*parataḥ*), he says: "of cognitions" (*jñānānām*).
The meaning of the genitive case is "being located in" (*ādheyatva*).
And its connection is with "having that as its qualifier in that which possesses it" (*tadvati tatprakārakatve*). And that [connection]...
In the same way, [the definition] is "having that as its qualifier (tatprakārakatva) as delimited by having that as its qualificandum (tadviśeṣyakatva).
The referent of the word "that" (tat) is of the nature of potness (ghaṭatva) and so forth.
[The phrase] "to be grasped intrinsically" (svato grāhyam) means:
The meaning is: "the object of a cognition produced by the causal complex that apprehends knowledge. Regarding the term *parataḥ* (from another): the word "object" (*grāhya*) is to be supplied;
the meaning is "the object of a cognition produced by inference and so forth. In that regard:
In the phrase "vicāre," the meaning of the locative case is "being the motivator" (prayojakatva), which connects with "disagreement" (vipratipattau).
If it is asked how that [disagreement] serves as the motivator for investigation, they say the following:

For *vipratipatti* (conflict) consists of two statements that convey contradictory meanings. Through this, a doubt is produced in the neutral observer by means of a comprehension of the respective meanings of those statements which is overwhelmed by a suspicion of invalidity; thus, inquiry—in the form of the application of logic (*nyāya*) and so forth—is undertaken for the sake of ascertaining one of the two alternatives.
Thus, the utility of conflicting views (*vipratipatti*) for inquiry remains intact, as they give rise to the doubt that is necessary for inquiry.
[Regarding] "the validity of cognition" (*jñānaprāmāṇya*):
The statement of the subject (*pakṣanirdeśa*):

here, the subject (*pakṣa*) is validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself in the form of being a cognition that possesses a particular qualifier with respect to its qualificandum, and not validity in the form of being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramiti*).
The word "knowledge" (jñāna) serves to indicate the intended meaning;
however, in reality, it refers to the state of having that [object] as its qualifier when it possesses that [object].

Since it is impossible for any validity (*prāmāṇya*) to be apprehended by the entire causal complex that apprehends the cognition— given that [validity] is differentiated by the distinction of objects such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*)—
therefore, when a validity constituted by a particular property (*dharma*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), at that time...

What must be proven is precisely that [the cognition] is apprehended by all those factors that apprehend a cognition having that specific property (*dharmaprakāraka*) as its object; it is not merely that it is apprehended by all those factors that apprehend a cognition in general. It is the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) that serves to indicate this intended meaning (*tātparya*).
This is expressed in the passage beginning with "its invalidity" (*tadaprāmāṇya*), and so forth.
The meaning is: whether or not that [cognition] is the object of a grasping produced by whatever causal complex (sāmagrī) grasps the cognition while not grasping its lack of validity.
In the Guru’s system, such a grasping is the "determination" (vyavasāya).
In the view of Murārimiśra, it is reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*);
and in the view of the Bhāṭṭas, it is an inference based on the mark of cognizedness (*jñātatā*).

In this regard, according to the Guru’s view (*gurumata*), all cognition manifests this triad of the means of knowledge (*miti*), the knower (*mātṛ*), and the object of knowledge (*meya*). In that system, [the cognition] "I [know] the pot as a non-pot" [is explained as follows].
Because only a determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) of the form "I know" arises;
and thus, since the determinative cognition is self-luminous by nature, its own validity is apprehended by itself. Therefore, [the validity] is established.

The self-evident apprehension of validity; because they do not accept that the cognition of the qualifier is a cause for a qualified cognition, [they hold this] even regarding a validity that is not present [to consciousness].
Because of the impossibility [of such a manifestation],
according to the Miśra school, immediately after the cognition "this is a jar," there arises [the cognition] "I know the jar as being a jar-ness."
A worldly mental cognition (mānasa) having knowledge as its object arises,
and by that, there is the apprehension of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
However, in the Bhaṭṭa school's view, since knowledge is supersensible (*atīndriya*), [the apprehension of validity occurs] only through inference based on the mark of cognizedness (*jñātatā*).
Validity is apprehended by that [cognition] through its nature as the grasping of the initial cognition.
The formulation of the inference, however, is as follows:
the jar is the object of a cognition that has "jar-ness" as its qualifier and a substrate possessing "jar-ness" as its qualificandum.

"Because it possesses a cognizedness (jñātatā) characterized by the mode 'pot-ness'; for that which is not so, is not so. And the distinction between views is this: cognizedness is an additional category (padārtha), produced by knowledge and possessing an object. — *Bālapriyā* The argument is as follows: A pot possesses a specific property called "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), which is produced by the cognition of that pot and is characterized by the cognitive mode "pot-ness. Whatever lacks such a property does not possess it. Regarding the nature of this *jñātatā*, the distinction between philosophical schools is that it is an additional ontological category (*padārtha*) distinct from substance, quality, and action, which arises from a cognition and has an object (*saviṣayaka*). This is the view of the Nyāya school. The phrase *matavivekaḥ* refers to the differentiation of these various doctrinal positions. The commentary *Bālapriyā* explains this point.
By this much of the treatise, the four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been examined;
and thus, when the means of valid cognition are known, [the nature] of that which constitutes them—
He says,

"By reason of the context of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇaprasaṅgāt*), meaning that since the presence of validity (*prāmāṇya*) occurs, it prompts an inquiry into the subject of validity through the logical connection (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*) consisting in the fact that what has been brought to mind cannot be neglected.

The meaning is: "by way of the connection of a logical consequence (prasaṅga) as determined by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). "About to establish" means: "about to prove [it] after first refuting the views of others."
The meaning of the genitive case is "the state of being located" (ādheyatva), and so forth;
thus, it resides in cognitions such as "this is a jar."

The meaning is that it is being investigated whether validity— consisting of such forms as "having potness as its qualifier" (prakāraka) delimited by "having a pot as its qualificand" (viśeṣyaka)— is graspable intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or extrinsically (*parataḥ*).
This is because even the Mīmāṃsakas accept that the validity residing in [cognitions such as] desire is graspable extrinsically.

In that regard, since there is no dispute [regarding it], its investigation is not necessary; this is indicated by the inclusion of the qualification "established in knowledge" (*jñānaniṣṭham*) with respect to validity. [Note:
1. Regarding the phrase *taddhaṭakasya*:]...
The intended meaning is that the word *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition) signifies that which produces a cognition qualified by validity (*pramātva*). [Objection:
There is no single validity common to all cognitions, because [validity] is not something distinct from a universal (*jāti*).

The plural form "of cognitions" (*jñānānām*) is used to indicate that each cognition, being constituted by its respective object such as "pot-ness," is distinct. [The term] "cognizer of cognition" (*jñānagrāhaka*)...

The meaning is: that which is the object of the cognition produced by that causal complex (sāmagrī) which generates a cognition having [another] cognition as its object. The manner in which this [definition] is to be applied will be explained later.
In the phrase "inference and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes verbal testimony (*śabda*) in the form of authoritative speech (*āptavākya*).
Thus, there are two types of statements.
"Validity is apprehended intrinsically" is one statement;
"validity is apprehended extrinsically" is another statement. Regarding these:
The first [is that] of the Mīmāṃsaka,
and the second of the Naiyāyika.
For the neutral person hearing these two sentences which set forth mutually contradictory meanings, the first...
A cognition of the respective sentence-meanings arises as an object of doubt regarding its validity; from that,
a doubt arises as to whether the status of being a valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇya) is apprehended intrinsically (svataḥ) or extrinsically (parataḥ).
Then, for the neutral observer, first arises a cognition of the respective sentence-meanings that becomes the object of doubt regarding its invalidity;
thereafter, [the cognition of] its validity [arises].
A doubt arises as to whether [the object] is to be apprehended by oneself or apprehended by another;

therefore, for the sake of producing a definitive determination toward one of the two alternatives in the mind of a neutral observer, there is the application of the method of reasoning (*nyāyaprayoga*).
An investigation is conducted; and thus, with respect to the investigation in the form of a formal logical argument (*nyāyaprayoga*), the doubt of a neutral observer is the cause.
With respect to the doubt of a neutral observer, conflicting testimony (*vipratipatti*) is the cause. Thus, [the role] of the conflicting testimony...
The intended meaning is that it serves as the motivator for deliberation (*vicāra*).
In this context, "deliberation" (*vicāra*) refers to debate (*jalpa*),
which consists of the application of formal reasoning (*nyāya-prayoga*) with the intent to defeat an opponent by exposing their errors.

The passage from Gadādhara’s work should be understood as follows: "By means of accomplishing the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), [it refers to] the conflicting views (*vipratipatti*) which give rise to the doubt of a neutral observer—an auxiliary factor that is useful for that [inquiry].
The statement of conflicting views presented in the *Dīpikā* consists of a restatement of those respective doctrines.
They say it belongs to the author of the *Dīpikā* itself.
Regarding the phrase "of that which generates doubt," it means "that which causes doubt."
This is the meaning.
Now, an objection is raised: "But was it not stated that 'the validity of knowledge' is the statement of the thesis?"
In that regard, one might ask: "Let the definition of the thesis simply be 'validity' (*prāmāṇya*);

for what purpose is the word 'cognition' (*jñāna*) included? To this objection, he says: "In this context, [it refers to] that which possesses it. This is because the word *pramāṇa*—derived from the root *mā* with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*)—is here used to denote the state (*bhāva*) of the resulting cognition.
The meaning of the word *prāmāṇya* is "being an instrument of valid cognition" (*pramākaraṇatva*).

The meaning of the word *prāmāṇya*, which is derived from the noun *pramāṇa* (formed by adding the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an action) with the addition of the suffix *pyañ* in the sense of an abstract state, is "the state of being valid cognition" (*pramātvam*).

And in the present context, the term "cognition" (*jñāna*) is used to indicate that the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*) is the category of validity itself, which consists in being a means of valid cognition (*pramātva*), and not the state of being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatva*).
Nor should it be argued that "the state of being an instrument of valid cognition" (*pramākaraṇatva*) itself should be the subject (*pakṣa*);

for in that case, there would be a contradiction (*bādha*), since the probandum—namely, the quality of being graspable intrinsically (*svatogrāhyatva*)—is absent therein. Nor can it be asked how the inclusion of the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) excludes the state of being an instrument of valid cognition.

It should not be said that the state of being a means of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatva*) resides in cognitions such as the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the knowledge of similarity (*sādṛśya*),
because it resides in cognition alone.
Since the intended meaning of the restriction "validity is the validity of cognition" is that validity residing in all cognitions is what is intended as the subject (*pakṣa*),
validity in the form of being an instrument of valid knowledge (*pramākaraṇatva*) [is not the subject].
But it does not function as mere cognition, because that [mere cognition] functions in the mind and so forth; rather,
its nature is that of a knower (*pramātṛ*).
The intention is that since validity (prāmāṇya) resides in cognition in general, the word "cognition" (jñāna) serves to exclude the instrument of valid knowledge (pramitikaraṇatva).
Now, [one might object]: "But [validity] resides in cognition in general..."

If it is asked: "Even when the qualification is given, how is there an exclusion of that [instrumentality] which resides in the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth— namely, the status of being an instrument for valid cognitions such as inference— which subsists in all cognitions in general?"— to this they reply:
Since it is a general rule that the qualifier is construed with the qualified under the delimitation of the delimitor of the qualificandhood,

in the present case [the qualifier] is construed under the delimitation of the delimitor of the qualificandhood, which consists in the nature of being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatvatva*).
Alternatively, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with "subsisting in cognition alone" must be stated;

for [if it were not so], there would be a sublation of "subsisting in cognition alone" in respect to being a means of perceptual valid cognition, which is itself encompassed by the property of being a means of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatva*).

Therefore, in this context, validity (*pramātva*) alone is the meaning of the term "authoritativeness" (*prāmāṇya*). However, with respect to that which is delimited by the nature of validity— namely, being a cognition whose mode is present in that which possesses it (*tadvati tatprakāraka-jñānatva*)— ...

There is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the property of residing solely in cognition; since this is possible, by the force of that [concomitance], it is precisely validity (*prāmāṇya*) in the form of being a means of valid cognition (*pramātva*) that is apprehended here. Now, one might object:

If the subject (*pakṣa*) were the category of "validity" (*prāmāṇya*) in its capacity as the referent of the term "validity," then there would indeed be a redundancy with the word "cognition" (*jñāna*). However, this is not the case when the subject is specifically "the state of being a cognition that possesses a particular qualifier in a locus where that qualifier resides."
He states that the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is not redundant because it serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*), saying "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*).
This refers to "of any validity whatsoever" (*kasyāpi prāmāṇyasya*) in the case of [the cognition] "possessing potness" (*ghaṭatvavati*).
Even though validity— consisting in being a cognition having "potness" as its qualifier— is apprehended by the causal complex that apprehends the cognition which is its locus,

there is a sublation [of the opponent's position] because it is not apprehended by the causal complex that apprehends all cognitions included within the class of those that do not have that [validity] as their locus, such as the cognition of a cloth.

It may be so. Therefore, when the subject (*pakṣa*) is validity consisting in the nature of a cognition that has "potness" as its qualifier and is delimited by having a "pot" as its qualificandum—which is constituted by potness—then the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply being apprehended by the causal complex that apprehends the cognition qualified by potness; it is not, however, [the probandum]...

The point is that the word "jñāna" (knowledge) is used to indicate that being apprehended by the causal complex which apprehends knowledge consists in being constituted by knowledge through its general property of being knowledge (*jñānatva*);
however, it is not [meant] in a general sense.

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood that this is intended to secure the result that "being apprehended by the entire causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that apprehends a cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is another property" is not the probandum (*sādhya*).
1. “Beginning with the mind” (*manaḥ prabhṛti*): the meaning is that the mind is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the valid cognition (*pramā*) consisting of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
— [Regarding the phrase] “the invalidity of that,” etc.:

By the very same causal complex through which a cognition is known, validity (*prāmāṇya*) residing in that cognition is also known; the meaning is that within the very cognition whose object is the [primary] cognition, validity residing in that cognition is likewise an object.
In this regard, according to the Prābhākara school, cognition is accepted as being threefold in form (*tripuṭī*).
The meaning of "tripuṭī" (the triad) is that it has as its object this triad consisting of the knower, the knowable, and the knowledge.
According to that view, at first [there arises the cognition] "this is a jar."
Thus, it is not accepted that there is first a cognition consisting of a determinative judgment (*vyavasāya*), followed by a subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) consisting of "I know the jar";
rather, [the cognition] occurs from the very beginning.
Cognition arises in the very form "I know the jar"; that [cognition] is of the nature of determinate perception (vyavasāya).

In that cognition, there are three objects: the pot as the objective content, the "I" (ahamartha) as the knower, and the cognition which is the meaning of the verbal root *jñā*. These three constitute the object.
Therefore, the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) of cognition consists in its having itself as its own object;
and thus, there is a cognition that has cognition as its object, which is identical to itself.
It also takes its own intrinsic validity (svagatapramātva) as its object, just as it likewise takes the nature of cognition (jñānatva) residing in the cognition itself as its object.

Just as the objectivity of a cognition qualified by "cognitiveness" (jñānatva) is accepted for the determinative cognition (vyavasāya), so too is the objectivity of a cognition qualified by "truth" (pramātva) accepted. Nor is it the case that,
because the knowledge of a qualifier is a cause for a qualified cognition...
It must be explained how there can be the manifestation of validity (*prāmāṇya*) when it has not previously been present;
for such a causal capacity [is required].
Because [the opponent] does not accept that; and thus,

since according to the Guru's (Prabhākara) view the nature of self-validity (*svatastva*) consists precisely in being the object of a cognition whose object is cognition, the cognition that has cognition as its object is itself the locus of that objectivity (*viṣayatva*) belonging to truth (*prāmāṇya*).
The proof of self-validity [is as follows]:
in the view of Murārimiśra, first there arises a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) in the form "this is a jar."
From that [perceptual cognition], there arises the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form "I know the jar as being a jar.
Its meaning is: "one who possesses a cognition having 'jar-ness' as its qualifier (*prakāra*) and the 'jar' as its qualificand (*viśeṣya*)."
And thus, according to that view,
anuvyavasāya is the cognition having cognition as its object;
by means of it, when the cognition is made the object, [the object of that cognition is also apprehended].

By virtue of being a qualifier of that [cognition], validity— consisting in having a pot as its qualificandum (viśeṣya) as delimited by having "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) as its mode (prakāra)— is also made an object [of the introspective cognition]. Therefore, self-validity (svatastva), in the form of being the object of a cognition whose object is the cognition itself, is established.
In the view of the Bhāṭṭas,
since cognition is supersensible (*atīndriya*), the sensory perception of a jar or similar object does not have cognition itself as its object; therefore,
first of all, the cognition arises simply as "this is a jar."
By that cognition, a certain property characterized as "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), which has an object, arises in the jar; by means of that cognizedness—
Knowledge is inferred;
thus, in that view, the cognition of the object of knowledge is simply an inference characterized by the mark (liṅga) of "cognizedness" (jñātatā).

By that inference, the validity residing in the cognition is also made an object; thus, there is the establishment of "self-validity" (svatastva) in the form of being an object of the cognition itself.
This definition—that self-validity consists in being the object of the apprehension of the initial cognition—is common to all three philosophical positions.
It is to be defined as follows: by the qualification "being the first" (*prāthamikatva*) in the apprehension of knowledge,
the apprehension of a second cognition— consisting of an inference based on signs such as purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), which is accepted by the Naiyāyikas— is excluded.
"By virtue of determination having the nature of self-luminosity" means "by virtue of having itself as its object."
"Because of apprehension" means because of making [the object] an objective domain.
[This refers to] a mundane mental cognition having knowledge as its object.

The meaning is that this is a mental perception (mānasapratyakṣa) produced by the ordinary sense-contact (laukikasannikarṣa) consisting of the conjunction between the self and the mind, having knowledge as its object.
This very [perception] is called mental introspection (anuvyavasāya).
"By that, there is the apprehension of validity" means that by that mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), the state of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) is made an object.
That is to say, it is the objectivity residing in truthfulness (prāmāṇya) as determined by a mental perception whose object is knowledge;
by means of that [objectivity], truthfulness is apprehended through inference.
Validity is made the object [of cognition],
namely, as having a potness-possessing thing as its qualificand; and thus, in this inference...
The object [of the cognition] is a cognition that has "possessing potness" as its qualificandum and "potness" as its qualifier;

furthermore, validity— consisting in the state of having "possessing potness" as its qualificandum and "potness" as its qualifier— is also an object, insofar as it serves as a qualifier of the cognition.

In the *Dīpikā*, the purpose of including the word "itself" (*svataḥ*) in the definition is to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of its being apprehended through inference and other such sources; the word "as far as" (*yāvat*) is used for this reason. This...

In order to exclude sublation (*bādha*)—since the validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not apprehended by the cognition "this cognition is invalid"—the phrase "not apprehending invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyāgrāhaka*) is included [in the definition]. [For example:
"This cognition is invalid."

Thus, since even that which apprehends validity residing in the *anuvyavasāya* lacks the absence of apprehending invalidity, it would not possess "self-validity" (*svatastva*). Therefore, the term "that" (*tad*) refers to that which does not apprehend invalidity with respect to the locus of the apprehended validity.

In the case cited, since even that which apprehends the invalidity of the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) does not apprehend it within the subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), the self-validity (*svatastva*) of knowledge is established.

Intending that the portion ending with "agrāhaka" (non-apprehender) is meaningful only when the qualification "as much as there is" (*yāvattva*) is present, [the author] first states the purpose of that very [qualification].
He demonstrates this with the words "by inference," beginning with "of validity," and "proving what is already established."
In the view of the Naiyāyikas as well, [the inference is]: "This cognition is valid (pramā), because it generates successful purposive activity.
1. Regarding the term *prāthamika*:
the meaning is that it is the state of being the object of that first cognition which has the [initial] cognition as its object.
The sense is that [the cognition] is graspable by means of inference as well as by the authoritative statement (āptavākya) "this cognition is valid.
It should also be understood that even in the Nyāya school, this is stated in order to avoid the fallacy of sublation (bādhavāraṇa) when a negation is to be proven.
Regarding the phrase "as far as" (*yāvaditi*):

[one might object] that the qualification "as far as" applied to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is improper, because the apprehension of what is produced by the entire causal complex is not established.
For indeed, a single cognition is not produced by all the causal complexes of knowledge;
nor [is it produced] by taking up as many specific causal complexes as there may be.
If it is argued that one must state that what is being proven is the status of being the object of a cognition produced by this or that [specific cause],

because if the causal complexes (sāmagrī) such as the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya) were included in their specific forms, the consistency across the three philosophical systems could not be maintained— [we reply]: no.
The phrase "as far as" (*yāvat*) functions as a qualification of the apprehension in terms of its result;
thus, it means "being the object of every apprehension produced by the causal complex that apprehends cognition."

The result is as follows: the essential point is that [the property] is the counter-correlativity of a subjectivity that pervades the state of being grasped by a cognition produced by a causal complex capable of grasping a cognition having that specific property as its qualifier; this is the summary.

"Because validity is not apprehended" means that it does not take validity as its object, as expressed in the passage beginning with "resting upon the primary cognition" (*vyavasāyaniṣṭha*). This is the meaning.
The phrase "not grasping invalidity" means this:

since such a causal complex for cognition does not enter into the category of the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no sublation (*bādha*) even if validity is not grasped by it; this is the intended meaning.

"Ending in the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*)," and so forth. This refers to the validity— consisting in having as its qualifier the state of having non-validity as its qualifier, which is qualified by having as its object (the qualificand) that which possesses non-validity— which resides in such a subsequent cognition.
The meaning is "of that which apprehends it. The neuter gender is used because of the rule "the neuter is used for general categories" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*).
[The phrase] "there would be no self-nature" (*svatastvaṃ na syāt*) [is the intended sense].

When that which has its validity ascertained is the subject (*pakṣatā*), then it is precisely the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that apprehends validity without apprehending invalidity that is included within the category of the probandum (*sādhyakoṭi*).

The meaning is that because such a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not established as something to be introduced [into the definition], its being graspable by itself (*svato-grāhyatva*) cannot be proven.
Intending a locative *tatpuruṣa* compound, he says "in that" (*tasmin*). Of this very [same thing]...
The commentary states that the locus of the validity of the apprehended object is such a validity as is intended for the inferential cognition under discussion.
The meaning of the term "agrāhaka" (non-apprehending) is: that which does not produce a cognition having as its qualificandum a locus of such validity and as its qualifier non-validity;
[for example], "This cognition is invalid."

Thus, although the causal complex that apprehends validity residing in the *anuvyavasāya* (after-cognition) generates an apprehension of invalidity having the *vyavasāya* (primary cognition) as its qualificandum,
it does not generate an apprehension of invalidity having the *anuvyavasāya* itself as its qualificandum, and because it is a grasper of the cognition [itself].

He states that the intrinsic graspability (*svatogrāhyatva*) of validity—which is constituted by having as its qualificandum something possessing invalidity (*aprāmāṇyavad-viśeṣyakatva*), and so forth—is established in the cited case; that is to say, in the case of [the cognition] "this cognition is invalid. For further detail...
This should be understood from our commentary, *Maṇidīdhiti*. According to the *Bālapriyā*,
self-validity (*svatastva*) consists in being apprehended by that entire causal complex which apprehends all cognitions, provided it does not apprehend the non-validity of that cognition.
Thus it is stated in the *Dīpikā*:

"The meaning of that [definition] is: being the object of a cognition produced by whatever causal complex (*sāmagrī*) apprehends knowledge, provided that such a complex does not apprehend its lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*)."
The phrase "not apprehending invalidity" (aprāmāṇyāgrāhaka) means "not producing a cognition that has invalidity as its qualifier" (aprāmāṇyaprakārakajñānājanaka).

Within the term "cognition" (jñāna), which is a single part of that [compound], there is the syntactic connection (anvaya) of the meaning of the locative ending in "in that" (tasmin)—namely, having that [invalidity] as its qualificandum (tadviśeṣyakatva).
By the word "that" (tat-), [the invalidity is referred to].
That which is the locus of such validity as is apprehended by inference is called [the object of the definition]. And thus,

[the definition is] the state of being the object of a cognition produced by all those causal complexes (sāmagrī) that produce a cognition having as its object a cognition which does not generate a cognition whose qualificandum is the locus of the apprehended validity and whose qualifier is invalidity.
This results in [the property of] being self-evident (*svatastva*).

In the cognition "this is a jar," that which is grasped by the inference— "this cognition is valid because it generates successful activity"— namely, the presence of jar-ness in what possesses jar-ness...
When validity— consisting in having "pot-ness" as its qualifier—

exists in the cognition "this is a pot," then the causal complex that produces a cognition having that [pot] as its qualificandum and having "invalidity" as its qualifier (in the form "this cognition is invalid") does not produce a cognition having that [cognition of the pot] as its object; for it is not by that [complex] that [such a cognition is produced].
The cognition "the cognition of the jar is non-valid" arises;
and the cognition produced by such a causal complex is a cognition having [another] cognition as its object, according to the manner previously described.
According to different philosophical views, [valid knowledge] consists of cognitive determination (*vyavasāya*), reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), and inference (*anumiti*);
the application [of the definition] is that the state of being the object of these constitutes validity (*prāmāṇya*).

In this context, while discussing the purpose of the "petals," the *Dīpikā* first states the purpose of the word "as far as" (*yāvat*), and subsequently states the purpose of the phrase "that which apprehends its invalidity" (*tadaprāmāṇyagrāhaka*).

In this regard, having first stated the purpose of the term *agrāhakānta*, which presents itself first, it is logical to state the purpose of the term *yāvat*, which presents itself immediately thereafter.

In response to the doubt—“Having abandoned that [definition], for what purpose has a definition by way of contrariety (*viparyaya*) been stated?”—he says: “Only when the qualification ‘as long as’ (*yāvat-tva*) is present.
However, this [contrariety] is [intelligible] only when the purpose of both qualifications is understood.
In order to clarify this, the purpose of these two [definitions] is first set forth.

If the qualification "not apprehending invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyāgrāhaka*) were not included, then "self-validity" (*svatastva*) would mean simply being apprehended by whatever causal complex (*sāmagrī*) apprehends the cognition.
And likewise, even the cognition in the form "this knowledge is invalid" (idaṃ jñānam apramā) is included among all cognitions that have knowledge as their object; therefore,
its being apprehended by such [a cognition] exists only in its invalidity (apramātva).
However, there would be a contradiction regarding the status of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*).

To prevent this, the qualification "not grasping invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyāgrāhaka*) is included [in the definition] of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). This refers to the causal complex that produces the apprehension of a cognition in the form: "This cognition is invalid."
It would necessarily be a grasper of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), because such a cognition has invalidity as its object,
and it follows that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) producing such a cognition must necessarily be a grasper of invalidity. Consequently,
since that causal complex lacks the property of not grasping invalidity, it is [defined as] "not a non-grasper of invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyāgrāhikā*).
The causal complex that apprehends a cognition (*jñānagrāhakasāmagrī*) is indeed the very complex that constitutes subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) and so forth;

since the state of being an object of the apprehension of a cognition—such as the subsequent reflective awareness produced by that complex—exists in the case of validity (*prāmāṇya*), there is no sublation (*bādha*). If the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) were not employed, [the definition would fail] because there exists a causal complex that apprehends a cognition which does not apprehend invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).

By this [statement], having taken as the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) either an inference in the form "this cognition is valid because it produces successful activity" or an authoritative statement in the form "this cognition is valid," there arises— produced by that [complex]— an inferential or verbal comprehension in the form "this cognition..."

The Naiyāyika also accepts that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is the object of the two cognitions and apprehensions having the form "this is valid"; therefore, in proving [validity] in that manner, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
To avoid this, the word "as far as" (*yāvat*) is used.

This being the case, since even the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), and so forth, are included within the apprehension of the cognition itself, their being objects thereof is not admitted as constituting "truth" (*pramātva*);
thus, there is no proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is the purpose of the two clauses [of the definition].
In this context, the qualification "provided that there is no grasper of invalidity" is meaningful only as far as the locus [of the cognition] extends; otherwise,
if self-validity were defined merely as being the object of a grasping produced by the causal complex that grasps the cognition, no contradiction would arise.

By the phrase "grasping of knowledge," there is the possibility of [defining] truth as having that [knowledge] as its object, through the grasping of either a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), a subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), or an inference based on the mark of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*).
And thus, since no sublation (*bādha*) can occur, [the definition holds].
Otherwise, the entire section up to the mention of the apprehension of the absence of the apprehender of the result (i.e., the apprehension of non-apprehension) would be useless;
for as long as the term "all" (*yāvat*) is present,
even an apprehension of the form "this cognition is invalid" is included within the apprehension of all cognitions.
Since the state of having that [object] as its domain does not exist in the case of validity, the fault of sublation (*bādha*) would follow; therefore,
with the intention that the phrase ending in "non-apprehender" (*agrāhaka*) is meaningful as a means to avoid that [fault], it is only when the qualification "as far as" (*yāvat*) is present...

It has been stated in the *Pramāṇasiddhi* that [the definition] is meaningful because it ends with "not grasping [the object]," in order to prevent sublation (*bādhā*) when a negation is the probandum (*sādhya*).

The Naiyāyika’s thesis to be proven (*sādhya*) is the absence of being apprehended by the entire causal complex that apprehends all cognitions except for those that apprehend its own invalidity (*tadaprāmāṇyāgrāhaka-yāvaj-jñāna-grāhaka-sāmagrī-grāhyatvābhāva*).
In this regard, if the term "all" (*yāvati*) were absent [from the definition],...

Because it is apprehended by the words of a reliable person (*āptavākya*), which serve as the mark (*liṅga*) for an inference based on the capacity to produce purposeful activity (*samarthapravṛttijanakatva*),
there is a sublation (*bādha*) due to the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), which consists in the non-existence of that [capacity]. To exclude this, [the qualification is added].
The meaning is "up to the word" (yāvatpada).
This is stated with the intention that, in a case where non-existence is the probandum, the very presence of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) in the subject (pakṣa) constitutes sublation (bādha).

Regarding the phrase "nanu sāmagryām": if the word *yāvat* functions as a qualifier for the word *sāmagrī*, it refers to all those causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) that produce the apprehension of cognition.
It follows that the probandum (*sādhya*) is "being the object of a cognition produced by that [cognition].

This being the case, since a single apprehension of a cognition produced by the entire causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is unestablished, the fallacy of the unestablished probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) results; for:

Since every one of the causal complexes— namely, that which produces an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), that which produces a cognition whose mark is *jñātatā* (the state of being known), and that which produces an inference whose mark is successful activity— is individually a grasper of knowledge, there does not exist a single grasping of knowledge produced by all such causal complexes collectively.
It is not by way of being the totality of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) that [self-validity] is established,
but rather specifically; and thus,
self-validity (*svatastva*) consists in being the object of a specific apprehension produced by a specific causal complex that generates the apprehension of that particular cognition.

The meaning of the passage expressing the doubt is that even if the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) is avoided by means of the equipment (*pariṣkāra*), the consistency with all three views (*matatrayasādhāraṇya*) is still not achieved.
He provides the response:
"From which... as far as. [Objection: But even if the probandum is the state of being an object of apprehension as far as it is produced by the causal complex that grasps the cognition;

Anticipating the objection that sublation (*bādha*) is unavoidable— since the truth (*prāmāṇya*) consisting in the possession of the property "pot-ness" is not grasped by the cognition of the cognition of the cloth, which is produced by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) grasping the cognition of the cloth and is not included within the totality of what is grasped—

it is replied that there is no such fault, because the term "cognition-grasper" (*jñānagrāhaka*) is qualified by the attribute of "having that property as its qualifier" (*taddharmaprakārakatva*) with respect to the cognition.

Desiring to provide a resolution and also intending to indicate the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) whereby the word "as far as" (*yāvat*) conveys the pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) of the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the referent of the words co-uttered with it, he states the resultant meaning: "tattaddharma... (the respective properties...).

The meaning is: "that which has the mode of that property whose validity is constituted by that property. And thus, [it refers to] having the mode of potness as delimited by the state of being a qualificandum possessing potness.

The proposition is: "It is the determiner of an objectivity that pervades the state of being a cognition produced by the causal complex which apprehends a cognition having 'pot-ness' as its qualifier.
The cognition having "pot-ness" as its qualifier is the cognition in the form "This is a pot."

The causal complex that generates the knowledge of that [object], such as the causal complex of after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) and so forth, produces a grasping; wherever such a grasping occurs within after-cognition and the like, there exists a "subject-object relation" (*viṣayatā*) determined by truth (*pramātva*), which consists in having the potness as its qualifier and the locus of potness as its qualificand.
And since such a state of being the determiner of a subject-object relation (viṣayitā) exists in validity (prāmāṇya), the definition applies.
Now, [one might object]: even in the Nyāya system, there is a subject-object relation determined by validity...

Even though there is an absence of pervasion of such a grasping (graha) by the property of being a qualificative-ness (prakāritā) toward potness as delimited by having a potness-possessor as its qualificandum, there is nonetheless pervasion of the grasping produced by the causal complex of after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) and so forth by the property of being a qualificative-ness toward potness; thus, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).

Furthermore, it is not possible to intend for the objectivity of truth (*prāmāṇya-viṣayatā*) to be pervaded by the state of being a qualifierhood (*prakāritā*) determined by potness (*ghaṭatva*), which is itself delimited by having a substratum possessing potness as its qualificandum;
for in the system of the Naiyāyikas, the probandum (*sādhya*) would be unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).
In the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) of the form "I know this as a pot-ness," such subjecthood (prakāritā) appears precisely as the subjecthood qualified by pot-ness, and not otherwise.

Anticipating the objection that [the cognition] is characterized by the state of being a qualificative content of potness (ghaṭatva-prakāritā) as delimited by the state of having a substrate possessing potness (ghaṭatvavad-viśeṣyakatva-avacchinna), he says:
"In brief" (saṃkṣepa).
Here, in the case of that which possesses potness...

The proposition— that "the state of having potness as its qualifier (ghaṭatvaprakārakatva) is the determiner of a subject-object relation (viṣayitānirūpaka) possessing a property that is not a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absence residing in a cognition produced by the causal complex that grasps the cognition having potness as its qualifier"— is not what is intended.

By this, the aforementioned fault would not arise; rather, the counterpositiveness of the absence residing in the apprehension produced by the causal complex that grasps the cognition having "pot-ness" as its qualifier is not delimited by the property of being the objectness of validity, which consists in having "pot-ness" as its qualifier as delimited by the state of having a substrate possessing pot-ness as its qualificandum.
Thus, this is the intended thesis (*pratijñā*).
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no such fault as the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) and so forth.
For further details, one should consult the *Prāmāṇyavāda* section of the *Gādādharī*.
In the *Dīpikā*,
this is explained by the phrase "by the cognition that 'this knowledge is invalid,'" and likewise by the term "not apprehending invalidity."
If the qualification of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) were not included,
then "self-validity" (*svatastva*) would mean being the object of whatever apprehension is produced by the causal complex that apprehends the cognition.
This being the case, immediately after the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) "this is silver" regarding a piece of silver, that which is...

If "knowledge" (*jñāna*) were defined as "invalidity" (*apramā*), then since erroneous knowledge is of the nature of a cognition, it would be included among all cognitions produced by its own causal complex;

consequently, the property of being the object of such a cognition would reside only in invalidity (*apramātva*) and not in the subject (*pakṣa*) which is validity (*pramātva*). Thus, there would be a contradiction (*bādha*).
To exclude that [case], the qualification "not apprehending invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyāgrāhaka*) is added;
its meaning is "that which does not produce the apprehension of non-validity."
Since the apprehension of the aforementioned cognition has the nature of an apprehension of invalidity (*apramātva*)— insofar as it has invalidity as its object—

the causal complex that produces the apprehension of the aforementioned cognition necessarily produces the apprehension of invalidity; therefore, because [the causal complex] does not fail to produce that [apprehension of invalidity],
by the term "apprehension of cognition" (*jñānagraha*), one refers to an apprehension of cognition in the form "this cognition is invalid."

It is not the [object] that is apprehended; rather, it is precisely the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "I know this as silver" that is apprehended. Since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) producing that [after-cognition] is what apprehends the invalidity, the property of being the object of an apprehension consisting of the after-cognition produced by that complex exists in the case of validity; thus, there is no contradiction.
The state [of being];
as it says in the *Prakāśikā*: "the culmination of resolve," and so forth.

The meaning is: because it does not have as its object that truthfulness (prāmāṇya) residing in the erroneous cognition "this is silver," which consists in having silverness as its qualifier in relation to that which possesses silverness.
And thus, the sense is that there is a contradiction (bādha) because [the object] is not the object of such a cognition included within the scope of validity;
[this refers to] "by the causal complex of such a cognition" (tādṛśajñānasāmagryā).
This means: by the causal complex that produces a cognition of the form "this knowledge is invalid";
because [the object] does not enter into the category of the probandum (*sādhya*).
The meaning is that [the cognition] is not encompassed by the qualifying condition consisting in the non-apprehension of invalidity, because it apprehends invalidity.
Regarding the phrase "apprehending its invalidity":
