The purpose of that term, as stated in the *Dīpikā*, is as follows:
following the erroneous determinative cognition "this is silver," there arises [the reflective awareness] "this cognition is invalid" (*apramā*).

Thus, for one who maintains that validity consists in being a cognition whose content is the absence of invalidity (*apramātva*), there is a sublation of "self-validity"— defined as being apprehended by a causal complex that does not apprehend invalidity— because such validity is apprehended by the very same causal complex that apprehends invalidity, namely, the state of being a cognition whose content is invalidity within that which possesses invalidity. This applies to such validity.
To exclude that [possibility], the phrase "not apprehending its invalidity" (*tadaprāmāṇyāgrāhaka*) is included;
its meaning is "that which does not apprehend invalidity with respect to it."

The meaning of the phrase "not apprehending its invalidity" (*tadaprāmāṇyāgrāhaka*) is that it does not produce a cognition which has as its qualificandum the locus of that specific truthhood (*pramātva*) for which self-validity (*svatastva*) is asserted, and which has invalidity (*aprāmātva*) as its qualifier.

By the phrase "this cognition," what is intended is that cognition which takes the form "this is silver," [and] which is the object of the causal complex (sāmagrī) that apprehends the status of being a valid cognition (pramātva) residing in the cognition which takes the form "this cognition is not a valid cognition."

Even though it apprehends the non-validity (apramātva) having that [second cognition] as its qualificandum, it possesses the capacity to generate a cognition that has non-validity as its qualifier and that second cognition as its qualificandum— namely, the cognition "this cognition is invalid"— because the subject under discussion is the substratum of the validity consisting in having non-validity as its qualifier, which resides in that which possesses non-validity.
"There is no such fault" means that this knowledge has as its object the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that "this [prior] knowledge is invalid.
Because this knowledge has the [prior] knowledge as its object, it is designated by the term "reflective awareness" (*anuvyavasāya*). Therefore...
One should not raise the objection: "How can this [cognition] be an *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent reflective awareness), given that it lacks the form 'I know' and so forth?
Indeed, following the word *sāmagrī* (causal complex) which serves as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), one ought to say: "even of that which apprehends validity."
Anticipating the objection— "How can it be said that [this applies] even to the grasper of validity?"— the author states in the *Dīpikā*:
"The neuter form is used for the general sense," referring to the nature of being a grasper (*grāhakatva*).

The intention is that because of the grammatical rule stating "the neuter gender [is used] when there is a desire to express the locus of a general property (sāmānyadharma) while not desiring to express the specific locus of that [property]," the neuter gender is applied here.

"Of the aforementioned validity" (*niruktaprāmāṇyasya*): the meaning is "of the validity consisting in having as its qualifier invalidity, which is itself qualified by having as its qualificandum that which possesses invalidity.
"Of that" (*tasya*): the meaning is "of the aforementioned validity."
"It would not be established"; the sense is that there would thus be a contradiction (*bādha*). [This refers to] the establishment of being apprehended through itself (*svataḥ*).
Because the causal complex that generates the knowledge having as its object the subsequent cognition (anuvyavasāya) in the form "this cognition is false"— which is the locus of such invalidity—
does not produce a knowledge in which validity is the qualifier and the aforementioned subsequent cognition is the qualificand of its own locus.

The sense is that there is no sublation (bādha), because such a causal complex is well-known, and because the property of being the object of a cognition whose object is the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya) produced by that [complex] exists within the validity residing in the subsequent reflective awareness.
The *Dīpikā*:
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the theory that validity is known intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
Now, [it may be argued] that it is indeed intrinsically...
Validity is apprehended,
because by the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) "I know the jar," there is the objectification of that relation as well, just like [the object] the jar and [its property] jar-ness.
If it is argued that this is because the proximity consisting in the form of determination (*vyavasāya*) is equal [in both cases],
and because the very relation of the qualifier (*prakāra*) with the object present before one constitutes the meaning of the term "valid cognition" (*pramā*).
Having thus presented the conflicting views, the *Prakāśikā* introduces the Mīmāṃsaka position with the words "nanu" (but surely). [The validity is] intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

"Thus," and so forth. The meaning is that validity—consisting of the property of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) and so on—is apprehended by that very aforementioned causal complex (*sāmagrī*). By the particle *eva* (only), which has the sense of "also," inference and other means of knowledge are included.
[The phrase] "by the after-cognition" (*anuvyavasāyena*)...
And this is stated with the intention of the mixed view;
however, it should be understood that according to the commonality of the three views, it is by means of the apprehension of the initial cognition.
"Of that relation as well" means:
of the relation between the jar and jar-ness as well. [Objection: But how [is it perceived] in the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*)?

Anticipating the objection that the relation [between the object and its qualifier] must also appear, he says "vyavasāya... (by means of the determinate cognition), explaining that just as the pot and pot-ness appear through the proximity consisting of the determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), so too does their relation, because there is no difference in the nature of that proximity consisting of the determinate cognition.
To the question, "How then is validity manifested by that much?", he says: "Of the relation to the qualifier in the object present before one.
This means: of that which is constituted precisely by the relation to the qualifier existing in the object present before one.

The intention is this: even the Naiyāyikas accept that both the state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) and the state of being the qualifier (*prakāratva*) appear in the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), for they hold that the after-cognition takes precisely the form, "I know the object standing before me as a jar."
This is because they accept that [the relation is apprehended];
however, they do not accept the manifestation of the relation with a qualifier such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) in the case of a pot or other object present before one. Therefore, in that case—
Since nothing remains to be established regarding the manifestation of the relation between the qualifier and the qualified, the manifestation of validity is proven,
because there is a manifestation of the status of being the qualified and the status of being the qualifier even when these two are not themselves presented [to consciousness].
"Because it is accepted by all" means that its validity is constituted by [the presence of] potness and so forth.
The meaning is that validity— consisting in having "pot-ness" as the qualifier (prakāra) delimited by having the "possessor of pot-ness" as the qualificand (viśeṣya)—

is apprehended by the very same complex of conditions (*sāmagrī*) that apprehends the cognition which is its locus; namely, the cognition in the form "I know the pot," which has as its object the determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) in the form "This is a pot."

In that [perception], the object consisting of the "I" (ahamartha), the self (ātman), and knowledge (jñāna) appear through the conjunction of the self and the mind (ātmamanassaṃyoga) and through the inherence in what is conjoined with the mind (manassaṃyuktasamavāya); thus, in those respects, it is worldly (laukika).
However, the pot and the pot-ness appear through the cognitive proximity characterized by the nature of knowledge (jñānalakṣaṇā pratyāsatti).

Because prior to such a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), there exists the primary awareness (*vyavasāya*) in the form "this is a jar," and because that primary awareness has both the jar and jar-ness as its objects; thus,
by means of the contact characterized as cognition consisting of the primary awareness whose objects are the jar and jar-ness, [one perceives] "I [know] the jar."

In the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) "I know," there is the manifestation of both the jar and its jar-ness; likewise, the manifestation of their relation— specifically the relation of inherence (*samavāya*)— is also necessarily required.

Because that [relation] also appears in the determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), it necessarily follows that the relation with that [object] must appear due to the contact (*sannikarṣa*) whose nature is determinate cognition. Nor can it be argued that "let the relation between the jar and jar-ness appear," [for that would be untenable].

It must be stated that, since validity does not appear [in the cognition] to that extent, how could the "self-validity" (svatastva) of validity— defined as being the object of a cognition whose object is the cognition itself— be established?
Because the very relation with the object present before one constitutes the meaning of the term "valid cognition" (*pramātva*),
and because the manifestation of that relation is itself the nature of the manifestation of valid cognition.
If it is asked, "How is this so?"—
Listen: when the validity of knowledge is being refined, it culminates precisely in the suchness of the object— that is,
the object as it appears in the determinative cognition (vyavasāya) by virtue of possessing such-and-such a property.
The "suchness" (*tathātva*) of the object consists precisely in its relation to such a property (*dharma*);

and since that very [suchness] is what constitutes validity (*pramātva*), and because it is made an object by the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), validity is apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
This is the intention of the Mīmāṃsakas; it has been restated in both the *Dīpikā* and the *Prakāśikā*.
Although...

The following objection arises: since it is impossible for the truthfulness (*prāmāṇya*) residing in a cognition to consist in the suchness (*tathātva*) of the object as it exists in its objective domain,

truthfulness must instead be defined as "the state of being a cognition that possesses a qualifier residing in that [object], while simultaneously being the determiner of a qualificandum residing in that [same object]."

Nevertheless, the Naiyāyikas maintain that in the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya), there appears the state of being a determiner of the qualifierhood residing in "silverness," while simultaneously being a determiner of the qualificandhood residing in the object present before one.
It is accepted that in that case, even though the qualificandumness and the modehood are not presented [by a separate cognition], they appear;
the [objects] "that which is present before one" and "silver-ness" appear through the proximity consisting in the nature of the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*).
It is accepted that the possession of silver-ness does not appear in the object present before one; however, the Mīmāṃsakas [hold otherwise].

The distinction is as follows: having established that even the possession of silverness (rajatatvavattva) appears due to the similarity of its proximity in the form of a cognitive determination (vyavasāya), they further establish that the truth-value (pramātva) constituted by that [silverness] is made an object by the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya). This refers to the form: "I know the object present before me as a jar."

The meaning is: "I am one who possesses a cognition that has as its qualifier (prakāratā) the property of being a jar (ghaṭatva), which in turn is determined by a qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the object present before me.
This is the established conclusion (siddhānta) regarding the theory of the apprehension of validity (*prāmāṇyajñaptivāda*) according to the *Dīpikā*.
If intrinsic validity were apprehended, then in the state of non-habituation, there would be no doubt regarding the status of a cognition as valid— such as "Is this cognition of water valid or not?"—
because its validity would have been ascertained by the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya). Therefore:
Because there is an absence of being apprehended by itself, it is indeed apprehended through another.
For instance, when, following the initial cognition of water, one acts and subsequently obtains water, the previously arisen cognition of water—

Validity is ascertained by means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*): "A cognition is valid because it generates successful activity; that which is not so [i.e., does not generate successful activity] is not so [i.e., is not valid], just like an invalid cognition."

In the case of the second and subsequent cognitions, it is apprehended by means of a probans that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatirekin), namely, the mark of being of the same class as those [cognitions] based on the example of the preceding cognition.
The "illuminator" (prakāśikā) is the cognition of water, and so forth; it takes the form: "Is this cognition of water valid or not?"
In the state of non-habituation— that is,
in the stage following the initial apprehension of the cognition of water—
the doubt regarding its validity established by experience does not arise.
The meaning is "it might be so.
Regarding the phrase "because of being ascertained":
the cognition of the absence of that [property] in a locus is [prevented] by the ascertainment of its presence there.
The sense is that [it is not accepted] because it would constitute an obstacle.

In this regard, since the cognition "the jar is known" can be accounted for simply by postulating that its object is the state of being an object of knowledge (*jñānaviṣayatā*), there is no need for an additional *jñātatā* (cognizedness).

It should be understood that the method for refuting [the opponent's view] is as follows: [it is] not to be postulated because of [its] complexity and because of the absence of evidence. The phrase "therefore" (tasmāt) means:
because doubt is experienced during the stage of non-habituation. Of this...
In the absence of being graspable by itself, there is the positive concomitance (anvaya) [with the reason] "being graspable by another," because validity [is established] through inference.
The meaning is that there is thus the state of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatva*). By the phrase "when activity exists," this [is indicated].
An instance of deviation has been shown regarding the Mīmāṃsakas' accepted view that the ascertainment of validity is the cause of purposeful action;
nor does the ascertainment of validity [function] only in the case of unshakable action.
Regarding the state of being a cause: in the case of a wavering activity, there is doubt concerning its validity;

thus, both the state of being unwavering and the state of being wavering are simply specific modes of objectivity (*viṣayitā*). And so, even if one accepts that such wavering activity occurs therein, [the status of the cognition remains intact].
It must be stated how there could be a deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the status of the ascertainment of validity as a cause; nevertheless,
in a case where there was no cognition of either validity or invalidity,
yet there occurred a mere cognition of water and so forth, the demonstration of activity therein [establishes] that doubt regarding validity is the cause [of such activity].
Because deviation [of the cognition from reality] would be unavoidable;
nor should it be suspected that, in this way, activity would occur at the time of determining the invalidity of a cognition of water and so forth.
The summary is as follows: there is no fault because its status as a cause is accepted on the basis of being a cognition of water and so forth whose lack of validity has not been apprehended.
"When there is the attainment of water" means:

By this much, the doubt regarding the unestablished nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) of the reason that will establish the validity of what is about to be stated has been dispelled. Now, because the subject (*pakṣa*) does not exist, he says: "arisen previously" and "capable."
The meaning is: "having that as its qualificand and having that as its qualifier.

Since a positive (anvayi) example is impossible [in this case], he states a negative (vyatireki) example along with an illustration: "that which is not thus is not thus. That which is non-valid cognition...
The meaning is that it does not produce an activity capable of accomplishing that [effect].
"By the negative" means by that which possesses negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*).
"Is ascertained" means it is inferred (*anumīyate*).
"In the cognitions of the second [instance] and so forth" means in the cognitions of water in the second [instance] and so forth;
"by the mark of being of the same class as that" means by the mark consisting in being of the same class as the previous cognition;
that is to say, by virtue of generating a successful activity.
"It is apprehended" means that its validity is inferred.
Regarding the phrase "at the stage following the apprehension of the initial knowledge of water":
that which is initial...
The meaning is: at a time subsequent to that apprehension which has water as its object and takes the form "I know water," which constitutes the knowledge of water.
And likewise, if, upon the apprehension of the initial cognition of water, the truthfulness (prāmāṇya) residing in that cognition of water is also apprehended, then [the doubt arises]:
"Is this cognition of water true or not?"

The meaning is that there would be no doubt regarding the truth (pramātva) of the cognition of water, because the certainty (niścaya) regarding the truth of the cognition of water— which functions as an obstacle— would already exist; for instance, in the case of a person who,
having observed water in a reservoir on one day and performed bathing, drinking, and so forth therein, [encounters it] again on the following day.
The perception of water there from a distance at midday is called the second cognition of water, which has reached the stage of practice (*abhyāsadaśāpanna*).
Because it is recognized as being of the same class as the previous cognition whose validity was already grasped, this cognition is [determined to be] valid (*pramā*).
Having reflected that the doubt "or not" does not arise [in that case], it was stated: "after the apprehension of the initial cognition of water";
this refers to the cognition of the absence of that [water].

The meaning is that when there is doubt regarding validity (*prāmāṇya*), the absence of validity (*prāmāṇyābhāva*) also appears as one alternative; therefore, the ascertainment of validity acts as an obstacle to the cognition of that [absence] aspect.
"The method for refuting that" refers to this.
The meaning is: "the manner of refuting [the existence of] cognizedness" (*jñātatā*).
"By this" means:
by the statement that activity occurs immediately after the initial cognition of water.
Regarding the phrase "as accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas":
when some object has been known and a cognition has arisen, activity toward that object does not occur without a determination of the validity of that cognition.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that, with respect to an inclination toward an object, the certainty regarding the validity of the cognition having that object as its content is the cause. That is not tenable.

Because there is a deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), since activity arises even without the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇya-niścaya*)— in the form "this cognition of water is valid"— regarding the subject, which is that very cognition of water, immediately following the cognition of water.
This is the state.
And it is not "unwavering.
Activity is of two kinds—
It is both unshakable and shaky;
intense activity is unshakable, while non-intense activity is shaky.
The two types of objectivity (*viṣayatā*)—intense and non-intense—correspond respectively to intense and non-intense modes of activity (*pravṛtti*).

In this regard, the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇyaniścaya*) regarding the cognition of a given object is the cause for an intense activity directed toward that object; however, doubt regarding validity (*prāmāṇyasaṃśaya*) is the cause for a non-intense activity directed toward that same object.
The effect-determiner (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the ascertainment of validity is unhesitating activity,

while the effect-determiner for doubt regarding validity is hesitant activity. In cases where activity occurs immediately after the cognition of water even without the ascertainment of its validity, that [activity] is hesitant.
It is accepted that activity is accompanied by hesitation (*sakampa*).

Since that [activity] lacks the property of being "unhesitating activity" (*niṣkampapravṛttitva*), which serves as the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there is no deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*), because unhesitating activity, as delimited by that property, cannot arise without the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇyaniścaya*).

The intention of the objector is that the determination of validity (*prāmāṇya-niścaya*) is undeniably the cause of purposeful action (*pravṛtti-hetutva*). Nevertheless, even in cases where there has been neither doubt nor certainty regarding either validity or invalidity, but only the cognition of water has arisen, one observes the occurrence of action— even if it is hesitant (*sakampā*).

The intention of the respondent is that, because such activity arises even without a doubt regarding validity, there is a deviation in the negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra); therefore, a doubt regarding validity cannot be the cause of activity. Nor is it the case that either the certainty of validity or the doubt regarding validity [is the cause] with respect to activity.

The meaning is that if the status of being a cause is not admitted, then even at the time when there is a certainty of invalidity regarding a cognition of water, activity would still occur, because the cognition of water— which is the cause of activity— would still be present.

Regarding the term "unapprehended" (*agṛhīta*): since it is accepted that only a cognition of water and so forth qualified by the absence of a cognition of its invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*) is the cause for activity directed toward water and so forth, at the time when there is a cognition of invalidity regarding the cognition of water and so forth, there exists precisely a cognition of water and so forth qualified by that cognition of invalidity; therefore [it does not function as the cause].

The meaning is that there would be the occurrence of activity [only when] the cause of activity—namely, a cognition of water qualified by the absence of a cognition of invalidity—is present; [otherwise], there is no such cause. Now, one might object:
Since unshakable engagement is not observed in Vedic transactions— which are accomplished through great expenditure of wealth and effort— without a determination of their validity,
it is logical that the cause of engagement is precisely the ascertainment of the object qualified by the apprehension of its validity.

This is because, if a determination of the object qualified by the absence of the cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*) is the cause of purposeful action (*pravṛtti*), then rather than requiring the inclusion within its constitution of invalidity— consisting either in being a cognition of a particular mode in that which lacks it, or in the absence of being a cognition of a particular mode in that which possesses it— ...
Anticipating the objection that there is simplicity (*lāghava*) in including the qualification "being characterized by the apprehension of validity," he says: "In brief.

Even if the apprehension of validity is somehow useful for purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), since the apprehension of validity can occur extrinsically (*parataḥ*), it follows that the apprehension of validity is indeed intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
The meaning is that one should not be dogmatic.
"By this much" means by the statement that water has been obtained.
"Of the reason that establishes the validity [of the scripture] which is about to be stated";
the meaning is: "of the reason consisting in the capacity to produce successful activity, which proves validity."
The doubt regarding the lack of establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*)—that is, the doubt that [the reason] does not reside in the subject (*pakṣāvṛttitva*).
For the efficacy of the activity consists precisely in the attainment of water; and thus:
The point is that by the mention of "attaining water," it is indicated that there exists a reason (hetu) consisting in being capable of producing purposeful activity regarding the cognition of water.
Now, [the word] "idānīm" (now).
The meaning is: "at the time of the inferential cognition of validity.
Regarding the phrase "being of the same class as the previous cognition," the meaning is:
"by means of the mark (liṅga) of being of the same class as the previous cognition whose validity has already been apprehended."
Furthermore, the fact that a second or subsequent cognition is of the same class as the preceding cognition consists in its being the producer of a successful activity;
thus, being the producer of a successful activity is itself the probans.
The phrase "of the same class as the preceding cognition" (*pūrvajñānasajātīya*) is stated to indicate that the preceding cognition serves as the positive instance (*anvayadṛṣṭānta*).

The formal application of the inference (*anumānaprayoga*), however, is as follows: the second and subsequent cognitions of water are valid cognitions (*pramā*), because they produce successful purposeful activity (*samarthapravṛttijanakatvāt*); whatever produces successful purposeful activity is a valid cognition, just like [the first cognition].
Regarding "the initial cognition of water":
the reality here is this— immediately after the cognition "this is a jar," there arises [the cognition] "I know this jar."
There arises the non-determinate cognition "I know this as a jar," but not [the determinate cognition] "I know the jar as a jar. This is the nature of validity (*prāmāṇya*).

However, it is not merely the state of having "potness" as its qualifier (prakārakatva) qualified by having the substratum (dharmin) as its qualificand (viśeṣyakatva), because that [latter] resides in both valid cognition (pramā) and error (bhrama). Rather, it is the state of having "potness" as its qualifier qualified by having "that which possesses potness" as its qualificand. And this...
It does not appear in the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*),

because in that case the objective character (*viśeṣyatā*) is not apprehended as residing in that which is qualified by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*); for in the primary awareness (*vyavasāya*), the pot is the object precisely in its aspect as "this" (*idantva*).

Because the jar cannot be the qualificandum (viśeṣya) by virtue of being qualified by "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva), it is impossible for the cognition of reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya) to apprehend the status of being a qualificandum as residing in that which is qualified by "jar-ness."

Therefore, some maintain that the intention of the Naiyāyikas is that validity is not apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*). Nevertheless, since it is established by experience that doubt arises regarding both the validity of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) and the possession of that object by its referent immediately following the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), the possession of that object [by the cognition] is not [intrinsically apprehended].

The *Maṇi* text, “Its object is that,” is consistent with their [the Naiyāyikas'] view. The author of the *Dīdhiti* also states: “Since the doubt regarding validity would otherwise be inexplicable, it is postulated that the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) lacks the capacity to apprehend the state of having that qualifier when it has that property as its locus; therefore—”

They say: "Even when there is a cognition that has 'silver-ness' as its qualifier with respect to the object present before one, there is no cognition that [the object] is silver having 'silver-ness' as its qualifier.

Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya, however, [says]: "By means of grasping the relation of the delimited and the delimiter (avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva) between the state of having that [object] as its qualificandum and the state of having that [property] as its qualifier..."

They say: "Since the doubt regarding validity and the doubt regarding the object's possession of that [quality], which is dependent upon it, are both possible, it is not appropriate to insist that [the cognition] does not have the object's possession of that quality as its object.
— *Dīpikā*
The determination of the extrinsic nature of the origination of validity:
the state of being extrinsic (*paratastva*) with respect to the origination of valid cognition (*pramā*) consists in its being produced by excellence (*guṇa*).
A quality (*guṇa*) is the uncommon cause of valid cognition (*pramā*), while a defect (*doṣa*) is the uncommon cause of invalid cognition (*apramā*).
In that regard, in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*), [the uncommon cause] is the contact between the qualifier and the qualified object (*viśeṣaṇavad-viśeṣya-sannikarṣa*).

The auxiliary factor (*guṇa*) is as follows: in inference, it is the knowledge of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) in that which possesses the pervader (*vyāpaka*); in comparison (*upamiti*), it is the knowledge of similarity according to reality;
in verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*), it is the knowledge of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) according to reality.
Thus, etc., is to be inferred.
Regarding "so they say":
even when a cognition is apprehended, doubt regarding its validity arises; therefore, in accordance with that [doubt]...

It must be stated that some constituent element of validity does not manifest in the cognition of a cognition; and the author of the *Dīdhiti* and others maintain that this constituent element consists in the possession of "pot-ness" (ghaṭatvavattva) in the object present before one.

Alternatively, it consists in the relationship of the delimited and the delimiter (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) between the state of having a pot as its qualificandum (*ghaṭatvavad-viśeṣyakatva*) and the state of having pot-ness as its qualifier (*ghaṭatva-prakārakatva*).
Thus concludes the *Viveka* by Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya. [End of section] — *Prakāśikā*:
Thus, regarding the cognition [of the object].
Having established extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) [in general], he defines extrinsic nature with respect to origination as "the uncommon cause of valid cognition" (*pramā*). This means:

possessing a causal efficiency (*kāraṇatā*) that is defined by an effect-ness residing in valid cognition (*pramā*) which is not delimited by any property whose locus exceeds that of the property of being valid cognition (*pramātva*).
By this, there is the exclusion of the contact between the self and the mind— which is the cause of mere cognition— and of defects such as bile (pitta) which produce error.
In this same manner, the status of being a non-common cause of invalid cognition (apramā) should also be refined.
In the phrase "therein," he sequentially establishes the quality that serves as the cause for the fourfold valid cognition (*pramā*) among the four types of valid cognition.
This is the meaning. One should infer [the rest] in this manner:
in an error such as "the conch is yellow," the defect is bile (*pitta*) and so forth.
The meaning is that in an error such as "this is silver," one should infer the presence of a cause such as glittering (cākacakyādi);
this is what is intended. *Bālapriyā*.
"Existing in a locus wider than truth" (*pramātvādhikadeśavṛtti*) means:

the causality (*kāraṇatva*) defined by that causal state (*kāryatā*) residing in valid cognition (*pramā*), which is not delimited by any property that pervades truth (*pramātva*); this is the [definition] of the excellence (*guṇa*) that is the productive cause (*prayojaka*) of truth.
The meaning is "the definition.

If one were to state merely that [pramāṇa] is the causality characterized by the effect-ness residing in the pramāṇa itself, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to the contact between the self and the mind (ātmamanassaṃyoga) and so forth, which serve as causes for cognition in general.

To exclude that [undesired consequence], one must include in the definition of "being an effect" (kāryatā) the condition that it is not delimited by a property that subsists in a locus wider than truth (pramātva).
This applies, for instance, to the contact between the self and the mind (ātmamanassaṃyoga).

However, there exists only a causality that is not defined by an effectness delimited by *jñānatva* (the property of being a cognition)— which is a property residing in a domain larger than validity (*pramātva*)— and not a causality defined by an effectness not so delimited; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Since the causes of error—the specific defects such as *pitta* (bile) and so forth—possess causality with respect to an effect that is not delimited by "cognitiveness" (*jñānatva*) and other properties which pervade truth (*pramātva*), there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to those cases; therefore, in order to exclude this, the property of residing in a true cognition (*pramāniṣṭhatva*) is introduced into the definition of the effect. [This applies] to *pitta* and the like.

Even though [the eye] possesses causality as defined by an effect residing in error, it does not possess causality as defined by an effect residing in valid cognition; therefore, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
Thus he says: "by that."
"It is to be refined in this way":

"The effect residing in invalid cognition (apramā), which is not delimited by a property occurring in a locus larger than that of invalidity, is to be refined. [This means] possessing the causality characterized by the effect-ness residing in invalid cognition, which is not delimited by a property occurring in a locus larger than that of invalidity.
The meaning is that this is the definition of a defect (*doṣa*).
[It is] the *Dīpikā* on invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).

The extrinsic determination of invalidity is due to the fact that the absence of a qualifier in the object present before one is not presented by the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*); thus, invalidity is indeed extrinsic.
It is apprehended that "other-dependence" (*paratastva*) regarding origination consists in being produced by defects such as bile (*pitta*).
— *Prakāśikā*

He demonstrates that the non-validity of cognition is extrinsic (paratastva) along with its logical justification, stating: "the object present before one," and "because it is not [otherwise] established."
The meaning is "because it is not made an object.
And thus, the sense is that due to the absence of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the apprehension of invalidity by the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) is not possible.
Invalidity (*apramātva*)—
defined as being qualified by having a qualificandum that lacks that [property] while possessing that [property] as its qualifier—
is apprehended only extrinsically (*parataḥ*).
The meaning is that it is apprehended precisely through inference and so forth.

The formulation of the inference, however, is as follows: "This cognition is non-valid (apramā), because it generates a non-corresponding activity; for whatever is not thus [i.e., does not generate a non-corresponding activity] is not thus, like a valid cognition (pramā)."
"Because of the absence of proximity" (*pratyāsatter-abhāvāt*) means "because of the absence of contiguity" (*saṃnikarṣābhāvāt*). [This refers to] the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

Since the relation to the qualifier (*prakāra*) is the object of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), it was previously refuted that the apprehension of truth— consisting of that relation to the qualifier— could somehow occur through the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) by means of the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) characterized by the knowledge in the form of the primary cognition.
Since the relation to the absence of a qualifier in the object present before one is the object of the determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*),

it is in no way possible for invalidity— which is constituted by that relation— to be grasped by the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of the error; therefore, invalidity does not possess "self-validity" (*svatastva*), which consists in being the object of the first apprehension of the cognition.
Rather, the sense is that it is like the extrinsic nature (paratastva) known as being cognizable through inference. "Divergent activity" means fruitless activity.
The *Dīpikā*: An Exposition on the Justification of Anyathākhyāti.
Now, for all [schools]...
Since all cognitions are in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*), there is no such thing as a cognition that is not in accordance with reality (*ayathārtha-jñāna*).
Nor is it the case that activity is observed to arise from the cognition "this is silver" in relation to a mother-of-pearl shell.
It should be stated that the proof of anyathākhyāti [the theory of misapprehension] is established,
because purposeful activity is possible through the memory of silver and the cognition of the object present before one alone.

If it is argued that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as "this is not silver" because, in all instances, it is precisely the non-apprehension of the difference between the independently presented [object] and the desired [object] that prompts action—
[we reply: no, for in the case of real silver, there exists a cognition having the object before one as its qualificandum and silver-ness as its qualifier.

Because it is simpler to assume that [the cognition] produces activity, and because even in the case of mother-of-pearl it produces the activity of one seeking silver, one must postulate that it is indeed a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*).
— *Prakāśikā*
Having set aside the doctrine of the Guru,
he establishes *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) with the words beginning "nanu" etc.;
because it conforms to reality—

Because it possesses the nature of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*). The meaning is that there is no such thing as "cognition that does not correspond to reality" (*ayathārthajñāna*); that is, the property of being non-correspondent—defined as having a qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) that lacks that qualifier—is not a resident property of cognition.
Therefore, there is no contradiction resulting from the [alleged] establishment or non-establishment [of such a cognition].
The well-known status of being non-correspondent to reality (ayathārthatva), however, should be understood in the case of desire and so forth;
it is what is meant by "misapprehension" (anyathākhyāti).
If that [definition] is not accepted,
then since a cognition whose qualificandum is the object present before one and whose qualifier is a property such as "silver-ness"— which serves as the delimitor of desirability—
generates activity common to both successful and unsuccessful cases, there would be no activity at all in that instance.
The intended meaning is "it might be so.
Regarding the phrase "recollection of silver," it refers to [the cause] consisting of those two—
[the perception of the shell and the recollection of silver]— which are established as the necessary antecedents, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "because of its occurrence":

the point is that, since there is no causality whatsoever with respect to activity by way of being a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), it is impossible to postulate the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) in order to account for that [causality].
[Objection: But in that case, even where there is a sublation-cognition such as "this is not silver," there would still be activity; to this he says: "upasthita" (presented).
By this much, there is a dependence upon the cause consisting of recollection.

It has been made clear that [the cause] is precisely the non-apprehension of the difference from the desired object— that is, the absence of the apprehension of the difference from the silver and so forth that constitute the desired object.
By the word "only" (eva), the capacity of distinguished knowledge to initiate action is excluded.
Regarding the term "everywhere":
The meaning is "in silver and in mother-of-pearl.
In the case of real silver, it must be accepted that the cause of activity toward an object is specifically the nature of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*).

Otherwise, there would be [the fault of] having to postulate multiple causes, such as the cognitions of the attribute and the substrate, and that which is delimited by the cumbersome property of being a non-apprehension of the difference from the desired object.
Because it would entail [the absurdity of] being the cause [of all activity].

And thus, since there is parsimony (lāghava) in establishing that specific cognition (viśiṣṭajñāna) is the cause of activity with respect to that [particular instance] through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), [activity] in general as delimited by the property of being an activity (pravṛttitva) [is caused by it].

He offers the following resolution: since a single, uniform causal relation must be postulated based on the nature of qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), and since even erroneous activity is subsumed under that specific causal factor, a qualified cognition must necessarily be postulated prior to it; thus, the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) remains entirely unassailable.

Regarding the phrase "satyarajata" (real silver): it refers to a cognition having "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) as its qualifier (*prakāra*). The meaning is: [it refers to] that which is delimited by such a nature of cognition (*tādṛśajñānatvāvacchinna*).
By way of being the generator of activity— that is,
by way of being the generator of that which is delimited by the nature of activity—
of the qualified cognition alone.

[This refers to] precisely that cognition which has as its qualificandum the object present before one and which possesses as its qualifier the property that delimits desirability (*iṣṭatāvacchedaka*). By this, the non-apprehension of a difference from the desired object is excluded.
"From conceptualization" means from inference (*anumāna*).

The formal argument for that is as follows: "This [activity] is produced by a cognition whose qualifier is the delimitor of desirability (iṣṭatāvacchedaka) with respect to the object standing before one, because it is an activity (pravṛtti)."
"...just like the activity directed toward silver in a silver-plate.

This might be argued: since sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) is the cause of perception, and that [contact] is absent with respect to the aspect of "silverness," how can there be the cognition "this" with regard to the mother-of-pearl?
If it is argued that "this is silver" is a perception,
do not say so; for it has been established that even extraordinary sense-contact (*alaukika-sannikarṣa*) possesses the capacity to produce perception.

Because, in the present context, only the proximity characterized by knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*) is possible; this is the view of the Guru (Prabhākara). This is the "Beloved of the Ignorant" (*bālapriyā*).
All cognitions possess the nature of validity (*pramātva*), which consists in having that [object] as its qualifier when it possesses that [qualifier];
there is no cognition whatsoever that possesses the nature of invalidity (*apramātva*), which consists in having that [object] as its qualifier when it does not possess that [qualifier].
This means it is the view of the Prābhākara school.
Now, one might object that it is not appropriate to repeat the position of the Guru (Prabhākara) in the *Dīpikā* by stating that "erroneous cognition (*ayathārthajñāna*) simply does not exist."

If false cognition (*ayathārthajñāna*) were not established, its negation would not be logical; and if false cognition were not established, its negation would likewise not be logical due to the non-establishment of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Since this results in a contradiction regarding both establishment and non-establishment, he says:
"Being devoid of that" means:
"inaccuracy" (ayathārthatva) is the subject (pakṣa), and "the absence of subsisting in cognition" (jñānavṛttitvābhāva) is the property to be proven (sādhya).
The reason is: "because it is contradictory to validity, which pervades the nature of knowledge.

"Non-acceptance of that" means the non-acceptance of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension), which consists of a cognition having as its qualificandum an object that lacks that [predicate] and as its qualifier that [predicate].
This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "having the present object as its qualificandum":

with respect to an activity having the present object as its qualificandum, the cause is a cognition that has as its qualifier the property delimiting desirability (iṣṭatāvacchedaka) and has the present object as its qualificandum.

For a person seeking silver, activity does not arise with respect to an object standing before him— the locus of the notion "this"— in the absence of the knowledge of silverness, which is the delimiting property of desirability (*iṣṭatāvacchedaka*). And thus:

Without an erroneous cognition (*anyathākhyāti*) consisting of a knowledge that has "silverness" as its qualifier and the "mother-of-pearl" as its qualificand, purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) is not possible;
therefore, by following from such activity, [one infers] that which is its cause.
The intention of the objector is that misapprehension (anyathākhyāti) must be accepted;
"concordant activity" refers to successful activity.
Misleading activity; fruitless activity.
Is it not indeed a qualified cognition?

Regarding the argument that there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanā*) to maintain that either the two cognitions are the cause of the activity or their cause is [the silver], and that activity is possible through the memory of silver and the cognition of the object present before one alone— this is what is addressed by the passage beginning with "by those two which are established as invariably preceding," and so forth.

Even by the Naiyāyika, who asserts that qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is the cause of purposeful action, it is admitted that prior to the qualified cognition there exist two cognitions: a perceptual cognition in the form "this" directed toward the object present before one, and the recollection of silver.
And thus,
since activity is possible through these two alone— the cognition of "this" and the recollection of silver— which have been established as its necessary antecedents;
The sense is that qualified cognition is not necessary.
"By way of being a qualified cognition" means by way of being a cognition whose qualificandum is the object present before one and whose qualifiers are properties such as "silver-ness."
"Is it not thus?

means that the acceptance [of the opponent] is that the causes of activity are simply the memory of silver and the cognition of the object present before one, whereas a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is not the cause of activity. Activity (*pravṛtti*).
"It may be so. The sense is that this is because both the memory of silver and the cognition of the object present before one exist.
"In the form of silver, etc.
means that which is desired in the form of silver and so forth.

The meaning is: "of the absence of the cognition of difference having that [silver] as its counter-correlative. And thus, when there is a cognition of the object present before one and a recollection of silver—both qualified by the absence of a cognition whose qualifier is the difference from the desired object (such as silver) having the object present before one as its qualificandum—[this occurs] with respect to the object present before one.

The meaning is that since it is the cause of the activity of one who seeks silver, there is no contingency of activity occurring at the time of the subverting cognition "this is not silver. This is said with respect to the three factors— the cognition of the locus (*idam*), the cognition of silverness, and the non-apprehension of their difference— being required as causes [for activity].

The intention of the root text is that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in positing a single qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) as the cause. This is stated by the passage beginning with "in the case of real silver" (*satyarajatasthale*), etc.
Although both the cognition of the attribute (*dharma*) and the cognition of the substrate (*dharmī*) [could be considered causes], [the author] says this...
Even one who maintains that [the cognition] is the cause of a qualified knowledge accepts this; nevertheless,
it is for the sake of preventing activity at the time of grasping the sublation, such as "this is not silver."
The Prābhākara asserts that causality belongs to that which is delimited by the absence of the apprehension of a desired distinction,
whereas the Naiyāyika asserts that causality belongs to that which is delimited by qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*). In this regard,
the sense is that the simplicity of the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) belongs to the Naiyāyika alone.
"In general" means with respect to activity as delimited by the property of being activity,
that is, with respect to activity as it is common to both successful and unsuccessful activity.
"By being pervaded by the delimitor of its effect-ness" means:
by being the locus of that which is the delimitor of the effect-ness of that qualified cognition, namely, the state of being an inclination (*pravṛttitva*).
"Prior to that" means prior to the activity based on non-correspondence. "By the absence of that [non-correspondence] regarding the aspect of silver-ness" means...
"Due to the absence of sensory contact" means due to the absence of inherence in a power conjoined with the eye.
"Characterized by cognition" refers to that very cognition which has silverness as its qualifier and consists of the recollection of silver.
The meaning is that the contact which causes the appearance of silverness [is the cause of error].
This concludes the *Tarkasaṅgraha*,
the definition of erroneous experience (*ayathārthānubhava*).
Invalid experience (*ayathārthānubhava*) is threefold, distinguished by the categories of doubt (*saṃśaya*), error (*viparyaya*), and uncertainty (*tarka*).
Doubt is a cognition that apprehends the qualification of multiple contradictory properties in a single substratum (*dharmin*);
for example, "Is it a post or a person?"
False knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is error (*viparyaya*), such as [the cognition] "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl.

Reasoning (*tarka*) is the attribution of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) by means of the attribution of the pervaded (*vyāpya*); for example, "if fire were not present, then smoke would also not be present."

Invalid experience (*ayathārthānubhava*) is of three kinds, distinguished as doubt (*saṃśaya*), error (*viparyaya*), and hypothetical reasoning (*tarka*). Doubt is the cognition of multiple contradictory attributes (*viruddhanānādharmavaiśiṣṭya*) in a single substratum (*dharmin*); for example, "Is it a post or a person? (*sthāṇurvā puruṣo vā*).
False cognition is error,
such as [the thought] "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl.
Tarka (reductio ad absurdum) is the attribution of the pervader based on the attribution of the pervaded; for example: "If fire were not present, then smoke would also not be present.
— *Dīpikā*
He analyzes non-correspondent experience (ayathārthānubhava) with the words "non-correspondent" (ayathārtha).
Since dreaming consists of mental error (mānasaviparyaya), there is no contradiction with its being threefold. He states the definition of doubt (saṃśaya) with the words "one... (eketi).
The term "single" (*eka*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a collective cognition such as "the pot and the cloth.
[An example of this is] "the pot is a substance."
The term "contradictory" (*viruddha*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as the aforementioned;
the term "multiple" (*nāna*) is used to exclude over-extension in the case of "that which possesses cloth-ness, which is contradictory to pot-ness."
He states the definition of error (viparyaya) as "false" (mithyā);
the meaning is: a determinate cognition (nirṇaya) whose qualifier (prakāra) is present in that which lacks that [qualifier].
He defines reasoning (tarka) as "pervaded by... (vyāpya).
Although reasoning (tarka) is included within error (viparyaya), it is nevertheless mentioned separately because it serves as an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The *Prakāśikā* [objects]: "Indeed, the statement in the root text that there are three types of invalid cognition (*ayathārthānubhava*) is inconsistent,
because of [the inclusion of] dream-cognition (*svapnajñāna*)."

Since it is established by experience that dreams arise from the recollection of previously perceived objects, from defects such as phlegm (kapha), bile (pitta), and so forth, or from virtuous and non-virtuous unseen forces (adṛṣṭa), and have as their object things that are sublated, he says: "of the dream.
Although a dream is indeed a conjunction of the mind with a particular location [within the body], nevertheless...
It should be noted that the term "dream" is used figuratively for a cognition whose non-inherent cause is that [desire];

this is because it is impossible for it to have the nature of visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*) and so forth. He says "mental" (*mānasa*) because that which consists of memory (*smṛti*)— [...is not a dream.]
The claim that it is "dream-cognition" has been disregarded as it contradicts the *Bhāṣya* and other authoritative texts.

This is stated in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a conjunctive cognition (*samuccaya*) regarding a single substratum (*dharmin*), which arises after the knowledge that the two extremes (*koṭi*) do not pervade [the locus] and which takes both the jar and its absence as its qualifiers (*prakāra*).

To show that even if "having as its object a contradiction" (*virodhaviṣayakatva*) were included [in the definition], the inclusion of "manifold" (*nāna*) is still necessary, he says: "contrary to pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvaviruddha*), etc., and "manifold," etc.

This is because there is an absence of having as its qualifiers manifold contrary properties residing in a single property-bearer (*dharmin*), which is itself determined by a qualificative state (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in that same single property-bearer.

The intended meaning is that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Nor should it be suspected that there is over-extension in the case of a cognition whose qualificandum is a single substratum (*ekadharmī*) but which possesses multiple contradictory properties as its qualifiers (*prakāra*) in distinct forms; for this is precluded by the refinement consisting in the inclusion of a qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by a single property (*ekadharmāvacchinna*).
"Because there is no fault"— this is the general direction [of the argument].
He says this because in another tantra (*tantrāntara*), the word "false" (*mithyā*) is seen to be used in this way for everything other than Brahman.
The phrase "possessing the absence of that" is intended to exclude valid cognition (*pramā*);

for by intending to express the meaning as "the state of having that as its qualifier, delimited by the state of having that which possesses the absence of that as its qualificandum," [the definition does not over-extend].
There would be an over-extension [of the definition] to a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*).
To exclude doubt (*saṃśaya*) and desire (*icchā*), the term "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) is used in the sense of knowledge other than doubt; this is the summary. [End of] the root text.

"By means of the superimposition of the pervader": the meaning is that *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) is a false cognition (*bhrama*) regarding the presence of the pervader, which is produced by a false cognition regarding the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*), both of which are induced (*āhārya*).
The term "produced" (*janya*) is included at the end [of the definition] to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to mere induced knowledge (*āhāryajñāna*).

For instance, when there is the certainty that "this is not a person," one might still have the erroneous cognition "this is a person" due to a delusion regarding the hands and so forth in a tree trunk or similar object.
This is an instance of voluntary (āhārya) superimposition; the first term, "voluntary," is included in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case.

At the time of grasping the absence of anything pervaded by silver-ness, there arises a voluntary cognition of the presence of something pervaded by silver-ness, and from that [cognition] is produced the [judgment]: "This is silver."

Thus, the second term "āhārya" (fancied) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to non-fancied knowledge (*anāhāryajñāna*). It should be noted that in the case of *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum), the cause consists of the certainty regarding the absence of the thing to be established (*āpādya*) and the certainty regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the thing to be established and the establishing factor (*āpādaka*). Since *tarka* is indeed of the nature of a mental error (*mānasaviparyaya*), how could it be [considered] non-erroneous (*ayathārtha*)?
He states that there is a description of its threefold nature with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).
"Being an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānugrāhakatva*) means being useful by way of removing obstacles in the production of a valid cognition by a means of valid cognition.

"By way of distinction" means by way of its difference in nature from reasoning (*tarka*). The intention is that it is stated thus in order to make known that reasoning serves as an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). — *Bālapriyā* (Commentary).
"Figurative" (bhākta) means that there is a metaphorical designation of the cause for the effect.
And thus, dream-consciousness—
The meaning is that it is included within the opposite case.
It is contrary to the Bhāṣya and other texts, as [it says]:
"For one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased and whose mind has dissolved, [the mind] occurs precisely through the doors of the sense-faculties."

This is because the nature of dream as a form of experience is established in Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya* and in explanatory works such as the *Kandalī*, which state: "That mental experience is dream-cognition."
[The definition of] doubt [is as follows]: Doubt is a cognition whose qualificandum is a single entity and whose qualifiers are multiple contradictory properties.
Since the cognition "a pot and a cloth" has multiple contradictory properties—namely, potness and clothness—as its qualifiers, there is over-extension (ativyāpti) of the definition to that case.
To exclude that [over-extension], it is stated that [the object] must have a single property-bearer as its qualificandum.
Since the cognition "a pot and a cloth" has multiple property-bearers— namely, the pot and the cloth— as its qualificanda, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
Because the cognition "the pot is a substance" has a single property-possessor (dharmin), namely the pot, as its qualificandum,
and possesses multiple properties (dharmas) such as potness and substanceness as its qualifiers, there is over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case. To exclude that:
The term "contradictory" (*viruddha*) is a qualification of the property (*dharma*).

Since there is no contradiction in the form of non-coexistence in a single locus between potness (*ghaṭatva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*), which both subsist in the same pot, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

There would also be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the cognition "that which possesses cloth-ness, which is contradictory to pot-ness," because this too has as its qualificandum the single substratum (the cloth) and as its qualifier the property of cloth-ness, which is contradictory [to pot-ness].
To exclude that [undesired case], it is stated that [the cognition] must have multiple properties as its qualifiers (*nānādharmaprakāraka*).

Although a cognition such as "this possesses cloth-ness, which is contradictory to pot-ness" also has multiple properties— namely pot-ness and cloth-ness— as its qualifiers, [it is excluded by the following condition].

Nevertheless, in that cognition, pot-ness is the qualifier (prakāra) with respect to the contradictory portion, whereas cloth-ness is the qualifier with respect to the cloth portion; thus, since these two do not function as qualifiers for a single substratum (dharmin), there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).

Is it not the case that the purpose of the term "not" (na-anu) is precisely to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the cognition "this possesses cloth-ness," since that cognition, in fact, has as its qualifier cloth-ness, which is contradictory to pot-ness?

Regarding the claim that it is improper for the *Dīpikā* to pursue the inquiry as far as the cognition "it possesses cloth-ness, which is contradictory to pot-ness," he says: "Of the two alternatives (*koṭyoḥ*).
This refers to [the case] immediately following the cognition that "the pot and its absence are non-pervasive occurrences (*avyāpyavṛttī*)," when [the cognition] "this... arises.
In order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in a cognition designated as a "conjunction" (*samuccaya*), such as "it possesses a jar and it possesses the absence of a jar"—

which, in reality, has as its qualifier the absence of a jar (which is in fact contradictory to the jar)— the condition of having as its object the contradiction between two alternatives (*koṭidvayavirodhaviṣayakatva*) must also be included.

It must be established that it is precisely in a disjunction (*samuccaya*) occurring at a time when there is no knowledge of the two alternatives being non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*) that the contradiction between the two alternatives is the object.
However, in a conjunction occurring at a time when there is knowledge that those two do not pervade [the locus], the contradiction between the two alternatives does not appear; and thus,
regarding such a conjunction as previously described:
There is no over-extension [of the definition], because there is an absence of having contradiction as its object.
Thus,
in the cognition "this possesses cloth-ness," although cloth-ness is in fact contradictory to pot-ness—

With the intention that over-extension (*ativyāpti*) cannot be asserted there because, even though it has that [the jar] as its object, it lacks the property of having contradiction as its object, the author pursues the cognition up to the point of "this [is] possessed of cloth-ness, which is contradictory to jar-ness."

The intention is that the qualifier "multiple" (*nāna*) is included in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) which might otherwise apply, because that [erroneous] cognition has as its object a contradictory [pair].
This refers to the phrase beginning with "the qualificandum residing in a single substratum" (*ekadharminiṣṭhaviśeṣyatā*), and so forth.
In the cognition "this possesses cloth-ness, which is contradictory to pot-ness," both pot-ness and cloth-ness are qualifiers (prakāra);
however—
The modehood residing in potness is determined by the qualificandhood residing in contradiction;

the modehood residing in clothness is determined by the qualificandhood residing in cloth. [The claim is that] there is a relation of being determined by a single substratum-qualificandhood for both these modehoods residing in potness and clothness.

The point is that there is no over-extension [of the definition] to such a cognition as "it does not exist," because such a cognition lacks the property of being a determiner of multiple dharma-locating qualifiers (prakāratā) that are themselves determined by a single dharmin-locating qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā).
"By way of distinct forms" means,

for example, in a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) having the form "The mountain possesses fire; the substance lacks fire," by way of the properties of being a mountain (*parvatatva*) and being a substance (*dravyatva*).

There is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) with respect to a [cognition] whose qualificandum is a single locus in the form of a mountain; the sense is that it is a determiner of multiple property-qualificative-nesses (*prakāratā*) residing in various properties—namely fire and its absence—which are themselves determined by the qualificandum-ness residing in the mountain. [The term] "delimited by a single property" means as follows: and thus...
The definition of doubt (*saṃśaya*) is: being a cognition that has as its qualifier multiple properties residing in a single subject delimited by one property.
For example: "The mountain possesses fire..."
In the cognition "the substance is devoid of fire," there are two [qualifications]: the qualification residing in fire, which is determined by the qualificandumness delimited by mountain-ness;
and the qualification residing in the absence of fire, which is determined by the qualificandumness delimited by substanceness.

The meaning is that since there is no relation between the two modes (prakāratā) being determined by a single substratum-ness (viśeṣyatā) delimited by one and the same property, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).
[Objection: But even so...

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the conjunctive cognition (*samuccaya*) of the form "the ground possesses both a jar and the absence of a jar," occurring at a time when one knows that the jar and its absence are non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*). For in that case as well,
there is a single subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by the single property of being "ground-ness" (*bhūtalatva*), which is related to multiple properties in the form of the jar and its absence.
Because it does not have as its determiner a state-of-being-a-final-mode (*niṣṭhaprakāratā*), he says "etcetera" (*dig*).

[That which is] the state-of-being-the-thing-to-be-prevented (*pratibadhyatā*) determined by that which is determined by the state-of-being-an-obstructer (*pratibandhakatā*) delimited by a property composed of itself (*svaghaṭita*),

and which is further determined by a state-of-being-an-object-of-opposition (*virodhaviṣayitā*) determined by a property delimited by the delimitor of the state-of-being-the-determiner-of-itself (*svanirūpakatāvacchedakadharmāvacchinna*).

Doubtfulness (*saṃśayatva*) is precisely the state of being a qualifier (*prakāritā*) as qualified by that [dual object], through the relation of co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*). And this is excluded from a cumulative cognition (*samuccaya*).

In a conjunctive cognition (*samuccaya*), because there is no appearance of contradiction, the two objective contents (*viṣayatā*) are not characterized by having contradiction as their objective content; whereas in doubt (*saṃśaya*),
it is admitted that at least the two alternatives (*koṭi*) appear in mutual opposition by way of being related (*saṃsarga*).
The meaning is that it is "endowed with the characteristics.

By this, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a conjunctive cognition (*samuccaya*), when the qualification "having as its object a contradiction" (*virodhaviṣayakatva*) is applied to "knowledge," for that very reason, the cognition "a pot and a cloth" [is excluded from being] a substance (*dravya*).

Thus, since it is possible to exclude such cognitions, the qualification "having a single property-possessor as their object" and the qualification "contradictory with respect to the property" are redundant;
for those two cognitions [do not possess these qualifications].

There is no occasion for the doubt that [the definition] is excluded simply by the absence of having contradiction as its object; for the intended meaning of the present text lies precisely in the aforementioned refinement. 1. Regarding "svaghaṭita" and so forth: [The term refers to] that which is constituted by itself, etc.

The property consisting of the state of being a cognition that possesses a qualificative objectness (prakāritā) directed toward the earth-surface as qualified by a jar— this qualificative objectness being grounded in the doubt "Is it one's own earth-surface or not like a jar?"—
is defined as: the state of being a cognition possessing a qualificandness (viśeṣyitā) directed toward the earth-surface, which is delimited by a qualificative objectness directed toward a jar.

The state of being a sublater residing in the cognition "the ground is possessed of a jar," which is delimited by that [cognition], has a state of being sublated (pratibadhyatā) defined by it, residing in the cognition "the ground is devoid of a jar.
That which delimits this [state of being sublated] is the state of being a qualifier (prakāritā) defined by the absence of a jar. Thus, "self" (sva) [refers to this].

The subjecthood (*prakāritā*) determined by the jar is that which is determined by it; its locus is the jar, and its delimiting property (*avacchedakadharma*) is "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). The opposition (*virodha*) determined by that [property] is such that the subjecthood residing in it—and determined by the subjecthood residing in that opposition—is the subjecthood determined by the absence of the jar, [existing] through the relation of subsistence in a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇavṛttitvasambandha*).

The application [of the definition] is as follows: "the state of being a qualifier specified by that" (tadviśiṣṭaprakāritā) refers to the state of being a qualifier as determined by the jar; thus, it exists in the doubt, "Is the ground possessed of a jar or not?"—as stated in another treatise:
In Advaita Vedānta,
it is stated that erroneous cognition (*viparyaya*) is knowledge whose object is false; thus,
[this definition applies] to everything whatsoever that has as its object anything other than Brahman.
In the Advaita view, since knowledge has a false object, it would follow that it is an error;
therefore, regarding the term "false knowledge" (mithyājñāna):

The intention is that the definition has been explained as "a determinate cognition (nirṇaya) which possesses a qualifier in a locus where that [qualifier] is absent. The phrase "this [is for the purpose of] excluding valid knowledge (pramā)" means that a determinate cognition possessing that qualifier is [otherwise] a misconception (viparyaya).

If only this much were stated, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such valid cognitions as "this is a jar," since that too possesses the qualifier-ness (*prakārakatva*) of "jar-ness" and so forth.
To exclude that, the qualification "that which [the object] lacks" (*tadabhāvavatī*) is added.

The point is that there is no over-extension [of the definition] to such valid cognitions as "this is a jar," because such a cognition has as its qualificandum that which possesses jar-ness, and thus lacks the property of having as its object that which lacks jar-ness. Therefore,
there is no undue extension to collective apprehension (samūhālambana).
The meaning is that there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) in the case of the valid cognition "these are lac and silver" regarding lac and silver;
[this applies] to that valid cognition.

Even though there is the state of having silverness as the qualifier while having a yellow conch-shell (raṅga) lacking silverness as the qualificandum, there is no state of having silverness as the qualifier as delimited by the state of having a yellow conch-shell lacking yellowness (raṅgatvābhāva) as the qualificandum.
Since the modehood residing in silverness is determined by a qualificandhood residing in silver that possesses silverness,
it lacks determination by a qualificandhood residing in a yellow conch-shell (*raṅga*) which lacks silverness; thus, with respect to the portion consisting of the yellow conch-shell...
The meaning is that silver-ness (*rajatatva*) is not a qualifier (*prakāra*).
With the intention that everything remaining has already been stated in the section on perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*), he says, "in brief" (*saṅkṣepa*).
Tarka (reductio ad absurdum) is the attribution of the pervader through the attribution of the pervaded.
The word "attribution" (āropa) here means a voluntary mental error (āhāryabhrama).
And "being produced" (*āhāryatva*) means being generated by a desire existing at the time of sublation.
The meaning of the third [instrumental case] is "being generated," and of that...
In the superimposition of the pervader (vyāpakāropa), there is positive concomitance (anvaya).
The superimposition of the pervaded (vyāpya) is "vyāpyāropa. The meaning of the genitive case here is "object-ness" (viṣayatva).

And thus, it follows that *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) is a misconception regarding the pervader (*vyāpaka*) produced by a misconception regarding the pervaded (*vyāpya*), both of which are produced by a desire existing at the time of sublation (*bādha*). For example: "If the mountain were devoid of fire, then it would be devoid of smoke."
Such is the nature of the tarka (reductio ad absurdum).

In that context, the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is the absence of fire; the superimposition (*āropa*) having that as its object—namely, the error "the mountain is devoid of fire"—is produced by a desire concurrent with the sublation (*bādhaka*). If [this were the case]...

The superimposition (āropa) of the pervader, namely the absence of smoke, which is produced by that [cognition]— in the form "the mountain would possess the absence of fire"— is precisely that [which takes the form] "then it would possess the absence of smoke. That alone.

*Tarka* (logical reasoning). If the qualification of "being voluntary" (*āhāryatva*) were not included regarding an error whose object is a pervader (*vyāpaka*), there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in a case where, due to an error concerning the presence of a hand—which is a pervader of "human-ness"—one has a voluntary superimposition (*āhāryāropa*) such as "this is a human" with respect to a tree branch; the qualification of "being voluntary" is therefore provided to exclude that.
The error of mistaking a branch for an elephant is not "artificial" (āhārya); thus, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
This is because, when superimposing a pervader, the qualification of being "artificial" is not applied.

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the non-imaginary error (*anāhāryabhrama*) in the form "this is silver," which arises from the imaginary cognition (*āhāryajñāna*) "this possesses the property of being pervaded by silverhood"; therefore,
that [qualification] is included to exclude such cases.

Regarding this, he says: "Possessing a superimposed pervader," and so forth. The phrase "the existence of the certainty that 'this is not a person'" is stated in order to bring about the superimposed nature of the error "this is a person."

The phrase "at the time of grasping the absence of what is pervaded by silverness" is intended to ensure that the cognition of the presence of what is pervaded by silverness is of the nature of an *āhārya* (voluntary or forced) cognition;
it refers to the certainty regarding the absence of the probandum (*āpādya*).
Thus: that which is to be established is the consequence; the absence of smoke is its negative concomitance (vyatireka);
the absence of the absence of smoke is the form of smoke; and the certainty thereof [is the conclusion].

The meaning is that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*āpādya*), which is the absence of smoke, and the probans (*āpādaka*), which is the absence of fire, as well as the ascertainment (*niścaya*) thereof, are the causes in a *tarka*.
[Objection: How can there be a statement of three types for that which is non-correspondent to reality (*ayathārtha*)?
The meaning is that it is more appropriate to speak of only two types, namely doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*).
[This is said] "by way of removing obstacles."
The meaning is: "by means of removing the doubt of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) that acts as an obstacle.
However, for errors other than *tarka*, there is no assistance to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas for *tarka* there is.
The meaning is that the separate mention of *tarka*, even though it is included within *viparyaya* (error), is for the purpose of indicating its distinctness by stating "that [error] exists.
Thus, in the case of *viparyaya*, there is the form of being *tarka*.

The meaning is that the distinction is made on the basis of "error-ness" (*viparyayatva*) and "reasoning-ness" (*tarkatva*) in order to indicate the difference: while [the former] is the delimitor of the state of being an auxiliary to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), "error-ness" is not so.
The Compendium of Reasoning:
Definition of Memory (AnTs 65). Memory is also of two kinds.

That which is produced by valid cognition (*pramā*) is "in accordance with reality" (*yathārtha*); that which is produced by non-valid cognition (*apramā*) is "not in accordance with reality" (*ayathārtha*).
Memory, too, is of two kinds: accurate and inaccurate. That which is produced by valid cognition (*pramā*) is accurate; that which is produced by non-valid cognition (*apramā*) is inaccurate.
The definition of pleasure and so forth: Pleasure is that which is experienced by all as something agreeable.
Suffering is that which is to be experienced as disagreeable by all.
Desire is longing.
Anger is hatred.
Action is effort.
Dharma is that which is produced by actions performed according to scriptural injunctions.
Adharma, however, is that which is produced by prohibited actions.
Intellection and the other eight are the specific qualities belonging solely to the self.
Intellect, desire, and effort are of two kinds:
eternal and non-eternal.
Those that are eternal belong to God.
The life-force is impermanent.
