That which is to be experienced as agreeable is pleasure;
that which is to be experienced as disagreeable is suffering.
Desire is longing;
anger is aversion;
action is effort.
Dharma is that which is produced by enjoined actions;
adharma is that which is produced by prohibited actions.
The eight qualities beginning with cognition (buddhi) are the specific qualities belonging exclusively to the self (ātman).
Intellect, desire, and effort are both eternal and non-eternal;
they are eternal in the case of the Lord (Īśvara).
The lamp [of knowledge] is impermanent for the living being. The Smṛti explains it as follows:

Regarding "memory" (*smṛti*): it defines pleasure (*sukha*) by the words "of all. The defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is precisely the quality of being pleasure (*sukhatva*) and so forth, which is apprehended through the subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) such as "I am happy.
However, according to the literal reading [of the text]:
It should be understood as a statement of its own nature. [The *Prakāśikā* says: "Now, of all..."

The root text beginning with "to be experienced as favorable" (*anukūlatayā vedanīyam*) cannot be intended to define pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, because even sages are observed to feel aversion toward the pleasure produced by the enjoyment of words, substances, and the like.

Anticipating the objection that [the definition] is too narrow (*avyāpti*), he states— “by the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) ‘I am happy’ and so forth”— that the very nature of happiness (*sukhatva*) and the like, which is established by such direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is indeed the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). By the phrase “happiness-ness and the like,” the inclusion of pain-ness (*duḥkhatva*) and so forth is intended.
"Yathāśrutam tu" (but according to what has been heard) means "in accordance with the favorability of all [the sources]" and so forth. —
*Bālapriyā* (The Beloved of the Ignorant).

Since pleasure (*sukha*) is that which is to be experienced as agreeable by all, it is understood from the root [of the etymology] that the definition of pleasure is "being the object of a cognition whose mode is agreeableness. Likewise...
Since there is observed aversion toward the enjoyment of another's property on the part of the virtuous,
that [enjoyment] is indeed the object of a cognition characterized by the mode "being contrary to virtuous conduct"; thus, for all [beings],...

He states— beginning with "Now, for all..."— the passage from the *Dīpikā* starting with "I am happy," etc., in order to dispel the doubt that this definition is incorrect because it would result in the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), since the quality of being experienced as agreeable (*anukūlatayā vedanīyatva*) is absent in such pleasure (*tādṛśasukhe*).
The Compendium of Reasoning:
Definition of Mental Impressions (saṃskāra). There are three kinds of mental impressions.
Velocity, mental impression, and elasticity. Velocity is a quality residing in the four elements beginning with earth, as well as in the mind.
Mental impression (bhāvanā), which is produced by experience and is the cause of memory, resides in the self alone.
Otherwise, *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity) is that which restores to its original state what has been altered; it resides in earth, such as mats and the like.
Formative force (saṃskāra) is threefold:
momentum (vega), mental impression (bhāvanā), and elasticity (sthitasthāpaka). Momentum is a function of the four elements beginning with earth, as well as of the mind.
Latent impression (*bhāvanā*) is that which arises from experience and is the cause of memory;
it subsists in the self alone.
Otherwise, [there would be no memory] of what has been done (or endured).
Furthermore, *sthitasthāpaka* (elasticity) is that which restores an object to its original state;
it resides only in the earth, such as mats and the like.
The *Dīpikā* analyzes the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) as follows: "The latent impression... [and so forth].
Impression (*saṃskāra*) is that which possesses the genus *saṃskāratva*.
Regarding the substratum of velocity, he says:
"velocity" (*vega*). Velocity is that which possesses the genus *vegatva*.
He defines *bhāvanā* (mental impression) with the words "anubhava" (experience), etc.
The term "smṛti" (recollection) is used to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the destruction of an experience.
The term "anubhava" is used to exclude over-extension to the self (*ātman*) and other such entities.
The generation of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by memory has also been stated by the Neo-Logicians (*navīna*).
He defines the elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*) as follows: "otherwise... [etc.].
Number and the other eight— namely, occasional fluidity, velocity, and elasticity— are general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*).
— *Prakāśikā*

Regarding the phrase "it experiences": this is the intention of the ancient masters who maintain that [experience] is the cause of both memory and mental impression (*saṃskāra*) precisely by virtue of being an experience— that is,
with respect to the memory of a particular object and the mental impression of that same particular object.
The causality [of memory] resides solely in its being an experience (*anubhava*) of a particular object, and not in its being a cognition (*jñāna*) of that particular object;

for since "experience-ness" (*anubhavatva*) is also a universal (*jāti*), it cannot be considered more cumbersome than "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*). Nor should it be suspected that there is a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) [to choose between the two], because...

Because when causality is possible on the basis of a pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*), the pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*) is merely a specifier of the "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*). Thus say the New School (*navīna*). However, others [the older school]—

Experience functions as the cause of its respective object-specific memory and its respective object-specific latent impression (saṃskāra) solely by virtue of being a cognition of that particular object,
and not by virtue of being an experience per se.
Since a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is destroyed by its fruit, the impression produced by an experience would be destroyed by that very first recollection;
consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that what was experienced once could not be remembered after that first recollection. Nor is this [the case].

If a recollection produced by itself were the destroyer of its own latent impression (*saṃskāra*), then even though the cause would be "cognition" (*jñāna*) in general— which is common to all types of memory— a latent impression produced by an experience that encompasses multiple objects such as a jar and a cloth would be destroyed even by a single recollection directed toward one object, such as the jar.
Subsequent recollection of cloth and other such objects would be impossible because of the absence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding those specific objects; furthermore,
a latent impression whose object is cloth and so forth produced by a recollection would have a different object [than the original perception].
Because it is impossible for a cloth or similar object to serve as a reminder [of a past experience], one must,

by necessity, accept that the destruction of each respective latent impression (*saṃskāra*) occurs through its specific individuality (*tattadvyaktitva*) by means of the final memory produced from itself.
It should not be argued that there is no fault even in [the view that] being an experience (*anubhavatva*) constitutes the capacity to produce [a result],
because the result must have exactly the same object-domain as its cause.
There is no fault, because we accept that [the impression] is perishable;
furthermore, through repeated recollection, the impression becomes more firmly established.
And firmness is a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*) residing within [the mind], which serves as the cause for the immediate arising of memory;
it is not produced immediately by the power of fate.

It should not be argued that since the restriction of immediate recollection is established solely through the presence of the excitant (udbodhaka), no specific genus (*jāti*) residing in the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) need be postulated as its cause;
for [the fact remains] that recollection occurs immediately.
For, having accepted that [the manifestation of memory] depends upon the sudden convergence of conditions governed by destiny (*daiva*),
there would follow the impossibility of even practicing the study of the scriptures and so forth, since that would merely destroy the excellence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, having abandoned...

They say that since it is impossible to conceive of a causal relationship between a perceived form that is certain and non-deviant and a perceived form that is deviant, it is not possible for recollection to be the cause of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) by virtue of being an experience (*anubhava*).
He shows this view with the words: "Even of recollection... (smṛterapi).
Furthermore, there is the inclusion of "experience" (anubhava).
In this view, in the definition, instead of the phrase "produced by experience," one should insert "produced by cognition" (jñāna).
Regarding the phrase "by means of the pervading property":
the pervading property is the nature of being an experience (*anubhavatva*).
The pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*) is "cognitivity" (*jñānatva*),
because it is the basis for determining "being established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhi*).
For indeed, [this does not apply] to the staff.
The sense is that, in its nature as a substance, it lacks the character of being the cause of a jar.
This is because a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is destroyed by its fruit.
The meaning is that [the impression] is destroyed by its fruit, which is in the form of recollection. And thus,

if experience (*anubhava*) is the cause with respect to the impression (*saṃskāra*), then in a case where a recollection of a jar has arisen from an impression produced by an experience whose object was a jar, [the impression is destroyed].
Furthermore, in that case,

there would be no recollection of the jar at a later time, because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the jar would have been destroyed by the initial recollection of the jar; nor [could it arise] again from the recollection of the jar.

In the view that [the impression] is the cause by virtue of being an experience (*anubhava*), you may argue that a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) arises from it, and by means of that, there is the subsequent recollection of the jar.

In the case of the recollection of a jar, since it lacks the nature of experience (*anubhavatva*)— which is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the causal status of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*)— it is impossible for that [recollection] to produce a mental impression. However, if [experience] were the cause by virtue of its being a cognition (*jñānatva*), then [the same would apply] to recollection as well.

Since that [subsequent cognition] also possesses the nature of knowledge and thus serves as a cause for the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), a new impression arises from the first recollection of the jar;
from that [new impression], another recollection occurs. Thus, it is established that a recollection can follow upon a recollection.
The state [of the matter] is as follows: "Nor [is it the case that] by its own production," and so forth.
If one accepts that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) perishes through the memory produced by that impression, then [there would be] knowledge having that [object] as its content.
Even if one accepts causality in the form of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) as the cause of the memory regarding that object,
nevertheless, following an experience directed toward multiple objects such as a jar and a cloth— which takes them collectively as its support (*samūhālambana*)—
there arose the individual recollection of each [object], such as the jar and the cloth, and not [a collective memory].
Regarding the recollection of all previously experienced objects: in that case,
because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) concerning multiple objects such as a jar and a cloth— which was produced by a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana-anubhava*)—

is destroyed by the recollection of the jar, the recollection of the cloth and other objects would be impossible, since the latent impression having the cloth and so forth as its object [would no longer exist].
Because it has perished. Nor should it be argued that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the recollection of a jar generates the recollection of a cloth or other objects;
for since the impression produced by the recollection of a jar has the jar as its object, it is impossible for it to generate the recollection of a cloth or other things.
Because a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) having a certain object as its content is the cause of a memory (*smṛti*) having that same object as its content,
and because it is impossible for a memory with one object to arise from a latent impression with a different object; and thus:
Since it is impossible for a recollection of another object to arise from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) based on the final recollection alone,

it must be stated that the final recollection itself, in its specific individuality, is the cause for the destruction of the latent impression. And thus, that which is delimited by the nature of experience (*anubhava*) is the cause of both the latent impression and the recollection.

The intention of the objection in the text is as follows: even in the case [of repeated recollection], since the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of a jar is not destroyed by the first recollection of the jar, it is possible for another recollection of the jar to occur through its power; therefore, let the status of being a cause of recollection belong to the experience itself, simply by virtue of its being an experience (*anubhavatva*).
"Only that which has an undiminished object," and so forth.

Regarding the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the destruction of that impression occurs only through a recollection whose objects are exactly as many as the objects [contained] in the impression. And thus—

A latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose object is as extensive as that produced by a collective cognition (*samūhālambana-anubhava*) regarding various objects such as a jar and a cloth is not destroyed by the recollection of the jar alone, since that recollection has a subject matter less extensive than the former; thus, [the process occurs] gradually.

The sense is that the recollection of a cloth and so forth is thus rendered possible. Furthermore, in the case of recollection, the property of having a narrower scope than the latent impression (saṃskāra) consists in its having a scope that is pervaded by the scope of the latent impression.
He states another argument for the fact that [the mind] is the cause of a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) precisely by virtue of being cognition: "And it arises," and so forth;
repeatedly.

It is established by experience that from the recollection of a jar, there immediately arises a latent impression (saṃskāra) characterized by a specific genus consisting of the firmness that serves as the cause for the recollection of the jar.

And that [cognition] is logically consistent with being a cause of a latent impression (saṃskāra) precisely by virtue of its being a cognition; for even memory can give rise to a latent impression from it by virtue of its being a cognition—this is the sense.
[The phrase] "due to the presence of an awakener" [means as follows].
The "awakening cause" refers to the perception of related objects and so forth.

The Tarkasaṅgraha: Definition of Action (karman). Action consists of motion.
Throwing upward is the cause of conjunction with an upper location; throwing downward is the cause of conjunction with a lower location;
contraction is the cause of conjunction with a location proximate to the body.
Extension is the cause of conjunction with a remote object;
all other [motions] are locomotion.
These [motions] reside only in the four elements beginning with earth and in the mind.
Action is characterized by motion.
Throwing upward is that which causes conjunction with an upper location; throwing downward is that which causes conjunction with a lower location.
Throwing downward;
contraction is the cause of conjunction with that which is proximate to the body;
extension is the cause of conjunction with that which is remote from the body.
Everything else is motion. Regarding the definition of the universal (sāmānya): the universal is eternal, unitary, and inherent in many.
It resides in substances, qualities, and actions.
It is of two kinds, distinguished as the higher and the lower.
The higher is existence (*sattā*).
Furthermore, there is substance-ness and so forth.
Generality (sāmānya) is eternal, unitary, inherent in many individuals,
and subsists in substances, qualities, and actions.
The higher is existence;
the lower is substantiality and so forth.
This is the definition of the particular.
Particularities (*viśeṣa*) are those which reside in eternal substances and serve to distinguish them.

there is a deviation (vyabhicāra), because even in that atom— which lacks the probandum consisting of the distinctness of atoms— the reason consisting of oneness is present.
To prevent that [fallacy],
the reason "because of this oneness" (etadekatvāt) should be employed.
This so-called "oneness of this" (etadekatva) means:

This is the unity inhering in this very atom. And this quality of "inhering in this very atom" within that unity consists in its inhering in this atom while not inhering in anything other than this atom; [this is stated] with respect to that [other] atom, in relation to this atom.
If the difference [between the subject and the example] is unknown, it is difficult to grasp;
likewise, because there is an absence of knowledge of the logical reason (*hetu*), there can be no inference (*anumiti*).
Furthermore, if the difference is already known beforehand, inference would be redundant.
The intention is that this is for the sake of establishing the distinction of inference.
Now, [one might ask]: "Is this atom distinct from that atom?"
The distinction between atoms is to be established by means of this reason: "because of this specific difference."

In this regard, without establishing a distinction between this particularity residing in one atom and the particularity residing in another atom, this particularity cannot serve as the means of proving the difference from that other atom.

To avoid the fault of infinite regress that would result from having to accept yet another particularity (*viśeṣa*) for the sake of that [first particularity], he says: "That very [particularity] [is the cause] of those things belonging to its own class.
Just as the particularity establishes the distinction between atoms, so too...
It also establishes the distinction from other particulars of the same class, because it is accepted that it brings about both itself and others;
thus, the implication is that there is no infinite regress.
Tarkasaṅgraha:
Definition of Inherence (Samavāya) Inherence is an eternal relation.
It is an inseparable relation (*ayutasiddhavṛtti*). When, between two things, one remains dependent upon the other without perishing, those two are "inseparably established" (*ayutasiddha*).
Examples include: part and whole, quality and the possessor of quality, action and the agent of action, genus and individual, and particularity and the eternal substance.

Inherent relation (*samavāya*) is an eternal connection; it subsists between things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*), such that, between two of them, one cannot exist without the other unless it is in a state of perishing.
Those two remain dependent on one another; they are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*),
just like a part and its whole, or a quality and its possessor.
Action and the possessor of action,
genus and individual,
and particularity and eternal substance.
The *Dīpikā* defines inherence (*samavāya*) as "eternal" (*nitya*). The term "eternal" is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
The term "relation" (*sambandha*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
He states the definition of inseparable existence (*ayutasiddha*) with the words "of which two... as in the case of "the pot is blue."

A qualified cognition has as its object the relation between the qualifier and the qualified, because it is a qualified cognition, like the qualified cognition "the man with a staff"; thus is the establishment of inherence (samavāya).
Regarding "the part and the whole":
the part is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of a substance, while the whole is the substance produced from it.

The *Avayavin-prakāśikā* establishes inference as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for inherence (*samavāya*), in accordance with the common tenets of the Vaiśeṣika school— beginning with "blue" (*nīla*).
Thus [it is defined]. It is specified as "substance" because the state of being an inherent cause exists in the ultimate whole (*antyāvayavin*).
It is specified as "produced" (*janya*) in order to exclude atoms (*paramāṇu*).
It remains precisely as it was, not yet having entered a state of destruction.

Considering that a thing in a state of perishing remains for a moment without support— just as a cloth and so forth remain when the threads and so forth have perished— the root text states "not perishing.
(Bālapriyā)

From the *Dīpikā*, "A part is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of a substance," it is understood that the definition of a part is "the state of being an inherent cause with respect to a substance.
Since the state of being an inherent cause of a substance such as the color of a jar exists in a potsherd (*kapāla*), the definition is applicable. In that regard:

If one were to state merely "being an inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇatva*), there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a pot, which is a composite whole (*avayavin*), because it possesses the status of being an inherent cause of the color and other qualities that are inherent in it.
To exclude that, the qualification "as defined by [the category of] substance" (*dravyanirūpita*) is added to "being an inherent cause."

Although the whole (avayavin), such as a jar, possesses the status of being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatva) as defined by its qualities (guṇa) and so forth, it lacks the status of being an inherent cause as defined by [other] substances; therefore, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti). Thus he says: "of the status of being an inherent cause."

The term "ultimate composite" (*antyāvayavin*) is stated to indicate that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to a skull, which is a composite (*avayavin*), since it is accepted as having parts; for,
according to the text "a produced substance is a composite," being a composite consists in being a substance that is produced.
The definition has been stated.
In that context, if only "being produced" were mentioned, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to produced qualities and so forth;
to exclude those, "substantiality" (dravyatva) is included.

If only "substantiality" (dravyatva) were mentioned, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to atoms (paramāṇu), which are parts; to exclude that, "being produced" (janyatva) is included. Thus he says:
Regarding the refutation of the theory of atoms (*paramāṇuvāraṇāya*):
in the *Paramamūla*, it is stated that "between two [substances], one remains in a non-decaying state while depending upon the other; these two are then *ayutasiddha* (inseparably established)."
By means of the word "inseparable" (ayuta), the definition [of inherence] has been stated.
Between two things—such as between a thread and a cloth—one, namely the cloth, exists only as dependent upon the thread; thus, those two, the thread and the cloth, are inseparable (ayutasiddha).
In this context, "the state of perishing" means the moment immediately preceding destruction;
"the state of not perishing" means existing in the moments prior to the one immediately preceding destruction.

The state of being in the process of perishing (*vinaśyadavasthatva*) means being characterized by destruction through the two relations of occurring in the immediately preceding moment and having itself as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Regarding this,
he states the purpose of the qualification "not in the state of perishing" (*avinaśyadavastham*):
By the words "not in a state of destruction" and so forth,
the following is the intended meaning here: if the qualification "not in a state of destruction" were not applied to the term "one," [the argument would fail].
In that case, the definition of *ayutasiddha* (inseparable) would be: "those two among which one exists only as dependent upon the other.
If that were so, there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the thread and the cloth.
Since there is no rule that between the threads and the cloth, one cloth must necessarily exist as being dependent upon the threads,
when the cloth is destroyed due to the destruction of the threads, at that very moment of the threads' destruction, the cloth—
Because it persists precisely while not yet dependent on the destruction of the threads,
the cloth is therefore qualified as being in a state of "not yet perishing. A cloth situated at the moment of the destruction of the threads is in a state of "perishing."

Because the cloth perishes in the subsequent moment, it is therefore characterized by the state of being in the process of destruction, which consists in its existence in the moment immediately preceding its destruction. Thus:

The "non-perishing state" refers to the cloth delimited by the moment immediately preceding the destruction of the threads; since that cloth exists precisely as being dependent upon the threads, there is no lack of pervasion [in the definition].
Thus, it is said: "the destruction of the threads, etc."
The meaning is: at the moment of the destruction of the thread and so forth.
This concludes the *Tarkasaṃgraha*, the section on the definition of non-existence (*abhāva*).
Prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is beginningless but has an end;
it pertains to an effect prior to its production. Destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) has a beginning but is endless.
After the production [of a cause],
there is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) characterized by a counter-correlativity delimited by a relation across the three periods of time;
for example, "there is no jar on the ground."
Mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) is that whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation of identity (tādātmya), as for example: "A pot is not a cloth."
Prior non-existence is beginningless but has an end;
it pertains to an effect prior to its production.

Antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is that which has a beginning but no end; it pertains to an effect immediately after its production. Non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is that which follows production.
Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is a non-existence delimited by a relation that exists throughout the three periods of time.
Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*):
for example, "there is no jar on the ground.
Mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by identity (*tādātmya*); for example, [the absence of a cloth in a jar].
"A pot is not a cloth"—
thus the *Dīpikā* defines antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

"Beginningless" (*anādi*): this is stated to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to space (*ākāśa*) and the like. "Having an end" (*sānta*): this is stated to exclude over-extension to jars (*ghaṭa*) and the like.
[It is] that which exists in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

Prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the cause for the linguistic usage "it will come into being," as it generates its counter-positive. He defines destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) as "that which has a beginning.
The term "endless" (*ananta*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to things such as jars.
The term "having a beginning" (*sādi*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to space (*ākāśa*) and other such entities.

Destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is that which is produced by its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), which subsists in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of that counter-positive, and which is the cause for the conventional usage of the term "destroyed."
He defines absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) with the words "pertaining to the three times" (*traikālika*).
The term "relation" (*saṃsarga*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
The term "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
He defines mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) with the words "identity" (*tādātmya*).

Due to differences in the delimitors of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) and the superimposed relations (*āropya-saṃsarga*), there is a distinction between absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), even when they have the same counter-positive.
The absence of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) arises from the cognition "there is an absence of the man with a staff" due to the absence of Devadatta alone;
the absence delimited by duality (*dvitvāvacchinnābhāva*) arises from the cognition "even when one exists, two do not exist";
and there is the absence of a jar through inherence (*samavāya*) in that which possesses a jar through conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Furthermore, the general absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "pot-ness" (ghaṭatvāvacchinnapratiyogitāka) is distinct from the absences of individual pots;
the same applies to mutual absence as well.
The *Prakāśikā* states the proof for prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as follows: "It will come to be."
"Conjunction" (saṃsarga) means a relation other than identity (tādātmya).
This is because even in the case of destruction (dhvaṃsa) and prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), there exists a relation that delimits the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha).
The qualification "pertaining to the three times" is intended according to our own view;

otherwise, since those two [types of non-existence] would already be excluded by the exclusion of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), that qualification would result in being redundant. If the meaning of the phrase beginning with "delimited by relation" (*saṃsargāvacchinna*) were "an absence other than mutual non-existence," then...
Even according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the term "pertaining to the three times" (*traikālika*) here is meaningful as having the nature of eternality (*nityatva*).
In the statement, "There is no jar on the ground," the ground is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the aspect of the jar’s absence, and [this] is the relation (*sambandha*).

Regarding the statement "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," the intention of the ancient masters—who maintain that in the case of the ground, the absence functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and its relation [to the ground] is *saṃsarga*—is as follows: being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) and being the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) are specific types of essential relations (*svarūpasambandha*), not specific types of objective content belonging to a cognition (*jñānīyaviṣayatā*). Nor is it the case that...
Let there be only one essential relation called "qualifierhood" (*viśeṣaṇatā*),
for the distinction between the cognition "there is no jar on the ground" and the cognition "the ground possesses the absence of a jar" [is accounted for otherwise].

It should not be argued that [the distinction] is established merely by postulating that the object of cognition is the locus-ness (ādheyatā) as delimited by the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*); for, in order to account for the difference between those two cognitions, in the first case,
the contact (*sannikarṣa*) is the locus-ness as delimited by the state of being a qualifier.
Is it accepted that the relation of qualification belongs to the second [case-ending],
or rather that the relation of qualification belongs to the first?

In the case of the second [cognition], because a determining factor (*vinigamaka*) is difficult to find for [the claim that] "the substratum-ness is delimited by its being a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatvāvacchinnādhāratā*),
and because there is no difference between those two cognitions regarding the aspect of the relation (*saṃsargāṃśa*).

It should be argued that since the distinction [between the two cases] is established through the difference in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), let the status of being a relation belong to the state of being a qualifier alone in both instances. Even so, [the expression] "the jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭaḥ*)...

This is because no distinction can be established between the two cognitions "there is the absence of a jar on the ground" and "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," nor between the two cognitions "the ground has the absence of a jar" and "the ground is in the absence of a jar.
Therefore, regarding both of these, which are termed the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) and the state of being the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*):
The relation between the intrinsic nature and the particular relation constitutes the relationality (*saṃsargatā*).

Thus, in the case of "the absence of a jar is possessed by the ground," the relation is the fact that the ground functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) with respect to the portion consisting of the absence of the jar.

And in the case of "the ground in the absence of a jar," the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) belongs to the absence with respect to the portion that is the ground; and since that [relation] is uncontradicted there, the status of the cognition as non-erroneous is maintained— this is the summary.

Is there a single uniformity between absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), which have a single counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), just as there is between destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)?
He says "no"— "pratiyogiteti" (regarding the counter-positive).
"Having superimposed"— this is according to the intention of the ancient [authorities]. In this case,
there is a distinction based on the limiting property (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma*) as appropriate.
It should be understood that the distinction between types of relational connection (*saṃsarga-bheda*) is the cause for the multiplicity of absolute non-existences (*atyantābhāva*),

whereas the distinction between the properties that delimit the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma-bheda*) is the cause for the multiplicity of mutual non-existences (*anyonyābhāva*).

He demonstrates that very point with the word "kevala" (mere): the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that because of the absence of mere Devadatta, the absence of the qualified [Devadatta] is something distinct.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition "the staff-bearer is not present" could not arise in a place containing only Devadatta;
for if the absence of both were something distinct [from the individuals], one would require a further cognition [of that absence].
He provides the proof: "even in the case of a single entity.
In such cases as "the two, pot and cloth, are not themselves," the triad consisting of potness, clothness, and duality is the delimitant of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedaka).
Because there is such a cognition in that which possesses only a jar, that which possesses only a cloth, and that which possesses both of them in some respect;
[the author] shows the distinctness of absence due to the difference in relations with the words "by conjunction" (*saṃyogena*).
He demonstrates the distinction between the universal (sāmānya) and the absence of a particular (viśeṣābhāva) with the words "tattad" and "atirikta.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "there is no jar" arising even in a place containing some other jar.
The same applies to mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

Due to the difference in delimiters (*avacchedaka*), there is the exclusion of this or that specific jar; from that, both types of exclusion and the exclusion of the jar itself are distinct [from one another]. This is the meaning.

The root text states: "An absolute absence (atyantābhāva) is a relational non-existence (saṃsargābhāva) pertaining to the three periods of time. Here, "relational non-existence" means an absence whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by a relation.

This is the meaning. In that context, if one were to state merely "existing in all three periods of time," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), because that too is eternal. To exclude that, it is stated that [the counter-positive] must have a counter-positivity delimited by a relation of connection (*saṃsargāvacchinnapratiyogitāka*). Not...

Nor should it be argued that even if the definition were to include "having a counter-correlativity delimited by a relation of conjunction," the defect of over-extension would remain unavoidable, because mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) has a counter-correlativity delimited by the relation of identity (tādātmya).
By the term "non-existence through non-conjunction" (saṃsargābhāva), what is intended is an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a relation other than identity (tādātmya).
Thus he says: "The meaning is 'a relation other than identity'.

If one were to state merely "the state of being an absence of relation," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); therefore, [the qualification "other than identity"] is added to exclude those.
Regarding the term "pertaining to the three times":
is it not the case that, while a jar exists in its locus by way of inherence (*samavāya*), the jar does not exist there by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*)?

In order to account for the cognition that "there is no jar by way of inherence in the locus of the jar [which is the ground] by way of conjunction," one must state the distinction between the absence of a jar delimited by the relation of conjunction and the absence of a jar delimited by the relation of inherence. For that purpose...
Furthermore, it is accepted that the counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā) belonging to absolute non-existence is delimited by a relation;
however, since such reasoning is impossible in the case of destruction and antecedent non-existence, their having a counter-positiveness delimited by a relation is unauthentic.

And since the exclusion of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is possible by the term "non-existence of relation" (*saṃsargābhāva*) alone, the qualification "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) would be redundant; therefore, he says: "even of destruction and antecedent non-existence."

According to the view that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) are incompatible with absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), in the cognitions "red does not exist by way of inherence in the unblackened jar" and "black does not exist by way of inherence in the red jar," it is precisely those two— prior non-existence and destruction— that are the objects; therefore, for them as well...

The sense is that, according to his view, since there exists a state of having a counter-correlativity delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*), the qualification "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) is added to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Otherwise... [the definition would fail].
The meaning is that one does not accept that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) have counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by a relation.
[This is stated] precisely by means of the phrase "by that which excludes mutual non-existence" (*anyonyābhāvavārakeṇaiva*).

The meaning is that by the very qualifier— namely, "having a counter-correlativity delimited by a relation other than identity" (tādātmyātiriktasambandhāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva)— which is employed [in the definition], the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti) regarding mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) is avoided.
Because of the exclusion of those two—since it is possible to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
Because that would result in futility—the consequence of the superfluousness of the qualification "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*). As for "if":
thus, the meaning of "relational non-existence" (*saṃsargābhāva*) is "an absence distinct from mutual non-existence" (*anyonyābhāva*).

The intention is that since even destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) possess the nature of being non-existences non-different from mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), the qualification "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) is added to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to those cases;
this applies even to impermanent entities.

Even if the qualification "pertaining to the three times" (*traikālika*) is given—on the grounds that it is possible for [the object] to exist in the three periods of time known as past (such as yesterday), future (such as tomorrow), and present (such as today)—the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) remains in that same state; therefore, he says: "In this context, 'pertaining to the three times' means having the nature of eternity."
Eternality (nityatva) consists in being a non-counterpositive of destruction while being a non-counterpositive of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva).
By the inclusion of the condition "non-counterpositive of destruction," prior non-existence is excluded.
By including the condition of "not being the counter-positive of prior non-existence," destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is excluded.

Now, in the cognition "there is no jar on the ground," the ground is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the portion consisting of the absence of the jar; [this is] the relation, [and] the ground...

Regarding the statement "like the absence of a jar," the claim made by the ancients— that the relation [in the cognition] "the ground possesses the absence of a jar" consists in the absence of the jar being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to the portion that is the ground— is not tenable.
[This is because] [the cognition] is "the ground possesses the absence of a jar."
Since, in the cognition [of "there is no jar on the ground"], the ground appears as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and the absence of the jar appears as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*),
the statement that the relation [between them] is the qualifier-status of the jar's absence with respect to the ground is indeed consistent;
however, [this does not apply] to the absence of the jar in the cognition "there is no jar on the ground."

Furthermore, because the ground appears as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and [the absence] as the qualifier (*prakāra*), the ground lacks the status of being the qualificandum; therefore, the statement that "the relation is the qualificandum-ness of the ground" is incoherent. Likewise...
Since such a cognition would result in being an error because it involves the apprehension of a relation in the form of a sublated qualificandum,
[the author] begins to state the intention of the ancients with the words: "In that regard, regarding the portion consisting of the absence of the jar," and so forth.

The states of being the qualified (*viśeṣyatva*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) are specific types of essential relations (*svarūpasambandha*). For example, in the case of "a man qualified by a staff," the state of being the qualified as determined by the staff— which resides in the man— is either the nature of being distinguished from the staff, or the very nature of the man who serves as the substratum.

Likewise, the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatva) residing in the ground as determined by the absence of a jar is also of the nature of being qualified by the absence of the jar; it is the very essence of the substratum, the ground.
Or, for example, [the qualificand-ness] residing in the staff...

The nature of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatva) is the very essence of the stick that is the substratum; likewise, the nature of being a qualifier residing in the absence of a jar is also the very essence of the absence of the jar.
The states of being a qualificand (viśeṣyatva) and being a qualifier, when spoken of as relations, do not [exist as separate entities].
It is not of the nature of specific objective relations known as the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) and the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) found in cognition;
rather, it consists of the relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*).
And thus, in the case of "There is no jar on the ground," [the absence is related to the locus by way of identity].

Even though the subjecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) form of objectivity does not exist in the ground (*bhūtala*), subjecthood in the sense of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) does exist; therefore, because the ground appears as the qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to the absence of the jar through that relation, the cognition is indeed valid (*pramā*).
It is an entity, and it is not called "qualification" (viśeṣaṇatā).
Thus, there is a state of qualification between the ground and the absence of the jar.
The relation is indeed one and the same.
Nor should it be asked: "If the relation is one and the same, and is the object of both cognitions, how can there be a difference between them?"

Even though the relation is one and the same, in the cognition "there is no jar on the ground," the object of awareness is the locus-ness (ādheyatva) as delimited by the relation of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatā),
whereas in the cognition "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," the object of awareness is the state of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatva). Thus it is.
The intention of the objector is that it is possible to state a difference between the two cognitions. He provides the resolution: "between such two cognitions" and "in the first [cognition]."
The meaning is: "in the cognition 'there is no jar on the ground'.
Regarding the phrase "in the second": "the ground..."
The meaning is: "in the cognition 'as the absence of a jar'. He raises an objection again: "And not [the case] of such two cognitions..."
And thus, in both cases, the object is one and the same relation called "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇatva*).
Nevertheless, in the cognition "there is no jar on the ground,"...

In the cognition "The ground possesses the absence of a jar," the objective relation termed "qualificandumness" (viśeṣyatā) resides in the absence of the jar, while the objective relation termed "qualifierhood" (viśeṣaṇatā) resides in the ground.

The intention of the objector is as follows: the objective relation termed "qualificandumness" (viśeṣyatā) resides in the ground, while the objective relation termed "qualifierhood" (viśeṣaṇatā) resides in the absence of the jar; thus, the distinction between those two cognitions arises solely from the difference in their objective relations, not from a difference in their underlying relations.

"Due to the distinction between the qualifier-qualified relation (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*)," means: due to the difference between the objective states (*viṣayatā*) known as "qualifierhood" (*viśeṣaṇatā*) and "qualifiedness" (*viśeṣyatā*).
He provides the explanation:
"Even by that much," [meaning] in the cognition "there is no jar on the ground," regarding the absence of the jar.

The objective relation called "qualificandumness" (viśeṣyatā) resides in the ground, and the objective relation called "qualifierhood" (viśeṣaṇatā) resides in the absence of a jar; since this is exactly the same in the case of the cognition "there is an absence of a jar on the ground," there would be no distinction between the two because of the lack of difference in their objective relations.

Thus, in the cognition "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," there is a subject-locus objective state (viśeṣyatākhyaviṣayatā) residing in the ground and an [objective state] residing in the absence of the jar.

The distinction between these two [cognitions] does not arise from a difference in their objective relations (*viṣayatā*), because even in the cognition "the floor [is] in the absence of a jar," there is likewise the objective relation known as *viśeṣaṇatā* (qualifierhood),
and thus there is no difference in their objective relations.
The sense is that [the distinction] is difficult to establish.

And thus, by accepting only a single relation called "qualifierhood consisting of the essential nature" (svarūpātmaka-viśeṣaṇatā), there is a difference in cognition due to the difference in objective status (viṣayatā).

Having accepted two types of relations consisting of essential nature— namely, the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) and the state of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*)— on account of their difficulty to establish, he began by asserting that the distinction in cognition must be accounted for solely through the distinction in relation.
He concludes that the cognition is non-erroneous with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
And thus, in the case of "There is no jar on the ground," the ground is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) in relation to the absence of the jar, and [the relation] is inherence (*saṃsarga*).
In the expression "the absence of a jar on the ground," the ground is a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) of the absence of the jar;
this constitutes the distinction between these two [cases].
In the cognition "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," the relation of the absence of the jar to the ground-aspect is that of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*).
In the cognition "the ground [is] in the absence of a jar," [the relation is that of being a locus].

The point is that there is a distinction between the two: in the case of the absence of a jar on the ground, the relation is the state of being the qualificandum (viśeṣyatva) of the absence with respect to the locus (bhūtalāṃśa).
[Objection: But even so, in the case of "the absence of a jar..."

There would be no distinction between the two cognitions "the ground" and "there is no jar on the ground," because both would have the same objective content regarding the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). Likewise, [in the case of] "possessing the ground"...

Otherwise, there would be no distinction between "the absence of a jar" and "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," because in both cases the object of cognition would be nothing but the relation in the form of qualification; therefore, he says: "In brief."

The difference between cognitions must be established through a distinction in the qualifier-qualified relationship (viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva) consisting of their own essential nature (svarūpa-sambandha), which is accompanied by a distinction in the qualifier-qualified relationship consisting of specific objective relations (viṣayatā-viśeṣa). This applies to those two cognitions...

There is no difference in objective status (*viṣayatā*) between those two, yet there is a difference in their relation (*sambandha*). Conversely, for those two between whom there is no difference in relation, there is a difference in objective status; thus it is said.
The meaning is that there is a distinction between cognitions;
therefore, because the relation [between them] is uncontradicted, its status as valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is also established.
Although I had repeatedly scrutinized this text, because I did not understand its intended meaning (*tātparya*), I questioned the venerable teacher;
he too [explained it] in many ways.
Having examined it in the *Prakāśikā* and performed a slight correction, [the author] explained the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
I have written it down here in exactly that same way,
because of the difference in the properties that delimit the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma-bheda*).

Furthermore, due to the difference in the relations that delimit the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha-bheda*), even an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) having a single counterpositive is differentiated. Likewise, due to the difference in the attributes that delimit the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma-bheda*), even a mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) having a single counterpositive is differentiated; this is illustrated with examples as follows.

In the *Dīpikā*, [this distinction] is examined; however, the distinction between destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) has not been examined in that manner. He states the reason for this: "of destruction and prior non-existence," and so forth.
The intended meaning is this:

it is not accepted that the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is either delimited by a relation (*sambandhāvacchinna*) or delimited by some property (*kiñciddharmāvacchinna*). Therefore...
Destructions having a single counter-positive and prior non-existences having a single counter-positive are each of only one kind; however,
this is not accepted in the case of absolute and mutual non-existence.
When absolute absences having a single counter-positive possess counter-positiveness delimited by different relations with different properties,
this is due to the difference in the properties that delimit the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma-bheda*).
Furthermore, there is indeed a difference [between absences] due to the difference in the relations that delimit their counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha*).
Although it may be impossible to assert a difference among mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*) having the same counterpositive on the basis of a difference in relation, [the distinction still holds].

This is because identity (*tādātmya*) itself serves as the relation that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakasambandha*). Nevertheless, the point is that a distinction can be asserted on the basis of the difference between the properties that delimit the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakadharma*). [The word] "superimposed" (*āropya*)...
According to the view of the ancients:
non-existence that is the object of a cognition produced by the superimposition of a relation is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

The ancients have stated that what is called "superimposition of relation" (*saṃsargāropa*) is the superimposition of a counter-correlative by means of a relation other than identity (*tādātmya*). Thus,

there is a distinction based on the types of relations— such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth— which serve as the objects of the superimposition that generates the cognition of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
The meaning of the *Dīpikā*— namely, that "the difference consists in absolute non-existence" refers to "the difference in the superimposed relation"— is the intended sense.
However, the modern [logicians] (*navīna*) maintain:
Since the view that the superimposition of the counter-positive is the cause of the cognition of absence is devoid of logical justification,
the nature of a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāvatva*) must consist solely in being an absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by a relation other than identity (*tādātmya*).
They say that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvatva*) is precisely that [non-existence] qualified by being present across the three times (*traikālika*).
According to that view, however:
It should be inferred that absolute non-existence differs according to the difference in the relation that delimits the counter-correlativity; however,
in the case of non-existence delimited by identity, there is no such difference because the relation of counter-correlativity consisting of identity is of a single uniform nature.
It should be noted that the difference in the relation delimiting counter-positiveness has not been stated as a cause for the difference between mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*).
[This is because] it is from the absence of Devadatta alone [that the distinction arises].

Although Devadatta alone is the counter-positive (pratiyogin) both for the absence of Devadatta and for the absence of Devadatta as qualified by a staff, nevertheless, in the former case, the property of being Devadatta (devadattatva) is the delimitor of counter-positiveness (pratiyogitāvacchedaka).

The difference between the absence of Devadatta and the absence of a man with a staff arises from the difference in the properties that delimit their counter-correlativity— namely, "Devadatta" in one case and "staff" in the other.
If, however, this difference between the two is not admitted, then [the following consequence would follow] regarding a ground where Devadatta alone exists.
Just as the cognition "Devadatta does not exist" does not occur [in the absence of Devadatta],
so too the cognition "the man with a staff does not exist" would not occur; yet it does occur.
Such is the cognition. Therefore,
the meaning is that the absence of Devadatta qualified by a staff is distinct from the mere absence of Devadatta.

Regarding the cognition "the two, pot and cloth, do not exist": in a location containing only a pot, or in a location containing only a cloth, there arises the cognition, "the two, pot and cloth, do not exist."
Neither the cognition "the jar does not exist" nor the cognition "the cloth does not exist" occurs;
therefore, this is because of the absence of the jar alone.
Furthermore, since there is no absence of the cloth alone, the absence of both the jar and the cloth must be admitted as something distinct.

In the case of the cognition "the jar and the cloth do not exist," neither jar-ness alone, nor cloth-ness alone, nor duality alone can serve as the delimiting factor of the counter-positive (pratiyogitāvacchedaka).
Because an absence is incompatible with its counter-positive as qualified by the delimiting property of counter-positiveness, on a ground possessing only a jar, there exists the jar—

which is the counter-positive qualified by the delimiting property of counter-positiveness, namely "jar-ness"— and thus [the absence] is contradicted; [therefore, one cannot say] "the jar and the cloth..."

This is because the cognition characterized by the form "they do not both exist"— which apprehends the absence of both— is untenable; likewise, because in a location containing only a cloth, as well as in a location containing some other pair distinct from both a jar and a cloth,
there exists the contradictory [factors] qualified by cloth-ness and qualified by pair-ness respectively.
Such a cognition would not occur;
therefore, the triad consisting of potness, clothness, and bothness is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedaka).

Since there is an opposition between an absence and its counter-positive as delimited by a property that is the locus of the complete distribution of the counter-positivehood-restriction, it is precisely the pair "pot-and-cloth" as delimited by such a triad that is the opponent of the absence of the pot-and-cloth pair; thus,
[the absence] exists only in a location where the pot-and-cloth pair is present.

The meaning is that the cognition "the jar and the cloth do not exist" does not occur [in the absence of a locus], whereas it is possible for such a cognition to occur when there is a mere jar or similar object present.

"By means of conjunction (saṃyoga)"—thus it is said. And so, one must accept that the absence of a jar delimited by the relation of conjunction is distinct from the absence of a jar delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya); otherwise, [the distinction between the two absences would not hold].

Just as the cognition "there is no jar by way of conjunction on the ground which possesses a jar by way of conjunction" does not occur, so too the cognition "there is no jar by way of inherence" would not occur. Likewise,
just as the cognition "there is no jar by way of inherence" occurs in that very same place, so [should it be understood].

The meaning is that there would also arise the cognition "the jar does not exist" by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Regarding the phrase "of the absence of the general and the absence of the particular," it means "of the absence of the general and the absence of the particular."
An absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a general property is a general absence (*sāmānyābhāva*).
An absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a specific property is a specific absence (*viśeṣābhāva*). For example:
"The pot does not exist."
Thus, the absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by potness (*ghaṭatva*), established through common cognition, is a general absence (*sāmānyābhāva*);
as in the case of "there is no blue pot."
A particular absence (*viśeṣābhāva*) is an absence whose counter-positivehood is delimited by [a property such as] "being a blue pot," as established by cognitions such as "there is no red pot."

If the absence of a universal were not something distinct [from the absences of its particulars], then, since there is the absence of a red pot on a ground that possesses a blue pot, it would necessarily follow that there is also the existence of the absence of pots in general— which is of the nature of the absence of a red pot— and thus one could not say, "There is no pot."
There would arise a cognition apprehending the absence of the universal "pot.

However, if the absence of the universal is held to be a distinct entity, then even when there is the absence of a red pot on a ground that possesses a blue pot, such a cognition does not occur because the absence of the universal "pot" is not present there; thus it may be said.
It is possible [to distinguish them]. Therefore, the sense is that one must accept a generic absence (*sāmānyābhāva*) as distinct from the absence of specific instances (*viśeṣābhāva*).
[This is] because of the difference in their delimiters (*avacchedaka*).
The property of being a blue pot is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity for the difference from a blue pot;
[likewise] for the difference from both a pot and a cloth...

The property of being both a pot and a cloth is the delimitant of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) for the absence of [the pair] "pot and cloth," whereas potness is the delimitant of the counter-correlativity for the absence of a pot; thus, due to the difference in these properties that delimit the counter-correlativity, there arise [distinct cognitions such as]:
"This is not a blue pot," "These two are neither a pot nor a cloth," and "This is not a pot."

The meaning is that one must state the distinctness of those things established by such cognitions as the difference between a blue pot and a pot, the difference between both a pot and a cloth, and the difference from a pot, and so forth. (Dīpikā)

Regarding the absence qualified by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadhar-māvacchinnābhāva*), such as the cognition "there is no cloth by way of being a jar," the absence qualified by a property residing in a different locus is not accepted [as a distinct category].
The meaning of that [statement] is that "pot-ness does not exist in a cloth.
If [the absence] were distinct [from its locus], it would be a purely positive (kevalānvayin) [absence].
— *Prakāśikā*
He states this as a consequence:
"by way of being a jar.
[The phrase] "is not accepted" [is used].

Because cognitions of absence are reinforced by the limit of apprehending a qualified relation (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhin*), a cognition such as "the cloth does not exist as a pot" (*ghaṭatvena paṭo nāsti*)—
which does not apprehend a qualified relation with respect to potness and so forth— is [distinguished from others].

The point is that there is no evidence for an absence qualified by a non-co-occurrent property, because there is an absence of any factor that could establish it as a delimitor of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*). [Objection:
"In that case, what is the status of such a cognition? To this, he says: "the cloth" (*paṭa*).
Now, it might be argued that the cognition "there is no cloth by way of potness" cannot possibly have as its object the absence of potness residing in the cloth.
In the absence of a subverting factor, since there is a cognition that explicitly mentions that word,
it is impossible to abandon its status as having for its object the meaning conveyed by that word;
this is the case with the absence of potness residing in a cloth, which arises from the expression "there is no cloth by way of potness."
For it is not cognized in any way [as such];
rather, there is simply the apprehension of "pot-ness" as independent within the portion consisting of the absence, by means of the relation of having a delimited counter-correlativity.
However, there is no such rule that "the cognition of absence does not exceed the limit of apprehending a qualified relation" (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhinī*);
and thus, an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*) is established as having valid proof.

If it is argued: "Let it be, then, that its counter-correlativity is distinct," he says: "In the case of being distinct. That [counter-correlativity] is one whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*).
[The term] "kevalānvayin" [is used here].
The meaning is that there is an absence of contradiction in the form of a counter-positive delimited by the delimitor of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). —
*Bālapriyā*

Now, one might object that in the context of defining the various types of absences (*abhāva*), it is improper to refute the absence qualified by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharmāvacchinnābhāva*); to this he replies: "by way of occasion" (*prasaṅgāt*). [This refers to] what has been brought to mind.
The meaning is: by way of the logical connection (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*) consisting in the undesirable consequence that [the object] would not be fit for equanimity (*upekṣānarhatva*).

[This is] as much as from the difference in the relation of the property delimiting the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma-sambandha-bheda*), etc., as from what pertains to the property delimiting the counter-correlativity itself.
Anticipating the objection that a distinction between absences also arises from the difference between counterpositiveness being co-located with its locus or not being co-located with it—
and that in this very way,

the distinction between two absences is established, namely those whose counterpositiveness is delimited by properties residing in different loci versus those residing in the same locus— it is argued as follows:
With the intention that there is no such thing as an absence qualified by a property residing in a different locus, how could there be a search for another distinction for its sake?
The venerable Nṛsiṃha Śāstri also stated that the refutation of the absence qualified by a property residing in a different locus is likewise appropriate;
as it says in the *Dīpikā*: "There is no cloth by way of being a jar," and so forth.
It has been stated that [the absence] is established by the cognition "there is no cloth by way of pot-ness";
however, we do not accept such an absence qualified by a property residing in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇadharmāvacchinnābhāva),
because of that very cognition.
The meaning is: because it has as its object the absence of potness in a cloth, which is an absence that is the counter-positive residing in a cloth as delimited by potness.
On this point, the teacher Saundada says: "Absence is of two kinds—"

[The absence] has a counter-positivity delimited by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*) and a counter-positivity delimited by a property residing in the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇadharma*).
A property that does not reside in the substratum of the counter-positive is a "property residing in a different locus."
A property that subsists in the locus of the counter-positive (pratiyogitāśraya) is a co-occurrent property (samānādhikaraṇadharma).
In the case of "There is no cloth by way of pot-ness," the cloth is the locus of the counter-positive; the property that does not subsist in it is pot-ness.

The absence that is the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of that counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) residing in the cloth as delimited by that [pot-ness] is the "absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a property residing in a different locus" (*vyadhikaraṇadharmāvacchinnābhāva*).
This is the case in the instance "the pot does not exist."

They say that the substratum of the counter-correlativity is the pot; the property residing therein is "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva); and the absence whose counter-correlativity resides in the pot as delimited by that [property] is an "absence delimited by a co-located property."
He states the manner of its refutation in the *Prakāśikā*:
"abhāvadhiya iti" (regarding the cognition of absence).
The cognition of absence [does not exceed] the limit of apprehending a qualified entity as possessing another qualification (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya*).
By the rule that "one does not exceed [the object]," every cognition having non-existence as its qualifier (prakāra) necessarily apprehends the relation of the counter-positive,
as qualified by its counter-positiveness-determinant (pratiyogitāvacchedaka), within that non-existence.
Thus it should be stated:

since, in the present context, a cloth qualified by potness is unestablished, the state of having that qualification as its object is impossible; therefore, [the cognition] is "there is no cloth by way of potness."
The cognition does not take as its object an absence whose counter-correlativity resides in a cloth delimited by pot-ness;
rather, just as the cognition "there is no rabbit's horn" [takes as its object] the horn itself, [so it is here].

Just as [the cognition] "the rabbit does not possess moonhood" takes the absence of moonhood as its object, so too the cognition "there is no cloth by way of potness" apprehends the absence of potness in the cloth;
therefore, this aforementioned cognition [is a case of non-apprehension].

The sense is that [the property of being a pot] is not capable of establishing itself as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) when it resides in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇadharma).
Now, regarding the phrase "by way of potness" (*ghaṭatvena*) and so forth:
provided there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
Because of the rule that a cognition delineated by a particular word must have as its object the meaning conveyed by that word,

it must be asserted that whatever object is conveyed by the sentence "There is no cloth by way of being a pot" is precisely the same object that serves as the object in the cognition delineated by that sentence.
The point is this: since from such a word there arises the cognition of only that absence whose counter-positive resides in a cloth as delimited by potness,
it is logical that even the cognition expressed by such a word has precisely that [absence] as its object.

However, [the word] "iti": the meaning of the instrumental case in "ghaṭatvena" (by way of potness) is "having a counterpositiveness delimited by [that property]," and the intention is that this [meaning] is construed with the absence (abhāva).
The connection [of a word] with another in the form of a case-meaning as a relation is indeed accepted.
For this very reason, in the *Dinakaryā*,
it is stated that in expressions such as "a jar on the ground," there is a connection between the jar and the ground even by way of the relation of locus-ness (*ādheyatā*).
It has been stated that [the term] *sākṣāt* (directly) is also included in the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of this [term]. Regarding that, in the *Rāmarudrī*:

"Even though it is sufficient for the explanation [of the cognition] by simply accepting a cognition whose qualifier (*prakāra*) is the state of being located on the ground (*bhūtalavṛttitva*) with respect to the jar..."
It is also inappropriate to accept that the ground (*bhūtala*) is a qualifier (*prakāra*) in respect to the jar by way of the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatā-sambandha*),
because it is not admitted that a word-meaning can appear as a mode of relation (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*).
Nevertheless, [in the cognition] "the jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭaḥ*)...

It has been stated that, because it is established by experience that doubt as to whether "the jar belongs to the ground or not" does not arise immediately after the knowledge born from such a sentence, the denotation of the case-ending is accepted as appearing even as a relation (*saṃsarga*). By this [it is shown that...]

The objection is that since having a delimited counter-correlativity (*avacchinnapratiyogitākatva*) is the meaning of the third case suffix (*tṛtīyāvibhakti*), it is more appropriate for it to appear as a qualifier (*prakāra*); therefore,
the expression "by way of the relation of having a delimited counter-correlativity" is not tenable.
[The opponent says: "Water [is the locus].
[The proponent replies: But is it not the case that in such instances as "the pot does not exist as a pot," the property of potness (*ghaṭatva*) is [unfit to be the counter-correlative]?
It must be stated that the absence [of the cognition] is construed with [the locus] through the relation of having a delimited counter-correlativity (*avacchinna-pratiyogitākatva*).
And thus, since there is no occurrence of "pot-ness" in the pot [in this case], there is no apprehension of the qualified by the qualifier (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya*) characterized by pot-ness.

He says "abhāvabuddhiḥ" [the cognition of absence] because there is a violation of the rule that "the cognition of absence does not transcend the limit of apprehending a qualified entity as possessing a further qualifier. [For example,
in the case of] "a pot by way of potness..."

Since the experience of a negative cognition (*abhāvapratyaya*) in the form "it does not exist" is well-established, the rule that a cognition of absence must involve the apprehension of the qualified relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*) with respect to that wherein the delimitation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) appears, is untenable. And thus:
The sense is that such a violation of the rule is indeed desired.
"Let it be so, then.
And thus, a jar by way of its nature as a jar...

Regarding the cognition "it does not exist," there is no such rule that the delimitor of counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) must belong exclusively to that which has attained the status of a qualifier of the counterpositive (*pratiyogi*), because when [a property] such as "pot-ness" appears independently, one apprehends it as the delimitor of counterpositiveness.
An absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a property residing in the same locus is established; likewise,
even by the cognition "there is no cloth through pot-ness," there is the apprehension of delimitation in pot-ness, which resides in a different locus.
The sense is that even an absence whose counter-positivehood is not delimited by a property residing in a different locus is established.
Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of a contradictory":
the locus of the substratum of the counter-positivehood, qualified by the delimitator of that counter-positivehood, [is absent] from the absence.
It is contradictory: since a pot qualified by "pot-ness" exists, the absence of a pot delimited by "pot-ness" is not possible;
such an absence occurs only in a place devoid of pots, and thus it is not a purely positive (kevalānvayin) property.

The meaning is as follows: the absence of a cloth (paṭābhāva) qualified by pot-ness (ghaṭatvena), however, does not exist because its contradictory—the form of a cloth qualified by a pot—is unestablished; therefore, since it exists everywhere, both where there is a cloth and where there is no cloth, it is a purely positive (kevalānvayin) [absence].
The Lamp:
A Refutation of the View that Occasional Absence is an Additional Category;
occasional absence as well.
It is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) itself that is perceived at a particular time; for when a jar is brought into a place where it was previously absent,
the absolute non-existence is not perceived [to have moved], even though it has not gone elsewhere.

Since cognition occurs when the jar has been removed, it is postulated that the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the conjunction between the ground and the jar are the determinants for the cognition of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar; [this applies] in the case of a place where a jar exists.
Because the prior non-existence and the destruction of that conjunction are absent, there is no cognition of absolute non-existence;
however, when the jar has been removed, because the destruction of the conjunction exists, it is cognized.
— *Prakāśikā*

Now, one might object: "Surely, when a jar is present on the ground or elsewhere, there is no cognition of its absence; however, such a cognition arises at other times. Therefore, a temporary absence (*sāmayikābhāva*) must be admitted as something distinct [from the absolute absence of the jar]. To one who argues thus:
To refute this, he says: "occasional" (*sāmayika*).
An occasional absence is simply an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is perceived at the time when its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is absent; it is not, however, [a separate category].
The collective meaning is that [the absence] is distinct from that which possesses arising and destruction.

Now, if this were so, then even at the time when a jar is being brought onto the ground, since its absence would be eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of that [absence]. Therefore—
He says: "possessing the absence of a jar.
He establishes the very nature of its being a regulator by saying: "possessing a jar.
