This is because the earth and so forth, as delimited by their respective times, possess the relation of the absence of a jar and the like, and at the time of the jar...

It should also be observed that, due to the absence of a relation with the form of the ground and so forth as qualified by that specific time [of emptiness], there is no cognition of its absolute non-existence at that time. *Bālapriyā* [comments: It should also be understood that because there is no relation with the form of the ground and other substrates as characterized by that particular time of emptiness, there arises no cognition of the absolute non-existence of that [jar] at that time.
But it is not something distinct from that which is subject to arising and destruction; rather,
it arises at the time when its counter-positive is absent.

An absolute non-existence that perishes at the time of its counter-positive is a situational absolute non-existence (*sāmayika-atyantābhāva*). Thus, the absolute non-existence of a jar and the like is a situational absolute non-existence,
whereas the absolute non-existence of a hare's horn and the like is [an absolute non-existence that is eternal].

Their intention is that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) pertains to all three times (*traikālika*). However, the authors of the *Dīpikā* maintain that occasional non-existence (*sāmayikābhāva*) is not distinct from absolute non-existence pertaining to all three times; it exists at all times.

Even though [an object] exists, it is called a "temporary absence" (sāmayikābhāva) merely by virtue of its being perceived at a particular time, and not because it possesses the quality of arising at that particular time. Now,
if temporary absence is not distinct from absolute absence (atyantābhāva), then [what happens] on a ground where there is an absence of a jar?
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the absolute absence of a jar even after the jar has been brought [into the room],
because the absolute absence of a jar is eternal and, being inactive, does not move elsewhere; thus,
immediately after the jar is brought, the object consisting of the absolute absence of the jar exists on the ground where the jar now stands.

If this is argued—no; because the absolute non-existence of the jar, although present immediately after the jar has been brought in, is not perceived, whereas it is perceived immediately after the jar has been removed; therefore:

It is postulated that, with respect to the perception of the absolute non-existence of a jar, the prior absence of the conjunction between the ground and the jar and the destruction of the conjunction between the ground and the jar are the causal conditions;
[this is so] after the bringing of the jar.

However, because the destruction of the conjunction between the ground and the jar exists, or because its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) or its destruction exists, there is no perception of the absolute non-existence of the jar due to the absence of the necessary cause.
But after the jar has been removed, since the destruction of the conjunction between the ground and the jar exists, [the absolute non-existence of the jar can be perceived].
The direct perception of the absolute non-existence of a jar occurs;
and thus, at a particular time, there is indeed the absolute non-existence of that which is eternal.

The meaning of this section is that they demonstrate that, since the existence and non-existence of cognition are established through reasoning, one should not accept conventional absence as a distinct entity for that purpose.
In the *Prakāśikā*, he states another solution: "delimited by such-and-such time.
This refers to that time when there is an absence of the jar.
The cognition of the absolute absence of a jar on the ground arises;
the relation between the ground and the absolute absence of the jar is simply the very nature of the ground as delimited by a time characterized by the absence of such a jar.
The point is that even though the ground and the absolute absence of the jar exist immediately after the jar has been removed,

there is no cognition of the absolute absence of the jar in the ground because of the absence of the relation consisting in the nature of the ground as delimited by that time, which is [the relation] characterized by being devoid of the jar.
*Dīpikā*:
Refutation of the view that non-existence (*abhāva*) consists of its locus (*adhikaraṇa*);
since the linguistic usage "it does not exist" is established by the locus alone, non-existence [as a separate category] does not exist.

The teachers [claim] that it is a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*). That is not so; for if non-existence (*abhāva*) is not accepted, it is impossible to define absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).
The *Prakāśikā* says: "Now, non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a distinct category of reality (*padārtha*)."
In whatever locus there arises a cognition such as "there is no jar," that cognition is accounted for simply by postulating the absence of cloth and so forth in that very locus;
for it is simpler to postulate a property (dharma) in a locus already established than to postulate an entirely unestablished locus (dharmin).
Anticipating the objection of the Guru-mata,
he refutes it with the word "kevala" (alone). Although there are infinite topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), [the point remains as follows].
Since it is far more parsimonious to postulate a single substratum (dharmin) than to postulate multiple dharmas [for each absence],
the aforementioned reasoning does not apply here.
Furthermore, if non-existence were of the same nature as its locus (*adhikaraṇasvarūpa*), then in the case of water and so forth...

Although objections such as the consequence that the non-existence of smell and so forth— which actually exists— would become perceivable by other sense organs because it would take the form of water and so on, clearly arise,
nevertheless [the objection is refuted] simply by the rejection of that statement: "from the locus alone" (*kevalādhikaraṇād eva*).
Considering that since their cessation is possible, why should these [causes] be required, he refutes that very point with the words: "the acceptance of non-existence.
This means the non-acceptance of a separate, additional non-existence (*atiriktābhāva*). Now...
What is this absolute isolation (*kaivalya*)?
If it is said to be the true nature of the ground— then since the ground, like the jar,

would itself be of the nature of that absence [of the jar], there would follow the undesirable consequence that even at that time, there would be the cognition of the ground as possessing the absence of the jar.

If it is argued that [the state of being alone] consists in possessing the absence of a jar, then the existence of a distinct absence is established; therefore, he states "of isolation" (kaivalyasya) to show that defining isolation is impossible.

*Bālapriyā* [comments]: [The opponent suggests that isolation is simply the presence of the absence of objects]. If this were so, then an independent absence would be proven to exist; hence, he says "of isolation" to declare that such a definition cannot be maintained.

Regarding the phrase "even though [the substrata] are infinite": rather than postulating the nature of the absence of a jar (*ghaṭābhāvatva*) in each and every substratum where the cognition of the absolute absence of a jar occurs, one should instead [postulate it] only in those already established substrata.
The sense is that the postulation of a single locus (*dharmin*) consisting of the absolute non-existence of a jar is far more parsimonious. [Objection:
But in the case of postulating a locus, both must be postulated: the locus in the form of non-existence and the property in the form of "non-existenceness."

But in the view that [non-existence] is a property (*dharma*), only the property consisting of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvatva*) would need to be postulated, since the substrata (*dharmi*), which are the loci (*adhikaraṇa*), are already established. Thus, how could there be room for parsimony (*lāghava*)?
For this reason, he states another refutation, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*).

If non-existence (*abhāva*) were of the same nature as its locus (*adhikaraṇasvarūpa*), then, since the absence of odor existing in water would be of the very nature of water, it would follow by the logical rule: "Whatever quality is perceptible by a particular sense organ, the genus residing in that [quality], and the absence of that [quality] are also perceptible by that same sense organ."
Since the absence of odor is perceptible by the olfactory faculty, it would follow that water— which consists of the absence of odor— is perceptible by the olfactory faculty; however,
because water is perceptible by the visual faculty and other senses, it is not perceptible by the olfactory faculty.

The sense is that there would be the consequence of the absence of odor— which is of the nature of earth— being perceivable by the visual faculty and so forth, or else the consequence of its not being perceivable by the olfactory faculty;
that is to say, there would be the consequence of its being perceivable by other sense faculties.
The meaning is that [the non-existent] would result in being perceivable by the nose, or by other [senses] such as the eye,
and so forth; these are the refutations [that follow] if non-existence were of the nature of its locus.

The *Dīpikā* states that the objection to be understood from the word "etc. (*ādi*) is as follows: the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) between the ground and the absence of a jar is untenable, because the relation of locus and located is pervaded by difference (*bheda*).
The non-existence of non-existence has the nature of existence;
the non-existence of non-existence is existence.
It is not something additional, because that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress;
[this applies to] both the prior non-existence of destruction and the destruction of prior non-existence.
The ancients maintain that it is simply the counter-positive itself.

The moderns hold that the absence of an absence is indeed distinct [from its counter-positive], because the third-order absence is of the nature of the first-order absence; thus, there is no infinite regress.
The Prakāśikā [objects]:
"But if non-existence were something distinct, then its non-existence would also be distinct."

If that [non-existence] were also non-existent in the same way, there would be an infinite regress; therefore, he says: "the non-existence of non-existence," and so forth, beginning with "destruction."
Destruction's prior non-existence (dhvaṃsaprāgabhāva) consists of the nature of its counter-positive and the nature of the prior non-existence of that [counter-positive].

The meaning should be understood as follows: antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the nature of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), and its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is likewise the nature of that [counter-positive]. By this—
The cognition "destruction will come to be" is possible even during the state of the prior non-existence of the counter-positive,
and the cognition "prior non-existence has perished" is possible even during the state of the destruction of the counter-positive.
Now, one might object that the cognition "substantiality does not exist in time" does not arise,

whereas the cognition "the absence of substantiality [in time]" does arise; to resolve this discrepancy, it must be maintained that in the cognition "it does not exist," there is the manifestation of a locus-ness (ādheyatva) delimited by a spatial relation.
This must be postulated;
for if the absence of the absence of a jar and so forth were identical in nature to the jar itself, then the cognition "there is no absence of a jar here" would necessarily be an error.

Because it is not accepted that a positive entity (bhāva) functions as a qualifier [of another entity], he shows the view of the moderns—that the absence of an absence (abhāvābhāva) is distinct [from its counter-positive] and not of the nature of a positive entity—with the words "abhāva... [etc.]. To the objection that this leads to an infinite regress (anavasthā), he says: "third... [etc.].
Indeed,

from the *Dīpikā*, it is understood that the prior non-existence of destruction and the destruction of prior non-existence are indeed the counter-positive itself; thus, the prior non-existence of the destruction of a jar and the destruction of the prior non-existence of a jar are both of the very nature of the jar.

If that were the case, then at the stage when the jar has not yet arisen, there would be no cognition regarding the prior non-existence of the jar's destruction— namely, the thought "the destruction of the jar will come to be"— because at that time the jar is absent. Likewise,
at the stage when the jar has been destroyed, [there would be no cognition] such as "the prior non-existence of the jar has perished."

Otherwise, there would be no cognition regarding the prior absence and the destruction of a jar, because the jar—which is of the nature of those two—is absent; therefore, he states the intended meaning: "destruction and prior absence."
The prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of the destruction of a jar is both the nature of the jar itself and the nature of the prior non-existence of the jar. Thus,
since the prior non-existence of the jar exists during the stage when the jar has not yet arisen,

the cognition "the destruction of the jar will occur"— which takes as its object that very prior non-existence of the jar's destruction which is identical with the prior non-existence of the jar— is [possible].
A cognition arises.

The cognition "the destruction of the jar will occur," which arises immediately after the production of the jar, takes as its object the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of the destruction of the jar, which is identical with the jar itself. Thus...
The destruction of the prior non-existence of a jar is the very nature of the jar, and it is also the very nature of the jar's destruction;
therefore, at the time of the jar—
The cognition "the prior absence of the jar has perished" takes as its object the destruction of the prior absence of the jar, which is identical in nature to the jar itself.
At the time of the jar's destruction, there occurs the cognition "the prior absence of the jar has perished."

It takes as its object the destruction of the prior absence of the jar, which itself has the nature of the destruction of the jar; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever—this is the intended meaning.
Now, [one might ask: does time possess substantiality (*dravyatva*)?
Regarding the phrase "it does not exist" and so forth:
the cognition that "substantiality does not exist in time" does not arise; rather, the cognition that "there is an absence of substantiality in time" arises.

For that purpose, one must accept the following linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*): the negative particle (*nañ*) denotes an absence that is construed with a locus-ness (*ādheyatva*) qualified by the relation of spatial qualification (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā*).

The statement "there is no cloth-ness in the pot" means that there is an absence of cloth-ness which possesses a locus-ness delimited by the relation of spatial qualification as determined by the pot.

Although the absence of substanceness exists at time by way of temporal qualification (*kālika-sambandha*), substanceness, by virtue of being the counter-correlative of the absence of substanceness through spatial qualification (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā-sambandha*),
stands in opposition to it through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*) at that same time.
Because of the existence of substanceness (*dravyatva*),

the absence of substanceness does not possess a locatability delimited by the relation of spatial qualification (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā*) as defined by time; therefore, the cognition "substance-ness does not exist in time" does not arise.
It must be stated that "it exists";
and thus, even the cognition that "there is no absence of the jar on the ground" occurs when there is an absence of the absence of the jar.
It must be stated that [the cognition] apprehends a substratum-ness delimited by the relation of spatial qualification as determined by the ground.
If the absence of the absence of a jar were of the same nature as the jar itself, then...
Since it is not accepted that entities (bhāvas) reside [in space] by means of the relation of spatial qualification (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā*),
such a cognition would be erroneous because it apprehends a jar— which lacks the property of being located as delimited by that relation— as possessing it.
However, validity (prāmāṇya) is accepted [as a positive property].
Therefore, the absence of non-existence (abhāvābhāva) is not of the nature of a positive entity (bhāvarūpa), but rather something distinct (atirikta).
And there is no infinite regress,
because even though the absence of the absence of a jar is distinct [from the jar], we accept that the absence of the absence of the absence of a jar has the nature of the absence of a jar itself.
Such is the view of the moderns;
however, the more recent [scholars] accept that even entities (bhāva) have occurrence by way of the relation of spatial qualification (daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā). In their opinion:
The absence of an absence is not something distinct [from the original entity].
This principle should be examined in the *Gādādharī* commentary on the definition of "kūṭaghaṭita."
The Compendium of Reasoning:
The inclusion of the sixteen categories within seven categories.
(AnTs 81) Since all categories are included, as appropriate, within those already mentioned, it is established that there are exactly seven categories.
Since all categories (padārtha) are included within those already mentioned, it is established that there are exactly seven categories.

[Objection: But surely [the Nyāya Sūtra lists]: "The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the objects of valid cognition (prameya), doubt (saṃśaya), purpose (prayojana), example (dṛṣṭānta), tenet (siddhānta), members of a syllogism (avayava), reasoning (tarka), ascertainment (nirṇaya), discussion (vāda), sophistry (jalpa), cavil (vitaṇḍā), fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa), quibble (chala), futile rejoinder (jāti), and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna)."

Since the sixteen categories (*ṣoḍaśapadārtha*) have been mentioned in the *Nyāyasūtra*— specifically in the aphorism "The attainment of the supreme good results from the knowledge of reality" (1.1.1)— how can it be said that there are only seven? To this, he says:
"Of all" means that all [categories] are included within these seven alone:
"self, body, sense-faculties, objects, intellect, mind..."
"Activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation are the objects of valid cognition"— thus the object of valid cognition is twelvefold.
Activity consists of merit and demerit.
Attachment, aversion, and delusion are the defects. Attachment is desire;
aversion is resentment.
Delusion (moha) is the misconception of the self (ātman) in relation to the body and so forth.
Rebirth after death (pretyabhāva) is dying. Fruition (phala) is experience (bhoga).

Apavarga is liberation (mokṣa). And that is the destruction of pain not co-existent with the prior non-existence of pain that has the same locus as itself. The purpose (prayojana) is the attainment of happiness and the removal of pain.
An example (dṛṣṭānta) is [such as] a kitchen hearth and so forth. A tenet (siddhānta) is an object accepted as being authoritative.
A conclusion (nirṇaya) is a certainty; and that—
The fruit of valid cognition;
the illuminator [composed] by the one of supreme compassion.
The Sage, desiring to lift up people submerged in the mire of suffering, composed the aphorism beginning with "the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa-prameya*).
To avoid contradiction with that, he raises an objection, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).

Since it is clear that perception is included within substance and inference and the others are included within quality, he states the inclusion of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and so forth within substance and the rest:
By the words "self" and so forth:
[the object] consists of the substances of the self, body, and sense-faculties, as well as the object in the form of earth and the other elements.
Among substance and the other categories, the internal sense-organ, the mind, is included within substance as a quality of cognition.
In the same way, even in what follows, the respective inclusion [of these factors] should be understood.
Regarding the phrase "dharma and adharma," the meaning is "that which produces them."
And this is clear in the source text:
passion (*rāga*) is a particular kind of desire (*icchā*).
"Death" (maraṇa) means birth occurring immediately after death;
such is the etymological derivation of the term.
"Pretya" means having died; "bhāva" refers to birth.
Death is the destruction of the final conjunction between the vital breaths and the body. Birth is the first conjunction between the body and the vital breaths.

In order to prevent the contingency that a jar— which possesses the destruction of its conjunction with a liberated soul— would itself become liberated, [the definition specifies] "destruction of suffering" (*duḥkhadhvaṃsa*).
[This excludes] those who possess the destruction of suffering...
The phrase ending in "kālīna" (occurring at that time) is included to prevent the undesirable consequence that people such as ourselves would also attain liberation.

[This is necessary] because there is the risk of the undesired consequence that the selves of Śuka and others— who possess the destruction of suffering co-temporal with the prior non-existence of suffering belonging to another— would also be considered liberated, [unless the destruction is qualified by being] "co-located with itself" (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*).
The qualification "the prior non-existence of suffering" is necessary;

for by the phrase "not coexisting with a suffering that has the same locus as itself," the destruction of suffering occurring at the time of deep sleep— which exists at a subsequent moment— is already excluded.
It should not be said that [the mention of] antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is redundant;
for there is no redundancy in the arrangement as it stands—this is the general direction.
Since doubt has already been defined, he now demonstrates the nature of the purpose (*prayojana*):
"The purpose" refers to that of the means of valid cognition known as perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).

Regarding the term "substance" (*dravya*): the sense organ (*indriya*) is the instrument for the valid cognition of perception (*pratyakṣapramā*). In that regard, the eye consists of fire (*tejas*), and the tongue consists of water (*jala*).

Because the nose is included within earth, the skin within air, and the ear within space, and because the mind is a distinct substance, [these are the objects] of the means of valid cognition known as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The meaning is that they are included within "substance" (dravya).
And as for inference (anumāna) and the others, they are qualities (guṇa);
for inference is the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti).

The meaning is that comparison (*upamāna*) is the cognition of similarity, and verbal testimony (*śabda*) is the cognition of words; thus, inference and the other means of knowledge are included within the quality (*guṇa*) consisting of cognition.
The same applies to what follows as well;
the meaning is that even activity (*pravṛtti*), defects (*doṣa*), and so forth, are included within the *samskāras* themselves, each according to its respective nature.
Now, since activity is of the nature of a specific effort (*prayatna-viśeṣa*), whereas merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)— [the objection continues:]...

Because [dharma and adharma] consist of the nature of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*), the passage in the *Dīpikā* stating that "activity (*pravṛtti*) is dharma and adharma" would be inconsistent; therefore, he says: "the meaning is 'that which produces them'.
The meaning is that activity is that which generates dharma and adharma.
The meaning is that there is a metaphorical designation of the cause by means of the effect. Thus, activity (pravṛtti) is included within the qualities (guṇa).
"Clearly stated in the source" [is the sense].

In the commentary on the second sūtra, it is stated: "Dharma and adharma, which are the means for worldly activity (*pravṛtti*), are expressed by the word 'activity' (*pravṛtti'), just as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) have food as their means.
[And: "Dharma and adharma are the fruits of activity."
In this sūtra, these two are called "pravṛtti" (activity).
Why? Because they are the means for that [activity], as it is stated in the Vārtika on the seventeenth sūtra: "Food is indeed the life-breath of living beings."
The sense is that the capacity of activity (*pravṛtti*) to produce merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) is clear in the foundational texts. "A particular desire" means an intense desire.
And thus, attachment (rāga) is included within the quality (guṇa) consisting of desire, while aversion (dveṣa) is [included] within the quality.
And delusion (moha), which consists of false knowledge (mithyājñāna), is included within the [guṇas].
False knowledge is that knowledge whose nature is error.
"Immediately after death" (*maraṇānantara*) means existence after having died;
by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "birth," it refers to that which is produced at the time immediately following death.
The meaning of the term *pretyabhāva* [is as follows]:
death is the destruction of the final conjunction between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the body;
birth is the first conjunction between the body and the vital breath.
And thus, rebirth (pretyabhāva) is included within the quality (guṇa) of conjunction (saṃyoga),
and its finality consists in the conjunction of the vital breaths and the body.
The state of being "first" (ādyatva) consists in not being the locus of the prior non-existence of the conjunction of the vital breath with a body belonging to its own class;
and the state of being "first" also consists in not being the locus of the destruction of the conjunction of the vital breath with a body belonging to its own class.
In the *Dīpikā*, it is stated that the fruit is experience (*bhoga*). Experience, by name, is the perception of pleasure and pain.
And thus, regarding the fruit...
Inclusion is within the class whose nature consists of knowledge in the form of experience. Regarding the phrase "co-located with itself":
it refers to that antecedent absence of suffering which is co-located with itself.
The meaning is that liberation is the destruction of suffering not co-temporal with that [liberated state].
It is the destruction of whatever suffering currently exists for us at this moment.
The destruction of suffering in liberation is not co-temporal with the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of future suffering;
the sense is that this is because suffering will not arise again.
The *Prakāśikā* states the purpose of the components of the definition of liberation (*apavarga*) with the words beginning "muktātmasaṃyoga" [and so forth].
Regarding the phrase "the destruction of suffering" (*duḥkhadhvaṃsaḥ*), if the word "suffering" (*duḥkha*) were not employed there...

If it were stated merely that "liberation is a destruction (dhvaṃsa) not co-existent with the prior absence of suffering (duḥkhaprāgabhāva) that has the same locus as itself," then even the destruction of the conjunction between a liberated self and a jar would be [included], since such a destruction of conjunction is also not co-existent with the prior absence of suffering; thus, for one who possesses such a destruction of conjunction...
A jar would also possess liberation;

to prevent this, it is stated that liberation is the "destruction of suffering. The point is that the destruction of a conjunction is not the destruction of suffering, and therefore it does not constitute liberation.

But surely, since the liberated self is omnipresent, as long as the jar exists, there must indeed be a conjunction of the liberated self with the jar; how then could the jar possess the state of having that [conjunction] destroyed?
But when the jar has perished,

even though the destruction of the conjunction between the liberated self and the jar exists, since the jar is absent, it is all the more impossible for the jar to possess liberation; so how can such a doubt arise?
To this it is replied: first, the jar exists in some particular location;
at that time, there exists a conjunction between the liberated soul and the jar delimited by that location. That...
In this way, if a jar is moved to another location, the self-conjunction delimited by the previous location perishes,
and another conjunction arises delimited by the new location. And thus, while [the former] has not perished—

For [the opponent] holds the intention that, since the destruction of the conjunction with the liberated self— delimited by a particular location— exists in the pot, it would follow as an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the pot itself is liberated.
Regarding the phrase "of those who possess the destruction of suffering":

if one were to state merely that liberation is the destruction of suffering, it would follow that transmigrating beings such as ourselves are liberated even during deep sleep, because the destruction of suffering exists for them at that time.
To exclude that [possibility],
the term "temporal" (kālīna) is included;
[it refers to] the destruction of our present suffering existing today.

The point is that because [the state in question] is simultaneous with the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the suffering that will occur tomorrow, it lacks the property of not being simultaneous with the prior non-existence of such suffering; therefore, it does not possess the nature of liberation (*muktatva*).
[The phrase] "belonging to another" [is used].

And likewise, if the qualification "co-existent with its own locus" were not employed regarding the prior non-existence of suffering (*duḥkhaprāgabhāva*), then the destruction of suffering belonging to liberated beings such as Śuka would [be considered] that future suffering which resides in the transmigrating selves (*saṃsāryātman*) other than Śuka and the rest.
Since that [destruction of suffering] would exist only at the same time as its own prior non-existence,
Śuka and others would be non-liberated because they lack the destruction of suffering that is not co-temporal with it;
to prevent this, the qualification "subsisting in the same locus" (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) is added.

And when that [destruction of suffering] is taken as the upādāna, one's own destruction of suffering—which exists in the self of Śuka—is the result; its locus is the self of Śuka, and its existence therein does not occur in the prior absence of another's suffering; thus, it is not by taking simultaneity with that [other's suffering] that [the fault arises].
The meaning is that the aforementioned fault [remains]. Now, one might object:
let it simply be "not co-existent in time with a suffering that has the same locus as itself";
what is the purpose of the qualification "not co-existent in time with the prior non-existence of such a suffering"?
Furthermore, the destruction of suffering that occurs for us during deep sleep does not possess simultaneity with that suffering,
because suffering is absent during deep sleep. And thus:

If it were stated that [liberation] consists in the destruction of suffering not simultaneous with [present] suffering, then because such a destruction exists even while we are alive, it would follow that we are liberated. However, if it is stated that it consists in the destruction of suffering not simultaneous with [present] suffering, and if it is further specified as "not simultaneous with the prior non-existence of suffering," then...

It cannot be argued that in deep sleep there exists the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of future suffering within us, and therefore the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of suffering at that time is excluded because it is simultaneous with the prior non-existence of suffering;
for [the destruction]...

Since destruction is impossible [for that which is eternal], the destruction of suffering occurring at the time of deep sleep continues even during the moment of waking; therefore, there exists a state of being simultaneous with the suffering that occurs during the waking period.
He raises an objection with the intention that prevention occurs because there is an absence of being simultaneous with a suffering that has a common locus [with itself],

and thus it is not necessary to extend the definition to the point of "not being simultaneous with the prior non-existence of suffering": "And it is not the case that [it is prevented] by [the phrase] 'having a common locus with itself'..."
He provides the resolution:
"according to their respective arrangement.
Even though there is an exclusion [of other cases] by means of the qualification "not being simultaneous with suffering,"...
The sense is that even if [the effort] does not exist at the same time as the prior non-existence of suffering, its purpose is not rendered futile because it is still possible to prevent [suffering];
nor can it be said that [the effort] is useless simply because there is a simpler way, namely, by [merely] not being co-temporal with suffering.
It should not be said that the qualification "not being simultaneous with the prior absence of pain" is redundant when excluding the heavy [property],
because in cases where the purpose is served by a light property that constitutes part of the heavy property, [the latter is unnecessary].
In that case, the qualification (*gurudharma*) would be redundant. However, in the present context,

the absence delimited by the property of "not being simultaneous with suffering" is "not being simultaneous with suffering," while the absence delimited by the property of "not being simultaneous with the prior non-existence of suffering" is [the latter].
The state of not being simultaneous with the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering.

And since these two absences are distinct due to the difference in their delimiters of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), [the absence of one does not entail the other] within a single absence.
The intention is that because there is no lack of inclusion (*aghaṭakatva*), there is no room for the charge of futility (*vaiyarthyavikāśa*). Now, one might object:

since "ownership" (*svatva*) is not a single recurring property (*ananugata*), the definition formulated by including it would also be manifold; thus, the term "liberation" (*mukti*) would result in having multiple meanings. To this, he says: "the direction" (*dig iti*).
In this context, ownership (svatva) is not intended to reside in the subject of the relation (anuyogin), but rather in the counter-correlative (pratiyogin). And thus:

Liberation (mokṣa) is the destruction of suffering characterized by the exclusion of each specific instance of that suffering which coexists with the prior non-existence of suffering having the same locus as itself. And thus,
[liberation] consists in the state of being the destruction of suffering, as qualified by the collection of such exclusions.
The sense is that, because it is common to all forms of liberation (*sakalamukti*), there is no resulting fallacy of attributing multiple meanings to the word "liberation" (*muktipada*).
Furthermore, in this context, *apavarga* (cessation) is included within *mokṣa* (liberation).
[This applies] to doubt (*saṃśaya*).

Since it has already been stated that [doubt] consists in an experience that does not correspond to reality, it was not mentioned in the root text with the intention that its inclusion is already implied within the quality (*guṇa*) of cognition (*jñāna*).
Thus he says: "Of doubt..."
Because it has been defined as such:
the attainment of happiness is indeed happiness itself, and the abandonment of suffering is likewise.
The destruction of suffering;
and thus, the purpose (prayojana) is included within either a quality (guṇa) or an absence (abhāva).
As for the example (dṛṣṭānta):
Inclusion occurs within substance, quality, and so forth, as appropriate;
the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is likewise of the very nature of substance and the rest,
because a tenet is precisely an object accepted on the basis of its being authoritative.
The inclusion of the conclusion (*nirṇaya*) within the quality of cognition (*jñāna*) is because the members of the syllogism (*avayava*) have already been stated to consist of sound (*śabda*).

Since it has been stated that *tarka* (hypothetical reasoning) consists in the nature of superimposition (*āropa*), its inclusion is within the category of "quality" (*guṇa*); and since it is essentially a form of erroneous cognition (*bhrama-ātmaka-jñāna*), its inclusion is within that; for these reasons, neither of them is mentioned here.
Debate (*vāda*), wrangling (*jalpa*), and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are included within the category of *guṇa* (excellence) because they consist of the nature of speech.
This concludes the definition of discourse (*kathā*) according to the *Dīpikā*.
Discussion for one desiring to know the truth is *vāda*;
debate possessing the means of proof for both sides is *jalpa*.
Vitaṇḍā (cavil) is that which lacks the establishment of one's own position and consists solely in the refutation of the opposing position. A discussion (*kathā*),
on the other hand, is a sequence of sentences consisting of various speakers who set forth the prima facie and the final positions.
The *Prakāśikā* possesses both means of proof;
that is, it possesses both the refutation of the opponent's position and the establishment of one's own position.
And it should be understood that this [qualification] is intended to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of cavil (*vitaṇḍā*).
Regarding the phrase "one's own position" (*svapakṣa*):
In this context, the phrase "the speech of one desiring victory" (vijigīṣukathā) carries over from the previous section.
The word "various" (nānā) [is used].
By one [verse] the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is established, and by another the resolution (samādhāna) is provided;
thus in this sequence.
The fact that the collection of sentences has multiple authors is to be understood.
(Bālapriyā)

Regarding the phrase "parapakṣa" and so forth: if one were to state merely that "jalpa is a discourse for the sake of victory," there would be the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti) to *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
Therefore, it is stated that it must "possess the proof of one's own position."

In the phrase "possessing the refutation of the opponent's position and the proof of one's own position," the inclusion of the refutation of the opponent's position is intended to indicate that it is also necessary in *jalpa*,
and not for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and other such fallacies.
Since the very term *vijigīṣu* (one desiring victory) serves to exclude debate (*vāda*),
fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)— which consist of defective reasons— are included, as appropriate, within the categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth.
— *Dīpikā*
Quibble (chala) is the refutation of a statement by imputing a different meaning to it than that intended by the speaker.
The "illuminator" (prakāśikā) defines quibble (chala) as follows: for example, [the statement] "This Devadatta has no blanket," which was uttered with the intended meaning of "he has no new blanket."

Having postulated a distinct entity characterized by the number nine, someone objects: "He does not possess nine blankets because of his extreme poverty," and so forth. *Bālapriyā* [comments: [This refers to the critique of the Vaiśeṣika category of *saṃkhyā* (number) as a separate *padārtha*.]
Deceit (chala), too,
being of the nature of speech, is included within the category of "quality" (guṇa). —
Dīpikā.
A *jāti* is a futile rejoinder (*asaduttara*) that consists in the pointing out of a genus (*jāti-nirūpaṇa*).
— *Prakāśikā*
Regarding the phrase "an invalid rejoinder" (*asaduttara*):

the invalidity of a rejoinder consists in its being self-defeating (*svavyāghātaka*), by virtue of establishing the opponent's lack of proof while simultaneously sharing the common property of failing to establish one's own position.
And thus, the definition of a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) results in: "an answer that involves self-contradiction."—
*Bālapriyā*.

Regarding the phrase "by way of being non-probative for one's own [position] and common [to both parties]": for it is precisely to prove that [the opponent's argument] is not probative of the [opponent's] own position that the reply in the form of a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is stated.
If that [reason] were to establish even the non-establishment of its own position,
then it would be a "jāti" (futile rejoinder); this is the meaning when one attempts to prove that another's reason fails to establish its own thesis.
The meaning is that a "futile rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*) is that by which one's own position fails to prove its own point, even for its own sake;
that is, if a response stated for the purpose of refuting another's view also destroys one's own position.
The established meaning is that *jāti* (the universal) is such a specific excellence of the subsequent [cognition];
this is the *dīpikā* on similarity (*sādharmya*).

The fallacies of the counter-example (*vaidharmya*), exaggeration (*utkarṣa*), minimization (*apakarṣa*), the commendable (*varṇya*), the non-commendable (*avarṇya*), the alternative (*vikalpa*), the unproven (*sādhya*), attainment (*prāpti*), non-attainment (*aprāpti*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*), the counter-example (*prati-dṛṣṭānta*), non-arising (*anutpatti*),
doubt (*saṃśaya*), the topic (*prakaraṇa*), the non-reason (*ahetu*), implication (*arthāpatti*), non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*), proof (*upapatti*), and perception (*upalabdhi*).
The characteristics of the *sādharmyasama* (balancing the similarity) fallacy are illustrated by the following types of sophistry: non-apprehension, eternal, non-eternal, effect, and non-effect.
He shows its internal subdivisions by means of the passage beginning with "sādharmya" (similarity),
[noting that] the word "samā" (equal) is heard at the end of the dvandva compound.
Each [of these] is a *yoga*.

There are twenty-four types of *jāti* (futile rejoinders), such as *sādharmyasama* (balancing the homogeneity) and *vaidharmyasama* (balancing the heterogeneity). *Sādharmyasama* is a rejoinder that refutes a reason by means of its similarity; for example, [the argument regarding] the self (*ātman*).
It is active because it possesses qualities that are the cause of action, like a clod of earth;
and the quality here which is the cause of action is...

Regarding the formal proof that [the soul] consists precisely of conjunctions with the wind that produces action and so forth, the response is as follows: "If it is active because of its similarity to that which possesses activity, then why should it not be inactive because of its similarity to that which possesses the quality of omnipresence (vibhutva)?"
"And there is no decisive factor here [to distinguish between them]," says the Bālapriyā commentary on the *Sādharmyasamā*.
He states the definition along with an example: "By way of similarity" (*sādharmyeṇa*).
When the proponent has employed a reason (*hetu*) for the purpose of establishing his own thesis, [the opponent's objection] is based merely upon the similarity of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The term *sādharmyasama* (balancing the homogeneity) refers to a rejoinder that establishes the opponent's stated reason as incapable of proving its own probandum by means of proving the absence of the probandum desired by the proponent;
for example, "the self," and so forth.
Whatever possesses a quality that has become the cause of action is itself possessed of action;
just as a clod of earth is possessed of action because it possesses the quality of conjunction with air which has become the cause of action, so too [is the subject].

When the proponent states that the self (ātman) is also possessed of action because it possesses such qualities, the opponent replies: "If the self's possession of action follows from its similarity to a clod of earth by virtue of its possessing qualities that cause action, then [consider] space (ākāśa), which possesses the dimension of infinite magnitude."

He refutes [the opponent's position] by stating: "In that case, since the self also possesses the quality of supreme magnitude (*paramamahatparimāṇavattva*), why should it not also be inactive? For it can also be said: 'The self is inactive because it possesses the quality of supreme magnitude, like space.'"
Such a refutation is the meaning of *sādharmyasama* (balancing the similarity).
— *Prakāśikā*
The definition of *vaidharmyasama* is:
a refutation by means of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) that is equal [to the original argument] is *vaidharmyasama*.
Just as in that very case, because of the similarity with a clod of earth possessing action, if the self were to possess action,
then it would follow from its dissimilarity [to the clod] in the form of omnipresence (*vibhutva*).
Why should it not be entirely devoid of activity?

For there is no reason why, because of its similarity to that [space], it must possess activity, nor why, because of its dissimilarity to that, it must not be devoid of activity; there is nothing [to prove] this.
"There is a determiner.

Thus, by means of the dissimilarity to the example—consisting in the presence of a property that does not occur in the example—the opponent [refutes] the reason stated by the proponent. This is indeed "dear to the ignorant" (*bālapriya*).
The statement that [the reason] does not establish its own probandum is the fallacy of "balancing the heterogeneity" (*vaidharmyasama*).
Regarding the phrase "having the nature of omnipresence" (*vibhutvarūpa*): omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is the state of possessing the dimension of the supremely great (*paramamahatparimāṇavattva*).
And likewise, when a proponent has stated, "The self possesses action because it possesses qualities that are causes of action, like a clod of earth," [the opponent replies:
"The self is devoid of action."
The opponent says: "Because it possesses a nature different from that of a moving clod of earth," since the property existing in a moving clod of earth [is not present here].

If the self were active like a clod of earth, then since the omnipresence (vibhutva) that is absent in the clod exists in the self, why should the self not be inactive? This objection is stated to be the "balancing the heterogeneity" (vaidharmyasama) fallacy.
The *Prakāśikā* states that the definition of *utkarṣasama* (balancing by superiority) arises from the very means of proof (*sādhana*) stated by the opponent.
The "balancing by addition" (*utkarṣasama*) is the application to the subject (*pakṣa*) of a property that does not pervade [the reason].
For example, in the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," someone might say: "If [sound] is [impermanent] by virtue of being produced..."
"If sound were impermanent like a pot because of that reason,
then for that very same reason, sound would also be inaudible like a pot."
The *Bālapriyā* states the definition of the *utkarṣasamā* [fallacy]: "From the very proof stated by the opponent... and so forth.

The meaning of *utkarṣasama* (balancing by addition) is the consequence (*prasañjana*) of a property— which is non-pervasive of that very reason stated by the opponent for the sake of establishing their own probandum— upon the subject (*pakṣa*).

For example, regarding the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," someone might say: "If sound is impermanent like a pot by virtue of the reason 'being produced,' then for that very same reason, sound should also be inaudible like a pot. In this case, [the fault lies] in the reason.
The property of being inaudible is a non-pervader of the state of being produced; its application to the subject (pakṣa) is what is being performed.
Such a rejoinder is "balancing by elevation" (utkarṣasama), which does not take the pervasion (vyāpti) into account.

*Utkarṣasama* (the equalization by addition) is the consequence of attributing a property that does not exist to either the subject (*pakṣa*) or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), by means of either the property to be proved (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*).
For example, in the formal argument "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," since impermanence and the state of being produced are accompanied by color in a jar,
sound must also possess color.
"Thus, by virtue of the common property of being audible, a pot would also be audible because it is produced,
since there is no distinction [between them]," so says Viśvanātha in the *Prakāśikā*.
The definition of the "balancing by subtraction" (apakarṣasama) fallacy is as follows:

it is the proof of the absence of another property desired by the opponent in the subject (pakṣa), by means of a similarity with the example cited by the opponent. This is the balancing by subtraction.
For example, in that very same inference: "If sound were impermanent like a jar because of its being produced, then by that same [reason], sound would also be inaudible like a jar."
The imputation of non-existent properties is exaggeration;
the negation of existent properties is disparagement.
This is the *apakarṣasama* (balancing by subtraction).
Thus it is said: "by means of the similarity with the example stated by the opponent"—that is, by the opponent, the proponent.

The *apakarṣasama* (balancing by subtraction) is the proof of the absence of another property desired by the proponent in the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of similarity with an example that has already been stated;
for example: "Sound is impermanent."

When the proponent has stated "because it is produced," the opponent says: "If sound is impermanent like a jar due to its similarity to a jar consisting in being produced, then for that very same reason, sound would also be inaudible like a jar."

In this context, the syntactical connection (*samanvaya*) is as follows: just as there is impermanence in the word [as the subject], another property (*arthāntara*) accepted by the proponent— namely, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*)— is introduced, and the consequence of its absence is then demonstrated.
“The *apakarṣasama* (balancing the subtraction) occurs when one points out the absence of the property to be proven in the example,” so says the *Bhāṣya*. The *Prakāśikā* [comments as follows].
The definition of *varṇyasama* (balancing the subject): *Varṇyasama* is the proving of a property of the example—which is to be established—in the subject (*pakṣa*). For example:

In the aforementioned inference, let the possession of motion belong to clods of earth and the like because they possess conjunction known as "impulsion" (nodanā) which produces action; however, as for the self, if it were to possess motion—
"It would also possess the conjunction called 'impulsion' (nodanā) which produces that [sound].
Thus [the author] defines *varṇyasama* (balancing the subject).
"— of the subject to be described (varṇya).
The "balancing the subject to be described" (varṇyasama) is the proof [of a property] that exists in the example but must be established in the subject (pakṣa).

When a proponent states, "The self possesses action because it possesses qualities that are causes of action, like a clod of earth," the opponent replies: "Let the clod of earth and so forth possess action because they possess conjunction called 'impulsion' (*nodana*) which generates action; however, as for the self..."
If [the self] were possessed of action, it would follow that—like a clod of earth—the self would possess a conjunction called "impulsion" (*nodana*) which generates action;
such a response is *varṇyasama*. [In this context], *varṇya* means "that which is to be explained."
"The opposite is the 'indescribable' (avarṇya)," says the Bhāṣya. The Prakāśikā provides the definition of the "equal-to-the-indescribable" (avarṇyasama) fallacy.
The *avarṇyasama* (balancing the unprovable) is the demonstration of the equality between the properties of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*) with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*).
For example, in that very same inference, the possession of qualities such as the cause of motion— namely, impulsion and so forth— which reside in clods of earth and the like,
is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of the self (*ātman*).
And likewise, by parity of reasoning, just as the possession of action in the self is established by means of a quality that is the cause of action— which is itself unestablished—
so too [is it established] by such possession of action.

"Why is it not also proved that [the subject] possesses the qualities that produce that [effect], since there is no restrictive factor? Thus he states the *avarṇyasama* (balancing the unprovable) fallacy: "Of the probandum and the reason," etc. [This refers to] the subject (*pakṣa*).
Because both the probandum and the reason are equal [in being unproven], that rejoinder which refutes the proponent is called *avarṇyasama* (equal to the unprovable).
For example: "The self possesses activity because it possesses qualities that are causes of activity, like a clod of earth."

Thus, in this inference, the possession of action (*kriyāvattva*) in the self is unestablished (*asiddha*), and the possession of conjunction called "impulsion" (*nodana*), which is the cause of action, is likewise unestablished; therein, by means of that which is unestablished...

If it is argued that the soul's possession of activity is established by means of the quality called *nodana* (impulsion), which is the cause of action, then why is its possession of conjunction— specifically the conjunction called *nodana* that generates action— not also established by means of [the equally unproven] possession of action?
Since there is no restrictive factor [to distinguish between the two], such a response is what is meant by the fallacy of *avarṇyasama*.
The *Prakāśikā* [explains] the definition of the "equal to the conceptual" (*vikalpasama*) fallacy and the "conceptual example" (*dṛṣṭāntavikalpa*).
*Vikalpasama* (balancing the alternative) is the statement of an alternative [case] after having shown an illustrative example;
for instance, in that very same inference, [the argument]: "Something endowed with the quality of being a cause of action is light."

Just as that wind, so too some thing endowed with the qualities that cause action would possess action, like a clod of earth and the like; while some thing would be devoid of action, like the self (ātman).
"What would be the guiding principle here [to determine] that 'the previous conceptualization exists, but this one does not exist'?"— thus [it is asked]. *Bālapriyā*.
He speaks of the non-conceptualization of examples by saying: "having demonstrated the various conceptualizations regarding the example.
That is, having demonstrated the manifold conceptual constructions concerning the example.

In the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well, the "display of various conceptualizations" means the collection of conceptual constructions (*vikalpasameti*). For example, in the aforementioned inference— "The self possesses activity because it possesses qualities that are the cause of activity"—
there is something heavy endowed with qualities that are the cause of activity, such as [the earth].
Just as a clod of earth or the like is somewhat light, such as air,
so too some things are endowed with causal qualities and possess activity, such as a jar or the like.
For example, [the claim that] the self (*ātman*) is inactive;
in this regard, there is no determining factor whatsoever as to why the former conceptualization alone is correct while this conceptualization is not. And thus:

The rejoinder which states that even though the possession of the quality of being a cause of action is equal [in both cases], it is possible for only one of them to possess activity— and therefore, by that same reason, let the self be inactive—
is called *vikalpasama* (balancing the alternative).
The *Prakāśikā* [states] that the definition of the "similar-to-the-probandum" (*sādhyasama*) fallacy applies to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The statement that [the reason] is equal to the subject (*pakṣa*) is *sādhyasama*.
Here, the word *sādhya* refers to the subject (*pakṣa*).
As in that very same [text]:

If you say, "As is a clod of earth, so is the self," then it follows that "as is the self, so is a clod of earth. And thus, if activity is being established as belonging to the self, [it must likewise belong to the clod].
If it is argued that [the property] must then be established for a clod of earth as well, [we reply: in that case,
one should not say "the self is like a clod of earth," but rather "the self is similar to a clod of earth."
In the case of the statement "a clod of earth is not like oneself," there is no restrictive rule [to determine otherwise].
*Bālapriyā* states that this refers to the statement that the example is equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*).
By the etymological derivation "that in which [the property] is to be established" (*sādhyate 'smin*),
the word *sādhya* denotes the subject (*pakṣa*).
Since the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is equal to the subject, the resulting fallacy is called *sādhyasama* (equal to the probandum).
The remainder is clear.
"A property that possesses the power of the members [of a syllogism], such as the reason (*hetu*), etc., is the *sādhya* (the probandum).
When that [property] follows upon the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) as well, it is *sādhyasama* (equal to the probandum)."
If the self is like a clod of earth,
then it follows that the clod of earth is like the self;
and this self is yet to be proven.
Granted that even a clod of earth could be established as "possessing activity" [if it were so defined];
but if it is not so, then it is not as [you claim].
"The clod [of earth] is like the self"— this is the *Bhāṣya*. The *Prakāśikā* states that this is a definition by way of similarity (*prāptisamalakṣaṇam*).
Objection based on attainment is the "attainment-parity" (prāptisama);
it consists in the attainment of both the probandum and the reason.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For example, in that very same context, why is the possession of action (*kriyāvattva*) established solely on the basis of possessing qualities that are the cause of action, and why is the possession of such qualities not [established] on the basis of the possession of action?
"Because there is no distinction between the two. [The author] states the *prāptisama* (balancing by acquisition) as follows: *Bālapriyā*:
He states the *prāptisamā*.

"Objection by way of attainment" (*prāptyā pratyavasthānam*) means that if the reason (*hetu*) exists in the same locus as the probandum (*sādhya*), then it must also exist in the same locus as the reason itself.
It must be admitted that the probandum also exists [in the locus];
and thus, if the probandum is established by the reason by means of prioritizing co-occurrence with the probandum, then [there must be] co-occurrence with the reason.
Let the reason be established by means of that very thing which is to be proven (*sādhya*).

And in this way, just as [the argument] "the self possesses activity because it possesses qualities that are the cause of activity," so too [one may argue]: "the self possesses qualities that are the cause of activity."

The meaning of *prāptisama* (balancing through attainment) is an objection based on the argument that "because of possessing activity," [the reason] must also be established as something to be proven (*sādhya*), since there is no distinction;
that is, because there is no distinction between the two. Between which two? Between both.
The meaning is: "because there is no difference in their grammatical coreferentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya). This is the definition of the *aprāptisama* fallacy according to the *Prakāśikā*.
The "balancing by non-attainment" (*aprāptisama*) is an objection based on non-attainment;
for example, as in that same case, [the argument] because of the previously mentioned fault, [the reason] has not been attained.
The capacity of the reason to prove the probandum must be stated;
and if that were so, since there would be no distinction in terms of non-attainment, everything would prove everything.

"Why should this very reason not establish the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) instead? Since there is no decisive factor (vinigamaka) to determine that it must establish the probandum itself," so [it is argued]. — *Bālapriyā* This very reason—why does it not prove the absence of the probandum? For there is no determining factor to show that it must prove the probandum alone.
— *Bālapriyā*
He states the "equal by non-attainment" (aprāptisama):
"Objection based on non-attainment. Non-attainment refers to the non-attainment of both the probandum and the reason.
There is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*).
In this regard, the following alternative must be considered:
the self possesses action (*kriyāvān*).
When it is stated, "Because of possessing the quality of being the cause of action," does this reason establish the probandum while being co-locus with the probandum,
or does it establish the probandum while not being co-locus with the probandum?

Or [is it because they are not]? In the first case, since there is no distinction in their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), why would the probandum (*sādhya*) itself not also be established by the reason? Because this constitutes an objection based on the attainment of the same status (*prāptisama*). In the second case, since there is no distinction in their lack of coreferentiality, why would everything else, just like the probandum, not also be the reason?
It would not establish [anything];
and likewise, everything would establish everything.
Thus, the reason is as follows:

The objection—i.e., the statement of a refutation—consists in the following line of reasoning: "If [the reason], even though not co-located with the probandum (*sādhya*), establishes the probandum, then why should it not establish the very absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), since it is likewise not co-located with the absence of the probandum? This is the method of opposition.
The meaning is "equivalence through non-attainment" (*aprāptisama*). The definition of the sophistical refutation known as "equivalence by consequence" (*prasaṅgasama*) is as follows:
The question regarding the succession of means of proof is resolved through a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅgasama);
for example, if [the opponent] asserts that the possession of qualities which are the cause of action is the means of proof for the possession of action.
In that regard, what is the means of proof?
For indeed, there is no establishment of anything without a means of proof.
Thus, even there, [the question arises]: "What is the proof? and so forth. This is the *prasaṅgasama* [fallacy]. *Bālapriyā*.
He identifies it as "the question concerning the sequence of means. A question regarding the sequence of means is [an instance of] *prasaṅgasama*.
“The *prasaṅgasama* [balancing the consequence] is an objection based on the implication that ‘the means of proof for the proof must also be stated’”— this is the *Bhāṣya*. The remainder is clear.
The *Prakāśikā* [describes] the fallacy of "balancing the counter-example" (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*) by means of another example.
The "equal to the counter-example" (pratidṛṣṭāntasama) is the proof of the absence of the probandum;

for example, when in that very same case [of proving motion] motion has been established by means of the example of a clod of earth, one argues that the self is indeed devoid of motion by means of the example of space, which is devoid of motion.
"Why could it not be so? For there is no determining factor [to establish] that it possesses activity by the example of a clod of earth, while it lacks activity by the example of space."
The *Bālapriyā* states an analogous counter-example: "by means of another example"— namely,
that the self possesses activity (*kriyāvān*).

If, by means of the example of a clod of earth, one seeks to prove that the self possesses action because it is endowed with the qualities that cause action— just like a clod of earth— one might instead employ the example of space to argue that the self is devoid of action because it possesses conjunction with the wind, which is the cause of action, just like space.

The *pratidṛṣṭāntasama* (balancing the counter-example) consists in pointing out a fault by demonstrating a counter-example that is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) under discussion— for instance,
[arguing] that "the self possesses action."

When it is stated that "it is like a clod of earth because of its connection with the quality of being a cause of motion," a counter-example is adduced: "space is seen to be devoid of motion despite being connected with the quality of being a cause of motion.
But what, then, is the [quality] of space?
"The quality of being the cause of action is conjunction with air," so says the Bhāṣya.
[This is from] the Prakāśikā.
The "equivalence of non-arising" (anutpattisama) is the counter-position based on non-arising, characterized by the sameness of non-arising.

For example, regarding such [arguments] as "The jar is not eternal, because it possesses produced oneness," someone might say: "If produced oneness is the proof for non-eternality, then since that [oneness] is absent in the jar prior to the production of its oneness, the jar would be eternal."
If it were eternal, then it would be unarisen; thus [it is said].
(Bālapriyā)
He states the [objection] regarding non-arising as equality:
"The counter-argument is based on non-arising," and "because the produced is one."
That which is produced and that which is unity is "produced-unity"; therefore,
[it exists] precisely as unarisen.
And thus, the meaning is that impermanence would be sublated.
"And likewise, [there would be a failure] of the members of the proof— the thesis, the reason, and the example— "
"Anutpattisama (the equalization by non-arising) is an objection based on non-arising, [asserting] that 'prior to arising, there is an absence of the cause';
for its very definition is the objection raised on the grounds that prior to arising, the cause and so forth are absent"— this is the meaning according to Viśvanātha.
The *prakāśikā* [is] the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) which has the same characteristic as doubt (*saṃśaya*).
The demonstration of the raising of a doubt is the "balancing by doubt" (*saṃśayasama*).
For example, in the argument "Sound is non-eternal because it is a product," [the opponent might raise a doubt] regarding the nature of being a product shared by sound with the non-eternal pot.

As for similarity (*sādharmya*): just as there exists a similarity with the eternal nature of sound (*nitya-śabdatva*) in terms of being an object of auditory perception (*śrāvaṇa-pratyakṣa-viṣayatva*), so too does this similarity exist; thus, from the observation of this similarity common to both [the eternal and the non-eternal], doubt would arise. [If one were to insist on] the exclusion of one side...
"Because there is no determiner," he says.
Bālapriyā states the [objection] consisting of doubt:
Having demonstrated the common property (sādhāraṇadharma),
for the sake of clarity:
"Because of the similarity to both the eternal and the non-eternal."
This is a characterization of the causes of doubt.

Therefore, "balancing the doubt" (*saṃśayasama*) is the opposition based on doubt through the force of any cause of doubt whatsoever, such as the perception of a common property (*samānadharmadarśana*). Thus it is said.
Viśvanātha:
The *Prakāśikā* on the definition of the *prakaraṇasama* fallacy.
*Prakaraṇasama* is the presentation of another reason that establishes the opposite of the probandum (sādhya) for the reason stated by the proponent.
It should be understood that the very example given for *satpratipakṣa* (the counter-balanced reason) serves as the example here.
The *Bālapriyā* states that [the author] mentions the *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized reason) with the words "of the reason stated by the proponent."

When the proponent has stated the reason "because it is produced" (*kṛtakatva*) in order to prove the impermanence [of sound], as in the argument "sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," there arises the opposite of that which is to be proven by such a reason— namely,
the contrary position that "sound is permanent because it is audible, like the nature of sound" (*śabdatva*).

The meaning is that "balancing the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) refers to the opposition raised by pointing out another reason called "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*), which is being employed in this manner.
*Prakāśikā*.
The "equal to the non-cause" (*ahetusama*) fallacy consists in asserting that something is a non-cause because its nature as a cause is impossible throughout the three periods of time; for example:
If the probans, such as "being an effect," exists at a time prior to the probandum, "impermanence," then since the probandum—

impermanence— does not exist at that time, of what would it be the prover? On the other hand, if it exists at a later time, then since the probans is absent at the earlier time, of what would it be [the prover]?
The probandum is impermanence.
And if both [the reason and the probandum] exist at one and the same time, then what would be the proof for what, and what would be the probandum for what?
"Because there is no means of determination.
However, if the reading is *hetusama*,
the meaning is that *hetusama* refers to the statement of the impossibility of being a cause even throughout the three periods of time.
*Bālapriyā* identifies the lack of a cause with the phrase "even in the three times."

The *ahetusama* (balancing the non-reason) consists in stating that [the alleged reason] cannot function as a cause at any of the three times, thereby asserting its lack of causality; for instance, asking, "Of what is it the prover?"
The meaning is that the fact of being an effect does not prove impermanence;
for how can something that was non-existent at a prior time serve as a reason for a probandum?
The intended meaning is that it would be the prover (*sādhaka*). Of what is impermanence the probandum (*sādhya*)?
Impermanence is the probandum of being an effect (*kāryatva*).
The meaning is "it does not exist.
By the term "the three times," the time of the effect, its preceding time, and its succeeding time are intended.
“The reason is not distinguished by a non-reason; the counter-argument based on similarity with a non-reason is ‘balancing the non-reason’ (ahetusama),” so says the Bhāṣya.
[This is] the Prakāśikā.

The definition of *arthāpattisama* (balancing by implication) is the pointing out of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) by means of an implication (*arthāpatti*). For example, in the previously mentioned inference: "If sound is non-eternal because it possesses the property of non-eternality, then..."

"By implication (arthāpatti), since it possesses the common property of being eternal [with ether], its eternity is also established; for if one were to determine only one [of the two properties], there would be no restrictive factor. — *Bālapriyā*
He defines the sophistry based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpattisama*) with the words: "by means of a presumption" (*arthāpattipuraskāreṇa*).
[For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced."

When it is stated that "sound is impermanent because of its similarity to the impermanent pot in terms of being produced," it follows by implication that [sound] is permanent because of its similarity to the permanent; and indeed,
there exists [similarity] with the permanent ether (*ākāśa*).

The meaning of *arthāpattisama* (balancing through presumption) is the raising of an objection based on a presumption, such as: "Since sound possesses the common property (*sādharmya*) of being intangible (*asparśatva*), why should it not be eternal? Thus, it is the formulation of a refutation preceded by a presumptive argument.
"Arthāpattisama (balancing the implication) occurs when one establishes a counter-position by means of an implication;
for example, if [one argues]: 'Because it possesses the property of similarity with the impermanent, namely, being produced immediately after an effort...'"
"When one says 'sound is impermanent,' it follows by implication that it is permanent because of its similarity to what is permanent;
for it does indeed possess a similarity with the permanent, namely, intangibility," so says the Bhāṣya.
"Ascertainment of one alternative" means the ascertainment that there is impermanence *only* because of the similarity in property with the impermanent.
The *prakāśikā* explains:
*aviśeṣasama* (the "balancing through non-distinction") is the pointing out of the consequence that everything would be non-distinct, which constitutes the definition of *aviśeṣasama*.
As it is stated in that very same work: "If the impermanence of sound is [established] through its similarity to an impermanent jar and so forth by virtue of its being produced and so on,
then by virtue of its similarity to those same things through the form of being knowable (*prameyatva*) and so forth, everything would necessarily be impermanent."
"There is no determining factor to show that it is established by the similarity stated by me, and not by that stated by you."—
Bālapriyā.
He defines the *aviśeṣasama* (balancing through non-distinction) as:
"the pointing out of the consequence that everything would be without distinction. For example: "Sound is impermanent..."

In the case of the argument "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*), since a single property such as "being produced" exists in both sound and a jar, if one were to claim that sound and the jar are indistinguishable on account of their impermanence, then it would follow that all things are likewise indistinguishable.

Because a single property, such as "existence" (*sattva*) or "knowability" (*prameyatva*), exists in all things, the induction of non-distinction by means of a property that subsists in "mere existence" (*sanmātra*) is the sophistical refutation called "balancing the non-difference" (*aviśeṣasama*).
And likewise, if there were no difference among all things, there would be no distinction between the thesis and other members of the argument;
furthermore, if all things belonged to a single genus, intermediate sub-species would be abolished.
Viśvanātha explains that since all things are impermanent, there is the dissolution of birth and so forth;
this is the definition of the *upapattisama* fallacy according to the *Prakāśikā*.
*Upapattisama* (the equal by proof) is the statement that the proof is established through similarity with both sides;
for example: "If [this] is a proof for impermanence..."

"If the state of being an effect is established, then the impermanence of sound is proven; likewise, if some proof for permanence were also established, why should permanence not be the case?"—thus [it is argued].
(Bālapriyā)
He characterizes "logical proof" (*upapatti*) as "by way of similarity to both sides," meaning that the proof is applicable to both positions.
This statement is an "establishment by reasoning" (upapattisama);
for instance, in the case of the position that sound is impermanent, it is established through reasoning how its status as an effect serves as a proof.

Likewise, even in the case of the position that sound is eternal, a proof such as audibility is established; thus, this is an objection raised by setting forth a common property— the establishment of the proof— in respect to both positions.
"Upapattisama" (the equal by proof) continues as follows:
"prakāśikā" (the illuminator) is the definition of "upalabdhisama" (the equal by apprehension).
*Upalabdhisama* (balancing the apprehension) is the statement that the probandum is apprehended even in the absence of the reason demonstrated by the opponent;
for example: "Sound is impermanent because it follows from effort, like a jar."

In this case, since sound produced by the breaking of a tree branch is perceived even without effort due to the force of the wind's impulse, sound does not possess the property of conforming to effort.
*Bālapriyā* defines "equivalence through apprehension" (*upalabdhisama*) with an example, beginning with the words "vādya-ukta-".
*Upalabdhisama* (the equalization by apprehension) is the opposition based on the observation of the probandum even in the absence of the reason specified by the proponent. For instance,
in an argument such as "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke," which is intended for the ascertainment of fire—
It is said: that is not possible, because fire is established even from light and so forth without smoke;
thus, it lacks the capacity to prove [the probandum], according to Viśvanātha, who calls this a "counter-reasoning" (*pratikūlatarka*).
The *prakāśikā* explains that the definition of the *anupalabdhisama* fallacy occurs when,
due to the opponent's non-perception, one does not accept some particular entity.
The "balancing by non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhisama*) is the proof of the non-existence of even some object intended by the proponent, solely on the basis of its non-apprehension;
for example: "Because of an obstruction, water and so forth, though existing, [are not perceived]."
Just as with non-perception, so too is this position of the proponents— that a sound, though existing prior to its utterance,
is not perceived due to the influence of an obscuration— refuted:
if the sound is not perceived because of an obscuration, [then...]
In that case, just as the covering of water and so forth would be perceived, the covering of sound and so forth would also be perceived.
To this, the reply is: if by you...
If an obscuration is not accepted on the grounds of non-apprehension,

then since the non-existence of that non-apprehension is established by the non-apprehension of it, and because of that [non-existence], the non-existence of the obscuration remains unestablished, the obscuration itself is thereby established.
*Bālapriyā* defines the "equivalence through non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhisama*) with the words: "by the proponent," and so forth.
The Naiyāyikas establish the non-eternality of sound as follows:
if sound were eternal, why would it not be perceived prior to its utterance?
For there is no obscuration of sound, such as that of a jar or other objects by a wall or similar barriers, because such an obscuration is not perceived;
thus says the proponent of the universal (jāti-vādin).
