An objection is raised: if the absence of an obstruction is established through the non-perception of the obstruction, then, because that very non-perception of the obstruction is itself not perceived, the absence of the non-perception of the obstruction would also be established. And in that case, the absence of the obstruction would not be established by the means of knowledge known as non-perception (*anupalabdhi-pramāṇa*), but rather...
"Since there would merely be the occurrence of an obstruction, the objection stated regarding the permanence of sound is not tenable.
Thus, Viśvanātha explains that "balancing through non-perception" (anupalabdhisama) means an opposition raised in such a manner.
The illuminator is the characteristic of dharma that is eternally present.
The *nityasama* (balancing the eternal) fallacy consists in establishing the eternality of the subject (*dharmin*) by means of the alternative between its being eternal or non-eternal. For example:
"Is this impermanence which you attribute to sound itself eternal or non-eternal?
If it is eternal, then because it would be constant due to its very occurrence within sound, sound too [would be eternal]."
It has thus reached its true state.
Now, if that [impermanence] were non-eternal, then there would occasionally be an absence of impermanence in sound; therefore, sound would indeed be eternal. Thus, in either case, as for sound—
"Perpetuity," thus [it is said].
[The author] defines the *nityasama* fallacy.
—Regarding the phrase "of dharma":
it follows that the same applies to sound as well;
thus, sound too possesses eternality.
The meaning is "it would follow.

Since a property cannot exist without a substratum (dharmin), if the property of impermanence were permanent—that is, eternal—then the substratum, sound, would also have to be permanent; this is the intended sense regarding sound.

The meaning of Viśvanātha is that *nityasamā* (the "balancing the eternal") is the objection (*āpādana*) that if impermanence were accepted eternally— that is, at all times— then there would be permanence in the impermanent sound.
*Prakāśikā*.

The "balancing by impermanence" (anityasama) is the pointing out of the consequence that everything would be impermanent, based on the similarity with the example of impermanence due to the common characteristic of being impermanent.

For example: "If it is argued that sound is impermanent because of its similarity to an impermanent jar, then since everything is similar to something by some property or other, it would follow that everything is impermanent."
*Bālapriyā* characterizes the "impermanent" as being like an illustration of impermanence— namely, "that which has impermanence as its example."
For one who asserts that "sound is impermanent because of its similarity to an impermanent jar" (by virtue of the property of being produced), there exists [the similarity] with the impermanent jar.
If the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of all entities— such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth—
is [the reason], then the impermanence of everything becomes undesirable [for the opponent].
This is the commentary: "It is called 'balancing the impermanent' (anityasama) because it is countered by means of impermanence," provided that one does not take the pervasion (vyāpti) into account.
The "balancing by the eternal" (*anityasama*) occurs because, by means of some similarity with the example, one brings about the consequence that everything possesses the property to be proven.

The exclusion [of the fallacy] from the "equal by non-distinction" (*aviśeṣasama*) is due to its difference from the "probandum-term" (*sādhyapada*). In that case, it results in a total lack of distinction (*sarvāviśeṣa*) rather than the possession of the probandum by everything; such is the meaning of Viśvanātha.
— *Prakāśikā*

The definition of the "equal to the effect" (kāryasama) fallacy is: the statement that the reason adduced by the proponent could also occur in connection with another effect; this is the "equal to the effect."

Just as in that very case, the property of conforming to effort is possible in both ways: in the production of the nature of sound, like a jar or similar object, and in the removal of an obscuration, like water or similar substances; thus it applies to both.
Because it is observed to follow from effort,
and because another effect in the form of the removal of its obscuration is possible, there is no necessary restriction to impermanence.
Thus [it is said]. In some places, the reading is "kāraṇasama.
For that [reading] as well, there is the conformity of the cause—namely, effort—to both cases: the production of sound and the removal of its veil.

It should be understood that the conclusion rests precisely upon the meaning stated in the manner of the expression "the designation of equality. Here, for fear of prolixity, the subtle modes [of reasoning] have not been shown; therefore, they should be investigated by the learned in other works.
*Bālapriyā* points out that [the word] *kāryasama* (balancing the effect) is based on the reason stated in the opponent's argument: "because of the reason stated by the opponent."

For example, in the argument "Sound is impermanent because it follows upon effort," the property of following upon effort exists in two ways: in the production of its own nature and in the removal of its veil.

In that context, when the proponent has stated [the reason] with the intention that it refers to the production of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), the proponent of the *jāti* (fallacy) says: "The utility of following effort lies only in the removal of an obstruction, not in the production of the essential nature; thus, the impermanence of sound is not established. In this manner...
The meaning of *pratyavasthānam* is "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*).
In this regard, it should be noted that in certain texts,
the word *sama* appears in the feminine gender in forms such as *sādharmyasamā* (balancing through similarity) and *vaidharmyasamā* (balancing through dissimilarity).
In some cases, however, it is used in the masculine gender in forms such as *sādharmyasamaḥ* (equal by similarity) or *vaidharmyasamaḥ* (equal by dissimilarity).
In that context, when there is an intention to express the genus (*jāti*) as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the word *sama* takes the feminine gender.
However, the author of the Nyāyasūtras states: "The two [futilities] are *sādharmyasama* and *vaidharmyasama*."

He indicates [the subject] in the masculine gender by such forms as "ityādi. His intention is this: indeed, the negation of what has been stated by the proponent is performed by the proponent of the universal (jāti-vādin).

In that context, since the word *pratiṣedha* (negation) is masculine, the word *sama* (equal) is also treated as masculine in accordance with it. This was stated by the Vedāntadeśikas in the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*: "And in the works of Akṣapāda..."

In the sūtras defining the specific characteristics of *jāti* (futile rejoinders), the designation using masculine gender endings refers to the nature of *jāti* as intended here: namely, its status as a refutation (*pratiṣedhabhāga*) within the division consisting of the establishment of one's own position and the rejection of the opponent's position, specifically in the context of counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*).
They say that this refers to a specific type [of negation] of the form thus described.

This is because the authors of the *Nyāyabhāṣya* and others also frequently employ the word "negation" (*pratiṣedha*) in the Sūtra; therefore, taking the word "negation," [the term] "same" (*sama*) [is used].

They consider this to be the resolution of the masculine gender; however, Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana maintains that "the varieties of *jāti* (fallacies), such as *sādharmyasama* and others, [are the subject]."

By stating, "The various [forms] are *kalpa*, *vikalpa*, and *prabheda*," he establishes the masculine gender of the word *sama* in accordance with the word *vikalpa*. When the proponent has thus established his argument, the opponent therein—
A *jāti* is a specific type of fallacious rejoinder (*asaduttara*) that is being pointed out;
its designation by the term *jāti* is based on its very nature of being produced (*jāyamānatva*).
And thus it is said: "A *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is an opposition based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between two parties engaged in debate.
Regarding those two who have entered into the discussion:

When the proponent has presented a proof between the proponent and the opponent, whatever [fault] emerges from the mouth of the desirous opponent— who lacks the flash of a response corresponding to the actual state of affairs— [is the point at issue].

The venerable Uttamūru Vīrarāghavācāryasvāmin explain that the word *jāti* (fallacy) is employed for the sake of emphasis (*avadhāraṇārthatayā*), with the intention that a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) exists only as it is being produced by force of necessity, and not as something already produced that performs a function.
Those very masters describe the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the composition of the word *sama*, which signifies equality, as follows:
[it refers to] the two reasons (*hetu*) employed by the proponent and the opponent.
Equanimity (*sāmya*), as well as the equality between the proponent and the opponent, is indicated by the word "equal" (*sama*);
this is the meaning of the word "equal" in the Sūtra.

The qualification of the reason in the form of a negation demonstrates the similarity residing in the reason. Furthermore, if the similarity residing in the speaker is also intended, then the author of the Vārttika says: "Prayogasama [the equalizing by application] is for the purpose of effecting equality."
"Similarity based on similarity (*sādharmyasama*) is that [fallacy] in which the similarity of that formal argument (*prayoga*) is equal.
Here, by the phrase "for the purpose of equalizing," it is meant that in reality...
Even in the absence of actual equality, the intention to equalize is indicated;
for indeed, there can be neither the refutation of a valid reason by an invalid one nor the production of equality between them.
If it is asked, "By whom is there an equalizing with whom?"— it is the proponent's equalizing with the opponent, and likewise the opponent's [equalizing] with the proponent.
It is stated that the employment of a *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is made for the purpose of avoiding one's own inferiority, or at least for the sake of achieving parity; however,
the venerable Deśika, in the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*, [states that] the employment of a *jāti*...
It is thus stated that [the fault] is committed.

However, the teachers (deśikacaraṇāḥ) in the *Nyāyapariśuddhi* maintain that, just as a reason (hetu) employed by a proponent of a universal class (jāti-vādin) possesses the quality of "striking down another" (paraghātakatva), it likewise possesses the quality of "striking down itself" (svavyāghātakatva).
They maintain that this very state of equality (*sāmya*) is expressed by the word "equal" (*sama*).
Thus, when the characteristics of certain classes among those twenty-four types of beings specified are examined, a state of similarity (*samānatva*) [is observed].
It is perceived through a coarse perspective;

from that, the suspicion arises that there is merely a difference in names. Even in that case, when examined through a subtle perspective, a difference can be understood within their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Keeping this in mind, he says: "In this [work], subtle modes have not been shown for fear of excessive length. Furthermore, these classes [of yoga] possess seven limbs.
Thus it is stated by Udayanācārya at the end of the *Nyāyapariśiṣṭa*:
"The object to be defined, the definition, the origin, the state of persistence, the root, the fruit, and the eradication..."
"All this has been clearly explained in detail in private for the sake of the various castes."
This is established by the half-verse;
therein, that which is stated as a fallacious rejoinder (*asaduttara*) by the opponent is precisely what is meant.
The *lakṣya* (the object to be defined) is that which is not included within the *sādharmya-sama* and other [futile rejoinders]. That very definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is the definition.
"Arising" (*utthiti*) means birth.
The "locus of subsistence" (*sthiteḥ pada*) is the locus of the subsistence of the futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*).
Since a futile rejoinder (jāti) cannot be applied when a proof lacking a real entity is being employed, it is the probans itself that is intended as the locus of the refutation;
such is the root of this application of a futile rejoinder.
The [inferential] cognition has the aspect of similarity and so forth;
the result, however, for the proponent, is the production of the opponent's misconception that his own stated reason is faulty.
*Śātana* is the refutation by the proponent of the opponent's fallacious rejoinder (*jāti*) that has been advanced; however,
the author of the Sūtras [treats] the fallacious rejoinder...
He has clearly set forth the method of refutation for each respective category;
as for the sevenfold nature [of the definition], it has indeed been indicated here and there in the Nyāyapariśiṣṭa.
The meaning is that all of this has been omitted here for fear of prolixity; thus says the *Dīpikā*.
The definition of the points of defeat: A point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is the cause of the disputant’s loss.
The *Prakāśikā* defines the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) with the words: "of the proponent" (*vādinaḥ*).

And although this [fallacy] is also present in cases such as *chala* (quibble) and so forth, there is no fault, because it is included within the *nigrahasthānas* (points of defeat) such as *arthāntara* (irrelevant matter).
It is mentioned separately because knowledge of it is useful even by way of its nature as *chala* and the like.
Like a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*),
the *dīpikā* is the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*).
Shifting the proposition,
contradiction of the proposition,
and abandoning the proposition.
A different reason, an irrelevant point, and the meaningless;
That which has an unintelligible meaning,
that which is meaningless, and that which is mistimed.
Deficiency, excess, repetition, and failure to restate.
Ignorance, lack of ingenuity, distraction, admission of the opponent's view, and neglecting to censure when one should.
The charging of one who is not to be charged, the departure from one's own tenet, and fallacious reasons are points of defeat.
The remainder is easy to understand.
The *Prakāśikā* [explains] the definition of the fallacy of abandoning one's thesis (*pratijñāhāni*).
He demonstrates its internal subdivisions with the words beginning "pratijñā" (the thesis), etc.:
where there is an admission of something contrary to the meaning of the thesis, or an abandonment of the meaning of the thesis, therein lies the "loss of the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*).

For example, in the case of the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is a quality perceived [by the senses]," when an opponent raises an objection based on the force of recognition— such as "This is that very letter *ga*"— the proponent, accepting the permanence of sound by saying, "In that case, let sound be permanent," [proceeds].
He abandons the thesis of impermanence;
this is what the foolish call "abandonment of a thesis."
He defines it: "In that case where the matter proposed... etc.
*Pratijñāhāni* (abandonment of the proposition) is either the acceptance of something contrary to the proposed probandum (*sādhya*) or the relinquishment of the proposed probandum itself. This...

And [the definition] following the *Bhāṣya* is: "When an opponent has countered with a property contrary to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), one abandons the proposition (*pratijñā*) by admitting the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭāntadharma*) into one's own example; this is the abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*).
However, Viśvanātha states: "The abandonment of the proposition is the admission of a property belonging to the opponent's position into one's own position. [He further says: "By oneself..."

The essential meaning is the abandonment of what has been specifically stated. This [fallacy] becomes fivefold through the distinctions of the abandonment of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the probandum (*sādhya*), and that which is other than these.
For example, regarding sound:

When it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," and the objection is raised that "the subject of this [inference] is sublated by recognition," the respondent replies, "In that case, let the jar itself be the subject. Similarly, when it is stated regarding that very same [jar], "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," [the same objection is raised].
When it is objected that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), one might reply: "Let the reason be 'because of being produced' (*kṛtakatvāt*).

Similarly, when it is stated, "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke, like a lamp," and it is objected that the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the probans (*sādhanavikala*), one might reply: "In that case, let the kitchen (*mahānasa*) be the example."

When it has been thus answered on this very point by means of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanena*), [the opponent might say]: "In that case, let it be 'possessing fuel' (*indhanavān*).
But [in that case], there is the loss of [your] other [position].
The fallacy of the loss of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇahāni*) and so forth;

for example, when it is stated in that very same context, "because of blue smoke," and one objects that the qualifier is ineffective (*asamarthaviśeṣaṇa*), [the proponent] replies, "In that case, let it be 'because of smoke'."

Thus he says, "from the reason. Following that, in the *Dinakaryā*, it is stated: "of the abandonment of the thesis and so forth, which were specifically asserted, in the form of 'abandonment of the thesis' (*pratijñāhāni*)."
It has been stated:
the *Prakāśikā* [explains] the definition of another type of proposition (*pratijñā*).
*Pratijñāntara* (shifting the thesis) is the restatement of the matter proposed, characterized by qualifiers not previously mentioned, with the desire to remove a fault pointed out by the opponent.
For example: "The earth and so forth are produced from qualities."

In the argument "because it is an effect," when the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) is raised on the grounds that [the world] is produced by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*),
the qualification "having an object" (*saviṣayaka*) is added as an attribute of the quality (*guṇa*). *Bālapriyā* [Commentary].
He defines "another proposition" (*pratijñāntara*) as follows:
"the addition of a qualification to the reason (*hetu*) after it has been stated by the opponent."

The probandum is "being produced by a quality that possesses an object. The point is that since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) lacks the property of possessing an object, there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) by taking its production into account.

The phrase "of the matter asserted" (*pratijñātārthasya*) is an elliptical expression; the reality is that it refers to "the matter distinct from the reason" (*hetvatiriktārthasya*). By this, another example [is provided]:
"Another *upanaya* and another *nigamana* are included within the category of a 'restatement of the proposition' (*pratijñāntara*)," says Viśvanātha.
However, the author of the Sūtras has specified *hetvantara* (a different reason) as a distinct point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). — *Prakāśikā*
The definition of contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*) is the statement of a reason that contradicts the probandum (*sādhya*) stated by oneself;
for example: "Substance..."

"Because it is not perceived as distinct from form and so forth, [it is] different from the qualities. [This is an example of] contradiction with one's own proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*). *Bālapriyā*: [The opponent states: "Because it is not perceived as distinct from form and so forth, [it is] different from the qualities. This is a contradiction with one's own proposition.
He indicates [the reason] with the words "svoktasādhyeti" (by the aforementioned probandum).
For indeed, the state of not being perceived as distinct from color and so forth is pervaded by non-difference from the quality.
It does not establish the difference from the qualities;
therefore, the meaning is that there is a contradiction with the thesis (pratijñāvirodha) because the reason is stated as being pervaded by the absence of difference from the qualities.
— *Prakāśikā*
The definition of the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāsannyāsa*) is the denial of one's own stated position when it has been refuted by the opponent.

For example, when it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and the opponent has refuted this by pointing out the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a universal (*sāmānya*), the proponent denies his own statement, saying, "By whom was it said that sound is impermanent?"
*Bālapriyā* defines the renunciation of a promise as follows: "In the matter of one's own statement," and so forth.

The distinction is that in the case of *pratijñāhāni* (loss of the proposition), there is the abandonment of the meaning of the proposition, whereas in the case of *pratijñāsannyāsa* (renunciation of the proposition), there is its concealment.
— *Prakāśikā*
The definition of a different reason (*hetvantara*) is: the addition of another qualification to the category of a previously stated reason with the desire to refute an objection raised by another.

For example, when the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is raised against the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible," the qualification "provided it possesses a genus" (*ajātimattve sati*) is added.
*Bālapriyā* identifies another reason [for the objection] with the words "parokteti": it is for the desire to refute the criticism raised by others.

The meaning is that "another reason" (*hetvantara*) refers to a statement characterized by a reason-delimiting property (*hetutāvacchedaka*) that is distinct from the previously stated reason-delimiting property.
However, when the qualification "provided it possesses a genus" (*jātimattve sati*) is added, [the fallacy does not apply] in the case of a universal (*sāmānya*).
There is no deviation [from the rule] because of the absence of the state of possessing a genus;
this is the definition of a different object, according to the *Prakāśikā*.
Arthāntara (irrelevance) is the statement of a matter that is not applicable to the subject at hand.
For example: "Sound is eternal because it is intangible. And the word "because" [is used].
It is established by means of the *niṣṭhā* suffix;
and a "word" (*pada*) is that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), and so forth— thus [it is stated] in the *Bālapriyā*.
It defines *arthāntara* (irrelevancy): "that which is not useful for the subject at hand.
This means the expression of a matter that is neither relevant nor required by the context.
The definition of the meaningless (*nirarthaka*) is as follows:
the employment of words that do not convey meaning is the meaningless.
For example: "Sound is impermanent because of having the letters ja, ba, ga, ḍa, da, and śa," and so forth; this is the definition of a statement whose meaning is not understood.

The use of words that cause the audience or the opponent to fail to understand is "the unintelligible" (*avijñātārtha*). This takes such forms as having a confused syntactical connection (*akliṣṭānvaya*), having an unfamiliar meaning (*aprasiddhārthaka*), or being uttered too rapidly (*tvaritoccārita*), and so forth.
— *Bālapriyā*
He defines "that whose meaning is not understood" as follows: "the assembly," [referring to] that which has been stated three times by the proponent but [remains ungrasped] by the opponent.
That which is not understood by the members of the assembly is "the meaning not understood" (*avijñātārtha*).

It is the employment of a declarative sentence that does not produce the required mental presence conducive to the understanding of the opponent, even when the assembly consists of attentive, non-distracted, and proficient individuals.

By the term "vācaka" (denotative), the exclusion of meaningless (*nirarthaka*) and nonsensical (*apārthaka*) expressions is intended; such a sentence is [called] *bhūstana*. Viśvanātha’s commentary states this. Such a sentence is "the earth's breast."
Regarding the phrase "himabheṣajavat" and so forth:
the word *bhūstana* means "mountain.
Fire is the medicine (*bheṣaja*) for cold (*hima*); thus, the meaning of *himabheṣajavat* is "possessing that [fire]."
According to the Vedic scripture, "Fire is the remedy for cold," this is the definition of the irrelevant (*apārthaka*).
A collection of words that are not mutually connected is *apārthaka* (meaningless).
For example: "Soundness, pot, cloth, eternal, non-eternal, and because of being knowable," and so forth.
*Bālapriyā* defines the "meaningless" (*apārthaka*) as follows:
"mutually," etc.
The meaning is that a collection of words devoid of the expectancy conducive to the comprehension of the intended sentence-meaning is "meaningless" (*apārthaka*).
— *Prakāśikā*
The definition of "untimely" (aprāptakāla) is the statement of the members [of a syllogism] in an inverted order; that is, it is "untimely."

For example: "Sound is impermanent because it possesses the nature of sound," and so forth. *Bālapriyā* [comments: 1) The thesis (*pratijñā*) is the statement of that which is to be proven (*sādhyavacana*). 2) The reason (*hetu*) is the statement of the property (*dharma*) that serves as the ground for proving that very thing. 3) The example (*udāharaṇa*) is the statement of that which is well-known (*prasiddhavacana*) as being similar to the subject (*pakṣa*) in its possession of that same property. 4) The application (*upanaya*) is the statement of the similarity between the subject and the example based on the aforementioned commonality. 5) The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the statement that, because of this very similarity, the subject also possesses that property. These five are called the members of proof (*sādhanāṅga*). Among these, the first three are the essential members (*mukhya*), while the latter two are auxiliary members (*gauṇa*). This is because the first three alone are capable of establishing the object to be proven. The latter two, however, merely serve to strengthen the argument by removing doubt regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Furthermore, the reason is of three types: the affirmative-positive (*anvayin*), the negative-positive (*vyatirekin*), and the affirmative-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*). Among these, the affirmative-positive is exemplified by: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced; whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, like a pot. He characterizes [the fallacy of] mistiming (*aprāptakāla*) with the words "of the members" (*avayavānām*).
[This refers to] the members, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, according to their respective definitions.
The sequence [of the members] is determined by the force of the meaning.
In that regard, speaking with a reversal of the members is "untimely" (aprāptakāla); this definition follows the *Bhāṣya*.

Viśvanātha, however, states: "The reversal (*viparyāsa*) of a 'member' (*avayava*), which is a single part of the argument (*kathā*), is its inversion (*vaiparītya*); thus, it results in an expression following a sequence that is contrary to the order of the argument as established by the formal agreement (*samayabandha*)."

In this regard, the sequence is as follows: after the proponent has stated the proof (*sādhana*), the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) must be removed; this constitutes the first stage (*pāda*). The second stage consists of the opponent's refutation (*upālambha*) of that proof.

The third quarter consists of the opponent's proof of his own position and the removal of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) therein; the fourth quarter is the determination of victory and defeat. Thus [is the treatment] of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and so forth.
The sequence: therein, he demonstrates that "speaking out of order" (*aprāptakāla*) consists in speaking in a confused manner due to the agitation or delusion of the assembly.
— *Prakāśikā*
The definition of deficiency (*nyūna*) is as follows: the statement of a member [of the syllogism] that lacks any one of its constituent parts is deficient; this is clear.
Now, the definition of excess (*adhika*):
"Excessive" refers to the statement of more than one reason and so forth;
for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is sound and because it is audible," and so on.
The definition of tautology (*punarukta*) is the restatement of what has already been said, except in the case of a restatement for the sake of clarification (*anuvāda*).
For example: "Sound is impermanent," "Sound is impermanent," and so forth. *Bālapriyā* [comments: This refers to the repetition of the same statement.
He defines *punarukta* (repetition): "without restatement. *Punarukta* is the purposeless utterance of what has already been said;
however, restatement (*anuvāda*) consists of the form of an explanation.
It possesses a purpose;
therefore, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to that case. Thus, the purposeless re-statement of a word that has the same meaning and the same sequence of phonemes—
Verbal tautology (*śabdapunarukta*): for example, "sound is impermanent, sound is impermanent.
It is the purposeless repetition of a word that has the same meaning but a different sequence of phonemes.
Tautology of meaning (*arthapunarukta*) is a restatement of what has already been expressed;
for example, saying "sound is impermanent" and then "sound is subject to cessation.
— *Prakāśikā*
The definition of non-reproduction (ananubhāṣaṇa) is the failure to reproduce [the opponent's argument] even after it has been stated three times by the assembly.
*Bālapriyā* defines *ananubhāṣaṇa* (non-reproduction) with the words: "by the assembly," etc.
The opponent's failure to repeat a statement that has been uttered three times by the proponent and understood by the assembly.
Regarding "non-reiteration":
in order to exclude its confusion with "ignorance," one should qualify it as "not manifesting ignorance";
and in order to exclude its confusion with "distracting interruption," one should qualify it as "not interrupting the discussion."
Thus say the teachers;
and there is no confusion regarding non-appearance, even in the case of the subsequent comprehension.
Viśvanātha [states] that non-reproduction may occur due to disturbances in the assembly (*sabhākṣobha*) and so forth;
the *Prakāśikā* [identifies] this as having the characteristic of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

Ignorance (*ajñāna*), characterized as a lack of confidence (*apratibhā*), is the failure to understand the meaning of a statement even after it has been uttered three times by the proponent and understood by the assembly.
*Apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity) is the state of remaining silent due to the failure of a response to manifest, even after having understood the opponent's statement which requires a reply.
*Bālapriyā*.
He defines *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity) as "that which is worthy of a reply.
And here, since non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) is necessarily required [as a preliminary], it is that very thing [which constitutes the fault].
It should not be said that "let there be a refutation," for that applies when one does not restate what has been stated by the opponent; however,
in the case of *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity), it is different.
Even when repeating what has been stated by another, there is a failure to provide a response; this distinction constitutes the definition of distraction (*vikṣepa*). This is the *Prakāśikā*.
*Vikṣepa* (distracting) is the interruption of the discussion by adducing an impossibility or a preoccupation with another task that would require a different time.
*Bālapriyā*.
He defines distraction (*vikṣepa*) with the words "asambhavat":
that which is impossible at another time, though it might be capable of being done, is unfit to exist in reality at this present moment.
Distraction (*vikṣepa*) is the interruption of the discourse by feigning preoccupation with some task. By this [definition],

it refers to going when summoned by royal officials and the like, or summoned by family members and others for necessary business, or when one perceives such things as a fire breaking out in one's own house.
Or, if there is an obstruction due to an actual headache or similar ailment, there is no distraction.
[Distraction occurs] when one, having interrupted the discussion that was to be carried out, says: "I have this duty to perform; once that is finished..."

"I shall speak later"—this is the point of defeat called distraction (*vikṣepa*); such is the Bhāṣya. The *Prakāśikā* considers this to be the definition of admission of the opponent's position (*matānujñā*).
Matānujñā (admission of one's own position) consists in pointing out a fault in the opponent's position without having first removed the fault from one's own position.
— Bālapriyā.
He defines *matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's position) as follows: "In one's own position," that is,
having accepted a fault stated by the opponent regarding one's own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*) and failing to refute it.
The meaning of *matānujñā* (admission of one's own position) is the pointing out that the same fault applies even to the opponent’s established doctrine (*parasiddhānta*).
For example: "If you are a thief because you are a human being, then for that very same reason, you yourself are also a thief," and so forth.
— *Prakāśikā*

The definition of "overlooking the censurable" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa) is the failure to point out an opponent's ground for defeat (nigrahasthāna) that is worthy of being pointed out; this is what constitutes overlooking the censurable.
*Bālapriyā* defines "neglecting one who should be questioned" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) with the words "fit to be pointed out" (*udbhāvanārha*).
One who is "to be questioned" (*paryanuyojya*) is one who should be urged because grounds for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) have arisen.
Neglecting him by saying "you have reached a point of defeat" constitutes a failure to pursue the argument;
and to whom does this defeat belong?
When the assembly has thus questioned him, he should say:
"One who has indeed incurred defeat should not expose his own private parts. This is the commentary.
"But how can this be pointed out by the proponent?
For it is improper to expose one's own private parts."
"If this is true, it should be pointed out only by a neutral observer; however, there is no fault even if one points it out oneself during a formal debate," says Viśvanātha.
The rest is clear. Herein...
Regarding the subject of *jāti* (futile rejoinders) and *nigrahasthāna* (points of defeat),
[the details] are found in the *Bhāṣya*, *Vārttika*, *Tātparyaṭīkā*, *Pariśuddhi*, *Nyāyapariśiṣṭa*, *Nyāyamañjarī*, *Tārkikarakṣā*, and other such works.
Much has been analyzed in various treatises and in the *Nyāyapariśuddhi* composed by Vedāntadeśika.
Having carefully reflected upon all of that, some great work should be written as a separate treatise.
In this manual (*prakaraṇa*), however, this much is sufficient; therefore, I desist for fear of excessive prolixity.
The *Prakāśikā* [states] the definition of "charging with what is not to be charged" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*) as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurring when one is free from such defeat.
Pointing out a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) where there is no ground for censure is "reproaching one who should not be censured" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*).
Regarding the definition of a "deviation from tenet" (*apasiddhānta*):
it occurs when a discussion proceeds by relying on the view of a specific established system of tenets.
An *upasiddhānta* (quasi-conclusion) is the offering of a reply by relying on a doctrine that contradicts one's own established tenet.
[The other points of defeat are: loss of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), failure to repeat (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), lack of understanding (*ajñāna*), and inability to respond (*apratibhā*).

In the absence of [the faults of] diversion, evasion of what is to be questioned, and indifference, and in the presence of other points of defeat distinct from fallacious reasons, as well as of the [actual] reasons.
Their inclusion within [the categories of] substance and so forth should be understood according to their respective cases.
With the intention that the meaning of the Sūtra regarding what is additional is easy to understand, he says: "The rest."

*Bālapriyā* explains the manner in which the *jātis* (fallacies of the reason) and the *nigrahasthānas* (points of defeat) are included within the seven categories (*padārthas*) as they have been established:
By the passage beginning with "pratijñāhāni" (loss of the thesis) and so forth,
the inclusion of each of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) such as loss of the thesis within those respective categories is clearly stated in the *Dinakarī* commentary.

Therefore, it is to be understood from the very word itself, because the class of fallacious rejoinders (asaduttara) consists of a verbal statement that, by its own nature, contradicts the proponent's intended meaning.
Inclusion within a quality (*guṇa*). [This is] the refutation of the view that *dīpikā* (the illuminating power) is a category distinct from the others. Now, an objection:

If it is argued that "power" (*śakti*) is a distinct category of entity because, even when there is contact with fire in the palm of the hand, burning does not occur due to the presence of an obstacle, we say: no;
for the absence of an obstacle is [the cause] in every effect whatsoever.
Because power (śakti) is not required as a cause,
since the very nature of being a cause constitutes the category of power.
— *Prakāśikā*

Now, since burning does not occur even when there is contact with fire if a jewel or similar object is present, it must be asserted that the jewel and such things possess the status of an inhibitor (*pratibandhaka*).
And that [obstructiveness] is established only by accepting a power conducive to burning in fire,
because obstructiveness consists in the destruction of a power conducive to an effect.
Therefore, since this power— established through the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*)— is an additional category, it follows that "there are only seven categories."
The Prābhākara raises the objection that this is inconsistent, saying: "But surely...
[nanv iti]. If it is argued that even if *śakti* (power) is thus established, its status as a distinct entity remains unproven—[we reply]: No;
for power cannot first of all be of the nature of a substance (*dravya*), because it subsists in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.
For this very reason, it is not of the nature of either a quality or an action, nor is it of the nature of any one among the categories beginning with generality (*sāmānya*), because of its arising.
Because it possesses the quality of perishability;
and thus, its status as a distinct category of entity (*atirikta-padārtha*) is established. Now, an objection:
is obstructiveness (*pratibandhakatva*) not the destruction of a power conducive to the effect, but rather—
It is the state of being the counter-positive of an absence that serves as the cause; and this is established precisely because the absence of the jewel (maṇi) functions as the cause.
Furthermore, in the state where the jewel is present, the non-occurrence of burning is possible precisely because of the absence of that other cause which consists in the absence of the jewel;
thus, the postulation of a distinct power (*śakti*) is improper.
He provides the resolution: "of the absence of an obstructer.

Now, one might raise the objection that a distinct *śakti* (power) must be established because the common usage, "fire is capable of producing burning," would otherwise be inexplicable; having raised this doubt:
He states that even though it takes the form of causality (*kāraṇatā*), there is no additional power (*śakti*) because [the causal relation] is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*):
"of causality" (*kāraṇatvasya*).
Now, if the absence of the jewel and so forth is the cause, then at the time when the jewel is present—
Even when the excitant is present, burning would not occur;
however, in my view, just as in the state where the jewel and other [obstructors] have been removed,
in the state of the presence of the excitant as well, another power conducive to burning arises in the fire.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the absence of the fire] is accepted [as the cause], we say: no.

For there is no fault in accepting that the cause is the absence of the gem and so forth, qualified by the absence of the stimulant. Nor is there a problem because stimulants are not uniform (ananugata).

It should not be argued that there is complexity (gaurava) because one must postulate the causality of the absence of the jewel and so forth, as qualified by the totality of the absences of their respective excitants;
for [this is simpler] with respect to the power conducive to burning.

The summary is as follows: since such causality is necessary for you as well, it is simpler [for us] not to postulate infinite potencies, their prior non-existences, and their destructions, which would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
*Bālapriyā*.
Even when there is contact between the palm of the hand and fire, if a jewel that acts as an obstacle is present, the burning of the palm does not occur;
therefore, *śakti* (power) is a distinct category of entity.

This was the doubt raised in the *Dīpikā*. In that regard, how could the existence of power (*śakti*) as a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) be established merely by the non-occurrence of burning? Therefore, this doubt is untenable; thus, stating the intended meaning of the passage containing the doubt, he introduces [the following]:
— "But surely, even when there is contact with fire":

even when there is contact of the palm of the hand with fire, if a jewel or similar object is present, burning does not occur in the palm; yet, in the absence of such a jewel or object, burning does occur.
Since an effect does not arise when something exists and arises when that thing is absent, that thing acts as an obstacle; therefore,
because burning does not occur when a jewel or the like is present, while burning does occur when it is absent,
it must be stated that the jewel and so forth possess the quality of being an obstacle to burning.
And obstructiveness (*pratibandhakatva*) consists in the disruption of the capacity conducive to the effect;
thus, that which resides in fire and is conducive to burning—
That power is destroyed by the jewel;
therefore, since it is fire characterized by power alone that produces burning,
when the jewel is present, the power to burn is destroyed, and thus it is fire characterized by power alone that produces burning.

In the case of a jewel (*maṇi*), because the power of burning has been destroyed, there is no burning due to the absence of the cause, which is fire characterized by that power. And thus, since [the absence] obstructs the power conducive to the effect, it cannot be accounted for otherwise; in this way, through the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), a distinct category of entity consisting of "power" (*śakti*) is established.
The intention of the objector is that the statement "the word-meanings" is thus consistent.

[The author replies: "But even so," etc.; for even if the word-meaning in the form of *śakti* (power) is established by the means of knowledge known as *arthāpatti* (presumption) according to the manner previously stated, of that...
The meaning is: how can it be something distinct from the seven categories? For it is not, first of all, of the nature of substance, and so forth.
Power is distinct from substance, because it resides in qualities and so forth, just like the universal "quality-ness" (guṇatva) and the like;
for power indeed exists in qualities such as color and in actions and so forth.

Because in the case of the color and other qualities of the parts, there exists a power conducive to them by virtue of their being the cause of the color and other qualities of the whole; because that power resides in the qualities such as color; because action possesses a power conducive to it by virtue of its producing conjunction and so forth; and because power resides in action. And thus:

The meaning is that just as the properties of being a quality (guṇatva), the property of being an action (kriyātva), and so forth— which reside in qualities and the like— are not substances, so too power (śakti) is not a substance because it resides in qualities and the like.

"From this very reason" means "precisely because it subsists in qualities and so forth. Power (śakti) is distinct from both quality and action, because it subsists in qualities and so forth, just like the nature of quality (guṇatva) and the like.
Considering that if the distinction between quality and action were the probandum, then— whether it be of the nature of a quality or of the nature of an action—

the distinction between both would be possible according to the maxim "thus it is not both," resulting in the non-establishment of the intended object; therefore, the status of being the probandum was adopted for the distinction of either one.
The sense is that only where there is both a distinction of qualities (*guṇa*) and a distinction of actions (*karman*) can a distinction between either quality or action possibly occur.
And it is not the case that...
"Having the nature of one among [the categories] such as the universal (sāmānya) and so forth":
power (śakti) is distinct from one among the universal and so forth, because it possesses arising and destruction, like a jar and other such things.
If "merely possessing origination" were the reason,
there would be a logical fallacy (vyabhicāra), because possession of origination exists in destruction (dhvaṃsa), which lacks any of the categories such as generality (sāmānya) and so forth.
To exclude that, [the reason] is stated as "because it possesses perishability."
Since destruction (dhvaṃsa) lacks further destruction, there is no deviation [in the logical reason].
If one were to state merely "possessing destruction," then [the reason] would be deviant with respect to antecedent absence (prāgabhāva), which lacks the aforementioned probandum.
There is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because of the existence of perishability [even in cases where the probandum is absent]. To exclude that, "origination" (utpatti) is introduced.
Since prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), being beginningless, lacks origination, there is no deviation. And thus:
The reason (*hetu*) is either "possessing both origination and destruction" or "possessing destruction qualified by origination.

In the phrase "sāmānyādi," the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes *viśeṣa*, *samavāya*, and *abhāva*. "In this way" means that *śakti* (power) is a distinct category (*padārtha*), supported by the aforementioned inferences and by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

The point is that the status of *śakti* (power) as a distinct category (*padārtha*) is established by the inference of elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*), namely: "because, while not being included among the [six] established categories, it is nonetheless a category. Now, one might object:
"Since the absence of an impediment (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is the cause for every effect, there is no need for *śakti*."
Thus the *Dīpikā* text proceeds to refute that *śakti* (potency) is a distinct category (*padārtha*).
Let it be granted, for the sake of argument, that the absence of an obstacle (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is the cause in every effect.

In response to the doubt as to why power (*śakti*) does not have the status of a category (*padārtha*) on that account, the author states the purport of the *Dīpikā*: "It is not an obstructive factor" (*pratibandhakatvaṃ na*).
The phrase "and that" means "and the state of being an impediment.
Regarding the expression "precisely because the absence of the jewel is the cause," the word "precisely" (eva) [serves to exclude other factors].
It is the exclusion [of the gem] from being an obstructer of the capacity conducive to the effect.
And thus, although the gem lacks the quality of being an obstructer of the capacity conducive to the effect, there is the absence of the gem, which is the cause.

The status of being an obstructer is established because it is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of that [non-existence]. Thus, the sense is that since there is no evidence of presumption (*arthāpatti*)—which consists in the impossibility of an otherwise inexplicable fact—the existence of *śakti* (potency) is not proven.
This is because there is simply no other cause in the form of its absence.
The meaning is: "precisely because of the absence of that other cause which consists in the absence of the jewel.
Here, by the use of the word *antara* (other), fire is [indicated] with respect to burning.
Both the absence of the jewel and [the presence of fire] are separate causes; however, fire qualified by the absence of the jewel is not the cause,
nor is the absence of the jewel qualified by fire the cause.

It is indicated that if fire qualified by the absence of a jewel were the cause, there would result two cumbersome causal relations— due to the lack of a definitive conclusion regarding the relationship between the qualificand and the qualifier. Now, [one might object]:...

He raises an objection: "Even if power (*śakti*) is not established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for its being an obstacle, it is nevertheless established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). [The author replies: "But [in the case of] the production of burning, even without a distinct category of entity called 'power,' it is possible [to explain everything] solely through the already established category of 'causality' (*kāraṇatva*)."
He says that there is no inconsistency in conventional discourse because it is established by reasoning:
"Even though it has the nature of causality.
If it is asked, "But how is it that causality is not something distinct [from the cause]?"—
On this point, they say: "Causality (kāraṇatva) is included within either positive existence (bhāva), negative existence (abhāva), or both.
This is clearly stated in the *Kusumāñjali* and other works.
He raises an objection: "But surely, the absence of the moonstone and so forth is the cause.
The moonstone (candrakāntamaṇi) is an inhibitor of burning.
The absence of that [non-contact] is the cause of burning.

When there is contact with a moonstone (*candrakānta-maṇi*) or contact with a sunstone (*sūryakānta-maṇi*), or when there is the state of being the intended object of a mantra, in relation to that fire, then burning occurs.

It arises. In that case, since according to your view there is an absence of a cause consisting in the non-existence of the moonstone (*candrakāntamaṇi*), how can there be burning? In my view, however, the non-existence of the gem is not the cause of burning; rather—
Fire characterized by potency alone is the cause;
for even when the potency residing in fire is destroyed by a moonstone (*candrakāntamaṇi*), it reappears upon the conjunction of a sunstone (*sūryakāntamaṇi*), mantras, and so forth.
By accepting that another power conducive to burning arises in the fire,
burning becomes possible because the fire, as qualified by that power, exists;
therefore, [this] is power (śakti).
"It must be accepted"— this is the thought of the objector. Here, by the term "excitant" (*uttejaka*),
that which causes the production of the effect even when an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*) is present— such as a sun-crystal (*sūryakāntamaṇi*) and so forth— is denoted.

It is stated that "incitatory power" (*uttejakatva*) consists in being the cause of the production of an effect at a time when there is a presence of an obstructing factor. He provides the resolution:
Regarding the phrase "qualified by the absence of an excitant": where both a gem and an excitant are present,
because the qualifier— the absence of an excitant— is absent, the cause in the form of the absence of that qualified [absence] does not exist.
The sense is that since the production of burning is not possible [in that way], there is no utility for the power (*śakti*).
"Because it is not concomitant" means because it is manifold (*anekatva*).

The meaning of "respect" (*gaurava*) is that multiple excitatory absences (*uttejakābhāva*) are included within the scope of the delimitors of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). This refers to [the view that] with respect to the power conducive to burning (*dāhānukūlaśakti*), [multiple conditions must be accounted for].
Because it is accepted that the power conducive to burning in a jewel is destroyed when the jewel is present, and such a power arises again when the jewel is removed.
By virtue of this admission,

the absence of the jewel (*maṇyabhāva*) is the cause of the power residing in fire that is conducive to burning; for even in that case, when the jewel is present, the power is destroyed, and when the intensifier (*uttejaka*) is present, the power arises.
It must be stated that the absence of the jewel qualified by the absence of an excitant is the cause of power (*śakti*).

The point is this: rather than postulating an infinite number of powers, as well as their antecedent non-existences, their destructions, and so forth, let its causality be directed toward burning itself; what is the use of these further assumptions? [Objection: But surely...
If the absence of a gem qualified by the aggregate (kūṭa) of absences of excitants is the cause of burning,
then even during the state of an excitant in the form of a mantra, since the mantra— which consists of sound— resides in space (gagana),
its absence would exist in the location where the fire resides, by virtue of the relation of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
There would be the undesirable consequence that burning does not occur because of the presence of the jewel qualified by the absence of its stimulator. Furthermore,
just like conjunction, since a substance also exists non-pervasively (avyāpyavṛtti) through conjunction, even when the jewel is present,
[the fire] might exist through conjunction in some delimited part.
Furthermore, because of the existence of the absence of the jewel (maṇi), there would be the undesirable consequence of the arising of burning; therefore, he says "in brief":
[this refers to] that which is delimited by the property of burning (dāhatva) with respect to [the effect], by way of the relation of being a qualifier of an absence.

The [absence] of the jewel and so forth, which is delimited by that specific qualification characterized by co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the respective absences of the excitants— these absences having as their counter-correlates (pratiyogin) those [excitants] whose counter-correlativity is delimited by either the relation of being the intended object (uddeśyatā) or the relation of spatial qualification (daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā).

The meaning is that the two aforementioned defects are to be avoided by postulating a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) according to the method stated by Dinakara: that the absence of an absence—whose counter-positive is delimited by the relation of either "being a qualifier of the indicator" (*daiśikaviśeṣaṇatā*) or "being the object of the thesis" (*uddeśyatā*)—is the cause [of the effect] by means of the relation of "absence-qualifierhood" (*abhāvīyaviśeṣaṇatā*). This much [is the point].
The innate power (*sahaja-śakti*) has been refuted;
the *Dīpikā* [now] effects the rejection of the dependent power (*ādheya-śakti*).

If it is argued that an inherent capacity (*ādheya-śakti*) must be admitted because purification is observed in bronze and other materials through the application of ashes and the like—[we reply]: no.

[For purification consists in] the destruction of the contact with ashes and the like, accompanied by the non-existence of all instances of contact with the untouchable that are co-temporal with that contact with ashes and the like.
Because it is the meaning of the term "purity.
[The *Prakāśikā* says: But even so...
When an object such as bell-metal comes into contact with something that should not be touched, it lacks the fitness for its intended function, such as eating;
for only bell-metal that possesses [unimpaired] capacity is fit for that purpose,
since the capacity is destroyed upon contact with the untouchable.
However, since power (śakti) is produced again upon contact with ash, there is fitness for that [power].
And thus, an inherent power (ādheya-śakti) must be accepted in the case of bell-metal and similar substances.

Nor should it be argued that since the fact of eating and so forth from bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and other such vessels is already accounted for by postulating that contact with the untouchable (*aspṛśya*) acts as an obstacle, one need not accept [the existence of *adharma*]; for in the present case, contact with the untouchable consists essentially in conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with that which is not to be touched.

He objects again: "If destruction were present, then because the absence of an obstructing factor would exist, [the object] such as bell-metal would become fit for eating and so forth even while ashes or other substances are being applied to it."
Regarding the phrase "by means of ash, etc.":
the first word "etc. includes sour liquids and the like, while the second includes copper and so forth.

He provides the resolution—that it is improper to postulate a distinct power (śakti) when the purity of bell-metal and other such objects is established by the very destruction of the prior [impurity]—in the words:
"By contact with ashes, etc. (bhasmādisaṃyoga).

In cases such as bell-metal where there is contact with an untouchable object again after the destruction of the contact with ash and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence of purity because the destruction of the contact with ash and so forth still exists; therefore, the term "accompanied by" (*sahitānta*) is an adjective qualifying the destruction.

And here, "literature" (sāhitya) refers to a coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) constrained by a specific relationship, since it is impossible to describe a form that would follow upon untouchable objects.

Because it is impossible to include the absence [of contact] as delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), and because the absence of contact with any untouchable thing whatsoever exists there, that undesirable consequence (*tadāpatti*) remains exactly as it was; therefore, the word "as many as" (*yāvat*) is used.

And thus, the sense is that there is no such fault because, in that case, there is an absence of instances of contact with the untouchable by means of the relation of unqualified qualification (*niravacchinna-viśeṣaṇatā*) for as many [instances] as exist;
and where the conjunction with ashes and the contact with an untouchable object arise and perish simultaneously.

Furthermore, in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of purity arising by taking into account the destruction of the contact with ashes and so forth, as qualified by the non-simultaneous co-location (*kūṭasāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the absence of contact with each respective untouchable;
therefore, [the phrase] "existing there at the time delimited by the contact with ashes and so forth" is intended to mean that which exists therein during that period.
The term "up to the end of the time" (*kālīnāntam*) is a qualifier of non-existence (*abhāva*).
Thus, for you,
since all those absences are non-existent at the moment delimited by the conjunction with ashes and so forth, there is no fault.
Such is the meaning.
Now, by means of sprinkling and so forth— *bālapriyā*.

In the *Dīpikā*, beginning with the words "Now, by means of ashes and so forth," the view that an inherent power (*sahaja-śakti*) or an adventitious power (*ādheya-śakti*) can be produced in rice and other grains, or in bronze and other vessels, is refuted.
Thus, there are two types of power: the innate and the adventitious.
Because the Mīmāṃsakas accept two types of capacity;
by the first word, "etcetera," [it refers to] sourness and so forth. [It is said:
"one is purified by ashes."
"Brass and copper are purified by acid;
the earth is purified by cow dung, and likewise a woman by her menses. Thus it is said.
It is mentioned merely by way of words in the *Dīpikā*:
"in conjunction with ashes and so forth.
[This refers to] as many [factors] as are simultaneous with the conjunction with ashes and so forth.

The meaning is that the purity of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and similar substances consists precisely in the destruction of the conjunction with ash or other materials, which is qualified by the collection of absences whose counter-correlates are the touch of those who are untouchable (*aspṛśya*).
This applies to that bell-metal or other substance in which [such conditions obtain].
First, there is contact with an untouchable object; then, contact with ashes and so forth;

then, after the destruction of that contact with ashes and so forth, there is again contact with an untouchable object. At that time, because the prior destruction of the contact with ashes and so forth exists, [the impurity arises] from the mere destruction of the contact with ashes and so forth.
If it were the meaning of the term "pure," then even at that time, the state of being pure would follow;
to prevent this,
the word ends with "sahita" (conjoined).
In the case of the destruction of the conjunction with ashes and so forth, the qualifier [is as follows]:
at the time of contact with an untouchable, there is no absence qualified by having contact with an untouchable as its counter-positive; thus, there is no fault.
And here, "co-occurrence" (*sāhitya*) consists in a co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) established through an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*). Therefore,

there is no possibility of purity at the time of such a touch by taking as the counter-positive of the absence the touch with an untouchable, whether that touch is located in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) or is co-referential (*sāmānādhikaraṇa*) by means of a temporal or other such relation.

It does not occur; for even at the time of touching some untouchable object in a vessel made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and the like, since there is an absence of contact with another untouchable object, the destruction of the prior contact with ashes and so forth—qualified by that [absence]—would exist, and thus the attainment of purity would follow. Therefore...
As for the inclusion [of the term] "up to" (*yāvat*):

at that time, since there is no fault because the absence of that which consists in the non-existence of whatever kind of contact with an untouchable object exists within the scope of "up to non-existence" (*yāvad-abhāva*), there is no problem. It is not so.
Nor should it be argued that, rather than specifying "as many as" (yāvattva) with respect to the absence [of contact], one should simply specify the absence of contact with untouchable objects;
for [this would fail] in the case of several heterogeneous [objects].
Because there is an absence of a property that pervades untouchable objects, a general property— which serves as the delimitant of counter-correlativity— is impossible here;
this is due to the fact that conjunction is non-pervasive.

Even at the time of contact with an untouchable object in the case of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and so forth, because the absence of that [untouchability] exists in some part [of the vessel] by way of the relation of spatial qualification (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā*), there would arise the undesirable consequence of [the vessel] being pure by taking as the basis the destruction of a prior contact with ash and so forth qualified by that [absence]. To prevent this, [the definition must include the qualification "not having been touched"].

In the definition of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the locus-ness (*ādheyatā*) that constitutes it must be specified as being delimited by the relation of non-mediated spatial qualification (*niravacchinnadaiśikaviśeṣaṇatā*). This applies in cases such as where [the food] is in a vessel made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) or similar materials.

The conjunction with ashes and the touch of the untouchable arise and perish at the same time; in that case, the destruction of the conjunction with ashes becomes qualified by the absence of the touch of the untouchable. Therefore, in order to prevent the attainment of purity for the vessel and its possessor, [the definition specifies] the absence whose counter-positive is the touch of the untouchable.
The qualification "simultaneous with the conjunction with ashes and so forth" means that it exists in the locus of the conjunction with ashes and so forth,
as delimited by the moment that delimits the conjunction with ashes and so forth.

And thus, although the absence of contact with the untouchable existing there is co-temporal with the destruction of the conjunction with ashes and so forth, there is no fault, because it does not exist at the time delimited by the moment of conjunction with the ashes and so forth. And so it is.

The result is that purification (*śuddhi*) consists in the destruction of contact with ashes and the like, which subsists in a locus delimited by the moment of contact with ashes and so forth, and which is determined by a substratum-ness (*ādhikaraṇatā*) that is itself determined by a location-ness (*ādheyatā*) related through an unconditioned spatial qualification (*niravacchinna-daiśika-viśe�ṣaṇatā-sambandha*), residing in all absences whose counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are contacts with the untouchable.
Thus he says: "In that which, such as bell-metal," and so forth;
[it is] "restrained by a specific relation."
The meaning is that [the relation] is constituted by a spatial non-particularized qualification (*niravacchinnadaiśikāviśeṣaṇatā*).
This is the *Dīpikā*’s refutation of the view that ownership (*svatva*) is a distinct category (*padārtha*).
Ownership (*svatva*) is also not a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*),
because its nature consists in being fit for disposal according to one's will.

And the delimiting factor for that [ownership] is precisely the state of having been acquired through acceptance and so forth; thus, [the expression] "this belongs to Caitra" [is used]. (The *Prakāśikā*:
"This belongs to Caitra."

In the verse beginning with "dhanam" (wealth), he refutes the view that the ownership (*svatva*) perceived in relation to wealth and so forth is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) by stating: "Ownership also... The word "also" (*api*) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.
This includes [the concepts of] counter-correlativity and so forth.
Now, one might ask: what is the essential nature of ownership (*svatva*)? To this, he says:
"As one pleases" (*yatheṣṭa*).
"And its delimitant" means that which is the cause of such fitness (*yogyatva*).

Whether counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) consists in the nature of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*), or in the nature of the delimitant of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), and so forth— [all these are included].
There is much more to be inferred: that which is perceived as one's own property [is what is meant by "belonging"]. This is the *Bālapriyā*.
Thus; the word "by the genitive" is to be supplied.
"That is a different category from the referent of the word" means that ownership (*svatva*) is not of the nature of a substance (*dravya*).
Because it subsists in qualities and so forth;
for this very reason, it is not of the nature of either a quality or an action; nor is it of the nature of a universal or the like.
Because it would follow that [ownership] is eternal;
for, through such cognitions as "my ownership has arisen" and "your ownership has perished," one understands that ownership is impermanent.
Because it is impossible to accept [that] as desired,
nor is it of the nature of non-existence, since it is [perceived] as an existence.
Because it is being perceived,
and because it is not included among the established categories of things (*padārtha*), ownership (*svatva*) is a distinct category of thing; such is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Ownership (*svatva*) is precisely the state of having acquired [an object] through acceptance or other means, which determines its fitness for being employed as one desires;
and that [ownership] consists of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.
The established conclusion is that there is no category of entity beyond these;
this is the *Dīpikā-vidhivāda*.
Now, injunction (*vidhi*) is defined: an injunction is the object of a cognition that produces the desire to act, which in turn produces effort;
it is that which communicates such an injunction.

Or rather, it is the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth. Since no inclination toward action is observed regarding what cannot be accomplished through effort, whereas inclination is observed regarding what can be accomplished through effort, the cognition that something is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is the motivator.
And this is not the case for such acts as eating poison.
There would be the consequence of [constant] engagement,

because in the case of optional rites (kāmya), the cognition that something is to be accomplished by an effort (kṛtisādhyatājñāna)— which has "being a means to a desired end" as its logical mark— is produced by the cognition of the occasion (nimitta) consisting in the prescribed time and being a pure person.
The Guru says: "Because [the Vedic injunction] functions as an instigator in the case of both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites;
nor is there a lack of commonality (*ananugama*), since the property of being produced by the recollection of the possession of its own qualifiers is common to all. This is not correct—

Because, by parsimony, it is the cognition that something is an end to be accomplished through effort (*kṛtisādhya*) and a means to a desired object (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) alone that generates volition (*prayatna*) via the mediation of desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).
And this is not the case in the instance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.

Because there would be no means of accomplishing what is desired, it would follow that one would not engage in action; for even in those cases, it is postulated that the avoidance of transgression and the destruction of sin constitute the fruit.
Therefore, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers is simply the state of being a means to accomplish a desired end that is achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhya*).
The *Prakāśikā* [is so called] because it demonstrates how all categories are included, as appropriate, within the categories already mentioned, thereby removing any deficiency in the root text.
Intending to determine the nature of injunction (*vidhi*) in order to refute [opposing views], he promises to define it for the attention of his students with the word "Now" (*atha*).
First, he provides a definition of the property of being an injunction (*vidhitva*) that is common to both his own and others' systems.
"—*prayatne* (with effort):

the meaning is that it is the object of that knowledge which produces the desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*), which in turn generates effort. According to the Guru’s view, this refers to the knowledge of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*); according to our own view,"

Since the cognition of being a means to a desired end qualified by being achievable through effort produces volition— and thereby produces exertion— through the mediation of that volition, the definition applies in their view to "being achievable through effort" (kṛtisādhyatva), and in our own view to "being a means to a desired end qualified by being achievable through effort."
He states the intention of the proponent of the injunction regarding the expressive [word]: "the cognition of that.
This means the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, which convey the fact that [the action] is an effect to be brought about, having as its object such a cognition.

By the phrase "liṅādi" (the optative suffix, etc.), the imperative (*loṭ*) and the gerundive (*tavya*) suffixes are included. The particle *vā* is used in the sense of non-commitment. He raises the objection of the teacher's view with the words "to be accomplished by an action" (*kṛtyasādhya*).

The meaning is that it is understood as being capable of being accomplished through action (*kṛtyasādhyatva*). "That which impels" (*pravartaka*) means that which generates activity by way of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). Nor is it the case that...

It should not be suspected that the mere absence of the cognition that an action is incapable of being accomplished by effort (*kṛtyasādhyatvajñānābhāva*) is the motivator for activity; for if that were the case, there would be unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) due to its being defined as the absence of such a cognition.

This is because, in the case of activity, [the causes] are the cognitions of the non-existence of "being accomplishable by effort," the difference from "being accomplishable by effort," and the perception of various pervaders (*vyāpaka*) and so forth of those [two].
And because there would be great complexity (*mahāgaurava*) in postulating [such] obstructiveness (*pratibandhakatva*); this is the general direction [of the argument].
Now, an objection: [if that were so], there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of engaging in activities such as consuming poison.
He dispels the doubt that the knowledge of being achievable through effort exists even in that case, by saying "na ca" and so forth.
[The phrase] "having as its logical mark the state of being a means to a desired end" refers to: "This..."

The meaning is that [the action] is inferential, based on the reasoning: "It is to be accomplished by my effort, because, while being otherwise impossible without my effort, it is a means to achieve what is desired by me."
"In the case of optional rites" (kāmyasthale) connects with the phrase "because it prompts action. This means, for instance, in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and similar rituals.
Regarding the passage beginning with "vihitakāle" (at the prescribed time):

in the case of obligatory rites such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*), there is a cognition that [the action] is to be accomplished by volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*), which depends upon the cognitions of the prescribed time, purity, and vitality.

The meaning is that [the cognition of duty] functions as the motivator for the occasional act, such as bathing, because it depends upon the knowledge of the occasion (nimitta) characterized by impurity and so forth. [For example: "I am one who must perform the sandhyā-vandana, which is to be accomplished by an effort at this time."

In this manner, it should be understood that the cognition of being achievable through action (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is produced by the cognition of factors such as being at the prescribed time and being pure (*vihitakālaśucijīvitva*).
"Non-concomitance" (ananugama) means that there is no single factor that serves as the common cause for the occurrence [of various cognitions]; this is the intended meaning.
"Like that which possesses its own qualifiers," and so forth.
The "own" [nature] is the person as he proceeds; its qualification is the property residing in him, such as desire and so forth.

The meaning is: "the state of possessing that" refers to the knowledge consisting in the recollection of that relation—such as its being a means for establishing its own object—and [the cognition] has the state of being produced by that [recollection] as its [cause].
[The phrase] "by way of parsimony" (lāghavena) [is used].
The meaning is "due to the parsimony of the delimiting condition of causality" (*kāraṇatāvacchedakalāghavena*).
The point is that, according to his view, there is complexity (*gaurava*) because the delimiting condition of causality is composed of elements such as "being produced" (*janyatva*) and so forth.

[The definition of an action as] "the means to a desired end achievable through effort. In this context, the quality of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) must also be included.
Therefore, it is not [defined] merely by way of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*).

If [an object] were understood merely as a means to a desired end in the form of satisfaction, there would be the undesirable consequence of engaging in activities such as eating food mixed with poison;
however, the statement by the ancients that [the cause] is "delimited by the nature of a qualified cognition" [avoids this].

According to the view of the Navya-Nyāya school, cognitions such as "being achievable through effort" (kṛtisādhyatva) and so forth function as causes independently, according to the analogy of the staff and the wheel;
this is why [the author] says "in the case of effort."
The meaning is "engagement.
Regarding "obstruction" (*pratyavāya*): the avoidance of obstruction is its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Of that...

The sense is that, because the destruction of suffering is itself desired by virtue of being the absence of that which produces suffering, it possesses the status of a result (*phala*). Nor should it be argued:

"How can its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) be a result, since it is not produced? For [the status of being a result] consists in a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), which is obtained through the conventional usage "when X exists, Y exists."

It should be noted that since the state of being employed for the purpose of the *sandhyāvandana* exists therein, there is no loss of its status as a result (*phala*). [This addresses] the deficiency in the root text. *Bālapriyā*.
"To avoid [this objection]"—

and it is not the case that the root text is deficient because of the failure to define injunction (*vidhi*), since the *Tarkasaṃgraha* is composed precisely by defining seven or sixteen categories (*padārtha*).
It must be stated that this is because the proposition is firmly established;
