for, in the absence of a formal investigation into the positive method (*vidhi*)— which has been explained in detail in the *Maṇi* and other treatises that encompass all objects of knowledge (*prameya*)— [the inquiry would remain incomplete].
This is because the intention is that there is indeed a deficiency [in the opponent's position].
Regarding the phrase "that which produces effort" and so forth:
with respect to effort in the form of engagement (*pravṛtti*).
The desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), which takes the form "I shall do this," is the cause [of action].

According to the Guru's view, with respect to that desire to act, the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*), which takes the form "this is achievable by my effort," is [the cause].
The cause: in the Nyāya school's view, the cognition in the form "this [action], being achievable by my effort, is a means to what is desired by me" is the cause;
[the object of the action] possesses the status of being its object (*tadviṣayatvam*).

The meaning is that since [the action] exists as being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and as being a means to a desired end qualified by being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatvaviśiṣṭeṣṭasādhanatva*), the two are consistent with the definition of an injunction (*vidhi*).

The phrase "of the denoter" means that this is stated with the intention of the view that even the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, which express an injunction (*vidhi*), are themselves denotable by the word "injunction."

And thus the *Vātsyāyana-bhāṣya*: “That sentence which is prescriptive and impelling (*codaka*) is an injunction (*vidhi*); and “That sentence which is prescriptive and indicative (*deśaka*) is an injunction”—this is the *vārttika* on that point.
The word “or” (*vā*) is used in a non-committal sense (*anāsthā*).

In accordance with the natural sense of Pāṇini’s sūtra beginning with "vidhinimantraṇa... (Pāṇini 3.3.161), the word *vidhi* (injunction) applies specifically to that which is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, and not to the expressive word itself.
The meaning is: "because of such understanding.
[Objection: It is incorrect to say, as stated in the *Dīpikā*, that "one does not observe activity toward that which cannot be accomplished by effort (*kṛtyasādhya*)."
Since we observe that activity occurs even toward what is not achievable by effort due to the delusion that it is achievable by effort, he says: "the meaning is 'known as not achievable by effort.

For even if there is activity toward what is not achievable by effort due to the delusion that it is achievable by effort, [this occurs] only when there is knowledge that it is not achievable by effort.
The meaning is that there is no [logical] inconsistency, and therefore no lack of connection.

Now, one might object: since desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) alone is the cause of activity, it is not appropriate to say that the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is what prompts action. To this [the author replies]:

He says: the meaning is that [the cognition of desirability] generates activity by means of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). Nor [is there a problem with] "incompatibility with being achievable through action" (*kṛtyasādhyatva*);
for it is precisely in order to prevent activity at the time of knowing that something cannot be achieved through action that [this qualification is stated].
It has been stated that the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is the cause of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).

By stating that the absence of the cognition of not being achievable through effort (*kṛtyasādhyatājñānābhāva*) is the cause with respect to purposeful activity, it follows that at the time when there is a cognition of not being achievable through effort...
It is possible to exclude [the undesirable] activity;
nor should it be said that there is no room for parsimony,
because the absence of an obstacle has already been established as a cause for effects in general.

The proponent's intention is that there is parsimony (lāghava) in not having to postulate the absence of the knowledge that an action is achievable by effort as the cause [of inclination], whereas there is complexity (gaurava) in having to postulate a causality for the knowledge that an action is achievable by effort that has not yet been established (akḷpta).
He explains:

"By way of the absence of the cognition that [the action] is achievable through effort," in comparison with the state of being a cognition that [the action] is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñānatva*).

The meaning is that the property of being the absence of the knowledge that an action is achievable by effort (*kṛtyasādhyatājñānābhāvatva*) is too cumbersome as a delimiting factor (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) for causality.
Regarding the phrase "the absence of being achievable by effort" (*kṛtisādhyatvābhāva*):
[it refers to] the knowledge of the absence of being achievable by effort with respect to purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).

Since the cognition of the difference from what is to be accomplished by effort (*kṛtisādhya*), the cognition of the presence of that which is pervaded by the absence of being to be accomplished by effort,

and the cognition of the presence of that which is pervaded by the difference from what is to be accomplished by effort, all act as obstructions, one must also state that their respective absences are causes; thus, there is great complexity.

The point is that, in comparison with that, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) if a single cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is held to be the cause; thus it is stated in the *Dīpikā*.
"Having 'being a means to a desired end' as its logical mark," and so forth.
With respect to engagement in optional rites (*kāmyakarman*),

[the cause] consists of an inference whose nature is that which has "being a means to a desired end" as its logical mark and which has "being achievable through volitional effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*) as its predicate (*vidheya*).
The cognition that [an action] is achievable through one's own effort (*kṛtisādhyatvajñāna*) is the cause [of inclination].
[For example: "This optional rite, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, is achievable by my effort, because—while being non-existent without my effort—it is a means to achieve what is desired by me."
One should understand the following inference: "That which is not thus is not thus, just like the worship of a *caitya*.

This consists of an inferential cognition whose object is the state of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), which is enjoined with respect to the engagement in daily and occasional obligatory rites such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*), and which is produced by the knowledge of a mark (*liṅga*) in the form of a [ritual] occasion (*nimitta*).
The cognition that [an action] is achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is the cause [of inclination].
In the case of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*), being alive while possessing purity at the prescribed time is the occasioning condition (*nimitta*).
In occasional rites (*naimittika-karma*) such as ritual bathing, the state of being impure is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), provided that one is alive;
and thus, in that regard, "I..."

[The inference: "The person performing the sandhyā-vandana rite at this time is one who will perform it as an action to be accomplished by an effort at this time, because while being pure, he is alive; for whoever is not thus [i.e., does not perform it], is not thus, like a Buddhist. [And: "I am one who will perform a bath as an action to be accomplished by an effort at this time, because while being impure, I am alive."

The inference "whoever is not thus is not thus, just like an atheist" proceeds; and there is no [instance] anywhere of a cognition of being achievable through effort (kṛtisādhyatājñāna) based on the mark of being a means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatā), nor of a cognition of being achievable through effort based on marks such as being enjoined, occurring at the proper time, or being pure and living.

If those two were the causes of activity, then because activity would arise even in the absence of one of them, there would be a deviation from the negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra); consequently, it is not possible for the cognition that [the action] is achievable through effort (kṛtisādhyatājñāna) to be the cause of activity in general.

It should not be said that there is no single delimiting property (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-dharma*) common to all [causes] for the production of fearlessness; for there exists a common delimiting property, namely, "being produced by a cognition of possessing its own qualifier" (*svaviśeṣaṇavattājñānajanyatva*).

Because of its existence: a person acting [toward an object] has that as a qualification; the property residing in it is the desire for the fruit; possession of that is the relation consisting in being a means to the fruit which is its object; the knowledge of that is of the form "the desired object is a means to a benefit"; and [the action] is produced by that.
The cognition that [an action] is to be accomplished by an effort, which has "being a means to a desired end" as its logical mark (liṅga);
likewise, a person who is about to engage in such [an action] possesses a life characterized by the purity prescribed for that specific time.

The state of being a living being qualified by impurity, the knowledge of possessing that [impurity], and the knowledge in the form "I possess such qualities"— the state of being produced by these [is present] in the knowledge that the specific obligatory and occasional duties, such as twilight prayers and ritual bathing, are to be accomplished by an effort directed toward them.

The point is that, in the case of an inference consisting of a sign (*liṅga*) and its mark (*nimitta*), the property of being produced by the cognition of the subject's possession of its own qualifier (*svaviśeṣaṇavattājñāna*) serves as the subsumer (*anugata*) for the causal determinant (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).
This [is stated] in the *Prakāśikā*.
"Accomplishable by my effort," and so forth.

This refers to optional rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. Here, if one were to posit "being a means to what is desired by me" alone as the reason (*hetu*), [the reason would reside] in that which lacks the probandum (*sādhya*)—namely, the state of being accomplishable by my effort.

In the case of rain and the like, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the reason—namely, the state of being a means to achieve what is desired by me—is present; therefore, the "existence" clause (*sattvanta*) is included [in the definition] to exclude that. Since rain and the like exist even without my action, they lack the property of "non-existence without my action."
"There is no deviation" means that when there is "inexplicability," this has the sense of "when there is non-existence."

Regarding the phrase "without my action" (*matkṛtiṃ vinā*): if the word *mat* (my) were not included, there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This is because, in the case of another person's cooking—which is a means to achieve what I desire—the reason (*hetu*), namely "being a means to achieve what I desire," is present; yet the probandum (*sādhya*), namely "being achievable by my action," is absent since that cooking is not achievable by my action. Thus, while the reason exists, the probandum does not, resulting in a deviation.
To exclude that [case], the term "my" (*mat*) is placed there [in the definition].

Since the ripening (*pāka*) produced by another can be accounted for by the actions of others even without my own action, the antecedent condition (*satyanta*) is absent; thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

There is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because, in the case of fatigue— which is a specific form of suffering and thus lacks the probandum (*sādhya*), namely being achievable by an action dependent on one's own will— the probans (*hetu*), namely not existing without my action, is nevertheless present. To exclude that [deviation]:

The term "because it is a means to achieve what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatvāt*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Since my enemy's labor is also a means to achieve what is desired by me, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was.
To exclude that [undesired consequence], [the reason] is "because it is the means of accomplishing what is desired by me.
Even though my own exertion may be a means of accomplishing what is desired by someone other than myself, [it does not follow that it is an action].
There is no deviation [in the logical reason], because the state of being a means to what is desired by me does not exist [in that case].
In this probandum, the qualification "being dependent on one's own will" should be applied to the effort (*kṛti*).

Otherwise, even in the case of a labor that is not invariably concomitant [with the result], since there exists a cognition of being achievable by an effort produced by the aforementioned cognition of the cause, it would follow that one would engage in activity directed toward that [labor].
The word "sva" (its own) refers to that toward which the activity proceeds.

However, in the case of unavoidable labor (*nāntarīyaka-śrama*), there is no cognition that it is to be accomplished by an effort dependent on a desire for that object; thus, there is no resulting inclination toward action (*pravṛtti*) therein. And likewise, even in the case of the reason [in the inference], in the phrase "without my effort" (*matkṛtiṃ vinā*), the qualification "dependent on one's own desire" (*svecchādhīnatva*) applies to the effort as well.

It must be that which is to be given; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of things such as the incidental contact with water, which are achievable by my effort (*madiṣṭasādhana*) but depend on the will of another.
And this being so...

It should not be argued that, since the deviation [of the reason] can be excluded by the very absence of reality in the case of an effort that is not invariably concomitant (nāntarīyaka-śrama) and which lacks an action dependent on one's own will, the qualifier "being a means to the desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) in the second part of the definition is redundant;
for such a consequence is accepted.

They say there is no fault because this is a different reason [for the action], namely: "that which depends on the knowledge of having lived at the prescribed time and being pure. This refers to that which pertains to the prescribed time (*vihitakālika*).
The meaning is: that which is produced by a cognition having as its object "livingness" qualified by purity;
[this refers to] impurity, i.e., the state of being impure.
[This concerns] the cognition of that [impurity] as being achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*).

"Of that which causes the commonality of activity" means: of that which delimits the causality as determined by the effectness delimited by the property of being an activity (*pravṛttitva*). It means: by virtue of the parsimony (*lāghava*) of the delimiter of causality.

The meaning is that, in comparison with being produced by a cognition of the possession of its own qualifier (*svaviśeṣaṇavattājñāna*), the delimiting condition of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*)— consisting in the nature of a cognition of being a means to a desired end qualified by being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatvaviśiṣṭeṣṭasādhanatvajñānatva*)— is simpler.
He establishes its very brevity with the words "tanmate" (in his view). This means "in the view of the Guru" (the author of the *Śābarabhāṣya*).
In the phrase "because it is composed of [the factors] such as being produced," the word "such as" (*ādi*) refers to "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) and "cognition" (*jñānatva*).
For instance, the mere state of being produced by a cognition of its own qualifier-possessorhood (*svaviśeṣaṇavattājñāna*) is not the delimitor of the causality of purposeful action (*pravṛtti*),
because this would also apply to the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) which has such a cognition as its object.
Otherwise, it would follow that [the cognition of being produced by that] is a cause for activity simply by virtue of being produced by it;

rather, causality must be stated as residing solely in the cognition that something is to be accomplished by an effort (kṛtisādhyatājñāna) which is itself produced by a cognition of the possession of its own qualifiers.

And in that case, because there is the inclusion of a "producedness" (janyatva) defined by a restrictive rule and the state of being a cognition that something is to be accomplished by an effort, [there is no over-extension].
The sense is that [this constitutes] respect.

Now, if a cognition having as its qualifier the state of being a means to a desired end—qualified by the state of being achievable through one's own effort—is the cause of inclination, then even in the case of eating food mixed with honey and poison, [the cognition would arise]: "This, while being achievable through my effort..."

Since there would be the consequence of activity arising from the cognition that "this is a means to a desired end which is not [yet] satiated," he says: "In this case, [there is the qualification] 'not producing a powerful undesired result'.

And thus, [the cause of activity is] a cognition whose qualifier is the state of being a means to a desired end, as qualified by the state of being achievable through effort (kṛtisādhyatva), which is itself further qualified by the state of not producing a powerful undesired result.
It is the cause of engagement.
However, in the case of eating food mixed with honey and poison, although it is a means to achieve a desired end— namely, satisfaction— at that time, [in another time...]
The point is that there is no inclination toward that [action] because of the existence of the cognition: "Death is a means to a powerful undesirable [consequence].

What is meant by "not being connected with a powerful undesirable [consequence]" is the state of not producing a suffering greater than the suffering that is necessarily concomitant with the arising of the desired [result].
Or [the object of desire] is that which does not produce suffering for one who possesses intense aversion. Now,
if the cognition of being a means— qualified by being achievable through effort and qualified by not producing what is intensely undesired—

is the cause [of activity], then regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified among the properties such as "not producing what is intensely undesired," [there would be a problem].
Anticipating the objection that, due to the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), many cumbersome causal relations would result,

and thus how the author of the *Dīpikā* could have asserted its causality, he states— following the view of the ancients— that it was said so with the qualification: "of that which is delimited by being a specific cognition" (*viśiṣṭajñānatvāvacchinnasya*).
Regarding the view of the Navyas:
because of the lack of appropriateness in what was stated previously, there is no causality for that which is delimited by the nature of qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñānatva*).

However, the causality of the cognition that [an action] is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvajñāna), the cognition that it is achievable through effort (kṛtisādhyatājñāna), and the cognition that it is a means to what is desired (iṣṭasādhanatājñāna) is each distinct.

The point is that just as the staff, the wheel, and so forth have distinct causalities toward a jar— by way of being a "staff" or a "wheel" respectively, and not by way of being a "wheel qualified by a staff"— so it is here.

Because there is no engagement with what is fruitless, the cognition that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) [is required]; for even when a thing is known as a means to a desired end, one does not engage in eating food mixed with honey and poison. Therefore, the cognition that it is not connected with a powerful undesired consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvajñāna*) [is also required].

The point is that since there is no inclination toward actions such as bringing Mount Sumeru’s peak—which cannot be accomplished by effort—the causal status of all three [factors], including the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*), is necessary for the arising of inclination (*pravṛtti*). The phrase "for the sake of inclination" is stated in order to exclude effort consisting of cessation (*nivṛtti*). It is not [the case that this excludes other factors].
The point is that the cognition of being a means to a desired end achievable through effort is the cause for an effort whose nature is cessation (*nivṛtti*).
"By way of being an absence of that which produces suffering" means by way of being an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is that which produces suffering.
Since transgression (*pratyavāya*) is a producer of suffering,
the absence of that [transgression] is an absence of a producer of suffering.
[The phrase] "of that which consists in a relation of essential identity" refers to that which is already established (*siddha*).

The intended meaning here is that what is meant by "being the cause" is the nature of protection; therefore, the sense is that well-being (*kṣema*), which consists in the existence of the prior non-existence of transgression (*pratyavāya-prāgabhāva*), is considered to be brought about by the performance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyāvandana*).
The Lamp:
A Refutation of the Novel Claim that the Optative Suffix Denotes [the Result]. Now, an objection: [is it not the case that...]
In the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the optative suffix (liṅ) conveys an apūrva as the task to be accomplished, which is the means to heaven;
for the sacrifice itself is subject to immediate destruction.

Since it is impossible for [an action] to be a means of achieving heaven that comes into existence at a later time, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is precisely the *apūrva*—the enduring effect suitable for that purpose.
An effect (*kārya*) is that which is to be accomplished by volitional effort (*kṛti*). Of volitional effort...

Because it possesses an object, when there is an expectancy for an object, the sacrifice (yāga) connects as that object. When there is an expectancy for a person to be enjoined (niyojya), expressed as "Whose is this task?", the word *svargakāma* ("one desiring heaven") connects as referring to that person to be enjoined.

The person to be impelled is one who is bound by the task; thus, the meaning of the sentence is established as: "For one desiring heaven, there is a task whose object is the sacrifice named Jyotiṣṭoma."

Because it possesses Vedic indicative power (*liṅ*), even in the obligatory injunction "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives," it is postulated that the *apūrva* alone is the expressed meaning.
If it is argued that in such worldly injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) as "one who desires health should take medicine," there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the performance of the action— no;
for even in the case of a sacrifice, since there is no certainty regarding its impossibility, immediately after it is understood as a means to a desired end, [the inclination to act arises].
Because the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is postulated as an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) for the sake of accomplishing that [result],
and because scripture declares its destruction through acts such as recitation (*kīrtana*), the destruction of the sacrifice itself cannot be the operative factor.

He raises an objection regarding the view of the Guru— that the expressive power of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth resides solely in the "task" (*kārya*)— with the words "But surely... (*nanu*).

He states that since it is impossible for a sacrifice—which consists of a particular desire and is subject to very rapid destruction—to appear as the means for attaining heaven due to its lack of fitness, one must admit that the causal potency (śakti) resides only in an effect in the form of the *apūrva*: "Because it is unfit [to be the means], the manifestation of a sacrifice—which is of the nature of a specific desire and perishes very quickly—as the means for attaining heaven is not possible; therefore, the causal potency must be admitted to reside only in an effect in the form of the *apūrva*."
Regarding the phrase "of the sacrifice": "perishing more quickly" means being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a destruction occurring in the third moment;
"enduring" means persisting until the attainment of the fruit.
He demonstrates the manner of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—the effect—[as follows]:

Regarding the phrase "to be accomplished by effort" (*kṛtisādhya*): it should be understood that in the case of the sacrifice (*yāga*), the state of being accomplished by effort is direct, whereas in the case of the *apūrva*, it is mediated through the sacrifice.
"Kāryaboddhā" means one who possesses the knowledge that "this is to be accomplished by my effort."
He demonstrates the verbal cognition (śābdabodha) in which the meaning of the injunction is the primary qualificand with the words "by that" (tena).

The meaning is: by means of the connection of the sacrifice with the sense of the optative suffix (liṅ), which is the "thing-to-be-done" (kārya), and with one part of that [thing-to-be-done] for one who desires heaven.

According to the Nyāya view, however, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning in that case is: "The one who desires heaven possesses an effort conducive to a sacrifice which is achievable by effort, does not produce a powerful undesirable [consequence], and is a means to a desired [end]."
If it is objected: "Since the *apūrva* has not been previously presented [to consciousness], how can there be an apprehension of its denotative power (*śaktigraha*)?"—
on this point, they say:

Regarding the higher cognitions (*abhijñā*): according to that view, with respect to the verbal cognition whose object is delimited by a particular property (*taddharmāvacchinnaviṣayaka-śābdabodha*), there is causality for the apprehension of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) whose object is delimited by that same property, as well as for such a mental presentation (*upasthiti*);
however, the relationship of cause and effect does not exist on the basis of having an identical object (*samānaviṣayakatvena*).
And thus, there is the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to "effectness" (*kāryatva*) in general, wherever it may be;
and by the force of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), the specific form of the effect [is understood] in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

[The word "bhāva"] denotes [the efficient force], for no other action (kārya) can have sacrifice as its object. Now, one might ask: since there is no fruit in the case of an obligatory rite (nitya), how can it convey an *apūrva*? To this, he says: "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) and "only the *apūrva*" (*apūrvam eva*).
"By way of being an effect," and so forth;
the meaning is "intellectual merit" (*paṇḍāpūrva*) in the case of worldly contexts.
He says "ārogya" because the manifestation of something previously non-existent is impossible;
"kriyākārye" means in the state of being an effect residing in the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha).

With the intention that the expressive power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth must be accepted as residing in "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and the like, which are common to both the mundane and the supramundane, he offers the resolution:
"Of the sacrifice," etc. Because of [logical] incompatibility (*ayogyatva*), the sacrifice does not appear as a means to heaven.
He refutes the objection that [the cognition] "is possible" by stating "inappropriate.
The point is that even when there is doubt regarding inappropriateness, since that doubt does not obstruct [the process], verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) indeed occurs.
Once it is understood from the sentence that [the action] is a means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), since that [action], being subject to immediate destruction,
cannot produce the result without an operation (*vyāpāra*), an unseen force (*apūrva*) is postulated to account for it.
Thus he says: "for the sake of its accomplishment.
Now, one might object: let the destruction of the sacrifice itself be the intermediate operation (vyāpāra);
what is the use of postulating an *apūrva*? To this he replies: "by means of recitation and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [other such acts are included].
"By touching the waters of Karmanāśā, by crossing the Karatoyā, by swimming across the Gaṇḍakī with one's arms,
and by reciting [the name], merit perishes."
In this context, there is the inclusion of the contact with the waters of the Karmamāśā river and so forth.

Furthermore, another refutation should be considered: if destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) were the mediating operation (*vyāpāra*), it would lead to the undesirable consequence of the continuous occurrence of heaven (*svarga*).
Karmanāśā, Karatoyā, and Gaṇḍakī are specific names of rivers.
(Bālapriyā)
"At the root, an unprecedented [result] is understood as the effect.
This means that the unprecedented is understood by way of being the effect. For the optative suffix (liṅ) indeed...
The potency resides in that which is delimited by being an effect (*kāryatva*).
As stated in the *Prakāśikā*, this is "due to lack of fitness" (*ayogyatvāt*);
the meaning is that there is an absence of fitness for the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with being a means to attain heaven (*svarga-sādhanatva*).
Since the Buddhists themselves accept momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) in the sense of being the counter-positive of a destruction occurring in the second moment, he says "in the third moment.
Because duration lasting for as long as a month and so forth is of no use [for the argument], he says "lasting until the fruit."
The meaning is that it exists until the attainment of heaven.
"Having the meaning of the injunction as its primary qualificand" means having the *kārya* (the thing-to-be-done) denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) as its primary qualificand.
"Of one desiring heaven," and so forth. The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is "that which is to be accomplished by volitional effort" (*kṛtisādhya*).
The desire for heaven is construed with that [action] through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) within the volitional effort.
The sacrifice is connected [to the result] by way of the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*).
Thus, [the meaning is]: that which is to be accomplished (*apūrva*) by the volition (*kṛti*) which has the sacrifice as its object and is inherent in one who desires heaven.
The intention is that the cognition takes such a form. Even though it has been stated that for one desiring heaven, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the "thing to be done" (*kārya*),
what is intended by the speaker is precisely the connection with the performance [of the action], by means of distinguishing between what is already obtained and what is not yet obtained.
"In one part of that" means "when [the operation] has been performed upon one part of the effect. Regarding "in the Nyāya view," however:

In his view, by means of the optative suffix (liṅ) in its capacity as an optative, there are expressed the state of being achievable through volitional effort (kṛtisādhyatva), the state of not producing a powerful undesirable consequence (balavadaniṣṭājanakatva), and the state of being a means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatva).

In its form as a verbal suffix (ākhyāta), the effort (*kṛti*) is denoted. When it is connected with the three properties—being achievable by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), and so forth—their connection with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) occurs through the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*).
The sacrifice (*yāga*) connects with the effort denoted by the verbal suffix through the relation of favorability (*anukūlatā*).

The connection with the meaning of the nominative case ending, *svargakāma* (one who desires heaven), occurs through the relation of being the locus (*āśrayatā*) of the effort (*kṛti*). Thus, the cognition is as follows: "One who desires heaven possesses an effort conducive to a sacrifice which is the locus of being achievable by effort, not producing a powerful undesired result, and being a means to a desired end."

But it is not by virtue of having the same object; for, with respect to a verbal cognition whose object is qualified by a particular property (taddharma), [the cause] is the knowledge of the expressive power (śaktijñāna) whose object is that which is not so qualified by that property.
The meaning is that it is not the case that the cause is the mental presentation (upasthiti) of that [object] as delimited by its specific property (taddharmāvacchinna).
"In some instance or other" means in an action such as a sacrifice (yāga), and so forth.
"By the force of fitness" (yogyatābalāt) means by the force of the fitness for connection with being a means to heaven.
"Intellectual apūrva" (paṇḍāpūrva) refers to this.
The fruitless *apūrva* is called *paṇḍāpūrva*;
the Prābhākaras assert that in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), it possesses intrinsic purposefulness (*prayojanatva*) in itself.

Since the effect in the form of an action is already obtained through the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, the statement of its definition there would be inappropriate; therefore, he says: "in the state of being an effect residing in the meaning of the verbal root. The meaning is that the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which possesses the capacity for an effect, has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding that state of being an effect.

"Nṛsiṃha Śāstrī says: 'The meaning is that the definition [of action] consists in a specific conjunction residing in the channels (nāḍī), which is the counter-positive of the medicine— the means of health— and is produced by the act of drinking the medicine.'"
"By means of the sentence [stating] that it is a means to the desired object," and so forth.
From the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," [one understands]: "The Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is a means to heaven."

First, verbal comprehension arises; immediately thereafter, because of the recognition of an inconsistency— namely, that the status of sacrifice as a means to heaven, as taught by the Vedic revelation, is untenable given that the sacrifice persists for only two moments— [the apūrva is postulated].

The intended meaning is that it is impossible for the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) to be the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), because a postulated *apūrva* cannot be the object of the first arising verbal cognition.
Regarding the term "karmanāśā": [it refers to] *karmanāśā*.
*Karatoyā* and *Gaṇḍakī* are the names of specific rivers;
thus [ends] the *Dīpikā*.

The establishment that a verb has "effort" as its meaning is based on the force of worldly linguistic convention; for it is only with respect to an action— specifically one achievable through effort— that there exists the status of being a means to a desired end.

The fact that it is understood through the optative suffix (liṅ) means that its function as an injunction (vidhi) consists in its being an optative; its function as denoting effort (yatna) consists in its being a verbal suffix (ākhyāta).

Because we observe the analysis [of the term] as "pacati" means "he performs cooking," and because the answer "he cooks" is given to the question "what does he do?", it is certain that the meaning of the verb (ākhyāta) is effort (prayatna).

In expressions such as "the chariot goes," there is a metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) of a favorable activity. This is also the case in expressions such as "Devadatta cooks" and "rice is cooked by Devadatta."
The agent and the object are not denoted by the verbal suffix;
rather, it is only their [respective] singularities and so forth that are denoted.
The two [agent and object] are obtained solely through implication (ākṣepa).
"An elucidation of worldly convention" means "worldly usage."

Furthermore, he who engages in an action toward a certain object is one who possesses the knowledge that the object is both achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhya*) and a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*). Some, however, say that the worldly convention is simply this: that whatever one engages in by desire is the means to that [desired end].

The meaning of the modern [view] is that, by virtue of the rule governing cases where there is co-utterance with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth— such as "one should cook" (*paceta*)— there arises in the world an understanding of the action itself, as qualified by being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), as possessing the status of a means (*sādhanatva*).
They explained that "in all cases" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Regarding the phrase "by way of being a verb":
that consists in possessing the status of a verbal form through the relationship of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).
The moderns, however, maintain that the suffix *tiP* and so forth alone constitute the delimitors of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).
The property of having effort as its meaning consists in being the denoter of that which is delimited by the nature of an action (*kṛtitva*).
"What does it do? [The answer is:
It is precisely the capacity to convey a relationship that is sought after with respect to that which is delimited by the property of being an agent (*kartṛtva*).
The sense is that its capacity to exclude that [other meaning] cannot be otherwise.
Now, in cases such as "the chariot goes," regarding the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)—

Since it is impossible for [the root] to denote the agent (*kartṛ*), one must state that the power (*śakti*) resides in the operation (*vyāpāra*) itself in accordance with that [agent]; therefore, he says: "In cases such as 'the chariot goes' (*ratho gacchati*)," etc. The mention of "conformity" (*anukūlatva*) regarding the operation, however, is [intended] to indicate that [the operation] exists in the operation by way of that relation.
In order to obtain the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with motion;

the Neo-Naiyāyikas (*navya*), however, maintain that in the expression "he goes" (*gacchati*), there is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) of the locus (*āśrayatva*) for the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), just as in cases such as "he knows" (*jānāti*).

Nor is it pointless to assume a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) for the locus-hood (*āśrayatva*), on the grounds that the requirement is already satisfied by the connection of the action of going and so forth with the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case through the relation of locus-hood alone.
This must be stated:

because, just as between a noun and its referent, it is unestablished in grammar that there can be a relation— other than identity— between the meaning of a verbal root and the meaning of a noun within that context.
Likewise, because [otherwise] there would be no possibility of syntactic connection (*anvaya*);

for in examples such as *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks slightly"), since *stoka* and so forth connect with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)— namely, the act of cooking— it should be understood that [the relation] is other than non-difference (*abheda*).
He refutes the view of the Grammarians with the words:
"In the case of 'Devadatta,' it is not the meaning of the verb."

If one accepts that the verb possesses a denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the agent and so forth, then one must admit that an infinite number of specific acts (*kṛti*) and the like serve as the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). However, if one accepts that the power resides in the act (*kṛti*) itself, then the universal (*jāti*) such as "act-ness" (*kṛtitva*) serves as the delimiter of denotability.

The meaning is "lightness" (lāghava). [The phrase] "of those very [factors] such as singularity residing therein" means that they possess the status of being the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyātārthatva).
The connection is with what precedes.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of gerundives (*kṛtya*) and so forth.
[Objection: In that case, [the rule] would apply to the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*).
To explain how [this] is established, he says:
"of those two," [meaning] "precisely from the implication," according to the opinion of others.
In our own view, however, since that [meaning] is obtained by the nominative case-ending itself,
in the sentence "Devadatta cooks rice," [the meaning is]: "Devadatta possesses an effort conducive to the cooking whose object is rice."
This is the understanding of the syntactic relation (*anvaya-bodha*).

However, in the case of "The rice is cooked by Devadatta" (*devadattena pacyate taṇḍulaḥ*), the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "The rice is the object (*karman*) of a cooking action produced by an effort (*kṛti*) inherent in Devadatta."
Furthermore, in the case of "Devadatta cooks," the instrumental case would not occur,
and in the case of "The rice is cooked," the accusative case would occur.

In this regard, it should be stated that the agent and the object are not expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). It should be understood that there is no fault here, because the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is prescribed for unexpressed agency and the second case (*dvitīyā*) for such an unexpressed objecthood.
Regarding the phrase "bālapriyā yo yatra": that person who engages in a sacrifice or the like is that person.

The meaning is that from worldly usage, which takes the form "one who possesses a cognition having sacrifice as its qualificandum and characterized by the modes of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*"), it is understood that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes both the state of being achievable through effort and the state of being a means to a desired end with respect to actions such as sacrifice.
Having explained the term "vyutpatti" (derivation) with reference to its conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
[we now address] those who explain the term "vyutpatti" with reference to its restrictive rule (*niyama*).
He states the view of the moderns: "The moderns [hold that] it is the verbal suffix (*pratyaya*)," and "that [connection] is by way of the relation of convention.
This refers to the specific intention of Pāṇini and others regarding the verbal suffix *ti* and so forth within the verbal form (*ākhyātapada*).

There is a convention, such as *ti* and so forth; it possesses verbal suffixes (*ākhyātapada*) by virtue of the relationship of convention. Possession of verbal suffixes resides in *ti* and so forth. That [is the case].

The meaning is "the delimitor of capacity. Just as there is a convention for the term *ākhyāta* (verb) among the eighteen forms such as *tiP* and so on— whether by Pāṇini or by someone else— so too is there a convention for other words.

Considering that since [the suffix] could belong to another person's word, the property of possessing such-and-such a specific sound-form (*tattacchabdavattva*) might also be the delimitor of expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) due to a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraheṇa*), the moderns assert that the property of being *tip* and so forth (*tiptvādi*) alone is the delimitor of the expressive power for the sense of "effort" (*kṛti*).
He states that view: "It is precisely *tiP* and so forth.

In this regard, where the apprehension of denotative capacity (*vācakatā*) occurs only with respect to *tiP* and the like, it is in accordance with that [apprehension] that the cognition of the sequence *pacati* and so forth, assisted by the mental presence (*upasthiti*) produced by *tiP* and the like, [functions].

"The *Vyutpattivāda* text should be consulted, which states: 'Since it is necessary to postulate that [the suffix] brings about verbal cognition, it is more appropriate to postulate that the *tiP* suffix and others alone possess the expressive power (*śakti*) in that specific form.

This is because, compared to having the agent as its meaning, there is greater parsimony (*lāghava*) in the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) when the meaning is effort (*yatna*)."
It has been stated that "indicative power" (sūcanā) consists in denoting that which is delimited by the property of being an action (*kṛti*).
In the *Dīpikā*, this is illustrated by: "He cooks" (*pacati*) means "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*).
*Vivaraṇa* (explanation) is the statement of the meaning of a word by means of another word having that same meaning.

In the word *pacati*, which is to be explained (*vivaraṇīya*), there are two parts: *pac* and *ti*. In the explanatory sentence (*vivaraṇavākya*) "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), by the word *pākam*, [the meaning] of the verbal root...
The commentary states: by the word "karoti" (he does), there is an explanation of the verbal suffix "ti.
Effort is the meaning of the root *kṛ*.
Thus, because it is explained by means of "karoti," [the meaning] of the verb (*ākhyāta*)...
The word *yatna* (effort) signifies the meaning [of the action].

Thus, to the question "What does he do?", the answer "He cooks" (*pacati*) is given. In that interrogative sentence, the meaning of the word *kim* is that which is delimited by a property that is the object of inquiry.
The meaning of the second case [suffix] is "object-hood" (*viṣayatva*).

Therein, the referent of the word *kim* (what) is construed with [the objecthood] by means of the relation of "being located in" (*ādheyatā-sambandha*). The objecthood, in turn, is construed with the action (*kṛti*) by means of the relation of "determiner-ship" (*nirūpakatā-sambandha*). And thus:

The cognition arises that "the effort has as its object that which is delimited by the property [dharma] which is the object of inquiry. From the sentence "he cooks" (*pacati*), the cognition arises that "the effort has as its object that which resides in the cooking (*pāka*)."

And thus, since a question whose object is delimited by a property that is desired to be known can only have as its answer a word that expresses an effort whose object is delimited by a specific property, the meaning is that the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) denotes effort.
In the *Prakāśikā*,

the phrase "indicating the relationship sought to be known" means indicating the relationship consisting of being the object [of knowledge] whose counter-correlate is delimited by the property that is the subject of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*).
"In the sense of making known the connection with cooking" means "in the sense of making known that [the action] has cooking as its object.
"Its exclusion" means...
The meaning is that it brings about the cessation of the desire to know. This is because [the word] cannot convey an action (*kṛti*) in the case of an insentient object, such as a chariot.
The intended meaning is that [the denotation of] effort is sublated by the nature of the action (*rūpakṛti*).

Now, one might object: the statement that in expressions such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the favorable operation (*anukūlavyāpāra*) is not tenable.

Having raised the objection that— since it is possible for "conformity" (*anukūlatva*) to appear as a relational qualifier (*saṃsarga*), there is no necessity for the primary function of the word (*śabdavṛtti*) in that respect, and it is therefore more appropriate to claim that the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) applies only to the "operation" (*vyāpāra*) itself— the *Dīpikā* also [responds].
He states that the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is exactly thus: "the proclamation of favorability toward the operation. "The moderns," however, means the authors of the *Dīdhiti* and others.
He raises an objection regarding the view of the author of the *Maṇi*: "No."
And [it is] only by way of the relation of substratum;
because it is not established otherwise. Otherwise, [the sentence] "Caitra is cooked" [would be incorrect].

The point is that in such cases, there would be the unwanted consequence of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), namely "cooking," being construed with Caitra through the relation of agency (*kartṛtā*),
and in expressions such as *taṇḍulaḥ pacati* ("the rice cooks"), the rice being construed with the cooking— the meaning of the root— through the relation of objecthood (*karmatā*).
Regarding the view of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇamata*):
in the sentence "Devadatta cooks rice" (*devadattaḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the meaning of the accusative case following the word *taṇḍula* is "object" (*karman*).
Therein, the rice (*taṇḍula*) is construed with [the action] by way of identity (*abheda*). Of the object...

The verbal root-meaning, *pāka* (cooking), is construed with the agent through the relation of being the specifier of its own ultimate objecthood (*svaniṣṭhakarmatānirūpakatva*). In the expression "pacati" (he cooks), the meaning of the suffix *tip* is the agent;
therein, Devadatta is construed as non-different from that agent. Of the agent...

The verbal root-meaning (pāka) is construed with the agenthood residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhakartṛtā*) by way of the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatva*). Thus, the resulting cognition has the meaning of the verbal root as its primary qualificandum: "a cooking whose agent is non-different from Devadatta and whose object is non-different from rice."
In the sentence "The rice is being cooked by Devadatta," the meaning of the third case (instrumental) is the agent (*kartṛ*).
Therein, Devadatta is construed non-differently (*abheda*) with the agent. And [the agent]...
In the case of cooking (*pāka*), there is a coreferential connection (*anvaya*).

The meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is the object (*karman*); therein, the rice (*taṇḍula*) connects non-differentially with the object, and the object connects with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "Cooking whose agent is non-different from Devadatta and whose object is non-different from rice.
However, in the view of the Naiyāyikas:
In the sentence "Devadatta cooks rice" (*devadattaḥ taṇḍulaṃ pacati*), the meaning of the accusative case is *karmatva* (objecthood).
Therein, the rice (*taṇḍula*) is construed with [the objecthood] by means of the relation of being the locus (*ādheyatā-sambandha*).
The objecthood, in turn, is construed [with the action] by means of the relation of being the determiner (*nirūpakatā-sambandha*).
The verbal root-meaning, "cooking," is the core meaning;
the meaning of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) is "effort" (*kṛti*);
and [this effort] is connected to that [root-meaning] by way of the relation of being conducive (*anukūlatā*).
The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which is "cooking" (*pāka*), is construed [with the object];

the effort (*kṛti*) is construed with Devadatta by way of the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*). Thus, [the sentence-meaning is]: "Devadatta possesses an effort conducive to cooking, which is the determinant of the objecthood residing in the rice."
The cognition has the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case as its primary qualificand.
In the sentence "rice is cooked by Devadatta," the meaning of the instrumental case is effort (*kṛti*).
In that context, Devadatta is construed with [the action] by way of inherence (samavāya).
The effort (kṛti) is construed with the meaning of the verbal root, namely cooking, by way of the relation of being produced (janyatā).
The meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) is the objecthood (karmatva).
In that context, the cooking (*pāka*) is construed by way of the relation of being determined (*nirūpitatva*);
the objecthood (*karmatva*) is construed by way of the relation of substratum (*āśrayatā*) with respect to the rice (*taṇḍula*), which is the referent of the word ending in the nominative case.
The cognition [according to] the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsakas is: "The rice has the status of being the object (karmatā) as defined by the cooking produced by an action similar to that of Devadatta."
In the sentence "Devadatta cooks rice" (*mate devadattaḥ odanaṃ pacati*), the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is *bhāvanā* (productive operation) in the form of effort (*kṛti*).
The meaning of the accusative case ending following the word *odana* is "objecthood" (*karmatva*), which is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).
Therein, the rice (*taṇḍula*) is construed through the relation of "being located in" (*ādheyatā*).

The property of being an object (*karmatva*) is construed with the agentive force (*kṛti*), which is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), by way of the relation of being conducive to the cooking, which is the meaning of the verbal root that defines itself;
Devadatta is also construed in that very same place.
The meaning of the verbal root, namely "cooking," is construed with the act (kṛti) by way of the relation of being an instrument (karaṇatva).

It results that the cooking (*pāka*) is construed with the effort (*kṛti*) by way of the relation of being intended for the boiled rice (*odana*), which is the object of that effort as defined by its own status as an instrument (*svaniṣṭhakaraṇatānirūpaka*).
And thus, [the effort] is inherent in Devadatta.

The understanding is: "An effort (kṛti) which has cooking as its instrument and is conducive to the cooking that is the action upon the rice. According to these [grammarians'] view, the effort denoted by the verb (ākhyāta) appears as the primary qualificand (mukhyaviśeṣya) in the verbal cognition. Furthermore, the status of cooking as the instrument (karaṇatva) with respect to the effort is due to its being the instrument for the rice, which is the intended object (uddeśya) of that effort. However, where...

When only "pacati" (he cooks) is uttered without an accusative ending, there the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), namely cooking, is construed with the action (*kṛti*) by way of the relation of being its object (*karmatā*). [The resulting cognition is:
"An action inherent in Devadatta which has cooking as its object."
The understanding is that [the suffix] denotes agency (*kṛti*).
In the sentence "rice is cooked by Caitra" (*caitreṇa odanaḥ pacyate*), the meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is likewise agency.

The verbal root-meaning, *pāka* (cooking), is construed with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*)— namely, the *kṛti* (effort)— by means of the relation of being conducive to the cooking as determined by itself.
The connection [of the object] occurs with the effort (kṛti) through the relation of being intended for the rice-porridge produced by its own instrument;
in that context, the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) consists of both the objecthood (karmatva) and the productive activity (bhāvanā).

The rice (*odana*) is construed with the objecthood (*karmatva*). That objecthood is construed with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) by way of the relation of being conducive to the cooking that defines it. And thus:

The verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is as follows: "There is an effort (*bhāvanā*) which is conducive to a cooking whose agent is Devadatta, conducive to a cooking whose object is rice, which has cooking as its instrument, and which has rice as its intended goal.
This is the connection with the preceding [verb].

And likewise, in this view, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) consists of the number— such as singularity and so forth— residing in the agent or the object, as well as the effort (*kṛti*) and time. According to this opinion, the meaning of the rule *anabhihite* is "when the number residing in the agent or the object has not been expressed."
Alternatively, the meaning is "when neither the agenthood nor the objecthood is expressed";
therefore, this does not apply in the case of *devadattaḥ pacati*.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of a third-case suffix following the word *devadatta*, or a second-case suffix following the word *taṇḍula* in the sentence "rice is cooked" (*taṇḍulaḥ pacyate*).
And this is clear at the outset:
in the phrase "the inclusion of kṛtya suffixes and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes time (kāla).
"According to the opinion of others" means according to the opinion of the Mīmāṃsakas;
as stated in the Nyāyaprakāśa and other works: "And the agent is obtained through implication."
Because it has been defined as such;
[this is] the *Dīpikā* on the prefixes.
In expressions such as *prajayati*, the expressive power (*śakti*) for excellence resides in the verbal root itself.
Prefixes possess only the quality of being indicators; they do not have semantic power (*śakti*) in themselves. This is the illuminator.
He refutes the view that prefixes possess denotative power in cases such as *prajayati* and so forth.
[Objection: But surely by the verbal root alone...
Since the prefix *pra* and others would be redundant if excellence (*prakarṣa*) and so forth were already understood [from the root], he says: "Of the prefixes" (*upasargāṇām*).
"Indicative function" (*dyotakatva*) means the capacity to make the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) known.
By this, it is indicated that "other particles possess denotative power.
To illustrate, such is the case with the particle *eka*.

The exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is the meaning in such cases as "the conch is indeed white," while the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is the meaning in such cases as "Pārtha alone is the archer"; much more of this kind should be inferred.
*Bālapriyā* on the function of indicating the intended meaning: Where the prefix *pra-* is uttered together with a verbal root, it indicates intensity (*prakarṣa*) of that root.
The apprehension [of meaning] arises as "this is the intended meaning" (tātparya).
Therefore, the sense is that prepositions (upasarga) function to generate the apprehension of the intended meaning within a specific sense of the verbal root (dhātu).
"Of other particles" means of particles other than prepositions (*upasarga*). Such points and many others should be inferred accordingly.
The meaning is that in such cases as "the lotus is indeed blue," one should infer that the word *eva* (indeed) has the sense of excluding absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*).
Here, this should be understood:
The meaning of the particle *eva* is threefold: exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*),
exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*),
and exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*).
The meaning of the particle *eva* when connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*),
as in "Pārtha alone is the archer," and so forth.

In the sentence "pārthānyasmin dhanurdharatvayogo vyavacchidyate," there are three distinct possible meanings for the particle *eva*: "otherness" (*anya*), "connection" (*yoga*), and "absence" (*abhāva*).

The meaning of another word is that which possesses difference (*bhedavān*). In the case of difference, *pārtha* is construed through the relation of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*). This occurs within the connection (*yoga*) whose nature is that of a relation.
In the case of the primary [relation], there is a further connection of the property-bearer (*dharmin*) as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) with that which consists in identity;
in the case of conjunction (*yoga*), there is a connection as the counter-correlate;
and in the case of absence (*abhāva*), [the connection] is by way of essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*).
In another case, there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Thus, the archer is positively concomitant with Pārtha through the relation of non-difference. And so, [he] is one who possesses a difference having Pārtha as its counter-correlative (i.e., one other than Pārtha).

The verbal cognition arises as follows: "Pārtha possesses the absence of identity with the counter-correlative of 'archer' (i.e., he possesses the absence of being an archer), yet Pārtha is non-different from the archer. Thus, Pārtha appears twice: once as the primary qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and once as a qualifier of another.

Thus, in the case of *dhruvamartha-dharaḥ*, there is a double occurrence of the particle *eva*: as a qualifier of the meaning of the word itself (*evakārārtha*) and as a qualifier of the object (*pārtha*).
The meaning of the particle *eva* when conjoined with a qualifier is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). For example: [Pārtha alone is the archer].
In such cases as "The conch is white indeed," the non-connection of whiteness with the conch is excluded.
In that context, the particle *eva* has its semantic power (*śakti*) regarding both the absence of connection and [the presence of] absence.
Regarding connection, which consists of a relation—
The connection [of the word "white"] occurs through its counter-correlativity with "pāṇḍara";
the connection [of the word "yoga"] occurs within the absence through its counter-correlativity with the absence of yoga.

The non-existence [of the connection] is connected to the conch by way of its own-nature relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*). Thus, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "The conch possesses the absence of the absence of connection with whiteness."
When the particle *eva* is connected with a verb, its meaning is the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*),
as in: "The lotus is indeed blue."
In such cases as this, the absolute non-connection of the blue lotus with the lake is excluded;
and therein, both "absoluteness" and "non-existence" [are negated].
This is the meaning of the particle *eva*.

Furthermore, "absolute-ness" (*atyantatva*) is pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), and that consists in being a non-limiting factor (*anavacchedakatva*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of difference (*bheda*). Regarding difference—
The lotus is construed through the relation of being the locus;
[the absence] is construed through the relation of counterpositiveness with respect to that which is not the delimitant of the counterpositiveness of difference.

In the case of non-existence, there is a connection; that is, there is a connection of non-existence through an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*). Thus, [there is a connection] of the coming-into-being whose agent is blue.

The relation, which has the nature of blueness, is construed as the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) with respect to its connection with a portion of the non-connection. Thus, the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is: "There is an absence of the relation having blueness as its counter-correlative, which [absence] possesses the absence of being a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in the lotus."

Since it is impossible for there to be a pervasion of "lotus-ness" (sarojatva) in the absence of a relation with "blueness" (nīlatva), it would be impossible to convey the absence of non-conjunction qualified by the pervasion of lotus-ness;
therefore, it is explained that there is a cognition of the exclusion of the pervasion of lotus-ness from non-conjunction. More on this [is found] elsewhere.
This should be seen in the *Dīdhiti* during the analysis of the meaning of the particle *eva*, and also in the *Padārthamālā* composed by Jayarāma Nyāyapañcānana.
*Dīpikā*.
The determination that the knowledge of the true nature of categories is the cause of liberation:
the supreme purpose of the knowledge of categories is liberation.
For instance, because the scripture— “The Self, verily, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon”—
teaches that hearing and the other [means] are causes for the direct realization of the Self, one who has heard [the scriptures] attains knowledge of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth.
Even though [the truth] exists, because the cessation of the lack of conviction is to be accomplished through *manana*— which consists of the investigation of reasoning—
the scripture (*śāstra*) also serves as a means to liberation by way of defining the categories of objects useful for *manana*.
Following that, when *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) has been performed according to the method of yoga taught in the scriptures, thereafter...

When there is direct realization of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, false knowledge in the form of the conceit "I am [the body]" regarding the body and so forth is destroyed; due to the absence of defects, there is an absence of activity,
which leads to the absence of merit and demerit, which results in the absence of birth, once the previously accumulated merit and demerit have been exhausted through experience.
Liberation, characterized by the destruction of the final suffering, arises.
Knowledge alone is the means to liberation, because the cessation of false knowledge is achievable through knowledge alone. "Him thus..."
For it is stated in the Śruti: "Having known [Brahman], one transcends death; no other path exists for the journey," and because other means are thereby prohibited.
— *Prakāśikā*
To ensure that wise persons engage with it,
he demonstrates that the purpose of the treatise is liberation, which is the object of all desires, by stating:
"of the knowledge of categories."
The meaning is "of the knowledge of the true nature of categories.
He says "supreme" because other intermediate purposes also exist.
This is the meaning of the Śruti: "O seeker of liberation, the Self must be seen by the seeker of liberation."
The phrase "the vision of the self is the means to achieve the desired goal" is what is intended.
He shows the means for attaining the vision of the self with the words beginning with "it should be heard."
The verbal sequence is set aside by the sequence of meaning,
as in the cases of "He performs the Agnihotra sacrifice" and "He cooks the gruel. This is for the purpose of removing doubt regarding the possibility [of the performance].
The meaning is: "due to the cessation of the cognition of invalidity.
Regarding the phrase "investigation through reasoning" (*yuktyanusandhāna*):
the intended sense is as follows—reflection (*manana*) is the contemplation by means of reasonings. And that...

The self is inferred as being distinct from others; and that [inference] is to be accomplished by the knowledge of the "other" which serves as the counter-correlate of the difference. For that purpose, there is the definition of all categories of existence.
It clarifies the utility for liberation with the words "immediately after that": the meaning is "immediately after reflection" (*manana*).
— *Bālapriyā* [Commentary]
Regarding the phrase "the object of all desires":
since it consists of the state of non-rebirth, it is desired by everyone; thus, the meaning is that liberation has this as its purpose.
That for the sake of which no other purpose exists is the supreme purpose;
that for the sake of which another purpose exists [is not].
That is the intermediate purpose.
Supreme purpose is the state of being a purpose while not being a means to another purpose.
Intermediate purpose (*avāntaraprayojanatva*) is the state of being a purpose while simultaneously serving as a means to another purpose.
Now, [it may be objected]: "The Self, indeed, my dear... [and so forth].

Fearing that, according to the sequence of words in the scriptural passage "He is to be seen, He is to be heard," it would be understood that vision alone is the means to hearing, and not that hearing and so forth are the means to vision, he says: "by the sequence of meaning" (ārthakrameṇa).
The sequence that arises by virtue of a purpose is "sequential order based on purpose" (*ārthakrama*).

For example, as in the case of the *agnihotra* oblation and the cooking of the barley-gruel (*yavāgū*). Here, because the barley-gruel serves the purpose of the oblation, its cooking occurs by virtue of that purpose.
First, the order of performance is established. That sequence which belongs to the sentences that convey the ritual elements is the "order of recitation" (pāṭhakrama).
And by means of that, the sequence of the ritual elements is adopted.

Regarding the phrase "due to the cessation of the cognition of invalidity": through *manana* (reflection), there occurs the cessation of the cognition of invalidity with respect to *śravaṇa* (hearing)— which consists of a verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) concerning the Self as distinct from the body and so forth, produced by the words of the Vedic revelation.

And reflection (*manana*) consists of inference (*anumiti*). One should observe the formulation of a negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*) as follows: "The self is distinct from the body and so forth, because it is the locus of knowledge, desire, and the like; for that which is not thus [distinct] is not thus [the locus of knowledge, etc.]."

The meaning is as follows: "To be established by a cognition of that which is other than the counter-correlate of the difference" means that reflection (*manana*), consisting of inference, is produced by a cognition whose object is those things other than the self that serve as the counter-correlates of the difference having the self as its substratum.
"For that purpose" means for the sake of producing knowledge regarding objects other than the self. "Having withdrawn" means having restrained [the senses].
The meaning is: having acted so that [the senses] are no longer joined with their objects;
having withdrawn the mind—that is, having acted so that the mind is no longer joined with the sense organs.
Yoga is the application and stabilization of the mind upon the Self that is to be realized;
this occurs precisely through the perception of its specific nature.
The meaning is: "by the very perception of the unique property (asādhāraṇadharma) residing in the mother-of-pearl, such as its shell-nature (śuktitva), which excludes it from being silver.
The same applies to the present case as well.

The meaning is that false knowledge in the form of the delusion regarding the body and so forth is removed simply by the perception of a quality residing in the self that distinguishes it from everything else.
The *Tarkasaṃgraha* was composed by the learned Annambhaṭṭa for the purpose of establishing the intellectual proficiency of beginners in the systems of Kaṇāda and Nyāya.
The Tarkasaṅgraha has been composed.
Thus ends the Tarkasaṃgraha.
[The] Dīpikā.
Refutation of the Doctrine of the Combination of Knowledge and Action:

If it is argued that there is a combination of knowledge and action because of the traditional teaching that "O Great Sage, both wisdom and action have been declared as the means for attaining that [liberation]," and thus action also serves as a means to liberation— no.
“By performing only the obligatory and occasional rites,
one effects the destruction of evil and [attains] knowledge.”
Purifying it through practice, one should bring it to maturity.
And through practice and,
in some cases, through knowledge, a person attains liberation.

Since [the scriptures] establish through such passages that action is a means to knowledge (*jñāna*), action is a means to liberation (*mokṣa*) only by way of knowledge, not directly. Therefore, the ultimate purpose of the knowledge of the true nature of categories is liberation; thus, all is resolved.
It is delightful.
Thus ends the *Tarkasaṃgrahadīpikā*. [End of] the *Prakāśikā*.
"By the passage beginning with 'the man attains isolation' (kaivalyaṃ labhate naraḥ)," and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), [is meant] the verse: "And his karmas are exhausted when That is seen."

This is a summary based on such scriptural passages as "In the high and the low" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4) and such traditional texts as "The fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes" (Gītā 4.37).
[The phrase] "only through the door of knowledge" [is thus established].
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:
through actions performed without desire for personal gain and solely for the sake of pleasing the Lord,
there arises purification of the self in the form of the destruction of evil.
From that, dispassion toward sense objects arises; from that, engagement in hearing and so forth;
and from that, upon the arising of the knowledge of reality through the sequence of hearing and so forth.
Liberation is accomplished through the sequence beginning with the destruction of the aforementioned false knowledge;
further details should be investigated by those preeminent in the skill of rigorous logical analysis within our *Cintāmaṇidīdhiti* commentary.
The scholar named Nīlakaṇṭha, born of the Kauṇḍinya lineage,
has offered this auspicious work to that Lord whose crest is the moon.
Thus ends the *Prakāśikā*. *Bālapriyā*.
And they "perish": the meaning is that when the Supreme Self— in whom the higher and the lower are one— is directly realized, the karmas consisting of merit and demerit are destroyed.
"Jñānāgni" means that the fire whose nature is knowledge reduces all actions, whether of the form of merit or demerit, to ashes.
In the *Dīpikā*, it says: "When there is the direct realization of the Self," and so forth; [it continues]:
"the defect of activity produced by suffering."
"From the successive removal of false cognitions, through the removal of that which immediately precedes it, liberation [apavarga] occurs"—
this is the *Nyāya-sūtra* intended here.
First, like an unbroken stream of oil...
When there is *nididhyāsana*, which consists of uninterrupted self-contemplation having the same object as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*),
the Self is directly realized as distinct from the body and so forth;
this very realization is [the goal].
This is called the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
By means of this knowledge of reality, false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)— which consists of the delusion of non-difference between the self and the body and so forth— is subverted.
When such defects do not arise, the defects consisting of passion, hatred, and delusion do not arise;
when such defects do not arise, regarding prescribed and prohibited actions...
Activity does not occur; and due to the absence of activity, merit and demerit— namely, dharma and adharma in the form of virtue and vice—
do not arise.
Furthermore, when merit and demerit do not arise, birth— consisting of the conjunction of the body and the vital breath—
does not occur for the self.

The sense is that, in the absence of further births, when the merit and demerit commenced in this life are exhausted through experience, liberation occurs in the form of the destruction of the final suffering.
This is expressed by the words "having known Him alone" (*tameva viditvā*). "Him" (*tam*)...
Only by knowing— that is, by realizing— the Supreme Self does a person transcend death, which is to say, the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
The meaning is that only one who possesses the knowledge of the true nature of the Self becomes free from the destruction of *saṃsāra*.
"For the sake of attaining liberation" means that there is no other path— that is, no other means— besides the knowledge of reality;
this is because all other means are excluded.
The meaning is that there is a negation of any means other than the knowledge of the reality of the Self;
[this is what is meant by] "the cause for attaining that."

The meaning is that until liberation is attained, both knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and action (*karman*) in the form of sacrifices and other rites pleasing to the Blessed One are the means; this is what is meant by "combination" (*samuccaya*). That is, the aggregate of knowledge and action is the means to liberation.
The meaning is that both knowledge and action are means to liberation through their mutual cooperation, and not knowledge alone; and [the text says] "purifying knowledge."

The meaning is: performing, through reflection (*manana*), the knowledge of the Self as distinct from the body, senses, and so forth, such that it is not assailed by cognitions of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*).
"By means of practice" (*abhyāsena*)... [means:]

The meaning is that one should ripen [the mind]— that is, make it ready for the fruit— by means of *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) in the form of repeated reflection preceded by the restraint of the senses.
In the *Prakāśikā*, it is described as "harsh with logic."
That which is rooted in logic— namely,
a harsh and most rigorous investigation or inquiry— in that regard, by means of the skill or cleverness [displayed] therein, or rather, by those who are preeminent or capable, is the meaning.
"Vimarśa" refers to the skill or proficiency therein; by that, or in that regard, "by the capable ones" (dhuviṇaiḥ) means by those who are competent.
"May there be auspiciousness for the Moon-crested One" (candracūḍāya maṅgalam).
"Maṅgalam" (auspiciously) is an adverbial modifier of the act of offering;
the meaning is that he offered it to the Moon-crested Lord in such a way as to be auspicious.

Just as sacrifices, gifts, and other such acts performed with the intention of dedicating them to the Lord bring about auspiciousness, so too does the dedication of this entire work— which enlivens everything through the gateway of the knowledge of reality— to the Lord bring about auspiciousness for oneself and for others.
Existence.
By the power of the grace of Him who dwells on the mountain of the collyrium for the stainless one (Śiva),
and by the side-glance of the true teacher,
this commentary has been brought to completion.
Whether this commentary produces satisfaction in the minds of mature scholars or not, it certainly delights the minds of the young.
"He will certainly attain supreme joy"—

thus [ends the work] of the son of Śrī Kṛṣṇatātācārya, who obtained the general and specific knowledge of the scriptures through the grace of Śrī Devanāthatātācārya, and who is the crest-jewel of those learned in the four systems of philosophy.
Of the ocean of knowledge,
Nāvalpākkam Śaṭhakopa Rāmānuja Tātācārya.
The commentary *Prakāśikā* on the *Kṛtis*,
entitled *Bālapriyā*, is completed.
Salutations to the two lotus feet of the venerable Guru.
The commentary *Prakāśikā* is being expanded.
Regarding the statement beginning with "nidhāya" and so forth, this is the meaning of the sentence:
namely, in the word *hṛdi*, the meaning of the locative case is "being the locus of determination" (*nirūpitatva*). And of that...
