The connection occurs with "subsistence" (vṛttitva), which is a constituent of the meaning of the verbal root *dhā* (to place) preceded by the prefix *ni*, and which takes as its qualifier the property of being an object of a forced cognition (*āhāryajñāna*).

In the expression *viśveśam*, the meaning is either "the state of being the qualificand" (*viśeṣyatva*) or "the state of being the qualificandumness" (*viśeṣyitva*), which relates to the cognition through the relation of being its content (*nirūpakatā*) or relates to that [cognition] through the relation of being its locus (*āśrayatā*).

When the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is the qualificand, or when it is qualified by being the locus [of an action], its connection occurs through the relation of "being determined" (nirūpitatva). This is because the suffix *lyap* has as its referent the state of occurring at a later time, accompanied by the condition of having a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*). Thus, the *lyap* suffix [expresses this].

The meaning is destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). In that context, the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is construed as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), and [the agent] is construed with the destruction.

In the expression "guruvandanam" (reverence to the teacher), there is an occurrence within the sense of the root *kṛ* (to do) in the phrase "kriyate," by way of both relations: having the same agent as its own counter-correlative (*svapratiyogisamānakartṛkatva*) and existing at the time of its own locus (*svādhikaraṇakālavṛttitva*).

Veneration (*vandanam*) is an activity performed by such a sentient agent, which is conducive to a cognition characterized by the state of being a terminus of inferiority residing in a sentient being delimited by a body possessing a genus that is indicated by the property of being a genus not residing in both [the speaker and the listener] at one and the same time, while being delimited by the state of being the utterer of [the word "guru"].
This is because the word *guru*, being part of a compound, has its genitive case-ending elided.
The meaning is that which is determined by the qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā). And its connection occurs with the modehood (prakāratā) through the relation of identity (abheda).
The meaning of the base (prakṛti) connects with the qualificandhood by way of being the locus (ādheyatā).

The meaning of the second case is either "being that which is to be enjoined" (*vidheyatva*) or "the state of being enjoined" (*vidheyitva*), as connected with the function of the verbal root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *vi*.
Here too, the meaning of the suffix *lyap* is exactly as before.

[1] In the expression *bālānām*, the meaning of the genitive case is "inherence" (*samavetatva*) as it relates to "cognition" (*bodha*). Therein, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed through the relation of "being characterized by" (*nirūpitatva*).
[1] In the expression *sukhabodhāya*, "pleasure" (*sukha*)...
"Bodha" (realization) is that which occurs in such a manner;
"sukhaś cāsau bodhaś ca" (and this realization is blissful) is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*). In the *Dīpikā*, it is explained as "realization through ease" (*sukhena bodhaḥ*).
This is intended merely to demonstrate the meaning;
otherwise, the formation of the instrumental compound would be untenable. And as for the word "sukha" (happiness) [it is used in this sense].
Just as in the expression "I have become happy upon the removal of the burden," [the term] is used metaphorically for the absence of suffering;
and here, it refers to the substratum (dharmin).
In the phrase "for the sake of awakening" (bodhāya), it has the sense of "he goes to fetch fuel."

Just as in the expression "he goes for fuel" (*edhebhyo vrajati*), the dative case ending prescribed by the rule *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ*— in the sense that "[it] is performed in order to produce cognition" (*bodhaṃ janayituṃ kriyate*) as expressed by "it is performed for the sake of cognition" (*bodhāya kriyate*)— conveys the desire whose object is the activity conducive to [the cognition's] arising.
Its connection with the effort (*kṛti*) occurs through two relations: having the same agent as its own object, and being the object of a desire prompted by itself;
and its connection with the cognition (*bodha*) occurs with respect to origination (*utpatti*).
The present moment, conjoined with the meaning of the verbal root as that which is to be located,
[is related to the verb] by way of being its locus.

The meaning is that which is connected with the referent of the nominative case-ending, and its status as the predicate (vidheyatva) is also the meaning. The specific cognition [of this] is clearly stated in the *Dīpikā* [1]: "Viśveśvara."

The commentary is non-different from that which causes a cognition whose object is the meaning conveyed by the *Tarkasaṅgraha*—a cognition characterized by its own effort, which is the uncommon cause for the performance of one's own duties; this effort is related [to the subject] through the relation of being the possessor of a body accompanied by a mother; it has as its qualificandum the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśvara), who is non-different from the teacher of all sciences; and it has as its mode the state of being the limit of one’s own inferiority. Furthermore, the commentary is non-different from the act of making known the categories such as substance (*dravya*), which are characterized by effortless ease and are inherent in the child [student], and which is itself characterized by the destruction of one’s own activity conducive to the production of such a cognition.
The cognition is: "I am the possessor of an activity belonging to the present time that is subject to the injunction.

Furthermore, the qualification by the destruction of the activity [of the past] occurs through both relations: having the same agent as its own counter-positive (the activity), and occurring at a time that is the locus of itself (the destruction).
In the *Prakāśikā*, "I bow to Śiva," etc.,
refers to the first half-verse.

The cognition is: "I am the possessor of an effort conducive to an activity that is favorable toward a cognition whose qualificandum is Śiva Dakṣiṇāmūrti—who is non-different from the Mother who is non-different from the Teacher—and which has as its mode the state of being the limit of one's own inferiority. [2] This refers to the meaning of the subsequent portion beginning with "by whose salutation... and so forth.

The meaning of the word "api" (even) is the cognition that even a dull-witted person is the locus of a relation which has as its counter-correlative a similarity defined by a guru who is the object of the act of salutation.
The contradiction consists in the dullness and other qualities that delimit the referents of the words co-uttered with it;
and this [contradiction] is the non-occurrence in a single locus at the delimitation of a single moment, which is connected with similarity.
Furthermore, instruction (*upadeśa*) is the making known of what was unknown, consisting in the form of a word qualified by a cognitive objectivity (*viṣayatā*).

The specific distinction [of the property] consists in its being related to [the locus] by way of both the relation of generating the cognition that determines it and the relation of co-occurrence in the same substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Within this, the final member [of the compound] (*vṛttitva*) constitutes the factor of co-occurrence.
[The relation is] by way of the absence of being an object of a cognition delimited by a time prior to itself.
In expressions such as "the teaching of this meaning," the meaning of the genitive case is the property of being a locus (ādheyatva). Of that...
It should be understood that the connection occurs within the objective state (viṣayatā) that constitutes the meaning of the word "copadadeśa.

In the *Dīpikā*, [the phrase] beginning with "of what is intended to be done" (*cikīrṣitasya*) is used; here, the root *kṛ* has "action" (*kṛti*) as its meaning, and the suffix *san* has "desire" (*icchā*) as its meaning.

And the meaning of *niṣṭhā* [the past participial suffix] is that which is the locus of a qualifierhood delimited by the relation of objectness, which in turn is determined by a qualificandhood residing in an action (*kṛti*).
The action (*kṛti*) is construed with the desire (*icchā*) by way of the relation of qualificandhood; and of that [desire]...

The connection occurs with the *prakāratā* (the state of being a qualifier) through the relation of being determined (*nirūpitatva*). And that [qualifier] has the form: "May there be an effort whose object is this text" (*icchā 'granthaviṣayakakṛtir bhavatu*).
[1] Regarding the phrase "for the sake of completion without obstacles," [it means] in such a way that it is without obstacles (*nirvighnaṃ yathā yathā*).
The analysis of the compound is "completion" (*samāpti*).
However, in the phrase "for the sake of completion without obstacles" (*nirvighnaparisamāptaye*),
as before, the meaning of the dative case is simply the desire for the activity of the producer.

The activity (*vyāpāra*) consists of such forms as intuition (*pratibhā*), and completion (*samāpti*) is the destruction of the final phoneme; this is the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) connected with that [completion].

In the phrase "of the treatise" (*granthasya*), the relationship consists in being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of the final phoneme (*caramavarṇa*) contained within it. This essential point should be seen in our composed *Samāptivicāra*.
[1] For the instruction of disciples—[that is, for] the disciples.
The meaning is "in order to teach.
The dative case is used according to the sūtra *tumarthācca bhāvavacanāt* ("and after words expressing an action [ending] in the sense of the infinitive suffix *tum*, the fourth case is employed").
This is similar to the expression *pākāya vrajati* ("he goes for the sake of cooking") in the sense of *paktum vrajati* ("he goes to cook").

In that context, the dative case-meaning is simply desire (icchā); and this [desire] is connected [to the object] by way of both the relation of having the same agent as its own object and the relation of being the object of a desire known to be prompted by itself.
The term *anvaya* refers to the verbal bond (*bandhana*) consisting of words that generates knowledge of the subject matter of the treatise (*nibandha*).
The term *śikṣā* refers precisely to the desire in the form of a benevolent intention (*anugraha*), characterized by the thought: "May the disciples also act in this manner."

In that context, the connection for the disciples is through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*). "Instruction" (*śikṣā*) is the knowledge characterized by the mode (*prakāra*) of its being necessarily to be performed.
This, however, has been refuted at great length in our *Dinakari* commentary.

The meaning of the suffix *-kta* is that which is the locus of the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) delimited by the relation of objectness (*viṣayatā*) as determined by the qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*).

The meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha) is the initial effort (ādyakṛti). And the state of being "not yet performed" (kṛtāvadyatva) is ultimately equivalent to being different from that which is qualified by destruction (dhvaṃsa).

This qualification [of destruction] occurs through two relations: being posterior to itself (svottaratva) and being qualified by an effort whose counter-positive is itself (svapratiyogikṛtiviśiṣṭatva).
The distinction of the composition [is established] by way of both relations: co-referentiality with itself and having as its object the text that is its own subject matter.
Here, because the fruit of both the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) and its composition is observed, [it follows that] in the performance of those two...

The inference— "because it has the nature of being a performance of auspicious rites (maṅgalācaraṇa), it is prompted by the error that it is a means for achieving a specific desired result associated with various religious duties (dharmika), like the practice of a deluded person striking water with a stick"— is refuted.
As for that which was [stated]:
The demonstration of the inference— "Auspicious rites and the like should be performed because they are fruitless"—
is trivial;
for it would result in sublation (*bādha*) due to the fact that such rites are the objects of performance by deluded persons.

Even when proving the absence of being qualified by volitional effort (*kṛti*)—which depends on the valid cognition that [the action] is a means to achieve what is desired—[the absence of such qualification] resides in the volitional effort itself. (Note 1: Regarding "absence of being qualified by volitional effort":
being qualified by volitional effort is here understood through the relation of objecthood [*viṣayatā*].)
Since the argument ultimately results in the very absence of dependence on valid cognition (*pramā*), our own position is indeed more logical in comparison; furthermore,
that inference which claims "the performance of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) and so forth generates demerit" is also to be rejected.

If an action were fruitless, then because its performance would lack a result, it could not be established as an error; for since activity is possible through the very knowledge that it is a means to a specific result among those who are non-deluded, there is no evidence to postulate the production of sin from performing such an action.

Although this is not the case in the thesis statement, even there, the phrase "one should not act" is merely a restatement of the absence of activity on the part of a non-deluded person, which is dependent upon the absence of a cognition that [the action] is a means to achieve a desired end.
Because even in cases where the object is already attained, such as in the expression "they eat" (*abhuñjate*) and so forth, an optative suffix is observed; and because an action (*kṛti*),
which takes forms such as "I do," "it is done," or "do," would otherwise be fruitless.
Although the doubt may arise that such conduct is improper, nevertheless, there is no fault, because it serves the purpose of securing the attention of the disciples.
For this very reason, the writings of various authors stating "he makes a formal promise for the sake of the student's attention" and so forth are consistent; [this refers to] *avadhāna* (attention).
And the absence of mental distraction (*manaso vikṣeparāhityam*) means the non-association of the mind with anything of a different class (*vijātīyamanoyoga*).
The meaning of the fourth case (*caturthyarthaḥ*) is the desire for an activity conducive to production.
The rest is as before. And that—
The function [of *vyāpāra*] is the teacher’s employment of words toward his disciples, such as: "I have made a vow; you must remain attentive."

[2] Regarding "of one's own work" (*svagranthasya*), "other works" (*itaragrantha*), and so forth: the resulting understanding of the syntactic connection (*anvayabodha*) is that [the author] possesses an effort consisting of words capable of producing a cognition whose qualifier is the absence of being a producer of a purpose generated by other works, and whose qualificand is one's own work.
In the *Dīpikā* [1], it is stated: "There is no status of being a means for completion (*samāptisādhanatva*) in auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). [This refers to] auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
The meaning is: "that which lacks the status of being a means for completion";
or, "the absence of such a status of being a means resides in auspiciousness (maṅgala)."
[1] Because of deviation through both positive and negative concomitance.
Deviation in positive concomitance consists in the non-arising of the effect even when the cause is present;
and the intensification thereof is as follows:

The state of having as its delimitor of the counter-positiveness—delimited by a relation that is the delimitor of the effectness belonging to an absence residing in a locus possessing a collection of causes delimited by a cause-delimiter that is not a non-delimiter of the pervasion delimited by itself—the state of having as its delimitor of the effectness the property delimited by itself, etc.
1. "Delimited by itself," etc.
By its own term (*svapadena*), that which is to be grasped is that [property] for the existence of which, even though delimited by it, the effect is not produced.

And that is the nature of the conjunction between the potsherd and space (*kapālākāśasaṃyogatva*); the nature of the conjunction between the two potsherds (*kapāladvayasaṃyogatva*) is the delimitor of the pervasion delimited by that [former property], while it is not the delimitor of the pervasion that delimits the causal efficacy (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).

The absence of a jar— which exists in a location devoid of the conjunction of two potsherds yet possessing the collection of causes delimited by stick-ness and so forth— has as its counter-positive-delimiter (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) the property of jar-ness;
since this property exists in the conjunction of a potsherd and a *kāśa* grass, the conjunction of the potsherd and the *kāśa* possesses that [delimiting property].

In this context, regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāritva*) [of the cause], if the term "non-delimiting factor of pervasion" (*vyāpyatānavacchedaka*) were not included within the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), then the positive concomitance of the conjunction between the potsherd and space (*kapālākāśa-saṃyoga*) would not be established.
Therefore, that [is] the apādāna.

[It is defined as: the state of possessing a property that is intended to be the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of such a delimiting relation as determined by the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).
And negative deviation (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*) consists in the production of an effect even in the absence of the cause.

The state of being a cause consists in possessing the delimiting property of the cause as qualified by the locus of that which is delimited by the delimiting property of the effect, through a relation that is the delimitor of the effect;

this is by way of a dual relation consisting of [the property's presence] and the state of being located, where the latter is delimited by the relation of possessing the aggregate of loci delimited by all [the properties].

And such possession of a limiting adjunct (*kūṭa*) is ultimately equivalent to being qualified by itself through the relation of possessing a difference whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, which delimitation is in turn delimited by the relation of being the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of a difference that is co-located with itself.

The state of being its own locus (*svādhikaraṇatā*) [is defined] by the relation of being the locus-hood (*adhikaraṇatātva*) as determined by a property that delimits the instrument-hood (*karaṇatā*) qualified by itself (*sva*). The qualification by itself (*svavaiśiṣṭya*)...

[The definition of positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*) is: by way of the relation consisting in possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, which [delimitation] is delimited by the relation of being a delimitation of the pervasion-delimitation of that which is delimited by itself; and the delimitation of the counter-correlativity [of the difference] is by way of the relation of inherence (*ādheyatā*). Positive concomitance is the possession of a property that delimits causality and is devoid of such inherence.

Negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) consists in the possession of a delimitor of causality that is distinct from the locus of the effect, as qualified by the relation of both [the cause and the effect] as defined by etymology.

The apprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*) is included in order to exclude the conjunction of the potsherd and space, which is afflicted by the fallacy of positive deviation (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*).

The apprehension of negative concomitance (vyatireka-sahacāra) is likewise the cause for grasping the state of being a cause; it serves to exclude things such as donkeys, which are subject to deviation in negative concomitance.
And the two apprehensions of deviation are, respectively, obstacles to the apprehension of concomitance;
thus, in the *Prakāśikā* [3].
The meaning is that the phrase "there is no deviation" connects with the preceding [statement],
and thus the meaning is that the subsequent sentence "therefore there is no deviation" connects with that.
Anticipating the complexity [gaurava] involved in taking the state of having fewer obstacles (*vighna*) as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for causality, he states another alternative:
"of that which is more powerful" (*balavattarasya*).
1. Regarding "svaniṣṭhābhāvīya" and so forth: the first term "sva" (itself) refers to the locus delimited by the delimitor of the state of being an effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).
The second occurrence of the term "sva" refers to the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*);
the same applies to the subsequent occurrences of "sva."
[The terms] refer to the properties that delimit the causal status [of the cause]. 2.
"And the apprehension of deviation" means the apprehension of positive deviation (anvaya-vyabhicāra).

The meaning is that the apprehension of a deviation in positive concomitance (anvaya-vyabhicāra) is an obstacle to the apprehension of positive concomitance (anvaya-sahacāra), and the apprehension of a deviation in negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra) is an obstacle to the apprehension of negative concomitance (vyatireka-sahacāra).
"By means of the door of the destruction of obstacles" means by way of the connection with the destruction of obstacles produced by itself;
the same applies hereafter. Precisely for this reason...
Even when there is a great multitude of obstacles, completion occurs even in that case where a single, more powerful auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) is present;
and this "more powerful" status is a specific distinction of a different genus (*vaijātyaviśeṣa*).
[3] They say that this is indicated by the absence of vowels;
its seed-syllable (bīja), however, is derived from the principle that "a word uttered once conveys its meaning only once. Therefore...
There is simply the impossibility of words such as "ityādi" (and so forth), when repeated, conveying two distinct meanings. Now,
by the phrase "that which has its duty to be performed indicated by a Vedic injunction inferred from the conduct of the learned," [it is shown that] the conduct of the learned...
It follows that [the Veda] would be inferred as a scripture indicating that auspicious rites ought to be performed;
however, that is not tenable,
because [such a practice] would be merely a custom of the learned (śiṣṭācāra).

It must be stated that [the injunction] "having bathed, one should eat" and so forth does not enjoin the duty (*kartavyatā*) of eating— since eating is common even to those acts devoid of the duty characterized by being an object of engagement prompted by the Veda;
rather, its purpose is solely to prescribe that eating occurs at a time subsequent to bathing.
Because food is already established by natural attachment, it is impossible for [the scripture] to be intent upon its injunction;
for "scripture is authoritative regarding what is not otherwise established."

With the intention that it is according to this principle, he raises an objection: "[1] But as for the necessity of performing the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*)"; "necessity of performing" means being subject to the injunction of an action (*kṛti*). The word "what" (*kiṃ*) is used in a derogatory sense (*kṣepa*). And thus:
The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever that serves as the instrument for the cognition of the necessity of performing auspicious rites (*maṅgala*).
The intention is that, according to the reasoning already stated, it is impossible for the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) to imply a Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
As for the claim that "the state of being something to be done" (*kartavyatva*) means "being the cause of being enjoined by an act of will" (*kṛti-vidheyatā-prayojakatva*), [that is not correct].
That is laughable;

for there is no evidence that the suffix *tavya* and others—which denote a secondary object (*gauṇakarma*) consisting of objective status (*viṣayatā*)—denote an object characterized by a property that brings about that objective status. Otherwise, [the following would occur]:
Because the same undesirable consequence would apply even to words such as "to be understood" (*boddhavya*).

For this very reason, it is also appropriate to provide an introductory statement (*avataraṇikā*) that raises the objection in order to establish that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) possesses the status of being something that ought to be performed (*kartavyatā*) as taught by the Veda (*śruti*).
Establishment (*vyavasthāpana*) is the statement of correct reasoning conducive to a certainty that is not overridden by a cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*).
The meaning of the suffix *-tumun* is simply desire; of that [desire]...
The connection [of the term] "doubt" (*śaṅkā*) occurs through the relation of both: having the same agent as its own object, and being the object of a desire prompted by itself.
1. Regarding the phrase beginning with "svaviṣaya" (its own object), etc.:

In the case of doubt (*śaṅkā*), there is the desire to establish one's own [position], the establishment having that [desire] as its object, and the state of having the same agent; likewise, there is the desire to establish one's own [position] which prompts the doubt, and the state of being the object of the desire regarding the doubt.

The sense is that the desire for the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) arises with the intention: "I shall establish that auspiciousness (maṅgala) has a mandatory status as enjoined by the Veda (śruti), and therefore I shall formulate the prima facie argument."
In the *Dīpikā*, he provides the following resolution: "[1] ‘Śiṣṭa’ and so forth.
The nature of inference is preceded by the demonstration of the reason (*hetu*), the probandum (*sādhya*), and so on."
He explains: "[1] For instance, because it is the object of the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa), which is both extraordinary (alaukika) and beyond reproach (avigīta).
Here, the intended meaning is: "because it is the object of the conduct of the learned, which is co-located with being extraordinary and co-located with being beyond reproach.
This refers to the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) heard following the *karmadhāraya* compound.

This is because of the grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) that [a compound] conveys the delimitor (*tāvacchedaka*) of the meaning of the subsequent member as being co-locative (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the delimitor of the meaning of the preceding member.
Now, regarding the phrase "from the Vedic revelation inferred from the practice of the learned" (*śiṣṭācārānumitaśruteḥ*),

the property to be enjoined (*vidheya*) in the Vedic revelation is the state of being the object of an inference produced by a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose content is an activity (*kṛti*) inherent in the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
This does not cohere with what is taught by scripture;
for the property of being the object of an inference whose predicate is "having its duty taught by scripture" exists only when there is the state of having its duty taught by scripture.
And because it is included within the category of qualifiers of that [object] according to scripture;
even though it is included within the category of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), its status as the thing to be enjoined cannot be accepted.

In response to the objection that, if this were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the conventional usage "fire-ness has been inferred," he establishes that what is to be enjoined is the *śruti* (the Vedic word), beginning with the words:
"[3] Here, the intention is as follows... and so forth.

"Because it is not established prior to the inference"—this means because it is not the delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*) for the objecthood (*viṣayatā*) of the cognition existing at a time prior to the inference. By this, even though the fire of the kitchen (*mahānasīyavahni*) and so forth are objects of the *parāmarśa* (the intermediate inferential cognition), there is no inconsistency regarding their being the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*). In this regard:

Furthermore, the specific form of the scriptural injunction regarding the performance of auspicious rites is possible merely through the establishment of the connection with the probandum in the subject,
as in the case of "the mountain possesses fire," and so forth.
It should be understood that this is like the fire and other phenomena found on a mountain.

Now, an objection is raised: by the word "only" (*eva*) in the sentence from the *Dīpikā*, "only the injunction inferred from the practice of the learned," the status of anything other than such a scriptural injunction as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the necessity of performing auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) is excluded.
And that is not tenable;

for the inference—"A rite of auspiciousness (maṅgala) must be performed because its fruit is completion"—is possible as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in that regard. Therefore, he says: "[3] The particle *eva* has the sense of 'only' (*api-artha*)."
They say this because it lacks internal consistency;
however, the seed of that [objection] lies in the fact that the relationship in question does not restrict the occurrence of a function (*vṛtti*).
There is an impossibility regarding the inclusion within the pervader (*vyāpakatā*) and the inclusion within the co-existence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);

In this context, the state of being the object of a particular cognition of relative number (*apekṣābuddhi*) is qualified by a qualifierhood residing in unity, which is itself determined by a qualificandhood residing in substance-ness;

nevertheless, the meaning is as follows: is the object cognized by valid cognition a property that distinguishes one category of object from another, or is it something distinct?

Furthermore, because such a locus of a collection (kūṭa) is unestablished and because "collection-ness" (kūṭatva) is difficult to define, the following interpretation is also not tenable:
that the meaning of the alternative (vikalpa) is whether or not the object known by valid cognition possesses a collection of distinctions (bheda) such as substance and so forth.

it is for the purpose of avoiding deviation with respect to qualities and so forth.
The inclusion of "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) in the definition of the cause is for the purpose of excluding [the property] from earth and the like;
the mention of "earth and the like" is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*vyabhicāra*).

As for the claim that "the probandum (sādhya) is substanceness (dravyatva) qualified by the aggregate of differences from earth and so forth, related through the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), while the reason (hetu) is substanceness qualified by non-inclusion within earth and so forth"— that is not correct.

In the view of the Naiyāyikas, because the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*) are not previously established prior to the inference, the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is difficult to apprehend;
thus it is stated in the *Dīpikā* [23]: "The term 'prauḍha'... and so forth.

Maturity (*prauḍhatva*) consists in excellence (*utkṛṣṭatva*), which is the state of being a substratum of magnitude (*mahattva*). Magnitude is included [in the definition] to exclude atoms of fire (*tejaḥ-paramāṇu*).
Excellence is included to exclude the infinitesimal particles of fire (*tejastruṭi*).
And luminosity consists in possessing a manifested form that is not overwhelmed;
the term "manifested" is used to exclude the eye and other such organs.
The term "unoverpowered" (*anabhibhūta*) is used to exclude gold and similar substances;
the word "light" (*tejas*) is used to exclude jars and the like.
Although, according to the method to be explained, [the quality of] manifestness (*udbhūtatva*)...

Because the collection of absences of the non-manifestation of each respective [quality] cannot be subsumed under a single non-delimiting counter-correlate, it follows that there would be a multiplicity of the category of *tamas*.
1. "By the absence of that" (*tadabhāvena*).
The meaning is: "by virtue of possessing the nature of constant motion.
Nevertheless, darkness is simply the absence whose counter-correlate is delimited by the state of possessing great radiance.

And with the intention that by the term "light of mature radiance" (*prauḍhaprakāśakatejas*) it is precisely great splendor (*mahāprabhā*) that is intended, the word "direction" (*diś*) was stated later;
thus it is said in the *Prakāśikā* [24].
"Not assisted by light" means that its ultimate sense is: "because it possesses a worldly objecthood as determined by a visual perception not produced by light.
Therefore, there is no contradiction even if elsewhere the eye is characterized by light as a cooperative cause.

If it is objected that [the reason] is unestablished because light is a cause even in the perception of darkness by way of being time, we say no; for what is introduced [as the reason] is the absence of having a generative power residing in light as delimited by the property of time (kālatva).
The term "visual" (*cākṣuṣa*) is included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as a jar when it is grasped by touch.
He states the purpose for including "locality" (*laukikatva*) within the objective relation (*viṣayatā*): "[24] even in the visual perception of darkness..."
By the phrase "of jars and so forth," etc.,

the meaning is as follows: even though jars and other objects are objects of the perceptual cognition "darkness in the jar" through the extraordinary cognitive proximity (*jñānalakṣaṇā pratyāsatti*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case.

Furthermore, the reading "tamovān ghaṭaḥ" (the pot possesses darkness) found in modern manuscripts is untenable; for [according to Pāṇini 5.2.121], the suffix *vini* is prescribed after the words *asmi*, *āmi*, *medhā*, and *sraj*.
Because by this rule (*sūtra*), the form is produced as *tasmāt svī* alone,
since the suffix *matup* and its quality (*guṇa*) are impossible.
Since it is a rule that what is presented [as an object] appears only as a qualifier,

it is impossible for jars and the like to appear as the qualificand through the extraordinary cognitive proximity (*alaukika-jñāna-pratyāsatti*); and because, by taking extraordinary objecthood (*alaukika-viṣayatā*) into account, there can be no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to jars and the like.
Therefore, let the learned understand that such a reading is most erroneous and interpolated. [24]

The absence of distinction refers to an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*); and this is for the purpose of dispelling the suspicion that there is no difference between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The intended meaning here is as follows: by accepting that "being distinct from darkness" (*tamobhinnatva*) is a qualifier of substance within the scope of the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), [it is established] that visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*) [arises] with respect to that which resides in a substance distinct from darkness, through the relation of ordinary objectivity (*laukikaviṣayatā*).
Although there is no fault in light being a cause by way of conjunction,

nevertheless, since the property of being distinct from darkness must be included within the delimiting condition (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) for the effecthood of darkness if it is a substance, [the definition would be over-extensive].
There is complexity (gaurava) even due to the postulation of infinite parts; for,
in order to prevent the visual perception of darkness from being accidental,
it is necessary to postulate another specific cause, which results in complexity.
[25] By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "prior non-existence, etc.," destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is included.
[25] Regarding the term "necessary":
this is [said] because one might ask, "Why should light not simply be the absence of darkness?"
This is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt regarding the lack of a decisive criterion;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the perception of hot touch could not be accounted for in the case of the statement, "Fire is hot."
The definition of substance (*dravya*) in the *Dīpikā* [31] is "the possession of the universal (*jāti*) of substanceness" (*dravyatva*).
Here, the word "universal" [is used] in the sense of [the relation of] inherence (*samavāya*) with substanceness.
This is for the sake of attaining the status of being a definition;
however, even that [property] does not constitute a part of the definition, because if it did,
it would involve another property that is a delimitor of pervasion co-located with itself.
Because it would result in the fallacy of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) due to the non-restriction of pervasiveness;
as stated in the *Prakāśikā* [31]: "by way of being the delimiting factor for the production of conjunction."

In this regard, the following inference is intended: the causality delimited by the relation of identity, which is the counter-correlative of the effect-ness delimited by the relation of inherence-in-the-conjunction (saṃyoga-niṣṭha-samavāya),
is delimited by some property, because it is causality.
This is like the causality of a jar residing in a staff and so forth;

for it is established through the assistance of the reasoning that "there is parsimony (lāghava) if the property [in question] is a universal (jāti)," as well as by the absence of any sublation to its being a universal.
From the act of conceptual apprehension (*parāmarśa*), the establishment of being delimited by the universal (*jāti*) of substance-ness (*dravyatva*) follows;
for if that which is delimited by some universal were the probandum (*sādhya*).
It might be argued that there would be a logical deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the causality residing in the absence of an obstructer; therefore, that [objection] has been set aside.

Nor should it be said that there is a shift in the subject matter (arthāntara), because the inference could be concluded by taking existence (sattā) or universals such as "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) as the probandum.

Because only a property that is coextensive with that [subject] can be its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), and since in the present case there exists the apprehension of [the reason] as being pervaded by [the probandum] such as existence (*sattā*) and so forth, it is impossible for the inference to terminate by taking that [existence] as the delimitor.

"By the force of the following reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*): 'If existence (*sattā*) and so forth were the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of the causality of conjunction and inherent causality, then they would be co-extensive (*samaniyata*) with that causality.'"
Because it is impossible to infer that [the effect] is delimited by a genus such as "existence" (sattā) and so forth;
this should be understood similarly in subsequent cases as well.
By means of inherence (samavāya), substance-ness (dravyatva) is the cause of conjunction (saṃyoga) with respect to identity (tādātmya) in qualities (guṇa) and so forth.
It should be understood that this is for the purpose of avoiding the consequence that [the definition] would become a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*).
[31] This is because there is no difference between the definition and the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
Such being the case, when the inference of the difference from others is made by means of the definition, at the time of the *parāmarśa* (reflective cognition)...

Because there exists a proof (*siddhi*) in the form "the exclusion of others (*itarabheda*) that is co-locatable with substanceness (*dravyatva*) is the exclusion of others that pervades substanceness," inference (*anumiti*) would be untenable;
for even a certainty (*niścaya*) of a different form acts as an obstacle [to inference].
The intention is that there would be excessive effort in pursuing the desire to prove [the conclusion].
As for what was said—

The claim that "the impossibility of verbal comprehension from the *upanaya* sentence due to the non-difference between the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is possible in the present case as well" is trivial; for [in the present case], the property of being a substance (*dravyatva*) [is grasped] by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).
Because [substance-ness] is the delimitor of the locus of the definition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*),

and because [the property of being a substance] serves as the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) by virtue of its nature as substance-ness (*dravyatvatva*), there is no sublation of the traditional formulation of the application (*upanaya*) in the form: "The substance possesses substance-ness."

For it must be stated that the difference from that property (*taddharmabheda*) is the cause of verbal cognition specifically with respect to the relation of being the delimitation-delimitation (*avacchedakatāvacchedakatā*)— which is determined by the subjectness (*viśeṣyatā*) determined by the mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in that property. Otherwise,
expressions such as "substance possesses a genus" (*dravyaṃ jātimat*) would be untenable.

The definition of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) and so forth means that [the property] does not subsist in any part of the definiendum (*lakṣya*) by way of the relation intended to be the delimiting condition of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka*).

The refined definition (*niṣkarṣa*) is as follows: non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) consists in the state of being a locus of that which is delimited by the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), while possessing a counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) delimited by the delimitor of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka*) that is co-locative with the delimitor of the definiendum; and [furthermore] it consists in the state of being resident (*ādheyatva*) in the locus of the delimitor of the definiendum by means of a relation delimited by the delimitor of the definition. Otherwise, according to the literal reading (*yathāśruta*), [the definition would be flawed].

Because it is difficult to state [a definition] that is common to only a portion of the objects to be defined (*lakṣya*), inclusive (*anugata*), and not over-extensive (*anatiprasakta*), there would be the consequence of impossibility; therefore,
the second member [of the definition] is for the purpose of excluding what is impossible.
The first limb is for the purpose of excluding [the presence of] smell and so forth as defining characteristics;
for, since there is an absence of smell and so forth in earth and the other elements due to conjunction and other relations, [smell] would otherwise be the counter-positive of that absence.

The inclusion of the property of being delimited by the relation that delimits the definition [of the probans] is for the purpose of excluding [the over-extension of the definition] to things such as a single hoof, which reside in a cow through the relation of time; this is done by [specifying] the locus-ness (*ādheyatā*) contained within the second part [of the definition].
The inclusion of the qualification "being delimited by that relation" [is necessary].

And even so, [the definition would still fail] in the case of a jar and the like, with respect to the absence of smell and so forth as qualified by the occurrence in a jar of the absence of both smell and a jar.
It should not be argued that the same defect persists because of existence (*sattva*),

for what is intended here is that property which serves as the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of such an absence and which also serves as the delimitor of such a locus-ness (*ādheyatāvacchedaka*) with respect to the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka*). Even though...

Although properties such as *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) and *gandhatva* (odor-ness) are also delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of such absences, there is no fault because the intention is to specify the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) where the delimitorhood (*avacchedakatā*) is fully resident (*paryāpti*).
[33] "Of the definition in that which is not the object of definition" (*alakṣye lakṣaṇasya*).

The meaning is: "the state of being located, as delimited by a relation that constitutes the definition-ness (lakṣaṇatā), which is qualified by a difference whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by the delimitor of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedaka), through a specific type of qualification.
Because the difference from a jar and so forth does not exist in a jar and so forth, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) to smell and the like.
Nor [is it] by taking the existence of odor in water and so forth, which are non-eternal (*kālika*). [Note:
The phrase "by way of a specific qualification" (*viśeṣaṇatāviśeṣeṇa*) is construed with the term "possessing distinction" (*bhedavatve*).

Nor is there the persistence of that same defect [of over-extension], because the distinction of earth and so forth exists in earth and so forth themselves through the relation of temporal succession (*kālika-sambandha*),
according to the statement in the *Dīpikā*: "the property of not occurring in the locus of definition (*lakṣya*)."

If the word *mātra* (only) were intended to exclude other things, then the definition would result in "the absence of occurrence in the locus while being qualified by non-occurrence in what is other than the locus," which is equivalent to *asambhava* (impossibility). And that is not tenable, because it would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the definition even to an overly broad property; therefore—
In the *Prakāśikā*, he explains the word "only" (*mātra*) as having the sense of "entirety," stating: "[33] The word 'only'... [and] "...the specific relation, etc.

Here, the "specific relation" is precisely the essential nature (*svarūpa*) characterized by being the counter-correlate of a locus-ness (*ādheyatā*) delimited by the delimiting condition of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka*).

The final conclusion is that *asambhava* (impossibility) is the absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the property of "subsisting in the definiendum" (*lakṣyavṛttitvatva*), where this subsistence is delimited by a relation-in-itself (*svarūpasambandha*) that stands in the relation of counter-correlativity to a locusness (*ādheyatā*) delimited by the relation that delimits the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedakasambandha*).

Because, in that case, the essential nature (svarūpa) which has as its counter-correlative a locusness delimited by duality and so forth is extrinsic (vyadhikaraṇa) with respect to subsistence in qualities and the like;
and here, the word "only" (mātra) [serves to exclude such cases].

By virtue of its meaning being the pervasion of the delimitor of the referent of the word uttered in conjunction [with it], the pervasion of the delimitor of the indicated (lakṣyatāvacchedaka) as delimited by the relation of being a qualifier (nirūpakatā) is obtained in the property of being a locus (ādheyatva). This being so, there would otherwise be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of the definition to over-pervasive properties.

Furthermore, the property of possessing a collection of absences of the respective individuality (*tattadvyaktitva*) in as many individual instances of the definiendum (*lakṣyavyakti*) as there may be is difficult to ascertain,
due to both the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) and other reasons.
Considering that this [definition] cannot be explicitly stated, it is intended to indicate the general absence of occurrence in the *lakṣya* (the object to be defined).
In reality, however,

it is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*)— delimited by the relation of being a definition (*lakṣaṇatā*) belonging to the absence that pervades the delimitors of *lakṣyatā* (the state of being the object to be defined)— [that constitutes the definition].
The presence of a property that delimits the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedakadharmavattva*) constitutes the impossibility (*asambhava*).

Furthermore, the pervasion of the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedakavyāpakatva*) consists in the possession of a property that is not the delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitānavacchedaka*) of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the delimitor of the definiendum.

But it is not the state of not being the counter-positive of such an absence; for that would result in the impossibility [of defining the universal], since everything indeed possesses counter-positiveness delimited by duality and so forth.
There is no harm even if one does not accept this specific form as being the nature of relation (*saṃsargatva*),
provided it is [understood] by means of a relation that constitutes the delimitor of the state of being the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedakatā*).
The locus enters [the definition] precisely through the qualifiers such as the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
Therefore, there is no fault in taking a locus of the delimitor of the definiendum and so forth by means of a different relation.
Nor is there an infinite regress;
for it is like the case of "having a single hoof," even though [the term] occurs in the word *śata*.
According to the logic of the "fifty," even for cows and the like, the possession of a single hoof remains unimpaired;
nevertheless, "oneness" here does not consist in the form of a number.

Rather, it should be understood as a technical definition (*pāribhāṣika*) consisting in being other than that which is qualified by a hoof, by way of the two relations of residing in its own substratum and being distinct from itself.
This applies to the body of the over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

With the intention that the inclusion of "subsisting in the locus" (*lakṣyavṛttitva*) is unnecessary, [the author states]: "[Even] in the case of a mixture of defects (*duṣṭasaṅkara*)," because of the principle (*nyāya*).

This means that even though the nature of the defective [locus] is one and the same, since the natures of the individual defects are mutually distinct, the inclusion of that [subsistence in the locus] is unnecessary.
This is the state of being.
In this regard, in some ancient texts, the word *diś* (direction) is seen [in place of *bhāva*].
And in this regard, the point is as follows:

since there is no conventional usage such as "this definition is over-extensive" with respect to properties like having only one hoof— which are impossible [in the subject]— it is not necessary to necessarily include the condition of "subsisting in the definiendum" (lakṣyavṛttitva).
In that case, there is scope for the aforementioned reasoning;
for since there is no sublation to the conventional usage [of a term] in one place even when it is impossible in another, there is scope for the aforementioned reasoning therein.
An investigation into the definition of a definition:

Now, from the statement in the *Dīpikā*, "A property (*dharma*) is that which is devoid of these three defects," it follows that the definition of a definition is simply the absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by the state of being those three defects.
That [definition] is not tenable;

for even in a property that is seized by individual defects such as under-extension (*avyāpti*), that [definition] exists, resulting in over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Therefore, he says: "[It is] distinguished by the three absences of the aforementioned defects."
The meaning is as follows:
the intention is that there is no fault because each individual locus itself constitutes the locus of the aggregate (kūṭa).
[38] By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "non-pervasion, etc.," the inclusion of "impossibility" (*asambhava*) is intended.
[38] Regarding the term "of another kind":
thus, the term "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) refers to the meaning that is about to be explained.
Regarding the term "technical" (*pāribhāṣika*):

by the etymological derivation that "that which is not common is 'uncommon' (*asādhāraṇa*)," the meaning of the word "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) is characterized by both subsisting in the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) and not subsisting in what is not the object to be defined.
Furthermore, since a derivative (yaugika) category in the form of the absence of that [definition]— namely, being afflicted by both non-pervasion (avyāpti) and impossibility (asambhava)—
exists, such a meaning is untenable; moreover,
"a definition is a property free from these three defects."

The purport of the introduction to the *Prakāśikā* is that one should also understand that the author provides a technical definition (*pāribhāṣika*) while keeping in mind these two points of lack of internal consistency (*asvārasya*), namely the contradiction with the aforementioned text.
The reading "the clause 'sat' [is included] to exclude those [definitions] that are afflicted by under-extension (avyāpti) or impossibility (asambhava)" is erroneous.

Since there is no possibility of [the definition] being over-narrow (avyāpti) in that case— because a non-existent property such as "having a single hoof" lacks the quality of being pervaded by the delimitor of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedaka), which consists in its being pervaded by that [property] itself.
[38] The reading *avyāptasya* is seen in ancient manuscripts; that alone is correct. As for the statement—“earth and so forth... [the rest of the sentence follows].
In cases such as "the definition by way of inherence," there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to non-existent things like the sky-flower,
because the property of being pervaded by the definiendum-delimitant (*lakṣyatāvacchedakavyāpyatva*), which consists in occurring in that which lacks the definiendum-delimitant, exists therein; thus,
the reading "of those seized by under-extension and impossibility" is also correct— this [objection] is not tenable.

Because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of inconsistency with what is to be stated later— namely, that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding "being denotable" (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth—

it is necessary to include "being pervaded" (*vyāpyatva*) in the sense of "having that as its own pervader" (*svavyāpakatatkatva*); therefore, the reading [of the definition] as it stands cannot be correct.
And if there is insistence on the grammatical correctness of that reading, then [the definition is as follows]:

the absence of the delimitor of the counter-correlativity residing in the delimitor of the indicatedness (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), which is delimited by the relation of "subsisting in what possesses its own absence," [is the definition]. This absence is co-extensive with itself.
This can be explained by incorporating a pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) consisting of a counter-positiveness delimited by the relation of being a delimiting factor of counter-positiveness;
that very thing is called the "uncommon property" (*asādhāraṇadharma*).

From this statement in the *Dīpikā*, it is obtained that [the definition] is "being a property (dharma) while being uncommon"; therein, the inclusion of the factor of "being a property" is fruitless, because non-occurrent entities such as space lack the quality of being a pervader of the delimitors of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), and thus the charge of under-extension (*avyāpti*) does not apply there. Therefore...

He states the meaningfulness of the term *tatpada* (that-word) as follows: "[38] The term *dharma-pada*"; [38] "by means of the relation that constitutes the definition" means by means of the relation that delimits the state of being the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka-sambandhena*).
That which is not the delimiting factor (anavacchedaka) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of an absence residing in the locus of the delimitor of the indicatedness (lakṣyatāvacchedaka),

with respect to the relation that delimits the definition-ness (lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha); and that which is not the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in the locus of its own delimited [counter-correlate], with respect to the relation that delimits the definition-ness.

The meaning is that one must intend to express the possession of that property which serves as the delimitor of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka-dharma*), while being itself the delimitor of the locus of the definition (*kṣyatāvacchedaka*).
By the phrase "because of being a pervader" (*vyāpakatvāt*) and so forth, the inclusion of "being pervaded" (*vyāpyatva*) is intended.

And thus, the final conclusion is that "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇatva) consists in the possession of the delimitor of the definition by that which is qualified by the delimitor of the locus of definition.
And as for this "qualification":

[The definition is] by means of both relations: (1) being the delimitor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference from its own occurrence (*svavṛtti*), and (2) possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimitorhood residing in itself, which is delimited by a relation that is the delimitorhood of such a counter-correlativity belonging to an absence (*abhāva*) occurring in its own locus (*svādhikaraṇa*).
Delimitorhood (*avacchedakatva*) [in this context] is [to be understood] as the relation constitutive of the definition (*lakṣaṇatā*).
1. *Avacchedakatvam iti*: This means the state of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) that constitutes the first relation.
And thus, in the case of the delimitor of the property to be defined (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), [the definition applies].
The difference that exists in "cowness" is the difference consisting in having a dewlap and so forth;
for its own nature, which is the form of having a dewlap and so forth,
is the delimitor of the definition (lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka), and it belongs to that which is delimited by it, namely the dewlap and so forth.

Since the property of being the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in that which is the locus of a cow— by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) as the delimitor of the definition— is absent in "cowness" (*gotva*),
[cowness] does not possess the property of having a dewlap, etc., by way of the relation of being the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of such a difference.

"Cowness" (gotva) is a particularity consisting in the subsistence of cowness, like the possession of a dewlap and so forth; the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedakatva) resides in that possession of a dewlap and so forth.
In this way, "self" (sva) refers to cowness.

The property of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence residing in that locus (the dewlap, etc. does not exist in "dewlap-ness" (*sāsnāditva*).
Thus, the difference from that which possesses "cowness" (*gotva*)—by way of the relation of being the delimiting factor of such counter-correlativity—exists in "dewlap-ness.
Consequently, by means of both relations, there is the state of being qualified by "cowness," which is the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
This is to be understood as applying to "possessing a dewlap" (*sāsnāditva*), which is the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). And thus,
the first, second, and third occurrences of the word *sva* refer to the delimitors of the definiendum, while the fourth occurrence of the word *sva* [refers to the delimitor of the definition].

The distinction is that [the term] refers to the delimitant of the definition (*lakṣaṇatāvacchedaka*). [The relation is] by way of the relation of being the delimitant of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in the locus delimited by itself. In order to exclude [the over-extension of] conjunctions and so forth to the absence of smell and so forth, [this is specified] regarding pervasion (*vyāpakatā*).
The inclusion of the property of being delimited by the relation constitutive of the definition [lakṣaṇatā] is for the following reason:
since smell and other qualities exist in water and so forth through relations such as the temporal (kālika), that [delimitation by the defining relation] is included in pervasion (vyāpyatā).
And other points should be inferred by oneself.
Regarding the phrase "those which disrupt the state of being uncommon" (*asādhāraṇatvasya vighaṭakāḥ*), here the verbal root *ghaṭ* is preceded by the prefix *vi*.
The meaning is "non-existence.

The suffix *ṇvul* functions as an agentive marker; thus, the sense is "that which brings about [the absence]. And such a non-existence is caused by the absence of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) due to over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Intending to show that the cases of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and impossibility (*asambhava*) are caused by the absence of a qualifier, he says: "[38] Regarding over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*) consists in the presence of the absence of the reason merely in co-inherence with the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

The distinction is that *svarūpāsiddhi* (essential unestablishment) consists in the absence of that [reason] in the subject as delimited by that [delimitor]. And here, [the distinction from] *bhāgāsiddhi* (partial unestablishment) is made by way of the delimitor.
Because both [types of fallacy] are opposed to the cognition of the presence of the reason in the subject—
either by way of being opposed to the cognition of the presence of the reason in the subject under the delimitation of the locus (svarūpāsiddhi),
or by way of being opposed to the cognition of the presence of the reason in the subject through co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) under the delimitation of the [subject's] delimitor.
It should be understood that a reason is a fallacy (hetvābhāsa) by virtue of its being an obstacle to the cognition of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā).
As for the phrase "only exclusion" (vyāvṛttireva),
this is the intended meaning:
"The purpose of a definition is either exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) or conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Exclusion means differentiation from others;
conventional usage means a word that generates cognition.
The purpose (*prayojana*) is that which is to be made known. Likewise, "differentiating" (*vyāvartakatva*) means being the inferential indicator of difference from others.
"Conventional usage" (*vyāvahārikatva*)...
It is the capacity to lead to empirical usage (*vyavahārānumāpakatva*).
And in the present context, one opinion holds that exclusion alone (*vyāvṛtti*) is what is made known by the definition.
Another view holds that both exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) are what is to be made known.

In that regard, according to the first position, since the property of being an excluder itself serves as the delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*), as will be explained by the method to be stated.
Regarding the phrase "of that which differentiates" (*vyāvartakasya*): [it refers to] that which is qualified by the nature of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*).
That is, the specific [property] whose nature is being pervaded.
They bring about the absence of that [definiendum].
2. Regarding "due to the absence of the qualificand" (*viśeṣyābhāva*):

the meaning is that it is caused by the absence of that which constitutes the "qualificand," namely, the state of being pervaded by the delimiting property of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedakavyāpyatva*).
Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of the qualifier":
the meaning is that it is caused by the absence of that qualifier which consists in being a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
The meaning of the verbal root *vṛt* preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ā-* is "distinction from others.
With the intention that the suffix *-aka* denotes "that which generates an inference," he says: "[39] the meaning is 'of that which generates the inference of distinction from others.
The state of being a generator of an inference (*anumitijanakatva*)...

It is the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅga-parāmarśa*) itself that [is the cause], and not the logical mark being considered; for if it were the latter, it would be impossible for smell and so forth to function as differentiators. Not so.
It should not be argued that there is no fault because "exclusion" (*vyāvartakatva*) consists in being the object of a cognition that produces an inference of difference from others; for even so,
there is the undesirable consequence (*udāsīna*) that neutral things would also be included as objects of a collective comprehensive reflection (*samūhālambana-parāmarśa*).
Furthermore, it would be inconsistent to state that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding [the definition] "being denotable" (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth,
because that too is a subject of the definition (*lakṣya*) according to the method already explained.

Nor should it be argued that [the definition] consists in being the locus of a subject-object relation (viṣayatā) delimited by such a generative capacity; for even so, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to absences and the like which constitute the pervasion (vyāpti) of the difference from others.
For example: "A cow possessing a tawny color is a cow delimited by cowness, which pervades the difference from non-cows."

Furthermore, since even the color of Kapila and other such attributes would result in being a differentiator by virtue of being the object of a misconception consisting of a reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*) having such a form as "it is [the subject]," there arises the following doubt:
that the very state of being a property (*dharmatva*) is itself the definition of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). In response to this doubt:

For the sake of extracting the essential meaning, he says: "[39] 'That which has as its object the subject-qualifier delimited by the locushood (pakṣatāvacchedaka) belonging to the cognition that generates an inference whose probandum is the exclusion of others,' and so forth.

This means: the objectness (viṣayatā) determined by the qualificandness (viśeṣyatā) delimited by the locushood belonging to the cognition that produces an inferential knowledge (anumiti) where the probandum is the difference from others.
As for the claim that— in order to exclude defects by taking into account the objecthood belonging to an error— one must include the condition "not being determined by an error"—
that is incorrect; because there is no difference in objecthood among cognitions of the same form, [this would apply] even to an indifferent portion [of the object].
Because, by taking a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) as the basis, the impossibility [of the definition] would be unavoidable; therefore,

in order to avoid the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to "difference from others" by taking the "qualificative-ness of the difference from others" (*itarabhedaprakāratā*)— which is determined by the subject-predicate-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) contained within the factor of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)— as the criterion.
The inclusion of "being delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood" (pakṣatāvacchedakāvacchinnatva) [is necessary].
Even if one were to include "being delimited by something," the defect would remain as it was, because the subject is included as a constituent of the relation of co-inherence (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
This is my view;

in reality, however, it is precisely the state of being determined by the primary qualificandhood (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*) that should be incorporated into the definition of the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*).

Otherwise, in the case of "the definition of a property (bhāva) is its being locatable (*ādheyatva*)," there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [the definition] to *ādheyatva*, by taking as the qualifier [in the cognition] the qualifierhood residing in the pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is the delimitant of the generative capacity for an inference caused by the absence of property-hood (*bhāvatvābhāva*). This is the point here.

If the property of having "difference from others" as its object were included in the definition of inference (*anumiti*), then, by taking into account the generative capacity of the inference "Difference from others is cognizable, because it is nameable," it would follow that "nameability" and other such properties would possess the status of differentiators (*vyāvartakatā*).
Therefore, the property of having "difference from others" (*itarabheda*) as its predicate (*vidheya*) is included therein.

What is intended to be expressed is the state of having a predication-ness (*vidheyatā*) delimited by the property of being "difference from others. For example: "A pot possesses denotability (*abhidheyatva*) by way of the relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*), because it is knowable (*prameyatva*)."

Thus, by taking into account the status of being a producer of the cognition "it is thus," one must include— in that very defect— the property of being delimited by an essential relation qualified by pervasion of the delimitor of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) within the state of being the predicate (vidheyatā). Otherwise...

Because there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to a property that is subject to non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), by taking into account the generative capacity belonging to a valid inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*)— which is of the nature of a true cognition and serves as the cause for an inference of the form "different from what is other than a cow" (*gaur-itara-bhinna*)— that [consideration] merely apprehends the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. [Therefore,

the definition must be qualified by] the generative capacity that has as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) a generativity delimited by the state of being an effect of an inference, which is conjoined with the state of having such a [cow-nature] as its predicate (*vidheyatā*).
It must be posited that [the probans] resides in the subject. Otherwise, even if there is merely a co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the property delimiting the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka),

the defect remains as it was, because one could still take into account the generative capacity of a "collective cognition" (samūhālambana) inference that apprehends the difference from others, which is based on a consideration of mere co-occurrence belonging to the "subsumptive reflection" (parāmarśa).
Now, even in this way,

by means of a temporal or other such relation, [the property] is common to the cognition of the possession of the difference from non-pots and so forth, which is pervaded by the difference from things other than earth.

Alternatively, by taking into account the generative capacity for inference— which is common to both the knowledge of "the earth's being distinct from others" and the knowledge of "pervasion by the earth's being distinct from others"—
the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the "earth's being distinct from others" and so forth remains unavoidable. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that there is no fault because the property of "being a cognition belonging to that which produces such an inference" is included within the objective content (*viṣayatā*); for even so,

[the fault remains] in the case of a cognition regarding the difference from non-earth (*pṛthivītarabheda*) and the like, which is overwhelmed by the knowledge of its own invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñāna*).

Because knowledge of the form "Earth possesses the difference from non-earth that is pervaded by the difference from non-earth, and it also possesses the difference from non-substance that is pervaded by that [difference]" has such a nature;
[this refers to] its subsisting in a cognition that does not produce such an inference.

If it is argued that [the definition] cannot be formulated because it is impossible to include the objectivity (*viṣayatva*) of smell and so forth—which is common to doubts and the like that do not produce such an inference—[we reply]: No;

for [the definition refers to] that which delimits the generative capacity (*janakatā*) as determined by the state of being produced (*janyatā*) delimited by the nature of such an inference (*tādṛśānumititva*).

This is because what is intended [by the definition] is the state of being the locus of that objective content belonging to a cognition which is not overridden by a cognition of falsity, and which subsists in the cognition that brings about such an inference.
The refined definition is: "having an objectivity qualified by such a state of being produced.

The qualification [of the objectivity] occurs through two relations: (1) having the property of being the delimiting condition of the generative capacity as determined by itself; and (2) being the property of a cognition that is not overridden by a knowledge of invalidity which serves as an auxiliary to the inference that has that [objectivity] as its locus.

The state of being unassailed by the cognition of invalidity consists in being other than what is qualified by error through the three relations of objecthood, coreferentiality, and temporal qualification.

The path uniquely cultivated by me alone is as follows: [the definition of the qualifier-ness of a relation] consists in being the determiner of a qualifier-ness other than that qualified by the relation through the three relations of: (1) residing in its own counter-correlative, (2) being determined by the qualificative-ness residing in its own sub-stratum, and (3) being delimited by itself.
[39] "Even so" means by the particle *eva*. Now, one might object:

how can the fact that dewlaps and so forth are the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of cows and so forth be the cause of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), following the maxim of "breaking the staff by striking the back"?

Therefore, he says: "[39] 'Having the stated definition' and 'being distinct from being denotable, etc. Here, this must be considered: if everything that merely serves as a differentiator were to be the definiendum (lakṣya) by virtue of having the stated definition, then, since the exclusion of conventional [non-definienda] is achieved simply by incorporating the property of being pervaded by the delimitor of definiendumhood—which consists in not occurring in that which lacks a delimitor of definiendumhood—[the inclusion of "distinctness from being denotable, etc. would be redundant.

Having introduced the property of being pervaded by the delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), which consists in its own pervader and the state of being that [pervader], one incurs over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*); yet, to exclude this,
the introduction of the condition "being different from that" is improper according to the maxim of "washing away [dirt with mud]" (*prakṣālanādi-nyāya*).

As for the objection that there is over-extension (ativyāpti) because [the definition] exists in water and so forth— which lack the delimitors of the definiendum (lakṣyatāvacchedaka) such as earthness— by means of relations like temporality (kālika), that is not correct.
Because, in the case of the definition of a jar and so forth, the definition applies only to that which is distinct [from the definiendum], just like the cognition [of it]; therefore,

there exists the state of being pervaded by the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), which consists in having a counter-correlativity delimited by a relation that constitutes the definition and belongs to an absence that pervades the absence of the delimitor of the definiendum.
"Because it is intended to be so stated":
first of all, there is no inference of difference in a general sense—
that is, as a difference in a general sense.

The meaning of *tasil* is "delimited by" (*avacchinnatva*). And its connection is with the "predicative-ness of difference" (*bhedavidheyatā*), which constitutes the factor that leads to the inference of difference.
[39] "Delimited by the duality of some x or y" (*yatkiñcidubhayatvāvacchinnapratiyogitāka*) refers to "the pot."

In that case, [the definition] applies by taking into account the capacity to generate such inferences as: "The pot-cloth-both-different is denotable, because it is denotable," and "Earth is different from the pot-cloth-both, because it is different from what is other than earth."
The intention is that the status of being a differentiator (*vyāvartakatva*) is easily established.

Although this could be easily stated by taking into account the generation of an inference such as "the jar possesses difference because it is nameable" (*abhidheyatvāt*), [this is not the case here].
The pursuit [of the definition] up to the point of the inference whose probandum is a difference delimited by duality is fruitless; nevertheless,

for the purpose of understanding how a fault arises even when the definition is formulated with the inclusion of a predication delimited by "difference-ness" accompanied by "having a counter-positivehood delimited by some property," [the following is stated].
The statement was made in that way also for the sake of ensuring the exclusion [of the subject] from the class of similar instances;
otherwise, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāpatti*).
This is how it should be understood. Now, one might object:

Since no fault arises from introducing as the predicate-property (vidheyatā) a difference qualified by some property other than those that occur distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti), provided it is accompanied by a counter-positivehood (pratiyogitā) delimited by some such property, he says: "[39] Because all negative properties (vyatirekidharma) are excluded by something or other. [The example is: "The cow."

[This occurs] by taking into account the capacity to generate such inferences as "the horned [animal] is different from a pot" and "the tawny cow is different from a pot because it possesses a tawny color," with respect to the state of being horned, the tawny color, and so forth.
The intended meaning is that it is possible to establish that. [39] Nor is it "in a qualified manner," etc.;
