[it refers to] earth-ness (pṛthivītva) as delimited by its own nature as qualified by the pervasion of earth, and so forth.

The meaning is: being the locus of the aforementioned objective content (*viṣayatā*), which is the delimitor of the generative capacity (*janakatā*) for an inference whose qualificandum-ness (*vidheyatā*) is delimited by the state of being different from others.

Although there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the reddish-brown color and so forth would possess the status of a differentiator (*vyāvartakatā*) by taking as an instance the inference: "A reddish-brown cow is different from a pot because it possesses a reddish-brown color," nevertheless...
There is no fault by virtue of the logical principle beginning with "the delimiting property of the locus" (*dharmitāvacchedaka*),
because the co-extension (*samanaiyatyam*) with cowness and so forth does not exist there.

The point is that because "coextensiveness with the state of being a category" (*padārthatva-samaniyatatva*) cannot serve as a definition due to the non-establishment of the definiendum (*lakṣya-aprasiddhi*), its existence therein is irrelevant.
[40] This is the probandum (*sādhya*) in the inference of the difference from others as delimited by cowness (*gotvāvacchinnetara-bheda*).
Thus, the meaning is that "cowness" (*gotva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*) by virtue of the relation of being the inferential indicator of the difference from others as delimited by itself.

By this, the subsequent mention of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth becomes consistent; otherwise, since "others" as delimited by "category-ness" (*padārthatva*) would be unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), the absence of the probandum—which is constituted by that [relation]—would likewise be unestablished.
Because it is even more unestablished, it is difficult to state the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), which consists in occurring in that which lacks the probandum;
however, in our position, [the probans] is related to "being a category" (*padārthatva*) by the aforementioned relation.
Since the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is well-established by virtue of having a different locus, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is indeed easy to state;
this applies to the case of "being distinct from 'nameability' (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth. Here, the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "or" (*vā*).
Otherwise, by merely introducing the condition of being distinct from what is different from that which is delimited by those properties (*taddharmāvacchinnetarabhedabhinnatva*),

since "other than the categories" (*padārthetara*) is unestablished, any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth would be excluded; thus, the inclusion of "being distinct from nameability" and the like within the scope of the reason (*hetu*) would be fruitless.
Because it is impossible for that [term] to be a collective indicator, there is a lack of coherence;

for in this case, regarding the locus of universal pervasion, there exists the presence of both the respective probandum and the reason, qualified by the absence of the apprehension of the pervasion of each respective probandum within the subject of that reason.

Intending to show that an inference is not possible in the present context— since the validity of inferential cognition has already been discussed in the *Siddhāntalakṣaṇa* and the *Prāmāṇyavāda*— he says: "[40] This is for the sake of further investigation" and "[40] without the knowledge of that which is to be designated by that form."
The meaning is: "without the parāmarśa (subsumptive reflection) whose object is the subject (*pakṣa*) by way of its distinction from others (*itarabheda*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "delimited by that form" (*tadrūpāvacchinna*): it means "that which does not convey [the property] as delimited by the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), such as 'earth-ness' (*pṛthivītva*)."
Because of the impossibility of linguistic usage— that is, because of the impossibility of inferring linguistic usage—

conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*) with respect to a given property is defined as the property of being the delimiting factor for the generative capacity of an inference whose object is a linguistic usage consisting of words that convey an entity delimited by that property.
And that [is as follows]: "A pot should be designated as 'earth,' because it is distinct from what is other than earth," and "A pot should be designated as 'an entity' (padārtha)."

The point is that by taking the inference beginning with "because of being denotable" (*abhidheyatvāt*), [the definition] remains unimpaired even in the case of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and denotability (*abhidheyatva*).
By this, [it is shown that] in the *Dīpikā*, regarding the purpose of the definition and its being made known by the definition...

The meaning should be understood as "because it is the means for establishing conventional usage" (vyavahārasādhanatvāt) or "because it is the inferential indicator of conventional usage" (vyavahārānumāpakatvāt).
This establishes that the possession of qualities (guṇavattva) is the definition of substance (dravyalakṣaṇa).

Since ancient authorities do not accept that absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) can reside in that which possesses antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) or destruction (dhvaṃsa), a pervasion (vyāpti) defined by absolute non-existence is not possible.

Alternatively, with the intention that there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) because the definition of pervasion includes only the state of being the counter-positive of an absence residing in the locus of the definiendum (lakṣyaniṣṭhābhāvapratiyogitva) as being non-co-located with its own counter-positive (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa), and because the absence of smell (gandhādyabhāva) is not such [an absence], he raises an objection in the *Prakāśikā* with the words "But surely" (*nanu*), etc. [53].
"The definition characterized by being the substratum of qualities" means that its nature consists of qualities.
The mention of "being a substratum" is for the purpose of demonstrating the relation that constitutes the definition. By this—
Because the locus-hood of being the substratum of a quality, as defined by its occurrence in relation to origination, is also non-pervasive;
[this is so] with respect to inherence qualified by having a quality as its counter-correlative.
Under the view that inherence (samavāya) is one, there is over-extension (ativyāpti) to qualities and so forth,
because the absence of inherence— qualified by having those [qualities] as its counter-correlate— exists at the time of their production; thus, there is non-pervasion (avyāpti).
The objection is without merit.
To prevent the misconception that "existence" (*sattā*) is the qualifier, it is stated that "the genus" (*jāti*) is the qualifier.
And in this context, there is the property of being co-located with a quality (*guṇa*).

The [intended] property is being the locus of inherence as delimited by the relation of inherence which is qualified by a substratumhood delimited by the relation of inherence residing in that which is established in a quality through the relation of inherence.

By this, there is the exclusion of *guṇatva* (the universal "quality-ness"), which, although it resides in a quality through the relation of inherence, resides in that which possesses qualities (i.e., substance) through the relation of time, and which resides in that which has the inherence of a quality through the relation of time.

[53] Regarding the term "existence" (*bhāva*): now, in the conventional expression "one form is distinct from taste," [the relation] resides in the quality (*guṇa*) by way of a relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

If it is admitted that [the property of being distinct] has as its object a quality (*guṇa*), then there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth could be designated as separate from itself;
for [distinctness] would then coexist with a distinctness delimited by itself.
If it is argued that [this is so] because there is no contradiction even with respect to itself— no;
for we do not admit that co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is a relation of separateness (pṛthaktva) having itself as its own limit.
And because both conceptualization and non-conceptualization depend upon their respective results;
for in reality, in cases such as "form is distinct from taste," and so forth—

There is no fault, because it is accepted that difference (*pṛthaktva*) appears [in cognition] by way of both relations: being distinct from that which is delimited by its own delimitors of definition (*svanirūpakatāvacchedaka*), and being co-located (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
[53] By the phrase "kālikādi" and so forth, there is the inclusion of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) constituted by both [the relation] inherence (*samavāya*) and its own nature (*svarūpa*).
[56] Regarding the term "hetudharmitāvacchedakaka":
The meaning is "having a qualificandum delimited by the reason. The intention is that there is no contradiction with an established cognition that has a different form. [56] This is the summary.
This is the intended meaning here:

there is no inconsistency whatsoever in negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) being a constituent part of inference. Furthermore, the alleged impossibility of verbal comprehension from the *upanaya* statement applies only to the context of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).
The fault does not apply even in the case of inference for oneself (svārthānumāna); thus, the establishment of the purpose of the definition is indeed free from objection.
Now, as for the state of being past (bhūtatva)...
Since there is an absence of being a universal (*jāti*), how can the confusion of that [universal] be a sublater?
For the confusion of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not a fault. To this, he says: "[57] That which is intended as a universal," meaning "that which has been established as a universal."
And thus, by the same reasoning,

since the genus *bhūtatva* (earthness) is established as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "earth" (*bhūta*), the fault of *saṃkara* (overlapping) does not apply; this is the intended meaning.

[57] In the verse beginning with "vyakterabheda," by supplying the word "iti," the understanding of the non-difference in the collection of the forms of the few sounds that produce cognition must be described;
this refers to the first triad.

The word *atha* is placed in the middle to indicate the specific distinction that, while [the first triad] constitutes a genus (*jāti*), the second triad serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*) of the state of possessing a genus (*jātimattva*).
Furthermore, this refers to the sublation of the genus as stated in the verse beginning with "of the individual" (*vyakteḥ*).

The definition of "absence of difference from the individual" (*vyaktyabheda*) is: being the object of a cognition that obstructs a cognition whose mode is either "being a universal" (*jāti*) or "possessing a universal" (*jātimat*);

or, [alternatively], being other than what is qualified by "knowable" (*prameya*) through the two relations of "inherence in itself" (*svasamavetatva*) and "inherence in something other than itself" (*svabhinnasamavetatva*).
Alternatively, it is the state of being other than that which possesses difference, by way of the two relations of "inherence in its own counter-correlative" and "inherence in its own substratum.
This is because the cognition of that [difference] functions as a cognition of being other than that which possesses it, by means of the aforementioned two relations.

The capacity to obstruct the cognition of "jātitva" (the nature of being a universal), which is constituted by its inherence in multiple entities such as being qualified by the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and so forth. [Note:
1. Regarding *svasamavetatva*: *sva* refers to the blue jar; *tatsamavetatva* is the state of inhering in that [jar], which resides in "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).]

Thus, "itself" refers to a blue pot, and "inherence in a yellow pot different from it" refers to potness. By means of these two aforementioned relations, potness is qualified by the object of knowledge (prameya) which is the form of a blue pot; likewise, the state of being different from that [blue pot] exists in ether-ness. Thus, itself...

The absence of a blue pot (nīlaghaṭabheda) [is present in potness]; the state of being inherent in its counter-positive (tatpratiyogin), namely the blue pot, also resides in potness; and the state of being inherent in its own (sva) substratum—the yellow pot—which is the locus of that absence (tadanuyogin), likewise resides in potness.
Thus, by virtue of these two relations, potness possesses such an absence—that is, it possesses the absence of a blue pot.
It should be understood that "being other than that" applies to space (*ākāśa*).
Equality consists in being co-extensive with a genus distinct from itself.
This results in being qualified by a universal (*jāti*) through the dual relation of being distinct from itself and being co-extensive with itself;
and that [qualification] is pervaded by the absence of *jātitva* (the property of being a universal).

The apprehension of that [absence], by way of being an apprehension of the possession of a property pervaded by its absence, constitutes an opposition to the acceptance of potness and so forth as being a universal distinct from the universal "jar-ness" and others; and of that [opposition]...

If *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) and *kalaśatva* (jar-ness) were distinct universals (*jāti*), there would be no other way [to account for the facts] than to postulate two powers (*śakti*) of the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth with respect to the two delimited properties, as well as the postulation of two causal relations (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Thus, by means of the cognition of parsimony (*lāghava*), assisted by intelligence...

This is established by the inference based on the reason "knowability" (*prameyatva*), which has as its probandum either the absence of "being a genus" (*jātitvābhāva*)— which is pervaded by the absence of that [genus]— or that [genus] itself, within the context of the thesis that [the object] is qualified by being a genus.
Furthermore, there is *saṅkara* (overlapping).

The state of being qualified by a universal (*jāti*) consists in its possessing a triad of relations: (1) co-occurrence with itself, (2) co-occurrence with its own absence, and (3) being the counter-positive of an absence that co-occurs with itself. Furthermore, this [state] is indeed pervaded by the absence of the nature of a universal (*jātitva*).
And its being such is established by the Dharmaśāstra:
[it concerns] the mutual pervasion of contradictory classes by means of a pervading class.
The inclusion of the three relations is for the purpose of avoiding the confusion of universals (jātisāṅkarya) between the pervading universal and the pervaded universal.

In this context, "infinite regress" (*anavasthiti*) and "endlessness" (*anavasthā*) are intended to mean the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasañjana*) consisting in an infinite series of causalities for the cognitions of various universals— cognitions determined by a conceptual awareness qualified by a universal that depends on a succession of property-qualifiers (*upādhi*) which serve as the differentiators of categories (*padārthavibhājakopādhi*) that do not reside in the universal itself.
And for that [universal], by way of the transgression that brings it about, there is the property of being opposed to a cognition in the form "the universal possesses the universal-possessor";
this is the loss of its nature (*rūpahāni*).

There would be a loss of the very nature of the definition, which consists in being excluded from others by itself. Furthermore, "being excluded from others by itself" for the *viśeṣas* means their possession of a mutual difference that is established intrinsically; [this] of those *viśeṣas*...
There is no logical possibility [for the ultimate particular] to possess a genus;

for according to the principle that the mutual distinction among entities belonging to the same genus is established either by perception or by another differentiator, if the particular (viśeṣa) were...

The particular (*viśeṣa*) serves as a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) against the existence of a genus (*jāti*) because it would entail the following undesirable consequence (*āpatti*): "If the particular possessed a genus, it would not be self-excluded (*svato-vyāvṛtta*).
This is established by the inference: "This atom is distinct from that atom, because of this particular. Thus, [the particular is proven].
If [the universal] were merely possessed of a genus, then by the rule that the substrate of a genus is a differentiator only by virtue of the genus itself,
it would follow that there is an instance of deviation regarding the fact that differentiation occurs only by virtue of the genus; thus,
there would be no connection.
Non-inherence;
and that, by virtue of the *bahuvrīhi* compound,
results in the absence of the general property of inherence.

The cognition of that [universal] possesses the property of being contradictory to the cognition of the possession of a universal that is eternal and inherent in many, by way of being a cognition of the possession of the absence of a universal whose nature consists in being eternal and inherent in many.
Intending all of this, it was stated in the *Dīpikā* [56]: "In brief, because lightness consists in the absence of heaviness. And as for heaviness...

It should not be argued that there is a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) by taking the absence of lightness (*laghutvābhāva*) as the defining nature [of gravity]; for the intention is that there is no fault, according to the maxim that "one who acts independently [is not to be questioned]. This concludes the analysis of action (*karmavibhāga*).
[62] Regarding the term "non-inherent" (*asamavāyin*):
it should not be argued here that, while being distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*), there must exist a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

The inclusion of the "conjunction" element is meaningful for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the first fall and other such instances;
this concludes the general classification.
[63] "With respect to existence in relation to substantiality," and so forth.
The meaning of the word *apekṣā* (relation) is that which determines the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*).
And as for the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*)...

Distinctness (*vaiśiṣṭya*) and subsistence in a larger locus (*adhikadeśavṛttitva*) consist in being qualified by an absence through the two relations of: (1) subsisting in the locus of its own counter-positive, and (2) subsisting in its own locus.
In the case of non-existence in a single location,
there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the property of being qualified by the state of being the counter-correlativity residing in the substance denoted by the word ending in the third case.
In the phrase "by way of existing in a larger locus" (*adhikadeśavṛttitvena*), the meaning of the third case is non-difference (*abheda*).

The meaning of the sentence is that "remoteness" (paratva) with respect to substanceness (dravyatva) is non-different from the possession of an absence whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) resides in substanceness.
Thus, substanceness and the like are "near" (apara) relative to existence (sattā).
And that [non-existence] consists in being the counter-positive of an absence residing in the locus of its own substratum.
This is the detailed classification.

In the statement "particular non-existents are indeed infinite," infinitude (*anantatva*) does not exist; for infinitude is a certainty inherent in ourselves and others, whose mode of presentation is delimited by a property pervaded by the nature of number (*saṅkhyātva*).

Based on the analysis of the compound *viśeṣyatāsambandhena yeṣu nāsti*, it means: the state of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) of such a certainty (*niścaya*) whose qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) is delimited by a property subsumed under "number-ness" (*saṅkhyātva*), which [certainty] does not exist in those [entities] by way of the relation of qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatāsambandha*).
(From the *Prakāśikā* [63])

1. Regarding the term *svāśraya*: "its own" (*svam*) refers to existence (*sattā*); its substratum (*āśrayaḥ*) is the quality (*guṇa*); the absence residing therein (*tanniṣṭhābhāvaḥ*) is the absence of substanceness (*dravyatvābhāvaḥ*); and the state of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitvam*) of that [absence] resides in substanceness (*dravyatve*).
Thus, the meaning is that substanceness is "lower" (*aparatvam*) than existence.
Regarding "discrimination" (*viveka*): likewise,
generality (*sāmānya*) is of three kinds— namely, the purely supreme (*kevala-param*), the purely non-supreme (*kevala-apara*), and [the mixed].
And regarding "the higher and the lower":
in the *Saṃgraha*, because only the higher and the lower are demonstrated, the category of the higher and the lower is clearly [established].
The sense is that it is not mentioned because of its being obtained [by implication].
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the statement of existence as being solely *paratva* (priority) is untenable?"

Because the universals such as "being affectionate" (premāyatva) exist, there is a further and ultimate existence (sattā); therefore, it is said in the *Dīpikā* [63]: "In the fourfold [category] beginning with the universal.
This refers to the definition of inherence (*samavāya*).

[64] Regarding the statement that inherence (*samavāya*) is indeed one: in this list of categories (*saṅgrahapaṅkti*), the oneness of inherence consists in its possessing a property that is not a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of any difference residing in inherence; it does not, however, consist in being a numerical form.
Because it does not reside in inherence (samavāya) and because it is non-excludent;
furthermore, the particle *eva* indicates the intention [of the author] regarding such technical terminology (*pāribhāṣikatva*).
Alternatively, oneness (*ekatva*) is a property that does not subsist in either [of two things].

And the state of not subsisting in either consists in being different from something qualified by any [property] through the relation of both "subsisting in its own counter-positive" and "subsisting in what is non-different from itself."

The meaning of the particle *eva* consists of two distinct components: the property of being the delimiting condition (*avacchedakatva*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the difference between the locus and the superstratum (*ādheyatā*), and non-existence (*abhāva*).
Regarding the superstratum, due to the peculiarity of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), even that which is presented by a word ending in the nominative case [is related].

Inherence (samavāya) is construed by way of the relation of being characterized (nirūpitatva). Furthermore, the state of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference— which is the locus of the substratumhood (ādheyatā) characterized by inherence— is related [to the absence] by way of the relation of being the counter-correlativity delimited by a delimitation that is itself delimited by the relation intended as the delimitor of the property-to-be-prescribed (vidheyatāvacchedaka).
There is no co-occurrence with non-existence;
rather, there is co-occurrence with such a non-existence within a single category-entity (padārtha),
and thus it is inherence (samavāya).

With the intention that the understanding is "identical with that which possesses an absence qualified by being the delimiting condition of the counter-correlativity of difference residing in the locus of the substratumhood (ādheyatā) as determined by inherence (samavāya)," he introduces the passage in the *Dīpikā* [64]: "He says that there is no difference of inherence.
And here, "difference" (bheda) refers to...
The term refers to a property that delimits the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the distinction between the locus and the superstratum (ādheyatā).
In the phrase "of inherence" (samavāyasya),
the meaning of the genitive case is "being characterized by" (nirūpitatva).
And its (the negative particle's) connection is with the locusness that constitutes the referent of the word denoting difference;
furthermore, by virtue of the diversity of grammatical usage, there is also a connection with the locusness that is the meaning of the verbal root *as* (to be).

And that [locusness] which is the meaning of the verbal root *as* is connected with the absence, which is the meaning of the negative particle, and that [absence] is connected with the referent of the word ending in the nominative case.
There is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with difference. And thus, the cognition is:

"The property that delimits the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in the locus of the substratum-ness (*ādheyatā*) as defined by inherence (*samavāya*), is that which possesses the absence of substratum-ness as defined by inherence."
1. Regarding "due to being proximate and remote":
existence (*sattā*) is proximate (*aparatva*) in relation to knowability (*prameyatva*), and it is remote (*paratva*) in relation to substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the like.
The intended meaning is that [the relationship of] being higher or lower is established by way of this method.

Since it is a grammatical convention (*vyutpatti*) that the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys the absence of a property as delimited by the delimiter of the locus (*anuyogitāvacchedaka*), the consistency of the stated sentence-meaning is maintained even under the view that inherence (*samavāya*) is dual.
Alternatively, "difference" (bheda) means mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva);
[this is the meaning] of the genitive case in the phrase "of inherence" (samavāyasya).
The meaning is "having a counter-correlativity delimited by a property that occurs in only one [locus]";
this applies again to "of inherence" (*samavāyasya*) through repetition.
The inherence of that object [the universal] is construed with the substratum-ness (ādheyatā) residing in the meaning of the verbal root; and thus,
it resides in inherence.

The cognition is as follows: mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) is that which is defined by a counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) delimited by a property residing in only one [of two things], and it possesses a subsistence (vṛttitva) characterized by inherence (samavāya).
The meaning of the word *iti* is the form "thus" (*ityākāraka*);
and its [connection] is by way of the relation of non-difference (*abheda-sambandha*).

The word *brū* (to speak), which is of the nature of sound and serves as the cause for the production of knowledge, is syntactically connected (*anvaya*) with "knowledge" (*jñāna*), which is a part of its own meaning. That [knowledge], in turn, is connected with the action denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*).
And in the present context, such knowledge is related [to the action] by way of the relation of "favorability" (*anukūlatā*).
It should be understood as having the form of a mental construct;
therefore, there is no harm even if its nature as a word-form is impossible in the present context.

In the *Prakāśikā* [64], regarding the phrase "to the inherence of form" (*rūpasamavāya*), this is the intended meaning: erroneousness with respect to a particular qualifier through a specific relation consists in having a qualifier delimited by that relation, while being delimited by a subject-ness (*viśeṣyakatva*) that is delimited by the absence of that [qualifier] as qualified by its counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) as delimited by that same relation.
And that [definition] remains entirely intact in the cognition "Air possesses color by way of inherence.

Furthermore, being a true cognition (pramātva) having that as its qualifier by way of that relation is not constituted by the property of having a qualificandum-ness whose relatum is that relation as characterized by that true cognition; rather, it is—

It is constituted by the property of having as its qualificandum a substratum of the relatum-ness (anuyogitā) of that relation, which is characterized by a relational determination (nirūpakatā) delimited by the state of being the counter-correlate (pratiyogikatva) of that [property].
In the case of air, which is devoid of color,
the relatum-ness of non-inherence (asamavāya) determined by a relational determination delimited by the state of being the counter-correlate of color is not admitted.
Thus, there is no contingency of such a cognition being a valid knowledge (*pramā*). Likewise,
because it is accepted that the state of being the relatum (*anuyogitva*)— qualified by being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of that [absence] and determined by that [absence]—
is pervaded by the existence of that [thing] through that relation, [the cognition] does not [arise] with respect to air.

With the intention that there would otherwise follow the consequence of possessing color by way of inherence in that which possesses inherence characterized by the counter-correlativity of color, the word "direction" (diś) was stated. This concludes the description of earth.
In the *Dīpikā* [65], it says "in accordance with the order of the enumeration," and so forth.
The meaning of the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is "being employed.

This refers to a cognition whose qualificandum is a specific earth-element—which is a constituent of the aggregate of earth and so forth that is non-different from the time prior to the statement of the definitions characterized by water and so on, which are themselves employed in accordance with such an enumeration—and whose mode is the definition.
The understanding is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to the word employed for the purpose of indicating knowledge.
In the *Prakāśikā*: [65] "In primacy" means in the state of being the first thing to be stated;
[66] "referring to the object to be defined."
The meaning is the complete enumeration of all things that serve as the basis for the primary characteristic under discussion.

Therefore, there is no persistence of the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), which denote jars and so forth that serve as the basis for the primary characteristic under discussion. And thus:

The intended meaning is that the qualification "cognition" (*bodha*) must be supplied with the property of having as its object everything up to the substratum of the primary definition (*prakṛtalakṣaṇāśraya*).
Regarding the phrase "the word 'only' (*mātra*)," some say: [66]...
The phrase "not having as its qualifier anything other than that which delimits the objecthood" (lakṣyatāvacchedaketarāprakārakatvam) is what is obtained by the word "only" (mātra).
The point is that since a definitional statement (lakṣaṇavākya) does not convey a definition other than that [specific one], there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case— so they say.
That is trivial;

for the word *mātra* has the function of conveying the exclusion of a connection with anything other than the object denoted by the word uttered in its proximity, as in the case of "here on this ground..."

In expressions such as "there is a jar" (*dhaṭo 'sti*), because of the established linguistic usage, what is obtained [from the word] is precisely its function of conveying a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is because [the word] conveys the exclusion of relations other than that which delimits the state of being indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
Because the contradiction with established linguistic usage is evident;

for the comprehension of the relation between two word-meanings alone constitutes verbal cognition, and thus, ultimately, even that which has the number of the base-meaning as its qualifier [is included].

Because a verbal cognition having earth (*pṛthivī*) and so forth as its qualificandum is possible, and because a verbal cognition that does not have anything other than the delimitor of the indicatedness (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) as its qualifier is unestablished; and thus,

[the definition is] the state of being a collection that pervades the phonemehood (*varṇatva*) which is the substratum of any objective content (*viṣayatā*) belonging to some knowledge that delimits the generality of the cause for producing a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the delimitor of the indicatedness.
This is the definition of the general indication (*uddeśa*);
therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to parts such as earth and so forth.
And suchness of being a collection—

It should be qualified by being the counter-correlative of a subsistence-inferiority residing in such a collection-ness (*samudāyatva*). By this, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in sentences such as those defining *lakṣaṇā*.
And such collection-ness [is defined] by means of the relation of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
This is the basis for the application of the term *uddeśapada*.

Therefore, there is no fault even if its locus (*āśraya*) is partially common [to other things], because the property of being a collection (*samudāyatva*) is introduced as residing distributively (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*). Hence—

Even if there is no commonality (*ananugama*) in that [property] consisting of being the object of a specific cognition (*dhīviśeṣa*), there is no harm. And if it is argued that this approach is not sound because "objecthood" (*viṣayatva*) does not subsist distributively (*avyāsajyavṛtti*), then one must state as the definition of the subject (*uddeśalakṣaṇa*) simply: "the possession of a property that pervades such phonemic-ness" (*tādṛśavarṇatvavyāpakadharmavattva*).

And because it is accepted that there is a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) whereby being such a property (*tādṛśadharmatva*) serves to convey the property that delimits the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakadharma*), there is no room for the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Even though, in order to avoid a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of verbal cognition dependent on another synonymous term, the state of being immediately subsequent to the knowledge of that specific term must necessarily be included within the defining property of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka), [if one were to] include the object (viṣaya) therein...
The cognition is: "one who possesses an effort conformable to the word that is to be applied for a purpose.
In the *Prakāśikā*: [65] "In being primary" means in being the first thing to be stated;
[66] "ending with the object to be characterized."
The meaning is the complete enumeration of all things that serve as the basis for the primary definition (prakṛtalakṣaṇā).
Therefore, there is no persistence of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), which denote jars and so forth that serve as the basis for the primary definition. And thus:
The meaning is that the qualification "cognition" (*bodha*) should be specified as "possessing an objectivity that culminates in all things which serve as the basis for the primary definition.
Regarding the phrase "the word 'only' (*mātra*)," some say: [66]...
The meaning of the word "only" (*mātra*) is the state of not having anything other than the delimitor of the object of definition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) as its qualifier.
The point is that since the definitional statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) does not convey a definition other than that [specific one], there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case— so they say.
That is trivial;
for in this context, the word "only" (*mātra*) conveys the exclusion of any connection with another object co-referential with the term it is uttered alongside.
Because, in cases such as "there is a jar on the ground," one is already proficient [in the usage], it is precisely the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that is conveyed by the word;
for [the word] does not convey the exclusion of any relation other than that which delimits the indicatedness (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
Because the contradiction with established linguistic usage is evident;

for verbal cognition consists precisely in the awareness of the relation between two word-meanings, and thus, ultimately, even that which has the number of the base-meaning as its qualifier [is included].

Since a verbal cognition (śābdabodha) having earth (*pṛthivī*) and so forth as its qualificandum is possible, and because a verbal cognition that does not have anything other than the delimitor of the indicatedness (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) as its qualifier is unestablished; and thus,

[the definition is] the state of being a collection pervading the phonemehood (*varṇatva*) which is the locus of any objective content (*viṣayatā*) belonging to some cognition that serves as the delimitor of the generality of the cause for producing a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the delimitor of the indicatedness.
This is the definition of the enumeration;
therefore, there is no over-extension to parts such as earth and so forth.
Such is the nature of the collection.
And it [the property] should be qualified by being the counter-correlative (*nirūpaka*) of a subsistence-in-a-less-extensive-locus (*nyūnavṛttitā*) residing in such a collection (*samudāyatva*).
By this, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in sentences such as those defining *lakṣaṇā*.
And such "collection-ness" (*samudāyatva*) is...
The basis for the application of the subject-term is by way of the relation of pervasion (vyāpti).
Therefore, there is no defect even if that [pervasion] is common to a portion [of the locus] by virtue of being its substratum.
The inclusion of "being a collection" (samudāyatva) is by virtue of its existing as a distributed property (vyāsajyavṛttitva);
therefore, [this applies] to that which consists in being the object of a specific cognition.
There is no harm even in following that [position].
And if it is argued that this approach is not sound because objecthood (*viṣayatva*) does not subsist non-distributively (*avyāsajyavṛtti*), then:
The definition of the subject (uddeśalakṣaṇa) must be stated as the possession of a property that pervades such color-ness.

And since it is accepted that there is a linguistic convention whereby [the definition] conveys the property that delimits the qualificand (viśeṣyatāvacchedaka) by virtue of being such a property, there is no room for the fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Even though...

In order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of verbal cognition arising from the study of synonyms or alternative words, it is necessary to include "the state of being immediately subsequent to the cognition of each respective word" within the definition of the effect-determinant (*kāryatāvacchedaka*). Since there is no purpose for including the object (*viṣaya*) therein [in that specific context], [it is not included].

It is impossible for the property of being delimited by the state of having "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) and so forth as its qualifier— which serves as the delimitor of the target— to reside in the producedness [of verbal cognition]. Nevertheless,
it is precisely the producedness delimited by the state of being a verbal cognition occurring immediately after the cognition of each respective word that must be included in the definition.

Therefore, there is no fault. [The definition is: that which pervades the phoneme-ness (*varṇatva*) residing in any object of a cognition that serves as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the generative power (*janakatā*)—which is itself delimited by the state of being a verbal cognition (*śābdatva*) produced immediately after the cognition of the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*).

And that very property which is defined by a subsistence-in-a-smaller-domain residing in such a collection of pervaders is to be understood as the definition for each respective subject (*uddeśa*), according to the principle that "the definition of earth is the property residing in such a collection of pervaders.
Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of uniformity (*ananugama*) due to the inclusion of the term "something-ness" (*kiñcitva*).
Because what is intended is the possession of a property qualified by a locushood (adhikaraṇatā) as determined by such a generative capacity (janakatā).

And this qualification [of the locushood] is by way of the relation of possessing a difference whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, which delimitation is delimited by the relation of being the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of a difference co-located with itself.
[The relation is] by way of the property of being a locus of its own [absence], which is the substratum of a subjectivity (*viṣayatā*) qualified by that [absence] and qualified by itself.

As for the "being qualified by that which is qualified by itself" (*svaviśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭya*) within that subjectivity, it is by way of the two relations: (1) being the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the generative capacity (*janakatā*) whose delimiting factor is itself, and (2) being resident in a cognition whose locus is itself.

And "being different from that which does not reside in what is subordinate to the locus of such a property" means being other than that which is qualified by such a property through the two relations of: (1) residing in something that possesses a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by itself (*sva*), and (2) being in co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with itself.

The relation that results [in the definition] is, by virtue of being a constituent of the qualification of the locus-hood (*adhikaraṇatā*), the relation of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimitorhood residing in itself, which is in turn delimited by the relation of being qualified by a property qualified by itself.

For this very reason, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in the statement "the earth possesses fragrance"; such is the path cultivated by me alone. Now, one might object: "But [the earth] is composed of parts that are both fragrant and non-fragrant."
In the sentence from the *Dīpikā*, by virtue of the analysis (*vigraha*) "begun by such parts," it is understood that there is the possession of an action (*kṛti*) produced by those very same parts;
this is because the root *rabh* is preceded by the prefix *ā*.
Because the suffix *kta* denotes an initial action,
its meaning as that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is inconsistent.
Because action (*kṛti*) is a property belonging solely to the self (*ātman*), he says: "[66] In the case of that which is begun, it is produced (*janya*); *u* (indeed) [it is so].
"[66] Because of mutual contradiction (*parasparavirodha*). Contradiction here means the state of being an obstacle (*pratibandhakatva*); in that regard—

And mutualness (*parasparatva*) consists in being related to that which is the locus of the obstruence (*pratibandhakatā*) as determined by its own locus; this amounts to being qualified by the obstruence, by virtue of the two relations of "subsisting in the locus of its own determiner" and "subsisting in its own locus."
[66] Regarding the case of "the foul odor in relation to the fragrant odor," and so forth;
here, in relation to the fragrant odor by way of inherence (*samavāya*)—

By virtue of the force of our cognition, [the absence of odor]— either as the absence of foul odor whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of inherence, or simply as the absence of fragrant odor whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of inherence— is understood to be the cause by virtue of its existence at the time of the effect.

The point is that when both a fragrant and a non-fragrant [substance] arise through inherence (*samavāya*) while remaining unrelated to one another, neither fragrance arises because of the absence of the cause— namely, the absence of an obstructing factor— at the time of the effect's production.

As for the description that, by means of inherence (*samavāya*), foul odor (*asurabhigandha*) and the like act as an inhibitor with respect to fragrant odor (*surabhigandha*) through the relation of inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-what-is-inherent-in-itself (*svasamavāyisamavetasamavāya*)— that, however, [is incorrect].
It is not to be accepted due to the complexity (*gaurava*) of the relation that delimits the state of being an obstructer (*pratibandhakatāvacchedaka-sambandha*),
such as "by way of the relation of inherence in what is inherent in its own locus" (*svāśraya-samavetatva-sambandhena*), and so forth.
In this context, [the property to be proved] possesses a delimited relativity (*avacchinna-saṃsargatākatva*).
This is the meaning of the third case (instrumental). And that [meaning] connects with "pratītau" in the phrase "tacca pratītisaṃbhavena.
The meaning of the third case is "being the instrument of accomplishment" (prayojyatva).
It should be understood that its role as a causal factor in the perception of smell through inherence (*samavāya*) functions by way of the defect of error (*bhramadoṣa*).

As stated in the *Dīpikā* [65]: "Because variegated smell (*citragandha*) is not admitted. Thus, the sense is that since variegated smell does not exist, there is indeed a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

In the *Prakāśikā*, however, it is said "let the wicked be satisfied" according to the maxim *tuṣyatu durjanaḥ*. Herein lies the intention: a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is produced from two atoms (*paramāṇu*), one possessing a fragrant odor and the other a non-fragrant odor.
Thereupon, [the substance] arises through the sequence beginning with the triad (tryaṇuka) up to the great composite whole;
in that case, the perception of odor in a jar is certainly not admitted, because of the absence of odor in its constituent parts, such as the potsherds.
Because odor is impossible [in that context] and because the odor of an atom is not an object of sensory perception;
however, in reality,
even though the odor of an atom lacks the status of being an object of ordinary sensory perception, [it exists].
Through a mediated relation consisting of its own inherence,

a non-ordinary (alaukika) perception of the smell of that atom is indeed possible there. And if you insist that an ordinary cognition in the form "this [substance] possesses smell" arises, then let it be a variegated smell (citragandha).

Thus [ends the section]. Regarding the phrase "co-referential with odor" (*gandhasamānādhikaraṇa*), the meaning here should also be understood as before; otherwise, there would be a fault according to the previous method.

Now, one might object: "Is not 'lower than substanceness' (dravyatvāparatva) simply 'the state of being different from that which is different from substance'? And if so, how does this avoid the fault of being impossible? To this, he says: "[66] It means 'subsisting in a narrower extension than substanceness'."

Why is it that "not occurring in that which lacks substanceness" (*dravyatvābhāvavadavṛttitvam*) is not introduced precisely for the purpose of excluding existence (*sattā*)? To this he says: "By that," and "the exclusion of substanceness."
Although *dravyatva* (substanceness) does not reside in that which possesses its own absence, it lacks the property of being the counter-positive of an absence that is co-locative with itself;

therefore, the term "universal" (*jāti*) is included in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by taking into account the possession of such a property through the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*).
Only eternity is intended here,
because the property of inhering in many things does not serve to exclude [the subject] in the present context.
Because the property of being either earth or water lacks co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) as constituted by the relation of inherence (samavāya);
[this is said] with respect to the temporal relation (kālika-sambandha).

In order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by taking into account the possession of such a property [in a general sense], it is necessary to intend the possession of such a property specifically through *samavāya* (inherence); for, since the aforementioned "either-or" nature (*anyataratva*) does not apply [to the definition], no fault arises.
Furthermore, even duality (*dvitva*) and so forth in earth and water consist essentially in being the object of a specific enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).
The exclusion [of the objection] should be understood as being due solely to the absence of permanence (*nityatva*),
namely through the relation of "being conjoined with its own substratum" (*svāśraya-saṃyuktatva*), and so forth;
here too, the meaning is exactly as before.
It is to be described by way of being concomitant—
meaning, by way of being distinct from the delimitor of the locusness residing in itself.
If the definition of a "constituent part" (lakṣaṇa) such as a potsherd were [defined] by a relation that is not a delimiter of the locus-ness (ādheyatā) of all ultimate entities,
there would be the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti) to things like the ground when a pot or similar object is conjoined with it;
the same applies to inherence (samavāya) and other relations.
In such a form, even the status of being a relation is without authoritative basis. "In reality," however— this is what is to be understood.
The meaning is that smell is the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of earth by way of inherence (samavāya), and a jar is the defining characteristic of its potsherd by way of inherence.
Regarding the classification of earth,
it is twofold— eternal and non-eternal— within the summary [of the elements].
That which has two kinds (vidhā) is "dvividhā"; "vidhā" means a classifying property (vibhājakadharma), that is to say,
a property directly pervaded by the delimitor of the scope of the subject (uddeśyatāvacchedaka), such as "earthness" (pṛthivītva) and so forth.

Since it is universally accepted that in a *bahuvrīhi* compound there is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) of the final member in the sense of another referent (*anyapadārtha*), in the present case, the word "vidhā" possesses a conventional metaphorical indication in the sense of that which possesses the class-property (*vibhājakadharma*) which is the substratum of the number two.
The word "dvi" serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*).

In the case of "eternal" and "non-eternal," there is a connection with the property of being either eternal or non-eternal in the instance of earth; for it is accepted that such an understanding applies everywhere in cases involving sentences of division (*vibhāga*). This concludes the [explanation of the] word.
It indicates a qualification containing a reason (*hetugarbhaviśeṣaṇa*).
And thus, the understanding is: "Since it is so, therefore the earth possesses such a property as being the locus of duality."
For this very reason, the feminine gender of the words *nityā* and *anityā* is justified, since they stand in grammatical apposition with the word *pṛthivī*.
As for the claim that the terms "eternal" and "non-eternal" refer respectively to eternality and non-eternality,
and that these two are connected by a relation of identity (abheda-sambandha) within the differentiating property (vibhājaka-dharma)— this is [incorrect].
That is trivial,
because the non-difference of both is impossible within a property that serves as a differentiator.

Because there is no word expressive of "either one of the two," it is impossible to convey the distinction between either permanence or impermanence; furthermore, there is no evidence for the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of those two.

Since the cognition of any given meaning through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is experienced as being produced even from a word possessing primary denotative power (*śakti*), there would result the undesirable consequence of using such an expression as "Earth is of two kinds: permanence and impermanence," [where the latter terms are understood through indication].

With respect to verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), [the cause] is the knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) denoted by some word co-occurring with the word *iti*, which is itself co-occurring with the word *vidhā*, [this knowledge being mediated] by the relation of subjectness (*prakāratā*)— delimited by the relation of non-difference (*abheda*)— which is in turn determined by the subjectness residing in the classifying property (*vibhājakadharma*) that delimits the meaning of the word *vidhā*.
Because it would entail a great complexity (mahāgaurava) in postulating [the atom] as an obstructer and so forth. Now, the atom is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.
Substance is of two kinds: earth and water.
If it is argued that this results in the application [of the suffix] *cvi*, we say no;
for in the bahuvrīhi compound beginning with "dvividha" (twofold),
as many properties as are perceived are understood as the referent of the word *vidhā*.

There is a conventional (nirūḍha) indication (lakṣaṇā) for that which possesses a property qualified by duality and so forth— where such qualification consists in being the object of a specific cognition whose object is merely the property itself.
And this "being qualified" [is as follows]:

There is no fault [in the definition], because it is based on the dual relation of being the locus of that which is directly pervaded by its own pervader—such as earthness (*pṛthivītva*)—and being the locus of itself.

Since it is accepted that there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with such a property (being a substance) delimited by the delimitor of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), namely earthness and so forth, [the objection] that "substance is of two kinds: earth and water" does not apply.
This is the application of the argument beginning with "ceti" and so forth.
Although permanence and impermanence, being common to water and other elements, are not pervaded by earthness and the like, nevertheless—

The status of those two [earth and water] as such is unimpaired by virtue of their relation to their own nature (*svarūpa*) as qualified by being any one of the [universals] such as earthness (*pṛthivītva*).
Furthermore, the word "directly" [is used because] "earth is of three kinds... [and so forth].
This is for the purpose of excluding such formal arguments as "the cloth is both eternal and non-eternal.
The same method applies even in cases such as "water is of two kinds— eternal and non-eternal."

And if, on the other hand, [the passage] beginning with "Furthermore, it is threefold— due to the distinction between body, sense-faculties, and objects" is considered to have as its purpose the classification of the general category of earth;

If it is considered that the cognition must be stated in the form "Earth is that which possesses a property directly pervaded by earthness, qualified by the number three induced by such a difference," then [properties such as] being a body and so forth would be inconsistent because they lack such a state of being pervaded. This is how it is analyzed.
The state of being directly pervaded by the delimitor of the intended object (uddeśyatāvacchedaka), such as earth-ness (pṛthivītva) and so forth, need not be included [in the definition].
This is because there is a linguistic convention for perceiving the mutual lack of co-location (vaiyadhikaraṇya) among the classifying properties (vibhājakadharma).
Since it is accepted that [earth] is of two kinds in such passages as "it is twofold," there is no occasion for the usage: "Earth is threefold: eternal, non-eternal, and a jar."
And thus, in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound,
there is a conventional (*nirūḍha*) secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for that which possesses the property of a substratum qualified by such duality.
As for "qualification" (*vaiśiṣṭya*):
By means of the two relations of identity and possession of distinctions such as "being one's own" (svaseta),

the delimitation of the counter-correlativity of difference is delimited by itself, which is qualified by its residing in that which is co-locative with the earthness (pṛthivītva) and so forth that serve as the delimiters of the subjecthood (uddeśyatā).

In that case, there is a single delimitorship (avacchedakatā) distinct from eternality, which is delimited by the relation consisting of both: (1) the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by that [specific] delimitorship, and (2) the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimitorship residing in that [specific] delimitorship.

[The relation is] by way of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, [the latter] being delimited by the relation of occurring at a time that resides in the locus of its own substratum.

Now, one might object: does the statement "earth is of three kinds" refer to a general classification of earth, or to a classification of *kārya*-earth (effect-earthen substances)? It cannot be the first.
The first [alternative] is not possible because eternal earth cannot be included within things such as bodies;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because it contradicts the natural force of the word "again" (punaḥ).
Therefore, since the prior division of that which is delimited by a certain property is indicated here as a division of that very same thing delimited by that property, but in another form,
he says "here" in the *Prakāśikā* [70].
And likewise, in passages such as "furthermore, it is of three kinds," there is a classification of earth in its general sense;
and in the statement "the object consists of clay, stone, and so forth," [it refers to that same general category].

Because it is possible for the word "beginning" (*ādi*) to include atoms (*paramāṇu*); and because of the division [of earth] into terrestrial (*bhauma*), celestial (*divya*), digestive (*audarya*), and mineral (*ākara-ja*), even in the context of the classification of the objects of light (*taijasa*), the term "terrestrial" (*bhauma*) is derived from the analysis "this belongs to the earth" (*bhūmeḥ idam*), and thus refers primarily to that which is related to the earth. By that very [term],...

The sense is that it is due to the collection of fiery atoms (*taijasaparamāṇu*). Regarding the phrase "they describe," the lack of naturalness (*asvārasya*) in this word is the seed for the subsequent objection.
This is what must be understood here: regarding the phrase "furthermore,
it is threefold due to the distinction between body, sense organs, and objects," [the term] "sense organ" is used here as the counter-correlative to "body."

The word "difference" (*bheda*), specifically in the sense of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), is construed with the body and so forth through any one of the following relations: (1) the relation of being the locus of the property of residing in that which possesses either the counter-correlativity or [the state of being] the counter-correlate; or (2) the relation of being the locus of the property of residing in that which possesses either the counter-correlativity of the object or the counter-correlativity of the counter-correlate—in accordance with the maxim "two things in one place.
The meaning of the ablative case is "being brought about by" (*prayojyatva*).

The understanding is that [the object] possesses a classifying property (vibhājaka-dharma) qualified by a threefoldness that resides in the difference specified by the body and so forth. Furthermore, the role of difference as the motivator [of the classification] occurs through the mediation of a conceptual cognition (buddhi) of expectation dependent upon its own knowledge. In the manner described, the understanding in other cases should also be inferred.
And "distinctiveness" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is as before. 1. Regarding the phrase "possessing a difference from its own [locus]" (*svasetyādibhedavattve*):

the meaning is "the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) has as its delimitation (*avacchedaka*) a delimitation residing in itself (*svaniṣṭha*), which is delimited by the relation of being the delimitation of the counter-correlativity of a difference that is co-locational with itself (*svasamānādhikaraṇabhedapratiyogitāvacchedakatvasambandhāvacchinna*)."
[69] "The object consists of earth, stone, and so forth.

By the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) of that which has earth, stone, and so forth as its beginning, the understanding is that the object consisting of earth is that which characterizes the state of being the substratum (*niṣṭhatā*) of earth, stone, and so forth.

The so-called "being the beginning" (*tadāditva*) of that which is delimited by a property (*dharmāvacchinna*) consists in its being qualified by the locus-ness (*ādheyatā*) relative to that [property], as residing in the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*). As for this qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*):
[The relation is] by way of the relation of possessing that property as qualified by the nature of the property residing in its own substratum (*svāśrayadharmatāviśiṣṭataddharmavattva*).

And the state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of the dual relation consisting of: (1) being the delimitor (*avacchedakatva*) of the denotability (*pratipādyatā*) of the word preceding the word that denotes [the property] as delimited by a property pervaded by itself (*svavyāpyadharmāvacchinnabodhakapadapūrvapadapratipādyatāvacchedakatva*), and (2) being pervaded by itself (*svavyāpyatva*).

Some, however, [define] "being the first" (*āditva*) as being a constituent of the aggregate that is the object of the knowledge whose own object it is. Here, "itself" (*sva*) refers to the object, such as the earth element (*pārthiva*). And thus:
The meaning is: that which is the object of a cognition whose content is a collection including clay, stone, and so forth,
and which is the determiner of the membership of that collection composed of clay, stone, etc., is the "earthly object" (*pārthiva-viṣaya*).

They explained [it thus]: because being a collection of threads consists in being the object of a particular cognition, when each individual substance is known specifically, it is impossible to define "collection-ness" itself;
furthermore, this is impossible for a non-omniscient living being with respect to each of those individual substances.
Because its own state of being pervaded is included within the scope of the relationship,
the statement "the object consists of clay, stone, water, and so forth" does not [apply].

Validity. And here, pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) consists in being co-located with that [the probandum], while being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference that is co-located with it.

But it is not [the definition] "not occurring in that which lacks it. Therefore, there is no inconsistency regarding the validity of such statements as "Earth and so forth are cognizable" (*prameya*).

Furthermore, because the condition of being a truth-constituent (*satyantāniveśāt*) is not met, sentences such as "Earth is a substance, etc.; it possesses odor, etc. lack validity. Moreover, because the condition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyaniveśāt*) is not met, the sentence "clay, stone, etc.
lacks validity. Enough of this excessive detail. [70] Thus ends the section.
Here, what is intended by "being a final whole" (*antyāvayavitva*) is the state of being different from that which is non-co-referential with substance (*dravyasamānādhikaraṇabhinnatva*).
Now, one might ask: why is the genus "body-ness" (*śarīratvajāti*) itself not stated as the definition of a body?
In the same way, a sense faculty (indriya) also possesses the universal (jāti) of being a sense faculty.
Nor is there a lack of evidence for the status of "bodiness" (śarīratva) and so forth as universals.

Since it is precisely the inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) is "being denotable by the word" that possesses such a nature, he says: "corporeality" (*śarīratva*). [This means: "Being denotable by the word 'body' is delimited by some property."
The meaning is that of the inference: "Because it is the state of being denotable by the word *pada*, like the state of being denotable by the word *ghaṭa*.

[In the definition of a sense organ] beginning with "other than sound" (*śabdetara*), the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is redundant, because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not pervaded by the genus (*jāti*) consisting of the property of being manifested (*udbhūtatva*).
Therefore, in order to make that term meaningful, he says:
"Being produced is not a genus."
[70] "Because of the confusion [caused] by the claim that [the caste] possesses white [complexion], etc."— *saṅkara* itself is *sāṅkarya*.
The suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of the base word itself, according to the rule governing words such as *cāturvarṇya*.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the preceding text which states that it is due to confusion (*saṅkara*) with respect to "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth;
for [otherwise] the status of being a cause would be untenable.

This must be considered here: even if one accepts that there are multiple non-manifest [qualities] subsumed under whiteness and so forth, it is easy to state that they possess a single causal efficacy toward visual perception by virtue of being "any one of those non-manifest [qualities].

This is because, regarding the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified among the individual differences (bheda) that constitute the property of being "any one of them" (anyatamatva), [the relation is established].
However, one should not suspect a lack of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*),

because even in the view that "manifestness" (*udbhūtatva*) consists of a collection (*kūṭa*) of the absences of each respective non-manifestness, [the same applies to] the nature of being a collection (*kūṭatva*).

Because there is an equal lack of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding the qualifier-qualified relationship among the various instances of "having that object" when they are defined as being of the nature of the objects of specific cognitions of those respective objects;

and because the property of "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) is required to exclude the visual perception of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth by taking conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other such relations into account.

Furthermore, because both *rūpatva* (the property of being color) and such *udbhūtatva* (manifestness) would have to be included within the scope of the delimiting condition (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) of causality, there would arise the fault of excessive complexity (*mahāgaurava*) due to the lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding which of these two should stand in the relation of qualifier and qualificand (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatāvacchedakabhāva*).
Regarding the term "viśeṣa" (particularity):
it means "distinct from general qualities" (*sāmānyaguṇa*).

It should be understood that the word "guṇa" (quality) is included in order to prevent the impossibility [of the definition's application] by taking "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth as the referent.
"In the absence of form" means in the absence of manifest form;
therefore, it does not [apply] to non-existence.
The impossibility of fitness [is due to its] being a constituent of the contact (*sannikarṣa*). This is the intended meaning here:
The state of being a cause of cognition consists in being invariably antecedent to cognition, and this remains entirely intact in the case of the contact between the eye and time; otherwise,
in the absence of the qualifier-relationship (viśeṣaṇatā) as determined by the contact with the eye, [cognition would not arise] with respect to time.
"Because the direct perception of the absence of form is untenable. [71] "The word 'mind' (manas) [is used];
there is no pleasure in time."
Perception, however, is simply not possible here,
because it is accepted that the contact between the self and the mind of a different class is the cause for cognition in general.

And thus, the intention is that the aforementioned qualification was introduced for the sake of universal applicability across all systems, out of fear of the excessive complexity (gaurava) involved in incorporating every distinct set of particulars.
This is stated with the aim of explaining the purpose [of the definition].

By this, the means of valid cognition consisting of inference regarding the olfactory faculty is also indicated. For instance: the direct perception of odor has as its instrument a sense-faculty distinct from the mind, because it is a direct perception of a general property other than mental [perception].

In order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)— since [the self] is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to the general class of visual cognitions such as those of a jar—

and in order to avoid the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of mental direct perception (*mānasasākṣātkāra*), the term "distinct from the mind" (*manobhinna*) is included in the body of the probandum (*sādhya*), while [the qualification] is placed within the scope of the reason (*hetu*).
"Thus it should be understood in the subsequent cases.
The phrase "co-inherent with cold touch" (śītasparśasamānādhikaraṇa) refers to "coldness" (śītatva), which is a specific universal residing in touch.
This is for the sake of indication.
It should be understood in the same way even in summary statements such as "water possesses the quality of cold touch" (*śītasparśavatya āpaḥ*). Not [otherwise].
But even that is included within the definition;
likewise for what follows. This concludes the examination of fire.
In the *Saṅgraha*, he explains the bahuvrīhi compound as "that for which lightning and so forth, being without fuel, are the waters that serve as fuel.
However, some explain it in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

If the word *indhana*, ending in a *lyuṭ* suffix, were to stand in grammatical apposition with the word *āp* (water), it would follow the gender of its substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*), resulting in a feminine form; consequently, the suffix *ṅīp* would be improperly applied according to the rule *aṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*.

Because [the term] "without fuel" (*abindhana*) would imply that form (*rūpa*) is not produced, it ought to be stated as "that which has no fuel" (*abindhanika*); furthermore, since the word "fuel" (*indhana*) does not possess such a status [of being a subordinate member], with the intention that the word "fuel" would otherwise result in being placed first [in a compound], [the author] employs a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi*.
He demonstrates this with the passage beginning "fuel by means of water" and so forth;
and thus they say that the word *indhana* (fuel) ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*, which denotes an abstract state (*bhāva*).
The doctrine that gold is of a luminous nature (suvarṇataijasatvavāda) [77], beginning with "of gold" and so forth;
this is the understanding, as well as the specific distinction (vaiśiṣṭya).

[The definition of a sentence is: by way of the two relations of being the object of the speaker's own desire to employ and having the same agent as its own object. With the intention that the statement "Gold is earthy" (*sūvarṇaṃ pārthivam*) from the *Dīpikā* contains an implicit restriction—based on the maxim that "every sentence, in the absence of a subverting factor, is restrictive"—he introduces it: 1. [The text follows...]

The meaning is: because it is not so [in reality], because it lacks coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "water," and because it lacks the quality of being dependent on the gender of its substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*).
2. Regarding the phrase beginning with "having as its object an operation" (*vyāpāraviṣayaka*), etc.:
The operation (*vyāpāra*) consists in the establishment of one's own position.
"Impelled by its own purpose" (*svaprayojya*) means:
its own [purpose] is the desire directed toward the object of the operation; it is impelled by that.

The desire in the form "I shall formulate the prima facie argument" has as its object that [act of formulation]; thus, it is the effort conducive to the prima facie argument. Likewise, one's own desire whose object is an operation has that operation as its object, as well as the state of having the same agent.
In such a construction:
"having gold as the qualificand," etc.;
[this refers to] the first [instance of] the end of the qualified [term].
The second qualified object is construed with the effort (*kṛti*) which is the operation conducive to the removal of doubt;
the first qualification [of that object] is by way of both the relation of being prompted by it and the relation of co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*);
the second qualification is—
[The definition is] by way of the two relations: being the object of the desire of one's own agent, and having the same agent as that which has oneself as its object.
[This is stated] with the words "proving earthiness," etc. Therefore, because gravity (gurutva) deviates in water, it is impossible for it to be a prover of earthiness.

The objection that it is improper to state a reason proving that [the object] lacks luminosity— since one must state precisely what proves the absence of luminosity, and that absence of luminosity is not obtained from the statement of the thesis— is without foundation.
Because the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*)— namely, that "gold is indeed earthen"— is what is to be expressed,
and because the word "only" (*eva*) therein conveys the absence of its being composed of light (*taijasa*). By this,
it means by the statement of the reason (*hetu*) that establishes the absence of its being composed of light.

[77] "Digi" means this: since it has been established that earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is the cause of yellow color (*pītarūpa*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*), through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), if gold were of the nature of light (*taijasa*), then its yellow color would be of a different genus (*vijātīya*).
A separate causal factor would have to be postulated;
however, if it were earthen (pārthiva), such a postulation would not be necessary—this constitutes parsimony (*lāghava*). Thus, supported by this reasoning (*tarka*), [the conclusion is that] gold...

The inference, "It possesses either earth-ness or its absence, because it is an object of cognition," is possible as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the earth-ness of that [gold]; thus,
gold is the substratum of yellowness and weight, and so forth.

The understanding is as follows: [the subject] possesses an effort conducive to establishing a favorable *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum), which is qualified by a desire for an operation conducive to removing a doubt regarding non-implication (*aprayojakatva*)—a doubt whose object is an inference qualified by the property of being a conclusion, and which is further qualified by a desire to state a reasoning conducive to a certainty that is not overridden by a grasp of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) having as its qualifier the state of being distinct from the locus of yellowness and heaviness, with gold as its qualificandum. [77] Regarding the phrase "provided there is no obstacle," etc.:
the meaning is "due to fluidity qualified by an absolute conjunction with fire, which is itself qualified by the absolute absence of obstacles."
The inclusion of "liquidity" (*dravatva*) is for the purpose of avoiding a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a pot conjoined with fire.
The two-fold relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) consists in the state of residing in a single locus delimited by a single moment.
[77] "That which is conjoined with an eternal fire is a yellow substrate," and so forth.
And herein, the phrase "conjoined with an eternal fire" [is used].

If the qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) were not included, then in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)— namely, with respect to a specific liquid substance that serves as the locus for a yellow color situated in the midst of water— the intended object of the inference must be an inference determined by a limiting condition (*avacchedakāvacchedena*).

The inclusion of that [term] is for the purpose of avoiding a contradiction (*bādha*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with turmeric insofar as it is the object to be spoken of;
likewise, there would be a contradiction through coreferentiality with ghee situated in the midst of water.

In order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), it must be stated that the intended object of inference is [the property] as delimited by its delimitor (*avacchedakāvacchedena*).
Furthermore, the property of being the locus of yellowness (*pītimāśrayatva*) is introduced to avoid partial sublation (*aṃśato bādha*) with respect to jars and the like.
Even so, there remains sublation with respect to such jars and other things that possess a yellow color; nevertheless...
Even so, there would still be a sublation (*bādha*) in the case of a jar or similar object possessing yellow color at a time immediately following [the destruction of the substrate]; nevertheless,

[the definition] refers specifically to the possession of yellow color qualified by a heterogeneous conjunction with fire (*vijātīyāgni-saṃyoga*), by way of the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) delimited by the moment immediately following that [conjunction].
The point is that there is no fault because the status of being the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedakatva*) is accepted.

The probans (*hetu*) is gravity accompanied by fluidity qualified by fire-contact, through the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which is defined as subsisting in the same substratum delimited by the moment immediately following [the contact].

The probandum (*sādhya*) is the state of being conjoined with another liquid substance which acts as an obstacle to the destruction of the liquidity inherent in itself. Nor is there a lack of comprehension regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), nor a deficiency in the probandum regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), due to the non-uniformity of "selfhood" (*svatva*) common to both the example and the subject.

Thus, regarding the phrase "by another liquid substance," it must be stated that if one intends to refer to a liquid substance that is the locus of its own mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), it is irrelevant and constitutes a case of being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*).
