Since it is accepted that the probandum (*sādhya*) consists in being qualified by a liquid substance (*dravadravya*) through a triad of relations— namely: (1) being conjoined with itself, (2) being the inherent locus of fluidity which is the counter-positive of a destruction that is itself obstructed by [the subject], and (3) possessing a cause that does not inhere in itself— the inclusion of the third relation within the body of the probandum is for the sake of establishing the intended object (*uddeśya*).
The inclusion of "heaviness" (gurutva) within the scope of the reason (*hetu*) is for the purpose of preventing deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to [ordinary] substance (*dravya*).
Even though, prior to the establishment of such a substance, [the property] therein...
Although there is no possibility of apprehending a deviation [of the reason], nevertheless,

if fluidity qualified by contact with an intense fire were pervaded by the aforementioned probandum, then it would establish that probandum within the delimitation of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka) of the present case.
To avoid an infinite regress, the term "gravity" (gurutva) is included; thus, water and so forth are taken as examples.
Here, "taking" (ādāna) means grasping, and that refers to the subject at hand.
It has the nature of being an object (*viṣayatā*).
The meaning of the suffix *lyap* is merely the identity of agent (*samānakartṛkatva*),
which is conjoined with the word-meaning that culminates in the nature of being an object.
And here, having the same agent means being determined by that which determines it.
In the expression "water and so forth," the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is the property of being located (*ādheyatva*).

And thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "the agent of an operation conducive to a cognition whose qualifier is possibility, which has as its locus a property other [than the subject], namely the state of being the object of an inference determined by that which determines the state of being the object residing in water and so forth.
[This refers to] the phrase beginning with "svasaṃyuktatva" (being conjoined with itself), and so on.

In the case of being supported [by water], its own substance is water, and its state of being conjoined with that [water] is maintained; in the case of being supported, its own water is that which obstructs it, the destruction of fluidity is its counter-positive, and its state of having that fluidity as its inherent cause (samavāyin) is maintained;
and in the case of being supported, its own water and its possession of the genus "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva-jāti), which does not inhere in that [water], are maintained.
The synthesis [of the example] consists in its being held within water; however,
in the case of the subject (pakṣa), it is the portion of luster residing in gold that is conjoined with the earthen portion.
The earthy portion possesses the quality of being the substratum of that fluidity which is the counter-positive of the destruction of fluidity obstructed by its own fiery portion;
the earthy portion also possesses the genus "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva), which does not inhere in that [fiery] portion, as it is the substratum of that genus.
Thus concludes the systematic exposition.
Now, regarding the definition of air (*vāyu*) in the *Dīpikā* [82]: "Air is to be inferred from touch."
And here, the term "contact" (*sparśa*) refers to the property of being contact (*sparśatva*);
by this, the conventional usage "the fire inferred from the mountain" is excluded.

The objection that "air is inferable from touch" would be inconsistent— on the grounds that the third case-ending must be accepted as having the sense of *prakāratā* (the mode of presentation) rather than the sense of *viśeṣyatā* (the qualificand)— is thereby refuted.
Alternatively, since it is intended that touch itself is the cause by way of the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), there is no inconsistency;
and the method of inference is as follows:
"The touch being perceived must be supported by something, because it is a touch, or because it is identical with its substrate,
like the touch of earth and so forth"— thus one infers air. And in this case:
In the word "vāyau" (in the air), the meaning of the locative case is "the sky" (*gagana*);
and that [sky] is construed with "perception" (*upalambha*) by way of the relation of being simultaneous (*samānakālīnatva*).

Although the statement of the reason and example as "because it is a quality, like color" is not appropriate— since that would contradict what was previously stated regarding its being inferable from touch— it is nevertheless intended as an illustration for inferences based on reasons such as "because it is tangibility."

It should be understood that another inference based on the reason of "being a quality" (*guṇatva*) has also been stated. In this context, it is argued: if that which is qualified by a perceptible touch were earth, then it would necessarily possess manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*).
If it were water and so forth, then it would not possess a touch that is neither hot nor cold;
if this [is] the touch...
If it were inherent in any one of the four [elements] beginning with space,
then it would be an object of ordinary perception for persons situated in another location;
if it were inherent in the mind, then it would not be an object of ordinary perception.
If this [air] possessed manifest touch and were inherent in earth, it would subsist where manifest color subsists;
if it were inherent in water and so forth, it would not be neither-hot-nor-cold;
and if the substratum of manifest touch were omnipresent, [it would follow that air is omnipresent].
If it were the mind, it would be the object of a tactile perception associated with a person located in another place;
[but] it is not the object of a tactile perception— by such logical arguments, this is "touch."
The point is that an inference of the form "there exists something inhering in something distinct from earth and so forth" arises.
[82] "Possessing manifested touch," and so forth.
And here, the word "manifest" (*udbhūta*) is used first in order to exclude deviation in the case of the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*);
for "manifestness" consists of an aggregate of absences (*abhāvakūṭa*).
Since that same fault would apply because [the quality of touch] exists even in the state of being a substance (*dravyatva*), the term "touch" (*sparśa*) is included.
To exclude that [quality of touch] from air (*vāyu*),
the inclusion of "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*) is made.
Since air also possesses non-manifest color and possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*), the inclusion of "manifest color" [in the definition of earth] is necessary.
And here, the fact that the substratum of the perceived touch is earth and so forth—
However, it is not the case that earth and the other elements are the substrata [of cognition].
Therefore, in order to avoid the fault of negating what is not even a candidate for such status, he provides the formulation beginning with "asya" (of this) and so forth.
In the *Dīpikā*, it says: "not the four all-pervading [entities]."
The meaning is that it is not any one of those [alternatives].

Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanaprasaṅga*), because both types of difference and so forth exist in a single instance; this is how it should be understood.
The moderns, however, describe air as being perceptible;
he restates their view in order to refute it: [83] "But surely, air is perceptible..."
By such [statements as] these. Now, an objection: perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) consists in being the object of perception;
and since it is admitted that air (*vāyu*) is also the object of extra-sensory mental perception (*alaukikamānasapratyakṣa*), this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
He says in the *Prakāśikā* [83]: "Perceptible" means an object of perception produced by the external sense organs.
Even though air also possesses the status of being an object of such extraordinary (alaukika) perception, that same defect remains as it was.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, because the intended meaning is that what is to be proven is the state of having a worldly object that is not determined by the mind (*mānasa*).
And the term "not determined" (*anirūpita*)...
This is stated in order to exclude other objects by taking "being an object of the mind" as the subject; for this very reason,
there is no room for the objection that the proposed upādhi lacks pervasion of the probandum (sādhya) with respect to the self (ātman), which will be discussed later.
Regarding the phrase "is perceived":

since the intended meaning is that it has as its locus an object belonging to the worldly domain (*laukika-viṣayatā*), there is no remaining state of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the tactile sense organ (*tvag-indriya*), which possesses touch as its object of worldly perception.
The term "touch-base" (*sparśapada*), however, refers to such categories as substantiality (*dravyatva*) which are the substrata of worldly objectivity (*laukikaviṣayatā*).
Even if one were to state "a quality that is the substratum of worldly objectivity," it would still include sound, which is the object of auditory perception (*śrāvaṇapratyakṣa*).
The mention of being a substratum is for the purpose of excluding deviation in the case of space (*ākāśa*),
and to indicate that touch (*sparśa*) is the cause by way of inherence (*samavāya*).

In the *Dīpikā* [83], regarding the phrase "of that which has manifested color" (*udbhūtarūpasya*), the word "manifested" (*udbhūta*) is an adjunct (*upādhi*) because certain ancient partial schools accept the existence of unmanifested color even in air (*vāyu*).
This is for the purpose of establishing that [the reason] does not pervade the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*).

As stated in the *Prakāśikā* [83]: "Because it is possible to infer the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the probandum (*sādhya*). This is because there is no deviation in relation to that which is not qualified by a form intended to be the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*).

Since deviation (*vyabhicāra*) as determined by a form that is intended to be the delimiting factor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*) serves as the inferential ground, and in the present case, it is precisely the deviation of perceptibility as qualified by the property of being a substance (*dravyatva*), which is the subject-attribute (*pakṣadharma*),
that can be inferred through the deviation of the pervader of the probandum as qualified by that [substance-property]; however, it is not [the case that...].
There is also deviation from the pure probandum (sādhya),

due to the absence of the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti). Nevertheless, when deviation from the qualified probandum is established through deviation from such a limiting condition (upādhi), [the probans is considered fallacious].

The sense is that, by means of the reason "occurring in that which possesses the absence of the qualified [subject] as characterized by the qualifier," one is subsequently able to infer "occurring in that which possesses the absence of the qualificand.
Alternatively, [this applies] when the subject possesses the property of the locus (*pakṣadharmin*).

By virtue of not pervading the probans (*sādhana*), it is possible to infer only the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the pure probandum (*sādhya*). Furthermore, "not pervading the probans" while residing in the locus of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmin*) consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that resides in a locus possessing the property of the subject which serves as the substratum of the probans. Thus...

And the state of being a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) consists in not being the counter-positive of an absence residing in that which possesses the property of the subject, which is the locus of the probandum. The same applies to other limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
It should be observed that,
in reality,
[it is characterized by] the emptiness of manifest form and substantiality (*dravyatva*).

The absence of both [the two conditions] is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), by virtue of the relation of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by its own absence— which itself has as its counter-correlativity a substratum-locus residing in substance, which is delimited by a locus-ness residing in itself, and which is further delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
Alternatively, manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is the limiting adjunct.
Because that [property] pervades the probandum (sādhya) by virtue of its existence even in form (rūpa) and so forth,
and because it does not pervade the probans (sādhana) by virtue of its non-existence in the subject (pakṣa), which is air (vāyu)—
this refers to the specific property (dharma-viśeṣa) as previously shown.

The mention of "pervading the probandum as delimited by the property of the subject" (pakṣadharmāvacchinnasādhyavyāpakatva) is intended precisely to indicate the status of being a limiting adjunct (upādhi).

Furthermore, the fourfold classification of limiting adjuncts is stated in various contexts for the purpose of securing the status of a limiting adjunct for a specific intended property, and for securing the status of a delimitor of the limiting adjunct for a specific intended relation.
Or rather, this is the path exclusively cultivated by me alone;
for some, however,
[it arises] from the apprehension of the pervasion of the qualified non-deviation, assisted by the ascertainment of the non-deviation of the qualifier.
They say that this establishes the deviation of the qualified [subject];
but that is incorrect, because the deviation of the qualified is simply the occurrence of the absence of the qualified, and not—
The deviation of the qualified [subject] that is not accompanied by the deviation of the qualifier;
for such [deviation] is impossible in cases such as "possessing perceptible touch."
Regarding the phrase "the absence of manifested color":
this is because, in qualities such as color, there exists the absence of both [manifested color and substance] due to the absence of substantiality;
and because, in substances such as a jar, there exists the absence of both [manifested color and substance] due to the absence of the absence of manifested color.
This [property] possesses pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) over the probandum (*sādhya*), which consists in being the object of a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) produced by an external sense organ.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the relation of inherence" (*samavāyasambandha*), etc.: the term "intrinsic" (*svābhāvīya*) means "as determined by its own absence" (*svābhāvanirūpita*).
The connection [of the property] resides in the substratumness that is grounded in substance (*dravya*).

Although the property of being defined by the absence of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) exists in the substratumness that is grounded in color (*rūpa*) and so forth, it does not possess the quality of being grounded in substance.
Since the state of possessing itself (*svavattva*)—
that is, the state of possessing manifest color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*)—

does not exist in color and so forth by virtue of the relation of being a locus residing in a substance as determined by its own intrinsic nature, [therefore] the state of being distinct from that which possesses itself [does not exist there] by that same relation.

The meaning is that because [the property] exists in color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, and because manifested color-form (*udbhūtarūpa*) exists there by way of the relation of being distinct from itself (as in the case of "like itself"), it pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*).
This refers to the locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) residing in jars and the like.

Even though there is the existence of being grounded in a substance (*dravyaniṣṭhatva*), there is no [existence] as qualified by the absence of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*). Therefore, since there exists the state of being different from itself (manifested color) by virtue of the relation of being a locus qualified by its own absence, it should be understood that manifested color exists in jars and the like through that same relation; thus, [the probans] possesses pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatā*).
And thus,

since we perceive no obstacle whatsoever to the establishment of a qualified pervasion through the aforementioned consideration, [the objection does not apply] to an upādhi that possesses a pervasion with the qualified probandum.
This results precisely in the failure to establish the indicator of deviation from a pure probandum (*śuddhasādhyavyabhicāronnāyakatva*).
As stated in the *Dīpikā* [82]: "Where is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) included? and so forth;
thus, the vital breath constitutes a tenth substance.
The sense is that even if [the object] were included within action (*vāyā*), it would follow that there would be either four types of objects or none at all.
However, because the definition of an object— consisting in being distinct from the body and the senses— is fulfilled by the qualifying term "body" and so forth, there is no fourfold division.

The intention is that because it is included within air (*vāyu*), it does not constitute a tenth substance; this is the underlying sense. Furthermore, in the summary statement—“And though it is one, it receives different designations such as *prāṇa* and so forth due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)”—the meaning of the ablative case in the phrase “due to the difference in limiting adjuncts” is "being employed by" (*prayojyatva*). Of that...
In the word "labhate" (obtains), there is a syntactic connection with the meaning of the verbal root;
and here, that [meaning] consists in being denotable.

In the phrase "even though one," "oneness" means the state of being devoid of any property that subsists in fewer instances than the property of being a living being (*prāṇitva*). The particle "api" (even) is used here [to indicate this].
It has the meaning of contradiction (*virodha*).

And contradiction is the absence of a distribution that is not delimited by a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) as determined by a substratum that is the locus of the unity which delimits the referent of another term co-occurring with it.
And its relation is positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Thus,

the understanding is that it (the self) is the substratum of relations defined by the designations "prāṇa," "apāna," and so forth, which are occasioned by the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) contradictory to oneness.
Some, however, claim that the word "api" (even/also) has the sense of contradiction;
that is incorrect, because [the context concerns] the locus (*dharmin*).

Because by the very manifestation of being the locus of such a relation, the absence of contradiction with oneness regarding that which is the locus of such a relation is obtained, making a separate statement redundant;
however, in our view...
This is because those [definitions] are meaningful insofar as they demonstrate the possibility of both contradiction and co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in a single locus.
In response to the doubt as to what these limiting adjuncts (upādhis) are, he states the meaning of the word "upādhi."
Regarding the word "place" (*sthāna*) in the *Dīpikā* [82],
the *Prakāśikā* [82] states the authoritative source for that as "the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the heart," and so forth.
Regarding the statement "by the force of the desire to create" in the *Dīpikā* on the process of creation and dissolution [85]:
although the will of the Lord (*īśvara*) is indeed eternal, [the manifestation occurs] by virtue of that desire.
Nevertheless, by the principle that "at this time,
let there be action in the atom," because that [time] is characterized by a specific temporal relation,
the restriction that action arises in it at that very time and not at another is logically established. Thus...
It should also be understood that [the reason] is due to the desire for reabsorption (*saṃjihīrṣā*).

Furthermore, regarding the argument "because it is a substance perceptible by the eye" (*cākṣuṣadravyatvāt*), if one intends the meaning to be "that which is a substance and is perceptible by the eye," then one must consider that the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was with respect to the self (*ātman*).
Intending the *karmadhāraya* compound with the word "substance" (*dravya*) and the maxim beginning with "above the *karmadhāraya*," he states the meaning: [85] "while possessing visibility," etc.,
and [85] "in the case of color-form (*rūpa*), etc."

And this is stated with the intention that "being a produced substance" (*janyadravyatva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*). However, it should be understood that if one were to prove "possessing parts" (*sāvayavatva*) in the sense of being inherent in a substance (*dravyasamavetatva*), there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the absence of a jar and so forth; thus, the word "etc. (*ādi*) should be regarded as including these cases.

[85] "Because of the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding its being an effect" means: because of the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasañjana*) that the gradation of magnitude (*parimāṇatāratamya*) found between Mount Meru and a mustard seed would be untenable, depending on an unstable succession characterized by having parts (*sāvayavatva*), which is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the state of being a constituent part (*avayavatva*).

And thus, the sense is that from the statement "the constituent part of a triad has parts, because it is the initiator of a large [object]," an inference arises— by the force of the aforementioned reasoning— that it is inherent in eternal parts.
This is what is meant by "in brief" in the *Prakāśikā*.
The point here is this:
although, if one accepts that the magnitude of an atom (*truṭi*) is eternal, there is no dependence upon the number of its parts.
The suspicion that the inference shown is inconclusive (aprayojakatva) is difficult to ward off; nevertheless—
"That subtle thing which is perceived within the rays of the sun through a lattice,"
"The sixtieth part of that is proclaimed to be an atom (paramāṇu).
On the strength of the authority of this Smṛti, the acceptance of both the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and the atom is necessary.
"Digiti"— here the intention is as follows: since the word "all" (sarva) signifies pervasion over the property-limiting factors (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) of the objects co-occurrent with it,
the intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*) possesses pervasion over the state of being a product-substance (*kāryadravyatva*).
The definition of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) is its being the effect of existence and its pervasiveness;
and as for this pervasiveness:
By the relation of being the counter-positive of a destruction residing in itself;
and "residing in itself" is by means of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*).

By this, the objection that the statement of this definition is inconsistent— on the grounds that it is impossible to fully comprehend the state of being a collection of such destructions because the infinite effects, including positive effects, are specifically difficult for one who is not omniscient to know— is thereby refuted.
[88] For the purpose of illuminating the determination of space (ākāśa),
it is likewise said that it has sound as its quality (śabda-guṇaka).

The intention is that, according to the maxim "the whole sentence [is the predicate]," it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which sound alone is the quality (*guṇa*) and specifically the specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*).
Now, an objection: in the summary statement (*saṃgrahavākya*), it is said, "And that is one."
It has been stated that space is one;
however, that is not tenable,
according to the principle beginning with "after a *karmadhāraya* compound," and so forth.

The meaning is that the maxim states: "A suffix expressing an abstract state (bhāvārthaka-pratyaya) occurring after a *karmadhāraya* compound indicates coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). [For example:
"the space of the jar" (*ghaṭākāśaḥ*), "the space of the hut" (*maṭhākāśaḥ*).
Because such linguistic usage exists as a proof for the multiplicity of space,
and because in the case of a difference in linguistic usage, the very difference in that which is to be designated is the regulating factor.

And likewise: "The linguistic usage of 'pot-space' has as its object of usage something distinct from that which is delimited by the nature of 'hall-space,' because it is a linguistic usage whose object of usage is delimited by a property other than the nature of 'hall-space'; whatever [is such]..."

In response to the objection that the proof here is an inference supported by a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*)— namely, "whatever linguistic usage has for its object of application a thing delimited by a property distinct from a certain property, that usage has for its object of application something residing in what is distinct from what is delimited by that [same] property"— it is said:

"Only the difference in the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the objects of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is the regulator of the difference in those usages; otherwise, the distinction between the linguistic usages of *prāṇa* (inhalation) and *apāna* (exhalation), for instance, would be untenable.
And thus, in the aforementioned inference..."
There would be a deviation [from the rule] by taking into account common usage such as "prāṇa" and "apāna.
Thus, in the present case,
since such usage is established through the distinction between the delimiters of the objects of usage— such as a jar or a hut— [the objection does not hold].

Intending the resolution that "it does not establish a division in space," he says: "[88] 'The space of a jar,' 'the space of a hut,' and so forth. [88] "Multiplicity" (anekatva) means possessing a property that subsists in less than the entirety of space (ākāśatva).
[88] "Means of knowledge" (pramāṇa) refers to valid cognition (pramā); of that...
The meaning is: "due to the absence [of such a property] whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation of being the qualificandum. And thus:

"Space is devoid of any property that subsists in a locus narrower than space-ness, because it lacks the state of being a qualificandum of a valid cognition (pramā) whose qualifier is the possession of such a property."
"That which is not thus is not thus" is the negative inference (*vyatirekī anumāna*) presented as the proof for the oneness of space;
[this is stated] because of its very oneness.
The meaning is: "precisely because of being devoid of any property that subsists in a locus narrower than [the property of] space-ness (*ākāśatva*).

However, some maintain that in the case of space, it is simply the state of having space-ness as its pervader, while being non-pervasive of a property that is contradictory to a property pervaded by space-ness.
Unity. Here, the following is the definition: it is the oneness qualified by the nature of space (ākāśatva) as delimited by difference.
And the qualification [of the difference] is by way of both the relation of being the delimitor of its own counter-correlativity and the relation of being its own locus.
The state of being a delimiting factor (avacchedakatā) [is established] by the relation of being qualified by a property that is pervaded by itself; and as for this qualification (vaiśiṣṭya),...
They say that [the relation] is by way of being qualified by a property contradictory to itself;
and this qualification is by way of the relation of possessing a difference from its own locus and so forth.
As for the claim that it is "that which is devoid of the two differentiating properties," that is trivial.

Because [the definition] would result in the fallacy of impossibility (*asambhava*), as both *dravyatva* (substancehood), which is a category-dividing property of categories, and *ākāśatva* (etherhood), which is a category-dividing property of substances, exist [in ether]; and because,
if one were to include the property of being a category-divider of ether, there would be a contradiction due to the simultaneous presence of proof and non-proof (*siddhyasiddhibhyām*).
The object of meditation: omnipresence (*vibhutva*), which is common to ether, time, space, and the self, is not a genus (*jāti*).
This is because a corresponding perceptual cognition (*anugatapratyakṣadhi*) that would establish it is impossible, and because color and other qualities are absent in them.
Because inference is impossible due to the non-perception of a mark that is not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*),

and because verbal testimony has its authority rendered doubtful by the lack of certainty regarding its being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), since otherwise the opposite could equally be asserted.

Nor should it be argued that the universal "all-pervasiveness" (vibhutva-jāti) is established by virtue of being the delimitor of the denotation of the term "all-pervasive," for by the same reasoning, the universal "elementality" (bhūtatva) would also [be established].

Because, through the occurrence of [the flaw of] non-establishment (*siddhyāpatti*), there exists a subverter of its status as a universal (*jātibādhaka*)— namely, the fact that being qualified by those three relations previously mentioned is pervaded by the absence of being a universal— and thus its status as a universal is not established.

As for the claim that omnipresence (*vaibhava*) consists in possessing the dimension of the infinitely great (*paramamahatparimāṇavattva*), that is not correct; [for it follows] from omnipresence [that there would be no distinction between the two].
For in the sūtra, "The self is likewise as great as space," Kaṇāda has stated all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for proving supreme greatness; therefore,
it is not the intention of the author of the sūtras that the nature of the self consists in possessing a dimension of supreme greatness.
With this intention, he defines omnipresence (*vibhutva*) by another method: "all corporeal...
Here, the word "all" (*sarva*) is used to exclude cases such as a jar that is conjoined with a cloth or other objects. Of the omnipresent entities...
The term "corporeal" (*mūrta*) is included to exclude the impossibility [of conjunction] due to the absence of mutual conjunction resulting from the absence of action;
this is because corporeality, in the view that it is a specific universal established as the delimiting condition for being the inherent cause of action, [is required].

The term *dravya* (substance) is included to exclude the impossibility [of the definition] by taking into account a substance that was previously accepted, produced, and then destroyed; it has the sense of "possessing conjunction.
For this very reason, the term *mūrta* (corporeal) is stated to avoid the aforementioned defect.
The claim that [space] is eternally formless (*nityāmūrta*) is an unacceptable prattle; for it would result in the redundancy of the term "substance" (*dravya*), and because,
according to the view that "formlessness is the possession of action" (*kriyāvattva*), one cannot accept a substance that has arisen and then perished.
Or rather, that [definition] is certainly not to be accepted. Now,
if the phrase "the state of being conjoined with all corporeal substances" means "possessing conjunctions whose counter-correlates (pratiyogin) are all those corporeal substances," [then...]

There is an impossibility [of the definition] because a single conjunction having all those things as its counter-correlates is not established. If the meaning were taken as "possessing a collection of conjunctions where each individual thing is a counter-correlate," then even the conjunction between a jar and a cloth would be included within such a collection.

Since the state of possessing a collection composed of a single conjunction with each of those [entities] does not exist in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, that same fault remains. As for the claim that it is "the state of possessing a collection composed of a single conjunction having as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) each and every corporeal substance (*mūrtadravya*)," this is not [the case].
This is a fault. And it is not [a fault] in the case of the universal *mūrtatva* (corporeality),
because— [as stated in the commentary]— “by the same reasoning” means by way of being the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of what is denoted by the word *bhūta*.

"Previously mentioned" means by way of this triad of relations: (1) coexistence with itself (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*), (2) coexistence with its own absence (*svābhāvasāmānādhikaraṇya*), and (3) being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that coexists with itself (*svasamānādhikaraṇātyantābhāvapratiyogitva*).
[This applies] even to earth and so forth that have arisen and perished, by virtue of their being the locus of that [universal].
It should not be argued that because space and the like are not included within any corporeal substance (*mūrta*), a conjunction having them as its counter-positive is unestablished;

and thus, since space and the like do not possess the collection of conjunctions defined by such [unestablished] relations, the definition remains subject to the flaw of being impossible (*asambhava*). This is because it has already been explained that the word "substance" (*dravya*) signifies that which possesses conjunction.

[The opponent argues: "Because such things as earth are not included [in the definition], and because there is no fault whatsoever if the term 'mūrta' (corporeal) is taken to mean 'possessing action' (kriyāvat)," [we reply:
that is trivial.

Since the "collection-ness" (samudāyatva)— which consists in being the object of a specific enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) and which resides pervasively (paryāpta) in the collection of conjunctions inherent in each individual member of the quartet beginning with space—
is distinct in each case, [the property of] possessing such a collection-ness delimited by each respective collection is likewise distinct.

Alternatively, if one accepts that "all-pervasive" (*vibhu*) is the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), because [the definition] does not exist in anything other than that which possesses the property of being denoted by the word "all-pervasive"—a property delimited by the state of being the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*)—through the relation of being the denotable object (*vācyatāsambandha*).
Furthermore, if the possession of those four respective collections were taken as the definition, there would be the consequence of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*). Of that...
Because it does not exist anywhere [as a single entity];
for if being "one of several" were to be such [a single entity],
then such "one-of-several-ness" would consist in being other than that which possesses a fourfold difference delimited by the respective collective states.
If one does not accept absences whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a property that exists distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti), the definition would result in being impossible;
yet if such absences are accepted, then even the conjunction of a jar with space and so forth would possess the nature of being a locus of such "anyone-ness" (anyatamatva),
leading to over-extension (ativyāpti) in the case of the jar and other such things— how, then, can this [definition] be consistent?

Furthermore, by the statement "the state of being conjoined with all corporeal substances," it is understood that there is no conjunction with [non-corporeal] substances such as space (gagana) in corporeal substances.

And thus, the resulting definition is: that which possesses a collection of differences whose counterpositiveness is delimited by its own individuality (tadvyaktitvāvacchinnapratiyogitāka), provided it is a corporeal substance not conjoined with itself.
Here, because a corporeal substance not conjoined with the ether (*gagana*) and so forth is unestablished, by the term "self" (*sva*), [the definition applies to]...
Because it is impossible for space and so forth to have a material cause (*upādāna*), the definition applies to space and the like.

Furthermore, the term "corporeal" (*mūrta*) is included to exclude the impossibility [of the definition] applying to space and so forth, since these are qualities and the like that are not conjoined with themselves.
In the view that "mūrtatva" (corporeality) is a universal (*jāti*),

the term "substance" (*dravya*)— which signifies that which possesses conjunction— is included in order to exclude the impossibility [of the definition] applying to things such as jars that have arisen and perished while not yet having come into conjunction with their own substratum.
Furthermore, since such things as a jar lack the property of being a conjunct (saṃyogitva) even when not conjoined with space and so forth, there is no impossibility [in the definition].
Nor, in this case, is the term "embodied" (mūrta) redundant.
It should not be argued that this is because qualities and the like do not possess such a nature;
for even so, space and the like are related to space and so forth through their own non-conjunction with them.
"To prevent that defect, it is necessary"— this too is incorrect,
because [it would apply to] the individual instances of corporeal objects belonging to other persons at other times.
Because it is impossible for us to know [all such particulars] individually, it is difficult to formulate a definition consisting of a collection of such differences;
[this is so] by virtue of the two relations of being conjoined with a corporeal object not conjoined with itself and identity (*tādātmya*).
Even though it is possible for a single, inclusive property— namely, "being other than that which is qualified by the object of cognition"— to serve as a definition,

a definition consisting of "being different from what is delimited by itself" (svāvacchinnabhinnatva) related through the relation of conjunction (saṃyuktatva) would over-extend to color and so forth, because such a correlate of conjunction (svasaṃyukta) is unestablished [in those cases].

Even if that [over-extension] were excluded by independently introducing "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) [as a qualifier], there would still be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of earth and so forth that have been produced and then destroyed;
and even if that were avoided by introducing "possessing conjunction" (*saṃyogitva*) in place of "substance-ness," it would result in extreme prolixity (*mahāgaurava*).

Furthermore, since it is improper— according to the principle that "one should not wipe away what has already been washed"— to abandon a faultless meaning obtainable from the words exactly as they are heard according to the method to be explained, and instead to postulate another meaning and introduce further qualifications therein merely to eliminate other faults.
By this [qualification],

namely "not conjoined with itself," there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) to produced and subsequently destroyed earth and so forth, because what is intended is an absolute absence whose counter-positivehood is delimited by the relation of being conjoined as residing in itself (svaniṣṭha-saṃyuktatva-sambandhāvacchinna-pratiyogitā).

Thus, by this [definition], "the state of possessing a property that divides substances and does not reside in action" or "the state of possessing a property that divides substances and is non-co-instantaneous with the universal *mūrtatva* (corporeality)" is intended to mean "the state of being in conjunction with all corporeal substances."
And the possession of such a property [is established] by way of either the relation of identity (*svarūpa*) or inherence (*samavāya*);
therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) with respect to time, the self (*ātman*), and so forth.
This is refuted, because the state of being "flowing upwards" (udakṣaratā) is unavoidable; furthermore,
there is no decisive criterion for determining the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two parts constituting either one [of the two options].
Furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence of there being two types of all-pervading entities (*vibhu*).
To this, it is replied:
the meaning of the passage beginning with "all embodied" (*sarvamūrta*) is that [the quality] pervades all material substances (*mūrtadravya*).

Because the word "all" (sarva) signifies pervasion over the property-limiting factors (*tāvacchedaka*) of the meanings of the words with which it is co-referential (*samabhivyāhṛta*); and this pervasion is as follows:
By means of the relation of being the counter-correlate of a conjunction whose correlate is itself;
it is precisely for the sake of obtaining this that the word "conjoined" (saṃyogin) was stated.
Although, by means of the relation of being the counter-positive of a conjunction having itself as its relatum,

the state of being a pervader of corporeal substances (*mūrtadravyatva*) is ultimately reduced to the absence of the counter-positiveness delimited by that same relation in the absolute non-existence residing in corporeal substances;

Although this [property] is not established under the view that a relation which does not restrict occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha*) cannot be a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), nevertheless,

it consists in the state of being devoid of the aforementioned delimitation (*avacchedakatā*) as delimited by that very relation, with respect to the counter-positiveness of the difference residing in corporeal substances (*mūrtadravya*).
This is what is intended here:

even for a relation that is not a restrictor of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha*), which serves as the delimiting adjunct of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), there exists the status of being a delimiting adjunct of the delimitation of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatāvacchedakatā*) of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
"By the maxim of washing away mud" means by the principle expressed in the saying: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off."
"Because it is agreed upon by all"—
this is the path cultivated exclusively by me.
Now, regarding measurement:
Being concealed does not consist in being inferior,
which would entail the aforementioned fault; rather,
it consists in not being inherent in any one of [the categories] such as space (ākāśa) and so forth.

As for the claim that "it is inherence in an omnipresent substance"— that is incorrect; for since omnipresence (vibhutva) is defined by the absence of corporeality (mūrtatva), it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).
Therefore, keeping in mind that there is no pervasion by parts within atoms, he says in the *Prakāśikā* [88]: "In reality... This is the determination of time (*kāla*).
[89] By the phrase "from the future, etc.," the present is included.
[90] Regarding the term "by way of being a constituent": with respect to the conventional usage of "past" and so forth.

The meaning is: by virtue of being the locus of a primary qualifier-nature (prakāratā) which is itself qualified by a qualifier-nature of "subsistence" (ādheyatva), which is in turn qualified by a qualifier-nature of "destruction" (dhvaṃsa), which is further qualified by a qualifier-nature of "counter-correlativity" (pratiyogitva)— the latter being the delimitor of the capacity to produce such linguistic usage (vyavahāra) based on a cognition whose mode is "pastness" (atītatva) and so forth.
Non-difference is the meaning of the third case suffix, conjoined with causality.
In reality, however, "pastness" [is established] by way of the relation of being the counter-positive of a destruction residing in itself; thus, "[it is] past."
Futurity consists in possessing the time that serves as the locus for the employment of a word;
and it is "will be" by virtue of the relation of being the counter-positive of a prior absence (prāgabhāva) residing in itself.
Presentness is the state of being possessed of the time that serves as the locus for the employment of a word;
and since presentness exists by way of the relation of inherence (*ādheyatā*), it is the state of being possessed of the time that serves as the locus for the employment of a word.
And thus, since in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) knowledge whose mode is the delimitor of the object to be used is the cause,
time’s status as a cause of linguistic usage— in the form of possessing a subject-object relation (*viṣayatā*) delimited by that [delimitor]— remains entirely intact.
The phrase "by way of being a constituent" (ghaṭakatayā) also means "by way of being the locus of such a cognitive objectivity" (viṣayatā).
Non-difference is the meaning of the instrumental case-suffix.
Furthermore, if prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is not accepted, then [the word] "will come to be" (bhaviṣyati) [is used].

It should be understood that [the definition] must be formulated as "having an origination at a time delimited by the destruction of the moment that serves as the locus for the employment of the word," which,
through the relation of "having an origination at a time delimited by its own destruction," results in being qualified by such a moment.

And the objectivity that delimits the status of being a producer (*janakatāvacchedikā viṣayatā*) consists in the nature of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) as determined by the primary qualificandum (*mukhyaviśeṣyatā*); this is the case in the former alternative, whereas in the latter alternative—

"Of the cognition having 'pastness' and so forth as its qualifier" means: of the cognition having the form "The pot is the counter-positive of a destruction residing in the present time. The phrase "the delimitor of the generativity of such conventional usage" is to be construed with "the final qualifierhood" (antimaprakāratā).

The temporal-qualifierhood residing in the present time, which is determined by the locative-qualifierhood residing in the locus, which is determined by the objective-qualifierhood residing in destruction, which is itself determined by the objective-qualifierhood residing in counterpositiveness.
The meaning is "by virtue of being its substratum.

[The property to be grasped] should be understood as having either of two forms: being the qualifierhood determined by the primary qualificandumhood, or being the objecthood determined by the objecthood of origination which is itself determined by the relationhood determined by the primary qualificandumhood; therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
[90] Regarding the phrase "of that which has followed," and so forth:

the meaning is that because each moment, day, and so on, is distinct from the others due to the distinctness of the sun's movements and so forth, the conventional usage of terms such as "past" and so on would be untenable therein.
[90] It is said: "Digi" (it is so).
Even if the conventional usage of "past" and so forth had as its object a single, underlying time (*kāla*), then such usage would also apply to the present and other times;
therefore, by necessity, it must have as its object limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the non-uniform revolutions of the sun.
It cannot be accepted that an additional entity called time is established by the aforementioned method; nevertheless,

because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) to restrict [the substratum] to any one among ether and the rest— since each of them could serve as the locus of the conjunction that acts as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for temporal priority and so forth— an additional time is established by means of the temporal relation (*kālikasambandha*).

He dispels the misconception that the property of being the substratum of all (*sarvādhāratva*) over-extends to action (*kriyā*) and so forth—by means of the passage beginning with "here" (*atretyādi*).
By the phrase "west and so forth" (*pratīcyādīti*), the inclusion of the north and south is intended. This is the definition of the Self (*ātmanirūpaṇa*).

The meaning is "by way of inherence (samavāya), like cognition. The intention is that otherwise, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to time and so forth, which possess cognition through temporal or other relations.
Regarding the phrase "there is a contradiction": [end of section 92].
The sense is that by this [statement], the fact that God has the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpatva*) is made known; for in the scriptural text "eternal consciousness" (*nityaṃ vijñānam*),
the word *vijñāna* is derived from the suffix *aṇ* (added to a word ending in *arśas*, etc.).

Alternatively, intending that the suffix *lyu* (aka) is applied in the sense of the agent because the word belongs to the *nandī* group and so forth, he says: "[93] ...having the meaning of 'one who possesses consciousness'.

Now, raising the objection: "Since there is an absence of pleasure (*sukha*) in the Lord (*īśvara*), how can the aforementioned scripture be authoritative?"—anticipating this, he says: "[93] Here... one who is happy" (*sukhī*).
The phrase "I have become" means it is like the word "happiness" (sukha) found within such a sentence; that is,
as used in the aforementioned scripture.

Ānanda says: "The word 'bliss' (ānanda) is used figuratively for the absence of suffering. The meaning of the locative case is the state of being contained within [the absence of suffering]. "Figurative usage" (upacāra) means metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).
The meaning of the verbal root *āśray* is "the qualifier" (*nirūpakatva*).
Thus, the result is that the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) occurring in the aforementioned scripture is the qualifier of the definition residing in the absence of suffering.

1. *Teyati* means "by the Śruti," namely by the text: "Brahman is eternally consciousness and bliss. Since there is no sublation [of the primary meaning], it is not appropriate to resort to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for a word occurring in a Vedic sentence; thus, regarding the word "bliss" (*ānanda*),...

He states the view of the moderns (*navīna*), who maintain that [the term "bliss"] refers to its primary sense (*mukhyārtha*), with the words: "But the moderns... Now, one might object: since there is an absence of produced pleasure (*janyasukha*) in God (*īśvara*), how can the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) have its primary sense [there]? To this, he says: "eternal happiness" (*nityasukha*).

"By the power of what has been shown and heard," and so forth. "Of a different class" means that otherwise, the supreme self would result in being perceived by another's mind through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This is the state of affairs.
Here, this is to be understood: "The self is devoid of the ordinary objecthood of external perception."
Because it is a substance devoid of manifested form,
[the self] lacks the status of being an ordinary mental object distinct from the pleasure and other qualities residing in the living being.
The intended two-fold inference is as follows: "Because it is devoid of being conjoined with a heterogeneous mind, being inherent in its substratum, and so forth, like the sky and other such things.
By this, [the argument] does not apply to the Cārvāka position.
The subject (pakṣa) is not unestablished;
since the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (sādhya) by way of its delimiting condition (avacchedaka),
there is no "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhana) in part.
Nor is there inference, because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*); for in this case as well,

the generality of the object of cognition (*prameyasāmānya*) possesses an absolute absence whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) resides in the living being and is delimited by the relation of being a prover of a self distinct from itself.
The inference "because it is a real entity" is to be understood; this is the direction.

The underlying point here is this: although the existence of a jar as delimited by its nature (ghaṭatva) occurs when there is existence delimited by being made by a potter, and its absence occurs when that [potter-made-ness] is absent—[nevertheless, the argument holds].
Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the causal relationship is established specifically between pot-ness and the act of creation by a potter;
nevertheless, this is so by virtue of the general rule that "whatever two particulars [are related], their general classes are likewise related."

It is also necessary that [volition] possesses causality toward that which is delimited by being an effect (kāryatva) by virtue of its nature as volition (kṛtitva). Likewise, it possesses such causality toward that which is delimited by being an effect by virtue of both its nature as knowledge (jñānatva) and its nature as desire (icchātva), because there is no difference in the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) in those cases.
And thus, just as the inference "an effect is produced by volitional effort (kṛti) because it is an effect," [one might argue] "an effect is produced by cognition (jñāna)..."

The two inferences intended are also "and that which is produced by desire, because it is an effect," and so forth; by the phrase "of immediate knowledge and the like" (*aparokṣajñānādeḥ*), the word "and the like" (*ādi*) includes the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*);
and by the phrase "the desire to act and the like" (*cikīrṣādikam*), the word "and the like" includes volitional effort (*kṛti*).

Now, one might object: since the status of the Lord as possessing knowledge of all objects is already obtained by the word "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) alone in the scripture, "He who is omniscient, all-knowing," the term "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*) is redundant. Anticipating this objection, he says:
[93] Regarding the term "sarvavit" (all-knowing): in reality, based on the etymological derivation of "sarvavit" as "those who know all," its meaning is "all-pervading."
It should be understood that this is because such a meaning is possible for the verbal root *vida* (to live) when the suffix *kvip* is applied.

Now, an objection is raised: since the *Dīpikā* states, "He states the definition of the individual soul (*jīva*)—'the individual soul... [92], and since the introductory statement to the summary verse says, "The individual soul, moreover, is distinct in each body" [91], [your interpretation] is incorrect.
Because distinctness with respect to each body is impossible as a defining characteristic of the individual soul (*jīva*) due to its commonality with the sense organs and other factors,
therefore, by virtue of the force of the frequent use of the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), [the term *bheda* is understood in this specific sense].

Relying on the derivation *lakṣyate idam* (this is characterized) and adopting the suffix *-lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), he explains it with the intention that it refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), stating: "[93] The meaning is 'it expresses the essential nature. Regarding the phrase in the root text, "distinct in each body," and here—
The meaning of the second case ending (dvitīyā) when co-occurring with the word *pratipad* consists of two parts:
the property of being the delimiting counter-correlativity of the difference between the substratum of the locusness (*ādheyatā*) and [the locus itself], and non-existence (*abhāva*).

Otherwise, it should be noted that because it is difficult to define pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) in a general sense as something not constituted by a specific pervaded (*vyāpya*), it would be untenable for it to be the meaning of the second [word].
Now, [one might object]: "In every body..."

From the statement "distinct" (*bhinna*), just as in the case of "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth— where existence pervades each substance— the word "body" (*śarīra*), when used in conjunction with each term,
signifies that which pervades "bodiness" (*śarīratva*); thus, its meaning is "that which has as its counter-positive a distinction pervading bodiness."
That [conclusion] is obtained, yet it is not tenable;
for even if one accepts the unity of the individual self (*jīvātman*),
the pervasion of corporeality by the plurality of selves remains unimpaired, since such a purpose can still be accomplished.
To this it is replied: for it is not intended that the pervasiveness of difference with respect to being the body is by way of an essential relation (svarūpa-sambandha),
such that [the aforementioned objection] would apply.

Furthermore, in the case of the body, the delimitingness (*avacchedakatā*) exists by way of a relation consisting of both: (1) being the delimitor of an experience that has the same locus as itself, and (2) being the delimitor of its own counter-correlate;

and [this delimitingness] exists in the body by way of a relation consisting of possessing an experience delimited by a body that is not produced by qualities such as those born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), which are themselves qualified by that [delimitingness].
And its own qualification [is established] by way of both relations: being distinct from itself and being simultaneous with itself; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

Intending this very point, he says: [93] "Simultaneous," and so forth. In response to the doubt, "What then is the characteristic of the living being (*jīva*)?", he states in the *Dīpikā* [92]: "Pleasure and so forth are the characteristics of the living being.
Here, the mention of "pleasure" (*sukha*)...
This is in accordance with the view of the ancients;
otherwise, according to the view of the moderns, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to God (*īśvara*), as stated above.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), suffering and hatred are included.
In the *Prakāśikā* [p. 93], it is stated: "Otherwise, if the self were distinct from the body;
[and] in our own tenet (*siddhānta*), regarding the term 'human' (*manuṣya*) and so forth..."

Intending to show that the cognition "I am a human" and so forth is possible by taking the self as delimited by a human body or similar, through the relation of possessing an effort that is the common cause for one's own activities and movements, it was stated: "[93] It is a conceit (abhimāna)."

[94] Regarding the passage beginning with "that which has a middling magnitude" (*yanmadhyamaparimāṇam*): "middling-ness" (*madhyamatva*) with respect to magnitude (*parimāṇa*) consists in being distinct from both atomicity (*paramāṇutva*) and supreme largeness (*paramamahattva*).
And thus, if the self (*ātman*) were of such a nature...
The sense is that, because it too would necessarily possess contraction and expansion according to the body, the consequence of its impermanence would follow.
"Dig" (the direction) indicates that the underlying point here is as follows: if, moreover...
If, in the context of the manifestation of the body (*kāyavyūha*), the emission of light is accepted in order to account for the direct perception of pleasure and so forth even within another body,
then it is untenable to postulate here what has not been observed elsewhere.
Because it is universally accepted that conceptualization must conform to what is observed—
since the radiance of a lamp situated in one house is not seen in another house—
even scripture that purports to establish all-pervasiveness serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this regard.
The definition of mind in the *Dīpikā* [98]: "provided that it is devoid of touch," [is stated] out of fear of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to air (*vāyu*).
The disregard for being devoid of form and so forth is because, in the *Saṃgraha*, it is said to be "restricted to each individual.
On this point, some say: as many as...
The specific meaning is that because the selves are expressible by as many minds as there are, the minds are infinite.
If one asks how that attainment occurs, it is as follows:
The word *ātman* (self), when uttered in conjunction with the term *pratipad* (each respective [locus]), refers specifically to each individual instance of a self.

Its "restriction to that" (*tanniyatatva*) consists in its non-connection with anything other than that; and this, in turn, consists in its not producing a cognition inhering in anything other than that. And thus:
The meaning is: "because it does not produce a cognition that is co-present with some self distinct from itself, which is the locus of the cognition produced by it.
The phrase "of each individual mind" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
In the context of infinity, the state of being cognized by a cognition is the meaning of the ablative case.
The claim that "it follows" is baseless;

for since the word *ātman* possesses a primary denotative power (*śakti*) qualified by the universal *ātmatva*, if it were intended to refer to each specific individuality (*vyaktitva*), it would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
This is because the self is characterized by infinity and is difficult to comprehend;
however, in reality,
"determinateness" here refers to being the substratum of difference.
And when there is a distinction regarding the self,

by the force of its co-utterance with each respective term, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) through a pervading relation (*vyāpakatā-sambandha*) consisting in the state of possessing distinctions such as "one's own" and so forth.
The state of having itself as its locus [is defined] by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). 1.
Regarding the phrase "possessing distinctions such as its own nature" (*svasetyādibhedavattva*):

The meaning is: by way of the relation of "possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity has as its delimitor a delimitor residing in itself, which is delimited by the relation of being a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference that is co-referential with itself.

[The term] *bheda* (difference) [is qualified] by the relation of "being the inherence locus of a cognition produced by the mind, which is the substratum of itself, and which has as its delimitor of counter-correlativity a delimitor of its own counter-correlativity, which is delimited by the relation of being the generator of a cognition inherent in something different from itself."
By virtue of both connections,
the primary sense of the word "self" (ātman) is also all the more appropriately established.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Saṅgraha-ṭippaṇī* that even the alternative view [of a single mind for all] is discarded from afar:
"But surely, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), there is only one mind for all selves."
Regarding the word "let it be," he says: "[99] Of all selves," and so forth.
Now, would the aforementioned fault not indeed apply only if the mind were atomic?
For we do not accept its atomicity (*aṇutva*),
but rather its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*).
And thus, even though the mind is one for all selves, [it can function] simultaneously with all the sense organs.

With the intention that, because conjunction is possible, there is no impossibility for another person during the state of knowledge of one person, he raises an objection in the *Dīpikā* [99] with the words beginning "But the mind...
and [99] "provided it is devoid of touch," and so forth.

The positive member (*satyanta*) is for the purpose of avoiding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to earth and so forth; the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is for the purpose of eliminating deviation with respect to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.
And here, if the mind were atomic (*aṇu*), there would be [the fault of] infinitude (*ānantya*).

It must be postulated; however, since there is no such [requirement] in the case of omnipresence, there is parsimony (*lāghava*). Because this logical reasoning (*tarka*) exists, this inference is not lacking in its probative force (*aprayojakatva*).
The state [of being a cause].

Since action is the cause of conjunction by way of inherence (samavāya), and since there is an absence of action in all-pervading substances (vibhus), the aforementioned conjunction is not possible; with this intention, he says in the *Prakāśikā*:
[99] Regarding "the two pervasive ones":
by the words "action, etc.," conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is included.
In the *Dīpikā*, it says: "[99] At that time, there is deep sleep."
This is what must be understood here: deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is not a conjunction between the self, as delimited by the region of the *purītat* vessel, and the mind.
But [if you claim] that there is a conjunction having such a location as its locus (anuyogin) and the mind as its relatum (pratiyogin),
then it would follow that sentences such as "Caitra sleeps" and "Maitra is in deep sleep" would be invalid. In that case:
Because the words *caitra* and so forth refer to the self as delimited by that particular body, and because such a conjunction is absent in the self;
and because the agentive suffix conveys the sense of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*). Therefore...

Thus it has been stated by Kṛṣṇambhaṭṭa in his *Vyutpattivāda-ṭippaṇī*: "In that regard, with respect to one [instance] of sleep, which consists of the conjunction of the mind delimited by the sleep-channel (*nidrā-nāḍī*), [the word 'sleep'] denotes the meaning of the verbal root."

And [it is stated] in the passage: "In the form of the self and the mind as delimited by the sleep-channel. As for the description of the cognition in cases such as "he sleeps" (*svapiti*) as "one who possesses an effort conducive to the conjunction of the mind with the region of the pericardium" (*purītat*):

That is incorrect— because in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), such an action does not exist in the self, and because the effort characterized as the "vital source" (jīvanayoni) is the cause of mere vital breath activity alone,
it lacks the capacity to be conducive to such a conjunction.

Furthermore, since Gadādhara has stated that the universal *pravṛttitva* (the state of being an inclination), which is the delimitor of being produced by the cognition that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), is itself the delimitor of the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*),
there is no possibility at all of the effort constituting the "life-force" (*jīvanayoni-yatna*) being the meaning of the verbal suffix. Even though...
If such a mental conjunction (*manoyoga*) were of the nature of sleep itself, it would follow that sentences such as "the mind sleeps" would be authoritative;
nevertheless, in that case, [sleep] is indeed the locus of the relation (*anuyogitā*).

Since it is accepted that [the suffix] has the meaning of a *pratyaya* (suffix) and since its status as a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is not admitted, the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not arise;
for although elsewhere it has been established that verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) and the like also have meanings such as "substratum" (*āśrayatva*).
Consequently, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that one could employ such expressions as "the mind sleeps" (manaḥ svapiti) with that very intention would be unavoidable. Nevertheless,

the expressive power (śakti) of the verbal suffix (ākhyāta) resides only in the action to be performed (kṛtyādi), whereas its conventional metaphorical indication (nirūḍhalakṣaṇā) applies to the substratum (āśrayatva) and so forth.
This is agreed by all.
In that regard, it is postulated that the intention regarding beginninglessness applies only to the suffix when it is mentioned in conjunction with the verbal root *svap* (to sleep).
Therefore, there is no fault.

Now, since [the relation] such as being the object of inquiry (*anuyogitva*) is accounted for simply by its appearing as a relation (*saṃsarga*), why should one admit that the verbal suffixes and so forth denote that meaning and accept its appearance as a qualifier (*prakāra*)?

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to assume that even the relation between those [two] is an object of verbal cognition, which would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor does this lead to an inconsistency regarding the connection of the absence— the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)— in cases such as "Caitra does not sleep," for the same applies to the locus-ness (*anuyogitā*) as it does to the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*).
It should not be argued that [the relation] is not the delimitator of the counterpositiveness of an absence because it does not restrict occurrence;
for there is no fault, since we accept that even a relation which does not restrict occurrence can serve as the relation constituting the delimitation of the counterpositiveness of an absence.
Nor is there [the problem of] a distinct absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a relation that does not restrict occurrence.
It should not be said that there is complexity (gaurava) in the conceptualization [of the absence],
because the absence of that [relation]— which has as its counter-positive (pratiyogitā) that which is delimited by such a relation—
is non-different from the absence of that very same relation, owing to their being co-extensive (samanaiyatyena).
Because there is no assumption of anything superfluous;
nor is there any complexity in assuming a counter-positiveness delimited by a relation that does not determine the occurrence [of the absence], even in this case.

This must be stated: for even in your own view, the two positions are equal due to the presence of the aforementioned complexity (*gaurava*). Nor should it be argued that, according to the reasoning stated regarding "the king's servant" (*rājapuruṣa*), the status of being the object of inquiry (*anuyogitva*) must necessarily be a qualifier (*prakāratva*) in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).
Because such arguments have been refuted by us at length elsewhere,
[the argument] regarding the mere expression "he sleeps" [is untenable].

This is because, for the sake of establishing the capacity to convey meaning, it is necessary that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) and other elements have "being the correlate" (*anuyogitā*) as their denotation.

Although there is no fault whatsoever in the case of sentences such as "Caitra sleeps," where even if being the correlate is the word-meaning, it appears as a relation within the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), nevertheless...
We have no insistence on whether the cognition there consists of that [object] as its qualifier or as its qualificand, depending on the specific intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Caitra...
The same should be understood regarding such usages as "he knows" (*jānāti*) and so forth.
Thus, in your view,
the validity of such expressions as "the pericardium sleeps" (*purītati svapiti*) would be unavoidable.
In our view, however, it is not so; this is the path exclusively cultivated by me alone:
that the mind (*manas*) is the sense faculty (*indriya*) which serves as the means for the apprehension of pleasure and the like. [98]

This is the summary: here, the term "pleasure and so forth" (*sukhādi*) is used to exclude the eyes and other [senses] which are the means for the perception of jars and the like; the qualifier is used to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the self (*ātman*). And if such being a means for perception—
It is the status of being a producer (janakatva) as defined by a productivity (janyatā) delimited by a property that is pervaded by the nature of experience culminating in such a perception;

otherwise, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) to the eyes and other organs which produce it by way of time (kālavidhayā). Thus, since there is no over-extension to the self (ātman), it is considered that the qualification "being a sense organ" (indriyatva) is redundant.
Regarding that, he says in the *Prakāśikā*: "From the conjunction of the self and the mind. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), pleasure and so forth are included.
And thus, with respect to [the cognition] delimited by being a mental perception of pleasure and so forth, [the cause is] the mind.

The meaning is that the instrumentality [of the mind] is necessary for the sake of explaining [the production of cognition]; since it is essential to postulate either the conjunction of the self and the mind as a specific quality inherent in the self, or the operation of pleasure and so forth, its purposefulness lies in precluding those [other possibilities].
[99] Regarding "the establishment of atomicity": this is the point here.

The inference accepted as a means of valid knowledge— namely, "the mind possesses either atomicity or its absence, because it is an object of cognition"— is supported by the following reasoning: if the mind were not atomic, then, according to the method already stated, deep sleep would be impossible.
The definition of visible form [100]:
"Visible form is a quality apprehended solely by the eye" is the summary statement.
And here, by the phrase "grasped by the eye alone," the understanding is that it is grasped as the substratum of a property qualified by the eye; and this qualification is as follows:

[The relation is] by way of worldly proximity, through a relation delimited by the counter-correlativity of the distinction between the function of the sense organ that grasps its own object-form and [the object],

[and which is] qualified by a counter-correlativity residing in itself (the eye) whose delimitation is [the property of] being the eye, [and which is further qualified] by both [the property of] being located in [the eye] and [the property of] being a locus.
This has been explained by us more extensively elsewhere in the *Prakāśikā* [101],
where it is stated that it is not possible in the case of form (*rūpa*).
The sense is that form (*rūpa*) is graspable by the self and the mind (*manas*).

Nevertheless, it is said "by the tactile faculty" (*tvagindriya*); for even though [form] is devoid of the ordinary objecthood (*laukika-viṣayatā*) belonging to a cognition which is the locus of a producedness not delimited by being a cognition determined by another [faculty] such as the eye, [it is still grasped by the skin].
There is no fault in intending to specify that your own form (tvarūpa) is not graspable by other [senses] such as the eye;
nevertheless, the skin and so forth function as conditions for visual perception in the manner of time and other factors.

In order to avoid the impossibility [of the definition] by taking into account the nature of being a producer (*janakatā*), one must either specify that the nature of being a producer is not delimited by time-ness (*kālatva*) and so forth, or else specify that the nature of being produced (*janyatā*) is delimited by a property subsumed under the category of knowledge-ness (*jñānatva*).

Considering that there would be the fault of impossibility if one were to include "inherence connected with the eye," and that there would be the fault of prolixity due to the necessity of qualifying the "other" as a substance distinct from the eye, he abandons that [qualification].
Regarding the phrase "not being perceivable by the skin," and so forth:

In this context, it must be stated that the qualifiers for the genus (*jāti*) are: being devoid of a worldly objective domain (*laukika-viṣayatā*) as determined by the sense of touch, and possessing a worldly objective domain as determined by the sense of sight.

Consequently, although the property of "being a cloth" (*paṭatva*) appears in tactile perception through the process of sublation (*upanaya*), [the genus remains qualified by the aforementioned conditions]. And [so too] of the skin...
There is no defect even if time, by way of its own nature, generates visual knowledge of color;
likewise, there is no over-extension [of the definition] even if gravity and so forth appear in visual perception through the operation of mental application (*upanaya*).
In this context, the term "visual" (cākṣuṣa) is used to exclude rasa and other such entities; the term "qualifier of qualities" (guṇavibhājaka) is used to exclude light and the like.
This means [the term refers to] that which is pervaded by the universal "quality-ness" (guṇatva).

Now, in response to the doubt—"Why not simply state the word *guṇa* (quality) as referring to *viśeṣaguṇa* (specific quality) in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the conjunction of light with a wall?"—he says: "For this very reason," and so forth. And thus, it serves to exclude the over-extension shown above.

Furthermore, since it is necessary to include a refinement involving a *jāti* (universal) in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the specific fluidity that is innate and perceptible by the eye alone, the inclusion of "specific-ness" (*viśeṣatva*) in the definition— when [the property] can be established simply as the qualifier "not perceptible by the skin" (*tvagagrāhyatva*) and so forth— is cumbersome.
The state [of the matter]: in the *Dīpikā* [100], it says "blue and so forth, which do not subsist by way of pervasion" (*avyāpyavṛtti-nīlādi*).
Here, the qualification "not subsisting by way of pervasion" (*avyāptivṛttitva*)—

In order to dispel the suspicion of mutual lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), what is intended here is spatially non-pervasive occurrence (*daiśikāvyāpyavṛttitva*). And that consists in being qualified by absence through a relation consisting of both: (1) having itself as the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) and (2) being located in some delimited part of its own locus (*svādhikaraṇanirūpitakiñciddeśāvacchinnādheyatva*).
[Objection: Is it not the case that the statement in the *Dīpikā*—"because color (*rūpa*) is necessarily pervasively present (*vyāpyavṛttitva*)"—is inconsistent?

For, according to the maxim "a substance is produced [simultaneously with its qualities]," it is necessary that color and the other qualities are temporally non-pervasively present (*kālikāvyāpyavṛttitva*). To this, he says in the *Prakāśikā*: "regarding pervasive presence" (*vyāpyavṛttitve*).
The meaning is "the state of being spatially pervasive" (*daiśika-vyāpyavṛttitva*).
And spatial pervasiveness is the state of being other than that which is qualified by the absence [of the counter-positive] through the two previously mentioned relations.
1. Regarding "its own counter-positiveness" (*sva-pratiyogitva*), etc.:
One's own absence of conjunction with a monkey (svaṃ kapisaṃyogābhāvaḥ) has that [conjunction] as its counter-correlate (tatpratiyogitva), which resides in the conjunction with the monkey;
likewise, one's own absence of conjunction with a monkey has the tree as its locus (tadadhikaraṇa).
