The application [of the definition] is as follows: the property of having its occurrence delimited by the foremost point (agradeśa) specified by that [tree] exists in the conjunction with the monkey.
Furthermore, in this context, the collection of blue and other [colors] possesses either the state of being the object of the cognition "this is color" or the absence thereof.

Regarding the inference "because it is an object of cognition," one must state a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) supported by the following reductio ad absurdum (tarka): "If the collection of blue and so forth were the object of a [unitary] cognition, then it would follow that [the collection] exists non-pervasively.
In that regard, concerning form...

He states another refutation against one who is in disagreement with the rule that [qualities] must be pervasively present (*vyāpyavṛttitva*), beginning with the words "this is an illustration" (*idamupalakṣaṇam*). And thus,
the meaning is that the aforementioned inference, assisted by the knowledge of the complexity [of the alternative], is itself the proof for the existence of a distinct variegated color (*citrarūpa*).

By the phrase "prior non-existence and so forth," the inclusion of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is intended. Now, one might object: since the perception of color in a variegated cloth is accounted for by taking the colors of the parts through the relation of co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is no need for a distinct variegated color (*citrarūpa*).

It is not accepted; for, due to mutual contradiction, even a collection of blue and other colors that occupy the same locus cannot arise there—this is the objection raised in the *Dīpikā* with the words "But in a variegated [image]," etc. To this, the *Prakāśikā* replies: because color exists there by virtue of being co-located (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of inherence" and so forth:

intending the parsimony (*lāghava*) that results from not postulating the nature of the relation of being inherent as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of causality, he says: "[101] Color [is the cause] by means of the relation of being inherent in its own substratum."
Since it is impossible for the universal of perceptuality residing in cognition (*jñāna*) to be the determinant (*prayojaka*), he says:
"[101] In the state of being an object of perception. Now, one might object:

If color (*rūpa*) were a cause of perception with respect to a substance by way of the relation of ordinary objective domain (*laukika-viṣayatā*) and the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), there would be great complexity (*mahāgaurava*) in the case of a variegated cloth due to the postulation of a distinct color, its prior absence, and its destruction; therefore, compared to that, [it is better to hold] that color [is the cause] precisely by way of the relation of being inherent in what is inherent in itself (*svāśraya-samavetatva*).

Since being a cause is appropriate, he states another refutation with the words beginning "citrāvayavāvayavaka" (Dīpikā 101), and "tasmāt paṭasya" (Dīpikā 101). The intended meaning here is as follows: this cloth—

By means of the inference, "This possesses either form or its absence, because it is an object of cognition," and supported by the reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*)—"If this were devoid of form, then it would be imperceptible"—form is established.
1. Regarding the phrase "and here":

The meaning is that there is an absence of variegated color (*citrarūpa*) in the collection [of parts] such as indigo; or alternatively, the meaning is that color possesses the property of being pervasively present (*vyāpyavṛttitva*).
Alternatively, the meaning is that the variegated form (*citrarūpa*) is something additional.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the relation of co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya-sambandhena*), the meaning is "by way of the relation of residing in its own locus" (*svādhikaraṇavṛttitva-sambandhena*).

Its own nature as the form of the constituent threads is the substratum; the threads are that substratum, and the cloth's existence therein constitutes its possession of the form of the threads by way of that relation.
This is the sense of "inherence."

If the state of being inherent in something possessing color (*rūpavatsamavetatva*) were the determinant of perceptibility, then it must be stated that its determinant role is fulfilled solely through the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*); thus, the relation of essential identity whose counter-correlative is the state of being inherent must be declared to be the delimiting relation of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedakasaṃbandha*).
But when color is the cause by way of the relation of inherence in its own substratum, however...
The relation that delimits the causal status is precisely inherence (*samavetatva*), and not its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*).
It should also be understood here that there is parsimony regarding the property that delimits the causal status.

Since its status as something distinct is established by the reasoning previously stated, it is designated as "variegated form" (citrarūpa). As for the non-establishment of variegated taste (citrarasa):
He states the reason: "[101] Substantial, worldly," and so forth.
And thus, this [subject] possesses either taste or the absence thereof.
The point is that the inference "because it is an object of knowledge" (prameyatvāt) is non-conclusive (aprayojaka) due to the absence of a supporting argument (anukūlatarka). Furthermore,

one should not raise the objection here that the acceptance of a "variegated flavor" (citrarasa) is necessary in order to account for the cognition "there is flavor here" in an object composed of two parts possessing different flavors.

In that case, it is because one accepts that only the taste of the constituent part (*avayava*) appears through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, in cases where a large composite whole has been produced through the sequence beginning with a binary atomic aggregate (*dvyaṇuka*) formed by two atoms possessing different tastes, the perception of [a single] taste is simply not admitted.
Because it is accepted that the subject (*dharmin*) appears in gustatory perception precisely through the function of the application (*upanaya*);
this applies even to the taste of an atom.

The first word "sva" refers to the initial falling;
the second word "sva" refers to the division characterized by that initial falling.

The coordination [of the definition] is as follows: the first falling possesses both the state of being the locus of a difference from itself—which is co-temporal with the destruction of that second falling which is co-locative with the first falling—and the state of being the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of that [difference]. Thus, both properties reside in the first falling.
3. Regarding "pratiyoginī" and so forth:
one's own second falling is co-located with the first falling; the state of being simultaneous with the destruction of that [first falling] and identity [with it] both exist in the second falling.
By means of the aforementioned dual relation, that very [action] is qualified by the second falling;
since its distinctness from that exists in the first falling, the grammatical connection (*samanvaya*) is to be understood. 4.
Regarding the phrase "simultaneous with itself" and so forth:
by the term *dhvaṃsa* (destruction), the destruction of the first falling is to be understood.
The application [of the definition] is as follows: being qualified by that [destruction] in the second falling, while being other than that [first falling], constitutes the first falling.
It should be stated as follows: the first occurrence of the word "fall" (patana) refers to the destruction (dhvaṃsa) of the first falling.
The state of being simultaneous with such a destruction is present in the second falling.
The second occurrence of the word "fall" [is likewise explained].
The second falling is the ultimate [end].
For the second falling exists in the destruction of the first falling by way of the relation of being the counter-positive of a falling that has the same locus as itself.

Thus, the locusness (ādheyatā) residing in the second falling, which is determined by the destruction of the first falling, is delimited by the relation of being the counter-positive of a falling that is co-locus with itself. And so,
the second falling is qualified by the destruction of the first falling through such a relation of locusness.
It should be understood that this refers to being other than that [state] at the time of the first falling.
The subtle analysis is that it is "otherness qualified by destruction.
In place of such "inherence" (ādheyatva),...
Alternatively, one may include the property of "having a common locus with the falling of its own counter-positive," and thus there is no fault whatsoever; the same applies elsewhere as well.
Even though, for example, in the case of a fruit or the like that has fallen from a tree onto a palace...
In the state of falling from the palace, that which was defined as "primordial" there is impossible;
nevertheless, the falling relative to the palace, as it pertains to such fruits and so forth, is not "primordial" in a general sense.

However, regarding falls with respect to a building (saudha), it is possible for a particular fall to possess "primacy" (ādyatva). This primacy consists in its being simultaneous with the destruction of another fall that has the same locus (svasamānādhikaraṇa) and the same building as its limit; thus, primacy must be defined as being constituted by a specific limit. And so it is with a fall having a tree as its limit.

The state of being "last" (caramatva) must be defined as consisting precisely of a specific limit (avadhi), such as the property of not being simultaneous with the prior absence of falling relative to a tree that exists in the same locus as itself.
As for the state of being "first" (ādyatva) mentioned by Prakāśika, however, it does not consist of a specific limit.
It should be understood that this refers to the place of occurrence and the intention;
thus, it is stated in the *Dīpikā* regarding the definition of sound: "the word 'quality' (*guṇa-pada*)."

Nor should it be argued that the word "quality" (guṇa) is redundant, because one might intend to specify "the cause of the state of being a solid mass" (piṇḍībhāva) as the uncommon cause in order to exclude such unobserved [entities].

This is because it is necessary to exclude things such as powder, which serve as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); for this reason, the *Prakāśikā* [113] states that "the state of being a solid mass (*piṇḍībhāva*) is a particular kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*)."
The meaning is that it is suitable for functions such as supporting and attracting. Since it is evident that space is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of sound alone, he says:
"In the first case, it is the non-inherent cause," and so forth.

The Definition of Intellect (buddhi): Now, in the summary statement, "Intellect is cognition that is the cause of all worldly transaction," it follows that being the cause of all worldly transactions is the defining characteristic of intellect.
And that is not tenable;
for the status of being the cause of linguistic usage uttered by parrots and the like is absent from the cognition [of the speaker].

Even though there is no deviation [in the definition] when one speaks of being the cause with respect to linguistic usage dependent upon the desire to communicate (*bubodhayiṣā*), [the definition still fails].

There is non-pervasion (avyāpti) in that case because the cognition by which no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) was produced due to the influence of an obstructing factor lacks the capacity to produce such usage.
This remains so even if "causality" is defined as "essential fitness" (*svarūpayogyatā*), as this applies to cognitions of jars and the like.

Since a single cognition lacks the status of being a cause for conventional designations such as "cloth" and so forth, it cannot be the cause for all conventional designations; therefore, he says: "[114] The definition is simply the nature of cognition.
But if that is so, then why does the *Saṃgraha* state that it is "the cause of all conventional designations"?
1. Regarding the term *svapratiyogī*: here, the word *sva* (self) refers to the destruction of the first fall;
its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is the first fall.

Regarding the phrase "its being in the same locus as that" in the case of the second falling, he asks, "For what purpose was this stated? and answers: "Because the latent disposition (*saṃskāra*) is of three kinds. [114]

And thus, the point here is that if "disposition" (*saṃskāra*) were intended to mean velocity (*vega*) and elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*), it would be impossible for it to exist in memory. Regarding the phrase "called cultivation" (*bhāvanākhya*): [114]...
And thus, since cultivation is the cause of memory, the sense is that this fault does not apply;
[this is stated] because [memory] possesses the quality of being produced by a formative impression (*saṃskāra*).

The intended meaning is this: due to its proximity to cognition, it is necessary that the cause [of memory] possesses as its object something other than the unawakened latent impression (*saṃskāra*); otherwise, the manifestation of jars and so forth in the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) of desire and the like would be untenable.
Thus, since even a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) functions as a cause by way of being a means of introduction (*upanaya*), it possesses the property of producing a mental impression; therefore,
there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the definition to inference and other such cognitions— this is the intended meaning.

Nevertheless, regarding the phrase "the eye and so forth": if the absence of being produced by the mind (*manojanyatva*) were not included here, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the mental recognition (*mānasapratyabhijñā*) such as, "I who saw the jar, I now touch it. However, when that [absence of being produced by the mind] is included...
This is impossible,
because the mind is the instrument for all cognition in general;
the same applies to the eye and other sense organs.
It should not be argued that [the definition] is impossible because memory is a cause [of knowledge] by way of being a temporal factor (*kāla*) and so forth;

for what must be included [in the definition] is either the possession of a collection of differences whose counter-correlates are delimited by universals (*jāti*) such as "being visual" (*cākṣuṣatva*) or "being mental" (*mānasatva*), or a difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by "being perceptual" (*pratyakṣatva*).
This must be considered here:
[the absence] of that which is obtainable from the word as heard, composed with the suffix *mātra*, namely,

the state of being devoid of a generative cause (*janyatā*) delimited by a property subordinate to "being a cognition determined by something other than a latent impression" (*saṃskāretaranirūpitajñānatvavyāpyadharmāvacchinnajanyatāśūnyatva*).
Since the definition is established by the inclusion of "lightness" (laghu) alone, the inclusion of "difference" (bheda) in the manner described would result in prolixity; thus,
the definition of valid cognition as "experience that accords with reality" [is preferable].
Since it is possible to exclude desire (*icchā*) and other such states by including "being a cognition" (*jñānatva*), he says "smṛti" (recollection).
[116] This result is the purpose of including "being an experience" (*anubhavatva*). [116] "Where... and so forth.

And here, the point is that since even cognitions such as "the pot-and-cloth-both is a pot" are accepted as having partial truth (āṃśikapramātva), there is no suspicion of over-extension (ativyāpti) in those cases.
Some, however, [say] "the pot-and-cloth-both..."

Even though cognitions such as "this is a jar" are not themselves the objects of definition (*alakṣyatva*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in that case, because the definition includes either: (1) a qualificative objecthood (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by a property that serves as the delimitor of the locus (*adhikaraṇatāvacchedaka*) of that [relation] as qualified by its connection with it;

or (2) a qualificative objecthood delimited by a property that serves as the delimitor of the substratum-ness (*anuyogitā*) of that relation which has that [property] as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*).

Because the property of being both a pot and a cloth (*ghaṭapaṭobhayatva*) and so forth is neither a delimiting factor for the aforementioned locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) nor a delimiting factor for the aforementioned relatum-ness (*anuyogitā*), such a property of being both is subordinate to (*nyūnavṛtti*) that locus-ness and so forth. And it is not the case that...
It should not be argued that there is no pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of a valid cognition where the delimiting factor of the locus (dharmitāvacchedaka) is absent;

for [the definition] incorporates a qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) that is not delimited by the property that delimits such a locus-hood (tādṛśādhikaraṇatā). Nor does this being the case lead to any fault.

It should not be said that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of an error whose delimiting property is non-existent, because such an error is not established by valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*). This [objection] is incorrect—so they say.
That is not right.

Because it is established by the experience of deluded people that there occurs a cognition in the form "there is silver here" which apprehends mother-of-pearl and the like as silverness and so forth, and which is devoid of a determiner of the subject (nirdharmitāvacchedaka) regarding the aspect of silverness; therefore, the aforementioned refinement suffers from over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case.
Because it is difficult to prevent;
others, however,
[hold that it is] due to the absence of both the state of not being delimited by the delimiting property of the locus as it presents itself and the state of being delimited by it.

By incorporating [the property] into the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to such errors as "both the jar and the cloth are a jar," according to the method stated; nor is there non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a valid cognition (*pramā*) that lacks a delimiting factor for the subject (*nirdharmitāvacchedaka*). As for what was said—

The claim that this over-extension does not occur because of the inclusion of a qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) that is not delimited by a property (*dharma*) residing distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) is trivial;
for [the cognition] "This pot and that pot, both are a pot" [would otherwise be excluded].
They say that [the definition] lacks pervasion (avyāpti) with respect to valid cognition;
but that too is incorrect,
because it merely obscures the very same lack of pervasion already mentioned.

This is because properties such as "being both this pot and that pot" (etad-ghaṭa-tad-ghaṭobhayatva) have a narrower extension than "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and the like; thus, there is no evidence for their being delimiters (avacchedaka) in the form of an essential relation (svarūpa-sambandha) defined by the locus-hood of pot-ness and so forth, since it is accepted that only that which neither under-excludes nor over-excludes [the property to be delimited] can be its delimiter.
Because there would be the consequence of excessive complexity (*mahāgaurava*) if such properties as "being both" (*ubhayatva*), which are infinite, were admitted as delimiters (*avacchedaka*); for,
in the case of introducing that delimiter as having the nature of "not occurring elsewhere" (*aniriktavṛttitva*).

[This definition] would be over-narrow (avyāpti) with respect to valid cognitions such as "The jar is a substance," which apprehend jar-ness and so forth merely through the coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of substanceness and so on.
Now, regarding the phrase "tadvatī" and so forth...

Since the relation of *nirūpakatā* (the state of being a determiner) is not a delimitor of occurrence (*vṛttyanavacchedaka*), it cannot be a delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence; consequently, its connection with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) would be untenable, and it is impossible for it to have the sense of a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). Therefore, he says: "[115] The meaning of the locative case is the state of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyitva*)."

Alternatively, in order to establish the distinction from a collective cognition (samūhālambana) such as "the ground possesses fire" or "the mountain possesses a pot," there must be a relationship of the defined and the definer (nirūpyanirūpakabhāva) between the objectness (viśeṣyatva) and the modehood (prakāratva) in a cognition such as "the mountain possesses fire."
One view holds that [the qualifier-qualified relationship] must be accepted [as a distinct relation].

Another view holds that it is so because there is a relationship of the delimited and the delimiting (avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva) between the qualificandness and the modehood, which consist of the objective-possessiveness (viṣayitā) determined by that [relation].
In that regard, following the second opinion, he says: "the state of being the qualificand" (*viśeṣyitvam*).

And here, since the locative case-ending signifies the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*), [the definition] is: the nature of experience (*anubhavatva*) which is the determiner (*nirūpaka*) of a qualificandhood qualified by a mode (*prakāratā*).

Validity (*prāmāṇya*). If, however, the object of that [validity] is the state of being a qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*), then it consists in being an experience possessing a qualificandum-ness qualified by a mode-ness (*prakāritā*). In the first case, the state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is as follows:

In the first case, [the relation] is by way of both the relation of being located in that which possesses its own locus (svāśrayavat) through its own delimiting relation (svāvacchedaka-saṃbandha), and the relation of being determined by itself (svanirūpitatva).

In the second case, the state of being qualified (vaiśiṣṭya) is by way of both the relation of being delimited by itself (svāvacchinnatva) and the relation of being determined by a qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) that is qualified by a modehood (prakāratā) determined by itself.

And it should be understood that the qualification by the modehood (*prakāratā*) is by way of the relation of its own delimiting relation (*svāvacchedakasambandha*) and by way of the relation of residing in that which possesses its own locus (*svāśrayavanniṣṭhatvasambandha*).
[116] "Possessing that" means having a relation to that. In the first case, it is the nature of experience as the determiner of a qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) qualified by a modehood (prakāratā).
And the state of being qualified is...

By means of both relations: (1) being determined by itself (*svanirūpitatva*), and (2) residing in that which is the locus of the correlatehood (*anuyogitā*) determined by a counter-correlateness (*pratiyogitā*) qualified by itself (*svaviśiṣṭa*).
[Note: 1. *Svāvacchedaka* etc.: The application is made in the cognition "This is silver" (*idaṃ rajatam*) with respect to the silver. *Sva* refers to...

The property-residing-in-the-silverness (*rajatatvaniṣṭhaprakāratā*) has as its delimiting relation (*avacchedakasambandha*) inherence (*samavāya*); by that relation, the silver possesses the silverness which is the locus of the property-residence. This "residing-in-that" (*tanniṣṭhatva*) resides in the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*). Likewise, "self" (*sva*) refers to the property-residence residing in silverness, and "being determined by that" (*tannirūpitatva*) also resides in the qualificandum.
The property of being an experience that has such a qualificandumhood (viśeṣyatā) exists in the cognition "this is silver.

In the second definition, "self" refers to the state of being a qualifier (prakāritā); it is the state of being delimited by that [qualificandumhood] residing in the cognition, which is itself determined by the qualifierhood residing in silverness.

It exists in the objectness residing in the cognition as determined by the objectness residing in silver; likewise, it [exists] through the relation of inherence, which is the delimitor of that silverness-residing qualifierhood which is itself determined by its own qualifierhood.
And since the state of being qualified by the qualificand-ness residing in silver— which is the locus of the mode (prakāratā)— exists in the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyitā),
that [silver] is the nature of the experience which is its locus.
The syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) is as follows: "This is silver" exists in the valid cognition (*pramā*).
Regarding the phrase "svanirūpitatva" and so forth: *sva* refers to the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in silverness; "nirūpitatva" means being determined by that [qualifierhood].
In the qualificand-ness residing in silver;
likewise, its own qualifier-ness is the counter-correlativity residing in silverness (as determined by the relation of inherence).

The relativity (anuyogitā) determined by that [silverness] resides in the silver, because the silver is the relatum (anuyogi) with respect to its inherence in silverness; thus, the property of residing in the silver, which is the locus of that [inherence], belongs to the qualificandum-ness (viśeṣyatā).

And the qualification by the modehood residing in silverness (*rajatatvaniṣṭhaprakāratā*) must be established as follows with respect to the counterpositiveness residing in silverness (*rajatatvaniṣṭhapratiyogitā*): "self" refers to the modehood; its locus is silverness; and the state of residing therein belongs to the counterpositiveness.
Thus, its own mode (prakāratā) has inherence-nature (*samavāyatva*) as its locus through the relation of being the delimitor of its own delimitorhood;
and the difference residing therein [in that inherence-nature] exists through the relation of being the delimitor of its own determinerhood (*nirūpakatāvacchedakatā*).
The difference from that which possesses counter-correlativity does not exist,
because inherence (samavāya) is the determiner of the counter-correlativity residing in silverness, [and thus] resides in the nature of inherence (samavāyatva).
Because there exists the state of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity residing in silverness,
it is impossible for there to be a difference from that [silverness] in the case of inherence (samavāyatva), which possesses that counter-correlativity through that relation; rather,
there is another difference, and the state of being the delimiting factor of that [other] counter-correlativity resides in the counter-correlativity itself.

The property "does not exist" consists in being distinct from itself by way of the relation of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference co-referential with itself;

and this property of possessing differences such as "difference from itself" exists within the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*). Thus, the counter-correlativity becomes qualified by the mode (*prakāratā*) through both of the aforementioned relations.
The same should be inferred for what follows hereafter.

In the case of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), its own qualification (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of both relations: [1] residing in that which has itself as its substratum (*svāśrayaniṣṭhatva*), and [2] possessing a difference from its own class and so forth (*svasajātīyādibhedavattva*).
And "having its own locus" [is defined] by the relation of being the delimitation of the delimitation of its own [absence's] counter-correlativity;
or by the relation of a unique delimitation belonging to that which is the counter-correlativity of the difference and is the determinant of its own [absence's] counter-correlativity.
Therefore, in the view of the ancient masters who maintain the oneness of inherence (*samavāya*), [the proposition] "Air possesses color by way of inherence" [is not a valid cognition].
There is no over-extension [of the definition] to error;

nor is there [over-extension] in such an erroneous cognition as "the quality is that which possesses existence qualified by being other than non-qualities," because [in that case] the inherence is not delimited by the state of being qualified by that [error].
There is over-extension (ativyāpti) regarding the view that relationhood (saṃsargatā) is [the nature of] relation;
for although conjunction, inherence, and so forth are impossible under the view that relationhood is their own essential nature (svarūpa), [the definition would still apply].
Nevertheless, according to that view,

it is precisely the state of being determined by the relation that constitutes its own delimitation (*svāvacchedaka-sambandha*) that must be included within the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*). However, in the erroneous cognition "possessing qualified existence" (*viśiṣṭa-sattāvān*),...

Since only a distinct locus-ness (*ādhikaraṇatā*), whose relatum-ness (*nirūpakatā*) resides in inherence (*samavāya*) as delimited by a specific property (*vaiśiṣṭya*), constitutes the relation (*saṃsarga*),
there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If...

And this being the case, it is said that there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a cognition having "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as its qualifier by way of both the relations of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*); for such an over-extension is unavoidable if one takes into account the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) delimited by those two relations. At that time—

And the qualification of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) by itself [the absence] occurs through both relations: (1) residing in its own locus (*svāśrayaniṣṭhatva*), and (2) possessing a difference from its own set and so forth (*svasetyādibhedavattva*).
[The term] *svādhikaraṇatā* [refers to] the state of being its own locus.
[The relation is] by way of the relation of being the relativity of the delimitor (*svāvacchedaka-saṃsargatā-sambandha*).
The delimitation of the counterpositiveness of the difference (*bheda-pratiyogitāvacchedakatā*) [is related] by way of the relation of being its own determiner (*svanirūpakatā-sambandha*).
As for that which was stated—

that in the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), one must introduce "the state of having an avacchedakatā pervaded by its own avacchedaka" as a constituent factor of its own specificity (*svavaiśiṣṭya*)— and that...
It culminates in the state of possessing distinctions such as being one's own limit (*svasīman*) and so forth;
furthermore, the delimitation of its own locus (*svādhikaraṇāvacchedakatā*) does not [exist] by way of the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatāsambandhena*).

Nor should it be argued that there is thus a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) is of an uninterrupted jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), etc.;
for [the definition] does not involve the relation of "being qualified by itself" (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) as previously described,

but rather involves the relation of "possessing an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in itself, whose counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the delimitor of the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of a difference (*bheda*) that is co-locative with itself."
Because there is no fault in introducing its own specific property (vaiśiṣṭya),
and because a relation already mentioned [as the qualifier] would be in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇa) with respect to an unqualified mode of presentation (anavacchinnaprakāratā).
And thus, there is no over-extension in the erroneous cognition "possessing qualified existence" (*viśiṣṭasattāvān*).

Alternatively, the relation of its own qualification (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) within the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) consists of a triad of relations: [1] residing in its own substratum (*svāśrayaniṣṭhatva*), [2] being determined by the relation that delimits it (*svāvacchedakasambandhanirūpitatva*), and [3] being the delimitation of the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhabhedapratiyogitāvacchedakatva*).
The property of being a delimitant (*avacchedakatva*) [is defined] by the relation of being delimited by a property qualified by itself.

And the qualification by itself [is defined] by the relation of possessing a difference whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, which is in turn delimited by the relation of being a delimitant (*avacchedakatā*).
Furthermore, it is not possible to include the condition "not being delimited by a property that does not delimit itself" [in the definition].

For if "not being its own delimiter" were defined as "being different from its own delimiter," then because its own delimiter would be unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), there would be an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in the previously mentioned valid cognition.

Even if [the absence] consists in an absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a relation that delimits itself, the aforementioned defect is not avoided because the counterpositiveness still possesses the property of being delimited by such a [delimiting] attribute.
That is not correct.

Because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such erroneous cognitions as "quality (*guṇa*) possesses a specific existence (*viśiṣṭasattā*)," since it is universally accepted that a cognition such as "quality possesses existence qualified by being other than quality and so forth" (*guṇādyanyatvopalakṣitasattāvān guṇaḥ*) is of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*),
[the property of] being qualified by being other than quality and so forth must also [be included].

Because the status of being a delimitor (*avacchedakatva*) of the locusness (*ādheyatā*) as determined by qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth does not disappear; for it is precisely the qualifier of the locusness that serves as its delimitor. For this very reason, [the relation] possesses the nature of being a relation that delimits the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭābhāva*).

Gadādhara, in his *Siddhāntalakṣaṇa*, accepts that the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) delimited by being specified by a qualifier (*viśiṣṭanirūpitatva*) serves as the delimiting relation for the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakasambandha*) of an absence characterized by a mere indicator (*upalakṣita*), whereas the undelimited inherence (*anavacchinnasamavāya*) is accepted [as such] otherwise; for [otherwise],
it would suffice merely through the presence or absence of the counter-positiveness-delimiting nature of the qualifier itself.

Because, according to the method demonstrated, it would follow that the explanation of the distinction between an absence qualified by a specific property (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) and an absence merely characterized by it (*upalakṣitābhāva*) is untenable;

for cognitions such as "that which possesses existence qualified by otherness from qualities" (where the relation is inherence characterized by otherness from qualities) lack any basis in valid experience.
In my view,
there is no room for the faults shown [in the opponent's position];
otherwise, as stated above, there would be the consequence of a lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*).
It should be understood that this is because it would result in a contradiction with the definition of a tenet (*siddhānta*).

Regarding the phrase "the consequence of being another means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntaratāpatti*): the meaning is that it would result in being a means of valid cognition distinct from the fourfold set beginning with perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The meaning is that [the definition] exists there because it possesses the status of being an uncommon cause while having an activity consisting of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
This concludes the examination of erroneous experience (*ayathārthānubhava*).
[119] Regarding the passage beginning with "In that case, it would lack that," etc.: here,

error (*bhramatva*) consists in being an experience (*anubhavatva*) qualified by having a qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) characterized by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*), or alternatively, qualified by having a qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyitā*) characterized by a modality-ness (*prakāritā*).

And the first [qualification] consists in the relation of being located in that which possesses an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a property residing in one and only that which is qualified by itself, combined with the relation of being characterized by itself.
And the qualification by itself [is as follows]:...

[The relation is] by way of the two relations: (1) residing in that which possesses an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a property residing solely in what is qualified by itself (*svaviśiṣṭaikamātravṛttidharmāvacchinnapratiyogitākābhāvavanniṣṭhatva*), and (2) being characterized by itself (*svanirūpitatva*).

And "being qualified by itself" (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of the two relations: (1) being delimited by the relation that delimits itself (*svāvacchedakasambandhāvacchinnatva*), and (2) residing in the locus of itself (*svāśrayaniṣṭhatva*). In the second [case]...
And the specific distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) should be inferred by oneself according to the method stated above;
for here, within the relation (*saṃsarga*), pervasiveness over its own locus (*svāśraya-vyāpyavṛttitva*) must be introduced.
There is no over-extension [of the definition] to a valid cognition whose qualifier does not pervade [its locus];
for, in reality,
because non-existence is introduced as being characterized by a locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) that is unconditioned (*niravacchinna*), there is no problem whatsoever.
The point is that this is a defect (*doṣa*).

Since an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not appear in an error (*bhrama*) by virtue of being its own delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), he says in the *Dīpikā* [120]: "the absence of conjunction" (*saṃyogābhāva*). Now, one might object:

He states— beginning with "In this regard, it should be noted that..."— that there is an over-narrow definition (avyāpti) of error, such as "the qualificandum being delimited by the locus of the absence of that [object]," in the case of an error where silver-ness and so forth are presented as pervasively present, such as "this is silver" in relation to mother-of-pearl.
This must be considered here:

since it is easy to state that the definition remains the same even when there is a difference between the qualifiers— whether they subsist pervasively or non-pervasively— by way of the formulation "the nature of an experience that determines a qualificandum qualified by a qualifierhood," [there is no need for a separate definition] based on that difference.
The description of a difference in characteristics is most improper;
and "qualifiedness" [is defined] by the relation of both being self-defined and residing in a locus qualified by itself.
And its own qualification [is established] by the relation of possessing an absence qualified by itself;
and that qualification of itself [resides] in the absence by means of the relation that delimits it.
[The relation is] by way of both [the following] relations: (1) residing in a locus that is not the locus of its own substratum; and (2) having a counter-correlativity qualified by itself.
And the qualification by itself (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of both [the following] relations: (a) being delimited by the relation that delimits itself; and (b) residing in the locus of itself.
1. Regarding the term *svaviśiṣṭa* ("qualified by itself"):
the term *svaviśiṣṭa* is construed with "the counter-correlativity delimited by a property residing in only one [of the two relata].
Thus, *sva* refers to the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) residing in silverness (*rajatatva*), and the relation is its delimiting relation (*avacchedaka-sambandha*).

The relation is inherence (*samavāya*); the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) residing in silverness, as delimited by that [inherence], likewise resides in the locus of the mode (*prakāra*). Thus, the counter-positiveness qualified by the mode is delimited by a single property residing solely in the form of "silverness" (*rajatatvatva*); [the absence] is its locus, being characterized by that [counter-positiveness].
The syntactic connection should be made according to the principle: "in [the relation of] qualificandness.
2. "To be inferred by oneself" means: error is the state of being an experience possessing a qualificandness qualified by a mode (prakāritā).

And the distinction [of the qualifier] is by way of both relations: being qualified by a subjectness (viśeṣyatā) that is itself delimited by [the qualifier] and determined by [that qualifier], and being determined by that [subjectness].
Furthermore, the qualification of the subjectness by the qualifierness (prakāratā) is as follows:

The meaning is as follows: [the absence] is related [to the locus] by way of both relations: (1) residing in a locus that possesses an absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a property residing in only that which is qualified by itself (*svaviśiṣṭa*); and (2) being self-referential (*svanirūpitatva*).

Furthermore, "being qualified by itself" with respect to the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*) should be understood as being determined by both relations: (a) being delimited by the relation that delimits itself (*svāvacchedaka-sambandha*), and (b) residing in the locus of itself (*svāśraya-niṣṭhatva*). 3.

Regarding the passage beginning with "svanirūpitatva" (being determined by itself), etc.: here, in the subordinate [definition], all instances of the word "self" (sva) refer to the mode-of-being (prakāratā).
The syntactic connection (samanvaya) is to be inferred as before.

As for that which was stated— that [the definition of memory] consists in being an experience that possesses a qualifierhood qualified by a qualifierhood, such qualifierhood being related to its own qualified-objecthood (viśeṣyatā) by both the relation of being determined by it and the relation of identity (tādātmya), as characterized by the aforementioned connection—
This is incorrect, because it would entail a great complexity due to the dual inclusion of the state of being a non-mode (*aprakāratva*) and the addition of identity (*tādātmya*).
Nor does the passage beginning with "by whatever delimitation" [apply here].
It should not be argued that such a description is made in accordance with the tone of the *Dīpikā* statement;

for if such a *Dīpikā* statement were intended to convey a difference in definition (*lakṣaṇabheda*), it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to valid cognitions such as "the tree characterized by the root is in contact with a monkey."
Because the definition of error pertaining to cases where the qualifier does not pervade its locus would be unavoidable;
and because, in the absence of a contradiction regarding the object, it is impossible to accept this as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Therefore, the aforementioned statement from the *Dīpikā*—

According to the method we have stated, with the intention of refining the definition of error, one might raise the objection that there is no coverage (*avyāpti*) in the case of an error whose qualifier is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*);
[we reply that] it is precisely a cognition that apprehends the qualification of a relation such as conjunction, where the locus is qualified by the root and so forth...
This is intended to demonstrate that error (*bhrama*) is the object of definition (*lakṣya*).
And thus, in the *Dīpikā* [120], the phrase "because it is intended" refers to [error] as the object of definition, and so forth; [120] "having been qualified," etc.

In this context, although it is possible to exclude *samūhālambana* [cognition] by incorporating the relationship of the defined and the definer (*nirūpya-nirūpaka-bhāva*) between the property of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) and the property of being the qualifier (*prakāratā*), nevertheless,
another method has been stated for the sake of clarifying the student's understanding; thus it should be understood.
Regarding the division of experience according to the object as stated in the *Dīpikā* [123], it is mentioned "incidentally" (*prasaṅgāt*).
Here, the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamy-artha*) is dependence upon the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) produced by cognition.
Regarding the inquiry, "What is the relevance of being accompanied by a distinction? he says in the *Prakāśikā* [123]:
"The state of that which has been remembered being unfit for neglect," and so forth. Of that which has been remembered...

The state of being unfit for neglect, which is the object of memory through its connection with a previously established entity, consists of a nature that is opposed to being the object of a cognition of aversion;
and in the present context, this is the state of being the instrument of valid cognition (*pramiti*). This...

Without including the fivefold classification beginning with *upodghāta*, and based on the conviction that even *upodghāta* and the others are included within *prasaṅga* itself— since they possess the nature of being modes of cognition that generate the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) which serves as the purpose for the subsequent statement— the definition of *prasaṅga* is formulated otherwise, as consisting in a specific difference from the general nature of causality (*kāraṇatā*), given that instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is a particular form of causality.
Because it is irrelevant due to its impossibility in the present context;
in reality, however,

[the term] is that which causes the recollection of a property that serves as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the object to be defined (*nirūpya*), thereby generating the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) that necessitates the immediate subsequent mention.

A relationship that is distinct from those such as the *upoddhāta* (introduction) and others, which are established through specific investigation, is *prasaṅga-saṅgati* (the connection of incidental relevance).

In the present context, since there are four types [of valid cognition], the similarity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) is precisely what constitutes such a relationship.
This is what must be noted here.

The connection (*saṅgati*) consists in the state of possessing a property that is qualified by another property; and this qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of the two relations of being different from itself and being qualified by a word qualified by itself.
And its own qualification (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) is as follows:

[The relation is] by way of both: (1) the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, which is delimited by the relation of being posterior to a word qualified by itself; and (2) the state of being posterior to the description of an object delimited by itself.

Furthermore, the qualification of "itself" [in the first relation] is by way of both: (1) the state of being posterior to the description of an object delimited by itself; and (2) the state of being a generator of a cognition whose qualificandum is delimited by a property different from itself and whose mode is a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), etc.
The qualification of the word [as the locus] is by way of both relations: being the locus (*ādheyatva*) and being qualified by the intention that motivates itself.
And the qualification of the intention is by way of both relations: being the locus and being the qualifier of the cognition that produces it.
As for being the locus...

[The relation is] by way of the property of having a qualificandumhood delimited by "cognition-ness," which is itself determined by a "determining-ness" (nirūpakatva-prakāratā), which is itself determined by a "qualificandum-ness" (prakāratva-prakāratā), which is itself determined by a "property-ness" (dharma-prakāratā), which is itself determined by a "pervaded-ness-ness" (vyāpyatva-prakāratā), which is itself determined by a "qualificandum-ness" (prakāratā) residing in itself (svaniṣṭha). Thus, in such cases as "inference is connected with perception," the referent of the word *saṅgati* (connection) is precisely a property qualified by another property.
In that context, perception is connected to the first property by way of the relation of "inherence-in-that-which-is-based-on-being-perceptual" (*pratyakṣatvaniṣṭhādheyatāsambandha*).
[The second property] consists in the capacity to convey a specific property that serves as the delimiting factor for the correlate of the connection (*anvayitāvacchedakadharma*).
The word *saṅgati* is established through its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).

Likewise, the capacity to convey the connection of a second property (*dvitīyadharmānvayabodhakatva*) resides in the substratum (*āśrayatā*), which is a part of the meaning of the suffix, by means of the relation of being qualified by the desired [property] as delimited by the relation that constitutes the ground for the application of the word conveying the positive correlate (*anvayisamarpakapada*). It is in this same manner.
In reality, however, *saṅgati* (relevance) is simply the state of being qualified by a property (*dharmaviśiṣṭatvam*).
And this qualification (*vaiśiṣṭyam*)...
By the relation of being qualified by a locus qualified by itself;

and the qualification of itself [is determined] by two relations: (1) being characterized by a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a property different from itself, and (2) being qualified by the word qualified by itself.
And the word’s own qualification [is established] as before.

Furthermore, the qualification of the word [in the cognition] occurs through the relation of both being the locus (*ādheyatva*) and being qualified by the intention that causes its own application. Locality (*ādheyatā*)...

[The relation is] by way of being the producer of a cognition whose qualificandum is delimited by a property that is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference determined by itself (the desire), and whose qualifier is definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth. And the state of being qualified by desire [is established] by way of both relations: (1) the relation of being located, as delimited by the state of being a cognition whose qualifier is a property pervaded by a property that is merely characterized (*upalakṣita*) by being the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference determined by itself (the desire); and (2) the relation of being qualified by a recollection that serves as the cause for such [cognition].

And the possession of this distinction [vaiśiṣṭya] is by way of both relations: (1) the relation of being located in [the locus] as delimited by the relation that motivates itself (*svaprayojaka-saṃbandha*), and (2) the relation of being the substratum (*ādheyatva*) as delimited by the relation consisting in having as its qualifier the property that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma*) of the difference (*bheda*) that characterizes itself;
and the possession of the locus-status (*adhikaraṇatā-vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of the relation of being the substrate of the substrate of itself (*svāśrayāśrayatva*). And here...
In expressions such as *saṅgatam* ("connected"), regarding the substratumhood (*āśrayatā*) which constitutes a part of the meaning of the suffix *-ta*,

the rule for syntactic connection (*anvaya-vyutpatti*) is that it occurs through the relation of "being characterized by its own substratum" (*svāśraya-nirūpitatva*), as delimited by that very relation by which the knowledge of the relation acts as a reminder of the relation itself.
It is to be accepted. The rest is as before.
Regarding the definition of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the inclusion of God (*īśvara*) is indicated by the phrase "from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth."

[124] Regarding the phrase "pervaded by the state of being an experience": although it is possible to exclude [factors such as] time and so forth even by introducing a causality defined by an effectness delimited by a property other than "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), nevertheless...
Because it does not exclude the self (*ātman*) and so forth, which serve as general causes for knowledge, there is disregard for them.
[The phrase] "in the occurrence of valid cognition" (*pramāvṛtti*) is intended to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to defects that produce error. Now, one might object:

The definition of valid cognition as formulated by Nirukta is over-extensive with respect to the conjunction of the eye [with its object] and so forth. Nor should it be argued that there is no such fault because of the inclusion of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*);
for if that were the case, [the definition would still apply] to the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the like.

Because the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would otherwise be untenable, he says: "even when there is the possession of an operation" (*vyāpāravattve sati*). And this "possession of an operation" is as follows:

The nature of an operation (*vyāpāratva*) consists in being qualified by something through the dual relation of being its own producer and being the producer of that which is produced by it. The phrase "being the producer of that which is produced by it" (while also being produced by it) is included in order to exclude the [original] cause itself.
The term "end" (*anta*) [in the definition] is for the purpose of excluding the fruit (*phala*). The qualifying attribute (*viśeṣya*) serves to exclude the result.
The inclusive meaning is "being qualified by the knowable (*prameya*)" through the two relations of being produced by it and being the producer of what is produced by it.
If it is argued that there is prolixity (*gaurava*) due to the inclusion of the additional category of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, [the response follows].
In that case, being qualified by "being produced" (janyatā) must be expressed;

and this qualification [is understood] through the relation of both "having its own locus" (svāśrayatva) and "being the producer of that which is produced by its own determiner" (svanirūpakajanyajanakatva). Alternatively, [it may be defined as follows].

The commonality (*anugama*) is to be understood as "being qualified by the state of being produced" through the relation of both: (1) being the producer of its own locus, and (2) being produced by that which determines itself.
In reality, however...
The nature of an operation (*vyāpāratva*) consists in being the determiner of a generative capacity that necessitates the production of a result.

By this definition, there is no room for the undesirable consequence that the son of a potter and the like would be considered the operation of the potter and so forth. Alternatively, it should be understood here as the state of being a generator produced by that [action], which takes the form of being a relation that delimits such a generative capacity.
But if this were the case, the validity of the auditory sense-organ (*śrotrendriya*) would be untenable;
for since *samavāya* (inherence) alone constitutes the contact (*sannikarṣa*) there, it cannot possess the aforementioned operation because it is not produced. To this, he says:

[124] Regarding the term "auditory organ" (*śrotra*): Is it not the case that being a cause consists in occurring immediately prior to the effect? And that must be stated in terms of the relation that delimits causal status (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-sambandha*).
Otherwise, [the causal status] of sacrifices and the like—
Because it would be untenable for [the sacrifice] to be the cause of heaven and so forth;

however, if it is stated in that way, there is no such untenability, since the sacrifice and other acts possess that status by virtue of their connection with the *apūrva* produced by themselves. And thus:

Instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is simply the state of being a cause delimited by its connection with an operation (*vyāpāra*). The separate qualification "provided it possesses an operation" is redundant, because the eye’s contact (*cakṣussaṃyoga*) and other such factors lack the aforementioned form [of instrumentality].
In that case, there would be no over-extension [of the definition].

Thus, with respect to audibility (*śrāvaṇa*), the ear is not the cause by way of the relation of its own occurrence as a mental conjunction (*manassaṃyoga*), but rather by way of the relation of being the object of worldly linguistic usage (*laukikaviṣayatā*).
Because it is possible, he says: "or sound. The sense is that, in this way, the ear's status as a cause is possible through its relation of identity with the sound residing within itself.
Regarding the phrase "they say," the word "the ancients" is to be supplied.
He states the new view [124]: "Because of its delay.

The essential point is this: uncommonness (*asādhāraṇatva*) consists in being the counter-positive of an absence that serves as the cause for the non-arising of an effect at a time when all other causes of the effect under consideration are present; this amounts to being characterized by the non-arising of the effect.
Therefore, there is no failure of the property of selfhood (svatva) to follow [the relation].

And the state of being qualified (vaiśiṣṭya) is by way of the two relations: being the counter-positive of an absence that serves as its own motivator (prayojaka), and being the delimiting factor of the counter-positiveness of a difference residing in a moment that is its own locus.
The state of being its own locus [is defined] by the relation of being the locus of the causes of the effect under consideration, excluding itself.
The delimitation of the counter-correlativity of difference [is defined] by the relation of inherence (*ādheyatva*).

As for that which [is defined] by the two relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and being the counter-correlate of an absence that is the causal factor for the non-arising of the effect under consideration occurring in a moment qualified by itself—

That [is] the state of being qualified by the object of cognition (*prameya-viśiṣṭatva*). [The phrase] "by the relation of being the delimitant of the counter-correlativity of a difference co-located with itself" means:
by the relation of being the delimitant of the counter-correlativity of a difference that is co-located with itself.

In this context, the coordination is as follows: in the expressions "svaprayojaka" (its own instigator) and "svādhikaraṇa" (its own locus), the word "sva" (self/own) refers to the absence of the production of the effect.

In the phrase "its own [cause] and so forth" (*svasetyādi*), the word *sva* refers to the cause, such as a staff; in the phrase "other than its own" (*svetara*), the word *sva* likewise refers to the cause, such as a staff.
And thus:

"self" refers to the absence of the production of the jar; the state of being qualified by that [absence] resides in the staff, and this constitutes its status as an uncommon cause. "Self" [refers to...].
The absence of the production of the jar is the non-existence that acts as its cause; this is the absence of the staff. The state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) resides in the staff.

Likewise, one's own [non-existence] is the absence of the production of the jar; the difference that exists at the moment which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of that [absence] is the "difference from the possessor of the staff" (*daṇḍavad-bheda*).
And the state of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-positiveness of that [difference] resides in the staff.
Here, by the term "difference from one possessing a staff" (*daṇḍavad-bheda*),

there is the difference from one possessing a staff [as the counter-correlate] related to the locus of the cause and effect of its own other [terms], through the relation of being delimited by the delimitorhood delimited by the relation of substratumness as determined by the counter-correlateness of the difference residing in the locus of the cause and effect of its own other [terms].
It is to be understood as follows:

because there is a rule that a location which is the substratum of causes other than the staff and the pot must exist at a moment that is the substratum of the absence of the pot's production, [the staff] exists in such a location.

The difference [in question]— namely, the difference existing in a moment that is the locus of the absence of the production of the jar by way of the relation of being the locus of the contained— is not [the same as] the difference [from the jar]; therefore,

it possesses the property of being the delimiting adjunct of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in the locus of the causes of the specific effect under consideration, other than itself.
Since such a moment does not exist [as possessing the staff], that moment is not "possessing a staff" by virtue of the relation of such a delimitation; therefore,
the absence of one who possesses a staff occurs in such a moment.
Since the state of being the delimiting factor of that counter-correlativity exists in the staff,

the staff’s status as the uncommon cause of the jar is established by virtue of its being qualified by the absence of the production of the jar through the aforementioned two relations. And as for this [qualification]...
The inclusion [of the definition] is achieved through the relation of being a distinction from "itself" (svasetar) and so forth;

the property of having itself as its locus and so on is to be understood in the manner previously described. However, that [method] is to be disregarded because it is vitiated by the fault of prolixity due to the introduction of identity (*tādātmya*) and other such relations.
Regarding the definition of a cause: surely, even by incorporating the condition of being distinct from itself (*svabhinnatva*), the exclusion of the self is possible;
likewise [in the case of] conjunction and so forth.
Since the absence of potsherds exists in the locus of a jar, such as the ground, by way of relations like identity (*tādātmya*),
it would follow that potsherds and the like could not be the loci of a jar; the same applies to the locus of an effect.

Since the absence of the cause is possible both at the time delimited by the period immediately preceding the effect and at the time delimited by the period following the effect, that very same fault applies;
thus it is for all [causes].
There is the impossibility [of the definition] because of the fact that [the pot] is the counter-positive of an absence delimited by duality and so forth.

However, the possession of a property that is not a delimiting factor for the counter-positiveness of such an absence would [apply] by taking such a property as "knowability" (prameyatva) and the like.

This would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga) even to a donkey; therefore, he states the refinement: "by the relation that delimits the state of being an effect," and so forth. And here, after the word "absence" (abhāva), [the word] "counter-positive-ness" (pratiyogitā) [is to be supplied].

It should be supplemented by the phrase "delimited by the relation intended to constitute the nature of being a prior cause. By this, it should be understood that no fault arises from taking into account the absence of a cause delimited by a different relation.
This concludes the definition of superfluous causality (*anyathāsiddhi*).
In the sentence from the *Dīpikā* beginning with "yena saha" (together with which),

the word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*) refers to that which is delimited by the nature of being a thread (*tantutva*) and so forth, which is intended as the delimitor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).
The word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) refers to the nature of being a thread and so forth, which is intended as being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*).

The final word ending in the second case (*dvitīyānta*) refers to that which is delimited by the property serving as the delimitor of the effectness of the subject under discussion (*prakṛtakāryatāvacchedakadharma*). 1.
Regarding "by the relation of possessing a difference [from itself] and so forth" (*svasetyādibhedavattvasambandhena*):

the meaning is "by the relation of possessing a difference whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a delimitor residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhāvacchedakatāka*), and whose counterpositiveness is further delimited by a relation that delimits the counterpositiveness of a difference co-resident with itself (*svasamānādhikaraṇabhedapratiyogitāvacchedakasambandhāvacchinna*)."
Keeping this meaning in mind, he says:
"By which thread," and so forth.
And here, the word *saha* denotes concomitance (*sāhitya*).
And that [concomitance] is the connection with a single action;
since the action is obtained from the verbal root itself, the meaning of the word "together" (saha) is precisely this connection.
According to the maxim "the meaning of a word is not obtainable through anything else," and since that [meaning] here consists in being the determiner of the mode (prakāratānirūpakatva),
the third case ending in the word "yena" [expresses this].
The meaning is the property of being a locus (ādheyatva) as qualified by the mode of presentation (prakāratā).
By virtue of the emphatic particle *eva* conjoined with the qualifier,

[the meaning is] that which is related through a relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) characterized by the pervasion of the nature of a cognition whose mode of presentation is the state of being an invariably antecedent factor to the action in question, having as its qualificandum that which is delimited by a particular property (*yaddharmāvacchinna-viśeṣyaka*).

In the cognition that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root *gam* preceded by the prefix *ava*, there is an occurrence of the property of being a determiner (*prakāratā*) as characterized by such [a relation].

The meaning of the verb suffix (*ākhyāta*) is "modehood" (*prakāratva*), which occurs in the cognition as the qualificandum-determinacy (*viśeṣyakatva*) delimited by the property denoted by the relative pronoun *yad* in the genitive case *yasya*.
And the state of being a qualifier (prakāratva) is related to the referent of the word ending in the nominative case;
thus, by the aforementioned relation.

The understanding derived from the sentence beginning with "yena saha" (with which) is as follows: the state of being a necessary antecedent to the action in question is that which serves as the qualifier in a cognition whose qualificandum is delimited by a certain property (yaddharma), and which is further characterized by being the determiner of the mode (prakāratā) that is the object of a specific relation (niṣṭhaprakāratānirūpakatva).
And thus:

The result is that one form of "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddha*) consists in the possession of a property (*dharmavatva*) such that there exists a general cognition which has as its qualifier the state of being invariably antecedent to the effect under discussion, with respect to an object qualified by that property, and which is the determiner of a mode (*prakāratā*) qualified by that same property.
The following is the analysis here:

[the definition] consists in the possession of a property qualified by another property; and this qualification is by way of the relation of "being located in" (ādheyatā). And that [relation of being located in] is by way of the relation of "possessing a difference consisting in its own set" (svasetyādibhedavattva).

The state of being its own locus (*svādhikaraṇatā*) is by way of the relation of being a cognition whose qualifier is the state of being invariably antecedent to the present operation, and whose qualificandum is delimited by itself (*svāvacchinna*).

The delimination of the counter-correlativity of difference (*bhedapratiyogitāvacchedakatā*) is by way of the relation of being the determiner of a qualifier delimited by itself (*svāvacchinnaprakāratānirūpakatva*).

And here, in order to prevent the charge of being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) by taking the collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of the "tanned-ness" (*tanatu-tva*) and so forth of cloth and other objects, the inclusion of the property of pervading the category of generality (*sāmānya-padārtha-vyāpakatva*) is introduced.

If one were to include merely the status of being an object (*viṣayatāmātra*), it would follow that a staff and the like would be "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*) by their own nature; therefore, the inclusion of the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) is necessary with respect to a cloth.
The yarn-form does not possess causality by virtue of being a color, precisely because of deviation;
therefore, even though the first type of extraneous sufficiency (*anyathāsiddhi*) is impossible at that time, there is no flaw.
It has been stated that the indication does not lead to over-extension;
it pertains specifically to the thread.
This is because when a suffix is applied to a word denoting a genus (jāti), the genus appears only in some form or other.

The point is that, in the present context, "threadness" (tantutva) is the qualificandum precisely as "threadness-ness" (tantutvatva), and "threadness-ness" consists in being inherent in all threads while not being inherent in anything other than the threads.
This is the summary.

Although the term "by which" (*yena*)— along with the necessary qualification used to prevent the over-extension (*anyathāsiddhi*) of the conjunction of threads by means of the threads themselves— prevents the over-extension of the thread [as the cause] by way of its nature as a thread (*tantutva*).
The qualification "possessing independent positive and negative concomitance" is redundant; nevertheless,
that qualification is necessary to exclude the case where the color of a thread (*tantu-rūpa*) is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) by its being a thread (*tantutva*).

[This is] for the sake of awakening. For this very reason, it is precisely by explaining the word *yat* as referring to that which is delimited by a particular property (*dharma*) that the possibility of precluding the "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) status of the thread [in relation to the cloth] arises;
because in the cognition "the thread is an antecedent invariably preceding the cloth," the property of being a thread (*tantutva*) appears in its own right (*svarūpataḥ*). Thus...
And thus, the suspicion that the qualification "ending in emptiness" (*śūnyānta*) is redundant is dispelled;

for it serves a purpose in order to prevent the charge of "otherwise-establishedness" (*anyathāsiddhi*) against the property delimited by being a color residing in its substratum as qualified by the nature of thread-ness (*tantutvatva*).

The state of possessing independent positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) consists in having positive and negative concomitance that is not dependent upon the positive and negative concomitance residing in anything other than itself. Furthermore, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is the state of possessing an existence that is the cause of the existence of the effect under consideration.

And negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consists in being the counter-correlative of an absence that is the cause for the absence of the effect under discussion. Here, the general definition (*anugama*) is: "being qualified by such a negative concomitance while being qualified by such an existence."

In the first case, the distinction [of the property] is by way of the two relations of being its own locus and being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in itself;
and the state of being a delimiting factor is by way of the relation of dependence on a positive concomitance residing in something other than itself.

In the second [definition], the specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of the relation consisting of both *svāśrayatva* (having itself as its locus) and *svavṛttibhedapratiyogitāvacchedakatva* (being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in itself).

The delimiting factorhood of the counter-correlativity of the difference is by way of the relation of being dependent upon the absence (*vyatireka*) residing in something other than itself (*svabhinnagata*).
And here, either the "existence" portion (*satyantam*) or the "qualificand" portion (*viśeṣyadalama*) alone should be adopted;
for there is no purpose in including both.
The very absence of such a qualified [property] is the state of being devoid of independent positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

[Regarding the phrase] "the existence of such" and so forth: it means that while possessing a qualification by way of an existence that is the cause for the existence of the effect under consideration...

The meaning is: "the state of being qualified by an absence that serves as the cause for the absence of the effect under consideration. For example, the cloth is the effect under consideration; the thread possesses the state of being a substratum for an existence that causes the existence of that [cloth]. Likewise, there is a difference residing in such an existence, [defined] by the relation of dependence on a positive concomitance (anvaya) residing in something other than itself.

The difference from that which possesses threads is the state of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) [of that difference], and this resides in the thread. Similarly, the absence of the effect in question is the absence of the cloth; the absence which acts as its causal factor is the absence of the thread, and the state of being the locus of that [absence]—in the form of being its counter-correlative—resides in the thread. Thus.

The application [of the definition] should be understood as follows: that which is grounded in such a negative concomitance (vyatireka)— namely, the difference from the possessor of the threads (tantumadbheda) by way of the relation of dependence upon a negative concomitance residing in something other than itself— possesses the property of being the delimiting factor (avacchedakatva) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) in the thread.

In reality, however, [the definition consists in] either (1) the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a deliminator residing in itself, where that [deliminator] is related to its own substratum through a relation delimited by positive and negative concomitance; or (2) the state of possessing both relations: (a) the state of possessing positive and negative concomitance qualified by itself, and (b) the state of being the counter-correlate of itself.
The inclusive definition is "the state of being qualified by a difference.
And its own qualification [by that difference] occurs through the relation of being dependent upon the positive and negative concomitance with something other than its own counter-correlative.
It is by way of the relation of possessing the difference from that which is delimited by itself (*svāvacchinnabheda*). However,
it should be noted that this [definition] is to be disregarded due to the complexity (*gaurava*) arising from the introduction of an additional category (*padārtha*), such as identity (*tādātmya*).

As for the objection that— since consistency is achieved by the very statement, "by which [agent], for whom, and with respect to what, the state of being antecedent is understood," the word *saha* (together) is redundant— that is not so; for if that were the case, [the word] *tasya* (of him) [would likewise be redundant].

Since the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) is that which is related to the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*), and the meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*) is "being delimited" (*avacchinnatva*), the definition is established as follows: "That general property of the qualificandumness residing in something (x), which delimits [the object], belongs to the knowledge of the invariable antecedence of the present effect. In that regard:

Furthermore, if one disregards the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for that which has entered into the scope of the delimiting factor, there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding "stick-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth;
whereas, by employing the word "together" (*saha*), the meaning arrives at what we have stated, and thus there is no such fault.

For this very reason, even the "otherwise-established" status (*anyathāsiddhi*) of color and other qualities—qualified by such properties as "inherence in a thread"—is established by means of "thread-ness" (*tantutva*).
The intended meaning is that it should be understood as "easily spoken.

He states the view of those who establish the first type of extraneous relation (*anyathāsiddhi*) even when thread-ness (*tantutva*) is a cause by virtue of its being that particular individual (*tadvyakti*), with the words: "[127] *itarānvaya*... (in the presence of others).

The refined definition (*niṣkarṣa*) is that "superfluity" (*anyathāsiddhatva*) consists in being qualified by something through both relations: having its own positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and being distinct from it.
This is stated in the *Dīpikā* as "in dependence on another," and so forth.
With respect to another [cause], namely with respect to an effect other than the effect under discussion;
in the phrase "pūrvavṛttitve," the locative case [is used] according to the rule "yasya ca... [Pāṇini 2.3.39].

By the principle stated as "by way of its nature," cognition is the object (*artha*). And its [the object's] presence in the apprehension through the relation of being produced (*janyatā-sambandha*) constitutes the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Thus, [the definition is]: the state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatva*) of a cognition whose qualifier is "being antecedent to the relevant effect," which is itself dependent upon a cognition whose qualifier is "being antecedent to effects other than the relevant effect."
It follows that this is the definition of the second type of "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha).
And in that case, the cognition of causality consists in the apprehension of a relation characterized by a specific correlate.
