With the intention that [the cognition] must necessarily depend upon a certain determination (*nirṇaya*) whose qualifier is the delimitor of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*), he says in the *Prakāśikā* (127), "And thus," and "inherence in multiple substances."
The meaning is "the state of being a substance distinct from atoms" [128].
"From its presence" means from the presence of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
1. In reality, however...
"Of its own substratum and its own class," and so forth.
In all instances, the word *sva* (own) refers to the specific distinctions of the body and so on. [This concludes] the section on the disjunction of causes.
Regarding the phrase "that which is inherent in the whole" (*saṃgrahe yatsamavetam*) and so forth:
in the word "effect" (*kāryam*), the phrase beginning with "that which" (*yad*) refers to the effect that is inherent in the whole.

By construing [the phrase] "it arises as a real entity" (*sadutpadyate*), the meaning is that it arises as something inherent in a substratum, such that it possesses an inherence relation having that [substratum] as its relatum (*anuyogin*) and [that substratum] as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
This is the meaning of the verbal root.
The meaning [of the locative case] is the state of being located as delimited by the first moment; the meaning of the verbal suffix is the state of being a substratum (āśrayatva);
and by virtue of the relationship between the subject and the predicate, such a state of being located is delimited by inherence (samavāya).
It shines forth; for there is a rule that the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the qualifier of the subject (*sadanta*) must be the delimitor of the property to be designated (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).

This is because, in cases involving the relationship between the subject and the predicate, there is a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) whereby the relationship of the delimited and the delimiting (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) is manifested between the delimitor of the subject and the predicate. Likewise...

And the meaning of the sentence is: that which has an effect, and which possesses such an inherence-based locusness (*ādheyatā*) delimited by an inherence relation whose relatum is that [effect], is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to that effect.
And here, regarding the two words "that which" (*yat*) and "it" (*tat*):

Considering that the focus on the manifestation of cause and effect refers to the final stage of the causal relationship, and intending to refer to those two as delimited by their respective properties (*dharmas*), the *Prakāśikā* states [at 134]: "that which is delimited by such-and-such a property," and so forth. And thus, it is the causality delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) as determined by the effecthood delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
The definition of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) has been established.
In that regard, in the perceptual cognition of a jar and so forth,
the object consisting of the form of the jar and so forth functions as the cause by way of the relation of identity (tādātmya).

The inclusion of the qualification "being delimited by the relation of inherence" (samavāyasambandhāvacchinnatva) within the state of being an effect (kāryatā) is for the purpose of excluding the status of being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatā) of the pot and other objects with respect to their own perception.

There is no fault, because the effectness (kāryatā) determined by the object that culminates in perception is delimited by the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā). To prevent over-extension to non-inherent causes (asamavāyikāraṇa), the condition of being delimited by the relation of identity (tādātmya) is introduced into the definition of causality (kāraṇatā).
Regarding "with the effect" or "with the cause" in the context of inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth:
here, that cause which exists as inherent in the same object as the effect is the single non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). With the cause...
The construction is by way of two distinct sentences: "That cause which, being inherent in a single object, [is a cause]—that is a non-inherent cause" (*asamavāyikāraṇam*).
The particle *vā* serves precisely to indicate this [division].
The meaning of the word "saha" (together) is concomitance (*sahitatva*), and in the present context, that takes the form of being restricted to a common substratum (*adhikaraṇa-niyapitatva*).
The term "samaveta" (inhering) is connected with "the state of inhering in that which delimits the category of the co-inherent object.
In the phrase "kāryeṇa" (by the effect), the meaning of the instrumental case is "being characterized by a substratumness that is itself related [to the effect]."
Whatever [word] is supreme even by a single syllable;
the meaning of the locative case following the word "artha" is the state of being determined (*nirūpitatva*). And thus:
One meaning of the sentence is that the cause is that which possesses an inherence determined by some object as specified by the locus of the effect;
this is to be understood likewise in the sentence beginning with "by the cause" (kāraṇena).

In fact, in the *Saṃgraha* [133], regarding the passage beginning with "together with the effect" (*kāryeṇa saha*), the meaning of the word "together" (*saha*) here is concomitance (*sāhitya*). And that consists in the state of being connected to a single action. In the present context...
This results in the definition of being inherent (*samavetatva*).
In the expression "by the effect" (*kāryeṇa*), the meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is the state of being located (*ādheyatva*).
The word *eka* refers to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
In the term *artha*, the meaning is "being qualified by that which is inherent [in the locus]. And thus:

The essential point is that the result is as follows: it means "that which possesses an inherence related to the substratum which is the determiner of the inherence residing in that which is identical with the effect.
This same understanding should be applied to the passage beginning with "by the cause" and so forth. This is the core meaning.
Regarding the phrase "by way of a cause" (*kāraṇena*), when there arises the expectation as to what the cause of what is, he says in the *Prakāśikā* [134]: "of its own effect" (*svakārya*).

This means: by way of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of its own effect. And here, the state of being a cause is defined as that which is delimited by either (1) the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*), or (2) the relation delimited by inherence in that which is inherent in the locus of its own inherence (*samavāya-svāśraya-samavetatva*), in relation to an effectness (*kāryatā*) delimited by the relation of inherence.
The definition of the generality of non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is as follows:

if one were to include merely the property of being delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha-avacchinnatva*) within the causal status (*kāraṇatā*), then [the definition would over-apply] to the first non-inherent cause.

When only the property of being delimited by the relation of inherence in its own substratum is introduced, that same definition should be understood as applying to the second type of non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) as well,
[namely] by way of the relation of ordinary objective presence (*laukikaviṣayatā*) residing in a substance.

Furthermore, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*) and the like— which serve as causes for perception (*pratyakṣa*) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) and through the relation of "inhering in that which inheres in itself" (*svāśrayasamavetatva*), respectively, with respect to the objective domain (*viṣayatā*) that resides in substances (*dravyasamaveta*)— in both definitions, [the qualification] must be applied to the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*).

The inclusion of the qualification "delimited by the relation of inherence" is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the second type of non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) within the definition of the first type of non-inherent cause, regarding the causal power (*kāraṇatā*).

The inclusion of the qualification "being delimited by the relation of inherence" is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the first non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) in the definition of the second non-inherent cause. Regarding that:

Regarding the inclusion of the condition "being delimited by the relation of inherence in its own substratum": here, in the context of being delimited by either of the two relations mentioned, [the definition consists in] the property of having a counter-positive delimited by a relation delimited by the locus-determinacy residing in itself (svaniṣṭhāvacchedakatā) which is delimited by the relation of inherence (samavāya), combined with the property of having a counter-positive delimited by a relation delimited by the locus-determinacy residing in itself which is delimited by the relation of inherence in its own substratum (svāśrayasamavetatva); [this is] a counter-positive delimited by a locus-determinacy residing in itself which is delimited by a relation delimited by both of these relations.
It should be noted that the property of being delimited by the relation of possessing a specific type of contact must be included;
this applies even to the conjunction of the third thread and the yarn, and so forth.

Considering that the inclusion of the condition "being distinct from that" in the general definition of an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) would result in an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*)— since the conjunction of three threads (*tūlapaṭasaṃyoga*), for example, serves as an *asamavāyikāraṇa* with respect to [the conjunction of two threads]— it was stated [as follows].
"Thus, it has the characteristic of being a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa)";
this refers to "space" (dik).
The intended meaning is as follows:

It is not correct to say that because the loom alone is accepted as the cause of the cloth by way of inherence (*samavāya*), while the shuttle is the cause by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the condition of "being different from that" need not be included even in the definition of a qualifier;
for [the definition of] causality is characterized by being an invariably antecedent factor (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*).
Because it remains unimpaired even when there is a conjunction with the threads of a loom;
yet, even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to the conjunction between a thread and space, and so forth.
Even if "being different from that" were included [in the definition], there would be great complexity;
nevertheless, [the property] consists in being inherent in the threads and so forth alone.
There is no fault, because the qualifier must be formulated as "not inhering in that [effect] and so forth.
In the *Saṃgraha* [verse 133], it says "distinct from both," and so on;
in the definition of the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), the term "both" refers to those two [the inherent and non-inherent causes].
He states that [the definition] refers to both the inherent (samavāyin) and non-inherent (asamavāyin) causes in the *Dīpikā* [133], beginning with "samavāyī" and so forth.
And here, the definition should be stated as: "that which, being qualified by its effect, is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) with respect to that effect."

And the distinction [of one cause from others] is by way of the threefold relation consisting of: (1) possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a deliminator residing in itself, which is in turn delimited by the relation of being an inherent cause as defined by itself; (2) possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a deliminator residing in itself, which is in turn delimited by the relation of being a non-inherent cause as defined by itself; and (3) the relation of being a cause as defined by itself.

Although there is a loss of the status of efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and so forth in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and the like— since, in the case of an effect that is a non-existence (*abhāva*), an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and so forth are not established— nevertheless...

The qualification of that effect must be introduced by way of a triple relation consisting of: (1) the absence of itself, where its own counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of being an inherent cause as defined by itself; (2) the absence of itself, where its own counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of being a non-inherent cause as defined by itself; and (3) the absence of itself, where its own counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of being a cause as defined by itself. Thus, there is no fault.
[This applies even to] destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and so forth.
Because [properties] such as being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) have a relation that resides in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇasambandha*),
it is easy to find their absence (*tadabhāva*) as having a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by such a relation. For this very reason...
Even though the fourth [category] and the others possess the status of being inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) with respect to their own qualities such as form,
there is no deficiency, because it is impossible for them to be distinct from inherent causes and so forth in a general sense.
This concludes the classification of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[136] Regarding the phrase "the state of being the specifier of the fourth [category] as its object": otherwise, due to the absence of having an object, the very nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) would be undermined for indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). As for this nature of cognition...

The sense is that, since having an object (*saviṣayatva*) is pervaded [by being a cognition], when the pervader is absent, the absence of the pervaded is necessarily entailed. [136] Regarding the phrase "as the qualificand, etc.": if taken according to its literal meaning, this [definition] would be impossible, as it would not include a cognition that does not apprehend the relation between the qualifier and the qualificand.
Just as a jar and so forth appear in non-conceptual perception due to the existence of visual contact (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyoga*), so too do "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and its inherence (*samavāya*) appear,

because of the existence of the respective sense-object contacts consisting of "inherence in that which is in contact with the eye" (*saṃyukta-samavāya*) and "qualification of that which is in contact with the eye" (*saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇatā*).
Because even the manifestation of that [relation] is unavoidable;
however, it has been supplemented with the intention that, regarding the pot, potness, and inherence, there is merely a fourth-order objecthood (*turīyaviṣayatā*) therein.
Regarding the phrase "the qualified object, etc.": by the word "etc.," the mode and the relation are included.
The meaning is "by way of being the qualified object, and so forth."

In the expression "not apprehending the qualificand and so forth," the meaning of the verbal root is "apprehension" (avagāhana), which is objectivity (viṣayatā); and the meaning of the suffix *ṇini* is the "determiner" (nirūpaka).

In the expression "vidhayā," the meaning of the instrumental case is non-difference (*abheda*), which is connected to the objective relation (*viṣayatā*). This [non-difference] is further connected to the difference denoted by the negative particle (*nañ*) in relation to the qualificand (*nirūpaka*).

Thus, there is obtained the sense of being distinct from that which qualifies the objective relation residing in the qualificand, such as the state of being the qualified (*viśeṣyatva*), while remaining non-different from it. In that context:

Since the portions concerning non-difference (*abheda*) and residing-in-that (*tādṛśaniṣṭhatva*) are redundant, he says "And thus" (*tathā ca*) with the intention that the definition is merely that which is non-different from the determiner of the qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*), etc.;
[he says] "consisting of the nature of cognition" (*jñānatvaghaṭita*).
This was stated in order to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to jars and the like.

In the sentence from the *Dīpikā*, "not apprehending the relation between the qualifier and the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyasambandhānavagāhī*), there is no copulative compound (*dvandva*); rather, the intention is that it refers to the relation which exists between the qualifier and the qualified.
He states the opinion of those who explain [the matter]: "[136] Some, however... [and] "bhāsamāna... [means] "that which is the locus of objectivity (*viṣayatā*)."

The meaning is that "being the counter-correlate of the relation to the locus of the objective reference (viṣayatā) belonging to that cognition" is what constitutes being a qualifier (prakāratva) in that cognition.
By this, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga). But [an objection]: nanu...
In the cognition "the conjunction of the jar and the ground," the jar would incur the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*).
Therefore, he says: "[136] delimited by a relation.
But surely, by the reasoning stated previously, this would apply even to indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*)?

Since the manifestation of a relation (*saṃsarga*) is necessary, [the definition] would be impossible; therefore, he says: "[136] *saṃsargatā*. The phrase "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*) means "in comparison with the definition consisting in the absence of a subject-matter delimited by a relation," and so forth. And thus:

Not involving a relation (*saṃsargānavagāhitvam*) means not being the non-referent of a subject-matter (*viṣayatva*) that resides in a relation. Furthermore, being devoid of a subject-matter delimited by a relation (*saṃsargāvacchinnaviṣayatāśūnyatvam*) means being devoid of a subject-matter that possesses a delimitedness (*avacchinnatva*) as determined by a relation. And in that regard:

Even though "being determined" (*nirūpitatva*) occupies the position of "being located in" (*ādheyatva*), the inclusion of the additional factor of "being delimited" (*avacchinnatva*) results in greater complexity compared to the definition beginning with "delimited by the relation" (*saṃsargāvacchinna*).
However, when compared to the definition characterized by "the absence of relativity" (*saṃsargatāśūnyatva*), the complexity of such a definition is indeed evident.
The meaning is: "it is to be understood.
Otherwise, as stated above, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*); such is the meaning.

[136] "Digiti" (As for this): the meaning here is as follows— regarding the phrase "not apprehending the relation between the qualified and the qualifier," if one resorts to a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, then by means of that relation...
The inclusion of the requirement that [the property] must reside in both the qualificand and the qualifier is useless; this is the underlying sense of the statement in the *Dīpikā*.
In our view, however, it is not so, because it serves the purpose of obtaining three definitions.
Regarding the statement "that [argument] is futile":
one might object that the inference— "qualified cognition is produced by the knowledge of the qualifier, because it is a qualified cognition"— is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

Anticipating the objection that there is a lack of supporting reasoning (*anukūlatarka*), he states the following with the intention of showing that this [reason] is not "unproven" (*aprayojaka*), because there exists here a form of reasoning characterized by the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of breaking the causal relationship between a qualified cognition and the knowledge of its qualifier: [136]
"Depending on a distinct cognition," and so forth.
Herein, if there is the state of being a distinct cognition...

With the intention that the intended reductio (*tarka*) is: "If [the cognition of a qualified object] were to deviate from being produced by the qualifier, then it would not be delimited by the property of being produced by the cognition of the qualifier," he says: "[136] *bhāva*.
In the *Dīpikā*, this is stated as: "[136] because of the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*)."
The property of being produced by a cognition that specifies itself (svanirūpakajñānajanyatva) pervades the state of being an effect-cognition (janyajñānatva);

this [pervasion] consists in being qualified by an objectivity (viṣayatā) through both relations: being produced by a cognition that specifies itself and being the specifier of a mode (prakāratā) that has the same locus as itself. [This conclusion follows] from an unstable chain of superimpositions.

Knowledge, being devoid of any specific mode (*niṣprakāraka*), appears in the inference accompanied by the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasañjana*) consisting in the impossibility of deep sleep and so forth;
or else, [it appears] in that which resides in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇaniṣṭhāyām*).

The point is that, by the force of the aforementioned reasoning, the property of being "unconditioned" (anavacchinnatva) with respect to the objective relation (viṣayatā)— which consists in the general absence of being determined by any objective relation— manifests itself therein. [136] Regarding the phrase "gauriti":
And this qualification regarding itself is stated in order to obtain the specific property to be proven (*sādhya*), namely, being produced by a cognition whose object is that [qualification].
Otherwise, [if it were not so stated], a cognition whose qualifier is that [qualification]...

The point is that this would result in the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntaratā), by taking as established the fact that it is produced by a cognition of a qualifier other than that [specific object].
In the *Saṅgraha* [135], it says "produced by the contact of sense-organ and object," and so forth;
and this refers only to produced perception (*janyapratyakṣa*).
This is intended with respect to that which is the object of definition;
therefore, since the perception of Īśvara is eternal,
any suspicion of non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding it is dispelled.

Because that [perception] is not a locus of definition (*alakṣya*). Otherwise, having introduced—by means of the relation of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by its own delimitation residing in itself, which is delimited by the absence of both the non-production and production [of perception] from the contact of sense-organ and object, and which resides in what is produced—the state of being qualified by the state of being produced from the contact of sense-organ and object; [one would fall into error].
Its inclusion [in the definition] must be understood as follows:

although, in this context, there is over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to inference and other such cognitions because the conjunction of the self and the mind is a cause for cognition in general, [this is not so] regarding the mind...

Although [the definition] applies to the sense organs because they are *indriyas* and to the self because it is the object (*artha*), there is nonetheless no fault, because "being produced" (*janyatā*) is specified as being delimited by a property that is pervaded by the nature of experience (*anubhavatva*).
In the literal reading, the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) serves to capture this intended meaning.
However, when both [the conditions] are intended [in the definition], the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is included to exclude space (*ākāśa*) and the like.
Some, however, hold that the definition is "the state of being knowledge while not having knowledge as its instrument," which is common to both produced and eternal perception.

Since inference and other such cognitions have the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth as their instruments, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to them. Furthermore, because the perception of the Lord (*īśvara*) is unproduced (*ajanya*), it is excluded;
however, in the case of produced perception (*janyapratyakṣa*), the sense organ alone [is the instrument].
Furthermore, there is a formal application of the definition because of its being an instrument (*karaṇa*).
They say that its status as an instrument is established because non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is the cause of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*).
The analysis of proximity (*sannikarṣa*) is found in the *Dīpikā* [137], beginning with "in the case of the direct perception of a substance" (*dravyapratyakṣe*). And here,

with respect to visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*), by means of the relation of being a worldly object residing in a substance (*dravyavṛttilaukikaviṣayatāsaṃbandhena*), [proximity] exists through inherence (*samavāyena*).
The causality of the conjunction with the eye must be stated.

In that regard, the inclusion of "subsisting in a substance" within the direction of the effect is for the purpose of excluding deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to color-form (rūpa) and other such qualities.

The inclusion of the term "extraordinary" (*alaukika*) is for the purpose of avoiding a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by taking as an example an extraordinary visual perception whose object is a past or future jar that is not in contact with the eye, such as one produced by the generalizing condition (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
Similarly, this applies to the aspect of the staff and so forth.
This should also be understood to apply to the visual perception "this was previously a staff-bearer," which is produced by proximity to knowledge (*jñānapratyāsatti*).
Likewise, [it applies] through the relation of being a locus of ordinary objectivity (*laukikaviṣayatā*) residing in that which is inherent in a substance (*dravyasamavetavṛtti*).

With respect to visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*), the inherence in that which is conjoined with the eye (*cakṣussaṃyuktasamavāya*) is the cause by way of its own-nature relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*). Here, in the case where the succession of parts comes to rest at the triad (*tryaṇuka*), the phrase "occurring in the direction of the effect" (*kāryadiśi vṛtti*) is included [in the definition] to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the triad. Although...
Even if one were to include the condition of "subsisting in what is not a substance," the same defect remains under the view that accepts atoms;
nevertheless, [this applies] to the case of being other than a substance.
There is no fault, because it is accepted that [the universal] is a qualifier inherent [in the substance].

Furthermore, the inclusion of "residing in" (*vṛtti*) at the end [of the definition] should be understood as a means to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the perception of universals such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*).

Inclusion of "laukikatva" (sensory immediacy) within the objective relation (*viṣayatā*) is for the purpose of excluding [the over-extension of the definition] by taking as an example the non-sensory visual perception (*alaukika-cākṣuṣa*) whose objects are past forms and so forth, which is produced by the universal proximity (*sāmānya-pratyāsatti*) such as "form-ness" (*rūpatva*).
The same applies to the aspect of blue and so forth.

Likewise, even in the case of the perception "this was previously possessed of a blue color," which is produced by proximity through knowledge (*jñāna-pratyāsatti*), there is an absence of inherence as qualified by visual contact; therefore, [the definition] is stated in that way to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Similarly, [it applies] with respect to the relation of ordinary objectivity (*laukika-viṣayatā*) residing in that which inheres in what inheres in a substance (*dravya-samaveta-samaveta-vṛtti*).
With respect to visual perception, the cause is the inherence-in-what-is-inherently-connected-with-what-is-conjoined (cakṣuḥ-saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya).
This applies to the yogic visual perception that has all things as its object, which is produced by the proximity consisting of the dharma born of yoga,
and to the visual perception of all universals, which is produced by the proximity consisting of the universal "universal-ness" (jātitva).
The inclusion of the term "empirical" (*laukikatva*) here is for the purpose of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
In the view that the triad (*tryaṇuka*) is independent,
the phrase ending with "subsistence" (*vṛtti*) is included to exclude deviation in the case of the triad itself, its color, and so forth.
Even according to other views,

that [relation] must indeed be included in order to prevent the contingency of such a subject-object relation being accidental with respect to auditory perception (*śrāvaṇapratyakṣa*) through the relation of being a worldly object of the operation of words.

The phrase ending in "vṛtti" (subsisting) is included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), which is the cause for the inherence [of sound] in the auditory organ.

The inclusion of the term "sensory" (*laukika*) is for the purpose of avoiding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a perception produced by the proximity of the universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva-sāmānya-pratyāsatti*) which has past and other sounds as its object, as well as in the case of such a perception produced by the proximity born of yoga (*yogaja-pratyāsatti*).

With respect to auditory perception (*śrāvaṇa*), inherence in that which inheres in the auditory organ (*śrotrasamavetasamavāya*) is the cause, by way of the relation of being a worldly object-locus residing in what inheres in sound. The qualification "residing" (*vṛttitva*) is included to prevent over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) to sound itself.

The inclusion of the term "sensory" (*laukika*) is for the purpose of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the perception of universals such as "being a *k*-sound" (*kakāratva*), which reside in past and future *k*-sounds due to the universal of "being a *k*-sound" (*jātitva*) serving as a means of proximity;
this should be understood similarly in other cases as well.
Now, an objection: since the types of qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*) are manifold—

due to distinctions such as "qualification of the conjoined" (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā*), "qualification of what is inherent in the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavetaviśeṣaṇatā*), and so forth— how can there be only six kinds of sense-object contact?

And if there is a unification of those [qualities] by way of their being qualifiers, then why should there not be a unification of "inherence-in-the-conjoined" (saṃyukta-samavāya) and so forth by way of their being inherence (samavāya)? He dispels this doubt with the words: "In this regard, the following should be noted," and so on.
[142] Regarding the refutation of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):

"the contact consisting of the relation between qualifier and qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāvasannikarṣa*) means the contact consisting of either the state of being the qualified (*viśeṣyatva*) or the state of being the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*).
[142] "At the time of the apprehension of a jar," and so forth.

Since the certainty regarding the presence of something (tadvattāniścaya) acts as an impediment specifically toward the cognition of the absence of that thing which is not produced by ordinary sensory contact (laukikasannikarṣa), [this applies to] the perception of the absence of a jar produced by ordinary sensory contact.
An undesirable consequence arises at the time when there is the ascertainment of the presence of a jar;

nor can it be argued that there is no such consequence of the perception of the absence of a jar in a location containing a jar simply because of the absence of the object consisting of the absence of a jar.
It must be asked: how can there be the possibility of a certain cognition of "possessing a jar" when the jar is absent?
Even in a place devoid of a jar, [such a cognition would arise].

Because it is possible for a certain cognition of the presence of a jar— though of the nature of an error— to arise through a sense-contact involving another property, there is the possibility of the unwanted consequence (prasaṅga) that the perception of the absence of a jar would occur even in a place where a jar is present.
This applies even to a location containing a jar and so forth.
And because there is the possibility of the undesirable consequence that the absence of a jar would be perceived through the force of a contact involving another property-possessor (*dharmī*).
Regarding the phrase "it is a separate means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntaratvam*) and so forth:
although another means of valid cognition is indeed a "separate means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntaram*), [the term here refers to a distinct category].
Through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the status of being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramitikaraṇatva*) apart from perception and the other means of knowledge is obtained;
furthermore, this is accepted by the Naiyāyikas as well for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) when it is admitted as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*).
This is because they accept that only that which is of the nature of absence (*abhāvarūpa*) can be the instrument for the valid cognition of absence (*abhāvapramā*).

Nevertheless, by accepting a transposition of the intermediate terms, the intended meaning is that the instrumentality of a valid cognition distinct from perception and the like—which results in the instrumentality of a valid cognition of a genus different from the cognitions produced by perception and so forth—is what is meant; thus there is no fault whatsoever. This is because the Naiyāyikas accept that the cognition of non-existence (abhāva) is indeed of the nature of perception.
For this very reason, it was stated earlier that there is the postulation of [the sense organ] as the instrument for a cognition of a different class. Now, one might object:

since the capacity [of the sense organ] has already been established by the portion ending with "one would see," the phrase "it does not exist because of the absence of perception" is redundant; having raised this doubt, the author introduces the next section.
— by the words "of reasoning" (*tarkasya*) and so forth;

in the case of the contrapositive (*viparyaye*), that is, when there is the absence of the pervader of the absence of the *āpādaka* (the subsumptive condition), there is the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitvam*).
The meaning of "accompanied by a limit" (*koṭyanvitam*) is the state of having that limit as its final point.
The "limit" (*koṭi*) of that *tarka* is the form of the consequence (*āpādya*); thus, the meaning is that it has that [consequence] as its object.
[142] Regarding "the perception which is opposed to the possibility of existence for the subject"—

this means that the perception possesses a quality of being opposed to the possibility of existence for the subject by way of subverting the certainty of the absence of the *apādya* (the thing to be established) which serves as the cause for the *āpatti* (the logical consequence), and not otherwise.
In its essential nature,
it is the state of being opposed to the possibility of existence;
that is, it is the state of being an obstacle to the certainty of the absence of the probandum (the thing to be established), which constitutes its cause.

Since the state of being an impediment (pratibandhakatva) is possible only for that which is non-artificial (anāhārya), it is precisely this quality of being non-artificial that must be intended by the qualification "contradictory" (virodhitva). Otherwise, [the definition would be flawed].

He states the extracted meaning with the words beginning "the existence of the counter-positive" (*pratiyogisattva*):
the meaning is "an object of an undesirable contingency (*apatti*) produced by an undesirable contingency whose object is the existence of the counter-positive.
[142] "In brief" (*saṅkṣepa*).

The intention here is this: in every case involving the perception of non-existence, there is no evidence for the occurrence of the following reductio (*āpatti*): "If the counter-positive were present here, it would be perceived.

The pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) characterized by the pervasiveness (*vyāpyatā*) residing in the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is what is intended to be expressed. For further details, one should consult the *Muktāvalī-prakāśa* and other such works.

For those who, without introducing the aforementioned qualification of "fitness" (*yogyatā*) into the definition of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), avoid the undesirable consequence of the perception of the absence of a jar by refining the notion of fitness in another way and then introducing it [into the definition].

He states the view of certain individuals who interpret the passage from the *Dīpikā* beginning with "tarkitā" (conceived) in a different way—namely, those who hold that [the absence of perception occurs] precisely because of the non-existence of perception (*upalambhābhāve*). [142] "But some... etc. Thus, in the absence of perception...
[This is] precisely because of the provision of the qualification "being prompted by such [a cognition].
The phrase "they say" indicates a lack of satisfaction (asvarasa).
The seed of that [dissatisfaction] is that, in the previous view, the qualification "being [cognitively] postulated upon the existence of the counter-positive" would be redundant.
However, in the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the term "presumed" (*tarkita*) is useful as a means of grasping the intended meaning regarding the requirement of suitability (*yogyatā*).
But according to this view:

Since the nature of fitness (*yogyatā*) consists precisely in being necessitated by the absence of the cause that is the existence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), and since this is already captured by the very term "opposed to the existence of the counter-positive," the word "supposed" (*tarkita*) serves no purpose whatsoever.
Thus, since there is no distinction in non-existence based on a distinction in locus, the undesirable consequence that the non-existence of a jar would be perceived in darkness cannot be avoided;
therefore, to remedy this deficiency, he says: "In this case, this... [143].

"that" (*tat*) means "a genus" (*jāti*).

The section on inference, concerning the definition of inference, is completed.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the connection of being dependent upon direct perception":
it refers to that which is the effect dependent upon direct perception— that is, the eye and other such sense faculties which constitute the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).
The meaning is: by way of connection through the definition of reality (*tattva*).
This refers to being prompted by the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) produced by a cognition that follows upon a formal investigation (*nirūpaṇa*).
The meaning of the third [case-ending] is as follows:
the sense of the base (prakṛtyartha) is construed with the cognition by way of being its object (viṣayitayā). This is the demonstration of the connection.

Furthermore, because there might be a lack of attention due to the suspicion that [the text] is the incoherent prattle of a madman— stemming from the fact that the preceding and following sections do not appear to be connected as a single whole— it is for the sake of dispelling that [suspicion] that the realization of the unity of the preceding and succeeding passages is also [stated].

It should also be understood that the purpose [of this section] is to demonstrate the connection [between the chapters]. Such a realization [is achieved by seeing that] "the chapter on inference forms a single syntactical unit with the chapter on perception."
"Because it establishes a meaning that is consistent with the subject matter propounded by the *Pratyakṣapariccheda*," and so forth; the details of this are found elsewhere.
This is understood from the statement in the *Dīpikā*: "it characterizes."
The meaning obtained is: "one who possesses the volitional effort conducive to words that produce knowledge characterized by the modes of definition.

In that context, since the divisions of essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth will also be explained further on, it would be deficient if they were not promised; therefore, he says "he defines" (*nirūpayati*).

And *nirūpaṇa* (ascertainment) is a word conducive to a cognition characterized by any one of the modes such as definition (*lakṣaṇa*), essential nature (*svarūpa*), or means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*); therefore, there is no deficiency [in the definition]. This should be understood similarly in what follows as well.
In the *Saṅgraha*, it is stated that "inference (*anumāna*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of inferential cognition (*anumiti*).

This is because the word *anumāna* functions as a *lakṣaṇika* term (one whose meaning is indicated by secondary implication) with respect to the property delimited by the referent of the word *anumāna*; this is so under the view that, in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is no secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the first member of the compound.
In this case, there is no lack of expectancy (nirākāṅkṣatā), as in the expression "the pot, the pot";
rather, [it refers to] being the instrument of inference (anumitikaraṇatva).

And [the definition of inference] consists in being the locus of a causality that is qualified by a property pervaded by the nature of experience (anubhavatva) residing in an inferential cognition (anumiti).
[Objection: Now, regarding the root text which states, "Inference is the instrument of inferential cognition" (*anumitikaraṇamanumānam*).
Since the word *anumāna* has the sense of "the instrument of inferential cognition" (*anumiti-karaṇa*),
as the meaning of the sentence "the instrument of inferential cognition is the instrument of inferential cognition" is ultimately established,

there must be a distinction between the delimitors of the subjecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicationhood (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) in cases of non-differentiation (*abhedānvaya*). [Otherwise, it would be like saying] "the pot..."

Since it must be accepted that the validity of the sentence "This is a jar" is excluded because the instrumentality of inference (*anumitikaraṇatva*) alone serves as both the delimitor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the delimitor of the predicate (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*), how can the stated sentence possess validity? To this, he says: "Of the word 'inference' (*anumānapadasya*). Thus:
Furthermore, since the instrumentality of inference (*anumitikaraṇatva*) is the delimitor of the object-to-be-indicated (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*),
and the nature of being the referent of the term "inference" (*anumānapadārthatva*) is the delimitor of the predicate-to-be-prescribed (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*), there is a distinction between the two.

The meaning is that there is no inconsistency in the sentence-meaning [of the definition] because the instrument of inference (*anumitikaraṇa*) is non-different from the category of inference (*anumāna*). 2. Regarding the position that the first part of the definition is absent:
In the case of the definition characterized by the first member of the compound, however,

the delimitor of the object-to-be-indicated (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is "the state of being a cause non-different from that which is related to inference," while the delimitor of the property-to-be-prescribed (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) is "the state of being the cause of inference"; thus, there is a difference between the two.
The point is that even if the word *anumāna* has the sense of "the instrument of inferential cognition" (*anumiti-karaṇa*), there is still no absence of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*).
Consequently, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to [the self] and so forth.
Now, for what purpose was the definition of inference stated as "cognition produced by a subsumptive reflection" (*parāmarśa*)?
Is it not because the cognition of the constituent parts [is required] for the cognition of the whole?

It should not be argued that the statement [defining inference] is purposeful because, since it is a cause, knowledge of the definition of inference— which includes that [inference]— is impossible without prior inferential knowledge;
for even by merely demonstrating the nature of inferential knowledge itself, that [definition] is established.
Anticipating the objection that there is no utility in stating its definition, he states that definition [only] because,

as long as the distinction between the cognitions of perception and inference is not known through their distinct definitions, the status of inference as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be established.

Because, in the inference whose probandum is "being a means of valid cognition distinct from perception and the rest" and whose reason is "being the instrument of inferential cognition," the suspicion of inconstancy (vyabhicāra) is unavoidable;
therefore, [it is stated] in the *Saṃgraha*:
With the intention that it is appropriate to state the definition of inference (*anumiti*), he expresses his view: "And so it is" (*tathā ca*).
[147] The definition of inference: [147] But is it not the case that [inference] is perception following doubt?
The statement in the *Dīpikā* is inconsistent,
because it fails to mention that there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) even to the case of a perceptual cognition following a contrary ascertainment such as "this is not a person."

Anticipating the objection that this would lead to an insufficiency [of categories], he says—[188] "perception subsequent to erroneous cognition"—with the intention that the word *saṃśaya* (doubt) found in the sentence of the *Dīpikā* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all erroneous cognitions in general, adding:
"[of those who] accept [this]. [148]
The phrase "of Miśra and others" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
By this, it is established that in the case of perceptual certainty,
the absence of the perception of a distinguishing feature (viśeṣadarśana) qualified by the absence of contrary cognition (viparītajñāna) constitutes the obstructive factor.

It has been indicated that, according to the view of the author of the *Dīdhiti* and others who maintain that the absence of that [cognition] is the cause [of doubt], there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Now, one might object: the statement in the *Dīpikā*, "immediately after the doubt between a post and a person," is inconsistent.

Since doubt is necessarily restricted to alternative possibilities (koṭi) such as "this or that absence," it is impossible for it to have both "post" and "person" as its alternatives; therefore, he says: "[148] *idam* (this).
The phrase "[148] *āhuḥ* (they say)" indicates a lack of full satisfaction with this position.

However, if the seed of that [doubt] is intended as the first instance of a doubt whose alternatives are "being a post" and "the absence thereof," then there is a contradiction with the subsequent text, which states that the perception "it is indeed a person" arises [from it].
For it must be stated that [the cognition] "it is indeed a post" arises from perception;
therefore, by reflecting upon such a passage...
In the sentence "immediately after the doubt concerning the atom and the person," two doubts are not intended;
rather, only one doubt is intended.
1. "By that" refers to the self (ātman) and so forth.
The point is that although [the probans] is the locus of the causality corresponding to the effectness delimited by "cognition-ness" as residing in an inference,
it is not an over-extension [of the definition], because it lacks the status of being the locus of the causality corresponding to the effectness delimited by "inference-ness."
And this does not hold true in this system.

Anticipating the objection—"Surely it must be said that [the cognition] 'it is a person' arises from perception; what is the purpose of employing the restrictive particle *eva*?"—he says: "[148] 'It is indeed a person'. Now, [the objection continues]: "But surely..."
Since there exists the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) "I infer the person," one would have to admit that the nature of an inference (*anumititva*) also resides therein; therefore, he says:
"[148] This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication)."
[148] This is the demonstration of a subverting argument (*bādhakayukti*).
[148] It is also an *upalakṣaṇa*, indicating other subverting arguments as well. Now, one might object:

In order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of perceptual cognition that follows a doubt, why was it not stipulated that the generative capacity (*janakatā*) included within the definition of "being produced by a *parāmarśa*" must be delimited precisely by the nature of a qualified *parāmarśa* (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśatva*)?
Furthermore, in the case of perceptual knowledge following from doubt— such as the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) "this person possesses hands and so forth, which are pervaded by humanity"—
the cause is accepted as being precisely the state of being a cognition qualified by another cognition, in accordance with the requirement that it be common to both [simple] dissociated cognitions.

Thus, if it were held that the perception of a distinguishing feature acts as an excitatory factor (*uttejaka*) by obstructing contrary cognition, then the aforementioned qualification would be redundant;
for there would be no occasion for the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to the perceptual cognition that follows a doubt. Anticipating this, he says: "By this... [148].

The meaning is that, instead of introducing the condition of being delimited by such a property (*tādṛśadharmāvacchinnatva*) into the causal capacity (*janakatā*), one simply intends to specify "being produced by a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) assisted by the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*)."

By the phrase "in the manner of a certainty (*nirṇaya*) whose mode is the delimitor of the qualifier," it is indicated that a cognition apprehending the qualifiedness of the qualified (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhibuddhi*) possesses a generative capacity delimited by the nature of such a qualified inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*).
Regarding the term "in brief" (*saṅkṣepa*):

the intention here is this— only a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) conjoined with the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) functions as a perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*), and thus serves as the cause for perceptual cognition following doubt.
The objection that the defect remains as it was must be answered by stating that its meaning is "being produced by parāmarśa while being produced by pakṣatā.
This is done in order to avoid over-extension (ativyāpti) to the perception of pakṣatā.
The inclusion of "being produced by *parāmarśa*" [is as follows]:
"Being produced by *parāmarśa*" means being that which is produced as characterized by a generative capacity residing in *parāmarśa*.
2. Regarding "analytical knowledge" (*viśakalitajñāna*):
[it consists of] the cognition that "hands and so forth are pervaded by being a person," and "this [person] possesses hands and so forth."
The meaning is: "in accordance with the commonality of the two cognitions. 3.
"By way of being a cognition qualified by a cognition" means:

by way of being a cognition whose qualificandum is the hand (or finger) etc., which is qualified by a cognition having as its qualifier the property of being pervaded by humanity (*puruṣatva*), and whose qualificandum is delimited by "this-ness" (*idantva*). 4.
Because there is no possibility of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

This is because, although there exists an effectness (*kāryatā*) characterized by an effectness that is defined by a causal capacity (*kāraṇatā*) delimited by "the state of being a cognition qualified by [another] cognition" (*jñānaviśiṣṭajñānatva*), there does not exist an effectness characterized by a causal capacity delimited by "the state of being a reflection" (*parāmarśatva*).
The meaning is "due to separation.

Although there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a collective perception (*samūhālambana-pratyakṣa*) that has both the subject-character (*pakṣatā*) and the subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) as its objects, even so...
Even so,

there is no fault, because what is intended is the state of being produced by a parāmarśa (subsumptive reflection) that is delimited by the property which delimits the state of being produced by pakṣatā (the subject-property). This is because the delimiters of pakṣatā and the perceptibility of parāmarśa are distinct.

The passage beginning with "due to the distinction" (*bhedāt*) and so forth should be consulted for a detailed explanation at the beginning of the section on inference (*anumiti*). Now, regarding the definition of *pakṣatā*:
why is it not included here that [the cause of inference] must be assisted by *pakṣatā*, which consists of doubt concerning the probandum (*sādhya*)?
With the intention that it is possible, he raises an objection with the words "even though" (yadyapi):
because in the case of inferring a cloud from one who has just woken up due to a deep thundering, there is an absence of the cause in the form of doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).

He provides the resolution with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), with the intention that because doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhyasaṃśaya*) would result in the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is impossible for such doubt to constitute the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), which is the cause of inference; therefore, it is not possible to intend that definition.
[Regarding the phrase] "of the desire for the inference of the probandum" (*sādhyānumitīcchāyāḥ*). Here:

If the existence of the probandum were established merely by the presence of a desire, then there would be the undesirable consequence of an inference occurring at the time of the desire "Let the pot come into being.
This consequence holds even if one does not include the [desire for] inference itself.
It is impossible to exclude the desire "May there be an inference of a jar.
Even if one includes in the definition a desire whose object is an inference of the probandum (sādhya), it remains impossible to exclude the desire "May there be an inference of a jar."

Because it is possible for there to be a desire whose objective is an inferential cognition (*anumiti*) that takes as its object a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of both the jar and the probandum (*sādhya*),

the meaning of the phrase "of a desire whose qualifier is the nature of being an inferential cognition specified by having the present probandum" should be understood in this way. Furthermore, regarding the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence, there is the property of being delimited by such a desire-nature (*icchātva*).
It must be so defined that no fault arises by taking the absence of both such a desire and a jar, and so forth.
Furthermore, "being delimited by such-desire-ness" means having a delimiting factor (avacchedakatā) that is pervaded by such-desire-ness;
and this, in turn, amounts to being not delimited by any property other than such-desire-ness.
Therefore, there is no fault in the case where Caitra possesses both the established [cognition] (*siddhi*) and the desire to establish (*siṣādhayiṣā*).

The point is this: although the state of being produced by a *parāmarśa* (inferential consideration), which resides in a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*) having a collective object (*samūhālambana*), is indeed delimited by the nature of a perception whose object is that *parāmarśa*, it is not delimited by that "pakṣatā-perceptuality" which serves as the delimitor of the state of being produced (*janyatāvacchedaka*) for the subjectivity (*pakṣatā*). This is the intended meaning.
2. Regarding "to be proved by the jar": the intention here is the desire expressed as, "May there be an inference of both the jar and fire.
3. "There is no fault."
The meaning is that there is no impossibility of *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject of inference) at a time when both the proof (*siddhi*) and the desire to prove (*sisādhayiṣā*) exist. 4.
Regarding the phrase "by suchness of desire" (*tādṛśecchātvāt*), etc.:
likewise, [this applies] to a desire such as "May there be an inference of both a jar and fire."

The intention is that since the absence [of the probandum]— namely, the absence of a pot other than that [intended one]— is delimited by the property of being the probandum of a pot other than that [intended one], which is distinct from the nature of such a desire, the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of that absence is not undelimited; therefore, such an absence does not possess the nature of the "absence of an intensifier" (*uttejakābhāva*).

There is no impossibility of inference by taking non-existence as the object, due to the desire to prove [the probandum] as qualified by the state of having a friendly disposition (*maitravṛttitva*). The same applies hereafter regarding the counter-positivehood (*pratiyogitā*).

The property of being delimited by either "qualified accomplishment" (*viśiṣṭasiddhi*) or its opposite must be introduced [into the definition]. By this, there is the exclusion of the absence of both "qualified accomplishment" and "pot," as well as the exclusion of the absence of such accomplishment qualified by its occurrence in some self (*ātman*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an inference occurring even when there is proof (siddhi) in the absence of a desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā). Although such a desire is a property other than [the mere absence of proof], namely, having the form of having the status of being an inferential cognition as its qualifier (tādṛśānumititva-prakārakatva), it follows that the absence of the desire to prove itself would not be included [in the definition].
The same applies to what follows as well; nevertheless,

[the definition consists in] not being the counter-correlative of a delimitorhood that is distinct from the delimitorhood residing in such-and-such a mode (*prakāraka*), and distinct from the delimitorhood residing in desire-ness (*icchātva*).
This is what must be intended to be said: likewise,

in the subsequent counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*), one should incorporate the property of not being the determiner (*anirūpakatva*) of a determinateness (*avacchedakatva*) that is distinct from the determinateness residing in "establishment" (*siddhitva*), which itself is distinct from the determinateness residing in the state of being qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣāvirahavaiśiṣṭya*).

The same should be understood in other cases as well. Regarding the statement "non-existence by way of inherence": this refers to the state of existence during both the desire to prove and the actual proof.

Since the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*)—whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of conjunction—is present in the self (*ātman*), inference would be untenable; therefore, it is stated "by way of inherence" (*samavāyena*).

The meaning of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyārtha*) is the state of having a counter-correlativity delimited [by a specific relation], which connects with the absence (*abhāva*). Now, one might object:

If the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) were qualified by *siddhi* through the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), then the problem of the impossibility of inference when both *siddhi* and *siṣādhayiṣā* are present would remain as it was; for *siṣādhayiṣā* exists only in the self (*ātman*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, he says: "By essential identity," and so forth.

And thus, the qualification by the absence of the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣāviraha) does not [reside] in the proof (siddhi) by way of an essential relation (svarūpasambandha), whereby the aforementioned fault would arise; rather, [it resides there] by way of...

The meaning is that there is no such fault because the relation is [defined as] the relation of inherence (samavāya) as qualified by the relation of being the locus, which is itself delimited by the relation of being the locus as delimited by the relation of identity residing in itself; thus,
"of the proof qualified by that" [is stated].
By Vyāsa’s writing, "the absence of proof qualified by the absence of the desire to prove" is established; thus,
the misconception that the entire compound word found in the sentence of the *Dīpikā* has "qualified" as a qualifier of "the absence of proof" is dispelled.
That being the case, regarding the established [cognition] (*siddhi*) and the desire to establish (*sisādhayiṣā*):

[the phrase] "having such a mode" (*tādṛśaprakārakatva*) means that it is distinct from the delimitation residing in the state of having as its mode the property of being an inferential cognition whose object is that locus (*pakṣa*) qualified by that probandum (*sādhya*).

The intended meaning is as follows: the term "absence of the desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣā-viraha*) refers to an absence whose counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*) is not determined by a delimitation (*avacchedakatā*) residing in the desire to prove that is distinct from the delimitation of the property of being the ultimate object of the desire (*icchātva-niṣṭha-avacchedakatā-bhinnā*).

It should be understood that in the case of a sentient being (*sattva*), the impossibility of inference remains as it was, because of the absence of the qualificandum in the form of the non-existence of proof (*siddhi*).
This means that there is an absence of proof by way of inherence (*samavāya*). [151]

The term "by way of inherence" (samavāyena) is stated in order to prevent inference at a time when there is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭasiddhi*), by taking into account the absence [of the probandum] through conjunction (*saṃyoga*)— an absence characterized by the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*). In this context,
within the body of the co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), regarding the first instance of "being contained in" (*ādheyatā*):

If the qualification of being delimited by the relation of identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) were not introduced, then even when the state of having established the probandum (*siddhi*) and the desire to prove it (*siṣādhayiṣā*) exist,
there would be the impossibility of inference because the absence of the desire to prove resides in the self through the relation of "having its own counter-positive" (*svapratiyogimattva*).
Therefore, its inclusion [is necessary].
Its meaning is "being delimited by a relation whose nature is undelimited.
By this, [it excludes] with respect to the delimitation of a jar and so forth.
There is no deficiency even when the absence of the desire to prove (*sisādhayiṣā-viraha*) exists within a self that possesses the desire to prove;

for at a time characterized by the absence of the desire to prove, the proof (*siddhi*) exists as a temporal qualifier (*kālika-viśeṣaṇatā*), and thus that very [undesired] fault remains. Therefore, the causality [of the proof] must be established through a second type of "unrestricted" (*anavacchinna*) essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

It must be stated that otherwise, since the absence of that [probandum] exists in the locus of the proof (siddhisattva) as delimited by a jar or the like, there would be the undesirable consequence of an inference occurring at the stage when the qualified [probandum] is already established. [151] This is the establishment of the probandum (sādhyasiddhi).
"Qualified by the delimiting property of the subject" and so forth.

This means: a cognition other than a doubt that possesses a qualifierhood delimited by a relation with the property delimiting the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka-dharma), which is in turn determined by a qualificandhood delimited by the delimiting property of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka).
And in this context, [the following is excluded]: "The stone is possessed of fire by way of conjunction," and so on.
For example, [the cognition] "The mountain possesses substance through conjunction," and "The mountain possesses fire through temporal relation (*kālika*), etc. and so forth.

Even if certainty exists, there would be the impossibility of inference; therefore, the delimitors of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) and so forth must be introduced, as well as the introduction of the relationship between the determined and the determiner (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*) between the qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) and the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*). [This applies to] the mountain...

It should be understood that this is for the purpose of avoiding the [undesired] exclusion of a collective judgment (*samūhālambana-nirṇaya*)— such as "the pot possesses [smoke], and the lake possesses fire"— from being a sublater of an inference such as "the mountain possesses fire. Furthermore, it is for the purpose of avoiding the exclusion of doubt (*saṃśaya*)— such as "does the mountain possess fire or not?"— from being a sublater [of the same inference].

The inclusion of "being other than doubt" [as a condition for a valid conclusion] does not mean being different from doubt in general; for if it were so, then [the following would be valid conclusions]:
"The mountain possesses fire by way of conjunction" and "The past possesses a jar."
Regarding the phrase "the possession of its own counter-correlative":

"its own" refers to the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā-viraha*); its "counter-correlative" is the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*); and "the possession thereof" is the self's (*ātmanaḥ*) having that [desire].

2. "That very same fault" means that even when there is both the established state (*siddhi*) and the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), inference (*anumiti*) would still be untenable. [The passage beginning with] "or not," etc., follows.
Because it would follow that a collective cognition (*samūhālambana-jñāna*) in the form of a partial doubt would not function as an obstacle [to valid knowledge], [the required property] is rather:
the state of not having as its qualifier an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation that delimits the probandum-ness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*).

Even though, in this context, a doubt such as "Is the mountain possessed of fire by way of conjunction?"— which involves other categories [of objects] through the property of fire-ness (*vahnitva*) and so forth— also possesses that same nature [of being a counter-example],

even when there is the intention to define [the required absence] as the absence of being a qualifier-nature (*prakāratā*) delimited by non-existence, which is itself qualified by a qualifier-nature determined by a subject-nature (*prakāratā*) delimited by the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-dharma*), and further delimited by a counter-positive-relation (*pratiyogitā-sambandha*) delimited by the relation that delimits the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that cognitions such as "the mountain possesses fire" and "the lake possesses the absence of fire" would not function as obstructions [to doubt]. Nevertheless, that which is the... characterized by the qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) delimited by the delimitor of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka)...
There is no fault, because it is intended that the qualifier-ness (prakāratā) delimited by suchness of absence (tādṛśābhāvatva) lacks its being the determiner (nirūpakatva) of that [absence].
Furthermore, the property of being delimited by the relation of identity (svarūpasambandha) must be included within the qualifier-ness delimited by absence-ness (abhāvatva).

Otherwise, there would result the undesirable consequence that even a certainty such as "the mountain possesses fire by way of conjunction" and "it possesses the absence of fire by way of a relation such as temporal connection (*kālika*) and so forth" would constitute a contradiction [with the sublation].

Furthermore, one must also include the absence of a qualifierhood (prakāratā) that is delimited by the nature of difference from the locus of the probandum (sādhyavat-bheda-tva) and is related through the relation of essential identity (svarūpa-sambandha), which is in turn determined by a qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka). Otherwise, there would result the undesirable consequence of opposition for a doubt such as "The mountain possesses fire, or is it different from that which possesses fire? Enough of this elaboration.

Is it not the case that the purpose of introducing the qualification "being distinguished by the absence of the desire to prove" when proof is already established— as stated in the *Dīpikā* passage beginning with "even when proof exists"— is precisely for the sake of the simultaneity of proof, the desire to prove, and the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*)?
That is possible;
yet that very thing is not tenable,
because of the specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) of a fit omnipresent substance (vibhu).
Since there is a rule that [cognitions] must be destroyed by qualities produced subsequently to themselves, it is impossible for them to exist simultaneously;

therefore, raising the objection that the statement of their purpose is irrelevant, he reconciles it with the case of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) consisting of a perfected cognition (*siddhi*)—[as follows]: "In this regard... [151]
By the words "and accomplishment" (*siddhiśca*) and so forth;
therefore, because of the pursuit [of the argument] up to the point of the collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*);
[the term] "subsequent reflection" (*parāmarśa*).

Otherwise, in a case where there is first a reflective awareness (parāmarśa), then proof (siddhi), then the desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā), and then inference (anumiti), the inference would simply not arise.
The sense is that because the *parāmarśa* (the subsumptive reflection) has already perished previously, no purpose [for inference] is possible here; and thus,

since a qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) can occur due to the absence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇābhāva*), there is no [need for] the desire to prove what is already established (*siddhi-siṣādhayiṣā*).
The sense is that there is a deviation [of the definition] with respect to a sentient being (*sattva*).
The definition of *parāmarśa* is found in the *Prakāśikā*.

[155] Regarding the acceptance of the seventh-case *tatpuruṣa* compound: now, why is a sixth-case *tatpuruṣa*— namely, "the property of the subject belonging to that which is qualified by pervasion" (*vyāptiviśiṣṭasya pakṣadharmatā*)— not adopted here?
And that alone is to be resorted to;

for, due to the lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*)— fearing the impossibility of a compound [if it were otherwise]— there is a co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the action contained within the compounded word, as derived from the rule *saptamyadhikaraṇe ca* belonging to the section on agents (*kāraka*).
If it is argued that the locative case is untenable because [the word *durvaca*] is difficult to be made subordinate, we say: no.

Even though a genitive case derived from a secondary suffix (*śaiṣika*) would be expected, the locative compound is respected here precisely to indicate that, in certain instances, the locative case is grammatically correct even after a word denoting a locus that is not a kāraka.
In this regard, the proof is precisely the inclusion of the word "and" (ca) in the aforementioned sūtra;
otherwise, its inclusion would be rendered purposeless. This is clear.
And this [is stated] in the *Vyutpattivāda*, in the investigation of the meaning of the locative case: "Now,

although it is possible to exclude the cognitions 'smoke is pervaded by fire' and 'the mountain possesses smoke' from the definition of *parāmarśa*— since *parāmarśa* consists in the knowledge of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) having as its object the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— nevertheless..."

The reason (*hetu*) is that which is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpya*), and the subject (*pakṣa*) is that which possesses the reason; thus, because there would be the consequence of regarding a collective cognition as a "subsumptive reflection" (*parāmarśa*), it would follow that an inference arises from it. Therefore, he states the refined definition with the words beginning "delimited by pervasion" (*vyāptyavacchinna*).
And here, in the case of a locus of deviation (*vyabhicāristhala*):

Since a qualified pervasion (vyāpti) characterized by the reason’s being a pervader and its co-occurrence with the probandum (sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya) is unestablished [in certain cases], one must instead posit as a constituent of pervasion a relation between objects that consists in a subject-object relationship (nirūpyanirūpakabhāva) common to both erroneous and non-erroneous cognitive states. And thus:
The phrase "delimited by pervasion" (vyāptyavacchinna) means:

delimited by the property-nature of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya), which is itself delimited by the property-nature of the probandum (sādhya), which is itself delimited by the property-nature of pervasion (vyāpakatva), which is itself delimited by the property-nature of the reason (hetu).

Furthermore, even for the constituent elements of the concept of pervasion, there exists only a state of objectivity characterized by the relationship of the determined and the determiner (nirūpyanirūpakabhāva).

The term *niveśyā* (to be included) is used in order to exclude inference such as "the lake possesses smoke pervaded by fire" or "the mountain possesses a pot," which arise from a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*).
The relation of the defined and the definer (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*) is introduced between the state of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatā*) and the state of being the qualifier (*prakāratā*).
This is for the purpose of precluding the inference "the mountain possesses fire" from the cognition "there is a substance which is smoke pervaded by fire."
Regarding the inclusion of the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*):
the term "certainty" (*niścaya*) is stated in order to exclude inference arising from a doubt such as, "Is the mountain possessed of smoke pervaded by fire, or not?"
Furthermore, certainty (*niścayatva*) is not merely the state of being different from doubt in general; for if it were, it would follow that even partial doubt could not produce [a cognition].

Rather, it consists in the absence of being a qualificand-determinant (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by the subject-locus (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), as characterized by a mode (*prakāratā*) whose object is the absence of the reason’s being pervaded by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpyahetutvābhāva*), and so forth.
The object of meditation is that which is characterized by pervasion,
wherein there is smoke.

In that regard, with the intention that the comprehension arising from the summary statement "there, fire" is that pervasion (*vyāpti*)— which is non-different from the restriction of concomitance (*sāhacaryaniyama*)— as that which is expressed by such a sentence, he says in the *Dīpikā* (at [157]) "where," and so forth.
[157] *Abhinaya* is the expression of words through intonation.

[157] Regarding the restrictive rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*), it is stated in the summary verse: "they move together" (*sahacarataḥ*); thus they are "concomitants" (*sahacarau*), and the state of those two is "concomitance" (*sāhacaryam*).

The meaning is "co-referentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya). According to the view of the ancients, its restriction (niyama) consists in the possession of properties such as "not occurring in that which lacks the probandum" (sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitva).
The definition of the *nīvīna* (the pervasion) consists in the determination of the probans (*hetu*), the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and the probandum (*sādhya*); its locus is the probans itself.

Or rather, since it must be stated that [the suffix] denotes [the property] solely through the indirect relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting in being the substratum of its own substratum, then in cases such as *vyāpya* ("pervaded"), that very [property] would have to be the meaning of the suffix; thus, the burden of the restriction (*niyama*) regarding its being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is unavoidable.
But if it is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), however—

Keeping in mind that, because the reason (hetu) resides in the locus of the qualified co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) specifically characterized by necessity through the relation of substratum-hood (*āśrayatā-sambandha*), there is no room for the aforementioned complexity (*gaurava*), it was stated as "necessary co-occurrence" (*niyata-sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
This takes the form of "not occurring in that which lacks the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvavad-avṛttitva*), etc.; by the word "etc. (*ādi*),...

The inclusion of "not occurring in what is other than the locus of the probandum" (sādhyavadanyāvṛttitva) means that the qualifier consisting of "not occurring in that which lacks the probandum" (sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitva) and so forth is the constituent element.

The meaning is that, by the etymological derivation "that in which such [a property] exists," it is constituted by the absence of occurrence in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitva*), and so forth.
Here, [the subject is] "possessing fire" (*vahnimān*).

The qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is for the purpose of excluding [the fallacy of] contradiction, such as "the sky-sun" and so forth; the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding deviant [reasons], such as "substance, because of existence" and so forth.

However, if the exclusion of the aforementioned contradiction is achieved by merely introducing the term "vṛtti" (occurrence), then the purpose [of the definition] should be understood to apply even to cases such as "smoke-possessing [is] because of fire.
Some, however, [define it as] the restriction of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*).

Regarding this, some have explained: "By the maxim that 'a state expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix appears as a substance,' the word *niyama* (restriction) refers to that which is restricted (*niyata*), and with the intention that it serves as a qualifier in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he says [in verse 157]:
'restricted coreferentiality'. This is incorrect.

If that were the case, it would contradict the explanation provided by the genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa), which interprets [the term] as "co-occurrence" (sāhacarya) being "grammatical coreferentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya), and that [coreferentiality] being "restricted" (niyama).
