Furthermore, because the word *niyata-paraniyama* would result in being placed first according to the rule "the qualifier [is placed before] the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣye*),
it follows that the intended meaning is stated as "constant co-referentiality" (*niyata-sāmānādhikaraṇyam*).
1. "The qualificand" (viśeṣya) means that which has the nature of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
2. "The qualifier" (viśeṣaṇa).
The meaning is that it is a qualifier in the form of a restriction;
the essential point is that it is not a statement of the word's primary meaning.

And thus, the meaning is that within the body of a definition consisting of restricted co-occurrence (*niyatasāmānādhikaraṇya*), a restriction—consisting in the qualification of "not occurring in that which lacks the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitva*) and so forth—cannot be stated. He states the fault in such a case as follows: [157]
This is stated by the words "idaṃ vācyam" and so forth. And here,

within the body of the definition consisting of "not occurring in that which possesses the absence of the probandum" (sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitva), is it an absence whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) resides in the probandum (sādhya) that is to be included, or rather...

Keeping in mind the alternative that [the absence] extends up to an absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by the delimitor of the probandumhood itself, and not delimited by any property other than that, [the author] first takes the absence of both "expressibility" (*vācyatva*) and "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*),
and then the absence of expressibility as qualified by its subsistence in a pot, and so forth.

Since it is evident that the non-deviation (*avyabhicāritva*) of a valid reason (*saddhetu*) would be untenable if one were to include the absence of "denotability" (*vācyatva*)— where the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth— the author states the refutation regarding the second [alternative]:
"[157] Because there is no cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)."
[157] The meaning is "not delimited by the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitānavacchedaka) and not delimited by the delimitor of the probandumness (sādhyatāvacchedaka).

The specific inclusion of the *sādhyatāvacchedaka* is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "smoky because of fire," where [the definition would otherwise apply] by taking properties such as knowability (*prameyatva*) or substantiality (*dravyatva*). Although...

The status of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absence of fire and so forth belonging to the kitchen (*mahānasīya*) is not impaired even for "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*) and the like, according to the maxim that "the property is [present] in addition.
Nevertheless, by the phrase "not the delimiting factor of such counter-correlativity," etc., [the point is established].

There is no fault by intending [the definition] to include the state of having a subject-matter (*viṣayatā*) delimited by the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) which is other than that qualified by an absence co-located with the reason (*hetu*). "Qualified" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of the relation of possessing a difference from its own locus (*sva-samānādhikaraṇa-bheda-vattva*), where "its own locus" (*svādhikaraṇatā*) [is as follows].
The delimitation of the counterpositiveness of difference [is related] by the relation of being the delimitation of its own counterpositiveness;
[the delimitation of the counterpositiveness of absence is related] by the relation of delimitation.
And thus, in the case of "belonging to the kitchen" (*mahānasīyatva*) and so forth...

The consistency with the definition [is established] due to the absence of such a delimitation of the objective determination (*viṣayatāvacchedakatā*). Furthermore, the property of being delimited by the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) in the objective determination belongs to a property that subsists in only one [individual].

The state of being the delimitor of the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedakatva*) consists in having a deliminatorship residing therein; this applies to two properties and so forth when they possess such a nature. 1.
That which is other than [the absence] qualified by an absence co-located with the reason (*hetusamānādhikaraṇābhāvaviśiṣṭa*).

The meaning is: "the state of possessing that [absence] which has as its objective content (viṣayatā) that which is delimited by the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka). By the term "itself" (sva), the absence of a jar or the like, which is co-locative with the reason (hetu), is to be understood. "Possessing a difference from the locus of itself" (svasetyādibhedavattva) means...

It is the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, which is itself delimited by the relation of being a delimitation of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in its own locus.

Here, "self" (*sva*) refers to the absence of a jar (*ghaṭābhāva*); the locus of that absence of a jar, by virtue of the relation of being the delimitation of its own counter-correlativity, is "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).

In that context, the difference which consists in being a difference possessing a subject-object relation (viṣayatā) qualified by "fire-ness" (vahnitva) through the relation of delimitingness (avacchedakatā), has its counter-correlate-delimitingness (pratiyogitāvacchedakatva) residing in the subject-object relation qualified by "fire-ness."

The objectivity (viṣayatā) delimited by "fire-ness" possesses the absence of a jar through the relation of being the delimitation of the counter-correlativity of such a difference; and the objectivity delimited by "jar-ness" is distinct from that which possesses the absence of a jar through that same relation— [this being so] by virtue of the relation of possessing a difference [defined as] "being in its own set," and so forth.

The coordination (*samanvaya*) should be understood as follows: the objectivity delimited by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvāvacchinnaviṣayatā*) is qualified by the absence of a pot, while the objectivity delimited by "fire-ness" (*vahnitvāvacchinnaviṣayatā*) is distinct from that.

However, [in other cases], there is a certain distinct [cognition] based on two properties (*dharmadvaya*) and so forth, through the relationship of qualifier and delimitor of the qualificandum (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatāvacchedakabhāva*).

Since being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) consists in being the counter-correlator (*nirūpaka*) of that [absence], there is no deficiency. Nor does this lead to an over-extension, for one cannot take as the [counter-positive] an absence of fire and so forth whose counter-correlativity is delimited by both the relations of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*).
It should not be argued that the defect remains as it was;

for what is intended [by the definition] is that [the absence] is delimited by the relation that serves as the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha) alone, which amounts to its being non-delimited by any relation other than that.

"Delimited by the delimitor of the probanshood (hetutāvacchedaka)" means: "delimited by a delimitor of the delimitinghood of the probanshood under discussion. Such a state of being the relatum (nirūpakatā) is to be construed with the locus (adhikaraṇatā).

By this, the objection— that because existence (sattātva) is also a delimiting factor of the causehood [of the reason] when that [existence] has qualified existence (viśiṣṭasattā) as its cause, that same defect remains— is refuted.

In reality, however, when a single property serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the causehood, it is precisely the state of having that [property] as its delimitation (*avacchedakatā*) which must be included within the locus-hood (*ādhikaraṇatā*). Where...

The suchness (*tathātva*) of the two properties (*dharmadvaya*) and so forth consists, according to the manner previously stated, in their having a distinct delimiting factor (*vilakṣaṇāvacchedakatā*); thus, nothing is lost.
In this very context, the phrase "that which is delimited by the delimitor of the causal state" (*hetutāvacchedakāvacchinna*) also applies.
This is what should be understood as the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Regarding the term "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*):

it means qualified by the property of being other than quality and action (*guṇa-karmānyatva*), through the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) which is constituted by both essential nature (*svarūpa*) and inherence (*samavāya*).

Now, one might object: "Since there is a difference between the qualified and the pure [locus], how can qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth be the locus of the reason? To this he says: "[158] 'Of the qualified'.
The construction is: "even though the absence of substantiality (*dravyatvābhāva*) resides in qualities and so forth, which are the loci of the reason."
By the phrase "qualities and so forth" (*guṇādi*), actions (*karman*) and the rest are included. Thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
That which delimits the property of being the specifier (*nirūpakatāvacchedaka*) of the locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) residing in that [substratum]—@
1. Here, by the term *nirūpakatā* (the property of being a determiner), *ādheyatā* (the property of being a locus) is intended.
And thus, that which pervades the delimitation of the status of being the reason under discussion—

The delimitation of the property to be located (*ādheyatāvacchedakatā*) is intended here as the state of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) that characterizes the location which, in turn, characterizes that [delimiting property].
Therefore, in the case of "Substance [is] because of qualified existence" (*dravyaṃ viśiṣṭasattvāt*), this applies to the delimitation of the probans-hood (*hetutāvacchedakatā*).

Regarding the state of being qualified existence (*viśiṣṭasattātva*), there is no delimitingness of the locus-ness (*ādhāratā*)—which is itself defined by the locus-ness residing in quality—with respect to the property of being resident therein;
for there is an absence of the cognition, "Quality possesses qualified existence [qualified by being other than quality and action]. Rather, however...

There exists a delimitation of the locusness (ādhāratā) qualified by the locusness residing in substance (dravya), as evidenced by the cognition: "Substance possesses existence qualified by being other than quality and action.
Therefore, [substance] possesses a locusness characterized by a locusness whose delimitation is pervaded by the delimitation of the probans-ness (hetutā).

The meaning is that it is indeed substance; since the property of not being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in it exists in substanceness (*dravyatva*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). 2.

Co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) constituted by both essential nature (svarūpa) and inherence (samavāya) means: being a subsistence delimited by the relation of essential nature, which is the state of residing in a locus that is the counter-correlative of a locativeity residing in itself and delimited by the relation of essential nature.
Of that very [co-occurrence]...

The meaning is that a quality (guṇa) and so forth do not possess the locus-hood (adhikaraṇatā) as determined by that [the smoke], because it lacks such a nature. Although, if the locus-hood of the reason were not specified as being delimited by the relation that delimits the state of being a reason (hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha),
then in cases such as a lake, which is a locus of smoke and so forth through a temporal (kālika) or other relation— [the definition would fail].

Because the absence of fire and so forth, as delimited by conjunction and the like, exists [in the locus], there is the possibility of the fault of non-pervasion (avyāpti). Nevertheless, this fault does not arise if one does not accept that everything produced possesses temporal existence; thus, he states the result of including that [temporal existence] in another way: "[158] There is no non-pervasion."

In the argument "that which is different from the self is like cognition because it is other [than the self]," etc., since the locus of the reason lacks any relation whatsoever with the self, the possibility of the definition's application is not precluded; thus, the fault of "impossibility" (asambhava) has not been demonstrated.

Since there is a dispute regarding the existence of the general absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sāmānyābhāva*) in a tree, he says "kapau" (in a monkey). Regarding the phrase "of the counter-positive's non-co-referentiality" (*pratiyogi-vaiyadhikaraṇyasya*):
although, if the counter-positive were introduced in a general sense, such an absence qualified by that particular attribute would be unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).

If "self" were introduced as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), then because "selfhood" would be restricted to each specific individual instance (*tattadvyakti*), it would follow that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) would be difficult for anyone who is not omniscient to know. Nevertheless, [the definition holds] by means of the two relations: identity (*tādātmya*) and subsistence in the locus of its own counter-correlative (*svapratiyogyadhikaraṇavṛttitva*).

The absence of being qualified by the counter-positive, either as "distinctness qualified by absence" through the two relations of being the determiner (*nirūpakatva*) and residing in the locus of its own substratum (*svāśrayādhikaraṇavṛttitva*), or as "distinctness qualified by counter-positiveness" (*pratiyogitāviśiṣṭānyatva*), should be included in the definition of absence in a way that conforms to both the gross and subtle methods; thus, there is no fault.

And here, if the meaning of the term "pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya" (non-coexistence with the counter-positive) were taken as "not occurring in the locus of its own counter-positive," there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to fallacious reasons (*vyabhicārin*), such as in the case of "this [tree] possesses monkey-contact, because it exists."

Because there is no difference in the absence [of the probans] corresponding to the difference in the locus (adhikaraṇa), it is impossible for the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) to be a constituent of its pervasion (vyāpakatā).

Furthermore, if one were to include the property of "subsisting in a locus that is not the locus of its own counter-positive" (svapratiyogyanadhikaraṇavṛttitva), [the definition would fail in the case of] "possessing conjunction with a monkey" (kapisaṃyogī).

However, since this [definition] remains subject to the same lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as the sun, one must incorporate the condition that "the locus of the reason (*hetu*) is not the locus of its own counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Bearing this and other points in mind, he says:
"[158] More... (referring to the *adhika* section).

1. By the term "non-existence" (abhāva), the absence of conjunction (saṃyogābhāva) is to be understood; that very [absence] qualified by its own counter-positive (svapratiyogin) through the relation of identity (tādātmya-sambandha) and the relation of subsisting in the locus of its own counter-positive (svapratiyogyadhikaraṇavṛttitva-sambandha), or something other than that.
The absence of a jar and so forth. Thus, the state of being a relatum (pratiyogitā) resides in the conjunction; that which defines it is the counter-correlate (nirūpaka).
The absence of conjunction is such that its counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) resides in itself, while the conjunction is its substratum;
furthermore, the absence of conjunction exists in the locus of that [conjunction]. Thus, it is qualified by counter-correlativity through the aforementioned two relations.
The non-existence of conjunction is distinct from that; thus the application [of the definition] should be understood as "the absence of jars and so forth.
[This concludes] the classification of inference, which begins with the words "by itself" and so on, as found in the *Saṃgraha* [verse 164].

The referent of this statement is that which is the locus of the substratum-ness (ādheyatā) as delimited by a transitive relation (*paramparāsambandha*)— consisting in being the substrate of its own substrate— as determined in the kitchen and so forth through repeated observation of dependence on others;
[this is expressed by] "wherever there is smoke, there is fire."
In that case where there is one who is the locus of an action of going toward a mountain occurring after a perception whose object is pervasion (vyāpti),
who possesses a doubt regarding fire residing in the mountain,
and who is the locus of a visual perception having smoke as its qualifier and the mountain as its substantive locus.
The undivided cognition (*akhaṇḍabodha*) is: "the locus of the recollection whose object is the pervasion, which has the form 'where there is smoke, there is fire'";
[this occurs] while one perceives smoke therein.
By the word "remembers" (*smarati*), the state of being produced by the perception of smoke is obtained in the case of the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

In instances involving the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), there is the manifestation of a causal relationship between the delimiting property of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) and the predicate; for example, as in the case of "the wealthy person... (*dhanavān*).
Because it was first observed through its association with pleasure;

and thus, in response to the doubt as to how the perception of smoke can be the cause for the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*), he establishes that in the *Prakāśikā* [165] with the words "ekasaṃbandhī" (connected with one).
Regarding the determination of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*),
the statement "having grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through repeated observation" indicates that repeated observation is the means of grasping pervasion.
It is obtained, yet that is not tenable;
for there is a deviation from the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Thus he raises the objection in the *Dīpikā* [164]: "But surely... (*nanu*) and so forth.

The Determination of the Means for Grasping Pervasion (*vyāpti*): Now, one might ask, "Why is it not possible to accept that even at a time when there is knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the certainty of pervasion is established through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*)? This would merely be an acceptance of what is already desired. To this, he says: "[165] 'At the time of the knowledge of deviation,' and so forth."
The sense is that this would likewise contradict experience.
Furthermore, if one were to disregard even such a contradiction with experience and accept the desired conclusion, he says: "[165] This is an illustration."
The statement regarding the over-extension (atiprasaṅga), which consists in the undesirable consequence of determining pervasion at a time when there is knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*),
is an *upalakṣaṇa*; that is, it indicates other faults that will be mentioned later.

"Because of the commonality of taste and so forth. This is an elliptical indication; for, in the view that does not accept generality as a means of proximity (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*), there is no such relation between the fire on the mountain and its smoke.

It should also be observed that because coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not present [at the time], it cannot appear in the perception of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in places such as the kitchen; consequently, the recollection of pervasion immediately after perceiving smoke and so forth on a mountain and the like would be untenable.

If pervasion (*vyāpti*) were defined as the property-limiting factor (*avacchedaka*) extending up to the cause itself, then smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*) and so forth would be both the delimiting factor and the delimited (*avacchedya*),
resulting in the undesirable consequence that the delimited and the delimiting are identical.
Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence;
for since a cognition whose qualifier is the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) is the cause of a cognition whose qualificandum is that which is delimited (*avacchedya*),
it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
And in the present context, self-dependence consists in the superimposition of a distinction upon one's own cognition, produced by the induction of one's own cognition as its cause.
If [it were] one's own cognition...

The meaning is that it would be a *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) as follows: "If [the self] were the cause of its own cognition, then it would be distinct from its own cognition"; or alternatively, it takes the form of a *tarka*: "If the self were its own cause, then it would be different from itself," and so forth.

Since the state of being the cause of one’s own cognition and so forth is pervaded by the state of being distinct from one’s own cognition and so forth, there exists a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*āpādya*) and the probans (*āpādaka*); thus he says: "[165] ‘of smoke-ness and so forth’" and "[165] ‘there is no harm’. And so, it is a cognition possessing a qualifier-state (*prakāratā*) delimited by such a property as smoke-ness.

The meaning is that there is no circularity (ātmāśraya) because of the difference between the effect and the cause: the effect is [the inference], while the cause is the cognition whose qualifierhood (prakāratā) is not delimited by [the property of] being smoke-ness (dhūmatva) and so on. This is stated because [otherwise] the fault of accepting what is undesired (iṣṭāpatti) would arise.

The meaning is that [the inference] does not arise from reasoning (*tarka*). Now, it has been stated that the absence of knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and the apprehension of concomitance (*sahacāra*) are the causes for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*);
in that regard, what role does each factor play in the apprehension of such a qualified pervasion?

Regarding the question of the utility of the absence of the apprehension of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and the utility of the apprehension of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he explains this with the passage beginning "And thus" (*itthaṃ ca*).
The reason is given as: "in the manner of being the cognition of the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇajñānavidhayā*).

The point is that without the cognition "co-occurring with the probandum" (*sādhyasamānādhikaraṇa*), it is difficult to apprehend the property of "subsisting in what is co-occurrent with the probandum" within the delimiting factor of the reason (*hetutāvacchedaka*).
He states "[165] In reality... to show that there is no fault even if co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*) is taken as the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
“*Taddharmadharmitāvacchedakake*”: the meaning is “that which has a qualificandumhood delimited by that property (*taddharma*)”. “*Ata eva*”:
the meaning is “precisely because it has been established that pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists only in co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) ending with that [delimitor].”

[166] "By the nature of being smoke-ness": the meaning is that the nature of being smoke-ness consists in its subsisting in all instances of smoke, together with its non-inherence in anything other than smoke.
[166] "Digi" means this:

by way of a certainty whose qualificandumness is delimited by the delimitor of pakṣatā (the subjecthood), which is determined by a qualificandumness that is delimited by the delimitor of the reason-property and is determined by a qualificandumness that is delimited by the relation of the reason-property-delimiter, which in turn is determined by a qualificandumness that is co-referential with the property to be proved (sādhya) as delimited by its own delimitor, which is determined by a qualificandumness that is the pervader, which is itself determined by a qualificandumness that is the reason as delimited by its own delimitor.
Since its status as a cause is accepted, there is no inconsistency in the qualified reflective awareness (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) being the cause of inference.

Thus, according to the former view, in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because of water," the definition of contradiction (*virodha*) is that which is a delimitor of the probans-ness (*hetutāvacchedaka*) and does not reside in what is co-locus with the probandum (*sādhyasamānādhikaraṇāvṛtti*).
And in this view,
the reason (*hetu*) does not reside in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyādhikaraṇa*);
likewise, in the previous view, [it does not reside there] in respect to the delimitor of the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedaka*).

Since it is necessary for the purpose of establishing the status of the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the essence (*svarūpāsiddhi*) that the [property] be included even by its own form (*svarūpataḥ*) as the delimitor of the qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*), there are three ways [of inclusion] within the definition of the reasonhood-delimitor (*hetutāvacchedaka*) residing in the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*).

In that view, there is the complexity of necessitating the inclusion of the delimiting property of the cause (*hetutāvacchedaka*); however, in this system, there is simplicity because [the relation] is of two kinds. Likewise, [it involves] the qualification of the probandum (*sādhya*) as qualified by the qualification of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*), which is itself qualified by the qualification of the reason (*hetu*).

In the previous view, the causality [of the inferential cognition] must be stated as residing in a certainty characterized by a subject-locus (viśeṣyatā) delimited by the pakṣatāvacchedaka, which is in turn characterized by a modehood (prakāratā) delimited by the hetutāvacchedaka, which is in turn characterized by a modehood of hetutāvacchedaka, which is in turn characterized by a modehood of subsistence (vṛttitva), which is in turn characterized by a modehood that is the qualifierhood (prakāratā) co-referential with the sādhya. Thus, there is complexity (gaurava). In this present view, however, it is not so.
Regarding "lightness" (*lāghava*):

here, the doubt concerning deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is an adversary specifically to the perception of pervasion (*vyāpti*), but not to the inference of pervasion and so forth, because in those cases it is actually favorable. And thus:

The very perceptibility of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the delimitor of the state of being obstructed by doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and not the status of being a cognition of pervasion common to inference and so forth; for if that were the case,
[the cognition would be obstructed] during the state of doubt regarding deviation.
Because pervasion and inference would otherwise be untenable; and thus, with respect to a single property-qualified object,
there is not a single obstructive factor characterized by the cognition of deviation that is common to both doubt and certainty.
It is possible;

likewise, the absence delimited by that [reason] also possesses the status of a logical reason (*hetu*). Furthermore, in the case of the obstructive function of doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*), *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) serves as the catalyst (*uttejaka*).
However, since that [doubt] is not such [an obstacle] with respect to the state of being an obstacle to certainty,
the doubt regarding deviation qualified by the absence of tarka functions as an obstacle to the perception of pervasion (*vyāpti*),
whereas the certainty regarding deviation unqualified by that [absence of tarka] functions as an obstacle to the apprehension of pervasion; thus, there is no [inconsistency].

The phrase "the possibility of a single obstructive power" (*pratibandhakatā-ekya-sambhava*) was stated with the underlying intention that it is not possible for the absence of a single thing to function as a cause; this is the "heart" (*hṛdaya*) of the matter.
This refers to the statement in the *Dīpikā* regarding the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti-graha*) in the passage beginning with "of smoke and fire," and so forth.

Anticipating the impossibility of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the word ending in the locative case, he completes the remainder [of the sentence]: "at the time when the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*) is about to arise.
Thus, by the rule "the locative case is used when a state is characterized by another state" (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*), the locative case is applied after the word *vyāptigrahe*.
It makes known the origination [of the cognition],
and it serves to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding that [origination]; here,
in the word "removal" (*nivṛtti*), there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by way of the relation of being prior in time to itself (*svaprākkālīnatva*).

Since that which is unknown is the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and that which is already known is the subject of reference (*uddeśya*), he states the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) by applying [the following] to the cited lamp-sentence, based on the cognition of some factor that generally removes the suspicion of deviation: [The sentence is: "In this lamp, there is smoke. Here, "in this" (*asmin*) refers to the lamp; "lamp" (*dīpa*) is the subject (*uddeśya*); "there is" (*asti*) is the verb (*ākhyāta*); "smoke" (*dhūma*) is the object (*vidheya*). In this context, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate proximity (*sannidhi*). Since the lamp is already known as the subject, it is not the object to be enjoined. However, because the lamp is not known to possess smoke, it becomes the object to be enjoined. Therefore, the word "here" (*atra*) is employed to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding the lamp's possession of smoke. Thus, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, there is smoke. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's location, thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its spatial proximity. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very place where the lamp is located, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its location. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's temporal proximity, thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its temporal relation. Consequently, the meaning is: "At this very time when the lamp exists, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its time. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's nature (*svabhāva*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its essential character. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which possesses such a nature, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its nature. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its functional capacity. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which performs such a function, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its causal efficiency. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its particularity. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which possesses such a specific characteristic, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its specific characteristic. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's universal (*sāmānya*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its general class. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which belongs to the class of lamps, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its universal. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its differentiation from others. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is excluded from non-lamps, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its exclusion. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's affirmation (*vidhāna*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its positive determination. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is affirmed as existing, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its affirmation. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's negation (*pratiṣedha*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its negative determination. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is negated as being otherwise, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its negation. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's identity (*tādātmya*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its ontological unity. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is identical to itself, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its identity. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's difference (*tadanyatva*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its distinction from others. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is different from non-lamps, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its difference. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's dependence (*apekṣā*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its relational requirements. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which depends on its causes, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its dependence. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's independence (*anapekṣā*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its lack of external reliance. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is independent, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its independence. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's permanence (*nityatva*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its eternal nature. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is permanent, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its permanence. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's impermanence (*anityatva*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its transitory nature. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is impermanent, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its impermanence. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's visibility (*dṛśyatva*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its perceptibility. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is visible, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its visibility. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's invisibility (*adṛśyatva*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its imperceptibility. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is invisible, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its invisibility. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its auditory nature. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is audible, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its audibility. This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's inaudibility (*aśrāvaṇatva*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its non-auditory nature. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this very lamp, which is inaudible, there is smoke. Thus, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to remove the suspicion of deviation regarding both the lamp and its inaudibility. This is the intended sense. Moreover, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the lamp's tangibility (*sparśanatva*), thereby removing the suspicion of deviation regarding its tactile nature. Consequently, the meaning is: "In this
[166] "It dispels the suspicion of deviation," and so forth.
In response to the question, "What is the form of this *tarka*? he says: [166]
"And that" refers to the passage beginning with "by non-proximity," and so forth.
The underlying sense is that being an object of perception is pervaded by [the presence of] sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*). This concludes the examination of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*).

[170] "The motivator of inference for others," and so forth. The underlying meaning is as follows: by the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) of *parārthānumāna* as a *bahuvrīhi* compound—since the latter member [of the compound] indicates the sense of another word (*anyapadārthalakṣaṇikatayā*)—the term *parārthānumāna* [refers to that which motivates inference for the sake of another].
Since it is understood as being delimited by its role as the motivator for the formulation of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), its status is merely figurative (*aupacārika*).
As for that which—

By relying on a *karmadhāraya* compound in the term "inference for others" (*parārthānumāna*), it is that which is delimited by being a five-membered statement itself that is conveyed by it through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of "being the instigator.
The expression "the instigator of inference for others," however, is intended to demonstrate the relationship between the primary meaning and the indicated sense.
That is trivial; for the Naiyāyikas do not accept the definition of a sentence as applying to the word *parārthānumāna* (inference for others) because it exists in the form of a sentence,
since the denotative power (*śakti*) of a sentence is not established [by them].
Because a definition (*lakṣaṇā*) consisting of a possible relation is impossible;
otherwise, in cases such as "the hamlet is on the deep river," the author of the treatise [would have to accept] the word "river" and so forth [as denoting the bank].
Because it would result in a contradiction with the statement that [the compound] indicates the bank of a deep river and so forth.
Here is the summary:
"In this context, the *bahuvrīhi* [compound] [functions as] a word for inference of the object..."
It is so proclaimed;
however, some say that it is a *karmadhāraya* compound in that context, but that is not correct.
If that were the case, since it would be a sentence, metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) would not be possible,
because the meaning of the sentence is not established [as a prior independent entity].
For metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) is indeed the connection of words.

"In our view, in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the final member is denotative; it is connected [to the meaning] through its relation to the primary sense (*śakya*), which consists in being the instigator (*prayojakatā*) [of the cognition]. Thus [it is said].
And here, the word "inference" (anumāna) refers to that which prompts the formulation of an inference for the sake of others;
the term "for the sake of others" (parārtha) serves to indicate the intended meaning.
According to the view of some,
the word "inference" (anumāna) refers to that which has inference as its purpose; thus,
it is the opinion of others that the referent of the term "for the sake of others" (parārtha) is connected with inference, which is a part of that [purpose].
Discrimination. [172] The definition of *nyāya* (the method of reasoning) must be understood as the determination of its constituent members (*avayava*). And thus:

The doubt that the definition to be stated— which consists in being a member of a syllogism (*nyāyāvayava*)— is difficult to understand if the definition of a syllogism (*nyāya*) itself is not fully known, has been dispelled. Now, [regarding] the summary statement beginning with "from the inferential mark (*liṅga*) established by this," etc.:

The meaning obtained is that "the other person" is also the locus of an inference produced by a mark (liṅga) which is the object of a cognition brought about by the employment of the collection of the five members beginning with the proposition;
however, that is not tenable.

Since it is impossible for the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) itself to be the cause of inference— otherwise, inference would be untenable in cases where the mark is past or otherwise non-existent— one might raise this objection; however, the word *liṅga* here refers to the "consideration of the mark" (*liṅgaparāmarśa*).

Therefore, intending to offer the resolution that the meaning obtained is "the other person also possesses an inference produced by the consideration of a logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) prompted by such a collection," he says:
"[172] By this," and so forth.

In the statement from the *Dīpikā*, "the statement of the subject as possessing the probandum" (*sādhyavattayā pakṣavacanam*), the word "probandum" (*sādhya*) refers to that which is delimited by the delimitor of the state of being a probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakāvacchinna*).
The meaning of the instrumental case suffix [in *vattayā*] is...
The term "pakṣa" refers to that which is delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). With this intention, he states the meaning as follows: [172]

By the phrase "delimited by the delimitor of the probandum" (*sādhyatāvacchedakāvacchinna*), etc., [the author] states the purpose of introducing the delimitant of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). By the phrase "example," etc., [he states it].
And this is done by accepting that the word "probandum" (*sādhya*) occurring in the example refers to the probandum alone. Therefore...

Since another interpretation will be stated later and that alone is logically sound, it is necessary— intending that [interpretation]— to include the pure delimiting property of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) in order to exclude the conclusion (*nigamana*); therefore,
regarding the word expressing the probandum (*sādhya*) found in the example (*udāharaṇa*), [the following applies].

If [the word "sādhya"] were intended to mean the probandum as qualified by being pervaded by the reason, then since there would be no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in that case— given that the word expressing the probandum in the example (*udāharaṇa*) would also refer to the probandum as qualified by being pervaded by the reason— the inclusion of the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) would be redundant.

[This is] refuted. He states the result of introducing the delimitors of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) and the relationship of the defined and the definer (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*) between the property of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) and the mode (*prakāratā*) in the passage beginning with "[163] ...and from the application (*upanaya*).
[The application is: "The mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire."

In cases where smoke (*dhūma*) and the like serve as the reason for a probandum (*sādhya*) such as "substance" (*dravya*), there is an absence of the property of being qualified by the delimiting condition of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*)— as it occurs in the cognition produced by the application (*upanaya*)— in relation to the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

The point is that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of the *upanaya* (application), because the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*)— which is determined by the subject-qualifierhood (*pakṣaviśeṣyatānirūpita-prakāratā*) in the cognition produced by an *upanaya* such as "possessing smoke that pervades the substance"— is not delimited by the delimitor of the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedakāvacchinnatva*).
This is the case in a situation where fire and so forth stand in the relation of the reason and the probandum through both temporal and spatial conjunction (*kālika-saṃyoga*).

The inclusion of the "delimiting relation of the probandum" (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha*) is for the purpose of excluding [the definition from] the *upanaya* (application). Now, one might object: "Let the definition simply be 'that which generates such a cognition'; what is the point of including the term 'sentence' (*vākyatva*)? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states its...
He states its purposefulness by way of excluding statements that fall outside the rules of logic (nyāya), saying: "[172] Of the word *vākya*.

The inclusion of the property of being a "member" (*avayavatva*) is for the sake of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the part consisting of the conclusion (*nigamana*), namely the portion "this [subject] possesses the probandum" (*sādhyavānayam*).
[173] Also at the beginning— in the definition of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth—

in the *Dīpikā* [172], it says "ending in the fifth case" (*pañcamyantam*) and so on; this is according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) meaning "that in which the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is the end (*antaḥ*)."

The state of having a fifth-case ending (*pañcamyantatva*) consists in being composed of a fifth case that lacks the property of being preceded by a word contained within itself; this results in the definition of being qualified by the fifth case. As for the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*):
[The relation is] by way of both the relation of being composed of itself and the relation of being the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in itself.
The delimitation [of the counter-correlativity] is by way of the relation of preceding the words that constitute it. The result of including that [relation] is as follows: from that...

Since the exclusion of the conclusion (*nigamana*) as "fire-possessing" is clear, he states the result of including the property of "being a communicator of the mark" (*liṅgapratipādakatva*) in the *Prakāśikā* with the words: "This is not from a staff," and so forth;
and "not produced by conjunction with a staff," and so forth.
The inclusion of both the qualifier and the qualificand is for the purpose of avoiding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as a jar or the color of a staff;
for, by the mere inclusion of the element consisting of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*), the example (*upanaya*) is already excluded.

The sole purpose of including the phrase "ending with that" (*tadantatva*) is to exclude the *nigamana* (conclusion). Since the proposition (*pratijñā*), such as "the mountain possesses fire," lacks the suffix of the fifth case (*pañcamī*), it is disregarded. As for expressions such as "this [is known] from the staff," they are not stated as "from the staff" because they contradict established tradition.
To prevent the misconception that the word *liṅga* refers to gender (*puṃstva*) and so forth, he says "hetu" (cause) [in verse 173].

Although in cases such as "because it is a substance not produced by conjunction with a staff" or "because it is not produced from a staff," the property of being not produced from a staff is not [the reason] for the [conclusion] "not from a staff"— that is, because it is a substance not produced by conjunction with a staff— [nevertheless...]

Even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*); nevertheless, [the definition] consists in being the generator of a cognition possessing a causal-objecthood (*hetu-viṣayatā*) that is determined by an objecthood of the probandum (*sādhya-viṣayatā*), which in turn is determined by an objecthood delimited by the locus-qualifier (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), and which is characterized by the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāpanna*) of the probandum as delimited by the locus-qualifier.
There is no fault, because it is intended to be expressed in that way.
1. That aggregate in which the fifth case-ending occurs as *antaḥ* (internal) is that aggregate; [it refers to] its own constituent part...
The state of being composed of that [collection] consists in the presence of a fifth case-ending which lacks a preceding word for "that" (yat).
Furthermore, both occurrences of the word "self" (sva) refer to the fifth case-ending.
3. *Svapadam* refers to a compound ending in the ablative case.
[Objection: Even so, however—

By means of an analysis of the meaning of the suffix *thāl*, and having first refuted it, the application (*upanaya*) and conclusion (*nigamana*) which contain that suffix are shown to be defective in other contexts; therefore, since in the present case the conclusion must be expressed in the form "therefore, not from a staff" (*tasmān na daṇḍāt*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in that regard.
If it is argued that [the status of] being the end of a fifth case-affix remains unimpaired there, we say no;
because in the definition of the "indicator" (*liṅga*)-producer, the property of being a *śruti* (direct statement) is included as a qualifier of the indicator,
[namely] the nature of producing a cognition whose object is an indicator not delimited by anything other than the delimitor of the indicatorhood of the subject under discussion.

Because there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of [the definition] being the indicator of a pure probans (*śuddhaliṅga*), since in the cognition produced by the conclusion (*nigamana*), the aspect of pervasion (*vyāptyaṃśa*) appears as something additional to the probans.
This is also the case for the application (*upanaya*) and so forth.
Because there is the presence of that which establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: [173] "The cognition of the reason under discussion," and so forth.
Since even natural metaphorical indication (*svārasikalakṣaṇā*) would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the opponent's statement, he says: [173] "Established" (*nirūḍha*).
This means: residing in an object that has been the referent of an intention (*tātparya*) since beginningless time.
Thinking that it is improper to assume meaninglessness when meaningfulness is possible, he says with this intention: "Alternatively" (*athavā*).
Now, [one might object]: if there is no comprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) from the example, then what of it?
Since it does not follow that [the statement] has as its primary purpose the pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "And thus" (*tathāca*).

And thus, by taking the subsequent mental cognition whose object is the pervasion produced by the example (*udāharaṇa*), there is the status of having the intention to convey the pervasion, which consists in being uttered with the desire for the cognition of the pervasion.
The sense is that what was intended by the phrase "establishing pervasion" (vyāptipratipādaka) must be demonstrated.
As for the word "dig" (direction/indication), the meaning is this: he does not [know it] from a staff.

In such cases as "because it is a substance not produced by contact with a staff," if in the illustrative sentence— "that which possesses the reason [of being a substance] is not [produced] from a staff"— the subject (*dharmin*) were not intended to be expressed, the negative particle (*nañ*) would have no power of signification at all. Likewise, [in the case of] "smokeless..."

In cases such as "because of the absence of fire," there would be an inconsistency if one did not intend to express the meaning of the pronouns *yat* and *tat* in the positive example (*anvayy-udāharaṇa*) such as "whatever does not possess fire does not possess smoke"; therefore,
it is said that [the example] "communicates the mark (*liṅga*) as qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*)."

Anticipating the objection that the definition of *upanaya* stated in the *Dīpikā* is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) with respect to the *nigamana*, he says: "[173] ‘That which has as its qualificandum (viśeṣya) that which is qualified by the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*)...
The sense is that there is no fault because of the inclusion of the relation of the "defined and the definer" (*nirūpyanirūpakabhāva*).
"[173] By supplementing the ellipsis with the word ‘is employed’ (*prayujyate*)."

And this [statement] is for the sake of the cognition of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*); it was stated thus because, under the analysis of the compound as *pakṣadharmatājñānārtham*, the dative case functions as an agentive case (*kārakavibhakti*), which necessitates dependence upon a verbal action.

If one accepts the etymological derivation "that from which the knowledge of the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatājñāna) arises," then there is no necessity for supplementing the sentence with the word "statement" (vacana) through ellipsis-filling.
It should be understood that this refers to the neuter gender.

Regarding the definition of the conclusion (*nigamana*) as "the statement of the subject (*pakṣa*) as possessing both the reason and the probandum," the compound *hetos-sādhyam* is a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound; thus, it means "the probandum of the reason. This is because of the rule concerning the fifth case (*pañcamī*).
It should be explained by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule).

Alternatively, in the expression "the probandum [is] of the reason" (*hetoḥ sādhyaṃ*), the genitive case is used in a secondary sense (*śaiṣikī*) to indicate that the probandum is that which is to be made known by the knowledge [of the reason].
Now, with the intention that the compound should be understood as *sup sup* (noun with noun), he states the meaning: [173] "by the knowledge of the cause."
[173] "Having as its object that which possesses the probandum" (sādhyavadviṣayaka) means:
having as its qualificandum (viśeṣyatā) that which is delimited by the locus-characteristic (pakṣatāvacchedaka) and characterized by such a probandum (sādhyaprakāraka). Now, an objection:
since the relation between the locus and the probandum and so forth are already obtained from the proposition (pratijñā) and other members, what is the purpose of the conclusion (nigamana)?
Having considered that [the argument] would otherwise be fruitless,

and having accepted that the word expressing the reason (*hetu*) situated in the conclusion (*nigamana*) possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) characterized by being "uncontradicted" (*abādhitatva*) and so forth, one reflects in the mind that it is improper to claim that the cognition of that [reason] is verbal (*śābda*), because secondary signification is the lowest [mode of meaning].
He states in the *Dīpikā* that the purpose of the conclusion (*nigamana*) is precisely the mental apprehension of non-sublation and so forth, saying: "non-sublation and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of "being unopposed by a counter-argument" (*asatpratipakṣitatva*) is intended.
"Non-sublated-ness and so forth" refers to the cognition of non-sublated-ness and so forth.
By that [term], in accordance with its literal sense, regarding the object—
The objection that there is an inconsistency because it is impossible for [the conclusion] to have "being produced" as its purpose is refuted;
in the phrase "at a later time," the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
Therefore, after the verbal cognition produced by the conclusion, the realization of the reason's being uncontradicted and so forth necessarily occurs.
It is understood that [the self] is born.
Since, according to the method stated above, its cognition cannot be verbal, the *Prakāśikā* [176] states: "It should be seen through the mind."
Regarding the establishment of qualified subsumption (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*) as the cause of inference,

the phrase "of that which is already established" (*kḷptasya*) indicates, according to the *Dīpikā*, that its status as an invariably preceding factor (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*) is accepted by both parties.
[176] For what purpose should it be accepted?
The sense is that it follows the principle: "from that very cause.
[177] Regarding the passage beginning with "here, however, as you maintain," etc., by this—
It has been indicated that for the Mīmāṃsaka as well, the state of being previously occurred must be postulated regarding the two cognitions.
Regarding the phrase "in verbal [cognition]," the intended meaning is that its manifestation is impossible without a word that makes it known.
By this, [it is shown that] in the case of perception, due to the force of sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*), someone’s...
It has been indicated that since the manifestation of the delimiting property of the cause (*hetutāvacchedaka*) is unavoidable, there is no possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case;
as stated in the *Dīpikā* [177]: "because of the necessity of the *parāmarśa*," meaning even without the two cognitions favored by you.

The meaning is that the qualified consideration (viśiṣṭaparāmarśa) must be accepted as preceding the inference. Now, one might object: "Let there be an inference from a qualified consideration in some cases; why must it be so in all cases?"
Because it is [achieved] through the postulation of a qualified *parāmarśa*, he says: "by way of parsimony" (*lāghavena*).
Anticipating the question, "Of what is there parsimony?", he states in the *Prakāśikā*: "the meaning is 'by way of parsimony of postulation'.

This refers to the two cognitions delimited by the nature of the cognition of pervasion (*vyāptijñānatva*) and the nature of the cognition of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñānatva*).

[177] Regarding "qualified reflective awareness" (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśa*), that is, reflective awareness delimited by the nature of apprehending the qualifiedness of what is pervaded (*vyāptiviśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhiparāmarśatva*): the sense is that, rather than postulating [the cause] as being delimited by a single property based on its being otherwise unestablished (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) and so forth, it is more cumbersome to postulate it as being delimited by the two previously mentioned properties. Now, one might object:

The causality of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the apprehension of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not accepted in their individual forms, for that would entail the aforementioned fault; rather, their status as such is accepted by virtue of being a cognition of the property of the subject as qualified by the apprehension of pervasion. Thus...
Furthermore, even in our view, the postulation of that [universal] occurs only as delimited by a single property; thus, parsimony (lāghava) is undeniable.
The lack of a decisive criterion (vinigamanāviraha) is exactly the same [for both sides].

As for the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the counter-example where there is a verbal reflection (*śābdaparāmarśa*), it must be avoided by incorporating "immediacy following a qualified reflection" (*viśiṣṭaparāmarśāvyavahitottaratva*) within the definition of the delimiting condition of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedakagarbha*). Otherwise,
[deviation would arise] because the qualified reflection— "possessing the reason delimited by the delimitor of the reasonhood that is pervaded by the probandum"— is present there.
Regarding the consequence of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he says: "[177] In reality... and "[177] It should be noted...".
This is the intended meaning:

In the Mīmāṃsaka view, it is necessary to include both "co-occurrence" (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and "twofold knowledge-ness" (dvidhājñānatva) within the delimiting factor of the causal efficiency of inferential cognition (anumitikāraṇatāvacchedakakoṭi).
In our view, however, this is not the case. Thus...

In that view, two distinct causal capacities must be asserted, because there is no decisive reason (vinigamanāviraha) to determine whether causality consists in the cognition of the subject-attribute (pakṣadharmatā) qualified by the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti), or whether it consists in the apprehension of pervasion qualified by the cognition of the subject-attribute.
In our view,

however, even though there may be an absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*), there is no room for two distinct causalities, because we accept the non-difference of those causalities that are co-extensive (*samaniyata*). Thus...

If the cause is taken to be a cognition possessing a qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) such as that of smoke, which is delimited by pervasion (*vyāpti*) and qualified by having a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by relations such as inherence (*samavāya*), then even the status of being a certainty (*niścayatva*) need not be included in the aspect of pervasion; for in our view,
there can be a cognition consisting of doubt regarding the aspect of the delimiting adjunct (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*).
"Because it is impossible for it to involve the apprehension of a qualified-qualifier relation (viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya), there is parsimony (lāghava).
[177] "Due to the absence of a deciding factor (vinigamanā-viraha)" means by way of the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) being qualified by the logical mark (liṅga).
The meaning is that, in this context, it must be stated that [inference] possesses causality; this is because there is no restrictive factor [to limit it otherwise].

[This refers to] its being a cause with respect to inference through the relation of being the intended object (uddeśyatā-saṃbandha), by means of a relation that delimits its causal status, such as conjunction (saṃyoga).
With the intention that it is difficult to establish the causality of reasons such as smoke, he says: "In that case also,
from inference," referring to the determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by means of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

And since it is "possessing pervasion" by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the word "concomitance" (*anvaya*) in the summary [verse] refers to positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*), which consists in the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the reason and the probandum.
[The phrase] "the state of being graspable by the grasper... [is used].
This is the meaning of the third case-ending (tṛtīyārtha).
For this very reason, there is a refutation of the purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) inference.
This also applies to the expression "by way of negative concomitance" (vyatirekeṇa).
Negative concomitance (vyatireka) is negative co-presence;
it consists in the co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the absence of the probandum and the absence of the reason.
The meaning of the third [element] is as before, namely "positive concomitance" (*anvaya-sahacāra*) and so forth, as stated in the *Prakāśikā*.
The first part of the definition (the "existence" clause) is included to exclude the purely negative inference (*kevala-vyatirekin*).
The qualifier is for the purpose of excluding purely positive (kevalānvayi) reasons.
If one were to include merely the possession of positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti), [the following would be a fallacy]:
"Earth is distinct from others because it possesses smell."
Thus, there is an impossibility of excluding the negative (vyatirekin) [type of inference] and so forth;

however, under the aforementioned refinement, because of the absence of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) that grasps positive concomitance (anvaya-vyāpti), there is no apprehension of the co-occurrence (sahacāra) between the reason and the probandum.

Thus, there is no fault. However, it should be understood that in the case of the qualified subject (viśeṣya), pervasion must be accepted as belonging to the qualified entity itself, and not merely by way of being apprehended by such a cognition.
Regarding the phrase "in the collection [of reasons], fire is the probandum":
the meaning is that "possessing smoke" is the determiner of the state of being a probandum as residing in fire.

In the illustrative sentence, the word *mahānasa* (kitchen) and so forth ends in the locative case (*saptamyanta*), in accordance with the requirement of the word *yatra* ("where"). Now, [begins] the definition of the purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) [inference]. Indeed...
"Why has the definition of a logical reason (hetu) not been stated as being merely positive concomitance (kevalānvayitva)? To this he says: "[182] 'Having a probandum that is purely positive'...
This means, for example, the reason in such cases as "A pot is nameable because it is earth" (*ghaṭo 'bhidheyaḥ pṛthivītvāt*). [182]

That very [definition] is indeed the state of being purely positive (kevalānvayitva). But is there not an over-narrowness (avyāpti) in cases such as "the sky is absent here, because it is cognizable" (gaganābhāvavān meyatvāt), since the probandum— the absence consisting of the sky— is itself the counter-positive (pratiyogin)?

Likewise, regarding cases such as "this [locus] possesses the absence of conjunction because it is knowable," since the probandum (sādhya) is the counter-positive of an absence consisting of conjunction and so forth, he says: "[182] ‘Unlimited’ (niravacchinna)."
The meaning is that it is devoid of that "distinctive non-delimitability" which is to be indicated by a co-occurrent term (*sapatamī-nirdeśya*).
Therefore, even though there is a rule that being a locus (*ādheyatā*) must be delimited by some property, [it does not follow that the absence of such delimitation is impossible].

The meaning is as follows: there is no deficiency; for since space (*gagana*) and the like lack the property of having a locus (*vṛttimattva*), and since the occurrence (*vṛtti*) residing in conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth lacks the quality of being non-delimited (*niravacchinnatva*), there is no room for the two aforementioned defects. However, some maintain that "being purely positive" (*kevalānvayitva*) consists in not being the counter-positive (*apratiyogitva*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that possesses a locus contradictory to itself.

Even if the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) were mentioned here by its own term (*svapada*), there would be the consequence of the [denotation] resting upon each individual instance (*tattadvyakti*),
and moreover, being "one among those" (*tāvadanyatamatva*) would be difficult to grasp.
If, however, the counter-correlate were mentioned...

Without the use of repetition (*vīpsā*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); if repetition were employed, it would be difficult to comprehend. Nevertheless, that [definition] consists in being other than that which is qualified by the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the possessor of the occurrence (*vṛttimat*). As for this qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*):

They say that there is no fault because [the relation] consists in the dual relation of being its own counter-positive and being the delimitation of the counter-positiveness of a difference residing in itself; furthermore, this delimitation is delimited by the relation of "subsisting in the locus of itself. However, this is to be considered.

Since the property of being purely positive (*kevalānvayitva*) as stated in the context of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*), it is necessary to include the condition "not occurring in its own locus" (*svānadhikaraṇavṛttitva*); consequently, the independent inclusion of the qualifier "possessing occurrence" (*vṛttimattva*) would result in redundancy.

Furthermore, if one were to include the condition of being devoid of an unconditioned locatability (niravacchinnādheyatā) as determined by its own locus (svādhikaraṇa), it would result in the collapse of the status of the absence of conjunction (*saṃyogābhāva*) as a purely positive entity (*kevalānvayin*),
because the absence of conjunction and other such absences [would fail to meet that criterion].

Because it is so; and because, even in the case of a [cognitive] state (*vṛtti*), if one were to include "unconditionedness" (*niravacchinnatva*), it would result in the fallacy of the maxim "washing away [the stain] with the very water that caused it.
This concludes the definition of the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*).

[183] Regarding the phrase "possessing only negative concomitance" (*vyatirekamātravyāptika*) in the summary verse, the meaning obtained is: "the state of possessing negative concomitance while being devoid of positive concomitance.
And here, the qualification is intended to exclude the *anvayavyatirekin* (reason that possesses both positive and negative concomitance).
It should be understood that the term "qualified" (viśeṣya) is included to exclude the deviant;
however, that [definition] does not hold up.

Because pervasion— whether defined as the reason’s co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*) or as its non-occurrence in that which lacks the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitva*)— is present in such reasons as "earth is distinct from others because it possesses odor."

With the intention that the definition should be stated as "the state of being the qualificandum of a certainty whose mode is positive pervasion (anvaya-vyāpti), while not being the qualificandum of a certainty whose mode is negative pervasion (vyatireka-vyāpti)," he explains [as follows]: [184]
Regarding the term "ascertained" (*niścita*):

here too, the qualifier and the qualified are intended to exclude those [reasons] that deviate in terms of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-vyabhicārin*). It is sufficient that there be the possession of negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāptimatva*) alone; thus, there is no lack of consistency with the definition.

The point is that because "earth-ness" as a whole is the subject (*pakṣa*), a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) distinct from it is difficult to find, and thus it is impossible to ascertain the positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*).

This is because the difference having something other than earth as its counter-correlate— which consists of differences delimited by [properties such as] "water-ness" and so forth— is already well-established.
Because of the impossibility of such a conceptual construction, he says: "delimited by otherness from earth" (*pṛthivītaratvāvacchinna*). Now, one might object:

if the probandum (sādhya) consists of a difference whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is delimited by otherness from earth, then the criticism stated in the *Dīpikā* regarding the first position—beginning with "where... (*yatra*) and so forth—is inapplicable, since the probandum would be well-established (*prasiddhi*) in that case.

1. One's own (sva) is the absolute absence of existence (*vṛttyabhāva*); the absence of the jar (*ghaṭābhāva*) is that [absolute absence]; being qualified by that is "being other than the jar" (*tadanyatva*), which belongs to "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth.
The jar's being qualified by the absence of the jar through the aforementioned two relations is as follows: one's own (*sva*) is the absence of the jar.
The absence of a pot is the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) of that [absence], which is the pot;
likewise, "self" refers to the absence of the pot, and the difference residing therein is the difference from that which possesses the pot, by way of the relation of subsisting in its own locus.
Since the absence of a jar does not reside in the locus of the jar, the jar is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of such a difference.

Since positive concomitance (*anvayitva*), which consists in possessing positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*), exists therein, it is impossible to bring that about; furthermore, since in the case of a reductio (*āpatti*) the determination of the absence of the probandum (*āpādya-vyatireka-nirṇaya*) is the cause, such a determination is impossible here—therefore, he says: [184]
Regarding the phrase "positive concomitance" (*anvaya-sahacāra*):
having raised the doubt as to why the acceptance of this [concomitance] is not possible, he states the reason with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*).
[184] Well-known inference (*prasiddhānumāna*) is an inference that has smoke and so forth as its reason for proving fire and so forth as its probandum.
This also includes such [inferences] as "earth is distinct from others because it possesses odor," and so on.

[184] Regarding the term *sapakṣa*: here, being a *sapakṣa* consists in being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of a certain cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), and not merely the state of possessing that property (*sādhyavattva*), because the latter would be impossible [in the case of the fallacy in question].
Thus, when the difference of earth from other things is the property to be proven, the possession of odor and so forth constitutes the fallacious reason known as the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).
The sense is that it would be so, but it is not a valid reason (*saddhetu*).

Now, [one might object]: even in the absence of knowledge of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is an inference having the probandum (*sādhya*) as its qualificandum, which arises from a negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) that does not include the probandum [as its locus].

There is no obstacle to the possibility [of inference] arising from the *parāmarśa* (reflective awareness) in the form: "Earth possesses odor, which is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the state of being other than earth"; therefore, he says: "[184] Because [the property] is unestablished," with this intention.
And thus, even in the case where the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished...

The sense is that this objection was stated precisely by accepting the position that an inference must have the probandum (sādhya) as its qualifier (prakāra). By this, inferences where the probandum is the qualificand (viśeṣya) are excluded.
[184] Regarding the phrase "of water, etc. and so forth:
It should be understood that "thirteen mutual absences" (*trayodaśānyonyābhāvāḥ*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound according to this [author's] view;
however, some maintain that it refers to the thirteen [categories], beginning with water.
Furthermore, it is a bahuvrīhi compound;
otherwise, the collective consisting of fourteen [elements] would not be obtained.
"Thirteen mutual absences" (*trayodaśānyonyābhāva*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
In the sentence from the *Dīpikā*, "delimited by thirteenthness" (*trayodaśatvāvacchinnā*), it is indicated that "thirteenthness" is a specific kind of collective state (*samudāyatvaviśeṣa*),
as shown by the passage beginning with "expectancy" (*apekṣā*).

The state of being delimited (*avacchinnatva*) is the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) residing in the difference (*bheda*). Now, one might object: "Even if fourteen are obtained according to the method stated in the passage beginning with 'the thirteen starting with water,' how is that obtained in a sentence such as 'merely thirteen'? To this, he says: "[184] 'Starting with water,' etc."
And thus, the sense is that such a [logical] infant is obtained by completing the remainder [of the definition].
Furthermore, there is the impossibility of establishing the status of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) as a constituent of inference in a manner common to other schools of thought. Thus...
Regarding the phrase "the thirteen beginning with water," there is the laborious effort of postulating another *bahuvrīhi* compound; and by supplying the word "each" (*pratyekam*),
there is the interpretive strain of explaining it as "those mutual absences which belong to each of the fourteen-fold collections."

Since the employment of words is within one's own control, such an indirect mode of expression is contrary to the author’s style; furthermore, there is an inherent awkwardness if the word *ādi* in the first compound is taken as referring merely to "primacy."

In the *Dīpikā* [184], it says: "Because of the absence of occurrence in a single substratum. This means that there is no prior ascertainment, through occurrence in a single substratum, of the [probans] before the inference [occurs].
Since a cognition whose object is the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)—which is not constituted by the probandum (*sādhya*)—is independent of the cognition of the probandum, he says:
"[184] *sādhyābhāve*," and so forth; rather, however...
"Jalādibhedakūṭam":
by this, the section of the *Dīpikā* ending with "melanam" has been explained.

Even if falsity (*kūṭatva*) consists in being another thing qualified by a particular [property], that same defect remains; however, if it consists in being the object of a cognition having that many objects, then regarding the objective relation (*viṣayatā*):

Since there is no evidence for [the property] existing as a distributed whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), it would follow that the aforementioned inference possesses a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by virtue of resting upon each individual [locus];
however, this is not the case because the absence of that which is delimited by such a delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
Furthermore, there is the impossibility of grasping the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*); nevertheless,

there is no fault, because we accept as the probandum (*sādhya*) the absence of fire qualified by the absence of air and so forth, through a relation characterized by having a locus distinct from water.
