The passage to be cited later, beginning with "a specific relative cognition" (*apekṣābuddhiviśeṣa*), proceeds on the assumption that objectivity (*viṣayatā*) is distributive (*vyāsajyavṛtti*);
otherwise, it would simply be a repetition of the aforementioned method.
The object of meditation (*dhyeya*). [184] Being a member of an inference (*anumity-aṅgatva*) means being a causal factor for inference (*anumiti-prayojakatva*).

[185] "Even later on"—in the phrase "of the probandum (*sādhya*) consisting of the difference delimited by the thirteen [categories] beginning with water," and so forth—it is because the literal meaning is established according to the method we have stated. "Water, etc. (*jalādi*)...
The unsuitability of completing the remainder [of the argument] is indicated by the phrase "it is said" (*āhuḥ*), which reflects a sense of dissatisfaction (*asvarasa*).
This is what should be noted here:
[the property of being the object of a cognition having that as its content] [is related] by way of pervasion (*vyāpakatā*) as delimited by the relation of superstratumhood (*ādheyatā*).

Since it must be admitted that [the property] is to be proven (*sādhyatva*), there is no contradiction even if objecthood (*viṣayatva*) is not distributed over its locus (*avyāsajyavṛtti*). This should be understood in other cases as well.
And such pervasion (*vyāpakatā*) is...

The definition of the subject (*pakṣa*) is: "that which possesses a difference whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a delimitation that is itself delimited by the relation of substratehood belonging to the counterpositiveness of a difference co-located with itself. [188] It is also defined as "that which possesses the probandum (*sādhya*) in a state of doubt."

From the statement defining the subject (*pakṣa*) as taught in the *Saṅgraha*, it is understood that the definition of the subject is "the state of possessing the probandum (*sādhya*) which has become the object of doubt.
And this [definition] applies in cases such as "the lake possesses fire," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that [the definition] does not extend to lakes and so forth, he says:
"by way of the relation of being the qualificandum" (*viśeṣyatāsambandhena*).
He further states: "the definition of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and so forth."

The definition of a *sapakṣa* (similar instance) is the state of possessing a certainty whose qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) is related [to the subject] by the relation of being the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyaprakāraka*).
The definition of a *vipakṣa* (dissimilar instance), which is to be understood by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), is also included.
By that relation, it is the state of possessing a certainty whose qualifier is the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).

Otherwise, in cases such as a lake during a state of error regarding fire and so forth, because of its being a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), [the definition would fail] in the case of a mountain and so forth.
Because, during the state of delusion regarding its being smokeless and so forth, it is impossible to present it as a counter-example (vipakṣa) for a person who is mistaken;
thus, the *Dīpikā* states: "by way of being ascertained" [188].
"By way of being distinct from others," and so forth;
"stated in the *Dīpikā*," and so forth.
Although such an absence of proof exists even in the case of a jar and other such things...
In cases such as "the mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And thus,

by means of the relation consisting in the possession of the property that serves as the delimiting adjunct (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) included within the scope of its own counter-positive-delimiter (*svapratiyogitāvacchedaka*),
[there would be an over-extension] of the absence of such a proof (*siddhyabhāva*).

There is no fault, as it is accepted that the basis for the application of the term "pakṣa" (the subject) is such a property; it should be understood that such a property, namely "being a mountain" (*parvatatva*) and so forth, is absent in things like a jar (*ghaṭa*). [This concludes] the definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).

Having examined the correct reason (*saddhetu*) contained in the *Dīpikā*, he states the purpose of the ultimate inclusion [of this section]: "In the examination of the incorrect reason (*asaddhetu*)," with the word "completed" (*kṛta*) being the ellipsis.
And thus, the effort (kṛti) is the meaning of the locative case;
its connection with remembrance occurs through the relation of being subsequent in time.
[189] This is connected by way of a relevant transition (prasaṅga).
The phrase "in the form of being non-existent reasons, etc. is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"That" means "non-existent reason. Regarding the expression "they appear like reasons": [190] they appear as if they were reasons.
And this is intended primarily to demonstrate the meaning, rather than to demonstrate the etymological analysis (*vigraha*).
As for the etymological analysis, however, it should be stated that they are "fallacies" (*ābhāsa*) because they resemble [valid] reasons (*hetu*).

The meaning is: the state of being the qualificandum (viśeṣya) of an error whose mode (prakāra) is a valid reason through identity (tādātmya). And the defect (doṣa) which is the cause of that error consists in the state of being conveyed by a word ending in the fifth case (pañcamyanta).

In the *Dīnapikā* [189], the phrase "having examined so as to believe" (*saddhentu nirūpya*) and so forth refers to that which is qualified by the destruction of a word that is the counter-positive of a cognition produced by a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and other such modes having a valid reason (*saddhetu*) as its qualificand, and which is also qualified by a desire directed toward a word that is the object of a cognition produced by a definition and other such modes having an invalid reason (*asaddhetu*) as its qualificand.

The indivisible cognition (*akhaṇḍabodha*) is: "He is the possessor of a present-time effort conducive to that [utterance], which is a word generating a cognition whose qualifier is a property pervaded by the state of having a false reason.
Here, regarding the term "having a false reason" (*asaddhetu*):
The connection with both [terms] occurs according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (*dehalīdīpanyāya*).
The first qualification [of the action] is by way of two relations: having the same agent as its own counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and occurring within the time that serves as its own locus.
The second qualification consists in the relation of being both the object of a desire prompted by itself and having the same agent as its own object.
Regarding the meaning of the word *sat* in the phrase *saddhetum*, the *Prakāśikā* [189] states: "qualified by pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is included.

Regarding the phrase "of such a kind" (*tādṛśasya*): it means [the absence] whose nature is the delimiting property of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka-dharma*) that has entered into the scope of the delimitor of its own counter-correlate (*svapratiyogitāvacchedaka*).
Granted that there may indeed be a necessity for stating general characteristics, nevertheless, it was specifically promised that the definition of the fallacious would be provided.
Since that very point ought to have been stated, it would be inconsistent to set it aside and instead state the definition of a fault; therefore, he says:
"The definition of a fault," and so forth.
[190] "Gain" (lābha) means understanding (bodha).
The intention is that a verbal root meaning "to obtain" (prāpti) has the sense of "to know" (jñāna).
Regarding the phrase "the word *anumiti*," etc., the underlying thought is as follows: the word *anumiti*...

It refers to either an inference (*anumiti*) characterized by the subject under consideration (*prakṛta-pakṣadharmin*) and having the property to be proven (*sādhya*) as its qualifier, or a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) characterized by the subject under consideration and having the reason (*hetu*)—which is pervaded by the property to be proven—as its qualifier; however, the subsumptive reflection is not included here by virtue of being the instrument (*karaṇa*) of inference.
Although the mountain...

In the inferential cognition "the lake possesses fire" (vahnimān hradaśca tathā), as well as in the sublating consideration (parāmarśa) such as "the mountain possesses smoke pervaded by fire and the lake is likewise," when these are apprehended as a collective object (samūhālambana), there exists an obstructive influence (pratibandhakatva) from contrary certainties such as "the lake does not possess fire, nor does it possess smoke pervaded by fire."

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding that [invalid cognition], because it is impossible to include a sublated object (*bādhya*) and so forth due to the fear of failing to encompass them;
for it is impossible to posit a state of being sublated (*pratibadhyatā*) that pervades either of those two [types of invalidity]. Nevertheless...

There is no fault, because the definition includes the state of being an obstructor as characterized by an obstructedness that possesses either the property of pervading the nature of the relevant inference (*prakṛtānumiti*) or the property of pervading the nature of the relevant consideration (*parāmarśa*). For this very reason, there is no need to include the consideration (*parāmarśa*) specifically as the instrument of inference (*anumitikaraṇa*).
The meaning is "distinct from error" (*bhramabhinnā*).

And being a qualifier (*bhramatva*) consists in being the determiner of a mode that is distinct from those qualified by the threefold relation consisting of: (1) being delimited by itself, (2) being determined by a qualificandum residing in its own locus, and (3) residing in its own counter-positive.
Therefore, there is no harm even if the cognition "the mountain is fireless" possesses validity regarding some of its parts;
this is because [the definition specifies] "having as its object that which is delimited by a particular form."

If one were to say "that which has as its object," then because there is no difference between the qualified and the pure [object], there would be the fault of impossibility by taking into account partial cognitions such as "the lake" (hrada); therefore, that [phrase] is disregarded. Then, in response to the inquiry "What, then, is this specific cognition?", [the definition is given] by way of demonstrating it.
He demonstrates the definition of the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) as it has been extracted: "And thus" (*evam ca*).
Herein, this is the inference:
1. by its own word, [it refers to] silver.

In the valid cognition "this is silver," the relation called inherence (*samavāya*), which serves as the objective content, is what is apprehended; the state of being delimited by that [inherence] exists in the qualifier-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in silverness.
Thus, "self" (*sva*) refers to inherence.
The silver is the correlate of that [relation], and the property of being qualified by the qualificand-ness residing in that [silver] exists in the subject-ness residing in silverness.
Likewise, "self" refers to inherence (*samavāya*), and its counter-correlative is [the self].
Silverness and its subsistence therein exist in the objectness (*prakāratā*);
therefore, by means of the aforementioned threefold relation,
the objectness belonging to what is cognized as true is qualified by the relation, whereas the objectness belonging to error is other than that.
Error (*bhrama*) is the state of being the determiner (*nirūpakatva*) of that [silverness] which resides as the mode (*prakāratā*) in silverness.
Defectiveness of the reason (*hetvābhāsatva*) consists in the existence of a form qualified by the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
And the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is...

By the relation of being qualified by the obstructiveness (pratibandhakatā) as determined by the state of being obstructed (pratibadhyatā) which is qualified by itself (*sva*). The qualification of *sva* [is defined as]:

being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference residing in an inference that possesses a mode (*prakāratā*) delimited by a relation belonging to the property delimiting the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakadharma*), which in turn is determined by a qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) delimited by *sva*.

[The definition of the object of the fallacy] is by means of both relations: (1) the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a deliminator residing in itself, which is not delimited by a relation [other than the one in question]; and (2) the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a deliminator residing in itself, which is delimited by the relation of being the deliminator of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in a *parāmarśa* (reflective judgment) that possesses a mode (*prakāratā*) of the reason—which is pervaded by the probandum—as qualified by a qualificandumhood delimited by itself.
The qualification by "obstructiveness" (*pratibandhakatā*) occurs through the relation of "residing in" (*ādheyatā*). And that [obstructiveness]...
[The relation is] by way of the relation of possessing distinctions such as "its own" (sva) and so forth;

[and] its own locus-ness (svādhikaraṇatā) is by way of the relation of being a certainty that is not overwhelmed by a non-validity-cognition and is non-artificial, having for its object that which is delimited by itself (svāvacchinna).

The delimitation of the counter-correlativity of difference (*bhedapratiyogitāvacchedakatā*) is by way of the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*). Therefore, in such cases as "there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) here in this [statement]," there is no syntactical split.
In this context, the determination of the relationship between the sublated (pratibadhyā) and the sublator (pratibandhaka) is as follows:

[the absence of] that which is qualified by a subjecthood (viśeṣyatā) residing in lake-ness (hradatva), etc., having an unconditioned delimiting factor (anavacchinnāvacchedakatā), and which is related to a relationality (saṃsargatā) qualified by conjunction-ness (saṃyogatva), and which has a qualificative-ness (prakāratā) residing in fire-ness (vahnitva), etc., having an unconditioned delimiting factor—[such an absence] with respect to a non-artificial cognition (anāhāryabuddhi) qualified by the state of being a cognition of that kind, [is the sublator].
That [absence] which is qualified by a subjecthood residing in lake-ness, etc., having an unconditioned delimiting factor...

The state of being an opponent [of a cognition] consists in its being a knowledge qualified by non-illusoriness and so forth, which possesses a qualificative content delimited by the nature of absence (abhāvatva) as determined by a qualificative content that is itself delimited by the nature of a relation— namely, the relation of essential identity (svarūpa-sambandha)— which is in turn determined by a qualificative content delimited by the relation of counterpositiveness (pratiyogitā) as delimited by a delimitor that is not delimited by anything else and residing in firehood (vahnitva) and the like.
In this context, [the cognition] "that which possesses a genus" (jātimān)...
The inclusion of the qualification "unconditioned" (anavacchinnatva) is for the purpose of excluding cognitions such as "it possesses fire" from the direction of the sublated (pratibadhya),
and for the purpose of excluding cognitions such as "it possesses a genus and lacks fire" from the direction of the obstructing (prati-bandhaka).

Thus, in order to account for the fact that an error apprehending conjunction (*saṃyoga*) by way of its temporal nature (*kālika-tva*) and so forth is not sublated with respect to the direction of the object to be obstructed, and in order to account for the fact that an error apprehending other categories of entities by way of "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*) and so forth is not sublated, [one must consider] by way of "conjunction-ness" and so forth...

And it should be understood that the inclusion of "conjunctionness" (*saṃyogatva*) as delimited by its own nature is for the sake of establishing the sublated status of an error that apprehends a distinct object-entity (*padārthāntara*).
Regarding the inclusion of a specific cognition (*jñānaviśeṣa*):
He states the purpose: "taneti" (by that); "aprāmāṇyajñānaviśiṣṭasyeti" (of that which is qualified by the cognition of invalidity);
and so forth, [meaning] by way of both the relation of being the object and the relation of coreferentiality.
1. *sva*—the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
Here, the word *sva* (self) is used in all these instances.
This refers to the nature that delimits the status of being a defect (*doṣatāvacchedakarūpa*).
[The author] presents the explanation of Miśra with the words "Others, however" (*pare tu*) and so forth,
beginning with "Of the defective ones" (*duṣṭānām*) and so forth.

And thus, the sense is that there is no contradiction with the thesis regarding the definition of the "defective" (duṣṭa). This— namely, being the object of a true cognition that obstructs inference— is what is meant.
[191] "Of the wicked alone"— by this very word, there is an exclusion of those who are not wicked. Now, as for the mountain...

In cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," there would be the over-extension [of the definition] by taking into account the erroneous sublation-cognition (bādhabhrama) that "the mountain lacks fire"; for that too, being a sublater of inferential cognition, would [otherwise] qualify as a fallacy in the reason.
Because it is possible for a cognition of that specific type to be true, he says: "[191] But rather...

Now, if one adopts the view that the defeaters such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*) are defeaters only when they are themselves cognized, then the formation of a *karmadhāraya* compound in the expression "true cognition of a defeater" (*pratibandhakayathārthajñāna*) would be impossible.
Because the meaning of the definition-sentence is untenable, he says: "[191] But its meaning...
This means: "But the meaning of the definition-sentence beginning with 'inference' (anumiti), etc. [191] "Single," etc.
The meaning is "having itself as its object";
this qualifies the cognition.
It causes the definition to be understood in the instance of the definiendum by means of the passage beginning with "possessing smoke," etc. [191] It is stated [in the following]: [191] "As stated."
The meaning is: "having the nature of being the delimiting property of the reason (hetutāvacchedakadharma) which is the subject under discussion (prakṛta) and is the object of a single cognition.
This applies likewise to the term "shown" (darśita) in what follows [at 191]. As for the word "that" (tad): [191] it refers to that.
The meaning is: "the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) consisting of fire and so forth, as qualified by subsisting in that which lacks smoke.
Now, since the general category of inference (*anumiti-sāmānya*) is introduced here in this definition, [as in the case of] "the mountain possesses fire,"...
There is over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "smoke,

fire, etc. [as a definition of fallacy], because the fallacy that obstructs the inference "the lake possesses smoke"— namely, that which consists of fire and the like qualified by subsisting in what lacks smoke— is [excluded].

He dispels the objection that, by the previously mentioned relation, the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) of a true cognition (*pramā*) having that [probandum] as its qualifier exists in valid reasons such as smoke—by stating "pertaining to the subject at hand" (*prakṛta*). This means: pertaining to the subject at hand, the probandum at hand, and the reason at hand.
[191] "In the case of 'having six causes,' there is no over-extension"— this is connected with the preceding statement.
[191] "If the term 'corresponding to reality' were not employed," and so forth.

Although it was stated immediately prior that there is no risk of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," since such [counter-examples of] deviation and so forth are unestablished;
How is this connected to the statement of the purpose?

Even so, in the very case of "this [hill] possesses smoke because of fire," one may take as the object of a delusion (bhrama) whose qualifier is a fault well-known in that context— such as the aforementioned deviation (vyabhicāra)— which has as its subject (dharmin) a donkey or the like, and which possesses the relation shown therein.

There is no fault, because the intention is that [otherwise] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to donkeys and so forth. Nor should it be said that the statement "and not so in the case of a valid reason" (*na caivaṃ saddhetau*) is improper;
for here, the term *saddhetu* [refers to...]
Because it refers to something other than the subject under discussion (prakṛta) and the reason (hetu).

And thus, even in the case of a valid reason (saddhetu), the remainder [of the sense] is that it would apply to things such as a donkey, which are distinct from the subject under discussion and the reason.
The word "api" (also) includes the reason under discussion;
the sense is that knowledge is introduced into the definition by way of being an example common to both error and valid cognition.
[191] "That" means:
the sense is "a word that accords with reality.
[191] "They say" means:

In this regard, the underlying intention is as follows: if "the state of being a defect" (doṣatva) is the definition of a defect, then "the state of possessing a defect" (doṣavattva) is clearly obtained as the definition of defective [instruments].
Thus, by defining inference and so forth through their defects, the definition of what is defective is readily established.

If, according to the stated method, that [pseudo-reason] possesses the definition of a fallacy (*doṣa*), then the definition of a fallacy cannot be established at all, and thus the clarification of the disciple's intellect would not be achieved.
This is because, although by the phrase "that which obstructs inference" [the definition is seemingly provided],...
Although the definition of that [fallacy] is obtained as "being an obstructer of inference," nevertheless,

since both [the definitions of fallacy and the nature of the object of knowledge] are consistent by merely stating "possessing an obstructer of inference" according to that school's view, there is a lack of natural elegance in the formulation beginning with "a true cognition of an obstructer."
The definition of the *savyabhicāra* (inconclusive) reason is stated in the *Saṃgraha* [195]: "that which occurs in that which possesses the absence of the probandum.
Regarding this, some say: "[the mountain] possesses fire..."

There is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of "smoke" and so forth; for the property of being located (*ādheyatva*), as defined by that locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) of smoke which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*), exists in smoke and the like. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that there is no fault because "the state of being located" (ādheyatva) intended here is that which is qualified by a locus-ness (adhikaraṇatā) residing in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvavat); for even so, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) in cases such as: "The locus-ness of smoke is different from [the locus-ness of smoke on] the mountain, because it is a locus-ness of smoke."

In that case, since the mountain possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*), and because the property of being the locus of smoke (*dhūmādhikaraṇatātva*) exists in the state of being the substratum (*ādheyatva*) as defined by the status of being the locus of smoke— which is the very exclusion (*niṣṭhatā*) of that [absence]— [the definition holds].

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault, because the intended meaning is: "that which is the locus-ness (ādheyatā) residing in a locus of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvavanniṣṭhā), while being qualified by being determined by [a locus] possessing the absence of the probandum."

Even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the following [inference]: "The locusness of smoke possesses both the property of being different from locusness and the property of being other than the mountain, because it is the locusness of smoke."
1. There is no fault;

for although the locusness of smoke residing in the locusness of smoke has the property of being qualified by the locusness of smoke residing on the mountain which possesses the absence of the probandum, [the definition still holds].
The meaning is that [the definition] lacks the property of being "defined by a mountain possessing the absence of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvavat-parvata-nirūpitatva*). 2.
Regarding the phrase "because of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) here":
for in that case, the mountain possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavān parvataḥ*).

Furthermore, when "that which possesses the absence of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvavat*) is used as a term to denote the mountain (*parvata*), the mountain's status as a locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) is established; that which is the locus-status residing therein is the locus-status of smoke (*dhūmādhikaraṇatā*).
The property of being defined by that [locus-status] exists in the "locatedness" (*ādheyatā*) residing in the locus-status of smoke itself. Thus, it is as follows:

The meaning is that if, by the term *sādhyābhāvavat* (the locus of the absence of the probandum), one were to take "locusness" (*adhikaraṇatā*)— specifically the locusness consisting in being the substratum of smoke— as the [counter-positive], then the property of being defined by that (*tannirūpitatvam*) would exist in the "inherence" (*ādheyatā*) residing in the nature of smoke-locusness; thus, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Nor is it intended that the locus-ness (ādheyatva) be qualified by the absence of the probandum; and as for this qualification—
It should not be argued that there is no fault because [the relation] consists of both the relation of being defined by itself and the relation of being defined by the locus-ness residing in itself;
for even so, the locus-ness of knowability (*prameyatva*)...

Because there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the following [pseudo-inference]: "The locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) residing in the locus-ness of knowability (*prameyatva*) is distinct from the locus-ness determined by the substratum-ness (*ādheyatā*) residing in the locus-ness of knowability, because it is the locus-ness of knowability.
This is because [the reason] exists in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*).

The locusness of the counter-correlate of the difference that constitutes the probandum; the locusness residing in that which possesses the absence of the probandum as determined by that [locusness]; and the locusness of knowability as determined by the locusness residing in such a locus.
Because there exists, in the locus-ness residing in the locus-ness of the property of being knowable (*prameyatva*), a substratum-ness (*ādheyatā*) determined by that [locus-ness];
and in a case where there is "being determined by the locus-ness residing in itself," there is not "being the determiner of the locus-ness residing in itself."

It must be said: since inherence (*ādheyatā*) does not have a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as its defining correlate (*nirūpaka*), the aforementioned fault has no place here; this is what must be stated. Even so, there remains the [problem of] inherence and locus-hood (*ādheyatva-adhikaraṇatā*).

Because there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the following [pseudo-reason]: "The locus-ness residing in the locus-ness of the property of being the substratum (*ādheyatātvaniṣṭhādhikaraṇatānirūpitādhikaraṇatā*) is distinct from the locus-ness of the property of being the substratum (*ādheyatvādhikaraṇatātva*), because it is the locus-ness of the property of being the substratum.
This is because the property of being the determiner (*nirūpakatva*) of the locus-ness determined by the universal locus-ness (*ādheyatāsāmānya*) resides in locus-ness in general.
Because of existence;
and not in a case where there is self-determination.

It should not be argued that there is no fault because of the inclusion of the property of having a locus-ness delimited by the relation of the reason-delimiting property— which is itself delimited by the delimitor of the self-determining [locus-ness];
for if that were the case, it would follow that the definition of pervasion as "not occurring in that which possesses the absence of the probandum" [would fail].

If [the nature of the probans] consisted in the absence of deviation as defined by etymology, then because it would follow that there is a distinction [between probanses] due to the difference in their causes,
there would result a contradiction with the treatise on *kevalānvayin* (purely positive) reasons;
for in that context, the non-difference of such a pervasion has been stated.

Nor is there any fault, for what is intended is the qualified subsistence (*ādheyatva*) in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*), by means of both relations: (1) being characterized by an absolute absence whose counterpositiveness resides in itself and is delimited by the relation of being its own determiner (*svanirūpakatva-sambandha-avacchinna*), and (2) being characterized by itself. Thus, no defect arises.
It should not be argued that [the relation] lacks the property of being a determiner of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-nirūpakatā*) with respect to the property of being the substratum (*ādheyatā*),

because, according to the view that a relation which does not regulate occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha*) cannot be a delimitor of the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitānavacchedakatā*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Because the aforementioned refinement is impossible;

nor is it the case that [the definition] consists merely in possessing a difference whose counterpositiveness is determined by a delimitor residing in itself, as delimited by the relation of being its own specifier (*svanirūpakatva*).
It should not be argued that there is no fault because [the relation] must be included [in the definition],

since it is universally accepted that even a relation which does not regulate the occurrence of a property (vṛttyaniyāmaka-sambandha) can serve as the delimitation of the delimitation of the counter-correlativity of mutual absence (anyonyābhāva). This is what must be stated.

If that were the case, there would be the consequence of impossibility in instances such as "this possesses smoke because of fire," [since the relation] would be by way of being a qualifier (*nirūpakatayā*).
They say that [the reason] is unestablished because it does not exist in things such as an iron ball.
To this it is replied: what is intended is the property of being a qualified locus of the absence of the probandum, by way of the relation of being determined by a distinct [locus].

And this distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) is an indivisible limiting adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*). Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of evidence for it, because [it is established] by the nature of being an effect (*kāryatā*).

Since Gadādhara, in his *Bādhagrantha*, has stated that the meaning of the genitive case is a distinct relation (*vilakṣaṇasambandha*), based on the fact that there is no linguistic usage such as "the cause of the cause" but there is usage such as "the cause of the effect," it follows by parity of reasoning that [the relation] resides in the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, it is necessary that the meaning of the locative case (saptamī) also be the state of being determined by something distinct from both the linguistic usage "it exists in the state of being a locus" and the non-usage [of such a term].
It should be understood that it is impossible to define "distinctness" (*vailakṣaṇya*) as anything other than an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).
Others, however, [say]:

They say that there is no fault because what is intended is "the state of being the determiner of a locus-ness residing in that which possesses the absence of the probandum. This, however, is to be examined—
the locus-ness of the knowable (*prameya*).
Because there is non-pervasion (avyāpti) in cases such as "mountains, because they possess the property of being the locus of the object of knowledge" (*prameya*),
since even the subject reason (*prakṛtahetu*)— by virtue of being an object of knowledge— is a determiner of such a locus-hood.

In the *Prakāśikā* [196], it says: "delimited by the relation that delimits the property to be proved (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-dharma-sambandha-avacchinna*. This means: "having a delimitorhood (*avacchedakatā*) that is pervasively distributed (*paryāpta*) over the relation that delimits the property to be proved. By this, [the definition applies even to cases involving] absences qualified by absences delimited by duality (*dvitva*) and so forth.

And there is the exclusion of an absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by both the relations of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*). Furthermore, being delimited by such a delimitorhood consists in being neither delimited by a property other than that [intended] property,
nor delimited by a relation other than those [intended] relations.

He states the purpose for introducing the relation (*sambandha*) between the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*niveśa*): "By that" refers to the inclusion of the relation that delimits the causal state (*hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha*). This is because, in an inference such as "that which possesses fire, because it possesses smoke," smoke and the like exist in a lake—which is a counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—by virtue of temporal or other relations.
In order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*):
regarding the state of possessing the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavattā*), that is, regarding the subsistence (*ādheyatā*) residing in the absence of the probandum.
[Objection: But is there not over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "this [tree] possesses conjunction with a monkey, because it is this very tree"?

For pure qualification (*śuddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) would be of that nature. To this, he says: "In the case of 'with a monkey'... [and so on]. The phrase "and so forth" (*dig*) [indicates that this applies to other similar cases].

In such cases as "The self possesses an absence whose counter-positive-ness is delimited by the relation of temporal qualification (kālika-viśeṣaṇatā) and further delimited by the non-existence of ether (ākāśābhāvatva)," it is indeed temporal qualification that constitutes such a relation. And if...
If it is argued that, by the principle of "adhikaṃ tu" (and so forth),

that defect remains as it was because one might take into account a certainty whose qualifier is the absence of conjunction with a monkey, related through an unconditioned qualifier-ness (*niravacchinnaviśeṣaṇatā*), then:

There is no fault, because [the definition] includes the property of being the delimitor of the locus-ness (ādheyatāvacchedakatā) as pervaded by that property [dharma], which is the delimitor of the relation-ness (saṃsargatā) determined by the qualificative-ness (prakāratā) of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) in a certainty.
Nor is there a persistence of that same fault even in this case, by taking into account such a collective cognition (samūhālambana-jñāna).

This must be stated; for the intended meaning is that such a general certainty (*niścaya*) is the sublator (*pratibandhaka*). And thus, what is to be included is the state of having an *avacchedakatā* (delimiting factorhood) that is pervasively instantiated (*paryāpta*) in a property residing in knowledge (*jñānatva*). Furthermore, "residing" (*vṛtti*) is by way of the relation of being possessed of a difference from its own locus (*svasetyādi-bhedavattva*).

The state of being its own locus [is defined] by the relation of being a certainty that is the determiner of the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) as determined by the object-ness (prakāratā) of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva), which has a relation whose delimitation is pervaded by itself;

and [the state of being the locus of the absence] is [defined] by the relation of being qualified by its own substratum, which is the delimitation of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the difference.

The state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [of the object] is by way of both relations: identity (*tādātmya*) and the relation of being the obstructor (*pratibandhakatva*) as determined by the obstructedness (*pratibadhyatā*) qualified by itself (*sva*).
The state of being qualified by itself (*svavaiśiṣṭya*)...

By means of the relation of "possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by its own [the pervasion's] own-inherence delimitation, which is itself delimited by the counter-correlativity residing in a non-illusory cognition possessing a qualifierhood delimited by a relation that is the delimitor of the probandumness as determined by a subjecthood delimited by the property that is the delimitor of its own subjecthood," there is no destruction of the unity of the qualified object in the case of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
This is because the inclusion of the general absence of subsistence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is necessary, and it is precisely for that reason [that the objection is avoided].

Anticipating the objection that by taking even a single instance of the similar class (*sapakṣa*), the fault is avoided and thus all terms [of the definition] would be redundant, he says: "[196] *Sapakṣavṛttitve*...
[He asks: "But if being a similar class (*sapakṣatva*) is merely the possession of the property to be proven (*sādhyavattvamātra*), then..."

[An objection: "There is no such impossibility, because in the case of 'sound-ness' (śabdatva) and so forth, there exists a co-referential relation (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with 'impermanence' (anityatva) and the like.
To this, he says: "[196] The term 'sapakṣa'..."

One might object: "In the proof of impermanence and other properties with respect to sound and so forth, 'being sound' (śabdatva) and the like are indeed valid reasons; how then can they be considered the fallacious reason called 'uniquely inconclusive' (asādhāraṇa-hetvābhāsa)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "[197] 'Sound,' etc."
The ancient masters who were conversant with the tradition stated this because the new doctrine is free from fault.

Considering that there is a contradiction—due to both proof and non-proof—between the definition stated in the summary as "the *anupasaṃhārī* is one devoid of examples of positive and negative concomitance" and its literal meaning, he says: "[197] *Anvayavyatireke*... etc.

Since the designation "non-conclusive" (*anupasamhārin*) is absent when there is either a certainty of the probandum or a certainty of the absence of the probandum regarding some locus (*dharmī*), both members [of the definition] are employed.

Regarding the definition of contradiction (*virodha*): one might object that there is the undesirable consequence of no distinction between contradiction and the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇya*) reason. To this, he says: "[203] *sādhyābhāve*...
[meaning] directly—that is, without mediating through the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*).
That is to say, by way of the cognition of the possession of that which is pervaded by its absence.
[203] The definition of the counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*):
that of which...

In the summary statement beginning with "that which proves the absence of the probandum" (*sādhyābhāvasādhaka*), the referent of the word *yat* ending in the genitive case is construed with the probandum (*sādhya*).
The word "in the subject" (*pakṣe*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
According to the view of the ancients,
since a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*) is considered an occasional defect (*anityadoṣa*), even a valid reason (*saddhetu*) may be designated as such; thus,
in the phrase "it exists" (*vidyate*), the meaning is "it is known," because the verbal suffix is understood in its passive sense (*karmākhyāta*).
According to the Navya school, however, the meaning is "it exists" by resorting to the agent as the referent of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*).
It is the means (*sādhaka*) by virtue of being the object of pervasion (*vyāpyatayā*).
The meaning is "that which is being grasped," according to the view of the Easterners; however,
in the view of the moderns, the meaning is "the pervaded."
With this intention, he explains:
"That which is related to... and so forth; and then:
"The moderns, however..."
A counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*) is a subject that possesses another reason which is pervaded by the absence of the probandum.
This pervasion should be understood through both positive (*anvaya*) and negative (*vyatireka*) concomitance.

The point is that the apprehension of that [reason] is an obstacle to inference by way of being an apprehension of the presence of something pervaded by its absence. This concludes the definition of the unestablished (asiddha).

[203] "The absence of the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) in the subject" means that the cognition thereof is an obstacle to the apprehension of the subject as qualified by the delimiting property of the subject. [203] "The absence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject."

Furthermore, it should be understood that the apprehension of that [upādhi] is opposed by the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) which grasps the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Now, one might object:
since an *upādhi* is a defect just like sublation (*bādha*) and so forth, [why is it not mentioned separately?]

It is necessary that a fallacy characterized by that [upādhi] be distinct from other fallacies, just like the "contradicted" (bādhita) and others, according to the principle that "even when there is a commingling of the things to be defined, they remain distinct.
Therefore, that which possesses an upādhi is a case of "unestablished pervasion" (vyāpyatvāsiddha).

This is inconsistent because it results in the contradiction of the fivefold classification of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). To this, he says: "[204] 'Of the adjunct' (*upādheḥ*). Now, one might object: "Since there exist two additional defects in the form of the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) and the unestablished nature of the probans (*sādhanāprasiddhi*), how can there be only five types of fallacious reasons? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "[204] 'Of the adjunct'."

He states that there is no contradiction with that [definition], because those two are included within the "unestablished due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*): "[In this regard, the following should be noted]," and so forth;
and the definition of the *upādhi* is given in the *Saṃgraha*: "While being a pervader of the *sādhya*," and so forth.

And here, in cases such as "this [mountain] possesses fire because it possesses smoke," the two components [of the definition] are introduced in order to exclude [properties like] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and [substances like] a pot (*ghaṭa*). Now,
if "pervasion of the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) consists in not being the counter-positive (*apratiyogitva*) of an absence residing in that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*), then—
It is non-existent;
for everything is the counter-positive of an absence delimited by duality and so forth. However—

[The definition of an *upādhi* is: "the state of possessing a property that is not a delimitor (*anavacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence residing in that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*). Consequently, in an inference such as "this [mountain] possesses fire because it possesses smoke," since a fire located in a kitchen (*mahānasīya-vahni*) is a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*) by virtue of the property "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*), it would follow that this fire is an *upādhi*. To address this, the *Prakāśikā* states: "Because of being a pervader of the probandum," and so forth.

That which, by means of the relation delimiting the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*), is not the deliminator of the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*)— as delimited by the relation constituting the nature of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhitā*) of the absence residing in that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*)— by means of the relation delimiting the probansness (*sādhanatāvacchedaka-sambandha*).

The meaning is: "the state of possessing that property which is the delimiting factor of the counter-positive, as delimited by the relation constituting the definition of *upādhi*, which occurs in the locus of the probandum (*sādhyaniṣṭha*) in the same way as it occurs in the locus of the probans (*sādhanavanniṣṭha*). This is the underlying generalization here: [The formal reconstruction of the definition: *sādhyavanniṣṭhābhāvīyapratiyogitānavacchedaka-sādhanavanniṣṭhābhāvīyopādhitāghaṭakasambandhāvacchinnapratiyogitāvacchedakadharmavattvam upādhitvam* (The state of being an *upādhi* is the possession of a property that is the delimiting factor of the counter-positive—delimited by the relation constituting the definition of *upādhi*—of an absence residing in the locus of the probans, [while] not being the delimiting factor of the counter-positive of an absence residing in the locus of the probandum. This is the method of unification (*anugama*) for this context.
The definition of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the possession of a property that serves as the delimitor of the status of being a limiting adjunct qualified by a difference.

This qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is established by two relations: (1) the relation of having itself as its locus (*svāśrayatva*), and (2) the relation of being the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of an absence residing in that which possesses the probans (*sādhanavanniṣṭhābhāvīyapratiyogitāvacchedakatva*), where this latter relation is delimited by a relation that is itself qualified by the status of being a limiting adjunct.

Its own specific property (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) [is defined] by the relation of being the delimitation of its own counter-correlativity (*svapratiyogitāvacchedakatāsambandha*). This delimitation (*avacchedakatā*) is [further] delimited by the relation of being the delimitation of the counter-correlativity of an absence residing in that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*) as delimited by itself (*svāvacchinna*).
Thus [it is said]. He states the result of introducing the relation that delimits the status of being a *upādhi* with the words "by that" (*tena*).
However, some [hold] that the definition is: the possession of a property that constitutes the *upādhi* as qualified by the relation that constitutes the status of being an *upādhi*.

Specificity (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [of the probans] consists in possessing a difference whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, which is in turn delimited by the relation of being the delimitation of the counterpositiveness of an absence residing in that which possesses the probandum as delimited by itself; and this [difference] is related [to the probans] through both of the following relations: (1) the state of being the delimitation of the counterpositiveness of an absence residing in that which possesses the probans as delimited by itself; and (2) [the aforementioned relation of being the delimitation of the counterpositiveness of an absence].
They say [that it is the state of possessing a property qualified by delimitation]. In reality, however, that [is] the state of possessing a property qualified by delimitation (*avacchedakatā*).

The state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of both relations: (1) the relation of being its own locus (*svāśrayatva*), and (2) the state of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) has as its delimitation residing in itself (*svaniṣṭha*) a delimitation delimited by the relation of being a delimitation qualified by itself (*svaviśiṣṭāvacchedakatvasambandhāvacchinna*).
1. "The property that does not constitute the status of being a condition" (upādhitāghaṭakadharma) means "the property that delimits the status of being a condition" (upādhitāvacchedakadharma).

Likewise, in the expression "the relation that does not constitute the status of being a condition" (upādhitāghaṭakasaṃbandha), the meaning is "the relation that delimits the status of being a condition" (upādhitāvacchedakasaṃbandha).

The qualification of *sva* (itself) [is determined] by the relation consisting of both: being delimited by its own delimiting relation (*svāvacchedaka-sambandha*) and being qualified by its own counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*).
The qualification of *sva* [is determined] by the relation of being qualified by the counterpositiveness that characterizes it (*svanirūpaka-pratiyogitā-viśiṣṭatva*).

The specific property (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [of the absence] consists in its being related to both [conditions] by way of the following two relations: (1) being delimited by the relation that delimits its own [locus], and (2) being the property of an absence that resides in the locus of the probandum as delimited by the delimitor of the probandumhood— which is itself delimited by a relation that delimits the residence [of the probandum] in something possessing the delimitor of the probans, where this latter relation is delimited by the relation that delimits the probanshood residing in the absence.
Therefore, there is no room for criticism by resorting to other types of relations.
Regarding the term "non-pervasion" (*avyāpti*):
in cases such as "air is perceptible," [the reason] such as "possessing manifest color" (*udbhūtarūpa*)...

The meaning is that there is an absence of pervasion by the pure probandum (sādhya) which is common to qualities and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the probandum qualified by whatever property" and so on: the essential point is the possession of that property which serves as the delimiting factor (upādhitāvacchedaka-dharma) for the status of being a condition (upādhi), as qualified by the property residing in the subject (pakṣadharma) and other such factors.

The specific distinction [of the probans] is by way of both relations: (1) being the delimitor of the pervasion delimited by that [relation] as determined by the probandum delimited by itself; and (2) not being the delimitor of the non-pervasion delimited by that [relation] as determined by the probans delimited by itself.
In reality, however...
What is intended is the state of possessing a nature qualified by the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatā*).

This qualification consists in both [the following]: (1) having the property of being the delimitation of the locus of its own substratum (*svāśrayāvacchedakatva*), and (2) having the property of being the delimitation of a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) that is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhāvacchedakatā*) which is delimited by the relation of being the delimitation of the counter-correlativity qualified by itself (*svaviśiṣṭapratiyogitāvacchedakatvasambandhāvacchinnasvaniṣṭhāvacchedakatākapratiyogitākabhedavattva*).
By way of a relation:

its own qualification [is established] by means of both relations— namely, being delimited by the relation that delimits its own locus, and belonging to an absolute absence residing in a locus of the probandum (sādhya) which is qualified by the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and so forth as defined by itself.
And the state of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) is delimited by the relation of "being the property of an absence residing in that which possesses the probans as qualified by itself.
Therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the statement "this is the *upādhi* here.
In reality, however...
The definition of a *upādhi* (limiting adjunct) is the possession of a property qualified by locus-hood (*adhikaraṇatā*).

This qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [of locus-hood] occurs through two relations: (1) being delimited by a relation that is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-sambandha*) of a difference whose counter-correlate is the locus-hood that characterizes itself (*svanirūpaka*), and (2) being characterized by a counter-correlativity that is itself qualified by the same [locus-hood].

The property of being qualified by itself (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) [is defined] by two relations: (1) being related to the absence residing in that which is determined by a locus possessing the probandum qualified by itself; and (2) being delimited by a relation that has as its substratum the locus of the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference whose own determiner (*svanirūpaka*) is [the said absence].
The property of being qualified by itself (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) [is further defined] by the relation of being delimited by a relation that has as its substratum itself.

In the second [definition], the qualification [of the counterpositiveness] is by way of both relations: (1) being delimited by a relation that delimits the counterpositiveness of a difference whose locus is the locus of the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of a difference that characterizes itself; and (2) being characterized by a counterpositiveness qualified by itself. The qualification of itself [is as follows]:...

[The definition is] by way of both relations: (1) being delimited by a relation that resides in the locus of the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the difference from the specifier of itself (*svanirūpaka*), and (2) belonging to an absence that possesses a location (*ādheyatā*) specified by a locus qualified by itself (*svaviśiṣṭa-sādhanavat*).
The qualification of "self" (*sva*) [in the second relation] is by way of the relation of being delimited by a relation residing in its own locus (*svāśraya*).
Herein, "possessing the probandum" (*sādhyavattva*)...
The property of possessing that which is delimited by the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) by means of the relation that delimits the probandum;

thus, there is no fault in taking a locus of the probandum through another relation. Nor is there the impossibility of [substances like] *dravyatva* being an adventitious condition (*upādhi*) in cases such as "that which possesses qualified existence (*viśiṣṭasattā*) has genus (*jāti*)," and so forth. In this way...

Possession of the means (*sādhanavattva*) also consists in possessing that which is delimited by the delimitor of the means (*sādhanatāvacchedaka*), by way of the relation that delimits the status of being a means;
it is not [possession] by way of some other relation.
There is no fault in taking the locus of the probandum (*sādhyādhikaraṇa*) as the basis;

nor does there arise the contingency of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth being adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) in cases such as "substance is not [excluded] because of its specific existence" (*viśiṣṭasattvāt*), and other exclusions should be understood in this same way.
"Of something" means of mountain smoke and so forth;
"this" refers to an external substance.
This is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

By this, it is indicated that when the state of being an object of external perception is the probandum (*sādhya*), the mere fact of being a substance (*dravyatva*) alone is the property of the subject.
Regarding the phrase "pervading impermanence":

since the word *anityatva* (impermanence) in the sentence of the *Dīpikā* is common to both being produced (*janyatva*) and being perishable (*vināśitva*), he says "perishability" (*vināśitva*) in order to accord with the subject at hand.

The point is that otherwise, it would be impossible for such a passage to have the purpose of establishing the pervasion of such a probandum (*sādhya*). This concludes the definition of the "sublated" (*bādhita*) [reason].
In the summary verse stating "that which lacks the probandum," the word "subject" (pakṣa) must be supplied. Thus,
[the definition refers to] that which is the qualifier of the certainty regarding the subject, produced by a means of valid cognition other than inference.
The meaning is that whatever is related to a reason is the probandum; its absence [is the non-existence of the probandum].
And the relation is characterized by the state of being the reason and the probandum.
In response to the doubt as to where and in what form the certainties regarding sublation (*bādha*) and so forth act as impediments, the *Dīpikā* states "of sublation," etc.
This is an investigation into the manner in which defects (*doṣa*) function as impediments to inference.

Since the term *bādha* (sublation) is also used for a specific type of defect (*doṣa*), the *Prakāśikā* [212] states: "of sublation, which is the ascertainment of the presence of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavattāniścaya*).
The *Dīpikā* [212] states: "because it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that generates a cognition of the contradictory (*virodhijñāna*) in the case of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*)."
Of the counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), that is, of the cognition of the counter-balanced reason;
by virtue of being a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that generates a contradictory cognition.
"By virtue of being the causal complex that generates the cognition of the possession of its absence.
On this point, the moderns [hold] that "being a causal complex" consists in one cause being qualified by another cause.

Including another cause within the determinant of the obstructive capacity (pratibandhakatāvacchedaka) is both fruitless and results in unnecessary complexity; therefore, it is more appropriate that the cognition which serves as the object of obstruction possesses its obstructive character precisely by virtue of being a cognition of the presence of something pervaded by the absence of that [cause], due to parsimony (lāghava).
Thus, since the absence of the probandum— which is pervaded by the counter-reason— resides in the subject (pakṣa) which possesses that counter-reason,

it is necessary that the contradiction [of the reason] occurs precisely through its being a cognition qualified by another cognition, owing to its commonality with two distinct, fragmented cognitions.
By this, they say that the view that "opposition consists in being a producer of a contradictory cognition" is also refuted; he demonstrates that position as follows:
In the *Prakāśikā* [212], regarding the phrase "in reality" (*vastutastu*):
one might object that the passage in the *Dīpikā* beginning with "of the common" (*sādhāraṇasya*) and so forth is inconsistent.

Since that very fallacious reason (duṣṭahetu), by virtue of being a common term, cannot possibly consist in the absence of non-deviation, he says: "by way of a designation in which the state [of being] is predominant. The instrumental case here denotes distinction (*vaiśiṣṭye*).
The same applies to what follows as well;
that is to say, it refers to the passage beginning with "of the contradictory," and so forth.
However, in reality:

In the phrase "of the contradictory" (*viruddhasya*), one should understand that it is easy to interpret the sense as "of contradiction" (*virodhasya*) by accepting the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
Now, [one might object]: what of the cognition of the presence [of the reason] in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadvṛttitva*), which has the reason as its locus?

It is established by experience that the pervasion— namely, "that which exists in the locus of the reason" (hetusamānādhikaraṇa) and so forth— is not grasped with respect to the reason itself; and yet,
this is not logically tenable.

Anticipating the objection that "the cognition of the presence [of the reason] in that which lacks the probandum cannot be contrary to the cognition of such pervasion, because it does not apprehend the absence of the object to be grasped," he says: "[212] Regarding the reason" and "Regarding pervasion."
The meaning is that the pervasion (vyāpti) is expressed by the phrase "having the same locus as the cause" (*hetusamānādhikaraṇa*), and so forth.
Regarding the expression "by way of the analogy of the jewel, mantra, etc.":
it is because [the cognition] does not apprehend the absence of the object to be grasped (*grāhyābhāva*).
The point is that even though the apprehension of such a deviation does not contradict the apprehension of such a pervasion, there is no occurrence of that [deviation] at that time.
This is expressed by the phrase "by way of the absence of the qualified pervasion," and so forth.

Now, in cases such as "this is smoky because it possesses fire," since the probandum (sādhya) which is the pervader of the reason is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), the qualified pervasion (*viśiṣṭavyāpti*) that incorporates it is likewise unestablished; consequently, its absence is all the more unestablished. How, then, can there be fallaciousness? Nor is it the case that—

There is no fault, for the "unestablishedness due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) residing in the reason is precisely the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in the reason, which has as its counter-positive (the reason) qualified by the relation of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) delimited by the delimitor of the pervader of itself and delimited by the delimitor of the probandum.
Thus, the subject (*pakṣa*) is that which possesses the reason as qualified by such a relation of co-occurrence.
It should not be argued that since cognition itself is the cause of inference, its status as a fallacy is untenable; for if that were the case,
it would be impossible to avoid the aforementioned fallacies such as deviation (vyabhicāra) and the rest.
Not so;

for the subject (pakṣa) is that which possesses the reason (hetu) as qualified by the delimitor of the property-to-be-proved (sādhyatāvacchedaka), through the relation of both being the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a particular occurrence within itself and being co-located with what is delimited by itself.

Cognition itself is accepted as the cause of inference; [the property of being] the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference resides [in it] by way of the relation of being a delimitor of its own set and so forth.

Only that reason which possesses an absence residing in the delimitor of the probandum—where the counter-correlativity is delimited by the aforementioned relation of being the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in itself—is [the cause].
Inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*).

*Vyāpyatvāsiddhi* (the unestablished nature of being pervaded) is precisely that probans which possesses an absolute absence whose counter-correlativity resides in the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), such absence being delimited by the relation of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with its own delimitor.
The intended meaning of the aforementioned text is also precisely this:
therefore, in cases such as "possessing smoke because of fire," there is no non-establishment [of the reason] according to the stated method; this is the path cultivated by me alone.
Some, however,

[define it as] the absence of both: (1) the state of being a delimitor of the pervasion of the reason residing in the delimitor of the probandumness, and (2) the state of being a delimitor of the subsistence in the locus of the reason.
They claim that because [the property] is intended to be expressed, there is no lack of established precedent; however,

this is trivial— [for instance, in the case of] "the mountain possesses smoke because it possesses fire," the subject (pakṣa) possesses the reason which is co-located with the probandum that pervades the reason.

The particle *u* [indicates] that since the delimiting condition of the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇavṛttitāvacchedakatva*) is not apprehended within the delimiting condition of the probandumness of knowledge (*jñānasya sādhyatāvacchedake*), the absence of both [conditions] shown [previously] is contradictory to that; therefore, its status as a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsatā*) is unavoidable.

In the case of perceptual cognition, there is no proof for its necessary manifestation by way of the principle that what is known by the same cognition must be manifested together, because there is a lack of evidence for such a rule.
In the form of perception...

Even if such an object appears in that manner in some way within that cognition, there is no restrictive factor for its appearance in an inference or verbal cognition; thus, at the time of apprehending such an absence—

Because such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is possible, and since the production of an inference is thereby possible, it is incorrect to regard such an absence as a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). [This is so] because of such a reflective awareness.
Because it does not apprehend both [terms] as having identical forms, it is impossible for it to be that which is sublated by the apprehension of the absence of such a pair;
[this applies] in the case of such a parāmarśa.
Furthermore, since the delimitor of the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), such as "smokiness" (*dhūmatva*), appears by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*),

it necessarily functions as a delimitor with respect to the aspect of being a delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedakatva*); therefore, it is even more impossible for there to be an obstruction by a contrary certainty (*viparītaniścaya*).
Furthermore, if one accepts that smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*) and other properties appear in the form of "smoke-ness-ness" (*dhūmatvatva*) and so forth,

it would follow as an undesirable consequence that an inference whose determinant of the predicatedness (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) is not delimited by "smoke-ness-ness" and the like could not be established.
As for that which was also [stated]:

It is claimed that there is no fault because the cause of inference (*anumiti*) is accepted as being the *parāmarśa*— the cognition that "the subject possesses the reason, which is qualified by both the property of being the delimitor of the pervasion of the reason and the property of being the delimitor of the subsistence in the locus of the reason"— where the delimitor of the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) is thus specified;
however, that too is not correct.

Because of the threefold inclusion of the objective determination delimited by the delimitor of causality within the interior of the delimitor of the causal condition, there is the fallacy of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*).

By the statement in the *Dīpikā*, "due to the absence of a qualified pervasion," it is understood that the defect resides solely in the absence residing in the reason (*hetu*); yet even by that much, the [proponent's] position is not established,
because in the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) which serves as the reason, there appears the relation— which is the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound— as an additional element.
"And because of great reverence"—thus everything is faultless.

In the *Dīpikā* [212], it says "by way of producing doubt regarding pervasion" (*vyāpti-saṃśayādhāyakatvena*). Here, "producing" (*ādhāyakatva*) means "causing" (*prayojakatva*). Now, one might object:

To explain how those two serve as the basis for doubt regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*), the *Prakāśikā* [213] states: "In the case of the reason (*hetu*), due to being uncommon (*asādhāraṇya*) and so forth. By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the "non-conclusive" (*anupasaṃhāritva*) fallacy is intended.
The word "prācīna" (ancient) implies that the new view has already been stated previously.
It is an obstacle to the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The object of a cognition that contradicts the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—
in the phrase "of one who looks to the face of another," this refers to the "obstruction" (*pratibandha*) and so forth— as stated in the passage beginning with "And thus" (*tathā ca*).
The intention here is this:
that which is included in the general definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)— namely,
the state of being an obstacle to either the inference or its instrument— is not, for the time being...
That [would mean] being the cause of the non-arising of that;
for there would be the over-extension [of the definition] to a reason qualified by a limiting condition (*upādhi*) through the relation of deviation (*vyabhicāritā*). And thus...

The claim that there is no over-extension because the absence of a cognition having the qualifier "limiting condition" (upādhi) as its mode lacks the status of being a cause for the inferential consideration (parāmarśa) is weak and untenable.

Since the definition of *āśrayāsiddhi* (unestablished locus) consists precisely in being non-opposed to the apprehension of the subject (*pakṣa*) as qualified by the delimiting property of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*),

such opposition is absent when the subject possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat-pakṣa*). Furthermore, because the inclusion of the element of doubt regarding the probandum in the aforementioned definition is fruitless, and because doubt has been refuted as being the nature of subjecthood (*pakṣatā*), the definition shown [by the opponent] is weak.

The meaning is as follows: it is included within the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). This is the sense—namely, in the *Dīpikā* [at verse 212]: "it is included within the unestablished locus.
This is the intended meaning.

The analysis of the compound is: "if there is the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the substratum (*āśraya*) as qualified by *pakṣatā*. And thus, at the stage when the probandum (*sādhya*) is certain, because the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*)—which consists in doubt regarding the probandum—is absent, that which is qualified by it (i.e., the substratum delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood) is then unestablished.
The sense is that it is appropriate for the subject (*pakṣa*) possessing the probandum (*sādhyavat*) to be included therein.
[This is] the factor that necessitates the inclusion of the "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) fallacy within the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

He establishes the fact that [the opponent's position] subverts the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*)—in the *Prakāśa*, "according to the ancient view. This means "according to the view of the ancients.
The underlying point is as follows: [it concerns] the subversion of the state of being a subject.

The state of being unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddhitva*) consists in being the object of a cognition that contradicts [the probandum]. Furthermore, the status of being the subject (*pakṣatā*) consists in a doubt regarding the probandum as having the property of the subject, qualified by the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
According to the view of the ancients,

this is because when there is a certainty regarding the absence of the *pakṣatāvacchedaka* (the delimiting property of the subject) residing in the subject, or when there is a certainty that the subject possesses the probandum (*sādhyavatpakṣa*), the aforementioned *pakṣatā* (subjecthood) is impossible.

Since the validity of both [positions] remains unimpeded, there is no occurrence of redundancy; for the "subject possessing the probandum" (*sādhyavat-pakṣa*), which takes the form of a "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*), is of the nature of a "non-establishment of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Thus, it is not the case [that one position is superior].
The meaning is that there is a suspicion of a contradiction regarding the division [of cases].

Wherever there is a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) either before or after the proof (*siddhi*), in that case, [the definition applies] by virtue of the proof being delimited by a time when the desire to prove is absent.

The term "merely" (*kevalam*) was stated in order to dispel the objection that, because the status of being an obstacle (*pratibandhakatā*) is necessary, the aforementioned position remains subject to the same over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
By this, [the author indicates] that [the proof] is established.
It is the exclusion of the absence of the coexistence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*).

Thus, in a case where the desire to prove has arisen both before and after the proof, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the proof is not yet established [at the time prior to its arising].
This is the meaning.
Thus ends the chapter on inference in the *Dīpikāprakāśa*, a commentary on [the work] titled *Prasaraṇa*.
The Chapter on Analogy (Upamāna-pariccheda) is completed.
[218] In the summary statement beginning with "from a certain forest-dweller," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used.
The meaning is "being caused to act" (*prayojyatva*). Its connection occurs within the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of the meaning of the verbal root *śru*.
Thus [is the function] of the word.
The meaning is "having the form of being connected with the word";
the rest is clear.
As for the word *iti*:
The claim that the root *śru* refers to a sentence delimited by such a sequence [of phonemes],
and that its meaning is auditory perception (*śrāvaṇapratyakṣa*),
with the sentence being construed therein as its object by way of being the content of that perception— this is trivial.

Since it is possible for the phrase "remembering" (*smaran*) to intend the presentation of a necessary verbal experience that has entered into the aforementioned collection of conditions for memory (*smṛtisāmagrī*),
it is improper to abandon that and instead intend the presentation of a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of a sentence that is irrelevant and established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*).

In the *Prakāśa* [p. 218], it is stated that the connection is by way of "occasion" (*avasara-saṅgati*). "Occasion" refers to the state of being necessarily to be explained at a time subsequent to the cessation of the student's obstructive desire to know.
All matters concerning the meaning of the instrumental case and so forth are as previously described.

Now, [218] it might be argued that by the summary statement— "Comparison is the cognition of the relationship between a name and the named"— the definition of comparison is stated as being a cognition whose object is the relationship between a word and its referent; however, this is not tenable,
because it would over-extend to such things as inference and the like.
Therefore, he states that such a summary statement is not intended to provide the definition of analogy (*upamiti*), but rather to demonstrate its essential nature alone:
"[218] The nature of analogy."
When the question arises as to what its characteristic is, he says: "But the characteristic... [218]
The phrase ending in "gamyā" is intended to indicate the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that the nature of analogy (*upamiti*) consists in being a universal (*jāti*).
By this, through the use of the present tense in the word "smarann" (remembering),
they say "āhuḥ" (they say).
And here, for the author of the compendium who has stated "from some forest[-text]" and so forth,

the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) concerning the meaning of the sentence of extended application (*atideśavākya*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the recollection (*smaraṇa*) concerning that [meaning] is [the operation].

The intended presentation of the view is that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the cognition of similarity and the result (*phala*) is the analogical knowledge (*upamiti*); it is not the presentation of the view that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is the perception of an object qualified by similarity and so forth, the operation is the recollection of such [similarity], and the result is the analogical knowledge.
If that were the case, since the employment of words is under one's own control, one could simply say, "he sees the lump while about to remember"; therefore,
considering the natural force of the expression "while remembering" and so forth, the former view alone is intended, and not the latter.
The second opinion is that, because it is intended to demonstrate that [view], it is inappropriate to provide an explanation of such a text; this is the seed of dissatisfaction [with the first view].
In the *Saṃgraha*, it says "in the sentence."
"The cow-like is the denotation of the word *gavaya*": this is an example of the transfer of essential nature (*svarūpātideśa*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by another stimulus" (*udbodhakāntara*): the meaning is that it refers to a stimulus such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) or the like, which is distinct from the perception of an individual object qualified by similarity (*sādṛśya*).
[219] "Immediately after seeing an object qualified by similarity," and so forth.
Herein, of this analogy (*upamiti*): this...
If one accepts that the form [of the cognition] is "that which is denoted by the word *gavaya*," then after seeing another individual *gavaya*,
there would be the impossibility of remembering the denotability of that word with respect to it;
for [the previously apprehended object was] "that which is denoted by the word *gavaya* and is similar to a cow."

And considering that if one accepts [the word] as having such a form, then— since similarity, defined as possessing properties residing in that [object] which are co-located with its difference from it, is cumbersome (guru)—
it cannot serve as the delimitor of the denotation of the word, and thus the [cognition] would result in being an error; so reflecting...

With the intention that analogy (upamiti) must be accepted as having the very form "the gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'," it was stated [in the text]: "in a light property such as *gavayatva*.
This means: "having a qualificandumhood delimited by such a property."

[219] This demonstration that the perception of similarity is the cause of analogical cognition (*upamiti*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative indication) pointing toward the meaning that is about to be explained.

[218] By the phrase "due to similarity, etc.," the inclusion of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is indicated. Thus ends the section on analogy (*upamāna*) in the *Dīpikāprakāśikā* commentary on the [Pramāṇavārttika] known as the *Prasaraṇa*. Now begins the section on verbal testimony (*śabda*).
