Regarding the connection based on the relationship between that which is dependent and that upon which it depends with respect to the definition of sound [222],
everything that needs to be said has already been explained in detail previously.
[222] "By being the basis for verbal cognition" means by being the cause of verbal cognition;
[222] "even though it resides in the result" means even though it is located in the fruit.
"By way of a direct relation with the nature of the substratum," and so forth;
"even of the two intrinsic natures"—
that is, even of the means of valid cognition consisting of verbal testimony and comparison.
By this, it is indicated that the state of being located in the instrument (*karaṇaniṣṭhatva*) is due to a direct connection (*sākṣātsambandha*) with the conjunction (*saṅgati*).
The phrase "of the two instruments" (*karaṇayoḥ*) and so forth expresses the meaning of the genitive case.
The state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) is that which is associated with the cognition of a portion of the meaning of the word denoting it;
and "immediacy" (*anantaratva*) is the state of being non-intervened.
And that [property] is common to both the preceding and the succeeding;

it should be understood as consisting in being either devoid of the state of having its own determination preceded by a prior determination, or possessing the state of having its own subsequent determination not preceded [by another].

Now, if it is argued that in the summary definition "verbal testimony is the word of a reliable person" (*āptavākyaṃ śabdaḥ*), since the property of being a word (*śabdatva*) serves as the delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), there would be an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in the case of unauthoritative sentences such as "one sprinkles with fire," because they lack the quality of being uttered by a reliable person;
therefore, he says: "it is authoritative verbal testimony" (*pramāṇaśabda*). Thus...
And the property of being a word that is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-śabdatva*) is the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
The point is that this property is excluded from sentences such as "one sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*).
[222] Regarding the definition:
the term "sentence-ness" (*vākyatva*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such groups as *ja-ba-ga-ḍa-da-śa*.

In the phrase "a sentence spoken by a reliable person" (*āptoktavākya*), the word "spoken" (*ukta*) signifies that the genitive case contained within the compound denotes the state of being uttered (*uccaritatva*).
Thus it has been indicated:
"in the form of being a speaker of things as they are.
By this, *āptatva* (authoritativeness) [is defined].

[The definition] "being desired" [is proposed]. However, in that case, the flaw of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) remains in a sentence such as "he sprinkles with fire," because it is possible for someone who utters it to desire it. This objection is refuted. Now, one might argue that even for the speaker of "he sprinkles with fire" and so forth, at some time...

Since it is possible for one to possess a true cognition that serves as the cause for employing a sentence whose meaning is sublated, how is over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) avoided? To this he says: "[222] Regarding the object of the sentence under discussion... and "[222] The final conclusion (*niṣkarṣaḥ*)."
The meaning is as follows:
1. "By its own expressed object," and so forth.
Its own [sentence] is "he sprinkles with water," and the object expressed by that is the meaning.

The state of being produced by that true cognition regarding water-jars, sprinkling, and the performer thereof— which resides in the speaker of such a sentence— is present in that sentence [by the rule]:
"having understood the meaning..."
The intended meaning is that this follows from the maxim "the arrangement of words [is the sentence].
[In this context,] the state of being a sentence qualified by another sentence [is defined] by the relation of both being produced by itself and expressing an object that has become its own content.
Alternatively, the definition of a word (*śabda*) is "a sentence characterized by knowledge corresponding to reality" (yathārthajñānaviśiṣṭavākyatva).
This refers to the fact that the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is the cause for the employment of words. This is the determination of *śakti* (linguistic potency).

One might object: "Is it not the case that the definition of the category of *śakti* (potency) in the *Dīpikā*, beginning with 'conducive to the recollection of the object' (*arthasmṛtyanukūla*), is improper?
For such a definition is irrelevant to the present context. Anticipating this objection, he says:
[225] "The Mīmāṃsaka," and so forth; "as the refuter" means as the purpose.

The third case ending is used because of the intention to express causality (*hetutva*). The word "in the foremost" (*agre*) is connected with "introducing" (*avatāraṇa*); "introducing" [refers to]...
It is an activity conducive to engagement;
and that is the engagement with the knot of doubt.
"That" refers to this.
The meaning is "a Mīmāṃsaka. "Tenet" (mata) refers to a matter accepted as being authoritative.
"By way of commonality" means that commonality consists in possessing the nature of subsisting therein.
It has been stated that "form" (rūpa) and "object" (artha), etc., [are the meanings].
The meaning of the third case (instrumental) is a specific relation (vaiśiṣṭya) characterized by the category of capacity (śakti).
The rest is clear.

Regarding the phrase "the power residing in the Dīpikā," the term "the category of power" (śaktipadārtha) was stated in order to indicate that this refers to the meaning of the word "power. In the Dīpikā—

The phrase ending with "anukūla" (conducive) is a qualification of the relation. Now, an objection is raised: even if "being conducive to the recollection of the object" is included as the definition of the category of *śakti* (power) as stated in the *Dīpikā*, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains as it was in the case of the inherence (*samavāya*) between a word such as "jar" and space.

Even if one were to include the qualification of being "distinguished by the word" through the dual relation of residing in itself and residing in its own meaning, it would still be redundant to exclude the inherence (*samavāya*) between the word "ether" (*ākāśa-pada*) and ether itself, because that too possesses both of those relations and because it is conducive to the cognition of the meaning; therefore, he says: "[225] ...that which generates verbal comprehension... (*śābdabodhajanaka*).
This is a qualification of "recollection" (smṛti). Accordingly,

since there is no over-extension [of the definition], because the recollection of objects such as space (*ākāśa*), which depends upon the cognition of inherence (*samavāya*), lacks the capacity to generate verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

This is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Favorability consists in being a producer, and that is sublated in the case of a relation, because it is the cognition of that [relation] alone which produces the memory. To this, he says: "[225] 'Favorability here...'"
[225] Regarding the phrase "the qualificandum":
although the state of being a relation exists in the self (ātman) with respect to the word "self" (ātmapada)— due to its possessing the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) that motivates it and so forth—

Nevertheless, there is no fault, because the refined definition is as follows: it is the state of being the locus of the relation that delimits the delimitorhood residing in cognition— which is itself delimited by the relation of being produced— as defined by that capacity to generate verbal comprehension which resides in memory.

1. Regarding "svajanyatva" and so forth: "sva" refers to the cognition whose object is the sentence-meaning of such sentences as "He sprinkles with water"; "tajjanyatvam" (the state of being produced by that) [refers] to such a sentence.

Thus, the coordination (*samanvaya*) is as follows: one's own cognition of such a sentence-meaning, the object of that [cognition] which is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), and the quality of being expressive of that [sentence-meaning] in that sentence— [all these are related] by the relation of being produced (*janyatā-sambandhena*).

The definition is consistent because it is accepted that the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is the recollection of a specific object as qualified by a cognition whose relation is *śakti* (denotative power), which has that specific word as its qualifier and that specific object as its qualificandum. Thus...
There is no fault, because the recollection of an object produced by the cognition of another relation lacks the status of being a cause for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

Now, [one might object]: by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "another word-meaning" (*padārthāntara*) means "an object distinct from [the other] word-meanings," the term *padārthāntara*—
It refers to something distinct from the objects already established;
for words such as "distinct" (*atirikta*), when not co-occurrent with a word that specifies a particular counter-correlate,
[denote] by virtue of being the substratum of the property-limiting the object-referent of the word with which they are co-occurrent.

This is because it has been observed in cases such as "the variegated [color] is a distinct form" that there is a capacity to convey a collection of differences (bhedakūṭa) having those respective substrates as their counter-correlates;
and thus, according to the Mīmāṃsakas, even in the case of power (śakti).

Anticipating the objection that, because such a collection of differences (*bhedakūṭa*) is not established as a category (*padārtha*) since it is not admitted to be a category itself, he says: "[225] *tattad*...
And thus, [the term refers to] those very categories such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, which are distinct from the nature of power (*śaktitva*).
The sense is that there is no lack of establishment because of its being apprehended;
"contradiction" (*vyāghāta*) means opposition, which is to say, non-establishment.

Alternatively, in the view of the Naiyāyikas, since *śakti* (potency) is not a distinct category (*padārthāntara*), its negation would be untenable due to the non-establishment of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). Therefore, he says: "The meaning is that it possesses the aggregate (*kūṭa*) of absences of the respective delimiters (*tāvacchedaka*) of those various categories. And in this regard:

Since the meaning "there exists here a collection of absences of the respective delimiters of those various categories" is obtained by accepting the suffix *ya* (in the sense of "possessing") as in *arśas-ādyañ*, the phrase "it is not a distinct category" (*na padārthāntaram*) [is justified] through the use of the negative particle (*nañ*).
Since it is observed elsewhere that the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) appear as intervening [meanings],
in the present case as well, the negation (*nañ*)— whose meaning is an absence—

is construed as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) with respect to the intervening category of absences; thus, [the referent] is the locus of the absence of the aggregate of the absences of the respective property-qualifiers (*tattat-padārthatāvacchedaka*) of those various meanings.
Having kept this meaning in mind, he says: "[225] There is no contradiction.
From this point, "contradiction" [is discussed].
The phrase beginning with "prior to [the establishment or non-establishment]" [refers to this].
"Another" means the Naiyāyika.
This is because the collection of absences of the respective delimiters of the categories (*padārthatāvacchedaka*) is individually well-known.

The point is that, according to the Naiyāyika position, negation is established because it is possible to have a cognition of the counter-positive as qualified by the delimitors of counter-positiveness.
Although, in this context, "being a collection" (kūṭatva) is difficult to define;
And because [the definition] is not established, there can be no inclusion of the absence of one thing as qualified by the absence of another. [Note:
The phrase "by the relation of being produced" (janyatā-sambandhena) is to be construed with "qualified by cognition" (jñāna-viśiṣṭa).]
Nevertheless,
there is no fault, because it is accepted that the meaning is "like being the object of a cognition whose content is the absence of this or that.
And the state of being an object is [defined] by the relation of being pervaded by itself, as delimited by the relation of inherence (*ādheyatā*).

Because the negation is established through the well-known existence of that absence, whose counter-correlativity is delimited by its relation to that [relation]; [225] "it is indeed distinct" means that,
in the absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamanā*) between two already established [entities], something else is postulated.
The sense is that it is established by the logical principle (*nyāya*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "yataḥ" and so forth: in this system, in expressions such as "vācya" (to be expressed), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) is such a qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
It should be understood that [the word "pratyaya"] has the substratum (āśraya) as its meaning. Now, if this is the case,
then in the verbal cognition produced by sentences such as "vācya" (denotable), there would be the manifestation of an additional category of meaning in the form of "substratum-ness" (āśrayatva).
There is weightiness due to the fact that it must be stated;

likewise, having raised the objection that the same applies because "being determined by the relation to a desire" must also be included within the definition of the qualificandum (viśeṣyatā), he states another alternative:
"Of such a kind" (tādṛśa) means residing in the state of being the object of the cognition produced by each respective word. "That" (tat) means God (Īśvara).
And thus, in this grammatical rule, the meaning of the base (dhātu) is simply the will of Īśvara, while that of the suffix (pratyaya) is as follows:

The meaning is that which possesses the objecthood (viśeṣyatā) as determined by the modehood (prakāratā) of being the object of the cognition produced by a word such as "pad" (word); and the intention is that the desire (icchā) is construed with this objecthood through the relation of being determined (nirūpitatva), so that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) regarding [the objecthood] of being the object of the cognition produced by words such as "ghaṭa" (pot).

The point is that since [the relation] appears only in the jar and so forth within the will of the Lord (īśvarecchā), the relationship of the defined and the definer exists only between those two objects.
Now, [one might object]: "In the case of 'there is a hamlet on the Gaṅgā'..."

In such cases, since the cognition of the riverbank (*tīra*) arises from the word "Gaṅgā" and so forth, it is necessary that even the property of being the object of such a cognition residing in the riverbank be made the content of God’s will;
for there is a rule that His will must have every existing property as its object.

And likewise, since that [cognition] also possesses the form "let the bank be the object of the cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā*," the aforementioned consequence of the total abolition of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) remains as it was; therefore, he says: "[226] Of the state of being produced by the word *gaṅgā*..."

It is accepted that the Lord’s will consists precisely in the form: "Let the cognition produced by the word *gaṅgā* have the bank as its object"; for by that much alone, the aforementioned rule regarding that [will] is established.

The meaning is that because it is possible for even the state of being the object of the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā" to appear there in the form of the nature of being the object of the cognition [of the word "tīra"], [it is not a case of non-existence].
Regarding the phrase "by way of non-existence": otherwise...
The sense is that there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence of no distinction between the desire for a specific form and the desire for a form that is not yet differentiated.

[226] Regarding the phrase "qualified by the mode-of-being (prakāratā) consisting in being produced by the word *gaṅgā*," etc.: by this, [it is meant] the property of having the form "let the bank be the object of cognition."
Because such a desire is admitted;
for the objective determination of the bank is characterized by being the object of the cognition produced by the word "Gaṅgā," as determined by the mode of being the object of that cognition.
The objection that the flaw of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains as it was because [the two properties] are unimpaired is refuted;
for since it is impossible for the particularization (*viśeṣyatā*) and the mode (*prakāratā*) belonging to a single [cognition] to be identical,
there can be no identity between the mode-forms of "being produced" (*janyatva*) and "being the object of cognition" (*bodhaviṣayatva*).
Because the relationship between the characterized and the characterizer is impossible,
there is no harm— that is,
no consequence of the abolition of defining characteristics.
"Manifestation as independence" means that when there is a relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*), the third case ending denotes manifestation,
which is to say, being a qualifier (*prakāratā*).
And autonomy (*svātantrya*) consists in the absence of being determined by a subjectness (*viṣayatāprakāratā*) that is itself determined by a qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) directed toward an object,
as well as the absence of being determined by a subjectness of cognition (*bodhaprakāratā*) that is itself determined by a subjectness of being produced (*janyatvaprakāratā*) residing in a word.
The connection of the term "independently" (*svātantryeṇa*), which has the meaning already stated, should be understood as appropriate to each case. This concludes the summary.
The intention here is as follows: without accepting that the will of God has the form "let the bank be the object of the cognition produced by the word 'Ganges'."
If one accepts that [the word] has a fragmented form as its expressed meaning, there is the complexity of having to postulate *lakṣaṇā* (indication) as a distinct mode of operation (*vṛtti*);
however, if one accepts that it has a qualified form as its expressed meaning, there is parsimony (*lāghava*). This is established by reasoning (*tarka*) supported by [the principle of parsimony].

Nor should it be suspected that the possession of a specific causal agency by that [Iśvara] is established by the inference: "The will of the Lord possesses either a specific causal agency or its absence, because it is an object of knowledge."
If that were the case, it would follow that for those who are not mistaken, there would be the conventional usage, "A jar is denotable by the word 'jar'";
[this is so] only when [the cognition] is qualified by the absence of subverting reasoning (*bādhaka-tarka*).
This is because it is accepted that the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghavatarka*) assists inference,
and that [parsimony] is not established in that case by the aforementioned inference.
Thus, in cases such as "the pot is the denoted object of the word 'pot'," the application of the meaning of the case-ending to the meaning of the suffix must be asserted;
yet that is contrary to experience. [This is why] the genitive...
The meaning is the mode-of-being (*prakāratā*) of being produced.

In that context, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is construed [with the suffix] by way of the relation of being qualified by a mode-of-being residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhaprakāratānirūpitatva*). *Vaca*...
The meaning of the verbal root is a desire qualified by being the determiner of the modehood of the objectness that is itself determined by the modehood of cognition.
The meaning of the genitive case is conjoined with the modehood of cognition through the relation of being determined (*nirūpitatva*).

And in the case of a qualified desire (*viśiṣṭecchā*), its occurrence as a qualifier— while having the referent of the suffix as its qualificandum— is construed with [the action] by means of the relation of being "determined" (*nirūpitatva*) by that which is delimited by the qualifier.
Thus, the first alternative is also established.
"It is indeed correct. Thus,
by not accepting the identity between the qualifierhood of the qualified (viśeṣyatā) and the modehood (prakāratā) belonging to the desire for distinction,
but rather accepting a relationship of the delimited and the delimiter (avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva), [the following applies] in a case where there is a modehood determined by another modehood.
By introducing the qualifierhood delimited by the qualificandhood that is itself determined by the qualifierhood (*prakāratā*),
the establishment of the power residing in the qualified (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*)— namely, "the power resides in the qualified," and so forth— is secured.

It is a word that produces a cognition having as its qualifier the impossibility (*anupapannatva*) of the Mīmāṃsaka doctrine— this word being qualified by a destruction whose counter-positive is a word that generates a cognition concerning the Mīmāṃsaka doctrine, which is itself qualified by a desire for an operation conducive to a certainty that is not overridden by a cognition of invalidity regarding the power [of the word] having a specific qualificandum as its object.
The indivisible cognition is: "one who possesses an effort conducive to that [action].
The second relation of qualification is by way of both the relation of having the same agent as its own counter-correlative and the relation of occurring at the time of its own locus.
The rest is clear.
Regarding "presumption" (*arthāpatti*): presumption consists in the [inference of] the state of being the object of the act of bringing.

It should be understood as having the following form: "Without the property of residing in a cow through a direct relation, it is impossible for [the universal] to reside in cowness through an indirect relation consisting in residing in what resides in its own locus. Now, one might object:

If it is accepted that the expressive power (*śakti*) resides only in the individual (*vyakti*) as the locus of the universal (*jāti*), how could there be the manifestation of the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and its relation within the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) produced by words such as "cow"? For [according to your view], nothing other than the individual is denotable, and thus the universal and its relation cannot appear in the verbal cognition.
This is because of the rule that there is no manifestation [of other objects]. Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of evidence for such a rule;
for if that were the case, then in the verbal cognition produced by words such as "cow," [there would be no manifestation] of jars and so forth.
This follows from the attainment of awakening.

As for the objection that, "if this were the case, non-difference (*abheda*) would not appear in the verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) of such instances as 'the pot is blue' (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*)," that is not so; for [in that case] there are two word-meanings—
Anticipating the objection that this is due to the qualification "other than association" (*saṃsargātirikta*), he states the solution favored by the ancients, beginning with:
"In this regard, it should be understood as follows," and so on. However, the new [scholars] (*navīna*)...
There is no evidence for such a restrictive rule;
nor does the aforementioned over-extension (atiprasaṅga) apply,

because it is precisely the capacities (śakti), their delimiters (avacchedaka), the relations constituting those delimiters, and relationhood itself that [determine] the verbal cognition (śābdabodha).
Because it is accepted that [the word] is the restrictor of the denotation,
they say that the expressive power (*śakti*) does not need to be admitted for both the universal (*jāti*) and its specific qualification (*tadvaiśiṣṭya*).
He presents that view with the words "the moderns, however" (*navyās tu*).
This is an exposition of the means for grasping word-potency (*śakti*); for indeed, in the *Ekadanta-kośa* and other works, the words "Ekadanta" and so forth [are used].

A *dvandva* compound is untenable here because a *dvandva* is grammatically correct only when there is mutual distinction (*bheda*) among the meanings of the words being compounded; since that is absent here, he says: "In that case" (*tatra*).
[235] From the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*);
that is to say, from the standpoint of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*).
[234] Even in the statement of the *Dīpikā*, "by means of the linguistic usage of elders" (*vṛddhavyavahāreṇa*), "elder" (*vṛddha*) refers to one who is proficient in language (*vyutpanna*).
The meaning is "by means of linguistic usage" (*vyavahāreṇa*) or "through engagement" (*pravṛttyā*).

Now, one might object: since the phrase "because it has a purposeful end" (*kāryaparatvāt*) in the sentence beginning with "nanu" found in the *Dīpikā* requires a genitive complement, and because it is impossible for the word "of linguistic usage" (*vyavahārasya*) to be construed with what follows, he says:
— "[237] Of linguistic usage," and so forth.
"[237] Of linguistic usage" means of the employment of sentences. Now, [it was said] "having observed activity and having seen the bringing of a cow" [at 234].
From the statement of the lamp (the *dīpikā-vākya*), it is understood that there is a cognition of the bringing of the cow immediately following the inference of activity;
however, that is not tenable,
because an inference is impossible without the prior cognition of the subject (*pakṣa*), and [thus] the cognition of the bringing of the cow [cannot arise].
Because it is the first [requirement] due to its necessity, he says: "Having seen the bringing of the cow," and so forth.
He says this because no other means of valid cognition (*pramiti*) for the apprehension of activity is possible.
Regarding the phrase "having perceived this":

he states the formulation of the inference—[235] "This action is produced; this effort is generated by a cognition of it being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) with respect to the property of bringing a cow, because it is an instance of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*)."
Another inference should also be understood here: "like one's own activity.
[235] Regarding the cognition of bringing a cow—that is, the cognition that bringing a cow is a means to achieve a desired end—[234] the word "having ascertained" [is used].

The intention here is as follows: the certainty in this case is inferential, [established by the reasoning] that such knowledge is produced by such a sentence because it is qualified by such a sentence.

And this distinctness [vaiśiṣṭya] is by means of both relations: having its existence dependent on the existence of itself, and being the counter-positive of an absence whose non-existence depends on itself. Now, [consider the case]: "Bring the cow."
Why is the power (*śakti*) of such a qualified sentence itself not accepted with respect to such a qualified meaning? To this he says: "of the sentence" (*vākyasya*).
Now, as for the word *yava*:
If one accepts that the meaning of the verbal suffix (*śakti*) is qualified by a long awn (*dīrghaśūka*), then there would be no usage of the word for *priyaṅgu* among the Mlecchas;
therefore, he says: "[235] But in the case of *priyaṅgu*, etc.
[235] "The verbal suffix [denotes] that which is qualified by effort," and so forth. The verbal suffix...

The capacity [of the root *kṛ*] to convey the meaning qualified by effort (*yatnatva*) should be understood through its function as an explanatory gloss (*vivaraṇa*), according to the principle that such a gloss [is authoritative] because it is explained by [the synonymous verb] *karoti*.
This is established by means of another word having the same meaning as that [root].
The sense is that exposition (*vyākhyāna*) consists precisely in the statement of the meaning of those [words].
This is the determination that words also have as their primary referent established entities (*siddha*).

[Objection: "But let one who has already achieved their goal also employ sentences; what does that matter for linguistic acquisition? To this, he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). [This means: otherwise—that is, in the absence of the necessity of grasping the word-potency (*śakti*) therein.
Regarding the definition of indication (*lakṣaṇā*):

[237] One might object that the statement in the *Dīpikā*, "nor is a primary denotative power (*śakti*) postulated for the bank," is untenable, because it is accepted that words such as 'bank' possess a primary denotative power with respect to the bank. To this, he says: [238] "of the word *gaṅgā*."
[238] "The remainder" means that the impossibility of having multiple referents is intended;
that is to say, the impossibility of possessing the capacity for multiple meanings.
But surely, a conjunction can somehow occur even between salt and a horse, and likewise, relations such as simultaneity and so forth are also possible.
Because there is no possibility of the expansion of the aforementioned faults, he says: "[238] This is an illustration.
[237] This refers to the postulation of various powers because there is no mutual relationship between salt and a horse.
[238] The meaning is: "of two things that are well-known and commonly used in similar applications.
By this, from words such as *gaṅgā*—
A distinction has been indicated there,
because the bank and the current do not possess that nature [of being the primary referent].
As for the expression "the man on the bed":
In this context, the word "bed" (*mañca*) refers to the person [on the bed],
while the expression "one who is on the bed" is used there to establish a possible relationship;
however, this does not apply to the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) of the bed itself.
It should be understood that [the denoted object] appears in the verbal cognition.
Herein is the definition of *ajahat-svārthā* (non-abandoning) indication (*lakṣaṇā*):
indication is that which generates a cognition whose object is the indicated alone, in its capacity as the delimitor of the state of being indicated (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
[238] By "api" means by the word "api. [238] By "being a single caravan-leader" means by being a constituent of a single collective.

The definition of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication) is: an indication that conveys both the denoted meaning and the indicated meaning by means of the form that delimits the state of being the object of indication (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).

The delimitor of the indicated (lakṣyatāvacchedaka) has been shown. Now, one might ask: since there is no lack of compatibility in the primary meaning of the word *chatrin* (the umbrella-bearer) being construed as the agent of the act of going, what here serves as the determinant for the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)? To this [it is replied]:
He says: "Regarding 'tātparya'";
by the phrase "possessing the sense of the suffix -mat," it is indicated that the suffix -in possesses the status of a word characterized by its expressive power (*śaktatva*).
"By its power" means by the power of the sentence. Intending the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, he says: [238]
Having explained this,
he says— according to his own intended view—
"otherwise": [238] "in another way" means that there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding a single object, namely, a single aggregate.
It consists of an indirect relationship (*paramparāsambandha*) characterized by being constituted by the person who is its own substratum.
The phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates a lack of satisfaction with this view;
the seed of that [dissatisfaction] is as follows: if that were the case...
This would be merely an example of *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication);
and thus it would be of no use for the present context, because in the *Dīpikā* that very [example] is stated to be an illustration of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-exclusive indication).
[239] Of that intense identity between Brahman and the individual soul;

[239] regarding the aspect of "that-ness," the passage beginning with "now" and so forth, the underlying meaning is this: the connection with this place and so forth is sublated in that which is qualified by the connection with that place and so forth.
Since it is necessary for a property being conjoined with a qualified entity to also be conjoined with its qualifier,
there would be a contradiction regarding its connection with that place and so forth which has become the qualifier; therefore, that word [is used].
It refers solely to the relation with place and time, but the aspect of "that-ness" (tattā) regarding the place and so forth is not intended to be expressed.
Thus, the indication by that word (*tacchabda*) is a "partial renunciation and partial retention" (*jahadajahallakṣaṇā*). Its definition, however, is as follows:
"Lakṣaṇā (indication) is that which causes a cognition whose object is the denotatum, but which does not have the delimitor of denotability as its qualifier.
This is the case when, in instances such as "This is that Devadatta," a verbal cognition apprehending the qualifiedness of the qualifier (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhi*) is accepted.
In that case, it would be as follows;

however, this is not accepted, but rather a cognition that apprehends a relation (vaiśiṣṭya) whose relatum (anuyogin) is characterized by its occurrence at that place and at that time. In that regard:
And thus, there is no room for sublation (bādha) by the manner previously stated, because the predicate does not connect with the qualifier. For this very reason,
immediately after the verbal cognition produced by a sentence such as "This is that Devadatta,"...
The non-arising of doubts such as "Is Devadatta present in that place and at that time, or not?"— which is also established by experience— is thus explained; therefore,
since the aspect of "that-ness" (tattā) is not abandoned, there is no room for *lakṣaṇā* (indication) here, and this is precisely what is accepted.
They say it is "indication by relinquishing and not relinquishing" (*jahadajahallakṣaṇā*).
He states that view with the words beginning "[239] others, however," etc.,
which is a refutation of the claim that figurative indication (*gauṇī*) and suggestion (*vyañjanā*) are distinct modes of operation (*vṛtti*).
[242] "Even for kings, it is by power alone" means that, according to the principle that one "bears" (dharati) and "protects" (rakṣati) the earth, it is solely through the power of yoga.
Now, as to where the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is included within the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he says—[242] "In the Gaṅgā," and so forth.
"By the sovereignty of indication" means by the power of indication. As for the word *ca* (and):
Because it is impossible for it to have the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), he says: "The word *ca* has the meaning of 'and' (*ca-artha*)," and "because of being a speaker of a distinct term."
The meaning is: "because it is qualified by the employment of a word with a distinct characteristic (*vilakṣaṇaśabda*).

The qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [between the word and its employment] is by way of both relations: having an effort (*kṛti*) conducive to itself, and being the locus of that [effort]. The state of being the locus (*ādheyatā*)...
[The definition is] by way of both relations: being produced by a desire whose object is a verbal cognition of this kind having one's own husband as its qualificandum.
Therefore, there is no deviation [of the reason], because the reason as stated exists even in cases such as ourselves.
By the phrase "conceit and so forth," the inclusion of mental factors is intended.
Regarding the term "to be thought":
the point is that, in that case, such a subsequent conceptualization (*anuvyavasāya*) is unestablished.
The examination of the seed of the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*): "the impossibility of the primary meaning" refers to the literal object, such as a staff (*yaṣṭi*) and so forth.
The intended meaning is that [the ritual] is possible through its connection with an action.
"At a fixed time" means at the specific time for the departure and so forth of the horse and other [animals].
By the phrase "because of the qualifier, etc.," the inclusion of concomitance (*sāhacarya*) and so forth is intended;
this is the refutation of the [necessity of] supplying an unstated meaning (*arthādhyāhāra*).
[246] *Adhyāhāraḥ* means "presence" (*upasthiti*). In the phrase "because it is for the sake of the knowledge of the meaning," "knowledge of the meaning" refers to presence.

"In whatever way" (*yathākathañcit*)— [246] Adhyāhāra means presence (upasthiti). In the expression "for the sake of the knowledge of the meaning," "knowledge of the meaning" refers to presence. "In whatever way"—
The meaning is "by means of another cognition.
Now, one might object that stating the specific purpose for including the requirement of being produced by words— as in the case of expressions such as "the jar is the object"— is futile.

Anticipating the objection that this [definition] is possible even in cases where objects are presented through perception and other means, he provides the following resolution— stating that this description of the purpose applies not only to the inclusion of "being produced by words" (*padajanyatva*) within the cognition, but also to the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*): "[247] ‘Also of the particular word’."
The instrumental case in "vṛttyā" denotes qualification (*vaiśiṣṭye*).

As for the word "direction" (*dig*), the intended meaning is this: although, in terms of the actual state of things (*vastugatyā*), a word such as "jar" is indeed qualified by its occurrence (*vṛtti*).

In order to prevent the occurrence of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) through the presentation of space (*ākāśa*) produced by a cognition of its inherence (*samavāya*), it must be stated that the cause [of such comprehension] is the presentation of a specific object produced by a cognition whose qualificandum is that specific word and whose mode (*prakāra*) resides in that specific stick (*daṇḍa*). Likewise...

[This applies] also to the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) of a specific object, which is produced by a cognition whose qualificandum is that specific object and whose mode is the specific mode residing in that specific word.
And thus, since inherence (*samavāya*) lacks the nature of being a relation (*vṛtti*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
[this restriction applies] only to *śakti* (denotative power) and *lakṣaṇā* (indicative function).

"Because it has the nature of a function" (vṛttirūpatvāt). The analysis of the compound is as follows: "component power" (avayavaśaktiḥ) refers to the power residing in the individual words that constitute it.
"By that alone" means by the power of the individual parts alone; the word "alone" (mātra) serves to exclude...

It is the exclusion of conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*). Thus, the definition of a derivative (*yaugika*) word is: that which, while lacking the capacity to produce a cognition whose object is the meaning generated by the knowledge of conventional power, possesses the capacity to produce a cognition whose object is the meaning generated by the knowledge of etymological power (*avayava-śakti*).
The conclusion is reached.
The first part of the definition (the "sat" portion) is for the purpose of excluding those terms that possess both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) meanings.
The phrase beginning with "by that alone," etc., follows.
The meaning is "by mere conventional usage" (*rūḍhimātreṇa*).

By the word "mere" (*mātra*), the exclusion of the power of the individual parts (*avayava-śakti*) is intended. And thus, [it refers to a word] which, while lacking the capacity to produce a cognition whose object is a meaning generated by the knowledge of etymological power (*yoga-śakti*), [is used].

The definition of a conventional (rūḍha) word is its capacity to produce a cognition whose object is a meaning generated by the knowledge of conventional power (rūḍhi-śakti). The first part of the definition (the "sati" clause) is included to exclude words that are etymological (yaugika).
[248] This is explained in the passage beginning with "by means of both etymology and convention" (yogarūḍhibhyām), etc.

The meaning is: "the state of being the generator of that verbal cognition which is produced by the knowledge of the power of yoga and is produced by the knowledge of the power of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
The first part, ending with "produced" (*janya*), is for the purpose of excluding conventional usage.

The second [element of the definition] is for the purpose of excluding purely etymological (yaugika) words. If the phrase "by mutual cooperation" were not included, then the definition would become: "being a conveyer of meaning through etymology while being a conveyer of meaning through conventional usage (rūḍhi). In that case—
And there is no distinction between the derivative (*yaugika*) and the conventional (*rūḍha*);
therefore, by including that [conventional power], one obtains in a single verbal cognition the state of being produced by the knowledge of two kinds of power.
And mutualness in the *sahakāra* consists in being defined by the locus of the *sahakāra* as determined by its own locus; this results in the state of being qualified by the *sahakāra*.

Distinctness (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [is defined] by way of both relations: subsisting in that which determines itself (*svanirūpakavṛttitva*), and being determined by its own substratum (*svāśrayanirūpitatva*).
The phrase "without mutual assistance" in the subsequent text means "in the absence of the aforementioned cooperation."

The relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) belonging to the meaning of the third case [the suffix -tva] is construed with *śakti* (denotative power) and so forth. Thus, [the definition of *yogarūḍhi* is]: that which, while being a producer of a cognition whose object is a meaning generated by the knowledge of *yoga-śakti* (etymological power) but not generated by the knowledge of *rūḍhi-śakti* (conventional power), is also a producer of a cognition whose object is a meaning generated by the knowledge of *yoga-śakti* but not generated by the knowledge of *rūḍhi-śakti*.
The definition of a term that is both etymological and conventional is thus concluded.
Both members of the compound are included to exclude terms that are purely etymological or purely conventional.
[249] "Etymological-lexical" (yogarūḍhi) means a lexical convention accompanied by etymological derivation.

In that case, if one resorts to an *itaretara-dvandva* (copulative compound of mutual conjunction) based on the principle "yoga and rūḍhi," there would be the undesirable consequence of the form ending in the dual number as "yogarūḍhī. If one resorts to a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective compound) based on the principle "the collection of yoga and rūḍhi," [there would likewise be the form] "yogarūḍhī."
There is no room for the objection that this would entail the consequence of being neuter;
for there is no contradiction, as one may resort to a compound with the middle term elided (madhyamapadalopisamāsa), such as in the case of "śākapārthiva" and similar expressions.

Precisely with this intention, since the term *kumuda* is employed for the *kumuda* flower later on, [the opponent might argue that] the desired conclusion is established; therefore, he says: "[249] *paṅkaja*, etc.
This is the refutation of the theory that the word's power resides in its syntactic connection (*anvita-śakti*).

The term "others" (itare) was stated for the purpose of securing the mutual connection between these two very categories; however, it does not imply that "otherness" (itaratva) itself is also a category.
With the intention that [the word's capacity] includes that which delimits its fitness (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), he says: "[251] *anvita* (connected).
Now, one might ask: "Let there be a power (*śakti*) even with respect to the aspect of connection;
what follows from that? To this he replies: "[251] *anvita*," and so forth.

Having kept in mind the lack of satisfaction— due to the possibility of the aforementioned reason for disregarding the "effect" portion and because the other word would incur the status of being figurative if it were intended to mean "effect"— the author says, "they say.
This refers to the state of occurring immediately after each respective cause.
The possession of that cause [is established] by way of the relation of "being produced in the moment immediately following itself, as delimited by its own co-referentiality.
By this, the exclusion of verbal cognitions that are non-co-referential is achieved.
Regarding the definition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth:
by the phrase "compatibility and so on" (*yogyatādīti*), the inclusion of words uttered without delay is intended.
Now, it might be argued that being produced by the absence of a word means being caused by that absence,
and this is not possible in the case of an absence which serves as the generator of verbal cognition. For that [absence]...
To the objection that [the definition] is too broad because of its permanence (*nityatva*), he says: "and being employed" (*prayuktatva*).

Now, since a verbal cognition arises even without the knowledge that [a word] does not produce a verbal cognition as defined above, how can that [knowledge] constitute the nature of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)? To this he says: "ending with non-productivity" (*ajanakatvāntam*).
[255] The indicator— namely, the awakener:
because the meaning of a sentence is difficult to grasp prior to verbal cognition due to its novelty, verbal cognition arises even from a doubt regarding semantic compatibility in certain cases.
With this intention, it was said: "[255] common to both doubt and certainty.
[255] "Existing in its own nature" means: "remaining unknown. [255] "The direction," etc.

The point is this: when the cognition of compatibility (*yogyatājñāna*) functions as a cause, it is precisely the absence of the ascertainment of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyaniścayābhāva*) that must be included within the delimiting condition (*hetutāvacchedaka*) of that causality.
In the view of the new school (Navīna), it is the absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the state of being a cognition of non-validity that is common to both doubt and certainty;
thus it is stated in the *Dīpikā*: "without delay," and so forth.
By this, the objection regarding the impossibility of verbal cognition in cases such as the verses of the Sage (Maunīśloka) is refuted;
otherwise, because there is an absence of the utterance of words therein, [verbal cognition would not arise].
Because the verbal comprehension [of the sentence] would be untenable.
Now, one might object that the examples cited in the root text, such as "cow," "horse," and "man," are irrelevant.
For instance: what kind of cognition is produced there?

Is it a cognition of oneness and so forth regarding a horse and the like, or is it a cognition of the syntactic relation of non-difference regarding cows, horses, and so forth? Not the first, because that would result in an undesired consequence (iṣṭāpatti).
The second [alternative] is not tenable,
because it is an inappropriate example; having raised such an objection, he states another example that lacks expectancy, beginning with "the jar," etc.,
regarding the non-human authorship of the Vedas.
Rather than postulating that two cognitions have different objects, it is more reasonable to postulate this for a single cognition;
and such is the case with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
The inference— "That [cognition] possesses either the apprehension of similarity (*sājātya*) or its absence, because it is an object of knowledge" (*prameyatva*)—

[establishes] the apprehension of similarity in recognition; [this is supported by] the parsimony (*lāghava*) consisting in the fact that the cognitions of production and destruction have as their objects merely the operations of the throat, palate, and so forth, which manifest the phoneme *ka* and others.
With the intention that "it might be so" refers to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) supported by reasoning (*tarka*), he says: "[259] *utpatti*...

And here, if recognition were to apprehend a commonality of kind (*sājātya*), then, because phonemes (*varṇa*) are impermanent, they would necessarily be the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of both destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
Thus, by means of the aforementioned inference— conjoined with the reasoning of respect—
it is established that recognition does not apprehend identity; consequently,
the postulation that the cognitions of arising and destruction have different objects is entirely unassailable.
Intending that it is precisely the reasoning already stated, he says "the heart" [251].
Out of dissatisfaction with this very point, he states another argument: "of the phonemes" [259].
Now, raising the objection, "If phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal, how can the Veda be non-eternal?", he explains this [in the *Prakāśikā*]: "In the case of 'Agni'... and "It is appropriate...";
the sense is that this is because it conforms to the cognitions of its production and destruction.
Regarding the authority of tradition and conduct:
is it not the case that "conduct" (ācāra) means...?

[Objection: Practice (anuṣṭhāna) consists of activity; therefore, if it were a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there would be a contradiction with the previously stated classification of the means of valid cognition. To this, he says: "[260] Regarding practices... [261]
By this, it is inferred that the term *ācāra* refers to a statement based on etymological derivation (*nirukta*). [260]
In this regard, the method of inference is as follows:
"This Smṛti is rooted in some Vedic Śākhā, because it is a Smṛti"— by means of this inference,
once a Śākhā that serves as the source for the Smṛtis of Vyāsa and others is established, such a Śākhā [is proven to exist].

[The reason why the Vedic texts] are now of interrupted recitation is because they are not being perceived at present; for that which is not so [i.e., not of interrupted recitation] is not so, just like the currently recited Śākhā.
This is shown by the passage beginning with "nadī-dīnādi" and so forth.
This includes examples such as *rājajarāsarorasa* and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "due to a specific meaning," this refers to words such as *nadī* (river) and the like.
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of understanding objects such as the poor and so forth [as the primary meaning].
And thus, the cognition of the expressive power (śakti) delimited by that form in which the co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra) with another word was apprehended [is what causes the understanding].
The denotatum is the cause of verbal cognition;
otherwise, even if the expressive power were grasped through such properties as "knowability" (*prameyatva*), it would follow that verbal cognition would arise [from those terms as well].

And thus, since the scripture inferred in this manner would have the form "one should perform the Aṣṭakā," there is no specific determination [of its meaning], and consequently, it lacks the capacity to convey understanding.
The sense is that one should understand that even in the place of the word *aṣṭakā*, there is the insertion of other synonymous words;
and this is because it leads to the comprehension of a specific meaning.
This refers to the reading [of the text];
however, if the reading were "because there would be no attainment of the understanding of the specific meaning," the meaning would be "because that necessity would be untenable."
The refutation of the status of presumption (*arthāpatti*) and other means as separate instruments of knowledge; they are, in fact, subsumed under inference (*anumāna*).
This method of inference should be understood as follows: "This person possesses an intention toward this specific meaning, because he possesses a distinct type of activity.
Regarding the phrase "having specified," etc., it applies even to the first speaker.
It is said "specifically" because it is already known in a general form;
"first" is an adverbial modifier of the action.
And "primacy" (prāthamya) with respect to speech consists in not being simultaneous with the destruction of the speech that expresses its own intended meaning;
this amounts to being other than what is qualified by such destruction. As for the qualification...
[The definition is] by way of the two relations: having the same time as itself, and being that which expresses the meaning expressed by the word denoting its own counter-correlative.
Thus ends the section on Word (*śabdapariccheda*) in the *Prakāśavyākhyā* titled *Dīpikāprasaraṇa*.
[Now begins] the *Prāmāṇyavāda* (Treatise on Validity).
In that regard,
the demonstration of misconceptions follows from the discussion on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is: "due to the logical connection (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*) consisting in the fact that [the property] resides in a function produced by itself, as determined by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Here, the word *pramāṇa* ends in the suffix *lyuṭ*, denoting the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Alternatively, the meaning is: "because of the connection (*saṅgati*) consisting of a nature that is opposed to being the object of indifference residing in the memory determined by that [object].
And that nature, in the present context, is the state of being graspable from another; and the memory is...
It arises by way of the relation of residing in its own occurrence (*svajanyavṛttiniṣṭhatva*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that valid cognition (*pramā*) is [defined] through the logical connection (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*) consisting of residing in its own occurrence as determined by that [valid cognition].
The meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is dependence upon a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) produced by a cognition;
this is construed with the act of establishing (*vyavasthāpanā*). Thus, [the definition of a treatise is:

one who possesses a future effort conducive to an operation favorable to a certainty—unassailed by a cognition of invalidity—that has as its object the quality of being extrinsically cognizable (*parataḥ-grāhyatva*), which is in turn a qualifier of the property of truth (*pramātva*) dependent on a desire to know produced by a cognition whose object is the topical connection (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*) as determined by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The understanding is that [the author] possesses an activity at the present time which is conducive to words not different from the text, and which is prompted by an effort whose object is knowledge (*jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "to be grasped by itself" (*svatogrāhya*), [it refers to] "that which grasps knowledge" (*jñānagrāhaka*).

Regarding the phrase "from another" (*parataḥ*), with the intention that the word "another" (*para*) refers to inference (*anumāna*) and so forth, he says: "[268] 'Inference and so forth' (*anumānādi*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the words spoken by authoritative persons (*āptokta-śabda*) is intended.
"Established by means of valid cognition," and so forth.

The term "established by means of valid cognition" is to be construed with "consistent. One's own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that [cognition] which produces a valid cognition (*pramā*); the state of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) is its property residing therein. If [the nature of a cognition] were to be apprehended from another [source], it would not reside in that [valid cognition].
And thus, the relationship between two things is of the nature of "connection" (*saṃgati*) when one is defined immediately after the other.

Since the fact that the status of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) is apprehended by another is defined immediately after the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the connection established by the definition of the means of valid cognition must be stated in relation to its being apprehended by another. And that [connection]—
The meaning is that it takes the form of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) consisting in residing in a function produced by itself.
2. Regarding "defined by that" (*tannirūpita*) and so forth: "defined by that" means defined by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Validity is traditionally defined as residing in that [cognition], consisting of a nature that is incompatible with being an object of indifference, and which is apprehended extrinsically; such is the *saṃgati* (logical connection).
Regarding "produced by itself" (*svajanya*) and so forth: "itself" (*sva*)...

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the valid cognition (*pramā*) produced by it, and the property of being valid (*pramātva*) residing therein—its being dependent on something else [for its apprehension] constitutes extrinsic apprehensibility (*parataḥ-grāhyatva*).
4. Regarding the phrase "defined by that" (*tannirūpita*) and so forth: "defined by that" means defined by that valid cognition (*pramā*).
The connection [of the words] is "conjunction" (*saṃgati*).

One's own [nature] is the cognizer and its function; "cognizer-ness" (*pramātva*) is the state of being resident in that [cognizer], which [is the case] when [the nature of the cognizer] is to be apprehended from another.

5. Regarding the term "its own word" (*svaśabda*): the sense is that here the term "its own" (*sva*) signifies what belongs to itself, and thus refers to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that apprehends cognition. [The opponent] raises an objection: "How so? [268]

The syntactical connection is as follows: "of that"—namely, of the misconception (*vipratipatti*); "here"—in the matter of being the motivator for the investigation that culminates in the refutation of that misconception; "[it is] unimpaired," so they say;
"for" (*hi*)—because.
He establishes this with the words beginning "contradictory" (*viruddha*) and so forth,
and the word "devoured" (*kabalita*).
The meaning is "having become the object"; it is an adjective qualifying "cognition. [268] Regarding the term "investigation" (vicāra):

The word "initiator" (*pravartaka*) is to be supplied as the remainder. And thus— meaning, when investigation proceeds in the manner described— it possesses utility for investigation (*vicāropayogitva*).
"Because of misconception," and so forth.

Here, "the validity of cognition" (*jñānaprāmāṇyam*) is the indication of the subject (*pakṣa*). The locative sense is that of being a constituent part, which is construed with the word "cognition" (*jñāna*).

[239] "Of such a kind" (*tādṛśa*) means: that which is produced by the entire causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that apprehends the cognition apprehending [the object], while not apprehending its invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).
[269] Here, in the aforementioned three views, the meaning of the locative case is "being a constituent part" (*ghaṭakatva*), which relates to the view of the Guru (Prabhākara).
"tat" means "heavy.
And "evam" means "in the manner described," that is, in establishing [the matter] according to the stated method. Now, one might object:

Since the knowledge of that [property] is the cause of a cognition possessing that mode, and since validity has not yet been presented prior to the aforementioned determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*), how could there be the possibility of the manifestation of validity in the indicated determinate cognition?
To this, he says: "[239] *viśiṣṭa*... (qualified).
Regarding the term "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*):
it refers to the phrase beginning with "of that nature" (*tadrūpa*) and so forth.
The word "as far as" (*yāvat*) is a qualifier of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). For this very reason, [it is stated] further on:

It was stated that "as far as the apprehension of knowledge" [is concerned]. Since opponents do not admit that validity—defined as the state of being the instrument of valid cognition—is apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*), and thus no investigation into it is possible for them, he says: "But in reality... [268].

As for the claim that the exclusion of being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramitikaraṇatva*) by means of the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is not possible [because it would also exclude] inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) and so forth—

The explanation—"because it is the instrument of valid cognition (pramiti-karaṇatva), therefore he says 'in reality' (vastutas tu)"—is incorrect. This is because the intended emphasis of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) "validity belongs to knowledge alone" is possible only through the exclusion of the commonality of being an instrument of valid cognition, which applies equally to the sense organs (*indriya*). [Otherwise] everything...

By the maxim that "the meaning is obtained through the word itself," such a meaning is secured by the word alone. Now, one might object: since it is impossible to apprehend all individual instances of qualified cognitions (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), their inclusion [in the definition] is not possible; therefore—
He says: "taddharma" (its property).
The meaning is that the phrase "yāvat" (as far as/as much as) has the sense of being a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the delimitor of the referent (*arthatāvacchedaka*) of the word co-uttered with it.
[274] *Phalataḥ*— that is, from the perspective of the intended meaning (*tātparya*). [268] *Samānyataḥ*— in the form of a generality (*sāmānya*).

That is to say, by "cognition-ness" (jñānatva) as qualified by the property of having that [object] as its qualifier (taddharmaprakārakatva). The suffix -tasil is used here in the sense of "in relation to" (vaiśiṣṭye) with respect to the cognition.
Otherwise, [there would be no distinction between] validity consisting of pot-ness and so forth...
Because there would be a contradiction in the positive formulation, due to the absence of being apprehended by that which apprehends a cognition having "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) etc. as its qualifier;
[as seen] in the cognition "this cognition is valid."

The statement in the *Dīpikā*, "because of the apprehension of validity residing in the self-referential after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), [and] because of the non-apprehension of validity," is inconsistent; therefore, he says: "[274] 'Residing in the primary cognition' (*vyavasāyaniṣṭha*), etc.
This is because it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) itself that apprehends validity, and thus it is the apprehender of validity residing in the after-cognition.
Thus, one might argue that the feminine gender alone should be employed; to this he says: "In the general sense" (*sāmānye*).
The meaning is that since the specific gender is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*), the neuter alone should be used for the designation, and therefore the aforementioned fault does not apply.
In order to prevent the misconception that "its invalidity" (*tasyāprāmāṇyam*) is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, it is stated as a locative:
"in such validity," and so forth.
Here is the essential point:
Validity as constituted by that property is something qualified;
this qualification [is defined] by the relation of both identity and being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in itself.
The delimitingness [of the counter-correlativity] is by way of the relation of being the delimitingness of the counter-correlativity of a difference that is co-locational with itself;
[this is] its own substratumhood.
By way of the relation of being produced by the causal complex that apprehends a cognition whose qualifier is that property as qualified by itself (*sva*).

The qualification by itself (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of the relation of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity has its locus of delimitation residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhāvacchedakatākapratiyogitākabhedavattva*). [Note:
In all these instances, the word *sva* refers to the cognition (*jñāna*).]
This is focused on the validity constituted by those properties.
The term "qualified by itself" (*svaviśiṣṭa*) is construed with the "cognitive-apprehending complex" (*jñānagrāhakasāmagrī*).

[The relation is] by way of the relation of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimitor residing in itself, which is delimited by the relation of being the generator of a cognition characterized by a subjecthood residing in its own substratum and a qualifierhood residing in invalidity.

The delimitingness (avacchedakatā), which is delimited by the relation of subjectivity (viṣayitā) as determined by itself, and which is defined by the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the difference residing in the cognition produced by that causal complex (sāmagrī) which apprehends the cognition having that property as its qualifier (prakāra), and which is qualified by itself.

The result is that validity consists in being qualified by some [property] through that relation— which is the delimitation of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in itself as delimited by its connection with that [object]— and through the relation of identity, [the property] being constituted by that [specific] attribute.
The manner of this concomitance is as follows:
validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in having "pot-ness" as its qualifier (*prakāraka*) with respect to that which possesses pot-ness; the locus of that [validity] is the true cognition, "This is a pot."

The capacity to produce a cognition having as its qualifier the lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*) with respect to that [object] does not exist in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that apprehends the cognition "this is a jar"; therefore,
that causal complex [is characterized by] its own substratum (*svāśraya*), etc., through the relation delimited by such a capacity to produce [the cognition of] validity (*pramātva*).
It possesses a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the state of being the ultimate limit (*niṣṭhāvacchedakatā*).

Therefore, that which is qualified by itself through the relation of possessing such a difference is the aforementioned causal complex; the cognition produced by that complex is the cognition having the cognition of a jar as its object, and the difference residing therein—
The absence of the truth-status (pramātva) consisting of "pot-ness" does not exist by way of the relation of subjectivity as defined by itself,
because it possesses such a truth-status through that very relation; rather, there is the absence of something else.

The state of being the delimiting factor of that counter-correlativity does not exist in the nature of valid cognition (*pramātva*) as constituted by "pot-ness"; thus, there is a difference residing in such a *pramātva*— in relation to which the counter-correlativity is delimited— by means of the relation of such delimitation,
[namely] in the *pramātva* as constituted by "pot-ness."
And since that identity exists therein, the establishment of the two relations [of inherence and identity] is possible;
this should be inferred in the same way for subsequent inclusions as well.

The delimitingness (*avacchedakatā*) [of the qualifier] is related by the relation of being the producer of a cognition possessing a qualificand-ness residing in itself and a mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).
The delimitingness of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the difference is related by the relation of the objectivity (*viṣayitā*) as determined by itself. Alternatively:
The state of being qualified by subjecthood (*viṣayitā*).

The state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of both relations: the relation of being its own determiner (*svanirūpakatva*), and the relation of being the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) of a difference residing in itself (*svavṛtti*).

The state of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) [is defined] by the relation of being the delimitation of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatā*) of a difference that is co-locus with itself.
The state of being its locus (*svādhikaraṇatā*) is the state of having its own substratum as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), and so forth, as previously explained.

And here, in this view that the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) consists of as many factors as there are, "being somewhat distinguished" refers to the coarse persistence (*sthūlānugama*); such is the distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*).
[The relation is] by way of both identity (*tādātmya*) and being the object of a cognition qualified by itself (*svaviśiṣṭajñānaviṣayatva*).

The qualification by itself (*svavaiśiṣṭya*) [is established] by way of the relation of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, which delimitation is in turn delimited by the relation of being the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of a difference that is co-located with itself (*svasamānādhikaraṇabhedapratiyogitāvacchedakatvasambandha*).
The state of having itself as the locus [is defined] by the relation of being a non-distributive (vyāsajyavṛtti) property that delimits the capacity to apprehend a cognition qualified by itself.
The qualification by itself [is as follows]:...

[The relation is] by way of possessing a difference whose counterpositiveness has as its delimitation a locus-delimitation residing in itself, which is delimited by the relation of being the deliminator of the capacity to produce a cognition having non-validity as its qualifier and having its own substratum as its qualificandum.
The delimitation of the counterpositiveness of that difference [is determined] by the relation of being the deliminator of the capacity to produce itself.
By this, [the fault of] infinite [regress] regarding the infinite...

Even if there is no fault in the difficulty of incorporating those respective causes— whether belonging to another place or another time— into the body of "self-validity" (svatastva) because they are difficult for one who is not omniscient to know,
such is the case according to the views of the Guru and others.

It is not easy to prove that this cognition possesses a specific qualification as defined by the statement "it is mutually heterogeneous," on the grounds that it is a collection of causes such as volitional effort (*vyavasāya*) and so forth.
He raises an objection: "[274] But surely... (*nanu*).
He establishes the lack of proof with the words "na hi" (for not).
[264] "Eka" means of one kind. [274] The syntactical connection is that "it is not produced. And in this case...

Insofar as all such properties possess the status of being objects of a cognition produced by that [definition], while simultaneously possessing the status of being objects of a cognition produced by that [definition]— in this manner, self-validity (*svatastva*) is the property to be proven; thus, there is no lack of locus for the probans (*aprasiddhi*).
He raises an objection: "If not," etc.

Now, one might argue that the purpose of the term *agrāhakānta* (ending with "non-apprehender"), which was mentioned first, ought to be stated first; yet, having set that aside, why is the purpose of the qualifier *yāvatva* (as-many-as), mentioned last, being stated first?
Desiring to dispel the doubt that it is inappropriate to state the purpose (*prayojana*), he says: "As long as... and so forth.
The underlying intention is this: for the purpose of that which lacks a grasper (*agrāhaka*) at its end...
The exclusion of the causal complex that apprehends invalidity cannot be accomplished unless "all-inclusiveness" (yāvattva) is included within that complex;
for [the doctrine of] the intrinsic nature of validity (svatastva-prāmāṇya) is established by taking into account the causal complex that apprehends validity.
Because it is easily established;

for if those qualifiers were present there, then since the causal complex apprehending non-validity would also be included among such [qualifiers], validity would not be apprehended by it, and thus there would be a contradiction (bādha).
[He states: "Insofar as the qualification 'all' (yāvattva) serves to establish the meaningfulness of the final term 'non-apprehender' (agrāhaka).

First—prior to stating the purpose of the term 'non-apprehender'—he demonstrates how the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) is to be avoided by means of the qualification 'all' applied to the causal complex (sāmagrī).

Regarding the term "Naiyāyika": although, in the affirmative alternative (*vidhikoṭi*), it is possible for the qualification "as many as" (*yāvattva*) to serve the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), such a possibility does not exist in the negative alternative (*niṣedhakoṭi*). Nevertheless...
He states that the avoidance of contradiction alone is possible as the result in the negative alternative: "naiyāyika...
By the phrase "and by the statement," the meaning of the word "etcetera" in "inference etcetera" is explained. [273–274]

In the statement, "This knowledge is not valid because validity is not apprehended by that knowledge," the meaning obtained according to the literal reading is: "because there is an absence of the apprehension of validity induced by such a cognition."
And that [objection] is irrelevant to the present context,
because it is sublation (bādha) alone that must be discussed here.
Therefore, he explains that "due to the non-apprehension of validity" means "due to the non-objectification of validity" with the words beginning "prāmāṇya...
and "tādṛśa...".
This means that it has the form "this is knowledge" or "this is valid.
By that aforementioned collection of conditions for knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*), it is "qualified," which means it is delimited (*avacchinna*). Even though...
In the cognition "this knowledge is valid," validity is the object by way of being its counter-correlative (*pratiyogitā*);

nevertheless, *svataḥ-prāhyatva* (self-validity) consists in being an object characterized by a relation of counter-correlativity that is grasped by a cognition produced by the very same causal complex that grasps the knowledge itself; or alternatively, [it may be defined as follows].

There is no inconsistency, because pervasion is intended here in the sense of being related to its own locus through the relation of having a qualificandum-ness residing in its own locus as determined by a qualifier-ness residing in itself (*svāśrayaniṣṭhaviśeṣyatānirūpitasvaniṣṭhaprakāratākatva*).
Thus, it is grasped by itself.
This must be considered here: by connecting the word *eva* immediately after [the verb], the meaning is "it is indeed grasped.
Thus, this *eva* is connected with the action, as in the case of "a blue lotus" (*nīlaṃ sarojaṃ*).
It is just like [the expression] "it exists indeed";
therefore, there is no contradiction, and thus his statement that [the suffix] has no meaning is untenable.
This is what should be understood here: when all the factors of the causal complex are included, the state of being qualified by knowledge is subtle conformity (*sūkṣmānugama*).
This is the specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*).

[The relation is] by way of both the relation of being an object (*viṣayatva*) and the relation of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference residing in itself (*svavṛtti*).

The delimitingness (*avacchedakatā*) [is defined] by the relation of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference co-located with itself (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*). The property of having itself as its locus (*svādhikaraṇatva*), etc., is as before. [274] Specifically—
By virtue of being the aggregate of those respective causes;
likewise hereafter as well.
Regarding the phrase "by way of having that form," it refers to [the object] in cognition.
The subtle investigation is that as long as there is non-inclusion, there is the state of being qualified by difference;
this qualification [of difference] occurs through the relation of both being the delimiting factor of its own counter-correlate and being its own locus.
The property of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is delimited by the relation of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference co-located with itself.
The state of being its locus (*svādhikaraṇatā*) is [defined] by the relation of being a cognition produced by the causal complex that grasps a cognition qualified by itself.

Its own specific property [is established] by way of the relation of possessing a difference whose counterpositiveness is delimited by a delimitation residing in itself, which is itself delimited by the relation of being the generator of a cognition having non-validity as its qualifier and having its own substratum as its qualificandum.
The delimitation of the counterpositiveness of that difference is [further] delimited by the relation of subject-matter (viṣayatā) as determined by itself.

He says: "Even when the two are not present.
The meaning is this:
the causality of the cognition of the qualifier is distinct for each instance according to the difference between the qualifiers.
In the present context, such a postulation of causality is not made merely to conform to the result.

Now, it may be argued that both the Guru and the Bhaṭṭa have established the apprehension of validity through two types of inference based on the marks of determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) and cognizedness (*jñātatā*). [242]
Having raised the doubt as to how the statement "by means of *anuvyavasāya*" appears in the *Dīpikā*, he states that it intends the opinion of Miśra— (namely, "And this...")—
and that the manner of its refutation is to be understood.

And this being the case, there is no inconsistency in the status of the jar and so forth as the object (*karman*) of the action of knowing in such cognitions as "I know the jar," because the nature of being an object consists precisely in possessing a result produced by the action.
In this regard, it must be stated that a second [application] is untenable;
for since possessing such a result constitutes the nature of primary objecthood (*mukhyakarmatā*), that [objecthood] is admitted only in cases such as "he goes to the village" (*grāmaṃ gacchati*).

This is because [the status of being an object] is not accepted in cases such as "he knows the jar," since in those instances only a secondary objecthood characterized by "object-sphere-ness" (viṣayatā) is admitted; otherwise,
[it would follow that the same applies to] "he desires the jar" or "he hates the jar."
"Because it would entail the postulation of another category of entity, such as 'desirability' (iṣṭatva) and so forth.
This is the summary;
the underlying point is as follows:
