The state of having its invalidity ungrasped (*agṛhītāprāmāṇyakatva*) means being unassailed by a cognition of invalidity; and that [state] is an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the property of "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*), as qualified by the relation consisting of both [the relation of] being the qualificandum as determined by the modehood of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-prakāratā-nirūpita-viśeṣyatva*) and the relation of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
In this same manner, the absence of a cognition of error (*bhramatva-jñāna*) and the absence of the grasping of truth (*pramātva-graha*) are also to be included.

Thus, regarding the cognition of invalidity, in a case where a cognition of invalidity has arisen, a distinct causal status must be postulated for it as "the state of being a cognition of invalidity whose locus is a cognition of invalidity," in order to account for the occurrence of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
More on this should be seen in the *Prāmāṇyavāda* and other works.
This refers to the reason that establishes validity (*prāmāṇya*), such as its being the cause of successful activity (*saphalapravṛttijanakatva*), and so forth;
for even the Mīmāṃsakas accept that validity is apprehended extrinsically (*parataḥ*).

Anticipating the objection that this would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), he explains by supplying the word "only" (*eva*): "The validity [of cognition] is [known] only from inference and so forth.
By this, he establishes the impossibility of the manifestation of validity in the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) and other such instances.
"Deviation" (vyabhicāra) refers to the section beginning with "negative concomitance" (vyatireka), etc. Likewise,
"in the case of cognition," etc.

The resulting cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvaya-bodha*) is as follows: it is the word that is conducive to a knowledge whose qualifier is "extrinsic validity" (*paratastva*) having as its subject a manifestation (*jñapti*) characterized by the previously mentioned mode; and it is the agent of that [word].
[287] Regarding the word *mātra*: the term *mātra* here signifies exclusivity (*evam-kevala*) and entirety (*kṛtsna*).

The meaning of "exclusion" (vyudāsa) is that [the definition] does not apply to cognitions such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and the like; this is the intended sense. Now, one might object: the state of being a unique cause of valid cognition (*pramā*) consists in being a cause as defined by an effectness delimited by a property other than the effectness residing in valid cognition.

And thus, even if time and so forth are excluded, it is impossible to exclude the self (ātman) and so forth; therefore, he says: "The state of being a cause... and so on. The essential meaning is: "the state of being a cause as determined by an effecthood qualified by the property of being a valid cognition (pramātva). As for the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*):...
By means of the two relations of "subsisting in its own locus" and "being delimited by a property qualified by itself.
1. Regarding "svādhikaraṇa," etc.: subsistence in its own locus—

The meaning is as follows: "the causality of a cognition that is common to all valid cognitions" refers to the causality defined by a specific effect-nature (*kāryatā*) which is qualified by "truth" (*pramātva*) through two relations: (1) being delimited by a property possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is determined by a deliminator residing in itself, and (2) being delimited by a property possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is determined by a deliminator residing in its own locus and residing in the locus of its own absence. Both these relations are delimited by the relation consisting of both: (a) residing in its own locus, and (b) residing in the locus of its own absence.
Its own validity, its locus is valid cognition; its being resident therein [is its presence] in the effect. Likewise, its own validity, its locus is valid cognition...

Cognitivity (jñānatva) exists in knowledge (pramā), which is its own validity (prāmāṇya); it also exists in error (bhrama), which is the locus of the absence of that [validity]. Thus, cognitivity is related [to both] by way of the two relations: subsisting in its own locus and subsisting in the locus of its own absence.
Like validity (*prāmāṇya*),
validity itself is not thus [subject to doubt],
because it lacks the property of residing in a locus where validity is absent; therefore...

The logical connection (*samanvaya*) should be understood as follows: validity (*pramātva*) possesses a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by a delimiting factor residing in validity itself, which is in turn delimited by both such relations; and this being delimited by that [difference] exists in the effectness (*kāryatā*) residing in valid cognition. Thus, through both relations, the effectness becomes qualified by validity.
Specificity (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [is defined] by the relation of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) has its own locus as the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*).
Delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*).
[The definition is qualified] by the relation consisting of both: (1) subsisting in its own locus, and (2) subsisting in the locus of its own absence.
He states the result of including "valid cognition" (*pramā*) within the property of being an effect (*kāryatā*) in the passage beginning with "[287] *bhrama*...
The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*) includes such cases as the delusion of a snake in a bamboo pole.
[287] By the phrase "bile, etc.," the application of frog-fat and so forth is included.
[289] Regarding "discrepancy":
it occurs in that which lacks that [object].
The meaning is "having that as its qualifier. By the phrase "to be understood," it is indicated that [the objection] arises because the locus (dharmin) is not established.
The doubt that "sitting down" (niṣedha) is untenable has been dispelled.
By the phrase "established as necessary," the doubt regarding the equality of postulation (kalpanā) is refuted.

[Objection: But surely, since it is possible for the mere non-apprehension of the difference from what is desired to function as the cause, the qualification "independently presented" (*svatantropasthitatva*) regarding the desired object is redundant;
to this he says: "[289] *etāvatā*... [Objection: But surely...
The use of the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only of the non-apprehension of the difference from the desired object" is inconsistent;
for since memory also requires [the apprehension of the object], it is impossible for that particle to exclude anything else.
To this, he says: "By the word *eva*... [289]
"Because of parsimony.

The sense is that otherwise, by including the additional factor of "having that as its qualifier in that which possesses it," there would be a lack of parsimony (gaurava) regarding the delimiting condition of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka).
[289] "Common" means in a common form. Non-difference is the meaning of the suffix, which is connected with the state of being a function. This is the definition of an invalid cognition.
[292] Regarding the phrase "a particular location" and so forth:
"a particular location" refers to a specific channel of sleep (*nidrā-nāḍī*).
The meaning is that the mind, being situated therein, is conjoined with the self. Regarding the phrase "having that as its non-inherent cause" and so forth, the intended sense is as follows:

The term "dream" (svapna) has a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) that refers specifically to a particular type of cognition; by the phrase "having that as its non-inherent cause," the relationship with the primary meaning (śakyasambandha) is indicated. Thus, it is figurative (bhākta), that is, based on secondary indication (lākṣaṇika).

The meaning is that this contradicts the commentary, because dream-cognition is observed to have as its object things never previously experienced, whereas recollection does not possess such a character.

Anticipating the objection that the purpose of introducing "manifoldness" (*nānātva*) could also be the exclusion of the cognition "it possesses cloth-ness" (*paṭatvavān*), and that therefore the pursuit of the cognition "it possesses cloth-ness which is contradictory to pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvaviruddhapaṭatvavān*) is fruitless, he says:

—[292] Regarding the phrase "of the two extremes": one might object that even in the cognition "that which possesses cloth-ness, which is contradictory to pot-ness," there exists the property of having multiple attributes (*dharma*) such as pot-ness and cloth-ness as qualifiers; how, then, is this [cognition] excluded?
To this, he says: —[293] "having a single attribute-bearer" (*ekadharmika*).
The meaning is this:
doubt consists in being a cognition qualified by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*). As for this qualification—

[The relation is] by means of both relations: (1) being qualified by its own [property] through the relation of being determined by a subjecthood that is delimited by its own [property], which is in turn determined by a subjecthood that is determined by a contradiction-ness which is determined by its own determiner; and (2) being determined by a subjecthood that co-exists with the qualificandumhood determined by itself.
Even so, "the mountain..."

He raises the objection that over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is unavoidable in the cognition "this possesses fire; it is a substance; like a person who produces what is incompatible with fire" — [293] no.
And so on; "delimited by a single property," etc.
This is the intended meaning:
in a case where there is co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by itself.

Having introduced the property of being "qualified by a qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) that is delimited by its own designated delimitor of qualificandumness," the rest should be understood as before. This concludes the "direction" (dig).
1. Regarding the phrase beginning with "prakāratāviśiṣṭa" and so forth: [The full definition follows].
In the doubt "Is the mountain fiery or not?", fire and its absence are the qualifiers (*prakāra*).
The contradiction between fire and its absence appears as the relation (*saṃsarga*).

The state of affairs is this: the qualificand-ness residing in the mountain (parvata) as determined by the qualifier-ness residing in fire (vahni) is one thing, while the qualificand-ness residing in the mountain as determined by the qualifier-ness residing in the absence of fire (vahnayabhāva) is another. Keeping this in mind, the consistency of the subsumption (anugama) is to be understood.

For instance: "svam" (itself) refers to the property-ness residing in fire (*vahniniṣṭhaprakāratā*); "tannirūpakatvam" (the state of being its determiner) resides in the cognition consisting of the aforementioned doubt. Likewise, "svam" refers to the property-ness residing in fire; that which is delimited by it is the object-ness (*viṣayatā*) residing in fire.
(The objectivity determined by the objectivity residing in contradiction):
the objectivity residing in contradiction as determined by that [objectivity] is the objectivity residing in the absence of fire.

The state of being delimited by that [mountain] resides in the qualificative-ness (prakāratā) residing in the absence of fire; it is co-extensive with that qualificative-ness which resides in the mountain and is determined by the mountain-residing qualificative-ness that is itself determined by the qualificative-ness residing in fire.
This [latter] qualificative-ness residing in the mountain is determined by the qualificative-ness residing in the absence of fire.

And since that [determinability] resides in the qualificative-ness (prakāratā) residing in the absence of fire, the state of being the determiner of that qualificative-ness— which is qualified by the qualificative-ness residing in fire through both relations—
exists in the doubt "Is the mountain fiery or not? In this regard:
The subjecthood residing in fire, which is determined by the objecthood called "the relation residing in contradiction," is delimited by the predicatehood residing in fire,

which is itself determined by the qualificandhood residing in the mountain; that which is the predicatehood residing in the absence of fire, determined by the qualificandhood residing in the mountain...

It should also be noted that this is because of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the objectivity residing in the absence of fire (*vahnayabhāva*), which is characterized by the objectivity residing in contradiction (*virodha*), is delimited by the objectivity residing in the intermediate appearing entity; thus, there exists a relationship of the delimited and the delimiting (*avacchedyāvacchedakabhāva*) between the two objectivities residing in the intermediate appearing entities.
2. The rest is as before. Thus, doubt is the state of being a cognition qualified by a mode (prakāratā). And this qualification (vaiśiṣṭya) is...

The meaning is as follows: [it consists in] being qualified by itself through two relations: (1) being delimited by the objectness (*viṣayatā*) which is determined by the objectness of contradiction (*virodha*), which in turn is determined by the objectness delimited by itself; and (2) being the determiner of a qualifierhood (*prakāratā*) that is qualified by itself through two relations: [the first being] being delimited by the delimitor of the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) determined by that [objectness], and [the second being] being determined by the qualificandhood determined by that [delimitor].
The intended meaning is this: although there is identity between each pair of properties, nevertheless [the relation] is by way of both of the following connections:

(1) having a qualifierhood residing in that [property] which is qualified by its own delimitor, and (2) having a qualifierhood residing in the absence of that [property] which is qualified by its own delimitor.
Doubtfulness consists in being a cognition qualified by a property, or alternatively, in being a cognition possessing a qualifierhood that is itself qualified by another qualifierhood.

In the second [definition], the distinction [of the counter-positive] is established by a triple relation consisting of: (1) being qualified by the subjecthood delimited by the delimitor of the subjecthood as determined by itself; (2) being qualified by the viṣayatā (cognitive content) of contradiction, which is itself qualified by the viṣayatā delimited by its own delimitor; and (3) not being delimited by that which is not the delimitor of itself. Therefore, there is no fault.
[293] In another tantra— that is, in the Advaitaśāstra—

by the phrase "tatprakārakatva" and so forth, there is the inclusion of the state of having a qualifier residing in that [object], which is determined by a qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in that which possesses the absence of that [qualifier].

[293] Regarding the term "in brief" (*saṅkṣepa*): this is the intended meaning— namely, that although there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in partial doubts such as "this is silver" or "is the ground possessed of a jar or not," [the definition still holds].
Nevertheless, there is no fault, because the exclusion of doubt with respect to that particular aspect has been included;
and the state of being a doubt with respect to that aspect [occurs] in a single [locus].
"Having as its modes both that [property] and its absence in the locus (*dharmī*).
[293] "In the case of a branch," etc.
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*)—for the purpose of establishing that the ascertainment of being a person (*puruṣatva*) is an artificial (*āhārya*) [cognition].

This is because the desire "May the ascertainment of being a person arise" must be expressible [as the object of the word]; otherwise, the definition of *āhāryatva* (the state of being a mental imposition), characterized as knowledge produced by a desire existing at the time of sublation, would be impossible in that case.
This is so according to the view that knowledge and desire arise simultaneously, precisely in such a state of error.
It should be understood that this is because of the possibility of desire and so forth;
"utility" means being the motivator.
By the phrase "to be experienced" (*vedanīyam*) and so forth, there is an inclusion of suffering (*duḥkha*) as that which is to be experienced through its disagreeable nature.
By the phrase "pleasure and so forth" (*sukhādi*), there is the inclusion of suffering.
[298] "Because it is not over-pervasive" (*avyāpteḥ*).
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*);
for [the rule] does not apply to the case of improper words (*asādhūnām*), which result in the suffering of hell and so forth produced by the enjoyment of another's property and the like.
Because hatred is not observed, there is also no pervasion— [this refers to] "delimited by itself" (*svāvacchinna*) and so forth; here,
"itself" (*sva*) is the nature of being a mountain (*parvatatva*).

The property of being the determiner of a fire-locusness-type (prakāratā) qualified by a qualificandumness (viśeṣyatā) delimited by that [mountain] exists in the doubt "Is the mountain fiery or not?"; likewise, "self" here refers to mountainhood.

The syntactic connection is as follows: "and the state of being the determiner of the qualificandumness delimited by that [mountain], which is itself determined by the fire-absence-ness residing in the fire-absence, belongs to such a doubt.
2. Regarding the phrase beginning with "svanirūpita" (determined by itself), etc.:
One's own [the smoke's] *prakāratā* residing in fire; the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the *viśeṣyatā* residing in the mountain as determined by that [fire], namely *parvatatva* (mountain-ness);
and the property of being determined by a *viśeṣyatā* delimited by that [mountain-ness] existing in the *prakāratā* residing in the absence of fire. Thus...
One's own [determinant] is the property of being a qualificand residing in fire (*vahniniṣṭhaprakāratā*); its delimitor is the nature of fire (*vahnitva*).
There is, then, a state of being determined by that which is the objectness residing in contradiction (*virodha*), which is itself determined by the objectness delimited by that [nature of fire].
This state of being determined resides in the property of being a qualificand residing in the absence of fire (*vahnyabhāvaniṣṭhaprakāratā*). Thus, one's own...

The property of being a qualifier residing in fire (*vahniniṣṭhaprakāratā*) has as its non-delimiter the nature of the absence of fire (*vahnayabhāvatva*); and this [non-delimitedness] by that [nature of the absence of fire] exists in the property of being a qualifier residing in the absence of fire (*vahnayabhāvaniṣṭhaprakāratā*).
Furthermore, that [property of being a qualifier residing in the absence of fire] is the nature of the cognition "it is a hill" (*tadālijñānatva*), which exists in the doubt;
thus is the formal application (*samanvaya*).
It should be understood that by the phrase "I am happy," and so forth, the notion "I am suffering" is included; the same applies to what follows.
The purpose of the definition of memory as "that which is produced by experience" is stated in the *Dīpikā* [299]:

Regarding the phrase "in the case of the self, etc.": one might raise the objection that if the exclusion of the self and so forth is achieved merely by including the property of being produced (*janyatva*), then the inclusion of the term "experience" (*anubhava*) is redundant; in response to this doubt, it is stated: "at the outset."
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), the conjunction of the self and the mind is included.
The nature of experience (anubhavatva) consists in being a cognition distinct from memory.

And thus, in response to the objection that it is more appropriate for [cognition] to possess causal efficacy by virtue of being merely "cognition" (jñānatva) due to parsimony— since there is complexity in including "distinctness from memory" (smṛtibhinnatva) within the body of the delimiting condition of causality— it is stated in the *Prakāśikā*:
[300] "Of experience as well" means "as a universal. As for the proof in that regard:

It should be understood that "I experience" is indeed a reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya), just as "I know" is a reflective awareness in the case of [the awareness of] the nature of cognition (jñānatva).

"Because it is the determiner of otherwise-establishedness (*anyathāsiddhi*)" means "because it is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to the difference from those respective properties. The underlying sense is that otherwise,
there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in accepting as causes those memories which are not actually causes at all.
[300] "Produced by itself" (*svajanya*): "itself" (*sva*) refers to the formative predisposition (*saṃskāra*). The same applies to what follows.
In order to dispel the doubt that memory arises from another subsequent experience, [the author uses] the words "at once" (*sakṛt*) and so forth, as well as "final" (*carama*).

In this context, "being the final [cognition]" consists in not being simultaneous with the prior absence of a memory that has the same object as itself and is produced by the saṃskāra (latent impression) produced by its own producer,
[defined] by the conjunction of three relations: being simultaneous with its own prior absence, being produced by the saṃskāra produced by its own producer, and having the same object as itself.

It culminates in the distinctness of that which is governed by memory. Regarding the phrase "by way of its own individuality in the future," this is what must be considered here: [is it] by way of an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*)?

There is no obstacle to accepting that, with respect to the destruction of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) having a certain object, the final recollection (*smṛti*) having that same object is the cause by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*); otherwise,
one would have to take into account factors such as contact with air (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) occurring at the same time as that [recollection].
Because it would result in the fallacy of lacking a determining factor;
for a formative force (*saṃskāra*) is destroyed by its fruit.

By this, the objection that the occurrence of a subsequent recollection after a prior recollection is possible through the operation of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the form of a mental trace from a previously arisen experience is refuted; for at that time, the operation consisting of the latent impression has already perished, and thus it cannot serve as such a medium.
This is because the original experience no longer exists at the time of the subsequent memory,
and it is universally accepted that an experience is the cause of memory only through its operation in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
[300] "Of that which has exactly the same object-domain" means:

the intended sense is by way of the two relations of being co-located (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and being a locus of inherence (ādheyatva) as delimited by the relation of possessing distinctions such as "being similar to itself," and so forth.

Alternatively, the causality of memory (*smṛti*) should be accepted as being established by a dual relation: (1) the state of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference (*bheda*) that is co-located with itself; and (2) the state of not being co-located (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the state of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in itself, which is delimited by the relation of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference co-located with itself.
[The term *svādhikaraṇatā* refers to the locus of "self."]
The relation is that of being the object as determined by itself;
the delimitation of the counter-correlativity of difference is also by that very same relation.
[300] "Immediately upon recollection," and so forth.

This is for the purpose of indicating the specific genus that serves as the probans (*pramāṇa*); the meaning is that it is the delimitor of the capacity to produce immediate recollection. And the probans should be understood as an inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) is the capacity to produce [recollection].

[300] *Saṃskārātiśayaḥ*—a specific type of latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing within the latent impression itself. Now, one might object that the definition of a latent impression as "that which is produced by experience" and so forth is under-extended (*avyāpti*) to a latent impression produced by another latent impression (such as memory). To this, he says: [300] *etanmate*—"in this view," namely, in the view of the Neo-Nyāya (*navya*) school.
This is the meaning.
The definition of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) begins with "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth.

The resulting definition is: *guṇatva* (the nature of being a quality) is that which possesses a *jāti* (universal) that does not reside in anything qualified by a *dravyavibhājakopādhi* (a property that divides substances), with respect to both relations: (1) residing in its own substratum (*svādhikaraṇavṛttitva*), and (2) residing in the substratum of a *dravyavibhājakopādhi* that is distinct from itself (*svabhinnadravyavibhājakopādhyadhikaraṇavṛttitva*).
Here, it is stated "respectively" (*pratyekam*) because there is no established instance (*aprasiddhi*) of a single substratum for such a pair of properties.
[303] Because it is of such a nature— that is, because it does not subsist in that which is qualified by the attributes that differentiate substances.
[303] "Intermediate" (avāntara) means "pervaded" (vyāpya).
The same applies to what follows.

Regarding the phrase "such two limiting adjuncts" (*tādṛśopādhidvaya*) and so forth: it refers to the state of being other than that which is qualified by the limiting adjuncts that differentiate substances (*dravyavibhājakopādhiviśiṣṭānyatvam*).
It is intended to be expressed by the end of the word *śūnya*.
The state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [is established] through the relation of possessing a genus that resides in what is qualified by itself and is co-extensive with a quality (*guṇatva*).

Its own specific property [is defined] by way of both relations: [1] subsisting in its own locus, and [2] subsisting in the locus of a category-delimiting attribute (upādhi) that divides substance and is distinct from itself;
for number-ness (saṃkhyātva) and so forth exist [in this manner]. [303]
The meaning is that because such numbers as duality (dvitva) and so forth exist as subsisting in those [entities].
[303] "Blue-ness and so forth," etc.
Although it is possible for the definition to apply even by taking color-ness (*rūpatva*) and so forth into account at this point, nevertheless,
color-ness and the like have been set aside in accordance with the refinements that will be explained later. Here...

The qualification "subsisting in fewer loci" (*nyūnavṛttitva*) is included in order to avoid the fallacy of impossibility (*asambhava*) by taking properties such as *guṇatva* (the nature of being a quality) and so forth;
this is expressed in the phrase "delimited by whatever form" (*yadrūpāvacchinna*), etc.
The meaning is as follows:

the definition of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is the state of being a quality that possesses a genus residing in both elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*) and those [qualities] qualified by the attributes that differentiate substances (*dravyavibhājakopādhi*).

And the specific distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [of the locus] is by way of the two relations: (1) being the delimiting factor of the occurrence in its own substratum, and (2) being the delimiting factor of the occurrence in the substratum of a property that distinguishes substances and is distinct from itself.
By this means, there is no complexity resulting from the necessity of introducing a collection of differences (*bhedakūṭa*).

Furthermore, there would be a lack of systematic consistency (ananugama) resulting from the introduction of some unspecified property as a differentiator for the natural application of co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya), which is delimited by the state of being those two such limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
If, instead, one were to introduce the negation of any single such [property], then, taking the negation of "oneness-ness" (ekatvatva) and so forth into account...
There would be the over-extension [of the definition] to duality and so forth;

for in this way, since duality in the form of number is impossible within a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), it must be expressed as having the nature of being an object dependent upon a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).
Because there is no lack of a single qualified meaning through the entry into the reality of that which possesses great respect,
and because there is no occasion for the consequence of a split in the sentence in cases such as "form is a specific quality" (*rūpaṃ viśeṣaguṇaḥ*),
[the definition] is formulated as being constituted precisely by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*); otherwise, [it would not be so].

[The opponent replies: "It should not be included," because this would lead to the fault of impossibility (asambhava) by taking into account a co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) constituted by relations such as those of time (kālika) and so forth.
The underlying point is that the property of elasticity (sthitasthāpakatva) cannot be grasped by the term "whatever form" (yadrūpa).

Now, since it has been stated that the earth and wind possess neither-hot-nor-cold [touch], and because "neither-hot-nor-cold" can be grasped by the word *rūpa*, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) regarding the touch that is neither-hot-nor-cold; to this, he says:
"[304] *pārthiva* (belonging to the earth)."
And thus, even in that case, the application of the definition is achieved by taking into account a specific difference in kind (*vaijātya*); this is the intended meaning.
"In that" refers to number and so forth.
The same applies further on.
"Such" means by way of the relationship already stated.
The meaning is "those qualified by the qualifiers that differentiate substances.
As for what has been stated by someone else—
that the definition should simply be "the state of being a quality (guṇatva) while possessing such a genus"— why [is this unnecessary]?

Regarding the phrase "by means of employing two negations"—that is not so; for if that were the case, there would be the over-extension [of the definition] to specific qualities such as color (rūpa) by taking the universal "color-ness" (rūpatva) and so forth.
However, when two negations are employed...
Since there is no possibility of over-extension (ativyāpti) due to the existence of such universals as blueness (nīlatva), that [definition] is necessary;
thus ends the definition of action (karmanirūpaṇa) as stated in the root text.
The meaning is that there is no pervasion (avyāpti) in the action of folding leaves and so forth; this is what is meant by "he says.
The phrase "he says" means he says with such an intention.
This concludes the definition of the universal (sāmānya).

Now, one might object that including "oneness" (*ekatva*) in the definition of universals (*sāmānya*) is fruitless; therefore, he says: "[309] the word 'one'. Now, regarding the definition of a universal...

Is the "oneness" that enters into the constitution of "manyness"— which consists of a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by oneness— of the nature of number, or is it a property residing in only one [individual]?
Not the first, because qualities and so forth are not admitted to possess further qualities and so forth.

Even if [the definition] applies to "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and so forth by means of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it is under-extended (*avyāpti*) with respect to "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth. Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable; for since such a property is purely positive (*kevalānvayin*), a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by it is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).

Not so; for in this context, "subsisting in many" means either being qualified by the object of cognition (*prameya*) or being qualified by difference (*bheda*). In the first case, the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of both the relation of subsistence in itself and the relation of subsistence in something other than itself. In the second case...
By means of both relations— namely, inherence in its own counter-positive and inherence in its own substratum— therefore there is no fault. This concludes the definition of *viśeṣa*.
[309] "Mutually" means:
the state of being mutual is the state of being determined by a locus that is itself determined by a difference residing in its own substratum.
This results in being qualified by difference through the two relations of "subsisting in the locus of its own specifier" and "being specified by its own locus.
Thus, they are called "provers of difference."

By this, it has been made clear that in the phrase "those which are differentiators" (*vyāvartakāḥ*), the meaning of the word *vyāvṛtti* is "exclusion" (*bheda*), and the meaning of the suffix is "that which establishes" (*sādhaka*).
And it is not easily grasped—this is the logical connection (*anvaya*).

And here, according to the method previously stated, there are particularities (*viśeṣa*) whose mutual difference is established by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the substratum (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*); [it is said that] "this is a particularity..."

He states that they possess intrinsic differentiators by saying, "[309] 'That very same...'," on the grounds that even through the inference— "it is distinguished from this particular by way of identity because of that particular"— the mutual distinction is established while depending upon the means of cognition for the substratum (dharmin). Thus, their nature as self-excluding differentiators is affirmed.
"Of those that are extremely intermingled" means "of those whose distinctions are extremely difficult to grasp," namely,
other particulars of the same class.
In this case of "mutually" as well, it should be understood in the same manner as before;
even there, since it refers to a specific instance, there is no infinite regress.
Regarding this, it must be said that what was already elaborated previously concerns the definition of inherence (samavāya),
starting with the argument that there is a qualified cognition such as "the pot is blue" and so forth.
The inferential apparatus here is as follows:

the qualifierhood (prakāratā) of blue color and so forth, as determined by the qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) of a jar and the like, is determined by a relationhood (saṃsargatā) residing in something [namely, conjunction], because it is a qualifierhood.

It should be understood in this manner: [the cognition] possesses a qualifierhood (prakāratā) of the staff and so forth, which is itself determined by a qualificandhood (viśeṣyatā) of the staff and so forth, which in turn is determined by a relationality (saṃsargatā) that is grounded in a conjunction (saṃyoga).
Here, [this occurs] by virtue of the supporting power of the certainty of sublation (bādhaniścaya) regarding the conjunction and so forth.

It should be understood that the establishment of a relation characterized by a connection residing in something distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like is precisely what is designated by the term "inherence" (*samavāya*).
Now, as for the existence of inherence:

One might argue that perception itself—such as "the pot is blue"—will serve as the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and thus the pursuit of inference to its ultimate limit would be futile; to this, he says: "[311] By the Vaiśeṣikas... and so forth, because the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that inherence (*samavāya*) is perceptible.

Regarding the state [of inherence]: first, in the *Saṃgraha* [verse 310], it says "two things that are not separately established" (*ayutasiddha*). Now, what is this "not being separately established"?
It cannot mean simply being different from "separately established" things.
For it is impossible to define what it means for things to be established as separate;
nor can it be conjunction, because that is impossible in the case of a jar and its shards, and so forth.
Nor should it be said that *ayutasiddhatva* (inseparability) is the state where, between two things, one remains dependent upon the other;
for, since the property of being real (*tattva*) does not pervade [all cases], the delimitor of the category of *ayutasiddha* objects would itself lack universal application (*ananugata*).
On this point, some [maintain]: duality itself as qualified by duality is what is inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*).

The qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [of the first duality by the second] occurs through both relations: identity (*tādātmya*) and being qualified by the individual instance that is its own substratum (*svāśrayavyaktiviśiṣṭatva*).
And "distinctness" (vaiśiṣṭya) is by way of the relation of subsisting in that which is qualified by itself;
and "its own distinctness" (svavaiśiṣṭya) is likewise.
[The relation is] by way of possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by its own locus;
and the delimitation [of that counter-correlativity] is by way of possessing an absolute absence whose counter-correlativity resides in itself.
And the counterpositiveness is delimited by the relation of being-located-in (ādheyatā).

When the duality residing in the potsherds and so forth is taken up by the term *sva*, [the absence of that duality] is related to the individual potsherd instances which serve as its substrata by way of the relation delimited by being-located-in and having as its counterpositive the duality itself; and [the absence of such an absence] is related to the subject by way of the relation of possessing a difference whose counterpositiveness has as its delimitation the property residing in itself and delimited by the aforementioned relation.
Since both subsistence (*vṛttitva*) and identity (*tādātmya*) exist in the aforementioned duality within specific objects such as a pot with a skull [on it], the definition is appropriately applied.
However, in the case of the ground and so forth...
Because at the time when a jar or other object is absent, there exists an absolute absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of being contained-in (ādheyatā), and because,
by virtue of that aforementioned relation, the state of being qualified by the ground or similar locus does not exist in the jar or other object.
The duality of the ground and the jar, etc., is not of that nature; therefore, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to the case of the ground and the jar, etc.

Although, by virtue of the relation of non-inherence delimited by the relation of conjunction, the potsherd and so forth do not exist in the jar, nevertheless, [the absence] has its own counter-positivehood delimited by the generality of inherence.
There is no fault, because [the definition] includes the state of possessing the absence of that very [thing].

Nor should it be argued that even so, there would be an over-narrowness (avyāpti) because, at the moment of the destruction of the potsherd and so forth, the potsherd and such are absent from the jar and so forth by means of the aforementioned relation.
Because the state of possessing an absolute absence qualified by itself must be introduced;

and the qualification by itself [is established] by way of both relations: being delimited by the time that is the locus of that which is delimited by itself, and having a counter-correlativity whose locus is itself, as delimited by the generality of the relation of being located therein.
Although even so there would be the undesirable consequence of non-separability (*ayutasiddhi*) between absence and the state of being an absence, nevertheless,
they say that there is no fault because [the definition] includes a locusness (*ādheyatā*) delimited by a relation distinct from its own substratum.

To avoid the over-extension [of the definition] by taking relations such as "being at that time" (tatkālika) and so forth, it must be stated that its status as a *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for the application of a term) is through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). Otherwise, according to the view of the ancients,
the sentence beginning with "the part and the whole are inseparably established" (*avayavāvayavināvayutasiddhau*) would result in being semantically deficient (*nirākāṅkṣatā*).

Even if duality were such [a universal] by virtue of its relation to a duality qualified by itself, since duality is of the nature of a number, there would be no pervasion (avyāpti) for qualities and their substrates;
and if it were of the nature of being the object of a specific enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi), then [the same problem would apply] to that enumerative cognition.
Because [the definition] would fail to be universally applicable due to being restricted to specific objects;

and because, if one seeks universal applicability by defining it as a cognition qualified by a property through both relations— namely, having a qualificandumness delimited by itself and a prakāratā (mode-of-presentation) of oneness, and having a qualificandumness delimited by a property different from itself and a prakāratā of oneness— then...

Because, by taking as the unifying factor the nature of a cognition qualified by difference— through the two relations of having a qualificandum-ness delimited by a property residing in its own substratum and being determined by a singular-mode-ness, and having a qualificandum-ness delimited by a property that is its own counter-positive and being determined by a singular-mode-ness— one would fall into the error of a lack of decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*), resulting in the undesirable consequence of a plurality of delimiters for the category of inseparable entities (*ayutasiddha*).
The detailed exposition of that [point], as well as the determination of non-existence (abhāva), has been elaborated by us elsewhere.

Now, one might object that since there is no evidence for the counter-positiveness of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and the like being delimited by a relation, the exclusion of destruction and so forth is achieved simply by including "being an absence through relation" (*saṃsargābhāvatva*); thus, the qualification "eternal" (*nityatva*) would be redundant. To this, he says: "[313] Destruction... and so forth.

In the view of the moderns (*navya*), who do not accept that the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of destruction and so forth is delimited by a relation (*saṃbandhāvacchinna*) when the non-existence is established, the author says "[314] In brief," keeping in mind what has been stated in another work.
[314] Regarding the phrase "of destruction and prior non-existence," and so forth:
even though destruction and prior non-existence have the same counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), they possess only a single form (*ekarūpatva*). The meaning here is that it is not so in this case.

In the *Dīpikā* [313], it says "the delimitors of counterpositiveness and the superimposed," and so forth. The meaning is: because of the difference between the delimitors of counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) and the superimposed relation (*āropyasaṃsarga*).
Furthermore, the superimposed (*āropya*) is the state of being the object of the superimposition of the counterpositive (*pratiyogyāropaviṣayatva*).

Since the moderns do not accept that the superimposition of the counter-positive is the cause for the cognition of non-existence, he says in the *Prakāśikā* (on verse 314): "it would be superimposed."
Now, in the case of the difference between mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*),
the difference in the relation that delimits the counter-positive-ness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakasambandhabheda*) is not the regulating factor for the mutual absence.
Because there is a rule that [the absence] must have a counter-correlativity delimited by a relation of identity (*tādātmya*).

Here, the phrase "as appropriate" (*yathāyogam*) connects with the statement "distinct due to the difference in delimiters" (*avacchedaka-bheda*). Regarding the term "by way of consequence" (*prasaṅgāt*): the "consequence" here consists in the state of possessing the nature of an absence (*abhāvatva*) that resides in itself.
"Depicted by that word" means having the same referent as the cognition produced by that word. "Independently" means by not appearing as a counter-correlative (pratiyogin).
The inclusion of the sixteen categories within the seven categories was first stated in the aphorism beginning with "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) and "objects of valid cognition" (prameya).

Regarding the objection that it is untenable to state the respective inclusion of the twelve kinds of objects of cognition (*prameya*) mentioned secondly within the already established categories—without first stating the inclusion of whatever remains unaccounted for—he says: "[331] *Pratyakṣa*...
and so forth; this refers to the nature of the sense organs such as the eye, and so on.
[331] Regarding the phrase "of inference and so forth" (*anumānādīnām*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes comparison (*upamāna*) and verbal testimony (*śabda*).
[331] The word "in substance" (*dravye*) is to be connected with the phrase "inclusion" (*antarbhāva*). [331] The same applies to what follows as well.

The meaning is: "even in the case of the object of cognition (*prameya*) consisting of activity (*pravṛtti*), defects (*doṣa*), and so forth. Now, one might object that since activity is a specific kind of effort (*prayatna-viśeṣa*), it is untenable to describe it as being of the nature of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); to this, he says: "That" (*tat*).
"Dharma and adharma" is the meaning.
He provides support from the earlier text regarding his own stated point:
"And this," which means that the statement "dharma and adharma" is an explanation of the sense of "that which produces them."
[331] Regarding the explanation of the *ākāra*:
Is it not the case that the statement in the *Dīpikā*, "transmigration (*pretyabhāva*) is death," is incoherent?
Since the meaning of the suffix *lyap*—

which constitutes the word *pretyabhāva*— and the word *bhāva* itself have not been explained [here], [the meaning of] the compound *pretyabhāva* is understood through the mere verbal root preceded by the prefix *prati*, which signifies death and birth.
And because it does not convey the meaning of the form of death, he says here: "immediately after death" (*maraṇānantara*).
"Immediacy" (*anantaratva*) means being subsequent in time.
Of the stated meaning—

He shows the conformity with the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the term *pretyabhāva*—that is, the meaning of the word *pretyabhāva* being as previously stated—with the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*). He shows the meanings of the words "death" (*maraṇa*) and "birth" (*janana*) in their respective order, beginning with "the final" (*carama*) and so forth. "The final" (*carama*)...
The term "particular conjunction" (*saṃyogaviśeṣaṇam*) applies here; likewise in what follows. The word "initial" (*ādyā*) is a qualifier of the conjunction.

The state of being "last" (*caramatva*) consists in not being contemporaneous with the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of such a conjunction that is co-located (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) with itself. Although,
in this context, the property of "selfhood" (*svatva*) is introduced as the relatum (*anuyogin*), [the definition remains valid].

The state of being the last (*caramatva*) is defined as that which is distinct from what is co-present with a prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the same kind that is co-locus with itself; however, because the individual instances of the final conjunctions (*saṃyoga-vyakti*) are infinite, there is a lack of commonality (*ananugama*).
[This applies] to the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

And upon the entry of ownership, when there is the entry of the difference from such a single individual— which is simultaneous with the prior non-existence of such a conjunction that does not reside in the same locus as the self— then even that which belongs to the present [time] [is included].
Such a conjunction would possess the quality of being "last" as previously described; therefore, by taking its destruction into account, death would occur even now.
Whatever [is] co-temporal with such a prior non-existence (prāgabhāva)...

Furthermore, if one were to include the entire collection of distinct individual instances (*tattadvyaktibheda*), the status of being "the last" (*caramatva*)— since it is constituted by "thatness" (*yattva*) and "thisness" (*tattva*)— would fail to constitute a single qualified entity; moreover, there would follow the undesirable consequence that those specific individual instances would be difficult for anyone who is not omniscient to discern.

Since the nature of being a "fraud" (kūṭatva) consists in being another thing qualified by a single [property], if "selfhood" (svatva) is included therein, then "being the last" (caramatva) is the state of being qualified by the knowable (prameya); this is the coarse (sthūla) formulation.
And as for the relation of qualification (vaiśiṣṭya):

The subtle method of subsumption (*anugama*) is as follows: [a thing] possesses a distinction (*bheda*) qualified by two relations: (1) identity (*tādātmya*), and (2) the state of being simultaneous with the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of such a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that is co-located (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) with it, where the locus of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by its own delimitation (*avacchedakatā*). This is the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*).
[The relation is] by way of both the relation of being its own locus and the relation of being the delimiting factor of its own counter-correlate.
Delimiting factorhood [is defined] by the relation of being simultaneous with a prior absence of such a conjunction that is co-locational with itself.
And when "selfhood" (svatva) is introduced as the counter-correlative, "lastness" (caramatva) consists in being other than that which is qualified by the prior non-existence of such a conjunction;
[this] is the state of being qualified (vaiśiṣṭya).
[The relation] is by way of both the relation of being co-temporal with itself and the relation of co-instantiation,

or else by way of the relation of co-instantiation delimited by a single moment (*ekakṣaṇāvacchinnasāmānādhikaraṇya*). And that [relation] consists in a substratum-ness (*ādheyatā*) delimited by inherence (*samavāya*), which is itself qualified by a substratum-ness delimited by the essential nature relation (*svarūpasambandha*) residing in itself.
And the state of being specific (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is by way of both relations: being determined by that which determines itself, and being delimited by its own delimiting moment (*kṣaṇa*).
And the state of being first (*ādyatva*) is the property of not being co-temporal with the destruction of such a conjunction that is co-locus with itself.
In this case as well, whether it be the state of being qualified by the object of cognition (*prameya*), the state of being qualified by difference (*bheda*),

or the state of being other than that which is qualified by the destruction of such a conjunction— this must be formulated by introducing "destruction" (*dhvaṃsa*) in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); the rest is as before.

And that is liberation (*mokṣa*). Although elsewhere it is stated that liberation is the destruction of that final suffering, in the *Dīpikā* [it is said]: [331] "And that is liberation. Even though the destruction of whatever final suffering exists is liberation, according to other sources.

Although it has been explained in that way, there is no contradiction, because by means of the qualification "suffering" ending with the word "kāla," only the final category (the last item) is elucidated.
The "concomitance" (anugama), however, should be understood as before:

it consists in being other than that which is characterized by the prior non-existence of suffering, through the previously mentioned relation of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). And in this regard—

Regarding the objection that, in the definition of liberation as "the destruction of any entity whatsoever that does not coexist with the prior non-existence of suffering that is in its own locus," the inclusion of the "suffering" portion as the counter-positive of that destruction is redundant, [the following is said] in response to that objection regarding its inclusion:

He states the purpose [in the *Prakāśikā* 331]: "the liberated self. And here, without taking into account the aspect of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), [liberation] consists in not being simultaneous with suffering that is co-located with itself, by way of the relation of co-location delimited by a single moment.

It is easy to state that "finality" consists precisely in the nature of being other than that which is distinguished by suffering; nor is there any lack of established proof for its being a qualifier of suffering,
since it exists at this very moment.
This is because [the absence of ignorance] is accepted as being a qualifier of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).
And such being the case, there is no consequence that people like us would be liberated even during the state of deep sleep.
At that time, because there is an absence of suffering in the self of ourselves and others,
[there is] the destruction of suffering belonging to that time.
It should not be suspected that [the definition] is over-extended due to the inclusion of specific qualifiers,
because such a destruction of suffering exists even at the time of deep sleep (suṣupti).
He raises the objection: "And not so," because there is no fault since it occurs at the same time as the suffering that follows the state of deep sleep;
this is indicated by the words beginning with "suṣupti" (deep sleep) and so forth. He anticipates the response with the word "agrima" (subsequent).
The meaning is "in the latter case.

That is, in the aforementioned formulation which incorporates prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as it is situated; and here, if prior non-existence is not admitted, then according to the stated method, [the definition] would consist in the state of not being simultaneous with such suffering.
Thus it is to be respected;

likewise, according to the method stated in the section on *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject), in a case where there is coexistence with the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering, there is the property of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) residing in suffering.
Intending that it should be included, he stated "Direction" [331]. Now, one might object:

since the Sūtra beginning with "The means of valid cognition... mentions doubt immediately after the objects of knowledge, it is improper for the *Dīpikā* to describe the nature of the purpose and so forth without first demonstrating the nature of doubt; to this, he replies: "Of doubt... [331].
He states the purpose of the phrase "possessing both means" (*ubhayasādhanavatī*) with the words "And this" (*idaṃ ca*). The meaning is:
"and this aforementioned qualification beginning with 'both'. Now, [one might ask], in the definition of debate (*kathā*):

The statement that there are multiple speakers is untenable, because neither the sentence of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) nor the subsequent sentence possesses multiple speakers; therefore, he says: "[335] By one," and provides an example of equivocation (*chala*).
"— 'yathā' (as) / — 'iti' (thus) / These two words have this meaning.
Another interpretation— "
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that there is no object distinct from the new form and its meaning; thus,
he refutes it— this is the logical connection.
[336] "By way of being common to the non-establishment of one's own [position]" (*svāsādhakatāsādhāraṇyena*):
"commonality" (*sādhāraṇya*) means the state of being contained (*ādheyatva*). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭye*). Of that...

In the expression *parāsādhakatāsādhakatayā*, there is an application [of the term] to the state of being the relatum (*nirūpakatva*) of the genitive case-meaning within the compound. Here, "self" (*sva*) refers to the one who states the refutation (*dūṣaṇavaktā*),
and "other" (*para*) refers to the one who states the inference (*anumānavaktā*).
[336] “Because it is self-contradictory”:
the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here in the sense of being employed (*prayojyatva*) with respect to that which is concomitant with non-existence (*asattvānvayin*).
And thus, according to the manner stated, of the subsequent [term]...
And regarding the establishment of its self-contradictory nature:
"that" means that which belongs to the aforementioned class of definitions; "each individually" means... [336] ...each one separately.
It is an indeclinable ending in the third-case plural;
the meaning is "by means of words such as *sādharmya* (similarity) and *vaidharmya* (dissimilarity).
*Yoga* means connection (*sambandha*).
Regarding the determination of the types (*jāti*), he states the definitions and examples of the types in sequence, beginning with "by similarity" (*sādharmyeṇa*) and so forth. Among these:

The section beginning with "by way of similarity" (*sādharmyeṇa*) and ending with "the answer" (*uttaram*) defines the sophistical rejoinder based on similarity (*sādharmyasama*). "Similarity" (*sādharmya*) means resemblance; "establishment" (*sthāpanā*) refers to the inferential argument that establishes [the thesis].
He provides an example of the *sādharmyasama* (balancing through similarity) with the word "yathā" (just as): "sakriyaḥ" means possessing action;
here, it refers to the body of the reason (*hetu*), which consists in the possession of qualities that are the cause of action.
The meaning of *trala* is the state of being a container (*ghaṭakatva*), which is endowed with qualities.
The term "janaka" (producer) is a qualifier for conjunction and so forth. [This applies] if it is active (*sakriya*).

The connection is with "tadā" (then/at that time); the connection is not with "na ca asti" (and it does not exist). Here, [the objection refers] merely to the state of being active, which is occasioned by the similarity to that which possesses activity.
Or [it may mean] merely the state of being inactive, which is applied by virtue of similarity with that which is inactive.
"The decider" means the determiner.
He states the definition of the *vaidharmyasama* (balancing the dissimilar).
—[338] "By way of dissimilarity" (vaidharmyeṇa): dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is the property of exclusion. "That" refers to the reason for the proof (sthāpanāhetu).
He provides an example of the *vaidharmyasama* (balancing through dissimilarity) with the words "for example" (*yathā*). In that very same case—
the aforementioned inference that "the self is active" and so forth—
it is countered by the claim that "it is indeed inactive."
The word "self" (ātman) is supplied [from the previous context].
The logical connection is that it "does not exist.
As for the word "that" (tat):
The meaning is "a clod of earth.
The same applies to what follows.
He defines the sophistry of parity through superiority (utkarṣasama):
[338] Regarding the phrase "stated by another" (*paroktā*): the word "that" (*tat*) means "the proof stated by another.
He provides this illustration:
"Yathā" means "it might be so that. This construction applies to what follows as well.
"Tenaiiva" means "by that very [fact]," namely, by the fact of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).
The same applies hereafter.
Regarding "having parts" (*sāvayava*): having parts consists in being qualified by the state of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatā*).
The essential point is that its distinctness [vaiśiṣṭya] is by way of the relation of substance-ness (dravyatva) as its own determiner;
and such is the state of having parts (sāvayavatva).

It should be understood that "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), in the form of being an effect, is indeed non-pervasive with respect to [the property of] being an effect, because it is excluded from things such as color (*rūpa*) which are effects. The word "thus" (*iti*) connects with the preceding phrase, "someone says thus."

He defines the *apakarṣasama* (balancing by subtraction) as follows: "By what is stated by the opponent," etc. "Of another property" (*dharmāntarasya*) means of a property other than the one intended to be established by the inference under discussion.

He states an example of this with the word "yathā" (as follows): "in that very [case]" means in the form already demonstrated, such as "sound is eternal," and so forth; the phrase "someone says thus" is to be supplied.
The same applies to what follows.
He defines *varṇyasama* as follows: "Of the subject of description (*varṇya*)... [340]
The same applies to what follows. He illustrates this with "just as," referring to what was stated previously.
The meaning is that [the fallacy] takes such a form as: "The self possesses activity because it possesses qualities that are the cause of activity, like a clod of earth.
The word "that" (tat) means "activity.
He defines *avarṇyasama* (balancing the unprovable):
[350] Regarding the term "to be proven" (*sādhya*): he illustrates it with "for example.
Precisely for that reason—namely, in the form "the self possesses activity," and so forth.
*Sādhana*—the rejoinder that establishes the occurrence of the probandum.
The same applies to what follows.
*Gata* and *rūpa* are qualifiers of the quality (*guṇa*). And thus:

And regarding the fact that the possession of the stated qualities is unestablished in the self: the connection with what follows is this— since it is equally the case that the proof has a reason unestablished in the self, why is [the opposite] not likewise established?
"By such"— that is, by that which is unestablished;
"that" means action.
He defines the "equal to the conceptual construction" (vikalpasama) with the words "[342] 'dṛṣṭānta' etc.";
he provides an illustration with "yathā" (for example).
But this—namely, the subsequent alternative—characterizes the *sādhyasama* (the "equal-to-the-probandum") fallacy: "[341] 'Of the example' (*dṛṣṭāntasya*)". Now, regarding this...

The name *pakṣasama* (equal to the thesis) is appropriate for that which consists in stating the equality of the two sides (*pakṣa*), but not for *sādhyasama* (equal to the probandum); in order to resolve this doubt, he states "sādhyeti," explaining that here the word *sādhya* itself denotes the *pakṣa* through its etymological derivation as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*)— that is, "that wherein [the property] is being proved" (*sādhyate atra*).
Here, in the word *sādhyasama*, the meaning of the suffix *-tra* is "constituent-ness" (*ghaṭakatva*), which is connected with the word *sādhya*.
He illustrates this with the words "for example" (*yathā*). It is said:
The connection is with the word "yadi" (if).
And thus, by means of scripture, the point that "as is the self, so is the clod of earth" is also established; the connection is with the word "yat" (that which).
That is: the state of possessing activity.
He states the definition of acquisition (*prāpti*) as follows: "[342] By acquisition... and so forth.
The third [case-ending] is used for the cause (*hetu*).
"Objection" (*pratyavasthāna*) means the statement of a counter-argument (*pratyuttara*).
The same applies to what follows;
that is to say, the subsequent answer is given by taking "attainment" (prāpti) as the reason.
Here, he states the meaning of the word "attainment" (prāpti): "and that which has been brought about. He provides an illustration: "as for example," and "of such a kind."
The meaning is "due to the cause of activity. The word "not" is to be supplied with the phrase "is being proven."

Because there is no distinction between the two— because there is no difference between the two [cases] regarding both possessing action and possessing the qualities that cause action, due to the equality of their grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
He defines non-attainment (*aprāpti*) as being equal [to attainment]:
"[343] By non-attainment.
As before, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a cause.
"Non-attainment similarity" (aprāptisama) refers to providing a counter-response by taking non-attainment as the reason;
it is illustrated as follows.
"Previously mentioned" means that which was shown earlier by the phrase "consisting of impulsion residing in a clod of earth," and so forth.
"Of that which has not been reached" [means...].

In this context, "non-attainment" (aprāpti) means being in a different locus from the probandum (sādhyavaiyadhikaraṇya). And likewise, when it is stated that such a reason is a prover of the probandum—
this very [point is what is meant].
It consists precisely in the state of possessing the quality of being the cause of an action.
He defines *prasaṅgasama* with the words "sādhaneti," and provides an example with "yatheti."
In this context—"kriyāhetuguṇavattve" means "in the state of possessing qualities that are causes of action.
To the question, "For what purpose is there a dependence on a means of proof (sādhana)? he says: "na hi" (not indeed).
The grammatical connection is with the words "nāsti hi" (for it does not exist).
In that case as well— even though there is possession of the quality that is the cause of the action—
he characterizes it as "equal to the counter-example" by means of another example.
The meaning is: "produced by an example other than those cited by the opponent. *Sādhana* is a rejoinder that establishes [the opponent's position] through the consequence of proof.
He provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (for example).
He characterizes non-arising as being equal:
"by non-arising.
Here too, the instrumental case is used in the sense of cause.
The meaning is that a reply is given by taking non-arising as the reason.
He provides an example with the words "just as" (*yathā*); the syntactical connection is: "if [it were] a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇam yadi*).
"‘That’ (tat) means:
by means of the proof consisting in the oneness of the produced [effect]. ‘Thus’ (iti) means:
this connects with what was said previously, namely, that ‘someone has said’."
He states the definition of that which is equivalent to doubt: "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), meaning "co-occurrence with both the probandum and its absence" (*sādhyatadabhāvasāmānādhikaraṇya*).
He provides an illustration: "as for example" (*yathā*). "Both" (*ubhaya*) means both eternal and non-eternal.
In the case of the elimination of one [of two possibilities], it refers to one [remaining].
When there is a certainty through elimination regarding either mere permanence or mere impermanence—
here, in the case of the "equal-to-the-point-at-issue" (prakaraṇasama) and the "equal-to-the-non-reason" (ahetusama).
He states the definition: "even in the three times.
This means even in the three times of past, future, and present.
He provides an illustration: "as follows. At that time...
At the time prior to the [property of] impermanence that constitutes the probandum;
of that— impermanence— it is not the prover.

The connection is with the phrase "the means of proof (sādhana) consisting of the nature of being an effect, etc. The word "afterwards" (paścāt) is connected with the beginning of the phrase "from the probandum, impermanence, etc.
The word "previously" (pūrva) is connected with the beginning of the phrase "the means of proof consisting of the nature of being an effect, etc."
"Because of the absence of proof" (*sādhanābhāvāt*): the term "proof" (*sādhana*) refers to [the property] having the nature of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth.

Of that—namely, the means of proof (*sādhana*) in the form of "being an effect" and so forth; both—namely, both the means of proof in the form of "being an effect" and the probandum (*sādhya*) in the form of "impermanence" and so forth;
[this constitutes] the "balancing by implication" (*arthāpattisama*).
He states the definition: "by means of placing *arthāpatti* (presumption) at the forefront.
This means: having made *arthāpatti*, which consists in the impossibility of being otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*), the logical reason (*hetu*).
"As previously stated" refers to sound (*śabda*).
The meaning is "in the form of 'eternal' and so forth.
If [the word] "probandum" (sādhya) is supplied, the connection is as follows:
"eternality also [is the probandum]."

The term "by means of presumptive testimony" (arthāpattyā) is to be supplied [to the previous sentence]. The word "would be established" (siddhyet) is the ellipsis. "Either one" (ekatare) means the determination of either non-eternality or eternality.
He defines the *aviśeṣasama* (balancing through non-distinction) with the words "sarva... [347]. *Aviśeṣa* means equality.
He provides an example with the words "tatraiva... [in that very same case].
"If there were impermanence," is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*); likewise for what follows.
The word "tat" means "sound";
that is, impermanence.
He characterizes the "concordant with the point to be proven" (*upapattisama*) as follows: "[348] 'In both positions' (*ubhayapakṣe*);
the meaning is 'in the two positions accepted by both the proponent and the opponent.
[The word] 'by similarity' (*sādharmyeṇa*) is an instrumental case used in the sense of non-difference."

The meaning is that an answer which establishes a logical justification (*upapatti*) by means of a probans (*sādhana*) not distinct from such a commonality (*sādharmya*) is an *upapattisama* rejoinder. He provides an example with "for instance" (*yathā*). In the following cases as well, the introductory remarks (*avatārikā*) should be understood in this same way.
"Has been shown" is a qualification of the probans (*sādhana*).
The connection is that "there is no state of conformity," which is to say, no state of being produced (*janyatva*).
The proof (sādhana) is the rejoinder that establishes the undesirable consequence (siddhyāpatti).
The same applies to what follows.
"If it is not perceived" constitutes the positive concomitance (anvaya).
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is: "if it is not accepted in this way.
[This applies] even to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
The meaning of the genitive case is counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*),

which is connected with the absence (*abhāva*) by way of being its determiner (*nirūpakatā*). Here, the particle *api* serves as a conjunction that includes the "covering" (*āvaraṇa*) as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The word "tat" means that which is not perceived.
"Tasya" refers to that impermanence.
"Sadātanatvāt" means because of its being eternal—that is, because of its permanence. [350]
"Tathātva" means eternality;
in either case— whether the operation of the word is non-eternal or eternal.
It is said that "yadi" (if) constitutes the logical connection (*anvaya*).
"Tat" means the term "impermanence.
In that very context: "Sound is impermanent."
It is precisely the inference [stated as]: "Because it follows effort, like a jar";
"in both ways" means by both methods.
By means of the two forms: the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpotpatti*) and the cessation of its obscuration (*āvārakanivṛtti*).
"Conformity" (*anuvidhāna*) means being produced (*janyatā*). And thus, since there is a possibility in both ways for the quality of conforming to effort (*prayatnānuvidhāyitva*), of that—
Regarding "conformity with effort":
the phrase "in another effect" means an effect distinct from the effect consisting of the production of its own nature (*svarūpotpatti*). "Necessity" (*niyatatva*) means pervasion (*vyāpyatva*).
"In some"—that is, in certain manuscripts.
"Of that too"—that is, even of such a reading as that. The connection with what follows is: "the meaning has indeed already been stated."
In this regard— that is, concerning the subject matter already mentioned—
the determination of the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is set forth in the Dīpikā.
[343] A point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is the cause of the speaker’s loss. Thus,
in the term *nigrahasthāna*, the word *nigraha* refers to the speaker’s defeat,
while the word *sthāna* refers to the cause.
This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, this constitutes both the nature of a reason that fails to establish the opponent's position and the definition of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
By the phrase "in the case of quibbling (*chala*) and so forth," the inclusion of the *jāti* known as *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-balanced) is intended.
By the phrase "in the case of shifting the subject (*arthāntara*) and so forth," the inclusion of the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) is intended. Now, if that is so—

Regarding the point that the separate mention of *chala* (quibble) and so forth in the sūtra beginning with "pramāṇa" is useless because they are already included within the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), he says:
"Even by way of being a quibble, etc. (*chalatvādināpi*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the *prakaraṇasama* [fallacy] is intended;
the particle "also" (*api*) serves to conjoin its status as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
This is by way of an illustration.
The phrase "the material cause of this knowledge" refers to [the fallacies] such as *chala* (quibble) and so forth.
This is because they are useful—that is, because they serve as causes for the opponent's defeat. The word "separately" means...
The meaning is: "in a form other than that of a point of defeat" (*nigrahasthāna*).
The term "as fallacious equivocation, etc. (*chalatvādinā*) is to be supplied [from the context].
*Upādāna* means "presentation" (*pratipādana*).
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "it has been established by the sūtra beginning with 'pramāṇa'.
The intention is that this follows the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*).
"Like a fallacious reason" (*hetvābhāsavat*).

The suffix *vati* is used after a word ending in the sixth case (genitive), meaning "like a fallacy of reason" (*hetvābhāsa*). This is the definition of the abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*).
Of that point of defeat as well— namely,
the acceptance of a proposition contrary to the meaning previously asserted— one must state its internal subdivisions, which are its specific sub-varieties.
The literal meaning of the term *pratijñāhāni* (loss of the proposition) is not possible [in this context],

because by the etymological analysis of its components— *pratijñā* being that which is proposed (*pratijñāyate*), thus the "proposition," and *hāni* being the loss of that— the term refers to the loss of the object proposed.
Because the abandonment of the proposed thesis is of such a nature, whereas such an admission is not, he says accordingly:
"or the abandonment of the proposed thesis."
The definition of a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*) is "previously," meaning "by the addition of a qualification not previously stated," and so forth; here, "addition" means stating.
The definition of the point of defeat consisting of an unintelligible meaning (avijñātārtha) is as follows:
it is an unintelligible meaning that constitutes a point of defeat,
and it is a consequence of affliction (kliṣṭānvaya).
[An example of] a word with a remote etymological derivation (*dūrānvaya*) whose meaning is not well-known (*aprasiddhārthaka*) is such as "the *bhūstana* is like a medicine for cold," and so forth.
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), [other examples are implied].
The summary of the mild and the exalted;
the characteristic of the untimely,
in reverse order— [357].
By means of a sequence exceeding the sequence established by the conventions of the treatises;
[this constitutes] an excessive definition, as indicated by the words "the reason (*hetu*) and so forth."
The inclusion of the example, the delimiting relation of the reason, and the two types of pervasion, etc.; here,
"statement" refers to the definition of *apasiddhānta* (contradiction with one's own tenets).
The phrase "of the jewel and so forth" is followed by the ellipsis "with regard to burning and so forth"—
this is the refutation of power (*śakti*) as a distinct category of entity— and that [power] resides in the jewel and so forth.
And [the question] "Why is there an obstructiveness toward burning and so forth? is answered by the words "of the obstructiveness.
Regarding "favorability": here, favorability means being the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of causality.

Regarding "the state of being a disruptor" (*vighaṭakatva*): the state of being a disruptor is the state of being a producer of destruction. "That" refers to the nature of an obstructer, which consists in disrupting the capacity conducive to the effect.
"By means of presumptive testimony" (*arthāpattyā*); the ellipsis is "by means of that which consists of the instrument of knowledge known as presumption.
The meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is "being produced" (*janyatva*) as accompanied by establishment (*siddhi*).
The proof here consists of the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
This should be understood as having the form: "Fire possesses a power conducive to burning."
1. "Bhūstana" means "mountain.
"Like snow and medicine" means "possessing fire."
"The fire is indeed the remedy for this," so says the Śruti.
They say that the sound of the earth belongs to Pavata.
Presumption (arthāpatti) is also of the nature of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
taking such forms as: "It is not possible for a fire to produce burning that is obstructed by a magnet and the like unless it possesses a power conducive to burning."
And "being obstructed" (pratibadhyatva) consists in being necessitated by the power [of the cause] that is to be destroyed.

However, some, following the text as it stands literally, have stated that there is a means of valid cognition based on presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), namely: that it would be logically untenable for a jewel to possess the nature of an obstructor—consisting in its obstructing the power conducive to burning—without fire itself possessing a power conducive to burning.
"That is trivial— because of the absence of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the probandum and the probans"—
this is the construction of the objection [introduced by] "it is suspected.
[The reason given is] "because of being distinct" (*atiriktatvāt*).
"From the prepared substances and so forth," and so on; likewise in what follows.
"In this way" means by the reasoning already stated.
Of that—of the power (śakti). For this very reason—precisely because it functions as the qualities (guṇas) and so forth.
"In its arising," and so forth.
