And its production is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

This *arthāpatti* consists in the fact that, without a production delimited by the removal of the jewel, it would be logically untenable for [the fire] to possess the capacity to bring about burning at a moment delimited by the moment immediately following such [removal].

In this way, destruction is also established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). And that [presumptive testimony] is as follows: the power [of the gem] cannot exist without its being characterized by destruction delimited by the removal of the gem.
The [objection] that it is untenable for there to be a lack of suitability for burning as delimited by the moment immediately following such a moment [is thus resolved].
Consequently, there is no possibility of the suspicion of the reason—such as arising and so forth—being unestablished (*asiddha*).
And thus, according to the manner stated:

And once it is established that power (*śakti*) is not included within substance (*dravya*) and the other categories, [the author states] "it is distinct" (*atiriktā*). Here, this inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*) is to be understood: Power possesses the entire set of differences from substance and the rest.
It is of the form "because it is not included among substance and the rest.
For here, being distinct [from others] consists in possessing the collection of distinctions such as substance and so forth.

And by the words "yataḥ" (since), etc., [the author] addresses the doubt regarding the non-establishment of the qualifier and the qualified, which have entered into the body [of the definition] as not being included within the substance and so forth that serve as the cause for such an inference.
This has been refuted; and that [refutation concerns] "the state of being the counter-positive of an absence that serves as a cause.
Under the view that the absence of the jewel and so forth is the cause, he explains how the non-arising of burning occurs at the time when the jewel is present: "maṇi... and so on.
The word "tat" means "the gem.
The phrase "by another cause" means by a cause distinct from causes such as fire and so forth.

This is the qualification "form" (rūpa). And thus— since, according to the stated method, being an impediment consists in obstructing the capacity conducive to the effect, and since it would otherwise be of a different nature.
By the impossibility of otherwise accounting for linguistic usage—

that is, by the impossibility of accounting for linguistic usage otherwise than by admitting a category distinct from the form of capacity (śakti), since [otherwise] it would be impossible for [cognition] to possess an object.

Now, one might object: "Even when both [the fire and] the stimulating gem are present, since the fire lacks the power conducive to burning, how can burning be accounted for even in your own view? To this he replies:
"My... This refers to the Prābhākara school.
The same applies to the subsequent cases as well.
"Another power" (*śaktyantara*) means a power distinct from the power existing at the time when the gem and other [obstructing factors] have been removed. "Qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*)...
This is an adjective qualifying "maṇi" (jewel); the same applies to what follows.
Because it is not included—meaning because it lacks the status of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absence in the form of a common property (*anugatarūpa*).
Because it is impossible to include [the counteracting agent] within the scope of the delimitor of the causal status (*kāraṇatāvacchedakakoṭi*). "Of such a kind" means:
delimited by the absence of the jewel and so forth, as qualified by the absence of each respective counteracting agent (*uttejaka*). "Even for you" (*tavāpi*):
furthermore, the word "also" (*api*) is used here to include the Naiyāyika as a corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The meaning is that this is because it is necessary;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) that the power conducive to burning would not arise during the state when both [the fuel] and the stimulating gem are present, and there would also be the undesirable consequence that the power would arise when only the gem exists. Now, [one might object]:

Desiring to refute the Mīmāṃsaka objection that "since the postulation of the aforementioned causality is equal in both systems, my own view alone should be accepted," he says: "ananta... and so forth.
"tattad... and so forth.
In this context, those two words refer to power (*śakti*).
Even so— meaning, even when the aforementioned reasoning excludes a favorable power— the term "contact" (*sparśa*) [applies].
In this context, "contact" (*sparśa*) everywhere consists of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), as is clear from the very text itself. The word "form" (*rūpa*) is a qualifier of the effect.
The term "by the Arhat" (*arhatā*) [is used].
The word "it exists" is to be supplied;
the logical connection is that "it does not exist. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because it possesses power."
The word "tat" means that which is fit for the function of eating and so forth.

Likewise, in the subsequent cases as well; and thus, in the case of bronze and other materials, once it is established that they possess or lack the fitness for functions such as eating, [the definition is proven].
And "in bell-metal and so forth" means by way of a proximity residing in the bell-metal and so forth; and that which is proximate...

It should be understood that the delimiting factor of the state of being obstructed (pratibadhyatā) is the state of being a substratum (ādhāratā), whereas the delimiting factor of the state of being an obstructor (pratibandhakatā) is inherence (samavāya).
Regarding the phrase "in the case of justification" (upapattau):

The phrase "the capacity and its absence for performing functions such as serving food in [vessels] like bronze" and so forth; "that" refers to [the capacity] in bronze and so forth; the meaning is "inherent power" (*ādheya-śakti*).
Now, one might object: "Since touch is a quality distinct from conjunction, how can it have the nature of conjunction? To this, he says: "And in the present case... (prakṛte ca).

The meaning is: "and in the section concerning the statement of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*) regarding the acts of eating and so forth occurring in vessels such as bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), and the touching of what is untouchable. The word "that" (*tat*) means: the touching of what is untouchable in the form of contact (*saṃyoga*).
To the objection that there is no fault if contact with ashes and so forth is possible— thereby resulting in the desired consequence— he says: "without" (antareṇa), which means "in the absence of."
"Attaining the fitness for food and so forth" means [the fitness] for bronze vessels and the like;
"in this manner" means in such a form.
Furthermore, "in a manner exceeding what was previously stated" means by the first method— that is, by entering [the cremation ground] with ashes and so forth.
"And by the second" [refers to] the word "and so forth" (*ādiśabda*), which is supplied from the previous context.
In the phrase "in bell-metal and so forth," the meaning is "having entered into. Regarding the term "established" (*kḷpta*):
The meaning is that [non-existence] is accepted as being included within the categories of reality (padārtha) ending with substance (dravya) and so forth, up to non-existence itself.
Regarding the phrase "by means of a specific kind of destruction" (dhvaṃsaviśeṣeṇaiva),
the "specificity" (viśeṣatva) resides in the destruction.

It is the state of being the counter-positive of the contact with ash and so forth, while being accompanied by the absence of all instances of contact with the untouchable that occurred at the time of that contact with ash and so forth. Regarding the phrase "there too," it is connected to the word "in bell-metal and the like."
The term "destruction" (*dhvaṃsa*) is used to prevent the misconception that [the word] functions as a qualifier for ash and so forth.
Here, within the body of the meaning of the word "purity" (*śuddhi*) as it has been shown,
[it refers to] a specific relation.
The meaning is: "the specific qualification of non-existence.
"Constrained" means "joined. Otherwise, [this would apply] to bronze and the like, which possess contact with the untouchable, by way of the relation of having its own counter-positive.

Because it is possible for there to be the absence of all counter-correlates of such a touch, and because in bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and other such objects— which possess all those absences but are not yet conjoined with ash or the like— the destruction of the conjunction with ash or the like exists by way of temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*) and so forth,
[there would follow] the destruction of the conjunction with ash or the like as qualified by all those absences.
Because the aforementioned [definition] would apply equally to bronze and other such materials, the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains as it was.
Regarding the term "co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*):
this must be introduced precisely in the manner of a relation.

This is because [the definition] is simpler by not introducing that specific relation. Thus, the final conclusion (*niṣkarṣa*) is as follows: "Ashes" and so forth are pure (*śuddha*) when there is a destruction of the conjunction [with them], qualified by all such absences through a relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting in a location-ness (*ādheyatā*) that is itself qualified by a location-ness determined by a locus which is the counter-correlative of a location-ness delimited by the relation of spatial inherence (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā*) residing in itself.
Now, since the [intended] establishment is possible by introducing merely the absence whose counter-positive is contact with the untouchable, what is the purpose of including "all" (yāvatva)?
Nor can it be argued that [the definition fails] because of taking such a particular absence.

Regarding the passage beginning with "yatra" (where), one might suspect that the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains as it was; however, he states "aspṛśya" (untouchable) to show that there is no such fault, because by defining the objects as untouchable things and then introducing the absence whose counter-positive is delimited by the property of touching such objects, the defect is avoided.
"Whatever it may be" (*yatkiñcit*) is a qualification of non-existence (*abhāva*). Regarding "as far as" (*yāvat*):
therein, by the words beginning with "wherein" (*yatra*), etc., [the meaning is established].
"In the previously mentioned bell-metal and so forth";
"that" means purification.
But surely, in the case of bronze and so forth mentioned in the passage beginning with "nanu yatra," the aforementioned over-extension remains as it was;
for [the definition] consists of the nature of conjunction.
Since such a touch is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), its absence also exists in that same locus; therefore, he says "therein" (*tatra*).
This means "in bronze and so forth," as previously mentioned by the words "wherein" (*yatra*) and so on.

Regarding the term "unrestricted" (*niravacchinna*): thus, the first locus-ness (*ādheyatā*) that constitutes the aforementioned co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is characterized by being delimited by the relation of unrestricted spatial qualification (*niravacchinnadaiśikaviśeṣaṇatā*).
The meaning is that it must be established.
"As stated" means in the form of the attainment of purity.

"Qualified by the non-existence of the aggregate [of causes] in a state of co-occurrence (sāmānādhikaraṇya)" means: qualified by the aggregate of absences through the relation of co-occurrence; this is a qualification of "destruction" (dhvaṃsa). "Ashes, etc. refers to that [destruction]. In that regard—
Regarding the performance of the application of ashes and so forth: although,
according to the literal sense, it consists of the state of being located (*ādheyatva*) as defined by a locus delimited by the time of contact with ashes and so forth—
wherever [that occurs]—

Regarding the contact with ash and so forth, which is mentioned as being among the instances of touching what is untouchable, there exists a commonality among all such absences; for even though at the time of the destruction of the contact with ash and so forth, such absences may be present there, those absences [would still] reside in other substrates, such as the ash.

The concern that the aforementioned over-extension remains intact is raised on the grounds that [the property in question] exists in its locus— that very locus which is the substratum of the prior conjunction with ashes and so forth— delimited by the moment of the destruction of the prior conjunction with ashes and so forth, which occurs within the time prior to [the subsequent conjunction] and is delimited by the [subsequent] conjunction. Nevertheless...
There is no fault [in our position], because the meaning of the word *kālin* (belonging to time) is the state of being qualified by connection with ashes and so forth.

This state of being qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya*) occurs through the relation of being a locus delimited by the relation of inherence residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhasamavāyasambandhāvacchinnādheyatāviśiṣṭa*), which is further delimited by the relation of being a locus characterized by an unconditioned qualifier-ship (*niravacchinnaviśeṣaṇatāsambandhāvacchinnādheyatāsambandha*).
The distinction [of the absence] is by way of both relations: being qualified by that which qualifies itself, and being delimited by the moment that delimits itself.
The term "absence" is included as a qualifier to prevent the misconception that [the contact] is a qualification of something untouchable and so forth. And thus—
And regarding the provision of the qualification "up to the end" (anta) for the time [period] whose meaning has been stated:
therein, "wherein" (*yatra*) and so forth refers to the bronze vessel (*kāṃsya*) and other such items already mentioned;
"as long as" (*yāvat*) is a qualification of non-existence (*abhāva*).
The word "that" (tat) means the touch of the untouchable. The word "defect" (doṣa) refers to the occurrence of impurity and so forth.
The refutation of ownership (*svatva*) as a distinct category (*atirikta-padārtha*) is understood;
the point is that a cognition arises therein in the form: "This possesses ownership as determined by Caitra."

By the aforementioned reasoning, it is not tenable that [the word] functions as a collective indicator of the stated meaning— namely, the power (śakti) residing in the substrate (upādheya) in the form of purity found in bronze and other such objects included within the category of "prepared substances" (kḷptapadārtha)— by way of being an illustration.
Intending to show that [the particle *api*] cannot function as a conjunctive particle for an unstated object when such a possibility exists, he says: "by the word *api*.
By the phrase "because of being a counter-correlate" (*pratiyogitvāt*) and so forth, there is the inclusion of being a sub-stratum (*anuyogitva*), being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*), and so on.
"Of such a kind," and so forth.

The word "tādṛśa" (of such a kind) refers to that which is determined by the intended application. By the phrase ending in "yogyatvāt" (because of fitness), there is an explanation of the meaning of the pronoun "tat" in the expression "tadavacchedakam" (the delimitant thereof).
The intention is that the word "limiting factor" (avacchedaka) refers to the instrumental cause;
this is indicated in the *Dīpikā* by the phrase "by means of acceptance and so forth."
The summary of the lineage beginning with the father is found in the *Vidhivāda* section of the *Prakāśikā*.
[370] "Of all," and so forth.
Here, this is the indivisible verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*):
having as its qualificandum the referent of the word "all" (*sarva*), and being determined by the aforementioned referents—

[He] is one who possesses an effort directed toward the future that is conducive to producing a cognition whose qualifier is a destruction (dhvaṃsa) having as its counter-positive an operation favorable to a comprehension characterized by the mode of inclusion according to what is appropriate; [and he is] one who possesses a word which generates a cognition whose qualificandum is an injunction and whose qualifiers are definitions and so forth, [this cognition being] qualified by a desire whose qualifier is an absence having as its counter-positive a deficiency consisting in the state of not being the specifier of an injunction whose qualificandum is the root [of the action].

The first qualification [of the speaker] consists in being a possessor of a present-time effort conducive to the sound that is non-different from the text beginning with "ayetyādi," which generates a cognition whose objective-mode (karmatva-niṣṭha-prakāratā) is determined by a subject-mode (prakāratā) delimited by present-time and residing in the determination of an injunction characterized by a desire for service associated with the disciples.
This [qualification] is established through two relations: (1) having a subsistence delimited by the time of its own locus, and (2) having the same agent as its counter-positive.
The second distinction [of the object] is by way of both relations: being the object of a desire prompted by itself, and having the same agent as its own object. The third is likewise.
In that definition, the word "that" (tat) refers to the injunction;
here, every term within its own context refers to the Naiyāyika.
"By effort" means by activity. "Distinguished" refers to this qualification of the instrumentality [of the action], beginning with the relation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
The same applies to what follows.
"Such" means that which produces the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), which in turn produces effort (*prayatna*).
This is a qualification of "knowledge.
By the phrase "because of being an effect, etc.," there is an explanation of the referent of the word "that" (tat) in the expression "the indicator of that."
By the phrase "tavyādi" and so forth, there is the inclusion of the suffixes *tavya*, *anīya*, and *ra*. Now,

it may be objected that in the world, activity is observed to arise from a misconception of "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatā*) with respect to that which is actually devoid of being achievable through effort.

Therefore, because activity is not observed toward that which is incapable of being accomplished by an action (*kṛtyasādhya*), the statement in the *Dīpikā*—“because of the non-perception of activity toward what is incapable of being accomplished by an action”—is incorrect; hence he says: “by way of its being incapable of being accomplished by an action.
This means: that which has become the object of a cognition characterized by the mode (qualifier) of being incapable of being accomplished by an action.
1. Its own destruction (sva-dhvaṃsa) is that which, delimited by the time of its own substratum, exists in space; sound (śabda) likewise [is delimited] by its own destruction.

Its counter-correlative is the verbal operation (*vyāpāra*) consisting of sound which is conducive to comprehension; and since the word shares the same agent (*samānakartṛka*) as that [operation], the two relations are established.
2. *Svaṃ* (one's own).
The desire to avoid deficiency; the desire prompted by that [desire];

the desire for the word that generates the knowledge of the injunction; the state of being the object of such a desire residing in that word. Likewise, "itself" refers to the desire to avoid deficiency; its object is the avoidance of deficiency; and [the word possesses] the quality of having the same agent as that.
And thus, there is the establishment of two relationships with the word "tādṛśa" (such).
3. Here, the term "svapada" (its own word) means the words belonging to the *Prakāśikā* commentary within this particular section.
The meaning is that the word "sva" (one's own) found in such phrases as "common to one's own and others' views" (*svaparamatasādhāraṇam*) and "in one's own view" (*svamate*) refers to the Naiyāyikas.
[This applies to] the phrase beginning with "by means of the desire to act" (*cikīrṣādvārā*), etc.
The sense is that this should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.
Regarding the phrase "kṛtyasādhyatve," the meaning is "due to the absence of being achievable through volitional effort (kṛti)."
The same applies to what follows.

By the word "only" (eva) in the phrase "the absence of the knowledge that [an action] cannot be accomplished by effort," the knowledge that it *can* be accomplished by effort (kṛtisādhyatājñāna) is excluded.
Because it would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava) if [non-existence] were to function as a real entity;
for [the definition of non-existence] is constituted by two types [of absence].

The phrase "the state of being the absence of the knowledge of the non-existence of the capacity to be accomplished by an effort" [is used] in comparison with "the state of being the knowledge that it can be accomplished by an effort," and so forth.
Regarding the term "tattad" (each respective):
The meaning is "the absence of being achievable through volitional effort" (*kṛtisādhyatvābhāva*) or "the difference from that which is achievable through volitional effort" (*kṛtisādhyabheda*).
By the phrase "by the pervader, etc. (*vyāpyādītyādinā*), [the author] intends to include other such factors.

This is a summary of the two contradictory properties: being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and being the opposite of that (unachievable through effort), each determined by its respective delimiting property (*avacchedaka-dharma*).

The phrase "and so forth" (*dig*) indicates the following intention: in cases where there was no prior cognition of either non-achievability through effort or achievability through effort, it is necessary for the cognition of achievability through effort to be the motivator (*pravartakatva*) in order to prevent the onset of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
"In that case too"— even in cases such as consuming poison—

"this"— the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and so forth— "without my doing" and so on; and this [qualification] is for the purpose of excluding deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of cooking and other acts performed by another person.
"Based on inference" (*ānumānika*) means that which is produced by inference. "Form" (*rūpa*) is a qualifier of the cause (*nimitta*).
In the phrase "sandhyāvandanā," the word "ādi" (etcetera) at the beginning must be supplied;
by this, bathing (*snāna*) is included.
In the expression "śucijīvitvādi," the meaning is "possessing purity of livelihood and so forth"; by the word "ādi" [other qualities are implied].
This is the summary of impurity for that specific time;
the same applies hereafter as well.
In the *Dīpikā*, it says "non-following."

The meaning is that it is impossible for the cognitions of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) regarding the three aforementioned types of objects of action to function as a single cause with respect to what is delimited by the nature of purposeful activity (*pravṛttitva*).
— *Prakāśikā*
He establishes [this] with the phrase "in the generality of activity" (*pravṛttisāmānye*).
This means: of that form which delimits the causality as determined by the effectness delimited by the property of being an activity (*pravṛttitva*).
"Of one"—that is, common to the knowledge of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) in the three aforementioned instances of action.
In the phrases "of that" (*tasya*) and "established in that" (*tanniṣṭha*), the word *tat* refers to the *puruṣa*.
By the phrase "desire and so forth," [the author indicates]...
This is a compendium of the states of having performed the prescribed purification and being possessed of temporary impurity.
In the phrase "tadvattāyāḥ" (of possessing that), the word "tat" (that) refers to desire and so forth.
The same applies here to the phrase "of its connection. Likewise, regarding the phrase "its own object": here, the word *sva* (own) refers to desire (*kāmanā*).
By the phrase "because of being a means" (*sādhanatvāt*) and so forth,
the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is included.
The term "form" (*rūpa*) is a qualification of the relation.
The final word "tat" (that) refers to knowledge,
because it is what is being pursued.
Furthermore, even in this way, since ownership rests upon each specific individual person,
there would follow the consequence of an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations due to the difference between individual persons; otherwise, [this would not be the case].

This is not so— because if "being an effort" (*pravṛttitva*) were taken as the inclusive delimitor of the effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Rather,

[the causal relation is such that] with respect to an effort directed toward a Vedic action delimited by "being an effort," [the cause is] the cognition that it is achievable through volition (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*), by way of both the relations of inherence (*samavāya*) and being the locus (*ādheyatva*).
There is no fault because its status as a cause is accepted;
its state of being "contained" [is established] by way of the relation of being produced by the recollection of its own qualification.

The phrase "the delimitor of the causal status" (kāraṇatāvacchedaka) should be followed by the word "relation" (saṃbandha); the meaning is "for the sake of parsimony" (lāghavena). The intention is that such an inherence relation (samavāya) is extremely simple. As for the word "that" (tat):
The meaning is "heavy.
Regarding the phrase "of the delimiting factor of causality," the word "of the relation" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Being produced" (*janyatva*) means having the nature of occurring necessarily at a subsequent time, and so forth.
By the phrase "being produced, etc. (*janyatvādītyādinā*), [the author] intends to include other such properties.
There is a comprehensive inclusion of the properties of being delimited by a relation, being a locus of inherence, and duality. Here—
in the body that is the object of the knowledge which generates effort—
it is also [the property of] not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence.

The meaning is that it must also be such that it does not entail what is undesirable (*aniṣṭa*). The word "powerful" (*balavat*) is used to exclude the undesirable— such as the expenditure of wealth and physical exhaustion— that serves as a cause for performing the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
In this context, "strength" (*balavattva*) consists in being distinct from [the cognition] existing prior to the time of the desired production.

The particle *api* serves as a conjunctive indicator, citing as examples the nature of the cognition that [an action] is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) and the cognition that it is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*).
Regarding that, he states the purpose of its inclusion therein with the words "by that":
[it is included] within the body, which is the object of the cognition that produces effort.
The meaning is: by including the condition of "not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence.
This is to be connected with the phrase "there is no risk of [unintended] activity."

“Desirable in form” (*rūpeṣṭā*) is a *karmadhāraya* compound. “Qualified” (*viśiṣṭā*) means: being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) that is to be accomplished by an effort (*kṛtisādhya*) which is not followed by a powerful undesired consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhi*).
[This applies] to the commencement of action (*pravṛtti*), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "because it is to be accomplished by effort" (*kṛtisādhyatvāt*): the word "etc.
(*ādi*) includes being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*).
[The term] "precisely separately" (*pṛthag eva*)...
The meaning is: "precisely by virtue of being the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñānatva*), and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "according to the logic of the staff, the wheel, and so forth": otherwise, if one were to accept causality on the basis of the aforementioned qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), [there would be an infinite regress] regarding the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

It should be noted that, in the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*), this would entail the acceptance of multiple causalities delimited by heavy properties (*gurudharma*). [The phrase] "in the sense of activity" (*pravṛtti*) means that otherwise, [the status of] effort (*prayatna*)...

The point is that if the property of being the object of an effort (kṛtisādhyatva) and so forth— which is common to both [the desire for] cessation and the desire for life— were the delimitor of the effect-ness (kāryatāvacchedaka) [of such knowledge], there would follow the fallacy of negative deviation (vyatirekavyabhicāra).
"Of the transgression" means "of sin.
"Prior non-existence" means "non-origination."
Otherwise, for one who performs the twilight prayers (*sandhyā-vandana*) and other such rites for as long as they live, no transgression (*pratyavāya*) would arise,
because the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) [of that duty] would be impossible.
The meaning is that [otherwise] his performance of the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*) and other such rites would result in fruitlessness.
Now, [one might object]: in the world, there is happiness and the cessation of suffering...

Since it is observed that only the cessation of the causes of suffering is desired as a fruit, how can there be the possibility of the previously mentioned antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) being a fruit?
For only that which is desired [can be a fruit].
Regarding the point "because it is a fruit," he says: "of that" (tasya).
[He explains] "by way of being the absence of that which produces suffering" (duḥkhajanakābhāvatayā);
[that is,] of that which produces suffering.
"Non-existence" means in reality;
"that" means that which produces suffering;
and "the state of being a fruit."

It should be understood that [the definition] beginning with "consisting of being the objective of engagement" and so forth, as well as the state of being desired as the absence of that which produces suffering, consists in being the object of a desire whose qualifier is the nature of such an absence. Now, one might ask:
how can there be [desire for] the prior non-existence of that [suffering], which is designated as the "avoidance of transgression" (pratyavāya-parihāra) and takes the form of its non-arising?
The state of being a result (*phalatva*) consists in being the intended object of purposeful activity (*pravṛttyuddeśyatva*) while being produced (*janyatve sati*).
However, one might object that the previously mentioned prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not produced; thus, he raises this doubt with the words "na ca" (and not).
The word "tat" means "pratyavāya" (transgression). "Tasya" refers to that non-existence of transgression (*pratyavāya-prāgabhāva*).

Of that which consists of a relation of essential nature—that is, not distinct from the essential nature of the substratum (dharmin). Therein—in the case of the prior non-existence of transgression. "Because there is no impairment of its status as a result" means that in the context of being produced, which constitutes the body of the definition of a result.

The sense is that it is precisely the state of being prompted (*prayojyatva*) that must be included [in the definition]. This concludes the refutation of the view that the *apūrva* is the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*).
"Specific desire" (icchāviśeṣa) means a desire characterized by the deity's ownership, preceded by the cessation of one's own ownership.
"Perishing very quickly" (āśutaravināśin) means...
The meaning of this will become clear further on.
"Appearance" (bhāna) is knowledge in the form of verbal cognition (śābda).
Alternatively, "appearance" (bhāna) means "objectivity" (viṣayatā); the same applies to what follows.
Regarding the phrase "as a means of proof" (sādhanatvena):
The third [type of] objectness (viṣayatā) consists in being determined by a mode (prakāratā) that is co-present with [the object].
The phrase "the appearance" (bhānam) refers to verbal cognition and so forth.
[378] "Because of inappropriateness" means because it lacks the status of being a means for attaining heaven.

And because the nature of being a means (*sādhanatva*) consists in possessing that property which is not a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absence residing in the locus of the effect, as delimited by the moment immediately preceding the effect.

The meaning is that there is an absence of sacrifice delimited by the moment immediately preceding heaven. Now, "perishing very quickly" means extreme rapidity of destruction; "destructibility" means being the counter-positive of destruction.

And since that [momentariness] is possible even for that which does not abide beyond its own fruit, because it is so in relation to what abides longer than that, he explains it with the words "the third" and "at the moment of its own arising," and so forth.

Otherwise, since the state of being the "third" in relation to some [preceding moment] would remain common to all moments without exception, the same fault would ensue. Furthermore, the state of being the third moment relative to its own moment of origination—

It is the state of being the locus of the destruction of the moment of its own production, which is itself the locus of the destruction of the production of the destruction of the moment of its own production. Nor is there a lack of uniformity here due to the inclusion of the concept of "selfhood" (svatva),
because [the definition] consists simply in being qualified by being an object of cognition (prameya-viśiṣṭatva) and being subject to extremely rapid destruction (āśutaravināśitva).
The broad definition [of pervasion] is as follows:

[the property of being the counter-positive of a destruction] residing in a moment that is the locus of the destruction of the moment which is the locus of the production of the destruction of the moment of its own production, by means of both relations: (1) identity with itself (*svatādātmya*), and (2) being the counter-positive of a destruction residing in a moment that is the locus of the production of the destruction of the moment of its own production.
1. It must be established that sacrifice and the like possess the property of being the counter-positive of a destruction occurring in the third moment of their own production.
In this regard, by the term "knowable" (*prameya*),...
Only the sacrifice (yāga) is to be grasped; its being qualified by that [the result] exists in the sacrifice through a dual relation.
For instance, the sacrifice itself is "self" (sva), and its identity with that exists in the sacrifice.
Thus, one's own sacrifice is [the object]; its moment of origination is the first moment;
the moment that is the locus of the origination of its destruction is the second moment;
the moment that is the locus of the origination of the destruction of that [second-moment destruction] is the third moment; and the destruction of the sacrifice that subsists therein [is the fourth].
The state of being its counter-correlative resides in the sacrifice;
this is the subtle analysis regarding the qualification by a moment.

The specific distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [of the moment] is by way of both relations: (1) being the counter-positive of a destruction residing in itself (*svavṛttidhvaṃsapratiyogitva*), and (2) being the locus of the production of a destruction of the moment that is the locus of the production of the destruction of the moment of its own production as defined by itself (*svanirūpitasvotpattikṣaṇadhvaṃsotpattyadhikaraṇakṣaṇadhvaṃsotpattyadhikaraṇatva*).
Therefore, there is no fault.
Considering that permanence (*sthāyitva*) consists in existing through multiple moments—
a property shared even by entities that exist for only a second moment— he explains it as "persisting until the attainment of the fruit."
The phrase "of that which bears fruit" (*phaletyasya*) refers to the following:

[it is] the state of subsisting throughout all moments that are substrata of the destruction of the moment of its own production, yet are non-substrata of the destruction of the moment of the production of the intended fruit (*prakṛtaphala*).
This results in being pervaded by the nature of such moments in terms of being the locus of [the action], which amounts to its persisting until the fruit is reached.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the statement in the *Dīpikā*—"the enduring effect is indeed the *apūrva*"—is incorrect?

For the nature of being an effect (*kāryatā*), in the form of being achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*), is possible only in the sacrifice (*yāga*) and not in the *apūrva*. To this, he replies with the words "In the sacrifice" (*yāge*).
"Directly" means without any mediation;

that is to say, by way of the relation of being a substratum (*āśrayatā-sambandha*). "By way of sacrifice" means by way of an indirect (*paramparā*) relation consisting in being produced by a sacrifice which has itself as its substratum.
The word "that" (tat) means "to be produced" (janya). The phrase "in one part" (ekadeśe) means:
The word "done" (*kṛta*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

In that regard—namely, in the sentence "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—the term ending in the instrumental case (*sādhanāntam*) is a qualifier of the sacrifice (*yāga*). "Previously" (*pūrvam*)...
"From the cognition produced by the sentence concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth.

"Because it is not present [to the mind]" means that since it is impossible for the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) to be established by any other means of valid cognition, it must be established by such a sentence alone.
The sense is that its establishment must be explained.
"Therein" refers to the *apūrva*;
"here" refers to the aforementioned objection.
"They say" means "the resolution," as is understood from the context;
"that" refers to it.
The meaning is "heavy. Regarding the term "of such a kind":
it means "having as its object that which is delimited by that property.
The state of having as its object that which is delimited by that property...
It is the state of being the determiner of the object-ness delimited by that property (*taddharmāvacchinnaviṣayatānirūpakatvam*).
But "not," [meaning] with respect to verbal cognition having that as its object.
Regarding the apprehension of the power (*śakti*) with respect to that [object]: 1.
By the first word "own" (*svapada*), the third moment of the production of the sacrifice (*yāga*) is to be understood.
The state of being the counter-positive of a destruction residing in that [yāga] exists in the sacrifice (*yāga*).
The second occurrence of the word "self" (*svapada*) refers to the third moment;
the third occurrence of the word "self" refers to the sacrifice.

The locusness (ādheyatā) residing in the sacrifice as determined by the third moment is delimited by the relation of being the moment that is the locus of the destruction of the moment which is the locus of the production of the destruction of the moment of its own production.
This is because, by virtue of that relation, the sacrifice exists in the third moment.
The syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) is that the sacrifice is characterized by the third moment through both [the relation of] such a locusness (*ādheyatva*) and [the relation of] inherence.
2. "Self" (*svam*) refers to the sacrifice.
Starting from the moment immediately following the destruction of the moment of its [the action's] origination,
as many moments as there are that do not constitute the locus for the destruction of the moment of origination of the intended fruit, such as heaven and so forth.
The meaning is that [the word] has as many occurrences as there are [instances];
the meaning is that the causality of an apprehension (*upasthiti*) having that as its object is not accepted.

And thus, according to the manner stated, if one does not accept the causal relation between the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*) and verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) on the basis of their having the same object (*samānaviṣayakatva*), but rather accepts it on the basis of their having the same mode (*samānaprakārakatva*);
This is the meaning.
"In some place"—that is, in something such as a jar. "Capability" means the capacity for the connection with having the sacrifice as its object.

Now, one might ask: why is it not possible for the effect itself, such as a jar, to appear in verbal cognition by virtue of semantic competency (*yogyatā*)? To this, he says: "For not... The syntactical connection is: "For it is not possible."
"Other" means [other than] the effect of a previously non-existent form, and so forth. "Eternal" means [eternal] with respect to action; this is the ellipsis.
"Because of the absence of a fruit.
Here, "fruit-ness" is defined by being produced (*janyatva*).
In that regard—namely, in the scriptural passage concerning obligatory rites (*nityakarman*)—it is stated in the *Dīpikā*:

[377] In the phrase "even in the case of an eternal injunction," the particle *api* serves as a conjunction to include injunctive sentences by way of illustration. The term "to be expressed" (*vācyam*) refers to the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.
Now, in what form is the *apūrva* [expressed]?
In response to the doubt that [the word "heaven"] might be denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth occurring in an eternal sentence, he says in the *Prakāśikā*:
"As an effect," and so on. [The term] "Paṇḍa" [is used].
In that system, the *apūrva* is of two kinds:

1) the *kalikāpūrva* and the *paṇḍāpūrva*. Among these, the first is the *apūrva* expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers found in sentences concerning optional rites (*kāmya*).

The second [type of injunction], expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth in an eternal statement (*nityavākya*), should be understood as "impotence" (*paṇḍatva*), which is to say "neuter-ness" (*napuṃsakatva*), meaning the non-productivity of a result. As it is said in the *Dīpikā* [377]: "It is postulated. This is the point here.

The mode of conceptualization is as follows: the optative suffix (*liṅ*) occurring in an eternal Vedic sentence denotes the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) by way of its being the nature of an effect, because it is an optative suffix found in a Vedic context, just like the optative suffix occurring in a sentence concerning optional rites (*kāmya*).
This applies to the statement beginning with "action" (*kriyā*).

To dispel the misconception that the phrase "in that which is the effect of the action, i.e., the meaning of the verbal root" refers to the fruit (*phala*), [the author] states in the *Prakāśikā*: "residing in the meaning of the verbal root.
Thus, in this context, the word "effect" (*kārya*) refers to the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*).
The intention here is that in the expression *kriyākārya*, it is indeed a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Regarding the term *alaukika*,
it means "Vedic."
The word "liṅādi" (optative suffixes, etc. is to be supplied [to complete the sentence].

Regarding the term "sādhāraṇyena" (by way of commonality): commonality here means the state of being the locus (*ādheyatva*); the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) that is connected with the capacity (*śakti*).
"In the case of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth" excludes the *apūrva* by the word "even" (*eva*). In the *Dīpikā*, it says: "Of the sacrifice (*yāga*) as well."
In this context, the word *api* (also/even) serves as an illustration and is intended to include that which is unprecedented (*apūrva*).
"Unfit" (*ayogyā*) means possessing the absence of being a means to attain heaven. "As a means" (*sādhanatayā*) [refers to the aforementioned].
"Beginning with heaven," and so forth. Regarding the word "that":
the term *kalikāpūrva* is derived from the etymology *kalayati* (it produces) *phalam* (the fruit). Thus, this word is established [in that sense].
He explains that the word *ūṣara* refers to the means for attaining desired fruits such as heaven;
the word *paṇḍa*, which denotes a neuter, signifies fruitlessness.

And thus, "fruitless *apūrva*" is the meaning of the term *paṇḍāpūrva*; [it means] "instrumentality. Even with such an explanation, [the word] "for the sake of its accomplishment" (*tannirvāhāya*) refers here to an "intermediate" [result].
The meaning is that it occurs during the intermediate period between the means and the fruit.

Regarding the phrase "because of the postulation of something unprecedented" (*apūrvakalpanāt*): this is the manner of postulation here—the sacrifice is that which produces the operation (*vyāpāra*) which, in turn, generates heaven.
Because it does not exist at a time immediately preceding heaven and yet is the producer of heaven;
for whatever does not exist at a time immediately preceding a certain thing and is its producer,
that is the producer of the operation which produces that thing.
Just as experience is the producer of memory through the medium of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Now, one might object:
let there be no certainty regarding the unfitness of the sacrifice; rather, doubt certainly arises.
Since doubt, like certainty, is an obstacle to the cognition of that [unfitness], how [can it be said that the cognition of fitness prevails]?
Regarding the possibility of understanding the sacrifice as a means for attaining heaven and so forth, he says in the *Prakāśikā*:
"incompatibility" (*ayogyatā*). This means the state of possessing the absence of being a means for attaining heaven and so forth. Of that—
"Because doubt regarding unfitness does not obstruct [the process];
that is to say, because it is non-contradictory."
The meaning is that the certainty of the absence of that [property] is precisely what opposes the cognition of its presence.

"In the cognition whose qualificandum is the sacrifice and whose qualifier is the status of being a means to heaven, etc. and so forth. "Cognition" refers to the cognition of the status of being a means to heaven, etc., derived from sentences such as those concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, and so forth.
"From the sentence" means from the *jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth. "Of that" refers to the sacrifice. [Objection:
But [what of] the *apūrva*?

If the destruction of the sacrifice (*yāgadhvaṃsa*) were the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the sacrifice, then both [of the following] would have to be postulated: its being produced by the sacrifice, and its being the generator of the result, such as heaven, which is itself produced by the sacrifice. However, in the case of the destruction of the sacrifice being the operation of the sacrifice, [it is established] by way of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

Since the property of being produced by the sacrifice has already been established in the destruction (dhvaṃsa) of the sacrifice, one need only postulate that it is the generator of results such as heaven; thus, the opponent raises the objection regarding the complexity of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by stating "nanu" [but surely], because both [the sacrifice and its destruction] would have to be postulated. By the word "eva" [only] in the phrase "of the destruction alone," the *apūrva* is excluded.
The term "the state of being an operation" refers to [the passage beginning with] "in the sacrifice," etc.,
and by the phrase "touching," etc.
In the *Dīpikā* [377], there is a summary of the two cases of crossing the Karatoyā and swimming across the Gaṇḍakī with one's arms:
"The destruction of the sacrifice is not the [actual] operation (*vyāpāra*)."
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is "there is no operation" (*na vyāpāraḥ*). The term "operation" (*vyāpāra*) refers to [the agent's activity] such as the sacrifice (*yāga*), and so forth.
Otherwise, the Vedic root *kṣarati* would have to be taken as meaning "perishes" (*naśyati*).

The sense is that because destruction (dhvaṃsa) lacks annihilation (nāśa), there would arise the undesirable consequence of contradicting scriptural statements regarding the destruction of [merit] through activities such as recitation;
and in this context, the root *kṣar* (to perish) does not apply.

It does not refer primarily to destruction or literal flowing away, but rather to a figurative "flowing away" consisting in the incapacity to produce a result. And thus, there is no contradiction even if the cessation of the sacrifice is considered the sacrificial operation (*vyāpāra*);
for that [cessation] possesses the quality of being incapable of producing a result.
This occurs because one must postulate that the proclamation of the Dharma and so forth act as an obstacle to results such as rebirth in heaven;

otherwise, there would be the aforementioned postulation— namely, the postulation of a destruction of the *dharma* in the form of the *apūrva*, and the postulation of the proclamation and so forth as the cause of that destruction— which would result in a great logical complexity (*mahāgaurava*).

Having reflected that the criticism stated in the *Dīpikā* is not withstandable under scrutiny, [the author] himself states an irrefutable criticism regarding the status of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) as an operation (*vyāpāra*), in the *Prakāśikā*, beginning with the words "of destruction" (*dhvaṃsasya*).
This is another criticism— a criticism distinct from those already established previously.

Regarding the establishment that the verb has effort as its meaning: [the objection] "But in the case of 'lokavyutpatti' (worldly linguistic convention), the convention [is established] regarding the state of being achievable through effort and so forth by means of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like."

Since it is not tenable to state that the nature of the apprehension of capacity (*śaktigraha*) serves as the regulator for the connection of "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and so forth with the action, he explains:
"[The meaning is] 'in worldly convention'"; and that...
"And worldly convention" connects with the phrase "of such a nature.
[The phrase] "by being achievable through effort," and so forth, [is explained as follows].

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) occurs when the object of cognition is a qualifier (*prakāratva*). The word *tat* (in *tatpada*) has the same meaning as the word ending in the suffix *tral*. Thus, the meaning is:
"one who possesses a cognition having as its qualifiers [the properties of] being achievable by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*)."
Regarding the phrase "for that purpose":
this refers to the fact that the word "that" here [functions] by the force of worldly linguistic convention (*lokavyutpatti*).
Regarding the phrase "in that": "in that" means in the world.
In the *Dīpikā*, after the words "by way of being the optative suffix" (*liṅtvena*), the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) is to be understood as an ellipsis.
Regarding the expression "the state of having an injunctive meaning" (*vidhyarthatvam*), the phrase "of the optative suffix and so forth" (*liṅādeḥ*) is to be supplied.
The term *vidhiratha* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which the chariot is an injunction. Thus,
since the word *vidhi* refers to the object of the impelling cognition (*pravartakajñāna*),
the meaning is that it denotes such an object.
Regarding the phrase "by way of being a verb" (*ākhyātatvena*), etc.: he explains that which is delimited by the property of being a verb in the *Prakāśikā* as "by way of being a verb."

"And that" refers to "the nature of being a verbal suffix" (*ākhyātatva*). "Convention" (*saṃketa*) refers to [the convention] of Pāṇini and others. "Power" (*śakti*) refers to [the power] residing in the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, as defined by the action (*kṛti*), and so on.
The meaning is "the characterization of the power. "In the delimited" means "in the qualified. The same applies hereafter as well.
Regarding "connection" (sambandha):
here, connection means suitability (anukūlatā); the same applies to what follows.
"That"—meaning that which consists of the form "What does it do?"—is the interrogative sentence "What does it do? The term "the state of being a remover" means... [end of fragment]
The word "is possible" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Otherwise" means:
in the absence of the capacity to convey the relation of cooking with respect to that which is delimited by the property of being an agent.
By supplying the phrase "the capacity to cause its cessation" (tannivartakatvam) from the preceding context, the syntactical connection is: "the capacity to cause its cessation is not possible.
This is because [the word] lacks the capacity to convey volitional effort (kṛti).
The meaning is that because the property of consciousness, namely volitional action (*kṛti*), is impossible in insentient things such as chariots and the like.
"That" refers to the chariot.
The meaning is that [the verb] "gacchati" (he goes) and so forth is explained by the principle of *sthālī-nayā* (the analogy of the cooking-pot).
By the word "anurodhena" (in accordance with),
the logical rule of the uniformity of the expressive power (*śakti*) of all verbal suffixes is indicated.
"It is precisely activity (*vyāpāra*). By the word "precisely" (*eva*), effort (*kṛti*) is excluded.
[Objection: But in cases such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*),...

Since the matter is fully accounted for simply by accepting a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) for that which is delimited by the light property of "the nature of being an operation" (vyāpāratva), the author of the Dīpikā is incorrect in asserting a secondary signification for that which is delimited by the heavy property of "the nature of being a favorable operation" (anukūlavyāpāratva).

Thus, since the connection of "going" and so forth with the state of being favorable must be expressed through the relation of being determined (*nirūpitatva*), there would be a great complexity in assuming that such an additional relation appears in verbal cognition; to this he says: "The operation" (*vyāpāra*). By this—

"In the form of being favorable" (*anukūlatvarūpeṇa*). "Established by convention" (*nirūḍha*) means residing in an object that has been the focus of intentionality since beginningless time. The same applies hereafter.

The particle *eva* (only) in the phrase "only by way of the relation of substratum-hood" (*āśrayatāsambandhenaiva*) is to be construed with the subsequent term "by way of positive concomitance" (*anvayena*). By this [use of *eva*], there is an exclusion of the possibility that the substratum-hood— conceived as the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*)— might be construed [with the agent] by way of the relation of being characterized (*nirūpitatva*).
"Like that of a name and its referent" means that just as the referent of one name does not have a connection with the referent of another name by way of a relation other than identity (*abheda*),
so too here, in the case of the referent of a name.
The meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha) is not admitted to be construed with another element through a relation distinct from identity; otherwise,

in cases such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's servant"), the meaning of the word "king" would be construed with the meaning of the word "servant" through a relation such as that of owner and owned, and in cases such as *taṇḍulaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is cooked"), [the same would apply] to the meaning of the verbal root.

The meaning is that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of the cooking and so forth being construed with the object such as rice, etc., through relations such as action and its object (*kriyākarmabhāva*) in their respective order;
this is because [such a construction] is unestablished (*avyutpanna*).
Because it lacks the constraint of knowledge regarding a specific co-utterance—
as in such cases as "the chariot goes" (ratho gacchati).
Likewise, [it applies] to the meaning of the word ending in the nominative case through the relation of being the locus (*āśrayatā*) of the action of going and so forth.
He states the result of introducing the qualification "being distinct" (*atiriktatva*) regarding that relation: "even in cases such as *stokaṃ pacati* (he cooks slightly)," and so on.

Since the author of the *Dīpikā* did not state the reasoning for the possibility that the agent and the object are the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), he himself states it therein: "of the verbal suffix," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in the agent, etc.": by the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of those specific actions (*karman*) consisting of various results such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*), which are intended to be the delimiters of the meaning of the verbal root.
The term "endless" (*ananta*) is stated to indicate great complexity (*mahāgaurava*).
By the phrase "beginning with *kṛtya*," etc., the inclusion of results such as *saṃyoga* (conjunction) and so forth is intended; the same applies hereafter.
The remainder of the argument is that since [the genus] must be accepted,

it follows that the delimitor of the delimitor of the denotability (śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka) for the genus "effort-ness" (kṛtitva) and so forth must also be accepted. By the phrase "effort-ness and so forth," conjunction-ness (saṃyogatva) and other such genera are included.
The point is that anything other than a universal (*jāti*) or an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) appears only in some form or another.
Regarding "simplicity" (*lāghava*):
because universals such as "effort-ness" (*kṛtitva*) are unitary, there is no infinite regress.

The sense is that, since it is accepted that the universal (jāti) appears by its very own nature in a cognition not delineated by another universal, no other property (dharmāntara) can be admitted as the delimitor of the delimitor of the denotative capacity (śakyatāvacchedakatāvacchedakatā).
In the *Dīpikā*, the word "that" (*tad*) refers to the agent and the object;
regarding the meaning of the phrase "oneness and so forth" (*ekatvādī*), the *Prakāśikā* states that "and so forth" (*ādinā*) includes "the gerundive and so forth.
The meaning of the expression "by 'and so forth'" (*ādinā*) is "by the word 'and so forth'."
The same applies elsewhere as well; thus, when a verb has the sense of a gerundive (*kṛtya*) and so forth.

Regarding the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ": this refers to examples such as "devadattaḥ pacati" (Devadatta cooks) and "pacyate taṇḍulaḥ" (the rice is cooked), and so forth; the word "iti" (thus) is to be understood as the remainder [of the context].
Acquisition (*lābha*) is apprehension (*pratīti*).
It consists, for example, of [the cognition] of Devadatta, rice, and so forth, by way of their respective agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*).
The same applies to what follows;
in the *Dīpikā*, regarding those two— the agent and the object—
it says "precisely by implication."
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is implication (*ākṣepa*).

It takes such a form as: "The fact that Devadatta and others are understood by words such as 'Devadatta' when co-occurring with verbs designated as *parasmaipada* (e.g., *karoti*), without [their] being agents and so forth, is otherwise inexplicable."

One might object: "Since [the author] does not accept the aforementioned form of implication (*ākṣepa*) in his own system, the statement in the *Dīpikā*, 'precisely because of implication' (*ākṣepāt eva*), is incoherent. To this, he replies: "[In the *Prakāśikā* it says] 'according to the opinion of others' (*paramatena*); but in his own system... (*svamate tu*).
The word "sva" (its own) here refers to the Naiyāyika;
by the very word "eva" (only), the aforementioned objection is excluded.

The word "tat" (that) means the agent and the object; desiring to state both the objection and its resolution regarding such cases as "Devadatta cooks," he [proceeds] by way of what is useful for that purpose.
He demonstrates the manner of verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) as appropriate in the example: "Devadatta cooks rice.
In that case—"Devadatta cooks"—[the analysis follows].
Regarding the two instances mentioned, such as "the rice is being cooked," [the rule does not apply] because of non-expression (anabhidhāna). Thus it is said.

The meaning is that this is because the two rules— the third [Pāṇini 2.3.2] and the second [Pāṇini 2.3.1], which establish the restriction— fall under the governing heading *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed").
Regarding the term *anabhihite*:
"By the letter *l* and so forth" means:
the meaning is "not being the object of a verbal cognition produced by the letter *l* and so forth.
"In such a case" means: when [the action] has not been expressed by the letter *l* and so forth.
The same applies to the root;
prefixes function as illuminators (dyotaka).
Regarding "of the prefixes" (*upasargāṇām*): the remainder [of the sense] is "of those beginning with *pra*, etc., which have been designated as 'prefixes' by the rule *upasargāt kriyāyoge*.
Regarding "in the state of being a word" (*vacanatve*): [this refers to their status as nominal stems].
"Specificity of meaning such as excellence" and so forth;
"intentionality" refers to the specificity of the meaning conveyed by the verbal root co-occurring with it, and so forth.
Regarding the term "grāhakatva" (the state of being a grasper): otherwise,

in expressions such as *guruḥ upāsyate* ("the teacher is worshipped"), the prefix *upa-* would have the sense of "proximate location," while the root *ās-* would have the sense of "being located upon."
Since the verbal root *upās* has as its specific meaning "that which is to be placed in a proximate location," it is intransitive;
therefore, according to the rule stated in Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.4.69, *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*, [the suffixes] are applied in the sense of the object and the state for intransitive roots.
Because it would otherwise follow that the verbal suffixes expressing action (*karmalakāra*) would be untenable;
therefore, the prefix *upa-* indicates that the verbal root *ās* has its intended meaning (*tātparya*) in a specific sense consisting of knowledge in the form of meditation (*upāsanā*).
"It must be stated exactly thus.

In the same way, this should be understood in other instances as well. In the *Dīpikā*, the author clarifies that the particle *eva* excludes [other meanings] by stating that in cases such as "excessiveness" (*prakarpa*) and so forth, there is only the sense of "indicating" (*dyotakatva*); he makes this clear with the words "not there."

"Power (*śakti*)" refers to [the capacity] regarding excellence (*prakarṣa*) and so forth. "By that" means by establishing the indicative nature (*dyotakatva*) of prefixes (*upasarga*) according to the manner described above.

The word "sūcitam" (indicated) is to be connected with this. "Itarā" means that which is devoid of the designation "upasarga" (prefix). "Nipātanāt" (by way of irregular derivation) implies "of the words 'eva' and so forth," as is the ellipsis.
The meaning is: of those items designated as *nipāta* by the rule "svarādinipātamavyayam" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.37),
such as the word *eva* and others.
He establishes the manner in which [the word] denotes by means of the passage beginning with "tathā hi" (for instance).

"Exclusion of non-connection" (*ayogavyavaccheda*) consists in being the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of that which serves as the delimitor of the subjecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), such as "conch-ness" (*śaṅkhatva*).
The phrase "anyayoga" (connection with another) and so forth is supplied from the word "eva" (only/exclusive),
as is the term "vyavaccheda" (exclusion).
The word "artha" (meaning) is supplied [from the previous context].

"Exclusion of connection with another" (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) means being pervaded by the state of being for the sake of others (*pārārthya*), which is the delimitor of the status of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), there is the "exclusion of absolute non-connection" (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) for the particle *eva* when it is connected with a verb.

It consists in the state of being co-located (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that which is intended as the delimitor of the object of reference (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), such as "lotus-ness" (*sarojatva*). This is the meaning of the phrase "the word 'object' (*artha*)," and so forth.
[This refers to] the knowledge of the true nature of categories (*padārthatattvajñāna*).
The determination of its being the cause of liberation [388]: "by a discerning person" means by an intelligent person. "Regarding the object," etc.
This is a qualification of liberation.
Since knowledge of earth and so forth by way of "waterness" and the like—which is not knowledge of reality—cannot be the cause of liberation, he says: "of the knowledge of the reality of categories."
The meaning is: "of the knowledge of objects in their state as they truly exist.
"Of others" refers to those for whom liberation is the purpose, and so forth.
"Intermediate" (avāntara) means situated in the middle. "Supreme" (parama):
supremacy consists in being distinct from any purpose to be accomplished by the knowledge of reality that arises immediately after it.
And "being the object to be established" (sādhyatva) should be understood as occurring either directly or indirectly;
the pervasion (anugama), however, is clear.
Regarding the word "śruteḥ": it refers to passages such as "The Self, verily... (ātmā vā are).

Now, since the means must necessarily precede the fruit, does it not follow that the portion of the text explaining the means must necessarily precede the portion explaining the fruit? How, then, should this be understood?
Regarding the phrase "the connection of such sentences," he says "ārtheti. This means "pertaining to the meaning.
Regarding the term "krameṇa" (in sequence), sequence means priority and posteriority.
The phrase beginning with "having spoken the words of the revealed scripture" and so forth; likewise in what follows. Regarding the word "sound" (śabda):

The meaning is "connected with words. The intention is that the construction is: "it becomes abandoned," [namely] "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*) and "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*). By means of logical arguments (*yuktibhiḥ*).
The meaning is: a stream of inferential cognitions (*anumiti-dhārā*) produced by a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose object is manifold logical reasons. "Of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*) means:

an inferential cognition having the self as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and "being distinct from others" (*itarabhinna*) as its qualifier (*prakāra*). And that—namely, the aforementioned form of inference—is as follows.
"Pratiyogītara" is a coordinate compound (samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa). "Tat" refers to that aforementioned form of inference;
"tat" [in the subsequent phrase] refers to the self (ātman).
The meaning is that [it serves] as an inference by way of being distinct from the other [means of knowledge].

With the intention that the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "immediately after that" (*tadanantaram*) refers to reflection (*manana*), he explains it with the words beginning "reflection," and so forth.
"Of what has been heard," and so forth.
"Uninterruptedness" (*nairantarya*) means being unseparated by heterogeneous cognitions (*vijātīya-pratyaya*).
The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭye*). [This applies] to the cognition (*pratyaye*).
And "being of a different class" (*vijātīyatva*) means having as its object a meaning in excess of the literal meaning [of the words].
Regarding the term "having withdrawn" (*pratyāhṛtya*):
withdrawal (*pratyāharaṇa*) is an activity conducive to the cessation of the [usual] connection [between the senses and their objects].
In the expression "from the objects" (*viṣayebhyaḥ*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of being the correlate (*anuyogitva*) of a relation;
likewise in the subsequent instance, "immediately after that" (*tadanantaram*).
Intending that the word "tat" refers to *nididhyāsana*, he says: "[388] *Nididhyāsana*.

Now, one might object: even if false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) alone is destroyed, as long as the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) dependent upon it persist, the possibility of defects remains; therefore, by the destruction of false cognition—
To show that the statement regarding the absence of defects is untenable, he explains: "accompanied by latent impressions" (*vāsanāsahita*).
This is a qualification of cognition (*jñāna*).
Latent impression (*vāsanā*) means a mental trace (*saṃskāra*).
By the phrase "attachment and so forth," the inclusion of hatred and delusion is intended.
Regarding the term "particular": it means the aspect that distinguishes [the object] from silver.
The phrase "having the form of mother-of-pearlness, etc. begins [the argument].
By the word "only" (*eva*) in the expression "by cognition alone," such [an object] is excluded.
